The gains are spread thinly across millions of households, each of which pays a little less for clothing, appliances or food, usually without noticing why. The losses fall heavily on a few: the workers of a particular mill, the shops that depended on their wages, the town whose tax base was the mill. A small saving that nobody notices is politically weightless; a closed factory is a photograph on the front page. Those who lose know exactly what they have lost and whom to blame, while those who gain rarely connect their small savings to a decision taken in a distant ministry. It is not surprising that the politics of trade so often seems out of proportion to its economics.

Economists have a standard reply. Because the total gains exceed the total losses, the winners could in principle compensate the losers and still come out ahead, so that everyone ends up better off. The argument is correct as arithmetic, and it is the foundation of the case that open trade raises national welfare. But the word that carries the weight is 'could'. A compensation that is possible but never paid is no comfort to the people who bore the losses, and to present it as though it settled the matter is to confuse a hypothetical with a policy.

Where governments have tried to pay, the record is unimpressive, though the reasons are instructive. Programmes reserved for workers who could prove that their jobs were lost to imports required them to establish a cause that is often impossible to isolate, since a plant may close because of foreign competition, new machinery and poor management all at once. Many eligible workers never applied; many who applied were retrained for occupations that were themselves shrinking. The failure lay less in the idea of compensation than in tying it to a cause that could not be reliably identified.

This suggests that the better course is not a trade-specific remedy at all but support that follows the worker regardless of why the job disappeared: insurance against lost earnings, help with moving to where work exists, and training linked to employers who are actually hiring. Such measures cannot be justified as payment for trade alone, and they will cost more than narrow programmes did. Yet the case for open trade has always rested on the claim that its benefits are broadly shared. If that claim is to be more than an assertion, the sharing has to be done by someone, and it will not happen by itself.
sets.difficulty_reason: The author accepts the economists' arithmetic while criticising its use, and the recommendation follows from a diagnosis of why past programmes failed.

sets.subtopic: Gross trade statistics credit the final assembler with value created elsewhere, so bilateral balances read as scorecards mislead policy, even though value-added figures are imprecise and leave overall balances unchanged.
paragraphs: Trade statistics were designed for a world in which goods were made in one place and sold in another. A customs officer records the full value of a shipment as it crosses the border and attributes it to the country from which it was sent. When a product is made from start to finish in a single country, this convention is harmless. When it is assembled from parts made in a dozen, the convention produces a curious distortion: the country where the last screw is turned is credited with the entire value of the product, including the much larger share that was created elsewhere and merely passed through.

Consider a hypothetical tablet computer assembled in one country from a display made in a second, chips designed in a third and fabricated in a fourth, and software written in a fifth. When the finished tablet is shipped to a sixth country, the statistics record an export of its full factory price from the assembling country, though the work done there may account for only a small fraction of that price. The bilateral balance between the assembler and the buyer swells accordingly, while the suppliers of the costlier components, whose contribution travels unseen inside the assembler's shipment, appear in the bilateral figures as having sold nothing to the final market at all.

Statisticians have responded by trying to trace value added: to ask, for each product, how much of its value was created in each country, and to tally trade on that basis. The striking feature of the results is not that a country's overall position changes, for it largely does not. Its balance with the world as a whole is much the same however one counts, since the value of each imported component is recorded once as an import and again inside the export, and the two entries cancel. What changes is the map: the bilateral balances that attract political attention are redistributed, often substantially, from assemblers towards the countries that supply the most valuable parts.

This matters because bilateral balances are routinely read as a scorecard of who is gaining at whose expense, and policy is sometimes made on that reading. A tariff aimed at the country with which a large deficit is recorded may, on the value-added view, fall chiefly on workers who contributed a modest share of what was bought, while leaving untouched the countries that contributed the most. The value-added figures are not beyond dispute. They depend on tables of who buys inputs from whom that are compiled infrequently and filled out with estimates, and they cannot replace the gross figures that customs administrations need for their own purposes. But one need not regard them as precise to see that they expose a habit of reading the gross bilateral figures as though they measured something they were never built to measure.
sets.difficulty_reason: Abstract accounting argument in which the key distinction (overall versus bilateral balances) is easy to blur, with a concession about the reliability of the alternative measure.

sets.subtopic: The infant-industry case for protection is sound in logic but fails in practice unless the exit is made credible in advance through fixed terms and performance tests such as exporting, which only capable states can enforce.
paragraphs: The argument for protecting infant industries is older than most of the arguments now made against it, and it is more respectable than its critics often allow. Its premise is that productivity in many industries is learned rather than given. A new steelworks or shipyard in a country without one begins with inexperienced workers, untested managers and suppliers who do not yet know what it needs; it will make costly mistakes for years before it reaches the efficiency of established foreign rivals. If it must meet those rivals at once, it may never survive long enough to learn. A period of protection, on this view, is not a subsidy to inefficiency but an investment in the learning that will eventually remove it.

The argument gains force from a further point. Much of what a pioneering firm learns does not stay inside it. Workers it trains move to competitors, suppliers it develops go on to serve other customers, and the mere demonstration that an industry can work in a given place lowers the risk for those who follow. Over time a cluster of related firms may form around the pioneer, each drawing on skills that the pioneer paid to create. Because the pioneer bears the cost of this learning but captures only part of its benefit, an unaided market will produce too little of it, and there is a case in principle for public support.

The difficulty lies not in the logic but in the ending. Protection is granted on the promise that it is temporary, yet every year it lasts it builds a constituency for its continuation: owners whose profits depend on it, workers whose jobs appear to, and officials whose standing is tied to the industry's survival. Worse, the protection itself weakens the motive to learn. A firm that knows its shelter will be extended whenever it fails to become competitive has little reason to bear the pain of becoming so, and the infant can remain an infant indefinitely, growing larger without growing up. The many cases in which protection outlived any plausible learning period are not accidents of bad administration; they are what the incentives predict.

It follows that the argument stands or falls on whether the exit can be made credible in advance. Protection whose duration is fixed and public, whose renewal depends on measurable progress, and whose beneficiaries are required to compete in some market where the shelter does not reach them, such as export markets, is a different policy from protection granted open-endedly. Export performance is especially revealing, because a firm cannot fake competitiveness in a market it does not control. A protected firm that must also sell abroad, at prices set by rivals it cannot shut out, learns quickly whether it has improved, and so does the government that shelters it. The interesting historical question is therefore not whether successful industrialisers protected their industries, since many did, but whether they attached conditions that forced the protected firms to improve.

None of this makes the conditions easy to impose. Withdrawing support from a large employer that has missed its targets requires a government able to bear the political cost, and the very constituency that protection creates is what makes that cost high. Protection also has victims who are easy to overlook: the firms that must buy the sheltered product at a higher price, and whose own competitiveness suffers as a result. The infant-industry case, then, is best understood not as a general licence but as a demanding bargain, sound in theory and available in practice only to states that can enforce its terms.
sets.difficulty_reason: A defended theory followed by a practical objection, a conditional rescue and a final qualification; the stance is clear but carefully hedged.

sets.subtopic: The objection that governments cannot pick winners misframes industrial policy, whose real task is to share the cost of discovering what an economy can produce and whose real danger is the inability to abandon failures.
paragraphs: The most familiar objection to industrial policy is that governments cannot pick winners. Officials, the objection runs, have neither the information nor the incentives to know which industries will flourish; investors risking their own money are better placed to judge, and when the state substitutes its judgement for theirs it will usually back the wrong horses and keep feeding them long after the race is lost. The objection has history on its side, in the sense that the record of state-backed ventures includes many expensive failures. But it rests on a picture of the problem that deserves closer inspection.

The picture is one in which the menu of possible industries is known and the only question is which item to choose. Investors, in this picture, already know what a country could produce profitably, and the government's error is to overrule them. Yet for an economy trying to move into activities it has never undertaken, no one possesses this knowledge. Whether a particular region can grow cut flowers for export, assemble electronic components or write software for foreign clients depends on a mass of local particulars, from the reliability of the roads to the habits of the workforce, that can be learned only by trying. An investor asked in advance would have no better basis for a forecast than an official; both would be guessing. The relevant knowledge is not hidden in investors' heads waiting to be consulted; it does not yet exist.

Producing it is costly, and here the market's usual advantages turn against it. The first entrepreneur to discover that a product can be made profitably in a given place bears the full cost of the experiment if it fails, but if it succeeds, others can copy the discovery cheaply, entering the industry once its viability has been shown. The pioneer thus bears the losses of failure while sharing the rewards of success, and rational investors will undertake fewer such experiments than the economy as a whole would want. The case for public involvement follows not from officials knowing more than investors, but from no one knowing enough and the cost of finding out being borne unevenly.

If this is right, the objection about picking winners is aimed at the wrong target. A policy of supporting discovery will back many ventures that fail; that is what experiment means, and a programme that never failed would be one that was taking no risks. Measured by the share of its bets that pay off, a sound programme of discovery may look worse than a timid one. The genuine danger lies elsewhere: support, once given, may become impossible to withdraw, so that the losers are kept alive at public expense. What matters is less the ability to pick winners than the ability to let losers go, and the second ability, though rarely discussed, is at least as hard to acquire as the first.

The approach has a cost of its own, and it would be dishonest to minimise it. Discovering what local firms could do requires officials to work closely with them, to learn what obstacles they face and what help would remove them. The same closeness that yields information also invites capture, in which those meant to be overseen come to set the terms. Officials who meet the same managers every month will find it hard to tell them, when a review date arrives, that support is ending. There is no formula that separates collaboration from collusion, only practices, such as public criteria and fixed review dates, that make the difference easier to see. That is a weaker guarantee than the advocates of industrial policy would like, but it is a stronger one than its critics usually assume.
sets.difficulty_reason: The author attacks the framing of an objection rather than its conclusion, relocates the risk, and closes with a concession whose balance must be read precisely.

sets.subtopic: The argument that private bargaining can settle pollution disputes efficiently is better read as a map of where bargaining fails and regulation is needed, and it leaves the question of who pays unresolved.
paragraphs: A familiar way of thinking about pollution treats it as a simple wrong: one party harms another, and the law should stop the harm or make the harmer pay. An influential argument in economics asks us to look at the situation differently. Suppose the smoke from a small factory soils the washing of a few households nearby. The harm, on this view, is reciprocal: to protect the washing is to restrict the factory, and to protect the factory is to burden the households. If the parties could bargain freely and cheaply, the argument runs, they would arrive at the efficient outcome whoever held the legal right. If the households had the right to clean air, the factory would pay them to tolerate some smoke whenever its gains exceeded their losses; if the factory had the right to emit, the households would pay it to fit a filter whenever the filter cost less than the damage it prevented.

The conclusion is often summarised as a reason for governments to stand aside: define property rights clearly, and private bargaining will do the rest. That reading takes the conditional for the claim. The striking result holds only when bargaining is nearly costless, and the more interesting lesson lies in how rarely that condition is met. A few households and one factory can meet around a table. A city of several million people breathing the exhaust of a million vehicles cannot. Each resident's share of the harm is small, working out who caused how much of it is difficult, and every resident has a reason to let others negotiate and pay while enjoying the cleaner air for nothing. The costs of finding the parties, measuring the damage and enforcing an agreement swamp whatever gains the bargain might bring.

Read in this way, the argument is less a case against regulation than a map of where it is needed. Where the parties are few, the harm is visible and agreements can be checked, private settlement may indeed work better than a rule imposed from outside; the neighbours of a noisy workshop may settle a dispute over evening hours more sensibly than any ordinance could. Where the parties are many and scattered, the same reasoning that praises bargaining in principle explains why it will not happen in practice, and why a tax, a standard or a tradable permit can stand in for a negotiation that no one is able to hold.

None of this makes the assignment of rights a matter of indifference. Even when bargaining would reach the same physical outcome, it matters a great deal who pays whom. A rule that gives the factory the right to pollute leaves the households poorer by the price of their clean air; a rule that gives them the right leaves the factory's owners poorer instead. Efficiency may be blind to that difference. Those who live downwind are not.
sets.difficulty_reason: A clear single line of argument built on one concrete example, with plainly signalled turns ('That reading', 'Read in this way', 'None of this').

sets.subtopic: Gains in energy efficiency are partly eaten up by increased use, by an amount that varies with circumstances, so efficiency should be paired with pricing if the aim is to cut total use.
paragraphs: In 1865 the economist William Stanley Jevons argued that Britain's growing skill at burning coal efficiently would not conserve its coal but hasten its exhaustion. Cheaper steam power, he reasoned, would make steam worth using in trades that had never used it, and the extra demand would more than swallow the saving. The idea has enjoyed a curious afterlife in contemporary environmental argument. It is invoked today, often with a note of triumph, by those who doubt that better lamps, engines and insulation can do much for the climate. It is dismissed, often with equal confidence, by those who regard efficiency as the cheapest source of clean energy there is. Both camps tend to treat the question as if it had a single answer, when the size of the effect plainly depends on circumstances.

The mechanism itself is not in dispute. When a service becomes cheaper to provide, people generally consume more of it, and the additional consumption offsets part of the anticipated reduction. A household that insulates its walls may heat more rooms, or keep them warmer; a driver whose car burns less fuel per kilometre may drive further, or buy a heavier car next time. Economists call the part of the expected saving that is eaten up in this way the rebound. What is disputed is its size. Where demand for a service is already close to saturation, as with lighting in a well-lit home, the rebound tends to be modest: few people want their rooms twice as bright merely because brightness has become cheap. Where energy is a basic input to production, and cheaper energy lets whole industries expand, the rebound can be large, and in the case Jevons studied it may well have exceeded the saving.

There is also a subtler and less visible channel of transmission. Money saved on fuel does not vanish; it is spent on something else, and that something else uses energy too. A family that spends less on petrol may take a holiday flight it could not previously afford. These indirect effects are considerably harder to trace than the direct ones, which is one reason why published estimates of the total rebound vary so widely across studies and sectors.

The sensible conclusion is neither that efficiency is futile nor that it is sufficient. Efficiency genuinely improves people's material circumstances: they obtain more warmth, light and travel for their money, and that is a gain in its own right. But if the aim is to reduce total energy use or emissions, efficiency works best when it is paired with something that keeps energy costly enough that the saving is not simply spent on using more of it, such as a tax on carbon or a cap on emissions. Efficiency then supplies the comfort, and the price makes sure that the comfort is not bought with the very fuel that was meant to be saved.
sets.difficulty_reason: Concrete everyday examples and an explicit, signposted conclusion; the only abstraction is the idea of indirect rebound.

sets.subtopic: The theoretical contest between carbon taxes and emissions trading matters less than it seems, because practical designs have converged and effectiveness depends on the level, coverage and credibility of the price.
paragraphs: Economists who agree that carbon emissions should carry a price often disagree, sometimes heatedly, about how the price should be set. One camp prefers a tax: the government announces a charge per tonne of emissions and leaves firms to decide how much to cut. The other prefers a cap with tradable permits: the government fixes the total quantity of emissions allowed, issues permits for that amount, and lets trading among firms determine what a permit costs. In a world without uncertainty the two would be equivalent. Any cap implies some price at which permits would trade, and any tax implies some level to which emissions would fall; a regulator who knew the costs of abatement could reach the same outcome by either route.

The difference appears once we admit that no one knows those costs in advance. A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain: if cutting emissions proves harder than expected, firms will pay the tax and emit more than was planned. A cap fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain: if cutting proves harder, permit prices will climb, perhaps steeply. Which uncertainty is more tolerable depends on the shape of the damage. If each additional tonne does roughly the same harm as the last, a fixed price tracks the damage well and a volatile price merely adds cost. If harm accelerates sharply past some threshold, a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price. Because the harm from carbon depends on the stock accumulated in the atmosphere over decades rather than on any single year's emissions, many economists conclude that year-to-year overshoots matter little and that a tax, or something that behaves like one, is the better instrument.

Advocates of trading reply that this argument, persuasive in the seminar room, neglects politics. A cap states its environmental goal openly, which can make it easier to defend, and the free allocation of permits to affected industries, though it hands them a windfall, has often been the price of getting a scheme adopted at all. A tax, by contrast, announces a cost to every voter and invites a fresh campaign against it with every scheduled rise.

The more telling fact is that, in practice, the two designs have drifted towards each other. Trading schemes have acquired price floors, to keep permits from becoming nearly worthless when demand falls, and price ceilings, to stop them from spiking; taxes have been given scheduled increases linked to emissions targets. The resulting hybrids are neither pure price nor pure quantity. This convergence suggests that the long debate was, in part, a debate about labels. What decides whether a carbon price works is less whether it is called a tax or a cap than whether it is high enough, broad enough in what it covers, and credible enough that firms invest on the expectation that it will last.
sets.difficulty_reason: Requires following a conditional theoretical argument about uncertainty and damage shape, then a political reply and a reframing conclusion.

sets.subtopic: Putting money values on nature is sound for decisions about small changes but misleading for whole systems, where outright limits serve better than prices.
paragraphs: Few proposals in environmental policy provoke as much unease as the suggestion that nature should be given a price. To put a figure in money on a wetland, a forest or a population of pollinating insects seems to many people a category mistake, as though one were to ask what a friendship is worth in rupees. Critics worry that once a forest has a price it can be sold, and that the language of valuation quietly concedes the very thing it was meant to resist: that everything can be exchanged for money.

Defenders of valuation reply that the choice is not between pricing nature and refusing to. Every decision to drain a marsh for housing, or to leave it alone, already implies a valuation; it merely leaves the valuation unstated. When a planning authority approves a road through a forest because the time saved by drivers is worth a stated sum, and counts the forest as worth nothing because no one has put a figure on it, the forest has in effect been priced at zero. Making the value explicit, on this view, does not turn nature into a commodity but protects it from being treated as free. A wetland that absorbs floodwater does work that would otherwise require embankments and pumps, and the cost of those replacements is a reasonable, if rough, guide to what the wetland does for the town beside it.

This reply seems to me largely right, but only within limits that its enthusiasts tend to forget. Valuation in money is a tool for comparing small changes: whether to drain this marsh or that one, whether to widen a road by a lane or route it elsewhere. It answers the question of what a little more or a little less of something is worth, given that most of it remains. It is far less suited to valuing whole systems on which economic life itself depends. To ask what all the pollinators in the world are worth is not like asking what one orchard's bees are worth and multiplying by the number of orchards. If the pollinators were gone, the prices used in the calculation, of fruit, of land, of labour, would themselves be different, and the figure would describe a world that no longer exists. Very large totals for the value of nature's services, however striking, should therefore be read as rhetoric rather than as accounts.

The practical lesson is to use valuation where it is strong and to set limits where it is weak. For decisions at the margin, an explicit figure is better than an implicit zero. For losses that would be large, irreversible or system-wide, a rule that simply forbids them, such as a minimum area of forest or a floor on water quality, may serve better than any price, because the price would become meaningless at exactly the point where it mattered most.
sets.difficulty_reason: Moves through a critique, a reply and the author's qualified position; the marginal-versus-total distinction in paragraph 3 is abstract.

sets.subtopic: A commodity boom can do lasting harm by destroying manufacturing capabilities that are not easily rebuilt, so the windfall should be managed rather than spent as if permanent.
paragraphs: Imagine a middle-income country that discovers large reserves of natural gas off its coast. Export earnings surge, foreign currency pours in, and the national currency rises in value. For a while the effects look wholly benign: imports become cheaper, the government collects more revenue, and wages climb as the gas sector and the services that cater to it compete for workers. Yet a decade later the country's manufacturers, who sell abroad against foreign rivals, may find themselves in serious trouble. A stronger currency makes their goods dearer in foreign markets, and the higher wages set by the booming sectors raise their costs at home. Factories close or move away, and the economy comes to rest ever more heavily on a single commodity. The pattern is common enough to have a name, Dutch disease, taken from the experience of the Netherlands after its large gas discoveries.

Some economists see nothing pathological in this. A country that finds itself rich in gas, they argue, should export gas and import the manufactures it once made, just as a country with fertile land should grow food. The movement of labour and capital out of factories is, on this account, the market reallocating resources to where they now earn most. To call it a disease is to mistake adjustment for illness.

The argument is coherent, but it assumes that the sectors lost can be regained whenever conditions change, and that assumption is doubtful. Manufacturing is not merely one way among others of earning foreign exchange. It is a place where workers acquire skills, where firms learn by doing, and where suppliers, engineers and managers accumulate knowledge that exists in no manual. Such capabilities take years to build and decay quickly once the firms that hold them have gone. Gas, meanwhile, is finite, and its price is notoriously volatile. When the price falls or the fields run down, the currency weakens and exporting becomes profitable again in principle, but the firms, skills and networks that would have taken advantage of the change no longer exist. The country finds that it cannot simply return to where it was.

The remedy, then, is not to leave the gas in the ground but to manage the boom so that it does not hollow out everything else. A government can save a large share of the windfall abroad, in a fund invested in foreign assets, which slows the rise of the currency and spreads the benefit across generations; it can spend at home at a pace the economy can absorb without bidding up wages across the board. Such measures are politically hard, because they ask citizens to forgo spending money they can see. But the alternative is to treat a temporary gift as permanent income, and to discover too late that the industries it displaced were not as replaceable as the theory assumed.
sets.difficulty_reason: A hypothetical case, a rival view and a rebuttal that turns on an unstated assumption; the mechanism is concrete but the rebuttal needs care.

sets.subtopic: GDP misrepresents environmental change by counting the depletion of natural assets as income and defensive spending as output, so it should be supplemented, not replaced, by accounts of natural assets.
paragraphs: National income statistics were designed to answer a question about production: how much an economy produces in a year. They were never meant to measure welfare, and some of those who built them said as much. But a statistic that is published every quarter, reported on the evening news and used to judge governments acquires a meaning beyond its design. Growth in gross domestic product has come to stand for success, and the blind spots of the measure have come to matter accordingly.

One blind spot bears directly on the environment. When a country fells a forest and sells the timber, the sale counts as production, and nothing is subtracted for the forest that is no longer there. When a country pumps oil from its fields, the revenue counts as income, though the oil in the ground was an asset and its extraction leaves the country with less of it. A household that sold a piece of its furniture every year and described the proceeds as salary would be judged to have misunderstood its own finances. National accounts already make a version of the necessary correction for machines and buildings, deducting their wear to arrive at net product; the same logic, applied consistently, would deduct the depletion of forests, fisheries, minerals and soil.

A second blind spot runs in the opposite direction. Spending that merely repairs damage counts as output. If a factory pollutes a river and the town downstream builds a treatment plant to make the water drinkable again, both the factory's production and the plant's construction add to GDP, though the town ends up with no more clean water than it had before the factory arrived. Defensive spending of this kind can make a deteriorating situation look like growth.

It does not follow that GDP should be abandoned, as some of its critics urge. For the purposes it was designed to serve, such as tracking output and employment through booms and slumps, it remains indispensable, and no alternative matches its consistency across countries and decades. Nor are the corrections straightforward. Valuing the depletion of a fishery requires assumptions about future prices and about the rate at which the stock regenerates, and different assumptions yield very different answers. The more modest and more defensible proposal is to publish, alongside GDP, accounts that record changes in natural assets, so that a country that grows by drawing down its capital can at least be seen to be doing so. A figure that is imperfect but visible is likelier to change behaviour than a correct one that nobody computes.
sets.difficulty_reason: Two parallel criticisms followed by a concession and a qualified proposal; the reasoning is clear but the final position is carefully hedged.

sets.subtopic: The green growth versus degrowth debate is misframed: absolute decoupling settles less than its champions think, past slowness proves less than its critics think, and both err in treating GDP itself as the target instead of limiting harm directly.
paragraphs: The quarrel between advocates of green growth and advocates of degrowth is usually staged as a dispute about a single empirical question: can economic output keep rising while the pressure it places on the planet falls? Green growth answers yes. Rich economies, it observes, have already shown that output and emissions can move apart, as electricity is generated from cleaner sources, heavy industry gives way to services, and the same goods are made with less material. Degrowth answers no, or not fast enough. Some of the apparent separation, it replies, reflects production moved abroad rather than pollution avoided; much of the rest is merely relative, a fall in emissions per unit of output that is swamped by the growth of output itself. On this view the only reliable way for rich countries to shrink their ecological footprint is to shrink their economies, or at least to stop enlarging them.

Both sides are right about something, and the way they frame the dispute obscures what it is really about. That emissions and output can diverge in absolute terms is no longer a mere hypothesis; it has happened in a number of countries, even after allowing for the carbon embodied in their imports. But the existence of absolute decoupling settles less than its champions suppose. The relevant question is not whether emissions can fall while output rises but whether they can fall fast enough, given how little more carbon the atmosphere can absorb before the damage becomes severe. A rate of decline that would be impressive in almost any other context may still be far too slow in this one. Equally, the degrowth case proves less than its champions suppose. That past decoupling has been too slow does not show that it must remain so; the pace of change in energy technology has repeatedly surprised forecasters, and the costs of some forms of clean power have fallen faster than most people expected a generation ago.

The deeper difficulty is that both camps take GDP as the variable of interest, one wishing to keep it rising and the other to see it fall. Yet GDP is neither the cause of environmental damage nor its cure. It is a sum of market transactions, some of which burn fuel and clear land and some of which, such as teaching, nursing or repairing, do very little of either. An economy could grow while its emissions fell sharply, if the growth came from activities of the second kind; it could shrink while its emissions rose, if a recession struck services harder than it struck heavy industry. To make the size of GDP the target, in either direction, is to aim at a proxy that is only loosely tied to the thing that matters.

A more productive stance would be indifference to growth as such. Policy would set limits directly on what does harm, through carbon prices, caps on extraction and the protection of land, and then let output rise or fall as it will within those limits. Such a stance asks something uncomfortable of each side. Advocates of green growth would have to accept that if the limits prove binding, slower growth may be the price, and that this would be not a failure of policy but a possible result of it. Advocates of degrowth would have to accept that if the limits are met while output rises, there is no further environmental case for shrinking the economy, whatever other reasons they may have for wanting a different kind of society. Neither concession is trivial, which may explain why the debate is so seldom conducted on these terms.
sets.difficulty_reason: The author corrects both positions in turn with fine distinctions (absolute versus sufficient decoupling, proxy versus target) and ends with a stance that neither side holds.

sets.subtopic: Border charges on the carbon in imports are hard to administer and may answer a smaller leakage problem than feared, but well designed they can act as a lever drawing other countries towards carbon pricing.
paragraphs: A country that puts a serious price on carbon faces an awkward possibility. If its steelmakers, cement works and chemical firms must pay for their emissions while their competitors abroad do not, production may move to places where emitting is free. The country's own emissions fall, but the world's do not, and some of its industry has been lost for nothing. Economists call this leakage, and fear of it has been among the most effective arguments against acting alone. The obvious answer is a border adjustment: a charge on imports equal to the carbon price that would have been paid had the goods been made at home, perhaps paired with a rebate for exporters. Domestic and foreign producers would then compete on equal terms, and the incentive to relocate would disappear.

The proposal is simpler to state than to carry out. To charge an import for its carbon, one must know how much carbon went into making it, and that depends on the plant, the fuel it burned and the electricity grid it drew from, none of which an importing government can observe directly. Default values can be assigned by product and by country, but these penalise clean producers in dirty countries and reward dirty producers in clean ones. Letting producers prove their actual emissions instead requires inspectors or trusted certifiers inside the exporting country, which raises questions of sovereignty as well as of cost. Trading partners, moreover, are apt to see the charge as protection dressed in green, and some have a further complaint: that countries which grew rich by burning carbon for two centuries are now taxing the goods of countries trying to do the same, and calling it fairness.

There is also reason to think the problem itself has been overstated. For most industries the cost of carbon is a small share of total costs beside labour, transport, access to markets and the quality of local institutions, and firms do not move plants lightly. A steelworks embodies decades of investment in a site, a workforce and a web of local suppliers, and escaping a modest carbon price would seldom justify abandoning all of that. The evidence from carbon prices so far suggests less relocation than the warnings predicted, though the prices in question have mostly been modest and some heavy industries have been shielded from them by free allowances, so the past may be a poor guide to the effect of prices high enough to matter.

If leakage is less of a threat than feared, why does the border adjustment matter? Its most important effect may lie not in the trade it reshapes but in the decisions it prompts elsewhere. An exporting country whose firms face a charge at the border has a reason to prefer that its own government levy an equivalent price at home, so that the revenue stays at home instead of flowing to a foreign treasury. A border adjustment can thus act less as a wall than as a lever, drawing other countries towards carbon pricing of their own. Whether it does so, or instead provokes retaliation, depends heavily on how it is designed and presented. A charge that credits carbon prices already paid abroad, that measures actual emissions where producers can show them, and that directs some of its revenue to helping poorer exporters cut their emissions has a chance of being accepted as what it claims to be. One that does none of these things will be read, not unreasonably, as the protectionism its critics allege.
sets.difficulty_reason: The passage proposes a remedy, undercuts both its feasibility and the size of the problem, then relocates its value; the stance is indirect and heavily qualified.

sets.subtopic: Heritability is a population statistic that depends on the environment and says nothing about how fixed a trait is or why groups differ.
paragraphs: When a trait is described as highly heritable, many readers hear a claim about destiny: if height or some aspect of temperament is 'mostly genetic', then upbringing can do little to alter it. The inference feels natural, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what heritability measures. Heritability is a statistic about a population, not about a person. It estimates what share of the variation in a trait, across a particular group living in a particular range of environments, can be statistically associated with genetic differences among the members of that group. It says nothing about how much of any one individual's height was produced by genes, a question that is not even coherent, since every centimetre of a person's height required both genes and food.

Two consequences follow, and both tend to surprise people. First, heritability depends on the environment in which it is measured. If every child in a group were given exactly the same diet, schooling and care, the remaining differences among them would be largely genetic, and the heritability of almost any trait would rise, not because genes had become more powerful but because the environmental differences had been taken away. Conversely, in a group where some children are well fed and others go hungry, differences in nutrition will account for much of the variation in height, and the measured heritability will fall. Second, a trait can be built almost entirely by genes and still show low heritability. Nearly everyone is born with five fingers on each hand because a developmental programme laid down in the genome builds them; most people who have fewer have lost them through injury. Variation in finger number is therefore mainly environmental, even though the fingers themselves are anything but.

The most consequential error concerns differences between groups. Suppose a trait is highly heritable within each of two populations. It is tempting to conclude that the average difference between the populations must also be largely genetic. It need not be. Picture two handfuls of seed taken from the same genetically varied sack, one sown in rich soil and the other in poor soil. Within each plot, differences in height will be largely genetic, since the soil is uniform; between the plots, the difference is due entirely to the soil. High heritability within groups is compatible with a gap between them that has no genetic basis at all.

None of this makes heritability useless. Breeders rely on it to predict how quickly a herd will respond to selection, and researchers use it to judge where genetic studies are likely to find something. The fault lies not with the statistic but with the habit of reading it as a measure of fixity. A highly heritable trait may still be changed by changing the environment; short sight is substantially heritable, and spectacles correct it all the same.
sets.difficulty_reason: Clear expository argument with concrete examples (fingers, seed plots, spectacles) and a signposted structure.

sets.subtopic: Costly ornaments can be explained as honest signals, but cost works only when it falls unequally, and not every ornament is honest.
paragraphs: For anyone who thinks of natural selection as a relentless editor of waste, the tail of a peacock is an embarrassment, since it is heavy, conspicuous and awkward in flight, and it makes its bearer easier for predators to spot and harder for him to escape. Darwin treated such ornaments as a problem of their own, and proposed that they spread not because they helped their owners survive but because they helped them mate: females preferred them, and the preference was enough to carry the trait forward. That answer, however, raised a second and more awkward question, namely why females should come to prefer an ornament that makes their mates less likely to survive.

One influential reply turns the embarrassment into the explanation. An ornament can work as an honest signal precisely because it is costly. A male in poor condition cannot afford to grow and carry an extravagant tail; only a male with ample reserves, and perhaps with sound inherited qualities, can bear the burden and still thrive. A female who chooses the most lavish display is therefore choosing, without knowing it, the male best able to pay. On this view the cost is not a side effect to be minimised but the very thing that keeps the signal reliable. A cheap signal could be produced by anyone, and a signal that anyone can produce soon carries no information.

The idea has been extended well beyond courtship. Some antelope, on spotting a predator, leap high into the air on stiff legs instead of fleeing at once, which looks like a waste of precious seconds. If the leap advertises that the animal is fit enough to outrun any chase, a predator that heeds it saves itself a fruitless pursuit, and the leaper is spared an attack. Here too, the display persuades because it could not be produced by an animal that lacked the quality it advertises.

It would be a mistake, though, to treat costliness as the whole story. Theoretical work suggests that what matters is not that a signal is expensive in absolute terms but that it is more expensive for weak individuals than for strong ones; a signal equally costly for all would sort no one. Nor need every ornament be honest. Some preferences may persist simply because females who hold them have sons who inherit the admired trait, a self-reinforcing loop that can carry ornaments well beyond any useful information. The costly signal, in short, explains why many displays can be trusted, not why every display exists.
sets.difficulty_reason: A familiar puzzle with a clearly signposted solution, an extension and a final qualification; concrete examples throughout.

sets.subtopic: The charge that natural selection is a tautology fails because fitness is a disposition that can be identified independently of reproductive outcomes.
paragraphs: A familiar complaint holds that the theory of natural selection is empty at its core. Its slogan, survival of the fittest, seems to define the fittest as those who survive, so that the principle reduces to the statement that survivors survive. A claim that cannot be false, the complaint continues, explains nothing; it merely relabels what happened. The objection is old, and it has a certain surface appeal, but it depends on running together two different things: the record of which organisms in fact left offspring and the properties that made them likely to do so.

Consider two moths of the same species, one pale and one dark, resting on bark darkened by soot. The dark moth is fitter in that setting, but not because it happens to have left more offspring. It is fitter because its colouring makes it harder for birds to see, and that is a fact one can establish independently, by measuring how often birds find each kind of moth on each kind of bark. Fitness, properly understood, is a propensity: an expected rate of reproduction given an organism's traits and its surroundings. Like the fragility of a glass, it is a disposition that holds whether or not it is ever displayed. A fragile glass may survive a lifetime on a shelf, and a well-camouflaged moth may die in an unlucky accident; neither fact refutes the disposition.

Seen this way, the theory makes claims that could turn out false. It predicts that when the propensities of variants differ, and the differences are heritable, the frequencies of the variants will shift in a direction one can anticipate from an engineering or ecological analysis of the traits. Such predictions are tested constantly, and some fail, which is precisely what a tautology could never do. The distinction also explains why biologists speak of drift: in small populations the lucky can outbreed the fit, and the actual record of reproduction can depart from the expected one. If fitness simply meant survival, drift would be unintelligible, since there would be no gap between expectation and outcome for chance to fill.

The critics are not wholly wrong, however. Biologists often measure fitness by counting offspring, because propensities are hard to observe directly, and careless writing can slide from the measurement to the definition. The remedy is not to abandon the concept but to keep the evidence for a disposition distinct from the disposition itself.
sets.difficulty_reason: Abstract philosophical argument (disposition versus record) carried by an analogy; needs the distinction held across paragraphs.

sets.subtopic: Kinship explains sterile insect workers, but the neat argument from their peculiar inheritance failed, and relatedness must be combined with ecological circumstance.
paragraphs: The sterile worker castes of ants, bees and wasps troubled Darwin as much as almost any feature of the living world. A creature that never reproduces cannot pass on whatever traits make it a good worker, so it was hard to see how natural selection could have refined the elaborate behaviour of workers over many generations. Darwin's tentative answer was that selection might act on the family rather than on the individual, much as a breeder who wants a good strain of cattle keeps the relatives of an animal whose worth became clear only after it was slaughtered.

The idea was given a precise form only in the twentieth century. A gene that disposes its bearer to help relatives can spread even if the bearer leaves no offspring of its own, provided the help raises the reproduction of relatives who are likely to carry copies of the same gene. What matters is the product of two quantities, the benefit to the relative and the probability that the relative shares the gene, weighed against the cost to the helper. Sterility, on this account, is not an anomaly to be explained away but an extreme point on a continuum of helping, reached when a helper can do more for its genes by raising siblings than by raising young of its own.

For a time, a further detail seemed to make the case almost too neat. In ants, bees and wasps, males develop from unfertilised eggs, and a peculiarity of inheritance follows: sisters who share both parents are, on average, more closely related to one another than a mother is to her daughters. If workers are more closely related to their sisters than to their own potential offspring, raising sisters is the better genetic bargain, and sterile castes should arise readily in exactly these insects. The argument was elegant, and it was widely taught. It has not survived well. Termites, whose inheritance has no such peculiarity, have sterile castes too; the queens of many ants and bees mate with several males, which dilutes the relatedness among their daughters; and the great majority of species with this peculiar inheritance are not social at all.

The lesson is not that kinship is irrelevant. Workers in social insect colonies typically do raise relatives, and the general principle remains the best account of why they can afford to forgo reproduction. The lesson is rather that relatedness is only one term in the calculation. Ecological conditions that make independent breeding hopeless, such as a scarce nest site that must be defended or food that only a group can gather, raise the benefit of helping and can tip the balance even where relatedness is modest. The special feature of inheritance made a good story, but the more durable explanation lies in the interaction of kinship with circumstance.
sets.difficulty_reason: History of an idea with a refinement that is introduced and then dismantled; the final position must be separated from the rejected one.

sets.subtopic: A shared toolkit of developmental genes shows deep common ancestry of control systems, but not a common design for the bodies they build.
paragraphs: Until late in the twentieth century, many biologists expected that animals as different as a fly and a mouse would be built by largely different sets of genes. Their bodies seemed to have little in common: one has a hard external skeleton, six jointed legs and compound eyes, the other an internal skeleton, four limbs and eyes with a single lens. If form reflects the genes that make it, the reasoning went, such different forms must be made by different genes. What came instead was one of the great surprises of modern biology. A small kit of genes that direct development, deciding where the head goes, where limbs sprout and which segments become which, turned out to be shared, in recognisable versions, across almost the entire animal kingdom.

The most striking demonstrations concerned eyes. Eyes had long been thought to have evolved independently many times, so different are the eyes of insects, squid and vertebrates. Yet a gene needed for eye development in mice has a counterpart in flies, and when the mouse version is switched on in the wrong tissue of a developing fly, the fly grows extra eyes, fly eyes, on its legs or wings. The gene does not carry a blueprint of an eye. It acts more like a switch that says, in effect, 'build an eye here', leaving the details of construction to the many other genes that each lineage has in its own repertoire.

It is tempting to conclude that the evolution of form is mostly a matter of rewiring old switches rather than inventing new parts, and there is much truth in that. Changes in when and where toolkit genes are turned on can alter the number of segments, the length of a limb or the pattern on a wing without any change in the proteins the genes make. Because a single toolkit gene acts in many tissues, a change to the gene itself would tend to disrupt many structures at once, whereas a change to one of its switches can alter a single structure and leave the rest alone. This helps explain why so much evolutionary change appears to lie in the regulatory regions of the genome.

Yet the shared toolkit should not be mistaken for a shared plan. That the same switch triggers eye-building in a fly and a mouse does not mean that their eyes are, in any useful sense, the same organ; the structures downstream of the switch were assembled separately, over hundreds of millions of years, from different materials. Common genes reveal a deep common ancestry of the control system, not a common design for what is controlled. The older view was wrong to assume that different forms require different genes; the newer enthusiasm risks the opposite error, of assuming that similar genes imply similar forms.
sets.difficulty_reason: Moves from a discovery to its correct and incorrect lessons; the control system versus controlled structure distinction carries the argument.

sets.subtopic: Mass extinctions select for traits that happen to matter in rare catastrophes, so life's history cannot be read as a simple record of design quality.
paragraphs: We tend to read the history of life as a long tournament in which the better designed win. On this view a lineage that disappeared must have had some flaw, and the dinosaurs, the textbook losers, are pictured as sluggish and outmoded long before their end. The picture is comfortable because it makes the present inhabitants of the earth look like deserving champions. For the most dramatic episodes in the record it is also misleading. During ordinary stretches of geological time, extinction does seem to track the qualities that adaptation produces: species with narrow diets, small ranges or slow breeding are more likely to vanish when conditions shift, and their places are taken by competitors that cope better. The great mass extinctions, in which a large fraction of species disappeared within a geologically brief interval, seem to follow different rules.

Consider the end of the Cretaceous period, when an asteroid struck the earth and the non-avian dinosaurs vanished along with many other groups. What determined survival in the aftermath was not, as far as can be told, excellence at the ways of life that had served well for millions of years. It was the possession of traits that happened to matter in a sudden catastrophe: small body size, a varied diet, the ability to shelter or to wait out a period of darkness and scarcity in a dormant state. Such traits had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe of this kind, which no living lineage had experienced. They were, from the point of view of the crisis, accidents.

The consequence is that mass extinctions can redirect the history of life in ways that ordinary selection would not. A group that had been flourishing, and that would probably have continued to flourish under normal conditions, can be swept away, while a group that had been marginal for tens of millions of years inherits an emptied world. The mammals, which had lived in the shadow of the dinosaurs for a very long time, are the familiar example. Their later success says little about whether they were superior to the non-avian dinosaurs in any absolute sense; it says that they passed through a narrow gate that the dinosaurs, for reasons unrelated to their earlier success, did not.

This does not mean that mass extinctions are pure lotteries. Survival in them is selective; it simply selects for different things. Nor does it mean that adaptation is unimportant, since the survivors went on to diversify through ordinary selection once the crisis had passed. What it does mean is that the long-run shape of life's history cannot be read as a straightforward measure of design quality. To understand why some groups are here and others are not, we need to know not only how well they fitted their world but also which rare disasters that world happened to contain.
sets.difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief with a case study and a careful final qualification separating selectivity from design quality.

sets.subtopic: Replicator-first and metabolism-first accounts of life's origin answer different questions and are better combined as successive stages than set up as rivals.
paragraphs: Debates about the origin of life have long been organised around a chicken-and-egg problem. In every living cell today, the information needed to build proteins is stored in nucleic acids, while the work of copying those nucleic acids is done by proteins. Neither seems able to arise without the other. One family of proposals breaks the circle by giving priority to the molecule that carries information: life began, on this view, when some molecule capable of copying itself appeared, however clumsily, and natural selection among its variants did the rest. A rival family gives priority to chemistry that sustains itself: life began as networks of reactions, perhaps on mineral surfaces near hot springs on the sea floor, that captured energy from their surroundings and kept themselves going long before any of their components stored heritable information.

The case for putting the replicator first gained great force from a discovery about RNA, a close chemical relative of DNA. RNA, it turned out, can not only carry information but also catalyse reactions, and the core of the machinery that assembles proteins in every cell is itself made of RNA. A world in which RNA did both jobs, storing instructions and doing chemical work, would dissolve the chicken-and-egg problem, and that protein-building machinery looks very much like a relic of such a world. Replicator theorists add a deeper argument. Without heredity, they say, there is no evolution in any serious sense: a chemical network that merely persists cannot accumulate improvements, because there is nothing to record which variants did better.

Metabolism-first theorists reply that the RNA world has a chemistry problem it has never solved. The building blocks of RNA are intricate molecules, hard to make without the help of enzymes and prone to fall apart in water; assembling them into long chains that can copy themselves requires a degree of order that seems unlikely to arise unaided. Self-sustaining reaction networks, by contrast, need only simple ingredients and a source of energy. These theorists also argue that heredity need not wait for a dedicated molecule. A network in which certain reactions reinforce one another could persist in several alternative states, and if fragments that break away from a network tend to restart the same state, something like inheritance exists before any gene.

It is worth noticing that the two camps are often answering different questions. Replicator theorists ask what made open-ended evolution possible, and their answer, a molecule that copies information with modest accuracy, is hard to dispute as an account of that threshold. Metabolism theorists ask where the materials and energy for any such molecule came from, and their answer, a geochemical setting that drives reactions without the help of life, is equally hard to dispute as an account of the prior stage. Presented as rivals, each side scores easy points against the other's weakest claim: that replicators could assemble themselves in a chemical vacuum, or that self-maintaining networks could evolve indefinitely without anything like genes.

The more promising view, then, treats the problem as one of sequence rather than of priority in the abstract. A chemistry able to sustain itself may have been the setting in which the first replicators formed and on which they depended, and the replicators may in turn have captured and refined the network that fed them. This does not settle the matter, since the details of each stage remain obscure and may never be recovered from a planet whose earliest rocks have been largely destroyed. But it changes what counts as progress. The question is no longer which came first, as though one of them had to be the true beginning, but how a world of self-maintaining chemistry could have given rise to one in which information was inherited.
sets.difficulty_reason: Two technical positions with their arguments and counter-arguments, followed by an authorial reframing that must be distinguished from both camps.

sets.subtopic: Convergence and contingency describe evolution at different levels of detail and are compatible, though neither settles whether something like human intelligence would recur.
paragraphs: Suppose the history of life could be rewound to some early point and allowed to run again. Would anything like the present living world appear a second time? One school answers no. Evolution, on this view, is a chain of contingencies, each step dependent on the particular steps before it and on unrepeatable accidents of climate, geology and mutation. Alter any early link, and the chain would run off in another direction entirely; the existence of vertebrates, of flowering plants or of our own species would be no more to be expected than a particular sequence of cards in a shuffled deck. On this view the tree of life is a record of accidents, intelligible after the fact but not predictable before it, and any search for a direction in it reads our own presence back into a history that never had us in mind. The rival school points to the remarkable frequency with which evolution arrives at the same solution independently. Camera-like eyes have arisen separately in vertebrates and in octopuses; streamlined bodies have evolved in fish, in extinct marine reptiles and in dolphins; flight has been achieved by insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats. If the same designs keep recurring, the argument runs, the outcome of a second run would be broadly familiar.

Each school has a strong case, and each tends to treat the other's evidence as anecdote. Convergence enthusiasts can list hundreds of cases, but the list is assembled after the fact from the solutions that did recur, and it says nothing about the far larger number of forms that appeared once and never again. Contingency enthusiasts can point to those unrepeated forms, but they often treat the mere fact that a lineage had a particular history as proof that its outcome depended on that history, which does not follow: a ball may take a unique path down a hillside and still come to rest in the only hollow at the bottom.

Much of the disagreement, I want to suggest, dissolves once we notice that the two schools are describing life at different levels of detail. At the level of broad functional solutions, a second run would very probably produce organisms that see, swim, fly and filter food, because the physical problems of moving through water or air, or of forming an image from light, admit only a few good solutions. At the level of particular lineages, the replay would almost certainly differ: there is no reason to expect that the flying creatures would be birds, or that the swimmers would have backbones. Convergence is a claim about the space of workable designs; contingency is a claim about which occupants of that space history happens to supply. The two are compatible, and both are probably true.

This reconciliation has a cost, and it is worth stating plainly. If the question that matters is whether a replay would produce something like us, a self-aware animal that makes tools and uses language, then neither school's best evidence is decisive. Intelligence of our kind has arisen, so far as we know, only once, and a single case cannot reveal whether it was a likely destination or a fluke. The recurrence of eyes and wings tells us that some problems have few solutions; it does not tell us that every capacity we value is among those solutions. On the questions that most excite the public, the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet discriminate between the two views.
sets.difficulty_reason: Abstract debate with a reconciliation by levels of description and a final limit on that reconciliation; stance is indirect and layered.

sets.subtopic: Counting saplings planted confuses an input with an outcome; forest recovery should be judged by lasting forest, which sometimes favours natural regeneration over planting.
paragraphs: Few environmental gestures are as photogenic as planting a tree. A minister kneels with a spade, a schoolchild pats soil around a sapling, and a campaign announces that so many million trees have gone into the ground this season. The appeal is easy to understand. A tree is a visible, countable object, and counting is what campaigns need: a target can be set, met and reported. Yet the habit of measuring forest recovery by the number of saplings planted has quietly confused an input with an outcome, and the confusion has consequences for the land it is meant to help.

The first problem is survival. A sapling planted in the wrong season, in compacted soil or without anyone to water it through its first dry months often dies within a year or two, and a campaign that counts plantings rather than living trees will never record the loss. The second problem is choice. Large drives tend to favour a few fast-growing species that nurseries can raise cheaply and in bulk, and the result, where the saplings do survive, may be closer to a plantation than a forest: rows of a single kind of tree, offering little to the insects, birds and fungi that a mixed woodland supports. In some places such planting has even been carried out on grasslands that were never forested at all, replacing one valuable habitat with a poor imitation of another.

An alternative, less dramatic and much harder to photograph, is to let forests come back on their own. On land where old roots, nearby seed-bearing trees and a living soil remain, simply protecting an area from grazing, fire and clearing can allow a varied forest to regenerate, often more cheaply than planting and with species suited to the site because they arrived there by themselves. Regeneration of this kind is slow at first, and for some years the land looks like scrub, which is one reason it is undervalued: it does not look like progress.

None of this means that planting is always a mistake. Where soils are badly degraded, where no seed sources survive nearby, or where a particular species must be reintroduced, careful planting may be the only way to begin. The objection is not to the spade but to the scoreboard. A campaign that measured success by the area of land that becomes, and remains, a functioning forest after ten or twenty years would sometimes plant and sometimes refrain, and it would be judged by what grew rather than by what was put into the ground.
sets.difficulty_reason: Clear problem and solution structure with an explicit concession; concrete examples and plain vocabulary.

sets.subtopic: Flagship species are a useful tool because protecting them often protects whole habitats, but they cannot set conservation priorities on their own.
paragraphs: Conservation has always had favourites. Appeals for money are illustrated with tigers, pandas, whales and elephants, animals with large eyes, recognisable faces and a reputation for grandeur, and rarely with a beetle, a freshwater mussel or a lichen. Critics have long complained that this distorts priorities. If donors give to what they find beautiful, the argument runs, then most of the living world, which is small, drab or simply invisible, will be neglected, and the species most in need of help will be the least likely to receive it. The objection is not merely aesthetic. Insects, fungi and the small organisms of soil and water do much of the work that keeps ecosystems running, yet they attract only a tiny share of public concern.

The complaint has force, but it is weaker than it first appears, because a charismatic animal rarely receives protection on its own. A large predator needs a large area, and the forest or grassland that is protected for its sake also shelters thousands of less appealing species that no donor would have paid to save directly. In this sense the famous animal works as a kind of advertisement for an entire landscape. The money is raised in the name of one face, but it is spent, at least in part, on soil, water and cover that serve everything living there.

The defence holds only up to a point, however. Some of the most threatened organisms live in habitats that no charismatic animal shares: a single cave, a spring, a patch of chalk grassland, the gravel bed of one river. Protecting a tiger reserve will do nothing for them. Moreover, money given in the name of a famous animal is sometimes spent on that animal directly, on breeding programmes, tracking collars or patrols against poachers, rather than on the wider habitat, and in such cases the advertising argument does not apply at all. A donor who pays for a radio collar has helped one tiger, and perhaps the scientists who follow it, but not the river below the reserve.

The sensible conclusion is neither to abandon flagship species nor to treat them as a complete strategy. They are a tool for raising attention and money, and a useful one. But a conservation movement that allowed the tastes of donors to draw its map of priorities would leave large gaps, and those gaps would fall precisely where the most unfamiliar forms of life are found. Some part of the effort has to be directed by need rather than by appeal, even when need comes in the shape of a mussel.
sets.difficulty_reason: A complaint, a defence and a limit to the defence, laid out paragraph by paragraph in plain language.

sets.subtopic: Conflict between farmers and recovering elephant populations is a problem of who bears the costs, not of attitudes, and appeals for tolerance ask the poor to subsidise everyone else.
paragraphs: When a population of elephants recovers, the news is usually reported as a conservation triumph, and in an important sense it is one. But the recovery is experienced very differently at the edge of the forest. For a farming household whose maize or paddy lies along an elephant's route, a single night's visit can destroy a season's income, and the danger is not only to crops: people walking home after dark, or guarding fields from makeshift platforms, are injured and sometimes killed. The benefits of a thriving elephant population are spread thinly across a nation, or across the world; its costs are concentrated on a few villages.

Discussions of the problem often frame it as one of attitudes. Farmers who retaliate, it is said, need to be taught to value wildlife, and coexistence is presented as a disposition that can be cultivated through awareness campaigns. There is something to this, since tolerance of wild animals varies a great deal between communities and is shaped by tradition as well as by loss. Yet to treat hostility as ignorance is to misread it. A farmer who has lost three harvests to elephants may understand their ecological importance perfectly well and still be unable to afford them.

The more honest framing is distributive. Coexistence is not a state of mind but an arrangement about who bears which costs. Compensation schemes acknowledge this in principle, but in practice they are often slow, demand paperwork that poor households struggle to complete, and pay for the market value of a damaged crop while ignoring the sleepless nights, the children kept from school to guard fields and the fear that hangs over every harvest. A scheme that pays a fraction of the loss, a year late, does not shift the burden; it documents it.

Practical deterrents have their place. Some communities have experimented with fences hung with beehives, which elephants tend to avoid, or with repellents made from chilli and with networks that warn villages of approaching herds, and where these work they reduce losses at modest cost. But deterrents move the problem as often as they solve it, pushing elephants onto the next village's fields. The underlying question remains political: whether the wider society that values elephants is willing to pay, promptly and in full, those who live beside them. Until it is, appeals for tolerance ask the poorest people in the landscape to subsidise everyone else's enjoyment of a recovered species.
sets.difficulty_reason: The stance is clear, but the argument turns on reframing a problem from attitudes to distribution, with a concession and a qualified remedy.

sets.subtopic: Suppressing every fire in dry forests let fuel accumulate into catastrophic fires, though the lesson depends on the ecosystem, and managers face incentives that favour continued suppression.
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, forest agencies in several countries treated fire as an enemy to be defeated wherever it appeared. The logic seemed unanswerable: fire destroys timber, threatens homes and kills animals, so every fire extinguished was a loss averted. Agencies measured their performance by how quickly they put fires out and how few hectares burned, and by those measures many of them succeeded remarkably well. Lookout towers, firebreaks and crews ready to move at short notice made it possible to reach most fires while they were still small.

The success contained its own reversal. In many dry forests, frequent fires of low intensity had once cleared the undergrowth, fallen branches and young trees that gather on the forest floor, while leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed. When such fires were suppressed year after year, that material was left to build up. The forest grew denser, and the fuel that would once have burned off in small, manageable fires accumulated until, in a hot, dry season, a fire that could not be stopped found enough of it to climb into the crowns of the trees. Such fires kill the very trees that the earlier, smaller ones had spared. By preventing many small fires, suppression had, in effect, been saving up for a few enormous ones.

The lesson is sometimes drawn too broadly. Not every ecosystem evolved with frequent fire; in some wet forests and many shrublands fire was historically rare, and a recent increase in burning there is a threat rather than a return to normal. Nor does the history of suppression explain every catastrophic fire, since drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land matter as well. The argument is not that fire is good, but that whether a given fire is harmful depends on the ecosystem in which it burns and on that ecosystem's history.

Recognising this has not made the remedy easy. Deliberately setting fires under controlled conditions, or allowing some natural fires to burn, can reduce accumulated fuel, but it carries risks that suppression appeared not to. Politically, a season without burning looks like competence. Smoke drifts over towns, and a planned burn that escapes is blamed on the people who lit it, while a wildfire that grows from decades of accumulated fuel is blamed on nature. A manager therefore faces an asymmetry. The harm of acting is visible and attributable; the harm of not acting is deferred and diffuse, and the easiest course is to keep doing what made the problem worse.
sets.difficulty_reason: Causal reversal explained through a process over time, then qualified by ecosystem type and complicated by incentives.

sets.subtopic: Fortress conservation rested on a false picture of untouched nature and imposes heavy costs, so excluding residents should be justified case by case rather than assumed.
paragraphs: The model of the national park that spread across much of the world in the twentieth century rested on a simple picture: nature is most fully itself where people are absent, and the task of conservation is to keep them out. Boundaries were drawn, guards were posted, and in many places the people who had lived within the new boundaries, herding, gathering, farming small plots or hunting, were moved elsewhere. Critics have come to call this approach fortress conservation, and the name captures both its method and its mood.

The picture of untouched nature was often historically false. Many landscapes that visitors admired as wilderness had been shaped for centuries by the people who were then removed: grasslands kept open by grazing and deliberate burning, forests whose composition reflected generations of selective harvesting and planting. Removing those people did not return the land to an original state; it began a new and unplanned experiment, and in some cases the very qualities that had made the place worth protecting began to decline. The costs to the displaced were, of course, more direct: the loss of homes, of access to food and medicine, of graves and sacred places, often with little or no compensation.

It would be too simple, however, to conclude that local residents are always the best stewards and that exclusion is never justified. Communities change, markets reach into forests, and a population that once harvested lightly may, under new pressures, begin to clear or hunt at rates the land cannot sustain. Some species, particularly those that are very sensitive to disturbance, may genuinely need areas where human presence is kept to a minimum. The romantic image of the timeless forest dweller can be as misleading as the image of untouched wilderness that it seeks to replace.

What the critique of fortress conservation establishes, then, is not a rule but a burden of proof. Exclusion imposes certain and heavy costs on identifiable people, while its benefits to wildlife are often assumed rather than shown.
