paragraphs: Few medical ideas seem as self-evidently right as early detection. A disease found sooner is a disease treated sooner, and a disease treated sooner, surely, is more often cured. Screening programmes, which look for disease in people who feel perfectly well, are built on this reasoning, and the figures they produce appear to confirm it. People whose cancers are found by screening typically survive far longer after diagnosis than people whose cancers are found because they caused symptoms. Patients who have been through screening often say as much, and public campaigns repeat the message with understandable conviction. It is hard to imagine clearer evidence that looking early pays.

The trouble is that the comparison is rigged, though by the arithmetic of detection rather than by anyone's intent. Suppose a tumour will kill a woman at seventy whatever is done. If it causes symptoms at sixty-eight, she survives two years after diagnosis; if a scan finds it at sixty-three, she survives seven. Nothing about her death has changed, but the survival figure has more than tripled, simply because the clock was started earlier. A second distortion arises from the different speeds at which tumours grow. A test repeated every few years is far more likely to catch a slow tumour, which lingers in a detectable but harmless state for a long time, than a fast one, which may appear and cause symptoms between two tests. Screened groups are therefore loaded with the gentler cases, and their better survival partly reflects what was found rather than what was done.

The most uncomfortable distortion takes this tendency to its limit. Some of the abnormalities found by screening, though they look like cancer under the microscope, would never have grown enough to cause harm in the person's lifetime. Detecting them is called overdiagnosis, and it is not an error in the usual sense, since the cells are what the pathologist says they are. The error lies in the prediction that they would have mattered, and since such a lesion is removed or destroyed once it is found, the prediction is never put to the test. People with such findings are treated, sometimes with surgery or radiation, and they then appear in the statistics as survivors, which of course they are, though they were never in danger. Because no individual can know that his or her own tumour was of this harmless kind, every overdiagnosed patient experiences the treatment as a rescue. Screening thus produces its own most sincere advocates, and the more it overdiagnoses, the more grateful survivors it creates.

None of this shows that screening is useless. For some cancers, carefully conducted trials comparing large screened and unscreened populations have found fewer deaths among those screened, and those programmes deserve their place. The point concerns the evidence, not the verdict. The question to ask of a screening programme is not how long its patients live after diagnosis but whether fewer people in the population it serves die of the disease, and whether that benefit outweighs the harm of treating people who were never going to be ill. Survival after diagnosis cannot answer that question, because it improves under the influence of lead time, slow tumours and overdiagnosis even when not a single death has been prevented. Doctors are not immune to the appeal of the survival figure, since it describes the patients they actually see; the deaths a programme fails to prevent, and the needless treatments it imposes, are visible only in comparisons between whole populations that no single clinic can make.
sets.difficulty_reason: A dense critique of a seemingly self-evident belief, built on three statistical distortions of increasing subtlety and a concession that separates the evidence from the verdict.

sets.subtopic: Trial averages should neither be applied as facts about each patient nor dismissed in favour of clinical intuition; they are the default, and departures need evidence as demanding as the average itself.
paragraphs: A randomised trial, for all its authority, answers a question about groups. It tells us that among patients like those enrolled, the people given a treatment did better on average than the people who were not, by an amount that can be estimated with known uncertainty. The doctor in a consulting room faces a different question, about a single person, and the gap between the two questions has produced two opposite errors, each of which presents itself as wisdom.

The first error is to apply the average as though it were a fact about each patient. If a drug lowers the risk of a stroke over five years from ten in a hundred to seven in a hundred, it is tempting to say that it reduces every patient's risk by three points. But the trial cannot show this. The same average would result if a small minority benefited a great deal and everyone else not at all, or if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed. An average is a summary of a distribution, and very different distributions share the same summary. Even afterwards the matter stays hidden: a patient who takes the drug and has no stroke cannot tell whether the drug or good fortune spared him. To promise a particular patient a reduction of three points is to claim knowledge the trial does not contain.

The second error starts from this observation and draws the wrong conclusion. Since every patient is different, it says, trial results do not apply to the person in front of me, and I must rely on my clinical judgement. The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. That patients differ is not news; what matters is whether they differ in ways that change how they respond to this treatment, and the clinician's impression is a poor instrument for discovering that. A doctor's experience is itself a kind of trial, but one without randomisation, with a small sample, no comparison group and a memory that favours vivid cases. If a large trial cannot reveal who benefits, a recollection of a few dozen patients is unlikely to do better.

Nor is the obvious remedy, examining subgroups within the trial, as reliable as it appears. Divide a trial's patients by age, sex, severity and a dozen other features, and some subgroups will show striking benefit or none at all purely by chance; the more divisions are made, the more such mirages appear. Findings of this kind have often failed to reappear when tested again. This does not mean that genuine differences in response do not exist. It means that claims about them need evidence as demanding as the evidence for the average itself, such as a plausible mechanism together with a difference that recurs in a fresh trial.

What follows is neither the tyranny of the average nor the licence of intuition. The average is the best default available when nothing more is known, and departures from it should be justified by reasons rather than by a sense that this patient is special. For some chronic conditions whose symptoms come and go quickly, it is even possible to run a trial within a single patient, alternating the treatment with a placebo over several periods and comparing the results. Such designs are not always practical, but they show what an answer to the individual question would actually require, and how little the bare assertion of individuality provides.
sets.difficulty_reason: An abstract argument on statistical reasoning that rejects two opposed positions and a tempting remedy before stating its own qualified view; several distinctions must be held at once.

sets.subtopic: Electronic computers inherited, rather than invented, a way of organising calculation that human computing offices had already worked out.
paragraphs: For most of its history the word 'computer' named an occupation rather than a machine. Observatories, survey offices and, later, engineering firms employed rooms of people whose work consisted of carrying out long calculations, often for tables of positions, tides or trajectories that others would use. It is tempting to treat these workers as a quaint prelude to the real story, a stopgap that lasted only until electronics arrived. That reading gets the relation backwards. The electronic computer did not introduce the idea of mechanical calculation into a world that lacked it; it inherited an idea that human computing offices had already worked out in detail.

The key feature of such offices was not the arithmetic skill of any individual but the way the work was organised. A planner with mathematical training would break a difficult problem into a sequence of simple steps, write those steps on printed sheets, and hand the sheets to workers who needed to know only how to add, subtract and look up values in a table. The workers did not have to understand why a step was there, and the scheme was in fact designed so that they would not need to. Errors were caught not by insight but by procedure: two people would compute the same column independently, and any disagreement sent the column back. What was being built, in effect, was a method in which correctness no longer depended on anyone grasping the whole.

Seen this way, much of what we think of as distinctive about programming was already present. The separation between the person who designs a procedure and the agent who executes it, the reduction of judgement to rules, the checking of results by redundancy rather than by understanding: all of these were practices before they were properties of machines. When the first electronic machines were built, their designers could borrow not only mathematical techniques from the computing offices but also a whole conception of what it meant to make a calculation reliable.

None of this is to say that the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly. Speed of the magnitude electronics provided changed which problems were worth posing at all; calculations that would have occupied a room of workers for years became routine, and whole fields grew up around them. But the continuity matters, because it reminds us that the habit of treating thought as something that can be divided, written down and handed to an executor who need not understand it is a social invention before it is a technical one. Its consequences, good and bad, were visible in offices long before they were visible on screens.
sets.difficulty_reason: Clear thesis stated early, concrete description of the offices, and an explicitly signalled concession in the last paragraph.

sets.subtopic: The characteristic risk of engagement-based recommendation is less the fragmentation of taste than the concentration of attention through feedback, a tendency older than algorithms but now faster and harder to see.
paragraphs: The most familiar complaint about recommendation algorithms is that they trap each of us in a private enclosure. Because a system learns what a user has clicked, watched or bought, the argument runs, it will keep offering more of the same, until every listener hears only the music that confirms their existing taste and every reader meets only the opinions they already hold. On this picture the danger is fragmentation: a public that once shared a common stock of songs, books and news splinters into millions of sealed niches, each tuned to one person.

The complaint is not baseless, but it may have the main tendency of these systems the wrong way round. Most recommendation engines do not learn from one user in isolation; they learn from the aggregate behaviour of very large numbers of users, and they rank items partly by how much engagement those items have already attracted. That design creates a feedback loop. An item that gets a slight early lead is shown to more people, which earns it more engagement, which earns it still more prominence. Imagine two songs of equal appeal released on the same day, one of which happens to be picked up by a few enthusiastic listeners in its first hours. Under such a loop the small, accidental difference can harden into an enormous gap, and the second song may effectively disappear, not because anyone judged it worse but because no one was shown it.

If this is right, the characteristic risk is less fragmentation than concentration: attention pooling ever more heavily on a few items, while the vast catalogue that digital distribution made available sits largely unvisited. The early hope that online platforms would let obscure work find its small audiences depended on people actually encountering that work, and a ranking system that rewards prior popularity makes such encounters rarer than the size of the catalogue suggests.

It would be wrong to present this as something algorithms invented. Bestseller lists, radio playlists and the front tables of bookshops have always amplified what was already selling, and cultural markets have long been marked by a few large successes and many neglected works. What is new is the speed of the loop and its invisibility. A bookseller choosing what to display is a person whose choices can be questioned; a ranking produced by continuous automated feedback appears simply to report what people want, when it is partly manufacturing it. The remedy, if there is one, lies less in protecting users from their own tastes than in asking how much of what looks like popular demand is an echo of earlier exposure.
sets.difficulty_reason: The author revises a familiar view rather than rejecting it, and adds a concession about older media; the stance is hedged ('may', 'if this is right').

sets.subtopic: Because personal data reveals others and supports inferences about non-sharers, privacy is partly a collective good that individual consent cannot secure on its own.
paragraphs: Debates about privacy in the age of large data sets usually begin from an image of ownership. Each person, on this view, holds a store of information about themselves, and the moral question is whether that information is taken with or without their permission. Hence the enormous weight placed on consent: the checkbox, the privacy notice, the setting that lets a user decline to share. If people are told what will happen to their data and agree to it, the transaction is treated as legitimate, and if they refuse, they are thought to have protected themselves.

The difficulty is that much personal information is not individual in the way the image assumes. A person who uploads their contact list discloses the names and numbers of people who agreed to nothing. Someone who submits a sample to a genetic testing service reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins, some of whom may not know the test was taken. More subtly, when enough people share information about their habits, a system can learn the patterns that link one trait to another, and then infer those traits in people who shared nothing at all. A person who declines to disclose, say, a health condition may find that it has been estimated, with fair accuracy, from purchases and movements that resemble those of people who did disclose it.

One might reply that the refuser has still kept their own data, and that what others choose to reveal is their own affair. But this misses what the refuser was trying to protect. Nobody declines to share a fact for the sake of a particular row in a database; they decline because they do not want the fact known. If it can be known anyway, through the choices of others, then the refusal has secured very little, and the consent framework, which places the whole burden of protection on individual decisions, has quietly ceased to describe what is actually happening.

This does not make individual consent worthless. Being asked still matters, and a person who is deceived about how their information will be used has been wronged in a way that the collective character of data does not erase. The point is that consent cannot carry the load it has been given. Privacy behaves in part like clean air or quiet streets: a condition that each person's conduct affects for others, and that no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone. Protecting it therefore requires rules about what may be inferred and done, not merely about who has clicked agree.
sets.difficulty_reason: A claim, an objection and reply, and a concession; the abstract notion of collective privacy is developed through concrete cases.

sets.subtopic: Failures blamed on human error in automated systems often arise from how automation leaves people the hardest tasks while eroding their skill, so systems should be designed around the people who must step in.
paragraphs: When an automated system fails and a human operator fails to rescue it, the official account usually ends with the words 'human error'. The phrase is accurate in a narrow sense, since a person did do the wrong thing, but it hides the way the situation was produced. Automation is typically introduced to take over the parts of a task that are routine and well understood. What remains for the human is whatever the designers could not automate: the rare, ambiguous, fast-moving situations in which the machine gives up or behaves strangely. The person is thus left with the hardest part of the job, and is expected to perform it suddenly, after long periods of doing almost nothing.

Those long periods matter. Skill at controlling a process is kept alive by exercising it, and an operator who has spent months watching a screen rather than flying, steering or adjusting will have less of it than one who did the work by hand. Worse, the automation removes the everyday experience through which people build an intuitive model of how the system behaves, so that when something goes wrong they must reason about it from first principles, under pressure, with alarms sounding. Monitoring is also something human beings do badly. Attention drifts when nothing happens for hours, and the more reliable the machine, the longer the stretches in which nothing happens.

The result is a curious inversion. The better the automation works in ordinary conditions, the less prepared its human supervisors may be for the extraordinary ones, and the more surprising their failure will look when it comes. Calling that failure human error locates the fault in the individual at the very moment when the design of the whole arrangement deserves scrutiny.

None of this is a case against automation, which has removed a great deal of tedium and many kinds of mistake. It is a case for designing automated systems around the people who must step in when they fail. That might mean having operators run the process manually at regular intervals so that their skill does not decay, building displays that show what the machine is doing and why rather than only whether it is working, or deciding deliberately that some tasks should remain shared even when they could be fully automated. Such measures cost efficiency in the short run. Their justification is that the moments they prepare for, although rare, are the ones in which the most is at stake.
sets.difficulty_reason: Concrete subject, a clearly signposted line of reasoning and an explicit concession; little abstraction.

sets.subtopic: The cloud metaphor fairly describes the user's experience but misleads public deliberation by hiding the material, located and concentrated infrastructure behind it.
paragraphs: Few technical metaphors have succeeded as completely as the cloud. To store files 'in the cloud' is to imagine them floating somewhere overhead, available from anywhere, belonging to no place in particular and weighing nothing at all. The image is not simply wrong; from the point of view of a user, it describes the experience rather well. A photograph taken on a phone appears on a laptop moments later, and the user neither knows nor needs to know where it has been in between. Yet the metaphor has migrated from describing an experience to shaping how whole societies think about a vast industrial system, and in that second role it misleads.

What sits behind the cloud is emphatically material. It consists of large buildings filled with servers, which consume great quantities of electricity and must be kept cool, often with water drawn from local supplies; of cables laid across sea floors and along railway lines; of particular sites chosen for cheap power, favourable taxes or stable ground. Each of these is somewhere, and being somewhere means being subject to the laws of a particular state, to the weather and geology of a particular region, and to the politics of the towns asked to host the buildings and supply their power. A data centre can strain a local grid or compete with farms for water, and a damaged cable can slow communication across a region.

The metaphor makes all of this hard to see. A cloud has no address, so questions about which country's courts can demand access to stored data come to seem technical rather than political. A cloud uses nothing, so the energy cost of keeping old files indefinitely available is easy to forget. And a cloud is diffuse, which suggests resilience, whereas in practice a large share of the services people rely on may depend on a small number of companies and sites, so that a single failure can ripple outward with surprising speed.

Defenders of the metaphor might point out that hiding complexity is precisely what good computing does. Nobody wants to think about the location of a server before sending a message, and abstractions of this kind are why ordinary people can use powerful systems at all. That is true, but it confuses two audiences. Abstraction is a gift to the user at the moment of use; it becomes a liability when it is carried over into the deliberations of citizens, regulators and planners, whose task is precisely to decide where the buildings go, who supplies their power and whose laws govern what they hold. For them, the useful question is not where the cloud is but how it came to seem to be nowhere.
sets.difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief with an objection and reply; the distinction between two audiences carries the argument.

sets.subtopic: The dispute over whether fluent machines understand rests on a shared all-or-nothing view of understanding, which should give way to mapping a cluster of separable abilities.
paragraphs: Whenever a machine produces fluent language, the question returns of whether it understands what it says. Two answers dominate. One holds that understanding is shown in behaviour: if a system answers questions, follows instructions and sustains a conversation in ways we cannot distinguish from a competent person, there is nothing further we could reasonably ask of it, and to withhold the word is mere prejudice in favour of our own kind. The other holds that behaviour, however impressive, can be produced by manipulating symbols whose connection to the world the system never grasps, and that understanding requires something behind the performance, some grounding of words in perception, action or experience.

The two camps disagree about almost everything except one assumption, and that shared assumption is where the trouble lies. Both treat understanding as a single property that a system either has or lacks, so that the only task is to decide which side of the line it falls on. Yet when we attribute understanding to people we do nothing of the kind. A student may understand a theorem well enough to apply it to textbook problems but not well enough to see why it fails when one condition is dropped; a mechanic may understand an engine thoroughly in practice while being unable to explain its thermodynamics. We judge understanding by a battery of loosely connected abilities: explaining, extending to unfamiliar cases, noticing one's own mistakes, connecting what one knows to what one does. These abilities can come apart, and people possess them in very different measures.

If understanding is a cluster of this kind, the all-or-nothing question about machines is badly posed. A system may display some of the abilities to a high degree and others hardly at all; it may extend a pattern brilliantly in one domain and fail, without any sign of noticing, at a trivial variation in another. Saying that it 'really understands' flattens this profile into a verdict that tells us little, and saying that it 'merely manipulates symbols' does the same in the opposite direction. The useful work lies in mapping which abilities are present, under what conditions, and how robustly.

This proposal will not satisfy everyone. Someone who believes that understanding involves an inner experience of meaning will say that mapping abilities, however finely, leaves the essential question untouched. Perhaps it does. But that question, whatever its answer, is a question about experience, and it arises equally for any being whose inner life we cannot inspect. It should not be allowed to stand in for the more tractable question of what a system can and cannot reliably do, which is, after all, the question on which most practical decisions about such systems depend.
sets.difficulty_reason: Abstract philosophical argument that rejects both reported positions by exposing a shared assumption, then partly concedes to a further objection; the stance must be separated from two reported views.

sets.subtopic: The mathematical incompatibility of fairness criteria under unequal base rates shows neither that fairness is incoherent nor that the choice is technical; it exposes a moral choice that human decision makers have always made silently.
paragraphs: Suppose a lender uses a scoring system to estimate how likely each applicant is to default, and suppose applicants belong to two groups that differ, for whatever historical reasons, in how often their members in fact default. There are several natural ways to ask whether the system treats the groups fairly. One may ask whether a given score means the same thing in both groups, so that among applicants scored as having a one-in-five chance of default, roughly one in five defaults whichever group they belong to. One may ask instead whether applicants who would in fact have repaid are wrongly refused at the same rate in both groups, or whether those who would in fact have defaulted are wrongly approved at the same rate. Each of these looks like a reasonable requirement, and each has been proposed as the meaning of fairness.

It turns out that they cannot, in general, all be satisfied together. When the groups' underlying default rates differ and the prediction is less than perfect, a score that means the same thing in both groups will produce different rates of error between them, in wrongful refusals, wrongful approvals or both, and equalising both kinds of error will make the same score mean different things in different groups. This is not a defect of any particular system that better engineering might remove; it follows from the arithmetic of prediction under unequal base rates. The finding was greeted in some quarters as a kind of scandal, and two conclusions were quickly drawn from it: that the idea of a fair algorithm is incoherent, or, conversely, that since some criterion must be chosen, the choice is a technical matter best left to the people who build the systems.

Both conclusions seem to me mistaken, and for related reasons. The impossibility does not show that fairness is incoherent; it shows that our everyday notion of fairness bundles together several demands that usually travel together and part company only under specific conditions. Discovering that two values can conflict is not the same as discovering that one of them is empty, any more than the occasional conflict between honesty and kindness shows that one of these is an illusion. Nor does the need to choose make the choice technical. Which criterion should give way depends on what the decision does to the people it touches: who bears the cost of being wrongly refused, how severe that cost is, and whether the different base rates are themselves the residue of earlier unfairness that the decision would perpetuate. Those are questions about harm and responsibility, not about arithmetic.

It is worth adding that the dilemma is not peculiar to algorithms. A loan officer who judges applicants by experience faces exactly the same trade-off whenever the groups differ in base rates; the officer simply does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know. In this respect the formal analysis has done something valuable. By making the conflict explicit, it has turned a choice that was always being made silently into one that must be made in the open, and has removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once. The danger is that the explicitness is squandered, that the choice is buried again inside the system, this time under a layer of technical vocabulary instead of a layer of personal discretion.
sets.difficulty_reason: Dense argument built on a formal result stated in words; the author rejects two opposite conclusions for related reasons and draws a further, qualified point about human judgement.

sets.subtopic: The persistence of digital information depends on incentives to copy it rather than on the medium, which reconciles the complaints that the internet never forgets and that digital records are fragile, and makes preservation an institutional task.
paragraphs: Two complaints about digital information circulate side by side, and at first sight they cannot both be true. The first is that the internet never forgets: an embarrassing photograph or an ill-judged remark, once posted, may resurface years later, copied onto sites its author has never heard of. The second is that digital records are alarmingly fragile: web pages vanish, links lead nowhere, and files saved in formats that no current program can read become, for practical purposes, meaningless strings of bits. One might expect a medium to be either durable or perishable, and it is puzzling to hear the same medium accused of both.

The puzzle dissolves once we stop asking about the medium and start asking about copying. A single digital copy is, if anything, more perishable than a sheet of paper. Paper survives neglect; a letter left in a drawer can usually be read a century later by anyone who knows the language. A file left on an old disk depends on the disk surviving, on a machine that can still read the disk, and on software that can still interpret the file, and each of these dependencies decays on its own schedule. What digital information has, and paper largely lacks, is the capacity to be copied perfectly, instantly and at almost no cost. Its persistence therefore depends far less on the durability of any one copy than on whether enough people, or enough systems, have reasons to keep making copies.

Seen in this light, the two complaints describe the same mechanism working on different material. The embarrassing photograph persists because it is the kind of thing people want to pass on, so it is duplicated faster than any single copy can be deleted. The municipal report, the small society's newsletter and the scholar's personal website persist only as long as someone pays for the server and remembers to renew the domain, because few people have any reason to copy them. Nothing about these documents makes them harder to store than the photograph; a newsletter occupies less space than most images. What they lack is a constituency of copiers. When the society disbands or the scholar retires, the single copy that existed sits on a server whose bills no one is paying, and one day it is simply gone, often without anyone noticing that it has happened. Digital persistence, in short, tracks attention and interest rather than value, and the material most likely to vanish is often the unglamorous record that matters most to a historian a generation later.

This suggests that preservation in a digital age is less a technical problem than an institutional one. Better storage media help, but no medium keeps information alive by itself; what keeps it alive is an organisation that has made copying it someone's duty, and that will go on paying for that duty when the material has ceased to be interesting. Libraries and archives have long performed this role for print, and some are trying to perform it for the web. It is tempting to hope that automated tools, which can gather enormous quantities of web pages without human effort, have made such institutions unnecessary. They have not: what such tools gather must still be stored, checked and kept readable as formats change, and someone must decide what deserves that continuing expense. Archives face a difficulty that print archives faced less acutely: the sheer volume of material means that they must choose, and every choice about what to copy is also, in effect, a choice about what to let disappear. The task cannot be avoided by declaring that everything is saved, because what is left to the accidents of attention is saved very unevenly.
sets.difficulty_reason: An apparent paradox resolved by a single mechanism, with a practical conclusion and a qualification; the reasoning is clear though the key idea is abstract.

sets.subtopic: Anonymous peer review is hard to defend chiefly where unsigned, secret reports also decide whether a paper is published, since anonymity combined with gatekeeping power removes accountability.
paragraphs: Few practices in science are defended as warmly, or examined as rarely, as anonymous peer review. A manuscript arrives at a journal, an editor sends it to two or three specialists, and their verdicts, delivered without signatures, decide whether the work enters the published record. The usual defence of the anonymity is straightforward and has real force. A young researcher asked to assess a paper by the most powerful figure in her field may hesitate to point out its flaws if her name is attached to the report, since that figure may one day sit on the committee that decides her promotion. Anonymity, on this view, is what allows candour to flow upward.

The trouble is that the same protection shelters other things as well. A referee who is quietly working on a rival theory, or whose own earlier results are contradicted by the manuscript, can recommend rejection without ever having to explain himself in public. Most referees, of course, do nothing of the kind; the difficulty is that nobody outside the editorial office can tell which ones do. Authors receive a verdict but not a reason they can contest, and readers never learn that a paper was turned away at all. A system designed to free the weak from the strong can thus end up freeing the established from scrutiny, because it is usually the established who are asked to referee, and a manuscript that challenges a reigning view is, by the nature of the case, most likely to be sent to the very people who hold that view.

It would nevertheless be wrong to infer from all this that anonymity is, in itself, the problem. What makes it dangerous is its combination with gatekeeping power. When a referee's report merely advises, when it is published alongside the paper as one reader's criticism that the authors can answer, the identity of the critic matters far less, because the criticism must persuade on its merits. When the report decides, in secret, whether anyone will read the paper at all, the absence of a name becomes the absence of accountability.

Some journals have begun to experiment along these lines, publishing papers first and attaching the referees' reports afterwards, sometimes signed and sometimes not. Such arrangements are not free of costs: they may let weak work into circulation, and they ask readers to do more of the sorting. But they reveal what the familiar arrangement conceals, namely that the case for anonymous review has always rested on an assumption about what review is for. If review exists to improve papers, a mask does little harm. If it exists to decide which papers exist, the mask deserves far more suspicion than it usually receives.
sets.difficulty_reason: A single thesis stated plainly in paragraph 3, a clearly signposted concession ('nevertheless'), and accessible vocabulary.

sets.subtopic: Null results stay unpublished less because journals reject them than because researchers abandon them as uninformative, so the remedy lies in designing studies whose null results would mean something.
paragraphs: Discussions of the so-called file drawer problem usually begin with journals. Editors, the complaint runs, prefer results that show something: a drug that works, an effect that appears, a difference between groups. Studies that find nothing are harder to place, and so they remain in researchers' filing cabinets while the published literature fills up with positive findings. A reader who surveys that literature will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print. The literature, in other words, is not a sample of the research that was done but a selection from it, made on the very quantity that readers most want to estimate.

There is truth in this account, and the remedy it suggests, journals that commit in advance to publishing well-conducted studies whatever they find, deserves the support it has received. But the account places the drawer in the wrong office. Ask a working scientist what became of her last inconclusive experiment and the answer is seldom that an editor turned it down. More often it was never written up at all. The study was abandoned before any journal had a chance to reject it, and it sits in the drawer because its own author put it there.

The reason is not laziness. A positive result, whatever its other defects, announces itself: something happened. A null result is mute about its own meaning. It may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol. The researcher who obtained it is often the person least able to tell which, and the most honest description she could offer, that she looked and did not see, is one that few colleagues would think worth the trouble of reading. Writing such a paper costs weeks and earns little, and the decision to move on is, from where she stands, entirely rational.

If this is right, obliging journals to accept null results treats the symptom at the far end. The drawer will empty only when null results become informative, and that depends on decisions made before any data are collected: samples large enough that a real effect would probably have been seen, procedures specified in advance so that a failure cannot be blamed afterwards on improvisation, checks built in to show that the apparatus was working. A null result obtained under such conditions says something definite, and researchers will publish it for the same reason they publish anything, because it tells their colleagues something they did not know.
sets.difficulty_reason: A critique of a common explanation with a concession in paragraph 2 and a causal argument that must be followed across paragraphs 3 and 4.

sets.subtopic: The reliability of citizen science depends less on volunteers' skill, which good design can manage, than on where and when they look, so sampling deserves as much attention as identification.
paragraphs: When professional scientists first began to rely on volunteers to record birds, butterflies or the timing of spring flowers, the objection most often raised was that amateurs would make mistakes. A trained ornithologist can tell two similar warblers apart by a fragment of song; a weekend walker may not know that there are two species to distinguish. Such worries were not idle, for a single confident error repeated across many records can manufacture a trend that does not exist. Data gathered by such walkers, the argument went, would be riddled with misidentifications, and conclusions drawn from it would be built on sand.

The worry was reasonable, but experience has shown it to be aimed at the lesser target. Well-run projects have learned to ask volunteers for the kinds of observation they can make reliably, such as whether any frog was heard calling at a pond on a given evening, rather than the kinds that demand years of training. Where identification is genuinely hard, volunteers can photograph what they see and leave the naming to specialists, and records that look improbable can be flagged and checked. Errors do not vanish, but when thousands of independent observations are pooled, isolated mistakes tend to be swamped by the many correct reports around them.

The more stubborn problem lies not in what volunteers see but in where and when they look. People record wildlife near their homes, along popular footpaths and on fine weekends, so that their records cluster wherever leisure, access and good weather happen to coincide. They visit nature reserves more often than industrial estates, and gardens more often than farmland. A map of volunteer sightings is therefore partly a map of the species and partly a map of the observers, and no amount of skill in identification will separate the two. A bird that seems to be thriving in the suburbs may simply be living where the watchers live.

This bias is harder to correct than misidentification precisely because it is invisible in any single record. Each observation may be impeccable; the distortion appears only in the pattern. Projects that take it seriously ask some volunteers to survey assigned locations at fixed times, accepting fewer and less convenient records in exchange for a sample whose shape is known. Such schemes demand more of participants, and they rarely attract the crowds that open recording does. But they show that the reliability of citizen science was never really a question about the competence of amateurs. It is a question about whether the people designing a project have thought as carefully about sampling as about skill.
sets.difficulty_reason: A clear problem and solution structure: an early objection, its partial answer, and a second problem signposted as 'more stubborn'.

sets.subtopic: The deficit model of science communication fails because public resistance often rests on judgements about trust and who bears the risk, though explanation remains right for some cases.
paragraphs: For much of the last century, efforts to explain science to the public rested on a simple picture. People who resisted a scientific conclusion, it was assumed, did so because they did not understand it; the gap between expert and lay opinion was a gap in knowledge, and it could be closed by supplying the missing facts. Critics later gave this picture a name, the deficit model, and the name stuck because it captured what was wrong with it: it treated the public as a vessel with a hole in it, defined entirely by what it lacked.

The model fails first on its own terms. If resistance came from ignorance, those who knew most about a contested subject would be the most accepting of the expert view, yet it is easy to find people who have read widely on a topic and still reject the consensus, sometimes with more conviction than before they began. Knowledge, it turns out, can be recruited to defend a position as readily as to change it. A person who already distrusts the source of a claim does not experience new information as enlightenment; she experiences it as further pressure from that source. The facts are heard, but they are heard as moves in a contest whose sides were chosen before the conversation began.

The deeper failure concerns what the model leaves out. Consider a village told by a team of engineers that a new dam upstream poses no danger. The villagers may follow the hydrology perfectly well. What they also know, and what the engineers' presentation omits, is that the last assurance they received from officials turned out to be wrong, that the benefits of the dam will flow to a distant city, and that if anything goes wrong it is they, not the engineers, who will bear the loss. Their scepticism is not a vacancy waiting to be filled. It is a judgement about whom to trust and who pays, and it may be quite rational even when the hydrology is sound.

None of this means that facts are irrelevant or that every misunderstanding is secretly a stance about power. Some people do hold mistaken beliefs simply because nobody has explained a matter clearly, and for them a good explanation is exactly what is needed. The error of the deficit model was to make this the whole story. Communication that begins by asking what an audience already knows, fears and has experienced will sometimes end in explanation. But it will at least explain the right thing, and it will treat the people it addresses as parties to a decision rather than as containers for information.
sets.difficulty_reason: A critique in two stages (an internal failure, then a deeper one) followed by a concession; the stance is clear but the distinctions need care.

sets.subtopic: There is no single scientific method, and the textbook sequence of steps does harm; what the sciences share is a set of communal norms for treating claims, not a procedure.
paragraphs: Generations of students have learned that science proceeds by a method, and that the method has steps. One observes, forms a hypothesis, designs an experiment, tests the hypothesis and draws a conclusion, after which the cycle begins again. The sequence is tidy, easy to examine and, as a description of what scientists actually do, very nearly useless. It is not that no scientist has ever followed it. It is that the sciences differ so widely in what they are able to do that any single recipe either excludes much of their work or becomes so general that it no longer guides anyone.

Consider the range. An astronomer studying a distant star cannot intervene in it; she can only watch, and her ingenuity lies in finding natural cases that differ in just the respect she wants to compare. A geologist reconstructing how a mountain range formed is not testing a hypothesis by experiment but assembling a history from traces, much as a detective does, and her standard of success is the coherence of a narrative that accounts for scattered evidence. A laboratory chemist may indeed run controlled experiments, but she spends much of her time on something the textbook sequence ignores entirely: making instruments and procedures work at all. To call all of this 'the scientific method' is to give one name to several distinct crafts.

The tidy sequence is not merely inaccurate; it does some damage. By making the controlled experiment the model of all good science, it encourages the view that sciences which cannot experiment are somehow lesser, as though reconstructing the history of the Earth were a provisional activity awaiting a proper laboratory. And by presenting science as a machine that turns hypotheses into conclusions, it leaves the public poorly prepared for the ordinary untidiness of research, in which results conflict, estimates are revised and experts disagree for long periods before they converge. People taught to expect the machine are apt to read each revision as a malfunction.

Is there, then, nothing that the sciences share? There is something, but it is not a procedure. What unites the astronomer, the geologist and the chemist is a set of habits about how claims are treated once they have been made: they are exposed to colleagues who are expected to attack them, they are stated in a form that evidence could tell against, and the people who make them are expected to give them up when such evidence arrives. These are norms of a community rather than steps for an individual, and that is precisely why they cannot be captured in a flowchart. A student who had absorbed them would understand science better than one who had memorised the steps, even if she could not say in what order they come.
sets.difficulty_reason: A critique of a common belief developed through three contrasting examples, a claim of harm, and a reply to the obvious objection in paragraph 4.

sets.subtopic: The Matthew effect is less an injustice to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates resources, arising when reasonable attention to reputation is converted into money.
paragraphs: When two researchers, one celebrated and one unknown, publish a discovery together, the discovery is very likely to be remembered as the celebrated researcher's. The same pattern appears when two people arrive at a result independently: the one who is already eminent tends to receive the larger share of the attention, the citations and the invitations that follow. Sociologists of science named this the Matthew effect, after the verse in the Gospel of Matthew about those who have being given more, and it is usually discussed as a problem of fairness. The unknown co-author did much of the work, and someone else collected the credit.

That description is correct within its limits, but it understates what is at stake, and it also misses why the effect is so persistent. Scientists face a literature far larger than anyone could read in a lifetime. A familiar name on a paper is a cheap signal that the paper is probably worth the reader's time, and in a world of scarce attention, readers who rely on such signals are not being foolish. To some degree, then, the effect is the by-product of a reasonable strategy for coping with abundance. Condemning it as mere snobbery does not explain why careful and fair-minded people take part in it every day.

The trouble begins when attention is converted into resources. A researcher whose papers are widely read finds it easier to win grants, which pay for students and equipment, which produce more papers, which are read more widely still. Advantage compounds. After a few rounds, the difference between two careers may bear little relation to any difference in the quality of their first ideas, and the field as a whole has placed a heavy bet on one line of work for reasons that are partly accidental. Ideas that happened to originate with the less visible researcher may wait years for a hearing, or never receive one, not because they were tested and found wanting but because nobody with the means to test them was looking in their direction.

Seen in this light, the effect is less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets, and the remedy is not to forbid readers from noticing names, which would be both futile and costly. It is to loosen the link between attention and money: to judge some grant proposals without knowing who wrote them, to set aside funds for researchers early in their careers, and to treat a famous name as a reason to read a paper rather than as a reason to believe it.
sets.difficulty_reason: The passage grants a common view, explains the phenomenon sympathetically, then relocates the harm; the shift from fairness to allocation must be tracked.

sets.subtopic: Allocating grants by lottery among proposals above a quality threshold is justified less by efficiency than by honesty, since ranking near the funding line already hides biased chance behind a show of judgement.
paragraphs: Every year, research funding agencies ask panels of scientists to read hundreds of proposals and rank them, and every year the money runs out long before the list does. The proposals near the bottom are usually easy to set aside: they are poorly argued, or unoriginal, or plainly unworkable. The difficulty lies higher up. Among the proposals that every member of the panel agrees are good, the panel must still decide which will be funded and which will not, and the line it draws often separates projects that no one present could distinguish with any confidence. It is in response to this predicament that a few agencies have begun to experiment with a once unthinkable idea: setting a threshold of quality and then choosing among the proposals above it by lot.

The proposal is usually defended on grounds of efficiency. Ranking is laborious; panels spend weeks producing distinctions that a lottery would produce in minutes. This is true, but it is the weakest part of the case, and resting on it invites the reply that good decisions are worth what they cost. The stronger argument is about honesty. Experience suggests that two independent panels given the same proposals will often disagree about which of them fall just above the funding line and which just below, a sign that, near the top, the ranking reflects the composition of the panel at least as much as the merits of the work. A ranking of this kind already contains a large element of chance. What it lacks is any acknowledgement of the fact, and so its outcomes are experienced, by winners and losers alike, as verdicts on quality.

Hidden chance is not neutral chance. When the members of a panel cannot tell good proposals apart on their merits, other preferences fill the gap: a taste for methods they themselves use, a wariness of projects whose payoff is uncertain, a familiarity with applicants they have met. Each of these is a mild bias, and none need be deliberate, but together they tilt the funding line toward the safe and the recognisable. A lottery among the proposals above the threshold removes this tilt at the margin. It cannot make the panel bolder, but it can stop the panel's caution from deciding cases that its judgement cannot decide.

The most serious objection is not that lotteries abandon judgement, since judgement is exercised in full at the threshold, where panels are reasonably good at separating the sound from the unsound. It is that scientists need to believe that reward follows merit, and that a lottery, by announcing that it sometimes does not, will corrode the motivation on which research depends. This deserves to be taken seriously. Yet the belief it seeks to protect is, at the margin, already false, and a system that preserves morale by concealing how it works purchases that morale at the cost of misleading the very people it rewards. A researcher whose proposal loses a draw has at least been told the truth: that her work was judged fundable and that the money ran out.

None of this recommends lotteries everywhere. Where proposals differ in ways that can be measured, as when an agency must choose a single design for a costly instrument, ranking is the right tool and chance would be an abdication. The argument applies only where judgement has reached its limit. Its real lesson concerns not lotteries but the pretence of precision, and agencies that decline to draw lots might still learn from it, for instance by publishing how close the decisions near their funding line actually were.
sets.difficulty_reason: Five paragraphs that set aside a weak argument, build a stronger one, answer the most serious objection and then limit the conclusion; the author's ranking of arguments must be tracked throughout.

sets.subtopic: Laboratory techniques depend partly on tacit skill that published methods cannot transmit, so making results checkable requires moving people and training as well as improving documents.
paragraphs: A scientific paper presents itself as a complete set of instructions. Its methods section lists the materials, the quantities, the temperatures and the timings, and the implicit promise is that anyone competent who follows them will see what the authors saw. This promise underwrites one of the most cherished ideas about science: that its knowledge is public, available in principle to anyone who can read, and independent of the particular people who first produced it. When a laboratory fails to reproduce a published result, the natural suspicion therefore falls either on the original claim or on the care of the people who tried to repeat it.

Anyone who has worked at a laboratory bench knows that the promise is only partly kept. Many techniques depend on skills that their practitioners cannot fully articulate: how firmly to tap a tube, how long a mixture should look cloudy before it is ready, which faint smudge on an image is signal and which is dirt. Such knowledge is not secret, and it is not mystical. It is simply of a kind that is acquired by doing and by watching others do, in the way that one learns to ride a bicycle rather than the way one learns a telephone number. A methods section can point toward it, but it cannot transmit it, any more than a manual can make its reader a competent cyclist.

It is not unusual for a group trying to build a new kind of instrument from published descriptions alone to fail again and again, while another group that has sent a member to spend some weeks in the original laboratory, or has received a visitor from it, succeeds, often without being able to say afterwards what the crucial difference was. In such cases the written instructions were not wrong. They were incomplete in ways that neither their authors nor their readers could have specified in advance, because the authors did not know which of the many things they did without thinking were the things that mattered.

Recognising this does not license complacency about how methods are reported. A great deal that is now left out of papers could be written down, and the habit of omitting it, whether to save space or to protect an advantage, deserves the criticism it receives. But the recognition does alter what we should expect from reform. Demanding ever longer methods sections will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was. If the goal is that results can be checked by people other than those who produced them, some of the effort now spent on documents might be better spent on movement: on funding researchers to visit one another's laboratories, on recording procedures as they are actually performed, and on treating the training of a replicator as part of the cost of a replication.

There is a larger consequence as well. The picture of scientific knowledge as a body of public statements, detachable from the people who hold it, turns out to be an idealisation. Much of what a field knows lives in the hands of its practitioners and moves only when they do. This is not a reason to distrust that knowledge, since skills can be tested by their results as surely as statements can. It is a reason to treat the communities that carry it, and the slow work of passing it on, as part of the infrastructure of science rather than as a private matter of training.
sets.difficulty_reason: Abstract claims about the nature of scientific knowledge, a concession about reporting that must be weighed against the proposed reforms, and a broader conclusion in paragraph 5.

sets.subtopic: The unreliable narrator matters less as a puzzle to be solved than as a device that makes readers aware of the trust they extend to all narration.
paragraphs: Discussions of the unreliable narrator tend to treat it as a game of detection. A narrator tells us one thing, the novel quietly lets us see another, and the pleasure lies in catching the gap: the jealous husband who insists he is perfectly calm, the child who reports adult quarrels without understanding them. Critics have catalogued the signals by which such narrators give themselves away, the protest that is too insistent, the detail that contradicts a claim made a page earlier, and readers have learned to watch for them. On this account the device is a kind of puzzle, and a reader who has spotted the discrepancy has finished the work the book asked of her. The narrator was wrong; the reader, standing above him, is right.

This picture is not false, but it is thin. It assumes that behind every unreliable account there stands a reliable one, which the attentive reader reconstructs and then keeps. Yet the clues by which we detect a narrator's distortions are supplied by the same narrator. We infer that the husband is jealous from what he notices, what he repeats, what he cannot stop describing; we have no other witness. The true story we assemble is therefore itself an interpretation, built from the materials of the account we have decided to distrust, and we hold it with a confidence that the novel has done nothing to guarantee.

What the best uses of the device achieve, then, is not the replacement of a bad narrator by a good reader but a change in how the reader regards narration as such. Having learned to read one voice against itself, we begin to notice how much we ordinarily grant to voices that give no sign of strain: the calm third-person narrator of a realist novel, the memoirist, the friend recounting a quarrel. None of them is lying, perhaps, but all of them select, arrange and omit. The difference is one of degree rather than kind; the narrator we call reliable is simply one whose selections we have not thought to question. The unreliable narrator makes visible a condition that reliable narration merely conceals.

It must be admitted that not every novel built on an untrustworthy teller rises to this. Some use the device as a trapdoor, a revelation held back for the final chapters that turns everything before it into misdirection. Such books can be thrilling once. On a second reading, however, they tend to go flat, because the only question they posed has been answered. The novels that survive rereading are those in which the distrust never quite settles, in which the reader, having caught the narrator out, is left wondering what she herself has failed to see.
sets.difficulty_reason: A clear critique of a common belief with one concession; concrete examples and moderate vocabulary.

sets.subtopic: The short story is not a smaller novel; it works by selection and omission, so judging it by the novel's standards mistakes its strengths for gaps.
paragraphs: A persistent habit of literary talk treats the short story as a smaller novel: the same materials of character, setting and incident, simply supplied in lesser quantities. On this view the story is where writers practise before attempting the larger form, and a collection of stories is a kind of portfolio of novels not yet written. The habit is reinforced by publishers, who have long regarded collections as harder to sell, and by critics who praise a story for being 'as rich as a novel', as though richness of that kind were the measure of success. Prizes and anthologies have sometimes followed suit, treating a writer's stories as preparation and the first novel as the real debut.

The comparison misunderstands where a short story does its work. A novel accumulates; it earns its effects through duration, letting the reader live alongside its people for enough days that change in them can be felt as change. A story has no such time to spend. What it has instead is selection, and selection pressed hard enough becomes a kind of meaning in itself. When a story shows a woman packing a suitcase, pausing over a single photograph and putting it back in the drawer, the eleven years of marriage that the story never describes are present precisely because they are withheld. The reader does not receive them; she supplies them, and the supplying is the experience.

This is why expanding a fine story so rarely improves it. Give the woman a history, a sister to confide in, a chapter on the courtship, and the photograph becomes one detail among many rather than the point on which everything turns. The gaps that had been doing the work are filled with information, and information, however well written, is less charged than implication. The reader who had been supplying the marriage is now simply told about it, and being told is a lesser kind of participation. The story's brevity was not a limitation it laboured under but the condition of its force.

None of this means that stories and novels never meet. Some writers have plainly used stories as sketches, and more than one long novel began as a few pages its author could not leave alone. Nor is brevity a virtue in itself; a weak story can hide behind its shortness, gesturing at depths it has not earned. The claim is narrower: that when a story succeeds on its own terms, it succeeds by a method the novel mostly cannot use, and that judging it by the novel's standards will reliably mistake its strengths for omissions.
sets.difficulty_reason: A single contrast developed through one concrete example; the concession is explicit and the vocabulary plain.

sets.subtopic: The suspicion of happy endings confuses closure with consolation; an ending is honest when the book's own pressures lead to it, whatever its tone.
paragraphs: Among serious readers there is a settled suspicion of the happy ending. A novel that closes with a wedding, a reconciliation or a recovered fortune is assumed to have flinched at the last moment, to have given its audience what it wanted rather than what its story required. An ending in death, separation or failure, by contrast, is credited with courage. The assumption behind the contrast is rarely stated but easy to reconstruct: life does not resolve itself neatly, so a book that resolves neatly must be telling a comforting lie. The suspicion is old enough to have become a reflex, and few readers who share it could say where they acquired it.

There is something to this, since the history of popular fiction is crowded with endings that arrive from outside the story, the unexpected legacy, the villain who repents in a paragraph, the rival who conveniently dies, and readers are right to feel cheated by them. Such endings resemble a rescue by a passing stranger: welcome, perhaps, but unconnected with anything the characters have done. But the fault in such endings is not their happiness. It is that nothing in the preceding chapters made them necessary. A catastrophe imposed in the same way, a heroine killed by a runaway carriage because the author wanted the book to feel weighty, is no less arbitrary and, being arbitrary, no more truthful.

The prejudice persists, I think, because it confuses two things that endings do. Every ending closes; it marks the point after which the story will not be told. Some endings also console; they leave the reader reassured about the world the book has shown. Closure is a formal necessity, since a story must stop somewhere, while consolation is a choice. The suspicious reader notices that happy endings console, objects to the consolation, and then mistakes the objection for an argument against closure itself, as though the honest book would be the one that refused to finish. Yet an unhappy ending closes just as firmly; it simply closes on a different note, and that note can be just as comfortably familiar to readers who have learned to expect gloom from serious fiction.

The better test, then, is an internal one: an ending is honest when it is the place towards which the book's own pressures have been carrying it, so that a reader looking back can see how the earlier pages prepared it, whether that place is a marriage or a grave. By this test some happy endings are among the hardest-won things in fiction, and some tragic ones are merely fashionable. The question to ask of an ending is not whether it pleases but whether it follows.
sets.difficulty_reason: A critique of a common belief that turns on a conceptual distinction between closure and consolation; the concession and the final test must be held together.

sets.subtopic: Genre conventions are not a cage but an instrument, like a fixed verse form; the real distinction is between books that use their conventions and books that merely obey them.
paragraphs: The line between literary and genre fiction is usually drawn in terms of freedom. The literary novel, it is said, invents its own shape, while the crime novel, the romance and the tale of space travel arrive with their shapes already supplied: a body in the first chapter, an obstacle between the lovers, a voyage, a crisis and a return. To write in a genre is, on this account, to fill in a form someone else designed, and the best a genre writer can hope for is to fill it in with unusual skill. Critics who accept this account tend to praise a crime novel by saying that it rises above its genre, as though the genre were something to be escaped.

The account has the logic of constraint backwards. Nobody thinks a sonnet a lesser poem because its length and rhyme scheme were fixed before the poet began. We understand that the fixed form is what makes certain effects possible: a turn in the ninth line registers as a turn only because the reader knows where turns are expected. Genre conventions work in much the same way. A reader of detective stories knows that the culprit must be among the people introduced, that the clues must be fair, that a solution will come. These expectations are not a cage around the writer but an instrument she can play, and the slightest departure from them, a detective who is wrong, a solution that satisfies the law but not the reader, is felt with a precision no unconventional novel can command, because the unconventional novel has no settled expectation to depart from.

This is also why devoted readers of a genre are often its most exacting critics. Having read a hundred novels built on the same frame, they are alert to the smallest variation in it, much as a chess player who knows an opening thoroughly notices a single unusual move that a novice would pass over. Such readers can tell at once whether a twist is earned or merely borrowed, and they are rarely generous to a writer who mistakes one for the other. Their pleasure is not the passive pleasure of repetition but the active one of comparison.

None of this rescues every genre book. Conventions harden into formula when a writer treats them as a checklist to be completed rather than an expectation to be worked against, and a great deal of genre fiction is written in exactly this way. But the same is true of literary fiction, which has its own conventions, the quiet revelation in the final paragraph, the fractured chronology, the unnamed narrator, and its own writers who complete them dutifully. The useful distinction is not between books that have conventions and books that lack them, since none lack them, but between books that do something with their conventions and books that merely obey them.
sets.difficulty_reason: An argument by analogy (verse form and genre) that reverses a common view, followed by a concession that redraws the distinction.

sets.subtopic: The line break in free verse is a unit of attention that can create double meanings and govern pace; the charge of chopped prose is fair against many poems but not against the form.
paragraphs: The commonest objection to free verse is that it is merely prose with the margins moved. Take away the rhyme and the regular metre, the objection runs, and nothing distinguishes a poem from a paragraph except the typographer's decision to stop each line short of the edge of the page. If that decision is arbitrary, the poem is a pretence; if it is not, the objector would like to know what principle governs it, and a vague appeal to the poet's ear or instinct will not satisfy him.

The question deserves a better answer than poets usually give it, and the principle, where there is one, is that the line is a unit of attention. A reader pauses, however slightly, at the end of a line, and in that pause whatever the line has said is briefly complete. A sentence broken across two lines is therefore read twice: once as the line presents it and once as the sentence finally does. Consider a line that ends 'she said she would not leave', followed by one that begins 'the house until the rain had stopped'. For the length of the pause the woman refuses to leave at all; the next line shrinks the refusal to a matter of weather. Neither reading cancels the other; the poem holds the larger refusal and the smaller one together, and prose, which delivers its sentences whole, cannot easily do this.

Line breaks also govern pace, since a poem made of short lines slows the reader, weighting each word with a pause, while long lines carry her forward faster than the sense alone would. Where metre once supplied a regular beat against which a poet could set the natural stresses of speech, the free verse poet works with the silence at the ends of lines, which is a cruder instrument than metre but not a negligible one, and which has the compensating advantage that it can be varied from line to line without breaking any rule.

None of this shows that the objection is always wrong. A good deal of what is published as free verse is broken into lines for no reason a reader could recover, and in such cases the objection is simply correct: the lines could be run together without loss. A fair test is exactly that: set the poem out as prose, read it again, and ask what has gone. If nothing is lost, if no meaning that the breaks created has vanished and no pace has been flattened, then the breaks were decoration. What the test cannot do is condemn the form as such, since in the poems that pass it the breaks turn out to have been doing work that the prose version cannot preserve.
sets.difficulty_reason: Claim and objection with a worked example; the author's partial concession must be weighed against the defence.

sets.subtopic: Flat characters are not a lesser achievement than round ones but a different tool, serving society, comedy and realism, so a criticism that prizes only roundness misreads novels.
paragraphs: Few critical preferences are as widely shared as the preference for round characters over flat ones. A round character, in the usual formulation, has an inner life complex enough that it can change, contradict itself and still remain recognisable; a flat character is built around a single trait and can be summed up in a sentence. The first is praised as lifelike, the second tolerated as a convenience, useful for filling a drawing room or delivering a message but not to be mistaken for the real achievement of fiction.

Yet the preference rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that the novel's central business is the representation of individual inner life. That has been the business of one powerful tradition, but it is not the only thing novels do. Many of the novels readers return to are as much about a society as about a self, and a society is felt in fiction partly through the people who never change: the aunt who has said the same thing at every family dinner for thirty years, the official for whom every request is a breach of procedure. Their fixity is not a failure of imagination. It is how the novel registers the pressure of a world that does not bend, against which its few changing figures can be measured.

Flat characters also carry much of fiction's comedy, which depends on repetition. A man who responds to every misfortune by consulting the same almanac is funny the third time precisely because he could not have done otherwise. Deepen him, give him a moment of doubt about the almanac, and the joke dissolves into pathos; this may be a gain, but it is a different book. There is, too, a case that flatness is closer to ordinary experience than critics allow. Most of the people we know, we know only by a few habits and phrases, and a novel that rendered every acquaintance in the round would misrepresent how other people actually appear to us, however much it flattered our sense of their depth.

This is not to invert the hierarchy. A novel peopled entirely by flat characters would be a cartoon, and the moment when a figure we had thought simple reveals unexpected depth remains one of fiction's great effects, though it depends on our having first taken him as simple. The point is that flat and round are not grades of achievement but different tools, suited to different tasks, and a criticism that rewards only one of them will misread every novel in which both are at work.
sets.difficulty_reason: Critique of a common preference by exposing its assumption, with three supporting functions and a closing concession.

sets.subtopic: The essay's distinctive value is thinking conducted in the open, which the thesis-first school essay has suppressed; provisionality is candour about a claim's limits, not a licence for formlessness.
paragraphs: The word from which the essay takes its name once meant an attempt or a trial, the act of testing something by weighing it, and the form has never quite outgrown that sense. An essay, in its original spirit, is not the report of a conclusion already reached but the record of a mind trying a thought to see whether it will bear weight. It may change direction halfway through, concede more than it intended, or end with a question sharper than the one it started with. These are not lapses. They are the form doing what it was invented to do, and the reader of such an essay is permitted to overhear a mind in conversation with itself rather than merely to receive the outcome of that conversation.

It is worth noticing how far the essay most people now encounter has moved from this. The essay that is taught in schools and demanded in universities opens with a thesis, marshals evidence in its favour, dispatches objections and restates the thesis at the close. It is, in effect, a miniature treatise, and its virtues are those of the treatise: clarity of claim, economy of proof, a structure the reader can grasp in advance. These are real virtues, and there are good reasons to teach them, not least that a writer who cannot state a claim plainly is in no position to test it. But the result is that a generation of writers has learned to regard any movement of thought within a piece of writing as a defect of planning, something to be removed in revision so that the finished text looks as though its conclusion had been visible from the first sentence.

What is lost is not merely a style. The provisional essay offers something the treatise structurally cannot: a view of how a conclusion is reached, including the paths that were tried and abandoned. A reader who watches a writer test an idea against an example, find that it fails, and adjust it, learns not only where the writer arrived but how much the arrival cost and what it excluded. She is reminded, too, that the conclusion was reached by someone who could have been wrong and who knows it. The treatise presents its conclusion as if it were the only place the evidence could lead; the essay, by showing the alternatives it passed through, leaves the reader better placed to disagree. In this sense its apparent modesty is a form of candour about the limits of its own claims.

The same candour explains the essayist's much criticised first person. The 'I' of the essay is often taken for self-display, and sometimes it is exactly that. More often it marks the scope of a claim: this is how the matter looks from here, to someone with this experience, and the reader is invited to test it against her own. The impersonal voice of the treatise, by contrast, claims a standpoint from nowhere in particular, and so makes its claims harder to locate and therefore harder to contest. Its objectivity is sometimes real, but it is always also a manner, and a manner can be adopted by writers whose claims have not earned it.

None of this licenses formlessness. Provisionality is easily counterfeited, and the meandering essay that circles its subject without ever risking a claim is as familiar as the rigid one, and less useful. A thought cannot be tested unless it is first stated with enough definiteness to fail. A genuine attempt is one that might not succeed, and an essay that cannot fail because it never claims anything has not attempted anything at all.
