What is obvious to someone who already knows the answer tells us very little about what an object communicates to someone meeting it for the first time, in a hurry, with a bag in one hand. A flat plate invites pushing and a vertical bar invites pulling, whatever the small sign above them says. When the hardware and the sign disagree, people follow the hardware, and they are not foolish to do so, since the shape of a thing is read faster than words are.

There is a practical cost to the blaming habit beyond the irritation it causes. Errors that are attributed to individuals are treated by asking individuals to try harder: more signs, more training, more warnings printed in red. Errors that are attributed to design are treated by changing the design, which removes the error for everyone at once. Imagine a hospital in which two different medicines are supplied in bottles of the same size and colour. If it blames the nurse who confuses them, it may discipline that nurse and still find the confusion repeated next year by someone else; if it makes the bottles look different, it removes the occasion for the mistake altogether.

This is not to say that every mistake is the designer's fault, or that objects can be made so clear that nobody ever misuses them. Some tasks are intrinsically demanding, and some carelessness is simply carelessness. But the sensible default runs the other way from the usual one. When many people make the same mistake with the same object, the repetition is itself a kind of evidence, and it points less at the people than at the thing they all share.
sets.difficulty_reason: Concrete everyday examples, a clear thesis stated twice and a plainly signposted concession.

sets.subtopic: Vernacular buildings are admired as stores of climatic wisdom, but the record is filtered and shaped by scarcity, so what deserves imitation is their method of patient local adjustment rather than their forms.
paragraphs: Admirers of vernacular building, the houses and barns put up by people who were not architects, often describe them as stores of climatic wisdom. The thick earth walls of a desert village keep rooms cool through the afternoon and release their stored warmth at night; the steep roofs of a snowy valley shed their load before it can crush the rafters; the raised floors of a flood plain let the water pass beneath. Each form, on this account, is the answer a community reached after centuries of trial, and modern builders, with their sealed glass boxes and mechanical cooling, would do well to copy it.

There is much truth in this, but the story is told too kindly. The forms that survive to be admired are the ones that worked well enough to be kept; the failures, the houses that collapsed and the villages abandoned after a bad decade, left nothing for us to photograph. What we see is therefore a filtered record, and it flatters the past. More important, vernacular forms were shaped by poverty and scarcity as much as by climate. People built with earth because earth lay underfoot and cost nothing to carry, not because they had compared it with every other material and found it best. A thick wall may be cool, but it may also be dark, damp in the rains and laborious to patch every year, and those who lived behind it bore those costs whether or not their admirers mention them.

None of this makes vernacular building less worth studying. It suggests, however, that the lesson lies in the method rather than in the forms. What village builders did well was to adjust slowly and continuously to the conditions in front of them, keeping what worked and changing what did not, with materials whose behaviour they knew intimately because they handled them every season. Their knowledge was local by necessity, and its strength was precisely that it never pretended to be anything else.

A modern builder who copies the outward shape of a courtyard house in a different climate, with different materials and a different way of living, has learned nothing from it, however picturesque the result. One who studies local sun, wind and rain with the same patience, builds, watches what happens and is willing to revise, has learned a great deal, even if the building that results looks nothing like a village house.
sets.difficulty_reason: A familiar topic with a clearly marked turn ('There is much truth in this, but') and a plainly stated conclusion.

sets.subtopic: The modernist charge that ornament is useless rests on a narrow idea of use, because ornament guides, measures and weathers for people at street level, so ornament should be judged by what it does.
paragraphs: For much of the last century it was an article of faith among progressive architects that ornament was a kind of lie. A building, they argued, should declare its structure and its purpose plainly; carving and moulding added cost without adding use, and they disguised what a building really was beneath a costume borrowed from some other age. The argument had moral force, and it produced buildings of great clarity. It also rested on a narrow idea of what counts as use.

Consider what ornament has traditionally done: a carved surround tells a stranger which of many openings is the entrance, so that nobody needs to read a sign to find the way in. A band of moulding at the level of the first floor breaks a tall wall into parts that a human eye can measure, so that a passer-by senses the height of the building in storeys rather than as an undifferentiated cliff. Projecting mouldings over windows throw rain clear of the glass and, as they weather, gather their stains in a pattern that reads as intended rather than as decay. Even purely figurative ornament, a row of leaves or a face above a door, offers the eye something to rest on at walking pace, which is the pace at which most people meet most buildings. These are uses, though not of the kind that appear in a structural calculation.

The critics were right about one thing: ornament applied without regard to any of these purposes, stuck on to a facade like a label on a jar, is as dishonest as they said, and much commercial building of their day was exactly that. But the remedy they chose, to strip surfaces bare, threw away the work along with the pretence. A blank wall is not neutral, for it tells the stranger nothing about where to go in, it offers no measure of scale, and it weathers into streaks that look like neglect because nothing in its design anticipated them. The plain building is honest about its structure and silent about almost everything else that a person on the street needs to know.

The more useful question, then, is not whether a building should be ornamented but what its ornament is for. Asked in that way, the question rules out a good deal of pastiche, the reproduction of historical detail for its associations alone. It also rules out a good deal of austerity that passes itself off as rigour, and it returns the judgement of a facade to the people who have to find their way past it.
sets.difficulty_reason: The author partly agrees with the view under attack; the stance turns on redefining 'use', which must be tracked across paragraphs.

sets.subtopic: Buyers now prize irregularity as proof of the handmade, but irregularity can be forged; what matters is the maker's responsive attention to particular material, a test some machine work can pass and some handwork fails.
paragraphs: A curious reversal has taken place in the market for handmade goods. For most of history, the aim of a skilled potter or weaver was regularity: bowls that stacked, threads of even thickness, a pattern that repeated without drift. Irregularity was the mark of an apprentice or of a hurried job, and the master's pride lay in eliminating it. Today, by contrast, the small wobble in a glaze or the slight lean of a hand-thrown cup is what many buyers are paying for. It has become the proof that a person, and not a machine, was involved.

The trouble with this proof is that it can be forged. A machine that can make a perfect cup can be programmed to make an imperfect one, and to vary the imperfection from piece to piece so that no two look alike. Tableware with deliberately uneven rims and glazes is already produced in quantity, and an ordinary buyer cannot tell it from the real thing. If what we value in the handmade is irregularity as such, then the handmade has no defence against its imitation, and the premium paid for it is a premium paid for a story.

But irregularity was never the point, and treating it as the point misunderstands what a craftsperson does. A turner working a piece of wood meets a knot, a change in the grain, a softer patch, and alters the cut to suit it; a weaver feels the tension of the warp change with the damp in the air and corrects for it. The handmade object is the record of many such small judgements, each a response to the particular material in front of the maker. Its variations, where they occur, are traces of that responsiveness, not ornaments added afterwards. A machine-made irregularity, however convincing, responds to nothing; it is a pattern generated in advance and imposed on material treated as uniform.

This distinction can be pressed too far. Machines can be built to sense and respond to their material, and a good deal of hand production is as mechanical as anything in a factory, the same motion repeated on identical parts without a thought. The line between craft and its imitation, then, is not drawn by the presence of a hand. It is drawn by whether the making involved attention to the particular, and by that test some machine work would count as craft while much of what is sold as handmade would not.
sets.difficulty_reason: The argument reverses twice (regularity to irregularity, then irregularity to responsiveness) and ends by detaching craft from the hand.

sets.subtopic: Written manuals cannot preserve a craft because craft knowledge is largely trained perception, which apprenticeship transmitted by guided practice; the remedy is to keep people practising together, not to romanticise the old system.
paragraphs: Every few generations someone tries to rescue a dying craft by writing it down. A retiring stonemason or bell founder is interviewed at length, his methods are photographed and measured, and the results are published as a manual that, it is hoped, will allow the craft to survive its last practitioners. The manuals are often admirable documents, careful, accurate and lovingly illustrated. They are also, as anyone who has tried to learn from one discovers, strangely inert: the reader can follow every step and still produce work that a practitioner would reject at a glance.

The reason is that much of what a skilled worker knows is not a set of steps at all but a way of perceiving. A smith judges the heat of iron by its colour, and the relevant differences of colour are ones that a novice literally does not see; a joiner hears in the note of a mallet whether a joint has seated; a plasterer feels through the trowel the moment at which the mix has begun to stiffen. Such judgements can be described, but the description presupposes the perception it describes. An instruction to work the metal when it turns the colour of straw is useful only to someone who already knows which straw, in which light, and how much variation is allowed.

Apprenticeship solved this problem not by explaining more but by arranging for the learner to perceive under guidance. The apprentice stood beside the master for years and was told 'now' and 'not yet' thousands of times, until he slowly came to see what the master saw. The words mattered, but chiefly as pointers to experiences the learner was having at that very moment. What passed from one generation to the next was less a body of information than a trained attention.

It would be sentimental to conclude that apprenticeship should simply be restored. It was slow, it was often exploitative, and the guilds that ran it guarded their knowledge as much to keep out competitors as to preserve standards. Nor are manuals useless: to a learner who has already begun to see, a good written account can organise and extend what practice has started. The lesson is narrower. A craft cannot be stored in a text in the way a recipe can, because what has to be preserved is a capacity of persons, and the only reliable way to keep it alive is to keep people practising it alongside others who already can.
sets.difficulty_reason: Abstract claim about perception supported by examples, followed by a concession that limits the conclusion; the 'narrower' lesson must be distinguished from a call to restore apprenticeship.

sets.subtopic: Conserving a building's accumulated layers is better than restoring it to an original state, not because conservation avoids interpretation but because it keeps its interpretations visible and reversible.
paragraphs: When an old building is to be repaired, those responsible must first decide what, exactly, they are repairing it to. One answer, long popular and still widely held, is that the building should be returned to its original state, or to the state its first builders intended. Later additions are stripped away, missing parts are reconstructed from evidence or from informed guesses, and the result is a building more complete and more consistent than it has been for centuries. The appeal is obvious: the visitor sees the church or the fort as it was meant to be seen, whole and coherent.

The opposing answer holds that a building's history does not stop at its completion. A medieval hall that later acquired a Georgian window, a Victorian staircase and a twentieth-century kitchen is a document of all those periods, and to strip it back to its first state is to erase most of what it records. On this view the repairer's duty is to keep what has survived, to intervene as little as possible, and to make any new work distinguishable from the old, so that no one mistakes a modern guess for an original fact. The restored building, by contrast, presents the restorer's idea of the past as though it were the past itself.

I find the second answer more persuasive, but it is not as neutral as its defenders sometimes suggest. Not every layer is worth keeping: a cheap partition put up in a hurry may hide a painted ceiling of real importance, and refusing to remove it is itself a choice about which history matters. Keeping everything is also an interpretation, one that values continuity over quality and treats the accident of survival as a kind of verdict. The conservator, no less than the restorer, decides what the building will say.

What separates the two approaches, then, is not that one interprets and the other does not. It is that conservation, at its best, leaves its interpretations visible and reversible, so that a later generation with better evidence or different priorities can undo them. Restoration tends to make its choices permanent and to conceal them, since a convincing reconstruction is one in which the seams cannot be found. Because every generation has been confident about the past and most have been wrong about some of it, the approach that allows its mistakes to be corrected deserves the benefit of the doubt.
sets.difficulty_reason: Comparison of two views in which the author sides with one but rejects its usual justification; the final ground of preference is stated only in the last paragraph.

sets.subtopic: Because buildings are now judged chiefly through photographs taken empty on opening day, both criticism and design have come to favour what a single frame can show over qualities that emerge through use and time.
paragraphs: Most people who hold opinions about celebrated modern buildings have never been inside them. They know them from photographs, and the photographs share a family resemblance. They are taken in the weeks after completion, before the occupants have moved in, on a day chosen for its light. Furniture, if there is any, is placed by the photographer; people, if they appear at all, are small and blurred, present to give scale rather than to show use. The building is caught at the single moment when it most resembles its architect's intention and least resembles the place it will become.

There is nothing sinister in this. The photographer is paid to show the work at its best, as a portrait painter is, and an empty room displays its proportions more clearly than a crowded one. The difficulty lies in what happens when such images become the principal medium through which architecture is judged. Reputations are made in magazines and, increasingly, on screens, and they are made quickly, long before anyone knows whether the roof leaks, whether the offices overheat in summer, or whether the grand atrium is a pleasure to cross on a wet Monday morning. Critics, who seldom have the time or the budget to return, write from the same images, and the first account of a building tends to become the account that is repeated. A building's reputation is thus fixed at the very moment when least is known about it.

The effect is not confined to critics. Architects are not naive about how their work will be seen, and a profession whose rewards follow the photograph will tend, without anyone deciding it, to design for the photograph. Qualities that register in a single frame, a dramatic cantilever, a pure white surface, a striking silhouette against the sky, come to be favoured over qualities that can be experienced only over time or through the other senses: the way a staircase feels under tired feet, the acoustics of a dining room, the dignity with which a material ages. White render photographs beautifully and often weathers badly; a brick that looks dull on the day of opening may look better in its fiftieth year than in its first.

Defenders of the photograph reply that it is the only way most of us can see buildings in distant cities, and that the alternative, judging only what one has personally visited, would make criticism parochial. They add that many buildings which photograph well also work well, and that architects idealised their work in drawings long before the camera existed. Each of these points is fair, yet none of them reaches the central point. The complaint is not that photographs flatter, which drawings did too, but that the moment of photographing has become the moment of judgement, and that the qualities a photograph can register have quietly become the qualities that count.

One modest remedy would be to make the second look as normal as the first. A building photographed and discussed again after ten years of use, with its occupants in it and its materials weathered, would be judged on evidence that the opening day cannot supply. Such a practice would not abolish the glamour of the new, and it is not meant to. It would simply give the slower virtues of a building a chance to be seen by those who will never walk through it, and it would give architects a reason to care about the tenth year as much as the first, since that is when they would next be judged.
sets.difficulty_reason: The author concedes every factual point made by the other side and relocates the complaint; the argument about incentives is implicit and the remedy is deliberately modest.

sets.subtopic: Buildings adapt best to their occupants' changing needs not when engineered for flexibility but when built with generous, simple slack, so for most ordinary buildings loose fit is a more durable virtue than precise fit.
paragraphs: Architects tend to speak of a building as finished on the day it is handed over, and most architectural criticism shares the assumption. For its occupants, however, the handover is a beginning. Within a few years the first partitions have gone up or come down, a porch has been enclosed, a garage has become a bedroom, and the building has started to diverge from its drawings. A family grows and then shrinks, a business expands into the floor above, a school changes the way it teaches, and each of these shifts leaves its mark on the fabric. Over a century the divergence can be so complete that little of the original arrangement survives except the outer walls and the structural frame. If we want to know how well a building has been designed, the question of how it absorbs such changes deserves at least as much attention as the question of how it looked when new.

The obvious response is to design for change, and for several decades architects attempted exactly that. Offices and schools were built as open floors with movable partitions, and houses with walls that could slide, fold or be unbolted, so that occupants could rearrange the interior at will. The results were often disappointing. Movable partitions were seldom moved, because moving them was laborious and disturbed the services concealed within them; the flexible plan turned out to be a plan that suited no particular use well; and the occupants, rather than enjoying their freedom, filled the space with improvised screens and cabinets to make the rooms that the design had declined to provide. Designing for every possible use, it emerged, had been a way of designing for none.

The buildings that have in fact proved most adaptable are frequently ones that were never designed with change in mind. Old warehouses and mills, with their regular grids of columns, generous ceiling heights and thick, plain walls, have been turned into flats, studios, schools and offices with surprising ease. Terraced houses built for one family have been divided into apartments and, a generation later, joined up again. What these buildings share is not flexibility in the engineered sense but a kind of slack: dimensions a little larger than any one use required, a structure simple enough to be understood by ordinary builders, and surfaces that can be cut into without catastrophe. The ordinary builder called in to knock two rooms together can see at once where the loads run and what may safely be taken away. They fit their first use loosely, and that looseness is what lets them fit their later uses at all.

The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a profession that prides itself on precision. A building tailored exactly to its brief, every room sized to its programme and every service routed to suit it, is admirable on the day of opening and brittle thereafter, because the brief will change and the building cannot. Generosity of this kind costs something at the outset, in floor area and in height, and clients are seldom eager to pay for space that nobody has yet asked for. This is not an argument against all precision; an operating theatre or a laboratory must fit its use closely, and a little slack in the wrong place is merely waste. But for most ordinary buildings, which will outlive the purposes for which they were commissioned, the more durable virtue is a certain generosity, together with a willingness on the architect's part to regard the occupants' later alterations not as defacement but as the building continuing to do its job.
sets.difficulty_reason: The argument turns on a paradox (designed flexibility fails, undesigned slack succeeds) and a fine distinction between flexibility and looseness, with a scoped concession about precision.

sets.subtopic: Kitsch is defined not by poor craft but by offering a feeling decided in advance that asks for no attention to the object, a habit that is harmless at home but dangerous where attention matters.
paragraphs: It is tempting to define kitsch as art that is badly made, but this will not do. Many objects that everyone recognises as kitsch are made with considerable skill: the porcelain shepherdess has been painted with a steady hand, the sunset over the lake is rendered with careful attention to the gradations of orange and violet, and the greeting-card verse scans perfectly. Conversely, a great deal of clumsy work, the amateur's lopsided watercolour or the child's drawing of a house, is not kitsch at all. Whatever makes an object kitsch, then, it is not a lack of craft.

A more promising account looks not at the object alone but at the transaction between the object and its viewer. Kitsch offers a feeling that has been decided in advance. The weeping clown, the kitten in a basket, the soldier embracing his mother on a railway platform: each announces the emotion it expects, and the viewer supplies that emotion without needing to look closely at anything. The image functions less as something to be seen than as a switch to be pressed. What is missing is not emotion, of which there is plenty, but resistance: nothing in the work pushes back against the viewer, complicates the feeling, or asks to be noticed for its own sake. A serious painting of grief may also move us to tears, but it usually makes us work for them, by showing grief in a particular face that does not quite match our expectation of what grief looks like.

This account explains why kitsch is so often associated with sentimentality, and also why the association is not quite exact. Sentiment as such is not the problem; a good deal of great art is openly sentimental. The problem is sentiment that has been detached from attention, so that the feeling comes first and the object is merely its occasion. The account also explains why kitsch tends to flatter. Because the emotion it calls up is one we already possess and approve of, tenderness towards the innocent or pride in sacrifice, we come away feeling good not about the work but about ourselves.

None of this requires us to despise those who enjoy kitsch, or to pretend that we never do. A cheap figurine on a grandmother's shelf may carry real memories, and those memories are not made false by the object's lack of ambition. Comfort is a legitimate thing to want from an object. The danger arises only when the habit of ready-made feeling spreads from the mantelpiece to places where attention matters more: to the way we respond to news of distant suffering, say, or to the way public ceremonies ask us to feel about history. There, the switch that kitsch trains us to press can stand in for the harder work of finding out what actually happened.
sets.difficulty_reason: Clear claim, illustration and concession in plain essay prose; the stance is stated directly.

sets.subtopic: The etiquette against spoilers rests on a mistaken theory that a story's value lies in not knowing its outcome, though it does protect one narrow, unrepeatable pleasure.
paragraphs: Few rules of modern etiquette are enforced as fiercely as the ban on spoilers. A friend who reveals the ending of a film that you have not yet seen is treated as though he had stolen something from you, and online discussions of new releases now arrive wrapped in warnings. Behind the etiquette lies a theory about what stories are for. On this view, the value of a narrative is concentrated in the not-knowing, and once the outcome is known the thing is used up, like a lottery ticket that has already been scratched.

The theory is difficult to square with how people actually behave. Children demand the same bedtime story night after night and object loudly if a single word is changed. Adults rewatch favourite films until they can recite the dialogue, and they reread novels whose endings they could describe in a sentence. Audiences at tragedies drawn from well-known legends have always known that the hero will die; for centuries this knowledge did not stop them from attending, and it may even have been part of the attraction. If knowing the ending destroyed the pleasure, none of this would make sense.

What these cases suggest is that suspense is not simply uncertainty about outcome. A viewer can know perfectly well that the hero survives and still grip the arm of the chair when the rope begins to fray, because attention is absorbed in the unfolding moment rather than in a calculation about the final scene. Much of what we enjoy in a story, moreover, lies in the manner of its telling: the rhythm of a scene, the turn of a phrase, the way a minor character reveals himself in a single gesture. None of this is spoiled by a summary of the plot, since a summary is precisely what leaves it out.

It would be too much to conclude that spoilers do no harm at all. Some stories are built around a single reversal, and the shock of the first encounter with it is a real pleasure that cannot be had twice; a mystery whose solution has been announced in advance loses something that rereading does not restore. The etiquette, then, protects something genuine. But what it protects is a narrow and unrepeatable pleasure, not the whole value of a story, and a culture that treats the ending as the only thing worth guarding may gradually forget how to enjoy everything that comes before it.
sets.difficulty_reason: A familiar topic argued in a straightforward claim, evidence, explanation and concession sequence.

sets.subtopic: Calling a pleasure 'guilty' looks modest but displays the speaker's taste and preserves an unexamined ranking of prestige; real unease about a pleasure should concern what it does, not its status.
paragraphs: The phrase 'guilty pleasure' has become one of the most common ways of talking about taste. A person confesses to loving a televised singing contest, a formulaic romance series or a song that dominated the charts in her teens, and the confession is offered with a smile that asks to be forgiven. On the surface the phrase is modest, even self-deprecating; looked at more closely, it does a surprising amount of work, and not all of that work is modest.

Consider what the speaker gains. By calling the pleasure guilty, she is able to enjoy the thing while signalling that she knows it is beneath her; she occupies the position of the enthusiast and the position of the critic at once. The confession is a kind of insurance: if her listener turns out to share the enthusiasm, nothing is lost; if the listener sneers, she has already sneered first. What looks like an admission of bad taste is therefore, very often, a display of good taste, since only someone who knows the rankings can confess to violating them.

This is why the phrase, for all its apparent humility, tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question. Every guilty pleasure implies an innocent one, a set of books, films and songs that may be enjoyed without apology because they are approved. The confession leaves that ranking intact; indeed it needs the ranking in order to mean anything. And the ranking itself is rarely examined. It is striking how often the pleasures labelled guilty are those associated with audiences who have little cultural prestige, the teenage, the provincial, the domestic, while the pleasures of the already respected are seldom described in this way, however predictable they may be.

It does not follow that no pleasure should ever make us uneasy. Some enjoyments really do deserve scrutiny: laughter at another person's humiliation, for instance, or the thrill of watching real suffering staged for entertainment. But in those cases the unease concerns what the pleasure does or endorses, not where its object sits in a ranking of prestige, and the honest response is to ask what we are enjoying and why. That question is worth asking of the singing contest as well. Perhaps the answer will be that it offers something real, the spectacle of ordinary people attempting something difficult in public. If so, the pleasure needs no apology; if not, a shrug and a smile will not settle the matter either.
sets.difficulty_reason: The argument turns on an indirect point (a confession that functions as a display) and ends with a qualified alternative.

sets.subtopic: Explaining a joke kills the laugh because it performs the listener's leap for him, but this shows humour can be analysed, and explanation that only supplies missing ground can even help.
paragraphs: It is often said that explaining a joke kills it, and anyone who has tried to rescue a failed pun by spelling out its double meaning knows that the saying is true as far as it goes. The listener nods, perhaps smiles politely, but the laugh that should have come does not. The usual inference drawn from this experience is that humour is a fragile, almost mystical thing, which analysis can only damage, and that the serious study of comedy is a contradiction in terms. The experience is real; the inference does not follow from it.

Consider why the explanation fails. A joke typically sets up one way of understanding a situation and then, in a single move, reveals that a second way was available all along. The pleasure lies largely in the listener's own discovery of the second meaning, in the sudden reorganisation that happens in his head rather than on the page. Explanation takes this work away from him. It hands over the result without the leap, much as being told the answer to a riddle deprives one of the satisfaction of solving it. The joke is not killed because it has been examined; it is killed because the examination has been done for the listener, before he could do it himself, at the very moment that was meant to be his.

Seen in this way, the failure of explained jokes tells us something about humour, namely that it depends on an active contribution from the audience, and this is exactly the kind of thing analysis can discover. There is nothing self-defeating in studying how jokes work, any more than there is in studying how riddles work. The student of comedy who analyses a routine afterwards does not expect to laugh at the analysis; he expects to understand the laugh he has already had. The two activities are simply different, and the second does not undo the first.

There is even a case for explanation in the moment, under certain conditions. A joke that turns on an unfamiliar word, a local custom or an allusion to a book the listener has not read cannot produce its leap, because one of the two meanings is not available to him at all. Here a brief explanation does not perform the leap on the listener's behalf; it only supplies the missing ground from which he can make it, and a listener who has been told what the allusion refers to will sometimes laugh a moment later, on his own. The skilled explainer, like the skilled comedian, knows how much to say and when to stop.
sets.difficulty_reason: A claim and objection structure with a fine distinction between performing the leap and supplying ground for it.

sets.subtopic: Signposted scenic viewpoints inherit a picture-making habit that values land by how well it composes, which harms unphotogenic places and thins experience, though framing can begin a wider attention.
paragraphs: Along many mountain roads there are small paved areas where drivers are invited to stop, and a sign, often bearing the symbol of a camera, announces that a view is available. People get out, look, photograph and drive on. The arrangement seems so natural that its assumptions pass almost unnoticed: that the beauty of a landscape is something seen, that it is best seen from a particular spot, and that the right relation between a person and the land is that of a spectator standing before a picture.

These assumptions have a history. The habit of judging terrain by whether it composes well, with a foreground, a middle distance and a far horizon arranged as a painter might arrange them, was cultivated by travellers who had learned to look at scenery through the conventions of landscape painting, and some of them carried tinted mirrors or framing devices so that the real view would more closely resemble a canvas. We no longer carry such devices, but the camera and the viewpoint sign perform much the same function: they select, frame and fix. A landscape that cannot be composed into a pleasing rectangle tends, under this regime, to count as no landscape at all.

The costs are not merely aesthetic. Places that photograph poorly, a marsh, a stretch of flat scrub, a slow brown river, are more easily dismissed as empty and therefore more easily drained, cleared or built upon, even when they are richer in life than the dramatic gorge that everyone stops to admire. The spectator's posture, moreover, shrinks what nature has to offer. The smell of wet earth, the sound of insects, the feel of a slope underfoot and the slow change of light over an afternoon cannot be gathered from a lay-by in the two minutes before the engine is restarted, and a beauty that is only looked at from a fixed point is a beauty with most of its dimensions removed.

It would be ungrateful to dismiss the viewpoint altogether. For many people a framed view is where an interest in landscape begins; the sign that says 'look here' has taught countless travellers to look at all, and a habit of attention begun at a lay-by can grow into something larger. The trouble lies not in framing as such but in treating the frame as the measure of value. An appreciation of nature adequate to its object would have to include the unspectacular and the unframeable, and it would have to be practised on foot and over time, with the whole body rather than with the eye alone.
sets.difficulty_reason: A history-of-an-idea structure with a practical consequence and a concession; abstraction is moderate.

sets.subtopic: Cuteness deserves serious attention because, detached from infancy, it becomes an ambivalent style that summons care and flatters power at once, disarming judgement before thought begins.
paragraphs: Cuteness is usually treated as the least serious of aesthetic qualities, if it is admitted to be an aesthetic quality at all. It belongs, we suppose, to stickers, toys and advertisements, and a taste for it is regarded as something to grow out of. Yet this dismissal sits oddly with the sheer power of the response. Few experiences in the visual world are as immediate or as hard to resist as the one produced by a large-eyed, round-faced, short-limbed creature stumbling towards us; we feel it before we have decided anything, and it is remarkably similar across cultures that agree on little else in matters of taste.

Students of animal behaviour noticed long ago that the features we find cute, a large head relative to the body, big low-set eyes, softness and clumsiness, are the features of the very young, and they proposed that the response is a mechanism for securing care. The explanation is plausible, but it accounts for less than it seems to. It tells us why infants elicit tenderness; it does not tell us why we find the same tenderness stirred by a cartoon kettle with eyes, or why the response is so readily extended to objects that need no care whatever. Once detached from the infant, the cute becomes a style, and a style can be applied to anything.

What makes the style interesting is its ambivalence. The cute object presents itself as small, soft and unable to resist, and our response to it is mixed in a way that tenderness towards a real child usually is not. Alongside the wish to protect, there is often a wish to possess and to handle, the half-joking urge to squeeze or pinch what one finds adorable, which people frequently admit to with some embarrassment. The cute flatters our power as much as it summons our care: it is an image of something that will never answer back.

This is why cuteness should be taken seriously rather than either indulged or sneered at. A quality that disarms judgement so quickly is a useful instrument for anyone who wishes to make something appear harmless, whether a product, an institution or a mascot standing in for an organisation whose activities are anything but soft. None of this means that delight in a kitten is a moral failing, and the pleasure is, in most of its forms, innocent enough. But an aesthetic that works by making us feel strong and kindly at once, and that does so before thought has begun, is not trivial; its very lightness is what gives it weight.
sets.difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief that partly accepts a reported explanation and adds an abstract point about ambivalence.

sets.subtopic: The maxim that taste cannot be disputed confuses preference with judgement; aesthetic argument aims at changed perception rather than proof, and treating views as mere taste withholds real respect.
paragraphs: The maxim that there is no disputing about taste is usually offered as a courtesy. When two people disagree about a film or a piece of music, one of them, sensing that the conversation is about to turn sour, observes that it is all a matter of taste, and the other, relieved, agrees. The maxim seems to express a modern and admirable humility, for who is anyone to tell another person what to enjoy? But the courtesy rests on a confusion, and the confusion has consequences for the way we talk about art and, in the end, for the way we treat one another.

The confusion is between preference and judgement. If you dislike the taste of coriander and I like it, there is nothing for us to argue about. Neither of us thinks the other has missed something; we simply report different reactions, and the reports do not compete, any more than your being cold and my being warm in the same room amounts to a disagreement about the room. Disagreements about novels or buildings are rarely like this. When I say that a novel is sentimental and you say that it is moving, each of us means to be saying something about the book, and each of us expects the other to be able, at least in principle, to recognise it. We point to passages, compare the novel with others, and draw attention to what the other may have overlooked. These are the moves of people who believe there is something to be right about, even if neither of them can prove it.

The relativist replies that this behaviour, however common, rests on an illusion. There is no fact about the book's sentimentality independent of readers' reactions, the argument runs, and so our disputes, unlike disputes about the boiling point of water, can never be settled; at most one party tires and gives up. This reply assumes that a dispute is worth having only if it can end in proof. Aesthetic argument, however, does not aim at proof. It aims at a change in perception, and its success is the moment when you look again at the passage I have pointed to and hear the false note I heard, or when I, rereading it at your insistence, find that what I took for manipulation is in fact restraint. Such moments are not rare. Most people can remember a friend, a teacher or a critic who showed them something they had not been able to see, and they do not remember the experience as having been talked into a preference; they remember it as having learned something.

It must be granted that some disagreements reach a floor. Two careful readers may agree about every feature of a poem, its rhythm, its imagery, its debts and its departures, and still differ about whether it is good, because one prizes austerity and the other abundance. At this point argument may genuinely run out, and it is sensible to say so. But the floor lies far lower than the maxim implies. Most disputes about taste break off long before they reach it, not because the parties have exhausted their reasons, but because one of them has invoked the maxim in order to end the conversation.

There is, finally, something less humble in the maxim than it appears. To tell someone that their view of a novel is merely a matter of taste is to decline to treat it as a view at all, that is, as a claim that might be true and from which one might learn. The maxim protects both parties from the risk of being wrong, but it does so at the price of the possibility of being changed. Real respect for another person's judgement would consist in disputing it.
sets.difficulty_reason: Abstract philosophical argument with a reported objection, a reply that reframes the aim of argument, a concession and a reversal of the maxim's claim to humility.

sets.subtopic: Both authors who call fan fiction trespass and fans who claim to own stories misdescribe the issue: a particular telling can be protected, but an imagined world has never really been ownable.
paragraphs: When readers began, in large numbers, to write and circulate their own stories about the characters of popular novels and television series, the reaction from some authors was indignation. The characters were theirs, they said; to send them on adventures their creators had never imagined, to pair them with new lovers or to bring the dead back to life was a kind of trespass. Defenders of the practice replied with equal heat that a story, once released into the world, belongs to those who love it, and that the fans who keep a fictional world alive with their own inventions have a better claim to it than the person who merely began it. Both sides, I think, have misdescribed what is at stake.

Consider first how unusual the authors' position is, historically speaking. For most of the history of storytelling, retelling was the ordinary way in which stories lived. The same heroes passed from one teller to another, gaining episodes, companions and endings along the way; a poet who took up an old legend was expected to change it, and was admired for the changes. The idea that a fictional person belongs to a single creator, and that others may not set that person in new situations, took shape alongside printing, markets for books and laws that made authorship a form of property. It is not a natural fact about stories, though it now feels like one. Fan writers, from this angle, are less the vandals of a settled order than the late heirs of a much older one.

Yet the fans' champions claim too much when they turn this history into a counter-theory of ownership. To say that a story belongs to those who love it is still to speak of belonging, merely moving the title deeds from one party to another. What the older practice suggests is rather that stories are not the sort of thing that is owned in the first place, though particular tellings are. An author can reasonably object to having her text copied and sold under someone else's name, or to having her own work altered and passed off as hers. It is much harder to see what she loses when a reader imagines her characters on another afternoon, so long as no one mistakes that afternoon for one she wrote. The distinction between a text and a world is precisely the one that both sides have blurred.

There is an irony here that deserves notice. Fan communities, which began by contesting an author's exclusive authority, have often developed authorities of their own. Long debates arise over what counts as 'canon', over which inventions are faithful and which are betrayals, and newcomers who ignore the accumulated rules can be treated with a severity that few authors would dare to show their readers. In such moments the community reproduces, on a smaller scale, the very proprietary attitude it set out to resist, as though the impulse to fix a story and guard its boundaries were not peculiar to authors but a temptation that comes with loving any story at all.

None of this settles every case, and there are surely retellings that wound in ways the distinction does not capture, as when a living author's characters are put to uses she finds degrading. But it does suggest a more useful question than the one with which the quarrel began, which asked whose story it is. The better question is what each kind of claim protects: the integrity of a particular telling, which deserves defence, or the boundaries of an imagined world, which, on the evidence of the long history of storytelling, have never been defensible for long.
sets.difficulty_reason: Comparison of two opposed views, both rejected, using a historical argument, a fine distinction between text and world, an irony and a hedged conclusion.

sets.subtopic: Narrow limits on given names can be justified by the child's interest, but stricter naming rules really protect a national stock of names and should be defended openly as cultural policy.
paragraphs: In a number of countries a newborn cannot simply be given whatever name the parents choose. A registrar may refuse a name that is judged offensive, that does not clearly indicate whether the bearer is male or female, that is spelt in a way the national orthography does not allow, or that does not appear on an official list. Defenders of such rules usually present them as a modest form of child protection. Parents, the argument runs, are fallible and sometimes vain; the child carries the name for a lifetime and had no say in choosing it; and the state, which already requires that children be schooled and vaccinated, may reasonably insist that they not be saddled with a label that will invite mockery.

There is something to this. A name is not a private ornament but a tool that other people use, and a name that cannot be pronounced, written on a form or read out in a classroom without laughter does impose a cost on the person who bears it. Cases in which parents have tried to register a brand name, a string of numbers or an insult are real enough, and few people would object to a registrar declining them. If the rules went no further than this, they would hardly be worth arguing about.

But they usually go much further, and the further they go, the less work the child-protection argument does. A rule that a name must indicate the bearer's sex protects no child from ridicule; it protects a social expectation. A rule that a name may use only the letters of the national alphabet does not shield the daughter of immigrant parents from mockery; if anything, it obliges her to carry an altered spelling of her grandmother's name, one that marks her at every roll call as someone whose family had to be corrected. An approved list, finally, protects children chiefly from novelty, and novelty is not a harm. Many names now regarded as solid and traditional were once eccentric inventions, and a register that had frozen the stock of names a century ago would have prevented most of them.

What the stricter rules actually defend, then, is the stock of names itself, treated as a piece of national heritage that private choices might erode. That is a coherent aim, and some will think it a worthy one. It should, however, be argued for openly as cultural policy and weighed against the interest parents have in naming their children as their own traditions require, rather than smuggled in under the language of protecting the young. A state that wishes to guard children from cruel names needs a short list of what is forbidden, not a long list of what is allowed.
sets.difficulty_reason: A clear claim and objection structure with a signposted concession in paragraph 2 and plain vocabulary.

sets.subtopic: Rules of usage are neither laws of the language nor mere prejudice but conventions of a register, whose authority is conventional and which should be judged by their usefulness.
paragraphs: The quarrel between those who lay down rules for English and those who merely record how it is spoken is usually staged as a contest between snobbery and science. On one side stand the guardians of usage, who object to split infinitives and sentence-final prepositions and who regard each new sense of an old word as a small act of vandalism. On the other stand the linguists, who point out that many of the rules are of recent and dubious origin, that admired writers have broken them for centuries, and that a grammar describing what speakers actually do is the only kind that deserves the name. Put this way, the linguists win easily, and in the universities, at least, they have been winning for a long time.

Yet the victory is less complete than it appears, because it rests on a confusion about what a rule of usage is. The linguist is right that no rule of this kind is a law of the language in the way that, say, the order of article and noun is: speakers who break it are still perfectly understood, and they are still speaking English. But it does not follow that such rules are mere prejudice. Beliefs about correctness are themselves part of the linguistic behaviour of a community. A speaker who avoids a construction in a job application while using it freely at home is not confused; she is responding accurately to a social fact, namely that certain readers will judge her by it. A descriptive grammar that ignored such judgements would be describing an imaginary community.

What the prescriptivist gets wrong is not the existence of the rules but their source. The traditional defence appeals to logic, or to the example of Latin, or to a clarity the condemned construction supposedly lacks. These appeals rarely survive inspection. The objection to splitting an infinitive, for instance, makes some sense in a language where the infinitive is a single word and cannot be split, and very little in one where it is two. The real authority of such a rule is conventional: it binds because enough educated readers expect it to be observed, and for no deeper reason.

Seeing the rules as conventions of a register, rather than as laws or as prejudices, changes the question we should ask about them. It is no longer whether a usage is correct in some absolute sense, but whether a given convention earns its keep: whether it marks a distinction readers find useful, or merely sets a test that excludes those who were never taught it. Some conventions pass that test; many fail it. The point is that they can be judged, and that judging them is neither the snob's work nor the scientist's alone.
sets.difficulty_reason: The author qualifies both sides of a familiar debate, so the stance must be assembled from paragraphs 2 to 4.

sets.subtopic: Switching between languages in conversation is usually a skilled, meaningful use of two grammars rather than a sign of incomplete mastery, though some settings may rightly require one language.
paragraphs: A parent who hears a child begin a sentence in one language and finish it in another often worries that the child has learned neither properly. Teachers have voiced the same anxiety, and so, at times, have bilingual speakers themselves, who describe their own mixing with a kind of apology, as though it betrayed a laziness they ought to overcome. The assumption behind the worry is simple: a speaker who switches must be reaching for a word he does not have, and a speaker who is constantly reaching has not finished learning.

The assumption is not absurd, and sometimes it is true. Anyone who has lived between two languages knows the moment when the word for a kitchen utensil, or for a form at the bank, has been acquired in one language and simply not in the other. But careful recordings of bilingual conversation suggest that such gaps account for only part of what happens, and not the most interesting part. Switches tend to fall at points where the grammars of the two languages fit together and to avoid points where they clash, so that a sentence begun in one language and finished in another is usually well formed by the standards of both. A speaker who was merely groping for words would not be so tidy. To switch in this way, one needs to know two grammars well enough to sense, without thinking, where they can be joined.

Nor is the timing of a switch random. Speakers move into the other language to report what someone else said, to mark a change of topic, to soften a refusal, to signal that a remark is a joke, or to draw a listener in or shut one out. A grandmother's proverb may be quoted in the language she used, not because the speaker cannot translate it, but because the translation would lose the grandmother. In such uses the switch itself carries meaning, much as a change of tone does within a single language; it is a resource that monolingual speakers lack, not a failure that they have avoided.

None of this means that every setting must welcome mixing. An examination set in one language, or a document that must be read by people who know only one, may reasonably require a speaker to stay within it, and a bilingual who could not do so would indeed have a problem. The error lies in treating the ability to keep languages apart as the measure of competence, and the habit of combining them as its absence. Most bilinguals can do both. Judging them by the first alone is like judging a pianist only by whether she can play with one hand.
sets.difficulty_reason: A critique of a common belief with a concession at each stage; the reasoning about grammar in paragraph 2 needs careful reading.

sets.subtopic: A word's earliest recorded meaning has no authority over its present meaning, though etymology remains valuable for what it reveals about a language's past.
paragraphs: Few arguments about words are made with more confidence than the appeal to origins. Someone uses 'decimate' to mean 'destroy most of', and a correspondent points out that the word comes from a Roman military punishment in which one soldier in ten was put to death, so that its proper sense is the loss of a tenth. Someone else describes an idea as 'nice' and is reminded that the word once meant 'foolish' or 'ignorant'. The assumption in each case is that a word's earliest meaning is its real one, and that later senses are errors which happen to have spread.

The assumption cannot be applied consistently, and nobody tries. If original meanings were binding, 'nice' would still be an insult, and so would a good many words now used without a second thought; the critic who insists on the Roman sense of 'decimate' does not, as a rule, insist on the earlier senses of the other words in his own sentence. Nor is there any principled place to stop. Most words have a history that runs back past the language in which they are now used, and the 'original' sense of any word is simply the earliest one of which we happen to have records. To treat that sense as authoritative is to give a vote to speakers who have been dead for centuries and to deny one to everyone now alive.

What a word means is settled, as far as anything settles it, by how the people who use it understand one another. This is not a counsel of indifference, for a shift in meaning can have a cost: if a word that once marked a fine distinction comes to be used loosely, the distinction may become harder to express, and a writer may reasonably prefer to keep it. But that is an argument about present usefulness, and it has to be made on those terms. It gains nothing from the fact that the stricter sense came first.

Etymology is not thereby made worthless. The history of a word can explain an odd spelling, reveal a forgotten link between two words that now look unrelated, or show how a community's way of life left its traces in the vocabulary, and it is one of the pleasures of knowing a language well; what it cannot do is serve as a court of appeal. To know where a word came from is to know something about the past of a language; it is not to know what the word must mean today.
sets.difficulty_reason: A single clear thesis developed with familiar examples, a signposted concession and a closing limitation.

sets.subtopic: Documenting an endangered language preserves a record rather than the language, and treating documentation as rescue diverts effort from supporting transmission to children.
paragraphs: When a language is said to be endangered, the response that attracts the most attention is documentation. Linguists record the last fluent speakers telling stories, explaining how to build a house or prepare a medicine, conjugating verbs on request; the recordings are transcribed, annotated and deposited in archives designed to outlast the people who made them. Such projects are routinely described as saving the language, and the phrase is meant sincerely. Something irreplaceable is, after all, being kept from disappearing.

But what is kept is not quite a language. A language, in the sense that matters to its speakers, is a practice: it is what people do when they greet one another, quarrel, court and console, and its existence consists in the fact that children acquire it from those around them. An archive holds evidence of that practice, often superb evidence, but it no longer holds the practice itself. To say that a recorded language has been saved is a little like saying that a photographed forest has been conserved. The photographs may be invaluable to someone who later tries to replant; they are not the trees.

The distinction would be pedantic if it did not affect what gets done. It does. Documentation produces outputs that funders and universities know how to count: hours of recording, entries in a dictionary, a published grammar. Supporting transmission produces almost nothing of the kind. It means paying for a language nest in which grandparents look after toddlers, defending a family's decision to speak the home language against the advice of a doctor or a teacher, or making it possible for young adults to earn a living without moving to a city where the language is of no use to them. These efforts are slow, uncertain and hard to evaluate, and when resources are short, the countable work tends to win.

None of this is an argument against archives. Where a community later sets out to bring back a language that has ceased to be spoken at home, the quality of the earlier documentation can decide how much of it can be recovered, and descendants have had reason to be grateful for the patience of a recorder who wrote down what their grandparents' generation did not pass on. The mistake is to treat documentation as the rescue rather than as insurance against the rescue failing. Where speakers still exist and children could still learn from them, the record is the second-best outcome, and a policy that spends most of its effort on it has quietly accepted defeat.
sets.difficulty_reason: A problem and solution argument built on a distinction (record versus practice) that the questions require applying, with a concession in the last paragraph.

sets.subtopic: The emergence of new sign languages shows that full grammar arises from learners' predispositions amplified by transmission across a community and its generations, not from an isolated mind or mere convention.
paragraphs: Few natural experiments in linguistics are cited as often as the birth of a new sign language. Where deaf people who have had no shared language are brought together, at a newly founded school, say, or in a village where hereditary deafness is common, they do not remain without one for long. A system of signs takes shape among them, and within a few decades it has acquired the apparatus of a full language: consistent word order, ways of marking who did what to whom, devices for referring back to something already mentioned. The case is regularly offered as decisive evidence that the capacity for grammar is built into the human mind and needs only an occasion to express itself.

The evidence is real, but it supports a more interesting conclusion than the one usually drawn from it. A deaf child raised among hearing people who do not sign will typically invent gestures to communicate with her family, and these home signs show some structure of their own: distinct gestures for actions and for things, and a tendency to place them in a regular order. What they do not become, however long the child uses them, is a full language. The leap appears only where there are many signers, and it appears in stages. The first cohort, who created the system as adolescents or adults, typically use it with more variation and less regularity than the children who learn it from them; and it is those children, receiving a still untidy system and reproducing it more consistently than they found it, who drive it towards full grammatical form.

If grammar were simply waiting inside each mind for an occasion, the solitary home signer would have occasion enough. She has a lifetime of need, a willing family and an intact brain. What she lacks is other people who share her system and, above all, a younger generation to learn it from her. The emergence of a sign language thus looks less like the unveiling of a finished structure than like a process distributed across minds and generations, in which individual predispositions are amplified by repeated transmission until regularities that were faint in any single user become fixed in the community.

This is not to deny that the mind brings a great deal to the task. The speed of the process, a matter of decades rather than centuries, and the resemblance between the regularities that emerge and those found in long-established languages both point to strong biases in how children learn. But the case tells against the picture of language as an organ that grows in isolation, as surely as it tells against the picture of language as a mere convention on which people agree. A language turns out to need both a particular kind of learner and a particular kind of crowd.
sets.difficulty_reason: A case study leading to a general point that rejects two rival pictures; the key contrast between home sign and community sign is spread over paragraphs 2 and 3.

sets.subtopic: Everyday metaphors are productive and therefore live as tools of expression, but whether they shape thought beyond speech can be settled only by non-linguistic evidence.
paragraphs: It has become a commonplace that the metaphors buried in ordinary speech reveal the structure of ordinary thought. We speak of arguments as if they were battles, defending positions, attacking weak points, winning or losing; we speak of time as if it were space, with deadlines approaching, holidays behind us and the future ahead. On the view that has made this observation famous, such expressions are not decorations added to a literal meaning but the surface of deep conceptual mappings, in which one domain of experience is understood in terms of another. We do not merely talk about argument as war; to a large extent, it is claimed, we think about it that way, and we would argue differently if our language had taught us to think of it as, say, a dance.

The opposing view is equally simple. Most of these expressions, it holds, are dead metaphors, idioms whose figurative origin is no longer felt by anyone who uses them. A speaker who says that a table has legs is not thereby thinking of the table as an animal, and a speaker who defends a position need not have soldiers anywhere in mind. On this account, inferring a mental mapping from a pattern of idioms is like inferring a belief in sorcery from the fact that people say 'bless you' after a sneeze: the history of an expression is mistaken for its present psychology.

Each view, I think, gets one thing right and one thing wrong. The sceptic is right that the evidence most often cited for the mapping view is weaker than it looks. If the existence of the mapping is inferred from the expressions, and the expressions are then explained by the mapping, the argument has gone round in a circle; the sheer number of warlike expressions for argument cannot by itself show that anything in the mind corresponds to them. But the sceptic is wrong to treat these expressions as a collection of fossils. Dead metaphors are inert: one cannot extend the legs of a table into talk of its knees or its gait and expect to be understood. The metaphors of argument and time are not inert in this way. A speaker who says that her opponent's case was all ammunition and no target, or that next week is already breathing down our necks, may be using a phrase she has never heard, and she is understood at once. Something is generating these extensions, and a list of frozen idioms cannot be it.

Productivity, then, rather than frequency, is the better test of whether a metaphor is alive, and by that test many everyday metaphors are alive, at least in the sense that speakers can use them as patterns for making and understanding new expressions. That is a real result, and it is more than the sceptic allows. It is also less than the mapping view claims. To show that a pattern is available for making expressions is not to show that it governs how people reason when they are not speaking, still less that a different language would leave them reasoning differently. Those further claims are empirical, and they can be settled only by evidence that does not itself consist of the very expressions in question: by watching how people solve problems, judge situations or remember events, and asking whether the metaphor leaves its mark there.

The debate has often been conducted as though one had to choose between seeing language as a window onto thought and seeing it as a heap of dead habits. The more modest position is less exciting but easier to defend: our metaphors are living tools of expression, and their influence on thought beyond expression is an open question that the metaphors themselves cannot answer.
sets.difficulty_reason: Compares two views and adopts an intermediate position whose limits are drawn finely; the key distinction between availability for expression and influence on reasoning is abstract.

sets.subtopic: The line between a language and a dialect is drawn by social institutions rather than by mutual intelligibility, but a socially drawn line is still real and matters.
paragraphs: Ask most people how to tell a language from a dialect and they will offer a test that sounds admirably objective: if two groups of speakers can understand each other, they speak dialects of one language; if they cannot, they speak different languages. The test has the appeal of turning a question that looks political into one that looks empirical. One need only sit speakers down together, the thought goes, and see whether conversation succeeds. The test promises, moreover, to spare the linguist from taking sides in quarrels that are seldom really about grammar.

Unfortunately the test does not deliver what it promises, and the reasons are instructive. Intelligibility is a matter of degree, not of yes or no; it varies with the topic, the speed of speech and the listener's experience; and it is frequently lopsided, so that speakers of one variety follow their neighbours more easily than their neighbours follow them. Worse, it is not transitive. Across many regions, a traveller passing from village to village finds that each community understands the next without difficulty, while communities at the two ends of the chain cannot understand each other at all. Where on such a chain does one language stop and the next begin? Intelligibility alone gives no answer, and the boundaries actually drawn on maps tend to coincide with something else entirely: the borders of states, the reach of a written standard, the language of schooling and broadcasting.

Everyday usage of the two words confirms this. The Scandinavian languages are counted as several, though their speakers can often converse, each using their own; the spoken varieties of Chinese are commonly called dialects, though many of them are no more mutually intelligible than languages that everyone agrees are distinct. In each case the label tracks not the distance between the varieties but the presence or absence of a shared written form, a shared state, a shared sense of belonging together. A dialect, in ordinary usage, is very often simply a variety that lacks the institutions which would have entitled it to be called a language.

It is tempting to conclude that the distinction is therefore empty, a piece of politics dressed up as science, and some writers have drawn exactly that conclusion. It does not follow. That a boundary is drawn by institutions rather than by sound systems does not make it unreal, any more than the border between two countries is unreal because no river marks it. Whether a variety has a standard spelling, a literature, a place in the classroom and a name its speakers use with pride makes a large difference to how it is learned, how it changes and whether it survives. A variety used in schools and courts acquires words for law and science; one confined to the kitchen and the field tends to borrow such words, or to give way to a variety that has them. Those are facts about the social life of a variety, not about its grammar, but they are facts.

The mistake, then, lies not in drawing the distinction but in where we locate it. The difference between a language and a dialect is not a property of the speech itself, waiting to be measured; it is a property of the arrangements a society has made around that speech. To see this is not to abandon the distinction. It is to understand that when a community campaigns to have its dialect recognised as a language, it is asking not for a correction of the linguistic facts but for a change in those arrangements, and that the request should be judged on those terms.
sets.difficulty_reason: Critique of a common belief that turns on a concession and then rejects the obvious sceptical conclusion; the final position (social but real) is abstract and easily confused with the view the author rejects.

sets.subtopic: Handwriting instruction remains worthwhile because forming letters by hand aids learning in ways an efficiency-based objection overlooks.
paragraphs: Few school subjects have lost their defenders as quickly as handwriting. When most adult writing passes through a keyboard or a touchscreen, the hours once devoted to forming letters on lined paper can look like a ritual preserved out of institutional habit rather than educational necessity. Why, the argument runs, should a child labour over the loops of a joined script that she will rarely use after leaving school, when the same time could be given to typing, programming or simply reading more widely? The objection has the considerable appeal of common sense, and part of it is right. But it rests on a narrow idea of what handwriting lessons were ever for.

The narrow idea treats handwriting as a delivery system, a way of getting words from a head onto a surface, and judged by that standard alone it has plainly been outpaced. Yet for a young child, forming a letter by hand is also a way of learning the letter. To write a b rather than a d, the child must attend to direction, proportion and the small differences that distinguish one shape from its neighbours, and that sustained attention seems to help fix the shapes in memory in a way that pressing a key does not. A keyboard presents every letter ready-made; the hand has to build each one. Several researchers have suggested that this building is part of how early readers come to recognise letters at all, though the evidence is still being argued over and is far from settled.

There is a second, quieter benefit, which concerns older students rather than beginners. Students who take notes by hand cannot transcribe a lecture word for word, because the hand is too slow. They are forced to choose, compress and rephrase, and that compression is itself a kind of thinking, an early and private interpretation of what the lecturer actually argued. The student with a laptop can capture far more, and may understand far less, since verbatim copying can proceed without the words ever being weighed. The slowness that makes handwriting look obsolete is, in this setting, precisely its use.

None of this is an argument for preserving every feature of the old curriculum. The insistence on one elegant joined style, and the marks lost for an untidy loop, had more to do with the manners of an earlier age than with learning, and they can be abandoned without much loss. Nor should typing be neglected in the name of tradition; children need both. The case for handwriting, properly made, is modest: not that it is beautiful or traditional, but that the hand teaches the eye and slows the mind in ways that are useful precisely because they are inefficient. A curriculum that drops it to save time may find that it has saved the wrong thing.
sets.difficulty_reason: A clearly signposted critique of a common belief with an explicit concession in the last paragraph; plain vocabulary.

sets.subtopic: The codex replaced the scroll less because it was cheaper than because it made texts navigable, which changed how books could be used.
paragraphs: The replacement of the scroll by the codex is one of the quiet revolutions in the history of reading. In the Mediterranean world of the early centuries of the common era, a book was usually a long roll of papyrus, wound on itself and read by unrolling one column at a time; within a few hundred years the dominant form had become the codex, a stack of folded sheets bound along one edge, which remains the shape of most books today. The customary explanation for the change is economy: a codex uses both sides of its writing material, it packs more text into less volume, and it is easier to carry. All of this is true, and none of it is quite enough.

The economic story struggles with timing. If thrift alone had driven the change, one would expect the codex to have spread fastest where writing material was scarce and to have triumphed as soon as its savings were obvious. Instead it lingered for generations as a humble format for notebooks, accounts and school exercises, while prestigious literature stayed on the roll. Its adoption was uneven in ways that cost does not explain; some communities, early Christian ones among them, seem to have taken it up well before their neighbours, for reasons that probably had as much to do with identity and use as with price.

A more illuminating difference lies in how the two forms allow a reader to move through a text. A scroll is constructed for continuous reading from beginning to end: to find a passage near the middle, one must wind through everything that precedes it, and comparing two distant passages is awkward enough that readers leaned heavily on memory instead. A codex, by contrast, can be opened anywhere. A finger can hold one place while the eye checks another; a page can be marked, numbered and returned to. The codex, in other words, made the text navigable, and navigation changed what reading could be. A legal compilation, a book of scripture to be cited in argument, a technical manual to be consulted rather than recited: these are works one enters at a point rather than travels through, and they suit the codex far better than the roll.

It would be a mistake to convert this into a narrative of inevitable progress. Readers of rolls were not deprived; they cultivated habits of memorisation and recitation that served their purposes admirably, and something of that intimacy with a whole text may have been lost when books became places in which to look things up. Nor did the codex create consultative reading out of nothing. But the form encouraged certain practices and discouraged others, and over centuries the encouragement told. The later apparatus of the book, page numbers, tables of contents and indexes, would have been nearly pointless on a roll. It is the codex's logic worked out in full.
sets.difficulty_reason: History of an idea that accepts the standard explanation's premises while rejecting its sufficiency, followed by a concession against a progress story.

sets.subtopic: A good dictionary is neither a court that rules on meaning nor a neutral mirror, but an argument from evidence whose authority is that of a careful witness.
paragraphs: When people settle an argument about a word by 'looking it up', they treat the dictionary as a court whose ruling ends the case. The image is understandable, since a dictionary speaks in the flat, confident voice of a statute, but it misrepresents how the better dictionaries are made. A serious dictionary does not decide what words mean; it reports, as carefully and as comprehensively as it can, what speakers and writers have been observed to mean by them.
