option_rationales.D: A poor view bears on the ordinary question of whether she 'had a clear view'; the passage ties the decoy question only to the ranger's announcement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the birdwatcher is not ordinarily asked about decoys, but 'If a park ranger has just announced that decoys have been placed along that stretch of river, the question changes'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the ordinary checks (care, expertise, clear view) with the special circumstance that makes the decoy relevant.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the author says the sceptic 'changes the subject'. This most nearly means that the sceptic

options.A: introduces a new topic, dreaming, that has no bearing on whether someone is really sitting in a room reading.
options.B: uncovers a hidden flaw in ordinary claims to know that the people making those claims had failed to notice.
options.C: replaces the standard that governs ordinary claims to know with a far stricter one and then judges those claims by it.
options.D: abandons the question of what we know and turns instead to the practical question of how we ought to act.

questions.correct_answer: (C) replaces the standard that governs ordinary claims to know with a far stricter one and then judges those claims by it.

option_rationales.A: This reads the phrase literally; dreaming bears directly on the sceptic's challenge, and the author's complaint is about the standard, not the topic.
option_rationales.B: The same sentence denies this: the sceptic 'does not discover a hidden flaw in our ordinary claims'.
option_rationales.D: Turning to how we must act is the 'shrug' response of paragraph 2, made by those who concede the argument, not the sceptic's own move.

questions.explanation: The full sentence reads that the sceptic 'changes the subject by importing a standard that no ordinary claim was ever meant to satisfy'. The subject changes because the question being answered is no longer the ordinary one about knowledge but one set by a different, stricter standard.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'changes the subject' as a change of topic rather than a change of standard.
questions.difficulty_reason: The literal sense of the idiom is a tempting wrong option; the correct answer needs the rest of the sentence.

questions.question: The author's attitude to the response that would 'concede the argument and shrug' (paragraph 2) is best described as

options.A: approving, because the response rightly sees that the sceptic's conclusion leaves practical life entirely untouched.
options.B: critical, because the response grants the sceptic's standard a correctness that it has never been shown to have.
options.C: dismissive, because the response overlooks the real possibility that we are in fact dreaming at this moment.
options.D: ambivalent, because the response is generous to the sceptic in one respect but unfair to him in another.

questions.correct_answer: (B) critical, because the response grants the sceptic's standard a correctness that it has never been shown to have.

option_rationales.A: The author calls the concession 'too generous' (paragraph 2), which is a criticism, and never endorses the claim about practical life.
option_rationales.C: The author's complaint is the opposite: the response takes the sceptic too seriously, not too lightly, and the author never treats dreaming as a live possibility.
option_rationales.D: The passage finds the response too generous and identifies no respect in which it is unfair to the sceptic.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'This concession is too generous' and explains that it treats the sceptic's standard 'as if it were simply the correct standard, which we happen to fall short of'. The author then argues that the standard is not the one we actually apply.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's agreement that scepticism has some value (paragraph 4) as approval of the shrug.
questions.difficulty_reason: Tone must be read from the reason the author gives, not from the word 'concede'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of which alternatives a knower must exclude?

options.A: Experienced birdwatchers misidentify herons far less often than beginners do, even when they view the birds from a considerable distance in poor light.
options.B: Many trained philosophers find the sceptic's argument very hard to refute, and some of them regard every refutation proposed so far as unsuccessful.
options.C: On rivers where decoys are known to be common, careful observers routinely check for them before they report a sighting of any wading bird.
options.D: In everyday conversation, people readily withdraw a claim to know as soon as an unlikely alternative is merely mentioned, even with no reason to think it obtains.

questions.correct_answer: (D) In everyday conversation, people readily withdraw a claim to know as soon as an unlikely alternative is merely mentioned, even with no reason to think it obtains.

option_rationales.A: This concerns ordinary checks such as knowing one's birds, which the author already accepts; it says nothing about what fixes the relevant alternatives.
option_rationales.B: The author grants this in paragraph 1 ('the air of a lawyer winning on a technicality') and argues that it does not show the sceptic is right.
option_rationales.C: This fits the author's account: decoys become a live alternative in those circumstances, exactly as in the ranger case of paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: The author claims that the alternatives to be excluded are fixed by 'something other than bare conceivability', namely what is live in the circumstances, and supports this by saying 'we nowhere apply that standard outside the philosophy seminar'. If ordinary speakers in fact abandon knowledge claims whenever a mere possibility is raised, then the sceptic's standard is applied in ordinary practice, and the author's main evidence fails.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about philosophers' difficulty, which the author has already conceded and answered.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying that the author's account rests on a claim about ordinary practice and finding the option that contradicts it.

questions.question: According to the passage, a majority of experts counts for more when

options.A: its members were all trained by the most eminent teacher working in that particular field.
options.B: it outnumbers the dissenting minority by a wide margin and has done so for a long time.
options.C: its members defend their position more fluently and confidently than the dissenters can.
options.D: its members arrived at their views independently of one another rather than from one common source.

questions.correct_answer: (D) its members arrived at their views independently of one another rather than from one common source.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: a majority counts for less when its members 'all learned them from the same teacher'.
option_rationales.B: The size and duration of a majority are never discussed; the passage makes its weight depend on independence.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 treats fluency and confidence as 'only loosely connected with being right', so they do not add weight.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'a majority counts for more when its members reached their views independently than when they all learned them from the same teacher'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that the size of a majority, rather than its independence, is what matters.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as evidence a layperson can use in judging between disagreeing experts EXCEPT

options.A: whether either expert has made checkable predictions, and how those predictions turned out.
options.B: the number of years each expert has spent working in the field concerned.
options.C: how the other members of the field divide on the question in dispute between them.
options.D: whether either expert stands to gain money or reputation from being believed by the public.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the number of years each expert has spent working in the field concerned.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 lists this first: 'whether either expert has a record of predictions that can be checked, and how those predictions fared'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists this third: 'how the rest of the field divides'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists this second: whether one 'stands to gain from being believed, through money, reputation or loyalty to an institution'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists three kinds of evidence: track record of predictions, interest in being believed, and how the field divides. Length of experience is never mentioned.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that paraphrases a listed method because its wording differs from the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: A straightforward check against the list in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The contrast between the careful scientist and the confident charlatan in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: argue that experts ought to hedge their claims and admit uncertainty more often than they now do.
options.B: illustrate how an expert's financial or institutional interests can be hidden from the public.
options.C: explain why an expert's fluency and ease are poor guides to whether that expert is right.
options.D: suggest that scientists are, on the whole, less trustworthy than other kinds of experts on most questions.

questions.correct_answer: (C) explain why an expert's fluency and ease are poor guides to whether that expert is right.

option_rationales.A: The passage gives no advice to experts; it warns audiences against rewarding confidence.
option_rationales.B: Hidden interests are mentioned in paragraph 4; the contrast in paragraph 3 concerns manner of argument, not interests.
option_rationales.D: The careful scientist is the more trustworthy figure in the contrast; the passage makes no comparison between scientists and other experts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says fluency and ease are 'skills of performance' that are 'only loosely connected with being right'; the scientist who hedges and the charlatan who brushes doubts aside show how an audience that rewards confidence can be misled.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the contrast as advice to experts rather than a warning to audiences.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence before the example.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the indirect methods described in paragraph 2

options.A: can make some lay beliefs about an expert dispute more reasonable than others without guaranteeing a correct choice.
options.B: allow a layperson to become as certain about the dispute as the experts themselves are about it.
options.C: are of no use when the question in dispute is among the questions that matter most to the public.
options.D: are most useful to a layperson who can also follow the technical arguments that each expert puts forward.

questions.correct_answer: (A) can make some lay beliefs about an expert dispute more reasonable than others without guaranteeing a correct choice.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the methods 'narrow the range of reasonable belief; they rarely close it', which rules out expert-level certainty.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says track records are 'often unavailable' for such questions, which concerns one method, not all of them, and stops well short of calling the methods useless.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'None of these questions requires understanding the dispute itself'; each concerns the circumstances of a claim 'rather than its technical content', so their value is not tied to following the technical case.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the methods 'narrow the range of reasonable belief; they rarely close it', and that a choice made on such grounds 'is not a coin toss'. They improve the reasonableness of lay belief without settling the dispute.
questions.common_misconception: Overreading the qualifications of paragraph 4 into a claim that the methods are useless.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the claim of paragraph 1 and the qualification of paragraph 4 together; one wrong option exaggerates the qualification.

questions.question: According to the passage, discounting a dissenter because she dissents is faulty reasoning because

options.A: it shows disrespect towards a colleague whose competence and care one has already acknowledged.
options.B: it uses the disputed conclusion itself as the only evidence that the dissenter has gone wrong.
options.C: it ignores information that the dissenter possesses and that the person discounting her lacks.
options.D: it gives the dissenter's view more weight than one's own view on the question under dispute.

questions.correct_answer: (B) it uses the disputed conclusion itself as the only evidence that the dissenter has gone wrong.

option_rationales.A: The passage objects on grounds of reasoning, saying it 'assumes what is in question'; respect for colleagues is never raised.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 stipulates that 'Neither of you has information the other lacks', so ignored information is not the fault identified.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the move: discounting the dissenter gives her view less weight than one's own, not more.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that 'If the only evidence that she has lost her way is that she disagrees with you, the reasoning simply assumes what is in question'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a moral objection where the passage gives a logical one.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in the last sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The example of the two auditors in paragraph 3 functions in the argument primarily to

options.A: show that auditors and similar specialists are seldom true peers, because one of them is usually more careful than the other.
options.B: show that the equal-weight principle must be given up, since some disagreements between equals call for no change of view.
options.C: show that one may hold firm against a peer whenever one is confident that one's own conclusion is correct.
options.D: show that the equal-weight principle applies only where one lacks dispute-independent grounds for thinking the other party erred.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that the equal-weight principle applies only where one lacks dispute-independent grounds for thinking the other party erred.

option_rationales.A: The example stipulates 'two equally able auditors'; the argument depends on their being peers, not on doubting it.
option_rationales.B: The author says 'The equal-weight principle survives', merely restricted in scope; the example qualifies the principle rather than refuting it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the first auditor's confidence 'does not rest on her own conclusion about the ledger' but on the absurdity of the other's, so confidence in one's own view is not what licenses holding firm.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 concludes that what licenses holding firm 'is not that a view is one's own but that one has grounds, independent of the dispute, for locating the error on the other side', and that the principle is 'a claim about what to do when such independent grounds are absent'. The example restricts the principle's scope.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the first wrong option, which mistakes the auditor's ground for confidence in her own view, the very ground the principle forbids.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to the correct answer: one misidentifies the ground for holding firm, the other overstates the qualification into refutation.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's view of the objection that the equal-weight principle undermines itself?

options.A: It is decisive, because a principle that recommends doubting itself cannot coherently be held by anyone at all.
options.B: It succeeds only if the principle's critics outnumber its defenders among the thoughtful people who have considered it with care.
options.C: It does not show that the principle is false, though it does show that conciliation cannot be all there is to rational belief.
options.D: It is beside the point, because the principle governs disagreements about particular bodies of evidence and not disagreements about principles themselves.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It does not show that the principle is false, though it does show that conciliation cannot be all there is to rational belief.

option_rationales.A: The author says the objection is 'less damaging than it first appears' and that such a principle may recommend doubting itself 'without thereby becoming false'.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about counting critics and defenders; the reply turns on whether self-directed doubt makes a principle false.
option_rationales.D: The author never restricts the principle in this way, and grants that the objection 'does reveal' something important.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 calls the objection 'less damaging than it first appears' because reduced confidence would not make the principle false, but adds that 'What the objection does reveal is that conciliation cannot be the whole story about rational belief'. The author's view is partly dismissive and partly concessive.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the concession in the second half of paragraph 4 and treating the author's reply as a complete rejection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's view has two parts, and each wrong option misstates one of them.

questions.question: In which of the following situations would the author most clearly hold that a person ought to move towards a disagreeing colleague's view?

options.A: Two equally careful historians, working from the same documents, date the same undated letter to different decades, and neither can fault the other's reasoning except by its conclusion.
options.B: Two equally careful chemists disagree about a reaction, but one of them knows that the other's sample was contaminated in a way the other has not noticed.
options.C: Two equally able judges disagree about a verdict, and one of them maintains that the accused was in two different cities at the same moment.
options.D: Two students disagree about a proof, one of whom has studied the topic for years while the other first met it in yesterday's lecture.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Two equally careful historians, working from the same documents, date the same undated letter to different decades, and neither can fault the other's reasoning except by its conclusion.

option_rationales.B: The first chemist has information the other lacks and a ground, independent of the dispute, for locating the error, which paragraph 3 says licenses holding firm.
option_rationales.C: The other judge can recognise the absurdity of this claim independently of the disputed reasoning, which is the auditor case of paragraph 3.
option_rationales.D: The students are not equals in competence, so the case falls outside the peer disagreement to which the principle applies (paragraph 1).

questions.explanation: The principle applies to peers with the same evidence when one has 'no reason, independent of the dispute itself, to think the error is hers rather than yours' (paragraph 1), and paragraph 3 limits it to cases where 'such independent grounds are absent'. Only the historians meet both conditions: they are equals, share the evidence, and can fault each other only by the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking either the requirement that the parties be peers with shared evidence or the exception for dispute-independent grounds.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option violates a different condition of the principle, so all the conditions must be held in mind at once.

questions.question: According to the passage, the shopper's explanation of her choice cannot be true because

options.A: she was not paying attention to the scarves at the moment she made her choice.
options.B: the scarves she chose among did not differ in the respects that she cited.
options.C: an onlooker would have given a quite different explanation of the very same choice.
options.D: she gave it without hesitation, which shows that she had rehearsed it in advance.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the scarves she chose among did not differ in the respects that she cited.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about her attention; her explanation fails because the scarves were identical, not because she was distracted.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: an onlooker 'could have produced the same explanation'.
option_rationales.D: Her lack of hesitation is mentioned to show her sincerity, not to suggest rehearsal; it is not why the explanation is false.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'Since the scarves really are identical, her explanation cannot be true', because she cites 'the richer colour or the finer weave', differences that do not exist.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the detail about hesitation as evidence of insincerity.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the onlooker mentioned in paragraph 2 as

options.A: unable to explain the choice at all, since he has no access to the inner states that caused it.
options.B: likely to explain her choice more accurately if he had first watched her shopping on other occasions.
options.C: better placed than the shopper to explain her choice, since he is free of the biases that distort her view of herself.
options.D: no worse placed than the shopper herself to say why she chose the scarf she did.

questions.correct_answer: (D) no worse placed than the shopper herself to say why she chose the scarf she did.

option_rationales.A: The passage says he 'could have produced the same explanation', so he is able to offer one.
option_rationales.B: The passage never considers what further observation would add; this goes beyond anything it supports.
option_rationales.C: The passage says the onlooker would be 'no more and no less likely to be right', which denies that he is better placed; biases are never mentioned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the onlooker 'could have produced the same explanation, and would have been no more and no less likely to be right', and paragraph 3 adds that about the causes of past choices the shopper 'may well be no better placed than anyone else'. The onlooker is therefore no worse placed than she is.
questions.common_misconception: Inferring that the outsider is better placed, which goes further than the passage's claim of equality.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases an equality claim; one wrong option turns it into superiority.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: First-person authority is genuine but lies in settling our own commitments, not in discerning the causes of our past actions.
options.B: People ought to be far more sceptical than they are about their own reports of bodily sensations such as pain.
options.C: We know our sensations with certainty, but we can know our beliefs and intentions only by inference from what we do.
options.D: Our sincere explanations of our own choices are usually false, and so self-knowledge is for the most part an illusion.

questions.correct_answer: (A) First-person authority is genuine but lies in settling our own commitments, not in discerning the causes of our past actions.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 treats sincere pain reports as a case where special access is 'plausible'; the passage's doubts concern reasons, not sensations.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says intentions about tomorrow are settled 'by deciding', not by studying evidence about oneself, so they are not known by inference.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls the conclusion that 'self-knowledge is an illusion' an overreach, so the author rejects this view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the lesson: 'not that the first person has no privilege but that its privilege has been misplaced'. We are 'poorly placed to discover, by looking inward, the forces that moved us' but 'well placed to settle what we will stand by'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the overreaching conclusion the author rejects in paragraph 3 for the author's own thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option states the view the author reports and rejects; another distorts the contrast between kinds of self-knowledge.

questions.question: Which of the following questions would a person answer with the kind of authority the passage describes in paragraph 3?

options.A: Whether the ache she has been feeling in her shoulder since the morning is still there now.
options.B: Why she chose ten years ago to study law rather than medicine when she left school.
options.C: Whether she will accept the post she has just been offered, now that she has had time to think it over.
options.D: Whether her irritability over the past week has been caused by her lack of sleep.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Whether she will accept the post she has just been offered, now that she has had time to think it over.

option_rationales.A: She may well have authority here, but it is the kind paragraph 1 grants to sensations; paragraph 3's authority comes from the answer being 'up to her', and an ache is not.
option_rationales.B: This asks for the causes of a past choice, about which paragraph 3 says she 'may well be no better placed than anyone else'.
option_rationales.D: This asks about the causes of her state, a matter on which the passage denies special access.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the authority in question 'derives from the fact that the answer is, in part, up to her': she answers 'by deciding'. Whether to accept a post she has been offered is settled by her decision, so it is the only question of that kind.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the shoulder ache because the passage grants authority over sensations, without noticing that it is a different authority from the one in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating two kinds of first-person authority the passage mentions, one of which a wrong option exploits.

questions.question: The examples of the pharmacist and the traveller in paragraph 1 are used to

options.A: show that whether someone deserves blame depends on how her action turns out rather than on what she intended.
options.B: illustrate cases in which a person's ignorance properly excuses her from blame for what she did.
options.C: suggest that most appeals to ignorance are counterfeit and should be met with suspicion by those who hear them.
options.D: show that people who handle goods on behalf of others ought to inspect those goods far more carefully.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate cases in which a person's ignorance properly excuses her from blame for what she did.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: ignorance matters because it breaks 'the link between what a person did and what she intended'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 calls the excuse 'often among the best'; the counterfeit form is introduced only in paragraph 2 as a contrasting case.
option_rationales.D: The passage says no inspection could have detected the contamination and that the traveller had no reason to suspect anything; it recommends no extra care.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the excuse is 'often among the best' and presents the pharmacist and the traveller as people nobody would blame, because ignorance 'breaks the link between what a person did and what she intended'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the examples as a call for vigilance rather than as cases of legitimate excuse.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentences around the examples.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the manager in paragraph 2 is responsible because he

options.A: deliberately kept himself from learning facts that he foresaw he might be obliged to act on.
options.B: lied when he later claimed that he had not known how the results were being achieved.
options.C: personally instructed his staff to falsify the safety records in order to meet their targets.
options.D: failed to check every record that his staff produced, as any responsible manager must.

questions.correct_answer: (A) deliberately kept himself from learning facts that he foresaw he might be obliged to act on.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says he can say 'truthfully, that he did not know', so his claim was not a lie.
option_rationales.C: He told his staff only that he did not want to hear how results were achieved; the passage never says he ordered the falsification.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 rejects a duty to investigate everything; his fault lies in arranging his ignorance, not in failing to check exhaustively.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'his not knowing was not something that happened to him; it was something he arranged', because 'He foresaw that there might be facts he would be obliged to act on, and he took steps to ensure that he would never be in possession of them'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the manager must have lied or given the order, when the passage insists his claim of ignorance is true.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases two adjacent sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'counterfeit form' of the excuse refers to

options.A: a version of the excuse that is used chiefly by people who hold positions of power over others.
options.B: a version of the excuse that courts and other authorities almost never accept in practice.
options.C: a version in which the person lies about what he knew at the time he acted.
options.D: a version that looks like the genuine excuse but lacks any title to the force the genuine one has.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a version that looks like the genuine excuse but lacks any title to the force the genuine one has.

option_rationales.A: The manager happens to be a superior, but nothing in the passage restricts cultivated ignorance to people with power.
option_rationales.B: The passage does not discuss courts or how often the excuse is accepted; it argues that the excuse should not be accepted.
option_rationales.C: The manager's claim not to have known is true (paragraph 2 says he speaks 'truthfully'), so the counterfeit lies in how the ignorance arose, not in a lie.

questions.explanation: A counterfeit resembles the real thing without its value. The manager's 'I did not know' is literally true, like the genuine excuse, but paragraph 3 says cultivated ignorance 'does not cancel responsibility', so it lacks the excusing force of real ignorance.
questions.common_misconception: Equating 'counterfeit' with 'false', when the passage stresses that the manager's statement is true.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is tempting because counterfeit suggests falsehood; the passage blocks it explicitly.

questions.question: Which of the following people would the author most likely regard as guilty of cultivated ignorance?

options.A: A tourist who dines at a popular restaurant without knowing that its kitchen recently failed a hygiene inspection carried out by the local authorities.
options.B: A shopper who buys a cheap shirt at a busy market without first researching the conditions in the distant factory where it happens to have been made.
options.C: A landlord who, after a tenant reports a smell of gas, decides against having the boiler inspected because a fault would oblige him to pay for repairs.
options.D: A clerk who routinely files a forged contract whose forgery an expert examiner later needed specialised laboratory equipment to detect at all.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A landlord who, after a tenant reports a smell of gas, decides against having the boiler inspected because a fault would oblige him to pay for repairs.

option_rationales.A: Nothing gave the tourist a reason to suspect the kitchen, so her ignorance is suffered, not cultivated, on the test of paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says that without 'some particular reason to suspect a problem', not inquiring is 'the normal condition of finite beings'; the shopper has no such reason.
option_rationales.D: This resembles the pharmacist of paragraph 1: the problem could not reasonably have been detected, so the ignorance excuses.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the charge is fair 'only where a person had some particular reason to suspect a problem and chose not to look because looking might oblige him to act'. The landlord has a specific warning and avoids inspection precisely to avoid the obligation to repair.
questions.common_misconception: Treating any failure to investigate as culpable, forgetting the limit the author sets in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying both conditions of paragraph 4 (a particular reason to suspect, and avoidance to escape obligation) to new cases.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as things with which intellectual humility is sometimes confused EXCEPT

options.A: an indifference to receiving public credit or recognition for one's own intellectual achievements.
options.B: a habit of introducing one's claims with an acknowledgement that one might be mistaken.
options.C: a tendency to hold every one of one's opinions with only a low degree of confidence.
options.D: a readiness to yield on questions of fact to those people who know more than oneself.

questions.correct_answer: (A) an indifference to receiving public credit or recognition for one's own intellectual achievements.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 names 'a modest manner', described as the habit of prefacing one's claims with an admission that one may be wrong.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says humility is sometimes 'equated with low confidence, as if the humble thinker were one who held every opinion loosely'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says humility is sometimes 'identified with deference, the willingness to yield to those who know more'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 lists three things humility is blurred with: low confidence, deference and a modest manner. Indifference to credit is a common association of humility in general, but the passage never mentions it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that paraphrases one of the three listed confusions because its wording differs from the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: A direct check against the list in paragraph 1; the correct answer is plausible from general knowledge but absent from the text.

questions.question: When the author says that 'I may be wrong' is 'cheap to say' (paragraph 2), the point is that

options.A: it is a vulgar or careless form of words that thoughtful and well-educated speakers usually take care to avoid.
options.B: saying it costs the speaker nothing and so is no evidence that she really holds her views open to correction.
options.C: it is now said so often in ordinary discussion that it has quite lost the meaning it once had for speakers.
options.D: it undervalues what the speaker knows and so misrepresents how much confidence her evidence actually warrants.

questions.correct_answer: (B) saying it costs the speaker nothing and so is no evidence that she really holds her views open to correction.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no judgement about the phrase's refinement; 'cheap' refers to how little the phrase reveals, not to its social standing.
option_rationales.C: The passage gives a different reason: the modest manner 'can coexist with a private conviction that one is never mistaken'; it says nothing about overuse.
option_rationales.D: This describes timidity, which paragraph 2 discusses under low confidence; the point about the phrase is that it may conceal overconfidence, not express underconfidence.

questions.explanation: The sentence before says the modest manner 'concerns how one presents oneself to others, and it can coexist with a private conviction that one is never mistaken'. The phrase is 'cheap' because uttering it requires no actual openness, so it proves nothing about humility.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'cheap' as a remark about style or overuse rather than about the absence of any real cost or commitment.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options offer familiar senses of 'cheap'; only the preceding sentence fixes the intended one.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the account the author favours, a person who is highly confident about many matters

options.A: ought to defer to recognised experts on every one of the matters about which she happens to feel confident.
options.B: is unlikely to be intellectually humble, since humility consists largely in holding most of one's opinions loosely.
options.C: can be intellectually humble only if she expresses her opinions to others in a suitably modest and tentative manner.
options.D: may still be intellectually humble, if her confidence rests on good grounds and she attends to where her grounds are weak.

questions.correct_answer: (D) may still be intellectually humble, if her confidence rests on good grounds and she attends to where her grounds are weak.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says a thinker who deferred to every apparent authority 'would be credulous rather than humble'.
option_rationales.B: This is the first of the confusions the author rejects; paragraph 2 says one may be 'entirely certain' of something 'without any failure of humility'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the modest manner concerns self-presentation and can coexist with arrogance, so it is not required for humility.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says humility 'is compatible with great confidence where her grounds are good', and that awareness of 'where her grounds are poor' makes her confidence elsewhere deserve to be taken seriously.
questions.common_misconception: Equating humility with low confidence, one of the confusions paragraph 1 identifies.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option restates one of the three accounts the author rejects, so the item tests whether the reader separates them from the favoured account.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the objection raised at the start of paragraph 4?

options.A: Most people find it considerably easier to detect errors in the reasoning of others than to detect errors in their own reasoning.
options.B: Some thinkers who are paralysed by self-scrutiny are nonetheless excellent judges of the arguments that other people put forward in their fields.
options.C: Whenever people fail to notice how their ambitions colour their judgements, their weighing of evidence about the world is distorted to the same degree.
options.D: Many people whom their colleagues regard as intellectually humble are no better than average at weighing evidence about the world.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Whenever people fail to notice how their ambitions colour their judgements, their weighing of evidence about the world is distorted to the same degree.

option_rationales.A: This fits the author's view that attention to oneself as a source of error is a distinct capacity, so it does not weaken the reply.
option_rationales.B: This concerns humility overdone (paragraph 5) and, if anything, again shows self-directed and world-directed judgement coming apart.
option_rationales.D: This supports the reply, since it shows humility and skill at weighing evidence coming apart in the other direction.

questions.explanation: The objection is that the account makes humility 'indistinguishable from good reasoning in general'; the reply is that 'the two can come apart', as in the scientist who weighs evidence well yet is blind to her own ambitions. If blindness to one's own biases always brings an equal distortion in weighing evidence, the scientist case cannot occur and the reply fails.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is about bias or self-scrutiny but leaves the claimed separation intact.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying that the reply depends on a dissociation and finding the option that denies it; the wrong options are on topic and two of them actually support the reply.

questions.question: The author's remark that humility 'can be overdone' (paragraph 5) implies that

options.A: humility is valuable only in moderation, and so it matters less to a thinker than the capacity for good reasoning does.
options.B: a thinker who ignores her own limitations is less at fault than one who is paralysed by attention to them.
options.C: the right relation to one's limitations requires judging their extent accurately, not merely attending to them as much as possible.
options.D: the account set out in paragraph 3 must finally be abandoned in favour of the view that humility is a kind of low confidence.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the right relation to one's limitations requires judging their extent accurately, not merely attending to them as much as possible.

option_rationales.A: The passage never ranks humility against good reasoning; it says only that excessive self-scrutiny misjudges one's limitations.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says the paralysed thinker has misjudged her limitations 'as surely as the one who ignores them', which treats both as faults without ranking them.
option_rationales.D: The author presents the point as 'a further merit' of the account, which strengthens it rather than abandoning it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says 'Owning one's limitations includes keeping them in proportion', and that the paralysed thinker 'has misjudged them'. Humility therefore requires an accurate estimate of one's limitations, not maximal preoccupation with them.
questions.common_misconception: Ranking the two failures, when the passage treats them as equally misjudgements.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer generalises from the final sentence; one wrong option turns 'as surely as' into a ranking.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: showing that scientific models are false, and that science therefore yields understanding of the world but never knowledge of it.
options.B: criticising educational systems for testing how well students remember statements rather than how well they can apply them.
options.C: defending the view that understanding is knowledge of causes against the objection that some causes cannot be known.
options.D: arguing that understanding differs from knowledge both in requiring a usable grasp of dependencies and in its more selective relation to truth.

questions.correct_answer: (D) arguing that understanding differs from knowledge both in requiring a usable grasp of dependencies and in its more selective relation to truth.

option_rationales.A: The passage says many models are 'taken literally, false', but never claims science yields no knowledge; this extends a point about models into a sweeping conclusion.
option_rationales.B: This is the subject of the short final paragraph only, which draws a consequence of the main argument; it is too narrow to be the passage's concern.
option_rationales.C: The passage argues against the view of paragraph 1 that understanding is 'knowledge all the same', and no objection about unknowable causes is discussed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the view that understanding is knowledge of causes; paragraph 2 argues against it with the memorising student; paragraphs 3 and 4 argue that understanding tolerates selective falsehood; paragraph 5 draws a practical consequence. The correct answer captures both lines of difference.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the educational point because it is concrete and comes last.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must cover two distinct claims; each wrong option is too narrow, too sweeping or a reversal.

questions.question: The student who has memorised the explanation of the seasons (paragraph 2) serves primarily to

options.A: present someone who seems to know why something happens without understanding it, against the view stated in paragraph 1.
options.B: show that the student does not really know why the seasons change, since an answer that is merely memorised is not knowledge.
options.C: illustrate how idealised models allow students to reason about cases for which their explanations were never originally stated.
options.D: show that what is learned from textbooks and teachers is less reliable than what a student works out through her own reasoning.

questions.correct_answer: (A) present someone who seems to know why something happens without understanding it, against the view stated in paragraph 1.

option_rationales.B: The passage says that 'by most accounts of knowledge she knows why the seasons change'; the case works only if she has knowledge but lacks understanding.
option_rationales.C: Idealised models are the subject of paragraph 3; the student in paragraph 2 cannot extend her explanation, so she illustrates the opposite.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 calls her sources 'a reliable textbook and a reliable teacher', and her answer is accurate; reliability is not what she lacks.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 holds that understanding is 'knowledge all the same'. The student has knowledge 'by most accounts' but cannot answer new questions, because she lacks 'a grasp of how the facts she already has depend on one another'. She is a case of knowing why without understanding, which is the 'difficulty' for the view.
questions.common_misconception: Concluding that the student lacks knowledge, which would dissolve the counterexample the author needs.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option denies her knowledge, a reading many students find natural but that the passage explicitly rules out.

questions.question: The passage suggests that part of understanding the simple model of a gas consists in

options.A: knowing a more accurate description of gases that the simple model was introduced to replace in teaching.
options.B: recognising the conditions under which its simplifications stop being harmless and the model begins to mislead.
options.C: being able to state the model correctly in the words used by a reliable textbook or a reliable teacher.
options.D: believing, as the model assumes, that actual gas molecules occupy no space and exert no forces on one another.

questions.correct_answer: (B) recognising the conditions under which its simplifications stop being harmless and the model begins to mislead.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says someone who memorised a more accurate description but could do nothing with it would not understand more.
option_rationales.C: Reproducing words is what the memorising student of paragraph 2 can do, and the passage says this falls short of understanding.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says 'no actual molecule does' this; believing it would be a false belief about molecules, not part of understanding the model.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the model 'serves well for gases at ordinary densities and misleads at very high ones, and part of understanding the model is knowing where it stops working'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing using a model with believing it literally.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases a clause in paragraph 4; two wrong options borrow ideas from paragraphs 2 and 3.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author be most likely to accept?

options.A: Knowledge, like understanding, can tolerate falsehood in respects that are irrelevant to the question being answered.
options.B: A person who understands a phenomenon must hold at least some false beliefs about that phenomenon.
options.C: Any explanation that can be applied fluently to new cases yields understanding, whether or not it gets the dependencies right.
options.D: A person can come to understand a phenomenon partly by means of a representation that she knows is not literally true.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A person can come to understand a phenomenon partly by means of a representation that she knows is not literally true.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says knowledge 'is usually held to require truth: one cannot know what is false', and paragraph 4 contrasts the two on exactly this point.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says understanding 'tolerates distortion' in irrelevant respects; tolerating falsehood is not requiring it, and the model can be used without being believed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says a story that 'got the dependencies wrong, however fluently it could be manipulated' would give only 'a skilful illusion' of understanding.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says understanding is often achieved through models that are 'taken literally, false', and paragraph 4 adds that 'part of understanding the model is knowing where it stops working', which implies awareness that it departs from reality. So a person can understand through a representation she knows is not literally true.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'tolerates' into 'requires', or extending to knowledge the looseness the author reserves for understanding.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four options deal with the relation between understanding and truth; separating 'tolerate' from 'require' and understanding from knowledge needs paragraphs 3 and 4 together.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards educational systems that measure success by the reproduction of correct statements is best described as

options.A: neutral, because the passage describes how such systems operate without passing any judgement on them.
options.B: contemptuous, because the reproduction of correct statements has no educational value of any kind.
options.C: critical, because such measures cannot detect the gap between possessing an explanation and understanding it.
options.D: approving, because such measures reliably identify the students who know why the things they study happen.

questions.correct_answer: (C) critical, because such measures cannot detect the gap between possessing an explanation and understanding it.

option_rationales.A: Saying the systems 'may never detect what she is missing' and that testing for understanding 'requires' other questions is evaluative, not neutral.
option_rationales.B: The author grants that the memorising student has knowledge; the complaint is that such tests miss understanding, not that correct statements are worthless.
option_rationales.D: The author says these systems 'may never detect what she is missing', which is a criticism; the passage never praises them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says such systems 'will reward the memorising student and may never detect what she is missing', and that 'Testing for understanding requires, at least in part, asking questions the student has not been prepared for'. The attitude is critical, on the specific ground that they miss understanding.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating measured criticism into contempt.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tone is measured, so the reader must reject both the neutral and the extreme readings.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: accept that tools can do memory's work while arguing that this reveals a new reliance on trust, not a larger mind.
options.B: show that biological memory is more trustworthy than notebooks and phones because it cannot be distorted by anyone.
options.C: defend the claim that the mind includes every device its owner consults, against critics who would confine it to the brain.
options.D: warn people who keep their appointments in phones that strangers are likely to tamper with what they have stored.

questions.correct_answer: (A) accept that tools can do memory's work while arguing that this reveals a new reliance on trust, not a larger mind.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says biological memory 'is fallible, and it too can be distorted by suggestion'; the contrast drawn is about who can revise it, not about immunity to distortion.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says this 'stronger conclusion' 'moves too quickly', and paragraph 4 says calling the device part of the mind explains nothing, so the author opposes it.
option_rationales.D: The passage gives no warning or advice and never says tampering is likely; the phone example in paragraph 1 opens a philosophical question about the boundary of the mind.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 accepts much of the argument ('much of it should be accepted'), paragraph 3 rejects the stronger conclusion because devices can be edited by others, and paragraph 4 states 'The better lesson': 'trust has become a part of cognition'. The purpose is to accept part of the thesis and redirect its lesson.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the thesis the author reports in paragraph 1 for the author's own conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's stance is announced in signposted sentences ('much of it should be accepted', 'Yet', 'The better lesson').

questions.question: According to the passage, devices differ from biological memory in that

options.A: they store information more accurately, whereas memory steadily loses and distorts what it holds over time.
options.B: others can routinely change what they hold, whereas memory is not open to such revision in the same way.
options.C: they let a person retrieve stored facts with no effort at all, whereas memory always requires some work to search.
options.D: they influence what a person does only when consulted, whereas memory guides action without being consulted.

questions.correct_answer: (B) others can routinely change what they hold, whereas memory is not open to such revision in the same way.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 calls memory fallible but never says devices are more accurate; the stated difference is 'not one of storage but of authority'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 mentions retrieving 'with less effort', not no effort, and presents this as no principled difference at all, so it is not the distinction the author draws.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says of both stored facts that they 'guide what I do'; no contrast about consultation and action is drawn.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: devices 'can be edited by other people', whereas memory 'is not open in the same routine way to the revisions of strangers'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a difference that sounds true in the world (accuracy, effort) instead of the one the passage states.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated directly in two sentences of paragraph 3.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'authority' refers to

options.A: the degree of confidence a person places in her own recollections.
options.B: the legal ownership of a device and of the data that are stored in it.
options.C: who is entitled to revise the information on which a person's beliefs rest.
options.D: the expertise that makes a particular source of information worth trusting.

questions.correct_answer: (C) who is entitled to revise the information on which a person's beliefs rest.

option_rationales.A: Self-confidence is not discussed; the sentence contrasts authority with storage and defines it by who can change beliefs, not by how sure the believer feels.
option_rationales.B: Ownership is never mentioned; the people who can alter a phone include whoever 'manages the service', which concerns the power to change contents, not title to them.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph is not about expertise or reliability of sources; it glosses authority as 'who has the standing to change' what a person takes to be true.

questions.explanation: The sentence explains itself: 'The difference is not one of storage but of authority, of who has the standing to change what a person takes to be true.'
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'authority' in its everyday sense of expertise rather than in the sense the sentence defines.
questions.difficulty_reason: The word is glossed in the same sentence.

questions.question: Based on the passage, the author would most likely describe the case of a woman whose diary has been secretly rewritten by a colleague as

options.A: a real injury to what she knows, best understood as a betrayal of the trust on which her beliefs had come to depend.
options.B: evidence that the diary had become part of her mind, which is the full explanation of why the change feels so harmful.
options.C: proof that the diary was never part of her mind, since nothing belonging to a mind can be altered by someone else.
options.D: an inconvenience no worse than mislaying a shopping list, since the true entries in her diary can usually be reconstructed later from other records.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a real injury to what she knows, best understood as a betrayal of the trust on which her beliefs had come to depend.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the thesis is 'right to notice the injury' but 'wrong to think that calling the device a part of the mind explains it'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says biological memory 'can be distorted by suggestion', so being alterable by others does not by itself exclude something from the mind, and the author never speaks of proof.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the alteration of a device 'can feel like an injury to the self and not merely an inconvenience', and nothing is said about reconstructing entries.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 notes that a notebook 'can be altered while its owner sleeps' and locates the difference in 'authority'; paragraph 4 says that once we lean on external stores, the soundness of our beliefs depends on the people who maintain them, and that alteration is 'an injury to the self'. The woman's case is a failure of that trust.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that echoes the extended-mind thesis, which the author says notices the injury but does not explain it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options use the passage's own vocabulary; the correct answer requires applying paragraph 4's distinction between noticing and explaining the injury.

questions.question: The example of the man and the cake in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate how tiredness at the end of a day corrupts a person's judgement of what is good for him.
options.B: present an ordinary lapse whose puzzling features the rest of the passage sets out to explain.
options.C: establish the old view that nobody ever knowingly chooses the worse of two courses.
options.D: show that most people lack the willpower needed to keep their resolutions about food.

questions.correct_answer: (B) present an ordinary lapse whose puzzling features the rest of the passage sets out to explain.

option_rationales.A: No paragraph says tiredness corrupts judgement; paragraph 3 says the man 'does not abandon his judgement so much as stop looking at it'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 reports that view as 'One very old answer' that most people find 'too clever by half', and paragraph 3 rejects the idea that the lapse is 'a simple change of mind'.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no claim about how many people lack willpower; the example is used to raise a puzzle about acting against one's judgement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the episode's 'strangeness is easy to miss' and asks 'what moved him to do otherwise?'; paragraphs 2 to 4 then weigh answers to that question. The example sets up the puzzle.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the opening example as evidence for one of the views instead of as the puzzle all the views address.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by the sentence that follows the example.

questions.question: According to the passage, the muscle picture of the will has the merit of

options.A: treating a lapse as something internal to the person rather than as something imposed on her.
options.B: showing that people who give in to temptation have, for the moment, changed their minds about what is best.
options.C: explaining why putting temptations out of sight helps people keep their resolutions.
options.D: fitting the way lapses feel and accounting for why they are more frequent late in tiring days.

questions.correct_answer: (D) fitting the way lapses feel and accounting for why they are more frequent late in tiring days.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: the picture 'makes the lapse strangely external to the person'.
option_rationales.B: That is the 'very old answer' of paragraph 1, not the muscle picture, which assumes judgement points the way and the will fails to follow.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'the muscle picture has trouble explaining why such strategies work', so this is a weakness of the picture, not a merit.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The picture has the merit of matching how lapses feel, and it explains why they cluster at the end of tiring days.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the merits the author grants with the advantages claimed for the rival account in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, according to the attentional account, the man who eats the cake

options.A: still holds that refusing is better but has, in the moment, stopped keeping that reason vividly before him.
options.B: has temporarily concluded that eating the cake is the better course after all.
options.C: lacks the strength to act on a judgement that remains clear and vivid to him as he reaches out.
options.D: will certainly give in again unless someone else removes the cake from his sight.

questions.correct_answer: (A) still holds that refusing is better but has, in the moment, stopped keeping that reason vividly before him.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the lapse is not 'a simple change of mind', and the man 'does not abandon his judgement'; this is the old answer from paragraph 1.
option_rationales.C: This is the muscle picture; paragraph 3 says he does not 'go on thinking, clearly and vividly, that he should refuse while his hand reaches out'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 lists arrangement as one possible remedy, including steps he can take himself, and concedes that not every lapse is a matter of attention; the option's certainty and its reliance on someone else are unsupported.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'He does not abandon his judgement so much as stop looking at it', and the lapse is 'a failure to keep one's own reasons in view'. He still judges refusal better, but that judgement has become 'abstract and distant'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the muscle picture because it matches the everyday description of being 'overcome'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the three views of paragraphs 1 to 3, each of which a wrong option restates.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the practical advantage the author claims for the attentional account?

options.A: Lapses of resolution are considerably more frequent in the evening than in the morning, especially after demanding work.
options.B: People who give in to temptation usually report afterwards that they felt overcome at the time by a desire that seemed stronger than they were.
options.C: People who kept tempting food out of view and planned their responses in advance lapsed as often as people who did neither.
options.D: Some temptations prove strong enough to defeat even people who have planned carefully how they will respond.

questions.correct_answer: (C) People who kept tempting food out of view and planned their responses in advance lapsed as often as people who did neither.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 accepts that lapses 'cluster at the end of tiring days' and paragraph 4 grants that this 'does not mean that fatigue is irrelevant'; the finding is compatible with both accounts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 already grants that the muscle picture matches 'how lapses feel'; the attentional account does not deny the feeling, so the report leaves the advantage untouched.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 concedes that 'some temptations are simply strong' and claims only that lapses are 'often' failures of attention, so occasional failures of planning do not weaken it.

questions.explanation: The claimed advantage (paragraph 4) is that if lapses are often failures of attention, 'the remedy can be arrangement', and that this explains why such strategies work. If arrangement made no difference to lapse rates, the advantage would collapse.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a finding that sounds like evidence for the muscle picture but is something the author has already conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches a point the passage concedes; the solver must see that concessions cannot weaken the claim.

questions.question: According to the passage, the argument from analogy concludes that another person is in pain on the basis of

options.A: a direct perception of the person's distress in the expression on her face.
options.B: a link between pain and behaviour that one has observed in one's own case.
options.C: what the other person reports, in words, about the feelings she is having.
options.D: a large number of observations of many different people who were in pain.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a link between pain and behaviour that one has observed in one's own case.

option_rationales.A: That is the author's own alternative in paragraph 3, offered against the inferential picture, not the argument from analogy.
option_rationales.C: Verbal reports are never mentioned; paragraph 1 says the inference rests on what one observes 'In my own case' together with the other's wincing and crying.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the argument 'generalises from a single case', which is exactly why critics call it fragile.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'In my own case I observe that pain is regularly accompanied by wincing and crying; when I observe wincing and crying in you, I infer that pain is present in you as well'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the argument from analogy with the author's perceptual alternative.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument is stated explicitly in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The example of the seeds in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: argue that inductive reasoning in general cannot be trusted when it is applied to living things.
options.B: suggest that the minds of other people differ from one another as much as seeds in a sack do.
options.C: show that the conclusion about other minds can never be confirmed by any further observation.
options.D: illustrate why a conclusion drawn from one instance would be rejected in ordinary reasoning.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate why a conclusion drawn from one instance would be rejected in ordinary reasoning.

option_rationales.A: The example appeals to ordinary induction as a standard the analogy argument fails to meet, so it presupposes that induction is normally acceptable.
option_rationales.B: The passage draws no comparison between seeds and the variety of minds; the example concerns the strength of an inference.
option_rationales.C: That is a separate objection, introduced by 'Worse' after the seed example; the seeds illustrate only the fault of generalising from one case.

questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that the argument 'generalises from a single case to every other person, which is the kind of reasoning we would reject anywhere else'. Concluding that every seed is fertile from one seed is such reasoning.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the example to the second objection ('Worse, the conclusion can never be independently checked'), which comes after it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two objections sit side by side in paragraph 2; the solver must see which one the example supports.

questions.question: The author's comparison between seeing that the mother is upset and seeing 'that the cup is full' suggests that

options.A: recognising another person's feeling can be as direct as perceiving an ordinary fact about an object.
options.B: children learn to read emotions by first reasoning carefully about the behaviour of physical objects.
options.C: children understand other people's emotions before they understand facts about physical objects.
options.D: feelings, like the contents of a cup, can be measured precisely by a sufficiently careful observer.

questions.correct_answer: (A) recognising another person's feeling can be as direct as perceiving an ordinary fact about an object.

option_rationales.B: This reverses the point: paragraph 3 denies that a child does 'first register a contraction of facial muscles and then hypothesise distress'; she sees the feeling 'as immediately' as the cup's state.
option_rationales.C: The comparison concerns how direct the two kinds of seeing are, not which is learned first; no order of development is discussed.
option_rationales.D: Nothing is said about precise measurement; paragraph 4 even grants that we 'can be badly wrong' in hard cases.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'she sees that her mother is upset, and she sees it as immediately as she sees that the cup is full.' The comparison makes the point that expressions are not 'evidence from which feelings are deduced' but the form in which feelings are visible.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the comparison as a claim about developmental order or precision rather than about immediacy.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the image to the claim it supports in the next two sentences.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's reply to the sceptic?

options.A: People frequently misjudge what strangers from unfamiliar backgrounds are feeling, even when they try hard to understand them.
options.B: Some people can keep a calm and composed face while concealing intense grief or anger from those around them.
options.C: Young children recognise their own mothers' feelings much more quickly than they recognise the feelings of strangers.
options.D: Adults turn out to identify what others feel only by consciously working from observed movements to conclusions about hidden states.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Adults turn out to identify what others feel only by consciously working from observed movements to conclusions about hidden states.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 concedes that 'When a stranger's expressions are unfamiliar' we reason and 'can be badly wrong', so this is a case the author already allows for.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 lists deliberate concealment among the special cases in which we must weigh evidence; it does not touch the claim that most feelings are simply seen.
option_rationales.C: This is consistent with the author's view, since familiar expressions are the clearest cases of seeing; paragraph 4 treats unfamiliar faces as the harder cases.

questions.explanation: The author's reply (paragraph 3) is that knowledge of other minds does not ordinarily 'arise' as an inference: we see feelings 'as immediately' as ordinary facts, and inference is confined to 'special cases' (paragraph 4). If even ordinary recognition were conscious inference from movements to hidden states, the reply would fail at its core.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about errors in reading minds, which feels like a blow to the author but describes cases paragraph 4 already concedes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options describe real limits on mind reading and the third is a plausible fact about children; the solver must see that each is compatible with paragraph 4's concession and only the correct answer attacks the general claim.

questions.question: The passage presents the judgement view of emotions as explaining each of the following EXCEPT

options.A: why an emotion can be appropriate or inappropriate to its circumstances.
options.B: why a friend can sometimes be argued out of her jealousy by being shown a misreading.
options.C: why a fear can persist after the person has concluded that there is no danger.
options.D: why emotions are directed at objects instead of being mere sensations about nothing.

questions.correct_answer: (C) why a fear can persist after the person has concluded that there is no danger.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the view 'explains why emotions can be appropriate or inappropriate to their circumstances'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 lists this explicitly: 'why we can sometimes argue a friend out of her jealousy by showing her that she has misread a situation'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 ends its list with 'why emotions are directed at objects rather than being mere sensations'.

questions.explanation: The three wrong options are the three explanations listed in paragraph 1. Persistent fear is precisely what the judgement view cannot explain: paragraph 2 says it would make the traveller's condition 'a straightforward contradiction'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing that the correct answer describes the difficulty of paragraph 2 rather than a merit from paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three supported options are listed in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, if the judgement theory were correct, the frightened traveller would have to be described as

options.A: perceiving the aircraft as dangerous while judging that it is in fact quite safe.
options.B: both believing and denying, at one and the same time, that flying is dangerous.
options.C: simply ignorant of how safe air travel is compared with the drive to the airport.
options.D: undergoing a mere sensation, like an itch, that is not directed at anything.

questions.correct_answer: (B) both believing and denying, at one and the same time, that flying is dangerous.

option_rationales.A: This is how the perceptual model of paragraph 3 describes her; it is offered precisely because the judgement theory cannot describe her this way.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 stipulates that she 'may know perfectly well' that flying is safer, so the theory cannot treat her as ignorant.
option_rationales.D: The judgement theory is credited in paragraph 1 with explaining why emotions are not 'mere sensations'; it would treat her fear as a judgement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'If fear were a judgement that flying is dangerous, the traveller would be simultaneously affirming and denying the same proposition'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the perceptual model's description, which is the author's view, for the judgement theory's.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is the rival model's description of the same case.

questions.question: The illusion of the two lines in paragraph 3 serves primarily to

options.A: suggest that emotional conflicts can be ended by a decisive measurement, as the ruler ends doubt about the lines.
options.B: prove that emotions and perceptions are mental states of exactly the same kind in every respect.
options.C: show that a state can present things one way while the person believes otherwise, without contradiction.
options.D: demonstrate that emotions are usually unreliable guides to what is actually valuable in the world.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that a state can present things one way while the person believes otherwise, without contradiction.

option_rationales.A: In the illusion the ruler does not end the appearance: one line 'continues to look longer'; and paragraph 4 says emotions cannot be dismissed by a single act of judgement.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'The analogy should not be pressed too far' and names a difference: we are answerable for emotions but not for illusions.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says such presentations are 'usually reliable and usually agree with our considered views'; the illusion is the exceptional case.

questions.explanation: The illusion persists after measurement, yet 'Seeing is not believing, so the conflict involves no contradiction.' The author uses it to model the traveller's fear as a presentation that conflicts with belief without contradiction.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the analogy as a full identification of emotion with perception, which paragraph 4 explicitly limits.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing what the analogy is meant to explain and where the author stops it.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the perceptual model of emotion can best be described as

options.A: endorsement, qualified by the recognition that the model leaves part of emotional life unexplained.
options.B: neutrality, since the passage sets out the two models side by side without preferring either of them.
options.C: unqualified enthusiasm, since the model removes every difficulty that faced the judgement view.
options.D: scepticism, since emotions are answerable to the person who has them in a way that perceptions are not.

questions.correct_answer: (A) endorsement, qualified by the recognition that the model leaves part of emotional life unexplained.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 opens 'A better model is perception', a plain preference for the perceptual model over the judgement view.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the model 'must be supplemented', so the author's support is explicitly qualified.
option_rationales.D: The author says 'A better model is perception' and that the model 'explains why emotional conflict is not contradiction'; answerability marks a limit, not a reason to doubt the model.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens 'A better model is perception'; paragraph 4 says it 'should not be pressed too far' and 'must be supplemented to explain why it is nevertheless an occasion for responsibility'. That is endorsement with a stated limit.
questions.common_misconception: Over-reading the final paragraph's limitation as rejection of the model.
questions.difficulty_reason: The scepticism wrong option uses the author's own limiting point, so tone must be judged across paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, the second difficulty for the memory theory is that

options.A: most people forget their early childhood, so memory cannot reach the first years of anyone's life.
options.B: memories might be transferred into another body, which would make two quite different people one and the same person.
options.C: identity must hold from one end of a chain to the other, whereas direct memory need not.
options.D: telling a genuine memory from a convincing false one seems to require knowing already who the rememberer is.
