questions.correct_answer: (D) telling a genuine memory from a convincing false one seems to require knowing already who the rememberer is.

option_rationales.A: Forgetting childhood figures only in the first difficulty's example; the second difficulty concerns distinguishing genuine from false memories.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 cites memory transfer as an imaginary case the theory appears to handle well, not as a difficulty for it.
option_rationales.C: This is the first difficulty, about chains and the rule that if A is B and B is C then A is C, not the second.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: to tell a genuine memory from 'a vivid but false impression of having sat it, we seem to need to know already that the rememberer is the person who sat it. Memory, apparently, presupposes the identity it was supposed to explain.'
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up the two difficulties, which are presented one after the other in the same paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in the last three sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred that allowing 'overlapping chains of memory' (paragraph 3) to carry identity would let the memory theorist say that

options.A: a vivid but false impression of an examination can now be told apart from a genuine memory of it.
options.B: the old woman is the child, because the teacher links the two even though the old woman recalls nothing of the child.
options.C: the old woman is not the child, since only a direct memory of an earlier stage of life can establish identity with it.
options.D: the teacher and the child are two different people, since the old woman remembers only the teacher.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the old woman is the child, because the teacher links the two even though the old woman recalls nothing of the child.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the chain solution meets 'The first objection' while the second, about false impressions, 'is much harder to escape'.
option_rationales.C: That is the strict criterion that produces the problem in paragraph 2; overlapping chains are introduced precisely to replace 'direct memory'.
option_rationales.D: The teacher does remember the child's accident, so on any memory criterion the teacher is the child; the old woman's memories do not affect that link.

questions.explanation: On a chain view, A is the same person as C if A remembers B and B remembers C. The old woman remembers the teacher, who remembers the child, so the old woman is the child, restoring the transitivity paragraph 2 demands.
questions.common_misconception: Thinking the chain solution also answers the circularity objection, which paragraph 3 says it does not.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the chain idea to the case in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Personal identity consists in memory, provided memory is understood as overlapping chains rather than direct recall.
options.B: Memory cannot settle who a person is, but it does measure how closely she is tied to her own past.
options.C: Personal identity is ultimately a matter of the body, since memory presupposes the very identity it was originally meant to explain.
options.D: Because memories fade over time, a person gradually ceases to be the same person she once was.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Memory cannot settle who a person is, but it does measure how closely she is tied to her own past.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the chain move answers only the first objection, and paragraph 4 says the theory 'fails as an account of identity'.
option_rationales.C: The author never endorses a bodily criterion; paragraph 3 contrasts the past remembered with one 'I share only bodily' to the disadvantage of the bodily.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says connection weakens but identity, 'being all or nothing', cannot; 'The old woman is the child she once was'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the conclusion: the theory 'fails as an account of identity and succeeds as an account of something else: the degree to which a person is connected to her own history'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the chain repair from paragraph 3, which is a step in the argument rather than its conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures a stage or a rival position mentioned along the way.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the distinction the author draws in paragraph 4?

options.A: A man who has forgotten his early years is identified by fingerprints, showing that bodily continuity is what personal identity consists in.
options.B: Two people both claim to remember winning the same prize as children, and the dispute is settled by checking records of which of them was actually present.
options.C: A woman who has lost all memory of her past is told by her doctors that she is now a different person from the one who was admitted.
options.D: A man accepts that he made a promise decades ago but feels it binds him only weakly, having lost almost every link to the life in which he made it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A man accepts that he made a promise decades ago but feels it binds him only weakly, having lost almost every link to the life in which he made it.

option_rationales.A: The passage never endorses a bodily criterion, and the case involves no difference in degree of connection, which is the other half of the distinction.
option_rationales.B: This illustrates the circularity objection of paragraph 2, that genuine memory presupposes identity, not the distinction between identity and connection.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 holds that identity does not lapse when connection weakens; the doctors' verdict applies the memory criterion the author says fails as an account of identity.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 separates identity, which is all or nothing, from connection, which 'comes in degrees and can weaken', and suggests that practical concerns such as 'the keeping of old promises' may track connection. The correct answer keeps identity fixed (he made the promise) while connection, and with it the felt force of the promise, has weakened.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a case about memory loss that ignores the second half of the distinction or adopts the criterion the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options each echo a different part of the passage; only the correct answer holds identity constant while varying connection.

questions.question: The example of the manager in paragraph 2 is used to show that

options.A: a person can decide each case fairly while the pattern of what she notices remains unfair.
options.B: assertive employees receive better treatment because they complain more often and more loudly.
options.C: managers in general are much less fair than they believe themselves to be.
options.D: applying identical rules to everyone leads, sooner or later, to unjust outcomes for some of the people affected.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a person can decide each case fairly while the pattern of what she notices remains unfair.

option_rationales.B: The passage says only that the manager noticed when an assertive colleague 'appeared dissatisfied'; complaining is never mentioned, and the point concerns her attention, not their tactics.
option_rationales.C: The example concerns one manager and makes no claim about managers in general; its point is about where the defect lies.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says her decisions 'may be beyond reproach'; the fault is placed 'upstream', not in the uniform rules.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Her decisions, examined individually, may be beyond reproach. The defect lies upstream, in a pattern of attention that has made some people's difficulties vivid to her and rendered others' invisible.'
questions.common_misconception: Blaming the rules or the employees instead of the manager's pattern of attention.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point of the example is stated in its last two sentences.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the word 'upstream' refers to

options.A: the earlier policy decisions that fixed the rules she now applies to every request for leave.
options.B: the pressure that more senior managers exert on the way she treats her own team.
options.C: the shaping of what a person perceives before she weighs any of the options before her.
options.D: the reserved employee's failure to tell anyone that he was anxious and withdrawn.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the shaping of what a person perceives before she weighs any of the options before her.

option_rationales.A: The rules are not said to be at fault; paragraph 1 places the relevant stage in what 'we attend to' before 'any choice is considered', which concerns perception, not earlier policy.
option_rationales.B: No senior managers appear in the passage; the defect is located in her own 'pattern of attention'.
option_rationales.D: The passage locates the defect in the manager's attention, not in the employee's silence, which is never mentioned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 argues that what a situation is taken to be 'is settled largely by what we attend to' before choice. The word 'upstream' in paragraph 2 names that earlier stage: 'a pattern of attention' that determines whose difficulties become visible at all.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'upstream' as any earlier decision, such as the rule-making, rather than the stage of noticing.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option names something genuinely earlier in time; the solver must connect the word to paragraph 1's claim about attention.

questions.question: The objection stated at the start of paragraph 3 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Attention is formed over time by habits and stories that a person is able to influence.
options.B: Moral life is located chiefly in what a person notices rather than in what she decides.
options.C: Every lapse of attention is, when examined closely, really a deliberate choice of some kind.
options.D: A person can rightly be blamed only for what lies within her voluntary control.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A person can rightly be blamed only for what lies within her voluntary control.

option_rationales.A: This is the author's reply to the objection, introduced by 'But', and it undercuts the objection rather than supporting it.
option_rationales.B: This is close to the author's own thesis, which the objection is raised against; the objection does not need it.
option_rationales.C: The objection holds the reverse, that noticing 'is not something we do at will', and the author agrees no single lapse 'is a choice'.

questions.explanation: The objection moves from 'Noticing is not something we do at will' to 'we cannot be blamed for failing to perceive what never came to our notice'. That inference needs the premise that blame requires voluntary control, which the hearing analogy reinforces.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the author's reply because it is the most prominent claim in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the objection, the concession and the reply within one paragraph.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Moral improvement consists solely in learning to see better and never in learning to choose better.
options.B: Since changes in attention are invisible from outside, they cannot be judged morally by other people.
options.C: Someone may be answerable for a failure to notice even if that particular failure was not something she chose.
options.D: Because attention is shaped by habit, each single lapse of attention deserves the same blame as a deliberately bad decision.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Someone may be answerable for a failure to notice even if that particular failure was not something she chose.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says improvement is 'frequently less a matter' of choosing than of seeing, a comparison of degree; the option turns it into an exclusive claim and denies choice any role.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says such work 'rarely earns admiration' because it is hard to see, not that it cannot be judged; the passage itself judges the manager's attention.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says 'No single lapse of attention is a choice, and it would be unjust to treat it as though it were'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 concedes that no single lapse is chosen but argues that attention is formed by things 'over which, across time, we have considerable influence'. Responsibility thus attaches to the pattern even where the individual lapse was unchosen.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the restatement of paragraph 4 without noticing that 'frequently less' has been hardened into an exclusive claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options differ from the author's view only in degree; the correct answer needs the concession and reply of paragraph 3 held together.

questions.question: According to the alternative view described in paragraph 2, attitudes such as resentment and gratitude are

options.A: feelings that a careful moral philosopher should try to exclude from judgements of blame.
options.B: part of living among persons, not conclusions drawn from a theory of causation.
options.C: suspended whenever it can be shown that a person's choice had antecedent causes.
options.D: justified only after the question of whether every choice is determined has been settled.

questions.correct_answer: (B) part of living among persons, not conclusions drawn from a theory of causation.

option_rationales.A: The alternative treats these attitudes as 'constitutive' of life among persons and warns against supposing a thesis could oblige us to 'relinquish them'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says suspensions occur in particular cases such as duress or ignorance, and 'none of them amounts to a general verdict on human agency'; causes as such are never a ground.
option_rationales.D: That is the traditional order of paragraph 1, which the alternative 'reverses'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'These attitudes, the alternative maintains, are not conclusions derived from a theory about causation. They are constitutive of what it is to live among persons rather than merely alongside objects'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the alternative view with the traditional order set out in paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The reference to compulsions, illnesses and conditions of upbringing in paragraph 4 serves to

options.A: show that the practice of blame has been revised by applying its own excusing principles to new cases.
options.B: illustrate how metaphysical arguments eventually forced societies to soften their harsh moral judgements.
options.C: establish that most societies have gradually come to accept the thesis that every human choice is causally determined.
options.D: suggest that people affected by such conditions should no longer be held responsible for anything they do.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that the practice of blame has been revised by applying its own excusing principles to new cases.

option_rationales.B: The passage explicitly denies this: the revisions 'arose when people learned more about how particular capacities can fail', not from metaphysics.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says these revisions 'were not imposed by metaphysics'; nothing is said about societies accepting determinism.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 speaks of conditions 'diminishing responsibility', not removing it altogether, and the author draws no such sweeping conclusion.

questions.explanation: The examples answer the worry that a self-answerable practice is 'immune to criticism': 'The history of the practice tells against such complacency.' They show revisions made by applying 'excusing principles the practice already contained to cases it had previously judged harshly'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that any softening of blame must have come from accepting determinism.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the examples against the claim they rebut in the first sentences of paragraph 4.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the most sweeping sceptical arguments overreach because

options.A: reactive attitudes are natural to human beings and so can never be shown to be mistaken in any case.
options.B: the evidence that every choice has antecedent causes is considerably weaker than sceptics usually suppose.
options.C: the general fact that choices have causes does not show that any particular excusing condition applies.
options.D: people outside philosophy continue resenting and forgiving whatever the latest argument happens to conclude.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the general fact that choices have causes does not show that any particular excusing condition applies.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 rejects the idea that the practice is 'beyond question' and describes cases in which the practice has been revised.
option_rationales.B: The author never questions the causal claim; paragraph 3 grants it for argument's sake ('from the bare claim that choices have causes') and denies that it has the consequences sceptics draw.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 cites this to explain why the debate 'seems unreal' to outsiders; that people ignore an argument does not show the argument overreaches, and the author gives a separate reason.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'from the bare claim that choices have causes, nothing follows about whether a particular person was acting under duress, or in ignorance, or as a child acts.' The excusing conditions the practice recognises are particular, so a general causal thesis cannot trigger them.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the point about outsiders, which sits in the same paragraph but answers a different question.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is a true statement from the same paragraph that explains something else.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: The free will debate is unreal, and findings about self-control are therefore irrelevant to the question of when people deserve blame for what they do.
options.B: Whether anyone is responsible depends on whether determinism is true, a question that the sciences of the mind will eventually settle.
options.C: Because responsibility is a shared practice answerable only to itself, its present standards of blame and excuse are beyond rational criticism.
options.D: Responsibility rests on a shared practice rather than on metaphysics, yet that practice can be corrected, partly with help from the study of the mind.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Responsibility rests on a shared practice rather than on metaphysics, yet that practice can be corrected, partly with help from the study of the mind.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says only that the debate 'seems unreal' to outsiders, and paragraph 5 says findings about self-control can reveal excusing conditions, so they are relevant.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says 'No general thesis about determinism will tell us whether blame is ever deserved'; this is the traditional view the passage rejects.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 calls this a case of the reversal being 'taken to establish more than it can' and says history 'tells against such complacency'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 endorse grounding responsibility in shared attitudes rather than metaphysics; paragraph 4 denies that the practice is therefore beyond criticism; paragraph 5 gives 'inquiry into the mind' a role in holding the practice 'to its own commitments'. The correct answer holds all three moves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that stops at the alternative view's insight and ignores the author's limits on it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is a position the passage mentions or nearly endorses; the correct answer requires the full argument across five paragraphs.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 5?

options.A: A rigorous philosophical proof that every human choice is determined leaves most people's feelings of resentment entirely unchanged.
options.B: Findings that a condition once dismissed as laziness impairs planning led schools to stop punishing pupils who have it.
options.C: Judges who were taught the general philosophical arguments for determinism became noticeably more lenient toward every kind of offender.
options.D: Societies have differed widely, across history and across regions, in which conditions they treat as diminishing responsibility.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Findings that a condition once dismissed as laziness impairs planning led schools to stop punishing pupils who have it.

option_rationales.A: This supports paragraph 3's point that the debate seems unreal to outsiders; it says nothing about detailed findings revealing excusing conditions.
option_rationales.C: This shows a general metaphysical thesis changing blame wholesale, which is the route paragraph 5 sets aside; the author's claim concerns specific findings about capacities.
option_rationales.D: Variation alone does not show that scientific findings about self-control drove any revision, which is the specific mechanism paragraph 5 claims.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 claims that 'detailed findings about how self-control develops, or how it is impaired, can reveal that the conditions our practice already counts as excusing are more common, or less conspicuous, than we had assumed'. The correct answer is a case of exactly this: a specific finding about an impaired capacity extends an existing excuse to cases previously blamed.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the judges, which links science-like argument to leniency but through the general thesis the author says cannot settle blame.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are closely related to the passage's themes; separating them requires the distinction between general theses and specific findings.

questions.question: According to the passage, the normative form of the narrative view holds that

options.A: a life that cannot be gathered into a coherent story is in some way deficient.
options.B: stories should be used only for making promises, recovering from loss and understanding others.
options.C: a person is a thing that persists unchanged beneath the experiences she has over a lifetime.
options.D: human beings do in fact come to understand themselves through stories about their lives.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a life that cannot be gathered into a coherent story is in some way deficient.

option_rationales.B: These uses are the author's own list of genuine goods in paragraph 4, and the author never says stories should be limited to them.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the narrative view denies exactly this: a person 'is not a thing that persists beneath her experiences'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 identifies this as 'The descriptive form'; the normative form 'adds' a claim about what people ought to do.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The normative form adds that they ought to, and that a life which cannot be gathered into a coherent narrative is in some way impoverished or broken.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the two forms defined in consecutive sentences of paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Defined directly in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The reference to a novelist at the end of paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: contrast fiction, in which leaving out what does not fit is harmless, with a life, in which it can be costly.
options.B: recommend that people model their understanding of themselves on the methods of skilled writers of fiction.
options.C: show that novels give a more truthful picture of human experience than the stories that people tell about their own lives.
options.D: argue that people who tell stories about their lives are deliberately deceiving those who listen to them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) contrast fiction, in which leaving out what does not fit is harmless, with a life, in which it can be costly.

option_rationales.B: The comparison works the other way: what is legitimate for a novelist is said to be harmful in a life: 'a life conducted on the same principle may lose precisely the evidence it most needs'.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not compare the truthfulness of novels and life stories; it says only that a novelist may 'legitimately omit' material.
option_rationales.D: The forgetting described is a pressure on the teller's own memory, 'a flattering kind of forgetting', not deliberate deception of an audience.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that the demand for coherence makes a person drop episodes that do not fit. The novelist 'may legitimately omit whatever does not serve the plot', but 'a life conducted on the same principle may lose precisely the evidence it most needs'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the comparison as praise of fiction or as an accusation of lying.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function depends on the contrast drawn in the final sentence of the paragraph.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard a person who does not experience her life as a plot as

options.A: evidence that the descriptive claim about narrative is false of most human beings.
options.B: having a different way of being a self rather than a defective one.
options.C: probably concealing a story about herself that she would prefer not to acknowledge.
options.D: unreflective about her own past in a way that limits what she can know about herself.

questions.correct_answer: (B) having a different way of being a self rather than a defective one.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the descriptive claim is 'plausible for many people' and doubts only its 'generality', on the basis of what 'Some people report'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'It would be rash to assume' that such people are 'concealing a narrative they would rather not acknowledge'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 also calls it rash to assume such people 'are simply unreflective'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 concludes that such testimony 'suggests that narrative self-understanding is one way of being a self rather than the condition of being one', and paragraph 5 objects to turning 'a difference in temperament into a deficiency'.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the author's doubt about the descriptive claim, which concerns its generality, into a claim that it fails for most people.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the author calls rash; the third overstates the scope of the author's own doubt.

questions.question: In the final paragraph, the claim that the narrative view 'turns a difference in temperament into a deficiency' means that the view

options.A: shows that temperament rather than narrative is what a person's self really consists in.
options.B: regards living by stories and living in the present as mere differences of temperament, neither better than the other.
options.C: explains differences of temperament between people as the outcome of the better or worse life stories they have told.
options.D: treats people who do not live by stories as lacking something when they merely differ in disposition.

questions.correct_answer: (D) treats people who do not live by stories as lacking something when they merely differ in disposition.

option_rationales.A: The author offers no account of what the self consists in, preferring a 'more modest view' that treats narrative as an instrument.
option_rationales.B: That is close to the author's own 'more modest view'; the narrative view, which says the self 'simply is its story', does the reverse and counts the non-narrative temperament as a deficiency.
option_rationales.C: The phrase is about how the view evaluates people who lack a narrative, not about what causes differences of temperament; no causal explanation is offered.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes people who live 'with their attention fixed on present tasks' and calls narrative 'one way of being a self'. Paragraph 5 says that making the story the self 'makes the instrument indispensable', so those who do not use it are wrongly counted as deficient.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'turns' as a causal claim about where temperament comes from.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase must be connected to the episodic people of paragraph 2; the causal wrong option is close in wording.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's position on the two forms of the narrative view?

options.A: The descriptive form is false, but the normative form remains valuable as an ideal toward which to work.
options.B: The descriptive form is true of everyone, but the normative form wrongly places value on coherence.
options.C: The descriptive form fits many people but probably not all, and the normative form is the more troubling of the two.
options.D: Both forms are false, since narrative has no genuine part to play in a life that is lived well and truthfully.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The descriptive form fits many people but probably not all, and the normative form is the more troubling of the two.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 calls the descriptive form 'plausible for many people', and paragraph 3 calls the normative form 'more troubling', the reverse of this option.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 doubts the descriptive form's 'generality' because of people who do not experience life as a plot.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 lists 'genuine goods' of narrative, such as promising and recovering from bereavement, and says lacking it entirely would be 'a real disadvantage'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the descriptive claim 'is plausible for many people, but its generality is doubtful'. Paragraph 3: 'The normative claim is more troubling', because the demand for coherence encourages 'a flattering kind of forgetting'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the comparative 'more troubling' and treating both forms as equally rejected, or neglecting the concession in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option gets one form right and the other wrong; the correct answer requires the author's graded verdict on both.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that blame rightly responds in part to outcomes, while granting that the control principle captures one strand of moral judgement.
options.B: show that the second driver deserves greater blame because he drove more recklessly than the first driver did on the same road.
options.C: defend the principle that people should be blamed only for what lies within their control against our emotional reactions to outcomes.
options.D: argue that the driver who arrived home safely should be treated as blameless because his careless drive harmed no one.

questions.correct_answer: (A) argue that blame rightly responds in part to outcomes, while granting that the control principle captures one strand of moral judgement.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the two drivers' 'recklessness were identical'; the author's case for the difference rests on the outcome, not on any difference in carelessness.
option_rationales.C: This is the view the author calls 'too quick' in paragraph 3; the passage argues against treating our responses to outcomes as mere emotional noise.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 rejects exactly this 'opposite error': the lucky driver 'did something seriously wrong', and his good outcome is 'no credit to him'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 sets out the control principle and its conclusion that the drivers deserve equal blame; paragraph 3 calls this 'too quick' because responsibility includes 'what our actions actually bring about'; paragraph 4 concedes that the principle captures 'one important strand' of blame but 'is not the whole of moral life'. The correct answer states both the thesis and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the view the author reports in paragraph 2 for the author's own position.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated outright in paragraphs 3 and 4; each wrong option contradicts an explicit sentence.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, if the principle that we should be blamed only for what lies within our control is correct, the two drivers

options.A: should each be judged by the harm that their careless driving might have caused on some other night.
options.B: deserve different penalties in law but should feel exactly the same degree of guilt about the drive afterwards.
options.C: deserve exactly the same blame, because their choices, states of mind and recklessness did not differ.
options.D: deserve no blame at all, because neither of them could control whether a child would be on the road.

questions.correct_answer: (C) deserve exactly the same blame, because their choices, states of mind and recklessness did not differ.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says they should be blamed 'for the risk each of them imposed on others' on this drive; other nights are never mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 draws no distinction between legal penalty and guilt; it concludes that the two deserve 'exactly the same blame', not different treatment of any kind.
option_rationales.D: The principle removes blame only for what was outside their control; their recklessness was within it, which is why paragraph 2 says both should be blamed 'equally, and severely'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states: 'If that principle is right, the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, since their choices, their states of mind and their recklessness were identical.' The correct answer restates this sentence.
questions.common_misconception: Concluding that luck cancels all blame, when the principle cancels only the blame attached to the outcome.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a paraphrase of one sentence.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the driver who arrived home without incident

options.A: ought to feel the same guilt as the second driver, since the two of them drove with equal recklessness.
options.B: owes an apology to the family of the child, since he imposed the same risk that led to the child's death.
options.C: deserves no criticism, because the control principle captures only one strand of our thinking about blame.
options.D: has no ground for taking credit for the fact that his careless drive happened to end without harm.

questions.correct_answer: (D) has no ground for taking credit for the fact that his careless drive happened to end without harm.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 defends the difference in the second driver's situation; it says his relationship to his own past is altered 'in a way that the first driver's is not'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says explicitly that the first driver 'has no one to apologise to'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says he 'did something seriously wrong'; calling the control principle incomplete does not make the lucky driver blameless.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says of the lucky driver that 'the fact that his drive ended well is no credit to him'. He did something seriously wrong, and luck in the outcome earns him no merit.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the author's rejection of the control principle as total, so that the lucky driver escapes all blame.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in a single sentence of paragraph 4.

questions.question: In the last sentence of the passage, the claim that a certain theory has 'impoverished' our moral concepts means that the theory

options.A: makes our moral concepts harder for ordinary people to apply, because it depends on abstract principles about control.
options.B: strips out features of moral life, such as owing an apology for harm actually done, that those concepts rightly contain.
options.C: removes from our moral judgements the emotional confusion about outcomes that had previously distorted them.
options.D: gives too much weight to the outcomes of actions and too little weight to the character of the agent.

questions.correct_answer: (B) strips out features of moral life, such as owing an apology for harm actually done, that those concepts rightly contain.

option_rationales.A: Difficulty of application is never raised; the complaint is about what the theory cannot 'make sense of', namely the apology owed by the second driver.
option_rationales.C: That is the 'purified' reading the author denies in the same sentence: the theory 'has not purified our moral concepts'.
option_rationales.D: The theory in question is the control principle, which gives outcomes no weight at all; the author's complaint is the reverse of this option.

questions.explanation: The theory is one 'that cannot make sense of why the second driver should apologise to the family'. To say it has impoverished our concepts is to say it leaves out something real, the responsibility that extends to outcomes, which paragraph 3 defends.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the direction of the criticism, or taking 'impoverished' to mean merely 'made harder to use'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying which theory is meant and linking the word to the contrast with 'purified'.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the simple form of consequentialism described in paragraph 2 would regard a bystander who declined a rescue that was the best act available to him as

options.A: having acted wrongly, since on that view the best available act is always the one required.
options.B: having performed a supererogatory act of his own by choosing to stay on the riverbank and call for help.
options.C: having done nothing open to criticism, since on that view heroic rescues are never required of anyone.
options.D: having acted permissibly, as long as he did nothing to obstruct anyone else who attempted the rescue.

questions.correct_answer: (A) having acted wrongly, since on that view the best available act is always the one required.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the view leaves 'no room above duty', so it can classify no act as supererogatory, least of all the refusal to rescue.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: on this view 'the person who fails to be a hero becomes a wrongdoer'.
option_rationales.D: On this view the best available act is required, so any alternative to it is wrong; the passage allows no merely permissible option beside the best act.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'the best available act is always the required one. If plunging into the river was the best thing she could do, she was obliged to do it; if it was not, she acted wrongly.' Declining a rescue that was the best act is therefore wrong on this view.
questions.common_misconception: Importing the ordinary view of paragraph 1 into the consequentialist view of paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference follows directly from two sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The remark that rescuers 'rarely say that those who held back did wrong' (paragraph 3) serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that rescuers who say that they 'had no choice' are mistaken about the real nature of what they did.
options.B: confirm the defenders' point that people are reluctant to blame others for practical reasons such as usefulness.
options.C: establish that the simple consequentialist is right about what the rescuer ought to have done in the river.
options.D: show that the rescuer's sense of obligation is personal rather than general, which the defenders' reply does not account for.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that the rescuer's sense of obligation is personal rather than general, which the defenders' reply does not account for.

option_rationales.A: The passage says rescuers speak 'sincerely' and builds on their self-understanding; it never says they are mistaken.
option_rationales.B: The remark follows 'But it leaves the rescuer's own understanding of her act unexplained'; it supports the author's objection to the reply, not the reply.
option_rationales.C: The remark tells against the consequentialist reading, since the rescuer does not treat her act as a duty binding everyone.

questions.explanation: The defenders say the rescue was what everyone in her position ought to do, and only blame is withheld. The author answers that rescuers feel they 'had no choice' yet do not condemn those who held back; their 'sense of being called is personal, not a verdict on everyone'. The remark shows what the reply cannot explain.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the remark as support for the reply because it concerns reluctance to blame.
questions.difficulty_reason: The remark mentions blame, which makes the defenders' point about blame a tempting but wrong home for it.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best fits the author's description in paragraph 4 of the region beyond duty?

options.A: A citizen pays his taxes in full, although he could probably have evaded part of them without ever being detected.
options.B: A doctor feels that she must volunteer in an epidemic zone, though she does not think that colleagues who stay at home are at fault.
options.C: A lawyer handles a case without charging a fee because the court has assigned the case to him under its standing rules.
options.D: A shopper chooses one brand of soap over another for no reason except habit, and would be equally content with either.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A doctor feels that she must volunteer in an epidemic zone, though she does not think that colleagues who stay at home are at fault.

option_rationales.A: Paying taxes honestly is a demand that applies to everyone; the region beyond duty is where morality 'stops issuing demands to everyone'.
option_rationales.C: This is an act required of him by an assigned obligation, which is 'duty' in the passage's terms, not an invitation addressed to him personally.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'merely permitted' choice of paragraph 1, like 'choosing tea over coffee'; paragraph 4 says the region beyond duty is not one to which morality is indifferent.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes the region as one where morality issues 'invitations to particular people' rather than demands on everyone, and where acts are admired as moral achievements. The doctor feels personally called but issues no verdict on her colleagues, exactly the pattern of paragraph 3.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an admirable act that is in fact a duty, such as honest tax payment.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each option must be sorted into the passage's categories of duty, permission and the region beyond duty.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the defenders' reply in paragraph 3 is best described as

options.A: neutral, since the author reports the reply without offering any judgement on whether it succeeds.
options.B: wholly persuaded, since the author thinks it reconciles consequentialism with the experience of rescuers.
options.C: appreciative of its ingenuity but convinced that it leaves something important unexplained.
options.D: dismissive, since the author treats it as a confusion that captures nothing of how we actually blame.

questions.correct_answer: (C) appreciative of its ingenuity but convinced that it leaves something important unexplained.

option_rationales.A: The author judges the reply explicitly, praising it and then stating its limit with 'But'.
option_rationales.B: The author says the reply 'leaves the rescuer's own understanding of her act unexplained', so it does not reconcile the two.
option_rationales.D: The author says the move 'is ingenious, and it does capture something', which rules out dismissal.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls the reply 'ingenious' and grants that 'it does capture something', then says 'But it leaves the rescuer's own understanding of her act unexplained'. The attitude is qualified appreciation.
questions.common_misconception: Fixing on either the praise or the criticism and ignoring the other half.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both halves of the attitude must be held together; one-sided options are tempting.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: When a promise conflicts with a stronger duty, the stronger duty prevails and the promiser owes compensation for the breach.
options.B: The firmness of promises is an illusion, since a promiser can always claim that his situation was not foreseen.
options.C: Promises bind only within limits set by a shared, reasonable understanding of the circumstances in which they were made.
options.D: A promise must always be kept, because the person who made it freely chose to create the obligation.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Promises bind only within limits set by a shared, reasonable understanding of the circumstances in which they were made.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'outweighed' explanation that paragraph 2 says 'misses something'; the author also says compensation is not owed.
option_rationales.B: This is the objection raised in paragraph 4, which the author answers with the standard of the reasonable promisee.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the obligation 'can seem absolute', but paragraph 2 at once says 'no one seriously believes that every promise binds whatever happens'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives the author's account: a promise carries 'an implicit understanding of the conditions under which they were made', and paragraph 4 fixes those conditions by 'what a reasonable person in the promisee's position would have taken them to be'. The correct answer captures this account.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the objection of paragraph 4 or the rejected explanation of paragraph 2 as the author's view.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is a position the passage states and then sets aside.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the author's account, a person who misses a promised lunch in order to take an injured cyclist to hospital

options.A: has committed a minor wrong against the friend, which is excused by the greater urgency of the cyclist's need.
options.B: owes the friend compensation for the lunch, though the friend should not think less of him for missing it.
options.C: need offer the friend no explanation, since both parties already understand that emergencies fall outside promises.
options.D: has not violated any right that the friend acquired when the promise was accepted.

questions.correct_answer: (D) has not violated any right that the friend acquired when the promise was accepted.

option_rationales.A: This is the outweighing picture, on which one obligation is broken for a heavier one; paragraph 2 says the promiser owes 'certainly not a confession of wrongdoing'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the promiser owes an explanation and perhaps an apology, 'but not compensation'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'I owe you an explanation'; the shared understanding removes the debt, not the need to explain.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the friend acquired 'a right against my changing my mind for reasons of my own convenience', not a right to my presence 'under every conceivable circumstance'. Helping the cyclist is not a matter of convenience, so 'the promise never extended so far' and no right is violated.
questions.common_misconception: Holding on to the outweighing picture, in which some obligation to the friend is still broken.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be drawn from paragraph 3, while two wrong options restate positions from paragraph 2 that look reasonable.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply in paragraph 4 to the worry that promises lose their firmness?

options.A: Some promisers privately intend, at the very moment of promising, to break their promise if it becomes inconvenient.
options.B: For most promises, reasonable people in the promisee's position disagree sharply about which emergencies would excuse the promiser.
options.C: Many people readily forgive a broken promise when the reason they are given for it is a genuine emergency.
options.D: In a few unusual cases, even careful observers cannot agree whether a promise was meant to cover a particular emergency.

questions.correct_answer: (B) For most promises, reasonable people in the promisee's position disagree sharply about which emergencies would excuse the promiser.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the conditions are 'not whatever the promiser privately had in mind', so private intentions to break a promise leave the reply untouched.
option_rationales.C: This is consistent with the author's account and says nothing against the claim that the reasonable-promisee standard keeps exceptions public.
option_rationales.D: The author already concedes that the standard 'will not settle every case', so a few hard cases do not weaken the reply.

questions.explanation: The reply is that the reasonable-promisee standard 'keeps the exceptions public'. If reasonable people disagreed sharply about most promises, the standard would fix no shared limits, and the escape route the objection describes would remain open.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about a few hard cases, which the author has already conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer and the strongest wrong option differ in scope ('most' against 'a few'), and only the correct answer defeats the reply.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The duty to help the cyclist overrides a right to the promiser's presence at lunch that the friend had acquired.
options.B: A promise gives the person to whom it is made a kind of authority over part of the promiser's future conduct.
options.C: Missing a promised lunch may call for an apology for the friend's wasted time even when missing it was right.
options.D: Letting the promisee's reasonable understanding fix the limits of a promise keeps those limits open to public view.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The duty to help the cyclist overrides a right to the promiser's presence at lunch that the friend had acquired.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says that in promising 'I hand you a kind of authority over my future conduct', so this is supported.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the promiser owes 'perhaps an apology for your wasted time', although he was right to help the cyclist, so this is supported.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the reasonable-promisee standard 'keeps the exceptions public', so this is supported.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the friend 'did not acquire a right to my presence at lunch under every conceivable circumstance' and that 'the cyclist does not outweigh the promise'. The correct answer describes the outweighing picture, which the author rejects, so it is the one statement the passage does not support.
questions.common_misconception: Remembering the word 'outweighed' from paragraph 2 and forgetting that the author replaces that explanation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported statement is the explanation the passage reports and then rejects, and it uses the passage's own terms.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards a wholesale dismissal of moral intuitions as

options.A: self-undermining, since the dismissal itself appears to depend on judgements of the kind it rejects.
options.B: sound for intuitions about harm, but mistaken for intuitions about which features of a case matter.
options.C: decisive, since it shows that every moral intuition has causes that are unrelated to moral truth.
options.D: irrelevant, because the empirical sciences face no comparable difficulty about the judgements they start from.

questions.correct_answer: (A) self-undermining, since the dismissal itself appears to depend on judgements of the kind it rejects.

option_rationales.B: The author distrusts some particular intuitions about harm, not a whole class; a wholesale dismissal is rejected for all classes alike.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says having such causes proves little, 'for every belief has causes'; the author does not find the dismissal decisive.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the sciences face a comparable situation, relying on perceptual reports checked 'only by further perception'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the debunker 'owes us an account of the standpoint from which the dismissal is made, and it is hard to find one that does not rely on some judgement of the same kind'. The dismissal thus seems to rely on what it dismisses.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's concession in paragraph 2 that some intuitions are distorted as acceptance of the wholesale dismissal.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer rests on one sentence of paragraph 4.

questions.question: The reference to the empirical sciences in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: show that moral intuitions can be checked against perception in the same way that scientific reports can.
options.B: suggest that relying on starting judgements that are not questioned at the outset is not a defect peculiar to moral inquiry.
options.C: illustrate how an intuition about harm can come to ignore the quantity of harm that is actually done.
options.D: concede that moral philosophy is less rigorous than science, because its starting judgements can never be checked at all.

questions.correct_answer: (B) suggest that relying on starting judgements that are not questioned at the outset is not a defect peculiar to moral inquiry.

option_rationales.A: The passage draws a parallel in structure, not a claim that intuitions are checked by perception; perception checks only perceptual reports.
option_rationales.C: That illustration comes later in the paragraph and concerns a different point, the grounds for suspecting a particular intuition.
option_rationales.D: The comparison is used to defend the moral method, and paragraph 2 goes on to say that particular intuitions can be found distorted.

questions.explanation: The sentence says 'Every method of inquiry begins with some judgements it does not, at that moment, question', and offers the sciences as an instance. The point is that the critics' complaint, if it worked, would condemn every inquiry, not just ethics.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the analogy to claim more than structural similarity.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing the role of an analogy within a reply to an objection.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about the debunker in paragraph 4?

options.A: Intuitions about the same cases differ considerably between cultures and between historical periods.
options.B: Moral theories have in the past overturned several reactions to cases that were once very widely shared.
options.C: A debunker could justify discarding all moral intuitions from purely non-moral premises, with no judgement about which features of cases matter.
options.D: Philosophers who reject intuitions in their writing still rely on them when making their everyday decisions.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A debunker could justify discarding all moral intuitions from purely non-moral premises, with no judgement about which features of cases matter.

option_rationales.A: This supports the critics' premise about the origins of intuitions, which the author grants; it does not show that the dismissal avoids relying on intuitions.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 itself says moral thought has done this before; the fact bears on the defender's obligation, not on the debunker's standpoint.
option_rationales.D: This, if anything, fits the author's point that it is hard to escape judgements of the kind being dismissed; it does not weaken it.

questions.explanation: The author claims that it is hard to find a standpoint for dismissing intuitions 'that does not rely on some judgement of the same kind'. If the dismissal could be justified entirely from non-moral premises, such a standpoint would exist and the claim would fail.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about cultural variation, which attacks intuitions in general but not the specific claim about the debunker's standpoint.
questions.difficulty_reason: The strongest wrong option is relevant to the debate but not to the precise claim; the correct answer requires isolating that claim.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the remark that 'the circle is wide' is best understood to mean that

options.A: the method takes a long time to arrive at a state of balance, although it does arrive there in the end.
options.B: the method admits so many intuitions that it is able to endorse almost any moral theory whatever.
options.C: critics have exaggerated the circularity, because in the end principles hold final authority over judgements about cases.
options.D: the adjustment ranges over a great many judgements and principles, so its circularity does not leave it empty.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the adjustment ranges over a great many judgements and principles, so its circularity does not leave it empty.

option_rationales.A: This reads 'wide' as a matter of duration, and the passage makes no claim about how long the process takes.
option_rationales.B: This turns the remark into a criticism, whereas the author offers it as a defence of the method against the charge of circularity.
option_rationales.C: The same paragraph says 'Neither level has final authority', so this misstates the method the author describes.

questions.explanation: The author concedes the method is circular 'in a sense' and replies that 'the circle is wide'. Because principles and case judgements, each supported 'elsewhere', support one another across a broad range, the circle is not the empty, self-confirming kind the critics fear.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the figurative phrase as a criticism or as a remark about time.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative phrase must be read as a reply to the charge of circularity, using the rest of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining how a victim can stop thinking about a wrong once the person who committed it has died.
options.B: arguing that forgiveness remains possible without an apology, although an apology often makes it easier and more apt.
options.C: showing that genuine forgiveness requires the wrongdoer to acknowledge the wrong, express remorse and make amends.
options.D: criticising people who forgive quickly on the ground that they lack both self-respect and moral seriousness.

questions.correct_answer: (B) arguing that forgiveness remains possible without an apology, although an apology often makes it easier and more apt.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 mentions ceasing to think about a wrong only to say that this is not forgiveness; the passage does not explain how to do it.
option_rationales.C: This is the view reported in paragraph 1, whose 'awkward consequence' paragraph 2 then exposes; the author rejects it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says only that forgiving every injury at once 'may' show a lack of self-respect; this qualification is a detail, not the purpose.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 objects that the earned view bars the victim from forgiving an unrepentant or dead wrongdoer; paragraph 3 says that 'Without an apology, forgiveness remains possible'; paragraph 4 concludes that apology is 'one route to forgiveness rather than its gatekeeper'.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the reported view of paragraph 1 for the author's thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is restated in the last sentence of the passage.

questions.question: According to the account the author favours, to forgive is to

options.A: excuse the wrongdoer, on the ground that he could not in the circumstances have acted otherwise.
options.B: accept the wrongdoer's apology and restore the relationship to what it had been before the wrong.
options.C: decide that the wrong no longer matters, so that it need no longer be judged as a wrong at all.
options.D: give up resentment and the claim to repayment while still judging that the act was wrong.

questions.correct_answer: (D) give up resentment and the claim to repayment while still judging that the act was wrong.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says that forgiveness, so understood, 'does not excuse anything'.
option_rationales.B: The passage says forgiveness is possible without any apology, and restoring the relationship is never mentioned.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says forgiveness continues 'to judge that the act was wrong' and that 'the judgement of wrong remains in place'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'To forgive is to give up resentment and the claim to repayment while continuing to judge that the act was wrong.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing forgiving with excusing or forgetting.
questions.difficulty_reason: A near paraphrase of one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: If the woman described in paragraph 2 forgave her former friend although he refused to admit anything, the author would most likely regard her forgiveness as

options.A: genuine, though offered as a gift and for reasons of her own rather than in answer to his remorse.
options.B: a sign that she lacks self-respect, since anyone who forgives without receiving an apology lacks it.
options.C: impossible, since on any sound account the conditions for forgiving depend on the friend's change of heart.
options.D: a way of excusing the wrong, since nothing in the friend's conduct has changed to make forgiving him fitting.

questions.correct_answer: (A) genuine, though offered as a gift and for reasons of her own rather than in answer to his remorse.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 limits that worry to forgiving 'every injury at once, before she has even registered that she was wronged', not to every unapologised forgiveness.
option_rationales.C: That is the consequence of the earned view which paragraph 2 calls 'strange'; the author's own account in paragraph 3 says forgiveness 'remains possible'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says forgiveness 'does not excuse anything', with or without an apology, because the judgement of wrong remains.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that without an apology forgiveness 'remains possible, but it is a gift rather than a response, and it is offered for the victim's reasons rather than the wrongdoer's'. The woman's case is exactly this.
questions.common_misconception: Stretching the caution of paragraph 4 to cover all forgiveness given without apology.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying paragraph 3 to the case of paragraph 2 while keeping paragraph 4's qualification in its narrow scope.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that forgiveness must be earned is best described as

options.A: approving, since the author holds that wrongs rightly make demands on wrongdoers.
options.B: contemptuous, since the author holds that it confuses forgiveness with forgetting.
options.C: respectful of its moral seriousness but critical of what it implies for victims.
options.D: indifferent, since the author's real concern is the danger of forgiving too readily.

questions.correct_answer: (C) respectful of its moral seriousness but critical of what it implies for victims.

option_rationales.A: The author praises this feature but then rejects the view because of its 'awkward consequence', so the overall attitude is not approval.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the view 'refuses to let forgiveness become a soft word for forgetting', which the author counts in its favour.
option_rationales.D: The author engages with the view at length in paragraphs 1 to 3; paragraph 4 is a qualification, not the main concern.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 grants that the view 'has an attractive moral seriousness'; paragraph 2 says it 'puts the victim's moral recovery in the hands of the person who harmed her'. The attitude combines respect with criticism.
questions.common_misconception: Reading only paragraph 1 and choosing approval.
questions.difficulty_reason: Praise and criticism sit in different paragraphs, and the one-sided options each match one of them.

questions.question: The author suggests that, if relativism is true, a tolerant culture faced with a culture that prizes conquest could

options.A: persuade the conquering culture to stop by showing that its own standards in fact forbid conquest.
options.B: do no more than report that tolerance is valued in its own culture, without giving the other a reason.
options.C: justify intervening by force to protect the peoples that the conquering culture threatens.
options.D: condemn conquest as wrong by appealing to a moral standard that both cultures are bound to accept.

questions.correct_answer: (B) do no more than report that tolerance is valued in its own culture, without giving the other a reason.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 describes a culture 'whose standards prized conquest', so its own standards cannot be shown to forbid it.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage says relativism licenses forcible intervention; the relativist argument is meant to support non-interference.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says that under relativism there is no such shared standard; appealing to one would mean helping oneself 'to a non-relative principle'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'If relativism is true, the most a tolerant culture can say to such a culture is that tolerance is valued here, which is a report about itself rather than a reason addressed to anyone else.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that the tolerant culture can still appeal to a shared standard.
questions.difficulty_reason: Paraphrase of one sentence in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author makes or accepts each of the following points EXCEPT that

options.A: the argument of paragraph 2 establishes that moral relativism is false.
options.B: doubt about moral matters can leave people unable to object to anything at all.
options.C: the case against intervention can rest in part on the poor record of forced conversion.
options.D: certainty that one's own customs embody universal truth has been used historically to justify coercion.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the argument of paragraph 2 establishes that moral relativism is false.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says doubt 'can also leave them unable to object to anything at all'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 lists 'the dismal record of forced conversion' among the grounds against intervention.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 accepts this when explaining the appeal of relativism: such certainty 'licensed them to remake others by force'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens: 'None of this shows that relativism is false'. Paragraph 2 shows only that relativism cannot support a universal duty of tolerance, so the correct answer is the one point the author does not accept.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that an argument against relativism's support for tolerance is an argument against relativism itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is denied in one sentence, but the denial must be connected back to paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following positions is closest to the view the author describes in paragraph 4?

options.A: A visitor declines to judge her hosts' customs at all, believing that their rightness depends only on the standards of her hosts.
options.B: A visitor judges her hosts' custom to be unjust and supports forcing them to give it up, since moral truths bind everyone alike.
options.C: A visitor praises her hosts' customs in public to avoid giving offence, while privately condemning them as barbaric.
options.D: A visitor judges one of her hosts' customs to be unjust, says so when asked, and still opposes any attempt to abolish it by force.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A visitor judges one of her hosts' customs to be unjust, says so when asked, and still opposes any attempt to abolish it by force.

option_rationales.A: This is the relativist attitude the passage criticises, not the view of paragraph 4, which holds that 'some moral claims are true for everyone'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the grounds it lists 'count strongly against intervention in most cases'; holding universal truths does not license force.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the view 'obliges one to say that some practices are wrong'; concealing that judgement behind public praise is not the view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes holding that 'some moral claims are true for everyone' while counting humility, respect for self-government and the record of forced conversion against intervention, a view that obliges one 'to say that some practices are wrong even while declining to stamp them out'. The visitor in the correct answer does exactly this.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that anyone who believes in universal moral truths must favour intervention.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must combine judging, saying and not intervening; each wrong option drops one element.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the author's argument?

options.A: It concedes that the objection of paragraph 2 fails, since believing relativism does in practice make people more tolerant.
options.B: It presents historical evidence that cultures holding relativist beliefs have been more tolerant than other cultures.
options.C: It considers a revised version of the relativist's case and argues that this version abandons the claim that relativism grounds tolerance.
options.D: It shows that relativism is false by demonstrating that doubt always leaves people unable to object to anything.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It considers a revised version of the relativist's case and argues that this version abandons the claim that relativism grounds tolerance.

option_rationales.A: The author grants only that this 'may be true as a matter of psychology' and says the reply 'changes the subject'; the objection of paragraph 2 is left standing.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'the historical record is mixed' and presents no evidence that relativist cultures were more tolerant.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 begins by saying the argument does not show relativism false, and it says doubt 'can' have this effect, not that it always does.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces the defender's reply that believing relativism 'tends to produce tolerant people', then argues that the reply 'defends relativism as a useful belief rather than a true one' and 'concedes that the case for tolerance must be made on other grounds'. That is the function the correct answer describes, and it prepares paragraph 4.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's partial concession about psychology as a concession that the earlier objection fails.
questions.difficulty_reason: The first wrong option uses the author's own concession; seeing why it does not rescue relativism needs paragraphs 2 and 3 together.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Moral progress is best pictured as a single line along which every society advances in the same direction.
options.B: Moral progress is real but is better understood as a series of corrections than as the widening of a circle of concern.
options.C: Moral progress consists in extending moral concern to those beings who were previously left outside its boundary.
options.D: Talk of moral progress is largely the self-congratulation of each age as it looks back on the ages before it.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Moral progress is real but is better understood as a series of corrections than as the widening of a circle of concern.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says progress is 'less like a single line along which societies advance and more like a series of corrections'.
option_rationales.C: This is the circle picture of paragraph 2, which paragraph 3 calls 'incomplete in a way that matters'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 reports this worry, and paragraph 5 says 'None of this means that we should abandon the idea of moral progress'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states the conclusion: progress is 'less like a single line along which societies advance and more like a series of corrections'. Paragraphs 3 and 4 show why the circle image is incomplete, and paragraph 1 establishes that progress is real in particular cases.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the circle picture because it occupies a whole paragraph and is described as appealing.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion is stated in paragraph 5; the wrong options are views the passage reports or denies.

questions.question: The author's discussion of the beating of wives in paragraph 3 suggests that

options.A: the reform of such practices came about by extending moral concern to people who stood outside the circle.
options.B: attitudes to wives have changed far less over time than attitudes to the treatment of children have.
options.C: a practice can be gravely wrong even when those it harms are fully recognised as objects of moral concern.
options.D: in the societies that permitted such beating, wives were not regarded as being morally considerable at all.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a practice can be gravely wrong even when those it harms are fully recognised as objects of moral concern.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'Reform came not from widening the boundary but from revising the terms within it'.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no comparison of degree; it says both attitudes changed, and treats children as a parallel case.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: wives 'were very much inside the circle'.

questions.explanation: The example shows that wives 'were very much inside the circle' yet were 'assigned a place in it that we now regard as degrading'. The wrong lay in the terms of inclusion, not in exclusion, which is what the correct answer states.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that any serious wrong must rest on exclusion, which is the circle picture the example is meant to correct.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing the purpose of the example against the circle picture of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Any extension of moral concern to new beings is an advance, whatever form the extension takes.
options.B: Changes in moral attitudes, like changes in fashion, are neither better nor worse than what they replace.
options.C: The inclusion of animals within moral concern is the clearest case of moral progress in recent times.
options.D: An age may rightly judge some earlier practices mistaken without being able to state a complete moral theory.

questions.correct_answer: (D) An age may rightly judge some earlier practices mistaken without being able to state a complete moral theory.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 denies this: 'concern can be extended in ways that are themselves harmful'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says it is hard to describe the abolition of slavery 'merely as changes in fashion'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 describes the extension to animals as made 'more recently and more contentiously'; the passage never calls it the clearest case.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says corrections 'can be recognised as improvements without a finished theory of the good', as a scientist recognises an error 'without possessing the final truth'.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the circle picture's implication that every extension is progress.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases paragraph 5, and each wrong option is contradicted elsewhere, so the whole passage must be in view.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's criticism of the circle image in paragraph 4?

options.A: Some movements that extended concern to distant peoples used that concern chiefly as grounds for ruling them against their wishes.
options.B: Many people who doubt the idea of moral progress in theory still accept it when they consider particular cases.
options.C: Concern for the welfare of animals has grown steadily in many countries over the course of the last century.
options.D: Several societies that once excluded foreigners from moral concern later came to include them fully and fairly.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Some movements that extended concern to distant peoples used that concern chiefly as grounds for ruling them against their wishes.

option_rationales.B: This repeats a point from paragraph 1 and has no bearing on the danger described in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: This is a further widening of the circle and says nothing about whether widening can itself be harmful.
option_rationales.D: This is the kind of case the circle image handles well; it supports the image rather than the criticism of it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that 'Inclusion that comes with a presumption of authority over the included is not obviously better than the indifference it replaces'. Evidence that extended concern was used mainly to justify unwanted rule is a direct instance of this danger.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option about widening concern that is on topic but fits the circle picture.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are true to the topic of progress; only one bears on harmful inclusion.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures what the author means by 'the vanity of the present' in paragraph 5?

options.A: the preference of each generation for its own fashions, such as the length of coats, over older ones
options.B: the belief of present societies that they are more prosperous and comfortable than those of the past
options.C: a society's pride in how wide its own circle of concern is compared with the circles of its neighbours
options.D: an age's habit of treating its own standards as the measure by which earlier ages are found wanting

questions.correct_answer: (D) an age's habit of treating its own standards as the measure by which earlier ages are found wanting

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 mentions coats only to contrast moral change with fashion; the vanity in question concerns moral judgement, not taste in dress.
option_rationales.B: Prosperity is never discussed; the passage is concerned only with moral judgements of the past.
option_rationales.C: The charge in paragraph 1 concerns an age looking back on 'its predecessors', a comparison across time, not with neighbouring societies.
