option_rationales.A: The passage never ranks misleading above lying; within relationships of trust it says only that true words offer 'almost no moral shelter'.
option_rationales.C: This is the reasoning that paragraph 3 allows only where listeners are on guard by convention; paragraph 4 places dealings with doctors among relationships of reliance.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 locates the harm in the unchosen false belief and the betrayed trust, both present at once, not in later discovery or distress.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists 'doctors' among relationships in which listeners may rely on a speaker's cooperation, where misleading 'offers almost no moral shelter'. Both harms named in paragraph 2 are present, so the doctor's choice of true words 'changes the technique, not the result'.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying the used car reasoning (shared responsibility for inferences) into a relationship of trust.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires placing a new case in the author's two-setting scheme; one wrong option overshoots the author's claim.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the widely shared intuition described in paragraph 1 as

options.A: tracking a real difference, though one that matters only in certain kinds of relationship.
options.B: correct in its ordinary moral form but mistaken in the form that legal systems have given it.
options.C: a rationalisation invented by people who want to deceive others without feeling guilty about it.
options.D: a reliable guide in every setting, although people like the employee sometimes misapply it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) tracking a real difference, though one that matters only in certain kinds of relationship.

option_rationales.B: The passage cites moral thinking and legal systems together as sharing the intuition and never distinguishes between them.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the intuition 'is not merely self-serving', and paragraph 3 grants that the distinction 'earns its keep' in one setting.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says that in cases like the employee's 'the distinction begins to look thin', so the author does not think it holds everywhere.

questions.explanation: The author grants in paragraph 1 that the intuition is 'not merely self-serving', argues in paragraph 2 that it looks 'thin' when trust is exploited, and concludes in paragraphs 3 and 4 that it matters where listeners are on guard but offers 'almost no moral shelter' in relationships of reliance. So it tracks a real difference with limited scope.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the dismissive reading because the author criticises the employee.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the author's net view across all four paragraphs, with a partial concession.

questions.question: According to the passage, the appeal of substituted judgement lies mainly in the fact that it

options.A: spares relatives the need to discuss treatment decisions with doctors and with other members of the family.
options.B: tends to produce outcomes that are medically better for patients than the outcomes of the best-interests standard.
options.C: lets the patient's own values keep governing her care after she has lost the ability to decide.
options.D: gives doctors, rather than relatives, the final responsibility for decisions about an unconscious patient's treatment.

questions.correct_answer: (C) lets the patient's own values keep governing her care after she has lost the ability to decide.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 presents shutting down discussion as a cost of the fiction, not as the source of the standard's appeal.
option_rationales.B: The passage compares the standards on autonomy and honesty, not on medical results, which are never mentioned.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the surrogate is 'usually a close relative'; nothing suggests the standard shifts decisions to doctors.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the standard 'extends the patient's autonomy beyond the point at which she can exercise it', so that 'her values rather than anyone else's continue to govern what is done to her body'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing a cost described in paragraph 3 with the appeal described in paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer located in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The example of the trial of dialysis in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: demonstrate that the best-interests standard leads to kinder outcomes than substituted judgement does.
options.B: illustrate a decision on which a patient's known views give the surrogate no real guidance.
options.C: show that patients who wish to die at home generally refuse treatments that may prolong their discomfort.
options.D: illustrate a clear prior instruction that a surrogate who respects the patient's autonomy is bound to follow.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate a decision on which a patient's known views give the surrogate no real guidance.

option_rationales.A: No outcomes are compared; the example concerns whether there is anything for the surrogate to reconstruct.
option_rationales.C: The example says the patient had views about dying at home 'but none about' dialysis; it denies, rather than asserts, a link between the two.
option_rationales.D: That is the role of the ventilator example earlier in paragraph 2; the dialysis case is introduced with 'Far more often, however' as its contrast.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 contrasts the ventilator case, where the patient 'has left a clear instruction', with situations 'the patient never considered'. The dialysis trial is such a situation: her firm views about dying at home do not settle it, so asking what she would have chosen may have 'no fact of the matter'.
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up the two examples in paragraph 2, which play opposite roles.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two examples in one paragraph play contrasting roles; the reader must keep them apart.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about the second cost of substituted judgement?

options.A: Relatives who later doubted their reading of a patient's wishes were, on the whole, no more distressed than relatives asked from the start to decide what was best for her.
options.B: Patients who left written instructions were more likely to have their wishes followed than those who expressed them only in conversation.
options.C: Many relatives say that they found substituted judgement a real comfort when they were required to make difficult treatment decisions on behalf of patients who had lost the capacity to decide.
options.D: Doctors and relatives frequently disagree about what an unconscious patient would have wanted, and such disputes are seldom openly resolved.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Relatives who later doubted their reading of a patient's wishes were, on the whole, no more distressed than relatives asked from the start to decide what was best for her.

option_rationales.B: The form in which wishes are recorded is irrelevant to whether relatives who doubt their reading suffer more than relatives told to judge best interests.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 already grants that families find the standard 'consoling'; the finding is consistent with the author and does not touch the claim about later suffering.
option_rationales.D: This bears, if anything, on the first cost (decisions hidden from discussion), and it would support rather than weaken that cost.

questions.explanation: The second cost (paragraph 3) is that relatives who later doubt they read the patient correctly 'may suffer more than they would have' if told from the start they were judging what was best for her. A finding that such relatives are no more distressed than the comparison group removes the predicted difference.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a finding about consolation, which the author already concedes, instead of one about the comparative suffering the claim predicts.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires isolating the comparative claim within the 'second cost' and distinguishing it from the first cost.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that a surrogate who has no reliable knowledge of a patient's wishes on the matter at hand should

options.A: reconstruct her wishes as carefully as possible from scraps of earlier conversation and follow that reconstruction.
options.B: abandon substituted judgement in this case and also in cases where her wishes are clearly known, for the sake of consistency.
options.C: refuse to take part in the decision, leaving it to doctors who can judge the patient's interests more objectively.
options.D: acknowledge openly that he is choosing what seems best for the patient rather than what she would have chosen.

questions.correct_answer: (D) acknowledge openly that he is choosing what seems best for the patient rather than what she would have chosen.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 calls this 'extrapolating from scraps' shaped by the surrogate's 'own hopes and fears', which is the fiction the author criticises.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'The remedy is not to abandon substituted judgement' and keeps it where the patient's wishes 'are actually known'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 assigns the surrogate the task of 'choosing on the patient's behalf what seems best for her'; it does not ask him to withdraw.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 proposes that outside cases where the patient's wishes are known and relevant, one should 'say plainly' that 'the surrogate is choosing on the patient's behalf what seems best for her', calling such honesty 'a form of respect'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating careful reconstruction as respectful, when the author regards confident reconstruction without a basis as a fiction.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option describes the very practice the author criticises in sympathetic terms.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'directed wrongs' are best understood as wrongs that

options.A: consist in what is done to some particular person, so that benefiting someone else cannot repair them.
options.B: are committed deliberately and with full knowledge, as opposed to harms that are caused by accident or neglect.
options.C: are ordered by one person but carried out by another, as when the unfaithful man pays his friend.
options.D: cause damage only through the total amount of similar harm that everyone together has committed.

questions.correct_answer: (A) consist in what is done to some particular person, so that benefiting someone else cannot repair them.

option_rationales.B: Intention is never discussed; the contrast in paragraph 3 is with 'aggregate' harms, not with accidental ones.
option_rationales.C: The friend in paragraph 1 is paid to be faithful, not to commit a wrong; 'directed' refers to the target of the wrong, not to who gives orders.
option_rationales.D: This describes the aggregate harms that paragraph 3 sets against directed wrongs, so it reverses the meaning.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says infidelity 'wrongs a particular person, and the wrong consists in what is done to her', which is why another couple's faithfulness cannot repair it. Paragraph 3 names such cases 'directed wrongs' and gives a further example: an insult to a colleague cannot be offset by kindness to a stranger.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'directed' in an everyday sense (deliberate, or ordered) instead of the sense fixed by the contrast with aggregate harms.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contrast with 'aggregate ones' in the same sentence fixes the meaning.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would describe a scheme that credits travellers for planting trees that would have been planted anyway as one that

options.A: is morally no different from buying a pardon, which confirms the critics' charge against offsetting in general.
options.B: still partly undoes the harm of the flight, since the traveller paid in good faith for what she was promised.
options.C: shows that offsetting is incoherent even for aggregate harms once it is actually put into practice.
options.D: leaves the harm unrepaired, a failing to be exposed by checking the scheme rather than by condemning offsetting.

questions.correct_answer: (D) leaves the harm unrepaired, a failing to be exposed by checking the scheme rather than by condemning offsetting.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says such an offset 'is not a pardon; it is simply a fraud', and the author denies that failures of this kind vindicate the critics.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 makes whether 'the trees would have been planted anyway' a test the offset must pass; good faith does not create any subtraction from the stock of harm.
option_rationales.C: The author separates principle from practice: offsetting is 'coherent for aggregate ones', and failures are practical questions for an audit.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists 'whether the trees would have been planted anyway' among the practical tests and says an offset that fails them 'is simply a fraud, and the right response to it is an audit, not moral disdain'. Nothing is subtracted from the shared stock of harm, so the harm is not undone.
questions.common_misconception: Taking a failed offset as evidence for the critics' philosophical charge, which the author keeps separate.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires keeping apart the author's two levels: offsetting in principle and particular schemes in practice.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the worries described in paragraph 4 is best described as one of

options.A: full endorsement: the worries show that offsetting ought to be discouraged until conduct has changed.
options.B: qualified acceptance: the worries are genuine, but they do not show that offset harms remain unrepaired.
options.C: detached neutrality: the worries are reported without any judgement of their weight or of their relevance.
options.D: dismissive contempt: the worries are rhetorical tricks that do not deserve a serious reply from anyone.

questions.correct_answer: (B) qualified acceptance: the worries are genuine, but they do not show that offset harms remain unrepaired.

option_rationales.A: The author confines the worries to character and politics and says they should not be 'dressed up as proof' against offsetting; the passage draws no conclusion that it should be discouraged.
option_rationales.C: The author does judge them: they are real but concern 'the character of the offsetter and the politics of reform, not the question of whether the harm itself has been undone'.
option_rationales.D: The author calls them 'real worries' and opens by denying any claim that 'nothing remains of the critic's unease'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 grants the worries ('These are real worries') and then limits their reach: they concern character and the politics of reform, not whether the harm is undone. That is acceptance with a qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Overshooting in either direction: reading the 'But' as dismissal, or the concession as endorsement.
questions.difficulty_reason: Concession followed by limitation; both extreme readings are partly suggested by the paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim that offsetting emissions is, in principle, a genuine undoing?

options.A: Investigations of several offset schemes have found that the forests they credited to their buyers were later cut down to make way for timber and farmland.
options.B: Most people who hear both the fidelity case and the author's reply to it continue to find the original objection to offsetting by far the more persuasive of the two.
options.C: The damage done by a tonne of emissions depends on how long it stays in the air, so carbon absorbed decades later cannot cancel the harm done meanwhile.
options.D: Travellers who regularly buy offsets tend to fly more often than they did before they began buying them, and say they feel less guilty about it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The damage done by a tonne of emissions depends on how long it stays in the air, so carbon absorbed decades later cannot cancel the harm done meanwhile.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 already treats survival of the trees as a practical test and calls failures fraud; such findings attack particular schemes, not the claim about principle.
option_rationales.B: How persuasive people find an argument does not show that it is unsound; the finding leaves the structure of the harm untouched.
option_rationales.D: This is the worry about the offsetter's conduct that paragraph 4 already concedes; it bears on character and reform, not on whether a given tonne is cancelled.

questions.explanation: The in-principle claim in paragraph 2 rests on interchangeability: 'A tonne removed in one place cancels a tonne added in another as far as the eventual damage is concerned.' If damage accrues while the carbon remains in the air, later removal is not equivalent to the original addition, so the harm is not fully undone even by an honest scheme. The other options attack practice or character, which the author has already set aside.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a fact that discredits offsetting in practice, which the author has already separated from the question of principle.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are genuine criticisms of offsetting; the solver must see that the author's argument has already absorbed them and find the one that strikes interchangeability itself.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a possible source of special obligations EXCEPT

options.A: being the parent of the child whose needs are in question.
options.B: living within the same municipal boundary as the people one might help.
options.C: having harmed the people who are now in need of help.
options.D: sharing with others an institution that one sustains and benefits from.

questions.correct_answer: (B) living within the same municipal boundary as the people one might help.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 opens its list with a parent who 'owes more to her own children than to children in general'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'We also owe more to those we have harmed', so this is presented as a source.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 names 'those with whom we share institutions that we sustain and from which we benefit', such as a school or cooperative.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists parenthood, past harm and shared institutions as grounds of special obligation. Paragraph 3 describes living 'within the same municipal boundary' as an 'accident' that creates no special relation, so it is the exception.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a shared city is a shared institution, which paragraph 3 explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three sources are listed together in paragraph 2; the exception is marked as an 'accident' in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that the resident in paragraph 3 who gives to a shelter in his own city

options.A: can be justified only if he has personally harmed some of the people whom the shelter helps.
options.B: acts wrongly, because all money given to charity ought to go wherever it will do the most good.
options.C: fulfils a special obligation, because he shares the institutions of his city with the people in the shelter.
options.D: is moved mainly by nearness, which does not create the kind of duty he may believe it does.

questions.correct_answer: (D) is moved mainly by nearness, which does not create the kind of duty he may believe it does.

option_rationales.A: Harm is one source of obligation among several, and paragraph 4 adds knowledge as a further consideration, so 'only' overstates the passage.
option_rationales.B: The author never calls local giving wrong; paragraph 4 calls the preference 'understandable' and objects only to mistaking it for 'an obligation'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says he 'shares no institution with them beyond the accident of living within the same municipal boundary'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'What draws him is proximity, and proximity by itself has little moral force', and paragraph 4 says such a preference is 'understandable but ... should not be mistaken for an obligation'.
questions.common_misconception: Concluding that the author condemns local giving, when the author only denies that nearness creates a duty.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option attributes the first camp's view to the author, who says each camp 'misidentifies' what it has hold of.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage functions mainly to

options.A: weigh the strongest remaining case for local giving and show that its force depends on circumstances.
options.B: establish that donors should always give where they are able to watch the results of their giving.
options.C: introduce a further reason why the first camp's arithmetic would dissolve the bonds that make moral life recognisable.
options.D: restate the author's earlier conclusion that special obligations arise from dependence, history and reciprocity.

questions.correct_answer: (A) weigh the strongest remaining case for local giving and show that its force depends on circumstances.

option_rationales.B: The author says the knowledge advantage 'cuts in both directions' and calls the wish to watch results something that should not be mistaken for an obligation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the knowledge argument is 'not about loyalty at all'; it does not return to the second camp's charge against the first.
option_rationales.D: That conclusion belongs to paragraph 2; paragraph 4 sets relationships aside and turns to a different consideration, knowledge.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 calls knowledge 'the strongest argument for local giving', grants that it is 'serious', and then shows it is 'empirical' and 'cuts in both directions', shrinking or disappearing depending on how well distant and local charities can be assessed.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the paragraph as an endorsement of the knowledge argument rather than a qualified assessment of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph concedes before limiting, so an endorsement reading is tempting.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's position on the dispute described in paragraph 1?

options.A: The local camp is right about loyalty but wrong about knowledge, since distant programmes can now always be assessed more reliably than local ones.
options.B: Both camps are equally mistaken, because how much one should give locally depends solely on how well donors can verify what their money achieves.
options.C: Partiality in giving can be justified by genuine relationships, but the local camp tends to mistake mere nearness for such relationships.
options.D: The camp that favours giving wherever money does the most good is right, because special obligations are sentiment that a rigorous ethics should discard.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Partiality in giving can be justified by genuine relationships, but the local camp tends to mistake mere nearness for such relationships.

option_rationales.A: The author argues that the local camp is wrong about loyalty when it rests on proximity, and says assessment advantages vary by case, not that distant programmes are always better assessed.
option_rationales.B: Knowledge is one consideration in paragraph 4, alongside relationships in paragraph 2; 'solely' reduces the author's position to a single factor it does not rest on.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'There really are special obligations' and that no plausible ethics asks a parent to put a stranger's schooling first.

questions.explanation: The author grants the local camp its real insight, special obligations from relationships (paragraph 2), but argues that local giving usually 'trades on these relationships while asking for something else', namely proximity, which 'has little moral force' (paragraph 3). The knowledge argument is assessed as circumstantial (paragraph 4).
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the knowledge-based option because paragraph 4 is the last word, or the first camp's view because the author criticises local giving.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures part of the passage; the correct answer requires holding the concession of paragraph 2 and the critique of paragraph 3 together.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the usual response to uncertainty about insect suffering is mistaken chiefly because it

options.A: relies on outdated evidence about how the nervous systems of insects are organised.
options.B: assumes that insects feel pain in exactly the way that dogs and birds feel it.
options.C: treats not knowing whether insects suffer as though it were knowing that they do not.
options.D: ignores the economic importance of the industry that farms insects for animal feed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) treats not knowing whether insects suffer as though it were knowing that they do not.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says the evidence is outdated; it says the evidence is 'likely to remain inconclusive', which is a different point.
option_rationales.B: The usual response assumes nothing about insect pain; it treats the lack of proof as permission, which is the reverse of this assumption.
option_rationales.D: Insect farming appears only to show how large the numbers are; its economic importance plays no part in the author's criticism.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 replies to the usual response: 'Uncertainty about whether a being can suffer is not the same as confidence that it cannot'. The builder example makes the same point, and the last sentence speaks of mistaking 'the absence of certainty for the presence of a licence'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option that mentions passage details (nervous systems, insect farming) without addressing the logical error.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in the first two sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 contributes to the argument of the passage mainly by

options.A: conceding that the weighing in paragraph 2 proves too much, and then replacing it with a quite different argument from shared physiology.
options.B: showing that bacteria and plants deserve moral consideration for the same reasons that insects do.
options.C: demonstrating that insects possess the same capacity for pain as the animals whose suffering we already accept.
options.D: defending the weighing in paragraph 2 against a charge of proving too much, by setting insects apart from bare possibility.

questions.correct_answer: (D) defending the weighing in paragraph 2 against a charge of proving too much, by setting insects apart from bare possibility.

option_rationales.A: The author grants the objection force only 'against arguments resting on probabilities so small that they amount to mere logical possibility' and keeps the weighing for insects.
option_rationales.B: The bacteria and plants appear in the objection as a reductio; the author's reply distinguishes insects from them rather than grouping them together.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph ends by saying insects share the relevant features 'only partially', and paragraph 4 denies they deserve 'the same consideration as mammals'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states 'The obvious objection is that this style of reasoning proves too much' and replies that it applies to 'mere logical possibility', whereas the insect case 'rests on specific behavioural and physiological features'. It defends paragraph 2's reasoning rather than abandoning it.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the concession ('That objection has force') as abandonment of the expected-value argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing how a concession is confined to one class of cases.

questions.question: Which of the following would best fit the practical conclusion of the passage?

options.A: A government bans the use of all agricultural pesticides until scientists have shown that insects are unable to feel pain.
options.B: An insect farm adopts, at little extra cost, a quicker killing method that would cause less suffering if its insects can suffer.
options.C: A campaign urges households to take care never to step on ants because each ant killed is a serious moral loss.
options.D: An insect farm keeps its present methods unchanged until research establishes beyond doubt that insects feel pain.

questions.correct_answer: (B) An insect farm adopts, at little extra cost, a quicker killing method that would cause less suffering if its insects can suffer.

option_rationales.A: This demands far more than the 'modest' precautions of paragraph 4 and extends the conclusion from deliberate farming to all pest control.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that 'every crushed ant is a tragedy'; the conclusion concerns deliberate mass rearing and killing.
option_rationales.D: This is the stance the passage rejects: refusing precautions 'on the grounds that sentience has not been proved'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that where we 'deliberately bring insects into existence in vast numbers and kill them, as in insect farming', we should prefer methods that 'would minimise suffering if suffering is present, provided the cost of doing so is modest'. The farm's cheap switch fits each condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a more sweeping precaution, missing the conditions of cost and deliberate farming.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option violates one specific condition of the conclusion, which must be read closely.

questions.question: The author's reply to the objection in paragraph 3 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: How likely an organism is to be sentient can be judged, at least roughly, by which pain-related features it shares with animals known to feel pain.
options.B: Bacteria and plants certainly cannot feel pain, so any argument that assigns them moral weight must rest on a premise that is simply mistaken.
options.C: Expected suffering ought to be the only consideration in deciding how any kind of organism, large or small, may be treated by human beings.
options.D: Insects possess every behavioural and physiological feature that is found in the animals whose capacity for pain we already accept without hesitation.

questions.correct_answer: (A) How likely an organism is to be sentient can be judged, at least roughly, by which pain-related features it shares with animals known to feel pain.

option_rationales.B: The reply needs only that their sentience is a 'mere logical possibility', which is weaker than certainty that they feel nothing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 adds the proviso that the cost of precautions must be 'modest', so the argument does not treat expected suffering as the only consideration.
option_rationales.D: The reply explicitly allows that insects share the features 'only partially', so it cannot depend on their sharing every feature.

questions.explanation: The reply separates insects from bacteria and plants by saying the insect case 'rests on specific behavioural and physiological features that insects share with animals whose capacity for pain we already accept'. This works only if sharing such features raises the probability of sentience above bare possibility, which is the assumption in the correct answer.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a stronger claim (all features, certainty about plants) than the argument needs.
questions.difficulty_reason: Necessary-assumption reasoning: two wrong options are stronger versions of what the argument requires, and the solver must find the minimal premise.

questions.question: According to the passage, the growth argument for discounting holds that

options.A: continued economic growth will in time repair whatever harm present policies impose on later generations.
options.B: outcomes in the distant future are less certain to happen and should therefore weigh less in present decisions.
options.C: the same resources will do less good for future people if they turn out to be richer than we are.
options.D: the well-being of future people matters less than ours simply because it will occur at a later date.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the same resources will do less good for future people if they turn out to be richer than we are.

option_rationales.A: The growth argument concerns how much difference a sum makes to richer people; paragraph 3 denies that a larger economy makes good every loss.
option_rationales.B: This is the third reason, the appeal to uncertainty, described at the end of paragraph 2.
option_rationales.D: This is pure time preference, which paragraph 2 lists as a separate reason and paragraph 3 rejects across generations.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'If future people will be considerably richer than we are, then a given sum of money ... will make less difference to their lives than it would to ours'. Paragraph 3 restates it: 'the same resources will do them less good'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the three rationales, which the passage lists one after another.
questions.difficulty_reason: The definition is given in two sentences; wrong options are the other two rationales.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement that each component of a discount rate 'encodes a substantive view' is best understood to mean that the rate

options.A: states its moral assumptions openly before arriving at a figure that can be applied to any decision.
options.B: carries a moral judgement inside what appears to be a neutral technical setting.
options.C: reflects the private opinions of the economists who first proposed using discount rates in policy.
options.D: turns a moral view into a precise figure that experts can then check against the evidence.

questions.correct_answer: (B) carries a moral judgement inside what appears to be a neutral technical setting.

option_rationales.A: This reverses the point: the rate is 'presented as a neutral parameter', so its assumptions are hidden rather than stated.
option_rationales.C: No economists or origins are discussed; the views at issue are about time, growth and repairable losses, not anyone's private opinions.
option_rationales.D: The author's complaint is that the verdict is 'reached without the argument such a verdict requires'; nothing suggests the figure makes the view checkable.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the choice of rate 'is not the technical matter it is often taken to be' and that a rate 'presented as a neutral parameter is, in effect, a verdict on what the present owes to the future'. To 'encode' a view is to carry it in a form that does not announce itself.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'encodes' to mean 'makes precise' rather than 'contains without stating'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is metaphorical, and one wrong option gives a plausible but opposite sense of encoding.

questions.question: The comparison in paragraph 3 between discounting by time and discounting by distance implies that, in the author's view,

options.A: when a person lives is no more relevant than where a person lives to how much that person's suffering counts.
options.B: people living in distant countries today have a stronger claim on us than people who will be born in later centuries.
options.C: discounting the suffering of distant people is acceptable in practice, though discounting the suffering of future people is not.
options.D: a person's preference for a pleasure today over a larger one next year is as indefensible as discounting future generations.

questions.correct_answer: (A) when a person lives is no more relevant than where a person lives to how much that person's suffering counts.

option_rationales.B: The comparison treats the two cases as equally indefensible grounds for discounting; it ranks neither group above the other.
option_rationales.C: The passage calls discounting by distance 'indefensible' and uses it as the benchmark for why discounting by time is wrong.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls such a person merely 'imprudent' and says the impatience 'is his own and so are its costs', setting this case apart.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says discounting the unborn for being born later treats 'a position in time as a reason for counting someone's suffering as less, in just the way that it would be indefensible to count suffering as less because it occurs in a distant country'. Position in time and position in space are equally irrelevant.
questions.common_misconception: Extending the author's verdict to the individual's own impatience, which paragraph 3 explicitly sets apart.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading an analogy correctly and noticing the contrast case placed just before it.

questions.question: Suppose analysts assess a policy that would prevent the permanent loss of a stretch of inhabited coastline two centuries from now, and they discount that loss at the expected rate of growth in consumption. On the passage's reasoning, the most fitting objection is that

options.A: the loss lies too far in the future for its size to be estimated with enough confidence for it to enter any calculation at all.
options.B: the growth rate hides a pure time preference within it, and such a preference has no defence across generations.
options.C: any discount at all is forbidden for harms this far ahead, including the small discount the passage allows for the chance that no future people will exist.
options.D: a loss of this kind is not made good by greater wealth, so discounting it at the growth rate treats it as repurchasable.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a loss of this kind is not made good by greater wealth, so discounting it at the growth rate treats it as repurchasable.

option_rationales.A: The passage never argues that far-future harms are too uncertain to estimate; it worries about harms 'we are confident will occur' being discounted away.
option_rationales.B: The passage treats the growth argument as distinct from pure time preference and says it 'does not deny the equal standing of future people'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'a small discount for that possibility is defensible', so a blanket ban on discounting contradicts the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the growth argument 'applies only to losses for which wealth can compensate' and that 'A flooded coastline or an extinct species is not made good by a larger economy, and to discount such losses at the rate at which consumption grows is to treat them as though they could be bought back.' The case fits this objection exactly.
questions.common_misconception: Reaching for the author's rejection of pure time preference, which targets a different rationale from the one the analysts use.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must match the case to the correct one of three rationales and to the specific limit placed on it; two wrong options use real claims from the passage aimed at the wrong target.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Someone who rejects pure time preference entirely could still defend applying a low discount rate to some future outcomes.
options.B: A discount rate of zero is the only rate consistent with treating future people as having the same moral standing as ourselves.
options.C: Once pure time preference has been set aside, nothing remains that could justify discounting future harms at all.
options.D: The rates commonly used are too low, because they give too little weight to the chance that there will be no future people.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Someone who rejects pure time preference entirely could still defend applying a low discount rate to some future outcomes.

option_rationales.B: The author accepts a 'small discount' for uncertainty and calls the growth argument 'respectable' because it does not deny equal standing, so zero is not the only consistent rate.
option_rationales.C: Paragraphs 3 and 4 grant some force to both the growth argument and the argument from uncertainty after pure time preference is rejected.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the rate supported by uncertainty is 'far lower than the rates commonly used', so this reverses the author's comparison.

questions.explanation: The author rejects pure time preference (paragraph 3) but allows that the growth argument holds 'on its own assumptions' for losses wealth can repair, and that 'a small discount for that possibility' of there being no future people is 'defensible' (paragraph 4). So a low rate can be defended without any pure time preference.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that an attack on high discount rates amounts to rejecting discounting altogether.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the verdicts on all three rationales; the zero-rate wrong option matches the author's sympathies but not the author's concessions.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the identified lives that communities rush to save are often

options.A: those of people living close to the engineers and machines that are needed to rescue them.
options.B: those of victims whose danger happens to be reported, not all who face similar danger.
options.C: those of people who are already personally known to the rescuers or to their communities.
options.D: those whose rescue costs less per life than the measures that would prevent similar deaths.

questions.correct_answer: (B) those of victims whose danger happens to be reported, not all who face similar danger.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says engineers are 'flown in', so closeness to rescuers is not what selects the victims; paragraph 2 points to reporting.
option_rationales.C: Personal acquaintance is never mentioned; 'identified' in the passage means known to be in peril, and paragraph 2 says identification is often 'by chance'.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the passage, which says rescue may cost 'a hundred times more per life' than prevention.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the identified lives are 'often identified by chance: they are the victims whose plight happens to be reported, while others in similar danger elsewhere receive nothing, because no one is watching'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'identified' as 'personally known' rather than 'publicly noticed'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 serves mainly to

options.A: concede that, from that standpoint, prevention is always to be chosen over rescue whatever the cost of either.
options.B: show that the assurance rescue provides is worth more than all the lives that prevention could save.
options.C: argue that the standpoint used to favour prevention can also make room for the value of rescue.
options.D: explain why advocates of prevention are wrong to reason from the position of someone not knowing his fate.

questions.correct_answer: (C) argue that the standpoint used to favour prevention can also make room for the value of rescue.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says prevention is 'usually' preferred from that standpoint and goes on to say rescue would also be wanted, so 'always' misstates it.
option_rationales.B: No such ranking is made; the paragraph speaks of choosing 'the proportion in which to buy them', which assumes both are worth having.
option_rationales.D: The author adopts that position ('Nor need this good conflict with the analyst's preferred standpoint') and argues from inside it rather than rejecting it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'Nor need this good conflict with the analyst's preferred standpoint', grants that this standpoint 'usually' favours prevention, and adds that someone in it 'would also want the assurance that rescue provides'. The choice becomes one of proportion: the paragraph reconciles the value of rescue with the critic's framework.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the paragraph as a rejection of the critics' standpoint, when it argues from within it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph's function is relational (reconciling paragraph 3 with paragraph 1's critique), not stated outright.

questions.question: The remark that statistical accounting 'has no column for' assurance (paragraph 3) suggests that such accounting

options.A: is right to ignore assurance, because a benefit of that kind cannot be given any value at all.
options.B: shows that the value of assurance is greater than the value of the lives that each rescue saves.
options.C: has been designed by economists deliberately to conceal the value of rescue and favour prevention.
options.D: omits a benefit of rescue that is enjoyed even by people who are never themselves in danger.

questions.correct_answer: (D) omits a benefit of rescue that is enjoyed even by people who are never themselves in danger.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a person 'would be willing to pay something for it', so the author thinks assurance can be valued.
option_rationales.B: No comparison of size is made; the point is that the good is left out, not that it outweighs the lives saved.
option_rationales.C: The passage attributes no motive to anyone; the image of a missing column points to an omission, not to concealment.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls assurance 'a real good' that accounting 'which counts only lives saved' cannot record, and adds that 'It is enjoyed by people who are never in danger'. The missing column is an omitted benefit.
questions.common_misconception: Reading an omission as a judgement that the item has no value, or as deliberate concealment.
questions.difficulty_reason: Figurative phrase whose sense is fixed by the surrounding sentences; wrong options overread it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3?

options.A: Residents feel equally sure of being helped in an emergency whether their town spares no expense on rescues or strictly caps what any rescue may cost.
options.B: Most people greatly overestimate the chance that they themselves will ever be trapped, lost or stranded in a disaster that requires a costly rescue.
options.C: Some rescues fail despite enormous expense and effort, and the people who were trapped die long before the rescuers are able to reach them.
options.D: Measures such as guardrails, better lighting and screening save many more lives for each rupee spent than even the best-run rescues do.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Residents feel equally sure of being helped in an emergency whether their town spares no expense on rescues or strictly caps what any rescue may cost.

option_rationales.B: If anything, this would make people value assurance more; it does not show that rescue fails to provide it.
option_rationales.C: The assurance in paragraph 3 is that a community will not 'abandon' a person in peril; a rescue that tries and fails still expresses that commitment.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 already grants this; it supports the critique of present spending but leaves the claimed value of assurance untouched.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that unlimited rescue produces 'an assurance, to everyone' that is 'a real good' felt even by those never in danger. If willingness to spend on rescue made no difference to people's confidence that they would be helped, rescue would not be producing the good the argument credits it with.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a true point about cost-effectiveness that the author has already conceded and that does not touch the assurance argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are on topic and one is already conceded in paragraph 2; the solver must target the specific causal claim that rescue spending produces assurance.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's overall position?

options.A: Communities spend too much on rescue and should move that money into prevention until the spending per life saved is equal.
options.B: Rescue and prevention serve such different values that neither can sensibly be judged by the standard that is used to judge the other.
options.C: Rescuing identified people has a real value that its critics miss, but that value offers no excuse for how little is spent on prevention.
options.D: The preference for identified lives is a costly bias that consistent accounting should remove, though the assurance that it brings to everyone deserves a little weight.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Rescuing identified people has a real value that its critics miss, but that value offers no excuse for how little is spent on prevention.

option_rationales.A: The author says 'We do not rescue too much' and rejects equalising for consistency's sake, locating the fault in too little prevention.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 judges both from a single standpoint and treats the question as one of 'the proportion in which to buy them'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 rejects abandoning rescue 'in the name of consistency'; the author defends the impulse to rescue, 'rightly valued', rather than seeking to remove it.

questions.explanation: The author accepts much of the critique (paragraph 2), defends the assurance that rescue provides (paragraph 3), reconciles it with prevention (paragraph 4), and concludes 'We do not rescue too much; we prevent too little' (paragraph 5).
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the first wrong option, which echoes the critics' view with a small concession, because the author agrees with 'much of this critique'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The first wrong option blends the reported critique with the author's concession; telling it apart requires the final paragraph's reversal.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that models in economics and biology idealise more heavily, and therefore less reliably, than the models used in physics.
options.B: recast the falsehoods in scientific models as claims about which factors matter, claims that can be checked by relaxing them.
options.C: defend the familiar view that idealised models are convenient fictions whose missing details ought to be restored once better methods allow it.
options.D: show that every idealisation is eventually exposed as harmful once a model is carried into conditions it was not built for.

questions.correct_answer: (B) recast the falsehoods in scientific models as claims about which factors matter, claims that can be checked by relaxing them.

option_rationales.A: Calling economics and biology 'worse offenders' is a passing remark in paragraph 1; the passage never ranks disciplines by reliability, and its argument applies to all models alike.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 reports this view and paragraph 2 opens by saying it 'gets the matter backwards'; paragraph 2 also says adding every missing factor 'would not improve such a model'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says only that not every idealisation is innocent, and paragraph 4 describes an assumption of infinity that 'was doing no harm', so 'every' overstates the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says an idealisation is 'a claim about relevance', paragraph 3 says such claims can fail outside their range, and paragraph 4 proposes testing them by relaxing the idealisation, ending with the frictionless plane as 'a hypothesis' that 'can be checked'. The correct answer states this purpose.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'useful fiction' view because it is described at length in paragraph 1, without noticing that the author rejects it at the start of paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated plainly at the start of paragraph 2 and the end of paragraph 4; the reported view is clearly rejected.

questions.question: The examples of the feather and the parachutist in paragraph 3 serve to

options.A: suggest that the motion of falling objects can never be modelled usefully without including the effect of the air.
options.B: demonstrate that air resistance is the most common source of error in the models that physicists actually use.
options.C: illustrate the earlier claim that adding missing factors to a model buries the very pattern it was built to display.
options.D: show that an assumption that some factor does not matter can hold in one setting yet fail in another.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that an assumption that some factor does not matter can hold in one setting yet fail in another.

option_rationales.A: The same sentence says treating air as absent is 'harmless for a stone dropped from a window', so the option contradicts it.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about which source of error is most common; the examples illustrate a pattern of failure, not a frequency.
option_rationales.C: That claim belongs to paragraph 2; the feather and the parachutist make the opposite point, that leaving a factor out can be disastrous.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says an assumption 'that holds well within one range of conditions fails outside it' and then contrasts the stone, for which ignoring air is harmless, with the feather and the parachutist, for which it is 'disastrous'.
questions.common_misconception: Linking the examples to the nearest general claim about models in paragraph 2 rather than to the sentence that introduces them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is announced by the sentence immediately before the examples.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, the phrase 'an artefact of the simplification' refers to a result that

options.A: survives unchanged when the population is treated as very large rather than as infinitely large.
options.B: owes its existence to the model's simplifying assumption rather than to any feature of the world being modelled.
options.C: was first reached through a simplified model and was later confirmed by more detailed observation of the world itself.
options.D: is valuable chiefly as a historical record of the way in which an earlier model was put together.

questions.correct_answer: (B) owes its existence to the model's simplifying assumption rather than to any feature of the world being modelled.

option_rationales.A: This describes the harmless case in paragraph 4, where 'the assumption of infinity was doing no harm', which is the opposite of an artefact.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 contrasts an artefact with 'a discovery about the world'; an artefact is precisely the kind of result that is not confirmed when the assumption is loosened.
option_rationales.D: This reads 'artefact' as a relic of the past; the passage uses it for a result produced by the model's assumptions, and says nothing about historical records.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that if a result 'vanishes as soon as the assumption is loosened, it was an artefact of the simplification rather than a discovery about the world'. The phrase therefore names a result created by the simplifying assumption itself.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'artefact' in its museum sense, or confusing the artefact with the robust result described one sentence earlier.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is defined by the contrast in the same sentence.

questions.question: A traffic model treats all drivers as having identical reaction times, which is plainly false. On the passage's reasoning, which of the following would best show that this idealisation is harmless for the model's prediction of where queues form?

options.A: Every traffic engineer consulted agrees that no real population of drivers has identical reaction times.
options.B: Treating drivers as identical lets the model's equations be solved far more quickly than any more realistic formulation would allow.
options.C: The model's predictions about where queues form have been presented to city planners for many years without any complaint.
options.D: Rerun with a realistic spread of reaction times among drivers, the model still places the queues in the same spots.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Rerun with a realistic spread of reaction times among drivers, the model still places the queues in the same spots.

option_rationales.A: This only confirms that the assumption is false, and paragraph 4 says literal truth is not the test, 'since almost none are' true.
option_rationales.B: Ease of calculation is the virtue claimed by the 'useful fiction' view in paragraph 1, which the author rejects; it says nothing about whether the omitted variation matters.
option_rationales.C: An absence of complaint does not check whether the result depends on the assumption; the passage's test is what happens when the idealisation is relaxed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the test is 'whether its conclusions survive when the idealisation is relaxed'. Rerunning the model with varied reaction times relaxes the idealisation; if the queues are unchanged, the assumption was 'doing no harm'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about the assumption being false, as though the passage judged models by literal truth.
questions.difficulty_reason: The test must be transferred from the population example to a new case, and one wrong option restates the rejected view.

questions.question: According to the passage, the barometer reading is able to predict the storm because

options.A: the reading and the storm are both produced by the same fall in atmospheric pressure.
options.B: a falling reading is the only reliable sign that the weather is about to deteriorate.
options.C: forecasters have learned to adjust their barometers so that the readings anticipate the storm.
options.D: the fall in the reading brings about a change in the air that causes the storm a short time later.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the reading and the storm are both produced by the same fall in atmospheric pressure.

option_rationales.B: The passage calls the reading 'an excellent predictor', not the only one; 'only' is an extreme claim the passage never makes.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage mentions adjusting instruments; the predictive power comes from a common cause, not from calibration.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says both are 'effects of a drop in atmospheric pressure'; the reading causes nothing, and paragraph 3 adds that a broken barometer 'would not have prevented the storm'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that the reading and the storm 'are effects of a drop in atmospheric pressure, and the reading earns its predictive power by riding on that common cause'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the predictor as a cause of what it predicts, which is the very confusion the example is meant to expose.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The example of the hillside in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: show that something can be a reliable predictor of an event without explaining that event at all.
options.B: suggest that geological events are too irregular for any scientific account of them to be given with confidence.
options.C: show that an event can be adequately explained even when it could not have been forecast beforehand.
options.D: illustrate the claim that a theory which explains everything and forbids nothing deserves suspicion.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that an event can be adequately explained even when it could not have been forecast beforehand.

option_rationales.A: That is the point of the barometer; the hillside is introduced with 'Conversely' to make the reverse point, that explanation does not require prediction.
option_rationales.B: The passage says the geologist's explanation 'is sound', pointing to saturated soil and weak clay, so it denies that no account can be given.
option_rationales.D: That remark comes in paragraph 4 and concerns testing; the hillside example in paragraph 2 has nothing to do with theories that forbid nothing.

questions.explanation: The hillside follows 'Conversely, we can often explain what we could never have predicted', and paragraph 2 ends: 'The explanation is sound even though the forecast was out of reach.' It is the second half of the claim that 'the symmetry fails in both directions'.
questions.common_misconception: Merging the two examples, so that the hillside is read as a second case of a predictor without explanatory force.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both examples in paragraph 2 attack the same symmetry, so the reader must keep their opposite directions apart.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that, in the author's view, a factor helps to explain an outcome when

options.A: the factor and the outcome are both effects of some deeper cause acting on them both.
options.B: knowing the factor in advance would have allowed someone to forecast the outcome before it occurred.
options.C: the factor has been observed, reliably and in many cases, to occur shortly before the outcome.
options.D: a different value of that factor would have led to a different outcome.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a different value of that factor would have led to a different outcome.

option_rationales.A: This describes the barometer and the storm, the passage's example of a factor that fails the test of explanation.
option_rationales.B: This is the symmetry view of paragraph 1, which the author rejects; the barometer allows a forecast yet explains nothing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says this kind of reliable connection is all a predictor needs, and the barometer shows that it does not make something explanatory.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says an explanation identifies 'the factors such that, had they been different, the outcome would have been different too', and applies the test: firmer clay 'would have held the slope'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the forecasting criterion because it sounds like good science, without noticing that it is the view under attack.
questions.difficulty_reason: The criterion is stated abstractly and must be separated from the predictor criterion in the same paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's case against the view described in paragraph 1?

options.A: Had the soil and clay been fully measured in advance, the relevant laws would have fixed the very week the slope failed.
options.B: Geologists frequently revise their published accounts of particular landslides as new information about the slope comes to light later.
options.C: Barometer readings quite often fall without any storm following, so their forecasts are rather less reliable than is commonly claimed.
options.D: Working scientists routinely test a proposed explanation by checking whether the predictions it implies about other conditions are actually borne out in practice.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Had the soil and clay been fully measured in advance, the relevant laws would have fixed the very week the slope failed.

option_rationales.B: Revising accounts in the light of new information does not show that explanation and prediction coincide; it is irrelevant to the symmetry.
option_rationales.C: The author's point is that even a reliable predictor need not explain; a less reliable barometer leaves the gap between predicting and explaining exactly where it was.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 already concedes this: checking implications 'is how such claims are tested'. It is consistent with the author's view that testing is 'a check on an explanation, not its substance'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the symmetry 'in principle'. The hillside case attacks it by saying the forecast 'was out of reach'. If complete measurement would have allowed the failure to be derived beforehand, the obstacle was only practical, and the hillside no longer shows an explanation that could not in principle have been a prediction. One half of the author's case collapses.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the barometer option because it attacks one of the examples, without seeing that the example does not depend on the barometer being perfect.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer works only if one notices the phrase 'in principle' in paragraph 1 and sees that the hillside case concerns a practical limit; two wrong options are consistent with the author's own concessions.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the investigator who measured one adult's height drew no general conclusion because

options.A: a single measurement of any quantity, however carefully it is taken, is never enough to support a general conclusion.
options.B: the investigator knew that adults vary in height, so one case could not stand in for the rest.
options.C: human height is too difficult to measure with the precision that a melting point allows.
options.D: the investigator lacked the principle of uniformity that the other investigator had managed to find.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the investigator knew that adults vary in height, so one case could not stand in for the rest.

option_rationales.A: The melting-point investigator draws a general conclusion 'from a single careful trial' and is said to reason well, so 'never' contradicts paragraph 2.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about difficulty of measurement; the difference lies in what each investigator knows about the uniformity of the domain.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says they differ 'not because one has found the universal principle and the other has not', which directly rules this out.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says each investigator 'knows something about the kind of thing being studied', namely 'that people are not uniform in their heights'. Paragraph 3 adds that such facts tell us 'how far a sample can be trusted to stand in for the whole'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the single-case contrast to be about the number of measurements rather than about what is known of the domain.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is spelled out at the end of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Because every inductive step depends on earlier inductions, scientific knowledge rests in the end on nothing more than habit.
options.B: A single careful trial is more trustworthy than a large sample whenever the substance under study is chemically pure.
options.C: Inductive steps are licensed by knowledge of particular domains, and the regress this creates does not make scientific practice irrational.
options.D: The sceptical argument about induction fails, since a principle of uniformity can be supported by the record of past successful inferences.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Inductive steps are licensed by knowledge of particular domains, and the regress this creates does not make scientific practice irrational.

option_rationales.A: The passage admits the regress but argues it is 'less damaging than it looks' and does not prevent science from being rational, so this reverses its conclusion.
option_rationales.B: This inflates one illustration in paragraph 2 into a general rule and leaves out both the domain-based thesis and the reply to the regress.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 explains that support from experience would be circular, and paragraph 4 says the author's view 'does not answer the sceptic on the sceptic's own terms'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that 'there is no such thing as inductive inference in general', paragraph 3 says inductive steps are licensed by 'particular facts about particular domains', and paragraph 4 grants the regress but argues science need not meet the sceptic's demand 'in order to be rational'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that claims to defeat the sceptic, when the author explicitly declines to do so.
questions.difficulty_reason: The main point combines a thesis and a qualified reply to an objection; wrong options overstate in both directions.

questions.question: Which of the following reasoners proceeds in the way the passage regards as sound?

options.A: A pollster who simply assumes that nature is uniform concludes that every future election will go the way the last one did.
options.B: A botanist, knowing that a certain trait hardly varies within a plant species, judges a new population's trait from a handful of specimens.
options.C: A physician who tests a new drug on one patient and, finding it effective, prescribes it to all patients alike.
options.D: A geologist who refuses to generalise from any finite set of rock samples, on the ground that induction can never be justified.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A botanist, knowing that a certain trait hardly varies within a plant species, judges a new population's trait from a handful of specimens.

option_rationales.A: This rests on a general principle of uniformity, which paragraph 3 says is not what licenses an inductive step.
option_rationales.C: Generalising from one case is sound only where the domain is known to be uniform, and nothing suggests patients respond uniformly; this resembles drawing conclusions from one adult's height.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the regress 'never requires us to justify all our inductive habits at once'; refusing all generalisation is the sceptical paralysis it argues against.

questions.explanation: The botanist generalises from few cases because of background knowledge that the trait is uniform within the species, which is the pattern of the melting-point investigator in paragraph 2: a sample is trusted to the extent that facts about the domain allow.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the physician because a single-case generalisation also appears in the passage, while ignoring that it was licensed only by knowledge of the domain.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires transferring the domain-knowledge condition to new cases, one of which copies the surface form of the passage's example.

questions.question: The author would accept each of the following EXCEPT the claim that

options.A: any single item of background knowledge can be questioned while the rest of it is held fixed.
options.B: two investigators may both reason well while drawing very different conclusions from a single observation.
options.C: the background knowledge that licenses an inductive step was itself acquired by inductive means.
options.D: a domain-based account of induction makes the regress that the sceptic describes disappear altogether.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a domain-based account of induction makes the regress that the sceptic describes disappear altogether.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'any item can in turn be questioned while the rest is held fixed', so the author asserts this.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says of the melting-point and height investigators, 'Both are reasoning well', though one generalises from a single trial and the other draws no conclusion at all.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 raises this point, and paragraph 4 calls the objection 'fair', so the author accepts it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'The regress it describes is real'; the author's claim is only that it is 'less damaging than it looks' because we never have to justify everything at once. The author does not say the regress disappears.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because the author defends the domain-based account, the author must think it dissolves the sceptic's regress.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is the one claim the author stops short of; it sounds like the author's own position and must be separated from 'less damaging than it looks'.

questions.question: According to the passage, a curve that passes exactly through every measured point is usually a poor guide to the next measurement because

options.A: in fitting every point it has also reproduced the errors that the measurements happen to contain.
options.B: complicated curves are harder to calculate with, so that mistakes creep in when they are used to predict.
options.C: nature is simple, so a complicated curve cannot correspond to the way things really are.
options.D: such a curve can be drawn only when the measurements are entirely free of error.

questions.correct_answer: (A) in fitting every point it has also reproduced the errors that the measurements happen to contain.

option_rationales.B: Ease of calculation belongs to the 'convenience' answer of paragraph 1; paragraph 2 explains the poor prediction by noise, not by calculating mistakes.
option_rationales.C: This is the second answer in paragraph 1, which the author calls unsatisfactory; paragraph 2 is offered precisely as an alternative to it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says any set of measurements 'each carrying some error' can be fitted perfectly, so the option contradicts it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says such a curve is a worse guide 'because much of what it has faithfully reproduced is noise'.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying over one of the two rejected answers from paragraph 1 instead of reading the reason given in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated directly in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a preference for the simpler of two well-fitting models is most clearly justified when

options.A: the more complex model has already been tested against new data and has predicted them better.
options.B: the data are abundant and precise enough to reveal fine structure in whatever is being measured.
options.C: the data available are few in number and each measurement carries a substantial margin of error.
options.D: the simpler model is the one that scientists find easier to state, to teach and to calculate with.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the data available are few in number and each measurement carries a substantial margin of error.

option_rationales.A: If the complex model predicts new data better, the statistical reason for preferring the simpler one has failed in that case.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the value of simplicity 'should shrink as data become more abundant and more precise', so this is where the preference is weakest.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says convenience 'explains why we might enjoy simple theories but not why we should believe them', so it does not justify the preference.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents simplicity as 'a policy for estimating well from limited and imperfect evidence', and paragraph 3 calls it 'a discount applied in proportion to our ignorance'. The justification is strongest where evidence is scarce and noisy.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the convenience option because it describes a real reason scientists give, though the author says it does not justify belief.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining paragraphs 2 and 3 to see that the justification varies with the quantity and quality of data.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the statistical justification of simplicity is best described as one of

options.A: studied neutrality, laying out its strengths and its costs without ever indicating which way the balance falls.
options.B: polite scepticism, because in the end it leaves simplicity a matter of taste, like a preference for a tidy desk.
options.C: qualified endorsement: it is more promising than the alternatives, but it supports less than is often claimed for it.
options.D: enthusiastic acceptance, because it finally demonstrates that the simpler hypotheses are the ones more likely to be true.

questions.correct_answer: (C) qualified endorsement: it is more promising than the alternatives, but it supports less than is often claimed for it.

option_rationales.A: The author does commit: the answer is 'more promising', it shows a 'reliable way to be less wrong', yet the principle has an authority 'borrowed rather than earned'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens: 'None of this returns us to the view that simplicity is mere taste.' The author credits the argument with showing a 'reliable way to be less wrong'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the argument does not show 'that the simpler hypothesis is, for that reason, more likely to be true', which is the opposite of this option.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the statistical answer 'more promising' than the two in paragraph 1, paragraph 3 notes 'a cost that its admirers do not always acknowledge', and paragraph 4 both defends it against the charge of taste and denies that it shows simpler hypotheses are more likely true.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the critical last sentence as rejection, or the defence against 'mere taste' as full endorsement, instead of holding both together.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude has two sides spread across three paragraphs, and two wrong options each capture only one of them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that simplicity is 'a discount applied in proportion to our ignorance'?

options.A: With small and noisy samples, models with fewer adjustable parameters predict new data better than models that have many.
options.B: Even where data are vast and highly precise, simpler well-fitting models keep predicting new measurements better than complex ones.
options.C: Scientists in many fields report that they choose simpler models chiefly because these are easier to teach to students.
options.D: Whether one model has more parameters than another sometimes depends on the variables in which both of them happen to be written.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Even where data are vast and highly precise, simpler well-fitting models keep predicting new measurements better than complex ones.

option_rationales.A: This is the situation in which the author says simplicity earns its keep, so it fits the claim rather than weakening it.
option_rationales.C: This concerns scientists' motives, which bear on the 'convenience' answer; it says nothing about whether simplicity's value shrinks as data improve.
option_rationales.D: The author makes this point in paragraph 3 as a further problem about measuring simplicity; it does not touch the claim that simplicity's value depends on how much we know.

questions.explanation: The claim implies that simplicity's advantage shrinks as data become 'more abundant and more precise' (paragraph 3). If simpler models kept predicting better even with vast, precise data, simplicity's value would not be tied to ignorance, which undercuts the claim directly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the parameter-counting option because it is a criticism, without noticing that it is the author's own point and targets measurement, not the discount claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The claim is metaphorical and must be unpacked into a testable implication; one wrong option is the author's own separate objection.

questions.question: According to the passage, when a prediction derived from a theory fails, logic alone establishes that
