options.A: at least one element of the theory and its accompanying assumptions is mistaken, though not which one.
options.B: the theory itself is false, whatever assumptions were made about the instruments and the conditions of the experiment.
options.C: the instruments used in the experiment were faulty or had been wrongly calibrated.
options.D: the theory must be replaced by another one that also explains its earlier successes.

questions.correct_answer: (A) at least one element of the theory and its accompanying assumptions is mistaken, though not which one.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says logic shows only that 'something in this whole bundle is wrong', so it cannot single out the theory.
option_rationales.C: Instruments are one part of the bundle, but logic 'does not tell us which part' is at fault.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in paragraph 1 says logic requires replacement; the Uranus case in paragraph 2 shows a theory surviving a failed prediction.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'When a prediction fails, logic tells us that something in this whole bundle is wrong; it does not tell us which part.' The bundle includes the theory and the assumptions about instruments, conditions and other forces.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the refutation slogan of the opening sentence, which the author says is 'too simple'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of the last sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The case of Mercury in paragraph 3 is introduced mainly to

options.A: prove that Newtonian mechanics was mistaken whenever it postulated an unseen planet to explain an irregular orbit.
options.B: demonstrate that astronomers of the period clung to Newton's theory out of a dogmatic reluctance to abandon it.
options.C: suggest that the general theory of relativity was devised chiefly in order to explain the orbit of Mercury.
options.D: show that the strategy that worked for Uranus does not always work and so carries no guarantee.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that the strategy that worked for Uranus does not always work and so carries no guarantee.

option_rationales.A: The Uranus case shows the same strategy succeeding, with Neptune found near the predicted position, so a claim about every such case contradicts paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 ends by saying 'the decision to treat both in the same way was reasonable', which is the opposite of a charge of dogmatism.
option_rationales.C: The passage says only that relativity eventually accounted for the discrepancy; it says nothing about why the theory was devised.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'The same strategy, however, does not always succeed', and the Mercury case shows the unseen-planet move failing. Together with Uranus, it supports the lesson in paragraph 4 that 'there is no rule which tells us in advance' how to treat an anomaly.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the Mercury case as a criticism of the astronomers rather than as a counterpart to the Uranus case.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by the opening sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The author's remark that, at the time, the two anomalies 'looked much the same' suggests that

options.A: the anomalies of Uranus and of Mercury had the same underlying cause, though this was not yet recognised.
options.B: astronomers of the period lacked the instruments they needed to tell a real planet from an imagined one.
options.C: the discovery of Neptune owed more to luck than to the soundness of the calculations that preceded it.
options.D: the astronomers who looked for a planet near Mercury cannot fairly be faulted for reasoning as they did.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the astronomers who looked for a planet near Mercury cannot fairly be faulted for reasoning as they did.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says one was explained by a new planet and the other only by a new theory of gravitation, so their causes were different.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about the limits of instruments; the point concerns how the anomalies appeared before their outcomes were known.
option_rationales.C: The passage presents Neptune as found 'close to the predicted position', a success of calculation; nothing suggests luck.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the anomalies look different in hindsight but looked alike at the time, 'and the decision to treat both in the same way was reasonable'. Treating Mercury like Uranus was therefore a defensible choice, even though it failed.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'looked much the same' to mean the anomalies really were alike, ignoring the contrast with 'In hindsight' at the start of the previous sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the contrast between hindsight and the view at the time, with one wrong option that misreads appearance as reality.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards scientists who keep a theory despite an anomaly is best described as

options.A: conditional approval, since such tenacity is reasonable but becomes dogma when it rests on assumptions invented only to save the theory.
options.B: firm disapproval, since a theory that has met a clear anomaly ought to be given up rather than protected further.
options.C: unreserved admiration, since holding on to a theory in the face of anomalies is always what good science requires.
options.D: detached indifference, since whether to keep or abandon a theory is a question the author leaves entirely to historians.

questions.correct_answer: (A) conditional approval, since such tenacity is reasonable but becomes dogma when it rests on assumptions invented only to save the theory.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 rejects the idea that theories 'should be given up at the first sign of trouble' and calls tenacity 'a virtue in science'.
option_rationales.C: The author warns that tenacity 'shades into dogma' when a theory is propped up by one convenient assumption after another, so the approval is not unreserved.
option_rationales.D: The author takes a view, calling tenacity a virtue and dogma a danger, and says the matter is one of scientific 'judgement', not something left to historians.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'Tenacity is a virtue in science' but 'shades into dogma when a theory is protected by one convenient assumption after another, each invented for no reason except to save it'. The approval is real and conditional.
questions.common_misconception: Seizing on 'Tenacity is a virtue' and overlooking the qualification that follows the semicolon.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option matches the first half of the author's sentence; the correct answer needs the whole sentence.

questions.question: The solvent example implies that a laboratory which judged harm to workers to be far worse than lost revenue should

options.A: report only the cost of withdrawing the solvent and leave every judgement about harm to the firm's managers.
options.B: demand more evidence of harm than usual before declaring the solvent dangerous to the workers who use it.
options.C: be prepared to declare the solvent harmful on less evidence than it would require if both errors seemed equally serious.
options.D: refuse to reach any conclusion until the evidence about the solvent leaves no room for any doubt at all.

questions.correct_answer: (C) be prepared to declare the solvent harmful on less evidence than it would require if both errors seemed equally serious.

option_rationales.A: The example is about how the weighing of errors sets the evidential threshold; nothing in it suggests reporting costs alone or handing the question to managers.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the logic: if wrongly calling the solvent safe is the worse error, the laboratory should require less evidence, not more, before declaring harm.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'evidence rarely settles a question outright', and the example concerns how much evidence to demand, not waiting for certainty.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says how much evidence to demand 'before declaring the solvent harmful' depends on which of the two errors is worse. If wrongly calling it safe is much worse, the bar for declaring harm should be lower.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that taking harm seriously always means demanding more evidence, which reverses the direction of the trade-off.
questions.difficulty_reason: One step of reasoning from the example in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's response in paragraph 3 to the suggestion that scientists simply report probabilities?

options.A: Probabilities reported by scientists are now usually accompanied by a full statement of the statistical model that was used to obtain them.
options.B: Teams analysing the same borderline samples classified them differently according to which error they most wanted to avoid, changing the probabilities they reported.
options.C: Most of the laboratories that test industrial chemicals are funded, directly or indirectly, by the firms that manufacture those chemicals.
options.D: Officials who receive probability estimates from scientists often misread them and, as a result, make poorer decisions than they otherwise would.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Teams analysing the same borderline samples classified them differently according to which error they most wanted to avoid, changing the probabilities they reported.

option_rationales.A: Disclosing the model makes the choice visible but does not show that the choice involved weighing errors; if anything it suggests the problem is manageable.
option_rationales.C: Funding and possible bias are outside the argument, which concerns unavoidable choices about errors, not conflicts of interest.
option_rationales.D: This is a practical objection about the users of probabilities; the author's response is that the weighing of errors already enters before any probability is produced.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that before any probability is reported, decisions about classifying 'ambiguous tissue samples' and other choices can 'err in either direction', so 'The weighing of errors does not disappear'. A case where such a classification depended on which error the team wanted to avoid, and changed the reported probability, confirms this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about officials misreading probabilities because it also criticises the proposal to report probabilities, though on different grounds.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options criticise or complicate the proposal; only one does so for the author's reason.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It limits the conclusion of the argument by separating a proper role for values from an improper one.
options.B: It concedes that the argument built on the solvent example fails, and restores the picture of objectivity in paragraph 1.
options.C: It answers the reply in paragraph 3 by showing that probabilities can after all be reported without any judgement of value.
options.D: It introduces a new example in order to show that researchers often discount results that they find unwelcome.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It limits the conclusion of the argument by separating a proper role for values from an improper one.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph keeps the argument's conclusion that values 'can properly bear on how much evidence to require', which the picture in paragraph 1 denies.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 has already rejected that reply; the final paragraph does not return to probabilities at all.
option_rationales.D: No new example is given, and the paragraph says only that the argument does not 'license' discounting results; it makes no claim about how often this happens.

questions.explanation: The final paragraph opens 'It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that anything goes', grants that values bear on 'how much evidence to require', and denies that they bear on 'what the evidence is'. It marks the limit of the argument.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'It would be a mistake' as a retreat from the whole argument rather than as a limit on how far it reaches.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph both keeps and restricts the earlier conclusion, and one wrong option reads it as a reversal.

questions.question: In the final paragraph, 'moving the evidence' refers to

options.A: raising or lowering the amount of evidence required in the light of what is at stake if one errs.
options.B: transferring the weighing of errors to an earlier stage of the research where it is harder to see.
options.C: presenting the evidence to the people who must act instead of accepting or rejecting the hypothesis oneself.
options.D: allowing a preference for one conclusion to alter what the results are taken to be, for instance by setting aside an unwelcome finding.

questions.correct_answer: (D) allowing a preference for one conclusion to alter what the results are taken to be, for instance by setting aside an unwelcome finding.

option_rationales.A: This is 'setting the bar', which the paragraph calls a proper role for values and contrasts with moving the evidence.
option_rationales.B: This echoes paragraph 3, where the weighing 'moves to a stage where it is less visible'; that describes method choices, not the improper act named in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: This is the proposal in paragraph 3 that scientists report probabilities, not what the final paragraph means by moving the evidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says values may not 'bear on what the evidence is, or license a researcher to discount an inconvenient result because it is unwelcome', and then labels this 'moving the evidence' as opposed to 'setting the bar'. The choices about ambiguous samples in paragraph 3 are a weighing of errors, part of setting the bar; moving the evidence is letting a wished-for conclusion decide what the results are.
questions.common_misconception: Matching the verb 'moves' in paragraph 3 to 'moving' in paragraph 4, though the two describe different things.
questions.difficulty_reason: A wrong option reuses a near-identical word from the previous paragraph with a different meaning.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Thought experiments are arguments in disguise, whose vivid imagery adds persuasive force but nothing to the logical content of their conclusions.
options.B: The best thought experiments give direct insight into the necessary laws of nature, as Galileo's case of the falling bodies shows.
options.C: Thought experiments inform by bringing unstated expectations into conflict with explicit theory, and are only as reliable as those expectations.
options.D: Thought experiments should not be trusted in modern physics, since its subject matter lies far outside everyday experience.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Thought experiments inform by bringing unstated expectations into conflict with explicit theory, and are only as reliable as those expectations.

option_rationales.A: This is the first of the two views in paragraph 2, and paragraph 4 says thought experiments 'cannot be reduced to an argument that someone might have written down beforehand'.
option_rationales.B: This is the second view, which paragraph 3 says 'makes the result mysterious'; the author uses Galileo's case against it, not for it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 warns about imagined cases of the very small, fast or distant, but the passage does not dismiss a whole field; this inflates one caution into the thesis.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says thought experiments draw on 'knowledge we have but have never made explicit', exposing a tension with explicit theory, and paragraph 5 concludes that the method 'is exactly as reliable as that knowledge'. Paragraphs 2 and 3 set up and reject the two rival views.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the two views the passage describes at length, or turning the closing caution into the main claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The central claim spans two paragraphs and must be separated from two rival views given equal space.

questions.question: According to paragraph 3, the supposition that heavier bodies fall faster contradicts itself because the two bodies tied together should fall

options.A: more slowly than the light body alone, since the air around them drags the heavier of the two bodies back.
options.B: more slowly than the heavy body alone, since the light one holds it back, and yet faster, since the pair is heavier.
options.C: at exactly the speed of the heavy body alone, since the light body, being so much lighter, adds nothing to the pair.
options.D: faster than either body alone in the imagined case, while in actual trials the pair is observed to fall more slowly.

questions.correct_answer: (B) more slowly than the heavy body alone, since the light one holds it back, and yet faster, since the pair is heavier.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the light body holds back the heavy one; air enters only in the closing qualification about 'a resisting medium', not in the contradiction.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'the pair is heavier than the heavy body', so the light body does add weight; the contradiction comes from two opposite predictions, not from one equal speed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says a thought experiment 'collects no new data'; the contradiction in paragraph 3 lies inside the supposition itself, not between imagination and observation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'the light body should hold back the heavy one, so that the pair falls more slowly than the heavy body alone; but the pair is heavier than the heavy body, so it should fall faster'. The same supposition yields both predictions, so it 'contradicts itself'.
questions.common_misconception: Thinking the contradiction is between the imagined result and an observed one, when it arises wholly within the supposition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The two halves of the contradiction are set out in consecutive clauses of paragraph 3.

questions.question: On the passage's account, which of the following imagined scenarios would produce a conviction that deserves the least confidence?

options.A: Imagining what a traveller moving at nearly the speed of light would see in a mirror held at arm's length.
options.B: Imagining whether a tall stack of books would topple over if the bottom book were pulled out very quickly.
options.C: Imagining whether a ladder leaning against a wall would slip if a heavy person climbed all the way to its top.
options.D: Imagining how two carts of equal weight would move after rolling into each other at walking pace.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Imagining what a traveller moving at nearly the speed of light would see in a mirror held at arm's length.

option_rationales.B: Books and the speed of a hand lie within the 'narrow band of experience' of moderate sizes and speeds where tacit expectations were formed.
option_rationales.C: Ladders and climbing are familiar everyday situations, so the expectations drawn on here have been tested in experience.
option_rationales.D: Carts at walking pace are exactly the moderate objects and speeds among which, paragraph 5 says, our expectations were formed and tested.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says tacit expectations were formed 'among objects of moderate size moving at moderate speeds' and that imagining 'the very fast' applies them 'where they were never tested'. Travel at nearly the speed of light is the only such case among the options.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the fast-pulled book because 'very quickly' sounds like the 'very fast' of paragraph 5, though a hand's speed is still everyday.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the stated limit to new cases; one wrong option borrows the word 'quickly' as a lure.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following claims EXCEPT that

options.A: a thought experiment collects no new data, so what it teaches cannot come from fresh observation.
options.B: the premises of a successful thought experiment may be discovered only in the course of running it.
options.C: the tacit expectations on which thought experiments draw were formed among objects of moderate size and speed.
options.D: the argument reading is unable to reconstruct Galileo's scenario as a set of premises and a conclusion.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the argument reading is unable to reconstruct Galileo's scenario as a set of premises and a conclusion.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says a thought experiment 'by definition, collects no new data', and the puzzle it raises is where the information comes from.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'the premises are found by running the scenario, not before it'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says our expectations 'were formed in a narrow band of experience, among objects of moderate size moving at moderate speeds'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The argument reading can reconstruct this, but only by writing in premises that no one had formulated before the scenario was imagined'. The reconstruction is possible; the author's objection is to what it leaves out.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's criticism of the argument reading as a claim that the reconstruction is impossible.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer distorts a qualified sentence ('can reconstruct this, but only by') into an outright denial.

questions.question: The author's criticism of the insight reading in paragraph 3 implies that an adequate account of Galileo's result must

options.A: show that the result could have been set out as a complete argument before the scenario was ever imagined.
options.B: trace the result to what Galileo and his readers already believed rather than to a newly perceived law.
options.C: establish that the result holds for all bodies, including those moving through a resisting medium.
options.D: explain why the scenario had to be carried out with real bodies before its conclusion could be trusted.

questions.correct_answer: (B) trace the result to what Galileo and his readers already believed rather than to a newly perceived law.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says thought experiments 'cannot be reduced to an argument that someone might have written down beforehand', so the author's own account denies this.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 limits the conclusion to bodies falling 'in the absence of a resisting medium', and the criticism of the insight reading is not about the result's scope.
option_rationales.D: The author's account explains how thought experiments inform 'without new data'; nothing requires a real trial.

questions.explanation: The insight reading is faulted for making the result 'mysterious, as though Galileo had glimpsed a law rather than noticed a contradiction in what he and his readers already believed'. An adequate account must therefore locate the source of the result in existing belief, as paragraph 4's account of tacit expectations does.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about a prior argument because the argument reading also grounds the result in existing beliefs, without noticing the author rejects the claim that the premises were available beforehand.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer and the strongest wrong option both appeal to prior belief; they differ on whether that belief was explicit beforehand, which requires paragraphs 3 and 4 together.

questions.question: According to the passage, one merit of the frequency view is that it

options.A: identifies chance with a physical tendency that each particular set-up possesses on its own.
options.B: assigns a definite chance to a single toss even when no long run of tosses ever takes place.
options.C: ties chance to something countable and so explains why observed frequencies serve as evidence about chances.
options.D: removes the need to decide which class of similar cases a particular event belongs to.

questions.correct_answer: (C) ties chance to something countable and so explains why observed frequencies serve as evidence about chances.

option_rationales.A: This describes the propensity view of paragraph 3, not the frequency view.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the frequency view's 'difficulties begin with the single case'; handling the single case is the merit claimed for the propensity view.
option_rationales.D: The need to choose a class is exactly the reference class problem that paragraph 2 raises against the frequency view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the frequency answer 'has the great merit of tying chance to something that can be counted, and it explains why observed frequencies are our main evidence about chances'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the merits of the frequency view with those of the propensity view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The merit is stated in the last sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The example of the toss 'described down to the exact force and angle of the flick' (paragraph 3) serves to

options.A: illustrate how a physicist with suitable equipment can measure the propensity of any set-up directly.
options.B: show that the propensity view meets its own form of the problem that the choice of class raised for frequencies.
options.C: show that a coin toss is really deterministic, so that its chance of heads is not truly one half.
options.D: explain why the frequency view cannot assign any chance to a coin that is tossed only once.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that the propensity view meets its own form of the problem that the choice of class raised for frequencies.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says it is 'unclear what a propensity is'; nothing in the passage claims propensities can be measured directly.
option_rationales.C: The author does not say the 'fair coin' chance is wrong; paragraph 4 says that description is 'the relevant one' for a gambler. The example shows dependence on description, not that one half is false.
option_rationales.D: That difficulty is raised in paragraph 2 about the frequency view; the flick example concerns the propensity view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the propensity view 'does not escape the problem it was meant to solve', because 'The tendency of a set-up depends on how the set-up is described'. The two descriptions of one toss give two propensities, just as two classes gave two frequencies.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the near-certain propensity as the author's verdict that the coin's true chance is not one half.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example's role depends on seeing the parallel with the reference class problem of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the account of chance given in paragraphs 4 and 5?

options.A: The beauty of a painting depends on the taste of whoever happens to be looking at it.
options.B: The age of a fossil can be estimated, but never exactly, because every dating method carries some error.
options.C: A hill's height is definite once one says whether it is measured from sea level or from the plain below.
options.D: The colour of an object is the one it shows under the single lighting that best reveals its true nature.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A hill's height is definite once one says whether it is measured from sea level or from the plain below.

option_rationales.A: This makes the property depend on the observer's taste, which is the subjectivity paragraph 5 says relativity to a description does not involve.
option_rationales.B: This is about uncertainty in measurement; the author's point is that chance is fixed once the specification is fixed, not that it is hard to measure.
option_rationales.D: This posits a single privileged condition, which is exactly what paragraph 5 says the account gives up.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 4 and 5 say chance is relative to a specification, the question is 'incomplete' without one, and 'Once the specification is fixed, the chance is fixed too'. The hill's height has the same structure: relative to a baseline, and objective once the baseline is stated.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the painting because it also involves relativity, without noticing that the relativity there is to taste, not to a stated description.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each capture one wrong reading of 'relative' (subjective; privileged frame).

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard two doctors who state different chances of recovery for the same patient as

options.A: both mistaken, since no chance can properly be assigned to the recovery of a single patient.
options.B: certainly in conflict, since the patient has a single chance of recovery that at most one of them has identified.
options.C: both merely expressing their own degrees of confidence, since chance is in the end a matter of perspective.
options.D: possibly both correct, if each is relying on a different specification of the patient's circumstances.

questions.correct_answer: (D) possibly both correct, if each is relying on a different specification of the patient's circumstances.

option_rationales.A: The author treats single-case chances as meaningful relative to a specification, and paragraph 2 notes that such judgements 'guide real decisions'.
option_rationales.B: This assumes a single privileged description, which paragraph 5 says the account gives up; on the author's view the patient has different chances relative to different specifications.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says 'relativity to a description is not the same as subjectivity', so the author would not reduce the doctors' statements to personal confidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a chance is a property an event has 'relative to a specification of the circumstances', and paragraph 2 lists several classes the patient belongs to with differing recovery rates. Two doctors using different specifications can therefore both be right; paragraph 5 adds that they would conflict only if they adopted 'the same description'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that disagreement about a chance always means at least one party is wrong, or overcorrecting into subjectivity.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the relativity thesis with the qualification in paragraph 5 about observers who share a description; wrong options capture the two opposite errors.

questions.question: On the author's account, the choice of which specification of the circumstances to use, unlike the chance given a specification,

options.A: is settled by the purposes of whoever needs the chance rather than by facts about the world.
options.B: can be settled only by gathering longer runs of observed frequencies for the event in question.
options.C: is left wholly open, so that any figure anyone proposes for the chance is as good as any other.
options.D: is fixed by nature, which singles out one description of each event as the correct one.

questions.correct_answer: (A) is settled by the purposes of whoever needs the chance rather than by facts about the world.

option_rationales.B: Frequencies are evidence about the chance under a description; paragraph 4 says the choice of description is settled by purposes, as with the gambler and the physicist.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the choice 'must be settled by our purposes', and paragraph 5 says that once a specification is fixed the chance is fixed, so not every figure is acceptable.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says the account gives up 'the idea that there is a single privileged description, the one nature itself would choose'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'What remains open, and must be settled by our purposes rather than by the world, is which specification to use', illustrated by the gambler and the physicist. Paragraph 5 adds that once the specification is fixed, 'the chance is fixed too'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'remains open' to mean anything goes, ignoring that purposes settle the choice and the world then fixes the chance.
questions.difficulty_reason: The distinction between choosing a description and the chance given a description is subtle, and one wrong option exaggerates 'remains open'.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: establish that whenever a population's expectations rise, the satisfaction it reports will fall regardless of its conditions.
options.B: urge governments to abandon measures of wellbeing and return to judging their success by economic output and income.
options.C: argue that life-satisfaction scores record expectation-dependent judgements and so should supplement, not replace, other measures of wellbeing.
options.D: show that life-satisfaction surveys are unreliable because respondents cannot accurately report how they feel from moment to moment.

questions.correct_answer: (C) argue that life-satisfaction scores record expectation-dependent judgements and so should supplement, not replace, other measures of wellbeing.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says such a population 'can report' falling satisfaction; the option turns one possibility into a rule and takes one illustration for the whole purpose.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 calls income 'at best a means to living well', and paragraph 4 recommends using the scores 'as one instrument among several', not going back to output.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says answering is 'quite unlike reporting a sensation'; the problem is that the score is an evaluation, not that feelings are misreported, and paragraph 3 says the surveys are not worthless.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows that the score is 'an evaluation' that depends on 'the standards brought to' it, paragraph 3 concedes the surveys have value but warns against 'treating them as a complete reading', and paragraph 4 recommends treating them as 'one instrument among several'. The correct answer states that argument and its scope.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that sounds most critical of the surveys and missing the concession in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis and concession are signposted ('Yet', 'None of this makes the surveys worthless'), and the wrong options are clearly too strong or off course.

questions.question: According to the passage, two people whose days contain the same mixture of pleasure, worry and boredom may report different scores because

options.A: one of them misunderstands the scale on which the answer is meant to be given.
options.B: they bring different expectations to the judgement of their lives.
options.C: one of them earns more and therefore has more of the means to living well.
options.D: one of them remembers the worrying parts of recent days more vividly than the other does.

questions.correct_answer: (B) they bring different expectations to the judgement of their lives.

option_rationales.A: The passage never suggests respondents misread the scale; it treats both answers as genuine evaluations made against different standards.
option_rationales.C: The two are stipulated to have the same daily experience, and income appears only in paragraph 1 as a means; it is not the explanation given.
option_rationales.D: Memory is never mentioned; paragraph 2 explains the difference by the fact that 'one expects more from life than the other'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the two people 'may give very different scores because one expects more from life than the other', which is a difference in the standards each brings to the evaluation.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible outside explanation instead of the one the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The warning that a government 'could succeed by teaching its citizens to want less' (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: governments that adopt satisfaction scores usually set out to lower their citizens' expectations on purpose.
options.B: people who have learned to want less are genuinely better off than those whose expectations remain high.
options.C: lowering expectations is the only reliable way for any government to raise the scores it reports.
options.D: average reported satisfaction could rise without any improvement in how people actually live.

questions.correct_answer: (D) average reported satisfaction could rise without any improvement in how people actually live.

option_rationales.A: The passage says a government 'could' succeed this way; it attributes no such intention to any actual government, so 'usually set out' distorts a possibility into a practice.
option_rationales.B: The author treats this as a way of gaming the measure, not of improving lives: the scores 'reward whatever lowers expectations as readily as whatever improves lives', which separates the two.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 names improving lives as another way scores rise; nothing says lowering expectations is the only or the most reliable route.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that scores depend on expectations, so lower expectations can yield higher scores for the same circumstances. Paragraph 4 draws the consequence: a government steering by the scores alone could raise them by lowering expectations, which means the average could rise without lives improving.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the ironic 'succeed' as a claim about actual government intentions, or as approval of lower expectations.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking paragraph 2's mechanism to the final sentence and resisting a wrong option that reads the remark as a description of real policy.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the phrase 'cut out the middleman' refers to

options.A: asking people about their lives directly instead of judging how well they live through income, which is only a means.
options.B: removing the cost of commissioning economic statistics by replacing them with cheaper surveys of opinion.
options.C: ignoring the standards that respondents use and recording only the sensations they feel during the day.
options.D: allowing citizens to report their satisfaction to researchers without any government official being involved in the process.

questions.correct_answer: (A) asking people about their lives directly instead of judging how well they live through income, which is only a means.

option_rationales.B: Cost is never discussed; the phrase concerns what the measure tracks, not what it costs.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says answering the question is 'quite unlike reporting a sensation', so this reverses what the survey involves.
option_rationales.D: No officials or intermediaries in the survey process are mentioned; the 'middleman' is income, which the previous sentence calls 'at best a means'.

questions.explanation: The sentence reads: 'Income is at best a means to living well, and a measure that asks people directly about their lives seems to cut out the middleman.' The middleman is income, the means standing between policy and the end of living well.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'middleman' literally as a person or institution.
questions.difficulty_reason: The referent is supplied by the first half of the same sentence.

questions.question: The example of a friend's illness in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: illustrate the popular claim that worry comes from caring about outcomes that one is quite unable to change.
options.B: prove that a person's goodness depends partly on whether the people he helps actually recover.
options.C: suggest that the Stoics regarded the recovery of friends as a matter of no importance whatever.
options.D: show that judging an outcome to be not up to us is compatible with caring about it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that judging an outcome to be not up to us is compatible with caring about it.

option_rationales.A: The popular reading is set out in paragraph 1 and corrected in paragraph 2; the example belongs to the correction, saying the Stoic is not 'indifferent' to the illness.
option_rationales.B: The example says goodness 'does not depend on whether she recovers, but on whether I act well toward her', which reverses the option.
option_rationales.C: The example says the opposite: denying the outcome is up to me 'is not to say that I should be indifferent to it'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that the distinction is a claim about where one's good lies, not a recommendation of indifference. The illness example makes this concrete: the outcome is not up to me, yet I should still 'act well toward her'; only my worth is not staked on her recovery.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the example to the popular reading in paragraph 1 instead of the correction in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence that contains the example.

questions.question: Which of the following lawyers acts most fully in the spirit of the doctrine as the author interprets it in paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: One who stops taking difficult cases, reasoning that since verdicts are not up to her she has no reason to expose herself to them.
options.B: One who prepares every case thoroughly, argues it as well as she can, and judges her own conduct by the quality of that work rather than by the verdict.
options.C: One who works on each case with great intensity and full seriousness because she believes her worth as a lawyer is measured by how many of her cases she wins.
options.D: One who stays calm in court by deciding that her clients' fates are no concern of hers, since she cannot control how judges rule.

questions.correct_answer: (B) One who prepares every case thoroughly, argues it as well as she can, and judges her own conduct by the quality of that work rather than by the verdict.

option_rationales.A: This is the withdrawal the author rejects: the doctrine 'offers no permission to withdraw', and the voter who stops voting has 'discarded the half that mattered'.
option_rationales.C: She does serve with full seriousness, but she stakes her worth on outcomes, which the Stoic is said to decline: 'declining to stake his worth on how any of it turned out'.
option_rationales.D: This is the popular version of paragraph 1, stopping caring in order to be calm; paragraph 2 says not being up to me does not mean being 'indifferent'.

questions.explanation: On the author's reading, the doctrine asks for full engagement (the Stoic serves 'with full seriousness') while locating one's good in 'the quality of one's own choosing' rather than in results. Only the correct answer combines full effort with judging oneself by conduct rather than verdict.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the calm, detached lawyer because calm is the popular association of Stoicism, or the intense lawyer because she does not withdraw.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures one half of the doctrine; the correct answer needs both halves together.

questions.question: The remark about someone who uses the doctrine 'to stop voting because elections are not up to him' suggests that the author regards the popular version of the doctrine as

options.A: open to being used as a justification for disengagement that the original doctrine does not allow.
options.B: an accurate account of how the ancient Stoics themselves behaved in public life.
options.C: mistaken in claiming that the outcome of an election is not up to any single voter.
options.D: more demanding than the original, because it requires a person to give up caring about results.

questions.correct_answer: (A) open to being used as a justification for disengagement that the original doctrine does not allow.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the Stoic was expected to 'serve in public life', so the abstaining voter departs from Stoic practice rather than describing it.
option_rationales.C: The author does not dispute that elections are not up to one voter; the mistake lies in drawing withdrawal from that fact.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: the careful reading is 'more demanding than the popular version, not less'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the doctrine 'offers no permission to withdraw' and that the abstaining voter 'has learned a convenient half of the lesson'. The popular version, which recommends ceasing to care, is what allows that convenient half to be used as an excuse for not acting.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the author disputes the factual premise about elections rather than the conclusion drawn from it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The stem's quotation needs to be connected to the contrast between the popular and the careful readings across paragraphs 1 to 3.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the Stoic doctrine when it is read in the careful way the passage recommends?

options.A: Dismissive, since the author regards it as a recipe for withdrawing from public life and private obligations.
options.B: Approving without reservation, since the author accepts the Stoic decision to treat partly controllable outcomes as indifferent.
options.C: Respectful of its coherence and its demands, but doubtful that sorting outcomes into two classes fits how they actually matter to us.
options.D: Admiring of its demands, and confident that its main difficulty disappears once the popular misreading of it is corrected.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Respectful of its coherence and its demands, but doubtful that sorting outcomes into two classes fits how they actually matter to us.

option_rationales.A: That charge applies to the misuse in paragraph 3; the careful reading 'offers no permission to withdraw' and is called more demanding.
option_rationales.B: The author says this decision 'seems false to how they matter' and doubts it 'describes a life anyone actually leads', which is a reservation.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the difficulty is one 'that the more careful reading does not remove', so the author is not confident it disappears.

questions.explanation: The author defends the careful reading against the popular one (paragraphs 2 and 3) and ends by saying 'One can admire the clarity of that choice and still doubt that it describes a life anyone actually leads.' That is respect combined with doubt about the two-bin sorting of the 'middle region'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the admiring wrong option because paragraphs 2 and 3 defend the doctrine, and missing that paragraph 4 says the careful reading does not remove the difficulty.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's attitude shifts between paragraphs 3 and 4, and the closest wrong option differs from the correct answer only on whether the final difficulty survives.

questions.question: According to the passage, the usual moral drawn from the story of the tree is that

options.A: every question about what a thing is good for is unreasonable and should be dropped altogether.
options.B: things that are of no use to anyone have no value and are rightly passed by without a second glance.
options.C: people with conspicuous gifts are likely to be exploited, so wise people avoid drawing attention to themselves.
options.D: craftsmen should learn to find uses even for timber that seems useless at first sight.

questions.correct_answer: (C) people with conspicuous gifts are likely to be exploited, so wise people avoid drawing attention to themselves.

option_rationales.A: This is neither the usual moral nor the author's view; paragraph 3 says each such question 'is reasonable on its own'.
option_rationales.B: That is the carpenter's attitude, which the tree rebukes; the usual moral sides with the tree, recommending that the wise 'keep their heads down'.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage recommends finding new uses; the story praises the tree for escaping use, and the usual moral concerns survival.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states the usual moral: 'in a dangerous world, conspicuous talent invites exploitation, and the wise keep their heads down'. The correct answer paraphrases this.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the carpenter's view, which the story rejects, with the moral readers draw from the story.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of the first sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'the carpenter's glance' refers to

options.A: a refusal to attend to anything that does not bear fruit or produce food.
options.B: a careful study of an object that eventually reveals its hidden and unexpected value.
options.C: the skill of quickly judging the quality of timber that comes from long practice in a trade.
options.D: a habit of looking at things only for what they can contribute to some purpose beyond themselves.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a habit of looking at things only for what they can contribute to some purpose beyond themselves.

option_rationales.A: Fruit trees are mentioned only as trees that get 'stripped and broken'; the glance concerns any kind of usefulness, not food in particular.
option_rationales.B: The carpenter passes the tree 'without a second glance' and misses its value, so the glance is the opposite of careful study.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 uses the phrase figuratively for institutions that 'measure things by their contribution to some further end'; it is not praise of craft expertise.

questions.explanation: In paragraph 3, 'we have grown skilled at the carpenter's glance' follows the remark that institutions 'measure things by their contribution to some further end', and the examples (study judged by jobs, land by revenue) show the glance is the habit of seeing things only as means.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the phrase literally as a craftsman's expertise.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is glossed by the sentence it completes and the examples that follow.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's main claim about the story of the tree?

options.A: It is mainly practical advice that talented people should hide their gifts in order to survive in a dangerous world.
options.B: Its chief target is a way of seeing that reduces things to their usefulness to someone, not usefulness itself.
options.C: It shows that things are valuable in proportion to how little they can be used by people.
options.D: It demonstrates that modern institutions are wrong to ask what subjects of study or land are good for.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Its chief target is a way of seeing that reduces things to their usefulness to someone, not usefulness itself.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 grants that this reading 'has support in the text' but says it 'makes the story smaller than it is', so it is not the author's main claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 rejects reading the story 'as a rejection of usefulness as such'; nothing ranks things by uselessness.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says each such question 'is reasonable on its own'; the warning is only against letting one become 'the only question'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the carpenter's real mistake is assuming that 'the only question worth asking about a tree is what it is good for to a carpenter', and paragraph 4 names the target as 'the habit of mind that cannot see a tree as anything other than timber not yet cut', explicitly not usefulness as such.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the prudential reading because the passage admits it has textual support, or overstating the author into rejecting usefulness.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the passage mentions and then limits; the correct answer requires keeping both limits in view.

questions.question: Which of the following, if it were added to the end of the story, would most weaken the author's reading of it?

options.A: The tree admits it would gladly have become timber had that been safe, and values its uselessness only as a way of staying alive.
options.B: On waking, the carpenter tells his dream to the apprentice, who doubts whether a tree could ever really speak to anyone.
options.C: The carpenter, waking from his dream, refuses to let his apprentice cut the tree down and reflects at length that he had misjudged it from the start.
options.D: Travellers continue to rest in the shade of the great tree for many generations after the carpenter's death.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The tree admits it would gladly have become timber had that been safe, and values its uselessness only as a way of staying alive.

option_rationales.B: Whether the dream is credible as an event has no bearing on what the story is criticising; the doubt neither confirms nor undermines the author's reading over the prudential one.
option_rationales.C: A carpenter who comes to see the tree differently fits the author's reading, which concerns his way of seeing; it does not weaken it.
option_rationales.D: This merely shows the tree surviving and offering another kind of benefit; it is consistent with both the prudential and the author's readings.

questions.explanation: The author argues that the story is more than prudential advice: it criticises seeing things only by their usefulness. If the tree itself said it valued uselessness only as a survival strategy and would happily have been timber, the story would reduce to the prudent moral that the author says 'makes the story smaller than it is'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an ending that changes the plot dramatically rather than one that bears on the competing interpretations.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the author's reading competes with the prudential one and picking the addition that favours the latter.

questions.question: According to the passage, the mirror argument is most effective against

options.A: the dread of the physical pain that people expect to suffer in the course of dying.
options.B: the fear of missing the future events and achievements that a longer life would have brought.
options.C: the fear of death imagined as a condition in which one will somehow find oneself.
options.D: the regret people feel about the many centuries of history that passed before they were born.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the fear of death imagined as a condition in which one will somehow find oneself.

option_rationales.A: Pain in dying is never discussed; the argument concerns non-existence after death, not the process of dying.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says that against this fear 'the symmetry breaks down'; it is the fear the argument fails to remove.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the time before birth 'did not trouble you then and does not trouble you now'; there is no such regret for the argument to address.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that 'against one target it is decisive': the picture of death as 'a condition they will find themselves in: a darkness, a silence, an interminable wait'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the fear of missing future goods, which the passage discusses at greater length.
questions.difficulty_reason: Paragraph 2 names the target explicitly.

questions.question: The final sentence of paragraph 3, contrasting being born earlier with dying later, is used to support the claim that

options.A: the fear of death as a dark and silent condition is a confusion that the mirror argument exposes.
options.B: the goods lost by dying would have belonged to this very life, whereas the goods of earlier centuries could never have been ours.
options.C: our attitudes in ordinary life to the pleasures that are still to come differ from our attitudes to pleasures that are already over.
options.D: people are inconsistent when they dread the time after their death but feel nothing at all about the time before their birth.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the goods lost by dying would have belonged to this very life, whereas the goods of earlier centuries could never have been ours.

option_rationales.A: That point belongs to paragraph 2; the sentence in paragraph 3 concerns the loss of goods, not the picture of death as a condition.
option_rationales.C: This is a separate, earlier point in paragraph 3; the sentence marked 'More importantly' adds a further reason, about whose goods are at stake.
option_rationales.D: That is Lucretius' charge in paragraph 1; the sentence is part of the author's reply explaining why the two periods differ, so it undercuts the charge of inconsistency.

questions.explanation: The sentence comes after the claim that 'the goods of the centuries before our birth were never ours to lose'. Because the same person could not have been born much earlier but could easily die later, only a later death would add goods to this very life; so losing them is a real loss, while missing the earlier centuries is not.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the sentence to the nearby point about ordinary attitudes to past and future, which it follows but does not illustrate.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are claims that appear in the passage, one of them in the same paragraph; the correct answer needs the precise link the sentence supports.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's objection to the symmetry argument in paragraph 3?

options.A: Many people who say they fear death admit, when questioned closely, that they picture it as a dark and silent condition they will endure.
options.B: Epicurus and Lucretius both wrote in the hope of freeing their readers from fears they considered groundless.
options.C: Some people who are dying report that they fear the process of dying far more than they fear being dead.
options.D: On reflection, people regret the goods they missed by being born late as much as the goods they will lose by dying.

questions.correct_answer: (D) On reflection, people regret the goods they missed by being born late as much as the goods they will lose by dying.

option_rationales.A: This concerns the fear the author already concedes the argument removes (paragraph 2); it leaves the objection about lost future goods untouched.
option_rationales.B: Their intentions do not bear on whether the author's distinction between past and future goods holds.
option_rationales.C: The process of dying is outside the argument altogether; neither Lucretius nor the author is discussing it.

questions.explanation: The objection depends on an asymmetry: we fear losing future goods but do not regret the goods of the time before birth, and the author explains why this is reasonable. If reflective people in fact regretted the goods they missed by being born late just as much, our attitudes would be symmetrical after all, and the mirror would apply to the fear of loss too. The author's further point about whose goods are at stake would still need answering, but this is the only option that bears on the objection at all; the others concern fears the author has already conceded or set aside.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about picturing death as a dark condition because it mentions the mirror's target, though the author has already granted that point.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying the asymmetry as the premise the objection rests on.

questions.question: The last sentence of the passage implies that

options.A: any argument that wholly removed the fear of losing one's future would also weaken a concern that the author regards as legitimate.
options.B: no argument about death can offer any genuine consolation, since every fear of death reflects care for the future.
options.C: Lucretius intended his argument to teach readers to care less about the future, and the author shares that aim.
options.D: grief in advance for a life cut short is a confusion that a better argument than Lucretius' could dispel.

questions.correct_answer: (A) any argument that wholly removed the fear of losing one's future would also weaken a concern that the author regards as legitimate.

option_rationales.B: The author says Lucretius 'removes part of the fear, and that is no small gift', so some consolation is possible and not every fear is of this kind.
option_rationales.C: The author says only what a perfect consolation 'would have to' do; nothing attributes this intention to Lucretius, and the author clearly does not share it.
option_rationales.D: The author says such grief 'is not a confusion to be argued away', which is the opposite.

questions.explanation: Grief in advance is called 'the shadow cast by caring about one's own future'. A consolation that removed it completely 'would have to work by teaching us to care less', that is, by weakening that care. Since the author treats the grief as no confusion and the care as natural, such a consolation would cost something the author values.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'teaching us to care less' as a description of Lucretius' project, or overlooking the concession that part of the fear can be removed.
questions.difficulty_reason: The implication depends on combining the final sentence with the claim that the grief 'is not a confusion' and the concession earlier in paragraph 4; the extreme wrong option is tempting.

questions.question: It can be inferred that those who accuse the teaching of 'moral recklessness' understand it to recommend

options.A: meeting success with pride and failure with an equally strong sense of shame.
options.B: refusing to act at all whenever the outcome of an action is uncertain.
options.C: acting without weighing what one's actions are likely to bring about.
options.D: choosing whatever action will be most visibly successful and most widely praised.

questions.correct_answer: (C) acting without weighing what one's actions are likely to bring about.

option_rationales.A: The teaching asks for 'the same evenness of mind' in success and failure; neither the teaching nor the objection concerns pride and shame.
option_rationales.B: The objection concerns an agent who acts but 'will not count the cost'; it does not say the teaching recommends inaction, and the teaching itself says one 'should act'.
option_rationales.D: This is the distortion paragraph 3 says the teaching guards against, not what critics take it to recommend.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the objection: 'An agent who does not care about outcomes ... is an agent who will not count the cost of what he does.' The critics therefore read the teaching as recommending action without weighing consequences, which paragraph 2 says confuses 'attending to consequences' with 'depending on them'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the critics' reading with the teaching's actual demand for evenness of mind.
questions.difficulty_reason: The critics' interpretation is stated in the sentence after the accusation.

questions.question: Which of the following teachers best shows the relation to results that paragraph 4 says the teaching can sensibly ask for?

options.A: One who gives up teaching a difficult class altogether once her first method fails, concluding from the failure that she simply lacks the talent for the work.
options.B: One who keeps using a method she believes is right without checking whether her pupils are learning anything from it.
options.C: One who chooses whichever methods will produce the most impressive results for visiting inspectors, whether or not her pupils actually benefit from them.
options.D: One who sees that a new method is not helping her class, changes it, and does not take the failure as proof she is a poor teacher.

questions.correct_answer: (D) One who sees that a new method is not helping her class, changes it, and does not take the failure as proof she is a poor teacher.

option_rationales.A: She treats the result as a verdict on her worth and abandons the course 'the moment it begins to fail', both distortions the passage describes.
option_rationales.B: This is the 'blindness to results' that paragraph 4 says the teaching does not ask for; the physician 'has to watch whether the treatment is working'.
option_rationales.C: This is the agent 'fixed on fruits' of paragraph 3, choosing 'the action whose success will be visible over the one that is right'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says results should be 'information to be used rather than verdicts on one's worth'. The correct answer teacher uses the result to adjust her method (information) but does not read it as a judgement of herself (not a verdict).
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the steadfast teacher because she seems unattached to results, missing that the passage rejects blindness to them.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches one distortion in the passage; the solver must hold both halves of the 'information, not verdict' relation.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 contributes to the argument chiefly by

options.A: restating the objection of paragraph 1 in a stronger form before the author's final reply in paragraph 4.
options.B: going beyond showing that detachment is compatible with good action to claim that it actually helps action go well.
options.C: conceding that anxiety about results is sometimes useful because it keeps agents attentive to what they do.
options.D: introducing the difficulty that most actions unfold over time and so must be adjusted as their effects gradually appear.

questions.correct_answer: (B) going beyond showing that detachment is compatible with good action to claim that it actually helps action go well.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 does not restate the objection; it continues the defence begun in paragraph 2 by naming benefits of detachment.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says anxiety about results is 'notoriously bad for performance'; it makes no such concession.
option_rationales.D: That difficulty is raised in paragraph 4, which begins 'It would be too quick, however'; paragraph 3 is still part of the defence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows only that the teaching does not forbid attending to consequences. Paragraph 3 then argues that detachment is 'a condition for acting well', because anxiety harms performance and fixation on fruits tempts agents toward visible rather than right action. It moves from compatibility to positive benefit.
questions.common_misconception: Assigning paragraph 4's qualification to paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing how paragraph 3 advances beyond paragraph 2, not merely what it says.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's stance toward the teaching by the end of the passage?

options.A: Sympathetic, having rejected the charge of recklessness, yet unwilling to claim that the teaching removes every difficulty.
options.B: Neutral, since the author declines to say whether the objection that the teaching is reckless succeeds or fails.
options.C: Sceptical, since the author ends by doubting that anyone could actually live by the teaching under real pressure.
options.D: Dismissive, since the physician example shows that the teaching cannot be followed by anyone whose work has consequences.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Sympathetic, having rejected the charge of recklessness, yet unwilling to claim that the teaching removes every difficulty.

option_rationales.B: The author does say: 'The objection rests on running together two different things', which rejects it.
option_rationales.C: The author says this is 'a question the teaching poses rather than settles'; leaving a question open is not doubting the answer.
option_rationales.D: The physician example is used in the teaching's favour in paragraph 2 and to refine it in paragraph 4, not to show it cannot be followed.

questions.explanation: The author answers the recklessness objection in paragraphs 2 and 3, then says it would be 'too quick ... to declare the tension dissolved' and leaves open whether ordinary people can sustain the required relation. That is sympathy with an acknowledged open question.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the open question at the end as scepticism.
questions.difficulty_reason: The closing qualification tempts solvers toward scepticism; the correct answer requires weighing it against the defence in paragraphs 2 and 3.

questions.question: According to the passage, loneliness differs from solitude in that loneliness

options.A: is a painful sense of having too little connection, which can be felt even in the company of others.
options.B: is always chosen by the person who suffers it, while solitude is always imposed by others.
options.C: is a circumstance of being physically alone, whereas solitude is a feeling about the state of one's relationships with others.
options.D: arises only when a person lives alone for a long period with no prospect of company returning.

questions.correct_answer: (A) is a painful sense of having too little connection, which can be felt even in the company of others.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says solitude is good 'because it is chosen', and nothing says loneliness is chosen; the option reverses and overstates.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the passage: solitude 'is simply being alone', a circumstance, and loneliness is 'the painful sense' of thin connections.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says loneliness 'can be felt in a crowded room' and within marriages, so it does not arise only from living alone.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines loneliness as 'the painful sense that one's connections are fewer or thinner than one needs' and says it 'can be felt in a crowded room', while 'Solitude is simply being alone'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing which term names the circumstance and which names the experience.
questions.difficulty_reason: The definitions are given directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The claim that 'Friendship is richer between people who could survive without it' (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: the best friendships are those in which the friends spend long periods apart from each other.
options.B: people who are capable of solitude have comparatively little need of friends and seldom go out of their way to seek them.
options.C: people who depend on others for company cannot form friendships of any kind.
options.D: a relationship held together partly by an inability to bear one's own company is, to that extent, less freely chosen.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a relationship held together partly by an inability to bear one's own company is, to that extent, less freely chosen.

option_rationales.A: Nothing links richer friendship to time spent apart; 'could survive without it' concerns capacity, not actual separation.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'Nor is the capacity to be alone a substitute for company'; the claim concerns the quality of friendship, not a reduced need for it.
option_rationales.C: The passage says such dependence makes relationships 'less free', not impossible; 'cannot form friendships of any kind' is extreme.

questions.explanation: The preceding sentence says a person who 'can never bear his own company depends on others in a way that makes his relationships less free'. The claim about friendship draws the positive side: where neither friend needs the friendship merely to escape being alone, it is chosen more freely and so is richer.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'could survive without it' as a claim that capable people need fewer friends, or that friends should spend time apart.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the aphorism to the sentence before it and resisting a literal reading.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The value of an evening spent alone depends partly on the state of the person who spends it.
options.B: Solitude remains valuable however long it continues, provided the person chose it at the outset.
options.C: Programmes that tackle loneliness should aim to improve people's connections with one another.
options.D: A person can be lonely while spending most of each day in the company of others.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Solitude remains valuable however long it continues, provided the person chose it at the outset.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says solitude's 'quality depends on what one brings to it', and the empty evening is a lack for one person and a good for another, so the author agrees.
option_rationales.C: The final sentence says 'The cure for loneliness is better connection', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says loneliness 'can be felt in a crowded room' and among colleagues who meet every day, so the author agrees.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says solitude is good 'because it is chosen and because it comes to an end', and that one which 'stretches on with no prospect of return' turns into loneliness. Being chosen at the outset is therefore not enough; the correct answer contradicts the author.
questions.common_misconception: Remembering only the 'chosen' condition and forgetting the second condition, that solitude must come to an end.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer states one of the author's two conditions while dropping the other, so it sounds familiar.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's warning in paragraph 4 about policies and technologies that aim to reduce time spent alone?

options.A: Programmes against loneliness substantially reduce the suffering of those who take part in them, as their organisers had hoped.
options.B: Some contemplatives in the past found their early periods of retreat painful before they came to value them.
options.C: People who spend less time alone because of such measures keep as much chosen, undivided time as before, since the hours they give up were mostly unwanted ones.
options.D: Many people who are lonely remain so even after they have begun to spend much more time in company.

questions.correct_answer: (C) People who spend less time alone because of such measures keep as much chosen, undivided time as before, since the hours they give up were mostly unwanted ones.

option_rationales.A: The author already agrees loneliness causes 'real suffering' and needs a cure; the warning is about crowding out solitude, which this finding does not address.
option_rationales.B: This concerns how solitude is learned; it does not show that reducing time alone leaves the good of solitude intact.
option_rationales.D: This supports paragraph 2's claim that loneliness can persist in company; it says nothing about whether solitude is being crowded out.

questions.explanation: The warning is that measures which only reduce time alone 'may ... crowd out a good that most people need'. That assumes the time removed includes valuable solitude. If the hours given up were unwanted and chosen solitude is fully preserved, nothing good is crowded out, and the warning loses its force.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the finding that programmes reduce suffering, as if showing their benefit refuted a warning about their side effect.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option praises the programmes, which feels like a reply to the author; seeing that it leaves the specific warning untouched requires isolating its assumption.

questions.question: According to the passage, Aristotle placed amusement with work rather than with leisure because amusement

options.A: is pursued in modern societies mainly for the skills and stamina that it helps people to build.
options.B: provides the relaxation that we need because we cannot labour without a break, and so serves further activity.
options.C: was available only to citizens who were supported by the labour of slaves and artisans.
options.D: is an activity chosen for its own sake and is therefore the highest use of a person's free time.

questions.correct_answer: (B) provides the relaxation that we need because we cannot labour without a break, and so serves further activity.

option_rationales.A: That is the author's account of modern free time in paragraph 3, not Aristotle's reason for classifying amusement.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says this of leisure, not amusement, and it is not the reason given for classing amusement with work.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: amusement exists 'for the sake of further activity rather than as an end in itself', and contemplation is the highest activity.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'We need relaxation because we cannot labour continuously, and amusement provides it, so amusement exists for the sake of further activity rather than as an end in itself'. That is why it belongs with work.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that amusement, as a pleasant free-time activity, must be what Aristotle meant by leisure.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that free time is 'colonised by the logic it was supposed to interrupt' means that

options.A: activities once done for their own sake have been abandoned in favour of rest and sleep.
options.B: people have so little time off that work fills almost every hour of the day.
options.C: employers increasingly demand that their staff remain available for work during evenings and holidays.
options.D: standards drawn from work come to govern how free time is judged and spent.

questions.correct_answer: (D) standards drawn from work come to govern how free time is judged and spent.

option_rationales.A: Rest and sleep are themselves described as being valued for their effect on performance; the point is not that people now prefer rest.
option_rationales.B: The author says the result 'is not merely that people have too little time off'; colonisation concerns the character of free time, not its amount.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 describes no employer demands; its examples are hobbies, exercise and sleep that people themselves treat as investments.

questions.explanation: The preceding sentences say that once leisure is recovery for work 'it inherits the standards of work' and is 'used productively', even sleep being valued 'for its effect on the next day's performance'. The logic of work, which free time was meant to interrupt, now organises free time itself.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'colonised' to mean that work hours literally invade free time.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor must be decoded from the surrounding sentences, and the wrong option about too little time off echoes a phrase in the same paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It accepts the objection that Aristotle's leisure depended on others' labour and concludes that his account of leisure must be revised for modern use.
options.B: It shows that Aristotle's exclusion of most people from leisure discredits his account of what leisure is, along with his picture of the good life.
