options.C: It accepts a serious objection to Aristotle in full while arguing that it applies to who had leisure, not to what leisure is.
options.D: It argues that the objection to Aristotle is unjust, since modern societies have extended to nearly everyone the leisure he reserved for a few.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It accepts a serious objection to Aristotle in full while arguing that it applies to who had leisure, not to what leisure is.

option_rationales.A: The author says the objection 'tells against the distribution of leisure ... not against his account of what leisure is', so no revision of the account follows.
option_rationales.B: The author says the objection tells 'not against his account of what leisure is', so the paragraph denies exactly what this option says it shows.
option_rationales.D: The author calls the objection 'just' and says it 'should not be softened'; nothing claims modern societies have extended leisure to all.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the objection, says 'This objection is just, and it should not be softened', and then limits its reach: 'it tells against the distribution of leisure in Aristotle's city, not against his account of what leisure is.' The paragraph concedes fully but narrows the scope.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option saying his account must be revised for modern use, which sounds like a balanced concession but contradicts the distinction the author draws.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each capture half of the paragraph (the concession, or the objection itself); the correct answer needs both the concession and its limit.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as leisure in Aristotle's sense?

options.A: A retired engineer who spends his evenings studying the music of a tradition he loves, though he will never perform or write about it.
options.B: A musician practising scales for several hours each evening to prepare for a paid audition with an orchestra.
options.C: A factory hand who spends his weekends watching comedies to unwind before the start of the next working week.
options.D: An office worker who reads philosophy before bed because it helps her sleep and work more sharply the next day.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A retired engineer who spends his evenings studying the music of a tradition he loves, though he will never perform or write about it.

option_rationales.B: Music is named in paragraph 2, but here it is practised for the sake of paid work, which paragraph 3 identifies as the logic of work, not leisure.
option_rationales.C: This is amusement as relaxation for further work, which paragraph 2 says Aristotle placed 'with work' rather than with leisure.
option_rationales.D: Philosophy resembles contemplation, but she reads it 'for its effect on the next day's performance', exactly the instrumental use paragraph 3 describes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines leisure as being free for 'activities chosen for their own sake' and counts the enjoyment of music among them. The engineer studies music for its own sake, with no use in view. Each wrong option involves something that looks like leisure (music, philosophy, entertainment) but is done for the sake of work or recovery.
questions.common_misconception: Matching surface features (music, philosophy) to the passage instead of asking why the activity is done.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options contain activities the passage associates with leisure (music, philosophy as contemplation), so the solver must apply the 'for its own sake' test rather than match words.

questions.question: The author's claim that 'the language of rest and productivity has no words to state' the demand in paragraph 5 suggests that this language

options.A: was invented by employers to persuade workers that long hours are good for them and their families.
options.B: values free time only by its relation to work, so it cannot express the worth of activities done for their own sake.
options.C: is too imprecise to measure how much free time the people of a society actually have each week.
options.D: is used mostly by schools and cities, which ought instead to leave free time to the choices of individuals.

questions.correct_answer: (B) values free time only by its relation to work, so it cannot express the worth of activities done for their own sake.

option_rationales.A: No origin or motive is attributed to the language; this adds a claim the passage does not make.
option_rationales.C: The author says the measure of free time is 'not only how much of it there is'; the limitation concerns what the language values, not its precision about quantity.
option_rationales.D: The passage places a demand on schools and cities; it does not say they use this language or that they should stay out of free time.

questions.explanation: On the view in paragraph 1, leisure's value is 'explained by reference to the work it interrupts'. A vocabulary of rest and productivity can therefore praise free time only as recovery; the demand in paragraph 5, that people be able to fill free time with 'activities worth doing for their own sake', falls outside it.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'no words' to be about measuring quantity, or inventing a motive for the language.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the final sentence back to the picture of leisure in paragraph 1.

questions.question: In the exercise described in paragraph 2, each component of a person is examined to determine whether it

options.A: is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it lies under one's control.
options.B: can be perceived directly, whether it can be described in words and whether others share it.
options.C: existed before the person's birth and whether it will continue after the person dies.
options.D: is a cause of suffering, whether it can be removed and whether it is a form of craving.

questions.correct_answer: (A) is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it lies under one's control.

option_rationales.B: None of these tests appears; paragraph 2 lists permanence, reliable satisfaction and control.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 asks whether each component 'is permanent', not about its existence before birth or after death.
option_rationales.D: Suffering and craving appear later in paragraph 2 as the purpose of the exercise, not as the questions asked of each component.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the listener 'is asked of each whether it is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it is under one's control'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that uses the tradition's vocabulary of suffering and craving.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three tests are listed in one sentence.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'an unchanging owner standing behind it' refers to

options.A: the teacher in the early discourses who leads listeners through the components of a person.
options.B: the person regarded as a stream of experiences that has a history, makes choices and bears consequences.
options.C: the bodily form, which stays the same throughout a life while feelings and perceptions change.
options.D: a self thought of as something over and above the stream of experiences, to which those experiences belong.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a self thought of as something over and above the stream of experiences, to which those experiences belong.

option_rationales.A: The phrase concerns what stands behind a person's experiences, not any figure in the discourses.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the teaching does not deny this stream; the 'owner' is what is denied 'in addition to the stream'.
option_rationales.C: Bodily form is one of the components that fails the permanence test in paragraph 2, so it cannot be the unchanging owner.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the teaching denies 'that there is, in addition to the stream, an unchanging owner standing behind it', and the chariot analogy contrasts the assembly with a 'further chariot over and above the parts'. The owner is a self added to, and possessing, the stream.
questions.common_misconception: Identifying the owner with the stream itself, which the teaching accepts.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option uses the paragraph's own description of the stream, which is what the owner is contrasted with.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that the no-self teaching contradicts itself, since someone must exist to entertain the doctrine and to be disappointed by it.
options.B: defend the no-self teaching as a practical therapy that, because it aims only at reducing craving, stands beyond the reach of philosophical criticism.
options.C: show that the no-self teaching escapes a common refutation because it is chiefly practical, yet still rests on a contestable claim that deserves argument.
options.D: establish that the chariot analogy settles the question whether a person is anything more than an organised stream of experiences.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that the no-self teaching escapes a common refutation because it is chiefly practical, yet still rests on a contestable claim that deserves argument.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'easy refutation' that paragraph 3 says 'misses its target'; it is the critics' view, not the author's.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 rejects exactly this: it would be 'too convenient' to treat the doctrine as 'purely therapeutic and therefore immune to philosophical scrutiny'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the question remains open, 'without anyone having settled the matter'; the analogy only illustrates the doctrine's position.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 argue that the easy refutation attacks a claim the teaching does not make, since the teaching is an exercise against craving. Paragraphs 4 and 5 add that the teaching's authority 'rests on a claim about the self that may be true or false' and must be argued about. The correct answer states both halves of this 'double' lesson.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the defence of the teaching as pure therapy, which matches the first three paragraphs but ignores the reversal in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The first wrong option is the 'easy defence' that the passage spends three paragraphs approaching before rejecting; only the whole argument separates it from the correct answer.

questions.question: Suppose it were shown that a person is, after all, something more than the organised stream of experiences. Based on the passage, the author would most likely hold that

options.A: the tradition would also have to abandon its claims that the stream of experiences has a history, makes choices and bears consequences.
options.B: the easy refutation described in paragraph 1 would at last be vindicated as an objection to the teaching as the tradition states it.
options.C: the exercise of paragraph 2 would then lack the authority the tradition claims for it, since that authority depends on revealing how things are.
options.D: the exercise would remain fully justified, since it would still reduce craving whether or not the belief it induces is true.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the exercise of paragraph 2 would then lack the authority the tradition claims for it, since that authority depends on revealing how things are.

option_rationales.A: These claims concern the stream, which the teaching affirms; a person's being more than the stream would not undermine them.
option_rationales.B: The easy refutation attacks the claim that no one exists, which the teaching 'does not make'; showing the person to be more than the stream would refute a different claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says a therapy that works by inducing a belief 'earns its authority only if the belief is warranted'; otherwise it is 'a comforting fiction'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 holds that 'The exercise succeeds, by its own standards, because it reveals how things are', and that a belief-inducing therapy has authority 'only if the belief is warranted'. If the person were more than the stream, the belief would be false, and the exercise would lose its authority.
questions.common_misconception: Thinking that refuting the doctrine would vindicate the easy refutation, when that refutation attacks a claim the teaching never makes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are hard to separate from the correct answer: one needs paragraph 4's point about therapy and truth, the other needs paragraph 3's point about what the easy refutation targets.

questions.question: The chariot example in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: show that the tradition regards persons as fictions, since the word 'chariot' names nothing that really exists in the world.
options.B: illustrate how a name can pick out an organised whole without there being any further thing over and above its parts.
options.C: prove that the components of a person are permanent, since the parts of a chariot survive when it is taken apart.
options.D: settle the metaphysical question that paragraph 4 raises about whether a person is more than an organised stream.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate how a name can pick out an organised whole without there being any further thing over and above its parts.

option_rationales.A: The example says 'nothing is lost' by admitting there is no further chariot; the assembly is real, and the person is a 'functioning whole', not a fiction.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says none of the components is permanent, and the example says nothing about what survives disassembly.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says this question has not been settled; the example illustrates the doctrine's position without proving it.

questions.explanation: The example comes right after the claim that the teaching denies only an owner 'in addition to the stream'. The word 'chariot' names an 'assembly of axle, wheels and frame', and the person is likewise 'a convenient name for a functioning whole, not a hidden thing to which the whole belongs'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as saying that persons, like chariots, do not exist at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'likewise', but one wrong option turns the conventional name into a denial of existence.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how the defects of the retinal image, such as its blind spot, are corrected by the beliefs a viewer holds about the world.
options.B: defend the view that seeing is a form of conscious reasoning in which the brain, like a careful clerk, weighs the evidence.
options.C: show that visual illusions reveal how unreliable perception is, so that what we see should be checked against measurement.
options.D: argue that seeing actively interprets ambiguous evidence, while denying that this makes the senses untrustworthy.

questions.correct_answer: (D) argue that seeing actively interprets ambiguous evidence, while denying that this makes the senses untrustworthy.

option_rationales.A: The blind spot is one detail of paragraph 1, and paragraph 3 says the expectations at work are not 'the beliefs we hold and can revise', so the option is both too narrow and a distortion.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says these are 'not conclusions we reach', and the careful clerk belongs to the recording picture the author rejects in paragraph 1.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says it would be 'a mistake' to conclude that perception is unreliable, and that illusions are built in laboratories to exploit assumptions that rarely mislead us elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 rejects the picture of seeing as recording, paragraph 2 offers the inferential account, paragraph 3 answers an objection to it, and paragraph 4 concludes that the view overturns 'the idea that seeing is passive' but not 'our trust in the senses'. The correct answer holds both the thesis and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the illusion option because illusions are discussed at length, and missing that the author uses them to make a different point.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option turns the author's concession into its opposite; another borrows the clerk image from the view being rejected.

questions.question: According to the passage, the retinal image is ambiguous in the sense that

options.A: eye movements make it change from moment to moment, so that no single image can ever be relied on.
options.B: it is upside down and flat, so the brain has to turn it the right way up before anything can be seen at all.
options.C: the same pattern on the retina is consistent with more than one arrangement of things in the world.
options.D: the blind spot removes part of every image, leaving gaps that the viewer's expectations must fill in.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the same pattern on the retina is consistent with more than one arrangement of things in the world.

option_rationales.A: Jitter is mentioned as a separate defect, and the passage never says that no image can be relied on.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 lists inversion and flatness as separate defects before 'Above all, it is ambiguous'; ambiguity is illustrated by the size and grey patch examples, not by inversion.
option_rationales.D: The blind spot is another of the listed defects; the passage illustrates ambiguity with one image fitting two different scenes, not with missing parts of the image.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives two illustrations of ambiguity: a small retinal image 'could be a small object nearby or a large one far away', and dim grey 'could be a dark surface in bright light or a pale surface in shadow'. In each, one image fits two states of the world.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the other listed defects of the retinal image instead of the one the passage calls ambiguity.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is in two adjacent sentences; the wrong options are the other defects in the same list.

questions.question: The author explains that perceptual assumptions rarely mislead us outside the laboratory because they are mostly true of the environments in which they were formed. Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this explanation?

options.A: People who move into surroundings that violate their perceptual assumptions are, from the start, misled no more often than people who grew up there.
options.B: Laboratory illusions are deliberately constructed by researchers so as to exploit the assumptions that ordinary vision relies on.
options.C: Viewers who are told exactly how an illusion works go on seeing it just as strongly as they did before being told.
options.D: Some perceptual assumptions, such as the assumption that light comes from above, turn out to be shared by people raised in very different places and cultures.

questions.correct_answer: (A) People who move into surroundings that violate their perceptual assumptions are, from the start, misled no more often than people who grew up there.

option_rationales.B: This repeats what paragraph 4 already says about illusions being 'carefully built to exploit' the assumptions, so it is consistent with the explanation rather than a challenge to it.
option_rationales.C: This bears on paragraph 3's point that knowledge does not alter what is seen, not on the paragraph 4 explanation of why the assumptions seldom mislead.
option_rationales.D: Shared assumptions fit paragraph 3's suggestion that some were formed 'over the history of the species'; the option says nothing about whether the assumptions mislead when they are false of a setting.

questions.explanation: The explanation says the assumptions rarely mislead because they fit the settings that formed them. It predicts that people placed in settings where the assumptions are false will be misled more. If newcomers to such settings are misled no more often than natives, the fit between assumption and environment is not doing the work the author claims for it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about illusions surviving knowledge, which is true according to the passage but belongs to a different claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires isolating the specific causal explanation in paragraph 4 and seeing which result breaks its prediction; two wrong options restate claims the passage already makes.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that 'the guess is tightly disciplined by the evidence' most nearly means that

options.A: repeated correction trains the brain, over time, to stop guessing and simply register the signal as it is.
options.B: the interpretation perception settles on is held in check by what the incoming signal actually contains.
options.C: perception refuses to adopt any expectation that the viewer has not personally confirmed by experience.
options.D: the viewer consciously tests each perceptual guess against careful measurement before accepting it as true.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the interpretation perception settles on is held in check by what the incoming signal actually contains.

option_rationales.A: This brings back the recording picture of paragraph 1, which the author rejects; the passage says every glance remains 'a small act of interpretation'.
option_rationales.C: The passage allows that some assumptions may come from 'the history of the species', and it says nothing about perception refusing unconfirmed expectations.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the conclusions are 'reached on our behalf, before anything is presented to awareness', so conscious testing is the opposite of the claim; the measuring viewer of paragraph 3 still sees the illusion.

questions.explanation: The phrase answers the objection 'why do we not simply see whatever we expect?' The reply is that the evidence constrains which interpretation wins, so expectation cannot override the signal at will. The correct answer states this constraint.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'disciplined' as a conscious checking process rather than a constraint built into the inference.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase has to be read against the objection it answers in the preceding sentence.

questions.question: According to the passage, viewers fail to see the unexpected figure because

options.A: attention lets only part of what reaches the eye into conscious experience.
options.B: they do notice the figure faintly but forget the impression before they are questioned about the video.
options.C: the figure appears too briefly and too indistinctly to register clearly on a short recording.
options.D: the light from an unexpected object does not reach the retina while the eyes are busy tracking a moving ball.

questions.correct_answer: (A) attention lets only part of what reaches the eye into conscious experience.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says what does not pass the gate 'is not dimly seen but, for practical purposes, not seen at all', which rules out a faint impression later forgotten.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the figure strolls through the middle of the scene and 'pauses to face the camera', so it is neither brief nor indistinct.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the light 'reaches the retina as surely as the light from the ball'; the failure is not in the eyes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 locates the failure in 'the selection that decides which parts of the scene will be built into conscious experience', and compares attention to a gate. The correct answer restates this.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the problem is visual (the eyes or the recording) rather than attentional.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2, and each wrong option is ruled out by an explicit phrase.

questions.question: The remark that the driver's 'honesty is not in question; his access to his own lapse is' implies that

options.A: he is probably concealing his inattention at the junction in order to avoid being blamed for what happened.
options.B: cyclists who appear suddenly at junctions are among the most common causes of collisions with careful drivers.
options.C: he glimpsed the cyclist dimly at the junction but has since lost the memory of that fleeting impression.
options.D: his account is sincere yet mistaken, since a cyclist he never consciously saw left nothing in his experience to report.

questions.correct_answer: (D) his account is sincere yet mistaken, since a cyclist he never consciously saw left nothing in his experience to report.

option_rationales.A: The passage says he reports 'quite sincerely' and that his honesty 'is not in question', which is the opposite of concealment.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about the causes or frequency of collisions; the example illustrates how a lapse can be invisible to the person who makes it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says what fails to pass the gate of attention is 'not dimly seen but, for practical purposes, not seen at all', so there was no glimpse to lose.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the things we miss 'leave no trace in experience from which we could learn that we missed them'. The driver therefore tells the truth as he experienced it, but his experience lacks the cyclist, so the report is wrong without being dishonest.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the dim glimpse option, which sounds psychologically plausible but contradicts the gate image of paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is ruled out only by connecting paragraph 3 to the gate claim in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the selectivity of attention is best described as

options.A: alarmed, regarding it as a serious defect of the mind that ought to be corrected through training.
options.B: accepting, treating it as the price of focus while warning against trusting it where misses are costly.
options.C: dismissive, treating the experiments as amusing curiosities with little bearing on ordinary life.
options.D: admiring, holding that attention can be relied on to admit whatever genuinely matters in a scene.

questions.correct_answer: (B) accepting, treating it as the price of focus while warning against trusting it where misses are costly.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the finding 'should not be taken to mean that attention is simply defective' and proposes changing tasks and signals, not training attention away.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the finding matters 'less because of its surprise value' than for what it exposes, and paragraph 4 draws practical lessons for roads and warning signals.
option_rationales.D: The driver example in paragraph 3 shows attention excluding something that matters a great deal, and paragraph 4 warns against relying on it where misses are costly.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 calls selectivity 'the price of focus' and says the price is usually low, but advises against relying on 'the conviction that we would have seen it' where the cost of missing is high. The attitude is acceptance with a practical caution.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the warning about high-stakes settings as general alarm about attention.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is stated in the opening sentences of the final paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following design decisions best reflects the lesson drawn in the final paragraph?

options.A: Asking pilots how confident they are that they would spot an unexpected obstacle, and grounding those who report low confidence.
options.B: Training drivers to widen their attention so that they take in the whole visual field at once rather than one part of it.
options.C: Fitting a machine with an alarm that halts the task in progress, so that an operator is not relied on to glance at a light.
options.D: Placing a warning light directly in the operator's line of sight, on the grounds that anything plainly in view will be noticed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Fitting a machine with an alarm that halts the task in progress, so that an operator is not relied on to glance at a light.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'We are poor judges of what we would notice', so self-reported confidence is the conviction the author warns us not to rely on.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says a mind that admitted everything in the visual field 'would be overwhelmed'; the author does not propose abolishing selectivity.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 shows that a figure in the middle of the scene, facing the camera, goes unseen; being in view does not guarantee being noticed, so this rests on the very assumption the author rejects.

questions.explanation: The final paragraph says that where misses are costly we should design 'on the assumption that attention is already spoken for'. An alarm that interrupts the task does not depend on spare attention, so it fits the lesson.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the line-of-sight option because it seems to make the warning hard to miss, forgetting that the gorilla was in plain view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option sounds sensible and is refuted only by applying the opening experiment.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'conviction and correctness have come apart' means that

options.A: how sure people feel about these memories no longer tracks how accurate the memories are.
options.B: people remember the shocking event correctly but feel unsure about the details surrounding it.
options.C: people grow steadily less confident in these memories as the memories become less accurate over the years.
options.D: each memory splits into a true core and an invented portion, which the person can readily tell apart.

questions.correct_answer: (A) how sure people feel about these memories no longer tracks how accurate the memories are.

option_rationales.B: This reverses the passage: people are most certain of the surrounding details, 'the room, the messenger, the coffee cup', which are the ones that drift.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the later, changed accounts are given 'with complete assurance', so confidence does not fall as accuracy does.
option_rationales.D: The passage says people cannot tell: the woman feels 'that her present memory is the true one' even when shown her earlier account.

questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts 'accuracy' with 'the confidence and vividness with which they are held'. Saying conviction and correctness have come apart means the two no longer go together: confidence stays high while accuracy falls.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the two must move together, so that falling accuracy would bring falling confidence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the first half of the same sentence.

questions.question: The example of the woman who concedes that she wrote the earlier account suggests that

options.A: people readily give up a vivid memory once they are shown a written record that contradicts what they now recall.
options.B: evidence that a memory has changed need not shake the feeling that its present version is the authentic one.
options.C: she has knowingly revised her story over the years so as to make it more dramatic when telling it to others.
options.D: accounts written in the shock of the moment are less reliable than those formed after a period of calm reflection.

questions.correct_answer: (B) evidence that a memory has changed need not shake the feeling that its present version is the authentic one.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says she concedes writing the account 'while continuing to feel that her present memory is the true one', so she does not give the memory up.
option_rationales.C: The passage describes her later account as given 'with complete assurance' and explains change by unwitting reconstruction; nothing suggests deliberate embellishment.
option_rationales.D: The passage treats the early account as the check against which later ones are found to have changed, and says later versions are reconstructions; nothing suggests the early record is the weaker one.

questions.explanation: She accepts the documentary evidence yet still feels her present memory is true. The example shows that recognising a discrepancy does not dislodge the sense of authenticity, which paragraph 3 then explains: 'the most recent reconstruction is the one that feels like the original'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a rational person shown the evidence would revise the memory, and so choosing the first wrong option.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the concession together with what she continues to feel.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the final paragraph in the passage?

options.A: It turns to a separate subject, the use of memory as evidence in courts, for which the earlier paragraphs have not prepared the reader.
options.B: It withdraws the earlier claim that flashbulb memories are often inaccurate, in the light of evidence that emotion strengthens memory.
options.C: It grants a real effect of emotion on memory and shows that the grant leaves the main argument standing.
options.D: It offers readers a reliable technique for telling their accurate flashbulb memories apart from their inaccurate ones.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It grants a real effect of emotion on memory and shows that the grant leaves the main argument standing.

option_rationales.A: Courts are never mentioned; the remark about memory 'used as evidence' generalises the passage's own conclusion rather than opening an unprepared topic.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph keeps the claim: it says the proudly recalled details 'are precisely the peripheral ones', which emotion lets blur, and ends by restating that vividness is a weak guide to truth.
option_rationales.D: No technique is offered; the paragraph explains why the most vivid details are the least trustworthy, which is a caution, not a method.

questions.explanation: The paragraph opens with a concession ('None of this means that strong feeling has no effect on memory'), notes that emotion sharpens central detail, then shows that the details people are surest of are peripheral, so the concession does not rescue them. It ends by generalising the lesson.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the opening concession as a retreat from the thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: Students must see how the central and peripheral distinction turns the concession back in favour of the thesis.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: Emotion may improve memory for the features of an experience that were central to it.
options.B: Repeated retelling of an event can make a reconstructed version of it feel like the original memory.
options.C: A person can accept that her earlier account differs from her present one without ceasing to trust the present one.
options.D: How vivid a memory is and how certain its owner feels give no indication at all of whether it is true.

questions.correct_answer: (D) How vivid a memory is and how certain its owner feels give no indication at all of whether it is true.

option_rationales.A: Supported by paragraph 4: 'there is reason to think that emotion sharpens memory for whatever is central to an experience'. The hedge in the passage matches the hedge 'may'.
option_rationales.B: Supported by paragraph 3: each retelling is 'less a replay than a reconstruction, and the most recent reconstruction is the one that feels like the original'.
option_rationales.C: Supported by paragraph 2: the woman concedes she wrote the earlier account 'while continuing to feel that her present memory is the true one'.

questions.explanation: The final sentence says vividness and certainty 'are weaker guides to its truth than we are inclined to believe'. A weaker guide is still some guide, so the claim that they give no indication at all overstates the passage. The other three statements are each found in the text.
questions.common_misconception: Rejecting the hedged statement about emotion because it seems to cut against the thesis, and accepting the extreme statement because it sounds like the thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported option is an exaggeration of the author's own conclusion, while one supported option looks like a counterpoint; telling them apart needs attention to degree.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: describing the biological processes through which memories that are seldom used gradually decay in the brain.
options.B: recommending that people give up memory aids so that their minds can edit stored information more efficiently.
options.C: questioning the belief that an ideal memory would keep everything, by showing how forgetting helps memory work.
options.D: arguing that the fear of forgetting in old age is unfounded, since most memory loss turns out to be beneficial.

questions.correct_answer: (C) questioning the belief that an ideal memory would keep everything, by showing how forgetting helps memory work.

option_rationales.A: The passage describes no biological processes and says forgetting looks 'less like decay than like editing'.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no recommendation about memory aids; its conclusion is only that the capacity to forget is 'part of what makes memory useful'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the losses of 'brain injury or dementia are not editing but damage', so the author does not dismiss fears of decline.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 names the assumption 'that an ideal memory would keep everything', paragraphs 2 and 3 show why forgetting is useful, and paragraph 4 limits the claim. The correct answer captures the target and the method.
questions.common_misconception: Overextending the thesis to all memory loss, which the final paragraph explicitly blocks.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is announced in paragraph 1 and restated at the end.

questions.question: The example of recalling every parking space one has ever used serves to

options.A: show that people with very complete recall are unusually good at everyday tasks such as finding their cars.
options.B: demonstrate that most forgetting is caused by the brain running short of room in which to store information.
options.C: suggest that memories of places are forgotten more readily than memories of faces.
options.D: illustrate how holding every memory with equal force would bury the one that is needed.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate how holding every memory with equal force would bury the one that is needed.

option_rationales.A: The passage says such recall is described 'less as a pleasure than as a burden'; the example shows a cost, not a skill.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the problem 'would not be a shortage of information but a surplus of it', which is the reverse of a storage shortage.
option_rationales.C: Places and faces are two parallel illustrations of the same point; the passage never compares how quickly they are forgotten.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 uses the parking spaces to make the point that 'the memory you needed would be buried among the memories you did not'. The example illustrates the cost of total retention.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the point of the thought experiment and reading it as a claim about storage capacity.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated two sentences after the example.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the account of forgetting given in paragraph 3?

options.A: A library that withdraws books from its shelves once readers report that they contain factual errors.
options.B: A library that sends rarely borrowed books to a distant store, keeping much-borrowed titles on the open shelves.
options.C: A library that shelves every book it has ever owned in the main hall, arranged strictly in order of arrival.
options.D: A library that destroys a share of its old books at random each year to free space for new acquisitions.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A library that sends rarely borrowed books to a distant store, keeping much-borrowed titles on the open shelves.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 makes accessibility depend on 'past use', not on accuracy; withdrawing books for error is a different principle.
option_rationales.C: This is the keep-everything memory of paragraph 2, where nothing is moved back, which the author presents as the problem rather than the solution.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 describes memories becoming 'harder to reach' according to how often they are used; random destruction is neither selective by use nor a matter of reduced access.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 compares memory to a filing system that keeps frequently consulted files near at hand and moves the rest 'to the back', betting that past use predicts future use. Moving rarely borrowed books to a store keeps them but makes them harder to reach, on the same bet.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the random-destruction library because it involves losing books, which seems like forgetting, while ignoring that the forgetting in the passage is selective by use and a matter of reduced access rather than loss.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two features must both match: selection by frequency of use, and reduced access rather than destruction.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Failing to recall a name at an important moment can be a genuine loss even when the forgetting comes from a sound design.
options.B: The memory losses caused by dementia are best understood as an extreme form of the useful editing that all memories perform.
options.C: A memory that held on to everything would be more useful, though less comfortable to live with, than the one we have.
options.D: Because forgetting is the price of a sensible policy, the cost of any particular memory lapse is more apparent than real.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Failing to recall a name at an important moment can be a genuine loss even when the forgetting comes from a sound design.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says such losses 'are not editing but damage', so the author explicitly rejects this view.
option_rationales.C: The last sentence says 'A memory that never let go would be a worse memory, not a better one'; the author denies that total retention is more useful.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls the forgotten name 'a real cost, even if it is the price of a sensible policy', which contradicts the claim that such costs are only apparent.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a system 'well designed on average' does not serve every case, and that the forgotten name is 'a real cost, even if it is the price of a sensible policy'. The correct answer restates this.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that defending forgetting as useful commits the author to calling every lapse harmless.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option draws a natural but wrong conclusion from the 'sensible policy' phrase.

questions.question: According to the passage, when chess pieces are arranged at random,

options.A: strong players recall them more accurately than real positions, since no familiar habits mislead them.
options.B: strong players reconstruct the positions little better than beginners do.
options.C: neither group can reconstruct a single piece of the position after it has been removed.
options.D: beginners outperform masters, because the masters try to force the pieces into familiar patterns.

questions.correct_answer: (B) strong players reconstruct the positions little better than beginners do.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the masters' advantage 'largely disappears'; nothing suggests they do better with random positions than with real ones.
option_rationales.C: The passage says the advantage disappears, not that everyone fails completely; novices manage 'a handful' even of real positions.
option_rationales.D: The passage says masters 'do little better than beginners', not worse, and gives no account of masters imposing patterns.

questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 1 says that with random arrangements 'the masters' advantage largely disappears, and they do little better than beginners'.
questions.common_misconception: Over-reading the result into a reversal of the masters' advantage.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of one sentence.

questions.question: The author calls the random-position result 'more instructive' than the first result most probably because it

options.A: shows that beginners could become strong players more quickly by studying random positions instead of real games.
options.B: proves that skill at chess depends entirely on perception and not at all on calculation.
options.C: reveals that the memory of strong players fails when they are given only a few seconds to look at a board.
options.D: rules out the explanation that masters simply have a greater capacity to store pieces in memory.

questions.correct_answer: (D) rules out the explanation that masters simply have a greater capacity to store pieces in memory.

option_rationales.A: The passage draws no lesson about training on random positions; paragraph 4 says learners need 'a great many cases', which in context means real ones.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'perception is not the whole of expertise' and that 'Masters still calculate', so the word entirely contradicts the author.
option_rationales.C: Masters are given the same few seconds in both conditions and succeed with real positions; the time limit is not what changes.

questions.explanation: If masters merely had better memories, they should excel with any arrangement. Their advantage vanishing with random positions shows the advantage depends on meaningful configurations, which paragraph 2 makes explicit: 'not a larger store for holding pieces but a different way of seeing them'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option claiming skill rests entirely on perception, which pushes the inference beyond what the author allows.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is an inference from the contrast of two results; one wrong option overstates the conclusion.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, 'knowledge that has been absorbed into perception' refers to

options.A: learning that now shapes what the specialist sees, without having to be called up step by step.
options.B: facts the specialist has forgotten that resurface without warning when she is under pressure.
options.C: a mysterious faculty that works independently of anything the specialist has studied or practised.
options.D: rules that the specialist silently recites to herself while she looks over an image or a board.

questions.correct_answer: (A) learning that now shapes what the specialist sees, without having to be called up step by step.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage concerns forgotten facts or pressure; the knowledge is in constant use, shaping 'what is seen in the first place'.
option_rationales.C: This is the account of intuition that paragraph 3 calls 'tempting' and then replaces; the author denies that it stands apart from knowledge.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the knowledge 'no longer needs to be consulted', which excludes reciting rules.

questions.explanation: The phrase is glossed in the same sentence: the knowledge 'no longer needs to be consulted, because it shapes what is seen in the first place'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the author's view with the view of intuition as a mysterious faculty the author sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is glossed in the rest of the sentence.

questions.question: On the passage's account, an experienced radiologist shown an image of a rare condition unlike any she has studied would be most at risk of

options.A: recognising the condition at once, because trained perception carries over to every image in her field.
options.B: performing exactly as a novice would, since her skill rests only on a larger memory for images.
options.C: forming a quick and confident first impression that turns out to be wrong.
options.D: failing to form any impression of the image until she had worked through written diagnostic rules.

questions.correct_answer: (C) forming a quick and confident first impression that turns out to be wrong.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 limits the trained eye to 'the territory that trained it'; a case unlike those it learned from is exactly where it is said to fail.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 rejects the idea that expertise is 'a larger store', and the passage says the risk is misrecognition, not a return to novice performance.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the trained eye responds 'within a second or two'; nothing suggests it falls silent on unfamiliar cases, and the risk named is speed, not hesitation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a pattern 'recognised instantly can also be misrecognised instantly' and that with 'a case unlike those it has learned from' the trained eye's 'speed becomes a liability rather than an asset'. A rare, unfamiliar image is such a case.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming expertise transfers across a whole field, ignoring the limit the author sets in the final sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Applying the final qualification to a new case; the tempting wrong option uses the radiology example of paragraph 3.

questions.question: According to the passage, while an interval is passing, the sense of how long it is lasting depends largely on

options.A: how pleasant or unpleasant the person finds the activity that fills the interval.
options.B: how much attention is being paid to the passing of time itself.
options.C: how many distinct memories the events of the interval are laying down.
options.D: how old the person is and how routine the rest of his life has become.

questions.correct_answer: (B) how much attention is being paid to the passing of time itself.

option_rationales.A: The passage contrasts boredom with absorption as states of attention; pleasantness as such is never given as the factor.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 makes the number of distinct memories the basis of the judgement made 'Looking back', not of the judgement made while the interval passes.
option_rationales.D: Age and routine are used in paragraph 3 to explain the retrospective complaint about years, not the felt length of an interval in progress.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'While an interval is passing, our sense of its length depends largely on how much attention we pay to time itself'.
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up the two kinds of judgement and choosing the memory-based factor.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence; the main wrong option belongs to the other judgement.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the middle-aged complaint that the years go faster

options.A: shows that the felt passage of a single afternoon speeds up steadily as people grow older.
options.B: is mistaken, because older people in fact keep more distinct memories of each year than young people do.
options.C: concerns how a past year looks as a whole, not how its hours feel while they are being lived.
options.D: arises because adults pay closer attention to clocks and calendars than young people usually do.

questions.correct_answer: (C) concerns how a past year looks as a whole, not how its hours feel while they are being lived.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'Few people find that a particular afternoon passes faster at fifty than at fifteen', which contradicts this.
option_rationales.B: The passage suggests the reverse: adult life has 'fewer firsts' and a routine year 'leaves less behind', and it does not call the complaint mistaken.
option_rationales.D: Attention to time governs the judgement made while an interval passes; the passage explains the complaint by remembered duration, not by attention.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The complaint is almost always retrospective' and contrasts the unchanged afternoon with last year 'viewed as a whole'. The complaint is about remembered duration.
questions.common_misconception: Applying the attention mechanism, which belongs to experienced duration, to a retrospective complaint.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attention wrong option is tempting because attention is the passage's first mechanism.

questions.question: In the last sentence, the quotation marks around 'really' serve to

options.A: cast doubt on the idea that there is one true fact about how long an experience felt.
options.B: express scorn for people who believe that novelty can be used to lengthen their lives.
options.C: signal the author's view that remembered duration is truer than the duration felt at the time.
options.D: show that the word is quoted from the cheerful advice that the author criticises earlier in the paragraph.

questions.correct_answer: (A) cast doubt on the idea that there is one true fact about how long an experience felt.

option_rationales.B: The author does question that advice in the preceding sentences, but the marked word concerns 'how long something' felt, and the sentence explains it with 'as though there were only one answer'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'there is no obvious reason to prefer one of these measures over the other', so the author ranks neither as truer.
option_rationales.D: Nothing indicates that the advice used this word; the marks flag a doubtful assumption in ordinary speech, explained by 'as though there were only one answer'.

questions.explanation: The sentence ends 'as though there were only one answer'. Having shown that duration is judged in two ways that can disagree, the author marks 'really' to question the assumption of a single true felt duration.
questions.common_misconception: Linking the marks to the nearby criticism of cheerful advice rather than to the clause that explains them.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options draw on genuine content of the paragraph and must be separated from what the marks themselves do.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the explanation offered in paragraph 3 for why the years seem to pass faster in middle age?

options.A: Middle-aged adults habitually plan further ahead than adolescents do, and many of them say that they spend more of their time thinking about the future.
options.B: Middle-aged adults report that individual afternoons pass at much the same rate as they did when they were adolescents.
options.C: Travellers returning from a varied holiday judge it to have lasted longer than a routine week at work of the same length.
options.D: Adults whose lives remain as full of first experiences as in youth report the same speeding up of the years as adults with routine lives.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Adults whose lives remain as full of first experiences as in youth report the same speeding up of the years as adults with routine lives.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 already lists 'how far ahead people habitually plan' among changes that 'probably play a part'; showing that another factor is present does not show that routine plays no role.
option_rationales.B: This matches what paragraph 3 says about afternoons and supports treating the complaint as retrospective, so it does not weaken the explanation.
option_rationales.C: This illustrates the principle that distinct memories lengthen remembered duration, on which the explanation rests, so it strengthens rather than weakens it.

questions.explanation: The explanation is that routine adult life, with 'fewer firsts', leaves fewer distinct memories, so years seem brief. If adults with as many firsts as the young feel the same speeding up, the proposed cause is absent while the effect remains, which undercuts it directly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the planning option because it names a rival factor, without noticing that the passage already accepts several factors and that a co-existing cause does not remove this one.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that only a case with the cause absent and the effect present tests the explanation; the rival-factor wrong option is the classic trap.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Mind wandering is better understood as a symptom of unhappiness than as its cause, contrary to what researchers at first believed.
options.B: Training in attention should be abandoned, since every attempt to suppress the wandering mind is futile and does real harm.
options.C: The opposed verdicts on mind wandering largely reflect the different occasions studied; its worth depends on when it occurs and whether it is noticed.
options.D: Mind wandering is chiefly productive work on plans and unfinished problems, and its costs have been exaggerated by narrowly designed experiments.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The opposed verdicts on mind wandering largely reflect the different occasions studied; its worth depends on when it occurs and whether it is noticed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says only that wandering 'may be as much a symptom of unhappiness as its cause', a point used to unsettle one argument; it is a detail, and the option hardens it into a claim the author does not make.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 redirects training rather than abandoning it, aiming 'to make wandering more visible to the wanderer', and calls abolition only 'probably unachievable and possibly harmful'.
option_rationales.D: This is the second interpretation reported in paragraph 2; the author says 'Each interpretation' makes the same mistake, and accepts that the costs on demanding tasks are real.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the author's thesis: both interpretations treat wandering 'as though it were one thing with one value', when their evidence comes from 'different occasions'. Paragraph 4 replaces the question with 'not whether the mind should wander but when, and with what awareness'. The correct answer combines the diagnosis and the proposal.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the second, more sympathetic interpretation in paragraph 2 for the author's own view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The longest paragraph presents a view the author rejects; the main point requires separating reported views from the author's and combining paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, researchers began to study mind wandering directly by

options.A: asking people at the end of each day to estimate how often their minds had drifted.
options.B: measuring the errors people made while reading or driving under laboratory conditions.
options.C: recording the solutions that came to people unbidden while they were in the shower or out walking.
options.D: interrupting people at random moments and asking what they had been thinking about.

questions.correct_answer: (D) interrupting people at random moments and asking what they had been thinking about.

option_rationales.A: The passage describes interruptions at random moments, not end-of-day estimates; this method is never mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Errors in reading and driving are mentioned in paragraph 2 as findings linked to wandering, not as the method that first studied wandering directly.
option_rationales.C: Unbidden solutions appear in paragraph 2 as part of the case for the benefits of wandering, not as a research method.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'When researchers began to study these lapses directly, by interrupting people at random moments in their day and asking what they had been thinking about'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a detail from paragraph 2 that concerns findings rather than method.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author's remark about a person who is worried implies that

options.A: a link between mind wandering and low mood does not by itself show that wandering makes people unhappy.
options.B: the studies that linked wandering with low mood were badly conducted and ought to be set aside.
options.C: worried people perform better than others on tasks that demand continuous attention.
options.D: mind wandering is always produced by unhappiness and never contributes to it in any way.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a link between mind wandering and low mood does not by itself show that wandering makes people unhappy.

option_rationales.B: The author accepts the association, reported 'in some studies', and questions only the direction of cause, not the quality of the research.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage compares the task performance of worried and untroubled people.
option_rationales.D: The author says wandering 'may be as much a symptom of unhappiness as its cause', which allows that it can also be a cause; the words always and never go beyond this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces the example with 'Nor does the link with low mood settle the matter': worry could produce both the bad mood and the wandering. The point is that the correlation leaves the direction of cause open.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'may be as much a symptom ... as its cause' into a claim that wandering is only a symptom.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the hedge exactly; the main wrong option overstates it.

questions.question: Which of the following outcomes of a course in attention training would the author regard as most successful?

options.A: A trainee now lets her thoughts roam freely during important meetings, on the chance that unbidden solutions may come to her there.
options.B: A trainee still lets her thoughts drift while gardening but now notices quickly when they drift in a meeting she needs to follow.
options.C: A trainee no longer lets her thoughts drift on any occasion, whether at work, at lectures or at home.
options.D: A trainee feels happier than before because she now spends more of her waking time thinking about her future plans.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A trainee still lets her thoughts drift while gardening but now notices quickly when they drift in a meeting she needs to follow.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 treats drifting during a demanding event one has chosen to attend as 'a cost'; a meeting she must follow is such an occasion.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the goal 'should not be to abolish wandering', calling that aim 'probably unachievable and possibly harmful'.
option_rationales.D: The author's goal for training is awareness of 'which kind of occasion she is in'; mood and time spent planning are not the measure of success the author proposes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 sets the goal of training as making wandering 'more visible to the wanderer, so that she can tell which kind of occasion she is in'. The trainee who drifts freely in an undemanding activity but catches herself in a demanding one fits that goal exactly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the trainee who never drifts, which matches the first interpretation's remedy but not the author's.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches one reported view or one detail; only the correct answer fits the author's stated goal.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the two bodies of research 'are, for the most part, looking at different occasions'?

options.A: Errors made while driving are more dangerous than errors made while reading, so lapses at the wheel matter more.
options.B: Studies reporting costs were run mainly in laboratories, while studies reporting benefits were often run in everyday settings.
options.C: People report that their minds wander more often when they are worried than when they are content.
options.D: A survey of the research finds that studies reporting costs and studies reporting benefits mostly used tasks of very similar difficulty.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A survey of the research finds that studies reporting costs and studies reporting benefits mostly used tasks of very similar difficulty.

option_rationales.A: This compares the seriousness of two costs and says nothing about whether the cost and benefit studies examined different kinds of task.
option_rationales.B: This describes another difference in the occasions studied, so if anything it supports the claim that the two literatures look at different situations.
option_rationales.C: This concerns the link with mood discussed later in paragraph 3, not where the evidence for costs and benefits comes from.

questions.explanation: The author's claim is that cost studies used demanding tasks and benefit studies used undemanding ones, so their verdicts differ because their occasions differ. If both used tasks of similar difficulty, the difference in verdicts could not be explained this way, and the claim fails.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the laboratory option because it mentions the two literatures, without seeing that it adds a further difference and so fits the claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The strongest wrong option names a methodological contrast that sounds like a challenge but actually supports the author.

questions.question: The comparison of a test to a thermometer in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that tests, like thermometers, are precise instruments that schools ought to use more often.
options.B: show that the effects of a test can be measured accurately only when a week has passed since it was taken.
options.C: capture the common assumption that testing records learning without changing it, which the passage goes on to reject.
options.D: illustrate how a student's anxiety rises during an examination much as a temperature rises during a fever.

questions.correct_answer: (C) capture the common assumption that testing records learning without changing it, which the passage goes on to reject.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the finding does not support the conclusion that 'schools should simply test more'; the image is introduced in order to be challenged.
option_rationales.B: The one-week interval belongs to the experiment in paragraph 2 and has nothing to do with the thermometer image.
option_rationales.D: The passage uses the thermometer for an instrument that measures without altering, not for rising anxiety; anxiety is a separate point in paragraph 4.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says a test, like a thermometer, 'is supposed to leave the thing it measures unchanged', then calls this understanding possibly 'false', since retrieval 'changes the memory'. The image states the belief under attack, and the final sentence turns it around.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the image as endorsing tests because the passage ends by praising a kind of testing.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence that introduces the image.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the advantage of retrieval practice was long overlooked partly because

options.A: measurements taken soon after study could make rereading look at least as effective as recall.
options.B: students who practised recall concealed their gains from researchers because they were anxious about being tested.
options.C: rereading produces stronger memories in the short run, which later decay into confidently held errors.
options.D: researchers regarded tests as too unpleasant to be worth studying as a method of learning.

questions.correct_answer: (A) measurements taken soon after study could make rereading look at least as effective as recall.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage says students concealed anything; anxiety appears only in paragraph 4 as a risk of high-stakes tests.
option_rationales.C: The passage says rereaders 'often do as well or better' at first; it never says their memories turn into errors, and confident errors are linked in paragraph 4 to uncorrected recall.
option_rationales.D: The unpleasantness of recall is offered in paragraph 3 to explain why students avoid it, not why researchers overlooked it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that after a few minutes 'the rereaders often do as well or better' and that the advantage of retrieval 'is easily hidden by the timing of the measurement, which may be one reason why it was overlooked'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the unpleasantness of recall, which explains students' choices, to the question of why the effect was overlooked.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options combine real passage elements in wrong causal roles.

questions.question: Which of the following study routines best matches the practice the author recommends?

options.A: A student sits one long, formally graded examination at the end of term, whose marked scripts are never returned to her.
options.B: After each chapter, a student shuts the book, writes out what she remembers and then checks her account against the text.
options.C: A student reads each chapter three times over, until every sentence feels familiar and slides past without effort.
options.D: A student answers practice questions from memory every evening but never looks up whether her answers were right.

questions.correct_answer: (B) After each chapter, a student shuts the book, writes out what she remembers and then checks her account against the text.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 warns that a high-stakes test 'followed by no feedback' may teach little; the recommended practice is 'frequent, low-stakes' recall.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says this feeling of fluency 'is readily mistaken for mastery'; rereading is the method the passage contrasts unfavourably with recall.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 requires each attempt to be 'followed by a chance to check', and warns that an uncorrected wrong answer 'may itself be strengthened'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 recommends 'frequent, low-stakes attempts to recall, each followed by a chance to check, built into ordinary study'. Writing out what one remembers after each chapter and checking it meets every element.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the daily practice questions, which satisfy frequency and recall but omit the check the author insists on.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option meets two of the three conditions; the solver must hold all three.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that what strengthens memory is 'the effort of retrieval, not the apparatus of examination'?

options.A: Students who reread a passage felt more confident about a coming test than those who practised recall, although a week later they remembered less of it.
options.B: Students who sat a formal, high-stakes examination reported feeling far more anxious than students who practised recall at home with their books closed.
options.C: Students who received feedback after each attempt at recall remembered more a week later than students who attempted the same recall without any feedback.
options.D: Answering recall questions improved memory a week later only when done under formal examination conditions, and not when done in an informal, ungraded session.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Answering recall questions improved memory a week later only when done under formal examination conditions, and not when done in an informal, ungraded session.

option_rationales.A: This restates the finding of paragraph 3 about confidence and fluency; it is consistent with the author and irrelevant to the effort versus apparatus claim.
option_rationales.B: This fits paragraph 4's warning that high-stakes tests provoke anxiety and says nothing about which element produces the memory benefit.
option_rationales.C: This agrees with the author's insistence on 'a chance to check'; it does not suggest that formal examination conditions are what matters.

questions.explanation: The claim credits the effort of recalling, not the formal trappings of a test. If the same recall effort helps only when done under formal examination conditions and not in an ungraded session, the apparatus is doing the work, which directly contradicts the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the feedback option because it adds a condition to the benefit, without noticing that the author already requires feedback.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every wrong option is consistent with the passage; only the correct answer separates effort from apparatus and comes out against the author.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The benefit of retrieval practice may fail to appear in a test given only a few minutes after study.
options.B: Attempting to recall material benefits memory only when the learner succeeds in producing the right answer.
options.C: A learner's confidence at the end of a study session can be a misleading guide to what the session achieved.
options.D: Students who are left to choose their own method of study will seldom choose to practise recall.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Attempting to recall material benefits memory only when the learner succeeds in producing the right answer.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says that tested 'a few minutes later, the rereaders often do as well or better', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'a learner's own sense of how well a session went is an unreliable guide to how much it achieved', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says recall is effortful and unpleasant, 'which is presumably why students left to themselves so rarely choose it', so the author agrees.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'What strengthens memory is the effort of retrieval', not its success, and recommends 'attempts to recall, each followed by a chance to check', which presupposes that attempts may fail and still be worth making; paragraph 3 even counts it a feature of recall that 'it exposes gaps'. Paragraph 4 also says a wrong answer recalled confidently 'may itself be strengthened', so retrieval acts on whatever is retrieved. The statement that recall helps only when it succeeds conflicts with all of this.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the unsupported statement as one the author would accept because it sounds like a sensible caution, without connecting it to the claim that the effort of retrieval, not its success, does the work.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported statement is plausible in itself and can be rejected only by linking it to one clause of paragraph 4.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how vivid news reporting manufactures public fear of dramatic accidents that are in fact very unlikely to happen.
options.B: argue that resources for safety should be allocated strictly in proportion to the number of deaths each hazard is expected to cause.
options.C: argue that public fear of some hazards partly expresses defensible values, while warning that such fear still needs to be examined.
options.D: show that expert rankings of hazards are mistaken and that policy should defer to the rankings the public prefers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) argue that public fear of some hazards partly expresses defensible values, while warning that such fear still needs to be examined.

option_rationales.A: Reporting appears only in paragraph 4 as one source of distortion; the passage is chiefly about the values dread can express, so this is too narrow.
option_rationales.B: This is the experts' view reported in paragraph 1, which paragraph 2 says has 'less than its confidence suggests'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says public fear should not be treated 'as a verdict', so deferring to lay rankings reverses the author's position.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that features such as consent, catastrophe and fairness make dread partly a matter of values, not arithmetic; paragraph 4 adds that 'None of this makes dread a reliable guide' and that fear must be taken apart. The correct answer holds both halves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the experts' view because it opens the passage, or the reporting point because it is vivid.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis and its qualification are both stated outright, and each wrong option is clearly one-sided or narrow.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following makes a hazard feel more frightening?

options.A: Its being placed on people by others rather than accepted by them through their own choice.
options.B: Its being so familiar from everyday life, like driving, that people rarely stop to think about it.
options.C: Its producing deaths a few at a time, spread out over many years, rather than all at once.
options.D: Its having been studied for a long time by experts who publish their estimates of the danger.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Its being placed on people by others rather than accepted by them through their own choice.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says people drive 'without a second thought', so familiarity is linked to a lack of fear, not to dread.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says risks feel worse when they 'could kill many people at once rather than a few at a time', the reverse of this option.
option_rationales.D: The passage never connects expert study or published estimates with how frightening a hazard feels.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists the features: risks feel worse 'when they are imposed rather than chosen', when they could kill many at once, when effects are delayed or invisible, and when creators and bearers differ.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the 'many at once' feature.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of one listed feature.

questions.question: The example of the rock climber who objects to a factory's chemical release serves mainly to

options.A: support the claim that legal systems ought to prohibit factories from releasing any untested chemicals into rivers.
options.B: show that a preference which ignores expected deaths can rest on a coherent distinction between risks that are chosen and risks that are imposed.
options.C: illustrate the kind of error in arithmetic that leads ordinary people to rank hazards differently from experts.
options.D: demonstrate that recreational activities such as climbing are in fact more dangerous than most forms of industrial pollution.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that a preference which ignores expected deaths can rest on a coherent distinction between risks that are chosen and risks that are imposed.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no legal proposal; it notes only that legal systems already recognise the distinction between consent and imposition.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the climber 'is not confused about arithmetic', so the example is offered against this reading.
option_rationales.D: The passage compares no levels of danger; the example is about consent, not about which activity kills more people.
