questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the climber 'is drawing a distinction between a risk she has consented to and one that has been placed on her by others', a moral distinction. The example shows that a ranking at odds with fatality counts need not be foolish.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about which activity is more dangerous.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentences that follow the example state its function directly.

questions.question: A town council meets strong local opposition to a planned waste incinerator whose expected effect on health is small. Which course of action is most consistent with the author's recommendation?

options.A: Sort the objections into those about consent, fairness or control, which deserve weight, and those that stem only from a recent alarming story.
options.B: Proceed as planned, since the expected toll is small and residents' fear is a problem of perception to be corrected with figures.
options.C: Abandon the incinerator, since strong public dread is itself a verdict that a council has a duty to accept without question.
options.D: Show residents vivid images of road accidents in the town, so that their fears are redirected toward the hazards that really matter.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Sort the objections into those about consent, fairness or control, which deserve weight, and those that stem only from a recent alarming story.

option_rationales.B: This applies the experts' view of paragraph 1, which the author says has 'less than its confidence suggests'; it treats fear as mere noise.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 explicitly rejects treating public fear 'as a verdict'; the author wants it examined, not obeyed.
option_rationales.D: The author does not recommend countering salience with more salience; paragraph 4 asks for fear to be taken apart into its components.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the sensible response is 'neither to dismiss public fear as noise nor to treat it as a verdict' but to 'take it apart', asking which components reflect values deserving 'a hearing in policy' and which reflect only 'the salience of a recent and alarming image'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking one of the two extremes the author rejects, or a clever communication tactic the author never proposes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options match positions the passage discusses; the solver must apply the middle course of paragraph 4 to a new case.

questions.question: According to the passage, later attempts to reproduce the early findings on choice overload

options.A: revealed that the early experiments had been badly designed and that their reported results could not be trusted at all.
options.B: consistently confirmed the early findings, although the effects they found were somewhat smaller than those first reported.
options.C: showed that larger assortments always made people more likely to buy, so that the early findings were simply reversed.
options.D: found the effect in some cases, found nothing in others, and sometimes found that larger assortments increased buying.

questions.correct_answer: (D) found the effect in some cases, found nothing in others, and sometimes found that larger assortments increased buying.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim about faulty design; it says only that later results varied with conditions.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 calls the picture 'far more mixed' and says the effect sometimes vanished or reversed, which is not consistent confirmation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says larger assortments 'sometimes' increased buying; the option turns one of three reported outcomes into an invariable rule.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'sometimes the effect appeared, sometimes it vanished, and sometimes larger assortments made people more likely to buy.'
questions.common_misconception: Overreading the mixed results as a simple reversal or as a verdict on the early work.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer restates one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the description of the novice as 'drowning' suggests that the novice

options.A: is enjoying the large selection even more than the wine enthusiast who is merely browsing.
options.B: cannot find a suitable fund because most of the forty funds on offer are poor choices.
options.C: is overwhelmed because he has no way of sorting the options in front of him.
options.D: is taking a dangerous financial risk by choosing a pension fund without professional advice.

questions.correct_answer: (C) is overwhelmed because he has no way of sorting the options in front of him.

option_rationales.A: The contrast with 'browsing' marks the novice's experience as a burden, not a greater pleasure, so this reverses the image.
option_rationales.B: The passage says the difference between the two choosers is 'whether the chooser has a way of sorting them', not the quality of the funds.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 locates the difficulty in sorting the options, not in financial danger or the absence of an adviser.

questions.explanation: The sentences that follow explain the image: 'The number of options is the same.' and 'What differs is whether the chooser has a way of sorting them'. The novice lacks settled preferences and a means of comparison.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'drowning' as a comment on financial danger rather than on being overwhelmed.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor is glossed by the next two sentences.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the author would regard shortening a restaurant's menu as most clearly justified when

options.A: diners take longer to order than the staff would like, even though they are satisfied with what they choose.
options.B: most diners are regular customers who know the kitchen well and have firm preferences among its dishes.
options.C: the dishes differ along many dimensions, such as price, cuisine and spice, that diners find hard to compare.
options.D: most of the dishes on it are mediocre or are barely distinguishable from one another.

questions.correct_answer: (D) most of the dishes on it are mediocre or are barely distinguishable from one another.

option_rationales.A: The passage never treats the speed of choosing as a reason to cut; its concern is the chooser's burden and satisfaction.
option_rationales.B: Such diners resemble the enthusiast of paragraph 3, whom a policy of reduction would 'deprive' of what she values.
option_rationales.C: Hard comparison is a condition under which large sets burden people, but for that problem paragraph 4 prescribes organising options, not cutting them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'Cutting still has its place, particularly when most of the options are poor or nearly identical.' For difficulties of comparison, it recommends structure instead: grouping, defaults, narrowing in stages.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the hard-to-compare menu because it matches a condition for overload, without noticing that the author's remedy for it is organisation.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option names a real overload condition from paragraph 3; the solver must connect it to the right remedy in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's account of choice overload?

options.A: Several shops that trimmed their product lines in the hope of raising sales found that their sales fell instead.
options.B: Shoppers faced with many nearly identical products were more satisfied after the range was reduced to a few.
options.C: Novices given forty pension funds sorted by risk level, with a default marked, were as reluctant to choose as novices given the same funds unsorted.
options.D: Wine enthusiasts reported enjoying a shop with forty bottles on offer more than a shop that offered only eight.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Novices given forty pension funds sorted by risk level, with a default marked, were as reluctant to choose as novices given the same funds unsorted.

option_rationales.A: The author already doubts that reduction is a general cure, so this finding is consistent with the passage.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 concedes that cutting helps when options are 'nearly identical', so this agrees with the author.
option_rationales.D: This fits the author's view that enthusiasts value abundance, so it supports rather than weakens the account.

questions.explanation: The author claims that what burdens novices is 'the absence of structure' and that grouping and defaults can remove the difficulty (paragraph 4). If structure made no difference, the account of what drives overload, and its remedy, would be undermined.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a finding that sounds critical of trimming but actually agrees with the author.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are consistent with the passage in different ways; the solver must test each against the specific causal claim.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pull of an anchor on people's estimates persists even when

options.A: the quantity being estimated is one that participants deal with every day and know well.
options.B: participants have seen for themselves that the number was produced at random.
options.C: participants have been told the correct answer to the question before giving their estimate.
options.D: the anchor is mentioned only after participants have already written down their estimates.

questions.correct_answer: (B) participants have seen for themselves that the number was produced at random.

option_rationales.A: The passage discusses estimates of quantities people 'do not know'; familiar quantities are not mentioned.
option_rationales.C: The passage never describes participants who know the answer; the effect concerns quantities people 'do not know'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 describes anchors given 'first', before the estimate; nothing is said about anchors that come afterwards.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The effect survives when participants have watched the number being produced at random, when they are told it is meaningless, and when they are paid for accuracy.'
questions.common_misconception: Guessing from general knowledge instead of the list in paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: A direct paraphrase of one clause in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The image of 'a reluctant traveller who halts at the nearest acceptable station' serves to

options.A: convey the older account's claim that anchoring results from adjustment that stops early for want of effort.
options.B: show that people resist arbitrary numbers until they are given a financial reason to care about being accurate.
options.C: express the author's own preferred explanation of how numbers supplied by negotiators and sellers distort judgement.
options.D: suggest that anchors work by making certain recollections more readily available than others to the person judging.

questions.correct_answer: (A) convey the older account's claim that anchoring results from adjustment that stops early for want of effort.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the effect survives payment for accuracy, so the image cannot mean that money overcomes the anchor.
option_rationales.C: For supplied anchors paragraph 4 says 'the evidence favours the selective account', so this image belongs to a view the author largely rejects for that case.
option_rationales.D: That is the second explanation in paragraph 3, which does not treat the anchor as a starting point at all.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 sets out the older account: people 'adjust away from it ... but they stop too soon', and 'anchoring is a failure of effort'. The traveller image dramatises that early stop.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a vivid image as the author's verdict when it illustrates a reported view.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the reported older account from the author's conclusion in paragraph 4.

questions.question: On the selective account described in paragraph 3, a person given an anchor and asked to deliberate longer before estimating would most likely

options.A: give the same estimate but feel less confident in it, because the extra search would raise doubts about the anchor.
options.B: disregard the anchor entirely, because longer reflection would reveal that the number was arbitrary and irrelevant.
options.C: stay close to the anchor, because the extra search would mostly turn up more evidence consistent with it.
options.D: move further from the anchor, because the extra time would let adjustment continue beyond its usual stopping point.

questions.correct_answer: (C) stay close to the anchor, because the extra search would mostly turn up more evidence consistent with it.

option_rationales.A: The selective account says the search gathers confirming evidence, which gives no reason to expect growing doubt.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the effect survives even when people are told the number is 'meaningless', so knowing it is arbitrary is not enough.
option_rationales.D: This is the prediction of the older account in paragraph 2; paragraph 3 says that on the selective view 'effort is no cure'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'a more diligent search conducted in the same direction only gathers more of the same evidence.' Longer deliberation therefore leaves the estimate pulled toward the anchor.
questions.common_misconception: Applying the older account's remedy to the newer account.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both accounts are described in neighbouring paragraphs and make opposite predictions about effort.

questions.question: A buyer receives an opening price from a seller. Which piece of advice best follows from the author's conclusion?

options.A: Before responding, ask the seller to explain in detail how the figure was reached, so that its basis becomes clear.
options.B: Before responding, take time to reflect carefully on the figure offered and decide calmly how far to move away from it.
options.C: Treat the figure as an obviously self-interested number that cannot influence the judgement of an experienced buyer.
options.D: Before responding, set out the reasons that might make the figure a poor guide to what the item is worth.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Before responding, set out the reasons that might make the figure a poor guide to what the item is worth.

option_rationales.A: Asking the seller to justify the figure invites reasons in its favour from the party who chose it, the opposite of the search against the anchor that paragraph 4 recommends ('asking what would make it wrong').
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the remedy for supplied anchors is 'not to think harder about the number one has been handed'; careful reflection on the figure is the remedy the author sets aside.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says anchoring appears 'among amateurs and professionals alike', so experience gives no such protection.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that for anchors 'supplied by others' the remedy is 'to think deliberately against it, by asking what would make it wrong'. Listing reasons the price might be a poor guide does exactly that.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing careful reflection, which sounds prudent but is the remedy the author rejects for supplied anchors, or asking for justification, which feeds confirming evidence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options sound like sensible negotiating advice; rejecting them needs both the mechanism in paragraph 3 and the remedy in paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, on tasks that are very hard, many people

options.A: rate themselves below average compared with others while still overestimating their own scores.
options.B: judge both their own scores and their standing relative to others accurately, because poor results are obvious.
options.C: rate themselves above average compared with others while underestimating how well they have actually done.
options.D: give much wider ranges for their estimates than they do on easy tasks, so that their overprecision disappears.

questions.correct_answer: (A) rate themselves below average compared with others while still overestimating their own scores.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says people on hard tasks still overestimate their own scores, so their judgements are not accurate.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 gives this as the pattern on easy tasks; on very hard tasks 'the pattern reverses'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says overprecision appears 'on easy and hard questions' and shows no tendency to reverse.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: on very hard tasks 'many people will rate themselves below average ... while still overestimating their own scores'.
questions.common_misconception: Swapping the easy-task and hard-task patterns.
questions.difficulty_reason: One sentence holds the answer, though the reversal needs careful reading.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that if people knew as much about others' performance as about their own, then

options.A: the tendency to give ranges that are too narrow when forecasting uncertain quantities would largely disappear.
options.B: the reversals between easy and hard tasks in how people rank themselves against others should become smaller.
options.C: people would place themselves above others on every kind of task, whatever its level of difficulty.
options.D: people would stop overestimating their own scores on very hard tasks such as juggling or composing verse.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the reversals between easy and hard tasks in how people rank themselves against others should become smaller.

option_rationales.A: Overprecision is treated separately in paragraph 4 as 'different'; paragraph 3's explanation is not applied to it.
option_rationales.C: Better information about others would remove the distortion, not produce uniform overplacement; the option has no basis in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 explains judgements of relative standing by the lack of information about others; it offers no such explanation for overestimating one's own score.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says judgements of others 'are pulled toward a vague middle' because people know more about themselves than about others, and that this produces the reversals in placement. Remove the information gap and that cause of the reversals weakens.
questions.common_misconception: Extending paragraph 3's explanation to overestimation or overprecision, which it does not cover.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option concerns the same hard tasks but a different form of overconfidence.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the claim that overconfidence is 'the most pervasive of the biases' is best described as

options.A: sceptical, because the claim treats as a single tendency several that behave quite differently.
options.B: dismissive, because the author holds that people are not in fact overconfident in any systematic way.
options.C: neutral, because the author only reports competing definitions of the term without judging any of them.
options.D: approving, because the author goes on to show how overconfidence underlies most of the other biases.

questions.correct_answer: (A) sceptical, because the claim treats as a single tendency several that behave quite differently.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 describes overprecision as robust across tasks and people, so the author accepts that real overconfidence exists.
option_rationales.C: The author does judge: lumping the forms together made the phenomenon seem 'more universal and more mysterious than it is'.
option_rationales.D: The author says the claim 'conceals' a great deal and never shows that other biases depend on overconfidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the claim 'conceals' much and that treating three things as one distorts the picture; paragraph 4 concludes that 'a single word has been doing the work of three'. The author doubts the claim without denying overconfidence.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking scepticism about a sweeping claim for denial of the phenomenon.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option overstates the author's doubt into outright denial.

questions.question: The passage makes each of the following claims about overprecision EXCEPT that it

options.A: appears among specialists in a field as well as among novices who know little about it.
options.B: reverses on very hard tasks in much the same way as the tendency to rank oneself above others.
options.C: is reduced only a little when forecasters are simply urged to be more humble about their estimates.
options.D: does particular harm when projects are budgeted against ranges too narrow to include the outcome.

questions.correct_answer: (B) reverses on very hard tasks in much the same way as the tendency to rank oneself above others.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says it appears 'among novices and among specialists', so the passage does make this claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'telling forecasters to be humble rarely widens their intervals much', which is this claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says it 'does most harm in planning' for exactly this reason, so the claim is made.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'Overprecision is different. It shows no comparable tendency to reverse'. The other three statements are all made in paragraph 4.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying the reversal pattern of paragraph 2 over to overprecision.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four options concern paragraph 4, and the false one borrows a pattern from paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, a problem 'dressed in unfamiliar clothes' is one that

options.A: is described in technical language that the participants were not taught to understand.
options.B: involves colleagues from a professional background different from that of the participants.
options.C: demands a decision far more urgent than any of the cases that were discussed in the session.
options.D: takes a form unlike the examples through which the biases were taught in the workshop.

questions.correct_answer: (D) takes a form unlike the examples through which the biases were taught in the workshop.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about unfamiliar terminology; the difficulty is recognising a familiar bias in a new setting.
option_rationales.B: The phrase concerns how a problem is presented, not who is involved; paragraph 2 explains it as the lack of a textbook label.
option_rationales.C: Urgency is never mentioned; the contrast drawn in paragraph 2 is between tidy labelled examples and messy real ones.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains the image: a textbook problem is 'labelled' by its chapter, while a real decision 'comes with no such label'. An unfamiliar dress is a presentation unlike the training examples.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the metaphor as a claim about people or language rather than about the form of the problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: The next paragraph glosses the metaphor.

questions.question: The contrast between a textbook problem about sunk costs and a real decision about a struggling project serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the tendency of people to see biases in their colleagues while believing their own reasoning to be sound.
options.B: argue that textbooks on decision-making ought to replace their tidy examples with problems drawn from real work.
options.C: explain why skill at recognising a bias in labelled examples does not readily carry over to actual decisions.
options.D: show that real decisions carry higher stakes than textbook problems and therefore produce stronger biases.

questions.correct_answer: (C) explain why skill at recognising a bias in labelled examples does not readily carry over to actual decisions.

option_rationales.A: That is the 'subtler obstacle' introduced afterwards in paragraph 2 as a separate point, not the point of this contrast.
option_rationales.B: No recommendation about textbooks is made; the contrast diagnoses a difficulty rather than proposing a reform.
option_rationales.D: The passage says real decisions lack labels and are messy; it never claims that their stakes make biases stronger.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 concludes from the contrast that 'Recognising a pattern in a tidy example is a different skill from noticing it in a messy situation, and teaching the first does not automatically produce the second.'
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the contrast to the neighbouring point about seeing bias in others.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is a genuine claim of the same paragraph, made for a different purpose.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a manager who has just attended a typical workshop on biases is most likely to

options.A: become more doubtful of their own conclusions than of the conclusions their colleagues reach.
options.B: make noticeably fewer errors on new problems that arise in the course of their own work.
options.C: become better at naming biases in colleagues' reasoning while remaining confident in their own judgement.
options.D: lose the ability to recognise biases even in the textbook examples used during the session.

questions.correct_answer: (C) become better at naming biases in colleagues' reasoning while remaining confident in their own judgement.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says instruction can sharpen the opposite asymmetry, leaving one's 'own sense of seeing clearly' undisturbed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says this is what participants 'far less often do', so the passage suggests the reverse.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says participants leave 'able to define the biases and to spot them' in descriptions, so recognition is gained, not lost.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says participants can spot biases 'in descriptions of other people's reasoning', and paragraph 2 says instruction can supply 'a vocabulary for diagnosing colleagues without unsettling one's own sense of seeing clearly'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that training produces the self-doubt it was meant to produce.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining a point from paragraph 1 with the asymmetry in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author's claim that redesigning procedures has 'the practical merit of not depending on each person's ability to catch themselves in the act' rests on which assumption?

options.A: That training built around practice and feedback never produces improvements that outlast the session in which it is given.
options.B: That procedures such as collecting independent estimates can still work as intended when the people following them are as biased as before.
options.C: That people who follow such procedures for long enough will gradually learn to recognise their own biases without help.
options.D: That biases are a form of ignorance which a well-designed procedure can cure by supplying the people involved with the knowledge they lack.

questions.correct_answer: (B) That procedures such as collecting independent estimates can still work as intended when the people following them are as biased as before.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 concedes that some such training has produced lasting improvements, so the author's case does not assume the opposite.
option_rationales.C: If the merit depended on members becoming self-aware, it would depend on individual self-correction, which is exactly what the author says it avoids.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 attributes the 'ignorance' view to approaches that inform individuals; procedural approaches treat bias as a 'standing feature' to be managed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says such a committee 'does not need its members to have become wiser. It builds the correction into the routine.' For this to be a merit, the procedure must deliver its correction even though individual tendencies are unchanged.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the extreme claim about training, which the passage's concession rules out, or the ignorance view, which belongs to the rival approach.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must separate what the argument needs from what it rejects or concedes, across paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, intuitive expertise can be learned only where

options.A: cues in the environment are linked to outcomes and practice comes with quick, clear feedback.
options.B: judgements are made rapidly and without the interference of slow and deliberate reasoning.
options.C: experts are able afterwards to explain step by step how they reached each of their judgements.
options.D: the person has received formal instruction in the theory that underlies the judgements of the field.

questions.correct_answer: (A) cues in the environment are linked to outcomes and practice comes with quick, clear feedback.

option_rationales.B: Speed describes how intuition works, not a condition for learning it; paragraph 2 names regularity and feedback.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 names only regular cues and quick feedback as conditions, and the nurse of paragraph 1, who 'cannot say how they knew', was nonetheless right.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 names only regular links between cues and outcomes and practice with quick feedback; formal instruction in theory is never mentioned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The environment must contain regularities that link cues to outcomes, and the person must have had extensive practice with feedback quick and clear enough to reveal whether a judgement was right.'
questions.common_misconception: Adding a requirement, such as being able to explain the judgement, that the passage does not impose.
questions.difficulty_reason: The two conditions are stated together in one sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Intuitions in medicine generally merit trust, whereas the intuitions of those who forecast markets generally do not.
options.B: Experienced professionals' intuitions are usually right and should be preferred to formulas whenever the two disagree.
options.C: The confidence an expert feels in a judgement is a useful, though imperfect, sign of whether the judgement is correct.
options.D: Whether an intuition merits trust depends on whether the setting in which it was formed allowed valid patterns to be learned.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Whether an intuition merits trust depends on whether the setting in which it was formed allowed valid patterns to be learned.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 denies that intuition should be sorted by profession, noting that one clinician's intuitions may be valid for some tasks and not others.
option_rationales.B: This is the view of one camp in paragraph 1, which the author treats as partial; paragraph 3 says intuition can be confident and wrong.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'Subjective certainty therefore tells us almost nothing about whether to trust a judgement', which contradicts this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 sets out the conditions for learning, paragraph 3 says the environment, not confidence, tells us whether to trust a judgement, and paragraph 4 concludes that the question is 'whether the conditions for learning it were ever present'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the medicine versus markets contrast, which uses the passage's examples but turns them into the profession-based rule the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option generalises the paragraph 2 examples in a way paragraph 4 rules out.

questions.question: A weather forecaster has spent many years issuing next-day forecasts for a region whose weather follows recognisable patterns, checking each forecast against the next morning's weather. On the passage's account, this forecaster

options.A: deserves trust in a given forecast only if he feels highly confident that this particular forecast is correct.
options.B: cannot be trusted unless he is able to explain the reasoning by which he arrived at each of his forecasts.
options.C: has had the conditions needed to develop intuitions about next-day weather that deserve a measure of trust.
options.D: can be trusted to the same degree when making long-range predictions about the region's climate over the next decade.

questions.correct_answer: (C) has had the conditions needed to develop intuitions about next-day weather that deserve a measure of trust.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the feeling of knowing is produced 'whether or not the underlying patterns are valid', so confidence is not the test.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2's test is regularity and feedback, not the ability to explain; the nurse of paragraph 1 'cannot say how they knew' and was still right.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the same expert may have valid intuitions for one task and not another; decade-long outcomes arrive too slowly to give feedback.

questions.explanation: The case meets both conditions of paragraph 2: regular links between cues and outcomes, since the region's weather follows recognisable patterns, and quick, clear feedback, since each forecast is checked the next morning.
questions.common_misconception: Extending trust from a short-feedback task to a long-feedback one.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must apply both conditions and the task-specific point of paragraph 4.

questions.question: The claim that subjective certainty 'tells us almost nothing about whether to trust a judgement' implies which of the following?

options.A: Confidence in a judgement grows only in environments that lack regular links between cues and outcomes.
options.B: Experts who feel certain of a judgement are usually less accurate than experts who feel some doubt about it.
options.C: Wherever experts feel confident, their intuitive judgements should be replaced by simple statistical formulas.
options.D: Two experts who are equally sure of their judgements may nonetheless deserve very different degrees of trust.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Two experts who are equally sure of their judgements may nonetheless deserve very different degrees of trust.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says confidence 'grows with familiarity' in any environment, which is why the nurse and the forecaster can feel equally sure.
option_rationales.B: The passage says confidence carries almost no information about accuracy, not that it is inversely related to accuracy; this turns 'nothing' into a negative signal.
option_rationales.C: The author recommends judging the learning environment, not replacing intuition wherever confidence appears; the passage makes no such prescription.

questions.explanation: If certainty tells us 'almost nothing', equal certainty cannot settle equal trust; the nurse and forecaster of paragraph 3 'can feel as sure' as each other yet differ in whether their patterns are valid.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'tells us nothing' as 'tells us the opposite'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is a subtle overstatement; the distinction between no signal and a reversed signal is fine.

questions.question: The remark that 'descriptions do not fall from the sky' (paragraph 2) means that

options.A: descriptions are imposed by people in authority, so that listeners seldom feel able to question the way they are put.
options.B: descriptions are chosen by speakers, and the choice often reveals something about what the speaker knows or believes.
options.C: descriptions used in experiments are carefully designed by researchers so that each pair is exactly equivalent.
options.D: descriptions take on their meaning only once the listener already knows the numbers that they are describing.

questions.correct_answer: (B) descriptions are chosen by speakers, and the choice often reveals something about what the speaker knows or believes.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph is about speakers' choices carrying information, not about authority or listeners' reluctance to question.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 refers to how ordinary speakers such as doctors choose descriptions; experimental design is not the point here.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the paragraph makes meaning depend on prior knowledge of the numbers; the point concerns what the choice of frame reveals.

questions.explanation: The next sentences explain the phrase: 'Somebody chooses them, and the choice is rarely arbitrary', and the doctor's choice of frame reflects her view of the treatment.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the idiom as a point about authority or experimental design.
questions.difficulty_reason: The idiom is glossed by the two sentences that follow it.

questions.question: On the account given in paragraph 2, a listener told that a glass is 'half empty' could reasonably infer that

options.A: the glass probably held more at some earlier point and has since been partly emptied.
options.B: the glass now holds noticeably less than half of what it could hold when full.
options.C: the speaker would like the listener to refill the glass before anyone else drinks from it.
options.D: the speaker is gloomy by temperament and tends to see the worst side of most situations.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the glass probably held more at some earlier point and has since been partly emptied.

option_rationales.B: The phrases 'half empty' and 'half full' describe the same quantity; the inference concerns the glass's history, not a smaller amount.
option_rationales.C: The passage attributes no request to the speaker; this reads a purpose into the frame that the paragraph does not discuss.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 explains the choice of 'half empty' by the reference point from which the quantity moved, not by the speaker's temperament.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: speakers 'describe a quantity in terms of the reference point from which it has moved: a glass that was full and has been partly drunk is more often called half empty'. So 'half empty' signals a glass that was fuller before.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the everyday idea that 'half empty' signals pessimism, which the passage does not use.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option draws on a familiar saying; the solver must stay with the passage's reference-point explanation.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 functions in the argument chiefly to

options.A: defend the principle that logically equivalent descriptions must produce the same choice in every situation.
options.B: show that the classic demonstration was badly designed and that its findings should not be relied upon.
options.C: refute the information account by showing that framing effects persist even when the frame is plainly arbitrary.
options.D: limit the information account by showing that it explains framing effects only in part.

questions.correct_answer: (D) limit the information account by showing that it explains framing effects only in part.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a rational participant should set the inference aside only when the frame is visibly arbitrary; a requirement binding in every situation is far broader than that.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph questions how to interpret the findings, not whether the original experiments were sound.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the account 'explains a good deal of the phenomenon'; the persistence of a residue limits it rather than refutes it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'This rehabilitation should not be pushed too far', notes a residue that survives arbitrary framing, and ends 'it does not explain all of it'. That is a qualification, not a refutation.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a qualification for a refutation because the paragraph reports evidence against the account.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option gets the direction of the paragraph right but its strength wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the account of framing given in paragraph 2?

options.A: Participants who read the word 'die' reported stronger unease than those who read the word 'live', even when told the figures matched.
options.B: Framing effects were just as large when the descriptions were assigned by a visible coin toss as when a speaker chose them.
options.C: Speakers who favoured a treatment mostly cited survival figures, and listeners hearing survival figures more often guessed the speaker favoured it.
options.D: Speakers describing a quantity rarely chose their words according to whether the quantity had recently risen or fallen.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Speakers who favoured a treatment mostly cited survival figures, and listeners hearing survival figures more often guessed the speaker favoured it.

option_rationales.A: This supports the residual 'plain pull of words' described in paragraph 4, a reaction the information account does not explain, so it does not strengthen that account.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the information account predicts smaller effects when the frame is visibly arbitrary, so equal effects would weaken it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2's account requires that speakers 'describe a quantity in terms of the reference point from which it has moved'; this finding denies that regularity.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 rests on two links: speakers' choice of frame reflects their view ('A doctor who believes a treatment is worth trying tends ... to speak of the patients it saves'), and listeners read that choice. The correct answer confirms both links.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the emotional-reaction finding because it concerns framing, without seeing that it supports the rival residue.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option supports a different part of the passage; separating it requires tracking which mechanism belongs to which paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's position on the principle that logically equivalent descriptions should produce the same choice?

options.A: It is a fair standard only where the choice of description carries no information about the speaker or the situation.
options.B: It is a sound requirement of rationality that ordinary people violate whenever they respond differently to equivalent descriptions.
options.C: It is irrelevant to real choices, because framing effects in the end reflect only the emotional pull of particular words.
options.D: It is mistaken, because two descriptions that seem equivalent never really express the same proposition at all.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It is a fair standard only where the choice of description carries no information about the speaker or the situation.

option_rationales.B: This is the received view of paragraph 1, which the author argues 'is less obvious than it looks' because frames usually carry information.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 treats the pull of words as a 'residue', and the author says the information account 'explains a good deal of the phenomenon'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says 'The equivalence holds between the propositions'; what differs is the acts of uttering them, so this distorts the author's distinction.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that when the frame is 'visibly arbitrary' a rational participant 'should set it aside', and paragraph 5 says whether responding to a frame is a lapse 'depends on whether, in the situation at hand, the frame was a signal'. The principle binds only where the frame signals nothing.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the received view, or overcorrecting by denying that the propositions are equivalent.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options echo positions or phrases in the passage; the correct answer needs the conditional verdict assembled from paragraphs 3, 4 and 5.

questions.question: According to the passage, the first research tradition infers the shortcuts the mind uses from

options.A: comparisons of how well simple and complex rules predict cases that have not yet been seen.
options.B: the pattern in which people's answers depart from answers fixed by logic or probability.
options.C: people's own reports, given after the task, of the rules they believe they followed.
options.D: studies of the environments in which human judgement first developed and is now exercised.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the pattern in which people's answers depart from answers fixed by logic or probability.

option_rationales.A: Prediction of new cases is the rival tradition's concern in paragraph 2, not the method of the first tradition.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 describes no self-reports; the tradition infers shortcuts from errors on problems with fixed answers.
option_rationales.D: Attention to environments is what the rival tradition demands, and paragraph 5 says neither tradition has studied them carefully.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'record the ways in which their answers depart from it, and infer from the pattern of departures the shortcuts the mind must be using.'
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the rival tradition's interests to the first tradition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The method is set out in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the 'frame' to which the rival tradition objects is best understood as

options.A: the statistical techniques that researchers in the first tradition use to analyse their experimental results.
options.B: the theory that human judgement developed in environments quite unlike those of the modern laboratory.
options.C: the wording in which experimental problems are put to participants, which shapes the answers they give.
options.D: the practice of judging responses against logical and probabilistic norms on problems built in the laboratory.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the practice of judging responses against logical and probabilistic norms on problems built in the laboratory.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says nothing about data analysis; its complaint is that rules should be judged 'against the environment in which it is used'.
option_rationales.B: That idea belongs to the rival tradition's own argument, so it cannot be the frame the rival tradition objects to.
option_rationales.C: This reads 'frame' in the sense of a framing effect; the paragraph objects to how rules are judged, not to the wording of problems.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 contrasts 'the findings' with 'the frame' and then explains the objection: rules must be judged against their environments, whereas the laboratory problems of paragraph 1 judge them against fixed logical or probabilistic answers.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'frame' in its technical sense from framing research.
questions.difficulty_reason: The word has a familiar technical sense in this field that does not fit here.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, in a small and noisy sample, a model that weighs many cues will predict new cases worse than a simple rule because it

options.A: neglects the one or two strong cues on which the simple rule relies for its predictions.
options.B: contains more systematic error than the simple rule, which it trades for a gain in flexibility.
options.C: fits accidental features of the sample at hand that will not recur in the new cases.
options.D: requires more computation than people with limited capacity are able to carry out reliably.

questions.correct_answer: (C) fits accidental features of the sample at hand that will not recur in the new cases.

option_rationales.A: The complex model 'weighs many cues carefully', which includes the strong ones; its fault is fitting accidents, not neglecting good cues.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the reverse: the simple rule accepts 'a little systematic error' in exchange for less sensitivity to noise.
option_rationales.D: Limited capacity is the first tradition's reading of ignoring information; paragraph 2's explanation concerns fitting noise, not human limits.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the complex model 'will fit the data at hand closely, including its accidents', and paragraph 3 says the simple rule gains by a 'large reduction in sensitivity to noise'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing which model carries the systematic error.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option inverts the trade described in paragraph 3.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 serves chiefly to

options.A: argue that the case for simple rules appeals to a different normative standard rather than discarding normative standards.
options.B: concede that the first tradition was right to judge responses by their agreement with a probabilistic calculation.
options.C: establish that simple rules are superior to elaborate models in every environment in which decisions are made.
options.D: show that the rival tradition, by praising heuristics that ignore information, rejects the authority of statistical theory.

questions.correct_answer: (A) argue that the case for simple rules appeals to a different normative standard rather than discarding normative standards.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says that standard is replaced by another, 'accuracy in predicting cases one has not yet seen', which it calls the one that 'matters'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 limits the advantage to 'small, noisy samples' and says the exchange is 'often' good, so a claim about every environment overstates it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the advantage of simple rules 'is itself a result of statistical theory', which is the opposite of this claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'it is worth seeing why it does not abandon the idea of a norm' and explains that praise for frugal heuristics replaces 'one standard ... with another'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the paragraph as hostile to statistical norms because it defends heuristics that ignore information.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options invert the paragraph's relation to the norm or overstate its scope; the correct answer needs its exact move.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the rival tradition is best described as

options.A: endorsement of its main claims, including its further claim that minds reliably select whichever rules best suit the task at hand.
options.B: acceptance of its critique of how errors are judged, with doubt that people have been shown to fit their rules to their tasks.
options.C: approval of its success in refuting the first tradition's findings about the systematic errors people make.
options.D: rejection of its argument, on the ground that ignoring information is in the end a symptom of limited mental capacity.

questions.correct_answer: (B) acceptance of its critique of how errors are judged, with doubt that people have been shown to fit their rules to their tasks.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls that claim 'an empirical hypothesis' for which 'the evidence ... is uneven', and says the tradition 'overreaches' in making it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the rival tradition objects 'not to the findings but to the frame', so it has not refuted those findings.
option_rationales.D: That is the first tradition's reading; paragraph 3 calls the rival tradition's point 'sound'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls the rival point 'sound' and paragraph 4 says the tradition 'overreaches' in moving 'from what heuristics can do to what people actually do'. The author accepts the critique and doubts the further claim.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the author's support for one argument as support for all of the rival tradition's claims.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the whole argument: a mixed verdict across paragraphs 2 to 5, with wrong options that are each one-sided.

questions.question: The central argument of the passage is that boredom

options.A: is a state of the same kind as hunger, since both are unpleasant and both disappear once they are satisfied.
options.B: is harmless in most settings, because people can nearly always find some more engaging activity to turn to.
options.C: has become harder for people to tolerate because a constant supply of entertainment is now available to them.
options.D: is better understood as a prompt to change an unengaging activity than as a mere absence of feeling.

questions.correct_answer: (D) is better understood as a prompt to change an unengaging activity than as a mere absence of feeling.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 uses hunger only as a comparison to show that discomfort can serve a purpose; the passage never claims the two are the same kind of state.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says many situations offer no way to act on the signal and that boredom can then turn into 'frustration or something close to despair', so the option contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no comparison with the past; paragraph 4 says distraction 'muffles' the signal, not that tolerance for boredom has declined over time.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 rejects the view of boredom as 'emptiness' and calls it 'an active and often insistent signal' that an activity fails to engage us. Paragraph 2 supports this with the hunger comparison, paragraph 3 qualifies it, and paragraph 4 draws the consequence for how to respond. The correct answer states this thesis.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the hunger comparison, which is only a supporting illustration, as if it were the thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated outright in paragraph 1 and the wrong options are clearly contradicted or out of scope.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that boredom 'curdles into frustration or something close to despair' means that boredom

options.A: turns into a more painful state when the person has no means of responding to it.
options.B: slowly disappears once the person accepts that nothing else can be done.
options.C: is hidden from the person feeling it, who mistakes it for some other emotion entirely.
options.D: becomes a more useful signal the longer a person is prevented from acting on it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) turns into a more painful state when the person has no means of responding to it.

option_rationales.B: The sentence describes boredom becoming worse, into frustration or despair, not fading away; acceptance is never mentioned.
option_rationales.C: Nothing suggests the person misidentifies the feeling; the waiting patient and the delayed passenger are said to 'receive the message'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says a signal is useful 'only when there is some way to act on it', so being unable to act makes it less useful, not more.

questions.explanation: To curdle is to sour or go bad. The sentence says that people who receive the signal 'without being able to respond' find boredom turning into frustration or despair, so the correct answer captures the meaning.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'curdles' as a fading or concealment rather than a souring into something worse.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative verb is explained by the words that follow it in the same sentence.

questions.question: The reference to hunger in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: argue that people should be less worried about boredom than about the physical needs of their bodies.
options.B: suggest that boredom, like hunger, is a bodily need that must be met at regular intervals through the day.
options.C: show that a state can be unpleasant and still have a purpose, as the author claims boredom does.
options.D: illustrate that boredom is a more disagreeable experience than most of the other unpleasant states people know.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that a state can be unpleasant and still have a purpose, as the author claims boredom does.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph does not compare how much concern each deserves; it uses hunger to explain how boredom works, not to rank it.
option_rationales.B: The passage never treats boredom as a bodily need or speaks of regular intervals; the comparison concerns only the purpose of discomfort.
option_rationales.D: No ranking of unpleasantness is made; the point is that hunger's discomfort is 'the means by which it gets us to eat'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says hunger is disagreeable but not a defect, since 'its discomfort is the means by which it gets us to eat', and then 'Boredom works in a similar way'. The comparison supports the claim that boredom's unpleasantness 'is doing work'.
questions.common_misconception: Turning an analogy about function into a claim that boredom is a physical need.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is announced by 'Boredom works in a similar way' immediately after the comparison.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a person who never feels bored because every pause is filled with small distractions as

options.A: more likely than other people to fall into frustration and despair whenever they cannot act on the signal.
options.B: possibly missing information about parts of their life, such as work or routine, that no longer suit them.
options.C: confirming the common view that boredom is an empty space which can be filled with anything at hand.
options.D: having solved the problem that boredom poses, since the unpleasant feeling no longer arises for them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) possibly missing information about parts of their life, such as work or routine, that no longer suit them.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 links despair to being unable to respond to boredom, not to the habit of filling every pause; the option joins two separate points.
option_rationales.C: This is the view paragraph 1 says 'gets the state almost exactly backwards'; the author would not treat such a person as confirming it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such distraction 'does not answer the message; it merely muffles it', so the author would deny that the problem is solved.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says someone who 'reaches for a screen at every lull' may 'never learn what the boredom was pointing at: a job that has stopped stretching them, a routine that has outlived its purpose'. The correct answer paraphrases this, with 'possibly' matching the author's 'may'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about despair, which borrows a real phrase from paragraph 3 but attaches it to the wrong situation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying paragraph 4 while rejecting a wrong option that recombines a phrase from paragraph 3.

questions.question: The passage implies that the commuter in paragraph 2 now takes out her phone mainly because

options.A: the familiar features of the journey set off the action without any present decision by her.
options.B: she decided long ago that the journey was the right time for checking her messages.
options.C: she lacks the firmness of resolve that would allow her to keep the phone in her pocket.
options.D: she has a strong wish to look at it each time she sits down in the carriage.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the familiar features of the journey set off the action without any present decision by her.

option_rationales.B: The passage grants the act 'may have been chosen' at first but says that after many repetitions 'it no longer needs choosing', so the old choice is not the present cause.
option_rationales.C: This is the popular view the author rejects: 'resolve is not what produces the act. The cue is.'
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says she may find the phone in her hand 'before she has formed any wish to look at it', so a present wish is not what drives the act.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the seat, the motion of the carriage and the familiar stretch of the journey 'are enough to bring the hand to the pocket', and ends 'The cue is.' The correct answer restates this.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the original choice as the present cause, though the passage says the act no longer needs choosing.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answered by the last sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: According to the passage, people often find it easier to change their routines after moving house because

options.A: a new home usually brings with it a fresh set of goals and daily reminders of them.
options.B: people who choose to move are generally less attached to their old habits than others are.
options.C: moving house tends to strengthen a person's resolve to make a fresh start in life.
options.D: the cues that used to set off their old behaviour are no longer present in the new setting.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the cues that used to set off their old behaviour are no longer present in the new setting.

option_rationales.A: Goals and reminders belong to the 'motivational' remedy of paragraph 1, which is not how paragraph 3 explains the observation.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about the kind of people who move; it explains the effect through the loss of cues.
option_rationales.C: The author's explanation is that 'the old cues have simply disappeared', not that resolve is strengthened; the option substitutes the motivational view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'the account explains why: the old cues have simply disappeared, and with them much of the pressure to repeat old behaviour.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a motivational explanation that sounds plausible in everyday terms.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Someone habitually eats snacks while watching television each evening and wants to stop. Which approach would the author regard as most promising?

options.A: Writing down each evening the health reasons for cutting back on snacks before switching on the set.
options.B: Promising a friend to resist the snacks and reporting every lapse to that friend the next day.
options.C: Watching in a different room, where no food is kept and the usual armchair is absent.
options.D: Allowing snacks on the weekend only after a full week of successfully resisting them on weekdays.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Watching in a different room, where no food is kept and the usual armchair is absent.

option_rationales.A: Reminding oneself 'why they matter' is the motivational remedy paragraph 1 describes and the author considers a poor tool for a habit.
option_rationales.B: This relies on strengthening the will against the habit, which paragraph 3 says is less effective than changing 'the circumstances that trigger it'.
option_rationales.D: A reward for resistance is still an effort to strengthen will; it leaves the room, the chair and the programme, the cues, unchanged.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'the most effective way to change a habit is often to change the circumstances that trigger it, not to strengthen the will that opposes it'. Moving to another room removes the cues (the chair, the nearby food), just as sitting in a different carriage does in the passage.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a commitment device, which feels practical but works through will rather than through cues.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four options are sensible advice in general; the student must apply the author's specific mechanism.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's account of what a habit is?

options.A: Habits that people form during childhood are much harder to break than the habits they form as adults.
options.B: Strong intentions to stop a routine barely reduce it while its usual setting persists, but a changed setting reduces it sharply.
options.C: Many people who move to a new city report feeling more anxious during their first year in the new place.
options.D: People who write down specific goals are more likely than others to begin and keep up a programme of exercise.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Strong intentions to stop a routine barely reduce it while its usual setting persists, but a changed setting reduces it sharply.

option_rationales.A: The age at which a habit forms has no bearing on whether habits are context-cued responses rather than strong desires.
option_rationales.C: Anxiety after a move is irrelevant to the claim that habits are triggered by cues; the passage uses moving only to show that cues disappear.
option_rationales.D: This supports the role of goals and motivation, which is the popular picture the author argues against, so it does not strengthen the account.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 claims that 'the context itself, rather than any present intention, sets the behaviour going'. A finding that intention makes little difference while the setting stays, and that changing the setting makes a large one, supports both halves of that claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about moving because it mentions a change of place, without checking that it bears on the claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be matched to the precise causal claim; the wrong options are on topic but test nothing about cues versus intentions.

questions.question: According to the passage, conditions such as persistent noise resist adaptation probably because they

options.A: tend to arrive suddenly in a person's life rather than building up by degrees.
options.B: are usually more severe in their effects than the gains to which people adjust.
options.C: cannot be compared with any earlier state in the life of the person affected.
options.D: keep demanding attention instead of settling into the background of experience.

questions.correct_answer: (D) keep demanding attention instead of settling into the background of experience.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about how quickly such conditions arrive; the explanation offered concerns attention.
option_rationales.B: Severity is never compared; paragraph 2 explains the resistance by the fact that such conditions 'keep demanding attention'.
option_rationales.C: Comparison with earlier states is mentioned only for gains that become 'the new normal'; it is not offered as the reason noise resists adaptation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says noise, commuting and chronic pain remain unpleasant 'perhaps because they keep demanding attention and never settle into the background of experience'. The correct answer restates this; 'probably' in the stem matches the passage's 'perhaps'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible real-world reason (severity, suddenness) in place of the one the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the remark that the flat line 'describes almost nobody in it' implies that

options.A: the average wellbeing of such groups has usually been misreported in the studies that measure it.
options.B: individuals who return to their earlier level after a major life event are very rare in such studies.
options.C: an average showing no change can coexist with large changes, in both directions, for nearly everyone in a group of that kind.
options.D: most people in such studies are unwilling to report honestly how their wellbeing has changed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an average showing no change can coexist with large changes, in both directions, for nearly everyone in a group of that kind.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph does not say the average is wrong; it says a correct average 'can conceal very different individual paths'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph ends by saying only 'a substantial minority do not return', which implies that most do return; the option turns a point about averages into a false claim about rarity.
option_rationales.D: Honesty of reporting is never raised; the problem identified is how results are summarised, not how they are collected.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes a hypothetical group in which 'some people end up much happier and others much less happy', so that the average barely moves. In such a group the flat line fits almost no individual, which is what the correct answer says.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the remark as a general claim that almost nobody returns to baseline, which contradicts the paragraph's own last sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option sounds like the remark itself; the student must notice that the remark is about a hypothetical mixed group.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a person considering a move to escape a persistently noisy flat

options.A: should base the decision mainly on temperament, since it is temperament that fixes how content a person can be.
options.B: has good reason to expect a lasting improvement, since noise is among the conditions people fail to adapt to.
options.C: will find that the benefit of the quieter home fades about as quickly as the pleasure of a higher salary.
options.D: should expect to adapt to the noise in time, so that the trouble and cost of moving are probably not worthwhile.

questions.correct_answer: (B) has good reason to expect a lasting improvement, since noise is among the conditions people fail to adapt to.

option_rationales.A: This is the popular conclusion paragraph 1 says the research does not support, so the author would not offer it as advice.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 contrasts the quick adjustment to a higher salary with the persistence of noise, so treating them alike reverses the passage's distinction.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists persistent noise among conditions that 'resist adaptation stubbornly', and paragraph 4 warns against being discouraged from changing 'the noisy flat'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says noise remains unpleasant 'year after year', and paragraph 4 names 'the noisy flat' among conditions people should not be discouraged from changing. The author would therefore expect leaving it to make a lasting difference.
questions.common_misconception: Applying the set-point idea across the board, which is exactly the overreading the passage criticises.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining paragraph 2's distinction with paragraph 4's practical warning.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 3?

options.A: When the individual paths in such studies are examined, nearly everyone's wellbeing turns out to return close to its earlier level.
options.B: People adjust more slowly to living in a larger house than they do to receiving a substantial rise in salary.
options.C: Average wellbeing tends to rise in the year before a wedding and to fall back gradually in the years that follow it.
options.D: In most groups studied, average wellbeing returns almost exactly to its earlier level within a few years of a major event.

questions.correct_answer: (A) When the individual paths in such studies are examined, nearly everyone's wellbeing turns out to return close to its earlier level.

option_rationales.B: This concerns the unevenness of adaptation discussed in paragraph 2, not the argument about averages in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.C: This describes the timing of an average around one event and says nothing about whether individuals diverge beneath it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 already grants that averages return; its argument is that averages hide individual differences, so confirming the averages leaves that argument untouched.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that a flat average can hide divergent individual paths, and supports this with the claim that individual-level studies find 'a substantial minority do not return'. A finding that nearly every individual returns would remove the evidence that the average is hiding anything.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about averages returning, which sounds like support for set points and so seems to weaken the author, though the author concedes it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option contradicts the author's general sympathies but not the specific argument of paragraph 3; the student must locate exactly what that paragraph claims.

questions.question: According to the information gap account as the passage presents it, people are rarely curious about subjects they know nothing about because

options.A: they hold no earlier beliefs about such subjects that new information might overturn or correct.
options.B: such subjects seem too difficult to them to be worth the effort that learning would require.
options.C: curiosity needs a general appetite for novelty, which wholly unfamiliar subjects fail to satisfy.
options.D: they cannot notice what is missing in a field they are unable to see at all.

questions.correct_answer: (D) they cannot notice what is missing in a field they are unable to see at all.

option_rationales.A: Overturning beliefs plays no part in the passage's account; the explanation turns on noticing an absence.
option_rationales.B: Difficulty and effort are never mentioned; paragraph 1 explains the point by the impossibility of noticing a gap.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the account treats curiosity as 'not a general appetite for novelty', so this reverses the account.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the account explains this 'since we cannot notice a gap in a field we cannot see'. The correct answer paraphrases that clause.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the novelty option because 'appetite for novelty' appears in the paragraph, without noting that the account denies it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of one clause in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author's objection to the reply described in paragraph 3 implies that a good account of curiosity should

options.A: draw its evidence from observing classrooms rather than from studying puzzles, riddles and mysteries.
options.B: describe curiosity in terms of many small gaps closed in succession rather than one large gap.
options.C: be capable of ruling out some patterns of behaviour instead of fitting any pattern after the event.
options.D: treat the wandering kind of curiosity as more important than the kind that seeks a single answer.

questions.correct_answer: (C) be capable of ruling out some patterns of behaviour instead of fitting any pattern after the event.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim about where evidence should come from; classrooms appear only in the practical conclusion of paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: This is the defenders' reply, which the author says preserves the theory only 'at a cost'; the author does not recommend it.
option_rationales.D: The author ranks neither kind; paragraph 4 says 'Both have their place', and the objection concerns how the theory explains, not which kind matters more.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 objects that if 'any movement of attention whatever can be redescribed after the fact as the closing of a gap', the account 'no longer explains anything in particular' and becomes 'a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis'. The implied standard is that a real hypothesis must exclude some possibilities.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the many-small-gaps option because it is the content of paragraph 3, although it is the view being criticised.
questions.difficulty_reason: The student must extract the methodological principle behind the objection rather than restate the objection.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of the kind of curiosity that, in the author's view, the information gap account fits poorly?

options.A: Reading on in a detective novel to learn which of the suspects actually committed the crime.
options.B: Leafing through an old atlas in a second-hand bookshop with no particular place in mind.
options.C: Walking through a museum to find a painting a friend recommended, whose gallery has been forgotten.
options.D: Working steadily through a crossword in order to fill in the answer to the one clue that remains.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Leafing through an old atlas in a second-hand bookshop with no particular place in mind.

option_rationales.A: A 'mystery with a culprit' is named in paragraph 2 as a case where the account 'is at its strongest'.
option_rationales.C: Though it looks like browsing, the visitor is closing a specific, noticed gap, the location of one known painting, which is the case the account handles well.
option_rationales.D: A puzzle with a single solution is a well-defined gap, which paragraph 2 says the account explains well.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the account is weaker for curiosity 'that drifts without a target', as in wandering library shelves, where 'there is no specific question waiting to be answered'. Leafing through an atlas with no destination in mind is of this kind.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the museum visit because it involves wandering, though it is driven by a single definite question.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option disguises a targeted search as browsing; the student must apply the passage's criterion rather than surface features.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the information gap account is best described as

options.A: appreciative of what it explains but doubtful that it accounts for every form of curiosity.
options.B: dismissive, because the account turns curiosity into a vocabulary instead of a genuine hypothesis.
options.C: neutral, setting out the account and the objections of its critics without taking any side between them.
options.D: wholly approving, since it explains both the stimulating effect of partial knowledge and the end of curiosity.

questions.correct_answer: (A) appreciative of what it explains but doubtful that it accounts for every form of curiosity.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says this only of the account as stretched by its defenders; the author calls the unstretched account 'a good theory of the first' kind.
option_rationales.C: The author takes a clear position in paragraph 3, 'It seems more accurate to say that there are at least two kinds', so the stance is not neutral.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the account 'fits some cases far better than others', so the author's approval is plainly not whole.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the account 'has much to recommend it' and lists what it explains; paragraphs 2 and 3 limit its scope to targeted curiosity. The attitude is qualified appreciation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing 'dismissive' because of the sharp phrase 'a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis', which is aimed at the defenders' reply.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires telling apart the author's view of the account from the author's view of one defence of it.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 mainly serves to

options.A: explain why the experience of grief is much harder to study systematically than the experience of dying.
options.B: trace the familiar sequence back to an origin that differs from the use now made of it.
