options.C: argue that the stages of grief have never been observed in any patient or in any bereaved person.
options.D: present evidence that the sequence accurately describes how terminally ill patients respond to their diagnosis.

questions.correct_answer: (B) trace the familiar sequence back to an origin that differs from the use now made of it.

option_rationales.A: No comparison of difficulty is made; the paragraph says only that the shift to grief happened 'largely outside' testing research.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the sequence began as a description of some patients, so it does not deny that the feelings were observed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the sequence was 'drawn from clinical conversations' with such patients but makes no claim that it describes them accurately, and presents no evidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the sequence's current status and then, with 'It began, however', traces it to observations of dying patients and notes its 'migration from the dying to the grieving' and from observations to 'something closer to a timetable'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the reference to clinical conversations as a claim that the model is accurate for dying patients.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'It began, however'.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a bereaved person who feels deep sadness that eases over some months, without anger or bargaining,

options.A: is probably in a state of denial, which the model treats as the first of the five stages of grief.
options.B: is unusual, because most bereaved people report experiencing every one of the named feelings at some point.
options.C: may well be grieving in a way that is common and is not a sign of feelings being avoided.
options.D: will pass through the missing stages later, once the full reality of the loss has finally been faced.

questions.correct_answer: (C) may well be grieving in a way that is common and is not a sign of feelings being avoided.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'Resilience of this kind is not denial in disguise', so the author rejects this reading.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says many people report some of the feelings 'hardly at all', which contradicts the claim that most report every one.
option_rationales.D: This expectation is what paragraph 3 criticises when helpers 'wait for a stage that never arrives'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes people who experience 'intense sorrow that gradually eases over months without passing through anything resembling distinct stages' and says this seems 'for a good number of people' to be 'the ordinary course that grief takes'.
questions.common_misconception: Applying the model's own reading of an absent stage, which the passage presents as the error.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong options restate the model's expectations, which the student must recognise as views the author rejects.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a consequence of treating the stage model as a standard EXCEPT that

options.A: researchers stopped studying grief because the model appeared to have settled the important questions.
options.B: friends or professionals may urge a grieving person to move on to the next stage of the sequence.
options.C: a bereaved person may come to believe that something is wrong with his own reactions to the death.
options.D: a grieving person who does not feel an expected emotion may be told she has not faced her loss.

questions.correct_answer: (A) researchers stopped studying grief because the model appeared to have settled the important questions.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says helpers may 'press a grieving person to move on to the next one', so this is stated.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the son who feels relief 'may wonder what is wrong with him', which is this consequence.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 gives exactly this case: the widow who is not angry 'may be told that she has not yet faced her loss'.

questions.explanation: The three supported options are the widow, the son and the pressing helpers of paragraph 3. Paragraph 1 says only that the model's spread happened 'largely outside' testing research and paragraph 2 refers to grief being 'studied directly'; nowhere does the passage say research stopped.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'happened largely outside the kind of research that might have tested it' as a claim that research ceased.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are drawn directly from paragraph 3; the correct answer is a distortion of a phrase in paragraph 1.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's overall attitude towards the stage model of grief?

options.A: Hostile, regarding the model's popularity chiefly as evidence of how readily the public accepts unsupported ideas.
options.B: Ambivalent, unable to decide whether the research on bereavement supports the model or tells against it.
options.C: Sympathetic, holding that the model's inaccuracy matters little when set against the comfort it has given to many.
options.D: Critical of its use as a norm for how people should grieve, while granting that it once met a genuine need.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Critical of its use as a norm for how people should grieve, while granting that it once met a genuine need.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 explicitly says 'It would be unfair, though, to treat the model's popularity as mere credulity'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the sequence 'has not fared well' when grief is studied directly, so the author is clear about what the research shows.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the harm lies 'less in its inaccuracy' than in its use, but it still describes real harm, and the author wants its fixed order dropped; the author does not excuse the model.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that the sequence is poorly supported and harmful as 'a standard of what everyone ought to feel'; paragraph 4 concedes that giving people words for hidden feelings 'was a real service'. The attitude is critical but fair.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing 'sympathetic' because the author says the harm lies less in inaccuracy than in use, missing that this relocates the criticism rather than softening it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires weighing the concession of paragraph 4 against the critique of paragraphs 2 and 3, and reading the 'less in its inaccuracy' sentence correctly.

questions.question: According to the passage, praise that tells a child about the quality of the work may strengthen interest because it

options.A: feeds the child's sense of competence, which is what made the activity enjoyable.
options.B: removes the child's expectation that drawing will be rewarded again in the future.
options.C: comes unexpectedly and so cannot have been the child's reason for drawing.
options.D: is less tangible than a prize and so is harder for the child to treat as a payment.

questions.correct_answer: (A) feeds the child's sense of competence, which is what made the activity enjoyable.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage says praise removes any expectation; the stated reason concerns the sense of competence.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 gives this reason for the unexpected treat, not for praise about quality; the option transfers one explanation to the other case.
option_rationales.D: Tangibility is mentioned as a condition of the undermining effect, but the passage does not explain the benefit of praise this way.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says such praise 'may even strengthen interest, since it feeds the sense of competence that made the activity enjoyable in the first place'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the reason given for the unexpected treat with the reason given for informative praise, as both appear in one sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is in one clause of paragraph 2, next to a tempting neighbouring clause.

questions.question: A pupil already loves playing the piano. Based on the passage, which of the following is most likely to reduce the pupil's interest in playing?

options.A: Telling the pupil after a recital which passages were played with particular skill and feeling.
options.B: Giving the pupil an unannounced treat in a week when the practice had been especially long.
options.C: Announcing that the pupil will receive a small gift for every hour of practice completed.
options.D: Offering a reward only for practising scales, which the pupil finds tedious, and not for playing pieces.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Announcing that the pupil will receive a small gift for every hour of practice completed.

option_rationales.A: This is praise that conveys information about quality, which paragraph 2 says 'may even strengthen interest'.
option_rationales.B: An unexpected treat 'cannot have been the reason' for practising, so paragraph 2 implies it does not undermine interest.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says rewards cannot crowd out an enjoyment 'that was never there'; the reward is attached to the dull part, not to the playing the pupil loves.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the effect is most reliable when the reward is 'tangible, expected in advance and given for doing the task rather than for doing it well'. A gift announced in advance for each hour of practice meets all three conditions for an activity the pupil already enjoys.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reward for scales because it is a tangible, announced reward, without noticing it targets an activity with no prior interest.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each option must be checked against several conditions spread over paragraphs 2 and 3.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that rewards for a task that is dull at the outset

options.A: will always produce a lasting interest in the task once the necessary skill has been developed.
options.B: can sometimes keep a person at it until growing skill makes the task itself enjoyable.
options.C: work better when they are given for doing the task well than when they are given merely for doing it.
options.D: will reduce interest in the task as soon as the rewards are withdrawn, just as they do for enjoyed tasks.

questions.correct_answer: (B) can sometimes keep a person at it until growing skill makes the task itself enjoyable.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says a reward 'may' keep someone at the task long enough for interest to arrive; 'always' overstates this.
option_rationales.C: The contrast between rewarding the task and rewarding quality belongs to paragraph 2 and is not applied to dull tasks in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says rewards 'cannot crowd out an enjoyment that was never there', so the undermining effect does not apply to dull tasks.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a reward 'may keep someone at a dull task long enough for skill to grow and for the task itself to become absorbing, so that interest arrives because of the incentive'. The correct answer states this hedged possibility.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'may' into 'always', or carrying the undermining effect over to tasks that had no interest to undermine.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is a plausible extension from paragraph 2; the student must keep to what paragraph 3 supports.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the phrase 'converted from play into work and then left unpaid' suggests that the child

options.A: has been made to draw harder and longer than before, so that the activity itself has become tiring.
options.B: comes to enjoy drawing only when other children are drawing too and there is a prize to compete for.
options.C: resents the adults for withdrawing a payment that the child had been led to believe would continue.
options.D: now sees drawing as a job done for the prize, so that without the prize it no longer seems worth doing.

questions.correct_answer: (D) now sees drawing as a job done for the prize, so that without the prize it no longer seems worth doing.

option_rationales.A: Nothing suggests the child is tired; the image is about how the child understands the activity, as paragraph 2 confirms with 'a means to the prize'.
option_rationales.B: Competition with other children is never mentioned; the image concerns the loss of a reward, not rivalry.
option_rationales.C: The passage attributes no resentment to the child; the reduced drawing is explained by a changed view of the activity, not by a grievance.

questions.explanation: The phrase describes an activity that has been turned into paid work and then stripped of its pay; paragraph 2 explains that an expected prize 'invites the child to understand the drawing as a means to the prize'. Once the prize ends, the means has no point.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the image emotionally, as resentment, instead of as a change in how the activity is understood.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor must be connected to the explanation given in paragraph 2.

questions.question: According to the passage, in engineering the term 'strain' refers to

options.A: the relation between a load and the capacity of a body to withstand it.
options.B: the load itself, considered apart from the body that has to bear its weight.
options.C: the deformation that a load produces in the body that is subjected to it.
options.D: the internal force per unit area within a body that is subjected to a load.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the deformation that a load produces in the body that is subjected to it.

option_rationales.A: A relation is one of the senses the word 'stress' takes on in psychology (paragraph 1); it is not the engineering definition of strain.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says stress and strain 'are distinguished from the load itself', so strain is not the load.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 gives this as the engineering meaning of 'stress', from which strain is distinguished.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'stress is distinguished from strain, the deformation that the load produces'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing strain with stress, which is defined in the sentence just before.
questions.difficulty_reason: A definition stated in a single clause of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that borrowing the word 'stress' from engineering was a mistake that the sciences of living things should now correct.
options.B: demonstrate that claims about 'good stress' are false and are promoted mainly by people who have advice to sell.
options.C: explain how the breadth of the term 'stress' allowed researchers in several separate disciplines to discover connections.
options.D: argue that 'stress' is worth keeping but that claims using it must be clear about which sense they rely on.

questions.correct_answer: (D) argue that 'stress' is worth keeping but that claims using it must be clear about which sense they rely on.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says abandoning the word 'would be a mistake', and the author values the breadth the borrowing produced.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the first sense of 'good stress' is 'uncontroversial' and the second 'plausible within limits'; the author criticises a slide between senses, not the claims as such.
option_rationales.C: This is the point of paragraph 4 only, a concession within the argument rather than its purpose, so the option is too narrow.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 show how the word slides between the situation, the reaction and the relation, paragraph 4 rejects abandoning it, and paragraph 5 recommends asking 'which of its meanings is in play'. The correct answer combines the diagnosis, the concession and the recommendation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the paragraph 4 option, which is accurate but covers only one part of the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is true but too narrow and another overstates paragraph 3; the correct answer needs the whole structure.

questions.question: The remark in paragraph 2 that popular discussion 'acquires the authority of the first reading and the scope of the second' implies that such discussion

options.A: gets the effects of reactions right but goes wrong by leaving out the part played by how people interpret their situation.
options.B: borrows a certainty available only when the claim is nearly true by definition and applies it to demanding situations generally.
options.C: is more trustworthy when it concerns people's reactions to demands than when it concerns the demands themselves.
options.D: relies on the standing of experts to support claims that hold good only for the small number of people they have studied.

questions.correct_answer: (B) borrows a certainty available only when the claim is nearly true by definition and applies it to demanding situations generally.

option_rationales.A: The remark concerns moving between the reaction sense and the situation sense; the relational sense based on belief is not what is being combined here.
option_rationales.C: The 'authority' of the reaction reading comes from the claim being 'close to true by definition', which makes it empty rather than trustworthy; the author does not commend it.
option_rationales.D: 'Authority' here means the apparent certainty of the definitional reading, not the standing of experts, and no claim about small samples is made.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the reaction reading 'close to true by definition' (the first reading) and the situation reading 'plainly false as a generalisation' (the second). Discussion that moves between them sounds as certain as the first while claiming as much as the second, which the correct answer states.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'authority' to mean expert standing, or reading 'first reading' as praise.
questions.difficulty_reason: The compressed phrase must be decoded by matching 'first' and 'second' to the three senses set out in the same paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's criticism, in paragraph 3, of advice built on the phrase 'good stress'?

options.A: Most such advice states plainly that it concerns how people interpret their reactions, and it cites studies that test this claim.
options.B: Some demanding situations, such as training for a long race, are widely regarded as experiences worth seeking out.
options.C: Researchers in different disciplines use the phrase 'good stress' in noticeably different ways from one another.
options.D: Physiological reactions to demand improve performance only up to a moderate level and impair it beyond that point.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Most such advice states plainly that it concerns how people interpret their reactions, and it cites studies that test this claim.

option_rationales.B: This is the first sense, which the author already calls 'uncontroversial'; confirming it does not touch the charge that advice slides from it to the third.
option_rationales.C: Varied usage, if anything, supports the author's concern about confusion; it does not show that the advice avoids sliding between senses.
option_rationales.D: This fits the author's description of the second sense as 'plausible within limits', so it is consistent with the criticism rather than damaging to it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 charges that such advice 'slides from the first meaning, which everyone accepts, to the third' and that the third is 'a specific claim requiring specific evidence'. If the advice openly made the third claim and supplied that evidence, neither the slide nor the lack of evidence would hold.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about physiological limits because it sounds like a scientific qualification, when it matches what the author already grants.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options confirm points the author concedes; the student must target the precise charge of sliding without evidence.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 functions in the passage chiefly to

options.A: show that ordinary language cannot be reformed, so the word must simply be accepted as people use it.
options.B: concede that the confusions described in the earlier paragraphs have in practice done very little harm.
options.C: head off an apparently natural conclusion by pointing to a benefit of the word's looseness.
options.D: give an example of a substantive hypothesis about stress that research has since gone on to confirm.

questions.correct_answer: (C) head off an apparently natural conclusion by pointing to a benefit of the word's looseness.

option_rationales.A: The author says abandoning the word is a mistake 'not only because ordinary language is not so easily reformed', and the main reason given is the term's fruitfulness.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says that failing to keep the senses apart 'has cost a good deal of confusion', so the author does not concede that the harm was slight.
option_rationales.D: The link between working conditions and heart disease is offered as a connection the broad term drew attention to, not as a confirmed hypothesis.

questions.explanation: After three paragraphs on confusion, paragraph 4 raises the obvious remedy, 'abandon the word altogether', and rejects it because the term's breadth 'has allowed researchers' in several fields to see connections. It blocks that conclusion before paragraph 5 gives the author's own remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the ordinary-language option, which picks up a reason the author mentions only in passing.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading 'not only because' correctly to see which reason carries the paragraph.

questions.question: According to the passage, the blood sugar version of the resource theory faced the particular difficulty that

options.A: the coordinated replications could not include any measures of blood sugar.
options.B: people who thought willpower was plentiful consumed fewer sweet drinks.
options.C: sweet drinks were found to weaken rather than restore people's self-control.
options.D: effortful thinking seems to alter the brain's total energy use only slightly.

questions.correct_answer: (D) effortful thinking seems to alter the brain's total energy use only slightly.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about what the replications measured; the 'additional difficulty' is a physiological one.
option_rationales.B: The finding about beliefs in willpower is separate and says nothing about consumption of sweet drinks.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says sweet drinks weakened self-control; the difficulty named concerns the brain's energy consumption.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says this version 'met an additional difficulty: effortful thinking appears to change the brain's overall energy consumption only slightly, far too little for the proposed mechanism to work'.
questions.common_misconception: Running together the separate findings listed in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The difficulty is stated after a colon in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the findings about people's beliefs regarding willpower are 'awkward' for the resource theory because

options.A: they prove that the experience of mental fatigue after effort is an illusion created by people's expectations.
options.B: a physical store ought to run down with use whatever a person happens to believe about it.
options.C: they show that people who hold strong beliefs about willpower have larger stores of the resource to draw on.
options.D: they came from the same laboratories that had earlier failed to reproduce the basic depletion effect.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a physical store ought to run down with use whatever a person happens to believe about it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'it does not follow' that the experience is an illusion, since people 'do grow less willing to persist', and the findings are only 'reported' by some studies.
option_rationales.C: If beliefs enlarged a physical store the theory would survive; the awkwardness is that belief matters at all to something supposedly physical.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not link the belief studies to the replication attempts; the awkwardness lies in what the result implies.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the result 'awkward for any theory in which the resource is a physical quantity'. A physical quantity should be depleted by effort regardless of belief, so a depletion that disappears when people believe willpower is plentiful does not fit.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the belief findings as evidence that fatigue is imaginary, which the author explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason must be inferred from the phrase 'a physical quantity'; the passage does not spell it out.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the account of mental fatigue set out in paragraphs 3 and 4 EXCEPT:

options.A: A person's persistence at a dull task recovers only after rest, however the task is framed or rewarded.
options.B: A volunteer stays absorbed in demanding work for longer when he can see clearly how it helps the people he serves.
options.C: Two equally demanding tasks leave people differently tired, depending on how rewarding each of the tasks feels to them.
options.D: Someone who has worked hard on a report all afternoon feels a growing pull towards a film she has been looking forward to.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A person's persistence at a dull task recovers only after rest, however the task is framed or rewarded.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says tasks that 'feel meaningful or rewarding should be less draining', so this is just what the account predicts.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 contrasts tasks that feel rewarding with 'equally demanding tasks that do not', which is this case exactly.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says weariness nudges attention 'towards rest, pleasure or novelty' as the value of alternatives accumulates, which this describes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that 'changing how a task is framed, or what it leads to, may restore persistence where rest alone would not'. A case in which only rest helps, whatever the framing or reward, is what the fuel picture would predict and runs against the opportunity cost account.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the film case as inconsistent because it describes giving up, though the account explains giving up as a shift in priorities.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are close paraphrases of predictions in paragraphs 3 and 4; the correct answer echoes the rival model and must be recognised as such.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to what happens, on the account the author favours, when mental fatigue sets in?

options.A: A student stops revising for an examination because she has now covered everything that the syllabus requires.
options.B: A shopper who has spent an hour in one store grows restless as the other stores nearby seem ever more worth the time.
options.C: A car slows to a halt on the motorway because the petrol in its tank has finally run out after a long journey.
options.D: A runner's leg muscles weaken over the course of a long race and need several days of rest before regaining strength.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A shopper who has spent an hour in one store grows restless as the other stores nearby seem ever more worth the time.

option_rationales.A: Stopping because a task is complete involves no rising opportunity cost; the author's account concerns weariness while the task is unfinished.
option_rationales.C: This is the fuel-gauge picture of paragraph 1, the model that paragraph 2 says has 'fared badly', not the account the author favours.
option_rationales.D: This depicts a store used up by effort and restored by rest, which is the resource model rather than a shift in what one is 'willing to pay for'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says continued effort 'carries an opportunity cost, the value of everything else one might be doing instead', and weariness rises as that cost accumulates. The shopper's restlessness grows as alternatives look more valuable, not because anything has run out.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the runner, which looks like the everyday experience of tiredness but mirrors the depletion model.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options model the rejected theory in concrete form; the student must map the structure of the favoured account, not the surface experience of tiredness.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the 'evening collapse' mentioned in paragraph 1 as

options.A: something best prevented by rationing effort through the day, as the failure of the resource model now shows.
options.B: an illusion that came to seem real largely because the resource model became so widely accepted.
options.C: evidence that everyday wisdom about tiredness has been refuted by the replication studies described in paragraph 2.
options.D: a real experience that the resource model described vividly but explained wrongly.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a real experience that the resource model described vividly but explained wrongly.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 presents rationing as the strategy that follows if willpower is a fuel; the author favours the other picture, so the failure of the model does not support rationing.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'it does not follow' that this experience 'is an illusion'; people 'do grow less willing to persist'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says the model's decline 'is not a refutation of everyday wisdom about tiredness'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 offers the evening collapse as the experience the theory matched, paragraph 3 insists the experience is not an illusion, and paragraph 5 says 'a vivid metaphor can capture a real phenomenon while getting its mechanism entirely wrong'. The correct answer joins these.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing rationing, which sounds like sensible advice but belongs to the model the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer requires linking paragraphs 1, 3 and 5, and each wrong option misreads one of them.

questions.question: According to the passage, what must the child serving imaginary tea do?

options.A: Keep the cup from toppling over at any point, since a spill would break the rules that the game has set up for everyone taking part.
options.B: Copy the way she has seen adults receive guests, so that she gradually learns the social role of a host.
options.C: Treat the cup as full inside the game while knowing it is empty, and let events in the game have their fitting effects.
options.D: Believe for the length of the game that the cup really holds tea, so that the pretence feels convincing to her.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Treat the cup as full inside the game while knowing it is empty, and let events in the game have their fitting effects.

option_rationales.A: In paragraph 1 a toppled cup is part of following the game's consequences 'faithfully', leaving the bear 'wet'; a spill breaks no rule.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 reports the 'rehearsal of adult roles' reading only to say that it misses 'what is most remarkable about the scene'; it is not what the child must do.
option_rationales.D: This reverses paragraph 1, which says she must 'keep the game's version from leaking into the real one', which is why she does not try to drink.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the child must 'hold two descriptions of the world in mind at once' (the cup is empty; in the game it is full), keep the game's version separate from reality, and 'follow its consequences faithfully'. The correct answer states both requirements.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'rehearsal of adult roles' option because it is mentioned in the passage, without noticing that the author rejects it as incomplete.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is set out in the last three sentences of paragraph 1; the wrong options are each contradicted by a nearby phrase.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'double bookkeeping' refers to

options.A: keeping track of how things actually are and how they are within the pretence, both at the same time.
options.B: recording a child's play twice over, once in the child's own memory and once in the notes of a watching adult.
options.C: moving back and forth between pretending and ordinary activity several times during a single afternoon.
options.D: a child's habit of counting imaginary objects alongside real ones, such as the cups, the tea and the animals.

questions.correct_answer: (A) keeping track of how things actually are and how they are within the pretence, both at the same time.

option_rationales.B: No adult record keeping is mentioned; the phrase picks up the 'two descriptions of the world' that the child herself holds in paragraph 1.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 stresses that the two descriptions are held 'at once', which is simultaneous, not alternation between play and other activity.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage concerns counting; 'bookkeeping' is a figure for keeping two accounts of the world apart, not for tallying objects.

questions.explanation: 'This double bookkeeping' in paragraph 2 refers back to the end of paragraph 1, where the child must 'hold two descriptions of the world in mind at once', the real one and the game's, keeping them apart while following each.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'bookkeeping' literally as record keeping or counting instead of reading it through the sentence it refers back to.
questions.difficulty_reason: 'This' points straight back to the preceding sentences, which define the idea.

questions.question: The third paragraph primarily serves to

options.A: reject the suggestion, made in paragraph 2, that pretend play and counterfactual thought share a capacity.
options.B: argue that most make-believe is too repetitive and loose to be of any real value to a child's development.
options.C: narrow the author's claim by conceding what the link between pretence and reasoning does not establish.
options.D: present evidence that children who spend more time pretending go on to become better at reasoning about causes.

questions.correct_answer: (C) narrow the author's claim by conceding what the link between pretence and reasoning does not establish.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 accepts the shared capacity ('That play and counterfactual reasoning draw on a shared capacity') and only denies that this shows more play makes better reasoners.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'much of it is repetitive and loose' but goes on to defend a 'narrower' claim about its value, so saying it lacks any real value is too extreme.
option_rationales.D: This is the opposite of paragraph 3, which warns that the shared capacity 'does not show that more play produces better reasoners'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with 'Some caution is nevertheless in order', grants that the shared capacity does not prove a causal effect of play, admits that much pretence is loose, and states 'The claim worth defending is narrower'. Its role is to qualify and narrow the thesis.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a concession for a rejection of the whole argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph signals its function in its first and last sentences.

questions.question: The author's reservation about turning free play into guided activities with stated learning outcomes rests chiefly on the concern that

options.A: guided activities take time away from the reading and counting that young children need to master well before their schooling begins.
options.B: any adult involvement in a child's game interferes with the reasoning about suppositions that pretence exercises.
options.C: stated learning outcomes cannot be measured reliably in children as young as the ones who play such games.
options.D: a child who senses that a particular answer is expected will stop exploring suppositions and try to read the adult instead.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a child who senses that a particular answer is expected will stop exploring suppositions and try to read the adult instead.

option_rationales.A: This echoes the 'waste of time' view that paragraph 1 rejects; the author never worries that guided play crowds out reading or counting.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'Some guidance helps' and that an adult who asks what happens next 'can enrich' a game, so the objection is not to any involvement.
option_rationales.C: Measurement is never discussed; the worry in paragraph 4 is that a lesson-driven game 'changes character', not that its outcomes are hard to assess.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that when a game exists to deliver a lesson, 'the child who knows that a right answer is wanted stops supposing freely and starts guessing what the adult has in mind', destroying the 'freedom from consequence' that made pretence valuable.
questions.common_misconception: Overextending the author's caution into a rejection of all adult involvement, despite the explicit concession that some guidance helps.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option overstates the author's view; the concession in paragraph 4 must be weighed against the objection.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: The best form for a lesson depends on its subject matter, which is why maps are the natural way to teach geography.
options.B: The belief that matching lessons to a learner's style improves learning lacks support, and labelling learners by style can do harm.
options.C: Teachers should present every lesson in visual, spoken and active forms so that learners of every style are reached.
options.D: People do not really have preferences about how they take in information, so the idea of learning styles is a myth.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The belief that matching lessons to a learner's style improves learning lacks support, and labelling learners by style can do harm.

option_rationales.A: This is the point of paragraph 3 alone; it leaves out the central critique of the matching claim in paragraph 2 and the cost of labelling in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 defends variety for other reasons (attention, several routes back to an idea); delivering lessons so that every style is reached keeps the diagnosis the author rejects.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 states that 'That people report preferences is not in dispute'; the author denies only that preferences predict performance.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that the predicted crossover 'has generally failed to appear', and paragraph 4 concludes that labelling 'narrows expectations while appearing to widen them'. The correct answer captures both the lack of support and the harm.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about matching form to content, which is true to one paragraph but too narrow for the whole.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated directly; the wrong options are a contradiction, a prescription and a single-paragraph point.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, which pattern of results is the learning styles theory committed to predicting?

options.A: The advantage of one teaching method over another reverses depending on which style a group of learners has been assigned.
options.B: Learners who state a clear preference for one form of instruction learn faster than learners who state none at all.
options.C: Learners classed as visual outperform learners classed as auditory whatever form the lesson is delivered in.
options.D: Learners of every style do better when a lesson combines visual, spoken and practical elements in a single session.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The advantage of one teaching method over another reverses depending on which style a group of learners has been assigned.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 compares groups taught in both ways; it says nothing about learners with no preference learning more slowly.
option_rationales.C: A group that wins in every format shows no flip; paragraph 2 says the theory needs the visual group to do better with visual lessons and the auditory group with spoken ones.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the theory predicts that the better method 'flips' between groups; a uniform benefit from mixed lessons is not a matching prediction.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the theory needs a visual learner to learn more from a visual lesson 'while a learner labelled auditory will show the reverse', and that testing it means 'checking whether the advantage flips from one group to the other'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the claim that visual learners simply do better with the claim that the better method differs by group.
questions.difficulty_reason: The prediction is spelled out in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage gives each of the following as a reason the learning styles idea is appealing EXCEPT that it

options.A: fits the ordinary, everyday experience that people favour some ways of receiving information over others.
options.B: gives teachers something practical and concrete to do with their respect for individual difference among pupils.
options.C: has been borne out by studies teaching learners both in their own style and in another.
options.D: seems to show proper respect for the many differences between individual learners in a class.

questions.correct_answer: (C) has been borne out by studies teaching learners both in their own style and in another.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says it 'fits the everyday experience that people do prefer some ways of taking in information to others'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the idea 'gives teachers something concrete to do with that respect'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 lists this first: 'it seems to respect individual difference'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 names three 'honest reasons' for the idea's appeal, matching the other three options. Paragraph 2 says that when tested in the demanding way 'the predicted crossover has generally failed to appear', so the correct answer is not a reason given; it is contradicted.
questions.common_misconception: Rushing past paragraph 2 and assuming the idea's popularity reflects confirming evidence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are near paraphrases of one sentence; the correct answer contradicts paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 2?

options.A: Teachers who accept the theory of learning styles report feeling noticeably more confident when they plan lessons for mixed classes.
options.B: Students taught a stretch of coastline from maps remembered it better than students given only a spoken description of it.
options.C: Most learners, when asked, can readily name a way of receiving information that they prefer over the others available.
options.D: Learners sorted by style and taught in both formats showed a reversal: visual learners gained more from diagrams, auditory learners more from talk.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Learners sorted by style and taught in both formats showed a reversal: visual learners gained more from diagrams, auditory learners more from talk.

option_rationales.A: Teachers' confidence says nothing about whether matched teaching improves learning, which is the claim at issue in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: This supports paragraph 3, where form is matched to content 'whoever the learner is'; it does not show any crossover between kinds of learner.
option_rationales.C: The author already grants this in paragraph 2 ('That people report preferences is not in dispute'), so it leaves the argument about performance untouched.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 rests on the claim that, under a proper test, 'the predicted crossover has generally failed to appear'. A properly designed test that found the crossover would undercut exactly that claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about preferences because it sounds like support for learning styles, without noticing that the author concedes it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option sounds pro-theory but is a concession; solvers must locate the precise claim under attack.

questions.question: According to the passage, practising one type of problem at a time falls short because it

options.A: spares the learner the decision about which procedure a problem needs, a decision a mixed examination requires.
options.B: produces more errors during study than mixed practice does, and the errors discourage learners from continuing.
options.C: prevents the learner from becoming fluent in any one procedure before the examination arrives.
options.D: takes much longer than rereading the chapter, and so leaves the student too little time for review.

questions.correct_answer: (A) spares the learner the decision about which procedure a problem needs, a decision a mixed examination requires.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: it is mixing problem types that makes study 'more error-prone', while blocked practice feels easy.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says block practice lets the learner apply 'the same procedure again and again', which builds fluency rather than preventing it.
option_rationales.D: The passage never compares the time taken by blocked practice and rereading; both are described as methods that feel easy.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says block practice lets the learner apply one procedure 'without ever deciding which procedure the problem calls for, the very decision a mixed examination demands'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing which method is error-prone during study.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of one sentence in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a quiz given to students on a topic they have never been taught as

options.A: useful chiefly because it shows students how much of the topic still remains for them to learn later.
options.B: an unhelpful difficulty, since there is nothing learned for the effort of retrieval to consolidate.
options.C: a useful difficulty, because any effortful test is preferable to the familiarity produced by rereading.
options.D: no less valuable than spacing study sessions apart, provided that the quiz is followed by careful rereading.

questions.correct_answer: (B) an unhelpful difficulty, since there is nothing learned for the effort of retrieval to consolidate.

option_rationales.A: The passage never credits tests with this diagnostic value; paragraph 3 says such a test 'teaches little except discouragement'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 rejects the lesson 'that harder is always better' and says a difficulty helps 'only when the learner can, with effort, overcome it'.
option_rationales.D: Nothing supports this pairing; the passage treats spacing as useful because it calls on retrieval of learned material, which an untaught topic cannot supply.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'a test on something never learned teaches little except discouragement', and paragraph 2 explains that the benefit of testing comes from 'The effort of retrieving a half-forgotten fact'. With nothing learned, there is nothing to retrieve.
questions.common_misconception: Generalising paragraph 2 into the rule that testing always helps and missing the limit set in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option draws on paragraph 2; the correct answer needs the qualification in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward learners who prefer rereading and blocked practice is best described as

options.A: sympathetic to the reasons for their choice while holding that the choice is mistaken.
options.B: approving, since the fluency these methods produce is usually a reliable sign of real competence.
options.C: scornful, since they keep using poor methods despite clear information about which methods work.
options.D: indifferent, since the passage is concerned with how teachers judge lessons rather than with students.

questions.correct_answer: (A) sympathetic to the reasons for their choice while holding that the choice is mistaken.

option_rationales.B: The author grants that fluency usually tracks competence (paragraph 1) but says that for durable learning the rule is 'frequently misleading', so the methods are not endorsed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'they are not foolish to do so', and adds that information alone is not enough to change practice, so scorn is the opposite of the author's tone.
option_rationales.D: Most of paragraph 4 concerns learners' own judgement; teachers are mentioned as facing 'a similar temptation', not as the sole concern.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says learners 'systematically prefer the methods that serve them worst' yet 'are not foolish to do so', because costs are felt now and benefits arrive later. The tone is understanding but critical.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the criticism of the methods as contempt for the learners.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the author's view of the methods from the author's view of the people who use them.

questions.question: Which of the following practices best fits the passage's account of a useful difficulty?

options.A: A student copies out key passages with her non-dominant hand during revision, so that each line takes longer to finish.
options.B: A student attempts problems from next year's syllabus before learning this year's methods, so as to struggle as much as possible.
options.C: A student works through problems grouped by type, raising the difficulty steadily within each group as her confidence grows over the weeks.
options.D: A student revising for a mixed examination shuffles problems from last month's topics, so that each must first be identified before it is solved.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A student revising for a mixed examination shuffles problems from last month's topics, so that each must first be identified before it is solved.

option_rationales.A: This only slows things down, like the 'faint, awkward typeface' in paragraph 3; it calls on no process the student will later need.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says material 'pitched far beyond a student's grasp produces confusion rather than consolidation'; struggle for its own sake is not the point.
option_rationales.C: This remains blocked practice: it adds difficulty but never makes the student decide 'which procedure the problem calls for' (paragraph 2).

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says useful difficulties can be overcome with effort and 'call on processes the learner will later need, such as retrieval, discrimination and reconstruction'. Shuffling familiar problems demands discrimination (paragraph 2: deciding which procedure applies), and last month's material is within reach.
questions.common_misconception: Treating any added difficulty as useful, especially the graded blocked practice, which feels demanding but lacks the discrimination step.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option adds real difficulty; only one meets both conditions in paragraph 3, so the solver must apply two criteria together.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'confidence without accuracy' describes

options.A: a violinist who keeps playing wrong notes boldly because no teacher is present to correct the mistakes.
options.B: practitioners whom long experience has made sure of their judgements, although those judgements are not reliably right.
options.C: the excessive faith that researchers have placed in counting hours of practice as a measure of skill.
options.D: beginners who feel sure of themselves before they have done enough practice to justify that feeling.

questions.correct_answer: (B) practitioners whom long experience has made sure of their judgements, although those judgements are not reliably right.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the violinist 'hears a wrong note at once'; the violinist is the example of good feedback, not of misplaced confidence.
option_rationales.C: The phrase describes practitioners in fields with poor feedback, not researchers; the critique of hour counting comes in paragraph 2 and paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 attributes this state to 'long careers', not to beginners who have practised too little.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that in fields where feedback is slow and noisy 'long careers can produce confidence without accuracy': years of work make people sure of themselves without making their judgements correct.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the phrase to the wrong group (beginners, researchers) instead of reading the sentence it sits in.
questions.difficulty_reason: The surrounding sentence defines who has the confidence and why it is unearned.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the popular rule that a fixed number of hours will make anyone an expert as

options.A: a fair summary of what the research on practice has shown about how experts are made.
options.B: accurate for fields where feedback is slow and noisy, though misleading for games and sports.
options.C: an overstatement that stretches sound findings about practice into a promise they cannot keep.
options.D: evidence that talent, rather than practice, is what finally separates the great from the good.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an overstatement that stretches sound findings about practice into a promise they cannot keep.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the rule is 'in that form, hard to sustain', so the author does not think it a fair summary.
option_rationales.B: This reverses paragraph 2, where practice 'accounts for more' in games and sports and 'for less' where outcomes are delayed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this restores the old picture of talent as a fixed endowment'; rejecting the rule is not a return to talent.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the research 'was right that expertise is built' but cannot 'deliver the promise sometimes made in its name, that anyone who puts in the hours will arrive at the same place'. The rule is a strong version of findings that hold in weaker form.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that rejecting the hours rule means endorsing talent.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs paragraphs 2 and 4 together to see that the author keeps part of the view while rejecting its strong form.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's explanation in paragraph 3 of why practice accounts for less in some fields?

options.A: In sports with stable rules and quick feedback, some athletes who practise a great deal still fail to reach the elite level.
options.B: Top chess players began playing at an earlier age, on average, than the many chess players who never managed to reach the top level of the game.
options.C: In one profession, members who learn quickly whether they erred improve more with experience than colleagues who learn the results only years later.
options.D: Financial analysts with long careers earn considerably more, on average, than analysts with shorter careers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) In one profession, members who learn quickly whether they erred improve more with experience than colleagues who learn the results only years later.

option_rationales.A: This concerns the unexplained remainder within a field with good feedback; it does not test whether poor feedback is what limits practice elsewhere.
option_rationales.B: Starting age has nothing to do with the quality of feedback, which is the factor paragraph 3 uses to explain the difference between fields.
option_rationales.D: Higher earnings for seniority fit the remark about 'seniority' but say nothing about whether feedback governs how much practice improves skill.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that 'what practice builds depends on what the environment can teach', meaning on quick and reliable feedback. A comparison within one profession, where only the speed of feedback differs, isolates that factor and supports the explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that mentions a field from the passage (chess, finance, sport) without checking whether it bears on feedback.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options reuse the passage's examples; the solver must isolate the causal factor named in paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It grants that practice builds expertise but denies that equal hours bring equal results, without making talent decisive.
options.B: It introduces new evidence that talent is a fixed endowment that settles in advance who can become an expert.
options.C: It recommends that people who want to become experts should choose fields in which feedback on their efforts is quick and reliable.
options.D: It reverses the argument of paragraph 3 by conceding that hours of practice do in the end determine expertise.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It grants that practice builds expertise but denies that equal hours bring equal results, without making talent decisive.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens by saying that nothing in the argument 'restores the old picture of talent as a fixed endowment that settles everything'.
option_rationales.C: No advice is given; the paragraph only observes that some fields make demanding practice 'barely possible'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 denies that anyone who 'puts in the hours will arrive at the same place', so it confirms rather than reverses paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the research 'was right that expertise is built' and right about the manner of practice, but cannot deliver the promise of equal outcomes for equal hours; its first sentence rules out a return to talent as 'a fixed endowment'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the rejection of the hours promise as an endorsement of talent.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph balances concession and rejection in both directions, so the solver must track two contrasts.

questions.question: According to the passage, when adolescents estimate the dangers of various activities in a calm setting, their estimates

options.A: improve noticeably once they have received formal instruction about the risks involved in them.
options.B: are often not far from the estimates that adults give for the same activities.
options.C: are markedly less accurate than the estimates they give when they are in the company of friends.
options.D: show that most of them believe harm happens only to other people and never to themselves.

questions.correct_answer: (B) are often not far from the estimates that adults give for the same activities.

option_rationales.A: The effect of instruction on estimates is never reported; paragraph 1 says only that information campaigns have had modest results.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 contrasts calm and social decisions, not estimates of danger; nothing says estimates improve among friends.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'familiar explanation' set out in paragraph 1, which paragraph 2 says rests on a premise 'weaker than it looks'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that in a calm setting adolescents' answers 'are often not very different from those of adults'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the ignorance view because it is stated in the passage, without noticing that the author disputes it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of one clause in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage suggests that an important reason information campaigns about risk have had limited success is that they

options.A: have usually given adolescents information about risks that is inaccurate or deliberately exaggerated.
options.B: come from schools and governments, sources whose advice adolescents are inclined to distrust and ignore.
options.C: assume a capacity to apply general facts to one's own conduct that most adolescents do not yet possess.
options.D: try to supply missing knowledge, when the difficulty lies largely in how knowledge is used in certain situations.

questions.correct_answer: (D) try to supply missing knowledge, when the difficulty lies largely in how knowledge is used in certain situations.

option_rationales.A: The passage never questions the accuracy of the information; its point is that the information is largely already known.
option_rationales.B: Distrust of the source is never mentioned; paragraph 2 locates the problem in 'what happens to that knowledge in particular situations'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says many adolescents 'reason about risk in hypothetical cases about as well as their parents do' and that 'Decisions taken alone and at leisure look quite mature', so a missing capacity is not the author's diagnosis; the problem is the situation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes campaigns that 'Teach young people the facts'; paragraph 2 says the premise of ignorance 'is weaker than it looks' because what distinguishes adolescents is 'less what they know than what happens to that knowledge in particular situations'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reasoning-capacity option, which sounds developmental, despite paragraph 2's statement about hypothetical reasoning.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause must be assembled from paragraphs 1 and 2; one wrong option misreads the developmental point.

questions.question: Which of the following measures is most in keeping with the approach the author favours in paragraph 4?

options.A: A course trains teenagers to calculate the statistical risks of common activities, so that they can weigh dangers as carefully as adults do.
options.B: A programme asks each teenager to sign a private pledge never to ride with a reckless driver, so that the promise guides later choices.
options.C: A campaign shows teenagers vivid images of injuries caused by careless driving, so that the dangers of speeding are kept firmly in their minds.
options.D: A school arranges for evening events to end with a supervised bus home, so that riding with a newly licensed classmate becomes the awkward option.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A school arranges for evening events to end with a supervised bus home, so that riding with a newly licensed classmate becomes the awkward option.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says adolescents already reason about risk 'about as well as their parents do'; the course adds knowledge rather than changing situations.
option_rationales.B: A pledge made alone works on decisions 'taken alone and at leisure', which paragraph 2 says already 'look quite mature'; it leaves the social situation unchanged.
option_rationales.C: This tries to change 'the beliefs they carry into' situations, the information-based approach the passage says has had modest results.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 favours interventions that 'change the situations adolescents find themselves in' and that 'make the safe choice the socially easy one'. A supervised bus changes the situation and makes the safe choice the easy one in front of peers.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the pledge, which seems to address peer pressure, though it works only on calm, solitary decisions.
questions.difficulty_reason: The pledge wrong option is close; the solver must apply the distinction between calm and social decisions from paragraph 2.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the account of adolescent development given in paragraph 3 EXCEPT:

options.A: Some teenagers who spend most of their time among friends take fewer risks than many adults do.
options.B: The gap between sensitivity to reward and the capacity for restraint narrows as people move through their twenties.
options.C: The heightened response to reward in adolescence is limited to non-social rewards such as money or prizes.
options.D: A risky choice made by an adolescent among friends may reflect the circumstances as well as the state of the brain.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The heightened response to reward in adolescence is limited to non-social rewards such as money or prizes.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 itself says 'plenty of teenagers who are surrounded by friends behave with conspicuous care', and 'adolescents differ widely'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says restraint and planning 'continue to mature into the early twenties', so the gap would be expected to narrow in that decade.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 warns that 'Brains do not determine behaviour on their own', which allows circumstances a share in the explanation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the reward systems that become more responsive are those that make 'rewards, and especially social rewards, feel intense', and that the gap shows most when 'peers raise the value of a daring act'. Limiting the effect to non-social rewards contradicts this.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the hedges in paragraph 3 as contradictions of the account, when the author includes them as part of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options sound like objections to the developmental account but are the author's own qualifications; only the correct answer conflicts with a detail.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining why adults learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children usually manage to do.
options.B: replacing the image of a language window that shuts at a fixed age with a picture of gradual age effects that differ by component.
options.C: arguing that adult immigrants fall short in a new language chiefly because they are not immersed in it as children are.
options.D: showing that age has no real effect on how well a second language is eventually learned, once exposure is held equal.

questions.correct_answer: (B) replacing the image of a language window that shuts at a fixed age with a picture of gradual age effects that differ by component.

option_rationales.A: This is one point within paragraph 3, used to support the case against a single critical period; it is too narrow to be the passage's concern.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says it is 'hard to tell how much of the outcome' exposure and age each explain, so naming exposure as the chief cause overstates the author's view.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 grants that the belief 'has some foundation' and that early learners end up closer to native-like command; the author denies only the fixed window.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the thesis ('a slope rather than a window'), paragraph 2 adds the confound of exposure, paragraph 3 the differences between components, and paragraph 4 the cost of the window image. The correct answer covers both the slope and the component point.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the confound in paragraph 2 as the author's whole explanation, or overstating the critique into a denial of any age effect.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options overstate the author's view in different directions; one is a single supporting detail.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that a simple comparison between the final attainment of child and adult immigrants

options.A: cannot by itself show how much of the gap between them is due to age rather than to conditions of learning.
options.B: proves that adults who are immersed in a language learn it every bit as well as children who are immersed.
options.C: shows that differences in exposure, not age, account for the whole of the gap between the two groups.
options.D: tends to overstate the advantage that adult learners hold over child learners in vocabulary and memory.

questions.correct_answer: (A) cannot by itself show how much of the gap between them is due to age rather than to conditions of learning.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'some' immersed adults reach high levels; this is far weaker than equal success for all immersed adults, and 'proves' is too strong.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says only that it is 'hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains', which rules out attributing the whole gap to exposure.
option_rationales.D: Vocabulary and memory strategies are discussed in paragraph 3 and are not linked to the comparison of attainment in paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that in such comparisons 'differences in the quantity and character of exposure travel along with age, and it is hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains'. The comparison therefore cannot isolate the effect of age.
questions.common_misconception: Converting 'hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains' into the stronger claim that exposure explains the whole gap.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading a confound argument at its correct strength.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'a set of different sensitivities' most nearly means

options.A: the varying degrees to which a learner's first and second languages influence each other over many years.
options.B: several distinct stages of childhood, each of them especially suited to the learning of a different language.
options.C: different learners, each of whom responds to a new language with a different level of anxiety or confidence.
options.D: separate parts of language ability, each affected to a different degree by the age at which learning starts.

questions.correct_answer: (D) separate parts of language ability, each affected to a different degree by the age at which learning starts.

option_rationales.A: Interference between languages is never discussed; the phrase contrasts accent and grammar with vocabulary in their sensitivity to age.
option_rationales.B: The sensitivities belong to components of language 'declining at different rates', not to stages of childhood matched to languages.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 is about components of language (accent, grammar, vocabulary), not about differences in learners' feelings.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says accent is 'most sensitive to the age of first exposure', some grammar 'sensitive too', while vocabulary keeps growing; it concludes with 'different sensitivities, declining at different rates for different components'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching 'sensitivities' to learners rather than to components of language.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is defined by the contrast drawn earlier in the paragraph, which must be connected to it.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's position?

options.A: Adults beginning a language progressed faster over their first year of study than children beginning the same language.
options.B: Among learners matched for the amount and kind of daily exposure, attainment fell sharply at one particular age, with little decline before or after it.
options.C: Late learners who were immersed as fully as children still differed from them in fine judgements about word endings.
options.D: Some adults who began a language late reached native-like command of it after many years of intensive immersion.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Among learners matched for the amount and kind of daily exposure, attainment fell sharply at one particular age, with little decline before or after it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says adults 'often learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children do', so this agrees with the author.
option_rationales.C: The author already grants in paragraph 3 that some aspects of grammar 'seem sensitive too'; a gradual, component-specific age effect fits this finding.
option_rationales.D: This supports paragraph 2, where immersed adults reach levels that the stricter window theories say 'should be out of reach'.

questions.explanation: The author holds that age effects form 'a slope rather than a window' and that exposure is confounded with age. A sharp drop at one age, with exposure held equal, is exactly the discontinuity the window theory predicts and removes the confound the author relies on.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the grammar finding because it shows a lasting age effect, without seeing that the author concedes such effects and disputes only their shape.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option shows an age effect; the solver must see that the author's claim concerns the form of the effect, not its existence.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the gains in test scores were

options.A: far larger on abstract classification and pattern detection than on vocabulary and arithmetic.
options.B: confined to the countries that had introduced mass schooling earlier than their neighbours had.
options.C: roughly equal across the different kinds of task that together make up a standard intelligence test.
options.D: largest on the tasks that draw most heavily on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic.

questions.correct_answer: (A) far larger on abstract classification and pattern detection than on vocabulary and arithmetic.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says scores rose 'in country after country'; no comparison of early and late schooling countries is made.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the gains 'were not spread evenly across the tests'.
option_rationales.D: This reverses paragraph 2, which says gains were 'much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the gains 'were largest on tasks that ask for abstract classification and for the detection of patterns in unfamiliar material, and much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing which tasks showed the larger gains.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in two consecutive sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The discussion of the two answers about the spade and the shears suggests that

options.A: test makers once gave credit for practical answers of this kind but stopped doing so as mass schooling spread.
options.B: intelligence tests ought in fairness to award credit for practical answers as well as for abstract classifications.
options.C: an answer can earn no credit on a test while still reflecting a sensible way of thinking about the world.
options.D: people who give practical answers are less able than others to reason abstractly when a task requires it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an answer can earn no credit on a test while still reflecting a sensible way of thinking about the world.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage describes a change in scoring rules; the change described is in the habits of test takers.
option_rationales.B: The passage draws no such recommendation; paragraph 4 asks for caution in interpreting comparisons, not for changes to scoring.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the practical answer reflects a 'habit', not an inability; nothing is said about what such people can do when asked to classify.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'The first answer earns credit; the second does not. Yet the second is not stupid', since it reflects a habit 'well suited' to a practical life. An uncredited answer can still be a sensible one.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the descriptive point into a recommendation about scoring.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference is close to the text, but two wrong options are plausible extensions that the passage never makes.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 functions mainly to

options.A: establish that the Flynn effect is merely an artefact of the way intelligence tests were renormed at intervals over time.
options.B: pose a dilemma whose two obvious resolutions both look unacceptable, which the rest of the passage tries to escape.
options.C: describe the methods by which researchers in many countries first detected the rise in raw scores and confirmed it.
options.D: argue that earlier generations were less intelligent than is usually supposed by those who remember them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) pose a dilemma whose two obvious resolutions both look unacceptable, which the rest of the passage tries to escape.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 treats the artefact explanation as one horn of the dilemma and says it is 'hard to see why the artefact should be so large'; it does not establish it.
option_rationales.C: Apart from noting that tests were renormed, paragraph 1 says nothing about methods of detection; its focus is the puzzle the rise creates.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 calls the conclusion that our grandparents were of low intelligence 'absurd on its face'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that the rise 'presents an awkward dilemma': if the gains are real gains in intelligence, earlier generations were absurdly dull; if they are an artefact, the artefact is inexplicably large. Paragraph 2 opens 'The way out begins', confirming that the rest seeks an escape.
questions.common_misconception: Taking one horn of the dilemma for the author's claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that both horns are presented in order to be rejected.

questions.question: The author's position on the twentieth-century rise in scores is best characterised as holding that the gains

options.A: mark a genuine spread of one style of thinking, without amounting to a rise in general intellectual power.
options.B: are real, and this shows that the tests were never good predictors of how people would fare at school or work.
options.C: are an artefact of the way tests were constructed and reveal nothing about how people's thinking has actually changed.
options.D: show that people today have greater general intelligence than earlier generations, though the tests exaggerate the size of the difference.

questions.correct_answer: (A) mark a genuine spread of one style of thinking, without amounting to a rise in general intellectual power.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the tests 'remain good predictors of success in schools and workplaces', so this contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'The gains are therefore real, since the habit genuinely spread'; the artefact horn is rejected.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the century 'did not make people more intelligent in some general sense', so any rise in general intelligence, even a smaller one, contradicts the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the century 'trained a particular style of thought' and that the gains are real 'since the habit genuinely spread, but they are not gains in a single underlying power'. The correct answer holds both halves of this position.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting a hedged version of the 'more intelligent' horn because it sounds moderate.
