Together these support the reading that the child is close to, not yet in possession of, a new method.
questions.common_misconception: Upgrading 'on the verge of learning' into 'already understands'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option differs from the correct answer only in degree, so the precise wording of paragraph 3 must be held.

questions.question: According to the passage, the octopus's intelligence is said to have been 'assembled independently' because

options.A: octopuses learn their skills alone, without any parents or companions to teach them how to hunt.
options.B: each of its arms developed its own nervous system separately during the octopus's own evolutionary history.
options.C: the octopus has a far larger share of its neurons in its central brain than vertebrates have in theirs.
options.D: its lineage split from ours before either had developed anything like a complex brain.

questions.correct_answer: (D) its lineage split from ours before either had developed anything like a complex brain.

option_rationales.A: Learning without parents is not mentioned in the passage; the word 'independently' concerns evolutionary origin, as the preceding clause about the split between lineages makes clear.
option_rationales.B: The passage never says the arms evolved separately; 'assembled independently' refers to the octopus lineage as a whole compared with ours.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the reverse, that more of its neurons lie in its arms than in its central brain, and this fact concerns the plan of its intelligence, not its independent origin.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the octopus line 'separated from ours more than half a billion years ago, long before either lineage had anything resembling a complex brain, so whatever intelligence it now has was assembled independently'.
questions.common_misconception: Linking 'independently' to the arms or to solitary learning rather than to the evolutionary split stated in the same sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in the same sentence as the quoted phrase.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards describing the octopus as 'an animal with nine brains' is best described as

options.A: dismissive of the anatomy behind it, since the author doubts that octopus arms do much on their own.
options.B: critical, since the description inflates a real anatomical fact into a claim the facts do not support.
options.C: neutral, since the author reports the description without saying whether it is accurate or misleading.
options.D: approving, since the description captures in vivid terms what the observations of the arms have shown.

questions.correct_answer: (B) critical, since the description inflates a real anatomical fact into a claim the facts do not support.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts the anatomy, describing in paragraph 2 how each arm 'handles much of the detail of its own movement'; it is the slogan's conclusion, not the facts, that is rejected.
option_rationales.C: The author does take a side, stating that the slogan 'goes too far' and replacing it with the claim that one mind does much of its work 'at the edges'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says plainly that 'The slogan goes too far', which is the opposite of approval.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces the slogan and immediately says it 'goes too far', because the arms 'are not independent agents with purposes of their own'. The author accepts the anatomy but rejects the inflated reading of it.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the distinction between rejecting a slogan and rejecting the facts behind it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's judgement is stated in a short, direct sentence.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the octopus's way of distributing control is best explained by

options.A: the small size of the octopus's central brain, which leaves it unable to issue commands to its arms.
options.B: the very long period during which the octopus lineage has evolved apart from vertebrates.
options.C: the advantage to an animal that often loses arms of having limbs that can go on acting on their own.
options.D: the difficulty, for any single centre, of controlling flexible and boneless limbs that can bend at any point.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the difficulty, for any single centre, of controlling flexible and boneless limbs that can bend at any point.

option_rationales.A: The passage never calls the central brain small or incapable; paragraph 2 says it 'sets broader goals', so it does direct the arms.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 uses the long separation to show that the octopus's intelligence arose independently, not to explain why it is distributed; the explanation offered in paragraph 4 is the control problem posed by its body.
option_rationales.C: Losing arms and survival after injury are not discussed; the severed arm in paragraph 2 is evidence of local control, not offered as its purpose.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says an animal 'with eight flexible arms and no skeleton faces a control problem that no single centre could easily solve', and calls distribution 'a sensible answer to the body the animal actually has'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the evidence for independent origin, given early in the passage, as the explanation for the distributed plan, which comes only at the end.
questions.difficulty_reason: A true detail from paragraph 1 tempts because it sits near the anatomical fact; the explanation must be taken from paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements most closely resembles the organisation of the octopus as the author describes it?

options.A: A building firm whose director sets the goals of a project while each specialist crew decides for itself how to do its own part of the work.
options.B: A street market with no authority of any kind, in which whatever order exists arises entirely from many separate traders.
options.C: A loose federation of towns, each pursuing its own aims and cooperating with the others only when doing so happens to suit it.
options.D: An army in which a general issues detailed orders for every movement and each unit carries out those orders exactly as given.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A building firm whose director sets the goals of a project while each specialist crew decides for itself how to do its own part of the work.

option_rationales.B: The octopus does have a centre: paragraph 2 says the central brain 'sets broader goals', so an arrangement with no central role at all does not fit.
option_rationales.C: This matches the 'colony of minds' slogan that paragraph 3 rejects; the arms share 'a single course of action' and do not pursue purposes of their own.
option_rationales.D: This is the centralised 'commander and its troops' picture that paragraph 2 says the octopus does not fit.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 offers the image of 'a coordinator working with partners that each know their own business': the centre sets broad goals, and each arm handles the detail of its own movement. The building firm has exactly this structure.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the federation because it captures local independence, while overlooking the author's rejection of separate purposes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options capture half of the structure each (local autonomy or a centre); only the correct answer combines both as the author does.

questions.question: According to the passage, what must an animal grasp in order to pass the mirror test?

options.A: That a mirror is a flat surface which reverses left and right in the image it reflects.
options.B: That the figure in the mirror is not another animal but corresponds to its own body.
options.C: That the mark on its forehead was placed there by the researchers who are running the test.
options.D: That its past and its future belong to one continuing individual with a history of its own.

questions.correct_answer: (B) That the figure in the mirror is not another animal but corresponds to its own body.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage requires the animal to understand the optics of mirrors; paragraph 2 concerns recognising the reflection as its own body.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists what passing requires, and knowing who placed the mark is not part of it; the animal need only connect the reflected mark with its own body.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says that passing does not, by itself, show this richer capacity; it is precisely what the passage says should not be read into success.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'To pass, an animal must grasp that the moving figure in the glass is not another individual and that what it sees there corresponds to its own body.'
questions.common_misconception: Reading the richer capacities of paragraph 4 back into the requirements of the test.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The comparison with a person asked a question in an unfamiliar language (paragraph 3) is meant to show that

options.A: self-recognition depends on language, so that animals without language cannot recognise themselves in mirrors.
options.B: researchers have been careless in choosing marks and mirrors that suit the senses of the species they study.
options.C: a test that does not suit the subject's way of engaging with the world can produce failure that reveals little.
options.D: animals that fail the mirror test would pass if the test were explained to them in a form they could understand.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a test that does not suit the subject's way of engaging with the world can produce failure that reveals little.

option_rationales.A: The analogy is about a mismatch between test and subject, not a claim that language underlies self-recognition; the passage says great apes generally pass and nowhere ties passing the test to language.
option_rationales.B: The passage criticises the inference drawn from failure, not researchers' care in carrying out the procedure; carelessness is never alleged.
option_rationales.D: The analogy concerns what failure reveals, not a prediction that any animal would pass a better version; the author never claims to know how failing animals would do.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that the test presupposes a visual animal that cares about its appearance, so failing a test designed around 'one animal's priorities is weak evidence' about another. The unfamiliar language case is a parallel: failure there shows the format did not fit, not that knowledge is absent.
questions.common_misconception: Turning an argument about weak evidence into a confident prediction that the animals would pass.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options each misread the analogy in a different plausible way; the correct answer requires seeing it as a point about evidence.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument about what failure on the mirror test shows?

options.A: Animals that pass the mirror test also tend to live in large and complex social groups.
options.B: Some animals that pass the mirror test go on to use mirrors to inspect parts of their bodies that they cannot otherwise see.
options.C: Several species of monkey that fail the mirror test perform well on other tests of memory and problem solving.
options.D: Dogs that ignore their reflection sniff a sample of their own scent far longer when it has been altered with an added odour than when it is left unchanged.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Dogs that ignore their reflection sniff a sample of their own scent far longer when it has been altered with an added odour than when it is left unchanged.

option_rationales.A: A link between passing and social life concerns which animals succeed, and it says nothing about whether the animals that fail lack self-recognition.
option_rationales.B: This concerns what animals that pass go on to do; it says nothing about whether animals that fail lack the capacity, which is the point of paragraph 3.
option_rationales.C: Memory and problem solving are different capacities from self-recognition, so success on them does not show that the mirror test missed a sense of self.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that failure may reflect a test built around vision, using the dog that 'navigates its world largely by smell' as its example. Evidence that dogs distinguish their own altered scent from their unaltered scent suggests a form of self-recognition in their dominant sense, which supports the claim that visual failure is weak evidence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the monkeys' general competence, which shows intelligence but not self-recognition.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires matching the evidence to the precise claim (failure through mismatched senses) rather than to general animal ability.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the author's view of the mirror test EXCEPT:

options.A: A species whose members do not groom may fail the test without lacking the capacity it is meant to detect.
options.B: Animals that pass the test probably have some representation of their own bodies as objects among others.
options.C: Animals that pass the test can be credited, on that evidence, with thinking of themselves as having a past and a future.
options.D: The test remains worth running, provided its results are not allowed to settle on their own which animals are self-aware.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Animals that pass the test can be credited, on that evidence, with thinking of themselves as having a past and a future.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 makes this very point about 'an animal whose species does not groom', so it is consistent with the author's view.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says it is 'reasonable to think' this of animals that pass, so the option agrees with the author.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this makes the test worthless' and that the error is letting one procedure decide the category, which is exactly this view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that recognising one's body 'does not show, by itself, that the animal reflects on its past, imagines its future or thinks of itself as a person with a history', and calls that step 'a leap of interpretation, not of evidence'. The correct answer asserts exactly the inference the author rejects.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the author's critique as wholly negative and so picking the option that says the test is worth running.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every option sounds like a moderate claim about the test, so each must be checked against a different paragraph; the correct answer is rejected only by the distinction in paragraph 4 between recognising a body and having a history.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the critics' view that brain metaphors are 'fashions' is best described as

options.A: partial agreement, accepting that no metaphor was the whole truth while denying that they were merely fashionable.
options.B: firm rejection, holding that the computer metaphor, unlike earlier ones, describes the brain literally and exactly.
options.C: complete agreement, accepting that the computer image will soon look as quaint and empty as the hydraulic one.
options.D: indifference, treating the question of whether the metaphors are fashions as unimportant to understanding the brain.

questions.correct_answer: (A) partial agreement, accepting that no metaphor was the whole truth while denying that they were merely fashionable.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the current metaphor should not be treated 'as a literal description', so the author does not exempt the computer image.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 opens 'The lesson is half right', so the author does not agree completely, and denies that the old images were empty.
option_rationales.D: The author spends paragraph 2 answering the critics, which shows the question matters to the argument.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The lesson is half right.' The author grants that none of the images 'was the whole truth' but says calling them 'mere fashions' misses 'what each one got right'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the signal phrase 'half right' and choosing a whole-hearted position.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is named in a short opening sentence.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the main contribution of the computer metaphor as the idea that

options.A: the brain can be divided into hardware and software, with programs that run independently of the structures doing the work.
options.B: what matters about neural signals is the information they carry and how it is transformed, not the material that carries them.
options.C: signals must travel from the senses to the centre and back again to the muscles along definite routes.
options.D: memories are held in fixed locations in the brain, where each record remains unaltered until it is retrieved.

questions.correct_answer: (B) what matters about neural signals is the information they carry and how it is transformed, not the material that carries them.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says this division fits the brain poorly, because 'the program and the machine are hard to tell apart'; it is a misleading feature, not the lasting contribution.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 credits this idea to the hydraulic picture and the importance of routing to the switchboard, not to the computer.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 presents memory as storage as a feature of the metaphor that comes 'along unexamined' and probably misleads, so it is not counted as the metaphor's contribution.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'The computer captured the idea that what matters about these signals is the information they carry and the transformations performed on it, rather than the stuff that carries them', and treats each metaphor's captured idea as its surviving contribution.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a feature of the computer metaphor that paragraph 3 lists among its misleading baggage.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are genuine features of the computer image, so the reader must separate what it got right from what it carries unexamined.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the critics in paragraph 2?

options.A: Researchers who used the switchboard image also held many beliefs about the brain that later turned out to be false.
options.B: The ideas credited to each metaphor were already established by direct study of nerves before that metaphor came into use.
options.C: Some present-day researchers prefer to describe the brain using images drawn from biology rather than from machines.
options.D: The hydraulic picture of the nerves was far more widely accepted among scholars than the switchboard picture ever was.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The ideas credited to each metaphor were already established by direct study of nerves before that metaphor came into use.

option_rationales.A: The author already grants that none of the images 'was the whole truth', so additional false beliefs held by their users do not touch the reply.
option_rationales.C: Alternative images used today say nothing about whether the older technological metaphors contributed lasting ideas.
option_rationales.D: How widely each image was accepted is irrelevant to whether it made some feature of the nervous system thinkable.

questions.explanation: The reply in paragraph 2 is that each metaphor 'was adopted because it made some feature of the nervous system thinkable' and left a contribution. If those features were already understood independently before the metaphors arrived, the metaphors contributed nothing of their own and the critics' charge of fashion looks stronger.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that criticises the metaphors in a way the author has already conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying the precise claim the reply depends on and seeing which evidence removes it.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Machine metaphors for the brain have each made something real thinkable, and the risk is in mistaking them for literal descriptions.
options.B: The computer is the most accurate metaphor for the brain yet devised, because it is the most complex machine so far built.
options.C: Brain metaphors drawn from machines are passing fashions, and brain science would progress faster if it gave them up.
options.D: Memory is better described as reconstruction than as storage, contrary to what the computer image of the brain suggests.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Machine metaphors for the brain have each made something real thinkable, and the risk is in mistaking them for literal descriptions.

option_rationales.B: The author never ranks the metaphors by accuracy, and paragraph 3 lists ways in which the computer image misleads.
option_rationales.C: This is the critics' lesson that paragraph 2 calls 'half right', and paragraph 4 says thinking without any metaphor 'is not an available option'.
option_rationales.D: This is one example in paragraph 3 of a feature the metaphor brings unexamined; it is too narrow to be the passage's central claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that each metaphor 'made some feature of the nervous system thinkable', paragraph 3 locates the danger in unexamined features, and paragraph 4 concludes that the habit to avoid is 'mistaking the tool for the thing'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the critics' view, which the passage reports at length before qualifying it.
questions.difficulty_reason: A reported view, an example and an unsupported ranking compete with the correct answer; the reader must hold the author's two-sided verdict.

questions.question: According to the evolutionary explanation described in the passage, perception seems easy to us because

options.A: children practise it constantly in their earliest years, long before they begin any formal schooling.
options.B: it requires very little computation compared with abstract tasks such as algebra and chess.
options.C: the processes that carry it out operate almost entirely outside conscious awareness.
options.D: it is performed by a small and specialised part of the brain that works without needing effort.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the processes that carry it out operate almost entirely outside conscious awareness.

option_rationales.A: Childhood practice is not part of the explanation; paragraph 2 appeals to evolutionary history and to what reaches awareness.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: our sense of ease 'tracks how much of a skill reaches consciousness, not how much computation it requires', and the machinery is called 'vast'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 calls the machinery of perception 'vast, ancient and almost entirely hidden from awareness'; nothing in it describes perception as the work of a small brain region.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the machinery of perception is 'almost entirely hidden from awareness', so 'we notice nothing when we recognise a friend's face, and conclude that perception is easy'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing seeming easy with being computationally light, which the passage explicitly separates.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a mistake?

options.A: Holding that the skills of seeing, grasping and moving were refined over a very long period of animal evolution.
options.B: Recognising that machines now identify images and speech far better than early researchers expected.
options.C: Doubting that skill at chess and formal logic is the best measure of how intelligent a creature is.
options.D: Concluding that a skill must demand a great deal of computation simply because people perform it without any effort.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Concluding that a skill must demand a great deal of computation simply because people perform it without any effort.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 presents this as part of the explanation that paragraph 3 calls 'persuasive', so the author would not regard it as a mistake.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 states this itself ('Nor has the gap stood still'), so it is the author's own observation, not a mistake.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 calls the identification of intelligence with such activities 'parochial', so the author shares this doubt.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 warns that the evolutionary explanation 'should not be stretched into the claim that every skill we find effortless is computationally deep', because it explains 'a general tendency' and 'does not supply a rule'. Inferring depth from effortlessness alone is exactly that stretch.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the general tendency as a rule, which the author explicitly cautions against.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are positions the author holds in different paragraphs; the correct answer is a tempting overextension of the passage's own explanation.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the account of the paradox given in paragraph 2?

options.A: Upgrading the parts of a machine so that it completes in seconds a calculation that once took hours.
options.B: Judging the size of an iceberg from the part above the water, and so overlooking the far larger mass beneath it.
options.C: Finding a subject hard at school because it was taught badly, and later finding it easy under a better teacher.
options.D: Believing that a familiar walk is shorter than an unfamiliar one of equal length, simply because it is familiar.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Judging the size of an iceberg from the part above the water, and so overlooking the far larger mass beneath it.

option_rationales.A: This concerns making a task faster, not misjudging how demanding a task is, so it misses the structure of the explanation.
option_rationales.C: Here difficulty comes from poor instruction, whereas paragraph 2 explains the misjudgement by how little of a skill reaches awareness.
option_rationales.D: Familiarity is not the passage's explanation; perception seems easy because its machinery is 'hidden from awareness', not because it is well practised.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'our sense of difficulty tracks how much of a skill reaches consciousness, not how much computation it requires'. As with an iceberg, the visible part (conscious effort) is a poor guide to the whole, most of which is hidden.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the familiar walk, which also involves misjudgement but for a reason the passage does not give.
questions.difficulty_reason: The analogy must match the mechanism (visible part misleads about the hidden whole), not just the presence of misjudgement.

questions.question: Given the passage as a whole, the author's answer to whether the 'paradox' 'deserves the name' is best captured by which of the following?

options.A: It is a genuine contradiction in the science of machines, and recent progress in machine perception has now largely resolved it.
options.B: It is misnamed, because machines have in fact always found perceiving and moving easier than reasoning.
options.C: It deserves the name, since the evolutionary account cannot explain why some effortless skills are also easy for machines.
options.D: The finding is surprising only on the assumption that the effort a task costs humans measures how much intelligence it requires.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The finding is surprising only on the assumption that the effort a task costs humans measures how much intelligence it requires.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the gap has narrowed but that manipulating unfamiliar objects 'remains much harder', and the author locates the surprise in our assumptions, not in a contradiction.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the observation in paragraph 1, which says perception and movement 'proved stubbornly hard' for machines.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 treats such cases as limits on the evolutionary story as a rule, not as a failure that makes the finding a true paradox; the author still endorses the account as explaining 'a general tendency'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says whether it deserves the name 'depends on what we took difficulty to be'. Paragraph 2 explains the surprise as 'an artefact of introspection', and paragraph 4 says 'What humans find hard is a measure of human limitations'. The paradox dissolves once human effort is no longer taken as the measure of difficulty.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the exceptions in paragraph 3 as evidence that the paradox is real, or misreading recent progress as a resolution.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is never stated outright; it must be assembled from the framing question in paragraph 1 and the conclusions of paragraphs 2 and 4.

questions.question: The sentence 'If a language were a prison, its inmates would not so regularly be found outside the walls' functions in paragraph 1 to

options.A: introduce the weaker form of the view that the passage goes on to examine in paragraph 2.
options.B: suggest that translation between languages, however carefully attempted, is never fully possible.
options.C: sum up, in a single image, the objections that count against the strong form of the view.
options.D: concede that the strong view contains a real, if limited, truth about how language confines its speakers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) sum up, in a single image, the objections that count against the strong form of the view.

option_rationales.A: The weaker view is introduced only at the start of paragraph 2 ('From the ruins of the strong view'); the prison sentence closes the case against the strong view.
option_rationales.B: The objections say translation 'though imperfect, is possible'; the image is about people escaping the limits of their language, which is the reverse of this option.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls the strong view 'thoroughly discredited'; the image is a reductio of the view, not a concession to it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 lists three objections (people learn distinctions their language lacks, translation is possible, people think thoughts they cannot word) and then concludes with the prison image: if language confined thought, people would not so often think beyond it.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the final sentence as a transition to paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function depends on seeing the sentence as the conclusion of a list of objections.

questions.question: The finding described in paragraph 3 matters to the author's argument chiefly because it suggests that

options.A: the colour advantage reflects words being drawn on during the task, not a lasting change in how colours are seen.
options.B: speakers with only one basic word for blue tell blues apart by relying on spatial memory rather than on words.
options.C: the advantage reported in paragraph 2 was an artefact of careless experimental design and should be disregarded.
options.D: the verbal and visual systems draw on one shared store of memory, so that occupying either one weakens the other.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the colour advantage reflects words being drawn on during the task, not a lasting change in how colours are seen.

option_rationales.B: The spatial task is a comparison condition that left the advantage intact; the passage draws no conclusion about how speakers with one word for blue perform the task.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says of the effect 'it was there', treating it as real; paragraph 3 reinterprets its source, it does not dismiss it.
option_rationales.D: The passage reports only that occupying the verbal system removed the advantage while a spatial task 'left it intact'; it never tests the reverse, and it explains the result by words being 'recruited on the spot', not by a shared store of memory.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that occupying the verbal system made the advantage largely disappear while a spatial task did not, and concludes that the words 'were not permanently altering how the visual system sorted colours' but were 'recruited on the spot'. Paragraph 4 builds the author's thesis on exactly this.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a reinterpretation of the effect for a dismissal of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires understanding why the spatial control matters and how paragraph 3 feeds the thesis in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the interpretation the author offers in paragraph 4?

options.A: A larger study finds that lifelong speakers with two words for blue keep the boundary advantage even while their verbal system is fully occupied by another task.
options.B: Languages differ in how many basic words they have for shapes and textures as well as for colours.
options.C: The boundary advantage for speakers with two words for blue is larger when the two colours are shown side by side than when they are shown one after the other.
options.D: Speakers of a language with one basic word for blue quickly learn to tell lighter and darker blues apart when rewarded for doing so.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A larger study finds that lifelong speakers with two words for blue keep the boundary advantage even while their verbal system is fully occupied by another task.

option_rationales.B: Variation across languages is already granted in paragraph 2; it says nothing about whether words act as on-the-spot tools or as lasting influences on perception.
option_rationales.C: Changes in the size of the effect across display conditions do not bear on whether the effect depends on words being used during the task.
option_rationales.D: This fits the author's account, and the first objection in paragraph 1, that speakers can learn distinctions their language lacks; it does not show that language engraves categories on perception.

questions.explanation: The author's interpretation rests on the advantage vanishing when the verbal system is busy, which shows the words are used 'there and then' rather than having 'engraved' categories on perception. If the advantage survived verbal interference in lifelong speakers, it would point to a lasting perceptual change, the reading the author rejects.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the learning option because it concerns perception of the same blues, without asking whether it separates lasting effects from on-the-spot use.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must identify the evidence the interpretation depends on and construct the result that would undercut it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that defenders and critics of linguistic relativity alike

options.A: accept that the strong form of the view, though discredited, is still defended by many researchers.
options.B: agree that the effects of colour words on perception are too small to be worth studying further.
options.C: recognise that ordinary thought is often partly carried out in words even where it seems wordless.
options.D: judge the importance of language by whether it leaves a lasting mark on how speakers perceive.

questions.correct_answer: (D) judge the importance of language by whether it leaves a lasting mark on how speakers perceive.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the strong view 'is now defended by almost nobody', and nothing suggests either camp thinks otherwise.
option_rationales.B: Only the critics are said to read 'the smallness of the effects as deflation'; the defenders read the same results 'as vindication'.
option_rationales.C: This is the author's own conclusion in paragraph 4, which the author says both camps 'have both tended to miss'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says defenders treat the results as showing that language 'shapes thought' and critics take the small effects to mean 'language barely matters'. Both are measuring language by its effect on a mind it might 'reshape', the question the author replaces with how often thinking 'proceeds by borrowing words as tools'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the author's conclusion to the camps the author criticises.
questions.difficulty_reason: The shared assumption is not stated; it must be drawn from the contrast in paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, Morgan's canon was first proposed as a response to

options.A: a growing belief among scientists that animals were mere machines that lacked any mental faculties at all.
options.B: disputes over whether chimpanzees and humans rely on similar mechanisms when they behave in similar ways.
options.C: reports of animal intelligence in which observers read their own feelings into what animals did.
options.D: experiments on animals that had been designed so poorly that they could not rule out simpler explanations.

questions.correct_answer: (C) reports of animal intelligence in which observers read their own feelings into what animals did.

option_rationales.A: The passage describes the opposite excess, anecdotes in which 'dogs reasoned, cats planned and birds grieved'; denial of animal minds is not what Morgan was answering.
option_rationales.B: The chimpanzee case appears in paragraph 3 as part of the author's critique of the later presumption, not as the problem Morgan addressed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the problem was anecdote, not poor experiments; controlled experiments are presented in paragraph 2 as something the canon later encouraged.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the evidence of the time 'consisted of anecdotes sent in by pet owners and naturalists ... in which the observer's own feelings were read into whatever the animal happened to do', and the canon was a discipline 'Against this habit'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the later consequences of the canon, described in paragraph 2, as its original target.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in paragraph 1.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that, when two closely related species behave alike in similar circumstances, the author regards an explanation in terms of shared mechanisms as

options.A: certainly correct, since close kinship guarantees that similar behaviour arises from similar mechanisms.
options.B: possibly the more parsimonious account, contrary to what the rigid reading of the canon implies.
options.C: a kind of anthropomorphism that the canon was rightly designed to prevent scientists from adopting.
options.D: impossible to test, since the mechanisms behind behaviour can never be observed directly in either species.

questions.correct_answer: (B) possibly the more parsimonious account, contrary to what the rigid reading of the canon implies.

option_rationales.A: The author says only that it is 'arguably the simpler hypothesis'; paragraph 5 insists that rival hypotheses still be tested, so certainty is not claimed.
option_rationales.C: The author argues that insisting on a lower mechanism for the chimpanzee 'is to multiply explanations', which defends the shared-mechanism account rather than condemning it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 recommends designing 'observations that would tell them apart', so the author thinks such hypotheses can be tested.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the shared-mechanism assumption is, 'given their close kinship, arguably the simpler hypothesis', and that insisting on a lower mechanism for the chimpanzee alone multiplies explanations. The hedge 'arguably' rules out certainty.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the hedge 'arguably' and choosing the certain version.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option differs from the correct answer mainly in degree.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards Morgan's canon?

options.A: Critical of Morgan for having meant his rule as a ban on crediting any animal with a higher faculty.
options.B: Hostile, since the author holds that it set the study of animal minds back by encouraging excessive caution.
options.C: Approving of the presumption it later became, while regretting that it began as a reaction against anecdote.
options.D: Appreciative of what it achieved as a corrective, but critical of the fixed presumption it later hardened into.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Appreciative of what it achieved as a corrective, but critical of the fixed presumption it later hardened into.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says Morgan 'appears to have intended his rule as a guard against careless inference rather than as a ban', so the author does not blame Morgan for the hardened version.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'As a corrective, the canon did its work well' and credits it with pushing the field towards testable explanations, which is not hostility.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the author's view: the author calls the later presumption 'a bias that happens to look like' caution and does not regret the reaction against anecdote.

questions.explanation: The author praises the canon's original role (paragraph 2) and spares Morgan himself (paragraph 5), but argues in paragraphs 3 and 4 that the hardened presumption is 'not as neutral as it looks' and is in effect 'a bias'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating criticism of the later use as criticism of Morgan's own intention.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options confuse the canon's origin with its later use; the reader must keep the two apart.

questions.question: The author criticises the presumption in favour of the lowest explanation on each of the following grounds EXCEPT that it

options.A: can require separate explanations for similar behaviour in closely related species, rather than fewer.
options.B: relies on experiments that are unable, in principle, to tell lean explanations apart from rich ones.
options.C: equates a lower explanation with a simpler one, and a simpler explanation with a more probable one.
options.D: guards against crediting animals with capacities they lack while ignoring the error of denying capacities they have.

questions.correct_answer: (B) relies on experiments that are unable, in principle, to tell lean explanations apart from rich ones.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says that insisting on a lower mechanism for the chimpanzee alone is 'to multiply explanations, not to reduce them'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 makes exactly this criticism: the presumption takes a lower explanation to be a simpler one, and a simpler one to be 'more probably true'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the canon 'is silent about the opposite mistake, denying them capacities they have', which is this criticism.

questions.explanation: The author never says that experiments cannot separate lean and rich explanations; on the contrary, paragraph 5 recommends designing 'observations that would tell them apart'. The other three criticisms appear in paragraphs 3 and 4.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because the author criticises the canon, any criticism of animal research must be the author's.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each of the three supported criticisms is in a different place, so the reader must check all of them.

questions.question: A researcher wants to know whether crows that hide food take account of which other birds have watched them. Which approach best reflects the 'symmetrical standard' the author recommends?

options.A: State both an association account and an account in which crows track what others have seen, and design trials in which the two predict different behaviour.
options.B: Design an experiment to test the association account first, and accept the richer account only if the association account clearly fails.
options.C: Collect many careful reports from experienced bird-watchers, and accept whichever account the largest number of reports supports.
options.D: Accept the account in which crows track what others have seen, since crows are widely regarded as unusually intelligent birds.

questions.correct_answer: (A) State both an association account and an account in which crows track what others have seen, and design trials in which the two predict different behaviour.

option_rationales.B: Although it uses an experiment, it still makes the lean account the default that must be defeated, which is the asymmetry paragraph 4 calls 'a bias'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says 'None of this is a case for returning to the anecdote', and reports from observers are the kind of evidence the canon was meant to discipline.
option_rationales.D: This adopts the rich explanation by default, which is the 'opposite' of the canon that paragraph 5 says is not the better successor.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 describes the symmetrical standard as: 'state the rival hypotheses, rich and lean alike, and design observations that would tell them apart', with simplicity 'argued for in each case, rather than a verdict delivered in advance'. Only the correct answer treats both hypotheses on equal terms and seeks a discriminating test.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that tests the lean account first, because it sounds rigorous, without noticing that it keeps the lean account as the default.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options involve experiments and differ only in whether one hypothesis is privileged; the reader must apply the idea of symmetry exactly.

questions.question: The example of early thermometers in paragraph 4 is used to

options.A: suggest that the study of consciousness is still at the stage that the study of heat was centuries ago.
options.B: argue that no-report methods should replace reports entirely in the study of conscious experience.
options.C: show that a circle of mutual checking among imperfect measures need not be a vicious one.
options.D: show that bodily sensations are a more trustworthy guide to temperature than thermometers are.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that a circle of mutual checking among imperfect measures need not be a vicious one.

option_rationales.A: The comparison concerns the logic of calibration, not the maturity of the two fields; nothing is said about consciousness research being backward.
option_rationales.B: The example defends no-report methods against the charge of circularity; the author never says reports should be replaced, and treats them as evidence to be calibrated.
option_rationales.D: The example says the reverse: thermometers 'came to correct the very sensations against which they had first been checked'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 answers the critics' circle with the thermometer history and draws the moral directly: 'A circle of mutual calibration is vicious only if it never widens'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the analogy as a claim about relative maturity of sciences, or as a preference for instruments over reports.
questions.difficulty_reason: The moral of the example is stated in the sentence after it.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the masking experiments described in paragraph 3, holding the physical stimulus constant matters because it

options.A: shows that subjects' reports of what they have seen are accurate and can be accepted without checking.
options.B: rules out differences in the image itself as the cause of differences in brain activity between kinds of trial.
options.C: removes any influence that the act of reporting might have on the brain activity that is recorded.
options.D: ensures that the subject has actually seen the image on every trial, whatever her report says.

questions.correct_answer: (B) rules out differences in the image itself as the cause of differences in brain activity between kinds of trial.

option_rationales.A: Holding the stimulus fixed does nothing to validate reports, and paragraph 2 says reports must be 'calibrated against other evidence'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the reverse: even with the stimulus held constant, some activity 'may belong to reporting rather than to experiencing'.
option_rationales.D: The method depends on the image sometimes not being reported as seen; constancy of the stimulus does not make every trial a seen trial.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'Because the physical stimulus is held constant, differences in brain activity between seen and unseen trials can be attributed, at least tentatively, to the difference in experience rather than to the stimulus.'
questions.common_misconception: Thinking the control also removes the reporting confound, which the next sentences say it does not.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing what the control does and, from the following sentences, what it does not do.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a subject's sincere report that she saw nothing on a particular trial

options.A: is less reliable than the involuntary eye movements that are used to track which image is being experienced.
options.B: should be set aside, since reports are shaped too strongly by expectation and the wish to please to count as data.
options.C: settles that she had no experience of the image on that trial, since no one else is better placed to know.
options.D: is evidence about her experience that could, in principle, turn out to be mistaken.

questions.correct_answer: (D) is evidence about her experience that could, in principle, turn out to be mistaken.

option_rationales.A: The author never ranks such signs above reports; paragraph 4 notes they were 'validated by showing that they agree with reports' and defends a mutual calibration in which neither is simply superior.
option_rationales.B: This is the first attitude, and paragraph 2 says it 'draws the wrong conclusion'; reports are 'fallible but informative'.
option_rationales.C: This is the second attitude of paragraph 1, which paragraph 2 rejects because people 'are often wrong about their own experience'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a report 'can misdescribe the experience it is about' and should be treated 'as evidence about experience, fallible but informative'. A sincere report of seeing nothing is therefore evidence, but not beyond error.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the eye-movement option, which sounds like the methodological progress the passage describes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are the attitudes the author rejects, and the third misreads the calibration argument as a ranking; the reader must hold the author's middle position precisely.

questions.question: Which of the following most closely parallels the reasoning the author uses to answer the critics in paragraph 4?

options.A: A witness's account of an accident is accepted in full because the witness is sincere and had a clear view of what happened.
options.B: A measuring tape is thrown away for good once it is found to stretch slightly whenever the weather is hot.
options.C: Two independent methods for dating ancient timber, each with known errors, come to be trusted more once they agree across many samples, and each is then used to refine the other.
options.D: A new thermometer is trusted because it was made in the same workshop as an older thermometer that has always been reliable.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Two independent methods for dating ancient timber, each with known errors, come to be trusted more once they agree across many samples, and each is then used to refine the other.

option_rationales.A: This treats a sincere report as the last word, the attitude paragraph 2 rejects; there is no cross-checking of independent methods.
option_rationales.B: This discards an instrument for being fallible, which is the response paragraph 2 rejects: 'the usual response is to study its errors, not to throw it away'.
option_rationales.D: This borrows the thermometer but replaces mutual calibration among independent methods with trust in a shared origin, which is not the author's reasoning.

questions.explanation: The author's reply is that 'when independent methods, each imperfect, are tested against one another and turn out to agree, confidence in all of them can rise together', as with thermometers that later corrected the sensations that first checked them. The timber case has the same structure: independent, imperfect methods, agreement, and mutual refinement.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the thermometer option because it shares surface vocabulary with the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option copies the passage's example while changing its logic, and the others mirror the two attitudes the author rejects.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Reports are fallible evidence that can be calibrated, so doubts about them do not rule out a science of consciousness, whatever its final reach.
options.B: Sincere reports may misdescribe detail, but they remain the final authority on what a subject actually experiences.
options.C: Because reports so often misdescribe experience, consciousness research should rely on no-report methods instead of on reports.
options.D: A science of consciousness will explain why experience exists once its methods of measurement have been calibrated against one another.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Reports are fallible evidence that can be calibrated, so doubts about them do not rule out a science of consciousness, whatever its final reach.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 rejects treating a sincere report as 'the last word'; this option restates the attitude the author dismisses most easily.
option_rationales.C: No-report signs were 'validated by showing that they agree with reports', and the author defends both as mutually calibrating; the passage does not prefer one to the other.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says the doubt about explaining 'why experience exists at all' 'may be justified'; the author does not promise this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that reports are 'fallible but informative' and must be calibrated; paragraphs 3 and 4 show this in practice and answer the circularity objection; paragraph 5 separates doubts about the science's reach from doubts about its data. The correct answer captures both the claim and its limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that overstates the science's reach, overlooking the concession in paragraph 5.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures part of the passage but misstates its scope or reverses a qualification.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that secure tenure matters more to the residents of informal settlements than drains, water supply or paved lanes.
options.B: argue that improving informal settlements where they stand generally serves residents better than relocating them, while noting where this approach falls short.
options.C: argue that informal settlements, having been built by their own residents, should be left as they are rather than altered by public authorities.
options.D: explain why planners in the last century preferred to build replacement housing on cheap land at the edge of the city.

questions.correct_answer: (B) argue that improving informal settlements where they stand generally serves residents better than relocating them, while noting where this approach falls short.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists tenure among the things upgrading adds and calls it crucial, but it never ranks tenure above infrastructure; the option invents a comparison.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 calls the view that settlements are 'good as they are' a romantic one 'their residents rarely share', and paragraph 3 endorses adding lanes, drains and tenure.
option_rationales.D: The location of the new blocks is a detail of paragraph 1; the passage as a whole is about why upgrading in place is the better response, so the option is too narrow.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the old policy of clearance, paragraph 2 explains why it failed (location sustains livelihoods), paragraph 3 presents upgrading in place as the better alternative, and paragraph 4 notes its limits (hazardous land, demolitions, missing tenure). The correct answer captures both the thesis and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that settlements should be left as they are because the author is sympathetic to residents, and missing the explicit rejection of the romantic view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated plainly in paragraphs 2 and 3; the wrong options are a reversal, a detail and an invented ranking.

questions.question: According to the passage, the relocation blocks were often half empty within a few years because

options.A: the land chosen for the estates was prone to flooding and landslides during the heavy rains of the monsoon.
options.B: the new blocks lacked the drains and secure walls that the residents had been promised before they agreed to move.
options.C: the residents were ungrateful and did not understand which kind of housing would serve their interests best.
options.D: moving to them cut households off from the work, schools and markets that had made their earlier location valuable.

questions.correct_answer: (D) moving to them cut households off from the work, schools and markets that had made their earlier location valuable.

option_rationales.A: Flooding and landslides are mentioned in paragraph 4 about some informal settlements, not about the relocation estates.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says relocation 'improves the walls'; the problem was what the move destroyed, not missing facilities in the blocks.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 reports this as how officials 'read' the empty blocks; paragraph 2 rejects that reading as less persuasive than the author's own.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says families chose their sites 'because of what it is close to', and that relocation to a distant estate 'improves the walls while destroying the arrangement', costing travel time or income. The empty blocks were 'a verdict' on that loss.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the official explanation in paragraph 1, which the author reports only to reject.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in paragraph 2; the main trap is a view the author reports but rejects.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that the empty blocks were 'not a puzzle but a verdict' means that the empty blocks were

options.A: a judgement on relocation that residents delivered by moving out, once the costs of distance are understood.
options.B: a court ruling that later stopped the authorities from clearing further settlements across the city.
options.C: a mystery that planners could not explain, even after they had studied the residents' reasons closely.
options.D: an official finding that the new housing had been badly designed and poorly built by the authorities.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a judgement on relocation that residents delivered by moving out, once the costs of distance are understood.

option_rationales.B: The passage mentions no legal proceedings; 'verdict' is used figuratively for the residents' response.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'puzzle' reading the sentence explicitly denies; once location is understood, the empty blocks need no special explanation.
option_rationales.D: No official finding is mentioned, and the passage says relocation improved the walls; the verdict was passed by residents, not by officials.

questions.explanation: The sentence follows the account of what relocation cost households. By leaving the blocks, residents in effect pronounced judgement on the policy; their behaviour is explained, not mysterious, once the importance of location is seen.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'verdict' literally as a legal or official decision.
questions.difficulty_reason: Figurative phrase explained by the sentences just before it.

questions.question: The author would most likely describe a programme that paves the lanes and lays sewers in a settlement but gives residents no protection against eviction as

options.A: a romantic attempt to keep the settlement exactly as it was, against the wishes of most of its residents.
options.B: a successful upgrade, because residents stay where they are and the networks that sustain them are preserved.
options.C: an incomplete improvement, because residents would remain unwilling to invest in houses they might still lose.
options.D: worse than relocation, because improving such a settlement amounts to investing in a future disaster.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an incomplete improvement, because residents would remain unwilling to invest in houses they might still lose.

option_rationales.A: Paving lanes and laying sewers changes the settlement; the romantic view in paragraph 4 is the belief that settlements are good unchanged.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls secure tenure crucial to upgrading, and paragraph 4 says a programme that 'installs pipes but withholds tenure' leaves residents 'still insecure', so the author would not call it a success.
option_rationales.D: The 'future disaster' remark in paragraph 4 concerns settlements on land that floods or slides, not settlements lacking tenure.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says tenure is needed 'so that residents can invest in their houses without fearing' demolition, and paragraph 4 says a programme that 'installs pipes but withholds tenure leaves residents improved and still insecure'. The author would see such a programme as falling short.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'successful upgrade' option because staying in place is the advantage the passage stresses, and overlooking the tenure condition.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the tenure clause in paragraph 3 with the caution in paragraph 4; one wrong option states a real advantage of upgrading.

questions.question: According to the passage, density differs from crowding in that

options.A: density is a ratio of people or dwellings to land, while crowding concerns too many people for the room they have.
options.B: density is found mainly in large cities, while crowding is a problem that arises chiefly in villages.
options.C: density damages the health of residents, while crowding is merely uncomfortable for those who experience it.
options.D: density refers to how many people share a room, while crowding refers to how many live on a hectare.

questions.correct_answer: (A) density is a ratio of people or dwellings to land, while crowding concerns too many people for the room they have.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 uses the village only to show that crowding can occur without density; it does not confine either condition to one kind of place.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the lethal conditions were overcrowded rooms and bad sanitation, and that death rates fell even where districts stayed dense, which is close to the opposite.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the definitions in paragraph 1, where density is people 'on a given area of land' and crowding is 'too many people in too little room'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines density technically as 'the number of people, or of dwellings, on a given area of land' and crowding as 'too many people in too little room'; paragraph 2 sums up: 'Density ... describes land; crowding describes the conditions of daily life.'
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the two definitions under time pressure.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both definitions are stated directly in paragraphs 1 and 2.

questions.question: The comparison of two districts with the same number of residents per hectare (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that maps showing population per hectare are usually drawn from inaccurate or outdated figures.
options.B: show that areas equal in density can differ sharply in how crowded daily life within them is.
options.C: prove that tall apartment buildings are always better places to live than low houses on narrow lanes.
options.D: illustrate the method by which nineteenth-century reformers tried to spread the urban population out.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that areas equal in density can differ sharply in how crowded daily life within them is.

option_rationales.A: The passage treats the maps as accurate; the districts are identical 'On a map of density', and the point is that density measures land, not daily life.
option_rationales.C: The point is that density figures hide differences in living conditions, not that one building type is always superior; the word always goes beyond the example.
option_rationales.D: The reformers appear in paragraph 3; the two districts are a hypothetical comparison with no connection to their methods.

questions.explanation: The districts share a density figure but one offers generous flats among parks and the other packs several households to a building. The paragraph concludes that 'density ... describes land; crowding describes the conditions of daily life'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a recommendation of tower blocks.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the paragraph's closing sentence.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the nineteenth-century reformers mentioned in paragraph 3

options.A: deliberately exaggerated the dangers of density in order to win public support for large building programmes.
options.B: succeeded in lowering death rates in industrial cities chiefly by persuading residents to move to less dense districts.
options.C: were mistaken in thinking that anything about conditions in the industrial cities needed to be changed at all.
options.D: rightly sensed that the industrial cities were unhealthy but located the cause in density rather than in rooms and sanitation.

questions.correct_answer: (D) rightly sensed that the industrial cities were unhealthy but located the cause in density rather than in rooms and sanitation.

option_rationales.A: Nothing is said about the reformers' motives; the passage calls them 'imprecise', which implies an honest error, not deliberate exaggeration.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 credits improved water and drains with lowering death rates, and notes that districts 'often remained dense', so the fall was not due to dispersal.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'The reformers were right that something was wrong', so the author does not think their concern mistaken.

questions.explanation: The reformers blamed density and tried to 'spread people out', but the lethal factors were 'overcrowded rooms, contaminated water and absent sewers', and death rates fell with better water and drains even where density stayed high. They were 'right that something was wrong' but 'imprecise about what it was'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that credits dispersal with lower death rates, because reformers acted and death rates fell.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the cause of mortality with the observation that density often stayed high; one wrong option confuses sequence with cause.

questions.question: A city has a district in which several families typically share one room. Which approach would the author most likely recommend?

options.A: Capping the number of residents per hectare and moving those above the limit to new settlements on the edge of the city.
options.B: Replacing every low house in the district with high towers, because building upward removes crowding wherever it is tried.
options.C: Increasing the floor space available to each household and supplying water and drains, without necessarily reducing residents per hectare.
options.D: Leaving the district as it is, since residents' sense of being crowded counts for less than the measured density of the land.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Increasing the floor space available to each household and supplying water and drains, without necessarily reducing residents per hectare.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 warns that capping density to relieve crowding 'may achieve neither', pushing people into more crowded rooms or out to the city's edge.
option_rationales.B: The towers in paragraph 2 relieve crowding because their flats are 'generous'; the author never says height by itself removes crowding, and the claim that it works wherever it is tried overreaches.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'Perception counts' and the district described here is crowded in the literal sense, so the author would not leave it alone.

questions.explanation: Several families to a room is crowding, not merely density. Paragraph 4 says 'Crowding is relieved by more floor space per person and by services', and paragraph 3 shows sanitation lowering death rates without lowering density.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the density cap because the district sounds 'dense', which is exactly the confusion the passage criticises.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires classifying the case as crowding and applying the matching remedy; the tower option borrows the paragraph 2 example.

questions.question: The passage implies that, before walkability indices became common, walking was widely regarded in planning as

options.A: a fallback way of getting about for people who had no option of driving.
options.B: the most important consideration in the design of new residential districts.
options.C: a form of exercise that estate agents promoted in order to sell homes in the suburbs.
options.D: a leisure pursuit with little bearing on how people reached shops and schools.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a fallback way of getting about for people who had no option of driving.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says many districts were designed 'as if nobody would ever arrive on foot', the opposite of walking being the main consideration.
option_rationales.C: Estate agents are said to quote index figures now; nothing suggests they promoted walking as exercise before the indices existed.
option_rationales.D: The passage says walking was treated as what people did 'when they could not drive', that is, as transport of last resort, not as leisure.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the indices gave walking, 'long treated as what people did when they could not drive', a place in planning arithmetic. Walking was thus seen as a fallback.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the phrase 'long treated as' and reading the later enthusiasm back into the past.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference rests on one phrase in paragraph 1.

questions.question: Each of the following is a claim the author makes about walkability indices EXCEPT that they

options.A: rest on an assumption that the main purpose of walking is to reach some destination or other.
options.B: can be raised by a city without making the experience of walking in it any better than before.
options.C: tend to overstate the number of shops, schools and stops that lie within a short walk of a typical home.
options.D: have helped to bring walking into the calculations that planners use when they lay out districts.

questions.correct_answer: (C) tend to overstate the number of shops, schools and stops that lie within a short walk of a typical home.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the indices' blindness 'reflects an assumption that walking is chiefly a means of reaching places'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says a city can raise its score by adding shops while the hostile road remains: 'The number improves; the walk does not.'
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the indices 'gave walking ... a place in the arithmetic of planning', so the author does make this claim.

questions.explanation: The author never questions the accuracy of the counts. The complaint in paragraph 2 is that an accurate count of proximity still ignores 'the walk itself'. The other three claims appear in paragraphs 1, 4 and 3.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a critic of the indices must think their figures are wrong, when the author's point is that they measure the wrong thing.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are paraphrased from three different paragraphs, and the correct answer is a plausible criticism that the author does not make: rejecting it requires seeing that the critique concerns what is measured, not how accurately.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that two districts with identical scores can offer entirely different experiences of walking?

options.A: Many residents of districts with high index scores continue to own cars and drive for most of their journeys.
options.B: Homes in districts with high index scores tend to sell for more than similar homes in districts with low scores.
options.C: Narrow pavements beside fast traffic are found in about as many high-scoring districts as low-scoring ones.
options.D: Across a large sample of districts, residents' ratings of how pleasant their streets are to walk along closely match the districts' index scores.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Across a large sample of districts, residents' ratings of how pleasant their streets are to walk along closely match the districts' index scores.

option_rationales.A: Car ownership says nothing about whether the walks that are taken feel different in districts with the same score.
option_rationales.B: Prices bear on how the scores are used by estate agents, not on whether equal scores can hide different walking experiences.
option_rationales.C: If hostile streets occur regardless of score, the score fails to capture the experience, which supports rather than weakens the author.

questions.explanation: The author's claim is that proximity scores do not track the experience of the walk. Evidence that experienced pleasantness closely tracks the score would suggest that districts with equal scores tend to offer similar experiences, undermining the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the traffic option because it is on topic, without noticing that it supports the author.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option strengthens the claim and must be told apart from the correct answer by direction; the others are on topic but irrelevant.

questions.question: On the author's view, a city that wished to improve walking in a district, and not merely its walkability score, should begin by

options.A: abandoning composite indices and relying instead on residents' own descriptions of what their streets are like.
options.B: studying the routes residents actually use between their homes and nearby destinations, and the conditions they meet along them.
options.C: raising the share of homes that lie near public transport, since reaching transport is what walking is chiefly for.
options.D: permitting more shops, clinics and services to open within a short radius of the homes already in the district.

questions.correct_answer: (B) studying the routes residents actually use between their homes and nearby destinations, and the conditions they meet along them.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this argues for abandoning measurement'; the author wants a score treated as the beginning of an inquiry, not discarded.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 identifies the belief that walking is 'chiefly a means of reaching places' as the assumption behind the indices' blindness; the author does not hold it.
option_rationales.D: This is what paragraph 4 describes as the cheap way to raise the score while 'the hostile road ... remains untouched'; it improves the number, not the walk.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 locates the goods of walking 'en route, by the quality of the street', and paragraph 4 recommends treating a score as 'the beginning of an inquiry into a street'. Examining the actual routes and their conditions follows from both.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing to abandon the indices, which overstates the author's critique, or to add destinations, which is the very move the author warns about.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option reflects a position that appears in the passage (the score-raising move, abandoning measurement, the destination assumption); the correct answer requires combining paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, developers come to provide plazas, arcades and gardens open to the public because

options.A: the city pays them for the ground at a price well above what it would fetch on the open market.
options.B: building codes in most large cities require every new tower to include some open space at its base.
options.C: they are allowed to build larger or taller than the rules would otherwise permit in return.
options.D: open spaces attract tenants and shoppers, and so add to the rents that the developer can later charge.

questions.correct_answer: (C) they are allowed to build larger or taller than the rules would otherwise permit in return.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the city 'gains open space without paying for it'; the developer is compensated in floor area, not money.
option_rationales.B: The passage describes a voluntary exchange 'on condition that' open space is provided, not a requirement imposed on every building.
option_rationales.D: No commercial motive of this kind is mentioned; the passage names the extra floor area as what the developer gains.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Developers are permitted to build taller or larger than the rules would otherwise allow on condition that they provide a plaza, an arcade or a garden that anyone may enter.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming a commercial motive from general knowledge rather than reading the stated bargain.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, private managers tend to withdraw the permissions listed in paragraph 3 chiefly because

options.A: those permissions bring the owner a little risk and no income, rather than because owners dislike the public.
options.B: planning law in most cities forbids protest and leafleting on land that remains in private ownership.
options.C: few people who use such plazas actually wish to stay in them, meet others there or hand out leaflets.
options.D: owners regard the people who would linger or protest in their plazas with open hostility and contempt.

questions.correct_answer: (A) those permissions bring the owner a little risk and no income, rather than because owners dislike the public.

option_rationales.B: The passage mentions no such law; it says the permissions are withdrawn by management, often through 'unpublished' rules.
option_rationales.C: The passage gives no evidence about what users want; guards who appear 'the moment anyone lingers' imply that some people do wish to stay.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the permissions are withdrawn 'not out of malice', which rules out hostility as the explanation.
