questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the permissions are withdrawn 'not out of malice but because each of them is a small risk to the owner and none of them earns anything'. The motive is a calculation of risk and return.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing hostility because the plazas are described as discouraging, and missing 'not out of malice'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases a contrast in paragraph 3; the hostility wrong option tempts readers who infer motive from effect.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the practice of trading extra floor area for open space is best described as

options.A: weary indifference, because ownership settles very little and the resulting spaces will be much the same either way.
options.B: qualified approval: the exchange is sound in principle but worthless unless the city secures and enforces permissions.
options.C: warm enthusiasm, because the city obtains open space without spending any public money and owners keep it well maintained.
options.D: outright rejection, because a space in private ownership can never become genuinely public whatever rules are attached to it.

questions.correct_answer: (B) qualified approval: the exchange is sound in principle but worthless unless the city secures and enforces permissions.

option_rationales.A: That ownership 'settles very little' leads the author to focus on rules, not to indifference; paragraph 4 makes firm demands of cities.
option_rationales.C: The author accepts the critics' account of bleak, discouraging plazas and says a city that does not enforce permissions 'has not acquired public space at all'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says this complaint 'puts the matter in the wrong place', and paragraph 4 says the bargain 'need not be abandoned'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'the bargain need not be abandoned; it needs to be completed' by specifying, publishing and enforcing permissions. Without that, the city has paid for 'something that looks like a square and behaves like a lobby'. This is support conditional on enforcement.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the sharp final sentence as rejection of the whole practice.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tone is mixed: a sharp critique of current practice within acceptance of the bargain itself; one wrong option misreads 'settles very little'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the important question is who writes a space's rules and to whom the writers must answer?

options.A: A study in one city found that its privately owned plazas were, on average, smaller, darker and harder to find from the street than its publicly owned squares.
options.B: Surveys in one city found that visitors consistently rated its privately owned plazas as cleaner, quieter and safer than publicly owned squares of a similar size and age.
options.C: Over a period of several decades, developers in one city were granted progressively larger floor-area bonuses for each plaza, arcade or garden that they provided.
options.D: In one city, private plazas whose rules of use the municipality set and published were as open to loiterers and leafleters as its best squares; plazas with owner-written rules were not.

questions.correct_answer: (D) In one city, private plazas whose rules of use the municipality set and published were as open to loiterers and leafleters as its best squares; plazas with owner-written rules were not.

option_rationales.A: Size and visibility echo the critics' complaint in paragraph 1, but the finding says nothing about whether the author of the rules decides how public a space is.
option_rationales.B: Cleanliness and safety are not the permissions the author treats as defining publicness, so the finding does not bear on who writes the rules.
option_rationales.C: The size of the bonus concerns the terms of the bargain, not whether rule-making and accountability determine how public a space is.

questions.explanation: The correct answer holds ownership constant (all the plazas are private) and varies only who writes the rules; publicness then follows the rule-writer, exactly as paragraph 3 claims. The other options concern cleanliness, the bonus and physical design, none of which isolates rule-making.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the size and visibility finding because it matches the critics' complaints, which the author accepts but does not use to support this claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are on topic and echo points the passage makes; the correct answer requires seeing that only a comparison which holds ownership fixed and varies the rule-writer tests the claim.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how districts designed around the car leave the young, the old and the poor unable to reach shops on foot.
options.B: defend the suburb as a better form of settlement than the dense centre of a large city, in which families are denied space.
options.C: show that the residents of suburban streets lead far more varied lives than novelists and critics have claimed.
options.D: argue that criticism of the suburb should address its remediable design faults instead of condemning what its residents want.

questions.correct_answer: (D) argue that criticism of the suburb should address its remediable design faults instead of condemning what its residents want.

option_rationales.A: This is the concession in paragraph 2, one part of the argument rather than its purpose.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this requires us to admire the suburb', and the passage never ranks the suburb above the city centre.
option_rationales.C: The variety of suburban lives is one point in paragraph 3; the passage uses it within a larger argument about where criticism should aim, so the option is too narrow.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 questions the uniform indictment, paragraph 2 accepts its practical part, paragraph 3 rejects its cultural part, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'criticism be aimed at what can be changed': design, not desire.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the defence of suburban preferences in paragraph 3 for a defence of the suburb as such.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are accurate details; the correct answer requires holding the concession and the rejection together.

questions.question: The author treats the uniformity of the language used against the suburb (paragraph 1) as

options.A: evidence that many critics had studied suburbs closely and independently reached the same conclusions.
options.B: a sign that suburban residents themselves had come to accept the critics' description of their lives.
options.C: grounds for doubting that the indictment does justice to what suburban life is actually like.
options.D: proof that suburban streets really are as monotonous as the critics' descriptions make them out to be.

questions.correct_answer: (C) grounds for doubting that the indictment does justice to what suburban life is actually like.

option_rationales.A: The author says the uniformity 'ought to make us suspicious', which is the opposite of treating it as confirmation.
option_rationales.B: Residents' views of the critique are never discussed; the remark concerns the critics' vocabulary.
option_rationales.D: The author argues the reverse: a way of life chosen by millions 'can hardly be as simple as the language used to dismiss it'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the indictment's uniformity 'ought to make us suspicious', because a form of life chosen by many millions 'can hardly be as simple as the language used to dismiss it'. Uniform language suggests a stereotype rather than observation.
questions.common_misconception: Reading agreement among critics as evidence for their view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference turns on 'suspicious' and the sentence that follows; one wrong option reverses the author's inference.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It concedes part of the critics' case but casts those faults as products of design, preparing the later contrast between design and desire.
options.B: It dismisses the critics' practical objections to the suburb before the author turns to answer their cultural objections.
options.C: It raises a fresh objection to the suburb that the critics described in paragraph 1 had failed to notice or discuss.
options.D: It sets out the strongest evidence for the author's thesis that the suburb is a better place to raise children than the city.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It concedes part of the critics' case but casts those faults as products of design, preparing the later contrast between design and desire.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 begins 'Part of the indictment is sound' and calls the costs 'real'; it accepts the practical objections rather than dismissing them.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph opens 'Part of the indictment is sound', so these objections belong to the critique already described, not a new one.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists costs of the suburb, not advantages, and the author makes no claim that the suburb is better for children.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 concedes that car dependence and single-use zoning are 'real costs', then adds that they are 'the costs of particular design decisions'. Paragraph 4 builds on this when it says criticism should aim at 'what can be changed'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the concession and assuming that the author is answering every objection.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing how the paragraph's last two sentences set up paragraph 4; one wrong option reverses concession into dismissal.

questions.question: Which of the following proposals for an existing suburb would the author most likely regard as answering the objections accepted in paragraph 2, in the way the passage recommends?

options.A: Halting all further suburban building in the district, because development of this kind consumes land and fuel at a great rate.
options.B: Allowing a grocer and a clinic on a few corner plots, and making the main road safe for children to cross.
options.C: Replacing detached houses with blocks of flats, so that families learn to prefer shared space over private gardens.
options.D: Requiring new houses to have varied facades and materials, so that the streets no longer look monotonous to visitors.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Allowing a grocer and a clinic on a few corner plots, and making the main road safe for children to cross.

option_rationales.A: The author acknowledges these costs in paragraph 4 but does not propose a halt; a halt also does nothing for the stranded non-drivers and separated uses of paragraph 2.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the desire for privacy and space 'is not a defect to be corrected' and favours remedies that do not ask 'anyone to want a different life'.
option_rationales.D: Monotony of appearance belongs to the cultural charge the author calls weakest in paragraph 3; it is not among the costs accepted in paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 accepts that car-centred design strands non-drivers and that single-use zoning empties streets. Paragraph 4 recommends 'a small centre, mixed uses and streets that a child can safely cross'. Shops on corner plots and a safe crossing apply that remedy without changing what residents want.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing varied facades because monotony is the most familiar complaint, without noticing that the author rejects that complaint as a reading of form for life.
questions.difficulty_reason: The facade option answers a real complaint, but the wrong one; separating it requires distinguishing the practical charge of paragraph 2 from the cultural charge of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The author implies that the count of departures described in paragraph 1, if carried out carefully, would

options.A: be impossible to carry out in practice, because households that leave a district cannot be traced afterwards.
options.B: measure what it set out to measure, but would miss a kind of harm suffered by residents who stay.
options.C: show that long-standing residents of gentrifying districts leave much faster than residents of districts that have not changed.
options.D: prove that complaints about gentrification amount to little more than nostalgia for a vanished streetscape.

questions.correct_answer: (B) measure what it set out to measure, but would miss a kind of harm suffered by residents who stay.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the question is 'answerable, at least in principle' and describes how to follow households over time.
option_rationales.C: The passage supposes the opposite result, that residents left 'no faster', and the author's objection does not depend on disputing that result.
option_rationales.D: This is the conclusion that, in paragraph 1, many would draw, which paragraph 2 calls 'premature' and answers with the staying resident.

questions.explanation: The author does not challenge the count itself; paragraph 2 says the conclusion drawn from it 'assumes that the only way to lose a neighbourhood is to leave it', and the staying resident is someone 'no count of departures will register'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the nostalgia option, which is the reported view the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the reliability of the count, which is not disputed, from the scope of what it measures.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the 'loss of standing' that the author distinguishes from 'a loss of scenery' refers to

options.A: a fall in the market value of the resident's home as the neighbourhood around it changes and its prices rise.
options.B: the disappearance of familiar shopfronts, benches and buildings that once gave the street its particular look.
options.C: the resident's being compelled, sooner or later, to leave the district in which she has lived for many years.
options.D: the decline of the resident's accepted place in her street: her ease in using it and her claim to belong there.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the decline of the resident's accepted place in her street: her ease in using it and her claim to belong there.

option_rationales.A: Property values are not discussed; the examples are credit, sitting on a bench, conduct in the park and complaints to the police.
option_rationales.B: Changes of appearance are the 'scenery'; paragraph 4 confirms that what she lost is 'not a familiar shopfront but the practical standing she once had'.
option_rationales.C: The point of the example is that 'She has not moved'; the loss is suffered in place.

questions.explanation: Each example in paragraph 2 concerns how the resident may use her street and how others treat her: credit withdrawn, a guard watching her on the bench, strangers complaining about ordinary behaviour. Paragraph 4 names this 'the practical standing she once had in her own street'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'scenery' and 'standing' as synonyms for physical change.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase must be read against both the examples of paragraph 2 and the restatement in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the distinction the author draws in paragraph 4?

options.A: Planners report that judging which relations a place sustains is a good deal harder and slower than counting the households that leave it.
options.B: Newcomers to gentrifying districts frequently form close ties with one another through the new shops, schools and associations that open there.
options.C: Residents of many affluent districts that resist new housing object chiefly that newcomers would erode the informal ties and local voice they have built up over decades.
options.D: Later and more careful counts showed that departures from gentrifying districts were in fact somewhat higher than the earlier counts had suggested.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Residents of many affluent districts that resist new housing object chiefly that newcomers would erode the informal ties and local voice they have built up over decades.

option_rationales.A: The author already concedes that the distinction 'asks more of planners than a count of departures does', so this does not weaken it.
option_rationales.B: Ties among newcomers are consistent with the author's view that relations are what matter; they do not blur the line between the two kinds of claimant.
option_rationales.D: This bears on the measurement discussed in paragraph 1, not on whether character located in relations separates the staying resident from the exclusionary homeowner.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the exclusionary homeowner defends 'not a set of relations at all but the absence of people who might form new ones'. If such homeowners are in fact defending relations of use and voice, the relational test no longer separates them from the staying resident, which is the work the distinction was meant to do.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the planners option because it sounds like a real weakness, without noticing that the author has already conceded it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be seen to strike at the specific claim about the exclusionary homeowner; one wrong option restates a concession, another targets a different paragraph.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: A resident who stays in a gentrifying district loses more of her neighbourhood than one who is forced to leave it.
options.B: A count of departures, however careful, cannot register the losses of residents who remain in a changing district.
options.C: Judging character by the relations a place sustains demands more of planners than counting those who leave.
options.D: The same appeal to a neighbourhood's character can serve both to describe a genuine loss and to justify exclusion.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A resident who stays in a gentrifying district loses more of her neighbourhood than one who is forced to leave it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says of the staying resident that 'no count of departures will register her', so the statement is supported.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the distinction 'asks more of planners than a count of departures does', so the statement is supported.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the language of character is 'also the language most readily turned to the opposite purpose', so the statement is supported.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the place has been withdrawn from the staying resident 'as surely as if she had' moved: her loss is comparable to that of one who leaves, not greater. The passage never ranks the two losses, so the comparison is unsupported. The other three statements restate paragraphs 2, 3 and 4.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's insistence that the staying resident's loss is real as a claim that it is the greater loss.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported statement turns on the degree word in 'as surely as if she had' and sounds like the author's sympathy for the staying resident; the supported statements are paraphrases spread across three paragraphs.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, circular migration, when viewed on its own terms rather than through the one-way story, appears as

options.A: a way of spreading a household's risk across two places, so that a setback in one is softened by the other.
options.B: a choice made chiefly because wages in the city are so much higher than anything the village can offer.
options.C: a temporary stage in a longer journey, which comes to an end once the migrants' children have been absorbed into city life.
options.D: a means by which migrants avoid paying the school fees that the city charges to families who settle there.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a way of spreading a household's risk across two places, so that a setback in one is softened by the other.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 never compares wages; it explains circulation by the security of having 'the other place' when one fails.
option_rationales.C: This is the one-way reading of paragraph 1, which paragraph 2 contrasts with the pattern seen on its own terms.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says city earnings pay school fees in the village; nothing suggests migrants circulate to avoid fees in the city.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Seen on its own terms, the pattern looks rather different: a way of spreading risk across two places, so that a lost job in the city or a failed crop in the village need not be ruinous, because the other place remains.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the one-way reading because it is described in the same paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase in the stem leads directly to the answer in paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the remark that for some migrants circularity is 'less a strategy than a sentence' means that for them it is

options.A: a legal penalty imposed by the city's courts on workers whose residence there is irregular or unregistered.
options.B: a condition forced on them by the city's failure to offer a place, not a course they would choose.
options.C: a brief phase that will soon end as they save enough money to buy land and settle in their village.
options.D: a carefully planned way of spreading risk between a job in the city and a farm in the village.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a condition forced on them by the city's failure to offer a place, not a course they would choose.

option_rationales.A: The word 'sentence' is figurative; no courts or legal penalties are mentioned in the passage.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in paragraph 4 says the pattern is brief; the contrast is between choosing circulation and having it imposed.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'strategy' reading that the phrase says does not fit this group; it describes those who 'genuinely prefer' two places.

questions.explanation: The sentence describes migrants who 'would settle in the city if they could' and return 'only because the city offers them nothing to stay for'. For them circulation is imposed, as a sentence is, rather than chosen, as a strategy is.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'sentence' literally as a legal punishment.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative phrase is explained in the same sentence.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the persistence of circular migrants' village ties

options.A: will gradually disappear once the migrants' children have grown up speaking the idiom of the city.
options.B: shows that circular migrants have no wish to become part of the cities in which they work for months or years.
options.C: is partly a result of their exclusion from the city, and so cannot fairly be taken as proof that they do not belong there.
options.D: was the original reason why city governments decided to exclude them from housing, schools and the electoral roll.

questions.correct_answer: (C) is partly a result of their exclusion from the city, and so cannot fairly be taken as proof that they do not belong there.

option_rationales.A: That is the outcome of the one-way story in paragraph 1, which the author says does not describe this group.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says some circular migrants 'would settle in the city if they could', so the ties do not show an absence of that wish.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says governments acted on the one-way reading and that the ties are later 'cited as proof'; it does not make the ties the original cause of exclusion.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'The exclusion then produces the very evidence that justifies it. Denied a secure foothold in the city, the circular migrant has every reason to keep the village in reserve, and the persistence of his village ties is then cited as proof that he never really belonged.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'original reason' option and reversing the causal order the author describes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires following a self-reinforcing loop; one wrong option reverses cause and effect.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the one-way story of urbanisation is best described as

options.A: dismissive, since the author regards it as a myth that never described the experience of any real migrants.
options.B: neutral, since the author presents it only as one account among others and passes no judgement on its influence.
options.C: approving, since the author treats it as the proper goal against which circular migration ought to be measured.
options.D: critical of its use as a yardstick for all migration, while granting that it fits many families' history.

questions.correct_answer: (D) critical of its use as a yardstick for all migration, while granting that it fits many families' history.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says 'The story is not false; it describes what happened to many families in many countries'.
option_rationales.B: The author judges its influence explicitly, saying it has made another pattern 'difficult to see' and has shaped exclusionary policy.
option_rationales.C: The author objects that it 'has acquired the status of a norm, against which other patterns are measured and found wanting'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 grants that the story 'is not false' but objects that it has become 'a norm' against which other patterns are 'found wanting'; paragraph 3 shows the harm of acting on it. The attitude is qualified criticism.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing outright dismissal because the passage argues against the story's dominance.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession 'The story is not false' must be weighed against the criticism that follows it.

questions.question: The recommendations in paragraph 5 are suited to the difficulty raised in paragraph 4 chiefly because they

options.A: would help both migrants forced to circulate and those who choose to, without the city having to tell the two groups apart.
options.B: would end circular migration altogether by removing the hostility of cities that is its underlying cause.
options.C: would persuade migrants who prefer a life in two places to settle permanently in the city instead.
options.D: would identify which migrants wish to settle, so that each group could be offered a programme designed for it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) would help both migrants forced to circulate and those who choose to, without the city having to tell the two groups apart.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says some migrants 'genuinely prefer' two places, so hostility is not the cause of all circulation, and paragraph 5 does not aim to end it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says the measures would let 'those who wish to circulate ... circulate without penalty'; they are not designed to change that preference.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says that from the outside 'the two groups look identical', so sorting them is exactly what the city cannot do; paragraph 5 instead offers measures that 'would serve both groups at once'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the two groups 'look identical' from outside, so 'a policy designed for one will misjudge the other'. Paragraph 5 proposes measures that 'serve both groups at once', letting settlers settle and circulators circulate. The measures work without distinguishing the groups.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the sorting option because it seems the natural response to two groups with different needs.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the problem in paragraph 4 (the groups cannot be told apart) to the design of the remedy in paragraph 5; the sorting wrong option is the intuitive but wrong solution.

questions.question: The example of the tenant on a twelve-month lease in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: argue that strict limits on rent increases are the most effective single measure for improving the lives of tenants.
options.B: suggest that tenants ought to be allowed to knock down walls and alter the structure of the houses they rent.
options.C: show that a short, revocable and restrictive tenancy, not renting as such, keeps a person from making a home.
options.D: show that renters, whatever the terms of their tenancy, invest less of themselves in their rooms than owners do.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that a short, revocable and restrictive tenancy, not renting as such, keeps a person from making a home.

option_rationales.A: Unlimited rent rises are one feature of the example, but the passage ranks no single measure as most effective.
option_rationales.B: Knocking down a wall is listed in paragraph 4 as a distinctive good of ownership; the passage never proposes extending it to tenants.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 goes on to say that where tenancies are long and secure 'renters make homes much as owners do', which contradicts the claim that the terms make no difference.

questions.explanation: Right after the example, paragraph 3 says 'the cause of his condition is not that he rents. It is that his tenancy is short, revocable and hedged with prohibitions.' The example isolates insecurity and lack of control as the obstacles.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the example as evidence against renting in general.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentences that follow the example.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard the owner described at the end of paragraph 3, whose mortgage consumes most of his income, as

options.A: a person who has 'failed to arrive' at home because of the debts he took on in order to buy his house.
options.B: someone who holds title yet may lack the security on which making a home depends.
options.C: proof that owning a house is generally a worse arrangement than renting one on secure and long-term terms.
options.D: an exception that confirms the rule that ownership always supplies both of the conditions a home requires.

questions.correct_answer: (B) someone who holds title yet may lack the security on which making a home depends.

option_rationales.A: The phrase 'failed to arrive' belongs to the equation in paragraph 1, which describes renters, not indebted owners; the author rejects that equation.
option_rationales.C: The owner is offered as a case in which ownership fails to supply security, not as proof about owning in general; paragraph 4 affirms the real goods of ownership.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says ownership has 'usually' supplied both conditions; this owner shows that it does not always do so.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 names security as one of the two conditions of home-making, and paragraph 3 says this owner 'may know the very precariousness that the equation reserves for tenants'. Title has not given him the security that home requires.
questions.common_misconception: Overreading the example into a general verdict against ownership.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the owner example to the two conditions in paragraph 2; one wrong option generalises, another misattributes a phrase from paragraph 1.

questions.question: The argument of paragraph 5 depends on the assumption that

options.A: renters as a group take less interest in local schools than owners do, whatever the length and security of their tenancies.
options.B: the attachment residents feel to a neighbourhood depends mainly on the physical design of its streets and public spaces.
options.C: most households that rent would prefer to own their homes if the price of buying one were to fall far enough.
options.D: people are less willing to invest effort in places and relationships they expect soon to be separated from.

questions.correct_answer: (D) people are less willing to invest effort in places and relationships they expect soon to be separated from.

option_rationales.A: The author attributes thin attachment to the expectation of moving 'at a landlord's word', not to renting as such; paragraph 3 says secure renters make homes as owners do.
option_rationales.B: Street design plays no part in the argument; paragraph 5 links attachment to security of tenure.
option_rationales.C: The argument concerns the effects of insecurity, not tenants' preferences about tenure, so it does not need this claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 reasons that a household that 'expects to move at a landlord's word' will not join the school committee, plant a tree or learn neighbours' names. This holds only if expected separation discourages such investment.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'renters as a group' option, which states the equation the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option sounds like the paragraph's conclusion but contradicts paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: What people value in a home is above all security rather than control, so tenancy reform should give every tenant a lease without any end date.
options.B: Renting has become the usual tenure in cities, and tenancy law has failed to keep pace with the growing number of households that rent.
options.C: Ownership confers no real advantage over a secure tenancy, so public support for buyers should be ended and redirected entirely to tenants.
options.D: Home is made through practices that need control and security, which ownership usually but not necessarily supplies, so policy should not treat ownership as the only route to home.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Home is made through practices that need control and security, which ownership usually but not necessarily supplies, so policy should not treat ownership as the only route to home.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 names control and security as two conditions together, and the passage proposes no specific form of lease.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says only that 'a large and often growing share' rent; this detail serves the argument and is not its centre.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says ownership confers 'real goods' that many want 'for good reasons', and the author's objection 'is not to ownership'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 redefines home as a practice requiring control and security; paragraph 3 shows that tenancy terms, not tenure, decide whether these exist; paragraph 4 concedes the goods of ownership while rejecting it as 'the only door into home'; paragraph 5 adds the civic cost of that assumption.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that ends support for buyers, which turns the author's objection to an assumption into an objection to ownership.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are distorted versions of the thesis (one drops the concession, one drops a condition); the correct answer must keep both conditions and the 'usually but not necessarily' scope.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the policies mentioned in paragraph 1 can 'present themselves' as the extension of home rather than as choices among ways of housing people because

options.A: once home is defined as ownership, promoting ownership seems to need no defence against alternatives.
options.B: tenants who bought the public housing they had rented reported feeling far more at home there after the purchase.
options.C: their designers knew that renters could never make real homes and therefore saw no alternative to promoting ownership.
options.D: subsidised mortgages and the sale of public housing have in fact extended home to nearly all of those who lacked it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) once home is defined as ownership, promoting ownership seems to need no defence against alternatives.

option_rationales.B: No such reports appear in the passage, and the author's explanation lies in the definition of home, not in tenants' testimony.
option_rationales.C: The author argues that renters can make homes under secure tenancies, and says nothing about what designers knew; the point concerns how an equation frames choices.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such efforts leave the conditions of tenancy 'largely untouched', so the author does not accept that home has been extended to all.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the equation 'seems less a claim than a definition'. If owning simply is having a home, then a policy that spreads ownership looks like spreading home itself, and the question whether other arrangements (such as secure tenancy) could serve as well never arises.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that supplies a factual reason, when the passage's explanation is conceptual.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer depends on grasping how a claim disguised as a definition removes the appearance of choice; the wrong options offer motives or outcomes instead.

questions.question: According to the passage, in a teknonymous system the new name that a parent receives chiefly announces that

options.A: the parent has acquired property that will later pass to the child whose name now appears in the title.
options.B: the parent has reached the age at which the community grants full rights to take part in its decisions.
options.C: the parent's place among their kin has shifted, not that the parent has become a different individual.
options.D: the parent's earlier personal name has been formally prohibited and may no longer be spoken by anyone.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the parent's place among their kin has shifted, not that the parent has become a different individual.

option_rationales.A: Property and inheritance are never mentioned; paragraph 2 says the name marks a change in 'position in a web of kin'.
option_rationales.B: The passage links the new name to the birth of a child, not to reaching an age or to any grant of rights.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the personal name 'has not been forbidden'; using it is only 'mildly rude' in some communities.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'the new name announces not that the individual has changed but that their position in a web of kin has changed'. The correct answer restates this.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'outranked' or 'mildly rude' in paragraph 3 as a formal ban on the old name.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is one sentence of paragraph 2, nearly restated.

questions.question: The comparison with calling a judge by a childhood nickname in court (paragraph 3) suggests that addressing a parent by the old personal name would be

options.A: a mark of special intimacy that only the parent's closest relatives are entitled to claim.
options.B: a lapse of manners rather than a breach of any rule, since the old name is out of place but not banned.
options.C: acceptable in formal settings such as courts but quite inappropriate in ordinary daily conversation.
options.D: a serious offence that the elders of the community would be expected to punish severely.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a lapse of manners rather than a breach of any rule, since the old name is out of place but not banned.

option_rationales.A: The passage presents the old name as out of place, not as a privilege of intimates; the judge analogy points to awkwardness, not closeness.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the analogy: the nickname is out of place precisely in court, the formal setting.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls it 'mildly rude'; nothing suggests punishment, so the option exaggerates.

questions.explanation: The analogy makes the old name inappropriate rather than forbidden: it 'has simply been outranked by a title that carries more social information'. Using it is a social awkwardness, which the passage calls 'mildly rude'.
questions.common_misconception: Over-reading the analogy as a rule enforced by punishment.
questions.difficulty_reason: The analogy is explained in the sentence that follows it.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the statement that the personal name has been 'outranked' means that it has been

options.A: displaced in everyday use by a title that carries greater social weight.
options.B: forgotten entirely by the community soon after the birth of the first child.
options.C: replaced in law through an official ceremony of renaming the parent.
options.D: judged inferior in moral worth to the personal names of the parent's children.

questions.correct_answer: (A) displaced in everyday use by a title that carries greater social weight.

option_rationales.B: The name 'has not been forbidden' and can still be used, if rudely, so it has not been forgotten.
option_rationales.C: No legal or ceremonial procedure is described; the change concerns how people are addressed.
option_rationales.D: The ranking is between two ways of addressing the same person, not a moral comparison with the children's names.

questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts being 'forbidden' with being 'outranked by a title that carries more social information'. The old name survives but gives way in use to the more informative title.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'outranked' to mean abolished or erased.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contrast with 'forbidden' in the same sentence fixes the meaning.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Fixed personal names in the West are really a concealed form of teknonymy, since surnames identify people through their descendants.
options.B: Teknonymy is unjust to childless adults and should be judged a less humane way of naming people than the system of fixed names.
options.C: Naming parents through their children expresses a view of persons as made by their place among kin, differing from fixed naming in emphasis.
options.D: Teknonymy shows chiefly that the societies practising it value their children more highly than societies that use fixed names do.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Naming parents through their children expresses a view of persons as made by their place among kin, differing from fixed naming in emphasis.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says surnames announce a lineage, that is ancestry, and calls the contrast one of emphasis, not a disguised identity of the two.
option_rationales.B: The hardship on the childless is a concession in paragraph 4; the author draws no verdict that one system is less humane.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 grants 'something in this' but calls it the less interesting point; the passage's claim concerns how the person is understood.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives the central contrast (identity owned first versus identity given by relationship), paragraph 3 extends it, and paragraph 4 qualifies it as 'one of emphasis rather than of kind' while insisting 'the emphasis matters'. The correct answer holds both the claim and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'children are prized' reading that the author mentions only to move past it.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is the view the author sets aside and another inflates the concession; the correct answer must keep both claim and qualification.

questions.question: According to the passage, the opportunity-cost method values an hour of household work by

options.A: the wage that would have to be paid to someone hired to carry out the same tasks.
options.B: the price of the nearest service that can be bought, such as a meal eaten in a restaurant.
options.C: the number of hours recorded for that task in a national survey of how people use their time.
options.D: what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment in that hour.

questions.correct_answer: (D) what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment in that hour.

option_rationales.A: This is the replacement-cost method described in paragraph 2, not the opportunity-cost method.
option_rationales.B: Pricing by a bought equivalent is the logic of replacement cost; the restaurant meal in paragraph 1 illustrates what accounts count.
option_rationales.C: Time-use surveys supply the hours; paragraph 2 says turning hours into money then 'requires a choice' of method.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: opportunity cost 'asks what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment during those hours'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the two methods, which are defined in consecutive sentences.
questions.difficulty_reason: Direct definition in one sentence.

questions.question: The example of an hour of childcare by a surgeon (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: argue that the opportunity-cost method is in general more accurate than the replacement-cost method.
options.B: show that the two methods can disagree about the value of particular work, not merely about totals.
options.C: suggest that highly paid professionals tend to spend rather less time on childcare than most other parents do.
options.D: illustrate why early statisticians found household work too difficult to observe and record.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that the two methods can disagree about the value of particular work, not merely about totals.

option_rationales.A: The author does not prefer either method; paragraph 4 says 'Both methods' share the same limit.
option_rationales.C: How much time surgeons spend on childcare is never discussed; the example concerns how one hour is valued.
option_rationales.D: Early statisticians appear in paragraph 1; the surgeon example comes after the methods are defined and compares them.

questions.explanation: The example follows the statement that the methods 'can rank the same work differently': the same hour is valued highly by opportunity cost (a surgeon's earnings) and modestly by replacement cost (a childminder's wage).
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about surgeons rather than about methods.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence containing the example states its purpose.

questions.question: The author's remark that recording household care at zero 'is also a valuation' (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: the replacement-cost method ought to replace the zero convention in the national accounts of every country.
options.B: national accounts are generally so inaccurate that they should no longer be used to guide policy.
options.C: leaving such care out of the accounts is itself a contestable choice and not a refusal to choose.
options.D: the critics are right that every possible way of valuing household work is equally arbitrary.

questions.correct_answer: (C) leaving such care out of the accounts is itself a contestable choice and not a refusal to choose.

option_rationales.A: The author defends estimating but never chooses between the two methods, so this prescription goes beyond the passage.
option_rationales.B: The passage says estimates have improved policy debate; it does not reject the accounts as a guide.
option_rationales.D: The author calls the critics' conclusion 'too quick' and says zero is 'the least accurate available', so methods are not equally arbitrary.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 rejects the idea that zero is 'the neutral one': since conventions must be chosen anyway, choosing zero is one more valuation, and a poor one. Omission is therefore a choice open to challenge.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that reports the critics' view, which the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the remark answers the critics, not that it endorses a particular method.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reason the author gives in paragraph 4 for treating a figure for unpaid care as a floor rather than a measure?

options.A: Elderly people cared for by both paid workers and their own children often value the children's care for reasons unrelated to the tasks.
options.B: Families that pay for help with cleaning tend to report spending more of their own time on looking after children.
options.C: Hired carers are generally able to carry out most household and nursing tasks as efficiently as members of the family can.
options.D: Wages paid to professional care workers have risen faster in recent years than wages in most other occupations.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Elderly people cared for by both paid workers and their own children often value the children's care for reasons unrelated to the tasks.

option_rationales.B: This concerns how families reallocate tasks; it does not bear on care that has value because of who provides it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 already grants that 'Much of it can be' handed over; this adds nothing about the element that cannot be bought.
option_rationales.D: Rising wages would change the size of a replacement-cost estimate but say nothing about what a price cannot capture.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that part of family care is valuable because 'it is they who provide it', which no market price can capture. Evidence that recipients value relatives' care for reasons beyond the tasks performed directly supports that reason.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option about care and money that is on topic but does not touch the author's specific reason.
questions.difficulty_reason: The stem targets one reason, and two wrong options concern related economic facts.

questions.question: According to the passage, in some societies the bridewealth goods must be returned if a marriage ends before any children are born because

options.A: the groom's family is entitled to be repaid for the expenses it incurred in arranging the wedding.
options.B: what the goods secure is the attachment of the couple's future children to the husband's lineage.
options.C: the bride's father is obliged to give back whatever profit he gained when his daughter married.
options.D: colonial administrators insisted on such refunds as a way of discouraging couples from divorcing.

questions.correct_answer: (B) what the goods secure is the attachment of the couple's future children to the husband's lineage.

option_rationales.A: Wedding expenses are never mentioned; the return is tied to what the goods secure, the children's affiliation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the goods are usually 'not kept by the bride's father as profit', so there is no profit to refund.
option_rationales.D: Administrators appear only as observers who misdescribed the custom; the passage never says they imposed rules on it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'what passes with the goods is not the woman herself but the affiliation of her future children to the husband's lineage, which is why ... the goods must be returned if the marriage ends before any children are born'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying an outside explanation (refunded profit, costs) instead of the one the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The causal link is stated in a single sentence with 'which is why'.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author treats the chain in which the same cattle pass from family to family (paragraph 2) as evidence that

options.A: families in such societies cared more about their sons' marriages than about their daughters' marriages.
options.B: households joined by such chains usually knew one another well and met often to settle obligations.
options.C: the goods given as bridewealth had little or no economic value for the families who received them.
options.D: bridewealth sets up lasting connections among groups, which is the reverse of what a sale does.

questions.correct_answer: (D) bridewealth sets up lasting connections among groups, which is the reverse of what a sale does.

option_rationales.A: The chain links a daughter's marriage to her brother's, but the passage draws no comparison of how much families cared about either.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the chain links 'households that may never meet', which this contradicts.
option_rationales.C: Nothing suggests the cattle were worthless; they are valuable enough to secure another marriage, so the option is unsupported and extreme.

questions.explanation: Right after the chain, the author writes: 'A purchase ends a relationship between buyer and seller; this transfer begins several.' The chain is offered as proof that bridewealth creates ties, the opposite of a market sale.
questions.common_misconception: Drawing a conclusion about family preferences that the example does not support.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference needs the contrast sentence that follows the example, plus elimination of a contradiction.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards critics who see a market in cash-based bridewealth (paragraph 4) is best described as

options.A: wholehearted agreement, since their judgement is extended to bridewealth in every setting.
options.B: qualified acceptance: their judgement is granted for such cases without the older verdict being revived.
options.C: studied neutrality, because the author declines to say whether their judgement has any merit.
options.D: dismissive, because they are seen as repeating the early travellers' error in a modern form.

questions.correct_answer: (B) qualified acceptance: their judgement is granted for such cases without the older verdict being revived.

option_rationales.A: The author limits the market reading to settings where 'the web thins'; paragraphs 2 and 3 reject it for the older form.
option_rationales.C: The author explicitly credits the critics in paragraph 4, so this is not neutrality.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says these critics 'are not simply repeating the old error', which rules out dismissal.

questions.explanation: The author concedes that in cash-based, narrowly held transfers the payment 'can begin to behave much more like a price' and that the critics 'are not simply repeating the old error', while insisting that the lesson is not that 'the travellers were wrong and the custom is innocent' in general but that meaning depends on context.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the negation in 'not simply repeating the old error' and reading the author as dismissive.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is carried by a negated phrase and a contrastive final sentence.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a way in which bridewealth in its older form differs from a market purchase EXCEPT that

options.A: the transfer opened several continuing relationships instead of closing a single one.
options.B: the goods were shared out among many of the bride's relatives instead of being kept by one recipient.
options.C: the bride herself could take back the goods for her own use if her husband's family mistreated her.
options.D: the bride's kin kept an interest in how the marriage went and some reason to step in when it went badly.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the bride herself could take back the goods for her own use if her husband's family mistreated her.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'A purchase ends a relationship between buyer and seller; this transfer begins several.'
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the goods are 'distributed among a wide circle of her kin' rather than 'kept by the bride's father as profit'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the transfer gives 'the bride's family a continuing stake' and 'reason ... to intervene when it goes badly'.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the bride's family, not the bride, a stake in the marriage: the family 'may have to gather them again in order to return them' and has reason 'to intervene'. Nowhere does the bride reclaim the goods for her own use, so this is the one difference the passage does not present.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'continuing stake' option because it sounds like a consequence rather than a difference, or rejecting the correct answer because it resembles the family's stake in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer shifts the agent of a real idea from the bride's family to the bride; it must be separated from three accurate paraphrases, each located in one or two sentences.

questions.question: The reference to saints painted 'with golden discs around their heads' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: prove that medieval parents thought of their children as holy beings rather than as ordinary people.
options.B: illustrate how artistic styles changed between the medieval centuries and the early modern centuries that followed.
options.C: suggest that medieval artists cared far more about religious subjects than about painting children at all.
options.D: show that medieval images followed conventions and so are not plain records of how children were seen.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that medieval images followed conventions and so are not plain records of how children were seen.

option_rationales.A: The saints are an example of a non-realistic convention; nothing links them to how parents viewed children.
option_rationales.B: No change of style is described; the example is used to discredit the 'argument from paintings'.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no claim about how much artists cared for different subjects; the saints illustrate convention, not preference.

questions.explanation: The example follows 'Artistic conventions are not photographs': haloes were never seen, so medieval art did not simply depict what it saw, and the small-adult portrayal of children cannot prove an absence of the idea of childhood.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a supporting image as a claim about religion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Function is stated by the sentence before and after the example.

questions.question: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with

options.A: rescuing a defensible core from an influential thesis much of whose evidence has been overturned.
options.B: showing that medieval parents loved and grieved for their children just as much as parents do today.
options.C: explaining why historians should stop using paintings as evidence about the past for any purpose.
options.D: defending the claim that no notion of childhood existed in Europe before the early modern period.

questions.correct_answer: (A) rescuing a defensible core from an influential thesis much of whose evidence has been overturned.

option_rationales.B: This is the critics' finding, summarised in paragraph 2; the passage goes on to say the thesis still captures a real change.
option_rationales.C: The author criticises one inference from paintings, not the use of paintings as evidence in general.
option_rationales.D: The author accepts that 'Childhood as a feeling may be ancient', so the original strong claim is not defended.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 records what 'has not survived', paragraph 3 says 'it would be a mistake to conclude that nothing changed' and identifies the institutional change, and paragraph 4 reframes the debate. The passage salvages part of the thesis.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the critics' conclusion, which is only one stage of the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are each a stage of the argument; the correct answer must span the turn in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that the critics of the original thesis

options.A: were wrong to treat letters and court records as reliable evidence of feeling within families.
options.B: showed that schools divided into classes by age were common throughout medieval Europe.
options.C: failed to find any convincing evidence that medieval parents mourned their dead children.
options.D: settled one question while leaving open the one on which the thesis is still illuminating.

questions.correct_answer: (D) settled one question while leaving open the one on which the thesis is still illuminating.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts their findings from these sources; no objection to the sources is made.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 dates the spread of age-graded schooling to the early modern period; the passage never credits the critics with any such finding.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says they 'assembled a large body of material' showing that parents grieved, so this contradicts the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the critics 'established that medieval people knew children were different and loved them' but 'did not establish that childhood occupied the same place in social life'; paragraph 4 says the two sides were 'talking past each other' and that the second question is more fruitful.
questions.common_misconception: Inferring that because the critics were right on feeling, they were right on everything.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires joining paragraph 3's limit on the critics with paragraph 4's reframing.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that childhood 'as a segregated, age-graded stage, organised by institutions, is far more recent' (paragraph 3)?

options.A: Records from many medieval towns show most ordinary children attending age-sorted schools and barred by local rule from adult work until their teens.
options.B: Medieval sermons in many regions often urged parents to treat very young children with tenderness, patience and a particular kind of care.
options.C: Early modern painters increasingly showed children with body proportions, faces and clothing that were quite unlike those of the adults around them.
options.D: Many early modern families continued for generations to send young children to work beside adults in the fields for long hours.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Records from many medieval towns show most ordinary children attending age-sorted schools and barred by local rule from adult work until their teens.

option_rationales.B: This supports the critics' point about feeling, which the author already accepts; it says nothing about age-graded institutions.
option_rationales.C: This concerns painting conventions, which paragraph 2 treats as unreliable evidence; it says nothing about whether age-graded institutions existed before the early modern period.
option_rationales.D: The author speaks of a 'gradual spread' of institutions, so continued child labour in the period is consistent with the claim.

questions.explanation: The claim is about institutions: age-graded schooling and separation from adult work spread in the early modern period. Widespread medieval evidence of exactly such institutions would show that this form of childhood was not 'far more recent'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the sermon option because it contradicts the original thesis, without noticing that the author's claim is about institutions, not feeling.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong options attack the original thesis, not the author's narrower revised claim; the solver must isolate which claim is targeted.

questions.question: According to the passage, the old-age dependency ratio is calculated by

options.A: dividing the number of people drawing pensions by the number of people actually in paid employment.
options.B: counting how many older people in a population depend for their daily needs on unpaid care from relatives.
options.C: dividing the number of people above a set age by the number in the conventional working-age band.
options.D: comparing the years that a population can still expect to live with the years it has already lived.

questions.correct_answer: (C) dividing the number of people above a set age by the number in the conventional working-age band.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 defines the ratio by age bands alone; the author's complaint in paragraph 2 is precisely that it ignores who is actually employed.
option_rationales.B: Unpaid care is discussed as something the ratio overlooks; it plays no part in how the ratio is calculated.
option_rationales.D: This describes the prospective measure that 'Some demographers have proposed' in paragraph 3, not the ratio itself.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the ratio 'divides the number of people above a fixed age, usually sixty-five, by the number of people of working age, conventionally fifteen to sixty-four'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the ratio with the alternative measure or with the author's proposed corrections.
questions.difficulty_reason: A definition stated in one sentence.

questions.question: The mention of grandparents who look after small children (paragraph 2) is meant to suggest that the ratio

options.A: wrongly assumes that parents who depend on grandparents for childcare are less productive at their jobs.
options.B: treats as pure dependants some people whose work makes it possible for others to earn.
options.C: overlooks the fact that most grandparents would prefer to stay in paid work than to look after children.
options.D: ignores the many families in which working grandparents reduce the need for public spending on pensions.

questions.correct_answer: (B) treats as pure dependants some people whose work makes it possible for others to earn.

option_rationales.A: The ratio makes no assumption about parents' productivity; the passage criticises how it classifies the grandparents.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about what grandparents prefer; the point is how their existing work is counted.
option_rationales.D: Pensions saved by working grandparents are not discussed; the grandparents in the example provide unpaid childcare, not earnings.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says grandparents' childcare 'allows both parents to hold jobs', yet 'on the ratio's accounting, those grandparents appear only as a cost'. The example shows the ratio counting contributors as dependants.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about grandparents' preferences or pensions.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point must be drawn from the sentence's contrast between real contribution and the ratio's accounting.

questions.question: A planning ministry that fully accepted the author's argument would be most likely to forecast its future obligations to older citizens by

options.A: projecting actual rates of paid and unpaid work at each age and the number likely to need intensive care in very late life.
options.B: dropping all projections of spending on health care for older people, since ageing has turned out to be largely costless.
options.C: continuing to rely on the ratio as it is now defined but adding a generous margin to its forecasts to allow for error.
options.D: moving the threshold of old age from sixty-five to seventy and otherwise keeping the familiar ratio exactly as it stands.

questions.correct_answer: (A) projecting actual rates of paid and unpaid work at each age and the number likely to need intensive care in very late life.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this means that ageing is costless', so this reverses the author's concession.
option_rationales.C: A margin keeps the faulty measure; the author's objection is to 'calibration', which a uniform margin does not correct.
option_rationales.D: This answers only the second equation; it still counts 'heads by birthday', ignores who actually works and does nothing to locate the costs of very late life.

questions.explanation: The author objects to equating age with dependence (paragraph 2) and to a fixed threshold (paragraph 3), and wants concern directed to 'very late life, in which it is most acute' (paragraph 4). A forecast built on actual activity and on late-life care needs answers all three.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the raised threshold, which fixes one of the author's two objections but keeps counting by birthday.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option applies half of the argument; the correct answer needs both equations of paragraphs 2 and 3 and the concession of paragraph 4.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The objection is not to concern but to calibration' (paragraph 4), 'calibration' refers to

options.A: how pension payments are adjusted each year to keep pace with prices and the general cost of living.
options.B: how accurately the size of the problem and the point where it bites are gauged.
options.C: how soon governments should begin to respond to the rising number of older citizens in the population.
options.D: how the responsibility for caring for the old is divided between public services and private households.

questions.correct_answer: (B) how accurately the size of the problem and the point where it bites are gauged.

option_rationales.A: Indexing pensions is a sense the word can have elsewhere, but the passage never discusses pension levels.
option_rationales.C: Timing of a response is not discussed; the next sentence explains calibration as exaggerating one form of the problem and obscuring another.
option_rationales.D: The division of responsibility is not the subject of paragraph 4, which concerns what the measure gets wrong.

questions.explanation: The next sentence explains the objection: the ratio will 'exaggerate the problem in its general form and ... obscure it in the specific form, very late life'. Calibration is the accuracy with which the scale and location of the problem are measured.
questions.common_misconception: Taking a familiar technical sense of the word (adjusting payments) instead of the sense fixed by the following sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the sentence that follows, and one wrong option uses a plausible outside sense.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, under the older vocabulary, a tie between two children nursed by the same woman would have been classed as

options.A: real, because it carries the same bar on marriage that a tie of birth carries.
options.B: biological, because nursing involves the sharing of a bodily substance.
options.C: fictive, because it does not rest on birth or descent.
options.D: metaphorical, because it is modelled on the bond between brothers and sisters.

questions.correct_answer: (C) fictive, because it does not rest on birth or descent.

option_rationales.A: The older vocabulary counted as 'real' only ties 'resting on birth and descent'; the bar on marriage is the author's evidence against that vocabulary.
option_rationales.B: The older scheme equated biology with birth and blood; nothing suggests it treated nursing as biological kinship.
option_rationales.D: Metaphor is not one of the two categories of the older scheme, and the author denies that the milk tie is 'a metaphor for kinship'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the older vocabulary called 'fictive' all relations 'that did not ... rest on blood'. A milk tie is not a tie of birth, so it would have been fictive; paragraph 2 objects to exactly that.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the author's view of the milk tie with how the older vocabulary would have classed it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Applies a definition from paragraph 1 to an example from paragraph 2.

questions.question: The third paragraph functions chiefly to

options.A: withdraw the earlier claim that the label 'fictive' misdescribes many non-Western forms of kinship.
options.B: argue that new reproductive technologies have now made biological kinship an obsolete idea in the West.
options.C: introduce evidence that biology is the single most important idiom of relatedness in every society.
options.D: limit the scope of the argument and show that its point applies within Western kinship too.

questions.correct_answer: (D) limit the scope of the argument and show that its point applies within Western kinship too.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph narrows the claim but keeps it; it does not withdraw the charge made in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: Donated eggs and sperm are cited to show people choosing between birth and care, not to declare biology obsolete.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph calls birth 'one of the most powerful ways', not the most important everywhere, and stresses variation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens 'This is not an argument that biology is irrelevant' and says 'The point is narrower', then adds 'Nor is the West an exception', using adoption, remarriage and donation as Western cases. It qualifies the thesis and extends it.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a qualification for a retraction.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph both concedes and extends, and the solver must capture both moves.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a way in which, in some societies, people may become kin EXCEPT

options.A: inheriting a share of the same land from a common ancestor.
options.B: eating food that has been grown on the same land.
options.C: making their home together in the same house.
options.D: being nursed as infants by the same woman.

questions.correct_answer: (A) inheriting a share of the same land from a common ancestor.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 lists 'eating food grown on the same land' as a way of becoming kin.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists 'living in the same house' as a way of becoming kin.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists being 'nursed at the same breast' and gives the rule on children nursed by the same woman.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 names food from the same land, a shared house and shared nursing. Land appears only as the source of food; inheriting land from a common ancestor is never given as a way of becoming kin, and inheritance from an ancestor would in any case rest on descent.
questions.common_misconception: Matching the word 'land' to the first item in paragraph 2 without noticing the change from eating its food to inheriting it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer reuses a word from the passage, so it must be rejected by the relation, not the vocabulary.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the author's claim that kinship is 'something people do as well as something they are born into'?

options.A: A woman tracing her ancestry learns from a genetic test that she has a number of cousins living on another continent whom she has never met.
options.B: A girl orphaned in childhood is placed by a court with an uncle she has never met, chosen because he is her nearest living relative by birth.
options.C: A family insists that a long-serving household servant, though deeply loved by all of them, can never be counted as kin because she shares no blood.
options.D: A man raised from infancy by his stepfather comes to regard him, and not the father he never met, as the parent whose funeral rites he must perform.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A man raised from infancy by his stepfather comes to regard him, and not the father he never met, as the parent whose funeral rites he must perform.

option_rationales.A: This is kinship discovered through birth alone; nothing is done to make or sustain the tie, so it shows only the 'born into' half.
option_rationales.B: The placement is made on the basis of birth; the tie has not yet been formed through shared living, so it does not illustrate kinship made by doing.
option_rationales.C: The family applies the biological rule the author criticises; the example shows kinship withheld on grounds of birth, not made through conduct.

questions.explanation: The author says kinship can be made through care and shared life, and that people must decide 'whether a tie of birth or a tie of care should prevail when the two come apart' (paragraph 3). The stepson treats years of care as the tie that confers the duties of a son, which is kinship made by conduct.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the court placement or the genetic discovery because they involve a family relationship, without asking whether the tie is made by conduct.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four cases are about family; three rest on birth, and one of them (the servant) involves a strong tie of care that is denied kin status.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain why marketers, journalists and employers have come to depend so heavily on labels for each new generation.
options.B: argue that calendar-based generation labels misplace the causes of difference, while granting a narrower, event-anchored notion of generation.
options.C: show that differences in age and period matter less for explaining how people behave than differences of class and region do.
options.D: demonstrate that genuine differences between generations can never be detected in survey data, whatever methods researchers choose to use.

questions.correct_answer: (B) argue that calendar-based generation labels misplace the causes of difference, while granting a narrower, event-anchored notion of generation.

option_rationales.A: Why the labels persist is the subject of paragraph 5 only; it is one part of a larger critique, so the option is too narrow.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 compares variation within and between cohorts; the passage never ranks age and period against class and region.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says separating the effects requires 'some assumption from outside the data', not that detection is impossible, and paragraph 4 says cohort effects 'have been found'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 give two reasons the labels mislead (confounded effects, arbitrary boundaries), paragraph 4 concedes a 'serious idea' anchored to events, and paragraph 5 explains the labels' persistence and cost. The correct answer captures the critique together with the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating paragraph 2's method problem into a claim of impossibility.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are each tied to one paragraph; the correct answer requires the concession in paragraph 4 as well.

questions.question: A survey carried out in a single year finds that people then in their twenties change jobs more often than people then in their fifties. On the reasoning of paragraph 2, the survey

options.A: would separate age from cohort effects if it were simply repeated with a much larger and more representative sample.
options.B: has shown that the difference is a period effect, since every person surveyed was observed in the same year.
options.C: cannot by itself show whether the difference reflects age or a lasting imprint left on each group by its birth cohort.
options.D: has established that the difference is an age effect, because paragraph 2 says that young people change jobs more often.

questions.correct_answer: (C) cannot by itself show whether the difference reflects age or a lasting imprint left on each group by its birth cohort.

option_rationales.A: The obstacle is arithmetic ('once any two are known the third is fixed'), so a larger sample of the same design cannot remove it.
option_rationales.B: When all observations come from one year, the period is the same for both groups, so a period effect cannot explain a difference between them.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 offers the job-changing example only to illustrate what an age effect is; it insists that 'No set of observations can by itself pull them apart'.
