questions.explanation: In one year, period is held constant, so the observed difference must be due to age or cohort, and in a single cross-section age and birth cohort move together exactly. Paragraph 2 says no observations 'can by itself pull them apart; some assumption from outside the data is always required'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the illustrative example in paragraph 2 as a finding, or thinking that more data cures an identification problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the age, period and cohort logic to a new case and seeing that period is fixed in a single-year survey.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's objection to generational boundaries in paragraph 3?

options.A: People who came of age during a major war have been found to show lasting differences in their attitudes to saving and spending money.
options.B: Attitudes shift sharply among people born within a year or two of the usual dividing line between two named generations but change little within each span.
options.C: People born within any one fifteen-year span differ widely in their incomes and outlooks according to their class, region and schooling.
options.D: Different sources that use generational labels routinely disagree by four or five years about where each generation begins and ends.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Attitudes shift sharply among people born within a year or two of the usual dividing line between two named generations but change little within each span.

option_rationales.A: This supports the event-anchored cohort effects granted in paragraph 4; it says nothing about whether the conventional boundaries track real breaks.
option_rationales.C: This is the within-cohort variation that paragraph 3 uses against the labels; it strengthens the objection.
option_rationales.D: This is the disagreement paragraph 3 itself reports, so it supports the objection rather than weakening it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 objects that boundaries are conventional, that people a day apart are split while people fourteen years apart are joined, and that within-cohort differences exceed between-cohort ones. A sharp change exactly at the conventional line, with little change inside spans, would show the boundaries marking real breaks.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the war example because it shows that cohort effects exist, without noticing that the objection concerns where boundaries fall.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option answers paragraph 4, not paragraph 3; two others are restatements of the objection itself.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the idea that people who come of age during a war or a depression may carry its mark for life is best described as

options.A: respectful but restrictive, accepting it as real provided it is not stretched into a character shared by a whole cohort.
options.B: indifferent, mentioning it only so that it can be set aside as irrelevant to the argument against the labels.
options.C: enthusiastic, presenting it as proof that the calendar-based generational labels are broadly accurate after all.
options.D: dismissive, treating it as a piece of marketing that has merely been dressed up in the language of social science.

questions.correct_answer: (A) respectful but restrictive, accepting it as real provided it is not stretched into a character shared by a whole cohort.

option_rationales.B: The idea is the passage's main concession and is used to define what a defensible notion of generation would be, so it is not set aside.
option_rationales.C: The author says such effects are 'anchored to events rather than to calendars', so they do not vindicate calendar labels.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls it 'a serious idea buried under the marketing' and says such effects 'are not trivial', which rules out dismissal.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 grants that 'Such effects have been found, and they are not trivial', then limits them: they are tied to events, uneven within a cohort, and 'rarely produce a single character that an entire cohort shares'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the concession as an endorsement of the labels.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude combines acceptance with limits within one paragraph.

questions.question: With which of the following statements would the author be LEAST likely to agree?

options.A: Attributing young adults' insecure work to their temperament makes the problem seem less open to a remedy through policy.
options.B: A lasting difference between cohorts is more credible as generational when it can be traced to a specific event in their early years.
options.C: A difference between two cohorts observed at the same age in different decades must be a cohort effect, with no further assumption needed.
options.D: Some members of a cohort may be marked by a formative event far more deeply than others who were born in the same year.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A difference between two cohorts observed at the same age in different decades must be a cohort effect, with no further assumption needed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says this converts an economic question into one of character, which 'has no obvious policy answer', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says genuine effects are 'anchored to events rather than to calendars', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such effects 'mark some members of a cohort far more deeply than others', so the author would agree.

questions.explanation: Comparing two cohorts at the same age holds age constant, but they are observed in different decades, so the difference could be a period effect. Paragraph 2 says the three effects cannot be separated by observations alone: 'some assumption from outside the data is always required'. The author would therefore reject the claim that no further assumption is needed.
questions.common_misconception: Thinking that holding age constant isolates the cohort effect, forgetting that the period then differs.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer sounds methodologically careful; rejecting it requires applying paragraph 2's arithmetic to a new design.

questions.question: According to the passage, a joint household often divides when

options.A: the parents decide to divide the household's property among their daughters.
options.B: the eldest son marries and brings his new wife into his parents' home.
options.C: one of the sons migrates for work to a city hundreds of kilometres away.
options.D: the father dies and his sons set up separate hearths of their own.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the father dies and his sons set up separate hearths of their own.

option_rationales.A: Division of property among daughters is not described as a cause of partition; paragraph 5 mentions inheritance only as a contested question.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says this is when the household 'becomes joint', not when it divides.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says migration brings 'dispersal', which 'is not the same thing as dissolution'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the household 'often divides when the father dies and the brothers set up separate hearths'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the stage at which a household becomes joint with the stage at which it divides.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is one clause of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The population described in paragraph 2, in which every family follows the cycle exactly, is introduced in order to show that

options.A: nuclear households are more stable over time than joint households and therefore make up the larger share of any count.
options.B: a count made on one day can find mostly nuclear households even where joint living is a near-universal stage of life.
options.C: most families in South Asia do in fact follow the developmental cycle exactly as the paragraph describes it.
options.D: census officials have deliberately undercounted joint households in order to lend support to the story of decline.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a count made on one day can find mostly nuclear households even where joint living is a near-universal stage of life.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nuclear households are a phase that 'may in turn become joint', so it does not call them more stable.
option_rationales.C: The population is explicitly hypothetical ('In a population in which every family followed this cycle exactly'); it is a thought experiment, not a claim about real families.
option_rationales.D: The passage blames the method of counting at a single moment, not any deliberate bias on the part of officials.

questions.explanation: The thought experiment ends in the conclusion drawn in the next sentence: 'A high proportion of nuclear households, then, is not by itself evidence that the joint family is disappearing.' It shows how a snapshot can mislead about a cycle.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a hypothetical population as a description of real families.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'then' in the sentence that follows.

questions.question: As used in the last sentence of paragraph 4, 'the jointness that matters most to its members' refers to

options.A: the shared obligations and joint decisions that bind relatives even when they live apart.
options.B: the condition of several married couples sharing one roof, one kitchen and one purse.
options.C: the legal co-ownership of ancestral property by a group of brothers and their sons.
options.D: the authority that the eldest man in a family exercises over all its other members.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the shared obligations and joint decisions that bind relatives even when they live apart.

option_rationales.B: This is the residential definition that, the sentence says, a census uses and that 'will miss' the jointness meant.
option_rationales.C: Property is one subject of joint decisions in paragraph 4, but legal co-ownership is narrower than the obligations described.
option_rationales.D: Authority within the family is discussed in paragraph 5 as something being renegotiated, not as what jointness means here.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists what survives dispersal: money sent to parents, decisions 'still taken together', a son abroad 'bound by his family's expectations'. That is the jointness a residence-based census misses.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the residential definition because it is the usual meaning of joint family.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence contrasts the census definition with the intended sense, and one wrong option offers the census definition.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 2?

options.A: Many families living in nuclear households regularly send money to parents who remain in their home village.
options.B: In some regions brothers commonly divide their parents' household before their father's death rather than after it.
options.C: Studies following the same families for several decades find that most of their members never lived in a household with more than one married couple.
options.D: A count taken on a single day in one region finds that most of its households consist only of parents and their unmarried children.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Studies following the same families for several decades find that most of their members never lived in a household with more than one married couple.

option_rationales.A: This supports paragraph 4's point about jointness across distance; it does not touch the life-cycle argument of paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: This changes the timing of partition within the cycle but leaves the cycle, and hence the snapshot argument, intact.
option_rationales.D: The author predicts exactly this result from the cycle, so it is consistent with the argument and does not weaken it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that snapshot counts mislead because people pass through joint phases over a lifetime. If following families over time showed that most people never lived jointly, the life-cycle explanation would fail and a high nuclear share would again count as evidence of decline.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the single-day count because it sounds like evidence for the decline story, without seeing that the author has already explained it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must see that the argument depends on life-course experience and that a snapshot result is already accommodated.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The joint family is essentially unchanged, since migrants remain bound by their families' expectations wherever they live.
options.B: The contests over authority within joint households show that the story of decline was right after all, if for the wrong reasons.
options.C: Industrialisation in South Asia has had no effect of any kind on the ways in which households are formed and divided.
options.D: Whether the joint family is declining depends partly on whether it is defined by co-residence or by shared obligation.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Whether the joint family is declining depends partly on whether it is defined by co-residence or by shared obligation.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says it would be 'equally mistaken' to 'declare the joint family unchanged', so the author rejects this.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 calls these changes 'a transformation of jointness' rather than 'its end', so they do not vindicate the decline story.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says household form 'is not simply read off' the economy, which denies a simple link, not every effect.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a census defining jointness 'by shared residence' will record a dispersed but bound family as 'several nuclear ones'. So the verdict on decline turns partly on the definition used, which the author would accept.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the authority option because paragraph 5 concedes real change, or swinging to the claim that nothing has changed.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each take one of the author's concessions too far in opposite directions.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: defending superstition as a hidden form of practical wisdom that modern societies have been wrong to dismiss.
options.B: arguing that education will in time remove superstition by filling the gaps in people's knowledge of causes.
options.C: explaining superstition as a response to uncontrollable stakes and proposing that it be judged by what it displaces.
options.D: proving that skilled professionals are more superstitious than other people because their work involves greater danger.

questions.correct_answer: (C) explaining superstition as a response to uncontrollable stakes and proposing that it be judged by what it displaces.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says superstition is 'neither a quaint error to be laughed at nor a hidden wisdom to be celebrated', so this reverses the author's balance.
option_rationales.B: This is the view paragraph 1 rejects: superstition 'does not distribute itself the way ignorance does'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says such professionals are 'often among the most attached' to rituals, which is offered only to unsettle the ignorance view; nothing is proved about their being more superstitious than everyone else, and danger is not the stated cause.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 rejects the ignorance view, paragraphs 2 and 3 explain superstition as a response to high stakes that lie partly beyond control, and paragraph 4 sets the criterion: it 'deserves to be judged by what it crowds out'. The correct answer covers both the explanation and the evaluative criterion.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about professionals because paragraph 1 dwells on them, when that example only serves to clear away the ignorance view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure is signposted and the two wrong views are explicitly rejected in the text.

questions.question: According to the passage, the fishing communities mentioned in paragraph 2

options.A: gave up their rites for open-sea voyages once they had acquired enough skill to make those voyages reliable.
options.B: regarded lagoon fishing as more dangerous than open-sea fishing, even though the lagoon reliably yielded a catch.
options.C: used protective magic in the lagoon and on the open sea alike, since their beliefs about the world did not change.
options.D: used no protective magic in the sheltered lagoon but surrounded open-sea voyages with elaborate rites.

questions.correct_answer: (D) used no protective magic in the sheltered lagoon but surrounded open-sea voyages with elaborate rites.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about the rites being abandoned; it contrasts two kinds of fishing done by the same people.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the passage: the lagoon is 'sheltered' and skill 'reliably brings a catch' there, which is why no magic is used.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says they 'use no protective magic' in the lagoon; only their exposure to chance changes, not their beliefs, and the rites follow the exposure.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that these communities 'use no protective magic when they work in a sheltered lagoon' yet 'surround voyages into the open sea with elaborate rites'.
questions.common_misconception: Misreading 'the same beliefs about the world' as meaning the same practices in both settings.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the tennis player's routine is valuable to her chiefly because it

options.A: gives her a fixed action at the point where further deliberation could only unsettle her play.
options.B: allows her to skip some of the training she would otherwise need to complete before a match.
options.C: improves the physical accuracy of her serve through repeated rehearsal of the same muscular movement.
options.D: persuades her that she can influence the result of the point through forces beyond ordinary physics.

questions.correct_answer: (A) gives her a fixed action at the point where further deliberation could only unsettle her play.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the ritual fills only 'the space that preparation cannot reach', so it does not replace preparation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the ritual supplies 'not a causal lever over the outcome'; physical improvement of the serve is never claimed.
option_rationales.D: The author says she is 'not, in any serious sense, trying to bend the laws of physics', which rules this out directly.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the routine marks 'a boundary between deliberation and execution' and 'protects the execution from second thoughts'; it is an outlet for anxiety 'when no further useful action is available'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the routine must work causally on the serve itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The supporting sentences sit together at the end of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a superstition that has crossed the line described in paragraph 4?

options.A: A pilot touches the nose of the aircraft before each flight, after all the required safety checks are complete.
options.B: A farmer leaves a dry field unirrigated because he trusts a rite performed at sowing to bring enough rain.
options.C: A student who has prepared thoroughly for every examination wears the same small pendant into each of them.
options.D: An actor recites the same short phrase in the wings before every opening night, whatever role she is playing.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A farmer leaves a dry field unirrigated because he trusts a rite performed at sowing to bring enough rain.

option_rationales.A: Because the checks are complete, the gesture comes after all useful action; it does not displace anything that would improve the odds.
option_rationales.C: The preparation is done and the pendant occupies only the leftover uncertainty; it displaces no useful action, so it stays on the acceptable side of the line.
option_rationales.D: Opening nights are given in paragraph 2 as a case where the ritual fills space preparation cannot reach; nothing useful is crowded out.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 places the line 'where the ritual stops occupying the residue of chance and begins to displace action that would genuinely improve the odds'. Irrigation would improve the odds, and the rite displaces it. In the other three cases the useful action has already been taken.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing any ritual that looks irrational, instead of applying the author's specific criterion of displacement.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four options are superstitions; only the stated criterion separates the correct answer from the rest.

questions.question: According to the passage, the main work of the fixed days of traditional mourning was to

options.A: ensure that widows stayed away from celebrations for as long as the family remained in mourning.
options.B: settle in advance how relatives, neighbours and the bereaved household should conduct themselves after a death.
options.C: measure how long sorrow normally lasts, so that the bereaved would know when their grief ought to end.
options.D: give community elders a means of supervising how each family spent its money after a death.

questions.correct_answer: (B) settle in advance how relatives, neighbours and the bereaved household should conduct themselves after a death.

option_rationales.A: This is one custom mentioned in paragraph 1, and paragraph 4 treats it as policing; it is not given as the main work of the fixed days.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'The fixed days rarely claimed to measure how long sorrow lasts', which denies this directly.
option_rationales.D: Spending and supervision by elders are never mentioned; the passage speaks only of conduct and coordination.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the fixed days 'settle a set of practical questions' about visiting, speaking and resuming work, and paragraph 3 sums up: 'Its main work was coordination.'
questions.common_misconception: Taking a vivid custom from paragraph 1 for the general function the author assigns.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is named in so many words in paragraphs 2 and 3.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'the labour of inventing their own conduct' refers to

options.A: the strain of displaying more sorrow in public than one actually feels in private.
options.B: the task of devising new ceremonies that later generations of the community can follow.
options.C: the effort of working out, unaided, how to behave and what to do while newly bereaved.
options.D: the physical work of arranging the funeral and preparing the gatherings that follow it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the effort of working out, unaided, how to behave and what to do while newly bereaved.

option_rationales.A: Pretended feeling is not the issue in paragraph 2; the phrase concerns not knowing how to act.
option_rationales.B: The phrase is about the bereaved person's own behaviour at the time, not about creating traditions for others.
option_rationales.D: The surrounding questions are about when to visit, what to say and when to resume work, not practical arrangements for the funeral.

questions.explanation: The phrase follows the list of questions (when to visit, what to say, when to resume work) that 'A prescribed sequence answers' in advance. Without the sequence, the bereaved would have to decide these matters themselves while 'exhausted'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'inventing' as creating new rituals rather than improvising one's behaviour.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the questions listed immediately before it.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that, where shared mourning scripts have weakened,

options.A: people who want to support the bereaved are often held back by not knowing what is expected of them.
options.B: the bereaved now grieve for a shorter time, because no outward schedule keeps their sorrow going.
options.C: grief has become more authentic and more personal, even if it has also become somewhat lonelier.
options.D: communities have usually replaced the old customs with newer rules that are just as rigid.

questions.correct_answer: (A) people who want to support the bereaved are often held back by not knowing what is expected of them.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage says that schedules prolonged sorrow or that grief has become shorter; this is outside its scope.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the result 'has not obviously been freer grief'; the author grants loneliness, not greater authenticity.
option_rationales.D: The passage describes the absence of scripts, not new rigid rules; this contradicts paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes friends who 'hesitate' and colleagues who 'say nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing', because 'nobody else knows what part to play'. Paragraph 4 adds that abandoning shared forms 'removes the cues that let others accompany' grief.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the half-true option that grief is lonelier, without noticing that its other half (more authentic) is denied.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option pairs a supported claim with one the author rejects.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards traditional mourning customs is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality, setting out the case on each side without ever coming to a view of its own.
options.B: firm disapproval, on the ground that the customs forced private feeling to follow a public schedule.
options.C: nostalgic admiration, joined to a hope that the older rules will one day be restored in full.
options.D: qualified appreciation of their coordinating role, together with criticism of the coercion some of them involved.

questions.correct_answer: (D) qualified appreciation of their coordinating role, together with criticism of the coercion some of them involved.

option_rationales.A: The author takes a clear position: the objection 'misreads what the calendar was for', and a replacement should keep the coordinating function.
option_rationales.B: This is the modern objection reported in paragraph 1, which the author says 'contains a truth' but largely rejects.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 opens 'This is not an argument for restoring every old rule', which rules out a wish for full restoration.

questions.explanation: The author defends the customs' coordinating function (paragraphs 2 and 3) while conceding that some 'bore down hardest on those with least power' and policed widows (paragraph 4). Appreciation with a stated reservation is the attitude.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the objection the author reports in paragraph 1 for the author's own view.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires weighing the defence in the middle paragraphs against the concession at the end.

questions.question: The list of features at the end of paragraph 1 (seclusion, shaved heads, identical garments and so on) serves mainly to

options.A: show why the transitional phase of such rites has drawn more attention than the other two.
options.B: establish that every rite of passage, in every culture, uses exactly the same set of practices.
options.C: suggest that rites of passage are often cruel to novices and ought to be reformed for that reason.
options.D: contrast the transitional phase with the more elaborate ceremonies that mark incorporation.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show why the transitional phase of such rites has drawn more attention than the other two.

option_rationales.B: The list gives typical features; nothing claims that all cultures share every one of them, which would be an extreme reading.
option_rationales.C: The author never condemns the practices; paragraph 2 goes on to explain their function.
option_rationales.D: No ceremonies of incorporation are described, so there is nothing for the list to be contrasted with.

questions.explanation: The sentence before the list says the middle phase has attracted the most attention 'for good reason', and the list begins 'It is there that most of the strange features of such rites are concentrated'. The list supplies that reason.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a moral judgement into a descriptive list.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is announced by the sentence that introduces the list.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that removing the markers by which novices were ranked

options.A: is an unintended side effect of seclusion that the organisers of the rite neither foresee nor value.
options.B: permanently erases the differences of rank between the families from which the novices come.
options.C: helps to create bonds among novices that are not organised by the standing or wealth of their families.
options.D: makes novices less willing to accept instruction from elders who come from humbler families.

questions.correct_answer: (C) helps to create bonds among novices that are not organised by the standing or wealth of their families.

option_rationales.A: The author presents the stripping as the 'function' of these features, against the 'waiting room' reading, so it is not an accident.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the novices are indistinguishable only 'for a time'; nothing suggests family rank is erased for good.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: people 'deprived of their usual footing' become more 'receptive to instruction'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says levelling makes sons of rich and poor families 'indistinguishable', and that shared hardship then creates 'cohorts whose loyalty cuts across lineage and wealth'. Levelling is the precondition for those cross-cutting ties.
questions.common_misconception: Ignoring the qualifier 'for a time' and treating the levelling as permanent.
questions.difficulty_reason: The link between levelling and loyalty spans two sentences, and one wrong option ignores a qualifier.

questions.question: The passage attributes each of the following to the traditional liminal phase EXCEPT

options.A: firm limits on its duration and on the novices' conduct, set by the community's elders.
options.B: a temporary removal of the markers by which novices had previously been ranked.
options.C: a heightened readiness to learn among people deprived of their usual footing.
options.D: an open-ended freedom in which novices themselves decided when their transition was complete.

questions.correct_answer: (D) an open-ended freedom in which novices themselves decided when their transition was complete.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'Elders set its length, prescribed what novices could eat and say, and decided when it was over', so this is attributed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says stripping names, clothing and possessions 'removes the markers by which they were previously ranked', so this is attributed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says novices become 'receptive to instruction, since people deprived of their usual footing listen differently', so this is attributed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the elders 'decided when it was over' and that the openness praised by modern admirers is exactly what the traditional threshold did not have. This option describes the modern image, not the traditional phase.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying the modern celebration of liminality as 'freedom, creativity and play' back into the traditional rite.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are paraphrases scattered over two paragraphs, and the correct answer echoes language the passage uses about a different view.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's conclusion about what made liminality productive?

options.A: Many young people who drift between education and employment say that they feel disoriented, lack companions and cannot tell when, if ever, their transition will be over.
options.B: Young people passing through open-ended, unmarked transitions are found to form lasting ties and take on new roles just as well as novices in bounded rites do.
options.C: In some societies the period of seclusion during initiation lasted several years rather than a few weeks.
options.D: Elders in some traditional societies extended the seclusion of novices who had broken the rules of the rite.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Young people passing through open-ended, unmarked transitions are found to form lasting ties and take on new roles just as well as novices in bounded rites do.

option_rationales.A: This matches the author's description in paragraph 4 of the threshold 'without its discipline, its companions' and so supports the conclusion.
option_rationales.C: A long phase is still a bounded one, ended by elders; the length of the frame does not touch the claim that the frame is what mattered.
option_rationales.D: This shows elders controlling the threshold, which fits the author's picture of a 'firm frame' and does nothing to weaken it.

questions.explanation: The conclusion is that liminality was productive not because of its openness but because of 'the certainty that the openness would end'. If open-ended transitions with no exit produced the same goods (ties, new roles), the bounded frame would not be what made the difference.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about modern young people because it is on topic, without checking whether it supports or undermines the conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires isolating the causal claim in the final sentences and separating it from the modern admirers' view.

questions.question: According to the passage, what has happened in many places since modern transport made distant shrines easy to reach?

options.A: Pilgrimage has dwindled, because the effort that once gave the journey its meaning has disappeared.
options.B: The authorities at many shrines now require pilgrims to cover the whole route to them on foot.
options.C: Pilgrims have come to value the sight of the shrine far more than any hardship they might meet on the road leading to it.
options.D: Pilgrims have chosen to bring back some of the effort, for instance by walking the last part of the way.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Pilgrims have chosen to bring back some of the effort, for instance by walking the last part of the way.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 mentions this only as what 'One might have predicted'; it then says the effort 'has instead been reintroduced by choice'.
option_rationales.B: No requirement by shrine authorities is mentioned; paragraph 3 says the effort is reintroduced 'by choice'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 describes pilgrims adding hardship back, which is the opposite of valuing arrival alone.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the effortful element 'has instead been reintroduced by choice', with pilgrims leaving their vehicles 'to walk the final stretch, sometimes barefoot, sometimes on their knees'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the prediction the author mentions and rejects for what actually happened.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The contrast between blisters on a hiking holiday and blisters on the way to a sacred place (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: hardships on pilgrimage routes are usually more severe than those met with on ordinary walking holidays.
options.B: pilgrims value suffering for its own sake, wherever and for whatever purpose it is undergone.
options.C: the same bodily hardship can carry different meanings depending on the goal towards which it is directed.
options.D: hikers come to regard their discomfort as an offering once they reach the end of a long trail.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the same bodily hardship can carry different meanings depending on the goal towards which it is directed.

option_rationales.A: The passage speaks of 'the same blisters'; the difference it draws is one of meaning, not of severity.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says just before the example that 'The hardships of the road are not valuable in the abstract', which contradicts this.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the passage, which says that for the hiker blisters are 'an inconvenience'; only the pilgrim's become 'an offering'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the hiker's blisters are an inconvenience while 'the same blisters' become an offering for the pilgrim, and that 'What converts them is the fixed point towards which they are directed'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the difference must be one of physical severity rather than meaning.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the example together with the general claim that frames it.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The effort of the road and the fixed destination give each other their significance in pilgrimage, so neither can be understood on its own.
options.B: The chief value of pilgrimage lies in the inner change produced by long days of walking, whatever the destination happens to be.
options.C: Modern transport has emptied pilgrimage of its meaning, which can be recovered only by walking the whole of the route.
options.D: People who walk old pilgrim routes for reasons they would not call religious are deceived about the value of what they find.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The effort of the road and the fixed destination give each other their significance in pilgrimage, so neither can be understood on its own.

option_rationales.B: This is the second misunderstanding set out in paragraph 1, which the author says detaches the walking from the destination.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the effort has been 'condensed rather than abandoned', and nothing says only the whole route will do.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 opens by denying this: such a walker is not 'deceived about what he finds', and the change 'can be real'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states the thesis: both familiar views 'detach two elements that draw their meaning from each other'. Paragraph 3 supports it with the reintroduction of effort, and paragraph 4 with the point that the destination's being fixed 'lends the road its gravity'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the two views the author describes as misunderstandings.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options restate views the passage reports; the correct answer must be found in the author's reply to both.

questions.question: The author would most likely say of someone who walks an old pilgrim route with no fixed destination in mind that

options.A: his experience must be illusory, because a change in a person that is not religious cannot be a real one.
options.B: the walk may change him genuinely, though it lacks the gravity that a fixed and unchangeable destination helps to give a journey.
options.C: he is having the pilgrim's experience in a secular form, since the walking itself is where the value lies.
options.D: he would have the pilgrim's experience if he happened to end his walk at a famous shrine along the route.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the walk may change him genuinely, though it lacks the gravity that a fixed and unchangeable destination helps to give a journey.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'the change can be real without being religious', which this contradicts.
option_rationales.C: This is the second view in paragraph 1, which the author rejects; paragraph 4 says such a journey is 'a different thing' from the pilgrim's.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a visitor who arrives 'on a whim' sees what the pilgrim sees without the pilgrim's experience; the destination must be fixed from the start.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 concedes that such walks 'do change people' but says the walker gives something up 'when the destination becomes optional': the pilgrim's inability to change destinations 'lends the road its gravity'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the shrine option because it adds a destination, missing that the passage requires the destination to be fixed and binding beforehand.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option adds a destination after the fact and must be ruled out by combining paragraphs 2 and 4.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'a sudden demand for definition' refers to

options.A: the wish of each community to agree with the others on a single name and story for the saint.
options.B: an insistence by some outside authority that the site be formally assigned to one tradition.
options.C: a gradual build-up of disagreement between the different communities who visit the site.
options.D: a request by visitors that the custodians explain the meaning of the rites performed at the site.

questions.correct_answer: (B) an insistence by some outside authority that the site be formally assigned to one tradition.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the communities are not 'much troubled by the discrepancy'; the demand comes from 'some authority', not from the communities' wish to agree.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 contrasts the demand with 'the slow pressure of difference', so a gradual build-up is exactly what the phrase does not mean.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says custodians are not asked and do not ask about belief; the phrase is glossed in paragraph 3 as registering or claiming the site for one tradition.

questions.explanation: The same sentence explains the phrase: 'when some authority, a government department, a heritage body or a movement seeking to purify practice, insists that the site be registered, restored or claimed as belonging to one tradition alone'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'definition' as explanation of meaning rather than official assignment of identity.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is glossed in the sentence where it appears.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It supplies the observations of how sharing actually works on which the author's rejection of both stories rests.
options.B: It describes how shared shrines decline once the communities start to disagree about the identity of the saint.
options.C: It gives evidence for the harmony story, which the author then accepts subject to the qualifications in paragraph 4.
options.D: It explains how custodians from one community gradually come to take control of sites that were once shared.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It supplies the observations of how sharing actually works on which the author's rejection of both stories rests.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the communities are not 'much troubled by the discrepancy'; it describes stable sharing, not decline.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says observation 'rarely finds a single, blended faith', and paragraph 3 says the harmony story 'puts the emphasis in the wrong place'; it is rejected, not accepted with qualifications.
option_rationales.D: Custodians in paragraph 2 'accept offerings from all'; the possibility of one side enlarging its claim is raised only in paragraph 4.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 reports what 'Close observation' finds: parallel use, different names for the saint, custodians who do not ask about belief. Paragraph 3 then begins 'This is why the harmony story ... puts the emphasis in the wrong place' and goes on to reject the truce story as well.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because paragraph 2 describes real sharing it must support the harmony story.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing how paragraph 3 uses paragraph 2 against both stories.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements most closely resembles the kind of sharing the author describes?

options.A: Two clubs share a hall only after long meetings in which they agree on a common purpose for their activities.
options.B: Two clubs take turns in a hall after a court has ruled on which of them is its legal owner and on what terms.
options.C: Two clubs meet in the same hall on different evenings, each calling it by its own name, and the caretaker never asks which club owns it.
options.D: Two clubs merge into a single society with a common constitution so that they can make joint use of one hall.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Two clubs meet in the same hall on different evenings, each calling it by its own name, and the caretaker never asks which club owns it.

option_rationales.A: The author says the arrangement 'does not depend on people believing the same thing'; prior agreement on purpose is the opposite model.
option_rationales.B: Settling ownership is the 'demand for definition' that paragraph 3 says threatens sharing, not the basis of it.
option_rationales.D: A merger with a common constitution is the 'single, blended faith' model that paragraph 2 says observation rarely finds.

questions.explanation: The author's model is parallel use (different evenings, like different days), different names for the same thing, a custodian who does not ask, and the decisive question 'whose shrine it really is' left unposed (paragraph 2). The correct answer reproduces all of these.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option with harmony or a formal settlement, both of which the author says misdescribe sharing.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches one of the models the author rejects, so the analogy must be mapped feature by feature.

questions.question: The author's description of ambiguity as 'a social achievement in its own right' (paragraph 4) suggests that

options.A: the communities using shared shrines have, over many generations, quietly agreed among themselves to adopt one common interpretation of the saint and his story.
options.B: leaving ultimate questions unsettled is more valuable than agreement about them in every area of social life.
options.C: shared shrines have survived only where outside authorities protected their ambiguity through law and regulation.
options.D: the vagueness at shared shrines is actively sustained, for instance by custodians not asking about belief, and is not simply a lack of clarity.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the vagueness at shared shrines is actively sustained, for instance by custodians not asking about belief, and is not simply a lack of clarity.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says each group keeps 'a different name and a different story'; there is no common interpretation, agreed or otherwise.
option_rationales.B: The author says only that coexistence 'need not wait for agreement'; ranking ambiguity above agreement everywhere is an extreme reading.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 names government departments and heritage bodies as sources of the threat, not as protectors of the ambiguity.

questions.explanation: An achievement is something done, and the author calls the ambiguity 'carefully maintained'. Paragraph 2 shows how it is maintained: custodians 'refrain from asking visitors what they believe' and 'certain questions are never posed'. The correct answer links these two paragraphs.
questions.common_misconception: Treating ambiguity as the absence of something, and so missing the sense of active maintenance the word 'achievement' carries.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting a figurative phrase in paragraph 4 to the practices in paragraph 2, with a tempting extreme wrong option.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: demonstrate that religion has been confined to private life in most societies that have modernised.
options.B: show that the secularisation thesis was right after all, once the evidence of its critics is properly understood.
options.C: explain why religious movements revived in the late twentieth century in societies that were growing wealthier.
options.D: argue that the secularisation debate went astray by treating several independent claims as a single thesis.

questions.correct_answer: (D) argue that the secularisation debate went astray by treating several independent claims as a single thesis.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the privatisation thesis 'has fared worse still, since religious voices are plainly present in public debate', which contradicts this.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'It would be too quick to declare the older thesis vindicated', so the author explicitly declines this conclusion.
option_rationales.C: The revival is the starting point in paragraph 1, but the passage never explains its causes; it analyses what the revival does and does not refute.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that 'Both the confidence and the recantation' treated 'as one hypothesis what was really a bundle of several'. Paragraph 3 tests each strand separately, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'the debate has been conducted at the wrong level of generality'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the vindication option because paragraph 3 defends differentiation, without reading the refusal in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option follows from paragraph 3 alone; the concession in paragraph 4 decides it.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a society in which religious attendance is high but courts and hospitals operate free of clerical control as

options.A: consistent with the differentiation strand of the thesis while failing to fit the decline strand.
options.B: an unusual and unstable combination that the pressures of modernisation will sooner or later break apart.
options.C: proof that privatisation has taken place in that society even though decline has plainly not.
options.D: evidence that the secularisation thesis has now been refuted in every one of its forms.

questions.correct_answer: (A) consistent with the differentiation strand of the thesis while failing to fit the decline strand.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'that combination is in fact common', and nothing in the passage predicts it will break apart.
option_rationales.C: The case says nothing about whether religion is present in public argument, which is what privatisation concerns; the inference has no basis.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the strands are 'logically independent'; such a society refutes decline but fits differentiation, so not every form is refuted.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines differentiation as institutions such as law and medicine operating 'no longer answerable to religious authority', and decline as 'a fall in belief, membership and practice'. High attendance with independent courts and hospitals fits the first and contradicts the second; paragraph 2 calls this combination 'common'.
questions.common_misconception: Running the strands together, which is the very error the passage diagnoses.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying two of the three definitions to a case and keeping the third out.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the religious resurgence 'tends to presuppose' differentiation?

options.A: Some religious movements commission surveys and use the language of rights more skilfully than many secular campaigning groups.
options.B: Membership of religious organisations fell steadily in several wealthy countries over the same decades in which the resurgence occurred elsewhere.
options.C: In several countries resurgent movements won influence mainly by restoring clerical authority over courts and schools, not by competing within independent institutions.
options.D: Religious movements that lobby legislatures and contest elections tend to attract more members than those that stay out of politics.

questions.correct_answer: (C) In several countries resurgent movements won influence mainly by restoring clerical authority over courts and schools, not by competing within independent institutions.

option_rationales.A: This is further evidence that such movements act as 'one set of claimants among many', which supports the claim.
option_rationales.B: This bears on the decline strand, which the author already says 'has fared poorly as a universal law'; it says nothing about how resurgent movements operate.
option_rationales.D: Lobbying is one of the behaviours paragraph 3 cites as acting within differentiated institutions, so this fits the author's claim rather than weakening it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that resurgent movements act 'as one set of claimants among many within institutions they do not control'. If resurgence typically worked by putting institutions back under religious authority, it would undo differentiation rather than presuppose it, which directly counters the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the decline option because it seems to bear on secularisation, when the claim at issue concerns differentiation only.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires distinguishing the three strands and seeing which kind of evidence bears on the specific claim.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards those former defenders of the thesis who 'said as much' (paragraph 1) is best described as

options.A: approving, since the author agrees that the evidence of religious resurgence refuted the secularisation thesis as a whole.
options.B: critical of their recantation for sharing the confusion behind their earlier confidence, without endorsing their original prediction.
options.C: dismissive, since the author regards every question about secularisation as one that no evidence could ever settle.
options.D: sympathetic, since the author believes that their original prediction was correct and that they abandoned it too readily.

questions.correct_answer: (B) critical of their recantation for sharing the confusion behind their earlier confidence, without endorsing their original prediction.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the recantation rested on an error, and paragraph 3 says differentiation 'has held up remarkably well', so the author does not think the thesis was refuted as a whole.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the general question has 'no single answer' but that narrower questions are ones 'the evidence can actually settle'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the theory 'predicted the fading of faith and got that prediction wrong in much of the world', so the author does not think the original prediction was correct.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'Both the confidence and the recantation' rested on treating several claims as one, so the author faults the recantation. Paragraph 4 also says the decline prediction was wrong and the thesis is not 'vindicated', so the author does not side with the original view either.
questions.common_misconception: Inferring that because the author criticises the recantation, the author must think the original thesis was right.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are each half-right; the correct answer needs both paragraph 2 and paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, the fact that rulers have both funded and banned festivals of inversion

options.A: shows that rulers regarded these festivals as harmless entertainment with no political significance.
options.B: has been cited by supporters of each of the two dominant explanations as evidence for their view.
options.C: proves that the festivals tended to turn into riots wherever the authorities allowed them to continue for long enough.
options.D: indicates that such festivals were supported mainly by the elite and opposed mainly by ordinary people.

questions.correct_answer: (B) has been cited by supporters of each of the two dominant explanations as evidence for their view.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says banning suggests rulers 'found them dangerous', and funding suggests they found them 'useful'; neither implies no significance.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says riots occurred only 'on a few occasions'; nothing ties them to long toleration.
option_rationales.D: The passage contrasts different responses by rulers; it says nothing about ordinary people opposing the festivals.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'Supporters of each view can point to cases': funding 'suggests they found them useful' (the safety valve) and banning 'suggests they found them dangerous' (the subversive view).
questions.common_misconception: Reading the funding and banning as evidence for a single conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in the last two sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a historian asking why a particular carnival became an uprising should look first at

options.A: any changes in the masks, songs and other forms that the festival used in that particular year.
options.B: whether the festival belonged by its nature to the safety valve type or to the subversive type.
options.C: the economic and political conditions surrounding the festival in the year that it turned violent.
options.D: how much money the authorities had spent on funding and staging the festival in earlier decades.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the economic and political conditions surrounding the festival in the year that it turned violent.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the same festival, 'with the same masks and the same songs', could be harmless or rebellious; the forms do not explain the difference.
option_rationales.B: The author rejects the idea that a festival's meaning is 'fixed by its form', so there is no such fixed type to identify.
option_rationales.D: Funding appears in paragraph 2 only as evidence cited by one theory; paragraph 3 locates the cause in 'circumstances' such as harvests and taxes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The difference lay not in the ritual but in its circumstances: a bad harvest, a disputed tax, a quarrel between factions of the elite'. Inversion 'takes' its charge 'from the situation into which it is performed'.
questions.common_misconception: Looking for the cause in the ritual itself, which is the assumption the author attacks.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the paragraph's general claim to a new question.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 functions in the passage mainly to

options.A: introduce the account of inversion as a lesson in hierarchy that the final paragraph goes on to develop.
options.B: provide evidence that festivals of inversion generally increased the grievances of those who took part in them.
options.C: defend the second explanation by showing that the first cannot account for carnivals that turned into riots.
options.D: attack one of the two explanations on a ground distinct from the objection raised against both in paragraph 3.

questions.correct_answer: (D) attack one of the two explanations on a ground distinct from the objection raised against both in paragraph 3.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 begins its account afresh 'from a simpler observation'; paragraph 4 is about the steam image and does not set up that account.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says only that participants 'may feel more entitled'; its point is that no one has observed the mechanism, not that grievances generally grew.
option_rationales.C: Riots are not mentioned in paragraph 4, and paragraph 3 has already rejected the second explanation along with the first.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 criticises both theories for assuming that meaning is 'fixed by its form'. Paragraph 4 announces 'a further weakness' of the safety valve theory only: its hydraulic image of resentment has no observed basis. It is a second, independent objection aimed at one theory.
questions.common_misconception: Treating paragraph 4 as a bridge to paragraph 5, or as support for the rival theory, instead of as a second objection to one theory.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options describe plausible roles for a fourth paragraph; the correct answer requires tracking which theory each objection targets.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's criticism of the safety valve theory in paragraph 4?

options.A: Town records show that formal complaints against local officials rose rather than fell in the weeks after festivals mocking those officials.
options.B: Town records show that rulers who funded festivals of mockery seldom faced open rebellion during the years that followed.
options.C: Collections of songs that mocked local officials during festivals were later printed and read as a form of popular literature.
options.D: Some festivals of mockery were banned after riots in which participants had used their masks to hide their identities.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Town records show that formal complaints against local officials rose rather than fell in the weeks after festivals mocking those officials.

option_rationales.B: This is the kind of case paragraph 2 says safety valve supporters cite; it supports that theory rather than the author's criticism of it.
option_rationales.C: The later fate of the songs says nothing about whether resentment is released like steam, so it is irrelevant to the criticism.
option_rationales.D: This concerns why authorities banned festivals, not whether mocking masters leaves people less aggrieved afterwards.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that resentment does not behave like steam: participants 'do not obviously feel less aggrieved afterwards' and may feel 'more entitled to their grievance'. Complaints rising after the festival is direct evidence that grievance was not discharged.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about riots or bans because it sounds like evidence against the safety valve.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are all on topic; only one bears on the specific hydraulic claim.

questions.question: Which of the following best reconciles the account in paragraph 5 with the claim in paragraph 3 that inversion 'does not carry its own political charge'?

options.A: Because inversion always teaches the existing order by displaying it, it reliably conserves that order, whatever the circumstances in which it occurs.
options.B: Because inversion displays the hierarchy in a way that can be read as confirming or exposing it, the surrounding situation must decide which reading prevails.
options.C: Because inversion requires the active cooperation of the authorities being mocked, its effects depend on how willingly those authorities take part in it.
options.D: Because inversion shows rank to be a convention, it always weakens hierarchy in the long run, even when a festival passes off without any trouble.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Because inversion displays the hierarchy in a way that can be read as confirming or exposing it, the surrounding situation must decide which reading prevails.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says 'the lesson cuts both ways'; this keeps only the conservative lesson and contradicts the claim that the festival has no fixed charge.
option_rationales.C: 'The mock bishop presupposes a real one' means the parody depends on the existence of the hierarchy, not on the bishop's participation; this is a distortion.
option_rationales.D: This keeps only the subversive lesson; paragraph 5 says which lesson is learned 'depends, again, on what else is happening'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says inversion teaches the order 'in that sense' but also shows ranking to be 'a convention rather than a fact of nature', and that which lesson is learned 'depends, again, on what else is happening'. The word 'again' points back to paragraph 3: the charge comes from circumstances, and paragraph 5 explains why the form can carry either charge.
questions.common_misconception: Fastening on one of the two lessons in paragraph 5 and turning it into a fixed effect.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires synthesising paragraphs 3 and 5; two wrong options each keep half of the double-edged lesson.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'only nominally attached' most nearly means

options.A: committed to the group for a short trial period before full membership.
options.B: attached to the group through a name inherited from one's family.
options.C: belonging to the group in name while lacking any real commitment to it.
options.D: connected to the group informally, without ever having formally joined it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) belonging to the group in name while lacking any real commitment to it.

option_rationales.A: No trial period is mentioned; the phrase describes the kind of member that demanding rituals screen out.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in paragraph 2 concerns family names; the contrast is between real and merely apparent commitment.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the sense: the free rider is formally a member who takes the 'benefits of membership', but is not committed.

questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts someone willing to bear years of hardship with someone 'only nominally attached'; the preceding sentences describe people who 'take the benefits of membership without bearing its burdens'. Nominal attachment is membership in name only.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'nominally' literally as having to do with names.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is explained by the free-rider description just before it.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the signalling account, a group that lowers its demands may lose members because

options.A: the members who remain must take on a larger share of the cost of the rituals that are left.
options.B: outsiders conclude from the change that the group has quietly abandoned its central doctrines.
options.C: long-standing members resent losing practices that they had come to enjoy for their own sake.
options.D: belonging becomes less valuable once uncommitted people can enter more easily and draw on its benefits.

questions.correct_answer: (D) belonging becomes less valuable once uncommitted people can enter more easily and draw on its benefits.

option_rationales.A: The demands have been lowered, so the remaining costs fall rather than rise; this distorts the passage.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in paragraph 2 refers to outsiders' views of doctrine; the explanation offered concerns the value of belonging.
option_rationales.C: The signalling account treats costs as screens, not as enjoyable in themselves; this explanation is outside the theory.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says demanding rituals 'screen' out free riders so that members 'can extend trust', and that when demands fall 'the value of belonging falls along with its cost'. Lower costs let in the free riders the screen used to exclude, which reduces the value of membership.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible psychological reason not contained in the signalling account.
questions.difficulty_reason: The mechanism is implied by combining the screening idea with the final sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a limitation of the signalling account EXCEPT

options.A: its inability to explain why groups that relax their demands sometimes lose members.
options.B: its silence on why communities insist on the exact form of a rite.
options.C: its neglect of how a demanding practice can create the commitment it shows.
options.D: its difficulty with demanding practices imposed on very young children.

questions.correct_answer: (A) its inability to explain why groups that relax their demands sometimes lose members.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 gives this as the first gap: the theory explains why a ritual is costly 'not why it should take the particular form it does'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 gives this as the third and 'most important' gap: cost 'helps to manufacture' commitment.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 gives this as the second gap: a rite performed on an infant 'cannot be a signal of the child's own' commitment.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'The theory also explains' the pattern of groups losing members when they lower their demands; this is a success of the account, not a limitation. The other three are the three gaps listed in paragraphs 3 and 4.
questions.common_misconception: Remembering that the loss of members is discussed but forgetting that the theory is credited with explaining it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are the numbered gaps; the correct answer reverses a point the passage credits to the theory.

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates the 'third gap' described in paragraph 4?

options.A: A club refuses a generous donation from a new member offered as a substitute for the arduous initiation that it normally requires of everyone who joins.
options.B: Parents enrol their newborn in a demanding religious order partly to show their neighbours how devout the household is.
options.C: A volunteer who joined a relief group half-heartedly finds, after months of exhausting night shifts, that she is now deeply loyal to it.
options.D: A village extends credit only to those who have completed a long and difficult fast, judging them to be trustworthy.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A volunteer who joined a relief group half-heartedly finds, after months of exhausting night shifts, that she is now deeply loyal to it.

option_rationales.A: Refusing an equally costly substitute illustrates the first gap in paragraph 3, about the particular form of a rite.
option_rationales.B: A practice imposed on an infant that signals the parents' commitment illustrates the second gap in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.D: This illustrates the signalling account itself (paragraph 2), not any gap in it.

questions.explanation: The third gap is that the practice can change the performer, producing 'the conviction it was supposed to display' (paragraph 4). The volunteer's commitment grows out of the costly practice instead of preceding it.
questions.common_misconception: Matching the club example to the third gap because it involves cost, without checking which gap each case illustrates.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option illustrates another part of the passage, so the gaps must be kept apart.

questions.question: The claim in paragraph 4 that 'cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it' depends on the assumption that

options.A: people who take on demanding practices do so chiefly in order to impress observers with their devotion.
options.B: what people report about being changed by demanding practices is broadly accurate rather than a later rationalisation.
options.C: practices imposed on children produce a stronger commitment than practices that adults choose for themselves.
options.D: observers are generally unable to tell genuinely committed members apart from those who are free riding.

questions.correct_answer: (B) what people report about being changed by demanding practices is broadly accurate rather than a later rationalisation.

option_rationales.A: The author criticises the theory for treating ritual only as 'a message addressed to observers'; the claim does not need performers to be aiming at observers.
option_rationales.C: Children's rites belong to the second gap, and nothing in paragraph 4 compares the strength of commitment produced in children and in adults.
option_rationales.D: If this were assumed the signalling account would fail outright, yet paragraph 5 says the objections do not overturn it; the claim does not depend on it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 bases the claim on what people 'commonly report' and introduces it conditionally: 'If that is so, cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it.' The conclusion therefore requires that those reports be broadly true.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the conditional 'If that is so', which shows exactly what the claim rests on.
questions.difficulty_reason: Assumption questions require spotting an unstated premise; here it is signalled only by a conditional clause.

questions.question: The image of a crowd at a parade in which 'everyone stands on tiptoe' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: suggest that graduates are worn out by the number of years they have spent studying.
options.B: show that employers have quietly agreed among themselves to keep raising the qualifications they demand from applicants.
options.C: demonstrate that a degree gives an individual employer no useful information about applicants.
options.D: illustrate how choices that make sense for each employer combine into an outcome that helps nobody.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate how choices that make sense for each employer combine into an outcome that helps nobody.

option_rationales.A: This reads 'more tired' literally; the image is about the collective result of everyone raising the bar, not about the fatigue of students.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'Each employer is behaving sensibly' on its own account; there is no agreement or collusion among employers anywhere in the passage.
option_rationales.C: The passage says the degree is 'the cheapest filter available' and once selected a more persistent group, so it does carry some information; the image concerns the collective result.

questions.explanation: The image follows directly on 'Each employer is behaving sensibly' and 'the sum of these sensible choices'. When everyone stands on tiptoe, each person's move makes sense, but 'no one sees better than before, and everyone is more tired': raising the bar for all buys no advantage for anyone and only adds cost.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the image literally, or reading collusion into what the passage presents as separate sensible choices.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence introducing the image states its point outright.

questions.question: According to the passage, when few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one

options.A: was picking out a small group who tended, on average, to be more persistent and better connected.
options.B: was asking for a master's degree in order to separate the strongest applicants from ordinary graduates.
options.C: was ensuring that new staff had already been thoroughly trained in the particular tasks that the job would require.
options.D: was deliberately excluding applicants whose families could not afford fees, since that was the intended purpose.

questions.correct_answer: (A) was picking out a small group who tended, on average, to be more persistent and better connected.

option_rationales.B: Asking for a master's is what employers did later, once degrees had become common; it does not describe the period when few people held degrees.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 explains the selection in terms of persistence and connections, not task training, and paragraph 3 says much of what graduates studied 'is barely used in the job'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 describes exclusion as a result of the rising bar, a requirement 'introduced in the name of competence'; the passage never says exclusion was intended.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'When few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one was selecting a small group who were, on average, more persistent and better connected than the rest.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the early stage with the later stage of the process, or reading intention into an effect.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer sits in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Governments should prohibit employers from asking applicants for degrees unless the job needs specialist knowledge.
options.B: Most jobs now advertised for graduates involve exactly the same tasks that they involved fifty years ago, despite the new paperwork.
options.C: A rise in the education a job demands does not by itself show that the job has become harder.
options.D: The main value of a university education lies in the signal of persistence it sends to employers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A rise in the education a job demands does not by itself show that the job has become harder.

option_rationales.A: The passage proposes no regulation; paragraph 4 mentions employers who test applicants directly, but as a development that raises a question, not as a law the author recommends.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 concedes that 'Some occupations really have changed beyond recognition' and says only that the change in many jobs is 'often modest', which is far weaker than saying most jobs are exactly the same.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says education 'has goods that no labour market can measure', so the author does not reduce its value to a labour-market signal.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the explanation that work has become more demanding 'is offered far more often than it is checked', and paragraph 2 offers a rival account in which requirements rise because degrees stop separating applicants. So a rising requirement does not by itself show the work is harder.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the author's 'often modest' into 'no change at all', or crediting the author with a prescription.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the author's hedged position across paragraphs 1 and 2 and rejection of two plausible overstatements.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the 'more economical account' given in paragraph 2?

options.A: In a firm that began requiring degrees for clerks, graduates did the job's tasks markedly better, and the gap was traced to their coursework.
options.B: Employers who dropped their degree requirements found that screening applicants by other means took them longer and cost them considerably more.
options.C: The proportion of school leavers going on to university kept rising in the years after the requirement became common.
options.D: In a firm that began requiring degrees for its clerks, the new recruits came mostly from families able to pay for several years of study.

questions.correct_answer: (A) In a firm that began requiring degrees for clerks, graduates did the job's tasks markedly better, and the gap was traced to their coursework.

option_rationales.B: This supports the account, which says the degree is 'the cheapest filter available' to each employer.
option_rationales.C: More people seeking degrees is what the queue account predicts, as each tries to keep a place in line; it does not challenge the account.
option_rationales.D: This fits paragraph 3's claim that the rising bar rewards 'the capacity to pay for time'; it does nothing to show that the degree certifies skill.

questions.explanation: The account in paragraph 2 treats the degree 'less as a certificate of skill than as a ticket in a queue', valued for 'the signal rather than the substance' (paragraph 3).
