Evidence that graduates do the job better because of what they learned shows the degree certifying real skill, which cuts directly against the account.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is about degrees and access but is consistent with, or even supports, the signalling account.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying the core claim (signal, not skill) and seeing which option contradicts it rather than merely touching the topic.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the remark that 'a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to' most nearly means that

options.A: leisure became so expensive that most working families could no longer afford to enjoy the free time they had won.
options.B: employers could buy back their workers' Saturdays by offering them extra pay for working at the weekend.
options.C: workers were now free to sell their weekend hours to whichever employer offered them the best terms.
options.D: free time falling at the same hours for everyone became a market that businesses could plan to serve.

questions.correct_answer: (D) free time falling at the same hours for everyone became a market that businesses could plan to serve.

option_rationales.A: The passage says leisure came to be paid for, not that it became unaffordable; it calls guaranteed free time 'a real gain' for most working people.
option_rationales.B: The passage never mentions overtime; the sentence that follows lists football matches, excursion trains and resorts, which sell leisure to workers rather than buy their time.
option_rationales.C: The sellers in paragraph 3 are leisure businesses, and what changes is that leisure becomes 'something one went out and paid for'; workers are the buyers, not the sellers.

questions.explanation: The phrase is explained by the next sentence: football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts 'arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday'. Because everyone was free at the same time, businesses could sell leisure to that shared block.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'sold' as a sale of labour time rather than a sale of leisure to workers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The following sentence glosses the phrase directly.

questions.question: According to the passage, what did employers gain from the compromise that produced the weekend?

options.A: Influence over how workers spent their Sundays, since leisure was now organised and supplied by employers themselves.
options.B: Workers who could be relied upon to arrive, in a fit state, at the start of the week.
options.C: Lower wage bills, since workers accepted reduced pay in return for having all of Saturday free.
options.D: A longer total working week overall, since Saturday afternoons were exchanged for extra hours on the other weekdays.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Workers who could be relied upon to arrive, in a fit state, at the start of the week.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says leisure was organised by football, trains and resorts, not by employers, and gives employers no control over Sundays.
option_rationales.C: Wages are never mentioned in the passage; the employers' gain is stated as predictability, not savings on pay.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says workers 'wanted fewer hours' and gained guaranteed rest; nothing suggests hours were added elsewhere in exchange.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning.' Employers had wanted predictable hours, and this is what the compromise gave them.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible economic gain (hours, wages) that the passage does not state.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a single explicit sentence.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the weekend is best described as

options.A: grateful, crediting factory owners with the generosity that first gave workers a Saturday free of labour.
options.B: appreciative of what it won for workers, while noting how it reshaped the nature of leisure.
options.C: nostalgic, regarding the irregular rhythm of pre-factory work as a freer and healthier way of living.
options.D: dismissive, treating the weekend as a defeat for workers that was presented to them as a victory.

questions.correct_answer: (B) appreciative of what it won for workers, while noting how it reshaped the nature of leisure.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says free time 'was won against resistance', and paragraph 2 presents a struggle and a compromise, not employer generosity.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says plainly that 'The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better', noting its ties to poverty and overwork.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 opens by saying it would be 'wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls guaranteed free time 'a real gain' won against resistance, yet adds that 'the weekend also changed what free time was', turning it into a scheduled block that could be sold to. The attitude is appreciation with a critical observation.
questions.common_misconception: Picking up the critical note in paragraph 3 and overstating it into dismissal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong attitude is explicitly ruled out by a sentence in the passage.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely parallels the change described in paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: Workers in a factory strike for higher wages and win a large raise, though their daily hours of work stay exactly as they were.
options.B: A town council turns a disused railway yard into a public park so that residents have somewhere to spend their free afternoons.
options.C: A company abolishes its fixed holiday calendar and allows staff to take leave whenever they choose, provided that their work is done on time.
options.D: Musicians who rested whenever bookings dried up join an orchestra with a fixed August holiday, and travel firms begin selling August trips to its players.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Musicians who rested whenever bookings dried up join an orchestra with a fixed August holiday, and travel firms begin selling August trips to its players.

option_rationales.A: This concerns pay alone, whereas the passage stresses that the struggle over hours was 'also a struggle over the shape of time'.
option_rationales.B: This provides a place for leisure but changes neither who decides when free time falls nor its regularity, which is the heart of the passage's change.
option_rationales.C: This moves from fixed to discretionary time, the reverse of the passage's change from rest taken 'at the worker's discretion' to 'a fixed block'.

questions.explanation: The passage describes two linked shifts: irregular, self-chosen rest becomes guaranteed rest fixed for everyone (paragraph 2), and that shared block becomes something businesses sell to (paragraph 3). The orchestra case reproduces both: guaranteed, standardised holiday replaces rest taken when bookings ran out, and a market forms around the fixed period.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing any case that involves leisure or workers' gains without both the standardisation of time and the market that forms around it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The analogy must match two linked features at once; each wrong option matches one surface element only.

questions.question: The back staircases and basement bells mentioned in paragraph 1 serve primarily as

options.A: proof that servants in large houses were treated more harshly than those employed in small households.
options.B: illustrations of the technical improvements that made large households cheaper and easier to run in that period.
options.C: examples of how a house was laid out so that the work of servants went unseen.
options.D: evidence that nineteenth-century families valued privacy from one another as much as privacy from their servants.

questions.correct_answer: (C) examples of how a house was laid out so that the work of servants went unseen.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no comparison between large and small households, and it treats the features as concealment rather than harshness.
option_rationales.B: Cost and efficiency are never discussed; paragraph 1 presents these features as means of keeping servants out of sight.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about family members avoiding one another; the staircases kept maids from meeting 'the family', and the bells hid 'who answered'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the staircases and bells right after saying that 'the best servant was the one who was least noticed'; the staircases mean maids 'need never meet the family', and the bells let a summons be answered without anyone seeing 'who answered it'.
questions.common_misconception: Inferring a purpose (efficiency, privacy) that the surrounding sentences do not give.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is fixed by the topic sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author describes app designers' talk of 'removing friction' (paragraph 3) as revealing because the phrase

options.A: treats as a nuisance what is often simply the customer's meeting with the person doing the work.
options.B: shows that app designers have consciously modelled their services on the households of the nineteenth century.
options.C: suggests that technical faults in apps are now the main obstacle standing between customers and good service.
options.D: admits that delivery and cleaning apps make the work of couriers and cleaners physically harder than it used to be.

questions.correct_answer: (A) treats as a nuisance what is often simply the customer's meeting with the person doing the work.

option_rationales.B: The author claims a durable wish, not conscious imitation; nothing suggests designers have the Victorian household in mind.
option_rationales.C: This takes 'friction' as a technical glitch; the author's 'as though' clause says the friction is, very often, a human encounter.
option_rationales.D: Workers' physical burden is not discussed; 'friction' in the passage refers to the encounter between customer and worker.

questions.explanation: The sentence says designers speak of removing friction 'as though the friction in question were not, very often, the encounter with another person who is doing the work'. The phrase is revealing because it recasts contact with the worker as an inconvenience, echoing the old wish 'to receive service without meeting the server' (paragraph 4).
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's point as a claim about designers' intentions or about technical faults.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning lies in an 'as though' clause that must be connected to the thesis in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: A wish to keep social inferiors out of sight does not fully explain why servants were made invisible.
options.B: Comfort that seems to require no effort can depend on a great deal of labour deliberately kept from view.
options.C: The modern means of receiving service without seeing the worker reach many more people than the older means did.
options.D: Couriers and cleaners today work under essentially the same conditions as Victorian servants, though under a different name.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Couriers and cleaners today work under essentially the same conditions as Victorian servants, though under a different name.

option_rationales.A: Supported: paragraph 1 says 'snobbery explains less than it seems to' and that invisibility was 'one of the things the household was for'.
option_rationales.B: Supported: paragraph 2 says 'The ease was manufactured by a great deal of labour, and the labour had to be hidden for the ease to be believed'.
option_rationales.C: Supported: paragraph 4 says the means 'are now available to far more people than ever owned a back staircase'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 warns that 'The comparison must not be pressed too far': modern workers are not bound to one household, keep hours that end and have legal protections a scullery maid lacked, so 'to call such workers servants is to erase real gains'. The claim of essentially the same conditions contradicts this.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the passage's comparison between old and new service as an identity claim, missing the qualification in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three true statements are paraphrased from different paragraphs; the false one echoes the passage's own comparison.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Victorian families hid their servants out of snobbery, and apps have now made that same snobbery affordable for the middle classes.
options.B: The disappearance of large-scale domestic service shows that the social hierarchy it once supported has also come to an end.
options.C: Hiding the labour behind comfort once helped a class seem exempt from necessity, and the wish behind that concealment outlives the old form of service.
options.D: Modern delivery and cleaning work amounts to a revival of domestic servitude, and its workers ought to be recognised openly as servants.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Hiding the labour behind comfort once helped a class seem exempt from necessity, and the wish behind that concealment outlives the old form of service.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says 'snobbery explains less than it seems to'; the author's explanation is that concealment produced the appearance of ease and so produced hierarchy.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'it is easy to assume that its logic went with it' and then argues the opposite, that the logic survives by other means.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says that calling such workers servants 'is to erase real gains'; the author draws a qualified parallel, not an identity.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that hiding labour let a class 'appear exempt from necessity', and paragraphs 3 and 4 argue that 'the wish to receive service without meeting the server' survives in new forms, even though modern workers have real gains. The correct answer holds both halves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that echoes the passage's comparison most strongly, or the familiar snobbery explanation the author sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: All wrong options reuse the passage's own material; the correct answer needs both the functional claim and the qualified comparison.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the 'ownership' of emotion at work refers to

options.A: who sets the terms on which a worker's feelings are displayed, and for whose benefit.
options.B: the legal rights that a worker holds over the recordings her employer makes of her calls.
options.C: whether the worker genuinely feels the warmth or calm that she shows to the people she serves.
options.D: how much emotion a particular job demands in comparison with the emotional demands of other jobs.

questions.correct_answer: (A) who sets the terms on which a worker's feelings are displayed, and for whose benefit.

option_rationales.B: This takes 'ownership' literally; the passage never discusses recordings or legal rights over them.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says a scripted greeting 'can be delivered with real goodwill', so sincerity is a separate matter from who controls the display.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the distinction 'was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not', and paragraph 3 contrasts ownership with mere presence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 contrasts 'the presence of emotion at work' with 'its ownership', picking up paragraph 2's distinction between feeling a worker manages 'according to her own judgement' and feeling whose display is 'specified, monitored and sold by someone else', where 'the employer, not the worker, sets its terms'.
questions.common_misconception: Equating ownership with sincerity, or with the amount of emotion involved.
questions.difficulty_reason: The term is defined by the preceding paragraph's contrast.

questions.question: On the author's account, the builder in paragraph 1 who keeps his temper with clients would most likely count as

options.A: no emotional labourer, because the feelings of manual workers play no real part in how well they do their jobs.
options.B: no emotional labourer in the strict sense, provided nobody else scripts or monitors how his courtesy is displayed.
options.C: an emotional labourer, because every job that requires the management of feeling falls within the concept.
options.D: an emotional labourer, because he would lose business and income if he failed to manage his feelings with clients.

questions.correct_answer: (B) no emotional labourer in the strict sense, provided nobody else scripts or monitors how his courtesy is displayed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says a builder who loses his temper 'will not keep' his clients, so feeling clearly matters to his work; the author's criterion is control, not relevance.
option_rationales.C: This is the critics' reductio, which the author answers: the distinction 'was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not'.
option_rationales.D: Losing clients shows only that emotion matters to his work; on the author's test what counts is whether someone else specifies and sells the display.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 puts the line between feeling managed 'according to her own judgement' and feeling 'specified, monitored and sold by someone else'. The surgeon's calm 'is left to her; nobody scripts it'. The self-managing builder resembles the surgeon, so he falls outside the strict concept unless someone else controls his display.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the critics' broad criterion, or treating the commercial consequences of emotion as the test.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the author's criterion to a case the critics raised, and separating it from the critics' criterion.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's suggestion in paragraph 3 about where the cost of emotional labour lies?

options.A: In one chain of shops, staff whose greetings were scripted and scored were more exhausted than staff serving the same customers as they saw fit.
options.B: Surgeons report higher levels of stress at work than call-centre agents do, especially during long and difficult operations.
options.C: Workers whose jobs involve dealing with members of the public all day report more exhaustion than people who work largely on their own.
options.D: Customers rate scripted greetings as noticeably less sincere than greetings that shop staff are free to phrase however they like.

questions.correct_answer: (A) In one chain of shops, staff whose greetings were scripted and scored were more exhausted than staff serving the same customers as they saw fit.

option_rationales.B: Surgeons' stress arises from feeling that is 'left to her', so it says nothing about the cost of feeling produced on demand under supervision.
option_rationales.C: This compares contact with solitude, not controlled display with self-managed display, so it cannot isolate the factor the author identifies.
option_rationales.D: This concerns how customers perceive the greeting, whereas paragraph 3 is about the cost borne by the worker.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 locates the cost not in smiling as such but in a smile that 'must be produced on demand' and whose absence is 'a disciplinary matter'. A comparison that holds the customers constant and varies only who controls the display isolates exactly that factor.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a finding about emotion at work in general rather than about externally controlled display.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are on topic; only a controlled comparison tests the author's specific mechanism.

questions.question: The author's reply to the critics in paragraph 2 implies that

options.A: they are right that the concept is too broad, and that the remedy is to restrict it to occupations whose main task is serving customers.
options.B: they are right about how the term is often used, but wrong to infer that the concept itself picks out nothing distinctive.
options.C: their examples of the surgeon and the lawyer reveal that professionals perform more emotional labour than call-centre agents.
options.D: they have shown that the concept should be dropped and replaced with a narrower term that names only scripted forms of feeling.

questions.correct_answer: (B) they are right about how the term is often used, but wrong to infer that the concept itself picks out nothing distinctive.

option_rationales.A: The author narrows the concept by the test of who controls the display, not by occupation; a customer-facing worker left to her own judgement would fall outside it.
option_rationales.C: The author uses the surgeon to show feeling that 'nobody scripts', the opposite of the agent's case, so the reply reverses the critics' examples rather than ranking them.
option_rationales.D: The author keeps the concept and calls it 'narrower than its popular use suggests, but also sharper', so it is clarified rather than abandoned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens: 'The objection is fair against the loose use of the term, but it misses what the original idea was pointing at.' The author grants the point about usage while denying that the concept itself is empty, since it marks off feeling 'specified, monitored and sold by someone else'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the occupational restriction because it resembles the author's narrowing, without noticing that the criterion is control, not job type.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option narrows the concept as the author does but by the wrong criterion; separating them needs paragraphs 2 and 3 together.

questions.question: According to the passage, the older 'simple map' of taste held that

options.A: educated people enjoyed both high and popular culture, though they tended to enjoy the two in quite different settings.
options.B: elites marked themselves out mainly by how much they spent on concerts, exhibitions and other cultural events.
options.C: taste was largely a matter of individual preference, with only a loose and unreliable connection to social class.
options.D: a person's social standing could be read from where their preferences fell on a ladder from refined to popular culture.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a person's social standing could be read from where their preferences fell on a ladder from refined to popular culture.

option_rationales.A: This describes the omnivore pattern that surveys later found (paragraph 2), not the older map of paragraph 1.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says elites 'distinguished themselves by what they refused', not by how much they spent.
option_rationales.C: This is the conclusion that 'Some observers' draw from the omnivore findings in paragraph 2; the old map tied taste closely to class.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'a person's place in society could be read, with fair accuracy, from the position of their preferences on this ladder', a ladder running from opera, poetry and the old masters down to popular entertainments.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the old map with the later findings or with the observers' interpretation of them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author's discussion of the 'knowing, curatorial attitude' (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: omnivores secretly dislike the popular forms they claim to enjoy and consume them only in order to appear open-minded.
options.B: the manner in which something is liked matters more than breadth of taste in every form of social distinction.
options.C: two people may enjoy the same popular film while their way of enjoying it marks quite different social positions.
options.D: popular culture is transformed into high culture once educated audiences begin to adopt it and write about it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) two people may enjoy the same popular film while their way of enjoying it marks quite different social positions.

option_rationales.A: The passage says omnivores do enjoy popular forms, 'prizing a song' or 'enjoying a film', but in a distinctive manner; nothing suggests secret dislike.
option_rationales.B: The author offers manner as one marker beside breadth and selective dislike, and never ranks them, let alone for every form of distinction.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about popular forms changing their status; it is the manner of consumption, not the form, that marks distance.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says omnivores 'rarely consume popular forms in the same way as their usual audiences' and that 'this manner of liking can mark distance'. So the same object can be enjoyed by two audiences whose enjoyment signals different positions.
questions.common_misconception: Turning a claim about manner of enjoyment into insincerity, or into a ranking of markers.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires moving from the description of an attitude to its social implication.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely treat as an instance of the shifted boundary described in paragraph 4?

options.A: A graduate who boasts of enjoying every kind of music but finds one genre, loved chiefly by her town's least schooled residents, beneath notice.
options.B: A music critic who dismisses all popular music as worthless and attends only concerts of classical and early music.
options.C: A student who listens to a very wide range of music, from folk to jazz, because her friends keep introducing her to new things.
options.D: A retired factory worker who listens only to the songs he grew up with and has never felt any wish to attend an opera.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A graduate who boasts of enjoying every kind of music but finds one genre, loved chiefly by her town's least schooled residents, beneath notice.

option_rationales.B: This is distinction by refusal of the old kind described in paragraph 1, not the moved boundary of the omnivore.
option_rationales.C: Her breadth involves no excluded form associated with the least educated, which is the feature paragraph 4 describes.
option_rationales.D: He shows neither omnivorous breadth nor a highly educated person's selective dislike; paragraph 4 concerns the boundary drawn by the highly educated.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the forms 'most often rejected by the highly educated tend to be those most associated with the least educated', so that 'the boundary has moved rather than vanished'. A self-described omnivore who excludes the one genre of the least schooled fits this exactly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the classic snob, who also draws a class boundary but in the old way the passage contrasts with the new.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options involve taste and class; the correct answer must match the specific combination of openness and selective exclusion.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the final paragraph in the passage?

options.A: It introduces evidence showing that the omnivore pattern found in surveys is confined to a small number of wealthy countries and does not hold elsewhere.
options.B: It shows that the old snobbery of paragraph 1 has returned among the highly educated in exactly its earlier form.
options.C: It adds a further reason to doubt that hierarchy has ended, grants that real change has occurred, and then restates that distinction persists in a new form.
options.D: It withdraws the doubts raised in paragraph 3 by conceding that the loosening of cultural hierarchy is genuine after all.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It adds a further reason to doubt that hierarchy has ended, grants that real change has occurred, and then restates that distinction persists in a new form.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says nothing about the geographic spread of the pattern; its evidence concerns what the highly educated dislike.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 speaks of 'the decline of snobbery' and says distinction now works 'through openness', which is a new form, not the old one returned.
option_rationales.D: The concession is followed at once by 'But distinction has not disappeared', so it qualifies the argument without withdrawing paragraph 3's doubts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with 'Nor is the omnivore's appetite unlimited', adding the evidence of selective dislikes to paragraph 3's objections; it concedes that loosening 'is a genuine change'; and it concludes that distinction 'has learned to express itself through openness'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the concession as a reversal, or mistaking the moved boundary for a return of old snobbery.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph does three things, including a concession that can be misread as a retraction.

questions.question: The example of persistent unhappiness in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that psychiatrists have been steadily losing ground to clergy and social workers in the treatment of unhappiness.
options.B: demonstrate that licensing has failed to protect the public from practitioners who are not properly qualified to help.
options.C: illustrate that some human problems are too complex for any single profession to treat adequately on its own.
options.D: show that the profession to which a problem belongs is decided by rivalry among professions rather than by the problem itself.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that the profession to which a problem belongs is decided by rivalry among professions rather than by the problem itself.

option_rationales.A: The passage names the rival claimants but reports no winner or trend; it says only that the question is settled 'provisionally and repeatedly'.
option_rationales.B: Licensing is not discussed in paragraph 2, and the example concerns which profession owns a problem, not the qualifications of practitioners.
option_rationales.C: The point is not that the problem exceeds any one profession's ability but that its classification 'is not settled by the nature of unhappiness'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the boundaries of professional work 'are anything but given'. Unhappiness could be medical, psychological, spiritual or social, and which it is 'is not settled by the nature of unhappiness' but 'by contests' among professions. The example undermines the shared assumption that a profession's work is simply given.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a report on who is winning, rather than as a counter to the assumption that work is given.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function depends on the preceding claim about what the two accounts share.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the two accounts in paragraph 1 as

options.A: incompatible with each other, so that anyone who accepts one of them is bound to reject the other entirely.
options.B: each capturing a real effect of licensing, while sharing an assumption that prevents either from explaining professional change.
options.C: correct when taken together, since in combination they give a complete account of how professions rise and fall.
options.D: equally mistaken, since licensing in fact neither protects clients from charlatans nor raises the fees that professionals charge.

questions.correct_answer: (B) each capturing a real effect of licensing, while sharing an assumption that prevents either from explaining professional change.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 accepts the effect each account describes at once, so the author does not treat them as mutually exclusive.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'neither effect explains why some professions grow while others shrink', so together they remain incomplete.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'Clients are protected by licensing, and fees are raised by it', so the author grants both effects.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'each is right about something', and paragraph 4 confirms that licensing both protects clients and raises fees. But paragraph 2 says both 'look at one profession at a time' and treat its work as 'simply given', and paragraph 4 adds that neither explains growth and decline.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the concession in paragraph 4 and concluding that the author rejects both accounts outright.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires joining paragraph 1's framing, paragraph 2's diagnosis and paragraph 4's concession.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about how knowledge matters in contests over problems (paragraph 3)?

options.A: Practitioners in a profession that lost a problem to a rival were later found to have been entirely competent at treating it.
options.B: After one profession won control of a problem, licensing rules were rewritten so as to bar its rivals from treating that problem.
options.C: Across many contests over newly recognised problems, the winner was usually the group with the best record of treating them, whatever theories its rivals offered.
options.D: A profession with an abstract theory took over a problem that its rivals had long treated, and later lost it again when that theory fell from favour.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Across many contests over newly recognised problems, the winner was usually the group with the best record of treating them, whatever theories its rivals offered.

option_rationales.A: This supports paragraph 4's claim that people 'perfectly good at their work can find that work quietly reassigned'.
option_rationales.B: This fits the author's description of licensing as 'a weapon in a jurisdictional struggle', and says nothing against the role of theory.
option_rationales.D: This is consistent with the author's view: theory won the problem, and the loss fits a history 'of conquests and retreats'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that 'What wins a contested problem is often not superior skill in treating it but a more abstract body of theory'. A broad pattern in which practical success, regardless of rivals' theories, usually decided the contest directly contradicts this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a case that mentions theory or competence but is consistent with, or supports, the author's model.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is drawn from the passage's own model and supports it in a different way; only the correct answer reverses the specific claim about theory and skill.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The state's part in professional life is confined to certifying the competence of individual practitioners through licences.
options.B: A body of practitioners could become more skilled over a decade and still end it with a narrower field of work.
options.C: The size of a profession at a given moment is a reliable measure of how well it serves the clients who rely on it.
options.D: A profession armed with abstract theory will always defeat a rival whose knowledge is purely practical in a contest over a problem.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A body of practitioners could become more skilled over a decade and still end it with a narrower field of work.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 treats licensing as 'a weapon in a jurisdictional struggle', and paragraph 4 names the state among those a profession must persuade.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says a profession's fate 'depends less on how well it does what it does' than on its persuasiveness, so size does not track quality of service.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says theory 'often' wins and that a practical profession 'can be' displaced; saying always overstates a hedged claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says practitioners 'perfectly good at their work can find that work quietly reassigned', because fate depends 'less on how well it does what it does' than on claiming problems. Growing skill is therefore compatible with a shrinking jurisdiction.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'always' option because it echoes paragraph 3's claim about theory, missing the hedge.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is an unstated consequence of paragraph 4; the strongest wrong option overstates a hedged claim from paragraph 3.

questions.question: According to the passage, conspicuous display has lost much of its power to separate the advantaged from others because

options.A: rising taxes on imported luxury goods have made open displays of wealth far more costly than they were.
options.B: the wealthiest households now keep most of their wealth in savings rather than in goods of any kind.
options.C: satirists and moralists have made the owners of showy goods into figures of public ridicule.
options.D: cheaper production has put passable versions of once-rare goods within reach of most people.

questions.correct_answer: (D) cheaper production has put passable versions of once-rare goods within reach of most people.

option_rationales.A: Taxes are never mentioned; paragraph 2 says such goods became cheaper, not more costly.
option_rationales.B: Retirement savings appear in a list of inconspicuous spending, but the passage never says most wealth is held this way or that this caused the change.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says showy goods invited criticism, but the passage gives cheap imitation, not ridicule, as the reason display lost its power to separate.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'As mass production and global supply chains have made once-rare goods cheap, the handbag and the car have become available, in passable imitations, to almost anyone with a credit card. Display of this kind has lost much of its power to separate'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a detail from elsewhere in the passage that is not given as the cause.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause is stated in the sentence just before the claim.

questions.question: The contrast between a diamond and a childhood in good schools (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: advantages built into a person are passed on more securely than those held as saleable property.
options.B: diamonds are a poor financial investment compared with spending on a child's education, which yields a higher return.
options.C: parents who spend money on jewellery tend to care less about their children's futures than parents who pay for schooling.
options.D: the benefits of a good education can be gained just as readily in adult life as in childhood, given enough money.

questions.correct_answer: (A) advantages built into a person are passed on more securely than those held as saleable property.

option_rationales.B: The passage makes no comparison of financial returns; its point is that one can be sold or lost while the other 'becomes part of a person'.
option_rationales.C: Nothing is said about the motives or care of particular parents; paragraph 5 explicitly sets aside personal motives.
option_rationales.D: This contradicts the passage, which says such a childhood 'can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'A diamond can be sold', whereas a good childhood 'becomes part of a person and can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later', and concludes that such spending 'passes it on'. Advantage embodied in a person is transmitted more securely than property.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the contrast as one of financial value or of parental attitudes.
questions.difficulty_reason: The implication must be drawn from the contrast together with the sentence that follows it.

questions.question: The reference to gold-plated taps in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: suggest that inconspicuous consumption is simply conspicuous consumption carried on in more refined and tasteful forms.
options.B: concede that the turn away from showy spending is, in some respects, a genuinely welcome change.
options.C: illustrate the sort of quiet, hard-to-copy goods on which affluent households now prefer to spend their money.
options.D: argue that wealthy households ought to be discouraged by public policy from spending on luxuries of every kind.

questions.correct_answer: (B) concede that the turn away from showy spending is, in some respects, a genuinely welcome change.

option_rationales.A: The author argues that the new spending works differently, by passing advantage on and by looking like virtue; it is not the old display in new dress.
option_rationales.C: Gold-plated taps are the opposite of inconspicuous goods; they stand for the vulgar display that the rich have abandoned.
option_rationales.D: No policy is proposed, and the remark appears in a sentence granting that the new spending 'yields real benefits'.

questions.explanation: The remark comes in the concession 'In part it is': much inconspicuous spending 'yields real benefits', and 'few would wish the rich to return to buying gold-plated taps'. It grants the improvement before the author turns, with 'But', to the two concealed consequences.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the taps as an example of the new spending, or reading the concession as the author's main claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function depends on recognising the concession before the turn signalled by 'But'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that inconspicuous goods reproduce advantage more effectively than conspicuous ones?

options.A: Most affluent parents who pay for private tuition say that they do so out of concern for their children's learning and not out of any wish for status.
options.B: Households that spend on organic food and exercise classes report better health than households of similar income that do not.
options.C: Imitations of luxury handbags, cars and watches have continued to become cheaper and more widely available to ordinary households.
options.D: Children of wealthy families that spent heavily on schooling ended up no better placed as adults than children of equally wealthy families that spent on luxuries.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Children of wealthy families that spent heavily on schooling ended up no better placed as adults than children of equally wealthy families that spent on luxuries.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says 'most such choices are made sincerely' and 'The point is structural rather than personal', so motives do not bear on the claim.
option_rationales.B: This fits the concession in paragraph 3 that such spending 'yields real benefits', and it says nothing about transmission to the next generation.
option_rationales.C: This supports paragraph 2's explanation of why display lost its power to separate; it does not test which spending transmits advantage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that spending on schooling and upbringing 'does not merely display a position; it passes it on', more effectively than conspicuous goods. If equally wealthy families spending on schooling secured no better adult positions than those spending on luxuries, that claim would fail.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the sincerity option, which addresses motives that the author has already declared irrelevant.
questions.difficulty_reason: The strongest wrong option answers a different charge, one that paragraph 5 explicitly sets aside; seeing this needs the whole passage.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards inconspicuous consumption is best described as

options.A: critical of its social effects, while declining to impugn the motives of those who practise it.
options.B: approving, regarding it chiefly as a welcome advance in good taste over the vulgar display of earlier generations of the rich.
options.C: scornful, regarding it as a form of hypocrisy that disguises a hunger for status as healthy and responsible living.
options.D: neutral, describing a change in the spending of the rich without passing any judgement on what that change brings about.

questions.correct_answer: (A) critical of its social effects, while declining to impugn the motives of those who practise it.

option_rationales.B: The author grants the change is an improvement only 'In part', and devotes paragraphs 3 to 5 to consequences that 'the language of good taste conceals'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says 'None of this is an accusation of bad faith' and that 'most such choices are made sincerely, for the reasons people give'.
option_rationales.D: The author judges the consequences plainly: it reproduces advantage, leads to the poor being 'quietly judged', and makes inequality 'harder to argue about'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 3 and 4 criticise the effects (more effective transmission of advantage, moral cover, judgement of those who cannot afford it), and paragraph 5 adds that 'The point is structural rather than personal', explicitly declining to call the affluent hypocritical.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the critique for scorn of individuals, or overweighting the concession in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the critique, the concession and the disclaimer about motives together.

questions.question: The image of the escalator in paragraph 2 conveys that

options.A: a society can carry people downwards just as easily as it carries them upwards, depending on economic conditions.
options.B: people born near the bottom rise faster than those born near the top whenever the economy is growing quickly.
options.C: living standards can rise for everyone together while people's ranking relative to one another stays fixed.
options.D: moving up in society is automatic and calls for no effort or ability on the part of the individuals concerned.

questions.correct_answer: (C) living standards can rise for everyone together while people's ranking relative to one another stays fixed.

option_rationales.A: The escalator in the passage only goes up; downward movement is discussed in paragraph 4 as a feature of relative mobility.
option_rationales.B: The image says 'the order of people on it stays the same', so no group overtakes another.
option_rationales.D: Effort and ability are never discussed; the image concerns the difference between rising standards and unchanged rank.

questions.explanation: The escalator sentence sums up the preceding one: most children may outearn their parents 'even if the chance of a child born near the bottom reaching the top ... has not changed at all'. All rise, but 'the order of people on it stays the same'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the image as a claim about effort or about who rises faster.
questions.difficulty_reason: The image glosses the sentence immediately before it.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that people who conclude, when growth slows, that society has become less fair

options.A: have generally lived through a genuine fall in relative mobility that the usual measures have failed to detect.
options.B: are mistaken in believing that they are doing no better than their parents did at the same stage of life.
options.C: are reacting chiefly to a rise in downward mobility among the children of comfortable and well-placed families.
options.D: may be rightly sensing a real loss but wrongly attributing it to a decline in openness.

questions.correct_answer: (D) may be rightly sensing a real loss but wrongly attributing it to a decline in openness.

option_rationales.A: The passage says that on measures of relative position 'the chances may be much as they were', which points the other way.
option_rationales.B: The author says they feel something has closed 'reasonably enough' and that 'The sense of closure is real'; their experience is not in doubt.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 attributes the feeling to falling absolute mobility; downward mobility of the comfortable comes up only in paragraph 4, as something they resist.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'The sense of closure is real; its diagnosis is frequently mistaken.' What has disappeared 'is not openness but the rising tide', so the loss is in absolute mobility, while relative chances 'may be much as they were'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the author as dismissing these people's experience, rather than their explanation of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the experience the author accepts from the diagnosis the author questions.

questions.question: Which of the following would be a case of relative mobility rising while absolute mobility falls, in the passage's sense?

options.A: In a booming economy where most children outearn their parents, the order of families in the income ranking remains exactly what it was before.
options.B: In a booming economy where nearly all children outearn their parents, the income ranking is substantially reshuffled from one generation to the next.
options.C: In a stagnant economy where few children outearn their parents, children of poor families increasingly overtake children of rich families in the income ranking.
options.D: In a stagnant economy where few children outearn their parents, children remain in much the same place in the income ranking as their parents held.

questions.correct_answer: (C) In a stagnant economy where few children outearn their parents, children of poor families increasingly overtake children of rich families in the income ranking.

option_rationales.A: This is the escalator of paragraph 2: absolute mobility is high and relative mobility unchanged, the reverse of what is asked.
option_rationales.B: Here absolute mobility rises, since nearly all outearn their parents, so it is a case of both kinds rising, not of absolute mobility falling.
option_rationales.D: Absolute mobility falls here, but relative mobility is unchanged rather than rising; this is the situation described in paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Absolute mobility is 'the share of people who end up better off than their parents'; relative mobility concerns changes in 'position in the distribution'. A stagnant economy where few outearn their parents has low absolute mobility, and poor children overtaking rich ones in rank is a rise in relative mobility.
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up the two measures, especially choosing the paragraph 3 case in which relative mobility merely stays the same.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying both definitions to four cases that differ on two dimensions.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Relative mobility is the only true measure of whether a society is open, while absolute mobility merely reflects how fast its economy is growing.
options.B: Since absolute and relative mobility answer different questions and can diverge, running them together leads people to misread slowdowns and to ignore what fairness costs.
options.C: Social mobility has not stalled as its critics claim; it has simply become much harder to measure than it was in earlier generations.
options.D: Comfortable families use private tuition and housing choices to block relative mobility, and governments should act to prevent them from doing so.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Since absolute and relative mobility answer different questions and can diverge, running them together leads people to misread slowdowns and to ignore what fairness costs.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says 'None of this makes one kind of mobility the real one', and that the question absolute mobility answers also matters.
option_rationales.C: The author accepts that absolute mobility falls when growth slows, and the difficulty of measurement is a passing remark, not the thesis.
option_rationales.D: This narrows the passage to paragraph 4 and adds a prescription; the author asks for honesty about costs, not for action against families.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says argument goes astray 'because the two are run together'; paragraph 3 shows this leads people to read slower growth as closure; paragraph 4 shows it hides the fact that relative mobility requires some to fall; paragraph 5 says both kinds matter and draws both lessons.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that ranks one kind of mobility above the other, which the final paragraph explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures part of the passage or a plausible stance; the correct answer requires all four movements of the argument.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a government promising to raise relative mobility while ensuring that no family moves down the ranking

options.A: is promising something that cannot be delivered when positions are ranked, whatever the rate of economic growth.
options.B: is making essentially the same promise as a government that pledges to raise the living standards of each new generation.
options.C: could keep its promise provided that the economy grew fast enough to raise the incomes of every family at once.
options.D: could keep its promise by abolishing private tuition and other devices that comfortable families use to defend their position.

questions.correct_answer: (A) is promising something that cannot be delivered when positions are ranked, whatever the rate of economic growth.

option_rationales.B: That pledge concerns absolute mobility; treating the two promises as the same is the very confusion the passage criticises.
option_rationales.C: Growth raises absolute mobility, which can 'be enjoyed by everyone at once'; it cannot let one family climb the ranking without another falling.
option_rationales.D: Removing such devices might raise relative mobility, but paragraph 4 says that 'for one family to climb another must fall', so some would still move down.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'If positions are ranked, then for one family to climb another must fall', so relative mobility 'cannot' be enjoyed by everyone at once, unlike absolute mobility. Growth changes standards of living, not rankings, so no growth rate rescues the promise; paragraph 5 adds that it 'cannot be had at no one's expense'.
questions.common_misconception: Believing that growth can make relative mobility painless, which confuses the two measures.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option applies the logic of absolute mobility to relative mobility; spotting this needs paragraphs 2 and 4 together.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that collectors value the objects they gather for their beauty and rarity rather than for the places they fill in a set, whoever happens to have designed that set.
options.B: trace how private collections of timetables, matchboxes and editions gradually developed into the public museums of today, and to praise the collectors who began them.
options.C: show that collecting is a compulsion created by manufacturers, who profit by persuading buyers to complete sets that they never wanted until the empty spaces were shown to them.
options.D: distinguish collecting in which the collector defines the series from collecting in which a seller does, and to show that the latter's harm lies in removing that power.

questions.correct_answer: (D) distinguish collecting in which the collector defines the series from collecting in which a seller does, and to show that the latter's harm lies in removing that power.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: collecting is 'less a love of things than a love of completion', and a stamp matters for 'the place it occupies in a series'.
option_rationales.B: Museums appear in a single sentence of paragraph 3 as a supporting aside; the passage gives no history of their development, so the option is far too narrow.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 calls this conclusion one that 'goes too far' and offers collectors who pursue series 'that no company ever designed', so the option states a view the author rejects.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 identifies the love of completion, paragraph 2 shows sellers exploiting it, paragraph 3 rejects the conclusion that collecting is therefore a manufactured compulsion, and paragraph 4 states that the real difference is 'who holds the map', the danger being that commercial series take 'the act of definition' away from the collector.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the description of manufacturers in paragraph 2 for the thesis, and missing the concession in paragraph 3 that turns the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option restates paragraph 2 and the view the author rejects; the correct answer requires seeing the turn in paragraph 3 and the conclusion in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a collector would pay far more than an outsider for a particular stamp chiefly because

options.A: the collector has run out of space and must buy only the most valuable items.
options.B: the stamp fills a gap in a series that the collector is close to completing.
options.C: the stamp is an object of unusual beauty that only a trained eye can fully appreciate.
options.D: collectors usually know more than outsiders about how rare such stamps have become.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the stamp fills a gap in a series that the collector is close to completing.

option_rationales.A: Running out of display space is mentioned only to show that collectors keep buying regardless; it is not a reason for paying more.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says collecting is 'less a love of things than a love of completion', so the qualities of the object itself are not the reason given.
option_rationales.D: Rarity and expert knowledge are never offered as the reason; paragraph 1 ties the value to 'the place it occupies in a series' and to the series nearing its end.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that the stamp 'matters because of the place it occupies in a series, and its value to the collector rises sharply as the series nears its end, often far beyond anything a buyer outside the hobby would think of paying'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying an outside reason for high prices, such as rarity, instead of the reason the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is located in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: By saying that 'The empty album is the real product' (paragraph 2), the author means that

options.A: the stickers themselves are of such poor quality that only the album has any lasting value.
options.B: the albums are sold at a higher profit than the stickers that are later bought to fill them.
options.C: what the seller really offers is the outline of an unfinished whole, which makes each later purchase feel necessary.
options.D: buyers prefer to keep their albums empty because an unfilled album is worth more to other collectors.

questions.correct_answer: (C) what the seller really offers is the outline of an unfinished whole, which makes each later purchase feel necessary.

option_rationales.A: The quality of the stickers is never discussed; the remark is about the outline of a whole, not about the materials.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about relative profits; the sentence concerns how the printed spaces create desire, as the next sentence about 'every blank' shows.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the opposite: every blank 'becomes a small reproach' that the buyer wants to fill.

questions.explanation: The sentences around the phrase explain it: the buyer 'did not know he wanted' the whole 'until he was shown its outline', and once the spaces are printed 'every blank becomes a small reproach'. The album sells the gaps, and the gaps sell the stickers.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'product' in a literal commercial sense (profit, quality) rather than as a point about what creates the desire.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative sentence is explained by the sentences on either side of it.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates what the author calls the danger of the commercial version of collecting?

options.A: A woman who has long gathered old bus tickets from her town starts judging her collection against a numbered checklist that a company now sells with reproduction tickets.
options.B: A man who collects matchboxes from closed hotels becomes so absorbed in the hunt that he spends most weekends searching second-hand shops for the few he still lacks.
options.C: A collector of a minor poet's editions decides that pamphlet reprints do not count as part of her set and so stops looking for them.
options.D: A child buys a single plastic figure from a cereal box because she likes its colour, and never shows any interest in finding the remaining eleven.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A woman who has long gathered old bus tickets from her town starts judging her collection against a numbered checklist that a company now sells with reproduction tickets.

option_rationales.B: He defines his own series, as in paragraph 3, and paragraph 4 says intense passion is not what separates the two kinds; the danger lies elsewhere.
option_rationales.C: This is the collector exercising the 'act of definition' herself, which paragraph 4 treats as the healthy case, not the danger.
option_rationales.D: No series is being pursued here at all, so neither the desire for completion nor its definition by a seller is involved.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the danger is not that commercial collecting 'creates desire' but that 'it quietly takes the act of definition away from the person doing the collecting'. The bus-ticket collector had defined her own series, and now a seller's checklist defines what counts as complete.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the intensely passionate collector, although paragraph 4 says the passion 'can be equally intense' in both kinds.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the precise claim of paragraph 4 and rejecting an option that matches the passage's language about passion.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is curious about many buyers of retro goods?

options.A: They are mostly older people trying to recover the products of their own youth.
options.B: They are too young to remember the original products that the goods imitate.
options.C: They tend to prefer the reissued versions to the originals once they compare the two.
options.D: They usually know that the advertising behind such goods presents a false golden age.

questions.correct_answer: (B) They are too young to remember the original products that the goods imitate.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the reverse: many buyers know the period only from 'old films rather than lived', so it 'cannot be their own past'.
option_rationales.C: No comparison between originals and reissues by buyers is reported; the passage notes only that reissues remove the inconveniences.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 reports the opposite assumption, that buyers have 'no means of checking', and never says that they know the age is false.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 opens: 'A curious feature of the market for retro goods is how many of their buyers are too young to remember the originals.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that nostalgia must be for one's own past, which paragraph 1 explicitly rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in the first sentence.

questions.question: The examples of the record player with a phone socket and the camera that 'adds the scratches digitally' (paragraph 3) serve to

options.A: illustrate that retro design keeps the look of the past while removing the inconveniences that defined it.
options.B: prove that young buyers are deceived into thinking that the reissued goods are genuine antiques.
options.C: show that modern retro products are more fragile and costly than the originals that they copy.
options.D: suggest that the makers of retro goods are trying hard to preserve the technology of earlier decades.

questions.correct_answer: (A) illustrate that retro design keeps the look of the past while removing the inconveniences that defined it.

option_rationales.B: The examples concern how the products are designed, not what buyers believe; and the passage resists the view that buyers are simply 'fooled'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: 'the waiting, the expense, the fragility' are exactly what the reissues remove.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls retro design 'the opposite of preservation', so the examples work against this reading.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces the examples with 'how carefully the past is edited', then explains that the inconveniences 'are removed, and only the surface is kept'. The phone socket and the digital scratches are instances of keeping the look while modernising the substance.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the word 'opposite' and taking the examples as evidence of preservation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentences after the examples.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the buyers of retro goods is best described as

options.A: wholly indifferent, since the author describes the retro market without expressing any view about those who buy from it.
options.B: openly contemptuous, since the author regards them as gullible victims of advertisers who have invented a golden age.
options.C: warmly admiring, since the author presents their taste as a wise and successful rejection of disposable modern goods.
options.D: clear-sighted but not contemptuous: the author declines to scorn them while insisting on naming what they actually buy.

questions.correct_answer: (D) clear-sighted but not contemptuous: the author declines to scorn them while insisting on naming what they actually buy.

option_rationales.A: The author takes clear positions, correcting the usual explanation in paragraph 2 and stating what is really bought in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 begins 'None of this need be a cause for scorn', and paragraph 2 says the 'fooled' explanation 'misreads what the buyer is after'.
option_rationales.C: The author concedes that a taste for the durable 'is not foolish', but also says the buyer purchases 'a token of his unease', which is not admiration.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 rejects scorn and grants that some revived products are better made, yet insists 'it is worth being clear about what is being bought': not a recovered way of life but 'a token of his unease'. The tone is analytical and measured.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the final sentence about the market supplying 'tokens' as contempt for the buyers, when it is aimed at clarity about the purchase.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is signalled directly in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author's view of the explanation that buyers of retro goods are 'being fooled' (paragraph 2) is that it

options.A: applies to the buyers of drinks and cameras but not to buyers of record players, who know the originals well.
options.B: is entirely correct, since advertisers have invented a golden age that young buyers cannot check against memory.
options.C: contains some truth but wrongly assumes that buyers want an accurate past rather than an answer to a present mood.
options.D: has no basis at all, since advertisers make no claims about the past when they sell retro goods to the young.

questions.correct_answer: (C) contains some truth but wrongly assumes that buyers want an accurate past rather than an answer to a present mood.

option_rationales.A: The passage draws no distinction between kinds of retro goods or their buyers; this division is invented.
option_rationales.B: The author grants only that 'There is something in this' and adds at once that it 'misreads what the buyer is after', so it is not entirely correct.
option_rationales.D: The author concedes 'There is something in this', and paragraph 2 does not deny that advertisers invent a golden age.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'There is something in this, but it misreads what the buyer is after', and explains that nostalgia is 'less a memory than a mood': the buyer does not need the past to be accurate, since 'the feeling it answers is real'. The explanation is partly right but mistakes what is wanted.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the two extremes, when the author both concedes and corrects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the concession and the correction in paragraph 2 together.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 suggests that when reviewers call a dish authentic, their judgement depends chiefly on

options.A: the modest and unfamiliar setting in which the dish is served rather than the dish itself.
options.B: how much the critic has paid for the meal compared with similar restaurants.
options.C: whether the cook has been trained in the region from which the cuisine comes.
options.D: how closely the recipe matches the way the dish is cooked in its region of origin.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the modest and unfamiliar setting in which the dish is served rather than the dish itself.

option_rationales.B: Price appears only as one part of the scene ('nobody is getting rich'); the passage does not say reviewers compare prices across restaurants.
option_rationales.C: The cook's training is not mentioned; only the cook's halting speech is cited, as part of the scene.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says authenticity in this usage is 'less a property of the food than of the scene around it', so matching a recipe is not the basis.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 lists the cramped room, the halting speech and the low price, contrasts them with 'tablecloths and a wine list', and concludes that authenticity 'is less a property of the food than of the scene around it'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that 'authentic' must refer to fidelity to a recipe, which is the very assumption paragraph 1 exposes.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is in the last sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The hypothetical family restaurant in paragraph 2 functions in the argument mainly to

options.A: demonstrate that immigrant cooks change their recipes chiefly because they are pressured by reviewers who demand authenticity.
options.B: show that migration itself produces a distinct cuisine, which sets up the author's objection to the purists' idea of decline.
options.C: illustrate the kind of loss that occurs when cooks strip a cuisine of everything difficult so that it is recognised only by name.
options.D: provide evidence that restaurants which adapt to local tastes are commercially more successful than those that refuse to adapt.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that migration itself produces a distinct cuisine, which sets up the author's objection to the purists' idea of decline.

option_rationales.A: The changes in paragraph 2 come from missing ingredients, kitchen workload and early customers; reviewers' demands belong to paragraphs 1 and 3.
option_rationales.C: That loss is the concession of paragraph 4; paragraph 2 presents the adaptations as producing something new, not as a loss.
option_rationales.D: Commercial success is never compared; the case shows what the menu becomes, 'the food of the people who moved between them'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends with the menu becoming 'the food of the people who moved between them', a cuisine that 'exists nowhere else'. Paragraph 3 then says purists 'treat this history as a decline', which the author disputes. The case establishes the history that the purists misread.
questions.common_misconception: Merging the hypothetical case with the concession of paragraph 4 about harmful adaptation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing how paragraph 2 prepares paragraph 3, and separating it from the later concession.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the second menu is only 'one stage of a continuous adaptation'?

options.A: Many cooks who run such restaurants say they would like to cook more ambitious dishes than their customers will accept, and would do so if the rent allowed it.
options.B: Diners from the home community order mostly from the second menu, while other customers rarely know that it exists or how to ask for it.
options.C: Reviewers praise restaurants with second menus more highly than restaurants that offer only a single menu to all diners, whatever the cooking on either menu is like.
options.D: The dishes on such second menus are found to be prepared with imported ingredients and unchanged methods, and to match versions cooked in the home region.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The dishes on such second menus are found to be prepared with imported ingredients and unchanged methods, and to match versions cooked in the home region.

option_rationales.A: This bears on paragraph 4's point about the cooks' freedom, not on whether the second menu has itself been adapted.
option_rationales.B: Who orders from the menu says nothing about whether its dishes have been adapted, which is what the claim concerns.
option_rationales.C: This is consistent with the author's description of purists rewarding such restaurants and does not touch the claim about adaptation.

questions.explanation: The author says the second menu 'has passed through the same kitchen, the same suppliers and the same compromises' and is therefore not an unchanged original. Evidence that its dishes use unchanged methods and ingredients and match the home versions would directly contradict this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about who uses the second menu, which is on topic but irrelevant to whether it has changed.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires isolating the precise factual basis of the claim in paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following tests for judging a restaurant would the author most likely endorse?

options.A: Whether its adaptations were chosen by the cooks rather than prompted by complaints from customers.
options.B: Whether it has entirely resisted the commercial pressures that lead cooks to simplify a cuisine.
options.C: Whether those cooking its food have the latitude to make the dishes they themselves consider good.
options.D: Whether its dishes are prepared in the way they are still prepared in the region of origin.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Whether those cooking its food have the latitude to make the dishes they themselves consider good.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 counts dishes 'sweetened or softened because the first customers sent them back' as part of the legitimate history, so customer influence does not disqualify a menu.
option_rationales.B: The author objects only to pressure that narrows what cooks are 'free to make'; the passage never demands complete resistance to commerce and accepts adaptations made for customers.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 explicitly rejects asking 'whether its food matches some imagined source', so this is the purists' test.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 ends: 'The more useful question to ask of a restaurant is not whether its food matches some imagined source, but whether the people cooking it have the room to cook what they think is good.' The correct answer restates this test.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the test about customer complaints, which sounds like the cooks' freedom but conflicts with paragraph 2's acceptance of changes made for early customers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The test is stated in the last sentence, but one wrong option echoes it and is rejected only with paragraph 2's acceptance of changes made for customers.

questions.question: According to the trickle-down account described in the passage, those at the top abandon a style when

options.A: designers begin borrowing it from the clothing of a street subculture.
options.B: cheap copies of it begin to reach shops within a few weeks of its appearance.
options.C: it has spread so widely that it no longer sets them apart from others.
options.D: the people just below them stop copying it and turn to something new.

questions.correct_answer: (C) it has spread so widely that it no longer sets them apart from others.

option_rationales.A: Borrowing from subcultures belongs to the objection and reply in paragraphs 2 and 3, not to the trickle-down account of paragraph 1.
option_rationales.B: The speed of copying is the change described in paragraph 4, a later development, not part of the old account.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: it is the success of the copying, not its end, that makes the style lose its value.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'once the style has spread far enough to lose its power to distinguish, the people at the top abandon it for something else'.
questions.common_misconception: Importing the later material on subcultures or speed into the description of the old theory.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relation between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.A: Paragraph 2 raises an objection about the direction of influence; paragraph 3 replies that direction was never the theory's central claim.
options.B: Paragraph 2 refutes the theory's account of motive; paragraph 3 concedes the refutation but rescues the theory's account of direction.
options.C: Paragraph 2 presents the author's own view of fashion; paragraph 3 reports a rival view that the author goes on to reject in paragraph 4.
options.D: Paragraph 2 offers evidence for the old theory; paragraph 3 qualifies it by adding that styles sometimes move upwards from the street.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Paragraph 2 raises an objection about the direction of influence; paragraph 3 replies that direction was never the theory's central claim.

option_rationales.B: This reverses the passage: paragraph 2 challenges direction, and paragraph 3 rescues the account of motive while giving up direction.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 begins the author's own reply ('But direction was never the heart of the theory'), and paragraph 4 builds on it rather than rejecting it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 is presented as 'The obvious objection' to the theory, not as evidence for it, and the upward movement is its content rather than paragraph 3's.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens with 'The obvious objection' that much fashion 'did not begin at the top'. Paragraph 3 answers: 'direction was never the heart of the theory'; its real claim, the 'double motive', 'survives the reversal untouched'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing which part of the theory is challenged and which is rescued.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires tracking the objection-and-reply structure and what each side concerns.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, the movement of styles from subcultures to luxury houses

options.A: refutes the old theory entirely, since the theory depended on fashion always moving from the top downwards.
