options.B: shows that the wish to stand apart no longer plays any part in how the wealthy choose what to wear.
options.C: benefits the members of subcultures, who gain prestige when their clothing appears in expensive shops.
options.D: fits the motive that the old theory identified, even though it contradicts the direction that theory described.

questions.correct_answer: (D) fits the motive that the old theory identified, even though it contradicts the direction that theory described.

option_rationales.A: This is the objection of paragraph 2, which the author answers: the theory's core 'survives the reversal untouched'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the luxury house is 'not abandoning distinction but finding a new source of it', so the wish to stand apart persists.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says subculture members 'frequently drop the style once it appears in expensive shops', which does not suggest they welcome it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 grants that the direction is reversed but argues that the 'double motive' still operates: the luxury house seeks distinction through 'borrowed credibility', and the subculture drops the style 'for precisely the reason the old theory would predict'.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the objection of paragraph 2 as the author's conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is the view the author reports and answers.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of what has changed, as given in paragraph 4?

options.A: Copies sold in inexpensive shops are usually made of poorer materials and fall apart far sooner than the garments they imitate.
options.B: Even where cheap copies appear within weeks, the people most eager for status rely more than before on being seen in the newest visible styles.
options.C: Small releases that sell out in minutes are often bought by resellers who have no interest in fashion and want only to profit.
options.D: Members of street subcultures often abandon a style soon after a luxury house has adopted it and begun to sell it at high prices.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Even where cheap copies appear within weeks, the people most eager for status rely more than before on being seen in the newest visible styles.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 concerns what status-seekers do when looks are copied quickly; the durability of the copies does not bear on that claim.
option_rationales.C: Who else buys small releases does not show that status-seekers have stopped valuing early access, which is the claim at issue.
option_rationales.D: This repeats the observation of paragraph 3 and is consistent with the author's account; it does not weaken paragraph 4 at all.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 claims that because copies arrive quickly, 'visible novelty becomes a weak marker of status', so status-seekers turn to 'having had it first'. If status-seekers relied more than ever on visible newness despite fast copying, the claimed shift would be contradicted.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about resellers, which concerns small releases but leaves the author's causal claim intact.
questions.difficulty_reason: All wrong options are on topic; the correct answer requires identifying the causal claim in paragraph 4 and the evidence that would cut against it.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'a local flavour in a global grammar' suggests that

options.A: the chain's local dishes are so heavily modified that they no longer taste like anything eaten locally.
options.B: local cooks have learned to describe their traditional dishes in the vocabulary of international cuisine.
options.C: a locally adapted dish is delivered through a structure that is itself global and carries its own assumptions.
options.D: global chains succeed only when they combine local ingredients with recipes perfected in the home country.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a locally adapted dish is delivered through a structure that is itself global and carries its own assumptions.

option_rationales.A: The phrase grants that the flavour is local; the point concerns the system that serves it, not a loss of local taste.
option_rationales.B: The passage is not about how dishes are described; 'grammar' refers to the format of ordering, pricing and production set out in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no claim about what makes chains succeed, and the word "only" adds a condition found nowhere in the text.

questions.explanation: The sentence closes a paragraph arguing that the chain exports 'a format', the counter, fixed prices, consistency and the assembly-line kitchen, which carries 'assumptions about efficiency and predictability'. The patty supplies local content; the format is the global structure, the 'grammar', that organises it.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'grammar' as language about food rather than as a metaphor for the format.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor must be decoded from the paragraph it concludes.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Debates centred on a chain's menu miss that its format is what travels, while the meanings customers give it are made locally.
options.B: A chain's willingness to adapt its menu is the clearest sign of how far it respects the identity of the country it enters.
options.C: Local customers decide what global chains mean in their countries, so worries about cultural influence are largely misplaced.
options.D: Global chains erase local food cultures less through their menus than through a format that imposes foreign assumptions on customers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Debates centred on a chain's menu miss that its format is what travels, while the meanings customers give it are made locally.

option_rationales.B: This is the defenders' view in paragraph 1, which rests on the assumption that paragraph 2 says 'deserves more scrutiny'.
option_rationales.C: The passage treats the format as global and full of 'assumptions' that are 'far more foreign' than ingredients, so it does not dismiss cultural influence.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says it would be 'wrong to infer that the format simply imposes its meanings', so this keeps paragraph 2 and drops the qualification.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 shows both camps assuming the menu settles the question; paragraph 2 says the format is what is exported; paragraph 3 qualifies this with locally made meanings; paragraph 4 sums up 'three layers rather than one'. The correct answer holds both the global format and the local meanings.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that keeps the critique of the format but drops the qualification of paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The two strongest wrong options each keep one half of the argument; only the correct answer holds paragraphs 2 and 3 together.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as the strongest sign of a global chain's cultural influence on a country?

options.A: The chain adds several new regional dishes to its menu each year in response to suggestions made by its local customers and staff.
options.B: The chain's outlets in the country sell more of its standard home burger than of the dishes it has created for the local market, year after year.
options.C: Families in the country choose the chain's restaurants for birthdays and linger there long after they have finished eating.
options.D: Local family eateries begin taking orders at a counter, posting fixed prices and standardising their kitchens, while still serving their old dishes.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Local family eateries begin taking orders at a counter, posting fixed prices and standardising their kitchens, while still serving their old dishes.

option_rationales.A: This is menu adjustment, which the author treats as the easily changed middle layer and says reveals little about cultural influence.
option_rationales.B: This reads influence from the menu, which paragraph 2 calls 'the part that tells us least'; it says nothing about the format spreading.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 presents such lingering as customers bringing 'meanings of their own', which shows the limits of the chain's influence, not its reach.

questions.explanation: The author says the format's 'assumptions about efficiency and predictability' are 'far more foreign to many food cultures than any particular ingredient'. Local eateries adopting the counter, fixed prices and standardised kitchens shows the format, the deepest layer, spreading beyond the chain itself.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about sales of the standard burger, which looks like strong evidence of influence but is read from the menu.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the three-layer model to a new case and rejecting an intuitively strong menu-based option.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as part of the format that a global chain exports EXCEPT

options.A: a promise that a given meal will taste the same from one month to the next.
options.B: a set of new dishes devised specially to suit the tastes of the local market.
options.C: a counter at which customers place their orders without being served by a waiter.
options.D: a fixed price for each item that is displayed to customers before they order.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a set of new dishes devised specially to suit the tastes of the local market.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 includes 'the promise that the meal will taste the same today as it did last month' in the format.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists 'The counter at which one orders without a waiter' as part of what the chain exports.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists 'the fixed price displayed in advance' among the elements that 'travel intact'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists the counter, the fixed price, consistency of taste and the assembly-line kitchen as the exported format. Dishes made for the local market belong to the menu, which paragraph 2 calls 'the part that tells us least' and paragraph 4 places between the format and local meanings, 'adjusted constantly in response to both'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an element of the format because it sounds less global, without checking the list in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each listed element is stated in paragraph 2; the correct answer belongs to the menu, a different layer.

questions.question: According to the passage, households that live close to scarcity keep spare parts, old jars and oversized coats because

options.A: they wish to display their thrift to neighbours who might otherwise think them wasteful.
options.B: they cannot be sure of being able to buy such things again when they need them.
options.C: they reject the fashion for owning less as one more passing style of the wealthy.
options.D: they have more space at home than wealthier households living in crowded cities.

questions.correct_answer: (B) they cannot be sure of being able to buy such things again when they need them.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 gives no display motive for these households; it says accumulation is 'a form of insurance' against being unable to buy again.
option_rationales.C: Dismissing minimalism as 'one more passing style' is attributed to its critics in paragraph 1, not to these households.
option_rationales.D: Space appears only in the point about bare floors in crowded cities being expensive; it is not offered as the reason poorer households keep things.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: such households keep things 'because they cannot count on being able to buy them again; for them, accumulation is a form of insurance'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing to poorer households a view the passage assigns to minimalism's critics.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the point made in paragraph 2 about discarding objects freely?

options.A: A family living far from any market keeps old tins, spare buttons and broken tools in case they are someday needed.
options.B: A student keeps few books in her room because the rules of her hostel forbid students to own large amounts of property.
options.C: A wealthy collector displays rare porcelain in glass cabinets so that visitors can see how much he has spent.
options.D: A traveller sets out on long trips with only a small bag, confident that anything forgotten can simply be bought on arrival.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A traveller sets out on long trips with only a small bag, confident that anything forgotten can simply be bought on arrival.

option_rationales.A: This is the opposite case in paragraph 2, the household for which 'accumulation is a form of insurance'.
option_rationales.B: Her restraint is imposed by a rule, not made possible by an assurance that things can be replaced, so it does not match the point.
option_rationales.C: This is visible spending on display, the picture paragraph 2 attributes to Veblen, not the restraint that signals security.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'the confident discarding of objects depends on the assurance that they can be replaced when needed', so throwing away freely displays that one needs no insurance. The traveller with a small bag relies on the same assurance of easy replacement.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the porcelain collector because the passage mentions conspicuous consumption, when the point concerns display through restraint.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires abstracting the mechanism (restraint resting on assured replacement) and applying it to a new case.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author be most likely to accept?

options.A: A person who owns very little purely for the sake of calm may still, without intending it, be signalling financial security to others.
options.B: A person who owns very little purely for the sake of calm sends no social signal, since signals depend on what a person intends.
options.C: A person who owns very little for the sake of calm is probably deceiving herself, since the true motive of minimalism is to impress.
options.D: A person who owns very little can practise minimalism only if she is wealthy, so the poor can never adopt such a way of life.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A person who owns very little purely for the sake of calm may still, without intending it, be signalling financial security to others.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says a practice can 'still operate socially as a signal that its practitioners neither chose nor want', so intention does not decide the signal.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 rejects this as a confusion of 'motive with function' and says many 'are doing exactly what they say'.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the move is 'often' available only to the well placed and that 'most people cannot afford its preconditions'; it does not say the poor never can.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 separates motive from function: a sincerely chosen practice can 'still operate socially as a signal', because meaning 'is fixed by what the pattern makes legible to others', and what restraint makes legible 'is security'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the hypocrisy reading, which the author explicitly calls a confusion, or the absolute "only if" version of a hedged claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option distorts the motive and function distinction in a different way, and one turns 'often' and 'most' into absolutes.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the movement for owning less is best described as

options.A: approving of it as a sound ethical response to consumerism, though aware that a few practise it for show.
options.B: contemptuous of its followers, whom the author regards as status-seekers disguising their wealth as virtue.
options.C: doubtful of its claim to be a social critique, while accepting that many who practise it do so sincerely.
options.D: dismissive of it as a passing style that will soon give way to some newer fashion in consumption.

questions.correct_answer: (C) doubtful of its claim to be a social critique, while accepting that many who practise it do so sincerely.

option_rationales.A: The author argues that it is 'not, by itself, an exit' from the system of display and urges 'suspicion' towards its claim to critique, which is not approval.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'It does not follow that those who embrace minimalism are hypocrites' and grants that many 'are doing exactly what they say'.
option_rationales.D: Calling it a passing style is the critics' response in paragraph 1, which the author says takes the movement 'at its word' without asking what it communicates.

questions.explanation: The author defends the sincerity of many practitioners in paragraph 3 but concludes in paragraph 4 with 'suspicion towards any claim that a change in private taste can amount to a social critique'. The attitude combines scepticism about the movement's claim with respect for its followers' motives.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the critique of the movement's claim for contempt for its followers.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the passage reports (critics, advocates); the correct answer requires combining paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.A: Brand communities are an illusion created by advertisers, who borrow the language of tribes to make ordinary customers feel they belong.
options.B: Brand communities involve real solidarity, but because they gather around symbols a firm owns, the tribal comparison is only partly apt.
options.C: Brand communities are true tribes in every important respect, and firms that fail to see this lose the loyalty of their best customers.
options.D: Firms ought to give the members of their brand communities legal rights over the designs and emblems that the members care about.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Brand communities involve real solidarity, but because they gather around symbols a firm owns, the tribal comparison is only partly apt.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 names this as one of two tempting resolutions and says 'Neither will do', adding that 'The solidarity is real'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the analogy 'conceals as much as it reveals', listing ways in which brand communities differ from tribes.
option_rationales.D: The passage notes that wise firms consult their communities, but it proposes no legal rights; this adds a prescription.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 grants what the analogy captures, paragraph 3 says what it hides, paragraph 4 rejects both one-sided resolutions, and paragraph 5 concludes that a brand community is 'a genuine collective built on borrowed ground'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the two one-sided views that paragraph 4 explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must hold the concession and the critique together; two wrong options keep only one.

questions.question: According to the passage, how do the most loyal customers often respond when a company moves production to another country?

options.A: As enthusiasts who quietly accept the change because the product remains largely the same.
options.B: As disappointed consumers who decide to transfer their loyalty to the brand of a rival firm.
options.C: As owners who take legal action to stop the company from altering the products they bought.
options.D: As members who feel that something of theirs has been taken from them without their agreement.

questions.correct_answer: (D) As members who feel that something of theirs has been taken from them without their agreement.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 describes a strong sense of betrayal, and paragraph 4 describes 'anger', not quiet acceptance.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says they respond 'not as disappointed consumers but as betrayed members'; switching brands is not mentioned.
option_rationales.C: Their sense of ownership is described as 'not legal but moral', and no legal action is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'its most loyal customers frequently respond not as disappointed consumers but as betrayed members, as though something that belonged to them had been taken without their consent'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'disappointed consumers' option, which reuses the passage's words while reversing their sense.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a respect in which brand communities resemble tribes EXCEPT

options.A: the difficulty of leaving the group once one has joined it.
options.B: a shared body of lore that newcomers are expected to learn.
options.C: a habit of defining the group partly against outsiders.
options.D: the policing of boundaries between real and false members.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the difficulty of leaving the group once one has joined it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says members 'share a body of lore' that newcomers learn 'much as initiates learn a tradition'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says they 'define themselves partly against outsiders, often the owners of a rival brand'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says they 'police their own boundaries, distinguishing the real enthusiast from the person who has merely bought the thing'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists lore, opposition to outsiders, boundary policing and moral ownership as likenesses. Paragraph 3 makes the ease of exit a difference: a brand community 'can be abandoned at the price of another' purchase, unlike a tribe.
questions.common_misconception: Missing that paragraph 3 turns the point about leaving into a contrast with tribes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are listed in paragraph 2; the correct answer is a difference stated in paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 4 that the solidarity of brand communities is real?

options.A: Members of a computer brand's online forums spend considerably more each year on the brand's products than its other customers do, and buy new models sooner.
options.B: Owners of one brand of motorcycle are found to speak more unfavourably of a rival brand than the owners of that rival speak of theirs.
options.C: An owners' club for a long-discontinued car still meets, shares spare parts and helps members with repairs, decades after its maker stopped all promotion.
options.D: Attendance at events organised and paid for by a motorcycle maker rises sharply in the years when the firm spends heavily on advertising.

questions.correct_answer: (C) An owners' club for a long-discontinued car still meets, shares spare parts and helps members with repairs, decades after its maker stopped all promotion.

option_rationales.A: Higher spending shows commercial loyalty, not the friendship and mutual help that the author offers as evidence of real solidarity.
option_rationales.B: Hostility to outsiders is a tribal likeness from paragraph 2; it does not show that the bonds among members exist apart from the company.
option_rationales.D: Turnout that tracks the firm's spending is what the 'illusion manufactured by advertising' view would predict, so it does not support the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the solidarity is real because people 'form friendships, give one another practical help' and that 'much of this happens without the company's involvement'. A club that sustains mutual help long after all promotion ended is strong evidence of exactly this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about well-attended events, which shows activity but not activity independent of the firm.
questions.difficulty_reason: All options show attachment to a brand; only evidence of solidarity independent of the firm supports the claim, and the option about well-attended events looks strong until that criterion is applied.

questions.question: The author's remark that the anger after an unpopular redesign reveals 'the limits of an ownership they had felt but never possessed' (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: members' legal rights over the brand had been violated when the firm altered its design.
options.B: members' moral sense of owning the brand had outrun any power they actually held over it.
options.C: members had cared mainly about the product and not about one another all along.
options.D: the community had never been more than an illusion, which the redesign finally exposed.

questions.correct_answer: (B) members' moral sense of owning the brand had outrun any power they actually held over it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 calls their ownership 'not legal but moral', and paragraph 3 says they 'have no formal say', so no legal rights were violated.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'people form friendships, give one another practical help', so the remark does not imply that members cared only about the product.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 rejects the view that the community is 'an illusion manufactured by advertising'; the remark concerns limits of ownership, not the unreality of the group.

questions.explanation: The members felt the brand belonged to them, a moral ownership (paragraph 2), but the symbols are 'the legal property of a firm' over which they 'have no formal say' (paragraph 3). The redesign shows the gap between felt and actual ownership.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the anger as proof that the community was unreal, the view paragraph 4 rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the moral ownership of paragraph 2 with the legal facts of paragraph 3, while avoiding a rejected view.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the description of staged back regions as 'another front, built in the shape of a back' means that they are

options.A: presentations prepared for visitors that are designed to look like unstaged private life.
options.B: private spaces that hosts rebuild in a new style after visitors have finished their tours.
options.C: genuinely private spaces that visitors mistakenly believe were arranged for their benefit.
options.D: public monuments that are decorated so as to resemble the houses of ordinary villagers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) presentations prepared for visitors that are designed to look like unstaged private life.

option_rationales.B: The phrase concerns how spaces offered to visitors are arranged, not what hosts do afterwards; 'front' stands for the kind of presentation for visitors described in paragraph 1.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the phrase: the spaces are in fact arranged, as the tidied kitchens and placed looms show, not genuinely private.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 refers to homestays, kitchens and a cooperative presented as glimpses of the back, not to monuments made to look like houses.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 contrasts presentations arranged for visitors with the back region where people 'are simply living'. Paragraph 2 says the homestay, the lit kitchen and the arranged looms each 'presents itself as a glimpse of the back' but is in fact staged: a front made to look like a back.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the relation and taking the staged spaces to be genuine.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is explained by the examples in the same paragraph.

questions.question: The theatre audience mentioned at the end of paragraph 3 is used to suggest that

options.A: hosts who stage back regions for visitors should be regarded as artists and paid accordingly.
options.B: tourists enjoy staged performances more than they enjoy experiences that are genuinely unstaged.
options.C: knowing an experience has been arranged need not mean that one has been deceived by it.
options.D: tourists who believe they have found the real thing are no more foolish than people at a play.

questions.correct_answer: (C) knowing an experience has been arranged need not mean that one has been deceived by it.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim about how hosts should be regarded or paid; the comparison concerns the tourist's knowledge.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says nothing about comparative enjoyment; the point is that arranged experiences are 'not falsified' by being known as arranged.
option_rationales.D: The comparison works because the audience knows the actors are acting; it concerns knowing tourists, not those who believe the staging is real.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that many tourists know the homestay 'was prepared for them' and value 'the experience of being admitted', which 'is not falsified by the knowledge that it was arranged'. The theatre audience, which 'knows the actors are acting' yet is not deceived, illustrates that knowing participation is not deception.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the comparison as a defence of tourists who are fooled, when it describes tourists who are not fooled.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong option about believing tourists uses the passage's terms but reverses who the comparison describes.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about tourists in paragraph 3?

options.A: Some tourists say that they prefer an openly staged performance in a hotel courtyard to a visit to a village household, since the performance asks less of them.
options.B: Many families who run homestays say privately that they resent having to keep their own lives confined to a few back rooms during the months when guests arrive.
options.C: Homestays usually cost visitors considerably more than hotel rooms of a similar standard in the same town or village, even though they offer fewer comforts.
options.D: Most guests at homestays, on learning that the household had been prepared for their visit, say they feel cheated and would not have paid had they known.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Most guests at homestays, on learning that the household had been prepared for their visit, say they feel cheated and would not have paid had they known.

option_rationales.A: A preference for open performance does not bear on whether tourists who choose back-region visits are knowing or deceived.
option_rationales.B: This concerns the cost to hosts described in paragraph 4 and supports the author; it says nothing about whether tourists are deceived.
option_rationales.C: The price fits the critics' 'more expensive branch' but does not show that tourists believe the staging is genuine.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that many tourists are 'nothing of the kind' of dupes, knowing that the homestay 'was prepared for them'. If most felt cheated on learning this, they would be the dupes the critics describe, and the claim would be undercut.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about hosts' resentment, which is relevant to the passage but not to the claim about tourists.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires locating the precise claim of paragraph 3 and separating it from the cost argument of paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Since most tourists knowingly accept staged back regions, such tourism raises no serious ethical question that needs to be answered.
options.B: The ethical question raised by staged back regions concerns less the deception of tourists than the shrinking private lives of their hosts.
options.C: Critics are right that the search for unstaged life leads tourists only into more expensive staging, so visitors should stop seeking back regions.
options.D: Tourism inevitably destroys the authentic culture of the communities it reaches, replacing their ways of life with performances.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The ethical question raised by staged back regions concerns less the deception of tourists than the shrinking private lives of their hosts.

option_rationales.A: The author answers the tourist question in the tourist's favour but insists that 'The harder question concerns the hosts', so an ethical question remains.
option_rationales.C: The author calls the criticism 'mistaken about the tourists', and the passage never advises visitors to stop seeking back regions.
option_rationales.D: The passage concerns the hosts' loss of private life, not the destruction of their culture, and "inevitably" overstates its hedged 'can go a long way'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 accept that back regions are staged but deny that knowing tourists are deceived; paragraph 4 says 'If there is a cost in all this, it falls elsewhere', on the hosts; paragraph 5 shifts the question to 'how much of their lives they can afford to keep out of view'.
questions.common_misconception: Stopping at paragraph 3 and concluding that there is no ethical issue at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option captures paragraph 3 correctly but omits the relocation of the ethical question in paragraphs 4 and 5.

questions.question: Which of the following practices would best fit the author's view of what a tourism that 'respected its hosts' would do?

options.A: A village expands its range of homestays and kitchen tours so that more households can share in the income from visitors.
options.B: A regional tourism office prints leaflets explaining to visitors that homestays and craft demonstrations are arranged for their benefit.
options.C: A tour company guarantees in writing that every household its customers visit is unprepared and shown exactly as it is lived in.
options.D: A village keeps certain festivals and quarters closed to visitors, although tourists would readily pay to attend or enter them.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A village keeps certain festivals and quarters closed to visitors, although tourists would readily pay to attend or enter them.

option_rationales.A: Opening more back regions shrinks private life further, which paragraph 4 identifies as the cost the author is concerned about.
option_rationales.B: This addresses whether tourists are deceived, which the author says is the less important question and is usually answered in their favour.
option_rationales.C: This keeps the tourist's experience 'at the centre of the moral picture' and would open more private life, the reverse of what the author asks.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says a tourism that respected its hosts would measure itself 'by how much it is content to leave alone'. Keeping festivals and quarters out of view, even at a loss of income, protects the private life whose erosion paragraph 4 describes.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the leaflet, which sounds respectful but addresses tourist deception, the question the author sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options sound ethical but address the tourist's question; the correct answer requires applying the relocation of concern to the hosts.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a neighbour who returns a dish of sweets on the same evening she received one

options.A: treats the gift as repayment of a favour that she had done for the giver earlier.
options.B: shows that she values the friendship even more highly than the original giver does.
options.C: signals a wish to end the exchange rather than to keep a relationship going.
options.D: lacks the means to prepare a return of a different value at a later date.

questions.correct_answer: (C) signals a wish to end the exchange rather than to keep a relationship going.

option_rationales.A: No earlier favour is mentioned; paragraph 2 reads the speed of the reply as closing the account, not as settling a prior one.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the quick return means she 'declined a friendship', which is the opposite of valuing it more highly.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about her means; it interprets the timing as a message that 'she wants the account closed'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says such a neighbour 'has not discharged a debt so much as declined a friendship; the speed of her reply announces that she wants the account closed.' The prompt return signals an end to the relationship.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a prompt return as eager goodwill, which is the modern intuition the passage questions.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of one sentence in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author mentions anonymous donations in paragraph 3 in order to

options.A: suggest that the gifts usually called free earn that name by deliberately blocking a tie from forming.
options.B: illustrate how patrons use gifts that can never be repaid to bind those who receive them.
options.C: show that the most generous gifts in modern societies are those whose givers choose to stay unknown to the receiver.
options.D: recommend that anonymous giving be replaced by gifts matched to what the receiver can return.

questions.correct_answer: (A) suggest that the gifts usually called free earn that name by deliberately blocking a tie from forming.

option_rationales.B: Patrons appear in paragraph 4 and create binding ties; anonymous donations are cited for the opposite reason, because they prevent any tie.
option_rationales.C: The author never ranks gifts by generosity; paragraph 3 calls the free gift 'less an ideal than an anomaly', so praising anonymous gifts reverses the point.
option_rationales.D: The calibration point in paragraph 4 concerns gifts that bind the receiver, and the author makes no recommendation about anonymous giving.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that a gift demanding nothing 'would create no tie' and then notes that the gifts we call free, such as anonymous donations, 'are precisely those designed to prevent any relationship ... from forming'. The example supports the claim that freedom from obligation is bought by removing the relationship.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the example as praise of anonymous giving, when it is used to show why the 'free' gift is anomalous.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong options use ideas from nearby paragraphs; the function depends on the sentence before the example.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about what sustains the bond between neighbours who exchange gifts?

options.A: In one town, people say they feel mildly uneasy whenever they remain in a neighbour's debt for more than a few weeks at a time.
options.B: Households that exchange gifts often with their neighbours are more likely to help those same neighbours in an emergency.
options.C: In a village where gifts are always returned at once and in exactly equal value, friendships between neighbours prove as close and lasting as anywhere.
options.D: Among several farming communities, gifts sent by clients to their patrons are seldom returned in any form whatsoever.

questions.correct_answer: (C) In a village where gifts are always returned at once and in exactly equal value, friendships between neighbours prove as close and lasting as anywhere.

option_rationales.A: Unease is compatible with the author's view, which says one party is always 'a little in the other's debt'; it does not show that the bond fails to depend on the imbalance.
option_rationales.B: This links frequent exchange to strong ties, which fits the author's account rather than weakening it.
option_rationales.D: Client and patron relations belong to the unequal case of paragraph 4, not to the exchanges between neighbours whose bonds paragraph 2 explains.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 claims that the bond is sustained by a return that 'comes later and differs slightly in value', and that exact or immediate returns close the account. Close, lasting friendships among people who always return equal value at once would show that the imbalance is not what keeps the bond alive.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a fact about discomfort with debt, which is on topic but does not test the causal claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be identified by isolating the precise causal claim of paragraph 2; one wrong option sounds critical of it but is consistent with it.

questions.question: Suppose a wealthy household regularly sends a much poorer neighbour gifts far larger than the neighbour could ever return. On the author's argument, the main problem with this practice is that

options.A: it keeps the poorer neighbour always somewhat in the household's debt, an imbalance that harms the bond in itself.
options.B: the gifts close the account between the two households before a friendship can develop.
options.C: any gift given in the expectation of a return is tainted and falls short of real generosity.
options.D: it leaves the neighbour under an obligation he has no way of discharging, so that his thanks become reliance.

questions.correct_answer: (D) it leaves the neighbour under an obligation he has no way of discharging, so that his thanks become reliance.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says a slight, standing imbalance is 'the mechanism by which the relationship is kept running'; the trouble in paragraph 4 is not imbalance as such but a debt the receiver can never repay.
option_rationales.B: Closing the account is what a quick or exact return does in paragraph 2; a debt too large to repay keeps the account open permanently, which is the opposite.
option_rationales.C: This is the modern intuition described at the start of paragraph 1, which the author questions; the author holds that the obligation to return is part of what a gift is.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says: 'Where one party can give far more than the other could ever repay', the receiver 'is bound by a debt that cannot be cleared, and gratitude hardens into dependence'. The problem is not the expectation of return or imbalance itself but that the strings are not ones 'the receiver is able to hold'.
questions.common_misconception: Falling back on the intuition that strings spoil gifts, or treating any imbalance as the fault, when the author praises a slight, repayable imbalance.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to the passage's ideas (imbalance, the free-gift ideal) and must be separated from the specific objection of paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, barter tends to be found

options.A: where the parties lack the trust needed to leave a debt outstanding.
options.B: mainly in the earliest stage of a society's economic history, before credit develops.
options.C: chiefly in small villages where neighbours settle their debts at harvest time.
options.D: in societies that have not yet found a commodity that everyone will accept.

questions.correct_answer: (A) where the parties lack the trust needed to leave a debt outstanding.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 denies exactly this: barter is 'not the primitive condition out of which trust and credit later grew'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says villagers use running accounts rather than barter; harvest repayment is an example of credit, not of barter.
option_rationales.D: This is the textbook story of paragraph 1, which the author rejects; paragraph 3 says barter is not 'the primitive condition'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists strangers, distrustful groups and people cut off from money, and concludes that 'barter is a response to the absence of trust'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the textbook view, which the passage reports in order to reject.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in the last sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'running accounts' refers to

options.A: written ledgers kept by villagers to record the exact value of every item exchanged.
options.B: ongoing obligations between neighbours that are repaid loosely and over time, if at all.
options.C: arrangements in which every exchange between two neighbours is completed on the spot.
options.D: debts that are measured in coins and must be repaid by a fixed date each year.

questions.correct_answer: (B) ongoing obligations between neighbours that are repaid loosely and over time, if at all.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in paragraph 2 mentions writing or exact values; debts may be repaid 'never precisely at all'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: 'no one needs the exchange to be completed on the spot'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 describes repayment in grain or labour at no fixed time; coins belong to the textbook story.

questions.explanation: The phrase is explained by the example that follows: the woman takes the pot, 'both understand that something will be owed', and the debt may be repaid in grain, labour or 'never precisely at all'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'accounts' literally as bookkeeping.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the example in the next sentence.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the defence of the textbook story in paragraph 4 is best described as

options.A: treating it as irrelevant, since thought experiments have no place in the study of money.
options.B: dismissing it as a deliberate attempt by economists to mislead their students.
options.C: accepting it fully and so withdrawing the historical objection raised earlier.
options.D: granting it partial force while denying that it makes the story harmless.

questions.correct_answer: (D) granting it partial force while denying that it makes the story harmless.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts that a thought experiment can show why a medium of exchange is useful; the complaint is about what this one teaches.
option_rationales.B: No intent to mislead is alleged; the author grants that the reply is fair before qualifying it.
option_rationales.C: The author calls it 'a fair point as far as it goes' and then adds 'But the thought experiment is not idle', so the objection is not withdrawn.

questions.explanation: The author concedes that the reply is 'a fair point as far as it goes' and then argues that the thought experiment 'is not idle', because it teaches us to see money as a neutral token rather than a record of obligations. That is qualified acceptance.
questions.common_misconception: Seizing on 'a fair point' and missing the 'But' that follows, or overstating the author's criticism into an accusation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the concession and the reply together.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the double coincidence of wants is a serious obstacle mainly for

options.A: parties who need each exchange to be settled at the moment it takes place.
options.B: communities that already use money to keep a record of mutual obligations.
options.C: villagers who prefer to repay what they owe in labour rather than in goods.
options.D: neighbours whose harvests happen to fail in the same year as each other.

questions.correct_answer: (A) parties who need each exchange to be settled at the moment it takes place.

option_rationales.B: Money as a record of obligations is the author's account of what money is; it is not linked to the double coincidence problem.
option_rationales.C: Repayment in labour is one of the flexible forms of paragraph 2, among people for whom the problem 'scarcely arises'.
option_rationales.D: Failed harvests are never discussed; the passage ties the problem to the need for on-the-spot settlement, not to scarcity.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the problem 'scarcely arises' among neighbours 'because no one needs the exchange to be completed on the spot'. By implication it bites where exchange must be completed at once, as between the strangers of paragraph 3.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that mentions a detail of village exchange without seeing the condition the passage attaches to the problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer must be inferred from the 'because' clause that ends paragraph 2.

questions.question: The rituals listed in paragraph 2, such as the offering of water and the exchange of names, are presented as

options.A: customs so varied that no general account of hospitality can be given.
options.B: stages by which an uncertain stranger is turned into a guest with a defined position.
options.C: ways in which guests repaid their hosts for the food, water and shelter they received on arrival.
options.D: evidence that strangers were usually welcomed without any suspicion at all.

questions.correct_answer: (B) stages by which an uncertain stranger is turned into a guest with a defined position.

option_rationales.A: The author offers exactly such a general account; the rituals are cited as instances of one process, 'this conversion'.
option_rationales.C: The rituals are offered by the host and mark a change of status; nothing in paragraph 2 treats them as repayment.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 begins by describing the stranger as a possible 'spy or a raider'; the rituals manage that uncertainty rather than showing it was absent.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the rituals 'can be read as stages in this conversion', the conversion of an 'uncertain figure into a guest'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the rituals as gestures of pure kindness instead of reading the sentence that frames them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the same sentence as the examples.

questions.question: The passage implies that the customary limit on the length of a guest's stay

options.A: reflects the small amount of food that most households could afford to share.
options.B: shows that traditional hospitality was less sincere than its admirers have claimed.
options.C: helps keep intact the host's authority, on which the welcome itself depends.
options.D: exists mainly to prevent guests from being adopted into the host's kin group.

questions.correct_answer: (C) helps keep intact the host's authority, on which the welcome itself depends.

option_rationales.A: Scarcity of food is never mentioned; paragraph 3 explains the limit by the risk that the guest would 'unsettle the household's order'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the welcome 'is generous precisely because it is temporary', and paragraph 4 denies that the host's authority corrupts hospitality.
option_rationales.D: Adoption is listed in paragraph 3 as one of the statuses a guest may pass into after the limit, not as something the limit prevents.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a guest who could stay indefinitely 'would gradually unsettle the household's order, and the host would cease to be master of his own house'; paragraph 4 says the host's authority is 'the condition that allows a stranger to be received at all'. The limit therefore protects the authority that makes the welcome possible.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the limit as a sign of insincerity, which the author explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the explanation in paragraph 3 to the conclusion in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The passage associates each of the following with the acceptance of hospitality EXCEPT that

options.A: the guest who shares the host's food implicitly undertakes not to harm the household.
options.B: the host becomes responsible for protecting the guest against harm from third parties.
options.C: the guest may stay indefinitely on the same terms on which he was first received.
options.D: the guest submits, for a time, to an order of rules that the host administers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the guest may stay indefinitely on the same terms on which he was first received.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the guest who eats at the host's table 'has implicitly agreed not to harm the household'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 states that the host 'has made himself responsible for the guest's safety against third parties'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says accepting hospitality is accepting 'a place inside someone else's order', and paragraph 2 speaks of 'rules that the host administers'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that a guest may stay only 'a few days before his status must change', and that a guest who 'could stay forever on a guest's terms' would unsettle the household. Indefinite stay on the original terms is ruled out; the other three are stated in paragraphs 1 and 2.
questions.common_misconception: Remembering that a guest may become a kinsman and treating this as staying on the original terms.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each supported option must be located; the unsupported one is contradicted by paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Customary limits on a guest's stay show that hospitality was designed to protect the household, not the guest.
options.B: The host's authority over the guest is not a flaw in hospitality but what allows strangers to be received at all.
options.C: The ideal of unconditional hospitality is incoherent, so suspicion towards outsiders is fully justified.
options.D: Hospitality is better understood as a method of neutralising dangerous strangers than as an act of generosity towards those who are in need.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The host's authority over the guest is not a flaw in hospitality but what allows strangers to be received at all.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the host also becomes responsible for the guest's safety, and the time limit is only one supporting point.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 grants that the ideal 'has force' as a corrective to suspicion of outsiders; the author never defends that suspicion.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the generous picture 'is not false' but 'omits half'; the author adds authority to generosity rather than ranking control above it.

questions.explanation: The passage argues that hospitality includes an 'exercise of authority' (paragraph 1), explains that authority as the conversion of a stranger into a guest (paragraph 2) and its temporal limits (paragraph 3), and concludes that the authority 'is not a corruption of hospitality' but 'the condition that allows a stranger to be received at all' (paragraph 4).
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the cynical reading that replaces generosity with control, which overstates the author's correction.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option is a sharpened version of the thesis; it must be rejected on degree, using the qualification in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a way in which village commons have been regulated EXCEPT

options.A: imposing fines on offenders that increase each time the offence is repeated.
options.B: limiting a household's animals to the number it can feed through the winter.
options.C: moving grazing between sections of the hill in a fixed order of rotation.
options.D: auctioning the right to graze each season to whichever household bids the most.

questions.correct_answer: (D) auctioning the right to graze each season to whichever household bids the most.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 mentions 'fines that rose with each repeated offence'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says a household might graze 'only as many animals as it could feed through the winter from its own fields'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'grazing might move between sections of the hill in a fixed rotation'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists winter-fodder limits, rotation, a paid watchman and rising fines. Auctioning grazing rights is not mentioned anywhere.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that any sensible-sounding rule must be in the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each listed rule appears in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: According to the passage, what distinguishes a commons from 'open access'?

options.A: A commons belongs to a community that can make and enforce rules for its use.
options.B: A commons is owned by the state, while open access land is held privately.
options.C: A commons is always smaller and so easier to watch than an open access resource.
options.D: Open access resources are used only by outsiders who ignore the village's customs.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A commons belongs to a community that can make and enforce rules for its use.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 presents community management as a third possibility beside private property and state control, so a commons is neither.
option_rationales.C: Size is never mentioned; paragraph 2 distinguishes the two by the presence of rules, monitoring and punishment.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 defines open access as 'a resource that belongs to no community at all', not as one used only by outsiders.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the parable's herders have 'no such rules, no means of watching one another and no way of punishing those who cheat', and calls this 'open access, a resource that belongs to no community at all'. A commons is governed by a community's rules.
questions.common_misconception: Equating the commons with state ownership, which is one of the options the author calls too narrow.
questions.difficulty_reason: The distinction is drawn in the last two sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following developments would the author regard as most likely to lead to the collapse of a well-run village forest commons?

options.A: Households agree to change the order in which sections of the forest are used after a dry year.
options.B: A new road lets timber traders from distant towns enter a forest whose rules bind only villagers.
options.C: The village raises the grain it pays its watchman after a dispute over the forest boundary.
options.D: A village with a stable population raises the fines it charges for repeated offences.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A new road lets timber traders from distant towns enter a forest whose rules bind only villagers.

option_rationales.A: Revising the rotation by agreement is the community adapting its own rules, which the author sees as a strength.
option_rationales.C: Paying the watchman more strengthens monitoring, one of the rules paragraph 2 credits with keeping commons intact.
option_rationales.D: Rising fines for repeat offenders are among the working rules in paragraph 2; a stable population also removes the migration risk.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists the conditions under which commons fail, the first being 'when outsiders who are not bound by local rules can enter freely'. A road that brings in traders not bound by the forest's rules is exactly that case.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a change to the rules and assuming any change is destabilising.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires matching a scenario to the list of failure conditions in paragraph 3.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard a government scheme that replaces a village's grazing rules with uniform national regulations as

options.A: a risk to the commons if the villagers neither understand the new rules nor accept them as legitimate.
options.B: an unwelcome change, but one that cannot affect whether the commons survives, since that depends on human nature.
options.C: a fair remedy for the inequality of village arrangements that give larger shares to households holding more land.
options.D: a safeguard the commons needs, since local rules cannot restrain households once the resource rises in value.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a risk to the commons if the villagers neither understand the new rules nor accept them as legitimate.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says failures are 'not proof that shared ownership is doomed by human nature', and it counts an overriding distant authority as a cause of failure.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 mentions this inequality only to avoid romanticising village life; it proposes no remedy and warns that policy which ignores community management 'may destroy working arrangements'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 lists a rise in value as one danger among several and gives no hint that state rules answer it; it names a distant authority overriding local arrangements as a separate danger.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says commons tend to fail 'when a distant authority overrides local arrangements with regulations that villagers neither understand nor respect', and paragraph 4 warns that policy ignoring community management 'may destroy working arrangements'. The author would see such a scheme as a danger, conditional on its being imposed without local understanding or respect.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that rules imposed from above must be stronger than local ones, which is the narrow choice paragraph 4 rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires matching the scenario to one failure condition in paragraph 3 and the warning in paragraph 4, while rejecting a prescription the passage never makes.

questions.question: According to the passage, which kind of content in oral tradition is often transmitted with unusual fidelity?

options.A: The middle generations of a genealogy, since they serve no present interest of the community.
options.B: Accounts of who led an ancient migration, which communities have reason to remember exactly.
options.C: Fixed forms such as formulaic songs and ritual phrases, even when their meaning has been lost.
options.D: Stories that explain why one lineage holds the best land in the settlement.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Fixed forms such as formulaic songs and ritual phrases, even when their meaning has been lost.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the middle of the past is 'compressed', and paragraph 3 advises caution about 'its middle generations'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says a tradition 'may be quite wrong about who led it', the opposite of fidelity.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 gives these as stories shaped by present needs, which change 'when those needs change'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'formulaic songs, names of places and fixed ritual phrases are often transmitted with a fidelity that ordinary narrative never achieves, even when no one any longer understands what they mean.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing 'details that serve no present interest', which are judged trustworthy, with the compressed middle generations.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in the last sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The author's remark in paragraph 3 about 'details that serve no present interest' serves mainly to

options.A: argue that oral traditions are more reliable as sources than the written chronicles of the same period and region.
options.B: concede that most of the content of an oral tradition was invented to serve present interests.
options.C: explain why formulaic songs are handed down more faithfully than ordinary narrative.
options.D: show how knowing what a tradition is for lets a historian judge which of its parts to trust.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show how knowing what a tradition is for lets a historian judge which of its parts to trust.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says written sources face 'the same pressures'; the author never ranks oral above written sources.
option_rationales.B: The author does not say most content is invented; the point is that distortions are patterned, so the unaffected details can be picked out.
option_rationales.C: The fidelity of fixed forms is a separate point introduced by 'Nor is all content equally fluid', not the role of this remark.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that distortions 'that follow from a known function can ... be anticipated and read through'. The remark about details that 'serve no present interest and are therefore unlikely to have been invented' illustrates this method: the historian uses the tradition's function to sort reliable from suspect parts.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the remark as a general verdict on how much of a tradition is invented.
questions.difficulty_reason: The remark must be tied to the claim it illustrates two sentences earlier.

questions.question: The author's disagreement with the sceptics described in paragraph 1 is best characterised as a disagreement about

options.A: whether the founders named in genealogies were real persons or later inventions.
options.B: whether oral traditions change at all as they are handed down from one generation to the next.
options.C: whether the changes oral traditions undergo are of a kind that a historian can partly correct for.
options.D: whether societies without writing developed precise techniques for memorising long texts.

questions.correct_answer: (C) whether the changes oral traditions undergo are of a kind that a historian can partly correct for.

option_rationales.A: The passage never takes up the reality of founders; it discusses how the generations between founders and the present are compressed.
option_rationales.B: The author agrees that traditions change; paragraph 2 says 'it changes when those needs change'. The dispute is over the kind of change.
option_rationales.D: That claim belongs to the sympathetic current in paragraph 1; the author neither defends nor attacks it in answering the sceptics.

questions.explanation: The sceptics hold that errors accumulate like copying mistakes, so the historian cannot tell 'the accurate parts from the embellishments'. Paragraph 3 replies that the analogy 'is misleading' because distortions that follow from a known function 'can, at least in part, be anticipated and read through'. Both sides accept change; they differ on whether it is random or correctable.
questions.common_misconception: Thinking the author denies that traditions change, or confusing the sympathetic view with the author's own.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires locating the precise point of disagreement across paragraphs 1 to 3 while not crediting the author with the sympathetic view.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's case against the sceptic's manuscript analogy?

options.A: A tradition recorded at intervals over a century changed in ways that bore no relation to shifts in the community's alliances or landholding.
options.B: A tradition was found by excavation to be right about the route of an ancient migration but wrong about the leader it named.
options.C: Chronicles kept by a monastery were found to have been altered over time to support the land claims of the monks who copied them.
options.D: Singers in one community preserved ritual phrases word for word for many generations although none of them understood the words.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A tradition recorded at intervals over a century changed in ways that bore no relation to shifts in the community's alliances or landholding.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 predicts exactly this mix of accuracy and error, so the finding fits the author's account.
option_rationales.C: This supports paragraph 4's point that written sources face 'the same pressures'; it does not show that oral changes are random.
option_rationales.D: This confirms paragraph 3's claim about fixed forms being 'transmitted with a fidelity that ordinary narrative never achieves'.

questions.explanation: The author's reply to the sceptic rests on the claim that a tradition's 'changes are not random' because they follow present needs, and can therefore be read through. Evidence that a tradition changed without any relation to the community's political or economic arrangements would make its changes look like random copying errors, restoring the sceptic's analogy.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the monastic-chronicle option because it involves distortion, though it supports the author.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options are on topic and two involve distortion; only the correct answer attacks the premise that changes are patterned.

questions.question: The reference in paragraph 3 to knowledge about medicinal plants or fishing grounds being used by outsiders serves to illustrate

options.A: why communities have usually refused to share what they know with outside researchers.
options.B: how often local beliefs about medicine turn out to be mistaken once they are tested.
options.C: the claim that local knowledge must be translated into a form that evaluators can handle.
options.D: how validation can move control over knowledge away from the people who held it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) how validation can move control over knowledge away from the people who held it.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says communities refuse to share; the example concerns knowledge that was shared and then published.
option_rationales.B: The example concerns what happened after publication, not whether the knowledge was accurate; mistaken beliefs are discussed only in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: Translation into a manageable form is the first assumption, discussed in paragraph 2; the example in paragraph 3 concerns what outsiders did with knowledge after it was published.

questions.explanation: The example is followed by the conclusion 'Validation, in other words, can be a means of transfer as much as of recognition.' It shows knowledge, once published, being used 'in ways they had no say in'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a nearby point from paragraph 2 instead of the point the example is used to establish.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option borrows the neighbouring assumption from paragraph 2; the example's point is fixed by the 'in other words' sentence after it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that if one of the signs a farmer uses, tested on its own, predicted rainfall poorly, this result would

options.A: indicate that the sign ought to be dropped from the set she relies on in future.
options.B: fail to show that her overall judgement about when to sow is unreliable.
options.C: show that she had been taught a mistaken sign by older members of her community.
options.D: prove that knowledge of the weather held by farmers cannot be put into words at all.

questions.correct_answer: (B) fail to show that her overall judgement about when to sow is unreliable.

option_rationales.A: The author says the signs are weighed 'against one another', so a sign weak on its own may still contribute; no such recommendation is made.
option_rationales.C: Who taught her is never discussed, and paragraph 2 warns against reading the poor result of one sign as a failure of her knowledge.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says she 'could not easily put into words' how she weighs the signs; the claim that it cannot be put into words at all is an overstatement and does not follow from one test.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a sign tested 'in isolation' may predict poorly, but that concluding 'that the farmer's knowledge has failed would be to mistake a judgement for a list of rules'. The poor result tells us about a fragment, not her combined judgement.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a weak component means a weak whole, which is the very inference paragraph 2 rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying paragraph 2's distinction between a judgement and a list of rules to a stated result.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the practice of validating local knowledge is best described as

options.A: qualified approval: it improves on dismissal but rests on questionable assumptions.
options.B: outright hostility, since validation is nothing more than a disguised form of theft.
options.C: detached neutrality, describing the practice without passing any judgement on it.
options.D: unreserved enthusiasm for the respect it shows towards long-neglected expertise.

questions.correct_answer: (A) qualified approval: it improves on dismissal but rests on questionable assumptions.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 calls validation 'an improvement on simple dismissal', and paragraph 3 says only that it 'can be' a means of transfer.
option_rationales.C: The author judges the practice throughout, ending with the view that mutual testing is 'more honest'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 ends 'Yet the language of validation carries assumptions that deserve more scrutiny', which rules out unreserved enthusiasm.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 calls validation 'an improvement on simple dismissal' but adds that its language 'carries assumptions that deserve more scrutiny'. Paragraphs 2 and 3 examine those assumptions, and paragraph 4 proposes something better.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating paragraph 3's warning into outright hostility.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is signalled by two adjacent sentences at the end of paragraph 1.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements would best fit the approach the author recommends in the final paragraph?

options.A: Biologists test every claim that fishers make about spawning sites and publish only the claims that tagging data confirm, naming the fishers as their sources.
options.B: Fishers' knowledge is recorded in their own words and kept away from scientists, so that outsiders cannot misuse it.
options.C: Fishers are trained in tagging methods so that they can validate their own claims before offering them to scientists.
options.D: Fishers and biologists jointly choose which spawning sites to study, and the biologists' stock estimates are also checked against what fishers see on the water.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Fishers and biologists jointly choose which spawning sites to study, and the biologists' stock estimates are also checked against what fishers see on the water.

option_rationales.A: Crediting the fishers does not change the one-way direction of checking that paragraph 4 objects to; only the fishers' claims are tested.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'It would be wrong to conclude that local knowledge should be shielded from testing altogether'.
option_rationales.C: Science still sets the standard and nothing scientific is tested against the fishers' observations, so authority still runs one way.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 objects to 'a procedure in which only one side checks' and recommends one where local people 'help decide which questions are asked' and where 'scientific claims are also tested against their observations'. Only the joint arrangement has both features.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that credits the fishers, which sounds respectful but keeps the one-way validation the author criticises.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options look like improvements on validation; each must be checked against both conditions in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following does the passage present as an instance of earmarking that gives a household member a sphere of decision of her own?

options.A: Coins meant for the temple being kept apart from other money in a tin.
options.B: A woman spending her earnings from tailoring on her children's schooling.
options.C: A grandmother's gift to a newborn being placed in an untouched savings account.
options.D: A windfall being spent on a celebration that a salary would never fund.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A woman spending her earnings from tailoring on her children's schooling.

option_rationales.A: The temple tin is listed in paragraph 2 without any explanation linking it to a household member's control over spending.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 explains this case as preserving a relationship, 'the bond it expressed', not as giving anyone a sphere of decision.
option_rationales.D: The windfall appears in paragraph 2's list, but the passage never explains it in terms of decision-making within the household.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The tailor's earnings are spent on schooling because keeping them distinct allows her to claim, within the household, a sphere of decision that pooled money would not give her.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the grandmother's gift, which paragraph 3 also explains, but by a different function.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the statement that money 'renders them comparable' means that money

options.A: removes from goods any record of who made them or where they came from.
options.B: requires strangers to disclose the histories of the goods they exchange.
options.C: lets goods with different origins be measured on a single common scale.
options.D: makes all goods equally valuable regardless of how useful they are.

questions.correct_answer: (C) lets goods with different origins be measured on a single common scale.

option_rationales.A: This paraphrases the separate phrase 'strips goods of their particular histories'; being comparable is the further result of a common measure.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says money lets strangers trade 'without either needing to know anything about the other's life', the opposite.
option_rationales.D: Comparable does not mean equal; a common measure allows goods to be ranked against each other, as in 'a single ranking of needs'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says each sum 'can buy exactly what the others can' and that a rational person spends 'according to a single ranking of needs'. To render goods comparable is to place them on one scale of value.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the paraphrase of the neighbouring phrase about stripping histories.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option paraphrases the other half of the same sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's interpretation of the tailor's spending?

options.A: Women who earn money from tailoring spend more on their children's schooling than women who earn no money of their own.
options.B: Shopkeepers in the town accept the tailor's rupees on exactly the same terms as the rupees earned by her husband.
options.C: Women whose earnings are pooled with their husbands' say they have less influence over household spending than women who keep their earnings apart.
options.D: Households that earmark their money pay more interest over a year than households that pool all of their income together.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Women whose earnings are pooled with their husbands' say they have less influence over household spending than women who keep their earnings apart.

option_rationales.A: This shows an effect of earning, not of keeping earnings distinct, so it does not bear on the claim that separation gives her 'a sphere of decision'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 already grants this about the market; it concerns fungibility in trade, not decision-making within the household.
option_rationales.D: This concerns the financial cost of earmarking, which paragraph 3 concedes, and says nothing about why the tailor keeps her earnings distinct.
