questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that keeping her earnings distinct 'allows her to claim, within the household, a sphere of decision that pooled money would not give her'. Evidence that pooling reduces a woman's influence over spending directly supports that claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the income comparison, which is about the tailor but not about keeping money separate.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option confuses the effect of earning with the effect of earmarking.

questions.question: In responding to the objection raised in paragraph 4, the author

options.A: concedes that earmarking reflects only feelings and so leaves money's fungibility untouched.
options.B: argues that the market is itself a distortion of the money that people use at home.
options.C: denies that money is fungible even in impersonal trade between people who are strangers.
options.D: accepts its point about market exchange but argues that fungibility holds only in particular settings.

questions.correct_answer: (D) accepts its point about market exchange but argues that fungibility holds only in particular settings.

option_rationales.A: The author turns the objection around: fungibility 'fails' in the household and among friends, so it is not left untouched.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 rejects the picture of a natural money that is 'afterwards' distorted, and never calls the market a distortion of household money.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'The objection is correct about the shopkeeper' and that fungibility 'holds ... in impersonal trade'.

questions.explanation: The author grants the objection's premise ('correct about the shopkeeper') and then argues that it 'concedes the point that matters': fungibility 'holds where people have agreed to ignore the histories of sums ... and fails where they have not'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the concession, or reversing the author's claim about distortion in paragraph 5.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires following a concede-and-turn move and not confusing it with outright denial or with the reversal of paragraph 5's image.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Money behaves as one interchangeable medium only where people agree to ignore where sums came from; elsewhere they mark it deliberately.
options.B: Because money carries social meanings, the economic principle of fungibility is simply false and ought to be abandoned by economists.
options.C: Mental accounting is not an error at all, because keeping money in separate categories costs households nothing.
options.D: Households earmark their money chiefly because cognitive shortcuts are easier than ranking all their needs together.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Money behaves as one interchangeable medium only where people agree to ignore where sums came from; elsewhere they mark it deliberately.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says fungibility 'holds' in impersonal trade, and paragraph 5 calls the arrangement 'valuable'; the author limits the principle, not abandons it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'The errors are real' and gives the costly example of the wedding savings and the roof loan.
option_rationales.D: This is the standard response described at the start of paragraph 3, which the author says misses 'what it accomplishes'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 show that households label money to express relationships and claim control, paragraph 4 limits fungibility to settings where 'people have agreed to ignore the histories of sums', and paragraph 5 calls it 'a social achievement, and a local one'.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the thesis into a rejection of fungibility, or adopting the standard view the author reports.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme wrong option is a sharpened version of the thesis and must be rejected using paragraphs 4 and 5.

questions.question: According to the passage, in the bidding versions of a rotating association

options.A: the pot is awarded to whichever member has contributed the most over the whole cycle.
options.B: a member who wants the pot urgently takes a smaller sum, and the others share the difference.
options.C: the order in which members receive the pot is fixed by drawing lots at the first meeting.
options.D: members compete to receive the pot as late as possible in order to earn the most interest.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a member who wants the pot urgently takes a smaller sum, and the others share the difference.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says every member contributes 'a fixed sum', so no member contributes more than another.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 names lot as a separate method of fixing the order, distinct from bidding.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a late recipient's savings pay 'no interest at all'; bidding is for early access by the one who 'most urgently wants the money'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says that in bidding versions 'the member who most urgently wants the money' accepts 'a smaller pot and the difference shared among the rest'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing bidding with the other ways of fixing the order listed in the same sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one clause of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The argument of paragraph 4 implies that the association's two characteristic features, its protection of savings and its vulnerability to default, are linked because

options.A: dense ties among members reduce the size of the discounts that desperate members accept in the bidding versions.
options.B: members who refuse loans to their cousins lose the trust of the other members of the group.
options.C: early recipients default most often when relatives make claims on the pot they have received.
options.D: the ties that make a refusal to kin acceptable are the same ties that keep early recipients paying.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the ties that make a refusal to kin acceptable are the same ties that keep early recipients paying.

option_rationales.A: Discounts appear only in paragraph 5 and are never connected to the density of ties.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the refusal is 'an excuse that kin and neighbours recognise as legitimate', so it costs no trust.
option_rationales.C: No cause of default is given beyond weak ties and mobility; the passage never links default to claims from relatives.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'The same social pressure that makes a refusal to a cousin acceptable is what keeps the early recipient paying', so where ties are thin both the shelter and the protection against default fail.
questions.common_misconception: Inventing a causal link between kin claims and default that the passage does not draw.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the shelter function of paragraph 3 with the default risk of paragraph 2 through paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the explanation that associations supply discipline is best described as

options.A: accepting it as partly right while holding that it misplaces the chief difficulty.
options.B: regarding it as relevant only to the bidding versions of the association.
options.C: endorsing it as a complete solution to the puzzle raised in paragraph 2.
options.D: rejecting it entirely as a view that members themselves dismiss as mistaken.

questions.correct_answer: (A) accepting it as partly right while holding that it misplaces the chief difficulty.

option_rationales.B: The discipline explanation is discussed for associations in general; bidding is never mentioned in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.C: The 'But' that follows 'part of the answer' shows the author thinks it incomplete and adds the problem of other people's claims.
option_rationales.D: The author says 'This is surely part of the answer'; members describe the problem 'differently', but do not dismiss discipline.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls discipline 'surely part of the answer' but objects that 'it treats the problem as one between the saver and her own weaker self', whereas the real difficulty is 'other people'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the 'But' as outright rejection, or the concession as full endorsement.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options sit on either side of the qualified view.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the function the author attributes to rotating associations?

options.A: A man often asked for loans by his friends keeps his savings in a bank account that none of his friends knows about.
options.B: A trader borrows from a moneylender at a high rate of interest because no bank in his town will lend to him at all.
options.C: A shopkeeper tells relatives seeking loans that her cash is pledged to her suppliers' cooperative, a commitment they accept she cannot break.
options.D: A student joins a study group because she knows she will not work regularly unless others expect her to attend.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A shopkeeper tells relatives seeking loans that her cash is pledged to her suppliers' cooperative, a commitment they accept she cannot break.

option_rationales.A: Secrecy is not the mechanism in paragraph 3; there the money is openly committed and the refusal is 'an excuse that kin and neighbours recognise as legitimate'.
option_rationales.B: This treats an informal arrangement as a substitute for missing banks, the view of paragraph 1 that the author rejects.
option_rationales.D: This matches the discipline explanation, which the author grants is only 'part of the answer'; it involves no shelter from others' claims.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the association 'uses a debt to the group to shelter money from other debts that are harder to decline', and paragraph 3 calls the refusal 'an excuse that kin and neighbours recognise as legitimate'. A pledge to a cooperative that relatives accept as binding works the same way.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the hidden bank account, which also keeps money from friends but by concealment rather than by a recognised prior obligation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches a nearby idea (concealment, discipline, substitution); the correct answer requires the precise mechanism of paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of why people join rotating associations?

options.A: Some members who receive the pot early later stop contributing and leave the town without repaying the others.
options.B: Members whose relatives and neighbours make no claims on their money join as often, and pay as reliably, as members facing many such claims.
options.C: Associations formed among recent migrants to a city collapse more often than those in villages where members have lived side by side for several decades.
options.D: Members of bidding associations sometimes accept very large discounts when they need money urgently for an emergency.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Members whose relatives and neighbours make no claims on their money join as often, and pay as reliably, as members facing many such claims.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 already grants that 'stories of a member who vanished with the pot' show 'the risk is not imaginary'.
option_rationales.C: This fits paragraph 4, which says associations 'break down' where members can move away or barely know one another.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 concedes this; it concerns the costs of bidding versions, not the reason people join.

questions.explanation: The author's account is that associations shelter money from the claims of kin and neighbours. If people with no such claims join just as often and pay as reliably, the sheltering function cannot be what draws members, which undercuts the account.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about collapse or default, which the passage already concedes.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are all things the author grants; the correct answer tests the account's central causal claim.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: defend first come first served as the fairest principle for allocating any scarce public service among people who are strangers.
options.B: explain how some nations have produced more patient citizens than others through long traditions of waiting in line.
options.C: show that numbered tickets and railings are the most effective means available to offices for reducing conflict among customers.
options.D: argue that orderly queuing among strangers is better explained by how visible the rule is than by any national character.

questions.correct_answer: (D) argue that orderly queuing among strangers is better explained by how visible the rule is than by any national character.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the queue is not 'the fairest possible way' and that strict arrival order in a hospital would be 'indefensible', so this reverses the author.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 calls the national character explanation 'mostly wrong'; this presents the rejected view as the author's purpose.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 mentions tickets and railings as illustrations of legibility; the passage never ranks them as the most effective means, and they are not its purpose.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 rejects the character explanation and asks why the rule 'holds at all among strangers'; paragraphs 2 and 3 answer that the queue 'makes its own rule visible'; paragraph 4 restates that the rule 'survives among strangers because it can be seen'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the national character view because the passage opens with it, or an illustration from paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated in paragraph 1 and restated in the last sentence; the rejected view is flagged as wrong.

questions.question: According to the passage, people waiting at the doors of a bus often jostle because

options.A: waiting for a bus feels more urgent to them than waiting at a ticket counter does.
options.B: no official is present at the bus doors to punish those who push ahead.
options.C: no one can tell with confidence who arrived first, so there is no clear order to defend.
options.D: people in a crowd become more selfish than they are when standing in a line.

questions.correct_answer: (C) no one can tell with confidence who arrived first, so there is no clear order to defend.

option_rationales.A: Urgency is raised only in paragraph 4 about hospitals; paragraph 2 gives the absence of a visible order as the reason for jostling.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the queue too is 'enforced by no official', so the absence of an official cannot be what separates the bus crowd from the queue.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says they jostle 'not because they have become selfish', which directly rules this out.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the same people jostle at the bus doors 'because no one can say with confidence who arrived first' and that 'Without a visible order there is nothing to defend'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the selfishness option, which the passage explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The example of a hospital that treats patients 'strictly in order of arrival' serves mainly to

options.A: show that informal norms collapse wherever people are unable to see a line forming in front of them.
options.B: concede that allocating a service by order of arrival can be orderly and yet unjust where needs differ.
options.C: suggest that hospitals are generally less well organised than the ticket offices described in paragraph 3.
options.D: illustrate how numbered tickets can be adapted for use in settings where urgency matters to those waiting.

questions.correct_answer: (B) concede that allocating a service by order of arrival can be orderly and yet unjust where needs differ.

option_rationales.A: That is the point of the bus example in paragraph 2; the hospital example in paragraph 4 concerns fairness, not whether the norm holds.
option_rationales.C: No comparison of how well hospitals and offices are organised is made; the hospital is imagined, and called 'orderly'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says nothing about adapting tickets; it uses the hospital to mark a limit of the queue as a principle of allocation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with 'None of this means that the queue is the fairest possible way' and notes that it 'ignores urgency'; the hospital, 'orderly and indefensible', illustrates that concession.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the example to the argument about visibility instead of to the concession it introduces.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'None of this means' at the start of the paragraph.

questions.question: A popular food stall finds that customers push and argue at its counter at busy times. Which of the following measures would the author's account most clearly predict to reduce the problem?

options.A: Marking a single line on the ground leading to the counter, so that each newcomer's place is plain to everyone.
options.B: Inviting customers who believe they have waited longest to call out when the counter becomes free.
options.C: Asking each customer to state how urgently they need food so that the neediest can be served first.
options.D: Posting a notice at the counter reminding customers that patience is a civic virtue they should show to others.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Marking a single line on the ground leading to the counter, so that each newcomer's place is plain to everyone.

option_rationales.B: This leaves the order to competing claims, which is the situation of the bus crowd in paragraph 2 where 'no one can say with confidence who arrived first'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 mentions urgency only to say the queue ignores it; inviting claims of urgency adds doubt about order, the opposite of what paragraph 3 recommends.
option_rationales.D: The author rejects explanations from character and notes that offenders already know the rule; a reminder of virtue makes nothing more legible.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says measures such as 'painted footprints' and single lines 'succeed by removing doubt rather than by threatening punishment'. A marked line makes compliance and violation visible, which is the author's mechanism.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the urgency option because the author concedes that queues ignore urgency, without noticing that it would make the order less legible.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the legibility mechanism to a new case and rejecting options that sound reasonable but add ambiguity.

questions.question: The remark that the retired teacher 'has lost not her wages, which she never had, but her say' implies that

options.A: part of what volunteers value is control over how and with whom they contribute, which managerial roles can take away.
options.B: volunteers who leave reorganised clubs are mainly those who had hoped that the new arrangements would bring them some form of payment.
options.C: retired teachers are especially ill suited to working under coordinators because they are used to running their own classrooms.
options.D: the reading club ceased to be of any benefit to the children once it was turned into a programme with targets.

questions.correct_answer: (A) part of what volunteers value is control over how and with whom they contribute, which managerial roles can take away.

option_rationales.B: The remark says the opposite: she never had wages and did not lose any; what she lost was her say.
option_rationales.C: The teacher is a single hypothetical case; nothing is said about teachers as a group or their classroom habits.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not say the children lost out; paragraph 3 even allows that a reorganised body 'may deliver its service more reliably'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says volunteers are 'choosing what to do, with whom and on what terms, and that choice is part of what they value'. The teacher's loss of 'her say' is a loss of that choice.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the remark as being about payment or about teachers in general rather than about choice.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence just before the example states the principle the remark illustrates.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the professionalisation of volunteering is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality: reporting what supporters and critics claim without offering any judgement of the author's own.
options.B: outright hostility: treating any form of training or rules for volunteers as a betrayal of what voluntary life stands for.
options.C: qualified scepticism: accepting it for demanding tasks but doubting it as a general model for voluntary bodies.
options.D: warm approval: welcoming it as clear evidence that voluntary bodies have at last matured into reliable organisations.

questions.correct_answer: (C) qualified scepticism: accepting it for demanding tasks but doubting it as a general model for voluntary bodies.

option_rationales.A: The author judges plainly, describing losses and ending with what 'The sensible question' is and how it should be answered.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 begins 'None of this is an argument against training or rules as such' and endorses checks for those who work with children.
option_rationales.D: The author says the change is 'usually presented as simple progress' and then argues that 'neither is the whole story', which is not approval.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 set out two losses; paragraph 4 accepts rules for a mountain rescue team and child safety but objects when standards 'are applied across the board'. That is scepticism with a stated limit.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the strong criticism in paragraphs 2 and 3 for outright hostility and ignoring the concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession in the final paragraph settles the attitude.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the third paragraph in the passage?

options.A: It offers evidence that professionalised organisations deliver their services less reliably than informal groups of volunteers do.
options.B: It answers the objection that rules are needed for demanding tasks such as rescue work on a mountain or work with children.
options.C: It explains why funders prefer to support organisations that can report the hours their volunteers have given.
options.D: It identifies a second cost, beyond individual volunteers' loss of say, that falls on the practice of collective self-government.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It identifies a second cost, beyond individual volunteers' loss of say, that falls on the practice of collective self-government.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the reorganised body 'may deliver its service more reliably'; its point is about lost habits, not worse service.
option_rationales.B: That objection is taken up in paragraph 4, which concedes it; paragraph 3 does not address it.
option_rationales.C: Funders' preferences appear in paragraphs 1 and 4; paragraph 3 concerns what happens to self-government inside organisations.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'There is also a quieter loss', signalling an addition to the teacher's loss of say in paragraph 2, and describes how 'that practice of self-government shrinks'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the paragraph claims worse service, when it explicitly allows better service.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing the signpost 'also' and distinguishing the individual loss of paragraph 2 from the collective loss of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's suggestion that managerial practices lead some long-standing volunteers to drift away?

options.A: Some volunteers who left professionalised organisations later joined informal groups such as allotment societies and reading clubs.
options.B: Among comparable groups, long-serving volunteers left at the same rate whether or not their group had adopted role descriptions and supervisors.
options.C: Organisations that adopted role descriptions and supervisors reported more volunteer hours to their funders than they had before.
options.D: Many newly recruited volunteers say that clear role descriptions made them more willing to join an organisation in the first place.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Among comparable groups, long-serving volunteers left at the same rate whether or not their group had adopted role descriptions and supervisors.

option_rationales.A: If anything this fits the author's picture of volunteers who still want to give time but drift away from managed bodies.
option_rationales.C: Reported hours say nothing about whether long-standing volunteers left; the author even grants that such reporting helps win support.
option_rationales.D: This concerns newcomers joining, not existing volunteers leaving, and fits paragraph 1's point that the plausible claims are not 'the whole story'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says such volunteers 'simply drift away' when managed like employees. If departure rates are the same with and without those practices, the practices are not driving departures, which undercuts the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about newcomers because it praises role descriptions, without noticing that it concerns a different group.
questions.difficulty_reason: Only the correct answer tests the causal link; two other options are on topic but about other groups or measures.

questions.question: According to the passage, the tests on which early placement into streams is based measure

options.A: children's ability alone, although teachers later tend to misread what the results of those tests mean.
options.B: a mixture of ability and other factors, such as a child's maturity and the help she has had at home.
options.C: chiefly the quality of the teaching that each child has received in the school before the tests.
options.D: a child's real talent more accurately at the age of seven than it could be measured at fifteen.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a mixture of ability and other factors, such as a child's maturity and the help she has had at home.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the tests measure 'along with ability' maturity, familiarity with the task and help at home, so ability alone is wrong.
option_rationales.C: The passage names help 'at home', maturity and familiarity with the task, not the quality of earlier school teaching.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 implies the reverse: a small age gap that 'would be invisible at fifteen can look like a difference of talent at seven'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that placement 'rests on tests that measure, along with ability, a child's maturity, her familiarity with the kind of task being set and the amount of help she has had at home'.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the phrase 'along with ability' and treating the tests as pure measures.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of one sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the meaning of 'The door is open, but the corridor behind it grows longer every term' as used in paragraph 3?

options.A: The number of pupils moving up from the lower streams rises steadily as the school year goes on and they improve.
options.B: Schools deliberately add new requirements each term in order to keep pupils in the streams first assigned to them.
options.C: Pupils in the lower streams gradually lose their motivation and so stop trying to win a place in a higher group.
options.D: Movement between streams is formally permitted but becomes harder in practice as the groups' coverage drifts further apart.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Movement between streams is formally permitted but becomes harder in practice as the groups' coverage drifts further apart.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'movement is uncommon'; the image describes a growing obstacle, not growing movement.
option_rationales.B: Nothing suggests deliberate obstruction; the obstacle arises because a pupil 'who has covered less material cannot readily join a group that has covered more'.
option_rationales.C: The passage gives uncovered material and teachers' labels as the obstacles; it never mentions pupils' motivation.

questions.explanation: The door that is open stands for the formal possibility of moving that defenders cite ('in principle they can'). The lengthening corridor is the widening gap in material covered, which makes moving harder each term.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the image as about pupils' attitudes or about deliberate policy instead of about accumulating differences in curriculum.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative sentence must be connected to the explanation that precedes it and to the defenders' reply.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the later examination results of pupils in different streams

options.A: are determined mainly by the age at which pupils first entered school rather than by what they were taught.
options.B: prove that pupils who were placed in lower streams had equal ability to the others at the outset.
options.C: cannot be taken as straightforward confirmation that the original placements were accurate.
options.D: show that the original placement tests detected no real differences at all between the pupils who sat them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) cannot be taken as straightforward confirmation that the original placements were accurate.

option_rationales.A: Age is one factor in placement, but the author's point about later results is that teaching in different streams widens gaps; this reverses the emphasis.
option_rationales.B: The author says the results are 'partly' the product of streaming, not that initial abilities were equal; the option overstates both the certainty and the claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 speaks of 'The gap that the original test detected', so the author accepts there was some real difference, and denying any difference is too strong.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends by saying the later results 'seem to confirm the placement' but 'are partly its product'. So they are not clean evidence that the placements were right, though they are not meaningless either.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating 'partly its product' into a claim that the tests or the initial differences were wholly unreal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options are extreme versions of the correct answer; the solver must keep the author's 'partly'.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that streams partly produce the gaps they are said to detect?

options.A: Pupils with almost identical placement scores, assigned to adjacent streams only because a cut-off fell between them, differed markedly in attainment a few years later.
options.B: Pupils in the upper streams report enjoying school more, on average, than pupils who have been placed in the lower streams.
options.C: Teachers of classes with widely mixed attainment report that planning their lessons is far more demanding than teaching a single stream.
options.D: Pupils who were placed in lower streams at the age of seven also tended, on average, to obtain noticeably lower scores in their examinations at fifteen.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Pupils with almost identical placement scores, assigned to adjacent streams only because a cut-off fell between them, differed markedly in attainment a few years later.

option_rationales.B: Enjoyment is not attainment; the finding does not show that placement itself widened any gap in what pupils learned.
option_rationales.C: This supports the case for grouping that the author concedes in paragraph 4; it says nothing about whether streams create gaps.
option_rationales.D: This correlation is what both the author and the defenders of streaming would expect, since it fits accurate placement as well as self-confirming placement.

questions.explanation: If pupils who began almost equal diverge after being placed on either side of a cut-off, the divergence must come from the placement, which is exactly the claim that the gap is 'widened by the arrangement that was supposed to respond to it'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the age-seven to age-fifteen correlation, which looks supportive but cannot separate the author's explanation from the defenders'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option is consistent with the claim; only the correct answer isolates the effect of placement itself.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the usual explanation of why benefits go unclaimed

options.A: rests on accurate information about how many eligible people have never heard that the benefit exists.
options.B: is correct for most of those entitled but fails to account for a small group of the seriously ill.
options.C: overlooks the demands that the process of claiming itself places on the people entitled to the benefit.
options.D: was devised by governments in order to justify reductions in the money spent on welfare programmes.

questions.correct_answer: (C) overlooks the demands that the process of claiming itself places on the people entitled to the benefit.

option_rationales.A: The passage offers no information about awareness levels; it challenges the explanation rather than vouching for its evidence.
option_rationales.B: The author does not grant that the usual explanation holds for most people; paragraph 1 criticises it for never asking 'what claiming actually involves'.
option_rationales.D: No origin is given for the explanation; paragraph 3 discusses governments and spending, but about procedures, and hedges on intent.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the usual explanation 'locates the problem in the claimant' and 'rarely asks what claiming actually involves', then lists those demands.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about governments because paragraph 3 later discusses hidden cuts.
questions.difficulty_reason: The criticism is stated directly in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The hypothetical government in paragraph 3 that 'wished to spend less on a programme but did not wish to say so' serves to

options.A: show that governments routinely add documents to application forms as a deliberate way of cutting spending on welfare.
options.B: argue that all requirements to renew a claim should be abolished because they serve no legitimate purpose at all.
options.C: demonstrate that laws on welfare are usually drafted with far more care than the forms used to administer them.
options.D: illustrate how changes in procedure can narrow a programme's reach while its rules of entitlement remain unchanged.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate how changes in procedure can narrow a programme's reach while its rules of entitlement remain unchanged.

option_rationales.A: The case is hypothetical ('could add') and the author adds 'Whether or not anyone intends this', so no routine deliberate practice is claimed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens 'This is not to say that verification is illegitimate' and says that 'some checking sustains' public belief, so abolition is not argued.
option_rationales.C: The contrast with legislation concerns public debate, not the care of drafting; drafting quality is never discussed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says burdens 'can change who receives a benefit without any public decision'. The hypothetical shows the mechanism: recipients fall 'while the rules of entitlement stayed exactly as they were'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a hypothetical as a factual accusation, despite the author's explicit hedge about intent.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must notice both the conditional framing and the hedge 'Whether or not anyone intends this'.

questions.question: Which of the following reforms would best accord with the 'sound design' described in the final paragraph?

options.A: Hiring more officials to examine completed forms so that a greater share of fraudulent claims is detected each year.
options.B: Letting officials confirm eligibility from records already held by other public offices instead of asking applicants to collect them.
options.C: Requiring claimants to renew their claims more often so that any change in their circumstances is detected sooner.
options.D: Removing every check on eligibility so that anyone who applies for the benefit receives it without delay or question.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Letting officials confirm eligibility from records already held by other public offices instead of asking applicants to collect them.

option_rationales.A: This weighs only the office side of the ledger; the author complains that the costs borne 'in the lives of applicants' are not counted.
option_rationales.C: More frequent renewal adds exactly the kind of burden paragraphs 1 and 3 describe, and paragraph 3 notes that shortening renewal periods can cut recipients.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 accepts that 'some checking sustains' public belief in the programme; abolishing checks ignores the cost of errors the author wants weighed.

questions.explanation: The sound design would weigh 'the time and strain imposed on claimants as seriously as the cost of the errors it prevents'. Using existing records keeps verification while removing the applicant's burden of gathering documents 'held by three different offices'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the fraud-detection option because it sounds responsible, though it ignores the claimant's costs.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires balancing both sides of the final paragraph: verification is kept, but claimants' costs are reduced.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: Burdens on claimants are introduced chiefly by governments that want to cut spending without public debate.
options.B: The costs of verification fall partly on applicants, and these are often left out of the reckoning.
options.C: A requirement that is a minor nuisance for one applicant may be decisive for another applicant.
options.D: A fall in the number of people receiving a benefit need not reflect any change in the rules that define who is entitled to it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Burdens on claimants are introduced chiefly by governments that want to cut spending without public debate.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the costs are 'borne in two places' and 'only the first tends to be counted', so this is supported.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says a requirement costing one applicant 'an afternoon may cost a struggling one the benefit itself', so this is supported.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says that procedural changes can make 'the number of recipients' fall 'while the rules of entitlement stayed exactly as they were', so this is supported.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes what a government 'could' do and adds 'Whether or not anyone intends this'. The author never claims that burdens chiefly arise from such motives, so this is the unsupported statement.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the hypothetical in paragraph 3 as the author's account of where burdens come from.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each supported option paraphrases a different paragraph; the unsupported one turns a hedged possibility into a causal claim.

questions.question: In the example of the family that moves to a city, the people from its home district

options.A: find the family a permanent home in a neighbourhood where many different communities live.
options.B: refuse their help unless the family agrees to marry and to trade only within the group.
options.C: discourage the family from forming any friendships with neighbours from a different background.
options.D: help the family to secure a room, a loan and practical knowledge of offices and employers.

questions.correct_answer: (D) help the family to secure a room, a loan and practical knowledge of offices and employers.

option_rationales.A: They find it 'a room'; nothing is said about permanence or about a mixed neighbourhood.
option_rationales.B: The demand for conformity is described in paragraph 3 as a possibility for close groups generally, not as part of this family's experience.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the close circle often leads to a 'first friendship with a neighbour of a different background'; discouragement belongs to paragraph 3's other case.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Those people find it a room, lend it money, explain which offices to visit and which employers pay on time.'
questions.common_misconception: Importing the conformity demands of paragraph 3 into the family example of paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The detail is listed in a single sentence.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about bridging ties?

options.A: They can be created reliably by public policies that weaken networks within communities.
options.B: They are formed mainly by people who do not belong to any close group of their own.
options.C: They are often formed through contacts that bonding ties first make available to a person.
options.D: They are less valuable than bonding ties, which deserve the civic esteem that writers usually give to bridging.

questions.correct_answer: (C) They are often formed through contacts that bonding ties first make available to a person.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says such a policy 'would therefore risk destroying the very support' that lets newcomers form wider ties.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the first outside job or friendship 'frequently comes through someone who was met by way of the close circle'.
option_rationales.D: The author rejects the ranking itself ('The ranking is too quick') and makes bonding the 'precondition' of bridging, not its superior; paragraph 3 adds that close groups can become 'a closure'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 concludes that bonding is 'not the rival of bridging but its precondition', since outside contacts frequently come 'by way of the close circle'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that reverses the usual ranking, when the author rejects ranking the two kinds of tie at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option reverses the ranking instead of dissolving it.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that 'the closeness that was a resource becomes a closure' means that

options.A: the dense ties that once supported a group's members come to restrict what those members may choose to do.
options.B: the group's material resources are used up because too many dependent newcomers have relied on them.
options.C: the community stops offering help to its members and gradually dissolves as more and more of them leave.
options.D: outsiders become unable to learn what the community believes because its members refuse to speak to them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the dense ties that once supported a group's members come to restrict what those members may choose to do.

option_rationales.B: In the passage the word resource refers to support and ties, and nothing is said about anything running out.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not say the community dissolves; the network still exists and 'now stands in her way'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 is about constraints on members, such as the young woman, not about what outsiders can learn.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the density of ties 'that allows a community to support its members allows it to watch them', and the network 'which once sustained her family now stands in her way'. The resource has turned into a constraint.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'resource' literally as material goods, or 'closure' as the group shutting down.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wordplay must be decoded from the surrounding sentences.

questions.question: Judging by the criterion in the final paragraph, which of the following close groups would the author regard most favourably?

options.A: A community whose ties have loosened over the years, which leaves members free to make contacts elsewhere but gives newcomers little help.
options.B: A tightly knit association of traders from one region that helps newcomers open shops and encourages them to take partners from outside it.
options.C: A close neighbourhood community whose members help one another generously but expect their children to marry within it.
options.D: A group of families whose members have deliberately cut back their ties to one another in order to fit in better with the wider city.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A tightly knit association of traders from one region that helps newcomers open shops and encourages them to take partners from outside it.

option_rationales.A: Permeability without support loses what paragraph 2 values: the stability 'from which wider contacts become possible'. The criterion asks how a close group treats outside ties, not how loose it is.
option_rationales.C: Its help comes with 'a demand for conformity', the closure of paragraph 3; generous support does not make membership compatible with outside ties.
option_rationales.D: This is the weakening of community networks that paragraph 4 warns 'would therefore risk destroying the very support' newcomers need.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the test is not 'how tightly it binds but whether it lets its members go'. The traders' association binds tightly and supports newcomers, yet encourages ties outside, so it is both a resource and permeable.
questions.common_misconception: Equating permeability with loose ties and choosing the loosened community, when the author separates strength of ties from permeability.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer binds tightly, which seems suspect; the tempting option is permeable but lacks support, so the solver must hold both criteria.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, players' tolerance of refereeing errors before video review depended partly on

options.A: the lower stakes of professional matches in the years before cameras were introduced into the game.
options.B: rules that allowed teams to appeal against a decision once the match in which it was made had ended.
options.C: the expectation that, over a season, mistakes would not consistently favour or harm any one side.
options.D: players' belief that officials on the field were usually more accurate than replays would later turn out to be.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the expectation that, over a season, mistakes would not consistently favour or harm any one side.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about the stakes of earlier matches; the tolerance is explained by finality and by errors spread over a season.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 stresses that 'the decision would stand'; appeals after the match contradict the finality the author describes.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says players accepted decisions 'not because they trusted the official's eyesight', which rules out a belief in superior accuracy.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says error was tolerated as 'the price of finality', and 'since the errors fell, over a season, on all sides alike, the price seemed bearable'. The bearability depended partly on that even spread.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about trust in officials' accuracy, which the passage explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated as a subordinate clause and must be recognised as one of two supports for tolerance.

questions.question: The contrast in paragraph 3 between whether 'a challenge was reckless' and whether 'a toe was ahead of a defender's shoulder' serves to

options.A: illustrate the claim that officials on the field judge fouls less competently than the officials who watch replays.
options.B: argue that video review ought to be restricted to questions that can be settled as matters of measurable fact.
options.C: show that offside decisions are easier for officials to get right than decisions about how reckless a challenge was.
options.D: distinguish a question openly treated as judgement from one presented as fact that in truth rests on concealed choices.

questions.correct_answer: (D) distinguish a question openly treated as judgement from one presented as fact that in truth rests on concealed choices.

option_rationales.A: The passage says a trained official can judge recklessness 'in a moment'; it makes no claim about relative competence.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 restricts review to 'clear and obvious errors'; the author doubts that marginal measurement questions are settled facts at all.
option_rationales.C: The author says the toe question depends on hidden choices of frame and line, which makes it harder to settle, not easier.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls the first 'a matter of judgement' and says the second 'is presented as a matter of fact, yet the answer depends on which frame is chosen and where the line is drawn'. The contrast sets up the claim that 'A decision dressed as measurement invites challenge'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the author favours review for measurable facts, when the passage questions whether marginal measurements are really facts.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function depends on the second of two changes the paragraph describes, which is introduced as 'less obvious'.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The disputes that review provokes show that replays are less accurate than the eyes of a trained referee.
options.B: A replay system can remove real injustices and still weaken officiating if it is used to settle marginal calls.
options.C: Review would provoke no new disputes if the lines drawn on screens were made more precise than they are now.
options.D: Since finality matters more than accuracy in sport, cameras used for review do more harm to games than good.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A replay system can remove real injustices and still weaken officiating if it is used to settle marginal calls.

option_rationales.A: The author's complaint concerns finality and concealed choices of frame and line, not the accuracy of replays compared with referees' eyes.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the 'apparent precision of the image conceals' choices; greater precision would leave the choice of frame open, and 'every measurement can be disputed by another'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 opens 'None of this is a case for abandoning the cameras' and says replays remove blatant errors 'cheaply'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says replays remove plain errors such as a goal for a shot that 'plainly missed', but 'extended to the margins, it dissolves the very finality that made officiating possible'. Both halves of the correct answer come from that paragraph.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option against cameras because the passage stresses finality over accuracy, missing the concession; or the precision option, missing the point about frames.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are plausible extensions of the argument; rejecting them needs both the concession and the point about concealed choices.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why disputes over decisions now seem less settled?

options.A: In competitions that use review only for clear and obvious errors, supporters argue over decisions just as long as in those that review marginal calls.
options.B: Before video review was introduced, supporters often claimed that referees were biased against the team they followed.
options.C: Referees who work with video review report feeling less confident when making decisions during play on the field.
options.D: Supporters of teams that lose a match tend to argue about refereeing decisions for longer, and far more bitterly, than supporters of the teams that win.

questions.correct_answer: (A) In competitions that use review only for clear and obvious errors, supporters argue over decisions just as long as in those that review marginal calls.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 already grants that complaints are as old as officials; past accusations do not bear on why today's disputes seem less settled.
option_rationales.C: This fits the author's claim that review 'relocates authority' and makes the referee 'a provisional judge', so it supports rather than weakens.
option_rationales.D: This is true of disputes in general and says nothing about how review, or the type of question reviewed, affects them.

questions.explanation: The author attributes the new disputes to review being 'extended to the margins', where decisions are 'dressed as measurement'. If competitions that avoid marginal review have equally long disputes, that explanation loses its force.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about disputes or referees that is on topic but does not test the author's causal account.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must identify the precise explanation (marginal calls as disguised measurement) and find the option that varies it.

questions.question: According to the passage, the tendency of answers about quite different institutions to rise and fall together suggests that

options.A: the various institutions have tended to improve or to decline in their performance at the same times.
options.B: survey responses largely reflect a general disposition rather than considered judgements about particular bodies.
options.C: people trust the courts and the press for exactly the same reasons as each other.
options.D: respondents are much better informed about some public institutions than they are about others.

questions.correct_answer: (B) survey responses largely reflect a general disposition rather than considered judgements about particular bodies.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 draws the opposite conclusion: the pattern suggests the answers capture 'a general disposition' rather than each body's performance.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists several possible reasons for any answer and does not claim that the reasons for trusting different bodies are identical.
option_rationales.D: Differences in how well informed respondents are play no part in paragraph 2's interpretation of the shared movement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: answers about different institutions 'tend to rise and fall together, which suggests that much of what is captured is a general disposition rather than a considered judgement about any particular body'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about shared performance, an explanation the author does not adopt.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'well-calibrated trust' refers to trust that

options.A: stays at a moderate level, avoiding both complete confidence and complete suspicion of an institution.
options.B: is based on direct personal dealings with an institution rather than on its reputation alone.
options.C: rises or falls according to how reliable the institution in which it is placed actually is.
options.D: remains steady over the years regardless of how an institution's record happens to change.

questions.correct_answer: (C) rises or falls according to how reliable the institution in which it is placed actually is.

option_rationales.A: Calibration is defined as trust 'that rises and falls with the reliability of its object'; it can be high where an institution is highly reliable, so moderation is not the point.
option_rationales.B: Direct dealings appear in paragraph 5 as one kind of evidence to gather; they are not what paragraph 3 means by calibration.
option_rationales.D: This is the opposite of calibration, which requires trust to change as reliability changes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the phrase directly: 'trust that rises and falls with the reliability of its object', following the claim that 'trust is valuable only when it is placed in what is trustworthy'.
questions.common_misconception: Equating calibration with moderation, a natural reading of 'well-calibrated' that the passage's definition does not support.
questions.difficulty_reason: The moderate-level option is a plausible everyday sense of the phrase; the passage defines it differently.

questions.question: The example of people who distrust the courts yet 'continue to sign contracts that only courts can enforce' is used to suggest that

options.A: survey answers may be a weaker guide to trust, understood as reliance, than what people actually do.
options.B: people who express distrust of institutions while continuing to use them are being hypocritical.
options.C: trust in the courts is, in general, considerably higher than trust in the health service.
options.D: contracts would be signed far less often than they now are if the courts were trusted more.

questions.correct_answer: (A) survey answers may be a weaker guide to trust, understood as reliance, than what people actually do.

option_rationales.B: The author draws no moral conclusion about such people; the example is about which kind of evidence better reveals trust.
option_rationales.C: The courts and the health service appear as parallel examples of the same gap, and no comparison of their levels of trust is made.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the logic; the example shows people relying on courts despite professed distrust, not that more trust would reduce reliance.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'If trust is fundamentally a matter of what we are prepared to rely on, the survey and the behaviour can come apart, and it is not obvious that the survey is the better witness.' The contracts example illustrates that gap.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a criticism of respondents rather than of the survey.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence after the example, but the solver must connect 'reliance' to 'witness'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the explanation that a particular fall in measured trust records 'an improvement in the public's knowledge' of the institutions concerned?

options.A: The fall in measured trust coincided with the publication of several well-documented reports of misconduct within the police.
options.B: People who had dealt with the courts directly reported higher trust in them than people who knew the courts only by their reputation among friends and neighbours.
options.C: Information about the failures of these institutions became far more widely available during the period in which measured trust fell.
options.D: The fall was steepest among people who had seen no reports of the institutions' failures, while trust held steady among those who followed such reports closely.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The fall was steepest among people who had seen no reports of the institutions' failures, while trust held steady among those who followed such reports closely.

option_rationales.A: Publicised misconduct fits the information explanation, though it might also fit declining reliability; it does not count against the explanation.
option_rationales.B: This bears on paragraph 5's point about direct experience, not on whether the fall reflects better information.
option_rationales.C: Wider circulation of information is what the explanation predicts, so this supports it rather than weakening it.

questions.explanation: The explanation says the decline reflects information 'once hidden, now circulates freely'. If those exposed to the information did not lose trust while those unexposed did, the decline cannot be due to that information, which undercuts the explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that mentions information or scandal, which matches the explanation's vocabulary but supports it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must see which group the explanation predicts should lose trust and spot the option that reverses it.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A fall in measured trust in institutions is usually a sign that citizens have become better informed about them.
options.B: A sharp rise in measured trust in a police force would not, by itself, be a reason for satisfaction.
options.C: Public policy should aim to raise citizens' trust in institutions to the highest level that they are willing to accept.
options.D: Because survey answers about trust are unreliable, a decline in measured trust has no practical consequences.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A sharp rise in measured trust in a police force would not, by itself, be a reason for satisfaction.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 offers better information as one of several possibilities and paragraph 4 says the numbers cannot tell us which applies; 'usually' overstates.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'What we should want is not high trust but well-calibrated trust', which this contradicts.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says distrust 'has consequences of its own', such as tax evasion and unreported crime, and adds 'The point is not that the numbers are meaningless'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says trust in a corrupt police force would be 'a mistake' and that we should want calibrated rather than high trust; paragraph 4 says the figures cannot alone show what lies behind a change. So a rise in trust, without evidence of greater reliability, is not in itself good news.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the better-information option because the passage dwells on it, or the no-consequences option because it criticises the surveys.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is not stated anywhere and must be derived from paragraphs 3 and 4 together; two wrong options exaggerate genuine points.

questions.question: According to the passage, in the professionally managed organisations a member is typically

options.A: a person whose views on the organisation's policy are regularly sought and acted upon through surveys.
options.B: a person who gives time at the central office, working alongside the organisation's professional staff.
options.C: a person chosen by a local branch to represent it at the meetings of a regional or national body.
options.D: a person whose membership consists in having contributed money rather than in taking part in meetings.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a person whose membership consists in having contributed money rather than in taking part in meetings.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says supporters are consulted through surveys 'if at all', and says nothing of their views being acted upon.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says these organisations 'ask them for money rather than time'.
option_rationales.C: Elected delegates belong to the older federations described at the start of paragraph 2, not to the staff-run organisations.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'a member is someone who has made a payment, not someone who has attended a meeting'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the features of the federations with those of their successors, both described in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer is in one sentence; the wrong options draw on nearby sentences.

questions.question: The author's reading of the evidence implies that the remedies mentioned at the end of paragraph 1 are

options.A: unnecessary, since people already gather in online groups and networks that serve the same civic purposes.
options.B: suitable for older citizens but not for younger people who grew up absorbed in private amusements.
options.C: misdirected, since they target individuals' willingness to join when the change lay largely in what organisations offered.
options.D: sound in their aim but too gentle, since only shaming would be strong enough to bring people back to meetings.

questions.correct_answer: (C) misdirected, since they target individuals' willingness to join when the change lay largely in what organisations offered.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says such groups 'are seldom built to govern themselves', so they do not serve the same purposes.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no distinction between age groups; private amusements belong to the familiar story the author questions.
option_rationales.D: The author says the loss 'will not be repaired by urging individuals to join more', rejecting the approach, not its strength.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls the decline 'less a withdrawal from below than a transformation from above', and paragraph 5 says it 'will not be repaired by urging individuals to join more'. Remedies aimed at individuals miss the organisational cause.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the online groups option because paragraph 5 acknowledges that people still gather.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the remedies in paragraph 1 to the reinterpretation in paragraph 3 and the conclusion in paragraph 5.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It grants the faults of the older associations and the strengths of newer forms while restating what has been lost.
options.B: It abandons the earlier contrast and concludes that the old and the new organisations are of equal value.
options.C: It argues that excluding women and others was the main reason why the old federations went into decline.
options.D: It proposes that online groups be reorganised so that they can replace the federations of local branches.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It grants the faults of the older associations and the strengths of newer forms while restating what has been lost.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph still insists that newer forms are 'seldom built to govern themselves' and names 'the loss of a school of self-government'.
option_rationales.C: Exclusion is offered as a reason not to be nostalgic; the decline is explained in paragraph 3 by organisational choices.
option_rationales.D: No such proposal is made; the paragraph calls on organisations and funders to 'want members who turn up'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 concedes exclusion and stifling meetings, notes the new bodies' effectiveness and the ease of online gathering, and then restates that 'the loss of a school of self-government' is real.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the concessions as a change of position rather than as qualifications of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating concession from conclusion within one paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The fall in civic membership owes more to how organisations were rebuilt than to individual withdrawal, and it has cost citizens practice in governing themselves.
options.B: The decline of membership associations reflects organisations' choices about cheaper ways of raising money rather than any change in what ordinary people want.
options.C: Civic life has collapsed because people now prefer private amusements to the meetings and offices that earlier generations valued.
options.D: Professionally managed organisations are less legitimate than federations because they change laws without consulting their members.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The fall in civic membership owes more to how organisations were rebuilt than to individual withdrawal, and it has cost citizens practice in governing themselves.

option_rationales.B: This takes paragraph 3's reinterpretation but hardens its hedge ('may not have rejected participation at all') into a flat denial, and it leaves out the cost of the change that paragraphs 4 and 5 argue for.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'familiar story' of paragraph 1, which the author offers 'another way to read'.
option_rationales.D: The author grants that they are 'more effective at changing laws' and never calls them illegitimate; the loss is of self-government, not legitimacy.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the decline is 'a transformation from above', paragraph 4 says the federations taught skills of governance their successors do not, and paragraph 5 names the loss as 'a school of self-government'. The correct answer combines the cause and the cost.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the familiar story because the passage spends its first paragraph on it, or the legitimacy option because it echoes the critique of staff-run bodies.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures a view stated or touched on in the passage; the correct answer requires combining the causal reinterpretation with the claim about loss.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a step towards repairing the loss the passage describes?

options.A: A national charity doubles its number of supporters by advertising widely and begins to consult them through more frequent and detailed surveys.
options.B: A national charity gives local groups of its supporters budgets to manage and lets them elect delegates who vote on its policy.
options.C: An online forum lets supporters of a cause exchange views freely and at length, without officers, budgets or binding votes.
options.D: A public campaign urges every citizen to join at least one association in their town and to attend its meetings.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A national charity gives local groups of its supporters budgets to manage and lets them elect delegates who vote on its policy.

option_rationales.A: This deepens the model of paragraph 2, where supporters give money and are consulted 'through surveys', without meetings or elected officers.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says such groups 'are seldom built to govern themselves through elected officers and binding votes', which this forum lacks.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says the loss 'will not be repaired by urging individuals to join more'; this is the individual remedy the author rejects.

questions.explanation: The loss is of practice in running meetings, managing budgets and voting, and of a chain of elected representation from local to national (paragraph 4). A charity that gives local groups budgets and elected delegates restores both, and paragraph 5 asks organisations to 'want members who turn up'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the public campaign because it encourages attendance, without noticing that the author rejects remedies aimed at individuals.
questions.difficulty_reason: The campaign option sounds like participation; rejecting it needs the author's diagnosis that the cause lies with organisations.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how colonial clerks deliberately falsified reports in order to conceal the real causes of unrest from their superiors.
options.B: argue that the historians who read against the grain have mostly projected their own sympathies onto the people they study.
options.C: show that colonial archives are so distorted by official categories that historians should set them aside in favour of oral and material sources.
options.D: defend a way of reading official records while insisting that it has a boundary which honest historians must acknowledge.

questions.correct_answer: (D) defend a way of reading official records while insisting that it has a boundary which honest historians must acknowledge.

option_rationales.A: The passage says clerks recorded events in the administration's categories and 'declined to set down' causes; it never claims deliberate falsification or concealment from superiors.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls projection a 'quieter temptation', not the usual result, and paragraph 2 praises the method's achievements, so the claim that most such historians do this overstates the author's worry.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this is a reason to abandon the method' and that the archive 'can be cross-examined with great profit', so setting archives aside contradicts the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 praises reading against the grain for restoring 'motive and intelligence' to the governed; paragraphs 3 and 4 set out its limit ('Reading against the grain still reads the grain') and conclude that silences must sometimes be marked as absences. The passage therefore defends the method while drawing its boundary.
questions.common_misconception: Seizing on the critical paragraphs and missing that the author explicitly keeps the method.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options pick up the author's real worries but overstate them; the correct answer needs the praise and the limit held together.

questions.question: The statement 'Fear, in such documents, is a kind of evidence' (paragraph 2) suggests that

options.A: the anxious repetition of an official denial can show that the thing denied mattered to those involved.
options.B: officials' fears about rumours were usually justified, since most rumours in colonial districts later proved to be true.
options.C: the people who spread rumours did so mainly in order to frighten the officials who governed them.
options.D: historians should rely on emotional language in documents rather than on figures such as revenue collected or owed.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the anxious repetition of an official denial can show that the thing denied mattered to those involved.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the repeated denial shows the rumour 'mattered', not that it was true; whether rumours proved true is never discussed.
option_rationales.C: The motive of those who spread rumours is not given; the passage says only that the rumour probably mattered to them as well.
option_rationales.D: No ranking of emotional language over figures appears; the sentence concerns one kind of inference from official anxiety.

questions.explanation: The preceding sentence explains the point: officials' insistence, 'repeated across a dozen letters', that a rumour was baseless 'tells us that the rumour mattered a great deal to them'. Official anxiety is thus read as evidence of significance.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'mattered' into 'was true', or reading a motive into the rumour-spreaders.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence just before the quoted phrase explains it directly.

questions.question: Which one of the following best captures the meaning of 'Reading against the grain still reads the grain' as used in paragraph 3?

options.A: A critical reading of official records must begin with an uncritical reading, so that the historian first understands what the officials meant.
options.B: Historians who claim to read against the grain usually end up accepting the administration's categories without noticing that they have done so.
options.C: However critically the records are read, the method can only work with the people and events that those records happened to capture.
options.D: Records produced by the state are the only reliable source available for the lives of ordinary people under colonial rule.

questions.correct_answer: (C) However critically the records are read, the method can only work with the people and events that those records happened to capture.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph is about who is missing from the record, not about the stages of reading; nothing describes a preliminary uncritical reading.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 credits the method with genuinely restoring motive to the governed, so the author does not think it collapses back into accepting official categories.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 recommends other sources, such as songs and the remains of houses, so the author does not treat state records as the only reliable source.

questions.explanation: The sentence that follows explains the phrase: the method recovers only voices 'who left a trace by colliding with power', while those who never collided 'remain exactly where the archive left them, outside it'. The grain, the records themselves, still fixes what can be found.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the phrase as a charge that the method fails, rather than as a statement of its limit.
questions.difficulty_reason: The first wrong option is a plausible reading of the words that the rest of the passage rules out.

questions.question: A historian studying a colonial district finds that its records say almost nothing about the farm work done by women. Which response would the author of the passage most likely endorse?

options.A: Generalising about all the district's women from the few court cases in which women appear as defendants or as petitioners.
options.B: Stating plainly that the records are silent, and turning to evidence such as surviving tools, field layouts and remembered work songs.
options.C: Treating the silence itself as proof that officials deliberately suppressed women's resistance, and reconstructing that resistance from it.
options.D: Concluding that because the district's records rarely mention it, women's farm work was probably a minor part of the local economy.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Stating plainly that the records are silent, and turning to evidence such as surviving tools, field layouts and remembered work songs.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the voices recovered belong to those who collided with power; generalising from them to those who never collided is the error the author describes.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 warns that a silence 'is not always a hidden voice waiting to be decoded', and paragraph 3 warns against filling a thin record with the historian's sympathies.
option_rationales.D: This reads along the grain, treating the archive's categories as 'descriptions of reality', which paragraph 1 says reproduces the administration's view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that a silence may be 'simply an absence', that the honest response is 'to mark it as one', and that the historian can turn to sources not produced by the same gaze, naming 'remembered songs', 'tools' and 'the shape of fields'. The correct answer applies exactly this advice.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that sounds most critical of the archive (deliberate suppression), which the author treats as a temptation rather than a method.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option applies a different error the passage describes; the solver must map all three and see that only the correct answer follows paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, what a public statue records most precisely is

options.A: a choice, made by certain people at a certain time, to honour its subject in that place.
options.B: the settled judgement of an entire community about the moral worth of the person it depicts.
