options.C: the events that its subject took part in, as they were understood when those events occurred.
options.D: the main achievements of its subject, set down in a form that passers-by can easily read.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a choice, made by certain people at a certain time, to honour its subject in that place.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 attributes the decision to 'particular people', often committees with their own purposes, not to an entire community's settled judgement.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 notes that many statues were raised 'long after the events they commemorate', so they do not record how the events were understood at the time.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a statue records 'almost nothing about the life of its subject', only a name, dates and perhaps a line of praise.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states: 'What it records very precisely is a decision, taken at a particular moment by particular people, to honour that subject in that place.' The correct answer paraphrases this sentence.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a statue records its subject's life or a community-wide verdict.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The discussion of the explanatory plaque in paragraph 4 serves mainly to

options.A: show that plaques are the best available means of preserving a statue's value as historical evidence.
options.B: challenge the assumption that keeping a statue and adding text beside it is a choice free of anyone's judgement.
options.C: illustrate how committees in the past used inscriptions to assert the standing of a group or cause.
options.D: argue that statues of figures held in disrepute should always be removed rather than explained.

questions.correct_answer: (B) challenge the assumption that keeping a statue and adding text beside it is a choice free of anyone's judgement.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a museum 'may come closer to keeping the evidence', so the author does not rank plaques as the best means.
option_rationales.C: The plaque in paragraph 4 is a present-day compromise; the committees asserting standing appear in paragraph 2 and concern the statues themselves.
option_rationales.D: The author never says statues should always be removed; paragraph 3 warns that removal also loses useful evidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens by saying the plaque 'is often presented as the neutral option. It is not.' It then explains that a plaque 'is also an editorial act', requiring someone to decide what it says and whose judgement it expresses.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the plaque discussion as an endorsement of plaques, or linking it to the historical committees.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is announced in the first two sentences of the paragraph.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the claim that removing a statue 'erases history' as

options.A: correct only for statues raised soon after the events they depict, since later statues have no value as evidence of anything.
options.B: beside the point, because statues contain no evidence of any kind and their removal therefore costs a society nothing at all.
options.C: mistaken about what is lost, since removal ends an act of honour and some evidence of past values, not knowledge of the subject.
options.D: broadly correct, because a statue is the main means by which most ordinary citizens come to learn about the leading figures of their nation's past.

questions.correct_answer: (C) mistaken about what is lost, since removal ends an act of honour and some evidence of past values, not knowledge of the subject.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says later statues are good evidence 'about the people who raised it', so the claim that they have no evidential value is false to the passage.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says a removed statue 'also removes evidence of what an earlier generation chose to celebrate', so the author thinks removal has a real cost.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a statue 'is not a history lesson' and records almost nothing about its subject, which contradicts this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the charge 'loses much of its force' because removal 'does not alter what happened' and the sources that tell the subject's story remain. But it adds that removal 'also removes evidence of what an earlier generation chose to celebrate'. The author thus thinks the charge misidentifies the loss without thinking removal costs nothing.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that rejects the charge outright, missing the author's concession in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option matches the author's rejection of the charge but ignores the concession.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the views expressed in the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: The wording of an explanatory plaque reflects the judgement of whoever was given the task of writing it.
options.B: A statue raised long after its subject died may reveal more about its builders' concerns than about its subject.
options.C: A generation may legitimately decide to stop honouring a figure whom an earlier generation, with purposes of its own, chose to honour.
options.D: A statue moved from a public square into a museum gallery goes on honouring its subject much as it did before.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A statue moved from a public square into a museum gallery goes on honouring its subject much as it did before.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says someone must decide 'whose judgement it expresses', calling the plaque 'an editorial act', so this is consistent.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says such statues are 'better evidence about the people who raised it than about the person it depicts', so this is consistent.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'every generation is entitled to reconsider whom it honours', so this is consistent with the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a museum, which displays the date and purpose of a statue's making, 'may come closer to keeping the evidence without continuing the honour'. The claim that the moved statue goes on honouring its subject as before contradicts this.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the phrase 'without continuing the honour' and assuming relocation changes nothing.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three statements are paraphrases of the passage; the exception contradicts one clause in the last paragraph.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the critics mentioned at the start of paragraph 2 is best described as

options.A: studied neutrality: reporting their charge without indicating whether it is persuasive.
options.B: dismissive disagreement: treating their charge of anachronism as a basic misunderstanding of how history is actually written.
options.C: unreserved support: endorsing both their charge and the claim that national history is simply invented.
options.D: qualified agreement: accepting their central charge while rejecting one conclusion some of them draw from it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) qualified agreement: accepting their central charge while rejecting one conclusion some of them draw from it.

option_rationales.A: The author explicitly evaluates the critics, agreeing on the main charge and saying the criticism 'is often pressed further than it can go'.
option_rationales.B: The author says that 'on the main charge they are right', which rules out dismissive disagreement.
option_rationales.C: The author says the claim that the materials are 'simply invented' does not follow, so the support has reservations.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'on the main charge they are right' and then 'But the criticism is often pressed further than it can go', rejecting the inference that national history's materials are invented. That is agreement with a stated limit.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the 'But' and reading the paragraph as either full agreement or rejection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is stated in two consecutive sentences.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the 'coherence' of a national history of the kind it criticises is achieved chiefly by

options.A: omitting or condemning those parts of the past that pointed towards other political outcomes.
options.B: relying on poets and chroniclers who were themselves committed to the idea of a unified nation.
options.C: describing how rival political projects were peacefully absorbed into the nation once it was formed.
options.D: tracing real continuities of language, worship and trade over many centuries of the region's history.

questions.correct_answer: (A) omitting or condemning those parts of the past that pointed towards other political outcomes.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the poets wrote in dialects their descendants can barely read; nothing says they were committed to national unity.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says such projects become 'obstacles overcome' or are left out; nothing is said about peaceful absorption.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says noticing continuities is not the mistake; paragraph 3 attributes the coherence to narrowing the cast, not to the continuities themselves.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says whatever does not fit 'must be either left out or cast as a failure of loyalty' and concludes that 'The coherence of the story is purchased by narrowing its cast.' The regions, communities and rival projects it lists are all alternatives to the eventual nation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the continuities option, because the passage does accept them, without noticing that the author separates them from the source of coherence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The first wrong option uses the author's own accepted point in the wrong role.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that older continuities shaped which communities later found it easy to imagine themselves as one?

options.A: Some medieval rulers spoke several languages and held lands in regions that now belong to two or three different modern countries.
options.B: National histories in many countries trace the nation back to a legendary founder whose actual existence cannot be confirmed from any surviving written or archaeological source.
options.C: Studies of several regions found that national feeling formed just as readily within borders that cut across older zones of shared language, worship and trade.
options.D: Many modern states, once formed, required a single standard language in their schools and steadily suppressed regional dialects in all official business.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Studies of several regions found that national feeling formed just as readily within borders that cut across older zones of shared language, worship and trade.

option_rationales.A: This matches paragraph 1's point about rulers recast as founders and is consistent with the author; it does not bear on whether older continuities shaped later communities.
option_rationales.B: This supports the charge of backward projection in paragraph 1; it is silent on whether real continuities shaped later national communities.
option_rationales.D: This describes what states did after they formed; it does not show that older continuities failed to shape which communities could imagine themselves as one.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 claims that languages, worship, trade and songs 'plainly did shape which communities later found it easy, and which found it hard, to imagine themselves as one'. If national feeling formed just as readily across those older zones as within them, the continuities made no difference to which communities could imagine themselves as one, and the claim is undercut. The other options concern a different claim or a later period.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that criticises national histories, and so feels like it opposes something in the passage, without checking which claim it bears on.
questions.difficulty_reason: All options concern nationalism; the solver must isolate one specific causal claim and test each option against it.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the structure of the passage?

options.A: A criticism of national history is stated, the criticism is rejected as anachronistic, examples of its errors are given, and national history is defended.
options.B: A way of writing history is described, a criticism of it is accepted but limited, the harm of the error is traced, and an alternative proposed.
options.C: Two rival accounts of the origins of nations are compared, evidence for each is weighed, and the author concludes that both are partly mistaken.
options.D: A historical example is narrated in detail, a general principle is drawn from it, and the principle is applied to the teaching of history in schools.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A way of writing history is described, a criticism of it is accepted but limited, the harm of the error is traced, and an alternative proposed.

option_rationales.A: The author agrees with the critics' main charge in paragraph 2 and ends by proposing a different kind of history, not by defending national history.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not set out two accounts of national origins; it discusses one way of writing history and one criticism of it.
option_rationales.D: No single example is narrated; paragraph 1 describes a general practice, and schools are mentioned only in passing in paragraph 4.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the practice of reading the past backwards from the nation; paragraph 2 accepts the charge of anachronism but rejects the claim that the materials are invented; paragraph 3 explains the consequences of the teleological arrangement; paragraph 4 proposes a history that 'would keep the continuities and restore the alternatives'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the limited agreement in paragraph 2, or treating the brief mention of schools as the passage's destination.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires following all four paragraphs and recognising the partial concession.

questions.question: According to the passage, a mistake made independently by many witnesses differs from an individual slip of memory in that it

options.A: becomes a feature of shared understanding that needs to be explained rather than merely corrected.
options.B: can be corrected more easily, because the written records usually show where the witnesses went wrong.
options.C: is less likely to be an error at all, since agreement among witnesses usually indicates that they are right.
options.D: reveals the date of the event more reliably than an official document written at the time could do.

questions.correct_answer: (A) becomes a feature of shared understanding that needs to be explained rather than merely corrected.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 does not say shared mistakes are easier to correct; it says they call 'for explanation rather than mere correction'.
option_rationales.C: In the mining-town case the shared dating is 'simply wrong' about dates, so agreement does not make the account accurate.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'As evidence about dates, these accounts are simply wrong'; their value lies in meanings, not in dating.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 contrasts individual slips, 'scattered more or less at random', with the same mistake made by many people, which 'becomes a social fact, something that calls for explanation rather than mere correction'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that agreement among witnesses must make them right.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 3.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the phrase 'a social fact' most nearly means

options.A: an event that is confirmed by both oral testimony and official written records.
options.B: a falsehood that a community spreads deliberately in order to mislead outsiders.
options.C: something true of the community's shared outlook, as distinct from a single person's lapse.
options.D: a statistic about how often older people make errors when recalling dates.

questions.correct_answer: (C) something true of the community's shared outlook, as distinct from a single person's lapse.

option_rationales.A: The shared mistake is contradicted by the records, so 'social fact' cannot mean an event that the records confirm.
option_rationales.B: The witnesses err 'independently', and the passage gives no hint that the mistake is deliberate or aimed at outsiders.
option_rationales.D: The phrase describes one shared mistake that calls for explanation, not a general rate of error among the elderly.

questions.explanation: The phrase contrasts the shared mistake with individual slips 'scattered more or less at random'. Because it is shared, it reflects how the community understood events and 'calls for explanation', so it is a fact about the group rather than about any one memory.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'fact' as 'true event' and missing that the fact is the shared mistake itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning follows from the contrast in the same paragraph.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that, in the mining-town case, the records showing when the strike and the flood occurred

options.A: are of little further use to the historian once the residents' interviews have been recorded and analysed.
options.B: are needed to establish that the residents' dating is mistaken before that mistake can be interpreted.
options.C: should be doubted, since so many residents interviewed separately agreed on a different account of the dates.
options.D: show how the residents felt about the mine's owners during the years between the two events.

questions.correct_answer: (B) are needed to establish that the residents' dating is mistaken before that mistake can be interpreted.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the strongest work uses both kinds of source together, 'the record correcting the memory', so the records stay useful.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the residents' accounts are 'simply wrong' about dates, so the author trusts the records on that point.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says documents 'tend to record events' while the meanings people attached to them rarely reach an official file.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'An error can be interpreted only once it has been established that it is an error, and that usually requires the very documents' oral historians may dismiss. In the mining-town case, the records are what show that the strike and flood were years apart.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that credits documents with revealing feelings, which the passage assigns to testimony.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the general point in paragraph 4 to the case in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: In mining towns, residents tend to merge separate disasters because they blame the owners of the mines for both.
options.B: Oral testimony is more trustworthy than written records, because documents generally leave out the meanings that people gave to events.
options.C: Older people's memories of local events are usually inaccurate, so oral history should be confined to questions of meaning.
options.D: Shared mistakes in oral testimony can reveal how a community understood its past, once documents have shown them to be mistakes.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Shared mistakes in oral testimony can reveal how a community understood its past, once documents have shown them to be mistakes.

option_rationales.A: This generalises the hypothetical case, which the author offers only as an illustration of a wider point about patterned error.
option_rationales.B: The passage concedes that a single witness is 'frequently unreliable' and calls for the two sources to be used together, not ranked.
option_rationales.C: The passage never confines oral history to meaning; it says errors must first be established and that the two sources correct each other.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 turns the usual objection by showing that shared errors reveal meaning; paragraph 3 explains why patterned errors are evidence; paragraph 4 adds that interpretation depends on first establishing the error from documents. The correct answer holds both the claim and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that ranks oral sources above written ones, which overstates the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is too narrow (the illustration) and one overstates the thesis; the correct answer needs the condition in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The example of the harvest failure and the revolt in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the kind of speculative question that the author agrees has no place in serious history.
options.B: demonstrate that economic hardship is the most common cause of popular revolts in history.
options.C: show that an ordinary causal claim already contains a counterfactual within it.
options.D: suggest that historians usually overstate the importance of single events such as failed harvests.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that an ordinary causal claim already contains a counterfactual within it.

option_rationales.A: The author uses the example against the critics of counterfactuals; it is an ordinary causal claim, not idle speculation.
option_rationales.B: The example illustrates the logic of causal claims; the passage makes no general claim about the causes of revolts.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in paragraph 1 says historians overstate single causes; the example is about what any causal claim implies.

questions.explanation: Immediately after the example the author says: 'Every causal claim carries such a counterfactual inside it', concluding that the historian who rejects counterfactuals 'has not avoided them'. The example illustrates that point.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that any 'what if' example must be one the author disapproves of.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence after the example.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a book that traces how the whole of the following century would have unfolded had one particular battle gone the other way as

options.A: of little historical value, because the consequences it describes lie far beyond the horizon over which they could be judged.
options.B: legitimate history, since it does openly what every historian making a causal claim does implicitly.
options.C: valuable, provided the battle's outcome was something that people at the time actually contemplated as possible.
options.D: useful mainly for showing that the actual outcome of the battle was inevitable from the start.

questions.correct_answer: (A) of little historical value, because the consequences it describes lie far beyond the horizon over which they could be judged.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says causal claims imply counterfactuals, but paragraph 2 calls century-long alternatives 'closer to fiction than to history'.
option_rationales.C: Meeting the first constraint is not enough; paragraph 2 says the horizon must also be short, and a century fails that test.
option_rationales.D: A counterfactual is used in paragraph 4 to defeat claims of inevitability, not to establish them, so this reverses the author's view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 sets a short horizon as the second constraint, because contingencies multiply until 'the alternative world becomes as indeterminate as the future', and says imagining 'a whole century transformed by one changed battle is closer to fiction than to history'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that makes the book valuable because a contested battle seems to satisfy the plausibility constraint, forgetting the second constraint.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option satisfies one of the two constraints; the solver must apply both.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's position on how counterfactuals can defeat claims of inevitability?

options.A: Many causal explanations offered by historians rest on assumptions about the behaviour of societies that the historians never state explicitly.
options.B: Historians who use explicit counterfactuals have frequently disagreed with one another about what would actually have followed from an altered decision or battle.
options.C: Politicians often describe outcomes as inevitable mainly in order to discourage people from questioning decisions that have already been taken.
options.D: Options seriously debated at the time have often proved, on fuller evidence, to have been out of reach given the forces at work.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Options seriously debated at the time have often proved, on fuller evidence, to have been out of reach given the forces at work.

option_rationales.A: This is exactly what paragraph 3 asserts about ordinary causal explanation, so it agrees with the author rather than weakening the position.
option_rationales.B: The author concedes that 'nothing reliable can be said about where the alternative would have led', so disagreement about consequences does not touch the claim.
option_rationales.C: The motive behind claims of inevitability is irrelevant to whether showing an open alternative defeats them; if anything this supports the author's interest in testing them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that showing an alternative was 'open, contemplated and within reach' defeats a claim of inevitability, and paragraph 2 treats what contemporaries 'actually contemplated' as the mark of a plausible alternative. If contemplated options were often not really within reach, contemporary debate would be poor evidence of openness, and the method would lose its force.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about disagreement over consequences, which the author has already conceded and which does not bear on inevitability.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the criterion in paragraph 2 to the use in paragraph 4 and seeing that two wrong options restate or sidestep the author's concessions.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, for the author, the main advantage of an explicit counterfactual over an ordinary causal explanation is that it

options.A: allows the historian to establish with some confidence what would have followed from a different decision.
options.B: brings into the open the assumptions about how events connect that the causal explanation leaves tacit.
options.C: depends on fewer untested assumptions about which social pressures are strong and which choices are free.
options.D: lets the historian fill gaps in the evidence by reconstructing events that left no trace in the records.

questions.correct_answer: (B) brings into the open the assumptions about how events connect that the causal explanation leaves tacit.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the counterfactual is 'less a tool for discovering what would have happened', and that often nothing reliable can be said about it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the ordinary explanation rests on 'exactly the same assumptions', so the counterfactual does not depend on fewer of them.
option_rationales.D: Nowhere does the author recommend counterfactuals as a way of supplying missing evidence; their role is to test and expose, not to fill gaps.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'What the explicit counterfactual offers is not freedom from such assumptions but exposure of them, so that a reader can see what the explanation depends on and dispute it.' The ordinary explanation 'simply leaves them unstated'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing exposing assumptions with reducing them, which the author explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The leading wrong option differs from the correct answer only in degree (fewer assumptions versus exposed assumptions), a distinction the author draws in one sentence.

questions.question: According to the passage, the writers among whom the phrase 'The Middle Ages' took hold regarded the centuries it named as

options.A: a stretch of years grouped together merely for convenience, without any particular judgement implied.
options.B: a time of steady decline that began long before the ancient world had reached its height.
options.C: a gap between the learning of the ancient world and its revival in their own time.
options.D: the period in which universities, cathedrals and towns first laid the ground for later achievement.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a gap between the learning of the ancient world and its revival in their own time.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says most period names are 'compressed arguments' and that the period 'has been judged before it has been studied'.
option_rationales.B: The writers saw the period as an interval after ancient achievement, not as a decline that began before the ancient world peaked.
option_rationales.D: This is the view of later historians in paragraph 2, who showed that the original judgement does not fit the evidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says these writers believed they were reviving ancient learning 'after a long interruption' and 'saw the intervening thousand years as an interval, a middle that mattered chiefly as the gap between two moments of achievement'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the later historians' view to the writers who coined the name.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence; one wrong option is drawn from the next paragraph.

questions.question: The passage suggests that calling a period in the history of a region far from Europe 'medieval' is problematic chiefly because it

options.A: wrongly suggests that the region was less advanced than Europe during the same span of years.
options.B: may lead historians to seek a pattern such as decline and rebirth that the region's own evidence does not show.
options.C: implies that the region had no universities, cathedrals or growing towns during the centuries the label covers.
options.D: uses a European word for a period that the region's own historians had already named differently.

questions.correct_answer: (B) may lead historians to seek a pattern such as decline and rebirth that the region's own evidence does not show.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 objects to importing a chronology and its expectations, not to a comparison of advancement between regions.
option_rationales.C: Universities and cathedrals are mentioned in paragraph 2 as achievements of the European period, and paragraph 3 never says the label implies their absence elsewhere.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about names given by the region's own historians; its objection concerns the expectations the label carries.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the exported label imports 'a chronology built for one part of the world' and invites the historian 'to look there for whatever the label suggests, such as a decline and a later rebirth, whether or not the evidence of that region points to anything of the kind'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about relative advancement, which sounds like a common objection but is not the one the passage makes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options offer familiar objections to Eurocentric labels that the passage does not make.

questions.question: Which of the following practices would the author most likely regard as following the recommendation in the final paragraph?

options.A: A historian replaces all named periods with numbered centuries, so that no judgement about the character of an age enters the account.
options.B: A historian chooses a period name at the outset of a project and then organises the search for sources around the features the name suggests.
options.C: A historian refuses to group years together at all and narrates events year by year, leaving readers to form their own periods.
options.D: A historian keeps an established name for an era, checks whether its implied features appear in the sources, and drops it where they do not.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A historian keeps an established name for an era, checks whether its implied features appear in the sources, and drops it where they do not.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says centuries are 'as arbitrary as any label' and bring their own habit of assigning each hundred years a single character.
option_rationales.B: This is the danger named in the last sentence: 'letting the label arrive before the research and decide what the research will look for'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'History cannot be written without some way of grouping years together', so refusing all grouping goes against the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 recommends keeping period names 'while holding them lightly, treating each as a hypothesis ... to be tested against the evidence and abandoned where it fails'. The correct answer describes exactly that procedure.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the centuries option because it seems to remove bias, which the author explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option corresponds to a position the author considers and rejects in the last paragraph.

questions.question: Each of the following can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: Dividing the past into numbered centuries would avoid the distortions that named periods introduce into historical writing.
options.B: Achievements of the period called the Middle Ages contributed to developments that came after it.
options.C: A name for a period can go on shaping how the period is perceived after the view behind the name has been abandoned.
options.D: Some period names carry a judgement about the worth of the period that was made before the period was closely studied.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Dividing the past into numbered centuries would avoid the distortions that named periods introduce into historical writing.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says those centuries 'laid much of the ground on which later achievements stood', so this can be inferred.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the name 'has survived the demolition of the view that produced it' and 'continues to whisper', so this can be inferred.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says of 'The Middle Ages' that 'A period named in this way has been judged before it has been studied', so this can be inferred.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'the alternatives are not innocent either: centuries are as arbitrary as any label' and carry their own habit of giving each hundred years 'a single character'. So numbered centuries would bring distortions of their own rather than avoiding them.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because the author criticises named periods, a numerical scheme must be the author's preferred remedy.
questions.difficulty_reason: The exception sounds like a natural conclusion of the critique and is refuted only by a concession in the last paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Heritage is a legitimate celebratory use of the past, but it becomes objectionable when it passes off its selective story as historical knowledge.
options.B: Heritage falsifies the past for commercial ends, and historians are right to treat it with suspicion and to resist its growing popularity.
options.C: Public money should be moved from heritage attractions back to archives and libraries, which serve the purposes of serious historical study.
options.D: Heritage and history are in the end the same activity, since both make use of the same buildings, objects and stories from the past.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Heritage is a legitimate celebratory use of the past, but it becomes objectionable when it passes off its selective story as historical knowledge.

option_rationales.B: The author says the critique 'misses' the nature of heritage, and paragraph 5 rejects 'contempt' as the right relation, so this reverses the argument.
option_rationales.C: Redirected funding is one example in paragraph 4 of heritage claiming history's authority; the passage does not make a general funding proposal.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the two share materials 'but they put them to different uses', and paragraph 5 rejects 'merger', so they are not the same activity.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that heritage is commemoration and should be judged as such; paragraph 4 locates the trouble where heritage 'claims the authority of history'; paragraph 5 defends the line between 'celebration that knows itself to be celebration and celebration that presents itself as knowledge'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the historians' sneer in paragraph 1 as the author's own view, or treating one example as the thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the defence of heritage and its limit together across all five paragraphs.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the remark that heritage 'usually offers the past with the smell taken out' most nearly means that heritage

options.A: tends to attract visitors who have no real interest in the physical conditions of earlier times.
options.B: relies on modern materials and methods when it restores old buildings, cottages and other sites.
options.C: presents the past in an agreeable form from which its unpleasant realities have been removed.
options.D: concentrates on the visual appearance of old buildings rather than on how people actually used them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) presents the past in an agreeable form from which its unpleasant realities have been removed.

option_rationales.A: The phrase describes what heritage presents, not who visits; paragraph 3 even says visitors' curiosity can be awakened.
option_rationales.B: Restoration techniques are not discussed; the phrase follows a list of ways heritage makes the past 'comfortable'.
option_rationales.D: The phrase concerns removing what is unpleasant, as paragraph 3's example of open drains shows, not a preference for appearance over use.

questions.explanation: The phrase follows the statement that heritage does 'select, simplify and flatter' and the description of a past 'made comfortable ... stripped of everything that might disturb a family on a day out'. Paragraph 3's omitted 'open drains' illustrates the same point.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the metaphor too literally, as a remark about restoration or about the senses.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative phrase is explained by the sentences around it.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the historians described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: wholly approving: sharing both their observations about heritage and their conclusion that it is a falsification of the past.
options.B: partly sympathetic: granting that their observations are accurate while holding that they misjudge what heritage is for.
options.C: openly contemptuous: treating their objections as snobbery towards popular pleasures that deserves no serious reply.
options.D: indifferent: reporting their view without indicating whether it is accurate or mistaken in any respect.

questions.correct_answer: (B) partly sympathetic: granting that their observations are accurate while holding that they misjudge what heritage is for.

option_rationales.A: The author says 'What the critique misses is that heritage is not attempting to be history', which rejects their conclusion.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'The critics are not wrong about the facts' and replies to them at length, which is not contempt.
option_rationales.D: The author evaluates the critics explicitly, accepting their facts in paragraph 1 and rejecting their judgement in paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 ends: 'The critics are not wrong about the facts. Heritage does select, simplify and flatter', and paragraph 2 begins: 'What the critique misses is that heritage is not attempting to be history'. The author accepts the observations but rejects the verdict.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the word 'sneer' as the author's verdict on the historians, rather than a description of their stance.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two attitudes are expressed in adjacent paragraphs and must be combined.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that, in the author's view, a heritage display becomes objectionable chiefly when it

options.A: charges visitors for admission and earns most of its income from the sale of replicas and souvenirs.
options.B: draws large numbers of visitors who had shown no interest in the past before they arrived.
options.C: leaves out unpleasant features of the past, such as poor sanitation or the crowded quarters of servants.
options.D: offers its selective celebration as an account of what the past was really like.

questions.correct_answer: (D) offers its selective celebration as an account of what the past was really like.

option_rationales.A: Tickets and gift shops are part of the critics' complaint in paragraph 1; the author never locates the trouble in commerce.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 treats this as a possible service to history, since curiosity 'awakened there leads some of them on to the harder questions'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'The tidying that heritage performs is ... not itself the offence', and the restored village that omits drains 'is doing what celebrations do'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'The trouble begins' when heritage 'claims the authority of history', presenting its story 'not as a celebration but as an account of how things really were'. Paragraph 3 has already said that omission alone is not the offence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the omission option, because paragraph 1 lists it among heritage's faults, without noticing that paragraph 3 explicitly excuses it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The leading wrong option names a fault the author concedes exists but denies is the offence; the distinction needs paragraphs 1, 3 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's suggestion that heritage can serve history as a doorway?

options.A: Some heritage sites present events in ways that professional historians have shown to be inaccurate or misleadingly incomplete.
options.B: Several historians have said that their interest in the past first began during a childhood visit to a restored house or village.
options.C: Among visitors to heritage sites who later took up serious historical reading, nearly all had already been keen readers of history before they first visited.
options.D: Heritage sites in many countries attract far more visitors each year than public archives, libraries and university history departments combined.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Among visitors to heritage sites who later took up serious historical reading, nearly all had already been keen readers of history before they first visited.

option_rationales.A: The author already concedes that heritage selects and flatters; inaccuracy does not show that visits fail to lead people on to history.
option_rationales.B: This supports rather than weakens the doorway suggestion, since it describes curiosity awakened by heritage leading to history.
option_rationales.D: Visitor numbers say nothing about whether visits awaken curiosity that leads on to history; large crowds are compatible with the author's suggestion.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 suggests that 'the curiosity awakened there leads some of them on to the harder questions that history asks'. If those who went on to read history were almost all readers already, the visits did not awaken the curiosity; it was there before, and the causal claim is undercut.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the inaccuracy option because it criticises heritage, though it does not bear on the doorway claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying a causal claim and recognising that only a pre-existing interest breaks the causal link.

questions.question: According to the passage, what the peace agreements described in paragraph 2 actually established was

options.A: a requirement that citizens put the events of the conflict out of their minds.
options.B: a public record naming those responsible for the worst crimes of the conflict.
options.C: a ban on private remembrance of the dead in homes, kitchens and graveyards.
options.D: a limit on how past wrongs could be used in courts and in political life.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a limit on how past wrongs could be used in courts and in political life.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'No decree can make people forget' and that none of these arrangements 'tried to'.
option_rationales.B: The arrangements kept 'the question of who had done what to whom' out of the courts and assemblies, so they did not name the guilty.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the past 'continued to be remembered in kitchens and graveyards', so private remembrance was not banned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the agreements established 'something narrower: a rule about the public use of the past', under which crimes would not be prosecuted beyond a point and grievances would not become the basis of political campaigns.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the label 'forgetting', which the passage calls misleading.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in paragraph 2 after the author corrects a common description.

questions.question: The passage implies that those who treat remembrance as an unqualified duty after a conflict

options.A: take for granted that detailed public remembering always helps former enemies to live together.
options.B: generally belong to the side that lost the conflict and wish to see the victors punished.
options.C: would accept a temporary silence if they were shown that it had preserved the peace.
options.D: are mistaken in thinking that the truth about past crimes has any moral importance.

questions.correct_answer: (A) take for granted that detailed public remembering always helps former enemies to live together.

option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about which side holds this view; the injunction is described as almost universally taken for granted.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage indicates how such people would respond to evidence; the author only examines the assumption behind their view.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says 'The case for this view is strong, and nothing that follows is meant to deny it', so the author does not deny the moral importance of truth.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the view 'carries an assumption that deserves examination: that remembering, in public and in detail, is always what allows former enemies to go on living side by side'. The rest of the passage questions that assumption.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the author's examination of an assumption as a rejection of the whole case for remembrance.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong option that the author rejects truth is tempting because the passage questions the injunction; paragraph 1's concession rules it out.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the argument of the passage?

options.A: It shows that full public reckoning after a conflict has always reopened the war that it was intended to bring to an end.
options.B: It argues that the case for agreed silence turns on timing, being strongest soon after a conflict and weaker a generation on.
options.C: It explains why the victims of a conflict, rather than its perpetrators, bear most of the cost of an agreed public silence.
options.D: It offers historical examples of societies that made peace by agreeing not to prosecute those responsible for the conflict.

questions.correct_answer: (B) It argues that the case for agreed silence turns on timing, being strongest soon after a conflict and weaker a generation on.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says a reckoning 'may reopen the war', a possibility in fragile conditions, not something that has always happened.
option_rationales.C: The uneven distribution of costs is the subject of paragraph 4, which begins 'For the costs of silence do not fall evenly'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2, not paragraph 3, refers to such societies, and neither paragraph gives particular examples.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens: 'Whether such a rule is wise seems to depend less on the principle involved than on timing', then contrasts the fragile first years, when reckoning 'may reopen the war', with the situation 'A generation later'. This sets up the conclusion that silence is provisional.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the content of paragraph 3 with that of the paragraphs on either side of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options describe neighbouring paragraphs; one overstates the hedged claim.

questions.question: Thirty years after a civil war ended in an amnesty, the country's institutions are stable and the former combatants are elderly. The grandchildren of victims ask for the sealed records of the war to be opened, and the government refuses, saying that the peace was built on silence. The author would most likely regard the refusal as

options.A: justified, because an agreed silence that has kept the peace for thirty years ought to be preserved for as long as possible.
options.B: hard to justify, since the amnesty was defensible as a provisional arrangement and the conditions that once supported it have largely passed.
options.C: the predictable result of a mistake made at the start, since the records should never have been sealed in the first place.
options.D: acceptable only if opening the records were certain to lead to the prosecution of every surviving perpetrator of the war.

questions.correct_answer: (B) hard to justify, since the amnesty was defensible as a provisional arrangement and the conditions that once supported it have largely passed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 warns that 'A peace that rests indefinitely on such an asymmetry is unlikely to remain a peace in any full sense', and paragraph 3 says that a generation later 'the balance may look quite different', so the author does not favour keeping the silence as long as possible.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 allows that early silence may be wise when 'the institutions of the new order are fragile', so the author does not condemn the original sealing.
option_rationales.D: The passage nowhere makes prosecution a condition for breaking silence; the request here is for disclosure, which the author's argument supports in these conditions.

questions.explanation: The scenario matches paragraph 3's later stage: 'The armed men have grown old, the institutions have settled', and the children of victims 'may reasonably ask why the silence ... should still protect those who did the harm'. Paragraph 5 treats agreed silence as 'a provisional arrangement whose legitimacy depends on what happens to it later', and paragraph 4 warns against a peace that rests 'indefinitely' on the victims' silence. The author would therefore find the refusal hard to justify.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that condemns the original sealing because the author is sympathetic to the victims, forgetting that the author defends early silence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each capture half of the author's view (early silence defended, later silence questioned); only the correct answer holds both.

questions.question: The author's claim that the worst outcome is 'a silence that becomes permanent by default' implies that

options.A: whether a silence is acceptable depends partly on its remaining a deliberate and revisable choice rather than an unexamined habit.
options.B: a permanent silence is a worse outcome for a society than the renewed conflict that might follow a full public reckoning.
options.C: any silence is acceptable, however long it lasts, provided that every party to the conflict agreed to it at the outset.
options.D: the passing of the generation that fought a conflict automatically brings to an end any justification for continued silence.

questions.correct_answer: (A) whether a silence is acceptable depends partly on its remaining a deliberate and revisable choice rather than an unexamined habit.

option_rationales.B: The passage compares kinds of silence with one another; it never ranks permanent silence against renewed war, which paragraph 3 treats as a grave danger.
option_rationales.C: Agreement at the outset is not enough: paragraph 5 makes legitimacy depend 'on what happens to it later', and paragraph 4 warns that indefinite silence decays.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says only that 'the balance may look quite different' a generation later; making the change automatic turns a weighing into a rule.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 contrasts a silence 'that a society chooses, and later chooses to break' with one 'that no one ever decides to keep'. What makes the second the worst is that it was never chosen or reconsidered, so acceptability depends partly on silence being a deliberate and revisable decision.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'automatically' option, which matches the direction of the author's argument but turns the author's hedged weighing into a rule.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is close to the author's direction of thought but changes degree or scope; the correct answer depends on the phrase 'no one ever decides to keep'.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that unplanned uses of colonial railways by ordinary people show that the benefits of empire outweighed its costs.
options.B: demonstrate that, taken as a whole, colonial railways did more harm than good to the societies through which their lines happened to run.
options.C: explain why colonial governments chose railway routes that served export trade and military control rather than local need.
options.D: show that weighing empire as a ledger misleads, since imposed works are not gifts and the question of who decided is left out.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that weighing empire as a ledger misleads, since imposed works are not gifts and the question of who decided is left out.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says these uses cut 'against the ledger rather than in its favour', so the option reverses the author's point.
option_rationales.B: The author never totals the columns; paragraph 1 says the exchange 'can continue indefinitely', and the passage declines to settle it either way.
option_rationales.C: Route choice is one illustration in paragraph 2; it supports the argument about gifts but is far too narrow to be the purpose.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the ledger debate, paragraph 2 argues that its credits are not gifts, paragraph 3 concedes real local use but turns it against the ledger, and paragraph 4 names what the ledger omits: 'the question of who decided'. The purpose is to expose the flaws in the ledger approach itself.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author to be on the critics' side of the ledger, or mistaking the railway illustration for the point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must see that the author rejects the framing rather than joining one side; two wrong options take a side and one is a detail.

questions.question: According to the passage, the ledger debate 'can continue indefinitely' because

options.A: defenders and critics of empire agree about the facts but hold sharply different moral principles about foreign rule.
options.B: most of the benefits of colonial railways appeared only after the colonial period had come to an end.
options.C: each side chooses what to count, and neither can say what a fair price for a railway would be.
options.D: the records needed to total the two columns were largely lost or destroyed when the colonial governments finally withdrew.

questions.correct_answer: (C) each side chooses what to count, and neither can say what a fair price for a railway would be.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 traces the deadlock to each side choosing 'what to count' and to the lack of a fair price for a railway, not to a clash of moral principles over agreed facts.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage dates the benefits to the post-colonial period; paragraph 3 describes use during colonial rule.
option_rationales.D: Records are never mentioned; paragraph 1 gives a different reason, namely selective counting and the lack of a fair price.

questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 1 gives the reason directly: the exchange continues 'because each side chooses what to count, and because neither can say what a fair price for a railway would be'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible general reason instead of the one the passage states.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The distinction between 'being affected by something' and 'being given it' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: colonial railways had no real effect on the daily lives of the people who lived and worked along the routes they followed.
options.B: railways built by colonial governments were of poorer quality than those an independent society would have built.
options.C: colonised societies are owed compensation equal to the full cost of every railway built during colonial rule.
options.D: a railway's effects on a colonised population do not by themselves show that the railway was a benefit conferred on it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a railway's effects on a colonised population do not by themselves show that the railway was a benefit conferred on it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 describes people using the trains for pilgrimage, work and trade, so the author plainly accepts that the railways had effects.
option_rationales.B: The quality of construction is never compared; the distinction concerns whose purposes the railway served, not how well it was built.
option_rationales.C: The passage proposes no compensation; it argues only that such railways should not be entered as credits in a ledger.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that a railway built by one party, with another's money, for the first party's purposes 'is not a present'. Being affected by it, even favourably, is therefore not the same as having received it as a gift.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the distinction as a denial that railways had any effect at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning follows from the sentence and the one before it.

questions.question: The examples of passengers visiting shrines and attending political meetings (paragraph 3) serve mainly to

options.A: show that the colonial authorities used the railways mainly to prevent political meetings from taking place.
options.B: grant that local people put the railways to real use while showing that such use cannot be credited to the builders.
options.C: prove that colonial railways were designed chiefly with the comfort and needs of passengers in mind rather than freight.
options.D: confirm that the ledger records the benefits of empire correctly as long as unintended uses are added to its first column.

questions.correct_answer: (B) grant that local people put the railways to real use while showing that such use cannot be credited to the builders.

option_rationales.A: The passage says the meetings were ones the authorities 'would have preferred them not to attend', so the trains enabled them.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says routes served export trade and military control, and paragraph 3 says passenger numbers 'surprised the companies'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the point 'cuts against the ledger rather than in its favour', the opposite of confirming it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with a concession ('None of this means that colonial railways were useless'), gives the examples of use, and then argues that these uses 'were precisely the ones the builders had not intended and could not claim as their contribution'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a concession as support for the view the author is attacking.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph signals both the concession and its limit explicitly.

questions.question: In the final paragraph, the author calls the census 'closer to a mould'. This most nearly means that the census was

options.A: an invention that brought into being communities which had never existed before the enumerators arrived.
options.B: a faithful copy that reproduced the existing social order exactly as it was, without altering it in any way.
options.C: an instrument that gave a fixed shape to social distinctions which already existed but had been fluid.
options.D: a slow source of decay that gradually weakened the older identities until they disappeared from social life.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an instrument that gave a fixed shape to social distinctions which already existed but had been fluid.

option_rationales.A: That is the 'fiction' the author also rejects; paragraph 2 says the distinctions 'were not conjured out of nothing'.
option_rationales.B: That is the 'mirror' the same paragraph rejects; paragraph 2 shows the census changed distinctions by demanding a single answer.
option_rationales.D: This plays on another sense of the word; the passage says the categories 'outlived the governments', the reverse of decay.

questions.explanation: The sentence explains the image: 'existing and quite fluid materials were pressed until they set'. A mould does not create its material or merely reflect it; it fixes its shape, which matches the argument of paragraphs 2 and 3.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'mirror' or 'fiction' reading, both of which the author explicitly sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: The image is glossed in the same sentence.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, the double answers that the census treated 'as an error to be corrected' (paragraph 2) often

options.A: reflected the way many people had ordinarily understood their own belonging, rather than a mistake on their part.
options.B: showed that the older vocabularies of lineage, occupation and locality had already fallen out of use.
options.C: resulted from enumerators who lacked the training needed to record complicated answers accurately.
options.D: indicated that respondents were deliberately concealing their true identity from officials they distrusted.

questions.correct_answer: (A) reflected the way many people had ordinarily understood their own belonging, rather than a mistake on their part.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says people 'had long spoken of' these terms and used them for marriages and disputes, so they were in use.
option_rationales.C: Enumerators' training is not discussed; the problem lay in the census design, which 'demanded a single answer'.
option_rationales.D: The passage never suggests concealment; the weaver example shows several honest self-descriptions, none of them 'his real identity'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says older vocabularies did not require a person to belong to 'exactly one category of each kind, at all times and for all purposes', and the weaver used different descriptions in different settings. A double answer was thus often an accurate report of plural belonging that the census recast as an error.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that an answer the census rejected must have been false or careless.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the weaver example to the census's treatment of plural answers.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's interpretation of the petitions submitted in census years?

options.A: Many of the petitions were drafted by a small number of educated members of each group, acting on behalf of the rest of their community.
options.B: Some groups petitioned to be listed under names that had appeared in texts written long before colonial rule.
options.C: Petitions to change a recorded category were as frequent where categories had no bearing on recruitment, land or representation as where they did.
options.D: Census officials rejected most of the petitions that asked for a higher place in the order of precedence.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Petitions to change a recorded category were as frequent where categories had no bearing on recruitment, land or representation as where they did.

option_rationales.A: Even if a few people drafted them, the petitions still show groups campaigning over labels with consequences, so the reading stands.
option_rationales.B: This fits the author's claim in paragraph 2 that the distinctions were 'not conjured out of nothing'; it does not weaken the reading.
option_rationales.D: Whether petitions succeeded is irrelevant to why they were made, which is what the author's interpretation concerns.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 reads the petitions as evidence that the labels 'have begun to govern their lives', because recorded size and standing had consequences. If petitions were just as common where categories carried no consequences, they could not be explained that way, which undercuts the interpretation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a fact about the petitions that is interesting but leaves the author's causal reading untouched.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires isolating the causal link between consequences and petitioning and testing each option against it.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that colonial censuses did not so much count the peoples of the empire 'as invent them' is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality, reporting the thesis and the objections to it without taking a position of the author's own.
options.B: firm opposition, on the ground that the distinctions the census recorded were already present in the societies counted.
options.C: wholehearted endorsement, since the author agrees that the categories were creations of the administrative imagination.
options.D: qualified appreciation: crediting it with a useful corrective while holding that its strong form misplaces what was new.

questions.correct_answer: (D) qualified appreciation: crediting it with a useful corrective while holding that its strong form misplaces what was new.

option_rationales.A: The author takes a clear position, offering the 'mould' image in paragraph 4 as a better account than both rejected alternatives.
option_rationales.B: The author agrees the distinctions pre-existed but still credits the view with 'valuable work' and calls the census no 'mirror', so firm opposition overstates.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the view 'claims too much' in its strongest form, and paragraph 2 rejects the idea of categories conjured from nothing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the argument 'has done valuable work' before adding that 'in its strongest form it claims too much' and 'obscures what was genuinely new'. Paragraph 3 locates the novelty in what was done with the categories. That is appreciation with a specific qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Picking firm opposition because the author denies the categories came from nothing, while missing the praise and the rejection of the 'mirror' view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option states something the author does believe; separating it requires weighing paragraph 1's praise against paragraph 2's objection.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following distinguished indentured workers from slaves?

options.A: They were free to leave the estate whenever the work was not as they had been promised.
options.B: They could not be sold, and their status was not passed on to their children.
options.C: They were paid wages equal to those earned by free workers in the same colonies.
options.D: They were protected by the colonial courts from criminal penalties for absence from work.

questions.correct_answer: (B) They could not be sold, and their status was not passed on to their children.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says leaving without a pass was a criminal offence, so this contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.C: Wages are mentioned only as something recruits were 'misled about'; no equality with free workers is claimed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the courts enforced such penalties; the option reverses the role the passage gives the courts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that indentured workers 'were not property. They could not be sold, their children did not inherit their status'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because indenture was not slavery its workers enjoyed the freedoms of free labour.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in two short sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the author regards the enforcement of indenture contracts by the courts as

options.A: evidence that coercion operated through the contract itself rather than in spite of it.
options.B: the main reason that most indentured workers chose to return home when their terms had ended.
options.C: a departure from the contracts, which on paper had guaranteed workers the freedom to leave when they wished.
options.D: a safeguard that, though imperfect, limited the power that planters could exercise over their workers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) evidence that coercion operated through the contract itself rather than in spite of it.

option_rationales.B: The passage gives no reason for return migration and does not say most returned; it says 'many returned home'.
option_rationales.C: The author says the coercion 'was written into the contract', so enforcement applied the contract rather than departing from it.
option_rationales.D: The author says the contract was 'the instrument of their confinement' and the courts enforced penalties against workers, not limits on planters.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the coercion 'did not stand outside the contract and contradict it; it was written into the contract and enforced by courts', and that free agreement and compulsion 'were not opposed but fused'.
questions.common_misconception: Supposing that legal enforcement must protect the weaker party, or that the contract itself promised freedom.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is a subtle distortion of where the coercion lay relative to the contract.

questions.question: Which of the following present-day arrangements would the author regard as most clearly raising the question posed at the end of the passage?

options.A: A volunteer who works unpaid for a charity on weekends without having signed any written agreement at all.
options.B: A farm worker whose employer lent the recruitment fee and who may not change jobs until the loan, deducted from wages, is repaid.
options.C: A freelance designer who loses a client after missing a deadline that was set out in the signed contract.
options.D: A worker who is paid less than the contract promised but remains free to resign and look for other work at any time.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A farm worker whose employer lent the recruitment fee and who may not change jobs until the loan, deducted from wages, is repaid.

option_rationales.A: With no contract and no restriction on leaving, nothing here resembles compulsion presented as free choice.
option_rationales.C: Losing a client is an ordinary consequence of breach; the designer's freedom to stop working is not restricted at all.
option_rationales.D: The author's question concerns restrictions on the right to leave; this worker can leave, so the case is unfair pay, not compulsion through contract.

questions.explanation: The final paragraph names arrangements in which 'a worker's right to leave a job is restricted by debt, by the confiscation of documents or by a visa tied to a single employer'. A worker tied to the job by an employer's loan is restricted by debt, which is the closest parallel.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a case of unfairness that does not involve restriction on leaving.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the precise criterion (restriction on leaving through the contract) to new cases.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the structure of the argument in the passage?

options.A: It concedes that a system amounted to slavery and then argues that its contractual form made it less harsh than slavery.
options.B: It defends one of two opposing classifications of a system against objections and then applies it to present-day migration.
options.C: It narrates the history of a labour system from its origins to its abolition and then assesses its economic consequences.
options.D: It sets aside two opposed ways of classifying a system, identifies a feature both overlook, and draws a wider lesson from it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It sets aside two opposed ways of classifying a system, identifies a feature both overlook, and draws a wider lesson from it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 resists calling indenture slavery, and the author never ranks the two by harshness.
option_rationales.B: The author rejects both classifications in paragraph 2 ('the second classification fares no better'), so no classification is defended.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not trace the system to its end or discuss economic consequences; it analyses how the system should be understood.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 presents the two classifications, paragraph 2 rejects each in turn, paragraph 3 identifies what 'both classifications miss' (coercion written into the contract), and paragraph 4 draws the lesson for contemporary labour.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the final paragraph's warning about modern contracts as a defence of the critics' 'slavery' classification.
questions.difficulty_reason: The option about defending one classification is tempting because the author does apply the argument to the present; the solver must see that the author sides with neither classification.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason several multilingual states have kept the colonial language is that

options.A: its native speakers formed a clear majority in most of the newly independent states.
options.B: it is the language most widely spoken among the rural majority of the population.
options.C: doing so spares the state from declaring one community's speech superior to another's.
options.D: international bodies required its use as a condition of recognising the new state.

questions.correct_answer: (C) doing so spares the state from declaring one community's speech superior to another's.

option_rationales.A: The passage calls the colonial language 'equally foreign to almost everyone', so it has almost no native speakers there.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: the colonial language belongs to 'a small educated class', against the rural majority.
option_rationales.D: No such requirement is mentioned; usefulness 'for dealing with the wider world' is not a condition of recognition.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: retaining the colonial language 'spares the state from having to declare one community's speech superior to another's, which is one reason several multilingual states have kept it'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the colonial language's prestige with wide use among the population.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The statement 'equal foreignness is not equal access' (paragraph 3) means that

options.A: although the colonial language is native to almost no group, some citizens are far better placed to use it than others.
options.B: because the colonial language is foreign to everyone, every citizen finds it equally difficult to learn, to speak and to use well.
options.C: languages from outside a region are generally harder to learn than the languages spoken within it.
options.D: access to schooling in the colonial language was restricted by law to a small and wealthy class.

questions.correct_answer: (A) although the colonial language is native to almost no group, some citizens are far better placed to use it than others.

option_rationales.B: This is exactly what the sentence denies; the passage says the language is 'already the property of a small educated class'.
option_rationales.C: The sentence is not a general claim about learning difficulty; it contrasts the language's origin with who can actually use it.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the class already possesses the language, not that any law restricted schooling to it.

questions.explanation: The sentence turns from the advantage just named (the language is 'equally foreign to almost everyone') to its limit: an educated, often urban and wealthy class already commands it, so its retention entrenches that class.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'equal foreignness' to imply equal difficulty for all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The next sentence explains the phrase directly.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Policies that use several languages at different levels of government remove the inequalities that one official language creates.
options.B: Retaining the colonial language is the fairest option open to a multilingual state, since it disadvantages every group equally.
options.C: Debates about official languages after independence have been driven mainly by nostalgia for the colonial past or by national pride.
options.D: A rural citizen who natively speaks the chosen indigenous official language may gain more from that policy than from keeping the colonial language.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A rural citizen who natively speaks the chosen indigenous official language may gain more from that policy than from keeping the colonial language.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls such policies 'attempts to spread these costs rather than to escape them', so they do not remove the inequalities.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'equal foreignness is not equal access', and that retention entrenches an educated class against the rural majority.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says these debates 'have rarely been about nostalgia or national pride, whatever their rhetoric'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says choosing one indigenous language gives 'a lasting head start' to those who grew up speaking it, and paragraph 3 says retaining the colonial language works against 'the rural majority of every linguistic group'. A rural native speaker of the chosen language therefore gains under the first policy and loses under the second.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the surface appeal of the colonial language's neutrality, which the author qualifies.
