questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the two inequalities described in paragraphs 2 and 3 for a single case.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The colonial language should be kept in multilingual states because it is the only option that treats all language communities alike.
options.B: Language policy after empire has been shaped chiefly by the need to communicate with the wider world rather than with citizens.
options.C: Choosing an official language after independence is chiefly about how advantage is shared among citizens, not authenticity against convenience.
options.D: Newly independent states ought to replace the colonial language with indigenous languages as quickly as is practical, whatever the cost.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Choosing an official language after independence is chiefly about how advantage is shared among citizens, not authenticity against convenience.

option_rationales.A: The author qualifies this neutrality: equal foreignness 'is not equal access', so retention creates an inequality of its own.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the debates have been about who can 'read the forms, pass the examinations and understand the judge', which concerns citizens.
option_rationales.D: The author says recognising the dilemma 'does not settle what any particular country should do', so no such prescription is made.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the usual framing hides 'that every option distributes advantage and disadvantage among citizens', and paragraph 3 concludes that the choice is 'between two kinds of inequality'. That reframing is the central claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a policy recommendation when the author explicitly declines to give one.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options each take a side the author deliberately avoids; the correct answer requires seeing the reframing.

questions.question: According to the passage, the straight-line borders on the map of Africa

options.A: follow rivers, watersheds or the limits of existing states wherever the terrain made this at all possible.
options.B: are found mostly in deserts and thinly populated regions, where they divided relatively few people.
options.C: were drawn at the Berlin conference by diplomats who settled each boundary with a ruler on the map.
options.D: have caused most of the wars fought between African states in the decades since independence was gained.

questions.correct_answer: (B) are found mostly in deserts and thinly populated regions, where they divided relatively few people.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says many boundaries followed such features 'rather than lines of latitude', so these are the other borders, not the straight ones.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the conference 'chiefly agreed on rules' and that most boundaries 'were settled afterwards, over decades'.
option_rationales.D: This is the popular explanation that the author says 'is weaker than its popularity suggests'; the passage never attributes most wars to them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states: 'The straight lines are real, but they cluster in deserts and thinly populated regions, where they divided relatively few people.'
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the familiar image of partition that paragraph 2 corrects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The reference to the borders of Europe in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: show that the charge of artificiality, if accepted, would equally condemn borders not usually blamed for chronic conflict.
options.B: suggest that African states should redraw their inherited borders by the methods used in European peace conferences.
options.C: argue that the borders of Europe were drawn with far more care for local wishes than any colonial boundary was.
options.D: explain why the Organisation of African Unity chose to accept the boundaries that its member states had inherited.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that the charge of artificiality, if accepted, would equally condemn borders not usually blamed for chronic conflict.

option_rationales.B: The author makes no such proposal and notes that African leaders judged redrawing 'more dangerous than living with them'.
option_rationales.C: The passage says European borders were 'no more attentive to local wishes than any colonial commission', which is the reverse.
option_rationales.D: The decision is explained by the difficulty of defining natural borders and the danger of redrawing, not by the European example.

questions.explanation: The example supports the claim that the charge 'proves too much': European borders were also drawn without regard to local wishes, so 'If artificial borders caused instability by themselves, much of the world would be permanently at war'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a comparison meant to show equal artificiality as a claim that one side was better.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing how the example serves the 'proves too much' objection.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the decision of post-independence leaders to accept the boundaries they inherited as

options.A: evidence that the colonial borders in fact closely matched the boundaries of the states that existed before conquest.
options.B: a condition imposed on the new states by the former colonial powers before they agreed to grant independence.
options.C: a mistake that locked the new states into the conflicts that their artificial borders were bound to produce.
options.D: a considered judgement about the risks of redrawing, not a sign that they thought the borders were well drawn.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a considered judgement about the risks of redrawing, not a sign that they thought the borders were well drawn.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says only that 'many' boundaries followed existing polities; the leaders' decision is explained by the danger of redrawing.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the leaders 'chose' to accept the boundaries; nothing suggests the choice was imposed on them.
option_rationales.C: The author disputes that artificial borders produce conflict by themselves, so the author would not call the decision such a mistake.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the leaders were 'aware of these difficulties' (that no natural border exists and any line divides someone) and judged 'that an attempt to redraw them would be more dangerous than living with them'. The acceptance reflects prudence, not approval.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that keeping something implies thinking it good.
questions.difficulty_reason: The distinction between accepting and approving must be drawn from the reasons the passage gives.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about where the more serious colonial legacy lay?

options.A: Many European borders were also settled at peace conferences that made no attempt to consult the people living near them.
options.B: Most of the straight-line borders on the continent run through desert regions that had very few permanent inhabitants at the time.
options.C: Among former colonies, later instability tracks how extractive the colonial administration was far more closely than how straight or divisive the borders were.
options.D: Several boundaries fixed by survey commissions cut pastoral communities off from the grazing grounds they had always used in the dry season.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Among former colonies, later instability tracks how extractive the colonial administration was far more closely than how straight or divisive the borders were.

option_rationales.A: This supports the 'proves too much' argument of paragraph 3, not the comparative claim in paragraph 4 about what mattered more.
option_rationales.B: This supports paragraph 2's correction about where straight lines lie, but says nothing about extractive states being the graver legacy.
option_rationales.D: This supports the concession that some borders separated communities 'from their pastures', which concerns placement, not the legacy inside the lines.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 claims the graver legacy 'lay inside the lines rather than in their placement', in states 'built for extraction'. Evidence that instability follows the extractive character of administration more closely than border shape directly supports that comparison.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option that agrees with some part of the passage instead of the specific comparative claim asked about.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options are consistent with the passage; the solver must match evidence to the exact claim in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, under indirect rule, a ruler who had a genuine traditional claim to his office

options.A: became less constrained by those beneath him than he had been before colonial rule began.
options.B: kept exactly the position he had held before, since the policy preserved the existing institutions.
options.C: lost most of his authority to the warrant chiefs whom colonial officials appointed in his place.
options.D: was required to share his power with councils of elders, age-grades and religious associations.

questions.correct_answer: (A) became less constrained by those beneath him than he had been before colonial rule began.

option_rationales.B: This is the architects' claim; the author says 'Even where genuine rulers existed, their position changed'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says warrant chiefs were created where authority had been dispersed and no such ruler existed, not to replace genuine rulers.
option_rationales.D: These bodies are described as holding authority in places without kings; the passage says the checks on kings 'lost much of their force'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says such a king 'had once had to keep the support of title-holders and rivals' and faced possible desertion, but 'now had the backing of a colonial army, and the checks that had limited him lost much of their force'.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the policy's own description of itself as preservation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the consequence of colonial backing for the king's accountability.

questions.question: According to the passage, the written codes of customary law did all of the following EXCEPT

options.A: reflect the interests of the senior men who described the custom to colonial officers.
options.B: allow local communities to revise the rules themselves as their circumstances changed.
options.C: record as fixed a number of rules that had previously been flexible and open to dispute.
options.D: tend to favour men over women in matters such as marriage, land and inheritance.

questions.correct_answer: (B) allow local communities to revise the rules themselves as their circumstances changed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'the codes bear their fingerprints', and paragraph 3 that those men had 'an interest in the answer'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says flexible and contested rules 'were recorded as fixed', so the codes did this.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says rules were often recorded in the form most favourable to 'men against women', so the codes did this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 ends: custom 'became a code that could be changed only by the administration'. The codes therefore removed communities' ability to revise the rules, so this is the one thing they did not do.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the final sentence of paragraph 3 and assuming custom stayed flexible.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each listed effect is stated in paragraph 3 or 4; the exception contradicts the paragraph's last sentence.

questions.question: The author's disagreement with the architects of indirect rule is best captured by the claim that the policy

options.A: did not preserve existing authority but produced a new kind that answered to the colonial state rather than the governed.
options.B: was adopted mainly because it cost less than direct administration, not out of any real respect for local institutions.
options.C: should have been abandoned in favour of direct rule so that colonised peoples could adopt European institutions sooner.
options.D: replaced tradition with customs that colonial officials invented and imposed on subjects who had no part in shaping them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) did not preserve existing authority but produced a new kind that answered to the colonial state rather than the governed.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 notes the policy was cheaper, but the author never questions the sincerity of the moral claim; the disagreement concerns the effects.
option_rationales.C: The author makes no recommendation of direct rule; this assumes a preference the passage nowhere expresses.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says it 'would be wrong' to conclude this, since the elders' 'fingerprints' are on the codes.

questions.explanation: The architects claimed the policy would preserve existing institutions (paragraph 1). The author concludes that its lasting effect 'was not the preservation of old authority, nor its outright replacement, but the creation of a new kind of authority' answering 'upward to the state rather than downward to the governed'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the cost motive, which is true as a detail, or the invention thesis, which the author explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option uses a true detail about cost and another states the 'invention' view the author argues against; both must be separated from the actual point of disagreement.

questions.question: The final paragraph functions primarily to

options.A: introduce a fresh example of colonial invention, drawn this time from the record of post-colonial governments.
options.B: summarise the case that the defenders of indirect rule made for the policy before the author goes on to reject it.
options.C: reverse the argument of the earlier paragraphs by showing that tradition was in fact preserved by indirect rule.
options.D: qualify the preceding account by acknowledging the agency of local elders, then state the author's overall conclusion.

questions.correct_answer: (D) qualify the preceding account by acknowledging the agency of local elders, then state the author's overall conclusion.

option_rationales.A: The last sentence notes that later governments kept such authority; it is a consequence, not a new example of invention.
option_rationales.B: The defenders' case is set out in paragraph 1; the final paragraph gives the author's own qualified conclusion.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the lasting effect was 'not the preservation of old authority', so it does not reverse the earlier argument.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with 'It would be wrong, however, to conclude that tradition was simply invented', crediting the elders with shaping the codes, and then states the thesis: indirect rule created 'a new kind of authority that spoke the language of tradition'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the 'however' as a reversal of the whole argument rather than a qualification of one inference from it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph does two things; the solver must recognise both and their relation.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, which of the following would have counted as appropriating land under the view of property described there?

options.A: Moving across a region with the changing seasons.
options.B: Enclosing a field and ploughing it for crops.
options.C: Burning grassland at intervals to renew its growth.
options.D: Hunting over the same territory for many generations.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Enclosing a field and ploughing it for crops.

option_rationales.A: Land 'moved across with the seasons' is also listed as not yet appropriated on this view.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists land 'burned to renew its grasses' among land that 'had not yet been appropriated'.
option_rationales.D: Land 'hunted over' is listed as not yet appropriated, 'however long people had lived on it'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says property arose when a person mixed labour with the earth, 'enclosing it, ploughing it and improving it', and that 'Fences, fields and permanent buildings registered as use'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that long or careful use of land must have counted as ownership.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in paragraph 2; each wrong option is listed there as not counting.

questions.question: The remark that the settlers' error was 'not a failure to see but a theory of what was worth seeing' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: the land practices of the original inhabitants were in fact less productive than European agriculture.
options.B: the settlers were unaware of the methods by which the original inhabitants managed and used the land.
options.C: the doctrine could not be overturned merely by establishing that the land had been inhabited.
options.D: the settlers knowingly told a lie in order to justify taking land they knew belonged to others.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the doctrine could not be overturned merely by establishing that the land had been inhabited.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no comparison of productivity; it describes which practices a theory chose to recognise as use.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says those who invoked the idea 'were perfectly aware that others lived there'; the error was not ignorance.
option_rationales.D: The author says the doctrine is wrongly 'described as a lie'; settlers denied ownership by their own theory, not knowingly falsely.

questions.explanation: If the error lay in a theory about which relationships count as ownership rather than in a failure of observation, then showing that people were present does not touch it. Paragraph 1 says the familiar argument assumes the doctrine 'collapses' once the facts are acknowledged, which the author disputes.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'error' as ignorance or as deliberate deceit, both of which the author sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the remark in paragraph 2 to the argument the author rejects in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the 1992 repudiation of terra nullius and the native title regimes that followed is best described as

options.A: dismissive, since the author regards the decision as a symbolic gesture that changed nothing for claimants.
options.B: unreservedly celebratory, since the author treats the decision as the full dismantling of the doctrine.
options.C: indifferent, since the author holds that legal recognition has no bearing on the deeper question of title.
options.D: appreciative of the repudiation's significance but critical of the standard of proof attached to it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) appreciative of the repudiation's significance but critical of the standard of proof attached to it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 calls it 'a real achievement' that 'it would be ungracious to belittle', so dismissal is wrong.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says a doctrine 'is not fully dismantled' when the standard applied was shaped by the doctrine itself.
option_rationales.C: The author analyses the legal standard closely and says recognition is not 'worthless', which is the opposite of indifference.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 praises the repudiation, then turns with 'Yet' to the requirement of a 'continuing connection' weighed by courts that favour written records; paragraphs 4 and 5 develop the criticism while saying recognition is not worthless.
questions.common_misconception: Collapsing a mixed attitude into pure praise or pure dismissal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both halves of the attitude are signalled, but the solver must hold praise and criticism together.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: Native title courts routinely accept oral evidence of songs, hunting rules and fire practices as full proof of connection without any written record.
options.B: Some native title claims have succeeded where claimants could show long, unbroken written records of their occupation of the land.
options.C: Many claimant communities were forcibly removed from their land by government policy during the twentieth century and were never able to return.
options.D: Courts in most legal systems require evidence before they will recognise any claim to land, whoever the claimant happens to be.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Native title courts routinely accept oral evidence of songs, hunting rules and fire practices as full proof of connection without any written record.

option_rationales.B: Success through written records fits the claim that 'the forms most easily recognised are those that leave records', so this does not weaken it.
option_rationales.C: This supports paragraph 3's point that dispossession becomes 'evidence against them'; it strengthens rather than weakens the argument.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 already concedes that 'Any legal system must have rules of proof'; the argument concerns which forms are recognised, not proof as such.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that title 'still depends on displaying a relationship to land in forms that a court is equipped to recognise', chiefly 'those that leave records'. If courts fully recognised unrecorded practices of the kind listed in paragraph 2, the theoretical premise would not be surviving in this way.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the general point about rules of proof, which the author has already conceded and which leaves the specific claim untouched.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options agree with the passage and one restates a concession; only the correct answer attacks the claim about which forms count.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: The doctrine of terra nullius was a fiction that settlers adopted while knowing perfectly well that it was false and self-serving.
options.B: Native title regimes ought to be replaced by forms of restitution that do not require claimants to prove anything at all.
options.C: Rejecting the claim that the land was empty has not removed the doctrine's underlying view of which relationships to land amount to ownership.
options.D: European theories of property, from the early modern period to the present, have consistently undervalued pastoral and nomadic life.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Rejecting the claim that the land was empty has not removed the doctrine's underlying view of which relationships to land amount to ownership.

option_rationales.A: This is the familiar view of paragraph 1, which the author says 'misdescribes the doctrine's real strength'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says no 'purer form of restitution is readily available' and that claims without evidence 'would invite abuse'.
option_rationales.D: This is broader than the passage, which uses one strand of early modern thought to explain a specific doctrine and its legal afterlife.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the thesis: 'the factual premise of terra nullius has been abandoned while something like its theoretical premise survives', and paragraph 5 concludes that the doctrine 'is not fully dismantled'. Paragraphs 1 and 2 establish that the doctrine's real basis was a theory of ownership, not a factual mistake.
questions.common_misconception: Selecting the popular account the passage opens with, which the author corrects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The option calling the doctrine a knowing fiction states a view the author reports and rejects; the correct answer requires grasping the distinction between factual and theoretical premises.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author mentions the nationalisation of a foreign-owned mine (paragraph 3) as an example of

options.A: economic dependence coming to an end at exactly the same moment as the transfer of sovereignty.
options.B: a power that formal independence genuinely conferred, whatever the wisdom of exercising it in a given case.
options.C: one of the ruinous mistakes that showed many new governments were not yet ready for sovereignty.
options.D: a concession that former imperial powers demanded of new states during the bargaining over the transfer of power.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a power that formal independence genuinely conferred, whatever the wisdom of exercising it in a given case.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says other strands, including monetary arrangements, 'loosened over decades', so dependence did not end with sovereignty.
option_rationales.C: Mistakes are listed as a separate item in the same sentence; the author does not call nationalisation a mistake or judge readiness.
option_rationales.D: Nationalising a foreign-owned mine works against foreign interests; the passage lists it among powers of a 'sovereign government'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says sovereignty's ending 'was not trivial' and lists what 'A sovereign government could' do, beginning with nationalising a foreign-owned mine. The example shows a real power gained at independence, and the inclusion of 'ruinous mistakes' shows the author is not judging whether each use was wise.
questions.common_misconception: Treating every item in the list as a mistake, or confusing sovereignty with economic independence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example's role follows from the claim it illustrates.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, 'an unbundling' refers to

options.A: the deliberate dismantling by new governments of every institution that they had inherited from colonial rule.
options.B: the transfer of each colonial institution to new owners in a single ceremony on the day of independence.
options.C: the division of a single former empire into a number of separate and fully independent new states.
options.D: the separation, at different speeds and in different places, of relations that imperial power had held together.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the separation, at different speeds and in different places, of relations that imperial power had held together.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says some institutions 'were chosen, and defended' by new elites, so not every one was dismantled.
option_rationales.B: The point of the image is that the strands did not come apart together; only sovereignty 'ended at a stroke'.
option_rationales.C: The bundle in paragraph 2 is a bundle of relations such as sovereignty, trade and language, not of territories.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls empire 'a bundle of relations, held together by the power of the imperial state', and says the strands did not 'come apart at the same speed'. Paragraph 4 describes decolonisation as processes 'whose timing differed by strand and by place'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the image territorially or as a single event.
questions.difficulty_reason: The term is defined across paragraphs 2 and 4 rather than in one sentence.

questions.question: With which of the following statements would the author most likely agree?

options.A: The continuities that survived independence were for the most part imposed on the new states by their former imperial rulers.
options.B: The neo-colonial critique rightly saw that independence could coexist with dependence, but wrongly concluded that it changed nothing of substance.
options.C: The ceremonial picture is accurate about sovereignty and so remains the most useful framework for historians of decolonisation.
options.D: Because empire was a bundle of relations, the formal moment of independence had little real significance for the new states.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The neo-colonial critique rightly saw that independence could coexist with dependence, but wrongly concluded that it changed nothing of substance.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says some were imposed but 'Others were chosen, and defended' by new elites; the passage never says that imposed continuities were the majority.
option_rationales.C: The author accepts that the ceremony marks sovereignty but argues the useful question is 'which relations were transformed', not when empire ended.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the ending of sovereignty 'was not trivial' and lists powers that sovereign governments used, so the author disagrees.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 credits the critique with capturing 'something the ceremonial picture ignores', but the author rejects its claim that independence left 'substance intact', since paragraph 3 shows sovereignty was a real and consequential change.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that denies independence any real significance, which pushes the bundle idea toward the critics' conclusion that the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option takes one true element of the passage too far; the correct answer requires holding the author's partial agreement with the critique.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 5 that the governments of independent states must answer for some continuities?

options.A: Several former imperial powers kept military bases in their former colonies under formal agreements signed with the new governments at the time of independence.
options.B: Many members of the new governing elites had been educated in the former metropolis and admired its institutions.
options.C: The institutions that seemed to be kept by choice were in fact kept because foreign loans had been made conditional on keeping them.
options.D: Several newly independent governments wrote entirely new constitutions within a decade of gaining their independence.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The institutions that seemed to be kept by choice were in fact kept because foreign loans had been made conditional on keeping them.

option_rationales.A: Bases kept by agreement concern the strands former rulers held; nothing here shows that the apparently chosen continuities were not chosen.
option_rationales.B: This fits paragraph 3's description of elites 'formed by the old system' who found it 'congenial', so it supports the claim.
option_rationales.D: This illustrates sovereign power, which paragraph 3 already affirms; it does not bear on whether retained strands were chosen.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says 'If some strands were retained by choice, those governments must answer for the choosing'. The claim rests on the continuities being chosen. Evidence that the apparently chosen ones were in fact kept under financial pressure moves them into the category of strands kept 'by pressure', removing the basis for holding the new governments responsible.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that concerns continuity in general rather than the choice on which responsibility depends.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must identify the conditional on which the claim rests and see which option removes it.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Both standard accounts wrongly treat empire as one thing; its strands ended at different times, so the real question is which changed when.
options.B: Decolonisation was largely a ceremony, since the economic substance of imperial rule survived the formal grant of independence almost entirely intact.
options.C: The governments of newly independent states bear most of the responsibility for the persistence of colonial patterns after independence.
options.D: Formal sovereignty, which ended at a stroke, was the only part of imperial rule that independence was ever able to change.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Both standard accounts wrongly treat empire as one thing; its strands ended at different times, so the real question is which changed when.

option_rationales.B: This is the neo-colonial critique of paragraph 1, which the author says 'shares more with the view it attacks' than its holders admit.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 divides responsibility between new governments and former imperial powers; the passage never assigns the greater share to either side.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says other strands 'loosened over decades', so they changed too, only more slowly than sovereignty.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 identifies the shared assumption that empire is 'a single thing that either ends or persists' and replaces it with a bundle of relations; paragraph 4 draws the conclusion that the better question is 'which relations were transformed, when, by whom and at what cost'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the critique the author partly endorses, or overstating the point about sovereignty.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to positions the passage discusses; the correct answer requires the whole structure of the argument.

questions.question: The central argument of the passage is that

options.A: the preventive ideal behind modern policing was an illusion, since visible officers do not reliably reduce the crime that gets recorded.
options.B: police forces, founded on the aim of preventing offences through visible patrol, have drifted toward the countable arrest at some cost to that aim.
options.C: the uniformed police replaced watchmen and constables chiefly because they caught offenders far more efficiently than the older arrangements had.
options.D: patrols reduce crime far more than arrests do, so police forces ought to stop measuring the number of arrests altogether.

questions.correct_answer: (B) police forces, founded on the aim of preventing offences through visible patrol, have drifted toward the countable arrest at some cost to that aim.

option_rationales.A: This is the critics' view reported in paragraph 3, which the author rejects as 'too simple' because patrol was 'never only about deterrence'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: 'What was new about the reformed police was not that they caught criminals more efficiently.'
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 accepts scepticism about 'large claims about deterrence', and paragraph 4 says recovering the idea 'does not mean abandoning measurement'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 sets out the founding preventive idea, paragraph 2 explains why countable arrests displaced it, paragraph 3 defends the idea against the critics, and paragraph 4 draws the lesson that rewarding arrests 'may do so in ways that erode the trust on which prevention depends'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the critics' view in paragraph 3 for the author's, or inflating the author's case into a call to stop measuring.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is the reported view the author rejects and another overstates the conclusion; the correct answer needs the whole arc.

questions.question: According to the passage, what was new about the reformed police forces of the nineteenth century?

options.A: The claim that a paid, disciplined and constantly visible body of officers could stop offences before they happened.
options.B: Their greater success in recovering stolen goods and returning them to the people from whom they were taken.
options.C: Their practice of judging officers mainly by the number of people detained in the course of each year.
options.D: Their reliance on unpaid residents who served as constables and walked fixed rounds through the parish at night.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The claim that a paid, disciplined and constantly visible body of officers could stop offences before they happened.

option_rationales.B: Recovering stolen goods was the business of the private thief-takers described in paragraph 1, and the passage denies that efficiency was the novelty.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 presents judging officers by detentions as a later drift away from the founding idea, not as the founding idea itself.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 lists unpaid constables and night watchmen as the patchwork that came before the reformed police, not as what was new.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that what was new 'was the claim that a salaried, disciplined body of officers, visible on the street at all hours, could prevent offences from occurring at all'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a feature of the older arrangements or of the later drift because it appears near the relevant sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a quiet street is a poor measure of what a patrol has achieved because

options.A: officers on patrol tend to avoid quiet streets and spend their time in districts where arrests are more likely.
options.B: residents of quiet streets rarely report offences to the police, so the crime that occurs there goes unrecorded.
options.C: the streets that are quiet are usually those where officers have made many arrests in earlier years.
options.D: the quiet cannot show whether it was produced by the officer's visit or would have occurred without it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the quiet cannot show whether it was produced by the officer's visit or would have occurred without it.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says where officers choose to patrol; it says only that arrests came to be rewarded.
option_rationales.B: Reporting is mentioned in paragraph 3 as an effect of visible presence, not as a reason why quiet streets mislead.
option_rationales.C: No link between past arrests and present quiet is drawn anywhere in the passage; this is invented.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a street that stays quiet after an officer's visit 'looks exactly like a street that would have stayed quiet anyway', so its quiet cannot be credited to the patrol.
questions.common_misconception: Reaching for an outside explanation (reporting, past arrests) instead of the counterfactual point made in the text.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reasoning is given directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, the word 'legible' most nearly means

options.A: clearly printed or handwritten, so that a report can be read without difficulty.
options.B: lawful, in the sense of being permitted and approved by the public.
options.C: readily recorded, counted and reported to those who oversee the institution.
options.D: of greatest benefit to the residents whom the patrol is meant to protect.

questions.correct_answer: (C) readily recorded, counted and reported to those who oversee the institution.

option_rationales.A: This is the literal sense of the word; the passage applies it to an institution's output, not to handwriting or print.
option_rationales.B: This confuses 'legible' with 'legitimate'; the sentence contrasts what is easily measured with what the institution is for.
option_rationales.D: The sentence contrasts the 'most legible output' with the institution's 'purpose', so the legible output is not what benefits residents most.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 contrasts the 'most legible output', the arrest, which paragraph 2 calls 'countable', with the purpose of prevention. 'Legible' therefore means readily recorded and read off by those measuring the force.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the literal dictionary sense without reading the contrast in the sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contrast with 'purpose' and the earlier word 'countable' fix the meaning.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that the requirement to carry passports after the First World War

options.A: outlived the wartime anxieties that had first led governments to impose it.
options.B: was imposed mainly because railways had made travel too fast for frontier officials to manage.
options.C: was withdrawn once fears about spies had passed and was reintroduced only much later.
options.D: was resisted by most travellers, who regarded it as an unjustified intrusion on their liberty.

questions.correct_answer: (A) outlived the wartime anxieties that had first led governments to impose it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says faster railway travel led several countries to relax controls, not to impose them.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says plainly that 'when the war ended the requirement was not withdrawn'.
option_rationales.D: Travellers' reactions are never described; the passage says the expectation 'hardened into common sense'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says documents were demanded because of wartime fears about 'spies, deserters' and fleeing men, and that 'when the war ended the requirement was not withdrawn', so the measure outlasted its original reasons.
questions.common_misconception: Misreading the railway sentence as a cause of controls rather than of their relaxation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference follows from two adjacent sentences.

questions.question: The reference to stateless people in paragraph 3 serves primarily to

options.A: illustrate how documents issued by some states admit their holders to far more countries than those issued by others.
options.B: prove that passports were introduced mainly to protect vulnerable travellers rather than to control their movements.
options.C: suggest that every state ought to issue papers to all who live within its territory, whatever their origin.
options.D: show that the protection a passport confers is substantial, by indicating what a person without one is exposed to.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that the protection a passport confers is substantial, by indicating what a person without one is exposed to.

option_rationales.A: Unequal admission is the point of paragraph 4; stateless people have no document at all, so they cannot illustrate that comparison.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the passport's first purpose was selective closing of borders; paragraph 3 adds a protective side without reversing that history.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no recommendation about issuing documents; it uses the stateless only to show what the claim on protection is worth.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the passport is 'also a claim on protection', and the stateless, who 'can be refused entry everywhere', show 'how much that claim is worth'. The example establishes the value of protection by its absence.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the concession for a reversal of the passage's view, or attaching the example to paragraph 4's point.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing the paragraph as a concession and the example as evidence for it.

questions.question: According to the passage, two passports of identical design may differ in

options.A: how much personal information about the holder each records and checks at the frontier.
options.B: how long the issuing state allows each document to remain valid before it must be renewed.
options.C: how readily the countries a traveller visits will admit the person who carries the document.
options.D: whether each entitles its holder to return to the state that issued it in the first place.

questions.correct_answer: (C) how readily the countries a traveller visits will admit the person who carries the document.

option_rationales.A: The passage never compares the information recorded; paragraph 4 contrasts only what the documents are able to do.
option_rationales.B: Validity and renewal are not mentioned anywhere; the difference in paragraph 4 concerns admission and suspicion.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says a passport 'entitles the bearer to return home'; this is common to passports, not a difference between them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says identical-looking documents can have 'very different power, one admitting its holder to most of the world without a visa, the other inviting suspicion at every desk'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the right of return, which paragraph 3 attributes to passports in general.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 4.

questions.question: Each of the following is a claim the passage makes about passports EXCEPT that they

options.A: certify the identity of the bearer and which state answers for the person who holds them.
options.B: were first required in order to speed up travel once railways had made crossing frontiers routine.
options.C: entitle their holders to seek help from the officials of the issuing state when abroad.
options.D: reflect a ranking among states that the individual holder can rarely do anything to alter.

questions.correct_answer: (B) were first required in order to speed up travel once railways had made crossing frontiers routine.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the passport 'certifies who you are, and which state answers for you'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the passport entitles the bearer 'to seek help from the officials of the issuing state when abroad'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the passport records 'rank in an order of states', an accident of birth the individual 'can rarely change'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says railways led several countries to relax controls, and that documents were demanded because of wartime fears. The passage never says passports were required to speed up travel; it implies the reverse.
questions.common_misconception: Remembering that railways are mentioned and assuming they explain the requirement.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options must be checked against three different paragraphs.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Since frontline officials cannot avoid exercising judgement, reform should aim to expose and guide that judgement rather than to legislate it away.
options.B: Most of the unfairness in public agencies arises because officials are given more cases than they can handle in the time available.
options.C: Frontline officials should be given wide freedom to depart from rules, because they understand applicants' circumstances better than those who write the rules.
options.D: Detailed rules remain the fairest way to treat applicants alike, although officials sometimes apply such rules more rigidly than they should.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Since frontline officials cannot avoid exercising judgement, reform should aim to expose and guide that judgement rather than to legislate it away.

option_rationales.B: Heavy caseloads appear in paragraph 2 as one reason judgement is unavoidable; the passage does not make them the main source of unfairness.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'The case for discretion is not that officials can be trusted', and warns that latitude can be used to delay as well as to help.
option_rationales.D: The passage questions the remedy of more rules, arguing in paragraph 2 that tightened rules only drive judgement into 'less visible choices'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that judgement cannot be eliminated, paragraph 3 that the real choice is between 'discretion that is acknowledged and discretion that is driven underground', and paragraph 4 proposes recording, reviewing and guiding it.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the defence of discretion as trust in officials, which paragraph 3 explicitly disowns.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option praises discretion, which the author accepts only in a qualified way.

questions.question: The example of the clerk and the proof of address in paragraph 2 suggests that

options.A: clerks often misread eligibility rules on purpose in order to turn away applicants whom they happen to dislike.
options.B: rules about proof of address are usually drafted with little regard to how applicants actually live and where they stay.
options.C: applicants who live with relatives are more likely than others to be refused benefits by the clerks they deal with.
options.D: a rule can state what is required while leaving open how much effort an official spends helping an applicant meet it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a rule can state what is required while leaving open how much effort an official spends helping an applicant meet it.

option_rationales.A: The example concerns effort within the rule, not deliberate misreading, and the passage does not say clerks often act this way.
option_rationales.B: The passage does not criticise how such rules are drafted; it says only that no rule settles how hard the clerk should look.
option_rationales.C: No comparison of refusal rates is made; living with relatives is simply a case where the rule leaves a gap.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the rule requires proof of address but 'does not say how hard the clerk should look for an acceptable document', which is exactly the gap the correct answer describes.
questions.common_misconception: Turning an illustration of an unavoidable gap into a charge of bad drafting or bad faith.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated in the same sentence as the example.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the claim in paragraph 2 that judgement 'retreats into these less visible choices'?

options.A: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, supervisors begin publishing how often each caseworker's applicants are approved and refused.
options.B: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers come to differ chiefly in how quickly they schedule interviews for the different applicants they serve.
options.C: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers openly refuse to use it and carry on assessing applicants exactly as they did before.
options.D: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, fewer applicants are approved, because the new sheet is stricter than the assessments it replaced.

questions.correct_answer: (B) After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers come to differ chiefly in how quickly they schedule interviews for the different applicants they serve.

option_rationales.A: Publishing outcomes is the kind of reform paragraph 4 recommends to make discretion visible, the opposite of judgement retreating out of view.
option_rationales.C: Open refusal is visible defiance of the rule; the passage describes judgement that persists quietly inside a rule that is being followed.
option_rationales.D: This is an effect of the rule's content, not of officials' judgement; nothing here shows discretion moving anywhere.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that when rules are tightened judgement moves into choices such as 'whose file to open first'. Once a scoring sheet fixes the formal assessment, differences in how quickly applicants are scheduled are precisely such a less visible choice.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the publishing option because it involves the same scoring sheet, without noticing that it makes judgement more visible, not less.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each option starts from the same rule change; the solver must match the specific mechanism, and one wrong option is the passage's own remedy.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards frontline discretion is best described as

options.A: studied neutrality: the passage sets out competing views of it without favouring either side over the other.
options.B: warm admiration: it lets sympathetic officials rescue the families whom rigid rules would fail.
options.C: realistic acceptance: it is unavoidable and open to abuse, so it should be brought into view.
options.D: deep suspicion: it is chiefly a channel through which prejudice enters public administration.

questions.correct_answer: (C) realistic acceptance: it is unavoidable and open to abuse, so it should be brought into view.

option_rationales.A: The author takes a clear position in paragraphs 3 and 4, recommending that discretion be acknowledged and reviewed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 opens 'This is not to romanticise frontline discretion' and notes it also allows 'reasons for delay'.
option_rationales.D: The author grants that latitude may be exercised unevenly, but argues it is unavoidable rather than chiefly a channel for prejudice.

questions.explanation: The author accepts discretion as inescapable (paragraph 2), refuses to idealise it (paragraph 3), and proposes recording and guiding it (paragraph 4).
questions.common_misconception: Selecting suspicion because paragraph 3 mentions uneven treatment, and missing that the author's conclusion is acceptance with oversight.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two attitudes each match one half of paragraph 3; only the correct answer matches the whole.

questions.question: The analysis in paragraph 2 suggests that the soil principle

options.A: was adopted in some places for reasons of state interest that had little to do with openness to newcomers.
options.B: was abandoned by most states once their need for soldiers and taxpayers had declined over time.
options.C: was imposed on immigrant parents against their wishes and was widely resented by the families it affected.
options.D: is in practice more exclusive than the descent principle, despite its reputation for being open.

questions.correct_answer: (A) was adopted in some places for reasons of state interest that had little to do with openness to newcomers.

option_rationales.B: The passage gives no account of the soil rule being abandoned; it discusses only why it was adopted.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the children were claimed regardless of what their parents wanted, which means the parents were not consulted; it says nothing about resentment.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 concludes that 'Neither motive is obviously more liberal than the other', which is weaker than reversing the ranking.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the soil rule 'expressed less a generous conception of belonging than an interest in numbers', tied to the need for 'soldiers and taxpayers'.
questions.common_misconception: Overshooting the author's levelling claim into a reversal of the usual ranking.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option overstates 'neither ... more liberal' into 'more exclusive'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the soil and descent contrast is a misleading guide to how welcoming a society is?

options.A: Some children who acquire citizenship under the soil principle later renounce it in favour of the nationality held by their parents.
options.B: In several states that follow the soil principle, long-term residents must wait many years and pay high fees before they can naturalise.
options.C: States following the soil principle almost always offer quick, cheap naturalisation, while states following the descent principle almost always make it slow and costly.
options.D: Some states that follow the descent principle require applicants for naturalisation to pass a test of the national language before they are admitted.

questions.correct_answer: (C) States following the soil principle almost always offer quick, cheap naturalisation, while states following the descent principle almost always make it slow and costly.

option_rationales.A: Renunciation by individuals says nothing about whether the birth rule tracks how easy a country is to join, so it neither weakens nor supports the claim.
option_rationales.B: This is the very situation paragraph 3 describes, a soil state that keeps parents 'waiting at the door', so it supports the author rather than weakening the claim.
option_rationales.D: A language test in some descent states is compatible with the author's view that naturalisation rules, not birth rules, decide openness; it does not tie the two together.

questions.explanation: The author argues that the birth rule misleads because naturalisation, which matters more, can vary independently of it (paragraph 3). If soil states almost always naturalise easily and descent states almost always do not, the birth rule would reliably predict openness after all.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about naturalisation that merely adds detail, without seeing that only a systematic correlation undercuts the author's argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying that the argument depends on birth rules and naturalisation rules varying independently.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It summarises the historical motives for each principle that were set out earlier in paragraph 2 of the passage.
options.B: It grants a genuine merit of the soil principle while denying that this merit settles how open a society is.
options.C: It shifts the discussion away from nationality law towards the practical hardships of residents without secure status.
options.D: It reverses the earlier argument by admitting that the soil principle is after all the defining mark of an open society.

questions.correct_answer: (B) It grants a genuine merit of the soil principle while denying that this merit settles how open a society is.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 does not return to motives such as soldiers, taxpayers or emigrants; it weighs the value of the soil guarantee.
option_rationales.C: Residents without secure status are mentioned in a single clause to support the concession; the paragraph's subject remains nationality law.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the guarantee is 'better understood as one protection among several than as the defining mark of an open society'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'None of this means the choice of birth rule is unimportant', grants that the soil principle 'does guarantee something valuable', then limits that merit and restates the passage's question.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a concession as a reversal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Concession followed by a limit; the reversal wrong option catches readers who stop after the second sentence.

questions.question: According to the passage, the descent principle has been useful to countries that

options.A: needed to populate large and empty territories and to secure enough soldiers and taxpayers for the state.
options.B: sought to make naturalisation for adult residents quick, cheap and predictable.
options.C: wished to claim the children of newcomers automatically on the ground of their birth.
options.D: have many citizens living abroad and want their children to keep a tie to the homeland.

questions.correct_answer: (D) have many citizens living abroad and want their children to keep a tie to the homeland.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 gives this as the motive for the soil rule, not the descent rule.
option_rationales.B: Naturalisation speed is discussed in paragraph 3 as varying independently of the birth rule, not as a use of the descent principle.
option_rationales.C: Claiming newcomers' children by birth is the soil rule, as paragraph 2 explains.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'the descent rule has served countries with large populations abroad, allowing the children of emigrants to retain a connection to a homeland'.
questions.common_misconception: Swapping the motives the passage assigns to the two principles.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in one sentence.

questions.question: The passage as a whole is best described as

options.A: an account of how particular resource-rich states built competent institutions before their revenue arrived and so avoided its harms.
options.B: an examination of a thesis linking sources of revenue to accountability, which keeps a narrowed form of it after weighing objections.
options.C: a rejection of the claim that the way a state raises its money has any real bearing on how it treats its own citizens.
options.D: a defence of the thesis that resource revenue inevitably makes governments unaccountable, against critics who doubt that it does.

questions.correct_answer: (B) an examination of a thesis linking sources of revenue to accountability, which keeps a narrowed form of it after weighing objections.

option_rationales.A: Such states appear in one sentence of paragraph 3 as a counter-case; no particular states are described and they are not the passage's subject.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 retains 'a narrower but sturdier claim' about dependence, so the author does not reject the link outright.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls the thesis 'too mechanical', and paragraph 4 denies that 'resource revenue makes them bad'; the author qualifies rather than defends it.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 present the thesis, paragraph 3 qualifies it with two kinds of counter-case, and paragraph 4 keeps 'a narrower but sturdier claim' about dependence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'defence' option because the passage spends two paragraphs setting out the thesis sympathetically.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the author reports, qualifies and then narrows the thesis.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that a government living mainly on resource sales abroad

options.A: is unable to provide subsidies to its citizens, because its income depends on a few foreign contracts.
options.B: must negotiate constantly with its own citizens in order to keep its contracts with foreign buyers.
options.C: can sustain itself without detailed knowledge of who its citizens are or what they earn.
options.D: usually builds a larger administrative apparatus than a government that relies on taxing its people.

questions.correct_answer: (C) can sustain itself without detailed knowledge of who its citizens are or what they earn.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says such states buy 'acquiescence with subsidies and public employment', so subsidies are possible.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the revenue 'requires little cooperation from ordinary citizens', the opposite of constant negotiation.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 calls such states 'administratively thin' with 'no need to build an apparatus that knows the population'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says such a government has 'no need to build an apparatus that knows the population in detail', so it can run without that knowledge.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing one of the paragraph's several contrasts.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference restates a single clause.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most support the claim in paragraph 4 that 'it is the dependence, not the tax form as such, that does the work'?

options.A: Several resource-rich states that had strong institutions before their windfalls arrived went on to manage the revenue with notable openness.
options.B: Two governments equally dependent on their citizens' compliance, one funded by income taxes and the other by sales taxes, differ sharply in how openly they account for spending.
options.C: Citizens of states that tax heavily are more likely than others to tell survey researchers that they follow public affairs closely.
options.D: A ruler funded by customs duties collected at a few ports, needing no cooperation from most citizens, proves as unresponsive as rulers funded by mineral sales.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A ruler funded by customs duties collected at a few ports, needing no cooperation from most citizens, proves as unresponsive as rulers funded by mineral sales.

option_rationales.A: This supports paragraph 3's point about sequence, not the claim that dependence rather than tax form explains accountability.
option_rationales.B: This holds dependence constant and finds the form of the tax making the difference, which would undercut the claim that dependence rather than tax form does the work.
option_rationales.C: Interest in public affairs is not accountability, and the finding does not separate the effect of dependence from the effect of tax form.

questions.explanation: The claim separates two things that usually go together: taxing citizens and depending on them. A tax that requires no cooperation, yet yields the same unresponsiveness as resource revenue, shows that the tax form alone does nothing without dependence.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option that links taxation with openness without checking whether it separates dependence from the form of the tax.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must find the one case that pulls apart tax form and dependence; two wrong options support nearby claims.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: Raising more revenue from citizens is in itself a dependable way of making a government more accountable to them.
options.B: Taxation obtained by force need not bring the people who pay it any representation in return.
options.C: A government that needs its citizens' compliance has some reason to attend to what they demand.
options.D: The timing of a resource boom relative to the growth of institutions affects what the boom does to a state.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Raising more revenue from citizens is in itself a dependable way of making a government more accountable to them.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says many 'heavily taxed populations have obtained neither representation nor accountability in return'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says rulers 'who want a steady revenue have reason to listen' to those who pay.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says 'The sequence appears to matter as much as the source'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a reform 'that raised more revenue from citizens without increasing what citizens could demand in return would therefore miss the point entirely', so the author denies that more revenue is in itself a route to accountability.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the author endorses the original thesis in its simple form.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is a natural reading of paragraph 1 that paragraph 4 explicitly rejects.

questions.question: The reasoning in paragraph 2 implies that emergencies are commonly prolonged because

options.A: the threats that justify emergencies usually grow more severe the longer the emergency lasts.
options.B: officials fear being blamed for lifting powers too early more than they fear keeping them too long.
options.C: citizens demand that the powers stay in place long after officials would prefer to lift them.
options.D: leaders invent threats in order to dismantle the constitution gradually, one renewal at a time.

questions.correct_answer: (B) officials fear being blamed for lifting powers too early more than they fear keeping them too long.

option_rationales.A: The passage says only that the threat 'has not entirely disappeared', which implies a lingering threat, not a growing one.
option_rationales.C: The passage gives no evidence of public demand for renewal; it attributes renewal to officials' reluctance to be blamed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the common case begins with an emergency 'declared for a genuine reason'; deliberate abolition is the rarer, dramatic danger.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says emergencies are renewed 'because the threat has not entirely disappeared and no official wants to be blamed if it returns'. The asymmetry of blame is what keeps the powers alive.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the quiet pattern with the dramatic danger the paragraph sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires paraphrasing the stated reason and separating it from the dramatic case.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as the clearest sign that an emergency regime has failed?

options.A: A government declares an emergency during an epidemic and restricts movement for several months before the powers lapse.
options.B: Emergency powers are renewed three times in succession, each time by a larger majority of the legislature than the time before.
options.C: A constitution contains detailed provisions allowing the executive to rule by decree in time of war or invasion.
options.D: Detention powers first granted for a particular crisis are later moved into an ordinary statute and are no longer debated.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Detention powers first granted for a particular crisis are later moved into an ordinary statute and are no longer debated.

option_rationales.A: A genuine emergency whose powers lapse is the system working as paragraph 1 intends; it passes the test of whether the regime 'can end'.
option_rationales.B: Rising majorities for each renewal are exactly what the design in paragraph 3 demands, so this shows the safeguard working rather than failing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 defends such provisions as 'respectable', since without them governments would act 'outside the law'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 names the move of exceptional measures into 'ordinary statutes, where they no longer need renewal at all' as part of normalisation, and paragraph 4 says the purpose of safeguards is to stop exceptions 'slipping into permanence unnoticed'. The correct answer describes that failure exactly.
questions.common_misconception: Treating repeated renewal as failure, when renewals by growing majorities are what the author's design requires.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option looks like prolonged emergency rule but is the author's remedy in action; the solver must combine paragraphs 2, 3 and 4.

questions.question: The final sentence of paragraph 1 functions in the argument to

options.A: argue that emergency powers should be drafted so broadly that improvisation in a crisis is never necessary.
options.B: introduce the danger of normalisation, which the rest of the passage treats as the main problem with emergency powers.
options.C: explain why including emergency powers in a constitution is defensible despite the risks the passage goes on to describe.
options.D: show that governments in a crisis usually act outside the law even when emergency provisions are in place.

questions.correct_answer: (C) explain why including emergency powers in a constitution is defensible despite the risks the passage goes on to describe.

option_rationales.A: The sentence warns against powers with 'no defined limits', so it supports defined powers, not broad ones.
option_rationales.B: Normalisation is introduced in paragraph 2 as 'The more common pattern'; the final sentence of paragraph 1 concerns the case for having provisions at all.
option_rationales.D: The sentence says the absence of provisions would push governments outside the law; it makes no claim about what they do when provisions exist.

questions.explanation: The sentence follows 'The logic is respectable' and gives the reason: without provisions, governments would improvise 'with no defined limits and no defined end'. It justifies emergency clauses before the passage turns to their dangers.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the sentence to the next paragraph's topic rather than to the claim it supports.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the sentence as support for the preceding claim.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards sunset clauses is best described as

options.A: qualified approval: they help somewhat but leave renewal far too easy to secure.
options.B: strong endorsement: they are the most effective safeguard that a written constitution can provide.
options.C: grudging hostility: they are a distraction that has delayed the adoption of better designs.
options.D: outright rejection: they make abuse of emergency powers more likely than having no time limit at all.

questions.correct_answer: (A) qualified approval: they help somewhat but leave renewal far too easy to secure.

option_rationales.B: The author proposes 'A more demanding design' because sunset clauses turn renewal into 'a formality'.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says sunset clauses delayed anything; it says they are better than nothing but insufficient.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says 'Sunset clauses are better than nothing', which rules out outright rejection.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls sunset clauses 'better than nothing' but says they 'turn renewal into a formality', and proposes rising majorities instead.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the criticism of sunset clauses as total rejection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is mixed and the correct answer must match both halves.

questions.question: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

options.A: defend a formal understanding of the rule of law as naming a real but limited virtue that should be kept apart from other political goods.
options.B: compare the formal and richer conceptions of the rule of law and conclude that the choice between them is a merely verbal matter.
options.C: show that the formal conception of the rule of law prevents oppressive regimes from enacting and enforcing unjust laws against their subjects.
options.D: argue that the rule of law should be defined to include rights and fair distribution, since formal properties on their own are morally empty.

questions.correct_answer: (A) defend a formal understanding of the rule of law as naming a real but limited virtue that should be kept apart from other political goods.

option_rationales.B: The author holds that the choice matters, because the inclusive vocabulary 'cannot separate' different failings and is 'a poorer instrument'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says formal requirements 'forbid none of it outright', and paragraph 4 concedes that formal legality 'is compatible with deep wrong'.
option_rationales.D: This is the richer view the author argues against in paragraph 2, and paragraph 3 denies that the formal conception is 'morally empty'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues against folding every good into the phrase, paragraph 3 defends the moral worth of formality, and paragraph 4 limits that defence to the claim that formal legality is 'one distinct virtue'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'prevents' option because paragraph 3 praises formality, and missing paragraph 4's concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options catch readers who stop at paragraph 3 or who misread the author's interest in vocabulary as indifference.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the word 'congenial' most nearly means

options.A: familiar to them from long and settled practice.
options.B: warm, friendly and sociable in personal manner.
options.C: legally binding upon them in a time of crisis.
options.D: suited to their aims and convenient to use.

questions.correct_answer: (D) suited to their aims and convenient to use.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the sentence concerns familiarity; the following sentence shows the point is that such governments prefer other methods.
option_rationales.B: This sense applies to people's company; the sentence concerns whether oppressive governments find formal legality convenient, not friendly.
option_rationales.C: The word describes how governments regard legality, not whether it binds them, and crises are not mentioned in paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says oppressive governments 'rarely find formal legality congenial' and then lists the methods they 'prefer'. 'Congenial' therefore means agreeable or suited to their purposes.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the social sense of the word.
questions.difficulty_reason: The next sentence ('They tend to prefer ...') fixes the meaning.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a regime which publishes clear, prospective laws excluding a minority from public office, and enforces them impartially through independent courts,

options.A: is less unjust than it first appears, because formal legality prevents most of the harm that such laws are meant to cause.
options.B: satisfies the formal rule of law while committing a serious wrong that has to be condemned on other grounds.
options.C: shows that formal legality has no value whatever once the content of the law it applies becomes objectionable.
options.D: does not truly satisfy the rule of law at all, since its laws deprive a minority of rights it ought to enjoy.

questions.correct_answer: (B) satisfies the formal rule of law while committing a serious wrong that has to be condemned on other grounds.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says formality leaves 'some room' to anticipate and contest, and paragraph 4 says it is 'compatible with deep wrong'; it does not undo most of the harm.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the goods of formality are 'real goods even when the content of the law is objectionable'.
option_rationales.D: This is the judgement of the richer view in paragraph 1, which the author rejects in paragraph 2 because it cannot separate 'different failings'.

questions.explanation: On the author's narrow view the regime has the formal virtue, and paragraph 4 insists that questions of justice 'remain, on this view, as urgent as ever' but are 'different questions'. The regime is lawful in the formal sense and unjust on other grounds.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'less unjust' option by overextending paragraph 3's claim that formality obstructs injustice.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 together; two wrong options each exaggerate one paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author's formal conception classify as a failure of the rule of law, as distinct from a failure of justice or of democracy?

options.A: A state holds no national elections, but its laws are general, public, stable and applied by courts independent of the rulers.
options.B: A state whose courts are independent of the government faithfully applies a clearly drafted and stable law restricting public protest.
options.C: A state with generous welfare statutes lets local officials decide case by case, without any published criteria, which applicants will actually be paid.
options.D: A state publishes and impartially enforces a tax code that places the heaviest share of the burden on its poorest citizens.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A state with generous welfare statutes lets local officials decide case by case, without any published criteria, which applicants will actually be paid.

option_rationales.A: These are exactly the formal properties of paragraph 1; the absence of elections belongs to the richer package the author separates out.
option_rationales.B: Clear, stable law applied by independent courts satisfies the formal conception; whether the restriction is just is a different question.
option_rationales.D: The code is public and impartially enforced, so the formal properties are met; unfair distribution is a failure of justice, a separate question in paragraph 4.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives as a distinct failing 'excellent statutes on paper which officials ignore whenever it suits them'. Payment decided case by case without published criteria breaks the requirements that law be public and general, whatever the generosity of its content.
