questions.common_misconception: Treating any serious defect of a state, such as unfair taxes or missing elections, as a failure of the rule of law, which is the richer view the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options describe real wrongs; only one is a formal failure, and it is the only one with benevolent content.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a reason to value formal legality EXCEPT that it

options.A: tends to get in the way of the methods that governments bent on oppression usually prefer.
options.B: binds the officials who administer the law as well as the citizens who are subject to it.
options.C: allows people to know in advance what will be required of them and to plan their lives accordingly.
options.D: prevents governments from pursuing grave injustice through laws that have been properly enacted and published.

questions.correct_answer: (D) prevents governments from pursuing grave injustice through laws that have been properly enacted and published.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists secret directives and retroactive offences as preferred methods and says formal requirements 'get in the way' of much injustice.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says independent courts constrain 'the officials who administer it as well as the citizens who are subject to it'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says public, prospective law lets people 'know in advance what will be required of them and to arrange their lives around it'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says experience 'includes regimes that pursued grave injustice through meticulously drafted, publicly promulgated and impartially enforced laws', so the passage denies that formality prevents such injustice; it only obstructs much of it.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing 'get in the way of a great deal of injustice' (paragraph 3) with prevention, which paragraph 4 rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is a slightly stronger version of a true wrong option; the distinction between obstructing and preventing decides it.

questions.question: Within the author's argument, the example of the sailor in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: illustrate the self-binding defence of entrenchment, which the author then argues is a poor fit for constitutions.
options.B: show that a people, like a single person, can protect itself from its own passions by entrenching its rules.
options.C: explain why amendment rules often require the approval of most regions as well as of the legislature.
options.D: suggest that constitutions should be easier to amend in calm periods than in times of political agitation.

questions.correct_answer: (A) illustrate the self-binding defence of entrenchment, which the author then argues is a poor fit for constitutions.

option_rationales.B: This is what the defence claims; the author says the image 'does not fit the case', so the passage does not use it to show this.
option_rationales.C: Regional approval is mentioned in paragraph 1 as an example of entrenchment; the sailor does not explain it.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no proposal about timing amendments; calm and agitation belong to the image of self-binding only.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls self-binding 'The most familiar answer', illustrates it with the sailor, and then says 'The image is attractive, but it does not fit the case'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the view the example illustrates for the view the author holds.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'Just as' and the rejection that follows.

questions.question: The author's objection to the self-binding defence rests chiefly on the point that

options.A: a sailor tied to the mast can usually persuade his crew to release him once the dangerous song begins.
options.B: those whom a constitution binds are not, in any straightforward sense, the people who chose to be bound.
options.C: peoples, unlike individuals, are seldom calm enough to foresee the passions they will feel at a later time.
options.D: entrenchment protects a society against its own impulses less effectively than ordinary legislation does.

questions.correct_answer: (B) those whom a constitution binds are not, in any straightforward sense, the people who chose to be bound.

option_rationales.A: In the image the crew is ordered to 'ignore his later pleas'; the objection does not depend on whether they do.
option_rationales.C: The passage never questions whether peoples can foresee their passions; its objection concerns who is bound, not their foresight.
option_rationales.D: No comparison of effectiveness with ordinary legislation is made; the objection is that the analogy misdescribes who binds whom.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'The sailor binds himself' but 'A constitution binds people who were not present when it was adopted', so the defence assumes 'the continuity of the collective self that the objection calls into question'.
questions.common_misconception: Attacking details of the image rather than the identity point the author makes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires stating the logical flaw in the analogy in fresh words.

questions.question: The defence of entrenchment offered in paragraph 3 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: That a supermajority requirement will lead most proposals for amendment to win support from more than one faction.
options.B: That the present minorities who block amendments are usually right about the matters basic to their standing.
options.C: That amendment remains achievable in practice, so that whether a change passes is decided by the present balance of support.
options.D: That the framers of most constitutions intended amendment to be easy enough for any broad coalition to achieve.

questions.correct_answer: (C) That amendment remains achievable in practice, so that whether a change passes is decided by the present balance of support.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the requirement 'encourages' broader proposals, a tendency; the defence does not need most proposals to succeed in this.
option_rationales.B: The defence leaves open 'whether present minorities deserve such a veto'; it needs a living minority to be doing the blocking, not to be right.
option_rationales.D: The defence turns on who blocks amendments now, not on what the framers intended; framers' intentions play no part in paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that failed amendments are defeated 'by a present minority large enough to block it'. That is true only if a large enough present coalition could pass them; paragraph 4 confirms that the reframing 'succeeds only where amendment is demanding but genuinely possible'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the minorities option, although the author explicitly leaves their entitlement open as 'the real question'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The assumption is unstated in paragraph 3 and surfaces only in paragraph 4; two wrong options are near the text.

questions.question: In which of the following cases would the author most likely say that the objection from the 'dead hand' applies with full force?

options.A: An amendment backed by a narrow majority of citizens fails because a large regional minority votes against it.
options.B: A constitution requires two-thirds of the legislature and the approval of most regions for any amendment, and amendments have passed only rarely.
options.C: A constitution's amendment rules were drafted by framers who could not have foreseen the conditions under which citizens now live.
options.D: A provision declared permanently unamendable continues to bind citizens even though nearly all of them now wish to change it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A provision declared permanently unamendable continues to bind citizens even though nearly all of them now wish to change it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 treats exactly this as the work of 'a living hand', a present minority, not the dead.
option_rationales.B: Rare but real amendments under strict rules are the case of amendment that is 'demanding but genuinely possible', where paragraph 4 says the reframing 'succeeds' and any failure is the work of a present minority.
option_rationales.C: Unforeseen conditions alone are true of most constitutions; paragraph 4 limits the objection's force to cases where 'no present coalition, however broad, can alter the text'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a constitution that 'declares certain provisions unamendable altogether, really does impose the judgement of its authors on everyone who comes after'. Near-unanimous wishes thwarted by an unamendable provision are that case.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the unforeseen-conditions option because it echoes the objection as stated in paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option restates the objection's premise; the solver must apply paragraph 4's limit.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's stance towards the objection from the dead hand?

options.A: It is confused, because amendment rules never impose the judgement of a constitution's framers on anyone now living.
options.B: It is decisive, and shows that no generation may legitimately place any limits on the political choices of the next.
options.C: It fails as a case against entrenchment in general, though it has real force against constitutions that are effectively impossible to change.
options.D: It is best answered by the self-binding defence, provided that defence is stated with more care than usual.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It fails as a case against entrenchment in general, though it has real force against constitutions that are effectively impossible to change.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says an unamendable constitution 'really does impose the judgement of its authors on everyone who comes after'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 treats the objection 'not as a refutation of entrenchment as such but as a warning about its extremes', so the author denies it is decisive.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 rejects self-binding because it assumes the continuity the objection questions; the author prefers the defence of paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 calls the objection 'not as a refutation of entrenchment as such but as a warning about its extremes', which is the two-part stance of the correct answer.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'confused' option after reading only paragraph 3's reframing.
questions.difficulty_reason: The stance is two-sided and is completed only in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: defend elections against the charge that they systematically keep ordinary citizens such as shift workers and pensioners out of public office.
options.B: argue that selection by lot has genuine democratic merits but is better suited to supplementing elected bodies than to replacing them.
options.C: trace how the ancient Greek preference for filling offices by lot came to be abandoned in favour of the elections that modern states now hold.
options.D: show that randomly chosen citizens would legislate more competently than elected politicians and should therefore take their place in most chambers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) argue that selection by lot has genuine democratic merits but is better suited to supplementing elected bodies than to replacing them.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts the charge rather than rebutting it: paragraph 1 says an election picks 'a distinguished few', and paragraph 2 praises lot for including those usually 'spoken about rather than heard'.
option_rationales.C: The Greek view appears only in paragraph 1 as support for an intuition; the passage gives no history of how lot was abandoned, so this mistakes one detail for the purpose.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says only that the competence objection is 'weaker than it sounds', not that lot produces better legislators, and paragraph 4 rejects the idea that lot 'should displace election'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 make the case for lot, paragraph 3 dismisses the competence objection but accepts the accountability objection, and paragraph 4 concludes that lot 'can do something election does badly' without displacing it. The purpose is a qualified endorsement of lot as a complement to elections.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the strong case for lot in paragraphs 1 and 2 as the whole argument and missing the limit set in paragraphs 3 and 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer depends on holding the endorsement and the concession together; one wrong option captures only the endorsement.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the ancient Greek writers mentioned in paragraph 1 regarded election as less democratic than lot because election

options.A: favours people who already stand out from their fellow citizens, whereas lot gives everyone an equal chance.
options.B: allowed wealthy donors and party managers to decide in advance which candidates the citizens would be permitted to choose between.
options.C: required ordinary citizens to judge the competence of candidates on matters of law about which they knew very little.
options.D: made it impossible for those holding office to be removed by the citizens before their term of office had ended.

questions.correct_answer: (A) favours people who already stand out from their fellow citizens, whereas lot gives everyone an equal chance.

option_rationales.B: Donors and party managers belong to the modern case in paragraph 2, and nothing in the passage says they controlled who could stand in ancient elections.
option_rationales.C: Competence is raised in paragraph 3 as a criticism of lot, not of election, and it is not attributed to the Greek writers.
option_rationales.D: Removal is discussed in paragraph 3 as a strength of election, not a weakness, and the Greek writers' view is tied only to election's favouring of 'the prominent'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says winning requires a candidate to 'stand out from the crowd' and that the Greek writers saw election as 'a device that favoured the prominent'. Lot, by contrast, draws from everyone, which is why it was 'the characteristically democratic method'.
questions.common_misconception: Importing a modern reason from later paragraphs (donors, competence) into the ancient view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is located in the last two sentences of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author mentions that an elected representative who revises a position 'risks being called a turncoat' in order to

options.A: illustrate the problem of accountability that the author says the defenders of lot have never answered.
options.B: concede that selection by lot shares a weakness with election that its defenders usually prefer to overlook.
options.C: explain why members chosen by lot are in a better position to let evidence change their views.
options.D: criticise elected representatives for caring more about appearing consistent than about reaching the right answer.

questions.correct_answer: (C) explain why members chosen by lot are in a better position to let evidence change their views.

option_rationales.A: The accountability problem in paragraph 3 concerns members chosen by lot answering 'to no one', whereas the turncoat remark concerns elected members and supports lot.
option_rationales.B: The remark is part of the case for lot in paragraph 2, where a citizen chosen by lot 'has no platform to betray', so it marks a difference, not a shared weakness.
option_rationales.D: The sentence describes the pressure elected members face, not a fault of character; the author blames no one and uses it only as a contrast with lot.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists advantages of lot and ends with the claim that its members 'are free to change their minds'. The turncoat remark shows why elected members are not so free, which makes the advantage of lot concrete.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the remark as an attack on politicians, or linking it to the accountability objection because both concern representatives.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires placing the remark within the paragraph's list of advantages; one wrong option borrows the later accountability point.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the competence objection in paragraph 3?

options.A: Panels chosen by lot, unlike legislators, prove unable to judge which of their expert witnesses are reliable, and tend to adopt the view of whoever spoke last.
options.B: Legislators who disappoint their voters are often re-elected anyway, because voters remain loyal to the party under whose name they stand.
options.C: Elected legislators who depend heavily on staff and committees are often captured by those advisers, and end up voting as the advisers recommend.
options.D: Most elected legislators possess specialist knowledge of at least one policy area, usually drawn from the occupation they followed before entering politics.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Panels chosen by lot, unlike legislators, prove unable to judge which of their expert witnesses are reliable, and tend to adopt the view of whoever spoke last.

option_rationales.B: This bears on the accountability objection, and if anything it weakens the advantage the author grants to elections; it says nothing about whether a lottery body can legislate competently.
option_rationales.C: A weakness of relying on advisers would afflict elected and lottery members alike; the reply says only that there is 'no reason a randomly chosen body could not do the same', so a weakness shared by both leaves that parity intact.
option_rationales.D: The author already allows that legislators are expert in 'a sliver' of what they vote on; expertise in one area is consistent with that and leaves the reliance on advisers untouched.

questions.explanation: The author's reply assumes that a body chosen by lot could rely on 'staff, committees and witnesses' just as legislators do. If such panels cannot evaluate their witnesses, the parallel fails and the competence objection regains its force.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about expertise, about elections in general, or about a weakness of advice that legislators share, instead of the specific assumption that lottery members can use advice as well as legislators.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must isolate the unstated parity assumption in the reply, separate it from the neighbouring accountability argument, and see that a flaw in relying on advisers which legislators share does not break the parity.

questions.question: According to the passage, the laws that make voting compulsory typically require citizens to

options.A: pay a small fine each time they vote, which is returned if they can give a good excuse.
options.B: vote for one of the listed candidates, though the ballot itself remains secret from officials.
options.C: serve on a jury and complete the census form as well as attend the polling station on election day.
options.D: turn up to vote, while leaving them free to spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank.

questions.correct_answer: (D) turn up to vote, while leaving them free to spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank.

option_rationales.A: The fine in paragraph 1 is a penalty for failing to vote without an excuse, not a charge for voting; this reverses the relation.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says these laws require 'attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular', and a blank or spoiled ballot is allowed.
option_rationales.C: Jury service and the census are mentioned only as comparisons for the kind of duty involved; the passage does not say voting laws require them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states: 'What such laws typically require is attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular', adding that a citizen 'can spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the analogy (jury, census) or the penalty (fine) with the requirement itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, where voting is voluntary, campaigns tend to stir up anger against opponents mainly because

options.A: angry voters pay closer attention to policy, and so are more likely to reward a party that offers a well-argued programme.
options.B: getting likely supporters to the polls matters more than winning over the uncommitted, and anger is a cheap way to do it.
options.C: undecided citizens can be won over only by campaigns that frighten them about what the other side would do in office.
options.D: voters who are older and wealthier are, by temperament, more easily made angry or afraid than other citizens.

questions.correct_answer: (B) getting likely supporters to the polls matters more than winning over the uncommitted, and anger is a cheap way to do it.

option_rationales.A: The passage never links anger to attention to policy; paragraph 2 presents anger only as 'one of the cheapest ways' to make supporters 'turn up'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the undecided become the votes 'worth competing for' under compulsion; it never says fear is the way to win them, and fear is aimed at supporters.
option_rationales.D: The passage links the older, wealthier electorate to turnout, not to temperament; anger is used to bring supporters out, whoever they are.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says campaigns spend much of their effort getting likely supporters to 'turn up', and that 'one of the cheapest ways to do that' is to make them 'angry or afraid about the other side'. Under compulsion this 'loses much of its point' because everyone votes anyway.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the anger to the voters' character or to the undecided, rather than to the logic of mobilising turnout.
questions.difficulty_reason: The causal chain runs across several sentences of paragraph 2 and must be reconstructed.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the claim that compulsory voting 'produces wiser decisions' is best described as

options.A: sceptical, because a duty to attend a polling station does nothing by itself to inform the voter.
options.B: dismissive, because the author believes that most citizens forced to vote simply choose a name at random.
options.C: approving, because the author holds that a larger electorate makes better choices than a small and angry one.
options.D: undecided, because the author thinks the evidence about the quality of compelled votes is still inconclusive.

questions.correct_answer: (A) sceptical, because a duty to attend a polling station does nothing by itself to inform the voter.

option_rationales.B: The author says only that a resentful citizen 'may simply mark the first name'; this is a possibility, not a claim about most compelled voters, so 'most' exaggerates.
option_rationales.C: The author explicitly warns 'caution is needed' and says compulsion 'does not educate' the electorate, so approval of this claim reverses the stance.
option_rationales.D: No evidence on this question is discussed; the author reaches a clear judgement from the reasoning that attendance does not inform.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces the claim with 'Here caution is needed' and answers it: 'Compulsion enlarges the electorate; it does not educate it.' That is scepticism grounded in a stated reason, not outright dismissal or uncertainty.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the author's caution into contempt by seizing on the 'first name on the list' example.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sceptical and dismissive options both fit the negative direction; telling them apart needs attention to 'may'.

questions.question: Which of the following obligations is most similar to the kind of duty the author says compulsory voting imposes?

options.A: Members of a housing society must sign a declaration supporting the committee's plans before they are allowed to attend its annual meeting.
options.B: Members of a housing society must attend its annual meeting, but each may vote, abstain or leave the ballot blank on every motion.
options.C: Members of a housing society may attend its annual meeting only if they have first passed a short test on the society's rules.
options.D: Members of a housing society are encouraged to attend its annual meeting, and those who stay away face no penalty of any kind.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Members of a housing society must attend its annual meeting, but each may vote, abstain or leave the ballot blank on every motion.

option_rationales.A: This prescribes what members must endorse, which is the 'order about what to believe' that the author contrasts with compulsory voting.
option_rationales.C: This restricts participation by knowledge rather than requiring attendance; it resembles nothing the author describes.
option_rationales.D: This is a voluntary arrangement, the opposite of the fined duty described in paragraph 1.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the laws require 'attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular', with blank or spoiled ballots allowed. A duty to attend a meeting while remaining free to abstain on every motion has the same structure.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that keeps the compulsion but adds a required content, which the author says compulsory voting does not impose.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure of the duty is stated plainly in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The examples of the kitchen table and the telephone in paragraph 4 serve mainly to

options.A: suggest that the secret ballot was never as effective in protecting voters as its nineteenth-century supporters had claimed.
options.B: support the old liberal view that a vote seen by others is more likely to be cast for the good of the community.
options.C: show that newer ways of voting can recreate the exposure to pressure that secrecy was meant to remove.
options.D: argue that voting at home and voting with a telephone in the booth should both be prohibited in order to protect the ballot.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that newer ways of voting can recreate the exposure to pressure that secrecy was meant to remove.

option_rationales.A: The examples concern new methods that 'reopen the gap'; the passage never questions how well secrecy worked when it was introduced.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the point: the observers in paragraph 4 are a 'domineering relative' and 'whoever demands proof', the same kind of pressure paragraph 2 calls obedience, not responsibility.
option_rationales.D: The author says 'Neither practice is sinister in itself' and that both make voting easier; the conclusion is that secrecy must be maintained, not that these methods must be banned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says these practices 'reopen the gap that secrecy was designed to close' and concludes that privacy is 'an arrangement that has to be maintained'. The examples show how changes in the means of voting can expose voters again.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the author's call for vigilance into a call for prohibition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The option about prohibition is tempting because the examples are presented as dangers; the qualification 'Neither practice is sinister in itself' rules it out.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that secrecy makes a certain kind of corruption 'unenforceable' means that

options.A: voters who accept bribes are legally obliged to vote as they promised, though in practice few do.
options.B: corruption of every kind becomes impossible to prosecute once voters can no longer be observed.
options.C: officials can no longer enforce the laws against intimidation, because voters will not report it.
options.D: a corrupt bargain over a vote cannot be checked, so neither side can rely on it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a corrupt bargain over a vote cannot be checked, so neither side can rely on it.

option_rationales.A: The passage implies the opposite: the seller 'can take the money and vote as he pleases', because no obligation can be enforced.
option_rationales.B: The word concerns the corrupt deal between buyer and seller, not the law's ability to prosecute; and the claim about every kind of corruption exceeds the passage's 'a certain kind'.
option_rationales.C: Reporting by voters is never mentioned, and the paragraph says secrecy disarms bribery, not that it weakens the law.

questions.explanation: The surrounding sentences explain the word: buying a vote is a contract, and 'a contract is worthless if one party cannot check whether the other has kept it'. Secrecy makes the bargain impossible to verify and therefore impossible to enforce.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'unenforceable' in its legal sense (by the state) rather than as a property of the corrupt bargain itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is explained in the two sentences before the word.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the nineteenth-century liberals who opposed the secret ballot

options.A: correctly saw that being watched alters conduct but misjudged whose standards the watching would enforce.
options.B: were insincere when they described the vote as a trust to be exercised on behalf of the community.
options.C: rightly predicted that a secret vote would lead citizens to cast their ballots for more selfish reasons.
options.D: opposed it chiefly because they themselves gained from the ability to pressure the people who voted.

questions.correct_answer: (A) correctly saw that being watched alters conduct but misjudged whose standards the watching would enforce.

option_rationales.B: The author grants that the argument 'has a certain nobility', which does not fit a charge of insincerity.
option_rationales.C: The author never says secrecy made voting more selfish; paragraph 2 says publicity made votes 'more obedient', not more public-spirited.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 separates these liberals from 'those who profited from intimidation', saying the reform was resisted 'not only' by the latter.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 concedes that the argument 'rests on a real insight: people do behave differently when they are observed', but says its 'error lies in assuming that the observer will be the voter's conscience'; in fact the observers were landlords and employers.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the principled opponents with those who profited from intimidation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases a concession and a criticism from different sentences; one wrong option misreads the 'not only' clause.

questions.question: By the reasoning of paragraph 3, which of the following arrangements would best preserve the protection that secrecy gives against vote buying?

options.A: Ballots are cast openly, but any voter who reports an attempt to buy a vote is given full legal protection against the person who made it.
options.B: Ballots are marked in private, but each voter is handed a numbered slip, and the marked papers are published with their numbers after the count.
options.C: Voters may decide whether to keep their ballots secret, and those who choose to disclose their vote receive an official receipt recording the choice.
options.D: Voters may photograph their ballots, but any voter may later cast a fresh ballot that silently replaces the earlier one, so no photograph proves the final vote.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Voters may photograph their ballots, but any voter may later cast a fresh ballot that silently replaces the earlier one, so no photograph proves the final vote.

option_rationales.A: An open ballot lets the buyer check the vote, so the bargain is enforceable; legal protection for reporters does not restore the unverifiability that paragraph 3 relies on.
option_rationales.B: Privacy in the booth is not enough if the vote can be traced afterwards; a published, numbered paper lets a buyer demand the slip and check the vote, which the passage says destroys the protection.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says that if voters 'could choose to reveal their ballots', those under pressure could be made to prove compliance; an optional receipt does exactly this.

questions.explanation: The protection in paragraph 3 rests on one condition: no one 'can verify how a ballot was marked'. If any vote can be silently replaced, a photograph of one ballot proves nothing about the vote that counts, so a buyer still cannot check the bargain. Each other arrangement lets the buyer verify the vote.
questions.common_misconception: Treating privacy at the moment of marking as the essence of secrecy, rather than the impossibility of verifying the vote afterwards.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must extract the principle of unverifiability and apply it to an unfamiliar arrangement in which a photograph is permitted.

questions.question: According to the passage, hostility to elites cannot by itself serve as a definition of populism because

options.A: voters who distrust elites are often moved by real grievances that deserve a hearing.
options.B: many movements hostile to elites have promised to cut public spending rather than increase it.
options.C: criticising those in power is a normal activity of opposition in every democracy.
options.D: elites in most democracies have themselves adopted the language of their populist critics.

questions.correct_answer: (C) criticising those in power is a normal activity of opposition in every democracy.

option_rationales.A: Grievances belong to paragraph 4's warning about misusing the definition, not to the reason anti-elitism is insufficient.
option_rationales.B: Variety of programmes is discussed in paragraph 1 as a reason the term seems loose, not as the reason anti-elitism fails as a definition.
option_rationales.D: The passage never says this; the reason given in paragraph 2 concerns what ordinary opposition does.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the definition 'cannot be sufficient, since criticism of the powerful is the ordinary business of opposition in any democracy, and a definition that made every challenger a populist would be useless'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a true statement from another paragraph that answers a different question.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage serves primarily to

options.A: argue that populist movements are justified in their methods because the complaints of their supporters are real ones.
options.B: warn that a sound definition of populism can be misused to brush aside the complaints on which populist movements draw.
options.C: show that populism is, after all, merely a label for any style of politics the speaker happens to dislike.
options.D: withdraw the definition defended in the preceding paragraphs on the ground that it is unfair to the ordinary voters who support populists.

questions.correct_answer: (B) warn that a sound definition of populism can be misused to brush aside the complaints on which populist movements draw.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says grievances are real but still calls populism 'a threat to democratic competition'; it never justifies populist methods.
option_rationales.C: This is the conclusion that paragraph 1 calls 'premature'; the final paragraph does not return to it.
option_rationales.D: The author keeps the definition, calling it 'a tool for recognising a threat'; the paragraph limits its use, it does not withdraw it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with 'Yet the definition carries a hazard of its own' and ends by saying the definition 'is not a licence to stop asking why the threat finds an audience'. It qualifies how the definition should be used.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a qualification for a retraction, or sympathy for grievances for approval of populism.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option exaggerates the qualification into a retraction; the correct answer keeps both the definition and the warning.

questions.question: The passage implies that an analyst who treats every supporter of a populist movement as a victim of manipulation would be

options.A: showing that the definition based on a moral monopoly is too narrow to explain why populism attracts support.
options.B: acting reasonably, since the complaints that draw voters to populist movements are seldom ones that institutions could address.
options.C: applying the anti-pluralist definition correctly, even if without much sympathy for the voters concerned.
options.D: reproducing, in another form, the refusal to grant opponents the standing of citizens who disagree for reasons.

questions.correct_answer: (D) reproducing, in another form, the refusal to grant opponents the standing of citizens who disagree for reasons.

option_rationales.A: The passage faults those who misuse the definition, not its scope; it says the definition must not stop us 'asking why the threat finds an audience', not that it fails to answer.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says many such voters 'have real complaints' about distant decisions and unresponsive institutions, which contradicts this.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 presents this treatment as a misuse that the definition can 'tempt' people into; it is not a correct application of a definition meant only to recognise a threat.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines populism by its refusal 'to accept that the people may be divided in good faith'. Paragraph 4 says that treating populist voters 'as a symptom to be managed, rather than as citizens with reasons' denies them 'the standing that pluralism promises'. Such an analyst therefore mirrors the anti-pluralism the definition was meant to detect.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the critic of populism to be automatically on the side of pluralism.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the definition in paragraph 2 to the warning in paragraph 4 to see the reflexive point, which is not stated in one place.

questions.question: Which of the following movements would most clearly count as populist on the definition the author defends?

options.A: A movement that accuses the established parties of ignoring rural districts and asks the voters of those districts to judge it at the next election.
options.B: A movement that promises the largest programme of public spending in the country's history and draws its support mainly from the poorest voters.
options.C: A movement with cautious economic policies that calls its rivals' voters traitors to the nation and blames any election it loses on fraud.
options.D: A movement that campaigns fiercely against the influence of large banks on government and accepts the result whenever it loses an election.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A movement with cautious economic policies that calls its rivals' voters traitors to the nation and blames any election it loses on fraud.

option_rationales.A: This voices a grievance of the kind paragraph 4 calls real and submits to voters' judgement; it makes no claim that rivals are illegitimate.
option_rationales.B: This identifies populism by policy and by who supports it, the approach the passage says misses the point, since populism 'is not a programme at all'.
option_rationales.D: This shows only hostility to elites, which paragraph 2 says is 'the ordinary business of opposition'; accepting defeat is the opposite of the pattern in paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: On the author's definition the mark of populism is the claim that one movement alone represents the authentic people, so that opponents are 'illegitimate' and defeat 'must then be explained as fraud'. Only the movement that calls rivals' voters traitors and blames fraud makes that claim, despite its unremarkable policies.
questions.common_misconception: Identifying populism by fierce anti-elite rhetoric or by lavish policies, which the passage expressly treats as insufficient.
questions.difficulty_reason: The fiercely anti-elite option is the natural everyday sense of populism; rejecting it requires the passage's specific definition.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: For all their faults, parties do work democracy needs, so their failings call for improving them rather than bypassing them.
options.B: Parties deserve far more admiration than they receive, since the functions they perform show that they are fundamentally virtuous.
options.C: Open primaries, though meant to democratise parties, usually produce candidates with intense followings rather than broad appeal.
options.D: Parties have become so self-serving that reformers are right to replace them with independent candidates and direct votes on policy.

questions.correct_answer: (A) For all their faults, parties do work democracy needs, so their failings call for improving them rather than bypassing them.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says plainly 'None of this makes parties virtuous' and warns against confusing indispensability with innocence.
option_rationales.C: This is one example in paragraph 3 supporting the larger argument; as a summary of the whole passage it is too narrow.
option_rationales.D: The passage reports these reforms in paragraph 1 only to argue against them; paragraph 4 rejects 'a politics that tries to do without them'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists what parties do for democratic government, paragraph 3 shows that weakening them shifts power elsewhere, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'the cure for bad parties is better ones'. The correct answer states the claim with its qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the open-primaries detail, or overstating the defence of parties into praise of their virtue.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is a true but narrow detail, another an overstatement the passage explicitly denies.

questions.question: According to the passage, a legislature made up entirely of independents would be a problem for voters because it

options.A: would be unable to assemble the conflicting interests of millions of people into any kind of legislation.
options.B: would leave them without any collective body that they could reward or punish at the next election.
options.C: would be dominated by wealthy individuals who had paid for the campaigns of most of its members.
options.D: would contain members who had been screened too strictly by organisations remote from local life.

questions.correct_answer: (B) would leave them without any collective body that they could reward or punish at the next election.

option_rationales.A: The passage says parties assemble interests into programmes, but it does not claim independents could pass no legislation; the stated problem is accountability.
option_rationales.C: Wealthy individuals appear in paragraph 3 as those who gain when parties weaken, but the passage does not say they would dominate a legislature of independents.
option_rationales.D: Screening is a function of parties, which independents by definition lack; the passage says weak parties screen too little, not too strictly.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'a legislature of independents, each with a private bargain to defend, offers voters no one in particular to reward or punish'.
questions.common_misconception: Overextending another function of parties (assembling interests) into an absolute claim about independents.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in the last sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: When the author says that defenders of party government have 'mistaken the indispensability of parties for their innocence', the point is that these defenders

options.A: have confused the innocent intentions of party founders with the conduct of the parties they built.
options.B: have wrongly believed that democracy could function perfectly well without any parties at all.
options.C: have assumed that because parties are necessary to democracy, they must also be free of blame.
options.D: have argued that parties are guilty of misconduct only when they face no serious competition.

questions.correct_answer: (C) have assumed that because parties are necessary to democracy, they must also be free of blame.

option_rationales.A: The founders' intentions are not discussed; the contrast in the phrase is between being necessary and being blameless.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the phrase: the defenders overrate parties, believing them necessary and blameless, rather than thinking them dispensable.
option_rationales.D: The sentence before mentions parties without competition, but the phrase itself describes a confusion between necessity and blamelessness, not a theory of when parties misbehave.

questions.explanation: The word 'indispensability' means being necessary; 'innocence' means being free of fault. Paragraph 4 says that the defenders treated the first as if it implied the second, which is why the author adds 'None of this makes parties virtuous'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the phrase as being about party founders or as a claim that parties are unnecessary.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase can be decoded directly from its two central words and the sentence that frames it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 about candidates chosen in open primaries?

options.A: Where parties adopted open primaries, turnout in those contests was high among committed party activists and very low among everyone else.
options.B: Where parties adopted open primaries, the candidates who won were generally those whom uncommitted voters rated most highly in polls.
options.C: Party membership has fallen as steeply in countries that never adopted open primaries as in countries that adopted them early.
options.D: Candidates chosen in open primaries tend to spend more money on their campaigns than candidates chosen by party committees.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Where parties adopted open primaries, the candidates who won were generally those whom uncommitted voters rated most highly in polls.

option_rationales.A: This makes it more likely that candidates with 'the most intense supporters' win, so it strengthens rather than weakens the claim.
option_rationales.C: This concerns the separate point about dwindling membership; it says nothing about what kind of candidate primaries select.
option_rationales.D: Campaign spending is not part of the claim, which concerns whether winners have intense supporters or broad appeal.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that in open primaries 'the candidates who win are often those with the most intense supporters rather than those with the broadest appeal'. Evidence that winners were the ones uncommitted voters preferred would show broad appeal winning, which cuts directly against this.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the turnout option because it mentions primaries and activists, without noticing that it supports the claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options concern primaries or the same paragraph; the solver must see that one strengthens and one addresses a different claim.

questions.question: According to the passage, disruption is close to the centre of democratic protest because

options.A: the public has always come to regard the causes of disruptive protesters as just once their methods are forgotten.
options.B: protesters who cause no disruption are usually breaking the law, while those who cause disruption usually are not.
options.C: governments in most democracies treat every inconvenience caused by protesters as an emergency requiring a response.
options.D: groups lacking money, office or press access have few other ways of bringing an issue to public notice.

questions.correct_answer: (D) groups lacking money, office or press access have few other ways of bringing an issue to public notice.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'Many causes' now thought just were first raised by nuisances; a claim about every such cause, with a condition about forgotten methods, goes beyond this.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about the legality of quiet or disruptive protest; this is outside its scope.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 urges governments not to treat every inconvenience as an emergency; it does not say most governments do, and this is not the reason given in paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains: 'Groups without money, office or access to the press have few ways of placing an issue on the public agenda, and a temporary cost imposed on the wider community is one of them.'
questions.common_misconception: Overgeneralising the historical remark about causes later judged just into a reason that is always true.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated directly in the second sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The remark that 'A march that nobody notices, held where nobody has to walk around it, is hardly a protest' suggests that the author believes

options.A: imposing some cost on others is part of what lets a protest function as a public claim.
options.B: complaints about inconvenience caused by protests are unfair and should be ignored by those who govern.
options.C: protests should be held in the busiest places available, whatever inconvenience this causes to the public.
options.D: most protests fail because their organisers choose places where they will not be noticed by anyone.

questions.correct_answer: (A) imposing some cost on others is part of what lets a protest function as a public claim.

option_rationales.B: The author grants that the complaint 'has some force'; the objection is only to the assumption that legitimate protest causes no inconvenience.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the costs of a method should 'bear some relation' to its importance, so an unlimited tolerance of inconvenience contradicts the author.
option_rationales.D: The remark describes what makes protest meaningful, not why most protests fail; the passage offers no claim about failure rates.

questions.explanation: The remark follows the claim that the complaint about inconvenience hides an assumption 'that legitimate protest would cause no inconvenience at all'. The author answers that 'Part of the point of gathering in public is to make a claim that others cannot easily ignore', so some imposition belongs to protest itself.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the author's defence of some disruption into a defence of unlimited disruption.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the remark to the sentences around it and to the limit set in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: Disruption is legitimate whenever the cause it serves is later judged by most people to have been just.
options.B: Governments should avoid treating every inconvenience caused by protesters as if it were an emergency.
options.C: A protest may legitimately impose costs on people who bear no responsibility for the grievance concerned.
options.D: Protesters ought to weigh the harm that their methods cause against the importance of their message.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Disruption is legitimate whenever the cause it serves is later judged by most people to have been just.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says those who govern 'have a responsibility not to treat every inconvenience as an emergency', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 accepts that commuters and shopkeepers who 'have done nothing wrong' are inconvenienced, and paragraph 2 defends a 'temporary cost imposed on the wider community'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says protesters should 'choose methods whose costs bear some relation to the importance of what they are saying'.

questions.explanation: The author's tests of legitimate disruption are its aim (seeking a hearing rather than imposing an outcome) and its proportion. Paragraph 2 notes that many just causes were once called a nuisance, but nowhere makes later vindication the test; a protest that blocked a lawful vote would fail the author's test whatever history later thought of its cause.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the historical remark in paragraph 2 as the author's criterion of legitimacy.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported statement echoes paragraph 2, so it must be rejected by recognising that the author's criteria are aim and proportion.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most clearly regard as disruption that 'seeks to impose an outcome'?

options.A: Protesters occupy a public square for a weekend, holding speeches and handing out leaflets to passers-by.
options.B: Protesters chain shut the doors of a council chamber so that a scheduled vote cannot be held.
options.C: Protesters march through the city centre during the evening rush hour, delaying traffic for most of the evening.
options.D: Protesters stand silently outside a council chamber with banners while councillors arrive for a scheduled vote.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Protesters chain shut the doors of a council chamber so that a scheduled vote cannot be held.

option_rationales.A: An occupation that invites passers-by to listen seeks attention and persuasion; nobody is prevented from acting on a decision.
option_rationales.C: This imposes a cost to win attention, which paragraph 3 calls disruption that 'seeks a hearing'; at most it raises the question of proportion.
option_rationales.D: This disrupts very little and does not prevent the vote; it is an attempt to be noticed, not to impose an outcome.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says disruption that seeks to impose an outcome tries 'to make it impossible for others to act on their own decision, for instance by preventing a lawful vote from taking place'. Chaining shut the chamber so the vote cannot be held fits exactly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the most inconvenient option (the rush-hour march) rather than the one that blocks a decision.
questions.difficulty_reason: Paragraph 3 gives a near-identical example.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Local newspapers were the most trustworthy watchdogs that democracies have ever had, and their closure has left local government without any honest observers at all.
options.B: The closure of local papers matters mainly because communities lose the obituaries, sports results and notices that bound their members together.
options.C: The chief democratic loss when local papers close is routine scrutiny of local government, which must now be sustained by other means despite the papers' own failings.
options.D: The internet has replaced local newspapers as a source of information about councils, though it spreads rumours more quickly than facts.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The chief democratic loss when local papers close is routine scrutiny of local government, which must now be sustained by other means despite the papers' own failings.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says many local papers were 'timid', 'cosy' and 'weak' watchdogs, so calling them the most trustworthy contradicts the author.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 grants these are 'real losses' but says 'they are not the ones that matter most for self-government'.
option_rationales.D: The author denies that the internet has replaced the papers, saying it 'confuses the supply of commentary with the supply of attention'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 identifies 'the habit of attendance' as the main loss, paragraphs 2 and 3 explain why it mattered and why the internet does not replace it, paragraph 4 rejects nostalgia for the papers themselves, and paragraph 5 calls for the function to be 'supported deliberately'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a summary that keeps the subject (local papers) but adopts a view the author reports and rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option states a view mentioned in the passage; the correct answer requires combining the function argument with the concession.

questions.question: The comparison with a speed camera in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: show that most of what local reporters wrote led to fines or penalties for the officials they wrote about.
options.B: suggest that local reporters, like speed cameras, were resented by the officials whose meetings they attended.
options.C: argue that local governments should be watched by automatic recording devices rather than by journalists.
options.D: illustrate that the value of monitoring lies mainly in the misconduct it deters rather than in what it exposes.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate that the value of monitoring lies mainly in the misconduct it deters rather than in what it exposes.

option_rationales.A: The comparison makes the opposite point: the effect is measured 'not by the fines it issues', and paragraph 2 says most reports were 'unremarkable'.
option_rationales.B: Resentment is never mentioned; the comparison concerns how an observer's effect is measured, not how officials felt about it.
option_rationales.C: The comparison is an analogy for how monitoring works, not a proposal; paragraph 5's suggestions do not include automatic devices.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says monitoring works as a speed camera does: 'its effect is measured not by the fines it issues but by the careless driving it prevents'. The point is deterrence.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the analogy literally, as a proposal about devices or a claim about penalties.
questions.difficulty_reason: The analogy is explained in the sentence that contains it.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards a neighbourhood online forum as

options.A: quick to circulate claims about local government but poorly placed to scrutinise it in a sustained way.
options.B: a dangerous source of misinformation that local governments would be justified in regulating closely.
options.C: an adequate substitute for a local reporter wherever its members are willing to attend council meetings.
options.D: more useful than a national outlet, because it reports on local government before the damage is done.

questions.correct_answer: (A) quick to circulate claims about local government but poorly placed to scrutinise it in a sustained way.

option_rationales.B: The author mentions that a forum can spread a rumour, but proposes no regulation and does not call forums dangerous; this goes beyond the passage.
option_rationales.C: The passage says forums 'seldom' have such members and also lack 'the training to read a set of accounts', so attendance alone would not make them adequate on the author's account.
option_rationales.D: The passage compares neither in this way; it faults both, the forum for lacking attention and the national outlet for arriving after the damage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a forum 'can spread a rumour about the council in minutes' but 'seldom has anyone willing to spend three evenings a month in council meetings, or the training to read a set of accounts'. It supplies reaction, not the 'patient, unglamorous observation' on which reaction depends.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the forum example as a condemnation of online media rather than as a point about attention versus commentary.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires paraphrasing the contrast between commentary and attention; one wrong option overlooks the second requirement (training).

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the local newspapers of the past is best described as

options.A: nostalgic, since the author regards their disappearance as the loss of a better and more honest era of journalism.
options.B: appreciative of the observation they performed while critical of their deference to local power.
options.C: indifferent, since the author thinks any institution could have performed their work equally well or better.
options.D: contemptuous, since the author believes that their timidity with advertisers made their coverage worthless.

questions.correct_answer: (B) appreciative of the observation they performed while critical of their deference to local power.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 opens 'None of this should be allowed to turn into nostalgia' and lists the papers' failings.
option_rationales.C: The author cares a great deal about the work they did and calls its loss important; indifference does not fit, and the passage does not rank institutions.
option_rationales.D: The author calls them weak watchdogs, but says their function was performed 'however imperfectly' and was worth preserving, which is not contempt.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 value the 'habit of attendance' the papers provided, paragraph 4 criticises them as 'timid', 'cosy' and given to 'boosterism', and paragraph 5 says they performed their function 'however imperfectly'. The attitude is mixed: appreciation of the function, criticism of the institutions.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a one-sided attitude from either the praise or the criticism.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contemptuous option draws on real criticism in paragraph 4; it must be rejected through 'however imperfectly'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about how monitoring works in paragraph 2?

options.A: Officials in towns with a local paper said that they seldom read the paper's reports of their own meetings.
options.B: In their final decade, the papers that eventually closed had published very few investigative reports about their councils.
options.C: In towns whose papers closed, residents said they now read more news about their council online than they had before.
options.D: In towns whose papers closed, the cost of public contracts rose steadily over the next few years, although no new scandals were reported there.

questions.correct_answer: (D) In towns whose papers closed, the cost of public contracts rose steadily over the next few years, although no new scandals were reported there.

option_rationales.A: The author's mechanism depends on officials knowing 'that someone was taking notes', not on their reading the coverage, so this neither supports nor undermines it.
option_rationales.B: This fits the remark that most reporting was 'unremarkable', but it does not show that the papers' presence restrained conduct, which is the claim at issue.
option_rationales.C: This bears on the objection in paragraph 3 that the internet has compensated, and if anything it supports that objection, not the deterrence claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 claims that a reporter's presence restrains officials, and that removing it causes 'a gradual loosening of the restraint' without 'a wave of scandal'. Rising contract costs with no reported scandal is exactly the pattern this predicts, so it strengthens the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the officials-do-not-read option as a weakener or strengthener, missing that the mechanism is awareness of being observed.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is closely related to the passage; the solver must match the prediction of the deterrence claim precisely.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, 'rational ignorance' refers to

options.A: the tendency of voters to draw illogical conclusions from the political information that they already happen to possess.
options.B: ignorance that voters conceal by offering reasonable-sounding justifications for choices they made without any real thought.
options.C: a lack of knowledge that comes from sensibly weighing the cost of learning against a vote's tiny chance of mattering.
options.D: knowledge that governments deliberately withhold from voters in order to avoid the scrutiny that an informed public would bring.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a lack of knowledge that comes from sensibly weighing the cost of learning against a vote's tiny chance of mattering.

option_rationales.A: This reverses the passage, which says 'the problem is not that voters reason badly but that they have little reason to acquire' information.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in paragraph 1 concerns concealment or justification; the term describes why voters choose not to acquire knowledge.
option_rationales.D: The ignorance described is chosen by voters themselves in view of costs; government secrecy is not mentioned anywhere in the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 explains that ignorance 'is what a sensible person would choose if he or she treated the vote as a decision with private costs and a vanishingly small chance of making a difference', and that 'Economists call this rational ignorance'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'rational' as describing how voters reason about what they know, rather than the decision not to learn.
questions.difficulty_reason: The term is defined by the surrounding sentences, but one wrong option exploits the ordinary sense of 'rational'.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard the claim that a voter equipped with cues 'can vote much as she would if she were fully informed' as

options.A: true only under conditions, such as stable and distinct parties, that a democracy cannot assume will hold.
options.B: broadly true, because party labels, prices and endorsements together give voters a reliable picture of every government.
options.C: false, because voters are in general incapable of using simple cues such as party labels in a sensible way.
options.D: beside the point, because the author holds that what matters is who would set and mark a test of voters' knowledge.

questions.correct_answer: (A) true only under conditions, such as stable and distinct parties, that a democracy cannot assume will hold.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says this conclusion 'claims too much' and shows how each of these three cues can fail, so calling the picture reliable for every government contradicts the author.
option_rationales.C: The author says voters do not 'reason badly'; the problem in paragraph 3 lies in the reliability of the cues, not in voters' ability to use them.
option_rationales.D: The quarrel over the test is raised in paragraph 4 as an objection to weighting votes, not as a reason to set aside the question of how well cues work.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the shortcut argument 'claims too much': a cue works only if its connection to what the voter cares about holds, and that connection 'is not guaranteed'. Party labels, for example, are informative only 'when parties are stable and their programmes distinct'. The claim is therefore conditionally true.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the author's criticism of the shortcut argument as a rejection of voters' competence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author partly accepts and partly rejects the defenders' claim; the false and broadly true options each capture one half.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply in paragraph 4 to those who would weight votes by knowledge?

options.A: Voters who score highly on tests of political knowledge often disagree sharply with one another about which policies are best.
options.B: Political parties in many democracies have grown more fragmented over recent decades, making their labels less informative to voters.
options.C: Even in settings where cues are highly reliable, voters' choices still differ markedly from the choices they would make if fully informed.
options.D: Tests of political knowledge have proved very difficult to design without favouring the education of some social groups over others.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Even in settings where cues are highly reliable, voters' choices still differ markedly from the choices they would make if fully informed.

option_rationales.A: This casts doubt on the critics' assumption that the informed reach better decisions, so it tends to support the author rather than weaken the reply.
option_rationales.B: This is consistent with paragraph 3 and shows why cues may need improving; it does not show that improving them would fail.
option_rationales.D: This supports the author, who warns that a test would invite a quarrel 'unlikely ever to be settled impartially'.

questions.explanation: The reply assumes that the quality of popular judgement 'varies with the reliability of the cues', so that improving cues is a remedy. If voters choose badly even when cues are reliable, improving cues would not close the gap, and the case for an alternative remedy regains force.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is about cues or tests in general, without checking whether it attacks the assumption on which the reply rests.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must identify the assumption of paragraph 4 and recognise that two wrong options actually support the author.

questions.question: The reference to voters who punish an incumbent 'for a drought' serves to

options.A: support the critics' view that the franchise should be weighted towards citizens who know more about policy.
options.B: show how a reasonable-seeming cue can hold governments responsible for things they do not control.
options.C: suggest that governments are generally less competent than voters believe, but are rarely punished for it.
options.D: show that voters who rely on how things are going reason worse than those who follow the endorsements of trusted organisations.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show how a reasonable-seeming cue can hold governments responsible for things they do not control.

option_rationales.A: The example belongs to the author's criticism of the shortcut argument; the author goes on in paragraph 4 to reject weighting the vote.
option_rationales.C: The point is that the cue 'measures luck as much as competence', not that governments are incompetent or escape punishment.
option_rationales.D: The passage compares no cues in this way; paragraph 3 says each kind of cue, endorsements included, can fail.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says judging a government by how things are going is reasonable 'if the government controls how things are going', and the drought is an example of an outcome it does not control, a cue that 'measures luck as much as competence'.
questions.common_misconception: Linking the example to the critics' conclusion because it shows voters erring.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example could seem to support the critics; its function is fixed by its place in the author's paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the author's overall position?

options.A: Since shortcuts are too unreliable to depend on, democracies should do much more to make every citizen properly informed about policy.
options.B: Since voters' ignorance is rational, it poses no real threat to the quality of democratic decisions and requires no remedy.
options.C: Since uninformed voters can easily be misled, the critics of democracy are right to give greater weight to the votes of informed citizens.
options.D: Since voters' competence depends partly on institutions, democracies should make the cues voters rely on more reliable instead of restricting who may vote.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Since voters' competence depends partly on institutions, democracies should make the cues voters rely on more reliable instead of restricting who may vote.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says a democracy can make citizens 'wiser as voters without making any of them more learned', so the remedy is better cues, not more knowledge.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says shortcuts 'do not make ignorance harmless', and paragraph 5 grants that 'an uninformed electorate can be misled'.
option_rationales.C: The author accepts the first clause in paragraph 5 but rejects the conclusion in paragraph 4, so this combines a concession with a view the author opposes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'the natural remedy is to improve the cues rather than to disqualify the people who use them', and paragraph 5 adds that competence is 'partly a product of institutions'. The correct answer joins the two.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the education option, which shares the author's dissatisfaction with shortcuts but proposes the remedy the final sentence rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every wrong option uses a premise the author accepts; the solver must match the remedy as well as the diagnosis.

questions.question: The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: explain why small states usually prefer forming alliances with one another to relying on the protection of a great power.
options.B: show that neutral states have nearly always stayed out of wars, provided that they kept armies strong enough to deter invasion.
options.C: recast neutrality, which critics treat as moral evasion, as a costly strategy by which small states try to keep out of wars.
options.D: defend neutral states against the charge of profiteering by showing that very few of them have gained from wars nearby.

questions.correct_answer: (C) recast neutrality, which critics treat as moral evasion, as a costly strategy by which small states try to keep out of wars.

option_rationales.A: Alliances appear only in a comparison in paragraph 3 ('Few alliances ask as much'); the passage never discusses small states allying with one another.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens 'None of this guarantees success' and says even a well-armed record 'may count for little', so the claim of near-constant success contradicts the author.
option_rationales.D: The author concedes in paragraph 4 that a neutral that profits 'invites the suspicion its critics voice'; nowhere does the passage claim such profit is rare.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the critics' charge and says it 'rests on a misunderstanding'. Paragraphs 2 and 3 present neutrality as 'a strategy, and a demanding one' requiring armed strength and peacetime discipline, and paragraph 4 qualifies the claim while redirecting the question to whether neutrality keeps a state out of war. The purpose is to recast neutrality as a costly strategy.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the author's defence into a claim of guaranteed success, ignoring the concession in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is announced at the end of paragraph 1 and developed directly; wrong options are clearly off once paragraph 4 is read.

questions.question: According to the passage, a neutral state must arm itself

options.A: against all of its neighbours at once, since it must be ready to resist whichever of them crosses its frontier first.
options.B: only so far as is needed to reassure its neighbours that its forces pose no threat to any of them.
options.C: against the strongest of its neighbours, since that power is the one most likely to want its territory as a road or a base.
options.D: together with other neutral states, so that their combined forces make the occupation of any one of them expensive.

questions.correct_answer: (A) against all of its neighbours at once, since it must be ready to resist whichever of them crosses its frontier first.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 asks for 'an army strong enough to make occupation expensive'; a minimal, reassuring force is not what the passage describes.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the neutral must arm 'against all of its neighbours at once rather than against one', which rules out concentrating on a single power.
option_rationales.D: The passage calls neutrality a 'solitary commitment' in paragraph 3 and never mentions neutrals pooling their forces.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states that the neutral 'must be ready to resist whichever side violates its frontier first, which means it must arm against all of its neighbours at once rather than against one'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming a state should arm against its most dangerous neighbour, which is how an aligned state would reason.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the author describes a neutral that cannot defend its borders as 'simply unclaimed'. The word suggests that such a state is

options.A: free of any formal alliance with a larger power, which is exactly the condition that a policy of neutrality aims to secure.
options.B: thinly settled and of little economic value, so that its larger neighbours have no particular reason to want it.
options.C: not recognised as a sovereign state by the great powers of its region and so lacking any standing under international law.
options.D: outside any effective protection, its own or anyone else's, and therefore open to seizure by whichever power moves first.

questions.correct_answer: (D) outside any effective protection, its own or anyone else's, and therefore open to seizure by whichever power moves first.

option_rationales.A: A well-armed neutral is also free of alliances, so that cannot be what separates the 'unclaimed' state from a true neutral; the contrast drawn is between defended and undefended territory.
option_rationales.B: This reads the word literally as unwanted land, but the passage says such ground 'is soon claimed', the opposite of being of no interest.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about legal recognition; the next clause, 'unclaimed ground in wartime is soon claimed', shows the point is about being seized.

questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts a neutral that can defend itself with one that cannot. The second is 'unclaimed' in the sense that no force secures it, and the passage adds that 'unclaimed ground in wartime is soon claimed', that is, taken by someone.
questions.common_misconception: Equating 'unclaimed' with being non-aligned, which is true of every neutral and so misses the contrast the sentence draws.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the clause that immediately follows the word.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a neutral state's conduct in peacetime matters chiefly because

options.A: treaties of friendship signed in peacetime would legally bind a neutral to support its partner once a war broke out.
options.B: foreign governments read minor gestures as clues to its wartime loyalties, and its security rests on their believing it impartial.
options.C: critics of neutrality judge a state mainly by its peacetime record rather than by what it does once fighting begins.
options.D: a neutral that behaves impartially in peacetime can count on the great powers to respect its borders in any later war.

questions.correct_answer: (B) foreign governments read minor gestures as clues to its wartime loyalties, and its security rests on their believing it impartial.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says such a treaty 'can be read abroad as a signal'; the concern is how it is perceived, not any legal obligation it creates.
