option_rationales.C: The critics in paragraph 1 object to sitting out wars and trading with the winner, which is wartime conduct; the passage does not say they focus on peacetime.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 denies any such guarantee: even 'a well-armed and scrupulous record may count for little' when its territory becomes essential to someone.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the aim of neutrality is to persuade each neighbour that the territory will never serve the others, and that this persuasion 'has to be earned'. Paragraph 3 adds that a treaty, a trade deal or a 'careless remark' can be read abroad 'as a signal of where it would stand in a crisis'. So peacetime conduct matters because neighbours' belief in its impartiality is what neutrality depends on.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that promises respect for an impartial record, overlooking that paragraph 4 withholds any guarantee.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the purpose stated in paragraph 2 to the peacetime discipline in paragraph 3; one wrong option is tempting until paragraph 4 is applied.

questions.question: Paragraph 2 functions in the passage chiefly to

options.A: offer cases that the popular lesson cannot explain and to propose different factors that decide whether a settlement lasts.
options.B: prove that severe settlements are, as a rule, more durable than lenient ones and should therefore be preferred by victors.
options.C: describe in detail how the terms of the settlement after the First World War came to be evaded one by one.
options.D: explain why victorious powers find it comforting to believe that a generous peace is both noble and prudent.

questions.correct_answer: (A) offer cases that the popular lesson cannot explain and to propose different factors that decide whether a settlement lasts.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says severity and generosity 'are the wrong variables to watch', so it does not rank harsh settlements above lenient ones.
option_rationales.C: The evasion of harsh terms 'piece by piece' is described in paragraph 3, and paragraph 2 gives no detail about that settlement.
option_rationales.D: The appeal of the lesson, that it 'joins morality to prudence', is explained in paragraph 1, not paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens 'the record does not sort so neatly', gives severe settlements that held and lenient ones that failed, and concludes that a settlement lasts when its terms 'match the actual balance of strength' and are upheld. It supplies counter-cases and an alternative explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the mention of durable severe settlements as an argument for severity.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph's role is announced by its first sentence and summed up by its last.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a lenient settlement is likely to fail when

options.A: the defeated state resents being offered trade, membership of institutions and the eventual lifting of restrictions.
options.B: the defeated state takes the mildness of its terms as a sign that its defeat was not decisive.
options.C: the victors later conclude that their terms were too generous and try to impose harsher ones in their place.
options.D: the defeated state is too weak after the war to make use of the generous terms it has been offered.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the defeated state takes the mildness of its terms as a sign that its defeat was not decisive.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says such offers give the defeated 'a stake in the order', the opposite of a source of resentment.
option_rationales.C: The passage never describes victors revising lenient terms; this explanation of failure is not in the text.
option_rationales.D: Weakness of the defeated is cited in paragraph 2 as the reason some severe settlements held, not as a reason lenient ones fail.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says some lenient settlements failed 'because the loser read leniency as a sign that it had not really been beaten', and paragraph 4 adds that generosity works best 'after the defeat has been made unmistakable'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the weakness of the defeated, which the passage links to durable severe settlements, to the failure of lenient ones.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer restates one sentence of paragraph 2, reinforced by paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of what makes a peace settlement last?

options.A: A harsh settlement that the exhausted victors stopped enforcing was overturned by the defeated state within a decade of being signed.
options.B: A lenient settlement lasted for several decades after the victors made it clear that they had won decisively and would defend its terms.
options.C: Historians continue to disagree about whether the settlement that followed the First World War was in fact unusually harsh.
options.D: A settlement that matched the balance of strength and was firmly upheld by united victors still collapsed within a few years because its harshness was resented.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A settlement that matched the balance of strength and was firmly upheld by united victors still collapsed within a few years because its harshness was resented.

option_rationales.A: This is the case paragraph 3 calls the worst combination, harsh terms and weak enforcement, so it supports the author rather than weakening the account.
option_rationales.B: This fits paragraph 4, which says generosity works once 'the defeat has been made unmistakable' and the settlement is backed, so it strengthens the account.
option_rationales.C: The author holds that severity and generosity are 'the wrong variables to watch', so a dispute about how severe that settlement was leaves the account untouched.

questions.explanation: The author claims in paragraph 2 that a settlement lasts when its terms match the balance of strength and its makers uphold it. A settlement that met both conditions yet collapsed because of resentment at its severity would show those conditions are not enough and that severity matters after all, which strikes at the account directly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a case of failure without checking whether it actually fits the author's own explanation of failure.
questions.difficulty_reason: Students must state the author's two conditions precisely and see that two options are confirming instances.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the lesson described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: dismissive of it, since the author holds that magnanimity toward a defeated enemy is imprudent whatever the circumstances.
options.B: detached from it, since the author reports the lesson and the evidence about it without reaching any judgement of their own.
options.C: sceptical of it as too simple, while granting that generosity toward the defeated, properly timed, has real value.
options.D: approving of it, since the author agrees that a generous peace reliably turns former enemies into dependable partners.

questions.correct_answer: (C) sceptical of it as too simple, while granting that generosity toward the defeated, properly timed, has real value.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'Generosity has a real role' and rejects 'cruelty dressed up as realism', so the author does not think magnanimity always imprudent.
option_rationales.B: The author judges plainly: the record 'does not sort so neatly', and paragraph 3 names what the worst settlement is.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says some lenient settlements failed and that generosity is 'the wrong variable', so the author does not endorse the lesson.

questions.explanation: The author calls the lesson attractive but says the record 'does not sort so neatly' and that severity and generosity are 'the wrong variables'. Yet paragraph 4 insists 'Generosity has a real role' once defeat is unmistakable. The stance is qualified scepticism.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's criticism of the lesson for a rejection of generosity itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are the two extremes; the correct answer requires holding the critique and the concession together.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a sanctioned government can blame foreigners for shortages with some success partly because

options.A: its citizens generally trust their own rulers far more than they trust the governments of foreign powers.
options.B: the foreign governments imposing sanctions seldom explain in public why they have chosen to impose them.
options.C: the shortages really are caused in part by measures that foreign governments have chosen to impose.
options.D: the educated groups who might dispute the claim have already taken control of the country's press.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the shortages really are caused in part by measures that foreign governments have chosen to impose.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim about the relative trust citizens place in their rulers and in foreigners; this is outside its scope.
option_rationales.B: Nothing is said about how sanctioning governments explain themselves; the passage locates the regime's advantage elsewhere.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the government 'controls the press' and that the educated tend to emigrate or be silenced, the reverse of this option.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the regime presents shortages as 'the work of hostile foreigners, and the explanation is the more convincing for being partly true'. Sanctions are imposed by foreign governments, so the blame is partly accurate.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible general reason from outside the passage instead of the one the text gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of one clause in paragraph 2.

questions.question: According to the passage, each of the following can help a sanctioned regime keep or tighten its hold on power EXCEPT

options.A: its control over who receives imported medicine, fuel and spare parts once these goods have become scarce.
options.B: its ability to present shortages as the deliberate work of hostile foreign governments rather than its own doing.
options.C: the departure or impoverishment of the educated and commercially minded groups best placed to demand change.
options.D: the targeting of named officials' assets, which provokes ordinary citizens to rally in sympathy behind those officials.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the targeting of named officials' assets, which provokes ordinary citizens to rally in sympathy behind those officials.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says whoever controls distribution of scarce goods gains 'a means of rewarding loyalty and punishing dissent', so this does help the regime.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the regime 'can present the shortages as the work of hostile foreigners', so this is supported.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists this among the effects that let sanctions 'tighten' the regime's grip, so it is supported.

questions.explanation: Three options restate mechanisms from paragraph 2. Paragraph 3 discusses targeted sanctions but says their limit is that officials hide wealth through intermediaries; it never says targeting makes citizens rally behind officials. That claim is unsupported.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the rally effect described for broad sanctions must also apply to targeted ones.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires checking each option against paragraph 2 and noticing that the correct answer borrows the topic of paragraph 3 but invents its effect.

questions.question: Which of the following most closely parallels the kind of measure the author criticises at the end of paragraph 4?

options.A: A lender freezes a borrower's accounts without ever saying what payment would release them, and the struggling borrower stops negotiating altogether.
options.B: A landlord raises the rent for every tenant until one noisy tenant moves out, announcing that rents will fall again as soon as that tenant has left.
options.C: A club bars one member who broke its rules from its premises but still admits that member's family, sparing them while punishing the offender.
options.D: A lender freezes a borrower's accounts and states exactly what sum must be repaid to release them, and the borrower soon pays it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A lender freezes a borrower's accounts without ever saying what payment would release them, and the struggling borrower stops negotiating altogether.

option_rationales.B: Because this comes with a stated condition for lifting the cost, it is not a measure that 'hurts but promises nothing'.
option_rationales.C: This parallels the targeted measures of paragraph 3, which the author calls 'a genuine improvement', not the measure criticised in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: This measure is paired with 'a clear and credible offer of what will be lifted in return for what', which paragraph 4 says is what lets sanctions work.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 criticises 'A measure that hurts but promises nothing', which 'gives a government little reason to move, and some reason to dig in'. The lender who imposes pain without stating terms, and whose borrower then digs in, mirrors this exactly.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the targeted-sanction analogy because it is also about sanctions, without matching the specific flaw criticised in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each analogy maps onto a different part of the passage; the student must match the precise feature named in the stem.

questions.question: The author's remark that targeting 'reduces the moral cost of sanctions more reliably than it increases their effect' implies that

options.A: governments have largely abandoned broad sanctions because their moral cost became too high to defend in public.
options.B: the surer benefit of targeted sanctions is that they spare ordinary people, not that they bring a dependable gain in pressure on policy.
options.C: targeted sanctions usually fail because officials cannot be identified precisely enough to be named in them.
options.D: targeted sanctions are, on the whole, less effective than broad sanctions at persuading a regime under pressure to change the policies it pursues.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the surer benefit of targeted sanctions is that they spare ordinary people, not that they bring a dependable gain in pressure on policy.

option_rationales.A: The passage presents targeting as the usual response but says nothing about broad sanctions being abandoned or about public defence.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 locates the limit elsewhere: officials 'rarely hold their wealth in their own names' and route money 'through intermediaries'; naming them is not the problem.
option_rationales.D: The remark compares two benefits of targeting with each other, not targeted with broad sanctions; paragraph 2 suggests broad sanctions can even strengthen a regime.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls targeting 'a genuine improvement' because it spares ordinary people, then notes that officials hide wealth through intermediaries. Saying it reduces moral cost 'more reliably than it increases their effect' means the humanitarian gain is dependable while any gain in effectiveness is uncertain.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a comparison between two benefits of one policy as a comparison between two policies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option uses the same words of comparison; separating them needs a precise reading of what is being compared.

questions.question: According to paragraph 3, how strongly the stability-instability paradox operates depends on

options.A: how confident each side is that a limited clash can be prevented from escalating.
options.B: whether the rival states fight through proxies or commit their own regular forces to a clash.
options.C: whether small wars were already common in the region before nuclear weapons appeared there.
options.D: how many nuclear weapons each side possesses in comparison with the arsenal of its rival.

questions.correct_answer: (A) how confident each side is that a limited clash can be prevented from escalating.

option_rationales.B: Proxies are listed in paragraph 2 as one form a limited clash can take, not as the factor on which the paradox's force depends.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 mentions that small wars predate nuclear weapons only to deny that the weapons cause them; it is not offered as what governs the paradox.
option_rationales.D: The size of arsenals is never discussed; the passage assumes only that the two states 'can each destroy the other'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the paradox's 'force depends on how confident each side is that escalation can be controlled'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a detail mentioned in paragraph 3 for another purpose.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in a single sentence.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that stability at the top 'loosens the rungs near the bottom' most nearly means that

options.A: the lowest levels of military force become too expensive for states to keep up once nuclear arms exist.
options.B: the restraints that once discouraged minor acts of aggression grow weaker as fear of the largest war recedes.
options.C: minor clashes become more likely than before to climb rapidly into a general war between the two powers.
options.D: the weakest states in the system lose their capacity to resist the demands made on them by stronger states.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the restraints that once discouraged minor acts of aggression grow weaker as fear of the largest war recedes.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage concerns the cost of conventional forces; the rungs stand for levels of conflict, which become easier to start, not costlier.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the point: the passage says each side assumes a limited clash 'will stay limited', so rapid escalation is what is feared less.
option_rationales.D: The image is about levels of conflict on a ladder of escalation, not about weak and strong states; the passage does not discuss weaker states' capacity.

questions.explanation: The 'ladder of escalation' runs from small clashes at the bottom to nuclear war at the top. Paragraph 2 says the fear that once restrained limited ventures 'is weakened precisely by the confidence that catastrophe will be avoided'. Loosened rungs are weakened restraints on low-level conflict.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'loosens' as making the ladder easier to climb, which reverses the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor must be decoded through the sentence before it; one wrong option turns it inside out.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reasoning set out in paragraph 2?

options.A: Two rival states fought several border wars against each other in the decades before either of them acquired nuclear weapons.
options.B: Several non-nuclear states bordering a nuclear power reduced the size of their armies in the years after it acquired its arsenal.
options.C: After two rivals acquired secure nuclear arsenals, raids across their border grew more frequent, with officials on both sides expecting the raids to stay contained.
options.D: Soon after two rival states acquired nuclear weapons, a minor border incident between them led within hours to a nuclear alert on both sides.

questions.correct_answer: (C) After two rivals acquired secure nuclear arsenals, raids across their border grew more frequent, with officials on both sides expecting the raids to stay contained.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 grants that small wars 'were common long before such weapons existed'; earlier wars say nothing about whether deterrence weakens restraint.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph concerns two states that can each destroy the other; troop cuts by non-nuclear neighbours do not bear on that mutual reasoning.
option_rationales.D: Rapid escalation would undermine the confidence the paradox needs, and so would tend to restore caution rather than support the reasoning.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that confidence that neither side will risk a nuclear exchange leads each to assume limited clashes 'will stay limited', so it feels freer to provoke. More frequent raids after mutual deterrence, accompanied by stated confidence that they would stay contained, fits both the behaviour and the reasoning behind it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about border wars in general without checking whether it involves the confidence that drives the paradox.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires matching both the change in behaviour and the belief behind it.

questions.question: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Small wars in the nuclear age are caused mainly by the confidence that mutual deterrence gives to the leaders of rival nuclear-armed states.
options.B: The author regards nuclear deterrence as a failure, since it has not succeeded in removing organised violence between rival states.
options.C: The paradox shows that the largest powers have in fact become more willing to fight each other directly once both are armed.
options.D: Where leaders doubt that clashes can be contained, deterrence is likely to weaken restraint on low-level aggression less than where they are confident of control.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Where leaders doubt that clashes can be contained, deterrence is likely to weaken restraint on low-level aggression less than where they are confident of control.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says explicitly that the paradox 'does not say that nuclear weapons cause small wars', only that deterrence can remove 'one brake' on them.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 calls the prevention of catastrophe 'no small achievement'; the author asks only that it be described accurately, not that it be judged a failure.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says deterrence has a claim to have kept the largest powers from fighting 'each other directly'; the paradox concerns lesser conflicts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the paradox does not 'operate automatically' and that where leaders doubt a skirmish can be kept small, 'the old fear returns, and with it some of the old caution'. So under such doubt the loosening of restraint will be smaller than where leaders are confident that escalation can be controlled.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the causal option, which overstates the paradox in exactly the way paragraph 3 warns against.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close misreadings of the author's carefully limited claim; the correct answer needs paragraphs 2 and 3 together.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The laws of war should be revised so that soldiers who fight for an aggressor can be prosecuted for the killing of those who defend against them.
options.B: The critics of the laws of war are mistaken, since a soldier acting on lawful orders cannot fairly be compared with a robber acting on his own.
options.C: Because nearly every belligerent believes its cause just, the morality of a war cannot be judged, and its soldiers bear no moral responsibility for it.
options.D: Although soldiers fighting for an aggressor may lack a real moral right to kill, the laws of war are wise to treat combatants on both sides alike.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Although soldiers fighting for an aggressor may lack a real moral right to kill, the laws of war are wise to treat combatants on both sides alike.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 argues that such a rule would 'make war more savage without making it more just'; the author defends the existing symmetry.
option_rationales.B: The author says 'the critics are right about the underlying morality'; the disagreement concerns only what follows for the law, not the robber comparison.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the convention 'is not a certificate of moral innocence' and that soldiers sometimes 'ought to refuse', so the author does not relieve them of responsibility.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the thesis: the critics 'are right about the underlying morality and wrong about what follows for the laws of war'. The symmetry is 'a convention' justified because the alternative would make war more savage, and paragraph 4 adds that it is not a judgement of innocence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that rejects the critics outright, missing that the author accepts their moral argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis concedes one point and denies another; the wrong options each keep only one half.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a soldier who knowingly fights in a plainly aggressive war, while observing every rule of conduct, as

options.A: free of legal blame under the convention, but not for that reason morally innocent of the killing that he does.
options.B: morally blameless for as long as he obeyed his orders, since orders transfer responsibility to the government that issued them.
options.C: guilty of a crime under the laws of war, since those laws ought in principle to follow the justice of the cause.
options.D: free of both legal and moral blame, since the convention exists precisely to relieve soldiers of judging the cause they serve.

questions.correct_answer: (A) free of legal blame under the convention, but not for that reason morally innocent of the killing that he does.

option_rationales.B: The passage never says orders transfer responsibility; paragraph 4 says that in a plainly unjust war an ordinary soldier 'ought to refuse'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 defends laws that do not follow the justice of the cause, so the author would not call this soldier a criminal.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says a convention that 'withholds legal blame is not a certificate of moral innocence', so the author keeps moral blame in view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 holds that every soldier who follows the rules of conduct is legally equal, so this soldier is not a criminal. Paragraph 4 adds that the convention 'is not a certificate of moral innocence' and that where injustice is 'so plain that an ordinary soldier could see it' he 'ought to refuse'. Legal blamelessness and moral fault are kept apart.
questions.common_misconception: Collapsing the author's distinction between legal blame and moral innocence in one direction or the other.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the defence of the convention in paragraph 3 with its limit in paragraph 4; two wrong options each keep one half.

questions.question: The example of the robber and the guard in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: suggest that soldiers who kill on the orders of their government are more to blame than criminals who act alone.
options.B: demonstrate that the laws of war were originally modelled on the ordinary domestic law governing self-defence.
options.C: show, through an everyday case outside war, that an unjust attacker gains no right to kill those who resist him.
options.D: illustrate the author's own view that soldiers of an aggressor commit crimes under the laws of war when they kill defenders.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show, through an everyday case outside war, that an unjust attacker gains no right to kill those who resist him.

option_rationales.A: The critics ask 'Why should the matter change' for a soldier, claiming equal fault, not greater fault, for the soldier.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no historical claim about where the laws of war came from; the comparison is a moral analogy.
option_rationales.D: The example belongs to the critics' argument; the author accepts its moral point but denies in paragraph 3 that the laws of war should treat such soldiers as criminals.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 sets out the critics' case. The robber who may not 'shoot back and call it self-defence' is a familiar case in which an unjust attacker plainly has no right to kill a defender, and the critics then ask why a uniform should make a difference.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the critics' conclusion about criminality to the author.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example is reported, not endorsed in full, and the most tempting wrong option ignores that difference.

questions.question: The author's argument in paragraph 3 for treating combatants alike depends most on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Most wars are fought between sides whose causes are, on a fair reckoning, roughly equal in their justice.
options.B: No authority exists whose ruling on which side has the just cause would be accepted by the belligerents while the fighting continues.
options.C: The moral truth about killing in war is too uncertain for anyone, philosophers included, to determine.
options.D: Soldiers who believe their own cause to be just fight with greater restraint than soldiers who privately doubt the justice of their war.

questions.correct_answer: (B) No authority exists whose ruling on which side has the just cause would be accepted by the belligerents while the fighting continues.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the symmetry 'is not a judgement that both sides are equally innocent', so the argument does not need causes to be equal.
option_rationales.C: The author says the critics 'are right about the underlying morality', so the argument assumes the moral truth can be known, not that it cannot.
option_rationales.D: The argument concerns who could claim a right to kill under a rule, not how belief in one's cause affects restraint; this is not needed.

questions.explanation: The author argues that a rule giving the right to kill only to the just side 'would therefore be claimed by both sides'. That follows only if each side decides for itself which cause is just. If some authority's ruling on justice were accepted during the war, the rule could be applied and the objection would fail. The argument therefore assumes no such authority exists.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that both causes are equal, which the author explicitly disclaims.
questions.difficulty_reason: The assumption is unstated and must be reconstructed from the word 'therefore'; two wrong options contradict explicit disclaimers in the text.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, under a balance of power, a state is most likely to join a coalition against another state when

options.A: the international organisation to which it belongs has formally condemned the other state.
options.B: the other state is a close trading partner whose goodwill it needs in some other region.
options.C: the other state's growing strength threatens to let it dominate the states around it.
options.D: the other state has attacked a small neighbour without any justification that others accept.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the other state's growing strength threatens to let it dominate the states around it.

option_rationales.A: Formal condemnation belongs to the collective-security organisation of paragraph 2, whose members condemned aggression but did not resist it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 lists such partners as states collective security might require one to fight; under balancing this would be a reason to hold back, not to join.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the balance of power is 'indifferent to the fate of small states whose conquest does not upset the balance', so aggression alone does not trigger it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says states under a balance of power 'align against whichever power threatens to dominate', and paragraph 3 says the practice cares 'only about the rise of a power that could threaten them'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the trigger of collective security (any aggression) with the trigger of balancing (a threat of dominance).
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer restates paragraph 1, and the wrong options are clearly tied to the other principle.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward collective security is best described as

options.A: indifferent, since the author treats the choice between it and the balance of power as of little practical consequence.
options.B: respectful of the legitimacy its principle can confer, but doubtful that states will bear the costs it asks of them.
options.C: contemptuous, since the author regards its principle as a cynical cover for the interests of the great powers.
options.D: enthusiastic, since the author holds that its impartiality makes it superior to the balance of power in every respect.

questions.correct_answer: (B) respectful of the legitimacy its principle can confer, but doubtful that states will bear the costs it asks of them.

option_rationales.A: The author argues that lasting orders depend on combining the two and that reformers erred by relying on one, which is far from indifference.
option_rationales.C: The author calls it an idea that seems 'obviously right' and credits its norm with supplying legitimacy; the word 'cynical' is applied to the balance of power, not to it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says its impartiality is also 'its weakness', and paragraph 4 calls relying on it alone a 'mistake'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says its impartiality is both its appeal and its weakness, since governments would not 'pay the price'. Paragraph 4 credits its norm with giving resistance 'a public justification' while calling exclusive reliance on it a 'mistake'. The attitude is qualified respect combined with doubt about its workability.
questions.common_misconception: Transferring the word 'cynical', used of the balance of power, to the author's view of collective security.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's view of collective security is spread across paragraphs 2 and 4 and must be assembled.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organised?

options.A: A historical failure is described, its cause is traced to a single mistaken leader, and a remedy is proposed for future reformers.
options.B: Two principles are compared, the first is shown to be morally superior, and the second is recommended as the more practical guide.
options.C: One principle is defended against its critics, its failures in practice are explained away, and it is recommended without reservation.
options.D: Two principles are introduced, the weakness of each is examined in turn, and the author argues that orders which last combine them.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Two principles are introduced, the weakness of each is examined in turn, and the author argues that orders which last combine them.

option_rationales.A: No individual leader is blamed; the passage speaks only of 'reformers' and of states unwilling to pay the price.
option_rationales.B: The author does not recommend the balance of power on its own; paragraph 4 says the lesson is 'not that one principle should replace the other'.
option_rationales.C: Neither principle is recommended without reservation; the author criticises both and concludes that 'each supplies what the other lacks'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces both principles, paragraph 2 examines the weakness of collective security, paragraph 3 the price of the balance of power, and paragraph 4 concludes that lasting orders have 'combined the two'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that ranks the two principles, which the conclusion explicitly refuses to do.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option matches the first two paragraphs and fails only on the conclusion.

questions.question: Which of the following situations would the author most likely regard as an instance of the combination described in paragraph 4?

options.A: States already uneasy at a neighbour's military growth unite against it once it seizes a border province, citing a shared rule against conquest to win wider support.
options.B: Two great powers agree to divide a weak buffer state between them so that neither gains an advantage, and the arrangement keeps the peace between them for a generation.
options.C: A group of states pledges to defend any member that is attacked and honours the pledge even against a small aggressor that could never threaten any of them.
options.D: A worldwide body votes by a large majority to condemn the invasion of a remote island and calls on its members to resist, but no member sends any forces.

questions.correct_answer: (A) States already uneasy at a neighbour's military growth unite against it once it seizes a border province, citing a shared rule against conquest to win wider support.

option_rationales.B: This is balancing alone, the partition of 'a weak country' to keep the strong satisfied that paragraph 3 criticises; no norm against aggression is at work.
option_rationales.C: This is collective security acting on its own principle without any balancing motive, since the aggressor poses no threat of dominance; it is not the combination.
option_rationales.D: This is the failure described in paragraph 2, members 'ready to condemn aggression and reluctant to resist it'; the norm is present but the balancing motive is not.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says lasting orders borrow 'legitimacy from the first and their enforcement from the second'. In the correct answer, the motive comes from balancing (unease at a neighbour's growth) and the public justification from the norm against conquest, which helps 'assemble allies who would hesitate to act on calculation alone'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the case of collective security that works, without noticing that it lacks the balancing motive.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option isolates one principle; the student must identify both elements in the correct answer.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: arguing that recasting sovereignty as a responsibility shifts, rather than settles, the question of who decides on intervention, leaving a choice between risks.
options.B: defending the traditional doctrine of non-interference against those who would permit outside powers to intervene to stop atrocities.
options.C: proposing that no use of force across a border be permitted until a broad body of states has authorised it under common rules.
options.D: showing that interventions to stop mass killing have generally been pretexts used by powerful states to pursue their strategic interests.

questions.correct_answer: (A) arguing that recasting sovereignty as a responsibility shifts, rather than settles, the question of who decides on intervention, leaving a choice between risks.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 begins 'None of this is an argument for returning to the wall', so the author does not defend the old doctrine.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 warns that insisting on authorisation 'can become a reason for doing nothing', and the author makes no such proposal.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 notes a pattern in where interventions occur, but the author accepts that atrocities can be 'equally real' and that standing by can be wrong; calling them generally pretexts overstates this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states that the formula 'does not remove the hard question but relocates it' to who decides, and paragraphs 4 and 5 explore how procedure might answer that and how it too can fail, ending with the admission that 'we are choosing which of these failures to risk'. The concern throughout is that the new formula leaves the hard choice in place.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's procedural point in paragraph 4 for a firm proposal, ignoring the reversal in paragraph 5.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches one paragraph; the correct answer requires the arc of the whole passage.

questions.question: According to the passage, the traditional rule of non-interference was justified on the ground that

options.A: governments could on the whole be trusted to treat their own populations decently without supervision from outside.
options.B: it protected small states from being dominated by an international organisation acting in the name of all members.
options.C: it made every state responsible for protecting its own people, so that no outside protection was needed.
options.D: allowing any state to enter another whenever it disliked how it was governed would lead to constant intervention by the strong.

questions.correct_answer: (D) allowing any state to enter another whenever it disliked how it was governed would lead to constant intervention by the strong.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says non-interference was 'less a tribute to the virtue of governments' than a device for limiting quarrels.
option_rationales.B: No international organisation is mentioned in connection with the old rule; its rationale concerned interventions by other powers.
option_rationales.C: Responsibility to protect one's people is the basis of the new formula in paragraph 2, not the rationale of the old rule.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says a world in which any power could intervene whenever it disapproved 'would be a world of permanent intervention, in which the strong would always find reasons to correct the weak'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the language of the new formula to the old doctrine.
questions.difficulty_reason: The rationale is stated directly in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author's remark that the old doctrine gave 'a clear answer to the question of who may enter: nobody' suggests that the author

options.A: believes that powerful states in fact obeyed the old doctrine without exception for as long as it prevailed.
options.B: sees value in the old doctrine's refusal of discretion as a safeguard, even while rejecting the answer it gave.
options.C: considers the old doctrine preferable, on balance, to the new formula and would like to see it restored in full.
options.D: regards clarity as the most important quality that any rule governing intervention could possibly possess.

questions.correct_answer: (B) sees value in the old doctrine's refusal of discretion as a safeguard, even while rejecting the answer it gave.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about how faithfully the old doctrine was observed; the remark concerns the answer the rule gave, not compliance with it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this is an argument for returning to the wall', which rules out wishing to restore it.
option_rationales.D: The author goes on to say that procedure 'matters as much as the facts' and that no formula escapes the dilemma; clarity is not ranked above everything.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 contrasts the old rule's clear answer with the new formula, which 'replaces that answer with a judgement' made by interested parties. The words 'at least' credit the old rule with denying anyone discretion. Paragraph 4, however, rejects a return to the wall, so the author values the safeguard without accepting the rule.
questions.common_misconception: Reading praise for one feature of the old doctrine as endorsement of the doctrine.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase 'at least' must be read against paragraph 4; the option about restoring the old doctrine is the natural over-reading.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: A requirement of proper authorisation can itself contribute to inaction while a population is being killed.
options.B: The places where interventions have occurred are roughly what one would expect of a rule leaving the decision to interested parties.
options.C: The responsibility formula is valuable chiefly because it ends the conflict between sovereignty and the demand to stop atrocities.
options.D: Whether an intervention is legitimate depends partly on how the decision was reached and not only on what was happening.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The responsibility formula is valuable chiefly because it ends the conflict between sovereignty and the demand to stop atrocities.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says insistence on authorisation 'can become a reason for doing nothing while the killing continues', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls this pattern 'an observation about how a discretionary rule will be used', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'the procedure matters as much as the facts', so the author agrees.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the formula 'seems to dissolve the conflict', but paragraph 3 replies that 'The elegance is partly an illusion' and that the formula 'does not remove the hard question but relocates it'. The author therefore denies that it ends the conflict, while each of the other statements restates paragraphs 3, 4 and 5.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting this statement because paragraph 2 describes the formula as elegant, without noticing that the description is immediately rejected.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every option is close to the text; the correct answer echoes the formula's own claim, which the author reports and then rejects.

questions.question: In the final sentence, 'a change of vocabulary' refers to

options.A: the insistence that an intervention be called legitimate only when a broad body of states has approved it.
options.B: the habit of replacing the word 'intervention' with milder terms that conceal the use of armed force.
options.C: the shift from describing sovereignty as a wall to describing it as a shield behind which murderers can hide.
options.D: the redescription of sovereignty as a responsibility that a state can forfeit rather than a right it holds unconditionally.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the redescription of sovereignty as a responsibility that a state can forfeit rather than a right it holds unconditionally.

option_rationales.A: Authorisation is a procedure the author discusses in paragraphs 4 and 5, not a change of vocabulary, and the author does not claim it was meant to spare anyone the choice.
option_rationales.B: The passage never discusses euphemisms for intervention; the vocabulary in question is the redefinition of sovereignty.
option_rationales.C: The phrase 'a shield for murderers' is how atrocities made the old doctrine look in paragraph 2; it is a criticism of the old vocabulary, not the new formula itself.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents the new formula, 'Sovereignty, it was argued, is not a privilege but a responsibility', as something that 'seems to dissolve the conflict'. The last sentence says we should stop pretending that this redescription has spared us the choice between two failures.
questions.common_misconception: Linking the phrase to the nearest discussion, of authorisation, instead of to the formula the whole passage examines.
questions.difficulty_reason: The referent lies three paragraphs back and is described there in different words; two wrong options are closer at hand.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a state fearing entrapment would be most worried that

options.A: its adversary might decide that the alliance's commitment is hollow and choose to test it.
options.B: its partner might fail to come to its aid if the state itself were attacked by a third power.
options.C: its partner, sure of being supported, might start a dispute that the state would then be obliged to join.
options.D: its partner might begin looking for other friends and arming itself in ways that alarm its neighbours.

questions.correct_answer: (C) its partner, sure of being supported, might start a dispute that the state would then be obliged to join.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 raises this as a risk of ambiguity concerning the adversary; entrapment is a fear about one's own partner.
option_rationales.B: This is the fear of abandonment, defined in paragraph 1 as the worry that the partner 'will fail it when it is attacked'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 gives these as consequences of loosening a commitment, which is what a state does to reduce entrapment, not the entrapment itself.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines entrapment as the fear that the partner 'will drag it into a war it has no wish to fight', and paragraph 2 explains that assurance 'may embolden the partner to take risks'.
questions.common_misconception: Swapping the definitions of the two fears.
questions.difficulty_reason: Definitions are given in one paragraph; only the matching is tested.

questions.question: The example of the island partner in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate how a protecting power can leave a guarantee deliberately unclear in order to restrain both its partner and its adversary.
options.B: show that great powers often fail to think through how far their guarantees extend until a crisis forces the question.
options.C: demonstrate that ambiguous guarantees usually lead adversaries to test them, sometimes with disastrous results.
options.D: provide evidence from a particular historical case that a policy of ambiguity has in fact preserved the peace.

questions.correct_answer: (A) illustrate how a protecting power can leave a guarantee deliberately unclear in order to restrain both its partner and its adversary.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph insists the reverse: 'The silence is not an oversight. It is the policy.'
option_rationales.C: Testing by an adversary is raised in paragraph 5 as a possible cost, and only as something that 'may' happen, not as the usual outcome.
option_rationales.D: The example is introduced as 'a hypothetical great power', so it cannot serve as historical evidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that vague guarantees are 'a deliberate instrument' that makes both partner and adversary careful. The island case, where the great power 'declines to say' whether the promise covers a dispute the partner starts, illustrates this, and the author stresses that 'The silence is not an oversight.'
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as evidence from history, or as a failure, when it is a hypothetical illustration of deliberate policy.
questions.difficulty_reason: Function must be read from the claim the example follows and the sentences that close it.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the dilemma described in paragraph 2?

options.A: An employer who keeps the terms of a bonus vague so that staff keep working hard without counting on any fixed reward.
options.B: A parent's promise to pay all of a grown child's debts reassures but invites borrowing; withholding it curbs borrowing but leaves the child feeling deserted.
options.C: A shopkeeper who offers a generous guarantee on every item she stocks sells more goods but must then pay to repair the ones that break.
options.D: A teacher who sets a very difficult examination finds that the strongest students in the class rise to it while the weakest ones simply give up.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A parent's promise to pay all of a grown child's debts reassures but invites borrowing; withholding it curbs borrowing but leaves the child feeling deserted.

option_rationales.A: This parallels the deliberate ambiguity of paragraph 3, a response to the dilemma, rather than the dilemma of paragraph 2 itself.
option_rationales.C: This is a single trade-off between sales and repair costs; there is no protected party whose conduct is emboldened by assurance and restrained by doubt.
option_rationales.D: This describes different reactions of different students to one measure, not one relationship in which easing one risk aggravates another.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says tightening a commitment reassures the partner but 'may embolden' it, while loosening it restrains the partner but invites doubt. The parent's open-ended promise reassures but encourages risky borrowing, and withholding it restrains but leaves the child doubting support: easing one problem worsens the other.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the vague-bonus case because it resembles the alliance discussion, though it matches paragraph 3, not paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two analogies share surface features with the passage; only one reproduces the two-sided structure of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, deliberate ambiguity in an alliance commitment is most likely to succeed when

options.A: the commitment is made steadily firmer and more public in the years after the alliance is formed.
options.B: the partner is confident that its patron will support it whatever conduct it chooses to adopt.
options.C: the protecting power judges accurately how both its partner and its adversary will read the uncertainty.
options.D: the adversary concludes from the vague wording that the commitment is unlikely ever to be honoured.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the protecting power judges accurately how both its partner and its adversary will read the uncertainty.

option_rationales.A: Making the commitment firmer removes the ambiguity; paragraph 2 says firmer commitments 'may embolden the partner'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 names this belief as one way ambiguity fails, since the partner is no longer restrained.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 names this as the other failure: the adversary may 'test it, discovering too late that it was real'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says the value of ambiguity 'depends on each party reading the uncertainty in the way the protecting power intends' and that the strategy 'rewards a protecting power that understands both its partner and its adversary well'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking one of the two misreadings that paragraph 5 lists as failures.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are the failures described in paragraph 5; the correct answer restates its condition for success.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 that ambiguity gives the partner 'reason to be careful'?

options.A: Ambiguous guarantees are frequently attacked in the protecting power's own press as a sign of weakness or indecision.
options.B: Partners with vague guarantees generally act as boldly as those with firm ones, assuming that their patrons could never let them fall.
options.C: Protecting powers that gave firm guarantees often found that their partners began taking greater risks than before.
options.D: Adversaries facing vague guarantees have on several occasions decided to test them, only to find that the guarantees were honoured in full.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Partners with vague guarantees generally act as boldly as those with firm ones, assuming that their patrons could never let them fall.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 already notes that ambiguity is 'often criticised as a failure of nerve'; public criticism says nothing about the partner's conduct.
option_rationales.C: This supports paragraph 2's point that firm assurance 'may embolden the partner', and so, if anything, strengthens the case for ambiguity.
option_rationales.D: This concerns the adversary's reading of the guarantee, not whether the partner is restrained, so it does not bear on the claim in the stem.

questions.explanation: The claim is that a partner 'uncertain whether reckless conduct will be supported, has reason to be careful'. If partners under vague guarantees behave as boldly as those under firm ones, ambiguity does not restrain them in practice. Paragraph 5 raises this as a possibility; a finding that it is the general pattern would undercut the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about adversaries testing guarantees, which concerns the other half of the strategy.
questions.difficulty_reason: The student must isolate which of the two restraints the stem targets; the most tempting wrong option concerns the other one.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that the great fairs were never important as markets for goods, since most of their business was carried on in promises to pay rather than in coin.
options.B: describe the kinds of commercial news, such as distant prices and harvest failures, that merchants exchanged when they met each year.
options.C: explain how permanent shops in growing towns gradually took away the retail trade on which the great periodic fairs had always depended.
options.D: argue that the great fairs mattered chiefly as fixed meetings for settling credit and sharing news, functions that the view of them as large markets overlooks.

questions.correct_answer: (D) argue that the great fairs mattered chiefly as fixed meetings for settling credit and sharing news, functions that the view of them as large markets overlooks.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the market account 'is not wrong' and paragraph 4 says fairs continued to 'matter as markets', so denying that they were ever important as markets contradicts the author.
option_rationales.B: The news of paragraph 3 is one of two functions the author uses to support the thesis; the option takes a single supporting paragraph for the purpose of the whole.
option_rationales.C: This is the conventional account the author treats as incomplete; paragraph 4 calls the shift of retail business real but says 'the deeper loss' lay elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the market picture 'describes the visible part of the fair and mistakes it for the whole'. Paragraphs 2 and 3 describe the two hidden functions, settling credit and exchanging news, and paragraph 4 reinterprets the decline of fairs in their light. The purpose is to relocate the fair's importance.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the correction into a denial that fairs were markets, or choosing one supporting paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is announced in paragraph 1 and restated in paragraph 4; the other options are clearly too narrow or too extreme.

questions.question: According to the passage, relatively little coin had to change hands when merchants settled their accounts at a fair because

options.A: what one merchant owed another could be cancelled against debts owed among other merchants present.
options.B: most merchants preferred to pay one another in goods such as cloth and livestock rather than in money.
options.C: banks that kept accounts all year round had already settled most debts before the fair opened.
options.D: the merchants who attended were generally too poor to carry significant quantities of coin with them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) what one merchant owed another could be cancelled against debts owed among other merchants present.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says much of the fair's business 'left no bales behind'; settlement was by offsetting debts, not by paying in goods.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 presents such banks as later institutions that took over the fair's functions, not as something operating alongside the fair.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about the wealth of merchants; the reason given is the offsetting of obligations.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: merchants settled accounts by 'cancelling what one owed another against what a third owed the first, so that relatively little coin had to change hands'.
questions.common_misconception: Reaching for a plausible outside reason instead of the mechanism the passage states.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of one sentence in paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that a fair 'was a calendar as much as a place' most nearly means that

options.A: the fair was held in a different town each year, so that merchants had to follow a calendar to find it.
options.B: the fair was important chiefly as a holiday that broke the routine of the working year for ordinary townspeople.
options.C: much of its value lay in fixing recurring dates by which debts fell due and to which traders were expected to return.
options.D: merchants used the fair mainly to learn the dates of harvests and religious festivals in distant regions.

questions.correct_answer: (C) much of its value lay in fixing recurring dates by which debts fell due and to which traders were expected to return.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage says fairs moved; paragraph 1 describes a meadow outside a town filling and emptying until 'the following year'.
option_rationales.B: The passage discusses merchants' credit, not townspeople's leisure; the option replaces the commercial meaning with a festive one.
option_rationales.D: Harvest failures appear in paragraph 3 as news, but the calendar image in paragraph 2 concerns the dates 'on which obligations fell due', not festivals.

questions.explanation: The sentence continues: the fair 'fixed the dates on which obligations fell due and gave distant traders a reason to keep faith with one another'. Its value as a recurring appointment for settling credit is what the calendar image conveys.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'calendar' literally or as a reference to holidays rather than to the timing of obligations.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative phrase must be connected to the credit mechanism described just before and after it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why the great fairs declined?

options.A: Merchants in several regions kept settling their year's accounts at the fairs for decades after banks and regular posts were established there.
options.B: In several regions permanent shops had taken over most of the retail trade in cloth before the fairs themselves began to decline.
options.C: In several regions merchants who attended the fairs were sometimes ruined by false rumours about the solvency of trading houses.
options.D: In several regions the great fairs continued for centuries as the main places where farmers bought and sold livestock.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Merchants in several regions kept settling their year's accounts at the fairs for decades after banks and regular posts were established there.

option_rationales.B: The author accepts that shops 'took over much of the retail business'; this fact fits the account rather than undermining it.
option_rationales.C: Unreliable news shows that fair gossip had consequences, which supports its importance; it says nothing about why fairs declined.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 already concedes that many fairs 'survived for centuries as places to buy animals', so this is consistent with the author's account.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 claims that the fair's credit and information functions 'passed to institutions that did not depend on bodily presence', such as banks and posts. If merchants kept settling accounts at fairs long after those institutions existed, the functions did not pass to them, and the explanation is weakened.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a fact that sounds like a decline story but that the author has already conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options restate the author's concessions; the correct answer must attack the specific causal claim.

questions.question: According to the passage, in records of pre-industrial working households the word 'family' often referred to

options.A: the head of the household together with the wider community to which he was answerable.
options.B: the parents and children of a household, as distinct from the servants who worked for them.
options.C: the wider kin group of a village, including relatives who lived in separate dwellings nearby.
options.D: the whole group living and working under the household head, servants and apprentices included.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the whole group living and working under the household head, servants and apprentices included.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the head was answerable to the community, but the community is not described as part of the family.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 warns that a reader who takes the word to mean 'blood relatives alone will misread them badly'.
option_rationales.C: The passage ties the word to those under 'the same roof and the same authority', not to kin living elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: records 'often used the word family to mean this whole working unit', which included 'apprentices, servants and labourers who lived under the same roof'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the modern sense of the word.
questions.difficulty_reason: The definition is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It argues that the working household was a better arrangement than the modern family, since its hierarchy gave everyone a definite place.
options.B: It heads off a nostalgic reading of the argument by noting the working household's harshness and limited reach, while keeping the claim that it differed in kind.
options.C: It introduces the shift of production into mills and offices that the final paragraph goes on to treat as a decline of the family.
options.D: It abandons the earlier claim that home and work were once combined, conceding that most people in fact worked for wages outside the home.

questions.correct_answer: (B) It heads off a nostalgic reading of the argument by noting the working household's harshness and limited reach, while keeping the claim that it differed in kind.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says explicitly that 'The point is not that the old arrangement was better', and it stresses harshness rather than the benefits of hierarchy.
option_rationales.C: The move into mills appears only in paragraph 4, and the author there denies that the change was mainly a decline.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 mentions only 'the poorest labourers' as an exception and restates that the old arrangement was 'different in kind'; nothing earlier is abandoned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens 'None of this should be romanticised', lists the cruelty and the exceptions, and closes by saying the arrangement was 'different in kind'. It is a qualification that protects the argument from being read as nostalgia.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a concession for a retraction, or for the opposite claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph's opening and closing sentences state its role directly.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a feature of the pre-industrial working household EXCEPT that

options.A: people who were not related by blood lived and ate under the same roof and authority.
options.B: the place of production, such as a loom or a dairy, stood within the dwelling itself.
options.C: its members understood it chiefly as a private refuge governed by affection rather than by discipline.
options.D: its head was held answerable to the community for the conduct of those in his charge.

questions.correct_answer: (C) its members understood it chiefly as a private refuge governed by affection rather than by discipline.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 lists apprentices, servants and labourers at the table, so this is a stated feature.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'The looms or the dairy stood beside the hearth', so this is a stated feature.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 calls the head 'answerable to the wider community for the conduct of everyone in his charge'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the idea of the household as 'a private refuge, governed by affection rather than discipline' arose only after production left the home and was then 'projected backwards'. It is not a feature of the working household.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a listed feature because it sounds unfamiliar, while missing that the correct answer describes the later ideal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are stated in paragraph 2; the exception comes from paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author would most likely respond to the claim that families today care less for one another than families did three centuries ago by saying that the claim

options.A: mistakes a narrowing of the tasks households perform for a weakening of the affection within them.
options.B: is broadly correct, because the household lost its economic role when production moved into mills and offices.
options.C: is mistaken, because affection within families has grown steadily stronger since the household lost its working role.
options.D: is supported by the harsh discipline of the old working household, which made affection a secondary concern.

questions.correct_answer: (A) mistakes a narrowing of the tasks households perform for a weakening of the affection within them.

option_rationales.B: The author accepts the loss of economic role but denies that it amounts to a decline of the family, calling it 'mainly transformation'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says what changed was 'less the strength of family feeling' than the household's tasks; the author asserts no rise in affection, so this reverses the claim rather than correcting it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 mentions harshness only to block romanticisation; the author does not use it to rank past and present affection either way.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: laments about decline rest on a projection, and 'What changed over these centuries was less the strength of family feeling than the range of tasks the household was expected to perform'. The author would diagnose the claim as confusing the two.
questions.common_misconception: Replacing the author's diagnosis of a confusion with a counter-claim about affection in one direction or the other.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the author rejects the comparison of feeling rather than reversing it; one option reverses it.

questions.question: According to the passage, before the railways, differences between the local times of neighbouring towns went largely unnoticed because

options.A: most towns took their time from the same distant observatory, so that their clocks seldom disagreed by much.
options.B: travel between towns was too slow for a discrepancy of a few minutes to have any practical effect.
options.C: church authorities in each town insisted that the local hour be kept and discouraged comparison with other places.
options.D: few people owned clocks, so the hour of noon was a matter of rough guesswork in every town alike.

questions.correct_answer: (B) travel between towns was too slow for a discrepancy of a few minutes to have any practical effect.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says observatory time arrived only with standard time; before that each town set its clock by its own observation of the sun.
option_rationales.C: No such insistence is described; the passage explains the indifference by the speed of travel, not by any authority.
option_rationales.D: The passage mentions public clocks set by observation and says nothing about how many people owned clocks; the option supplies an outside reason.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Nobody minded, because nothing travelled fast enough for the difference to matter', and a several-day coach journey 'absorbed a quarter of an hour's discrepancy'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible historical reason in place of the one the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated with 'because' in paragraph 1; only light paraphrase is needed.

questions.question: The comparison with 'agreeing on a common gauge for the rails' in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: illustrate the author's own view that the change to standard time was, at bottom, a technical matter with technical consequences.
options.B: show that the railway companies regarded standard time and a common gauge as equally urgent problems requiring government action.
options.C: suggest that standard time, like a common rail gauge, was imposed on towns by distant astronomers who never consulted local opinion.
options.D: characterise the standard account as treating the new time as a neutral technical fix, a view the author goes on to call incomplete.

questions.correct_answer: (D) characterise the standard account as treating the new time as a neutral technical fix, a view the author goes on to call incomplete.

option_rationales.A: The next sentence, 'It was more than that', shows the author rejects this framing; the comparison describes a view the author qualifies.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about how the companies ranked these problems; the gauge is an image for how the standard account frames the change.
option_rationales.C: Astronomers set the time signal, not the gauge; the comparison is used to describe a merely technical view, not an imposition.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 begins: the account 'treats the change as a technical adjustment, like agreeing on a common gauge for the rails. It was more than that.' The comparison sums up the view the author finds true 'as far as it goes' but incomplete.
questions.common_misconception: Taking an image used to describe a reported view as the author's own position.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the comparison together with the sentence that immediately rejects its sufficiency.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the townspeople who resisted railway time is best described as

options.A: sympathetic reappraisal: they are credited with a real insight, though their preference for local time is not endorsed.
options.B: detached neutrality: their objections are recorded without any judgement about whether they understood the change.
options.C: wholehearted endorsement: they are presented as having been right that standard time did more harm than good.
options.D: affectionate condescension: their resistance is presented as a charming but finally foolish attachment to old habits.

questions.correct_answer: (A) sympathetic reappraisal: they are credited with a real insight, though their preference for local time is not endorsed.

option_rationales.B: The author does judge: they grasped what 'the language of convenience obscures'. The attitude is not neutral.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this is a case against standard time, whose benefits were real', so the author does not side with them on the outcome.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 rejects reading them as 'clinging to habit' and says they 'had grasped something'; that is not condescension.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 reinterprets the resisters as having understood that 'a shared standard is also a centre of authority'. Paragraph 4 then declines to argue against standard time. The author credits their insight without adopting their position.
questions.common_misconception: Collapsing the author's two-part stance into either agreement or dismissal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each capture one half of the stance; the correct answer needs both paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely parallels the change that paragraph 2 describes?

options.A: A town that has kept its own weights for centuries decides to keep them alongside the new national weights, using each for different purposes.
options.B: A group of market towns, confused by each using its own weights, agrees on a common weight so that traders moving between them stop being cheated.
options.C: A village replaces its old sundial with a more accurate mechanical clock that is still set each day by observing the sun overhead.
options.D: A village whose fields were measured in paces that anyone could walk out adopts a unit defined by a distant bureau and checked only against that bureau's instruments.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A village whose fields were measured in paces that anyone could walk out adopts a unit defined by a distant bureau and checked only against that bureau's instruments.

option_rationales.A: This parallels the two-clock compromise of paragraph 3, a response to the change, rather than the change itself.
option_rationales.B: This captures only the standard account of paragraph 1, a practical fix for confusion; it leaves out what paragraph 2 adds, that the standard's source moved out of local reach.
option_rationales.C: Here the standard remains local and checkable by anyone; accuracy improves but authority does not move, which is the opposite of paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2's point is that local time was set by an observation 'a curious citizen could, in principle, check', while standard time was 'a decision taken elsewhere and transmitted'. The correct answer reproduces both halves: a locally checkable measure replaced by one defined and verified at a distance.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about resolving confusion, which matches the familiar account but not the specific change paragraph 2 identifies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option fits the passage's topic and the standard account; only the correct answer carries the shift from checkable to remote authority.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason why voicing a text was a useful aid to early readers was that

options.A: silent reading was regarded as discourteous in households and monasteries where others were present.
options.B: texts were often written with no spaces separating one word from the next.
options.C: most readers had learned their letters by reciting them aloud to a teacher in a group.
options.D: books were so expensive that a single copy had to be shared among many listeners at once.

questions.correct_answer: (B) texts were often written with no spaces separating one word from the next.

option_rationales.A: No such attitude is described; the anecdote of surprise concerns unfamiliarity, not discourtesy.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about how readers were taught; the aid it names is the absence of word spacing.
option_rationales.D: Cost and shared reading are mentioned, but as reasons for the social setting, not as the reason voicing helped a reader decode a text.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Texts were frequently written without spaces between words, which made voicing them a useful aid'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a reason connected with the social setting rather than the one tied to voicing as an aid.
questions.difficulty_reason: One sentence in paragraph 2 gives the answer directly.

questions.question: The point made in paragraph 2 about the ancient writer's surprise implies that

options.A: silent reading must have been the usual practice among learned readers of the time, despite the writer's reaction.
options.B: the anecdote is unreliable as evidence, since the writer probably exaggerated his surprise for effect.
options.C: an observer's astonishment at a practice reveals what was customary around him, not what people could do.
options.D: the man the writer observed had invented a technique of reading that others later learned from him.
