questions.correct_answer: (C) an observer's astonishment at a practice reveals what was customary around him, not what people could do.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says silent reading 'was not the default'; the point is that it was unusual, not that it was usual.
option_rationales.B: The scholars' point concerns what the surprise proves, not whether it was sincere; nothing in the passage suggests exaggeration.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'late discovery' story the passage questions; the scholars found 'a fair number' of other silent readers.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'surprise at a practice is not evidence that it was unknown, only that it was unusual where it was observed'. The surprise tells us about local custom, not about capacity.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the critique as a charge of dishonesty, or overcorrecting into the claim that silent reading was normal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating 'unusual' from 'unknown' and from 'usual'.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Reading aloud survived well into the age of print, which shows that the move to private reading never really took place at all.
options.B: Silent reading was not a late invention; what changed was the setting of reading, from shared to private, and that shift still mattered for how readers held their thoughts.
options.C: Silent reading was a late discovery that transformed the inner life of the West, as an ancient anecdote of surprise clearly shows.
options.D: Because silent reading was always possible, the history of reading has no real bearing on how people came to think of the self.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Silent reading was not a late invention; what changed was the setting of reading, from shared to private, and that shift still mattered for how readers held their thoughts.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 mentions the survival of reading aloud as part of a 'gradual and uneven' shift, not as evidence that no shift occurred.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'familiar story' of paragraph 1 that the author says 'has been asked to carry more weight than it can bear'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says it 'would be too little to say that it changed nothing'; the option contradicts the passage's final claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 correct the popular story, paragraph 3 relocates the change in 'the setting', and paragraph 4 insists that the change 'matters' for readers' sense of their own thoughts. The correct answer holds the correction and the retained significance together.
questions.common_misconception: Keeping only the correction, and so concluding that nothing of importance changed.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each keep one half of a two-part argument.

questions.question: The last two sentences of the passage suggest that the author believes private reading

options.A: produced a private self whose influence on later habits of thought cannot now be traced or assessed.
options.B: had no real effect on how people thought of themselves, whatever historians have claimed.
options.C: was the decisive development that brought the modern sense of a private self into being.
options.D: contributed to people's sense of owning their thoughts without being the sole or sufficient cause of it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) contributed to people's sense of owning their thoughts without being the sole or sufficient cause of it.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim that the effect is untraceable; it commits to a moderate effect, which is an assessment, not a refusal to assess.
option_rationales.B: The author says 'It would be too little to say that it changed nothing', which rules out a denial of any effect.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'It would be too much to say that private reading created the private self', which rules out a decisive or creating role.

questions.explanation: The paired sentences set an upper and a lower bound: private reading did not create the private self, but it did change 'how people came to think of their thoughts as their own'. The author's view lies between, a real but partial contribution.
questions.common_misconception: Reading one of the two bounding sentences on its own and taking it for the author's whole view.
questions.difficulty_reason: A fine distinction of degree; the wrong options take each bounding sentence as the thesis or turn caution into agnosticism.

questions.question: The passage suggests that in older towns a smell was most likely to provoke sustained complaint when it

options.A: was linked in residents' minds with a particular trade or with neighbours they disliked.
options.B: was believed by physicians to carry disease, since every bad smell was then treated as a medical danger.
options.C: was stronger than the ordinary smells of household refuse and animal dung that residents lived beside.
options.D: came from the drains and sewers that reformers had recently built to carry waste away from the streets.

questions.correct_answer: (A) was linked in residents' minds with a particular trade or with neighbours they disliked.

option_rationales.B: The disease meaning arose 'from the late eighteenth century onwards'; the selective complaints of older towns are described before that shift.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says intolerability 'depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean', so strength is not the deciding factor.
option_rationales.D: The reformers' drains come later in the passage's chronology and are presented as reducing smell, not as a source of complaint.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: odours 'associated with particular trades or with neighbours who were disliked, drew sustained protest', while strong smells such as a dung heap were tolerated.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that stronger smells drew the most complaint.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contrast is stated in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The sentence 'The theory was wrong, but it was productive' (paragraph 3) functions in the argument to

options.A: concede that the reformers' achievements were largely illusory, since they acted on a mistaken account of illness.
options.B: argue that reformers understood the true causes of disease but used the language of smell to persuade the public.
options.C: introduce the point that a false belief about disease nonetheless drove reforms that really did improve health.
options.D: suggest that the germ theory which replaced the older view was itself productive only because it was wrong.

questions.correct_answer: (C) introduce the point that a false belief about disease nonetheless drove reforms that really did improve health.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the measures 'did reduce disease'; the achievements were real even though their rationale was wrong.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the measures worked 'for reasons they did not understand', which contradicts any claim that reformers knew the true causes.
option_rationales.D: The sentence refers to the foul-air theory; nothing in the passage calls the germ theory wrong.

questions.explanation: The sentence is followed by the explanation that the theory 'gave reformers a reason, and a sense of urgency', and that their works 'did reduce disease, though for reasons they did not understand'. It sets up the paradox of a productive error.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'wrong' as cancelling 'productive', or attributing hidden knowledge to the reformers.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the sentence together with the rest of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim that 'What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean'?

options.A: Records from one town show residents raising no objection to a strong stench from their own stables while petitioning against a fainter smell from a newly arrived dyeworks.
options.B: Records from one town show that complaints about smell rose sharply in summer, when heat made every source of odour noticeably stronger.
options.C: Records from one town show that covered sewers built by reformers sharply reduced both the smell of its streets and its rate of disease.
options.D: Records from one town show that its residents complained about smell far more often than the residents of a neighbouring town did.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Records from one town show residents raising no objection to a strong stench from their own stables while petitioning against a fainter smell from a newly arrived dyeworks.

option_rationales.B: Complaints that rise with the strength of smells support the view the claim opposes, that strength decided intolerability.
option_rationales.C: This bears on the productivity of reform in paragraph 3, not on what made a smell seem intolerable to residents.
option_rationales.D: A difference in the number of complaints says nothing about whether meaning or strength drove them.

questions.explanation: The claim is that meaning matters more than strength. A case where a strong familiar smell is tolerated while a weaker smell tied to an unwelcome trade is protested isolates meaning from strength and supports the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about smell and reform that does not separate strength from meaning.
questions.difficulty_reason: Only the correct answer varies strength and meaning in opposite directions; the others are on topic but not probative.

questions.question: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred about the social meanings of smell, as the passage presents them?

options.A: They faded as cities grew cleaner, because fewer residual smells remained to be attached to particular groups of people.
options.B: They did not begin with the germ theory, but they grew more prominent once smell no longer carried medical weight.
options.C: They were an invention of the period after the germ theory, having had no counterpart in the complaints of older towns.
options.D: They were a lingering form of the foul-air theory, and they disappeared once the germ theory had fully replaced it.

questions.correct_answer: (B) They did not begin with the germ theory, but they grew more prominent once smell no longer carried medical weight.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the reverse: 'The cleaner cities became, the more a lingering smell could serve as a mark of social distance'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 shows older complaints already aimed at 'neighbours who were disliked', so social meanings predate the germ theory.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says that after the germ theory smell 'did not lose its power', and paragraph 4 describes social judgements strengthening, not disappearing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows social meanings in older towns (disliked neighbours); paragraph 4 opens 'Freed from medicine, the vocabulary of smell attached itself more firmly to persons'. The phrase 'more firmly' implies continuity with intensification.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the social meaning of smell as wholly new after the germ theory, which ignores paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs synthesis of paragraphs 2 and 4 and attention to 'more firmly'; the first wrong option is tempting if paragraph 2 is forgotten.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason why goods from the far end of the chain were so costly was that

options.A: the producers who wove the silk demanded very high prices from the first merchants who bought it.
options.B: bandits and wars so often closed the route that most caravans were lost before arriving.
options.C: a margin was added each time the goods changed hands on their way along the chain.
options.D: the merchants who carried them had to make the entire long and dangerous journey in person.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a margin was added each time the goods changed hands on their way along the chain.

option_rationales.A: The passage says producers were not those who 'profited most', which tells against this explanation.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says closures caused trade to slow 'rather than stopped', because goods found other ways round; it does not cite losses as a reason for cost.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says 'very few goods, and fewer merchants, made the whole journey', which is the opposite of this claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Each exchange added a margin, which is one reason why goods from the far end of the chain were so costly'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the romantic picture of a single long, dangerous journey that the passage rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in a single clause of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage implies that buyers at one end of the chain held fanciful beliefs about the origins of their luxuries mainly because

options.A: the goods passed so quickly from one end of Asia to the other that no information could keep pace with them.
options.B: traders deliberately invented stories about distant origins so that they could charge higher prices for their goods.
options.C: the long-distance travellers who did reach the source left accounts that were exaggerated and widely misread.
options.D: no trader they dealt with had travelled beyond his own stretch of the route to see where the goods began.

questions.correct_answer: (D) no trader they dealt with had travelled beyond his own stretch of the route to see where the goods began.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says the goods moved quickly; it attributes the poor flow of knowledge to the structure of relationships, not to speed.
option_rationales.B: The passage gives no motive of deception; it attributes the beliefs to the structure of the chain, in which 'no one they dealt with had seen the source'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says such travellers shaped our modern picture of the trade; it does not blame them for the buyers' beliefs at the time.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 links the beliefs to the relay: 'knowledge travelled poorly along the chain', 'because no one they dealt with had seen the source'. Paragraph 1 adds that each trader 'knew little of what lay beyond' his own stretch.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a motive (deception) where the passage gives a structural cause.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires joining the 'because' clause in paragraph 3 with the description of traders in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a consequence of the relay structure of the trade EXCEPT

options.A: the wealth of cities at the junctions where neighbouring trading circuits met one another.
options.B: the lasting fame of a few pilgrims and envoys whose journeys spanned the entire distance.
options.C: the poor transmission of knowledge about the sources of goods from one end to the other.
options.D: the ability of goods to find alternative routes when war or banditry closed one segment.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the lasting fame of a few pilgrims and envoys whose journeys spanned the entire distance.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists the profits of 'middlemen at the junctions where circuits met' as the third consequence.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 lists this as the second consequence: 'knowledge travelled poorly along the chain'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 lists resilience as the first consequence of the system of overlapping circuits.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 enumerates three consequences of the relay: resilience, poor flow of knowledge and the profits of junction cities. The fame of exceptional travellers, in paragraph 4, arises because they were 'exceptional', not as a consequence of the relay structure.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is in the passage without checking whether the passage presents it as a consequence of the relay.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four options appear in the passage; the solver must track which ones paragraph 3 attributes to the structure.

questions.question: The contrast between seeing 'a road' and seeing 'a web' at the end of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that both pictures of the trade are equally valid, each being the natural result of the kind of sources a historian happens to prefer.
options.B: dismiss the written accounts of pilgrims and envoys as unreliable, since their authors misunderstood the routes they themselves had travelled.
options.C: argue that the exceptional travellers mattered more than ordinary traders to the trade, because only they ever saw the whole route from end to end.
options.D: trace the misleading picture of the trade to a reliance on memorable exceptional journeys, and to affirm that routine exchange explains how it worked.

questions.correct_answer: (D) trace the misleading picture of the trade to a reliance on memorable exceptional journeys, and to affirm that routine exchange explains how it worked.

option_rationales.A: The sentence ends 'it is the web that explains how the trade actually worked', which rejects equal validity; the author ranks the two pictures.
option_rationales.B: The author says such travellers were 'exceptional', not that their accounts were unreliable; the problem is unrepresentativeness, not inaccuracy.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the paragraph, which says the travellers' fame distorted 'our picture of the ordinary trade' and that the web explains how the trade worked.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains why the road image persists: the exceptional travellers left memoirs and the routine trade 'left few memoirs'. The road/web contrast links each picture to its source base and then endorses the web.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the parallel sentence as even-handed, or as an accusation that the travellers' accounts are false.
questions.difficulty_reason: The relativist option is tempting until the final clause is read; the unreliability option confuses unrepresentative with inaccurate.

questions.question: Which of the following does the passage mention as a way in which some cities reduced the burden that quarantine placed on households?

options.A: Feeding shut-up households at public expense and compensating them for goods that had been destroyed.
options.B: Allowing households that reported a case promptly to leave the city before the doors were sealed.
options.C: Excusing households that reported a case from having their bedding and clothing burned.
options.D: Rewarding neighbours who informed on a household that had concealed a death from the inspectors.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Feeding shut-up households at public expense and compensating them for goods that had been destroyed.

option_rationales.B: Slipping out of the city appears in paragraph 2 as a form of evasion, not as something authorities allowed.
option_rationales.C: Burning goods is listed among the costs of reporting; the passage says cities paid compensation, not that they waived destruction.
option_rationales.D: No reward for informers is mentioned; paragraph 2 says neighbours themselves had reasons to stay silent.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'Some cities fed shut-up households at public expense, paid compensation for goods that had been destroyed, or relied on clergy and charitable brotherhoods'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option built from words in paragraph 2 that describe evasion or costs rather than relief.
questions.difficulty_reason: The relief measures are listed in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Modern health authorities should provide generous relief to quarantined households, since history shows that coercion fails to contain disease.
options.B: Harsh punishment of concealment drove plague underground, and this is why the measures taken by early modern cities usually failed.
options.C: Plague measures relied on people reporting illness, so their success depended on how far authorities reduced what reporting cost.
options.D: Plague measures in early modern cities were essentially coercive, and their apparent humanity has been exaggerated by historians of public health.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Plague measures relied on people reporting illness, so their success depended on how far authorities reduced what reporting cost.

option_rationales.A: The passage draws a general lesson about disclosure but offers no prescription for modern authorities and does not say coercion simply fails.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 makes this point about force, but paragraph 5 denies the measures were 'futile'; the option takes one paragraph for the whole and overstates it.
option_rationales.D: This is the second of the two stories in paragraph 1, both of which, the author says, 'tend to overlook' the role of cooperation; it is reported, not adopted.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says both standard stories overlook cooperation; paragraphs 2 to 4 show that quarantine needed information from households, that relief changed their calculation and that severity deterred disclosure; paragraph 5 generalises that such measures 'are bargains' limited by 'what disclosure costs'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the reported coercion story, or the narrower point about force.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options use real material from the passage but are too narrow, reported views, or prescriptive.

questions.question: In the final sentence, the phrase 'make knowing bearable' most nearly refers to

options.A: limiting what authorities try to find out about households, so that people are not burdened by intrusive questioning.
options.B: lowering the price that people who reveal illness must pay, so that the information the authority needs reaches it.
options.C: helping officials to cope with the distress of learning how widely an epidemic had already spread through the city.
options.D: teaching the public enough about how disease spreads that the facts of an epidemic no longer seem frightening to them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) lowering the price that people who reveal illness must pay, so that the information the authority needs reaches it.

option_rationales.A: The sentence speaks of an authority 'that wishes to know'; the remedy is to lower the cost of disclosure, not to ask less.
option_rationales.C: The phrase concerns the cost of disclosure to 'the person who discloses', not the feelings of the officials who receive the news.
option_rationales.D: The passage is about the costs of reporting, not public understanding of disease; education is never discussed.

questions.explanation: The preceding clause says success 'is limited by what disclosure costs the person who discloses'. For the authority to know, disclosure must become bearable for the discloser, which is what relief did in paragraph 3.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching 'bearable' to the wrong party, the officials or the public at large.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is compressed; its referent must be fixed from the clause before it and from paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: Where penalties for concealment were sharply raised, early reports of cases increased, and no later rise in hidden deaths came to light.
options.B: Cities that imposed severe penalties for concealment usually provided relief to shut-up households at the same time.
options.C: Guards posted outside shut-up households were frequently bribed to let members of the household leave at night.
options.D: Cities that punished concealment most severely also recorded some of the highest plague mortality of any cities in their region during the same period.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Where penalties for concealment were sharply raised, early reports of cases increased, and no later rise in hidden deaths came to light.

option_rationales.B: This makes it hard to separate the effects of force and relief, but it gives no evidence that severity actually brought hidden cases to light.
option_rationales.C: Bribery of guards shows force failing in practice, which fits the author's scepticism about force rather than undermining it.
option_rationales.D: High mortality in harsh cities is consistent with the author's claim that severity drives an epidemic underground, so it does not weaken it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that severity 'could not make the unknown come forward' because fear of discovery strengthens the incentive to hide. Evidence that harsher penalties produced more early reporting without a rise in hidden deaths directly contradicts this mechanism.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is unfavourable to plague regulation in general but actually agrees with the author's view of force.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are on topic and seem critical of force, but both support the paragraph; the confound option is tempting but neutral.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the evidence about relief discussed in paragraph 3 as

options.A: conclusive proof that public relief lowered plague mortality in the cities that were able to afford it.
options.B: too unreliable to support any conclusion at all, since it comes mainly from the complaints of officials.
options.C: suggestive about relief's effect on whether families concealed illness, but insufficient to show its effect on the death toll.
options.D: evidence that relief was generous enough to remove the costs of reporting for most of the households affected.

questions.correct_answer: (C) suggestive about relief's effect on whether families concealed illness, but insufficient to show its effect on the death toll.

option_rationales.A: The author says the records 'do not allow us to say with any confidence how much difference they made to mortality', which rules out conclusive proof.
option_rationales.B: The author does draw a conclusion from the officials' complaints, that 'concealment rose when relief failed', so the evidence is not dismissed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls the provisions 'expensive and often inadequate', so the author does not think they removed the costs of reporting.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 separates two questions: the effect on mortality, which the records cannot settle, and the effect on concealment, which officials' complaints 'suggest'. The correct answer keeps both halves of that distinction.
questions.common_misconception: Merging the two questions, and so treating the evidence as either decisive or worthless.
questions.difficulty_reason: Hinges on the distinction between mortality and concealment within one paragraph; two wrong options each collapse it in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It returns to the history of liberation described in paragraph 1, which the author now accepts, after all, as the correct and complete account.
options.B: It offers evidence that the crowds who broke lamps in paragraph 3 were acting against the interests of most townspeople.
options.C: It withdraws the claim of paragraph 3 that street lighting extended policing, conceding that safety was the sponsors' only real aim.
options.D: It keeps the critique of paragraph 3 from becoming a new one-sided story, showing that lighting also widened access to the night.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It keeps the critique of paragraph 3 from becoming a new one-sided story, showing that lighting also widened access to the night.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph calls replacing one story with the other 'the opposite mistake', and paragraph 5 rejects both simple stories.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph does not mention the crowds or judge their interests; it describes groups who gained access to the night.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'Lighting did extend surveillance'; it adds a second effect without withdrawing the first.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens: 'to replace the story of liberation with a story of discipline would be to make the opposite mistake', and then describes women, families and the elderly gaining the night. It balances paragraph 3 before the synthesis of paragraph 5.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a balancing paragraph as a retraction of what came before.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph's role is signalled by its first sentence, but two wrong options misread it as retraction or reversal.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, the phrase 'a separate jurisdiction' most nearly means

options.A: a legal code written specifically for offences committed after dark, with harsher penalties than by day.
options.B: a zone of complete freedom in which no rules of any kind applied to those who were out after dark.
options.C: a period in which daytime authority held only loosely and different customs and people governed the street.
options.D: a district of the town placed under the control of the night watch rather than of the ordinary magistrates.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a period in which daytime authority held only loosely and different customs and people governed the street.

option_rationales.A: No special code is described; the passage says violence in the dark often 'went unpunished', the reverse of harsher penalties.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the night had 'its own rules', paragraph 2 describes curfews and questioning by the watch, and the dark 'was not freedom in any simple sense'.
option_rationales.D: The passage speaks of a time, not a place: 'a time in which the authority of the day ran only weakly'.

questions.explanation: The phrase is glossed in the same sentence: 'a time in which the authority of the day ran only weakly and in which much that could not be done openly was done'. Paragraph 1 adds that the night had 'its own rules, its own inhabitants'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'jurisdiction' literally as a place or a legal code, or as a total absence of rules.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative sense must be read off the gloss and squared with the curfew details.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how the author interprets the crowds who broke street lamps?

options.A: As probably sensing, even if they could not say so, that the lamps carried an authority they had grounds to oppose.
options.B: As vandals whose actions have been wrongly dignified by historians eager to find political resistance.
options.C: As giving clear proof that most townspeople opposed street lighting from the moment it was installed.
options.D: As defending the freedom that thieves and other night dwellers had enjoyed before the lamps were put up.

questions.correct_answer: (A) As probably sensing, even if they could not say so, that the lamps carried an authority they had grounds to oppose.

option_rationales.B: The author says it is 'tempting to dismiss this as mere vandalism' and then rejects that reading as less plausible.
option_rationales.C: The author offers a hedged reading of some crowds 'in moments of unrest'; paragraph 4 adds that many people gained from lighting.
option_rationales.D: The author does not say the crowds acted for thieves; the reading offered concerns resistance to authority, not any particular group's interests.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the lamp-breaking 'is more plausibly read as a recognition, however inarticulate, that the lamps were an extension of an authority that the crowd had reason to resist'. The correct answer keeps the hedge ('more plausibly', 'however inarticulate').
questions.common_misconception: Upgrading the author's hedged reading into a certainty, or attributing to the author the dismissal the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options differ from the correct answer mainly in degree and in whose interests are named; the hedge must be noticed.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to what the author says, in paragraph 5, that lighting did to the night?

options.A: A town holds a festival one night a year at which ordinary rules are suspended and people may behave as they never would by day.
options.B: A public library extends its opening hours into the evening so that its regular readers can stay and read for longer after work.
options.C: A council installs cameras in an empty square that nobody had used at night, so that the area can be monitored by the police.
options.D: A beach once used at dawn only by fishermen, under their own customs, becomes a public promenade with council rules, drawing families but ending the fishermen's ways.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A beach once used at dawn only by fishermen, under their own customs, becomes a public promenade with council rules, drawing families but ending the fishermen's ways.

option_rationales.A: This creates a distinct time with its own rules, which is the reverse of abolishing one.
option_rationales.B: This lengthens an existing activity for the same users under the same rules; it captures only the liberation story, not the replacement of a distinct time.
option_rationales.C: This captures surveillance only, and the square had no prior users or customs to displace, so there is no distinct time being abolished.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says lighting abolished the night 'as a distinct social time': 'the day's rules, the day's people and the day's activities spread into hours that had once belonged to others'. The beach case has a distinct prior use with its own customs, an extension of general rules, new users who gain, and the old users' ways lost.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an analogy for only one of the two stories the author rejects (liberation or discipline).
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option models one partial reading; the correct answer requires all elements of the paragraph 5 synthesis.

questions.question: The final sentence of the passage implies that the usual histories of light have gone wrong chiefly because they

options.A: neglect to measure how far lighting actually lengthened the hours that people spent working, travelling and shopping.
options.B: see the street through one kind of user's eyes, missing that a single change brought gain to some and loss to others.
options.C: count lighting as a gain when, properly understood, its effects on everyday life were very largely a loss for townspeople.
options.D: depend on the testimony of the officials who installed the lamps, and so repeat those officials' claims about safety without ever questioning them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) see the street through one kind of user's eyes, missing that a single change brought gain to some and loss to others.

option_rationales.A: The author's complaint is about whose experience is imagined, not about missing measurements of hours.
option_rationales.C: The author declines to call it simply gain or loss, saying the verdict 'depends largely on whom we imagine walking the street'.
option_rationales.D: The passage notes that sponsors 'spoke of safety, and they meant it', but it never says historians relied on their testimony.

questions.explanation: The sentence says the verdict depends on 'whom we imagine walking the street', and that 'the habit of imagining only one kind of walker' made the history easy to tell badly. The flaw is a single standpoint that hides divided effects.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author to have a hidden verdict (loss), when the point is that the verdict varies by user.
questions.difficulty_reason: The compressed final sentence must be unpacked; one option smuggles in a verdict the author refuses to give.

questions.question: According to the passage, the decoy effect is weakest when

options.A: the menu contains more than three options, so that no single comparison stands out.
options.B: buyers already know from experience what they want, or when the decoy is obviously inferior.
options.C: the products on the menu are expensive, so that customers take more care over every comparison they make.
options.D: the product on sale is cheap and bought on impulse, like the popcorn sold in a cinema.

questions.correct_answer: (B) buyers already know from experience what they want, or when the decoy is obviously inferior.

option_rationales.A: The number of options is never discussed as a limit; paragraph 3 names only experience and an obviously inferior decoy.
option_rationales.C: The price level of the products is never mentioned as a limit; paragraph 3 ties weakness to the buyer's experience and to a decoy 'so plainly inferior' that the trick is noticed.
option_rationales.D: The passage uses popcorn as its main example of the effect working, and it ties weakness to the buyer's experience, not to the price or kind of product.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives the two limits: the effect is strongest when buyers are 'unsure what they want and have little experience', so a regular 'is rarely moved', and it 'weakens when the decoy is so plainly inferior that customers notice the trick'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that sounds like a sensible marketing rule rather than one the passage states.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The 'regular who knows exactly how much popcorn she can eat' (paragraph 3) is mentioned in order to

options.A: show that a buyer whose preference is already settled gives the decoy little to work on.
options.B: prove that the standard economic account of choice is correct for most customers after all.
options.C: suggest that frequent cinema-goers resent being steered and therefore buy the smallest size available.
options.D: illustrate the claim that people lean on the easy comparison and let it settle the hard one.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that a buyer whose preference is already settled gives the decoy little to work on.

option_rationales.B: The passage treats the regular as an exception that marks a limit; it never says the standard account holds for most people, and to call the example proof overstates the point.
option_rationales.C: Resentment is a separate limit mentioned in the next sentence, about decoys that are noticed; the regular is unmoved because she knows what she wants, not because she resents anything.
option_rationales.D: That claim, from paragraph 2, describes buyers who are moved by the decoy; the regular is the opposite case.

questions.explanation: The sentence says the effect is strongest for buyers who are unsure and inexperienced, and the regular is the contrasting case: she 'is rarely moved'. She illustrates the first limit on the effect.
questions.common_misconception: Merging the regular with the resentment point that follows her.
questions.difficulty_reason: Function is signalled by the sentence the example sits in.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the standard account described in paragraph 2, adding the medium tub to the menu should

options.A: reduce total sales, since customers faced with more options take longer and buy less.
options.B: raise sales of the medium tub among customers who could not decide between the other two sizes.
options.C: make the large tub look like a bargain to customers who had previously preferred the small one.
options.D: leave unchanged the proportion of customers who prefer the large tub to the small one.

questions.correct_answer: (D) leave unchanged the proportion of customers who prefer the large tub to the small one.

option_rationales.A: Choice overload is not mentioned anywhere in the passage; this imports an outside idea.
option_rationales.B: The standard account says nothing about who would buy the medium; its prediction in paragraph 2 concerns only the ranking of the other two, which should stay 'untouched'.
option_rationales.C: This is what the decoy actually does in paragraph 1, the result the standard account cannot explain, not what it predicts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that on the standard account the decoy 'should be inert': an unwanted medium tub 'should leave my ranking of the other two untouched'. So the share preferring large to small should not change.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing what the decoy does with what the standard account predicts.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the reported view from the observed result and restating its prediction.

questions.question: The passage is mainly concerned with

options.A: showing that ordinary customers are easily fooled by marketers and should distrust every menu they see.
options.B: explaining how cinemas and software firms can raise their revenue by adding options that nobody buys.
options.C: using the decoy effect to argue that how options are arranged helps shape what people choose.
options.D: defending the standard economic account of choice against evidence drawn from experiments on pricing.

questions.correct_answer: (C) using the decoy effect to argue that how options are arranged helps shape what people choose.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 asks for a better explanation than 'customers are easily fooled', and paragraph 4 says not every arrangement is sinister.
option_rationales.B: The passage uses such firms as examples, but its concern is what the effect shows about preference and menus, not advice on raising revenue.
option_rationales.D: The passage challenges the standard account, saying the decoy suggests preferences are 'assembled on the spot'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the decoy, paragraph 2 explains it as preference assembled from easy comparisons, paragraph 3 sets limits, and paragraph 4 draws the main lesson that 'the background is part of the decision'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the commercial example, or the 'easily fooled' reading the author explicitly sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure of the passage points directly to the final paragraph's lesson.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the statement that the winning firm 'has been selected for its error' means that the firm

options.A: will be excluded from future auctions once the seller discovers that it has overpaid.
options.B: was chosen by the seller because its survey team had a reputation for careless work.
options.C: made a deliberate error in bidding above its own estimate in order to defeat its rivals.
options.D: won the tract mainly because its survey happened to overstate what the tract was worth.

questions.correct_answer: (D) won the tract mainly because its survey happened to overstate what the tract was worth.

option_rationales.A: Exclusion by the seller is never mentioned; paragraph 3 speaks only of firms that keep losing money being 'driven from the market'.
option_rationales.B: No seller judges the surveys; the firm wins simply by bidding highest, and paragraph 1 says each estimate 'may be honest'.
option_rationales.C: The firms in paragraph 1 bid 'what its own survey says the tract is worth'; the error lies in the estimate, not in a deliberate overbid.

questions.explanation: The preceding sentences say the contract goes 'to the firm whose survey was most optimistic', so that 'winning ... is itself evidence of having overestimated'. Being selected for its error means the overestimate is what made it win.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'selected' as a decision by the seller rather than as a statistical sorting.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is explained by the two sentences before it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of why the winner's curse is learned away only slowly?

options.A: Experienced bidders in many auction markets are observed to bid somewhat below their own estimates.
options.B: In most such auctions the losing bidders are told, soon afterwards, how much the tract actually yielded.
options.C: Firms that repeatedly overpay for tracts eventually run short of money and stop taking part in auctions.
options.D: The yield of a single tract often differs from its expected value because of geological chance.

questions.correct_answer: (B) In most such auctions the losing bidders are told, soon afterwards, how much the tract actually yielded.

option_rationales.A: The author concedes this in paragraph 3 ('seasoned bidders in many settings do shade their bids'), so it is consistent with the account rather than against it.
option_rationales.C: This is part of the objection, and the author already grants it ('There is truth in this'); it does not touch the reasons given for the learning being slow.
option_rationales.D: This supports the author, who says 'The outcome of any single auction is noisy' and a disappointing tract 'may simply have been unlucky'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives two reasons for slow learning: single outcomes are noisy, and 'the firms that lose never discover what the prize was really worth', so correcting information reaches only winners. If losers routinely learned the true yield, the second reason would collapse.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that restates the objection, which the author has already partly accepted.
questions.difficulty_reason: Students must locate the two specific reasons and see that two options merely repeat what the author grants or asserts.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph in relation to the rest of the passage?

options.A: It draws on the earlier analysis to locate a remedy in the auction's information structure, without ranking formats outright.
options.B: It abandons the claim of paragraph 2 that bidders should shade, in favour of the claim that only design matters.
options.C: It shows that sealed-bid auctions should be replaced by open bidding wherever the value of a prize is uncertain.
options.D: It introduces a second cause of the curse, the signalling between rivals, which the earlier paragraphs overlooked.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It draws on the earlier analysis to locate a remedy in the auction's information structure, without ranking formats outright.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says design matters 'as much as' bidders' wisdom, which keeps shading in place rather than abandoning it.
option_rationales.C: The author explicitly denies 'that one format is always superior' because open bidding 'has weaknesses of its own'.
option_rationales.D: Signalling is mentioned only as a weakness of open bidding, not as a cause of the curse, which the passage traces throughout to the information structure.

questions.explanation: Having said that bidders learn slowly (paragraph 3), the author concludes 'For this reason' that design matters, since the curse is 'a property of the information structure'. The concession about open bidding prevents it from becoming a blanket ranking.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the comparison of formats as a recommendation, ignoring the concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph contains both a conclusion and a qualification, and the wrong options each mishandle one.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that the winner's curse, as the author describes it, would be LEAST likely to arise when

options.A: bids are submitted in sealed envelopes and opened only at the end.
options.B: each bidder's survey is honest and, taken on its own terms, unbiased.
options.C: every bidder relies on one shared survey instead of commissioning its own.
options.D: a very large number of firms compete for the same tract of seabed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) every bidder relies on one shared survey instead of commissioning its own.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says sealed bids leave each bidder 'alone with a single survey', the condition under which the curse is hardest to correct.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the curse occurs even when 'each estimate may be honest and, taken alone, unbiased', so this condition does not prevent it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the highest of many estimates is 'more likely to be inflated', so a large field makes the curse worse, not less likely.

questions.explanation: The curse arises because separate estimates 'scatter around the true figure' and the winner is the one with the most optimistic estimate. If all bidders used the same estimate, winning would no longer select for an overestimate, so the mechanism the passage describes would not operate.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the honest, unbiased survey, which sounds protective but is exactly the case the author says still produces the curse.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reconstructing the mechanism and applying it to a case the passage never mentions, while two wrong options reverse explicit statements.

questions.question: According to the passage, for goods whose qualities can be inspected before purchase, advertising

options.A: is more likely than other advertising to manipulate buyers by associating products with glamour.
options.B: informs buyers directly, so that no signalling explanation of it is required.
options.C: works mainly as a signal that the maker is wagering on a long stream of repeat purchases from satisfied customers.
options.D: is largely wasted, since buyers can examine the goods for themselves before paying for them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) informs buyers directly, so that no signalling explanation of it is required.

option_rationales.A: Manipulation is linked in paragraph 1 to advertisements that carry no information, not to advertising for inspectable goods.
option_rationales.C: That is the account paragraph 2 gives for cheap experience goods; paragraph 3 says inspectable goods require 'no signalling story at all'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says such advertising 'informs directly'; it never calls it wasted, which was the critics' conclusion about contentless advertising.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'For goods whose qualities can be inspected before purchase ... advertising informs directly and requires no signalling story at all.'
questions.common_misconception: Transferring the signalling account to goods the passage explicitly excludes from it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a firm that knows its cheap, frequently bought product is mediocre

options.A: would always advertise exactly as heavily as a firm with a good product, so that the expense revealed nothing.
options.B: could not afford to advertise at all, since it expects most of those who try its product never to return.
options.C: would gain less from a lavish campaign than a rival whose product is good.
options.D: would do better to sell its product as something that customers buy only once in a lifetime.

questions.correct_answer: (C) would gain less from a lavish campaign than a rival whose product is good.

option_rationales.A: This contradicts paragraph 2's reasoning; paragraph 3 allows that imitators 'may' mimic expense, which is far short of saying they always do.
option_rationales.B: The passage says lavish advertising is 'worth far more' to the good firm, a claim about relative value; it never says the mediocre firm cannot advertise at all.
option_rationales.D: Nothing suggests a firm can choose how often its product is bought; once-in-a-lifetime goods appear only as a limit on the signal.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the good firm expects 'a long stream of returns', the mediocre firm expects most triers 'never to return', and so lavish advertising 'is accordingly worth far more to the first firm than to the second'.
questions.common_misconception: Turning a comparative claim (worth less) into an absolute one (cannot advertise).
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires restating a comparative conclusion and rejecting an option that overstates a hedged remark in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The signalling argument, as limited in paragraph 3, would most clearly explain which of the following?

options.A: An expensive, almost wordless campaign launching a new toothpaste, a cheap item that households buy every few weeks.
options.B: A costly campaign by a firm that installs home swimming pools, something most households buy at most once.
options.C: A furniture maker's printed catalogue that lists the dimensions and the price of every table in its range.
options.D: A railway company's advertisement announcing the fares and the timetable for a newly opened route.

questions.correct_answer: (A) An expensive, almost wordless campaign launching a new toothpaste, a cheap item that households buy every few weeks.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says a firm selling what people 'buy once in a lifetime gains little from the signal', because satisfied customers will not return.
option_rationales.C: These qualities can be inspected before purchase, and for such goods advertising 'informs directly' with no need of signalling.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 cites 'the fare for a train journey' as information advertising conveys directly, so no signalling explanation is needed.

questions.explanation: The argument fits experience goods that are cheap to try and bought repeatedly, where an advertisement says little and its expense is the message. A new toothpaste with an almost wordless, costly campaign matches every condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a costly campaign without checking whether repeat purchase is likely.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each option must be checked against two conditions from paragraph 3.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a limit on, or qualification of, the signalling account EXCEPT:

options.A: it does not settle whether advertising also manipulates the people who see it.
options.B: it applies most clearly to goods judged only after use and bought repeatedly.
options.C: a firm's heavy spending may reflect vanity or miscalculation rather than confidence.
options.D: ordinary consumers do not consciously reason about the economics of repeat purchase.

questions.correct_answer: (D) ordinary consumers do not consciously reason about the economics of repeat purchase.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the account 'leaves the question of manipulation entirely open', a limit on what it establishes.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says exactly this: the argument 'applies most clearly to ... experience goods' and 'only where repeat purchase is likely'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'a firm may overspend from vanity or miscalculation', so not every campaign is a reliable signal.

questions.explanation: The point about consumers not reasoning this way is raised in paragraph 4 as 'A familiar objection', and the author rejects it: 'The objection misunderstands what the argument requires', because a rule of thumb suffices. It is therefore not a limit the author accepts.
questions.common_misconception: Treating an objection the author reports and rebuts as one of the author's own qualifications.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four options appear in the passage; the correct answer differs only in the author's attitude towards it.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a nudge that stops working as soon as its purpose is explained as

options.A: evidence, though not proof, that it depended on people not understanding what they were doing.
options.B: no different in principle from one that survives, since every presentation of options influences choice.
options.C: conclusive proof that the institution using it has acted manipulatively and must abandon it.
options.D: a sign that disclosure is itself distracting and so should not be expected of institutions.

questions.correct_answer: (A) evidence, though not proof, that it depended on people not understanding what they were doing.

option_rationales.B: This is the defenders' argument from inevitability, which paragraph 2 says 'answers a weaker objection than the one that matters'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the test 'is not decisive in every case' and that some nudges 'might fail it for innocent reasons', so failure is not proof.
option_rationales.D: Distraction is offered in paragraph 4 as one innocent reason a nudge might fail, not as a reason to drop disclosure, which the author's test requires.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says failure after explanation 'is evidence that it relied on a gap between what people were doing and what they understood themselves to be doing'. Paragraph 4 qualifies this: the test is 'not decisive', since a nudge may fail for innocent reasons. Evidence, not proof, matches both.
questions.common_misconception: Ignoring the qualification in paragraph 4 and treating the test as a verdict.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer requires combining paragraph 3's claim with paragraph 4's qualification, while one wrong option states the defenders' view the author rejects.

questions.question: The author's claim that the argument from inevitability 'answers a weaker objection than the one that matters' assumes that

options.A: the critics who deny that any arrangement of options is inevitable are more numerous than the careful critics.
options.B: most of the nudges now used by public bodies would fail if their purposes were explained.
options.C: an influence's being unavoidable does not show that every way of exercising it is equally acceptable.
options.D: people who are paying attention are almost never affected by the way in which their options are presented.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an influence's being unavoidable does not show that every way of exercising it is equally acceptable.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the position that an unarranged menu is available is one 'nobody holds', so the author is not counting its supporters.
option_rationales.B: The author says only that 'many of the most effective nudges' rely on going unnoticed and that some 'would plainly survive disclosure'; no claim about most nudges is needed.
option_rationales.D: The argument needs no such strong claim; paragraph 3 even allows a disclosed arrangement to keep working, as 'a reminder'.

questions.explanation: The defenders show that some influence is inevitable. The author replies that the real objection concerns influence that works by going unnoticed. For that reply to work, the inevitability of influence as such must leave open whether a particular, concealed form of it is acceptable; otherwise the defenders' argument would settle the matter.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a factual claim about how many nudges fail, which the author never needs.
questions.difficulty_reason: Assumption questions require reconstructing the gap between the defenders' premise and the author's conclusion.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the defenders of nudging is best described as

options.A: suspicious: they are suggested to be hiding their real motives from the people whose choices they steer.
options.B: deferential: their reply to critics is taken to have answered the charge that nudging is manipulative.
options.C: dismissive: their reply to critics is treated as confused and as missing the obvious unavailability of any neutral menu.
options.D: partly sympathetic: their central argument is accepted, but not as settling the issue that matters most.

questions.correct_answer: (D) partly sympathetic: their central argument is accepted, but not as settling the issue that matters most.

option_rationales.A: The author questions nudges that work unnoticed, not the honesty of their defenders, whose argument is engaged on its merits.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the argument 'answers a weaker objection than the one that matters', so the author does not think the charge has been answered.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 calls their argument 'sound as far as it goes', and it is the critics who imagine an unarranged menu who are said to attack 'a position nobody holds'.

questions.explanation: The author grants the inevitability argument ('sound as far as it goes') and ends by saying the test 'concedes to the defenders everything their best argument actually establishes', while insisting it does not answer the more serious objection.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's criticism of unnoticed nudges for hostility to their defenders.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude is mixed and stated in measured terms at the start and end of the passage.

questions.question: Which of the following practices would most clearly pass the test proposed in paragraph 3?

options.A: A government form redesigned so that the most common answer appears first, its designers never having asked what would happen if the reason were stated.
options.B: A clinic's texted appointment reminders that keep cutting missed visits after patients are told they are sent for that reason.
options.C: A bank's default savings option, explained in the fine print of a long contract, whose take-up is unchanged though almost no customers read that section.
options.D: A website's pre-ticked box for marketing emails, whose sign-ups fall sharply once a notice explains that the box was ticked to raise them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A clinic's texted appointment reminders that keep cutting missed visits after patients are told they are sent for that reason.

option_rationales.A: The test asks whether the influence survives being explained; an arrangement that has never been disclosed cannot be said to pass it.
option_rationales.C: The arrangement has not survived disclosure in the relevant sense, since the explanation never reached the customers; the gap between what they do and what they understand remains.
option_rationales.D: This is the failing case of paragraph 3: the nudge stops working once explained, which the author treats as evidence it relied on concealment.

questions.explanation: The test asks whether a nudge 'continues to work' once its purpose is openly explained. The clinic's reminders keep working after patients know why they are sent, so their power 'did not depend on concealment'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the savings default, which looks like survival after disclosure but involves a disclosure nobody registered.
questions.difficulty_reason: The savings-default option mimics the passing pattern on the surface, and only a reader who grasps why disclosure matters will reject it.

questions.question: According to the passage, competition does little to hold down the price that users pay for free services because

options.A: the firms that provide such services face no rivals offering a similar product to the same users.
options.B: users generally prefer the services that absorb the largest share of their day.
options.C: users cannot readily tell how much of their time a service takes, or whether a rival would take less.
options.D: advertisers rather than users decide how much attention each service collects.

questions.correct_answer: (C) users cannot readily tell how much of their time a service takes, or whether a rival would take less.

option_rationales.A: The passage speaks of 'Firms competing for attention' and of rivals, so it does not say rivals are absent; the problem is that the price cannot be compared.
option_rationales.B: No such preference is claimed; the passage blames product design on firms' incentives, not on what users want.
option_rationales.D: Advertisers buy the attention that providers gather; the passage never says they set how much is taken.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A user cannot easily tell whether one free application takes ten minutes of her day or two hours, still less whether a rival would take less, and so the competitive pressure ... operates feebly, if at all.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming a monopoly explanation instead of the passage's point about an unstated price.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: When the passage says that 'the user is less a customer than a supplier of the commodity being traded' (paragraph 2), it means that the user

options.A: provides the attention that the service gathers and sells on to its advertisers.
options.B: is paid by the service, in the form of free features, for recommending its advertisers' products.
options.C: matters more to advertisers than to the firm that actually provides the service.
options.D: writes the articles, messages and videos that the service later sells to other users.

questions.correct_answer: (A) provides the attention that the service gathers and sells on to its advertisers.

option_rationales.B: The passage describes no payment to users for recommending products; the user simply gives attention in exchange for the service.
option_rationales.C: The phrase concerns the user's role in the exchange, not a ranking of how much the user matters to different parties.
option_rationales.D: The commodity named in paragraph 2 is attention, 'which the provider gathers and resells to advertisers', not content made by users.

questions.explanation: The sentence says a free service 'is paid for with attention, which the provider gathers and resells to advertisers'. The user is thus the source of what is sold, a supplier, rather than a buyer.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'commodity' to mean content, a common association with online services that the passage does not make.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is glossed by the clause just before it.

questions.question: The author would most likely describe a free application designed to absorb as much of its users' time as possible as

options.A: a reason for governments to prohibit services that are offered to their users at no charge.
options.B: a predictable response to a market in which the price paid in attention cannot be seen.
options.C: likely to lose many of its users to rival applications that take up less of their time each day.
options.D: evidence that people who use such free services are dupes who fail to understand the bargain they have struck with the provider.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a predictable response to a market in which the price paid in attention cannot be seen.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says it 'does not follow that free services should be prohibited'; the remedy proposed is making the price visible.
option_rationales.C: This is the opposite of the passage's claim: because the price is invisible, competitive pressure 'operates feebly, if at all', so such losses are not expected.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that 'their users are dupes', and paragraph 2 allows that the bargain 'may be a good one'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that, the price being unstated, 'Firms competing for attention are therefore rewarded not for charging less of it but for extracting more, and the design of their products follows accordingly'. The author treats such design as a result of incentives.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the moralising option the author explicitly sets aside in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the author rejects outright; the third reverses the effect of an invisible price.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the case for the remedy proposed in the final paragraph?

options.A: Advertisers pay providers more for the attention of users who spend long hours on a single service.
options.B: Most users say in surveys that they enjoy free services and would not want to pay money to use them.
options.C: Users shown regular reports of their screen time usually stop reading them within a few weeks.
options.D: Users given weekly reports of their time on each application shifted towards those that served the same purpose in less time.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Users given weekly reports of their time on each application shifted towards those that served the same purpose in less time.

option_rationales.A: This supports the account of why firms try to extract more attention, but it does not show that reporting time would help users.
option_rationales.B: Enjoyment of free services is consistent with the passage but says nothing about whether making the price visible would change behaviour.
option_rationales.C: This would weaken the remedy, since a figure nobody reads cannot let users compare prices.

questions.explanation: The remedy rests on the claim that a visible 'figure to compare' would restore the discipline of comparison. Evidence that users, once shown the figure, moved towards services that charged less attention directly supports it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that supports another claim in the passage rather than the remedy.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option supports a different part of the argument and must be separated from the remedy itself.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that unravelling harms employers chiefly because

options.A: candidates who receive early offers usually refuse them in the hope that better ones will follow.
options.B: it obliges candidates to conceal their real preferences and to rank a likely employer first.
options.C: competition for the strongest candidates pushes up the salaries that employers have to offer.
options.D: very early offers must be made on scant evidence of how able the candidates are.

questions.correct_answer: (D) very early offers must be made on scant evidence of how able the candidates are.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says early offers are refused; refusal under time pressure belongs to the separate failure of congestion, and even there the problem is missed offers.
option_rationales.B: That is strategic misrepresentation, a third and distinct failure described later in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not discuss salaries; paragraph 1 explains that in matching markets price does not do the work of allocation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the race for earliness 'can push offers so far forward that they are made before anyone knows how good the candidates are'. Employers therefore commit with little information about quality.
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up the three failures, which are described in consecutive sentences.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three failures are adjacent and similar in vocabulary; the correct answer needs a small inference about who bears the cost.

questions.question: The final sentence of paragraph 3 ('Such clearinghouses show ... freedom alone creates') serves to

options.A: generalise from the remedy to a claim about what markets can be, against the view that they only arise of their own accord.
options.B: summarise the three failures of matching markets described in the preceding paragraph and explain which one is most serious.
options.C: concede that clearinghouses restrict the freedom of applicants and employers and so carry a cost the designer must weigh.
options.D: establish that markets in which people trade freely will fail unless a clearinghouse is constructed for them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) generalise from the remedy to a claim about what markets can be, against the view that they only arise of their own accord.

option_rationales.B: The sentence does not summarise or rank the failures; it draws a general lesson about markets from the clearinghouse.
option_rationales.C: The sentence says freedom 'alone creates' certain problems, not that clearinghouses restrict freedom; costs of design are discussed only in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: The sentence says a market 'is not always' spontaneous and can be built; it makes no claim that free markets in general fail, and paragraph 1 says price works in most markets.

questions.explanation: After describing the clearinghouse, the author concludes that 'a market is not always a spontaneous order' but 'can be an artefact'. The sentence moves from a specific remedy to a general claim, and 'not always' marks it as a correction of a common view, not a blanket rejection.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the hedge 'not always' into a claim that markets are never spontaneous, or reading the sentence as a concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to the sentence's wording; the correct answer requires attention to the hedge 'not always' and to the sentence's function.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a limit on what clearinghouses can achieve EXCEPT that

options.A: no procedure gives both sides full reason for honesty while always producing stable outcomes.
options.B: the choice of procedure involves judging whose interests most deserve to be protected.
options.C: they cannot produce assignments in which no unmatched applicant and employer would both prefer each other.
options.D: they depend on enough applicants and employers choosing to take part in them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) they cannot produce assignments in which no unmatched applicant and employer would both prefer each other.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says this directly, as an example of why a procedure cannot 'deliver every desirable property at once'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the designer's choice 'reflects judgements about whose interests deserve protection', which is why the art is called political.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'A clearinghouse works only if enough of both sides join it', a limit the author states plainly.

questions.explanation: The correct answer describes stability, defined in paragraph 3 as the absence of an unmatched pair who 'would both prefer to be' matched, and it is the property clearinghouses are designed to deliver. Claiming they cannot produce it contradicts the passage; the other three are limits stated in paragraph 4.
questions.common_misconception: Being misled by the technical wording of the correct answer and failing to recognise it as the definition of stability.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is a disguised restatement of a concept defined in paragraph 3, negated; the solver must map it back.

questions.question: Which of the following is the clearest instance of the strategic misrepresentation described in paragraph 2?

options.A: A law firm, keen to secure the strongest graduates, makes its offers in their first year of study rather than their last.
options.B: In a ranked-list scheme for course places, a student puts a less popular course first, fearing that naming her favourite would lose her the safer place.
options.C: A graduate accepts the only offer she holds because it must be answered within hours, and later learns of a better one.
options.D: A prestigious hospital declines to join the clearinghouse and fills its posts by recruiting the doctors it wants privately.

questions.correct_answer: (B) In a ranked-list scheme for course places, a student puts a less popular course first, fearing that naming her favourite would lose her the safer place.

option_rationales.A: Making offers ever earlier to secure strong candidates is unravelling, not the concealment of preferences.
option_rationales.C: Being unable to learn of a better offer in time is congestion, the second failure in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.D: Staying out of the clearinghouse is the participation problem of paragraph 4, not a misreported ranking.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines strategic misrepresentation as 'ranking a likely option first rather than the one they actually want, because they fear that revealing their real wishes will cost them'. The student does exactly this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing another of the market failures, which are described in neighbouring sentences.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is a different failure from the passage, so the definitions must be held apart.

questions.question: According to the passage, the theory that located value in the costs of production had difficulty explaining

options.A: why a good as essential to life as water should nevertheless be so cheap in most places.
options.B: goods whose prices bear little relation to the effort that went into obtaining or making them.
options.C: why the same bucket of water is worth far more to a traveller in a desert than in a town.
options.D: why resources such as clean air are treated as having no value until they become scarce.

questions.correct_answer: (B) goods whose prices bear little relation to the effort that went into obtaining or making them.

option_rationales.A: The cost theory did offer an answer to this, that water 'merely has to be collected'; paragraph 2 places its difficulty elsewhere.
option_rationales.C: The bucket example appears in paragraph 3 to show what the marginal account achieved; the passage does not present it as the cost theory's difficulty.
option_rationales.D: This is the error in public argument described in paragraph 4, which the passage links to reading prices as importance, not to the cost theory.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the cost theory 'struggled with cases in which effort and price come apart', such as a pearl found by chance and a wine whose labour 'has been forgotten'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the original paradox, which the cost theory claimed to solve.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence and illustrated by two examples.

questions.question: The statement that the marginal account 'moved value from things to situations' (paragraph 3) means that it

options.A: shifted attention from the labour needed to produce a good to the situations in which that labour is performed.
options.B: showed that the value of a good depends mainly on the place where it happens to be produced and sold.
options.C: replaced the study of individual goods with the study of whole markets, in which many buyers and sellers meet together.
options.D: made value depend on a person's circumstances, such as how much of a good she already has, not on fixed qualities of the good.

questions.correct_answer: (D) made value depend on a person's circumstances, such as how much of a good she already has, not on fixed qualities of the good.

option_rationales.A: The marginal account 'abandoned the attempt to attach value to goods as such' and set labour aside rather than relocating it.
option_rationales.B: The bucket's location matters only because of the people's circumstances, a town 'beside a river' against a traveller 'lost in a desert'; place of production is not the point.
option_rationales.C: The passage contrasts goods 'as such' with the position of someone who already has a certain amount, not individual goods with whole markets.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the account looked at 'the usefulness of one more unit of it to someone who already has a certain amount', and paragraph 3 illustrates this with the same bucket being 'nearly worthless' in one setting and 'beyond price' in another although 'nothing about the water has changed'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'situations' literally as geographic location.
