questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase must be interpreted through the example that follows it and the definition in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about a resource that is cheap today because it is plentiful?

options.A: It will remain cheap because the price of a resource reflects the labour needed to collect it.
options.B: It should be withdrawn from markets so that prices cannot mislead the public about its importance.
options.C: Its present price may be a poor guide to what it would be worth if it were to become scarce.
options.D: Its low price shows that the resource contributes little to the welfare of the society that uses it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Its present price may be a poor guide to what it would be worth if it were to become scarce.

option_rationales.A: This applies the cost theory, which paragraph 2 says was superseded, and it ignores the warning that abundance 'is not always permanent'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says 'None of this is a case against prices'; the author recommends remembering what a price measures, not removing goods from markets.
option_rationales.D: This is the error paragraph 4 describes and the author rejects: 'The marginal theory does not license this inference'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 ends: 'Abundance, moreover, is not always permanent, and a price set while a resource was plentiful says little about what it will be worth once it is not.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the inference the author identifies as the common error.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases a sentence, while one wrong option states the very view the author attacks.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the marginal account of value is best described as

options.A: appreciative of how it resolved the puzzle, while insisting on the limits of what it can tell us.
options.B: regretful, since it is blamed for encouraging the public habit of treating cheap resources as worthless.
options.C: uncritical, since it is taken to show that market prices are a reliable ranking of what matters to a society.
options.D: sceptical, since it is presented as no real advance on the cost theory that it replaced in the later nineteenth century.

questions.correct_answer: (A) appreciative of how it resolved the puzzle, while insisting on the limits of what it can tell us.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the marginal theory 'does not license this inference' and even 'predicts the error'; the author blames public argument, not the theory.
option_rationales.C: The author says the account 'was never a theory of importance' and 'warns us against reading prices as a ranking of what matters'.
option_rationales.D: The author calls the resolution 'genuine' and says 'its elegance is rightly admired', and the cost theory is shown to have 'struggled' with important cases.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with praise ('genuine', 'rightly admired') and then says it achieved 'less' than usually credited, because it was never a theory of importance. Admiration combined with a statement of limits fits the correct answer.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's criticism of public argument as criticism of the theory itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The regretful option uses the passage's subject matter, and only a careful reading of 'predicts the error' rules it out.

questions.question: In the light of the passage as a whole, the eighteenth-century conclusion that exchange value 'must therefore have some source other than usefulness' is best regarded as

options.A: correct, because the later theory confirmed that the labour needed to produce a good is what fixes its price in exchange.
options.B: mistaken, because price does reflect usefulness, but that of one more unit rather than of the good as a whole.
options.C: mistaken, because water turns out to be worth more in exchange than diamonds once its total supply is taken into account.
options.D: correct, because the later theory showed that price reflects scarcity, which is quite separate from how useful a good is.

questions.correct_answer: (B) mistaken, because price does reflect usefulness, but that of one more unit rather than of the good as a whole.

option_rationales.A: The later theory 'abandoned the attempt to attach value to goods as such', and paragraph 2 shows labour failing to explain the pearl and the wine.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage says water is dearer than diamonds; the marginal account explains why water stays cheap despite being essential.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'Price tracks this marginal usefulness'; scarcity matters only through the usefulness of an extra unit, so the later theory keeps usefulness as the source.

questions.explanation: The writers compared total usefulness with price, found them inverted, and abandoned usefulness. The marginal account shows the inversion arises because price tracks 'the usefulness of one more unit of it to someone who already has a certain amount'. Usefulness was the right source; the error was looking at the total.
questions.common_misconception: Equating marginal usefulness with scarcity and concluding that usefulness has dropped out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The scarcity option is close to the truth, and rejecting it requires seeing that the passage keeps usefulness at the centre of the later theory.

questions.question: According to the standard interpretation described in paragraph 2, owners ask more for the mug than non-owners will pay because

options.A: owners come to regard the mug as stock to be sold, and so set a price as a dealer would.
options.B: the owners, though chosen at random, turn out to care more for mugs than the non-owners do.
options.C: parting with the mug counts as a loss, which weighs more than the equal gain of acquiring it.
options.D: owners suspect that the experimenter knows the true value of the mug and fear underpricing it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) parting with the mug counts as a loss, which weighs more than the equal gain of acquiring it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a dealer's parting with stock 'does not register as a loss', which would shrink the gap rather than explain it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says 'there is no reason to think that the owners care more for mugs', and the standard interpretation does not rely on any such difference.
option_rationales.D: This is one of the explanations offered by the rival interpretation in paragraph 3, not the standard one.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'giving it up registers as a loss, whereas acquiring it ... registers only as a gain, and since the loss weighs more heavily, the owner demands more in compensation'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching an explanation from the rival view to the standard one.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a paraphrase of one sentence in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The reference to investors who are reluctant 'to sell shares that have fallen in value' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: show that the endowment effect is found mainly among people who invest in shares rather than in ordinary goods.
options.B: suggest that professional traders, who deal routinely in what they hold, are as prone to the effect as anyone else.
options.C: support the rival interpretation that the gap in prices is an artefact of how experiments are conducted.
options.D: illustrate how far beyond the laboratory the loss-aversion account appears to reach.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate how far beyond the laboratory the loss-aversion account appears to reach.

option_rationales.A: The example widens the account's reach; it does not narrow the effect to investors, and the mug experiments involve ordinary people.
option_rationales.B: Investors here are not presented as professional traders, and paragraph 3 says traders show 'much less of the effect'.
option_rationales.C: The example appears in paragraph 2 as support for the standard interpretation; the rival view is not introduced until paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: The sentence says the account 'connects the mug experiments with a wide range of other behaviour, from the reluctance of investors ... to the stubbornness' of people defending entitlements. The investors are one end of that range.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking an example of the account's breadth for a narrowing or a counter-example.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the same sentence as the example.

questions.question: The author's reading in paragraph 4 implies that a person who bought a mug at a market stall intending to resell it the next day would most likely

options.A: show a smaller gap between the prices at which she would sell and buy such a mug than a person given one to use.
options.B: value it as highly as someone who had been given the mug to use and had kept it for some time.
options.C: ask far more for it than a buyer would pay, since owning the mug would make it seem more valuable to her.
options.D: show a larger gap than participants in the mug experiments, because she paid money for her mug instead of receiving it free.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show a smaller gap between the prices at which she would sell and buy such a mug than a person given one to use.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 contrasts exactly these two positions: one who holds a thing 'to use' is 'in a different position' from one who holds it for exchange.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'what matters is not ownership as such but the frame in which a thing is held'; held for resale, parting with it 'does not register as a loss'.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in paragraph 4 makes the gap depend on whether a thing was paid for; the author ties it to whether a thing is held 'to use' or 'to exchange', and she holds hers to exchange.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that for a dealer 'parting with one is the purpose of having it, and so it does not register as a loss'. A person buying to resell holds the mug as something to exchange, so the author's reading predicts a smaller gap for her than for someone holding a mug to use.
questions.common_misconception: Applying the bare idea that ownership raises value, which the author's synthesis refines.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the author's distinction to a new case and rejecting the option that applies the uncorrected effect.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the rival interpretation presented in paragraph 3?

options.A: Investors who hold shares that have fallen in value turn out to sell them as readily as shares that have risen in value.
options.B: Participants who are given mugs report liking them somewhat more after they have been given them than before.
options.C: Many first-time participants say afterwards that they found the instructions for stating a selling price hard to follow.
options.D: The gap stays as large as ever among participants who have practised the procedure and know that misstating their values cannot help them.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The gap stays as large as ever among participants who have practised the procedure and know that misstating their values cannot help them.

option_rationales.A: This would bear on the breadth claimed for loss aversion in paragraph 2, not on whether laboratory procedures produce the gap.
option_rationales.B: This might suggest a further explanation of the gap, but it does not touch the rival view's claim that confusion about procedure inflates it.
option_rationales.C: This would strengthen the rival view, which holds that participants 'may be unsure what is being asked'; it gives no reason to doubt the artefact explanation.

questions.explanation: The rival view says the gap is partly an artefact of unfamiliar procedures, and that it shrinks when participants 'practise the bidding mechanism and understand that misstating their values cannot help them'. If the gap persisted undiminished under exactly those conditions, the artefact explanation would lose its main support.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option that bears on a different part of the passage, or one that actually supports the rival view.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option touches the passage, and the solver must test which one strikes at the rival view's own evidence.

questions.question: On the author's reading in paragraphs 4 and 5, which of the following would be expected to show the LARGEST gap between the price asked to sell an item and the price offered to buy an identical one?

options.A: A student who bought a bicycle on a resale platform last week, planning to sell it on again for a profit.
options.B: A family asked to sell a bicycle given to them an hour ago, still unpacked, which they have not yet decided whether to keep.
options.C: A family asked to sell a bicycle given to them months ago, which their child has ridden every day since.
options.D: A bicycle shop owner asked to sell one of the identical bicycles displayed in the showroom.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A family asked to sell a bicycle given to them months ago, which their child has ridden every day since.

option_rationales.A: The student holds the bicycle 'as something to exchange', and paragraph 5 says resale platforms that encourage people to regard possessions as stock 'may weaken the effect'.
option_rationales.B: The author says the effect depends on 'how people come to think of what they have' and that encouraging people to regard what they hold as their own 'may strengthen it'; a gift an hour old, unpacked and not yet settled as something to keep, has barely begun to become 'part of her possessions', unlike one used daily for months.
option_rationales.D: The owner holds the bicycles as stock, and for a dealer 'parting with one is the purpose of having it, and so it does not register as a loss'.

questions.explanation: The author's reading makes the gap depend on the frame in which a thing is held: things held to use, and increasingly regarded as one's own, show it most, as the remark that long trial periods 'may strengthen it' indicates. Months of daily use make the bicycle most fully the family's own.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the new gift on the reasoning that any ownership produces the effect, without weighing how strongly each item is held as one's own.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options are excluded easily, but separating the two families requires applying the trial-period remark in paragraph 5 as a matter of degree.

questions.question: The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: establish that poverty and inequality are, in practice, the same thing, so that measuring one measures the other.
options.B: defend relative poverty lines against the charge that they only measure inequality, while showing why they need an absolute companion.
options.C: argue that absolute poverty lines mislead governments because they ignore what it costs to take part in the ordinary life of a society.
options.D: show that relative poverty lines are superior to absolute ones and should replace them in official statistics.

questions.correct_answer: (B) defend relative poverty lines against the charge that they only measure inequality, while showing why they need an absolute companion.

option_rationales.A: The author answers the inequality charge by redefining poverty as exclusion from a social standard, not by equating poverty with the spread of incomes.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 credits absolute lines with a real 'virtue', and paragraph 4 wants both read together; the author never calls absolute lines misleading.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says relative measures cannot 'stand alone', and paragraph 4 recommends reading the two together, not replacing one with the other.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the charge that relative lines 'confuse poverty with inequality' and rejects it; paragraph 2 defends them as tracking a 'moving threshold of participation'; paragraph 3 concedes their recession weakness; paragraph 4 concludes that both kinds of line should be read together.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about absolute lines, which borrows the author's participation idea but turns it into a rejection of absolute lines that the passage never makes.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is built from the author's own reasoning but reverses the conclusion about absolute lines.

questions.question: According to the passage, what can happen to a relative poverty count when median income falls in a recession?

options.A: A household whose income is unchanged may stop being counted as poor though it is no better off.
options.B: The count rises sharply, because the poorest households are the first to lose their jobs in a slump.
options.C: The count can no longer be calculated reliably, because the median becomes unstable during a recession.
options.D: The line stays fixed at an earlier standard, so the count simply follows changes in real purchasing power.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A household whose income is unchanged may stop being counted as poor though it is no better off.

option_rationales.B: Job losses are never mentioned; paragraph 3 describes the line falling with the median, which can reduce the count, not raise it.
option_rationales.C: The passage never questions whether the count can be calculated; its complaint is that the result is 'perverse', not unavailable.
option_rationales.D: That describes absolute lines, 'fixed in real terms at some past standard'; paragraph 3 says the relative line 'falls with' the median.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: when median income falls, 'the line falls with it, and a household whose income has not changed may be counted as having escaped poverty while its circumstances are no better'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the behaviour of relative lines with that of absolute lines.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The examples in paragraph 2 of school clothes, a returned dinner invitation and a telephone suggest that the author regards poverty as

options.A: essentially a shortage of the food and shelter that a person needs in order to stay alive and healthy.
options.B: a condition that disappears once a country passes a fixed level of national income per head.
options.C: a matter of spending choices that poor families could make differently if they planned more carefully.
options.D: an inability to take part in the ordinary life of one's society, judged by that society's own standards.

questions.correct_answer: (D) an inability to take part in the ordinary life of one's society, judged by that society's own standards.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 opens by saying poverty 'has never meant only lacking the calories and shelter needed to stay alive'; the examples go beyond survival.
option_rationales.B: The passage says the requirements 'rise as that society grows richer', so no fixed national income level ends poverty in this sense.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage blames spending choices; the requirements are 'set by the society one lives in', not by the family.

questions.explanation: The examples are of being 'unable to do what one's neighbours take for granted', and the author adds that these requirements 'are set by the society one lives in'. Poverty is exclusion from ordinary participation.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the examples as luxuries and concluding the author has a survival-based view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The examples are explained by the sentence that introduces them.

questions.question: Which one of the following best captures the meaning of 'moving threshold of participation' as used in paragraph 2?

options.A: A poverty line that governments revise downward whenever median income falls during a recession or a slump.
options.B: The income at which households begin to vote, join associations and take part in the civic life of their community.
options.C: The level of resources needed to live as others in one's society do, a level that rises as the society grows richer.
options.D: The share of a society's members who can afford goods, such as refrigerators, that were once luxuries.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The level of resources needed to live as others in one's society do, a level that rises as the society grows richer.

option_rationales.A: This mixes up the phrase with the recession problem of paragraph 3; the threshold in paragraph 2 moves because requirements rise with prosperity.
option_rationales.B: The passage's participation is social and economic, 'taking part in ordinary life', such as school and work; it says nothing about voting or associations.
option_rationales.D: The phrase names a level that a household must reach, not a proportion of the population; the refrigerator is an example of what that level comes to include.

questions.explanation: The phrase sums up the preceding sentences: requirements for ordinary life 'are set by the society one lives in, and they rise as that society grows richer'. The threshold is that level of resources, and it moves upward with general prosperity.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'participation' in its political sense, or treating the threshold as a population share.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options use nearby ideas (refrigerators, revision of the line) and must be ruled out on what the phrase refers to.

questions.question: The references to pensioners and tax refunds in paragraph 1 serve mainly to

options.A: show that the fear of misuse is applied selectively to the poor rather than to everyone who receives public money.
options.B: demonstrate that almost all public spending is already unconditional, so that conditions are rare in practice.
options.C: argue that cash transfers to the poor should be paid through the same offices that administer pensions.
options.D: suggest that pensions and tax refunds are themselves frequently wasted, so that the poor are no worse than others.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that the fear of misuse is applied selectively to the poor rather than to everyone who receives public money.

option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about public spending as a whole; it uses two examples to expose a double standard, not to survey spending.
option_rationales.C: Administration is never discussed; the comparison concerns attitudes to recipients, not delivery systems.
option_rationales.D: The passage never says pensions or refunds are wasted; its point is that pensioners 'are not asked to show receipts', that is, nobody suspects them.

questions.explanation: Right after the examples, paragraph 1 says 'The worry is reserved for people whose poverty is taken ... as evidence that they cannot be trusted'. The examples show that other recipients of public money escape the suspicion.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the comparison as a claim about the recipients' behaviour rather than about the suspicion directed at them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence that follows the examples.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author considers transfers in kind inferior to cash chiefly because they

options.A: are designed by officials who are, as a rule, indifferent to what poor households actually need.
options.B: apply one assumption about need to households whose most pressing needs differ from one another.
options.C: cost more to deliver than cash in remote places, where transport and storage of goods are expensive.
options.D: are usually resold by recipients at a loss, so that much of their value disappears before it is used.

questions.correct_answer: (B) apply one assumption about need to households whose most pressing needs differ from one another.

option_rationales.A: The author says officials know less about a household's constraint than the household does, not that they do not care; the option turns a point about knowledge into one about motive.
option_rationales.C: The passage never compares delivery costs; its remote-places point in paragraph 3 is a qualification about cash raising prices, not a cost of goods in kind.
option_rationales.D: Resale is never mentioned; the objection in paragraph 2 is that a transfer in kind 'has to guess'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a household knows 'its own most pressing constraint' better than an official, that 'the constraint differs from one family to the next', and that a transfer in kind 'guesses the same thing for everyone'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about officials' indifference, which sounds like the author's critical tone but misstates the ground of the criticism.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is a paraphrase across three sentences; one wrong option shifts from knowledge to motive.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the general presumption that poor people will misuse cash is best described as

options.A: contemptuous, dismissing anyone who holds the presumption as acting in bad faith towards the poor.
options.B: neutral, presenting it as one reasonable position among several without taking a side on the question.
options.C: sceptical, treating it as a suspicion that the evidence has largely failed to bear out.
options.D: approving, since the presumption protects public money from being wasted on drink and gambling.

questions.correct_answer: (C) sceptical, treating it as a suspicion that the evidence has largely failed to bear out.

option_rationales.A: The tone is measured; the author concedes that conditions have a place and that 'Paternalism is sometimes justified', and accuses no one of bad faith.
option_rationales.B: The author takes a clear side, calling for 'a reversal of the burden of proof' and saying paternalism 'should not, however, be the starting assumption'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 reports little sign of increased spending on alcohol or tobacco, and paragraph 3 rejects a 'general presumption' of misuse.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the suspicion 'has been tested' and evaluations 'have generally found little sign' of it; paragraph 3 calls it no ground 'for a general presumption'. The attitude is reasoned scepticism.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the author's criticism into contempt.
questions.difficulty_reason: Tone is clear from explicit evaluative statements.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the reasoning in paragraph 2 for preferring cash to transfers in kind?

options.A: In a few remote villages, cash transfers raised local prices because traders could not bring in more goods quickly.
options.B: Some households in cash programmes spent part of the money on livestock or tools rather than on food for the family.
options.C: Pensioners in richer countries spend a larger share of their income on alcohol than recipients of cash transfers do.
options.D: In several programmes, nearly all households spent their cash on the same few items that a standard bundle in kind would have supplied.

questions.correct_answer: (D) In several programmes, nearly all households spent their cash on the same few items that a standard bundle in kind would have supplied.

option_rationales.A: The author already grants this in paragraph 3 as a qualification for particular cases; it does not touch the reasoning of paragraph 2 about differing needs.
option_rationales.B: Spending on livestock and tools is listed in paragraph 2 as a sensible use; it fits the author's claim that needs differ.
option_rationales.C: This concerns the double standard of paragraph 1, and if anything it supports the author; it says nothing about cash versus goods in kind.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 prefers cash because 'the constraint differs from one family to the next', so a transfer in kind that 'guesses the same thing for everyone' guesses wrong. If households in fact all wanted the same items, the in-kind guess would be right and the advantage of cash would largely vanish.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the remote-villages option, which is a real limit on cash but one the author has already conceded and which targets a different argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires locating the exact premise of paragraph 2 and separating it from the paragraph 3 qualification.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the modest average effects found by careful evaluations of microcredit

options.A: prove that small loans to the poor are worthless and that the money would be better spent in other ways.
options.B: say more about a mistaken assumption regarding borrowers' aims than about whether the loans were of any use.
options.C: were caused mainly by competition among lenders, which drove many households into taking one loan to repay another.
options.D: show that poor borrowers were never as creditworthy as the early lenders and their repayment figures claimed.

questions.correct_answer: (B) say more about a mistaken assumption regarding borrowers' aims than about whether the loans were of any use.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says outright that 'The lesson is not that small loans are worthless', and paragraph 3 calls the service 'genuinely valuable'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 raises over-borrowing as a danger to guard against, not as the explanation of the modest averages, which paragraph 2 traces to a false picture of borrowers.
option_rationales.D: Creditworthiness is not questioned; the author's point in paragraph 1 is that the step from creditworthiness to prosperity 'proved longer than advertised'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that reading the evidence as failure 'mistakes what was being tested', because the original story wrongly 'assumed that most poor people are frustrated entrepreneurs'. Paragraph 3 adds that the loans did something valuable that average income does not capture.
questions.common_misconception: Linking two things the passage mentions (modest effects and over-borrowing) into a causal claim the author does not make.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the argument of paragraphs 2 and 3 together; one wrong option builds a false causal link from paragraph 4.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a use to which borrowers put their loans EXCEPT

options.A: paying for travel to a city to look for work.
options.B: meeting a bill from a hospital stay.
options.C: paying the costs of a family wedding.
options.D: putting a new roof on before the rains.

questions.correct_answer: (A) paying for travel to a city to look for work.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 lists 'a hospital bill' among the uses of loans.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 lists 'a wedding' among the lumpy expenses that loans were used to manage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 lists 'a new roof before the rains' among the uses of loans.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists a wedding, a hospital bill, school fees and a new roof before the rains. Travel to seek work is never mentioned; paragraph 2 refers to wage work only to explain why people run enterprises.
questions.common_misconception: Associating the passage's mention of wage work with a use of loans.
questions.difficulty_reason: The list is in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's view that microcredit is best understood as a financial service?

options.A: Borrowers who had run established businesses before their first loan saw clearly larger gains in profit than other borrowers did.
options.B: In districts where several lenders competed, a large share of households held more than one loan at the same time.
options.C: Within five years of their first loan, most borrowers in one region had doubled their household incomes.
options.D: Borrowers asked what losing access to loans would mean most often said they would struggle to meet sudden large expenses.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Borrowers asked what losing access to loans would mean most often said they would struggle to meet sudden large expenses.

option_rationales.A: This matches the minority noted in paragraph 4, for whom credit worked as capital for enterprise; it supports the qualification, not the financial-service view.
option_rationales.B: This bears on the danger of over-borrowing in paragraph 4, not on whether loans chiefly serve to manage expenses.
option_rationales.C: A large rise in income would suggest that credit was an 'engine of growth', the view the author sets aside, so it weakens rather than strengthens the claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that loans largely went into 'managing life's lumpy expenses' and that their value is turning small repayments into 'a single usable sum'. Borrowers saying the loss of credit would hurt their ability to meet large sudden expenses directly supports that account of what the loans do.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the established-business option because it is drawn from the passage and shows credit doing good.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are drawn from paragraph 4 and support other claims; the solver must match evidence to the precise claim.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do many poor people run tiny enterprises?

options.A: Running a stall allows them to fit paid work around school fees, weddings and other expenses that fall due together.
options.B: Steady wage work is not available to them, and many would accept such work if they could.
options.C: Microlenders require a business plan before they will lend, so borrowers start businesses in order to qualify for loans.
options.D: They are frustrated entrepreneurs who have been held back only by their lack of access to capital.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Steady wage work is not available to them, and many would accept such work if they could.

option_rationales.A: Those expenses are what loans were used for in paragraph 3; the passage does not offer them as a reason for running enterprises.
option_rationales.C: No lending requirement of this kind is mentioned; paragraph 3 says much of the money did not go into enterprises at all.
option_rationales.D: This is what 'The original story assumed', a view paragraph 2 rejects for many of the poor: 'Many are not.'

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'They run tiny enterprises because steady wage work is unavailable, and given the choice many would take a factory job at a fixed wage over the uncertainties of a market stall.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the view the author reports and rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is the reported view the author denies; the answer is in one sentence but must be separated from it.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Inequality in developing countries can be expected to fall only after episodes of war and inflation destroy concentrated wealth.
options.B: The inverted U is mathematically mistaken, since moving workers between two sectors cannot change the overall level of inequality.
options.C: The inverted U records some historical episodes rather than a law, and gives governments no reason to expect inequality to correct itself.
options.D: Recent rises in inequality in rich countries are passing disturbances that further economic growth will in time reverse.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The inverted U records some historical episodes rather than a law, and gives governments no reason to expect inequality to correct itself.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists war and inflation as one factor 'in several cases', alongside schooling, labour and taxation; the option makes one item a condition.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the mechanism 'is sound as far as it goes' and that the arithmetic does widen and then narrow inequality.
option_rationales.D: This is the complacent lesson paragraph 3 attributes to treating the curve as a law, which the author criticises.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 shows the idea hardening 'into something closer to a law', paragraph 2 shows the evidence failing to follow it, paragraph 3 shows the policy damage, and paragraph 4 gives the 'better reading' as 'a record of what happened in some places' that cannot assure a government 'that inequality will take care of itself'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the war-and-inflation option because it uses a detail from paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer needs the whole structure; one wrong option is the criticised view itself.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the author regards the historical declines in inequality as

options.A: having involved more than the shift of workers between sectors, since the fall usually came together with other changes.
options.B: having been caused chiefly by the destruction of concentrated wealth in wars and periods of high inflation.
options.C: having been produced by measures that governments adopted deliberately in order to reduce inequality.
options.D: evidence that the inverted U never actually described the experience of any economy at all.

questions.correct_answer: (A) having involved more than the shift of workers between sectors, since the fall usually came together with other changes.

option_rationales.B: The passage names war and inflation only 'in several cases' and as one of four accompaniments, so 'chiefly' overstates it.
option_rationales.C: War and inflation are on the list, and they are not measures that governments adopt in order to reduce inequality; the passage says the declines 'came alongside' these changes, without claiming that any of them was aimed at inequality.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 treats the curve as 'a record of what happened in some places', so it did describe some economies.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that in the episodes that showed a decline, 'the fall rarely arrived on its own' but 'came alongside' schooling, organised labour, taxation and the destruction of wealth. So the fall was not the work of the sectoral arithmetic of paragraph 2 alone; other forces usually accompanied it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about deliberate measures, which reads intent into 'came alongside' and overlooks that war and inflation are on the list.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to the text; one adds intent, one adds 'chiefly', and the correct answer must be preferred for its exact scope.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most clearly regard as an instance of the 'damage' described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A finance ministry turns down a plan to expand rural schooling, arguing that the inequality brought by industrial growth will correct itself.
options.B: A statistics office revises its estimates of national inequality after discovering errors in the household survey data.
options.C: A government expands public schooling in the hope of narrowing a growing gap between urban and rural incomes.
options.D: An economist assembles data from many countries and shows that inequality sometimes rises again after a long decline.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A finance ministry turns down a plan to expand rural schooling, arguing that the inequality brought by industrial growth will correct itself.

option_rationales.B: Revising estimates has nothing to do with treating the curve as a law; the damage in paragraph 3 is the encouragement of 'waiting'.
option_rationales.C: This is action, not waiting; paragraph 3 lists the spread of public schooling among the changes that accompanied falling inequality.
option_rationales.D: This is the accumulating evidence of paragraph 2 that weakened the curve, not a policy harm caused by trusting it.

questions.explanation: The damage is that if rising inequality is seen as 'a natural stage of development that growth will itself reverse', governments 'can be told to tolerate it'; 'Both lessons encourage waiting.' A ministry declining to act because inequality will supposedly correct itself is exactly this.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the evidence-gathering option because it concerns the curve, without asking whether it is a harm to policy.
questions.difficulty_reason: Applying the abstract claim to a case requires identifying 'waiting' as the mechanism of damage.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It introduces the inverted-U hypothesis and explains how the idea came to be proposed in the first place.
options.B: It offers an alternative reading of the curve as a record of particular structural shifts and political choices.
options.C: It grants that the mechanism is arithmetically sound and then argues that real economies have not reliably followed it.
options.D: It describes the consequences for policy of treating the hypothesis as a law of economic development.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It grants that the mechanism is arithmetically sound and then argues that real economies have not reliably followed it.

option_rationales.A: That is the work of paragraph 1, which states the hypothesis and its origin in 'a handful of national histories'.
option_rationales.B: That reading is given in paragraph 4, which begins 'A better reading'.
option_rationales.D: The consequences for policy are the subject of paragraph 3, which opens 'It was to policy.'

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens 'The mechanism at its core is sound as far as it goes', explains the arithmetic, and then says 'What does not follow is that this arithmetic governs the course of inequality in real economies', citing the evidence of later data.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the roles of neighbouring paragraphs.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option describes another paragraph accurately, so the right one is quickly found.

questions.question: The passage implies that a programme allowing firms to register online would mainly benefit

options.A: the poorest informal workers, whose earnings are too low to meet the obligations that formality brings.
options.B: owners of established informal businesses who have weighed the costs of registering and decided against it.
options.C: government agencies that hope to collect more in fines from firms that are found to be evading taxes.
options.D: formal-sector employers who are looking for cheaper suppliers among the many unregistered firms nearby.

questions.correct_answer: (B) owners of established informal businesses who have weighed the costs of registering and decided against it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says such programmes are 'largely irrelevant' to this group: 'For her, simplification changes nothing.'
option_rationales.C: Fines belong to the separate approach of campaigns that 'treat informality as evasion', not to programmes that ease registration.
option_rationales.D: Formal employers seeking suppliers are never discussed; the passage considers only the two groups of informal workers and firms.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that programmes that cut the cost of registration, including 'allowing firms to register online', are 'well designed for the second group', the owners of established firms described in paragraph 2 who 'could register' and 'have decided against it'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming any pro-formalisation measure helps the poorest most.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer follows from one sentence of paragraph 3 read with the description of the second group.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the description of informality as 'a waiting room' implies that informal workers

options.A: have chosen a refuge in which they can avoid the taxes and regulations that formal firms must bear.
options.B: are learning, while they wait, the skills that formal employers will later demand of them.
options.C: are passing through a stage that every economy must go through on its way to becoming industrial.
options.D: occupy their position only until a better opening, in this case formal work, becomes available.

questions.correct_answer: (D) occupy their position only until a better opening, in this case formal work, becomes available.

option_rationales.A: That is the second camp's view; the waiting room belongs to the exclusion view, in which people are there for lack of jobs.
option_rationales.B: The image concerns waiting to leave, 'its occupants would leave if a door opened'; acquiring skills is never mentioned.
option_rationales.C: The image describes workers waiting for jobs, not a stage in a country's development; no such stage is claimed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 completes the image itself: informality 'is a waiting room, and its occupants would leave if a door opened'. On the exclusion view people are there 'because the formal economy has too few jobs to absorb them'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the image to the choice view described a few sentences later.
questions.difficulty_reason: The image is explained in the same sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the error that paragraph 2 attributes to both camps?

options.A: One survey of renters interviews young professionals and calls renting a lifestyle choice; another interviews families refused mortgages and calls renters shut out.
options.B: Two surveys of the same group of renters reach opposite conclusions because one asks about preferences and the other asks about income.
options.C: A survey calls renting a lifestyle choice, but a later check of its own figures shows that most of the renters it studied had in fact been refused mortgages.
options.D: A city that cuts registration fees for landlords finds that the number of officially registered rental homes rises in the following year.

questions.correct_answer: (A) One survey of renters interviews young professionals and calls renting a lifestyle choice; another interviews families refused mortgages and calls renters shut out.

option_rationales.B: This is a disagreement produced by different questions about one population; paragraph 2 describes camps that draw on 'a different population' each.
option_rationales.C: Here one study simply got its own population wrong; the error in paragraph 2 is two camps each generalising correctly observed facts about a different subgroup to the whole.
option_rationales.D: This is a policy result, not an error of generalisation, and it echoes paragraph 3 rather than paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'each tends to generalise from the cases that suit it': the exclusion camp studies the poorest workers, the choice camp studies established firms, and each treats its group as 'the informal economy'. The renters case has the same structure: two accurate studies of different subgroups, each generalised to all renters.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the same-population option, which also has two studies disagreeing, without noticing that the source of disagreement is different.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires abstracting the precise form of the error and rejecting analogies with a different structure.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the two camps described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: approving of both camps, regarding their disagreement as a useful division of labour among researchers.
options.B: indifferent, because the author regards the informal economy as a collection of unrelated cases.
options.C: sympathetic to the exclusion camp and dismissive of the choice camp as a cover for the evasion of taxes.
options.D: even-handed but critical, granting each a real basis while faulting both for treating a part as the whole.

questions.correct_answer: (D) even-handed but critical, granting each a real basis while faulting both for treating a part as the whole.

option_rationales.A: The author faults both for generalising 'from the cases that suit it' and for pretending 'that one diagnosis fits all'; that is criticism, not approval.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'It would be wrong to conclude that the informal economy is merely a collection of unrelated cases'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 credits the choice view with 'real evidence' about established firms; the author criticises crackdowns that 'treat informality as evasion', not the choice camp's evidence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens 'Each camp marshals real evidence, and each tends to generalise from the cases that suit it', and compares their dispute to arguing whether a typical city resident is 'a banker or a street sweeper'. The attitude grants both and faults both.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's defence of the poorest in paragraph 3 as a rejection of the choice view.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option exploits the author's sympathy in paragraph 3; the solver must keep the attitude to the camps separate from the attitude to crackdowns.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that an earmarked grant is least likely to be diverted to other uses when

options.A: the donor attaches a plaque and a public ceremony to the project so that its role is widely seen.
options.B: the recipient government had already set aside its own revenue to pay for the same project.
options.C: most of the recipient's spending is locked into commitments that cannot easily be cut or moved.
options.D: the recipient government has sound priorities and is free to move money to where it is most needed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) most of the recipient's spending is locked into commitments that cannot easily be cut or moved.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 mentions 'the comfort of a plaque' to mock rigid earmarking; publicity is never said to limit diversion.
option_rationales.B: This is the case in paragraph 1 in which diversion is easiest: the government can 'release the money it had set aside'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says sound priorities make fungibility harmless, not rarer; freedom to move money is exactly what allows diversion.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says fungibility 'is also weaker when a government's budget is so stretched or so rigid that there is little slack to shift'. Spending locked into commitments that cannot be cut leaves exactly that lack of slack.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the sound-priorities option, which confuses whether fungibility is harmful with whether it occurs.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is a paraphrase of one clause, and the main wrong option turns on a distinction between occurrence and harm drawn across paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, studies comparing donors' allocations with recipients' overall spending have often found that aid labelled for a sector

options.A: raised spending in that sector by more than the amount given, because it attracted matching funds from governments.
options.B: raised spending in that sector, though usually by less than the full amount of the aid.
options.C: was mostly lost to corruption before it could be spent in any sector of the recipient's budget.
options.D: had no measurable effect at all on spending in the sector for which it was labelled.

questions.correct_answer: (B) raised spending in that sector, though usually by less than the full amount of the aid.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says spending rose by less than the amount given; matching funds are never mentioned.
option_rationales.C: Corruption is not mentioned; the passage concerns legitimate reallocation by governments, not theft.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such aid raises sector spending 'by less than the amount given, though rarely by nothing', so some effect was usually found.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: studies 'have often found that aid labelled for a sector raises spending in that sector by less than the amount given, though rarely by nothing'.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'less than the amount' into 'nothing'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that donors 'are funding governments, not projects'?

options.A: A government that received a grant for roads reduced its own road budget by almost exactly the amount of the grant.
options.B: Recipient governments seldom publish detailed accounts showing how their own revenue is divided among sectors.
options.C: Donor-funded vaccination teams reached regions left out of the health ministry's own plans, while the ministry's spending elsewhere was unchanged.
options.D: Donors that earmark their grants report greater satisfaction with the results than donors who give general budget support.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Donor-funded vaccination teams reached regions left out of the health ministry's own plans, while the ministry's spending elsewhere was unchanged.

option_rationales.A: This is a clear case of fungibility and so strengthens the claim rather than weakening it.
option_rationales.B: This makes fungibility harder to detect but gives no reason to think it does not happen; it neither supports nor weakens the claim.
option_rationales.D: Donors' satisfaction says nothing about what their money actually changed; paragraph 1 notes the donor 'may never learn' what it financed.

questions.explanation: The claim holds where aid replaces spending the government had planned. Paragraph 3 says that where a donor funds what the government 'would not have undertaken', there is 'no planned expenditure to release'. Vaccination in regions excluded from the ministry's plans, with no cut elsewhere, is aid that funded a project rather than freeing the government's money.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about secrecy, which feels damaging to the claim but leaves it untouched.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that only additional spending with no offsetting cut weakens the claim.

questions.question: The hypothetical clinic in paragraph 1 functions chiefly to

options.A: show that clinics paid for by donors are seldom actually built by the governments that receive the money.
options.B: illustrate how money given for one purpose can end up financing something quite different.
options.C: argue that recipient governments tend to divert aid money into military spending rather than social services.
options.D: demonstrate that fungibility is harmful whatever the priorities of the government that receives the aid.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate how money given for one purpose can end up financing something quite different.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says plainly that 'The clinic gets built either way'; the point is what else the aid pays for.
option_rationales.C: The 'extra battalion' is one of three possible uses listed, alongside a road and a pay rise; no tendency towards military spending is claimed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'Nor is fungibility in itself a scandal' and that it is an advantage where priorities are sound.

questions.explanation: The clinic case shows a donor that 'likes to believe that it has paid for a clinic' while its money actually finances 'whatever the government would otherwise have gone without'. Paragraph 2 then names this 'fungibility'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the disapproving tone of paragraph 1 as the author's final verdict.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option exploits the tone of the opening, which the author qualifies in paragraph 4.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the effects of geography described in paragraph 3 as

options.A: illusions created by comparing countries whose histories and political systems were quite different.
options.B: minor in comparison with institutional effects, which explain most of the differences between countries.
options.C: the only effects of geography that statistical exercises are able to measure with any reliability.
options.D: real constraints on prosperity that better laws and government cannot simply remove.

questions.correct_answer: (D) real constraints on prosperity that better laws and government cannot simply remove.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts them as 'direct effects', adding that 'no amount of constitutional reform makes a mountain range easier to cross'.
option_rationales.B: The author never ranks the two; paragraph 5 says the question 'which matters more?' should be dropped altogether.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 criticises such exercises for the question they ask, not for measuring some effects and missing others; reliability is never discussed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls these 'direct effects': transport costs persist 'whatever its laws say', good government 'can reduce but not abolish overnight' the burden of malaria, and 'no amount of constitutional reform makes a mountain range easier to cross'. The author does not dispute them, and paragraph 4 faults both camps, not the geographers' facts.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because the author criticises the debate, the author dismisses geography's direct effects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer follows from the plain wording of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The example of the two halves of a peninsula in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: show that large differences in prosperity can open up between places that do not differ in geography.
options.B: support the geographers' view that places with a shared climate and soils will tend to share outcomes.
options.C: illustrate how colonisers chose institutions according to the disease environment they met on arrival.
options.D: show that political division of a country makes both of its resulting halves poorer than they would have been.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that large differences in prosperity can open up between places that do not differ in geography.

option_rationales.B: The example is offered as 'The institutional camp's strongest card', and it shows shared geography producing different outcomes.
option_rationales.C: Colonisers' choices are discussed in paragraph 4 in connection with the reversal pattern, not the peninsula.
option_rationales.D: The example concerns divergence between the halves, not a loss common to both; nothing is said about what either would otherwise have been.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says geography 'changes slowly while fortunes can change fast', and the peninsula halves, with 'the same climate, the same soils' and a shared history, 'diverge dramatically' under 'different political systems'. Geography is held constant while outcomes differ.
questions.common_misconception: Merging the peninsula example with the colonial reversal discussed later.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options use material from elsewhere in the passage; the function is signalled by 'strongest card'.

questions.question: The author's claim that the reversal story is 'a story about geography working through institutions' implies that

options.A: the regions that were prosperous five centuries ago owed their early prosperity to good institutions rather than to geography.
options.B: statistical estimates of the effect of geography on income are too large, because they wrongly include effects of institutions.
options.C: evidence the institutional camp cites against geography is partly evidence of geography's indirect influence.
options.D: institutions have no influence on prosperity apart from what the underlying geography of a region has given them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) evidence the institutional camp cites against geography is partly evidence of geography's indirect influence.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about the source of the early prosperity; the claim concerns what colonisers did afterwards.
option_rationales.B: The author objects that such exercises treat 'links in a single chain' as rival causes and answer the wrong question; no direction of bias is claimed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the institutions 'later took on a life of their own', and paragraph 5 says the same land 'can support very different outcomes'.

questions.explanation: The reversal pattern was cited by institutionalists to show that geography 'did not flip' while fortunes did. Paragraph 4 argues that the colonial institutions themselves depended on disease and soils, so they 'were, in this sense, partly geographical in origin'. The institutional camp's evidence thus partly reflects geography acting through institutions.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the statistical-bias option, which sounds technical and close to paragraph 4 but adds a directional claim the author does not make.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that paragraph 4 turns one camp's evidence against the framing of the contest; two wrong options overstate or redirect that point.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: Public health campaigns have greatly reduced the burden of malaria in a number of tropical regions over recent decades.
options.B: Colonial records show that the choice between settling and extracting followed home-country policy, without regard to local disease or soils.
options.C: Several landlocked countries have reached high incomes despite the extra cost of moving their goods to distant markets.
options.D: Statistical studies that include both geography and institutions find that institutions account for more of the variation in income.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Colonial records show that the choice between settling and extracting followed home-country policy, without regard to local disease or soils.

option_rationales.A: This is consistent with paragraph 3, that good government can 'reduce' malaria; it says nothing about the origin of institutions.
option_rationales.C: This fits paragraph 5, that a country is 'not condemned by its latitude', and does not bear on how colonial institutions arose.
option_rationales.D: The author would say such a result 'answers a question that the history does not pose'; it does not touch the claim that the two are linked in a chain.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 rests on the premise that colonisers 'chose to settle or to extract partly according to how likely they were to survive the local diseases' and that soils suited coerced-labour crops. If the choice was made without regard to disease or soils, the institutions were not 'partly geographical in origin', and the chain linking geography to institutions breaks.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the statistical finding, which seems to settle the contest in favour of institutions but is exactly the kind of result the author says is beside the point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option looks like decisive evidence for one camp; the solver must see that the author's argument is about the framing, not the winner.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a way in which geography may affect a country's prosperity EXCEPT

options.A: by favouring crops suited to large estates worked with coerced labour, and so shaping institutions.
options.B: by raising the cost of moving the goods a country produces to the markets where they are sold.
options.C: by imposing a burden of disease that reduces the health of a country's workers.
options.D: by fixing the prices that the country's minerals and crops will fetch on world markets.

questions.correct_answer: (D) by fixing the prices that the country's minerals and crops will fetch on world markets.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'the soils of some regions suited crops that were profitable to grow with coerced labour on large estates'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 lists 'how cheaply goods can be moved', and paragraph 3 notes that a landlocked country 'pays more to export every tonne'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 mentions 'how healthy workers are', and paragraph 3 discusses endemic malaria.

questions.explanation: Transport costs (paragraphs 1 and 3), disease (paragraphs 1, 3 and 4) and soils that shaped labour systems (paragraph 4) are all mentioned. World prices for a country's products are never discussed.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that the indirect route through institutions does not count as an effect of geography.
questions.difficulty_reason: One mentioned effect is indirect and sits in a different paragraph from the others, so all must be checked.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: defend judging development by freedoms against the charge of arbitrary weighting, while warning against collapsing it into one index.
options.B: show that income per head is a worthless statistic that development agencies should stop reporting altogether.
options.C: propose a definite list of capabilities, with weights attached, that would improve on existing composite indices.
options.D: explain why market prices are the fairest available way of weighing very different goods against one another.

questions.correct_answer: (A) defend judging development by freedoms against the charge of arbitrary weighting, while warning against collapsing it into one index.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 calls income 'the most convenient measure' and 'a means'; the author questions its authority, not its existence, and proposes no ban.
option_rationales.C: The author offers no list; paragraph 5 warns that composite scores can 'reproduce the very problem the approach set out to solve'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 criticises market weights for letting 'a luxury bought by the rich' count for more than a staple; the author does not call them fair.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 state the case for judging development by capabilities; paragraph 3 gives the objection about weights; paragraph 4 replies that income has the same difficulty, hidden; paragraph 5 qualifies the conclusion by warning against single indices.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the extreme reading of the author's criticism of income.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must combine the defence and the qualification; each wrong option takes one strand too far or reverses it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the 'old' difficulty mentioned at the end of paragraph 4 is that

options.A: critics of the capability approach have long disagreed among themselves about which capabilities belong on the list.
options.B: the poor are frequently unable to afford staple goods that a market economy treats as being of low value.
options.C: figures for income per head cannot be meaningfully compared across different countries or across decades.
options.D: any summary measure of well-being must weight unlike things, and so embodies value judgments whether or not it states them.

questions.correct_answer: (D) any summary measure of well-being must weight unlike things, and so embodies value judgments whether or not it states them.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 reports what critics say, not any disagreement among them, and their objection is the form the weighting problem takes for capabilities; the 'old' difficulty is the one income measures already had.
option_rationales.B: This is a detail from the illustration of how market prices weight goods, not the difficulty that the illustration is used to reveal.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: income per head 'can be compared across countries and decades'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says income 'also aggregates very different things, and it also weights them', with value judgments 'made silently, by the market'. A framework that states its weights 'has not introduced a new difficulty. It has exposed an old one': the old difficulty is the unavoidable weighting of unlike goods.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the critics' objection itself as the old difficulty, or picking up the staple example.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading 'old' against the argument of the whole paragraph; the wrong options are taken from the objection and the illustration.

questions.question: Which of the following findings would best illustrate the central point of paragraph 2?

options.A: A district whose average income doubled over a decade saw adult literacy rise in roughly the same proportion.
options.B: Within a single district, households with higher incomes are on average better nourished than households with lower incomes.
options.C: Two districts with equal average incomes differ widely in girls' completion of secondary school, because only one has a school within walking distance.
options.D: Ranking districts by a composite index of capabilities places them in a different order from ranking them by income.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Two districts with equal average incomes differ widely in girls' completion of secondary school, because only one has a school within walking distance.

option_rationales.A: Here income and a capability move together; it does not show a difference 'in the rate at which resources become lives'.
option_rationales.B: This shows income tracking a freedom, which is what income measures assume; paragraph 2 is about the same income yielding different freedoms.
option_rationales.D: This concerns indices, the subject of paragraph 5; it gives no case of equal resources yielding unequal freedoms.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that 'The same income does not yield the same freedoms to everyone', because bodies, climates and 'Social arrangements' change how resources convert into what people can do. Equal incomes with unequal schooling outcomes owing to the distance of a school is such a case.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an income-and-outcome correlation, which mentions a capability but shows the opposite of differing conversion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires recognising that the point concerns equal resources with unequal results, not any link between income and well-being.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the objection set out in paragraph 3 is best described as

options.A: persuaded, concluding that freedoms cannot be measured and that income must remain the standard.
options.B: respectful but unpersuaded, treating it as a real question that tells against income measures as well.
options.C: indifferent, because the author holds that questions of measurement do not matter to judging development.
options.D: dismissive, regarding it as a misunderstanding raised in bad faith by the defenders of income measures.

questions.correct_answer: (B) respectful but unpersuaded, treating it as a real question that tells against income measures as well.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the objection 'is weaker than it looks' and turns it back on income; the author is not persuaded.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 discusses how composite scores can mislead, so measurement plainly matters to the author.
option_rationales.D: The author answers the objection with an argument and never questions anyone's motives; 'weaker than it looks' concedes that it looks strong.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'The objection is weaker than it looks, because it applies with equal force to the measure it is meant to defend'. The author takes the objection seriously enough to answer it, but rejects it as a reason to prefer income.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the confident rebuttal as contempt.
questions.difficulty_reason: Tone must be judged from how the rebuttal is framed; the dismissive option is close in direction.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a reason why the same income may yield different freedoms to different people EXCEPT

options.A: the use of market prices to weight goods when incomes are added up into a national figure.
options.B: a custom that prevents women from travelling alone, whatever the income of their household.
options.C: a bodily condition, such as pregnancy, that raises what a person needs to reach the same level of nourishment.
options.D: a climate that obliges some households to spend on heating what others can spend as they please.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the use of market prices to weight goods when incomes are added up into a national figure.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 gives the case 'Where custom keeps women from travelling alone' and a daughter's freedom stays 'exactly where it was'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'a pregnant woman needs more food than a man of the same age to be equally well nourished'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'a household in a cold climate must spend on heating what a household elsewhere can spend on anything it likes'.

questions.explanation: Pregnancy, cold climates and customs restricting travel are all given in paragraph 2 as differences in 'the rate at which resources become lives'. Market prices appear in paragraph 4, but as the way income per head weights goods in aggregate, a point about the measure, not a reason why one person's income yields fewer freedoms than another's.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the paragraph 2 examples because it seems too obvious, or treating everything the passage criticises about income as a conversion factor.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is something the passage does mention, but in a different role, so the solver must check function, not just presence.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that explaining firms as savings on market costs, though sound about their boundaries, overlooks the competence that firms themselves create.
options.B: reject the view that firms exist to economise on the costs of finding suppliers, bargaining with them and enforcing contracts.
options.C: explain the method by which a firm decides which activities it should perform itself and which it should buy from outside suppliers.
options.D: show that coordination by command inside firms is generally more efficient than coordination by prices in open markets.

questions.correct_answer: (A) argue that explaining firms as savings on market costs, though sound about their boundaries, overlooks the competence that firms themselves create.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this overturns the bargaining view' and calls it the best guide to boundaries, so outright rejection misstates the author's position.
option_rationales.C: The make-or-buy decision appears in paragraphs 2 and 4 only as what the standard view handles well; it is a supporting point, not the purpose of the passage.
option_rationales.D: The passage never ranks the two methods in general; it argues that firms produce something markets cannot supply, which is a different claim from overall efficiency.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 poses the puzzle of why firms exist, paragraph 2 gives the standard cost-saving answer and grants its 'real explanatory power', paragraph 3 identifies what it leaves out (knowledge produced by people working together for years), and paragraph 4 keeps the standard view for boundaries while denying that it is 'a complete theory of what firms are for'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the critique of paragraph 3 as a full rejection and missing the concession in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: One option overstates the critique and another picks a supporting point; the correct answer needs both the critique and the concession.

questions.question: According to the passage, the bargaining view correctly predicts that firms tend to

options.A: draw up longer and more detailed contracts for tasks whose requirements cannot be fully stated before the work begins.
options.B: buy routine tasks that recur daily from outside suppliers, since frequent purchases allow the buyer to compare terms more easily.
options.C: perform for themselves the activities peculiar to their own operations, where an indispensable supplier could exploit them.
options.D: keep expanding once internal organisation becomes cheaper than contracting, until no outside purchases remain in their accounts.

questions.correct_answer: (C) perform for themselves the activities peculiar to their own operations, where an indispensable supplier could exploit them.

option_rationales.A: For tasks that cannot be specified in advance, paragraph 2 says firms hire on 'open-ended terms', which is the reverse of detailed contracts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: when a task 'recurs daily' and cannot be specified in advance, market costs multiply and hiring someone becomes cheaper.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the firm grows only 'until the cost of organising one more activity internally equals the cost of buying it outside', which sets a limit.

questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 2 states that the account 'predicts, correctly, that firms tend to bring in-house the activities that are specific to their own operations, where a supplier who knew it was indispensable could hold them to ransom'. The correct answer paraphrases this.
questions.common_misconception: Misreading the argument about recurring tasks, which actually favours hiring over buying.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence; the wrong options reverse nearby details.

questions.question: When the author says that what the bargaining view leaves out 'is suggested by its own vocabulary', the implication is that

options.A: the technical terms of the bargaining view are too abstract for the managers who must decide whether to make or buy a component.
options.B: describing the firm only by the costs it avoids presents it as at best equal to a costless market, which hides what firms add.
options.C: the bargaining view uses the word 'cost' in different senses in different parts of its argument and so contradicts itself.
options.D: economists who use the bargaining view have deliberately excluded evidence about informal knowledge because it cannot be measured.

questions.correct_answer: (B) describing the firm only by the costs it avoids presents it as at best equal to a costless market, which hides what firms add.

option_rationales.A: Managers' understanding of the terms is never discussed; the point concerns what the theory's framing can and cannot describe, not its difficulty.
option_rationales.C: No inconsistency in the account is alleged; the author accepts its reasoning about boundaries and objects only to treating it as complete.
option_rationales.D: The passage attributes the omission to the logic of the account's framing, not to any deliberate exclusion of evidence by its users.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the remark at once: the account 'describes the firm almost entirely in terms of costs avoided, as if the best a firm could do were to match what an ideal market would have delivered at no expense'. A vocabulary of avoided costs has no place for the positive product described next, knowledge that 'no contract could have bought'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'vocabulary' literally as a point about jargon or word usage rather than about the framing of the theory.
