questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the phrase to the explanation that follows and seeing why a cost framing caps what the firm can be credited with.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely offer as an example of 'the most valuable thing a firm possesses'?

options.A: A long-term contract with a parts supplier that spares a firm the expense of renegotiating terms every few months.
options.B: A brilliant engineer whose personal expertise is so well known that rival companies regularly offer her a higher salary.
options.C: A detailed operating manual that records every procedure of a workshop so that a new hire can follow it from the first day.
options.D: A surgical team whose members, after years together, anticipate one another's moves in ways that equally qualified strangers could not.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A surgical team whose members, after years together, anticipate one another's moves in ways that equally qualified strangers could not.

option_rationales.A: This is a saving on bargaining, the benefit the standard view already explains; the author's point is about something produced, not a cost avoided.
option_rationales.B: Expertise that rivals can bid for is available on the market, whereas paragraph 3 says the valuable knowledge 'does not exist outside' the firm and belongs to a group.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the valuable knowledge 'is rarely written down and often cannot be'; a manual is precisely the codified, transferable kind the author contrasts it with.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 defines the phrase as 'the shared competence of people who have learned to work together', and paragraph 3 describes it as unwritten, living in 'habits and in the expectations people hold of one another', and unavailable outside the group. A team whose coordination strangers could not reproduce fits every part of that description.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the star engineer or the manual because both involve valuable knowledge, while missing that the author's value is collective, tacit and not purchasable.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options involve knowledge and are tempting; only the correct answer meets all three conditions (shared, tacit, not available on the market) drawn from two paragraphs.

questions.question: According to the passage, quarrels among third-generation owners arise mainly because

options.A: outsiders hired to manage the firm tend to side with those owners who want to reinvest rather than distribute the profits.
options.B: owners with different ties to the firm want different things from it, and those who wish to leave may find no agreed buyout price.
options.C: the grandchildren of the founder have grown up in comfort and are therefore unwilling to work as hard as their parents did.
options.D: the founder usually leaves the largest share of the firm to the child who has worked longest in the business.

questions.correct_answer: (B) owners with different ties to the firm want different things from it, and those who wish to leave may find no agreed buyout price.

option_rationales.A: Hired managers appear only in paragraph 4 as part of the remedy; they play no role in the quarrels described in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.C: This is the character explanation of the folk story that paragraph 2 sets aside; the author says the quarrels 'follow from the structure'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 describes shares being divided among children, not an unequal bequest; the source of conflict is dispersal, not favouritism.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that salaried owners want reinvestment, distant owners want dividends, owners who need cash want to sell, and 'there may be no agreed price at which the others can buy them out'. The quarrels 'follow from the structure'.
questions.common_misconception: Falling back on the folk explanation the passage is arguing against.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is set out in a single paragraph.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the folk wisdom described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: approving, since the author's examples of quarrelling cousins and absent heirs confirm what the saying predicts.
options.B: neutral, since the author reports the saying and the alternative account without indicating which is more convincing.
options.C: doubtful of the explanation it gives while allowing that it is not wholly false.
options.D: contemptuous, since the author regards it as a story with no basis whatsoever in how family firms actually behave.

questions.correct_answer: (C) doubtful of the explanation it gives while allowing that it is not wholly false.

option_rationales.A: The examples support the predicted outcome but replace the saying's explanation with a structural one, so the author does not endorse it.
option_rationales.B: The author plainly prefers the structural account, ending with 'less a triumph of virtue than of design', so the stance is not neutral.
option_rationales.D: The author calls it 'only partly true' and concedes in paragraph 4 that 'some heirs are indeed less driven', so it is not dismissed as baseless.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 calls the story 'satisfying' but 'only partly true'; paragraphs 2 and 3 offer structural causes in place of character; paragraph 4 grants that character is not 'irrelevant'. The attitude is sceptical of the explanation but not dismissive of the observation.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing agreement about the outcome (firms often fade) with agreement about the cause (soft heirs).
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are each half right about the author's response; the correct answer needs both the doubt and the concession.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a founder who wishes to improve the chances of a good succession should

options.A: make sure that the next chief executive is chosen from among the relatives who already work in the business.
options.B: stay at the head of the firm for as long as possible, so that the heirs gain experience under his direct guidance.
options.C: divide the ownership equally among the heirs, so that none of them feels unfairly treated when a successor is named.
options.D: settle the matter of who will lead the firm well before illness or conflict forces the question.

questions.correct_answer: (D) settle the matter of who will lead the firm well before illness or conflict forces the question.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 argues that limiting the choice to family members narrows the field and makes the best manager unlikely to be chosen.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 criticises founders who postpone the question, since succession then 'tends to arrive suddenly' and falls to 'whoever is standing nearest'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 concerns choosing leaders, not dividing shares; and paragraph 2 suggests that dividing ownership widely creates conflict rather than preventing it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says founders make matters worse by 'postponing the question altogether', so that succession arrives 'suddenly, through illness or a quarrel'. The inference is that planning early avoids this.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option that sounds like sensible family practice but is criticised in the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: Follows directly from the paragraph's description of what goes wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why family firms decline?

options.A: Firms whose shares passed to a single heir in each generation declined as often as firms whose shares were spread among many relatives.
options.B: Family firms that adopted written rules for selling shares within the family reported fewer disputes among owners than those that did not.
options.C: In many family firms, the grandchildren of the founder have spent a large part of their inheritance on personal consumption.
options.D: Some long-lived family firms are run by family members who were chosen only after competing openly with outside candidates for the post.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Firms whose shares passed to a single heir in each generation declined as often as firms whose shares were spread among many relatives.

option_rationales.B: This supports the author, who lists written rules for share sales among the features of firms that last in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 already concedes that 'some fortunes really are spent rather than lost', so this is consistent with the author's qualified position.
option_rationales.D: This fits the author's argument, since an open contest widens the field of candidates, which paragraph 3 says improves the choice of leader.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 blames decline partly on the dispersal of ownership among many relatives. If firms with ownership concentrated in one heir declined at the same rate, dispersal could not be doing the causal work the author assigns it, which weakens the structural explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a fact about spendthrift heirs as a weakener without noticing that the author has already conceded it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option matches the folk view but is absorbed by the author's concession; the correct answer attacks a causal claim directly.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the incumbent's 'careful attention to its best customers' contributed to its decline because

options.A: those customers demanded lower prices, which reduced the incumbent's margins until it could no longer compete with the newcomer.
options.B: the incumbent spent so heavily on serving them that it had no money left over with which to improve its existing products.
options.C: those customers judged the new technology by standards it did not yet meet, so their advice steered investment away from it.
options.D: those customers were secretly switching to the new technology while telling the incumbent that they had no interest in it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) those customers judged the new technology by standards it did not yet meet, so their advice steered investment away from it.

option_rationales.A: Thin margins in paragraph 2 belong to the new technology's market, not to sales to the incumbent's best customers, whose demands are never said to be for lower prices.
option_rationales.B: Nothing suggests the existing products went unimproved; the problem is that money went 'where its profits are' rather than into the new technology.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 implies the best customers genuinely did not want the new thing at first; it was other buyers, 'never well served', who took it up.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the new technology is at first 'worse ... by the measures that the incumbent's best customers care about', so when asked, 'they say no'. Following this advice, the firm invests elsewhere, and by the time the technology is good enough for the mainstream the incumbent has nothing to offer.
questions.common_misconception: Inventing a hidden motive or a price story instead of following the mechanism the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the customers' standards in paragraph 2 to the outcome at its end.

questions.question: In the argument of the passage, paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: introduce a new example of an incumbent that survived a shift in technology by setting up a separate unit.
options.B: concede that the complacency explanation offered in paragraph 1 is correct in most of the cases that matter.
options.C: argue that incumbents should invest in every cheap technology because any one of them might eventually displace the existing product.
options.D: raise an objection to the account and turn it into further support for the author's conclusion.

questions.correct_answer: (D) raise an objection to the account and turn it into further support for the author's conclusion.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 contains no example of a surviving firm; separate units are discussed in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 concedes that the account involves hindsight, not that complacency explains most cases; the author continues to reject complacency.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says an incumbent that chased all such technologies 'would have squandered its resources', which is the opposite of this advice.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'It may be objected', states the hindsight objection, calls it 'fair', and then says 'it strengthens rather than weakens the point', because if good managers cannot foresee which markets will matter, vigilance cannot be the remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the content of the objection with the author's own recommendation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph's signposts ('It may be objected', 'strengthens rather than weakens') reveal its function.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a reason the incumbent passes over the new technology EXCEPT that

options.A: its engineers lack the technical skills needed to work with the newer and simpler design.
options.B: the market for the new technology is too small to matter to a company of its scale.
options.C: its existing customers, when asked about the new technology, say that they do not want it.
options.D: the profit margins it could earn from selling the new technology look thin when examined.

questions.correct_answer: (A) its engineers lack the technical skills needed to work with the newer and simpler design.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the market is 'too small to move a company of its scale', so this too is given as a reason.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'The incumbent asks its customers whether they want the new thing, and they say no', so this is a stated reason.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'It examines the margins, and they are thin', so this is one of the reasons given.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists three correct judgements: customers say no, margins are thin, the market is too small. A lack of technical skill is never mentioned; indeed the passage insists managers were capable and 'doing, carefully and well, exactly what they had been trained to do'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming incompetence of some kind, which the passage explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three reasons are listed close together; the excluded one must be checked against the author's denial of incompetence.

questions.question: The author's recommendation in paragraph 4 depends most on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: A separate unit can reliably predict which of the many cheap new technologies will eventually improve enough to serve the mainstream market of the parent.
options.B: A large firm's criteria for funding projects reflect its size and costs, so a smaller unit with its own measures can value what the parent dismisses.
options.C: Parent companies usually leave their separate units free of interference, supply them generously with funds and allow them to set their own prices.
options.D: Managers placed in charge of a separate unit are generally more alert to emerging technologies and to new customers than the managers of the parent company.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A large firm's criteria for funding projects reflect its size and costs, so a smaller unit with its own measures can value what the parent dismisses.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says good managers 'cannot tell in advance' which small markets will matter, and the remedy is offered precisely because such prediction is not possible.
option_rationales.C: The author concedes that separate units 'can be starved or smothered by the parent' and calls the remedy 'no guarantee', so the argument does not assume this.
option_rationales.D: The author denies that the problem is one of alertness ('not a failure to look'), so the remedy cannot rest on the unit's managers being more vigilant.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the separate unit has 'its own costs and its own measures of success, small enough that a small market can still excite it', and that it escapes 'the scrutiny of the rules' that would have rejected it. This works only if the rejection stems from criteria tied to the parent's size and costs, rather than from the technology itself or from managers' alertness.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the alertness option, which restates the complacency view the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is a natural assumption for a remedy of this kind, but each is contradicted by an earlier paragraph; the correct answer requires seeing that the argument is about rules, not people.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: showing that the effect of chief executives on results is commonly overstated, and that the overstatement is costly.
options.B: explaining why business journalists prefer stories about individual leaders to accounts of markets and industries.
options.C: proving that chief executives have no measurable effect on the performance of the companies they are appointed to run.
options.D: recommending that company boards stop appointing outsiders as chief executives and promote only from within.

questions.correct_answer: (A) showing that the effect of chief executives on results is commonly overstated, and that the overstatement is costly.

option_rationales.B: The journalists' preference is explained only briefly in paragraph 1 as the starting point; the passage goes on to argue about leaders' real influence and its consequences.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this means that leaders are irrelevant' and names situations in which they 'can matter a great deal', so this overstates the author's claim.
option_rationales.D: The passage criticises boards that hunt for saviours but makes no rule about internal promotion; it suggests only spending 'less on heroes'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 identifies 'a systematic error about how much any one leader actually controls', paragraphs 2 and 3 show how other forces drive results, and paragraph 4 says the error 'lies in degree, not in kind' and describes its costs to boards.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the claim of exaggeration for a claim that leaders do not matter at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis and the concession are both stated openly.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement 'The error lies in degree, not in kind' means that the mistake consists in

options.A: blaming leaders for small declines in results while crediting them for large recoveries.
options.B: misjudging the kinds of decision that leaders make, rather than how often they make them.
options.C: attributing a firm's results to the wrong kind of leader, rather than to the right one.
options.D: exaggerating how much leaders matter, rather than in believing that they matter at all.

questions.correct_answer: (D) exaggerating how much leaders matter, rather than in believing that they matter at all.

option_rationales.A: The passage says leaders are both credited and blamed for movements they did not cause, with no contrast between small and large changes.
option_rationales.B: Frequency of decisions is not discussed; the sentence follows a concession that leaders can matter and limits the error to its size.
option_rationales.C: The passage never distinguishes right and wrong kinds of leader; 'kind' here refers to whether leaders matter, not to types of leader.

questions.explanation: The sentence comes right after the concession that leaders 'can matter a great deal' in some situations. The author thus accepts that leaders have influence (the 'kind' is right) and objects only to how much influence is assumed (the 'degree').
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'kind' as types of leaders or decisions instead of as the question whether leaders matter at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The surrounding sentences fix the meaning.

questions.question: The remark that 'the second firm has no story to tell' (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: unremarkable managers who have run a firm for many years usually achieve better results than celebrated leaders brought in from outside.
options.B: the comparisons that would reveal how much success owes to circumstances are seldom made, because unremarkable success draws little attention.
options.C: the second firm actually performed worse than the first, which is why its results were not reported in the business press.
options.D: journalists deliberately ignore firms with ordinary managers in order to protect the reputations of the celebrated leaders they admire.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the comparisons that would reveal how much success owes to circumstances are seldom made, because unremarkable success draws little attention.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no such comparison of performance; its hypothetical firms both prosper, and it draws no general conclusion about which type does better.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'Both firms prosper', so there is no suggestion that the second firm did worse.
option_rationales.D: Nothing suggests deliberate suppression; the passage explains the neglect by the absence of a dramatic narrative, not by any motive to protect anyone.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that the celebrated leader's firm will be credited for 'what was largely a rising market carrying both firms upward', and that such comparisons 'are rarely made' because the second firm 'has no story to tell'. The implication is that the evidence needed to correct the error is missing because steady, undramatic success is not reported.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that the second firm must have done worse, or that the neglect is intentional.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the remark as an explanation of why the error persists, not as a fact about the second firm.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most similar to the error the passage describes?

options.A: A scientist who makes an important discovery insists on sharing the credit with the laboratory team that performed the experiments.
options.B: A company promotes an employee who has outperformed colleagues doing the same work in the same conditions over many years.
options.C: A new head teacher is praised for rising examination results that stem from teaching reforms her predecessor introduced years earlier.
options.D: A town council blames unusually heavy rainfall for floods that were in fact caused by its own failure to clear the drains.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A new head teacher is praised for rising examination results that stem from teaching reforms her predecessor introduced years earlier.

option_rationales.A: Sharing credit accurately is not an error of attribution; if anything it avoids the error the passage describes.
option_rationales.B: Here credit follows a fair comparison under similar conditions, which is exactly what paragraph 3 says is usually missing; there is no misattribution.
option_rationales.D: This blames circumstances for what a person caused, the reverse of the passage's error, which credits or blames people for what circumstances caused.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 notes that many products a firm sells 'were conceived years earlier, under managers who have since left', yet results are credited to the current leader. The head teacher praised for her predecessor's reforms is a direct parallel: an individual is credited with an outcome produced by earlier decisions.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the flooding case because it also involves wrong attribution, without noticing that its direction is reversed.
questions.difficulty_reason: The flooding option shares the structure of misattribution, and its direction must be checked against the passage.

questions.question: According to the passage, defenders of forced ranking argue that it corrects which tendency?

options.A: Managers, out of kindness or to avoid awkward conversations, rate nearly everyone above average, so the ratings convey nothing.
options.B: Teams tend to hide the weak performance of individual members by presenting all of their results as joint work.
options.C: Managers rate their own friends more generously than other staff, so that ratings come to reflect loyalty rather than performance.
options.D: Employees overestimate their own performance and resent any rating below outstanding, which makes appraisals difficult to hold.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Managers, out of kindness or to avoid awkward conversations, rate nearly everyone above average, so the ratings convey nothing.

option_rationales.B: Joint work is raised in paragraph 2 as part of the author's objection, not as a problem that defenders of the system say it solves.
option_rationales.C: Favouritism towards friends is not mentioned; paragraph 1 describes generous rating of almost everyone, not of particular people.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 is about managers' ratings of staff, not employees' views of themselves, though awkward conversations are mentioned as a motive for managers.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the defenders' case: 'Left to themselves, managers tend to rate almost everyone above average, partly out of kindness and partly to avoid difficult conversations, and a scale on which everyone scores highly conveys no information at all.'
questions.common_misconception: Attributing to the defenders a point the author makes against them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in a single sentence.

questions.question: The passage implies that, under a permanent system of forced ranking, a team made up entirely of strong performers would most likely

options.A: become more cooperative than other teams, because its members would know that each of them was equally capable.
options.B: be recognised as exceptional and therefore exempted by senior managers from the requirement to rank its members.
options.C: find it harder to keep and attract able people, since some of its good members must still be rated poorly.
options.D: improve further, because competition among able colleagues for the top ratings would push each of them to work harder.

questions.correct_answer: (C) find it harder to keep and attract able people, since some of its good members must still be rated poorly.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 argues that ranking makes 'helping a colleague' a cost, which points away from greater cooperation, not towards it.
option_rationales.B: No exemption is mentioned; the passage's point is that the system forces a distribution even on a small team 'assembled precisely because all its members are good'.
option_rationales.D: The passage presents ranking among excellent colleagues as manufacturing distinctions 'the work itself does not support', not as a spur to better work.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says forcing a distribution on a team of good people 'manufactures distinctions', and paragraph 3 says able people 'learn to avoid strong teams, since a good performer is safer among weaker colleagues'. Together these imply that a strong team would lose or fail to attract able members.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a general belief about competition that the passage does not endorse.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining a point from paragraph 2 with its consequence in paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that forced ranking discourages cooperation?

options.A: Teams that shared ideas freely produced better results than teams that did not, whether or not their firms used forced ranking.
options.B: Where forced ranking is used, the rank of each employee depends chiefly on colleagues' accounts of how much that person helped them.
options.C: Managers in firms that use forced ranking report that appraisal meetings have become more uncomfortable than they were before.
options.D: Employees who left their firms after receiving a poor rating under forced ranking usually found comparable jobs within a few months.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Where forced ranking is used, the rank of each employee depends chiefly on colleagues' accounts of how much that person helped them.

option_rationales.A: This shows that cooperation is valuable, which the author would accept; it says nothing about whether ranking makes people less willing to cooperate.
option_rationales.C: Discomfort in appraisal meetings concerns managers' experience of the system, not employees' incentives to cooperate with colleagues.
option_rationales.D: What happens to departing employees has no bearing on whether those who remain are discouraged from helping one another.

questions.explanation: The author's claim in paragraph 3 rests on the premise that 'If my rating depends on being ranked above my colleagues, then helping a colleague is a cost to me'. If ranks were determined mainly by how much one helped others, helping would raise one's rank, and the mechanism the author describes would run the other way.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about the value of shared ideas, which is on topic and favourable to cooperation but does not touch the incentive the author describes.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option concerns cooperation's benefits rather than the incentive to cooperate; the correct answer requires locating the premise of the claim.

questions.question: The way the author treats the case made by defenders of forced ranking in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: ironic, suggesting that the defenders do not really believe the argument they put forward and have other motives for it.
options.B: dismissive, presenting the case only in order to show that it rests on a misunderstanding of what ratings are for.
options.C: approving, since the author ends by agreeing that managers should be obliged to say what they already know about their staff.
options.D: fair-minded, presenting the case as reasonable before examining what it takes for granted.

questions.correct_answer: (D) fair-minded, presenting the case as reasonable before examining what it takes for granted.

option_rationales.A: No hidden motives are attributed to defenders; the author engages with their argument on its merits in paragraphs 2 and 3.
option_rationales.B: The author calls it 'a reasonable case' and, in paragraph 4, accepts that a single round of ranking may expose real problems; the case is not dismissed.
option_rationales.C: The author ends by warning against a 'permanent regime' of ranking, so the defenders' conclusion is not adopted.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'Its defenders make a reasonable case' and sets it out without mockery; paragraph 2 begins 'The difficulty is that the system assumes far more than it appears to', moving to examine its assumptions. The treatment is fair before it is critical.
questions.common_misconception: Inferring from the author's overall criticism that the opposing case must have been dismissed.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's overall stance is critical, which tempts a choice of 'dismissive'; the question concerns the treatment of the case itself.

questions.question: The example of the chemical plant in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: demonstrate that the safety limits written into plant manuals are usually set lower than they need to be.
options.B: show that engineers at hazardous plants often disregard written procedures because they care more about cost than about safety.
options.C: provide an instance of the kind of individual culprit whom inquiries into disasters rightly hold responsible.
options.D: illustrate how a working standard can shift through decisions that are each sensible, without anyone choosing to change it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate how a working standard can shift through decisions that are each sensible, without anyone choosing to change it.

option_rationales.A: Whether the written limit was too low is never assessed; the point is that the working limit moved without a decision, whatever its merits.
option_rationales.B: The engineers judge 'correctly as it turns out' that the vessel is safe; the example concerns reasonable decisions, not carelessness or indifference to safety.
option_rationales.C: The example is offered against the culprit-finding approach of paragraph 1; its lesson is that 'No one decided to change it'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 claims that organisations 'walk towards' catastrophe 'by steps that each seemed reasonable at the time'. The plant illustrates exactly this: each night's decision is defensible, yet 'the limit has quietly moved' and 'No one decided to change it'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a story of negligence, which is the very interpretation the passage opposes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the example back to the claim in paragraph 1 rather than reading it on its own.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the outsider's question in paragraph 3 'sounds naive' to those inside the plant because

options.A: the outsider lacks the technical training needed to understand how the pressure vessel actually works.
options.B: running above the limit has become so habitual that insiders no longer perceive it as a departure from the rules.
options.C: insiders know that the plant has been running above its limit only for a few nights and see no cause for alarm.
options.D: the written limit in the manual has been officially revised and the outsider has consulted an old copy.

questions.correct_answer: (B) running above the limit has become so habitual that insiders no longer perceive it as a departure from the rules.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about the outsider's expertise; the question sounds naive because of what insiders have grown used to.
option_rationales.C: The phrase 'everyone inside knows that it always has' indicates a long-standing habit, not a brief episode of a few nights.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'the written figure still stands in the manual'; no official revision has taken place.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 ends: the question 'sounds naive, because everyone inside knows that it always has'. Repeated deviation has become normal practice, so a question about it appears to show ignorance rather than insight.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that the outsider must be ignorant, rather than that the insiders have adjusted their sense of normal.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in the same sentence.

questions.question: In the final sentence of the passage, the phrase 'drift answers to no one' most nearly means that

options.A: a gradual change in practice cannot be reversed once it has continued for long enough within an organisation.
options.B: informal departures from procedure are never reported to the senior managers who are formally in charge.
options.C: a change that accumulates without ever being decided leaves no one accountable for having made it.
options.D: staff who allow standards to slip usually refuse to explain their actions when an inquiry questions them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a change that accumulates without ever being decided leaves no one accountable for having made it.

option_rationales.A: Irreversibility is not the point; the contrast with 'a decision' that is 'argued over and formally adopted' concerns responsibility, not permanence.
option_rationales.B: The phrase is about the absence of any decision-maker, not about a failure to report; nothing in the passage concerns reporting lines.
option_rationales.D: No refusal to explain is described; the passage implies that no single person made the change, so there is nothing for anyone to answer for.

questions.explanation: The final sentence contrasts a departure that is 'noticed, argued over and formally adopted', which 'is a decision', with one that 'simply accumulates'. A decision has an author who can be held to it; drift, having no decider, has no one who answers for it. This echoes paragraph 2: 'No one decided to change it.'
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'answers to no one' as defiance by individuals rather than as the absence of anyone responsible.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative phrase must be interpreted through the contrast in the same sentence and an earlier echo.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The deviations most likely to end in disaster are those large enough to attract attention at the moment they are made.
options.B: The fact that a risky choice caused no harm is not, by itself, good evidence that the risk was small.
options.C: Some departures from written procedures improve the way an organisation works and are worth keeping.
options.D: An inquiry that names a person at fault may be accurate about the facts and still mistaken about the cause.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The deviations most likely to end in disaster are those large enough to attract attention at the moment they are made.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls mistaken the inference 'that a risk which has not yet produced harm has thereby been shown to be small', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'much good practice begins as a sensible exception', so the author would agree.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says such findings 'are rarely false, but they are often beside the point', so the author would agree.

questions.explanation: The author locates the danger in deviations that pass unnoticed: in paragraph 2 the excess is 'small' and the limit moves 'quietly', and paragraph 4 says the danger lies in 'deviation that is never recognised as such'. The statement that ties danger to conspicuous deviations reverses this, so it is the one the author would reject.
questions.common_misconception: Rejecting the statement about beneficial departures because the passage is about disasters, missing the concession in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every true statement is paraphrased from a different paragraph and must be verified; the false one sounds like common sense and is refuted only by the passage's central mechanism.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Organisations should always keep as much spare capacity as they can afford, because neither shocks nor useful experiments can be predicted in advance.
options.B: The savings claimed by efficiency programmes are largely illusory, because the costs they remove reappear later in other parts of the organisation.
options.C: Most of the slack found in large organisations shelters inefficiency and protects the privileges of the departments that hold it.
options.D: Much spare capacity serves real if irregular purposes, so slack should be held deliberately and judged by its use rather than cut wholesale as waste.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Much spare capacity serves real if irregular purposes, so slack should be held deliberately and judged by its use rather than cut wholesale as waste.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says 'The aim is neither to maximise slack nor to abolish it', so a policy of keeping as much as possible contradicts the author.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says of these savings that 'the savings are real'; the author's objection is that the programmes miss what slack was doing, not that the savings are false.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'Some slack is indeed waste', not most, and this concession is a qualification of the thesis rather than the thesis itself.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 show two functions of slack (absorbing shocks, permitting unplanned experiments), paragraph 4 concedes that some slack is waste and says the usual question is 'badly posed', and paragraph 5 concludes that slack should be held 'deliberately' and judged by 'what the slack is for'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that defends slack most strongly, which overshoots the author's balanced conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: One option overstates the defence of slack and another overstates the concession; the correct answer holds both sides of the argument.

questions.question: According to the passage, a supply chain that holds no spare stock

options.A: works smoothly in most weeks but is overwhelmed whenever demand rises above its usual average.
options.B: recovers from the failure of a supplier more quickly, because it has less unsold inventory to clear.
options.C: is cheaper to run on ordinary days but stops altogether when a single supplier fails.
options.D: costs more to run than one with reserves, because it must place smaller orders far more often.

questions.correct_answer: (C) is cheaper to run on ordinary days but stops altogether when a single supplier fails.

option_rationales.A: This describes the hospital ward staffed to average occupancy, not the supply chain, and the chain's stated weakness is supplier failure, not a rise in demand.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says it 'halts entirely' when a supplier fails, because 'there is nothing between the failure and the factory floor'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the opposite about cost: such a chain 'is cheaper to run on every ordinary day'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A supply chain that holds no spare stock is cheaper to run on every ordinary day, and on the day a single supplier fails it halts entirely'.
questions.common_misconception: Transferring the hospital example's details to the supply chain.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence; one wrong option borrows from the adjacent example.

questions.question: The author's statement that the critics of slack 'are answering a question that is badly posed' implies that

options.A: the critics of slack are chiefly motivated by a wish to reduce the influence of departments that compete with their own within the firm.
options.B: slack cannot sensibly be assessed as a single amount, since reserves serving a purpose and reserves sheltering comfort call for opposite treatment.
options.C: the critics are mistaken in believing that any part of an organisation's spare resources could reasonably be described as waste.
options.D: the amount of slack in an organisation cannot be measured at all, so organisations should stop trying to keep account of their spare resources.

questions.correct_answer: (B) slack cannot sensibly be assessed as a single amount, since reserves serving a purpose and reserves sheltering comfort call for opposite treatment.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 attributes self-interest to some defenders of slack, not to its critics; no motive is ascribed to the critics at all.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'Some slack is indeed waste' and that the critics 'are therefore not simply wrong', so the author does not deny that some slack is waste.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 recommends reserves 'whose size is reviewed and whose use is reported', which presupposes measurement and accounting rather than abandoning them.

questions.explanation: The sentence that follows explains the phrase: asking 'how much slack an organisation has' treats 'a heterogeneous quantity as if it were uniform'. Paragraph 4 has just shown that slack may shelter 'invention' or 'comfort', and paragraph 5 proposes asking instead 'what the slack is for'. The fault in the question is that it lumps together reserves that should be kept and reserves that should be cut.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that says the critics are simply wrong, overlooking 'not simply wrong'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the concession in paragraph 4 with the reframing in paragraph 5; one wrong option transfers the defenders' motive to the critics.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim made in paragraph 3?

options.A: In several firms, the most profitable products began as projects staff pursued with time or money not assigned to any plan.
options.B: Engineers who are given unscheduled afternoons report that they enjoy their work more than colleagues whose time is fully allocated.
options.C: Most of the informal experiments that engineers carry out in their free time are abandoned within a few months without any result.
options.D: Firms that eliminated their spare inventory reported large savings in the first year, with no rise in costs in the years that followed.

questions.correct_answer: (A) In several firms, the most profitable products began as projects staff pursued with time or money not assigned to any plan.

option_rationales.B: Job satisfaction is not the claim; paragraph 3 argues that new products and methods originate in unclaimed time, which enjoyment does not establish.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 already grants that 'Most of these experiments come to nothing'; repeating this does not show that the valuable innovations come from such margins.
option_rationales.D: This concerns the savings discussed in paragraph 1 and, if anything, suggests slack was unneeded; it says nothing about experiments or innovation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that new products and methods 'often began in precisely the margins that a thorough efficiency drive would have closed'. Evidence that the most profitable products began as unplanned projects using unassigned time or money directly supports this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about failed experiments because it matches a sentence in paragraph 3, without noticing that it adds no support to the conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting option restates a premise the author concedes; the correct answer must be chosen for supporting the specific causal claim.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the author says that 'To judge slack by ordinary days is to judge an umbrella by the weather on days when it did not rain.' The comparison suggests that

options.A: efficiency audits should not consider the cost of reserves at all, since a reserve's cost has no bearing on whether it is kept.
options.B: the worth of a reserve held against rare events cannot be seen by looking only at periods in which no such event occurs.
options.C: the main value of slack lies in protecting against shocks rather than in leaving room for the experiments that produce change.
options.D: reserves are worth holding only by organisations whose operations face disruptions that are frequent and can be predicted in advance.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the worth of a reserve held against rare events cannot be seen by looking only at periods in which no such event occurs.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 accepts that the savings from removing slack 'are real', and paragraph 5 wants reserves reviewed and 'trimmed' when they outlive their purpose, so cost still counts.
option_rationales.C: The comparison concerns shocks only and ranks nothing; paragraph 3 calls the second circumstance, room for experiment, 'perhaps more important'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the reserve is held 'against an event whose timing could not be known', so the comparison concerns unpredictable events, not frequent and foreseeable ones.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the value of a margin held against an unpredictable shock 'appears only in the period that the efficiency audit treats as an exception'. An umbrella judged on dry days looks useless for the same reason: its use lies in the days that such a judgement leaves out.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the comparison as a ranking of the two functions of slack, or as a rejection of all attention to cost.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative sentence must be connected to the claim just before it about when the value of slack appears.

questions.question: According to the passage, the records of failed firms are seldom examined because

options.A: their former managers are unwilling to discuss their mistakes with authors who intend to publish the findings.
options.B: the practices of failed firms were so different from those of successful ones that comparison seemed pointless.
options.C: readers of business books are interested only in success and would not buy accounts of companies that failed.
options.D: such firms leave little documentation and attract neither researchers nor opportunities for interviews.

questions.correct_answer: (D) such firms leave little documentation and attract neither researchers nor opportunities for interviews.

option_rationales.A: Unwillingness is not mentioned; paragraph 2 says failed firms 'give no interviews' because they no longer exist to give them, not because managers refuse.
option_rationales.B: The passage suggests the opposite: failed firms may have shared the very practices of the winners, which is why ignoring them matters.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 explains why the books sell, but paragraph 2 gives the reason failures are not studied as a matter of access to evidence, not readers' tastes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The graveyard of failed firms is not consulted because it cannot easily be visited: failed companies leave few records, attract no researchers and give no interviews.'
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible human motive instead of the reason the passage states.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in one sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It withdraws the objection made in paragraph 2, conceding that comparison with less successful firms fully solves the problem of selection.
options.B: It introduces the author's own preferred method of studying business success, which replaces the study of winners with the study of failures.
options.C: It grants that a proposed remedy improves the method, then shows that it leaves one objection standing and fails to address another.
options.D: It offers evidence that the companies praised in such books were in fact poorly run, which their later difficulties made clear.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It grants that a proposed remedy improves the method, then shows that it leaves one objection standing and fails to address another.

option_rationales.A: The author calls the comparison 'a real improvement' but does not withdraw anything; the paragraph's purpose is to show what the remedy does not fix.
option_rationales.B: The matched comparison is the defenders' answer, not the author's method, and it adds less successful firms rather than replacing the winners.
option_rationales.D: The author does not claim the companies were poorly run; the point about their later stumbles concerns how such failures are explained, not how the firms were managed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the defenders' answer (matched comparison), acknowledges it as 'a real improvement', then says it 'does not remove the second difficulty' and does not 'settle a third', the unfalsifiable explanation of later decline.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the acknowledgement as a full retreat, or treating the defenders' remedy as the author's proposal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires tracking which view in the paragraph belongs to whom.

questions.question: In saying that the explanation for the later stumbles 'can be given whatever happens', the author implies that

options.A: the explanation cannot be tested, because the abandonment of the principles is inferred from the very failure it is meant to explain.
options.B: the companies in fact kept the principles that had made them great, so the explanation offered for their decline is simply false.
options.C: matched comparisons with less successful firms would confirm that the companies that stumbled had abandoned their founding principles.
options.D: the principles identified by such books were sound but were applied by the companies in markets for which they were unsuitable.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the explanation cannot be tested, because the abandonment of the principles is inferred from the very failure it is meant to explain.

option_rationales.B: The author does not say the explanation is false; the objection is that it is immune to refutation, which is different from being shown to be wrong.
option_rationales.C: No such confirmation is suggested; the passage says matched comparison does not 'settle' this third difficulty at all.
option_rationales.D: The passage never suggests that the principles were misapplied in the wrong markets; this introduces an explanation of its own.

questions.explanation: The final sentences of paragraph 4 describe a theory that explains success by 'the presence of certain practices, and ... failure by their supposed absence'. The word 'supposed' shows that the absence is assumed after the failure, so no outcome could count against the theory: it 'has arranged never to be wrong'.
questions.common_misconception: Equating an explanation that cannot be refuted with one that is false.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option is close in spirit; separating unfalsifiable from false is a fine logical distinction.

questions.question: Each of the following is a criticism that the passage makes of the method described in paragraph 1 EXCEPT that

options.A: its account of why admired firms later decline is framed so that no outcome could count against it.
options.B: it cannot tell whether the practices it praises were also common among firms that failed.
options.C: it rests on too few companies for any of its conclusions to reach statistical significance.
options.D: its descriptions of a firm's practices may be coloured by what observers already know of its results.

questions.correct_answer: (C) it rests on too few companies for any of its conclusions to reach statistical significance.

option_rationales.A: This is the third difficulty in paragraph 4: such a theory 'has arranged never to be wrong'.
option_rationales.B: This is the selection objection of paragraph 2: the method 'has no way of knowing how many companies followed the same practices and failed'.
option_rationales.D: This is the objection of paragraph 3: traits are 'described after the fact, by people who already know the result'.

questions.explanation: The passage raises three criticisms: selection of winners only (paragraph 2), descriptions shaped by known outcomes (paragraph 3) and an unfalsifiable account of decline (paragraph 4). The number of companies studied is never criticised; the selection objection concerns which firms are studied, not how many.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the selection problem with a problem of sample size, since both sound like statistical objections.
questions.difficulty_reason: The excluded criticism resembles the selection objection; each of the three real criticisms is paraphrased and must be matched to a different paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following studies would avoid the first difficulty described in the passage while remaining open to the second?

options.A: A study of the ten most profitable firms in an industry, rating each firm's culture from staff surveys conducted years before its results were known.
options.B: A study of the firms that survived longest in an industry, rating each firm's culture from interviews with managers held after the firm had become well known.
options.C: A study of every firm founded in one industry in a given decade, rating each firm's culture from staff surveys conducted every year from its founding.
options.D: A study of every firm founded in one industry in a given decade, survivors and failures alike, rating cultures from interviews held after each fate was known.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A study of every firm founded in one industry in a given decade, survivors and failures alike, rating cultures from interviews held after each fate was known.

option_rationales.A: Studying only the most profitable firms keeps the selection problem of paragraph 2, while surveys taken before results avoid the second difficulty; this is the reverse pattern.
option_rationales.B: Studying only survivors falls into the first difficulty, so this study does not avoid it, although it is also open to the second.
option_rationales.C: Including all firms avoids the first difficulty, and surveys made before outcomes were known avoid the second as well, so this study is not open to the second.

questions.explanation: The first difficulty (paragraph 2) is studying only winners; including failures avoids it. The second (paragraph 3) is that traits are 'described after the fact, by people who already know the result'. Only the correct answer includes all firms while still relying on descriptions made after outcomes were known.
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up which difficulty concerns the choice of firms and which concerns the timing of descriptions.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each option combines two features; the solver must apply both objections separately to four designs.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that schemes such as early retirement and caps on weekly hours fail because firms refuse to hire young workers.
options.B: reject the idea that work is a fixed quantity while granting that technological change still harms particular workers.
options.C: defend the fears of displaced workers as a sound reason for slowing the spread of new technology across an economy.
options.D: show that labour-saving machines create more jobs than they destroy within the very trades into which they are introduced.

questions.correct_answer: (B) reject the idea that work is a fixed quantity while granting that technological change still harms particular workers.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 is one application of the argument, and it does not say firms refuse to hire; it says a firm 'may simply produce less'. The option is too narrow and distorts the reason.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 calls the anxiety understandable but never recommends slowing technology; it asks that policy be judged by what it does for those harmed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the new jobs 'are rarely the jobs that were lost' and appear in other places and trades, so the claim about the same trades contradicts the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 names the fallacy, paragraph 2 shows why the quantity of work is not fixed, paragraph 3 applies this to work-sharing schemes, and paragraph 4 concedes that change can 'ruin particular lives and places'. The purpose is to correct the fixed-work belief while keeping the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the application in paragraph 3, or turning the concession into a call to resist technology.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure is clearly signalled; the wrong options are a narrow detail, a distortion and an overreach.

questions.question: According to the passage, job losses are more visible than job gains because

options.A: losses tend to arrive as single identifiable events, while gains are spread thinly over many trades and places.
options.B: newspapers prefer stories about closures and deliberately ignore the slower growth of new industries elsewhere.
options.C: the new jobs usually pay less than the old ones, so workers who take them rarely describe them as gains.
options.D: the new jobs appear only a generation later, by which time the closures they replaced have been forgotten.

questions.correct_answer: (A) losses tend to arrive as single identifiable events, while gains are spread thinly over many trades and places.

option_rationales.B: The passage attributes no motive to the press; paragraph 2 says the expansions are 'reported, if at all, as ordinary growth', which is about how they appear, not about deliberate neglect.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 never compares the pay of new and old jobs; the option adds a claim that the passage does not make.
option_rationales.D: The 'generation' in paragraph 4 is how long transitions can take for workers; paragraph 2 explains visibility by concentration versus dispersion, not by delay and forgetting.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A closed mill is a single event with an address; the thousand small expansions that follow are scattered across an economy'. Concentrated losses are noticed, dispersed gains are not.
questions.common_misconception: Borrowing the 'generation' from paragraph 4 and attaching it to the wrong claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following arguments rests on the same mistaken premise that the passage criticises?

options.A: A town should not assume that the jobs created by a new factory will go to the people whose old jobs it replaced.
options.B: A town should expect a cheaper bus service to draw extra riders, some of whom will spend their savings in local shops.
options.C: A town should plan for retraining to take years, because laid-off workers rarely have the skills that new employers want.
options.D: A town should refuse a permit for a second cinema, since its filmgoers would merely be split between two halls and no new jobs could result.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A town should refuse a permit for a second cinema, since its filmgoers would merely be split between two halls and no new jobs could result.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says new jobs 'are rarely the jobs that were lost', so this is consistent with the passage rather than an example of the fallacy.
option_rationales.B: This is the reasoning the passage endorses in paragraph 2: a lower price raises demand and frees money for other spending.
option_rationales.C: This matches the concession in paragraph 4 that transitions are slow and costly; it involves no assumption of a fixed amount of work.

questions.explanation: The fallacy, defined in paragraph 1, assumes a set amount to be shared out, so that any addition simply takes from someone else. The cinema argument assumes a fixed number of filmgoers to be divided, ignoring that a second hall might increase total attendance, just as cheaper cloth increased the number of shirts bought.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that mentions job losses or slow transitions, which sounds pessimistic but does not assume a fixed total.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires abstracting the structure of the fallacy and recognising it in an unfamiliar setting.

questions.question: The author refers to 'a fifty-year-old weaver whose skills no longer have a buyer' most likely in order to suggest that

options.A: technological change reduces the total amount of work available in an economy once a transition is complete.
options.B: caps on weekly hours would protect older workers better than schemes that push them into early retirement.
options.C: an argument about the total amount of work can be correct and still say nothing to the people who lose out.
options.D: the lump of labour premise turns out to be correct whenever older workers are the ones who are displaced.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an argument about the total amount of work can be correct and still say nothing to the people who lose out.

option_rationales.A: The same paragraph says 'technology does not abolish work in aggregate', so this reverses the author's view.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 criticises both schemes as resting on the same error; the passage never prefers one to the other.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the argument about totals is 'correct'; the weaver shows its limits, not that the premise is right for some age group.

questions.explanation: The weaver appears in the sentence saying the fallacy 'concerns the total amount of work, not its distribution' and that a correct argument about totals 'is cold comfort' to him. He shows the gap between aggregate truth and individual loss.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the concession as a retraction of the main argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The surrounding sentence states the point the example makes.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'the employment bundle' refers to

options.A: the group of workers who share one employer and a fixed schedule, as clerks in an office traditionally did.
options.B: the set of protections and obligations that come together with the legal status of being an employee.
options.C: the package of fares, routes and passengers that a platform assigns to each driver who logs into its app.
options.D: the combined earnings that a single worker collects from the several apps for which she drives in a week.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the set of protections and obligations that come together with the legal status of being an employee.

option_rationales.A: The bundle is a set of terms 'designed around a fixed schedule and a single employer', not the workers themselves.
option_rationales.C: Fares and passengers belong to paragraph 1's description of platform control; the bundle is what employment law attaches to a status.
option_rationales.D: The phrase names what would be 'imposed' on platform work, such as 'fixed shifts, minimum hours', not a worker's income from several apps.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says an employee accepts direction 'in exchange for a wage and a bundle of protections', and paragraph 2 lists 'fixed shifts, minimum hours and the rest of the employment bundle'. The phrase means the package of terms that comes with employee status.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'bundle' literally as a collection of earnings or jobs.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is defined by its first use in paragraph 1.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the two dominant responses described in paragraph 2 as

options.A: each accurate about a feature of platform work that the other response neglects.
options.B: unequal in merit, the case for treating platform workers as employees being clearly the stronger one.
options.C: irreconcilable, since the platform's control over work and the worker's flexibility cannot both be protected.
options.D: equally mistaken, since neither gives an accurate description of the way platform work is organised.

questions.correct_answer: (A) each accurate about a feature of platform work that the other response neglects.

option_rationales.B: The author credits each side with one truth and ranks neither; nothing in the passage favours the first response.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 argues that some protections 'depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible', which is a way of reconciling the two concerns.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'Each side is right about what the other ignores', so calling both simply mistaken overstates the author's criticism.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that 'Each side is right about what the other ignores': the first sees the platform's control, the second sees that the employment bundle fits flexible work badly. Paragraph 3 then identifies their shared mistake, which shows the author thinks each is partly right.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the shared mistake identified in paragraph 3 as a verdict that both responses are wholly wrong.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option uses the author's later criticism; the correct answer requires reading paragraphs 2 and 3 together.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that some protections 'depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible'?

options.A: Paid holidays calculated over a working year proved very hard to arrange for drivers who worked for three different apps.
options.B: A minimum rate for time worked could be enforced only if platforms fixed in advance the hours a worker counts as available, ending free log-ins.
options.C: Firms that were offered a menu of separable protections lobbied, in several places, for the cheapest selection on the menu.
options.D: Many platform workers say they would prefer employee status if it could be combined with the freedom to choose their own hours.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A minimum rate for time worked could be enforced only if platforms fixed in advance the hours a worker counts as available, ending free log-ins.

option_rationales.A: The author already grants in paragraph 3 that such holidays 'are harder to translate'; the claim under test concerns the other protections.
option_rationales.C: This bears on the danger noted in paragraph 4, not on whether the named protections can coexist with a flexible schedule.
option_rationales.D: This concerns workers' wishes, not whether the protections are compatible with flexibility, so it leaves the claim untouched.

questions.explanation: The claim is that protections such as a minimum rate for time actually worked are compatible with flexible scheduling. If enforcing that rate required fixing hours in advance, the protection would after all depend on ending flexibility, which directly undercuts the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the paid-holiday option because it shows a protection is hard to provide, missing that the author has already conceded that case.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are on topic and one restates a concession; the correct answer must target the precise claim.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage primarily serves to

options.A: report that firms have already moved many employees into a new category created to accommodate the platforms.
options.B: withdraw the proposal to unbundle protections and recommend a third legal category of worker in its place.
options.C: summarise the two dominant responses to platform work and show that the courts have already chosen between them.
options.D: acknowledge the risks of the author's proposal while explaining why it remains preferable to the binary.

questions.correct_answer: (D) acknowledge the risks of the author's proposal while explaining why it remains preferable to the binary.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph describes what 'could' happen and what firms are invited to do; it reports nothing that has occurred.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph warns that a third category 'could become a convenient place' to move employees; it does not recommend one or withdraw the proposal.
option_rationales.C: The responses are set out in paragraph 2, and nothing in the passage reports any decision by courts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'Unbundling has dangers of its own', names two, and then says the case for unbundling 'is therefore not that it is free of risk, but that the binary has already failed'. It concedes and then defends.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the warnings as a change of position or as reports of fact.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conceding and defending moves are signalled, but one wrong option turns a warning into a recommendation.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pay of the musicians must rise over time because

options.A: the cost of running concert halls has increased faster than the general level of prices.
options.B: audiences now expect a higher standard of performance than listeners did a century ago.
options.C: they would otherwise move to other occupations, where wages have risen along with productivity.
options.D: innovations have allowed musicians to perform the same quartet more quickly than before.

questions.correct_answer: (C) they would otherwise move to other occupations, where wages have risen along with productivity.

option_rationales.A: The passage denies that the halls have become 'inefficient' and gives no figures for their running costs.
option_rationales.B: Audience expectations are never mentioned; paragraph 1 says 'nothing about the quartet has changed'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: the quartet still needs four players and 'roughly forty minutes', and no innovation has shortened it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The musicians' pay must rise too, or they would drift into other work', following the statement that manufacturing wages have risen with productivity.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the musicians' productivity has changed.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in a single sentence.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the comparison of a class of sixty pupils with a class of thirty is used to

options.A: show that raising output per worker in such services can change the service rather than supply it more cheaply.
options.B: illustrate that productivity in teaching has grown about as fast as productivity in manufacturing.
options.C: suggest that many schools waste money by employing more teachers than their pupils actually need.
options.D: argue that schools ought to keep their classes small, however much it costs the public budget to do so.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that raising output per worker in such services can change the service rather than supply it more cheaply.

option_rationales.B: The point of the paragraph is that productivity in such sectors 'lags'; the comparison explains why it cannot simply be raised.
option_rationales.C: The comparison works against the suspicion of waste mentioned at the end of paragraph 2, so this reverses its purpose.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no recommendation about class size; the comparison illustrates why compressing time 'often' degrades the service.

questions.explanation: The sentence before says that 'attempts to compress that time often degrade what is delivered', and the class example shows it: the larger class is cheaper per pupil 'but it is not the same product at a lower price'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading an illustration of a mechanism as a policy recommendation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the example to the general claim that precedes it and to the paragraph's later point about waste.

questions.question: Suppose a public hospital's costs have risen much faster than prices in general for several decades. The author would most likely say that this fact

options.A: shows that society can no longer afford hospital care at its present relative price and must ration it.
options.B: fits the pattern of the cost disease but does not by itself show that none of the increase is waste.
options.C: must be explained by the cost disease, because health care consists largely of a person's time and attention.
options.D: shows that the hospital's administrative layers must have multiplied, since the cost disease cannot account for it.

questions.correct_answer: (B) fits the pattern of the cost disease but does not by itself show that none of the increase is waste.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 argues that a richer society can afford services 'even at their higher relative price'; the passage nowhere calls for rationing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 warns that the argument 'should not be stretched into a blanket excuse'; the cost disease is consistent with the rise but does not rule out waste.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says administrative growth 'can' occur, not that it must explain any rise; paragraph 2 says such sectors' costs rise under the cost disease.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 places nursing and similar work under the cost disease, so rising relative costs are expected. Paragraph 4 adds that 'some cost growth in services is unavoidable' does not mean 'all of it is', so the rise alone cannot rule out waste. The correct answer holds both points.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that says the cost disease must explain the rise, which keeps paragraph 2 but drops the limit in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each keep one half of the author's position; only the correct answer holds both halves.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a limit on the argument or on its consolation EXCEPT that

options.A: public budgets that depend on unpopular taxes may cut services well before the arithmetic of affordability requires it.
options.B: the higher relative price of care weighs most on people whose incomes have not shared in the general gain.
options.C: manufacturing productivity may one day stop growing, which would remove the cause of the cost disease.
options.D: rising relative costs in a service may partly reflect administrative growth that the cost disease does not excuse.

questions.correct_answer: (C) manufacturing productivity may one day stop growing, which would remove the cause of the cost disease.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says such budgets 'may cut services long before the arithmetic says they must', so this limit is stated.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the higher price 'falls hardest on those whose incomes have not shared in the general gain'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says administrative layers 'can multiply' and that 'the cost disease offers them no defence', so this limit is in the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 names three limits: unavoidable growth does not excuse administrative bloat, the price falls hardest on those left out of the gain, and tax-funded budgets may cut services early. The passage never considers manufacturing productivity ceasing to grow.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting a plausible economic idea because it involves the mechanism described in paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options paraphrase paragraph 4; the correct answer is plausible but absent.

questions.question: The passage is mainly concerned with

options.A: arguing that the common debate about remote work overlooks how it affects the way juniors learn their jobs.
options.B: showing that experienced professionals produce less at home than they did when they worked in the office.
options.C: explaining why video calls are a less efficient way to settle routine matters than face-to-face meetings.
options.D: arguing that firms should require junior staff to return to the office for most of their working week.

questions.correct_answer: (A) arguing that the common debate about remote work overlooks how it affects the way juniors learn their jobs.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says that for many experienced professionals the answer to the productivity question 'appears to be yes', so this reverses the passage.
option_rationales.C: Efficiency of calls for routine matters is not discussed; calls appear only to show that remote contact is planned.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 begins 'This is not an argument for ordering everyone back to their desks', so the prescription contradicts the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the usual question 'says little about how anyone becomes competent', paragraphs 2 and 3 show what juniors lose and why the loss is hidden, and paragraph 4 says firms must build learning 'on purpose'.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the author's concern into a call to end remote work.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated in paragraph 1 and the tempting prescription is explicitly denied.

questions.question: According to the passage, remote arrangements tend to remove the learning described in paragraph 2 because
