options.A: most accounting problems are too complicated to be explained clearly in an email or video call.
options.B: juniors at home tend to spend the hours they save on commuting on matters unrelated to work.
options.C: senior staff working from home are generally unwilling to answer questions from their juniors.
options.D: that learning relies on unplanned exposure, while contact in remote work is mostly scheduled.

questions.correct_answer: (D) that learning relies on unplanned exposure, while contact in remote work is mostly scheduled.

option_rationales.A: The passage says some questions feel 'too trivial', not too complicated, to put in an email; complexity is not the reason given.
option_rationales.B: Saved commuting hours are mentioned only as a gain for experienced staff in paragraph 1; nothing is said about how juniors use them.
option_rationales.C: Seniors' willingness is never discussed; paragraph 3 blames the planned nature of remote contact, not reluctance.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: such learning 'depends on unplanned exposure and remote work is organised around planned contact'.
questions.common_misconception: Inventing a motive for seniors or borrowing a detail from paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated directly in the first sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: The passage implies that the partners of the hypothetical firm in paragraph 2

options.A: had trained their juniors mainly through formal courses before the firm sent everyone home.
options.B: found that the firm's billable work fell sharply in the years that followed the first year at home.
options.C: judged the move by a measure that could not register what their newest recruits were losing.
options.D: knew that their juniors were learning less but decided that the loss did not matter to the firm.

questions.correct_answer: (C) judged the move by a measure that could not register what their newest recruits were losing.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'almost none of it is deliberately taught', which is the opposite of formal training.
option_rationales.B: The passage says only that billable work did not fall in the first year; it reports nothing about later output.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the loss is something 'they cannot see', so the partners are not described as knowing about it.

questions.explanation: The partners see 'no fall in billable work', while the passage says of what juniors miss that 'None of this appears in any measure of output'. Their yardstick could not show the loss.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'cannot see' as 'chose to ignore'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Follows from two nearby sentences in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the cost of remote work is 'real but delayed'?

options.A: Billable work at firms that sent everyone home rose slightly during the first year after the change was made.
options.B: Juniors placed among seniors who kept their office doors shut learned little more than juniors working at home.
options.C: Experienced accountants report that working from home has made them more satisfied with their jobs than before.
options.D: Staff who joined remote firms as recruits took longer, years afterwards, to be trusted with difficult client work than earlier cohorts had.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Staff who joined remote firms as recruits took longer, years afterwards, to be trusted with difficult client work than earlier cohorts had.

option_rationales.A: This fits the partners' first-year impression in paragraph 2 but says nothing about a cost appearing years later.
option_rationales.B: This supports the point in paragraph 4 that offices do not guarantee learning, not the claim that remote work imposes a delayed cost.
option_rationales.C: Satisfaction of experienced staff is irrelevant to whether juniors suffer a later cost; it concerns the group the author sets aside.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 predicts that the cost 'shows up years later, as a cohort of mid-career staff who are slower to exercise judgement'. Evidence that remote-era recruits were later slower to be trusted with hard work matches that prediction directly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the shut-doors option because it comes from the passage, without noticing it supports a different claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option supports a neighbouring claim, so the precise claim must be isolated.

questions.question: According to the passage, early researchers in artificial intelligence assumed that

options.A: perception and movement would be the hardest faculties to build, having taken longest to evolve.
options.B: the tasks people find easy would also be the easy ones for a machine to master.
options.C: a machine able to play respectable chess would still be far from being able to fold laundry.
options.D: the difficulty of any task could be measured by the amount of computation it requires.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the tasks people find easy would also be the easy ones for a machine to master.

option_rationales.A: The evolutionary account is the passage's own explanation in paragraph 2, and it implies the opposite of what the researchers assumed, since they judged by what 'people find easy'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says they assumed such a machine 'would soon be able to fold laundry', so this reverses their assumption; it is closer to what actually happened.
option_rationales.D: That measure is the passage's own suggestion in paragraph 2; the researchers instead equated difficulty with what 'people find hard'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'They took easy to mean what people find easy and hard to mean what people find hard'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the researchers' expectation with what actually happened.
questions.difficulty_reason: The assumption is stated in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the word 'cheap' in 'the cheap ones to mechanise' most nearly means

options.A: requiring relatively little effort or computation to reproduce in a machine.
options.B: quickly and easily acquired by human beings during childhood.
options.C: poorly paid when people perform them in the labour market.
options.D: of little real value to the people who happen to possess them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) requiring relatively little effort or computation to reproduce in a machine.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says explicit reasoning is 'effortful' for people; the word describes how easily machines reproduce a faculty, not how easily people learn it.
option_rationales.C: Pay enters only in paragraph 4, and there it concerns skills that are hard to mechanise; in paragraph 1 'cheap' describes the cost of mechanising.
option_rationales.D: The passage calls these faculties 'higher', so it does not treat them as worthless; the word concerns machines, not value to people.

questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts faculties that are 'cheap ones to mechanise' with those that are 'expensive'. Given the board-game and grasping examples, the contrast is between what is easy and what is hard to build into machines.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'cheap' as a remark about wages because the passage later discusses pay.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option borrows paragraph 4's topic; the sense must be fixed from the local contrast.

questions.question: On the reasoning of paragraph 3, which of the following jobs would be hardest for a machine to take over?

options.A: Restoring antique chairs, each built differently and damaged in its own way, for private collectors.
options.B: Checking insurance claims against a written list of the conditions under which payment is due.
options.C: Allocating hospital shifts to nurses according to a fixed set of rules about rest and seniority.
options.D: Computing the interest owed on thousands of loans using a formula set by the lending bank.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Restoring antique chairs, each built differently and damaged in its own way, for private collectors.

option_rationales.B: This follows 'rules that can be written down', like the reconciliation in paragraph 3, which the passage says a machine finds easier.
option_rationales.C: Allocation by a fixed set of rules is a written procedure, so on paragraph 3's reasoning it is easier to mechanise than physical work in varied settings.
option_rationales.D: A fixed formula is exactly the kind of explicit procedure the passage treats as easy to mechanise.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the cleaner is hard to replace because she works in rooms 'never arranged twice in the same way' and handles 'objects of every shape and texture'. Restoring varied, individually damaged chairs has the same features, while the other three jobs follow written rules.
questions.common_misconception: Judging by how skilled or prestigious a job seems rather than by whether it follows explicit rules.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the criterion of paragraph 3 to new cases; the wrong options all look skilled.

questions.question: Which of the following conclusions would the author most likely regard as NOT warranted by the argument of the passage?

options.A: Ranking jobs as basic or advanced by how hard they seem to people may mislead forecasts of automation.
options.B: The present line between what machines can and cannot do may move as learning methods improve.
options.C: Since care work resists automation, care workers can expect higher pay as machines take over clerical tasks.
options.D: Some clerical jobs may well be automated before cleaning jobs are, contrary to many familiar forecasts.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Since care work resists automation, care workers can expect higher pay as machines take over clerical tasks.

option_rationales.A: This is the point of paragraphs 2 and 3: our 'sense of difficulty' is not a good guide to what machines find hard.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the paradox 'describes a stage of technology' and that it 'would be rash to assume the boundary will stay where it is'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says a machine finds reconciling accounts 'far easier to take over' and that forecasts 'may therefore have the direction partly backwards', so the author accepts this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4's second caution says 'being hard to automate is not the same as being well rewarded', because abundant skills keep wages low 'whatever a robot can or cannot do'. Expecting care workers' pay to rise because their work resists machines is the inference the author rejects.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting this conclusion because it seems to follow from paragraph 3, without reading the caution in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are warranted conclusions drawn from different paragraphs; the correct answer requires holding paragraph 3 and the second caution together.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the textbook view of unions described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: studied neutrality, setting it beside the voice view without preferring one account to the other.
options.B: acceptance of it as an account of one real effect, joined to rejection of it as a full account.
options.C: outright dismissal of it as an ideological error with no basis in the way labour markets work.
options.D: broad agreement with it, together with a complaint that it understates the inefficiency unions cause.

questions.correct_answer: (B) acceptance of it as an account of one real effect, joined to rejection of it as a full account.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls judging unions by the wage premium alone 'a category error', which is a clear stance, not neutrality.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the cartel face is real and can be 'what remains', so the author does not dismiss the view as baseless.
option_rationales.D: The author argues that the view leaves out a possible gain from voice, not that it understates the losses.

questions.explanation: The author grants that unions have a cartel face that can predominate (paragraph 3) but calls measuring them only by the premium 'a category error' (paragraph 4). The view is accepted as partial and rejected as complete.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking strong criticism of the textbook's completeness for a denial that it describes anything real.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the concession in paragraph 3 with the criticism in paragraph 4.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in a firm whose management treats the grievance procedure as an adversary to be outmanoeuvred, the union is likely to

options.A: lead more workers to quit than would quit a comparable firm in which no union had been organised.
options.B: make the firm more productive than its non-union rivals, though by less than under cooperative managers.
options.C: stop bargaining over wages, since its energy is absorbed by disputes conducted through the grievance procedure.
options.D: impose a higher wage bill while yielding little of the information that might have offset it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) impose a higher wage bill while yielding little of the information that might have offset it.

option_rationales.A: The passage compares quitting with and without voice in paragraph 2 but never says an adversarial setting raises departures above the non-union level.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 attributes productivity gains to management that treats the procedure 'as an early warning'; in the adversarial case only 'the cartel face' remains.
option_rationales.C: Nothing suggests the union stops bargaining; the cartel face, which is the wage premium, is precisely 'what remains'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: where management treats the procedure as an adversary, 'voice tends to harden into obstruction, and the cartel face is what remains'. The cartel face is the wage premium of paragraph 1, and the offsetting benefit of voice in paragraph 2 is lost.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that some productivity gain from voice survives in every setting.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking 'the cartel face' in paragraph 3 back to the premium in paragraph 1 and the information gain in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most undermine the reasoning of paragraph 2?

options.A: Some managers in unionised firms regard the grievance procedure as a nuisance to be kept to a minimum.
options.B: In firms without unions, workers who complain about safety or supervision are no more likely than silent colleagues to be dismissed or passed over.
options.C: Unionised firms pay noticeably higher wages than otherwise similar firms in which there is no union.
options.D: Workers who leave a firm often take with them skills that their employer finds slow and costly to replace.

questions.correct_answer: (B) In firms without unions, workers who complain about safety or supervision are no more likely than silent colleagues to be dismissed or passed over.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 already allows that some managers treat the procedure as an adversary; this is consistent with the argument.
option_rationales.C: Both the cartel view and the voice view expect a wage premium, so this finding leaves paragraph 2 untouched.
option_rationales.D: This supports paragraph 2's claim that firms which hear complaints 'may lose fewer trained workers', so it strengthens rather than undermines.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 rests on the premise that, without a union, an individual who complains 'marks herself as troublesome', so leaving is 'often the only safe course'. If complainers suffered no penalty, individual voice would be safe and a union would not be needed to convert departures into information.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about wages or managers' attitudes, which concerns other paragraphs, instead of attacking the premise of paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer attacks an unstated link in the argument; one wrong option actually strengthens it.

questions.question: The sentence beginning 'None of this establishes that unions are good for firms' in the final paragraph serves to

options.A: confine the conclusion to a claim about how unions should be judged rather than a verdict on their worth.
options.B: concede that the textbook view of unions as cartels is, after all, a complete and accurate account of them.
options.C: introduce new evidence that unions, on balance, reduce the productivity of the firms in which they organise.
options.D: withdraw the earlier argument that collective voice can make a unionised firm more productive than its rivals.

questions.correct_answer: (A) confine the conclusion to a claim about how unions should be judged rather than a verdict on their worth.

option_rationales.B: The next sentence repeats that the question 'cannot be answered by looking at the price of labour alone', which rules out the textbook view as complete.
option_rationales.C: No evidence is introduced; the sentence limits what has been shown, and paragraph 3 says the evidence is 'mixed'.
option_rationales.D: The sentence says only that the argument has not shown unions to be good for firms; paragraph 3's claim that voice 'can' raise productivity still stands.

questions.explanation: After arguing that the wage premium is the wrong single measure, the author states that this does not show unions are good for firms, and that it shows 'only that the question cannot be answered by looking at the price of labour alone'. The sentence narrows the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a limiting statement as a reversal of the author's argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'None of this establishes' and the 'only' in the next sentence.

questions.question: The central claim of the passage is that working hours stopped falling mainly because

options.A: people came to value income above leisure once competition for status made relative position matter most.
options.B: governments stopped legislating shorter weeks after the middle of the century, leaving the matter to employers.
options.C: the structure of jobs, rather than workers' free choices, has decided how productivity gains are divided.
options.D: forecasts made early in the twentieth century relied on mistaken estimates of how quickly productivity would grow.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the structure of jobs, rather than workers' free choices, has decided how productivity gains are divided.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'related account' the author reports in paragraph 2 and then criticises for treating hours as freely chosen.
option_rationales.B: The passage never says governments stopped legislating; 'rules on hours' appear in paragraph 5 only as one way the structure could be altered.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says productivity 'kept rising'; paragraph 5 locates the forecasters' mistake in how labour markets work, not in productivity estimates.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that 'the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want', and paragraph 5 concludes that 'The division has in fact been made largely by the structure of jobs'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the status account because it is described in detail, without noticing that the author rejects its premise.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is a view the author reports and then argues against.

questions.question: According to the passage, a firm may prefer fewer people working longer hours to more people working shorter hours because

options.A: workers on short hours tend to leave sooner, so that the firm must keep replacing them at great expense.
options.B: professionals demand long hours as a signal of commitment, and firms must satisfy them to retain talent.
options.C: employees who work longer hours are more productive in each hour than those who work fewer hours.
options.D: some costs of employing a worker, such as recruitment and training, arise per person rather than per hour.

questions.correct_answer: (D) some costs of employing a worker, such as recruitment and training, arise per person rather than per hour.

option_rationales.A: Turnover among short-hours workers is never mentioned; the reason in paragraph 3 is a fixed cost per hire.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says long hours are a signal that firms reward with promotion, not something professionals demand from firms.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says nothing about productivity per hour; the reason given is the 'fixed cost for each person it hires'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A firm that pays a fixed cost for each person it hires, in recruitment, training, benefits and supervision, has good reason to prefer fewer people working longer'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the direction of the signalling point that comes in the next sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in a single sentence.

questions.question: The example of the lawyer in paragraph 3 is used chiefly to

options.A: suggest that part-time work no longer exists in any of the professions in which long hours are common.
options.B: demonstrate that the long hours worked in professions such as law raise the quality of the work produced.
options.C: illustrate that a trade of income for time that a worker wants may be unavailable or heavily penalised.
options.D: show that professionals, when offered a genuine choice, prefer a higher salary to a shorter working week.

questions.correct_answer: (C) illustrate that a trade of income for time that a worker wants may be unavailable or heavily penalised.

option_rationales.A: The trade 'may' be 'not on offer at all, or' very costly; the passage does not claim part-time work has disappeared everywhere.
option_rationales.B: The quality of legal work is never discussed; long hours are described as 'a signal of commitment', not as a cause of better work.
option_rationales.D: The lawyer 'would gladly trade' salary for time, so the example shows the opposite preference, frustrated by the job.

questions.explanation: The lawyer would 'gladly trade a fifth of her salary for a fifth of her week' but may find the trade 'not on offer at all, or that it costs her far more than a fifth of her career'. This supports the claim that observed hours reflect what jobs offer.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the lawyer's long hours as evidence of her preference, which is the premise the paragraph attacks.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing how the example serves the argument against the choice premise.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that 'the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want'?

options.A: Where workers gained a legal right to cut their hours at proportionally lower pay, with no effect on promotion, very few used it.
options.B: Many lower-paid workers reported that they could not obtain as many hours as they wished to work each week.
options.C: Surveys found that most professionals working very long hours said they would prefer to work somewhat less.
options.D: The fixed costs that firms bear for each worker they hire, especially for benefits and training, rose over several decades.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Where workers gained a legal right to cut their hours at proportionally lower pay, with no effect on promotion, very few used it.

option_rationales.B: This shows actual hours departing from desired hours, which is consistent with the author's view and appears in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: A gap between preferred and actual hours supports the author's claim that observed hours do not reveal what workers want.
option_rationales.D: Rising fixed costs per hire strengthen the author's explanation of why firms prefer fewer people working longer.

questions.explanation: The author's claim is that workers who want shorter hours cannot get them. If a genuine, penalty-free option to work less were offered and hardly anyone took it, observed hours would after all reflect what workers want, which directly weakens the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option from the passage's own evidence, which supports rather than weakens the claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options are on topic and two are drawn from the passage; each supports the claim, so the student must notice the direction.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard a national average of weekly hours that has held steady for some decades as

options.A: evidence that workers' preferences about how much to work have stopped changing over that period.
options.B: compatible with longer weeks for some groups of workers and too few hours for others.
options.C: a sign that the old prediction of a much shorter week will come true once productivity rises further.
options.D: proof that the institutional account is mistaken, since the structure of jobs changed during those decades.

questions.correct_answer: (B) compatible with longer weeks for some groups of workers and too few hours for others.

option_rationales.A: The author denies that observed hours reveal preferences, and paragraph 4 says an average 'can conceal' opposite movements.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says whether people would work less is 'an open question', so the author makes no such prediction.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 names a limitation of the institutional account, but nothing about a steady average refutes it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'An average that holds steady can conceal one group working too much and another too little', following the example of professionals with longer weeks and lower-paid workers with too few hours.
questions.common_misconception: Treating an average as information about every worker or about preferences.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the last sentence of paragraph 4 to a described case while rejecting overreaching readings.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 functions in the passage chiefly to

options.A: argue that producing more graduates would reverse the shrinking of employment in the middle of the wage scale.
options.B: state the author's own account of how technology has affected the distribution of pay over time.
options.C: introduce the task-based view that the rest of the passage goes on to defend without any reservation.
options.D: present an earlier explanation whose prediction is contradicted by the pattern reported in paragraph 2.

questions.correct_answer: (D) present an earlier explanation whose prediction is contradicted by the pattern reported in paragraph 2.

option_rationales.A: Producing graduates is the remedy the skill story offered; the author reports it, and paragraph 2 shows the story missed the pattern.
option_rationales.B: The author describes the skill story as having 'the defect of predicting a smooth gradient', so it is not the author's own account.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 describes the skill story, not the task view, and paragraphs 3 to 5 criticise the task view, so it is not defended without reservation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 sets out the skill story and notes its 'defect of predicting a smooth gradient'. Paragraph 2 opens 'found instead was a hollowing out', which contradicts that prediction.
questions.common_misconception: Taking a view the author reports for the author's own.
questions.difficulty_reason: The word 'instead' at the start of paragraph 2 signals the relation, but the reported view is written in a confident voice.

questions.question: The objection raised in paragraph 3 implies that a forecast that a task is safe from automation because it is non-routine

options.A: proves that reading medical images was always a routine task, since it is now discussed as a candidate for automation.
options.B: is reliable for tasks that demand judgement, since such tasks can never be fully specified in advance.
options.C: fails because the task view cannot explain why employment grew at the bottom of the wage distribution.
options.D: may rest on little more than the fact that the task has not yet been automated.

questions.correct_answer: (D) may rest on little more than the fact that the task has not yet been automated.

option_rationales.A: The author criticises exactly this kind of relabelling 'after the event'; the passage does not endorse it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says tasks 'once thought to demand judgement' are now candidates for automation, so judgement offers no permanent protection.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the task view 'explains a pattern the skill view could not', including growth at the bottom.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: whether a task 'counts as routine is usually settled by asking whether it has in fact been automated', so using the label to predict automation is circular. A task called non-routine may simply be one that has not been automated so far.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the relabelling option, which describes the practice the author criticises as if the author accepted it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires understanding the circularity argument and rejecting an option that restates the criticised practice.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the point made in paragraph 4?

options.A: After computers spread through offices, the wages of graduates rose faster than the wages of workers without degrees.
options.B: A task long described as requiring judgement is automated and is then reclassified by analysts as having been routine.
options.C: Two insurers buy identical claims software; one cuts its claims clerks, while the other, whose tax rules favour keeping staff, trains them to settle complex claims.
options.D: A typing pool is closed once word-processing programs become cheap enough to install on every employee's desk.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Two insurers buy identical claims software; one cuts its claims clerks, while the other, whose tax rules favour keeping staff, trains them to settle complex claims.

option_rationales.A: This illustrates the skill story of paragraph 1, which paragraph 4 treats as sharing the task story's mistake.
option_rationales.B: This illustrates the circularity objection of paragraph 3, a different difficulty from the one raised in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: This illustrates the remark in paragraph 5 that some tasks 'really are cheaper to mechanise', not the point that firms choose how to use the same technology.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 argues that 'which tasks are automated is a decision made by firms' that depends partly on the tax system, and that 'The same software can be deployed to remove a clerk or to let her handle cases that once needed a specialist'. The insurers show the same technology used in opposite ways under different incentives.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the typing pool because it involves automation, though it illustrates the limit stated in paragraph 5.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option illustrates a different paragraph of the same passage, so the student must locate the precise point of paragraph 4.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 presents each of the following as affecting which tasks firms automate EXCEPT

options.A: how many years of schooling the workers in a task have typically completed.
options.B: what machines cost compared with the cost of employing people to do the same work.
options.C: how the tax system treats spending on equipment compared with spending on wages.
options.D: whether managers see their workers as a cost to cut or as a capacity to develop.

questions.correct_answer: (A) how many years of schooling the workers in a task have typically completed.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the decision 'depends on what machines cost relative to people'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 lists 'how the tax system treats investment in equipment compared with spending on wages'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 lists 'whether managers regard workers as a cost to be reduced or a capacity to be developed'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 names three influences: relative cost, tax treatment and managers' view of workers. Schooling belongs to the skill story of paragraph 1 and is not offered as an influence on the firm's decision.
questions.common_misconception: Recalling that schooling is discussed in the passage and assuming it must be among the listed factors.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options closely paraphrase one sentence; the correct answer draws on a different paragraph.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The task view should be abandoned in favour of an account that explains wages through institutions alone.
options.B: Changing how equipment is taxed could alter how far the middle of the wage scale shrinks, though not every task is equally easy to mechanise.
options.C: Polarisation is a result of choices made by firms rather than an effect of technology on the jobs available.
options.D: Because the idea of a routine task is partly circular, no useful prediction about automation can be made.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Changing how equipment is taxed could alter how far the middle of the wage scale shrinks, though not every task is equally easy to mechanise.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 begins 'None of this makes the task view wrong' and speaks of technology 'filtered through institutions', not institutions alone.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 warns against replacing one determinism 'with another in which every outcome is a choice', and paragraph 4 says polarisation is only 'partly' a matter of incentives.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 calls the category 'less solid than it appears', not useless, and paragraph 5 says some tasks 'really are cheaper to mechanise'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 names the tax treatment of equipment as one influence on which tasks are automated, so a change in it could alter the extent of hollowing out. Paragraph 5 adds that 'Some tasks really are cheaper to mechanise than others', which the qualification in the correct answer preserves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that turns the author's 'partly' into 'rather than', the overcorrection paragraph 5 warns against.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option overstates one of the author's criticisms; the correct answer requires holding the criticism and the limit together.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how the gold standard came to be adopted by trading nations and why it was eventually replaced by paper money.
options.B: argue that because governments cannot be trusted with money, its supply should be fixed by a rule that no authority can alter.
options.C: challenge the belief that a gold-backed currency protected people, while granting the concern for trustworthy money behind it.
options.D: show that the depression of the 1930s was caused mainly by countries that refused to abandon the gold standard in time.

questions.correct_answer: (C) challenge the belief that a gold-backed currency protected people, while granting the concern for trustworthy money behind it.

option_rationales.A: The passage gives no history of adoption or replacement; it evaluates the standard's effects and the case its admirers make for it.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the author's view: paragraph 4 says a rule no one made is one 'no one can sensibly adjust', and recommends accountable institutions instead.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 mentions the 1930s only to say that early leavers 'tended to recover earlier'; the passage makes no claim about what caused the depression, and the point is one piece of evidence, not the purpose.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the belief, paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that gold discipline transferred risk to debtors and did not really bind governments, and paragraph 4 concedes that the underlying wish for trust is 'a legitimate demand' while saying institutions serve it better. The correct answer captures both the critique and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 1930s detail as the main point, or misreading the closing sentences as praise for fixed rules.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated plainly in the topic sentences of paragraphs 2 and 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, under a metallic standard the quantity of money was governed by

options.A: how quickly metal was mined and how it moved between countries, factors largely unrelated to what trade needed.
options.B: the demands of savers, who exchanged notes for gold whenever they feared that prices were about to rise.
options.C: the volume of trade, since merchants brought metal to the mint whenever commerce expanded and more coins were required.
options.D: the decisions of governments about how much paper money their reserves of metal would allow them to issue.

questions.correct_answer: (A) how quickly metal was mined and how it moved between countries, factors largely unrelated to what trade needed.

option_rationales.B: Savers' behaviour is never described as setting the quantity of money; the passage mentions savers only as the people the standard was supposed to protect.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the determinants had little 'to do with the needs of trade', which is the opposite of this option.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 names mining and flows of metal as the determinants; the discretion governments had (paragraph 3) concerned suspending convertibility and the official price, not setting the money supply at will.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'the quantity of money depended on the pace of mining and on the flow of metal between countries, neither of which had much to do with the needs of trade.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about government issue because paragraph 1 says governments 'cannot issue what they do not hold'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of one sentence.

questions.question: The example of the farmer who borrowed against next year's harvest is used in the passage to

options.A: show that farmers were more careless borrowers than merchants and therefore suffered most under the gold standard.
options.B: illustrate how falling prices raise the real burden of a debt that is fixed in money terms.
options.C: suggest that harvests under the gold standard were smaller, which was why the farmer could not repay his loan.
options.D: prove that creditors deliberately kept the supply of gold scarce in order to profit from the borrowers who owed them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate how falling prices raise the real burden of a debt that is fixed in money terms.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about farmers being careless or about merchants; the farmer suffers because prices fell while 'the sum he owed stayed exactly the same'.
option_rationales.C: The harvest is said to have 'fetched less', a fall in price, not in quantity; the passage never says harvests shrank.
option_rationales.D: No deliberate scheme by creditors is described; the passage says only that debtors 'bore much of the cost', which is an effect, not a plot.

questions.explanation: The sentence before the example says that 'falling prices are hard on anyone who owes money'; the farmer's harvest fetches less while his debt stays the same, which illustrates that point and supports the conclusion that debtors bore the cost.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about the size of harvests or about the motives of lenders.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by the general sentence that immediately precedes the example.

questions.question: The final sentence of the passage, about a rule that no one made, implies that

options.A: gold was a poor standard mainly because its value had been decided arbitrarily by officials long ago and never revised since then.
options.B: any rule for managing money becomes harmful once it is applied by people rather than determined by nature itself.
options.C: supporters of the gold standard have been dishonest in claiming that their preferred system was never designed by anyone.
options.D: the impersonality that makes gold seem trustworthy is also what makes it unable to respond to changing conditions.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the impersonality that makes gold seem trustworthy is also what makes it unable to respond to changing conditions.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says governments did alter the official price of gold, and the 'rule that no one made' refers to the supply set by geology, not to a decision by officials.
option_rationales.B: The author prefers institutions 'whose conduct can be observed, questioned and corrected', so the passage favours human judgement under scrutiny rather than condemning it.
option_rationales.C: The author does not accuse supporters of dishonesty; the sentence grants that gold 'offers the comfort' of an unmade rule and then names the cost of that very feature.

questions.explanation: The passage presents the absence of a human author as gold's appeal ('the comfort of a rule that no one made') and, in the same breath, as its defect: no one can 'sensibly adjust' it. The same feature produces both, which is what the correct answer says.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the closing sentence as an attack on supporters, or as a general distrust of human judgement.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the final two sentences together as a single double-edged point and relating it to paragraph 4's preference for institutions.

questions.question: According to the passage, an insurer facing adverse selection raises its price because

options.A: medical examinations and questionnaires have made it more expensive to administer each policy it sells.
options.B: compulsory membership has forced it to accept risky customers whom it would otherwise have refused.
options.C: the customers most likely to claim are staying in the pool while safer customers leave it.
options.D: buyers have been concealing their past claims and medical conditions in order to obtain cheaper cover.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the customers most likely to claim are staying in the pool while safer customers leave it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 presents screening as a way to close the information gap; the passage never says that its cost drives premiums up.
option_rationales.B: Compulsion is offered in paragraph 3 as a remedy for unravelling, not as a cause of the price rises described in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says unravelling 'can happen even though no one has lied to anyone'; concealment is not the mechanism described.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the safe find the premium expensive and 'some of them leave'; the insurer, 'seeing claims rise relative to premiums, raises the price'. The pool is left with those more likely to claim.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that adverse selection requires dishonesty by buyers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sequence is set out in consecutive sentences of one paragraph.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'no insurance in any useful sense' indicates that

options.A: insurers who examine applicants are breaking the law that requires them to offer every person the same premium.
options.B: a premium matching one's own expected cost leaves nothing of the bad luck shared with other people.
options.C: the person with the costly condition would be refused cover outright by every insurer on the market.
options.D: the policy offered would exclude the costly condition and so pay nothing at all if treatment were ever needed.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a premium matching one's own expected cost leaves nothing of the bad luck shared with other people.

option_rationales.A: No law is mentioned; the passage is describing an economic effect of sorting, not a legal violation.
option_rationales.C: The person is 'quoted a premium', so cover is offered; the point is that the price removes its value, not that it is refused.
option_rationales.D: The passage speaks of the premium being close to the expected cost, not of exclusions; the policy would pay, but the buyer would have prepaid nearly all of it.

questions.explanation: Insurance is valuable because the lucky help pay for the unlucky. If the premium equals the expected cost of one's own condition, the buyer is simply paying for his own treatment in advance, so the risk is not pooled. Paragraph 3 makes the point that 'a pool sorted precisely by risk is no longer sharing much risk at all'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'no insurance' literally as a refusal to sell.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is explained by the sentence immediately before it.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely shows the process the passage calls unravelling?

options.A: A voluntary repair plan for old cars loses its owners of well-kept cars after each price rise, until only owners of failing cars stay enrolled.
options.B: A repair plan for old cars becomes cheaper after the law requires every owner to join, because careful drivers now share the cost with careless ones.
options.C: A repair plan for old cars collapses after many owners claim for faults they caused on purpose, once they learn the inspectors cannot detect it.
options.D: A repair plan for old cars inspects each vehicle and charges owners according to its condition, so owners of failing cars pay nearly the cost of repair.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A voluntary repair plan for old cars loses its owners of well-kept cars after each price rise, until only owners of failing cars stay enrolled.

option_rationales.B: This describes the compulsory remedy in paragraph 3, which keeps the pool mixed; it is the opposite of a pool shrinking.
option_rationales.C: Deliberate damage concealed from the insurer is dishonesty, whereas paragraph 2 stresses that unravelling 'can happen even though no one has lied to anyone'; the mechanism is the exit of safe buyers.
option_rationales.D: This is the first remedy, sorting by risk, which paragraph 3 says erodes pooling; it is not the spiral of exits and price rises that defines unravelling.

questions.explanation: Unravelling (paragraph 2) is a cycle: safe buyers leave, the price rises, the next safest leave, until only the riskiest remain. The correct answer reproduces that cycle without any dishonesty; the other options describe fraud, compulsion and risk pricing respectively.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing unravelling with the remedies described in paragraph 3, or with fraud.
questions.difficulty_reason: All four options concern the same kind of plan; the student must match the precise mechanism.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards pricing insurance according to each person's risk is best described as

options.A: firmly opposed: it destroys the pooling on which insurance depends and should be replaced everywhere by compulsory membership.
options.B: detached and neutral: the author describes how the method works but declines to say when, if ever, it would be fair.
options.C: broadly approving: it is the technically correct remedy for adverse selection and should be left to the judgement of actuaries.
options.D: conditionally accepting: fair for risks people take on by choice, but troubling for risks imposed by birth or chance.

questions.correct_answer: (D) conditionally accepting: fair for risks people take on by choice, but troubling for risks imposed by birth or chance.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says pricing by risk 'seems fair enough' for chosen risks, and paragraph 3 notes compulsion is not free either, so the author opposes neither remedy outright.
option_rationales.B: The author does take a view, calling it fair for chosen risks and like 'penalising people twice' for risks of birth or chance.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 rejects treating the choice as 'a technical matter for actuaries' and calls sorting by inborn risk penalising people twice.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 draws a line: for risks 'people largely take on by choice' pricing by risk 'seems fair enough', while for risks that 'arrive at birth or by pure chance' it looks like 'penalising people twice'. The attitude depends on the kind of risk.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the author's sympathy for those born with costly conditions as total opposition to risk pricing.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options take one half of the author's distinction and generalise it.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 1 that the sound bank fails because

options.A: its loans turn out to be less prudent than its managers had believed when they first approved them.
options.B: its depositors behave irrationally, withdrawing money out of fear when they have no reason to do so.
options.C: depositors acting sensibly on a rumour bring about the very trouble that the rumour had wrongly alleged.
options.D: the state has not guaranteed its deposits, and so its managers are free to take excessive risks with them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) depositors acting sensibly on a rumour bring about the very trouble that the rumour had wrongly alleged.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 stipulates that the loans 'are prudent and its borrowers will repay'; the failure happens despite this.
option_rationales.B: The passage says it is 'rational to run whether or not the rumour is true', so the depositors are not acting irrationally.
option_rationales.D: Deposit insurance is introduced only in paragraph 2, and paragraph 1 describes no risk-taking; the institution is sound throughout.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: each depositor is better off withdrawing first, so a run is rational 'whether or not the rumour is true', and 'once enough people run, the rumour becomes true'. Hurried loan sales create the losses, so it fails 'because it was believed to be' unsound.
questions.common_misconception: Equating a panic with irrational behaviour, when the passage stresses that each withdrawal is individually rational.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is set out in the last three sentences of paragraph 1.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, deposit insurance is said to look 'almost like a free lunch' because

options.A: insured depositors receive the protection of their savings without paying any premium for it at all.
options.B: a guarantee that is believed removes the motive to run, so the promised payment rarely has to be made.
options.C: the guarantee costs nothing in the short run, though it encourages reckless lending that is paid for later.
options.D: the cost of insuring deposits is borne by the banks themselves rather than by depositors or by taxpayers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a guarantee that is believed removes the motive to run, so the promised payment rarely has to be made.

option_rationales.A: Premiums are not discussed; the 'lunch' is free because the promise prevents the runs it insures against, not because depositors pay nothing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 presents the optimistic view before any objection; the hidden cost of recklessness is the critics' point in paragraph 3, not the meaning of the phrase.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says nothing about who pays for the scheme; the point concerns the guarantee seldom being called upon.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains the phrase in the same sentence: insurance is 'a promise that, by being believed, makes its own fulfilment unnecessary'. Because no one runs, 'the guarantee is seldom called upon', so it seems to deliver stability at almost no cost.
questions.common_misconception: Importing the objection of paragraph 3 into the meaning of a phrase that states the case for insurance.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option blends the phrase with the later objection, which students may find attractive because 'almost' seems to hint at a cost.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's reply to the objection in paragraph 4?

options.A: Surveys of insured depositors find that very few of them have ever read their bank's accounts or asked how it lends the money they deposit.
options.B: In several countries the limit on deposit cover has been raised more than once, usually after a crisis had already begun rather than before it.
options.C: Runs on banks without deposit insurance have often begun from rumours that later proved false, and sound banks closed as a result of them.
options.D: Before guarantees existed, depositors steadily moved money away from banks with weaker loan books, well before any panic, and these banks then lent more cautiously.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Before guarantees existed, depositors steadily moved money away from banks with weaker loan books, well before any panic, and these banks then lent more cautiously.

option_rationales.A: This confirms the premise of the objection, which the author grants; the author's reply is that such watching was never valuable, so showing that insured depositors do not watch leaves it intact.
option_rationales.B: When limits were raised says nothing about whether depositors once supplied useful scrutiny, which is the premise of the author's reply; the option is on topic but bears on neither side.
option_rationales.C: This supports the author: it confirms that depositor discipline was 'indiscriminate, striking prudent and imprudent banks without distinction'.

questions.explanation: The author's reply rests on the claim that ordinary depositors 'were never skilled readers of loan books' and so supplied only indiscriminate panic. Evidence that they once discriminated quietly and effectively between weak and strong banks attacks that premise directly, implying that guarantees do remove genuine scrutiny.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the survey of inattentive depositors, which sounds damaging to deposit insurance but only restates the objection the author has already granted.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the central premise of the reply to be isolated from its secondary points; one wrong option restates the granted objection, one supports the author and one is irrelevant.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a proposal to guarantee every deposit in full, with no upper limit, as

options.A: unwise, because it would remove the incentive of large creditors who are among the few equipped to scrutinise banks.
options.B: acceptable, provided depositors were also required to study the loan books of their banks before opening accounts.
options.C: sensible, because if partial cover stops runs, full cover would stop them even more completely at no extra cost.
options.D: pointless, because depositors had already stopped paying attention to their banks once partial insurance was introduced.

questions.correct_answer: (A) unwise, because it would remove the incentive of large creditors who are among the few equipped to scrutinise banks.

option_rationales.B: The author thinks ordinary depositors were 'never skilled readers of loan books', so requiring them to read the books is no remedy on the author's view.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'the limit on cover matters a great deal, since it decides who still has a reason to care'; removing the limit ignores this warning.
option_rationales.D: The author's worry is not about small depositors, whose attention the author thinks was worthless, but about the 'large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 assigns scrutiny to supervisors and to 'the large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake', and says the limit on cover 'decides who still has a reason to care'. Unlimited cover would leave those creditors with no stake.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because the author defends deposit insurance the author would favour more of it without limit.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the final clause of the passage to a case it does not mention.

questions.question: According to paragraph 1, the analogy between inflation and taxation is exact in that

options.A: in both cases the burden falls most heavily on the poorest households, who hold their wealth in cash.
options.B: in both cases a collector must visit the people who are being taxed and record what each of them owes.
options.C: in both cases resources pass from the public to the authority that collects or issues the money.
options.D: in both cases the measure must be approved by a law before any money can be taken from the public.

questions.correct_answer: (C) in both cases resources pass from the public to the authority that collects or issues the money.

option_rationales.A: The point about who bears the burden is made in paragraph 2 by critics; it is not the respect in which paragraph 1 calls the analogy exact.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says of the inflation tax that 'no collector calls', so this is a respect in which the two differ.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says of the inflation tax that 'No law is passed', and paragraph 2 contrasts it with taxes that must be voted upon.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'In one respect the analogy with taxation is exact: resources move from the public to the issuer of money'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the distributional point from paragraph 2 because it is the critics' main complaint.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated directly after the phrase quoted in the stem.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It explains the historical shift from coin clipping to money creation that made the inflation tax possible in modern economies.
options.B: It sets limits on the inflation-tax idea by noting cases in which inflation involves neither intention nor much gain.
options.C: It rejects the inflation-tax idea altogether by showing that inflation is caused by harvests and fuel prices rather than by governments.
options.D: It strengthens the critics' case in paragraph 2 by showing that the burden of inflation falls on savers who hold interest-bearing deposits.

questions.correct_answer: (B) It sets limits on the inflation-tax idea by noting cases in which inflation involves neither intention nor much gain.

option_rationales.A: The historical comparison is made in paragraph 1; paragraph 3 qualifies the analogy rather than tracing its history.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'much inflation' has such causes, not all of it, and paragraph 4 goes on to endorse the idea where inflation is high and persistent.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 makes the opposite point about deposits: because their interest rises with inflation, the state's revenue from mild inflation 'is modest'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with 'The analogy misleads, however, when it is pressed too far' and gives two limits: some inflation is unchosen, and with interest-bearing deposits the gain from mild inflation is small. Paragraph 4 then restores the idea for the cases where it applies, so paragraph 3 qualifies rather than refutes.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a qualification as an outright rejection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option overstates 'much inflation' into all inflation; the reader must notice that paragraph 4 restores the idea.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a reason critics consider the inflation tax worse than ordinary taxation EXCEPT that it

options.A: is collected mainly from people with large incomes, who are able to move their wealth abroad.
options.B: benefits debtors, including the state, whose obligations lose real value as prices rise.
options.C: falls heavily on households that keep their savings in cash or live on incomes fixed in money terms.
options.D: does not have to be proposed, debated and voted upon in the way a tax on incomes does.

questions.correct_answer: (A) is collected mainly from people with large incomes, who are able to move their wealth abroad.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says it 'benefits anyone whose debts shrink in real value', and that the state is often among the largest debtors.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 names exactly these households as 'least able to protect themselves', so this reason is given.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a tax on incomes 'must be proposed, debated and voted upon' while the inflation tax does not; this is a reason the critics give.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives three complaints: the inflation tax is hidden and unvoted, it hits cash savers and fixed incomes, and it benefits debtors including the state. Nowhere does the passage say it falls on people with large incomes; it says the reverse, that it falls on 'those least able to protect themselves'.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking that the correct answer reverses the passage's claim about who bears the burden.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each listed reason is in one paragraph; the correct answer contradicts that paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely accept?

options.A: Since modern deposits pay interest, the idea of an inflation tax is a historical relic best confined to the age of coin clipping.
options.B: Any inflation that reduces the real value of government debt should be described as a tax, whatever its original cause may have been.
options.C: Mild inflation that arrives through the price of imports is a hidden tax imposed by foreign governments on domestic savers.
options.D: Whether a period of inflation deserves to be called a tax depends on examining who gained from it, not only on how much prices rose.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Whether a period of inflation deserves to be called a tax depends on examining who gained from it, not only on how much prices rose.

option_rationales.A: The author says the language is 'accurate description' when inflation is high and persistent and the state is a heavy debtor, so the idea still applies today.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says calling inflation a tax attributes 'intention' where there may be none; inflation from a failed harvest also shrinks state debt, yet the author would not call it a tax.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says that for inflation that 'arrives from abroad' the language of taxation 'obscures more than it reveals'; the author would reject this description.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the concept is best treated as 'a tool of diagnosis rather than as a verdict reached in advance' and that the right question is 'who gains?'. The correct answer states this: the label depends on an inquiry into gain, which paragraph 3 shows is not settled by the bare fact of rising prices.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about government debt, which echoes paragraph 2 but ignores paragraph 3's insistence on intention.
questions.difficulty_reason: The option about government debt uses a true fact from paragraph 2 to reach a conclusion the author's qualification forbids; separating it from the correct answer needs both paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: According to the reasoning in paragraph 1, a pre-election loosening of money fails to raise output because

options.A: the higher inflation that follows reduces output by more than the loosening had raised it in the first place.
options.B: appointed officials at the central bank refuse to carry out the loosening that the government has ordered.
options.C: voters punish governments that loosen money, so the government reverses the policy soon after the election.
options.D: people expect the loosening and raise wages and prices beforehand, which cancels its effect on output.

questions.correct_answer: (D) people expect the loosening and raise wages and prices beforehand, which cancels its effect on output.

option_rationales.A: The passage says only that 'only the inflation remains', not that output ends up lower than before; the option adds a net loss that is not stated.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 describes what happens when governments control money; independence is offered as the remedy, not as the reason the boost fails.
option_rationales.C: No reversal or electoral punishment is mentioned; the passage says the boost 'never materialises' because it was anticipated.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Because the public comes to anticipate this, it builds the expected inflation into wages and prices in advance, so that the boost to output never materialises'.
questions.common_misconception: Supposing that the remedy of independence is part of the mechanism it is meant to cure.
questions.difficulty_reason: The causal chain is set out in a single sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements is most closely analogous to the settlement the author describes in paragraph 3?

options.A: A city council sets a target for reducing road deaths and then chooses each new speed limit itself, consulting the safety agency only for advice.
options.B: A city council sets a target for reducing road deaths, and a safety agency decides how to meet it and must explain any shortfall publicly.
options.C: A city council asks a safety agency to cut road deaths, ease congestion and raise parking revenue, leaving the agency to balance the three goals.
options.D: A city council lets a safety agency decide both how far road deaths should be reduced and how that reduction should be achieved.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A city council sets a target for reducing road deaths, and a safety agency decides how to meet it and must explain any shortfall publicly.

option_rationales.A: Here the elected body keeps the instruments too, so there is no delegation of means and no commitment device of the kind paragraph 3 describes.
option_rationales.C: Balancing several goals is the situation paragraph 4 warns about, in which the agency's choices become political; it is not the paragraph 3 settlement.
option_rationales.D: This delegates goals as well as instruments, which is precisely the independence of goals that paragraph 3 distinguishes from the settlement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A legislature can fix the target ... and require the central bank to explain in public whenever it misses; that body then decides how to reach the target'. The correct answer keeps exactly that division: elected body sets the end, agency chooses the means, with public explanation of misses.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the multi-goal option, which mirrors paragraph 4 rather than paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option alters one element of the settlement (who sets goals, who sets means, how many goals).

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Delegating only the means of monetary policy can reconcile credibility with democracy, though the reconciliation weakens as mandates widen.
options.B: Central banks should be made fully independent, since elected governments cannot be trusted to resist loosening money before elections.
options.C: Central banks have lost public trust because they have been given too many goals, such as climate risk and the direction of credit.
options.D: Decisions about interest rates are political and should therefore be returned to elected governments, who can be removed by voters.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Delegating only the means of monetary policy can reconcile credibility with democracy, though the reconciliation weakens as mandates widen.

option_rationales.B: This is the case reported in paragraph 1, and the author goes on to accept the democratic objection in part, so it is not the passage's conclusion.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 argues that wider mandates weaken the case for being 'left alone', not that trust has actually been lost; the option also omits the passage's main resolution.
option_rationales.D: This is the democratic objection of paragraph 2, which the author calls 'partly right' and then largely answers with the distinction between goals and instruments.

questions.explanation: The passage reports two views, reconciles them in paragraph 3 by separating independence in the 'choice of instruments' from independence in the 'choice of goals', and in paragraph 4 says the settlement 'is stable, however, only while the mandate remains narrow'. The correct answer holds both the resolution and its limit.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking one of the two reported positions for the author's own conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the passage presents faithfully but does not adopt; the third is too narrow and adds a claim about trust.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A central bank with a single inflation target faces stronger electoral temptation than a government does before an election.
options.B: Once the legislature fixes an inflation target, the democratic objection to central bank independence ceases to apply in any form.
options.C: A central bank told to support employment as well as stable prices has a weaker case against elected oversight than one with only a price target.
options.D: Asking a central bank to pursue financial stability shows that its officials are cleverer than elected politicians in economic matters.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A central bank told to support employment as well as stable prices has a weaker case against elected oversight than one with only a price target.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says independence 'removes the temptation'; an appointed body does not face voters, so the passage implies the reverse.
option_rationales.B: The author says the arrangement 'answers much of the democratic objection', not all of it, and paragraph 4 shows how the objection returns as mandates grow.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the gain from independence lies 'in credibility rather than in any superior cleverness', and paragraph 4 treats wider goals as a problem, not a sign of skill.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: when central banks are asked to pursue extra goals such as employment, trading them off 'is itself a political judgement', and 'The more a central bank is asked to do, the weaker its claim to be left alone'. A bank with the wider mandate therefore has a weaker claim to be left alone, that is, a weaker case against oversight by elected bodies, than one confined to a price target.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that overstates 'answers much of the democratic objection' into answering all of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs paragraph 4 to be read as reviving the objection of paragraph 2; the most tempting wrong option turns 'much' into 'any form'.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that

options.A: the usual moral view of debt is one-sided, since lenders who are paid to bear risk share responsibility for loans that fail.
options.B: bankruptcy laws that grant honest debtors a fresh start benefit creditors more than strict enforcement of debts would.
options.C: borrowers who default should not be blamed, since default is merely a risk that the lender was paid in advance to accept.
options.D: moral language has no proper place in discussions of debt, which ought to be treated as purely a matter of contracts and prices.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the usual moral view of debt is one-sided, since lenders who are paid to bear risk share responsibility for loans that fail.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 mentions this rationale as one part of the practical case, but it is a supporting point, and the claim that creditors gain more is not made.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this licenses casual default' and that a borrower who never meant to repay 'has done wrong', so the author does not excuse all defaulters.
option_rationales.D: The author keeps moral language and wants it 'more accurate', and paragraph 1 says the existing language 'is not wholly misplaced'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states the thesis ('assigns the whole of the responsibility to one side of what is a two-sided contract'), paragraph 3 draws out consequences, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'obligation runs in both directions' and calls for a moral language recognising both duties.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the author's critique into a defence of all defaulters or a rejection of moral talk.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are exaggerations of the author's position, which the concessions in paragraphs 1 and 4 rule out.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason bankruptcy law in many countries favours a fresh start for honest debtors is that

options.A: debtors who receive a fresh start are more likely than others to borrow again and so increase the profits of lenders.
options.B: courts find it too costly to enforce debts that have remained unpaid for a long time against debtors with few assets.
options.C: lenders who made the original loans were usually aware that their borrowers would be unable to repay them.
options.D: a person weighed down by unpayable debts is of little productive use to anyone, including the creditors.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a person weighed down by unpayable debts is of little productive use to anyone, including the creditors.

option_rationales.A: Future borrowing is never mentioned; the rationale given concerns the debtor's productivity, not new lending.
option_rationales.B: Enforcement costs and courts are not discussed; the stated ground is that the crushed debtor 'produces little for anyone'.
option_rationales.C: The passage says lenders priced in 'the chance of not being repaid', not that they knew particular borrowers would default.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: bankruptcy law treats a fresh start as a social good 'partly on the practical ground that a person crushed by debts that can never be paid produces little for anyone, creditors included'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that sounds like a plausible real-world rationale but is not the one given.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in one clause.

questions.question: The author's claim that lenders 'collect the premium for risk while disowning the risk itself' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: lenders are legally entitled to the premium, but borrowers are never morally obliged to repay the sums they have borrowed.
options.B: lenders who condemn every default are trying to keep the reward for bearing a risk without accepting what that risk entails.
options.C: lenders ought to return the interest they have collected from any borrower who later turns out to be unable to repay.
options.D: lenders charge interest rates that are higher than the actual chance of default can justify, and so profit unfairly.

questions.correct_answer: (B) lenders who condemn every default are trying to keep the reward for bearing a risk without accepting what that risk entails.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 grants that 'a promise to repay is a promise', and paragraph 4 says a borrower who never meant to repay 'has done wrong', so borrowers do have obligations.
option_rationales.C: No such remedy is proposed; the author asks only for a moral language that recognises the lender's duty of 'care in deciding to lend'.
option_rationales.D: The author's complaint is not that rates are too high but that, having been paid for risk, lenders treat its occurrence as the borrower's sin.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the higher interest rate pays the lender 'for bearing exactly the risk that sometimes comes to pass'; condemning default as a sin then disclaims that very risk. The correct answer restates this inconsistency.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the phrase as a complaint about excessive rates or as a demand for refunds.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option about unfair profit shares the passage's critical tone but misidentifies the target.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 3 about the practical effects of a strong moral framing of debt?

options.A: In regions where default carries heavy social stigma, borrowers on average take out smaller loans and repay them in fewer instalments.
options.B: In regions with generous bankruptcy laws, the rate of default is higher than in regions where debts are enforced strictly against debtors.
options.C: In regions where default carries heavy social stigma, lenders check borrowers' incomes less thoroughly, and struggling borrowers seek renegotiation later.
options.D: In regions where default carries heavy social stigma, many people say in surveys that repaying a debt is a matter of personal honour.

questions.correct_answer: (C) In regions where default carries heavy social stigma, lenders check borrowers' incomes less thoroughly, and struggling borrowers seek renegotiation later.

option_rationales.A: Loan size and number of instalments do not bear on the two effects the author predicts, careless lending and delayed renegotiation.
option_rationales.B: This concerns bankruptcy law and default rates, not the effects of moral stigma on lenders' care or borrowers' openness, and it might even be read against the author.
option_rationales.D: This merely confirms that the moral framing is strong there; it says nothing about the consequences the author claims follow from it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 predicts two effects of a strong moral framing: lenders face 'less pressure to judge carefully whether a borrower can repay', and distressed borrowers 'conceal their distress out of shame instead of seeking to renegotiate early'. Evidence of both effects where stigma is strong supports the claim directly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the survey option, which shows the framing exists but not that it has the claimed effects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires matching evidence to the two specific predicted effects rather than to the topic.

questions.question: The example of firms built around a new technology (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.A: establish that the size of the eventual fall in prices is the most reliable sign that a market was in a bubble.
options.B: show that investors in new technologies are especially prone to collective madness and so tend to pay too much.
options.C: argue that most firms built around new technologies fail, so investors should avoid such shares until a winner emerges.
options.D: show how a steep later fall in prices can be compatible with the original prices having been a reasonable wager.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show how a steep later fall in prices can be compatible with the original prices having been a reasonable wager.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the mark of a bubble 'is not the size of the eventual fall', and the example in paragraph 2 is meant to break exactly that inference.
