questions.common_misconception: Choosing a reason that sounds as if it would obstruct bargaining without checking whether the passage gives it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three supported reasons are listed in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: When the author says that a certain reading 'takes the conditional for the claim' (paragraph 2), the point is that this reading

options.A: assumes that property rights can always be defined clearly, when in practice they are usually disputed.
options.B: confuses the efficient outcome of a bargain with the fair outcome that the parties ought to reach.
options.C: treats a result that holds only under a stated condition as though it held in general.
options.D: relies on what the parties claim they would accept instead of on what they actually agree to pay.

questions.correct_answer: (C) treats a result that holds only under a stated condition as though it held in general.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says that property rights are usually disputed; the condition it says is rarely met is that bargaining be 'nearly costless'.
option_rationales.B: The contrast between efficiency and who pays is raised only in paragraph 4; the phrase in paragraph 2 concerns the condition of costless bargaining.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage contrasts stated and actual willingness to pay; the phrase is about ignoring the requirement of cheap bargaining.

questions.explanation: The next sentence explains the phrase: 'The striking result holds only when bargaining is nearly costless'. The reading that governments may simply stand aside drops that condition and treats the result as generally true.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the phrase to the later point about fairness in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence that follows the phrase explains it.

questions.question: The closing sentence, 'Those who live downwind are not', implies that

options.A: people exposed to pollution care how the legal right is assigned, even when the physical outcome would be unchanged.
options.B: households near a polluting factory rarely understand how the efficient outcome of a bargain is reached.
options.C: an efficient outcome is reached only when the households, not the factory, hold the right to clean air.
options.D: residents downwind of a factory will refuse to pay for a filter however cheaply it could be fitted.

questions.correct_answer: (A) people exposed to pollution care how the legal right is assigned, even when the physical outcome would be unchanged.

option_rationales.B: The sentence concerns what residents care about, not what they understand; the passage says nothing about their grasp of economics.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the efficient outcome is reached 'whoever held the legal right', so this contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.D: Nothing suggests such refusal; paragraph 1 describes households paying for a filter whenever it costs less than the damage it prevents.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that even with the same physical outcome 'it matters a great deal who pays whom', and that efficiency 'may be blind to that difference'. The final sentence contrasts that blindness with the residents, for whom the difference is real.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'downwind' as a point about knowledge or stubbornness instead of about who bears the cost.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the two preceding sentences.

questions.question: According to the passage, the rebound from an efficiency gain tends to be small when

options.A: the efficiency gain applies to an input that whole industries use in production.
options.B: people already consume nearly as much of the service as they want, whatever its price.
options.C: the money saved is spent on other goods and services instead of on more energy.
options.D: households are able to measure their savings precisely and can plan their spending around them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) people already consume nearly as much of the service as they want, whatever its price.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: where energy is 'a basic input to production', the rebound 'can be large'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says money spent on other goods still uses energy, so this describes an indirect rebound, not a reason for a small one.
option_rationales.D: The passage never links the size of the rebound to how precisely households measure their savings.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that where demand 'is already close to saturation, as with lighting in a well-lit home, the rebound tends to be modest', because few people want brighter rooms just because brightness is cheaper.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the condition for a small rebound with the condition for a large one.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The example of the family that takes a holiday flight (paragraph 3) serves to

options.A: illustrate how money saved on energy can lead to more energy use through spending on something else.
options.B: show that the rebound from efficiency gains in transport is usually larger than the original saving.
options.C: explain why the mechanism behind the rebound is now disputed by economists who study energy.
options.D: suggest that families who save money on fuel ought to spend it on goods that need less energy.

questions.correct_answer: (A) illustrate how money saved on energy can lead to more energy use through spending on something else.

option_rationales.B: The example illustrates a channel, not a size; the passage says estimates of total rebound 'vary so widely' and claims a rebound above the saving only for Jevons's case.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'The mechanism itself is not in dispute'; only its size is.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no recommendation to families; its recommendation in paragraph 4 is a tax or a cap.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces 'a subtler and less visible channel of transmission': money saved 'is spent on something else, and that something else uses energy too'. The flight is an instance of that indirect effect.
questions.common_misconception: Turning an illustration of a mechanism into a claim about magnitude.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentences just before the example.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the two camps described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: sympathetic to those who doubt efficiency, since the author concludes that it achieves little on its own.
options.B: supportive of those who favour efficiency, while regretting that the rebound has been overstated.
options.C: dismissive of both, because the author regards the rebound as too uncertain to be worth discussing.
options.D: critical of both, for treating as settled a question whose answer varies with the case.

questions.correct_answer: (D) critical of both, for treating as settled a question whose answer varies with the case.

option_rationales.A: The author rejects the view that efficiency is 'futile' and calls its benefits 'a gain in its own right', so the sceptics are not endorsed.
option_rationales.B: The author never says the rebound is overstated and concludes that efficiency is not 'sufficient', which the efficiency camp's confidence ignores.
option_rationales.C: The author discusses the rebound at length and draws a policy conclusion from it; the uncertainty concerns its size, not whether it matters.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'Both camps tend to treat the question as if it had a single answer, when the size of the effect plainly depends on circumstances', and paragraph 4 rejects both 'futile' and 'sufficient'. The author faults both camps for the same overconfidence.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's limits on efficiency as agreement with the sceptics.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the criticism in paragraph 1 with the two-sided conclusion in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following policies would best match the recommendation in the final paragraph?

options.A: A city pays for insulating older homes and cuts the tax on heating fuel so that poorer households can afford to keep warm.
options.B: A city raises the tax on heating fuel steeply and ends all of its support for insulation and efficient boilers.
options.C: A city pays for insulating older homes and, over the same years, raises the tax on the fuels used to heat them.
options.D: A city bans the sale of inefficient boilers and leaves the price of heating fuel to be set entirely by the market.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A city pays for insulating older homes and, over the same years, raises the tax on the fuels used to heat them.

option_rationales.A: Cutting the fuel tax makes energy cheaper still, which is the opposite of keeping it 'costly enough that the saving is not simply spent on using more'.
option_rationales.B: The author values efficiency for the comfort it brings ('a gain in its own right'), so dropping it does not match the recommended pairing.
option_rationales.D: This relies on efficiency alone, which paragraph 4 says is not 'sufficient' when the aim is to cut total use.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 recommends pairing efficiency with 'something that keeps energy costly enough', such as a tax on carbon. Funding insulation while raising the fuel tax combines the two.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option with the strongest price signal and forgetting that the author wants efficiency kept as well.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each keep one half of the recommended pair.

questions.question: According to the passage, if cutting emissions turns out to be harder than expected, a carbon tax will

options.A: lead the government to lower the rate so that firms are not burdened by unexpected costs.
options.B: keep the price per tonne where it was set while emissions end up higher than planned.
options.C: hold emissions at the planned level while firms pay more for each tonne they continue to emit.
options.D: cause the price of emitting a tonne of carbon to rise, perhaps steeply, until firms cut back.

questions.correct_answer: (B) keep the price per tonne where it was set while emissions end up higher than planned.

option_rationales.A: The passage nowhere says that a tax is lowered in response to high abatement costs; it describes firms paying the tax and emitting more.
option_rationales.C: Holding the quantity fixed is what a cap does; paragraph 2 says a tax 'leaves the quantity uncertain'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says this happens under a cap: 'permit prices will climb, perhaps steeply'. A tax 'fixes the price'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain: if cutting emissions proves harder than expected, firms will pay the tax and emit more than was planned.'
questions.common_misconception: Swapping the behaviour of the tax and the cap.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence; the wrong options swap the two instruments.

questions.question: Suppose a river pollutant does little harm at low concentrations but kills most of the river's fish once its concentration in any single season passes a known level. By the reasoning of paragraph 2, the better instrument for controlling it would be

options.A: a limit on the total quantity discharged, since keeping below the threshold matters more than a predictable cost.
options.B: either instrument equally well, since a regulator who chose the right level could reach the same outcome by both.
options.C: a fixed charge per unit discharged, since the harm depends on what accumulates over decades and not on any one season.
options.D: a limit on discharges paired with a ceiling on the permit price, since that keeps costs predictable if cutting proves hard.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a limit on the total quantity discharged, since keeping below the threshold matters more than a predictable cost.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the two are equivalent only in 'a world without uncertainty'; paragraph 2 shows that once costs are unknown the choice depends on the shape of the damage.
option_rationales.C: That is the reasoning paragraph 2 applies to carbon, whose harm depends on the long-run stock; here the harm turns on a single season's concentration, so the reason does not apply.
option_rationales.D: A ceiling lets discharges exceed the limit whenever cutting proves costly, which sacrifices the quantity to keep the price stable; paragraph 2 says that past a threshold 'a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says: 'If harm accelerates sharply past some threshold, a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price.' A pollutant that becomes lethal past a level within one season is exactly that case, so a quantity limit fits.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying over the conclusion for carbon without checking whether its premise (harm from a long-run stock) holds.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the conditional rule to a new case where its premise is reversed.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It shows that free allocation of permits to industries makes trading schemes unfair and therefore politically unpopular.
options.B: It extends the argument of paragraph 2 by showing how uncertainty over costs affects voters as well as firms.
options.C: It supplies the author's own reasons for preferring a cap to a tax, after the economic case has been weighed.
options.D: It presents an objection from supporters of trading that the economic case for a tax overlooks political feasibility.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It presents an objection from supporters of trading that the economic case for a tax overlooks political feasibility.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says free allocation, despite the windfall, 'has often been the price of getting a scheme adopted', which is a point in favour of feasibility.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 does not discuss uncertainty over abatement costs; it turns from economic theory to the politics of adoption.
option_rationales.C: The objection is attributed to 'Advocates of trading', and paragraph 4 goes on to play down the choice between the two, so the author does not prefer a cap.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens 'Advocates of trading reply that this argument ... neglects politics' and lists political advantages of a cap. It answers the case for a tax made in paragraph 2, before paragraph 4 reframes the debate.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a reported reply as the author's own conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attribution to advocates is explicit, but one option tempts readers who skip it.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Now that hybrids exist, uncertainty about the cost of abatement no longer makes any difference to carbon policy.
options.B: Because they state their goal openly, trading schemes are easier to defend and should be chosen over taxes.
options.C: A tax and a trading scheme that each set a low price on a narrow range of emissions would both do little.
options.D: The long debate between supporters of taxes and of caps was at bottom nothing more than a quarrel about labels.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A tax and a trading scheme that each set a low price on a narrow range of emissions would both do little.

option_rationales.A: The passage says hybrids are 'neither pure price nor pure quantity', not that uncertainty has ceased to matter; floors and ceilings are responses to it.
option_rationales.B: This is the view of the 'Advocates of trading' in paragraph 3; the author's conclusion is that the label matters less than level, coverage and credibility.
option_rationales.D: The author says the debate was a debate about labels only 'in part'; paragraph 2 shows a real difference under uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says what decides whether a carbon price works is 'whether it is high enough, broad enough in what it covers, and credible enough', rather than whether it is called a tax or a cap. Both instruments set low and narrow would fail that test equally.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that echoes the 'labels' sentence without noticing the qualifier 'in part'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close paraphrases of things the passage says, distorted by degree or by attribution.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the example of the road approved through a forest is used to show that

options.A: roads should not be built through forests unless the time saved by drivers is very large.
options.B: the cost of replacing a forest with embankments and pumps is a reasonable guide to its value.
options.C: planning authorities generally overstate the value of time saved by drivers in order to justify new roads.
options.D: declining to put a figure on nature can amount to valuing it at nothing.

questions.correct_answer: (D) declining to put a figure on nature can amount to valuing it at nothing.

option_rationales.A: The example makes no recommendation about roads; it illustrates how an unstated value becomes an implicit zero.
option_rationales.B: The replacement-cost argument in paragraph 2 concerns a wetland that absorbs floodwater, not the forest in the road example.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not say the drivers' time is overstated; the point is that the forest is counted 'as worth nothing'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the authority 'counts the forest as worth nothing because no one has put a figure on it' and concludes that 'the forest has in effect been priced at zero'. The example supports the defenders' claim that every decision already implies a valuation.
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up the road example with the separate wetland example in the same paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion of the example is stated in the same sentence.

questions.question: In saying that very large totals for the value of nature's services 'should therefore be read as rhetoric rather than as accounts' (paragraph 3), the author means that such totals

options.A: are usually calculated dishonestly by people who wish to exaggerate the importance of conservation.
options.B: may draw attention to nature's importance but cannot be treated as meaningful measurements of value.
options.C: should be replaced by totals built up from many small valuations, such as one orchard's bees multiplied out.
options.D: are accurate in principle but too large for governments to use when drawing up their budgets.

questions.correct_answer: (B) may draw attention to nature's importance but cannot be treated as meaningful measurements of value.

option_rationales.A: The author questions the meaning of the figures, not the honesty of those who produce them; the reason given is that prices would themselves change.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 rejects exactly that method: valuing all pollinators 'is not like asking what one orchard's bees are worth and multiplying'.
option_rationales.D: The author says such a figure 'would describe a world that no longer exists', so it is not accurate in principle.

questions.explanation: The word 'therefore' ties the sentence to the preceding argument: a total for a whole system uses prices that would be different if the system were gone, so the figure does not describe anything real. It may persuade ('however striking') but is not an account in the sense of a reliable measure.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'rhetoric' as an accusation of dishonesty instead of a judgement about what the figure can do.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the phrase to the reasoning about changing prices that precedes it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the defenders' claim in paragraph 2 that making the value of nature explicit 'protects it from being treated as free'?

options.A: Where explicit valuations are used, low estimates of a habitat's worth have often been cited to approve projects that would otherwise be refused.
options.B: Values in money calculated for the pollinators of the whole world turn out to be impossible to interpret in any useful way.
options.C: Estimates of what it would cost to replace a wetland with embankments and pumps differ considerably from one town to another, even within a single region.
options.D: Surveys find that many people regard it as distasteful to attach money values to forests, rivers and wild animals.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Where explicit valuations are used, low estimates of a habitat's worth have often been cited to approve projects that would otherwise be refused.

option_rationales.B: This supports the author's point about whole systems in paragraph 3; the defenders' claim concerns ordinary decisions such as draining one marsh.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 already calls replacement cost a 'rough' guide, and variation between towns does not show that explicit values leave nature less protected.
option_rationales.D: This restates the critics' unease from paragraph 1; it does not show that explicit valuation fails to protect nature in decisions.

questions.explanation: The defenders argue that an explicit figure protects nature because the alternative is an implicit zero. If explicit figures are in practice often used to justify approving damaging projects that would otherwise be refused, valuation is working against protection, which strikes at the claim directly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that echoes a criticism made elsewhere in the passage but does not bear on the specific claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is a criticism of valuation the passage itself makes or reports, but only the correct answer tests the protective effect.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard an explicit money value for a forest as most useful when the decision concerns

options.A: how much all the forests of a large country contribute to the economy that depends on them.
options.B: whether to allow a loss of forest so large that it could not be reversed for generations.
options.C: whether to clear a small part of a forest that will otherwise remain largely intact.
options.D: whether forests ought to be treated as things that can be bought and sold like other property.

questions.correct_answer: (C) whether to clear a small part of a forest that will otherwise remain largely intact.

option_rationales.A: This is a whole-system valuation of the kind paragraph 3 says valuation is 'far less suited to'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says that for losses that are 'large, irreversible or system-wide' a rule that forbids them 'may serve better than any price'.
option_rationales.D: This is the critics' worry in paragraph 1 about commodification; it is a question of principle, not the kind of marginal comparison valuation is said to serve.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says valuation 'answers the question of what a little more or a little less of something is worth, given that most of it remains', and paragraph 4 says that for 'decisions at the margin, an explicit figure is better than an implicit zero'. Clearing a small part of a forest that otherwise remains is such a marginal decision.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the irreversible-loss option because valuation seems most needed when the stakes are highest, which is exactly where the author says prices fail.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the marginal-versus-total distinction in paragraph 3 with the rule in paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, a gas boom makes life harder for a country's exporting manufacturers because

options.A: a stronger currency prices their goods out of foreign markets while the booming sectors push up the wages they must pay.
options.B: the government taxes manufacturing more heavily in order to fund the expansion of the gas sector and its services.
options.C: cheaper imports of raw materials allow foreign rivals to set up competing factories inside the country.
options.D: their most skilled engineers and managers are recruited to run the government's new fund invested abroad.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a stronger currency prices their goods out of foreign markets while the booming sectors push up the wages they must pay.

option_rationales.B: The passage says the government 'collects more revenue' from the boom; it never mentions heavier taxes on manufacturers.
option_rationales.C: Cheaper imports are listed among the benign effects in paragraph 1; nothing is said about foreign rivals building factories inside the country.
option_rationales.D: The fund appears only in paragraph 4 as a remedy; the passage does not say it draws staff away from manufacturing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'A stronger currency makes their goods dearer in foreign markets, and the higher wages set by the booming sectors raise their costs at home.'
questions.common_misconception: Picking a plausible economic story that the passage does not tell.
questions.difficulty_reason: The two causes are stated together in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the view reported in paragraph 2 against the author's objection to it?

options.A: Funds invested abroad have slowed the rise of the currency in several countries that export large amounts of gas.
options.B: Countries with fertile land have tended, over long periods, to export more food than they import from abroad.
options.C: Workers who moved from factories into the gas sector during booms have usually earned more than they did before they moved.
options.D: Countries whose factories closed during commodity booms have usually rebuilt comparable export industries within a few years of prices falling.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Countries whose factories closed during commodity booms have usually rebuilt comparable export industries within a few years of prices falling.

option_rationales.A: This supports the author's remedy in paragraph 4, not the view that the shift out of manufacturing is harmless adjustment.
option_rationales.B: This merely restates the analogy used in paragraph 2; it does not address whether manufacturing can be regained after a boom.
option_rationales.C: The author already grants that 'wages climb' in the boom; higher pay does not answer the objection that lost capabilities cannot be regained.

questions.explanation: The author's objection is that the paragraph 2 view 'assumes that the sectors lost can be regained whenever conditions change', and that this assumption is doubtful. Evidence that such industries are in fact rebuilt quickly would confirm the assumption and so defend the view.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is consistent with the reported view but does not touch the assumption the author attacks.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be matched to the specific assumption named in paragraph 3.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards a resource boom as most damaging when

options.A: manufacturers fail to raise their productivity as fast as the wages they pay to workers in their factories.
options.B: a country decides to extract and sell its gas at all, instead of leaving the reserves untouched for later generations.
options.C: the windfall is spent at home so quickly that it drives up the currency and wages until other exporters disappear.
options.D: the national currency rises in value, whatever the government does with the revenue from the new exports.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the windfall is spent at home so quickly that it drives up the currency and wages until other exporters disappear.

option_rationales.A: Productivity growth in manufacturing is never discussed; the passage locates the cause in the currency and in wages set by the booming sectors.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'The remedy, then, is not to leave the gas in the ground', so extraction itself is not the harm.
option_rationales.D: The author proposes saving the windfall abroad precisely because it 'slows the rise of the currency'; the outcome depends on policy, not on any rise at all.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 contrasts managing the boom, by saving abroad and spending 'at a pace the economy can absorb without bidding up wages across the board', with treating 'a temporary gift as permanent income'. The damage the author fears comes from the second course, which hollows out other exporters.
questions.common_misconception: Treating any currency rise as harmful, when the author's concern is unmanaged spending of the windfall.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the remedy in paragraph 4 back into a diagnosis of when the harm occurs.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the concern the author raises in paragraph 3?

options.A: A city builds a costly stadium for a single sporting event and then finds that the stadium stands empty for most of the year.
options.B: A town lets its orchestra disband while a cheap rival holds its audience, and when interest returns finds its trained players and teachers gone for good.
options.C: A firm pays out an unusually profitable year's earnings as bonuses to its staff and later finds that it cannot meet its debts once its profits return to normal.
options.D: A farmer switches from wheat to rice when rice prices rise and switches back when they fall, losing little each time he changes crops.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A town lets its orchestra disband while a cheap rival holds its audience, and when interest returns finds its trained players and teachers gone for good.

option_rationales.A: This concerns wasteful investment, not capabilities that are lost under a temporary condition and cannot be rebuilt when it passes.
option_rationales.C: This resembles the warning in paragraph 4 about treating 'a temporary gift as permanent income', but it involves no loss of skills or capabilities, which is the concern of paragraph 3.
option_rationales.D: This is the frictionless reallocation the paragraph 2 view assumes; the author's concern is precisely that the switch back is not easy.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that capabilities 'take years to build and decay quickly' once their holders have gone, so that when a temporary condition passes, the country 'cannot simply return to where it was'. The orchestra case has the same structure: a passing condition removes an activity, and the skills it held do not come back.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the firm's bonuses, which matches the passage's final warning but not the specific mechanism of paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options match other parts of the passage, so the analogy must be fixed to paragraph 3's specific mechanism.

questions.question: The example of the household that sells its furniture (paragraph 2) is used to

options.A: show that national accounts already deduct the wear on machines and buildings when they calculate net product.
options.B: argue that welfare cannot be measured at all, since households commonly misunderstand their own finances.
options.C: show by analogy why counting the proceeds of running down an asset as income gives a misleading picture.
options.D: suggest that national governments, like households, should avoid selling any of their natural assets at all.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show by analogy why counting the proceeds of running down an asset as income gives a misleading picture.

option_rationales.A: The deduction for machines and buildings is a separate point made in the next sentence, which the furniture example does not illustrate.
option_rationales.B: The household is a hypothetical that would be 'judged to have misunderstood'; the passage does not claim households commonly do so or that welfare is unmeasurable.
option_rationales.D: The analogy is about how sales are recorded, not about whether they should happen; the passage never says assets should not be sold.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that oil revenue 'counts as income, though the oil in the ground was an asset'. The household that calls the proceeds of selling furniture 'salary' makes the same error in a familiar setting, which is why it 'would be judged to have misunderstood its own finances'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the analogy as advice about conduct instead of a point about accounting.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function must be separated from the neighbouring sentence about depreciation of machines.

questions.question: By the reasoning of paragraph 3, which of the following would add to GDP while leaving people no better off than they were before the damage occurred?

options.A: Families in a city whose air has worsened buy air purifiers so that the air in their homes is as clean as it used to be.
options.B: A hospital builds a new wing that allows it to treat far more patients each year than it was ever able to treat before.
options.C: A factory installs equipment that cuts its discharges into a river to well below the level they were at when it opened.
options.D: A government replants with trees a stretch of land that had been bare and unproductive for as long as anyone can remember.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Families in a city whose air has worsened buy air purifiers so that the air in their homes is as clean as it used to be.

option_rationales.B: This raises capacity beyond any earlier level; paragraph 3 concerns spending that 'merely repairs damage' and leaves people where they were.
option_rationales.C: This leaves the river cleaner than when the factory arrived, whereas the town in paragraph 3 ends up 'with no more clean water than it had before'.
option_rationales.D: This adds a new natural asset instead of restoring a loss, so it is not the defensive spending paragraph 3 describes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'Spending that merely repairs damage counts as output', and its example leaves the town 'with no more clean water than it had before'. Buying purifiers to restore indoor air to its former quality is defensive spending of the same kind.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an environmental improvement, which counts as output but does leave people better off.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are all spending that adds to GDP, so the correct answer must be picked on the 'no better off' condition.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards those critics who urge that GDP be abandoned is best described as one of

options.A: agreement, since the author has shown in two paragraphs that GDP misrepresents what happens to the environment.
options.B: indifference, as the author thinks that whether GDP is kept or dropped matters little beside the problem of valuation.
options.C: contempt, because the author holds that only those who misunderstand national accounts could make such a demand.
options.D: disagreement, on the ground that GDP still serves well the purposes for which it was built.

questions.correct_answer: (D) disagreement, on the ground that GDP still serves well the purposes for which it was built.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 opens 'It does not follow that GDP should be abandoned', so the author rejects their conclusion despite sharing their criticisms.
option_rationales.B: The author argues actively that GDP 'remains indispensable', which is not indifference to whether it is kept.
option_rationales.C: The author disagrees in measured terms and accepts the criticisms that motivate the critics; nothing suggests contempt for them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'It does not follow that GDP should be abandoned, as some of its critics urge', and gives the reason: 'For the purposes it was designed to serve ... it remains indispensable'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because the author criticises GDP, the author must side with those who would abandon it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the author's criticisms of GDP from the critics' conclusion.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author be most likely to accept?

options.A: Corrections for depletion should be built into GDP itself, so that a single headline figure reflects natural capital.
options.B: An account of changes in natural assets is worth publishing even if its estimates of depletion rest on uncertain assumptions.
options.C: The depletion of a fishery could be valued exactly once the rate at which its stock regenerates is known.
options.D: A country whose GDP is rising while its natural assets are falling must be growing poorer as a result.

questions.correct_answer: (B) An account of changes in natural assets is worth publishing even if its estimates of depletion rest on uncertain assumptions.

option_rationales.A: The author proposes accounts published 'alongside GDP', and says GDP remains indispensable for its original purposes, so merging the two goes beyond the passage.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says valuation also needs assumptions 'about future prices', so knowing the regeneration rate alone would not make it exact.
option_rationales.D: The author says such a country can be 'seen to be' drawing down capital, but never that it is necessarily poorer overall; that would need a comparison the passage does not make.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 concedes that valuing depletion 'requires assumptions' and that 'different assumptions yield very different answers', yet still proposes such accounts, ending: 'A figure that is imperfect but visible is likelier to change behaviour than a correct one that nobody computes.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that merges the correction into GDP, which follows the logic of paragraph 2 but not the proposal of paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: One option follows paragraph 2's logic but contradicts the more modest proposal of paragraph 4; another overstates degree.

questions.question: According to the passage, advocates of degrowth explain part of the apparent separation of output from emissions in rich economies as the result of

options.A: costs of clean power falling much faster than forecasters had predicted only a generation ago.
options.B: electricity being generated from cleaner sources and heavy industry giving way to services at home.
options.C: recessions that struck services harder than heavy industry and so reduced output faster than emissions.
options.D: polluting production having been moved to other countries instead of being avoided altogether.

questions.correct_answer: (D) polluting production having been moved to other countries instead of being avoided altogether.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 offers this as the author's reply to the degrowth case, not as part of that case.
option_rationales.B: These are the reasons green growth gives for decoupling in paragraph 1, not the degrowth explanation of why it is partly illusory.
option_rationales.C: This is the author's hypothetical in paragraph 3 about an economy shrinking while emissions rise; it is not attributed to degrowth.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Some of the apparent separation, it replies, reflects production moved abroad rather than pollution avoided'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing to degrowth an explanation that the passage assigns to green growth or to the author.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly, though each wrong option is drawn from elsewhere in the passage.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the claim that much of the separation of output from emissions is 'merely relative' means that

options.A: each unit of output has become cleaner, but output has grown enough to keep total emissions from falling.
options.B: the separation can be seen only when emissions are measured relative to imports instead of to output.
options.C: emissions have fallen in some rich countries only in relation to the higher emissions of poorer ones.
options.D: emissions and output have separated in absolute terms, though rather less in some sectors of the economy than in others.

questions.correct_answer: (A) each unit of output has become cleaner, but output has grown enough to keep total emissions from falling.

option_rationales.B: Imports are the subject of the first degrowth point, about production 'moved abroad'; 'relative' refers to emissions 'per unit of output'.
option_rationales.C: The passage contrasts relative decoupling with a fall in totals, not one country's emissions with another's.
option_rationales.D: This contradicts the meaning given in the passage: a relative fall is one 'swamped by the growth of output itself', so totals do not fall.

questions.explanation: The passage glosses the phrase at once: 'a fall in emissions per unit of output that is swamped by the growth of output itself'. Emissions intensity falls while total emissions do not.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'relative' as a comparison between countries or sectors.
questions.difficulty_reason: The gloss follows the phrase, but the wrong options offer other natural senses of 'relative'.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Because the cost of clean power has fallen so fast, emissions in rich countries will now decline quickly enough.
options.B: Proof that a rich country's emissions fell while its output rose would not by itself show that green growth is an adequate response.
options.C: Once the carbon embodied in imports is counted, no rich country has reduced its emissions while its output grew.
options.D: Those who favour degrowth are mistaken in wanting a different kind of society from the one that now exists.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Proof that a rich country's emissions fell while its output rose would not by itself show that green growth is an adequate response.

option_rationales.A: The author says only that past slowness 'does not show that it must remain so'; claiming the decline will be fast enough goes well beyond that.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says absolute decoupling 'has happened in a number of countries, even after allowing for the carbon embodied in their imports'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 sets their 'other reasons' for a different society aside without judging them; the author's point concerns only the environmental case.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the existence of absolute decoupling 'settles less than its champions suppose', because the question is whether emissions 'can fall fast enough'. A single instance of absolute decoupling therefore does not establish that green growth is enough.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the clean-power option, which turns the author's 'does not show that it must remain so' into a prediction of success.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author qualifies both sides, so each wrong option overstates one of the qualifications in a different direction.

questions.question: The two hypothetical economies in paragraph 3, one growing while its emissions fall and one shrinking while its emissions rise, serve mainly to

options.A: show that policy should aim to shift output from heavy industry towards services such as teaching, nursing and repairing.
options.B: show that green growth is correct to hold that output and emissions can move apart in rich economies.
options.C: show that the size of GDP is only loosely tied to environmental harm, so making it the target in either direction is a mistake.
options.D: show that recessions do more environmental damage than periods of growth, which counts against the case for degrowth.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that the size of GDP is only loosely tied to environmental harm, so making it the target in either direction is a mistake.

option_rationales.A: The author's proposal in paragraph 4 is to set limits 'directly on what does harm' and let output adjust; steering the composition of output is never proposed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 criticises both camps for treating GDP as 'the variable of interest'; the examples are not offered in support of either side.
option_rationales.D: The shrinking economy is offered as something that 'could' happen under one condition, not as a general claim about recessions, and the point is aimed at both camps.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says both camps take GDP as 'the variable of interest', then gives the two cases to show that output and emissions can move in either relation, concluding that targeting GDP 'is to aim at a proxy that is only loosely tied to the thing that matters'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the examples as support for one camp, when they are used against the shared assumption of both.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the examples target an assumption common to both camps, with two wrong options that each enlist them for a particular conclusion.

questions.question: It follows from the stance proposed in paragraph 4 that an advocate of degrowth who accepted it

options.A: would have to give up any wish for a different kind of society once the environmental limits were being met.
options.B: could still argue for a smaller economy, but not on the ground that the environment requires it once the limits are being met.
options.C: would treat any fall in output within the limits as a failure of policy that ought to be corrected.
options.D: would have to agree that output must keep rising, since growth within the limits would then be the aim of policy.

questions.correct_answer: (B) could still argue for a smaller economy, but not on the ground that the environment requires it once the limits are being met.

option_rationales.A: The author says the concession holds 'whatever other reasons they may have for wanting a different kind of society', so those reasons survive.
option_rationales.C: The passage says a fall in growth would be 'not a failure of policy but a possible result of it', and that concession is asked of green growth, not degrowth.
option_rationales.D: The stance is 'indifference to growth as such': output may 'rise or fall as it will', so rising output is not required.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: advocates of degrowth 'would have to accept that if the limits are met while output rises, there is no further environmental case for shrinking the economy, whatever other reasons they may have'. The environmental argument is given up; other arguments are not.
questions.common_misconception: Overreading the concession as abandoning every reason for degrowth.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires keeping the scope of the concession ('environmental case') separate from other motives the author leaves open.

questions.question: According to the passage, the drawback of assigning default carbon values to imports by product and by country is that such values

options.A: are set so high that most imports from poorer countries are excluded from the importing country's market altogether.
options.B: allow exporters to claim rebates that are larger than the carbon price they actually paid at home.
options.C: penalise clean producers located in dirty countries while rewarding dirty producers located in clean ones.
options.D: can be observed directly only by the government of the country where the goods were made.

questions.correct_answer: (C) penalise clean producers located in dirty countries while rewarding dirty producers located in clean ones.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about defaults being set high enough to exclude imports; the complaint about poorer countries concerns fairness, not exclusion.
option_rationales.B: Rebates for exporters are mentioned in paragraph 1 only as a possible part of the scheme; no abuse of rebates is described.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the plant, fuel and grid cannot be observed by the importing government; defaults are offered as a way round that, and their stated flaw is different.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Default values can be assigned by product and by country, but these penalise clean producers in dirty countries and reward dirty producers in clean ones.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the problem defaults are meant to solve (unobservable emissions) with the problem they create.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Leakage has been greatly overstated, so a country can price carbon alone without any measures at its border to protect its industry.
options.B: A border charge on carbon is the obvious answer to leakage, since it puts domestic and foreign producers on equal terms and removes any reason to relocate.
options.C: Border charges on carbon are protection dressed in green and will provoke retaliation, so countries should avoid introducing them.
options.D: A border charge on carbon is hard to administer and may meet a smaller threat than feared, yet if well designed it could draw other countries into pricing carbon.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A border charge on carbon is hard to administer and may meet a smaller threat than feared, yet if well designed it could draw other countries into pricing carbon.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 adds that the evidence comes from modest prices and 'may be a poor guide' to higher ones, and paragraph 4 still finds value in the border charge.
option_rationales.B: This is the case stated in paragraph 1, which paragraphs 2 and 3 then qualify; the author locates the charge's main value elsewhere, in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.C: The author reports this as the view of trading partners and says a charge will be read as protectionism only if it does none of the things listed in paragraph 4.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows the charge is hard to carry out, paragraph 3 that leakage may be overstated, and paragraph 4 that the charge's 'most important effect' may be as 'a lever, drawing other countries towards carbon pricing', depending on design. The correct answer combines these.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the proposal set out in paragraph 1, or the critics' view in paragraph 2, as the author's conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures one stage of the argument; the correct answer must hold the qualification and the reframing together.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 that the problem of leakage has been overstated?

options.A: When one region's carbon price rose to a high level, its heavy industries moved a large share of their output to regions with no such price.
options.B: Managers of industrial firms report that access to markets is the main consideration when they decide where to build a plant.
options.C: Several heavy industries in countries with carbon prices have received free allowances that shield them from most of the cost.
options.D: Across most industries, differences in wages between countries turn out to be far larger than differences in the cost of carbon.

questions.correct_answer: (A) When one region's carbon price rose to a high level, its heavy industries moved a large share of their output to regions with no such price.

option_rationales.B: This is consistent with paragraph 3, which lists 'access to markets' among the factors that outweigh the cost of carbon.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 already mentions this; it explains why past evidence may understate leakage but shows no relocation having occurred.
option_rationales.D: This supports paragraph 3's point that carbon is 'a small share of total costs beside labour', so it strengthens the claim instead of weakening it.

questions.explanation: The claim rests on evidence from modest prices, and paragraph 3 warns that 'the past may be a poor guide to the effect of prices high enough to matter'. Evidence of large relocation once a price became high would show that leakage is a real threat where it counts.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the free-allowance option because it appears in the passage as a caveat, though it does not itself show relocation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options support the claim and one restates a caveat; only the correct answer provides contrary evidence.

questions.question: The exporting country's reasoning described in paragraph 4, which lets a border charge work as 'a lever', depends on the charge being one that

options.A: lets the importing country keep all of its revenue, so that it can be spent on reducing emissions at home.
options.B: applies only to trading partners whose own carbon prices are already as high as the importing country's price.
options.C: is set high enough to stop most imports from countries that have not yet introduced a price on carbon.
options.D: is reduced or waived for goods whose makers have already paid a carbon price in their own country.

questions.correct_answer: (D) is reduced or waived for goods whose makers have already paid a carbon price in their own country.

option_rationales.A: The author recommends directing 'some of its revenue to helping poorer exporters', and the lever does not depend on where the importer spends its revenue.
option_rationales.B: Partners already pricing carbon at that level have nothing left to be drawn towards; the lever is meant to act on those who do not yet price carbon.
option_rationales.C: A charge that stopped imports would be the 'wall' the author contrasts with a lever; the lever works by changing other governments' choices, not by blocking trade.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says an exporting country prefers 'that its own government levy an equivalent price at home, so that the revenue stays at home'. That reasoning holds only if a price paid at home spares exporters the border charge, which is why the author lists a charge 'that credits carbon prices already paid abroad'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the high-charge option, which treats the charge as a barrier, the very idea the author sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: The condition is not stated as such; it must be reconstructed from the exporter's incentive and the design features listed later.

questions.question: The phrase 'not unreasonably' in the final sentence indicates that the author

options.A: believes that poorer exporting countries would be right to retaliate against every carbon charge at the border.
options.B: would think the charge of protectionism justified against a border charge lacking the design features just listed.
options.C: considers the critics unreasonable in their accusation but understands why they feel aggrieved by it.
options.D: regards the charge of protectionism as valid against any border adjustment, however carefully it is designed and presented.

questions.correct_answer: (B) would think the charge of protectionism justified against a border charge lacking the design features just listed.

option_rationales.A: The author mentions retaliation only as a possible outcome that depends on design; no judgement that retaliation would be right is made.
option_rationales.C: 'Not unreasonably' means the reading is reasonable; this option reverses the phrase.
option_rationales.D: The preceding sentence says a well-designed charge 'has a chance of being accepted as what it claims to be', so the author limits the judgement to badly designed ones.

questions.explanation: The final sentence concerns a charge that 'does none of these things', and says it will be read 'not unreasonably' as protectionism. The author thus grants the critics' reading in that case, while the previous sentence shows a well-designed charge might be accepted.
questions.common_misconception: Extending the author's concession to every border adjustment.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading a litotes precisely and keeping its scope to the case described in the same sentence.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that average differences between human populations are environmental rather than genetic.
options.B: correct a widespread habit of treating heritability as a measure of how unchangeable a trait is.
options.C: explain how breeders use heritability to predict how quickly a herd will respond to selection.
options.D: show that heritability estimates are too unreliable to be of use to breeders or to researchers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) correct a widespread habit of treating heritability as a measure of how unchangeable a trait is.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says only that a gap between groups 'need not be' genetic; the passage never asserts that actual human group differences are environmental, so this overstates and widens its claim.
option_rationales.C: Breeding is mentioned in a single clause of paragraph 4 as an example of proper use; it is a detail, not the purpose of the passage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this makes heritability useless' and gives breeders and researchers as legitimate users, so the option reverses the author's view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 names the error of hearing heritability as 'a claim about destiny', paragraphs 2 and 3 show why the reading fails, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'The fault lies not with the statistic but with the habit of reading it as a measure of fixity'. The passage exists to correct that habit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about group differences, which magnifies one paragraph into a sweeping empirical claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option turns a careful 'need not be' into a positive claim; the correct answer needs the whole arc of the passage.

questions.question: According to the passage, if every child in a group received exactly the same diet, schooling and care, the heritability of most traits would rise because

options.A: the environmental differences among the children would have been removed, leaving mainly genetic ones.
options.B: identical upbringing would allow the children's genes to exert a stronger influence on development.
options.C: children raised in identical conditions come to resemble their parents more closely in every trait.
options.D: measurements taken in uniform settings are more precise than measurements taken in varied ones.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the environmental differences among the children would have been removed, leaving mainly genetic ones.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the rise would happen 'not because genes had become more powerful', which directly rejects this explanation.
option_rationales.C: The passage never discusses resemblance to parents; the explanation it gives is the removal of environmental differences.
option_rationales.D: Precision of measurement is not mentioned anywhere; the rise is explained by what varies in the group, not by how it is measured.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says heritability would rise 'because the environmental differences had been taken away', so the differences that remain are largely genetic.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'stronger genes' option, which the passage explicitly rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence and the main wrong option is explicitly denied there.

questions.question: The example of finger number in paragraph 2 is used to show that

options.A: accidents are the main source of variation in most human physical traits.
options.B: developmental programmes are more dependable than environmental influences on the body.
options.C: a trait built by a genetic programme can still show low heritability.
options.D: heritability rises whenever the environments of a group are made more uniform.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a trait built by a genetic programme can still show low heritability.

option_rationales.A: The passage says injury explains variation in finger number only; it makes no claim about most human traits, so the option overgeneralises.
option_rationales.B: The passage compares no such dependability; the example concerns what heritability measures, not which influence is more reliable.
option_rationales.D: That is the first consequence in paragraph 2, illustrated by identical upbringing; the finger example introduces the 'Second' consequence, which is a different point.

questions.explanation: The example follows 'Second, a trait can be built almost entirely by genes and still show low heritability': fingers are built by a genomic programme, yet the variation in their number is 'mainly environmental'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the example to the first consequence in the same paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence introducing the example states its function.

questions.question: A study finds that within each of two towns, differences in children's reading scores are highly heritable, and that the average score in one town is well above that in the other. Which conclusion is most consistent with the passage?

options.A: Reading scores in the lower town cannot be raised much by improving its schools or its libraries.
options.B: The gap between the towns must be largely genetic, since heritability is high within each town.
options.C: The study must be mistaken, since a trait cannot be heritable within towns that differ on average.
options.D: The gap between the towns could be produced entirely by differences between their schools or homes.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The gap between the towns could be produced entirely by differences between their schools or homes.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a highly heritable trait 'may still be changed by changing the environment', so reading heritability as fixity is the error the passage attacks.
option_rationales.B: This is exactly the inference paragraph 3 calls 'the most consequential error'; high heritability within groups is compatible with a gap that 'has no genetic basis at all'.
option_rationales.C: The seed example in paragraph 3 shows that high heritability within each plot and a large gap between plots can coexist, so nothing here is contradictory.

questions.explanation: The towns correspond to the two plots in paragraph 3: within each, variation can be largely genetic, while the difference between them may be due 'entirely to the soil', here the schools or homes.
questions.common_misconception: Treating within-group heritability as evidence about the cause of a between-group gap.
questions.difficulty_reason: A direct transfer of the seed-plot analogy to a new case.

questions.question: According to the passage, a signal that any animal can produce

options.A: is preferred by females because it costs its bearer very little to display.
options.B: soon stops telling the receiver anything about the animal that sends it.
options.C: is the kind most often found among antelope when they spot a predator.
options.D: is eventually replaced by an ornament that females come to find more beautiful.

questions.correct_answer: (B) soon stops telling the receiver anything about the animal that sends it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 argues the reverse: the cost is 'the very thing that keeps the signal reliable', so cheapness is no ground for preference.
option_rationales.C: The antelope leap is offered in paragraph 3 as a display that 'could not be produced' by an unfit animal, the opposite of a signal anyone can produce.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing of cheap signals being replaced by more beautiful ones; it says only that they 'carry no information'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends: 'A cheap signal could be produced by anyone, and a signal that anyone can produce soon carries no information.'
questions.common_misconception: Connecting the antelope example to cheap signals because both appear near the middle of the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in a single sentence.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'the embarrassment' that the reply 'turns ... into the explanation' refers to

options.A: the burden that an extravagant ornament places on the animal that carries it.
options.B: Darwin's failure to propose any explanation at all for why such ornaments exist.
options.C: the awkwardness of the courtship display that the peacock performs before females.
options.D: the difficulty that females face in judging which of many males is healthiest.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the burden that an extravagant ornament places on the animal that carries it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says Darwin did propose an explanation, female preference; the embarrassment is the cost of the tail, not a gap in Darwin's work.
option_rationales.C: The passage describes the tail as 'awkward in flight', not the courtship as awkward; the embarrassment is the tail's cost to survival.
option_rationales.D: Female difficulty in judging males is never called an embarrassment; the word in paragraph 1 refers to the heavy, conspicuous tail.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 calls the peacock's tail 'an embarrassment' for a view of selection as an 'editor of waste', because it is heavy and dangerous. Paragraph 2 makes that very costliness the reason the signal is reliable.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'embarrassment' as a personal failure of Darwin's rather than as the costly trait.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reference is fixed by the first sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The remark that 'a signal equally costly for all would sort no one' (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: the more expensive a display is in absolute terms, the more reliably it identifies the fittest males.
options.B: most of the ornaments seen in nature cost every member of a species roughly the same amount.
options.C: females are unable to tell males apart once every male in a population has an ornament.
options.D: a display reveals quality only if weaker animals find it harder to bear than stronger ones do.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a display reveals quality only if weaker animals find it harder to bear than stronger ones do.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says what matters 'is not that a signal is expensive in absolute terms', so tying reliability to sheer expense reverses the point.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about how costs are distributed among most real ornaments; the remark is about what would follow if costs were equal.
option_rationales.C: The remark concerns signals of equal cost, not the mere presence of ornaments; males with ornaments may still differ in how well they bear them.

questions.explanation: The preceding clause says a signal works when it is 'more expensive for weak individuals than for strong ones'. If the cost fell equally, every animal could bear it to the same degree and the display would not distinguish strong from weak.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'more expensive is more reliable' option, which keeps the theme of cost but misses the point about unequal cost.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option matches the general idea of paragraph 2 but contradicts the refinement in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the costly-signal explanation is best described as

options.A: neutral, setting out the explanation without indicating any judgement of its merits.
options.B: sceptical, regarding it as an ingenious proposal that has gathered little real support.
options.C: appreciative of what it explains while insistent that it does not explain everything.
options.D: unreserved, treating it as a complete account of why ornaments evolve in animals.

questions.correct_answer: (C) appreciative of what it explains while insistent that it does not explain everything.

option_rationales.A: The author judges the idea explicitly, both in its favour and in the qualification 'not why every display exists', so the stance is not neutral.
option_rationales.B: The author calls it 'influential', extends it to antelope and says it 'explains why many displays can be trusted'; nothing suggests it lacks support.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says it would be 'a mistake ... to treat costliness as the whole story' and gives a rival mechanism, so the author is not unreserved.

questions.explanation: The author presents the idea favourably in paragraphs 2 and 3, then limits it in paragraph 4: it 'explains why many displays can be trusted, not why every display exists'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking 'unreserved' after reading only the middle paragraphs.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires weighing the favourable exposition against the closing qualification.

questions.question: The comparison with the fragility of a glass in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that camouflaged moths are, in practice, as easily destroyed as glassware on a shelf.
options.B: show that fitness, like fragility, can be established only after the organism has died or survived.
options.C: argue that chance matters more than inherited traits in deciding which organisms survive.
options.D: show that fitness can be a real property of an organism even when outcomes fail to display it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that fitness can be a real property of an organism even when outcomes fail to display it.

option_rationales.A: This reads the analogy literally; the glass is compared to the moth only in that both have dispositions that may go undisplayed.
option_rationales.B: The passage says fitness can be established 'independently', by measuring predation, before any outcome; the option reverses the point of the analogy.
option_rationales.C: The passage allows that chance can override fitness in particular cases, but it never ranks chance above traits in general.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls fitness 'a disposition that holds whether or not it is ever displayed'. The glass that never breaks and the moth that dies by accident both show that a single outcome does not refute the disposition.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the analogy literally or as a claim about the power of chance.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence that introduces the comparison.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the existence of drift as

options.A: evidence that fitness and the actual record of reproduction are not the same thing.
options.B: the main reason why biologists usually measure fitness by counting offspring.
options.C: a difficulty that the propensity view of fitness cannot yet satisfactorily explain.
options.D: a sign that natural selection does not operate at all in small populations.

questions.correct_answer: (A) evidence that fitness and the actual record of reproduction are not the same thing.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says biologists count offspring 'because propensities are hard to observe directly'; drift is not given as the reason.
option_rationales.C: The author says the distinction 'explains why biologists speak of drift', so drift supports rather than troubles the propensity view.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says only that in small populations 'the lucky can outbreed the fit'; that chance can override selection does not mean selection ceases to operate.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that drift would be 'unintelligible' if fitness meant survival, because there would be 'no gap between expectation and outcome for chance to fill'. Drift therefore shows the gap between fitness and the reproductive record.
questions.common_misconception: Overextending 'the lucky can outbreed the fit' into the claim that selection is absent.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the drift sentence back to the definition of fitness in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the complaint that natural selection is a tautology?

options.A: Some predictions made by applying the theory of natural selection to particular populations have turned out to be false.
options.B: For most traits, the only available way to tell which variant raises expected reproduction is to see which variant has in fact left more offspring.
options.C: In some populations, the variants that ecological analysis rates fittest sometimes leave fewer offspring than other variants do.
options.D: Field biologists studying wild populations usually estimate the fitness of a variant by counting the offspring it leaves.

questions.correct_answer: (B) For most traits, the only available way to tell which variant raises expected reproduction is to see which variant has in fact left more offspring.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 cites failed predictions as proof that the theory is not a tautology, so this finding supports the author's reply.
option_rationales.C: The author expects this: paragraph 3 says 'the lucky can outbreed the fit' and treats such gaps as support for the propensity view, so it does not weaken the reply.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 already concedes that biologists 'often measure fitness by counting offspring' and argues that this is evidence for a disposition, not its definition.

questions.explanation: The reply depends on fitness being identifiable 'independently', by analysing traits as in the moth example. If, for most traits, fitness could be identified only through which variant reproduced more, the propensity would collapse back into the record and the complaint would regain force.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a fact that sounds damaging (unfit outbreeding fit, offspring counting, failed predictions) without checking that the author has already absorbed it.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options look like objections but are anticipated by the author; the correct answer targets the hidden assumption of independent identification.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: Loose writing about fitness can blur the difference between measuring it and defining it.
options.B: Whether a variant is fitter can, at least in some cases, be established without counting its offspring.
options.C: Predictions derived from natural selection have so far been confirmed whenever they were tested.
options.D: In small populations, organisms that are less fit can leave more offspring than fitter ones.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Predictions derived from natural selection have so far been confirmed whenever they were tested.

option_rationales.A: Supported: paragraph 4 says 'careless writing can slide from the measurement to the definition'.
option_rationales.B: Supported: paragraph 2 says the dark moth's advantage can be established 'independently, by measuring how often birds find each kind of moth'.
option_rationales.D: Supported: paragraph 3 says 'in small populations the lucky can outbreed the fit'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says predictions 'are tested constantly, and some fail', and treats those failures as the mark of a non-tautological theory. A claim that every prediction has been confirmed contradicts the passage.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that an author defending a theory must claim its predictions always succeed.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each supported statement paraphrases a different paragraph; the unsupported one reverses a short clause.

questions.question: Which of the following does the passage cite as evidence against the argument based on the peculiar inheritance of ants, bees and wasps?

options.A: A worker that never reproduces cannot pass on the traits that make it a good worker.
options.B: Males in ants, bees and wasps develop from eggs that have not been fertilised.
options.C: Termites, which lack that pattern of inheritance, have also evolved sterile castes.
options.D: Workers in social insect colonies typically raise relatives rather than unrelated young.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Termites, which lack that pattern of inheritance, have also evolved sterile castes.

option_rationales.A: This is the puzzle in paragraph 1 that troubled Darwin; it is not one of the objections listed against the later argument.
option_rationales.B: This is the starting point of the argument in paragraph 3, so it cannot be evidence against it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 offers this in support of the general kinship principle, not as evidence against the argument from inheritance.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists three problems for the argument, the first being that 'Termites, whose inheritance has no such peculiarity, have sterile castes too'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a statement that appears in the passage but plays a different role.
questions.difficulty_reason: The objections are listed in one sentence.

questions.question: In describing sterility as 'an extreme point on a continuum of helping' (paragraph 2), the author implies that

options.A: sterility in insects evolved earlier than the milder forms of helping seen among relatives.
options.B: helping relatives is common only in those insect species whose workers are sterile.
options.C: workers lose the ability to reproduce as a consequence of the effort spent raising siblings.
options.D: sterile workers differ from other helpful relatives in how far they help, not in the kind of explanation they need.

questions.correct_answer: (D) sterile workers differ from other helpful relatives in how far they help, not in the kind of explanation they need.

option_rationales.A: A continuum concerns degree, not chronology; the passage says nothing about which form of helping appeared first.
option_rationales.B: The phrase places sterility at one end of a range of helping, which implies that milder helping exists elsewhere; the option restricts helping to sterile species.
option_rationales.C: The passage treats sterility as a strategy favoured when helping pays more, not as damage caused by the work of helping, so the option reverses the relation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says sterility 'is not an anomaly to be explained away' but lies on a continuum, so the same calculation of benefit, relatedness and cost that explains ordinary helping explains sterility, which is simply its limit.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'continuum' as a sequence in time, or reversing cause and effect.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the metaphor against the preceding 'not an anomaly' clause.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 functions in the passage mainly to

options.A: present an appealing refinement of the kinship argument and then show why it proved inadequate.
options.B: show that biologists have since abandoned the general kinship argument set out in paragraph 2.
options.C: explain why Darwin's proposal that selection acts on the family was eventually rejected.
options.D: supply the decisive evidence that ecological conditions, not kinship, explain sterile castes.

questions.correct_answer: (A) present an appealing refinement of the kinship argument and then show why it proved inadequate.
