option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'The lesson is not that kinship is irrelevant' and that the principle 'remains the best account', so the general argument survives.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 criticises the argument from peculiar inheritance, a later refinement; Darwin's family idea is developed in paragraph 2, not rejected.
option_rationales.D: Ecological conditions are introduced only in paragraph 4, and there they are combined with kinship rather than set against it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 introduces the 'almost too neat' argument from inheritance, notes it 'was widely taught', and then says 'It has not survived well', giving three objections.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the rejection of the refinement with rejection of kinship explanations as a whole.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option overstates the rejection to cover paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Kinship plays only a minor part in explaining why workers in insect colonies forgo reproduction.
options.B: Two insect species with similar relatedness among nestmates might differ in whether sterile castes evolve, because of differences in their surroundings.
options.C: Sterile castes are unlikely to evolve in any species whose nestmates are only modestly related to one another.
options.D: Where a queen mates with several males, the colony cannot sustain a caste of sterile workers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Two insect species with similar relatedness among nestmates might differ in whether sterile castes evolve, because of differences in their surroundings.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the general kinship principle 'remains the best account' of why workers can forgo reproduction, so this understates its role.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says ecological conditions 'can tip the balance even where relatedness is modest', so the author would reject this.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 cites multiple mating only as diluting relatedness and weakening one argument; it never says sterile castes then become impossible.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 makes relatedness 'only one term in the calculation' and says ecological conditions raise the benefit of helping. Holding relatedness equal, different conditions could therefore lead to different outcomes.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the dilution of relatedness as fatal to sterile castes, which keeps the rejected argument's logic.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option echoes a real sentence but shifts its strength; the correct answer must be derived from the final paragraph's two-factor view.

questions.question: According to the passage, a change to one of a toolkit gene's switches can be less disruptive than a change to the gene itself because

options.A: switches are shared by almost all animals, whereas toolkit genes differ from lineage to lineage.
options.B: a change to the gene would alter where its protein is made but not the shape of the protein.
options.C: changes to switches arise far more often than changes to the toolkit genes that they regulate.
options.D: a switch can alter a single structure while leaving the others in which the gene acts untouched.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a switch can alter a single structure while leaving the others in which the gene acts untouched.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the toolkit genes themselves are shared 'across almost the entire animal kingdom', so the contrast is false.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says it is switch changes that alter when and where genes act 'without any change in the proteins', so this reverses the roles.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about how often switch changes arise; its reason concerns the range of structures each change affects.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'a change to the gene itself would tend to disrupt many structures at once, whereas a change to one of its switches can alter a single structure and leave the rest alone'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing which change leaves the protein intact.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in one sentence.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, 'a shared plan' most nearly means

options.A: an inherited timetable fixing the order in which each organ appears during growth.
options.B: a common design for the structures that the developmental genes bring into being.
options.C: an intention that guides evolution towards a fixed and predetermined final form.
options.D: a common set of genes that decide where the head, limbs and segments of a body form.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a common design for the structures that the developmental genes bring into being.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not discuss the order in which organs appear; it glosses the idea as 'a common design for what is controlled'.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the passage concerns purpose or direction in evolution; 'plan' refers to the design of the organs themselves.
option_rationales.D: That describes the toolkit, which the author accepts is shared; the sentence contrasts 'the shared toolkit' with 'a shared plan', so the two cannot mean the same thing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 contrasts the shared toolkit with a shared plan and then restates the point: common genes show 'a deep common ancestry of the control system, not a common design for what is controlled'.
questions.common_misconception: Equating 'plan' with the toolkit itself, the very thing the sentence distinguishes it from.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is the term the phrase is set against.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an example of 'the opposite error' described in paragraph 4?

options.A: Concluding that the hearts of two distant animals must be built alike because the same gene starts heart formation in both.
options.B: Concluding that the eyes of insects and vertebrates were assembled separately, since their structures differ.
options.C: Concluding that much change in animal form has come from altered switches rather than from new proteins.
options.D: Concluding that a fly and a mouse share no developmental genes because their bodies look so different.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Concluding that the hearts of two distant animals must be built alike because the same gene starts heart formation in both.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 itself says the structures downstream of the switch 'were assembled separately', so the author holds this view rather than calling it an error.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'there is much truth in that' and explains why, so the author accepts this conclusion rather than treating it as a mistake.
option_rationales.D: This is the older error, that 'different forms require different genes'; the opposite error runs from similar genes to similar forms.

questions.explanation: The opposite error is 'assuming that similar genes imply similar forms'. Inferring the same heart construction from a shared starting gene is exactly that, just as a shared eye switch does not make fly and mouse eyes 'the same organ'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the older error because it is also called wrong in the same sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the author endorses and one is the other named error; the correct answer requires matching the precise direction of the inference.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the organisation of the passage?

options.A: A discovery about eyes is described, its practical uses in medicine are listed, and objections to it are dismissed.
options.B: Two rival theories of animal form are set out, the evidence for each is weighed, and one is finally preferred.
options.C: An expectation is overturned by a discovery, whose lesson is then accepted in part and guarded against overextension.
options.D: A puzzle about form is posed, several proposed solutions are rejected in turn, and the question is left open.

questions.correct_answer: (C) An expectation is overturned by a discovery, whose lesson is then accepted in part and guarded against overextension.

option_rationales.A: No practical or medical uses are mentioned, and the final paragraph limits an inference rather than dismissing objections.
option_rationales.B: The passage does not stage two rival theories; it reports how one expectation was overturned and then qualifies the lesson drawn from that.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not reject a series of solutions or leave its question open; it grants that switch rewiring has 'much truth in' it and states a clear conclusion.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the expectation and the surprise, paragraph 2 gives the eye evidence, paragraph 3 accepts the rewiring lesson ('much truth in that'), and paragraph 4 warns against the 'opposite error'.
questions.common_misconception: Seeing the older view and the newer enthusiasm as two rival theories weighed evenly.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires an overview of all four paragraphs.

questions.question: According to the passage, during ordinary stretches of geological time the species more likely to vanish are those that

options.A: belong to groups that have long lived in the shadow of their competitors.
options.B: depend on a narrow range of foods, occupy small areas or breed slowly.
options.C: are large-bodied and unable to wait out a period of scarcity in a dormant state.
options.D: had flourished for a very long time under conditions that were stable.

questions.correct_answer: (B) depend on a narrow range of foods, occupy small areas or breed slowly.

option_rationales.A: The passage gives the marginal mammals as survivors of a mass extinction, not as typical victims of ordinary extinction.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 lists small size and dormancy as traits that mattered in the end-Cretaceous catastrophe, not as the factors at work in ordinary times.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says flourishing groups can be swept away in mass extinctions; it does not say this happens in ordinary times.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: in ordinary times 'species with narrow diets, small ranges or slow breeding are more likely to vanish when conditions shift'.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying the catastrophe traits of paragraph 2 back to ordinary times.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author calls the traits that aided survival at the end of the Cretaceous 'accidents' (paragraph 2) because they

options.A: show that survival in a mass extinction was decided by pure chance rather than by traits.
options.B: appeared suddenly in the surviving animals in the years just after the asteroid struck.
options.C: had not arisen as adaptations to the kind of crisis in which they turned out to be decisive.
options.D: gave no real advantage during the crisis to the animals that happened to possess them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) had not arisen as adaptations to the kind of crisis in which they turned out to be decisive.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says mass extinctions are not 'pure lotteries' and that survival in them 'is selective', so the option contradicts the author.
option_rationales.B: The passage says the traits were already present and 'had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe'; it never says they appeared after the impact.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says these traits 'determined survival in the aftermath', so they plainly gave an advantage.

questions.explanation: The sentence before the word explains it: 'Such traits had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe of this kind, which no living lineage had experienced.' They were accidents relative to the crisis, not useless or random in effect.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'accidents' as meaning that survival was a lottery.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option merges the trait's origin with the outcome of selection.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about the mammals in paragraph 3?

options.A: Large mammals with specialised diets also died out at the end of the Cretaceous, while small mammals with varied diets survived.
options.B: Some mammals of the late Cretaceous had larger brains in proportion to their bodies than dinosaurs of a similar size.
options.C: After the crisis, mammals diversified rapidly into many of the ways of life that the dinosaurs had once occupied.
options.D: Several groups of dinosaurs had already been declining in number of species for some time before the asteroid struck.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Large mammals with specialised diets also died out at the end of the Cretaceous, while small mammals with varied diets survived.

option_rationales.B: This hints at a general superiority of mammals, the very reading paragraph 3 says their success does not support, so it does not strengthen the claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 already says a marginal group 'inherits an emptied world'; rapid diversification says nothing about whether their survival reflected superiority.
option_rationales.D: This suggests the dinosaurs were failing before the crisis, which supports the 'tournament' picture the author rejects and so weakens the claim.

questions.explanation: The claim is that mammals survived because they 'passed through a narrow gate', not because they were superior. If being a mammal did not protect large specialised mammals, while the crisis traits of paragraph 2 did, survival tracked those traits rather than any general mammalian superiority.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the diversification option, which is consistent with the passage but neutral on the claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is neutral and two point the wrong way; the correct answer needs the claim stated precisely.

questions.question: The author would be LEAST likely to accept which of the following?

options.A: Explaining which groups exist today requires knowing both how well they were adapted and what catastrophes occurred.
options.B: The diversification of groups that survive a mass extinction proceeds through ordinary natural selection.
options.C: The extinction of a lineage need not show that it was poorly suited to the conditions it normally faced.
options.D: Because the traits that mattered in mass extinctions were accidents, the survivors of those events were not selected at all.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Because the traits that mattered in mass extinctions were accidents, the survivors of those events were not selected at all.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts this: it restates the last sentence, which calls for knowing 'how well they fitted their world' and 'which rare disasters' occurred.
option_rationales.B: The author accepts this: paragraph 4 says the survivors 'went on to diversify through ordinary selection once the crisis had passed'.
option_rationales.C: The author accepts this: paragraph 3 says a flourishing group 'would probably have continued to flourish under normal conditions' and yet was swept away.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 insists that 'Survival in them is selective; it simply selects for different things.' The traits were accidents only in that they had not evolved for catastrophes; selection still acted on them, so the correct answer contradicts the author.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'accidents' to mean that no selection took place.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the origin of a trait from whether selection acts on it, a fine distinction drawn across paragraphs 2 and 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, the discovery that strengthened the replicator-first case was that RNA

options.A: is the molecule in which the cell stores most of its instructions for building proteins.
options.B: can copy itself with high accuracy in water without the help of any protein at all.
options.C: forms readily from simple ingredients and a source of energy near hot springs on the sea floor.
options.D: can speed up chemical reactions as well as carry information.

questions.correct_answer: (D) can speed up chemical reactions as well as carry information.

option_rationales.A: The passage says information is stored in nucleic acids and calls RNA a relative of DNA; it does not say RNA stores most instructions, and that is not the discovery reported.
option_rationales.B: No such ability is reported; paragraph 3 says RNA building blocks are 'prone to fall apart in water', and paragraph 4 speaks only of 'modest accuracy'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the reverse: RNA's building blocks are 'hard to make without the help of enzymes'; simple ingredients describe reaction networks.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'RNA, it turned out, can not only carry information but also catalyse reactions', which is why a world in which RNA did both jobs would dissolve the chicken-and-egg problem.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that attributes the metabolism camp's ingredients to RNA.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In arguing that 'something like inheritance exists before any gene' (paragraph 3), metabolism-first theorists are responding chiefly to

options.A: the discovery that the cell's protein-building machinery is made largely of RNA.
options.B: the claim that a network without heredity has no means of building up improvements.
options.C: the claim that the building blocks of RNA are difficult to make without enzymes.
options.D: the proposal that life began on mineral surfaces near hot springs on the sea floor.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the claim that a network without heredity has no means of building up improvements.

option_rationales.A: The discovery supports the RNA world, but the inheritance point addresses heredity, not the evidence of the protein-building machinery.
option_rationales.C: That difficulty is the metabolism camp's own objection to the RNA world in paragraph 3, so they are not responding to it.
option_rationales.D: That setting belongs to the metabolism camp's own account in paragraph 1; they would not be answering it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends with the replicator camp's 'deeper argument' that a network 'cannot accumulate improvements, because there is nothing to record which variants did better'. The reply that heredity 'need not wait for a dedicated molecule' answers precisely that.
questions.common_misconception: Matching the reply to the nearest preceding point (the chemistry problem) instead of to the argument it answers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reply and the argument it answers are a paragraph apart, with other material between them.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the phrase 'in a chemical vacuum' refers to

options.A: the absence of any earlier chemistry to supply materials and energy.
options.B: a stage of history in which no selection among competing molecules had yet begun.
options.C: a setting without the RNA molecules on which all later living things came to rely.
options.D: a region of space entirely empty of matter, where no molecules could exist.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the absence of any earlier chemistry to supply materials and energy.

option_rationales.B: The phrase concerns where materials and energy came from, as the preceding sentence on metabolism theorists makes clear, not whether selection had begun.
option_rationales.C: The weak claim concerns replicators assembling themselves, so the missing element is the supporting chemistry, not RNA itself.
option_rationales.D: This reads the phrase literally; paragraph 4 uses it for the replicator camp's weakest claim, that replicators formed without a supporting chemistry.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says metabolism theorists explain 'where the materials and energy for any such molecule came from'. The replicator camp's weakest claim is that replicators could form without such a setting, that is, 'in a chemical vacuum'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the phrase literally, or confusing the missing chemistry with RNA.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning must be built from the contrast drawn in the preceding sentences.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Replicator and metabolism theorists often address different questions, which is why each wins easy points against the other's weakest claim.
options.B: Because replicators could not have assembled themselves unaided, the metabolism-first account of life's origin is the more plausible one.
options.C: Accounts giving priority to replication or to self-sustaining chemistry are better read as describing successive stages than as rivals.
options.D: Because the earliest stages of life left almost no record, the question of which came first should be set aside as unanswerable.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Accounts giving priority to replication or to self-sustaining chemistry are better read as describing successive stages than as rivals.

option_rationales.A: This is the point of paragraph 4 only; the passage uses it as a step towards the claim in paragraph 5 that the two describe a sequence, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.B: The author does not choose a side: paragraph 4 calls each answer 'hard to dispute' for its own stage, and paragraph 5 combines them.
option_rationales.D: The author does set aside 'which came first', but because it is the wrong framing, not because it is unanswerable; the lost rocks are mentioned only as limiting the details.

questions.explanation: The passage sets out both camps, shows in paragraph 4 that each answers a different question, and concludes in paragraph 5 that the problem is 'one of sequence rather than of priority', with self-maintaining chemistry giving rise to inherited information.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the paragraph 4 summary, which is accurate but only a step in the argument, or the 'unanswerable' option, which gives the right conclusion for the wrong reason.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to the author's own words; one is too narrow and the other supplies a false reason.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the 'easy points' mentioned in paragraph 4 are won by

options.A: attacking claims that a staged account combining both views would not need to make.
options.B: raising questions about the earliest stages of life that can now never be answered.
options.C: the metabolism camp alone, through its criticisms of the chemistry of the RNA world.
options.D: showing that the central thesis of the opposing camp is mistaken about life's origin.

questions.correct_answer: (A) attacking claims that a staged account combining both views would not need to make.

option_rationales.B: The unrecoverable details are mentioned in paragraph 5 as a limit on the author's own view; the easy points concern weak claims, not unanswerable questions.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'each side scores easy points' and names a weak claim on each side, so the points are not won by one camp alone.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls each camp's central answer 'hard to dispute' for its own stage; the points are scored against the 'weakest claim', not the central thesis.

questions.explanation: The two weak claims are that replicators formed 'in a chemical vacuum' and that networks evolved 'indefinitely without anything like genes'. The sequence proposed in paragraph 5, chemistry first supplying the setting and replicators then taking over, asserts neither, so the points count only against the rival framing.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the points refute a camp's main thesis, when the author says each thesis is hard to dispute.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the weak claims of paragraph 4 to the synthesis in paragraph 5.

questions.question: The image of the ball in paragraph 2 implies that

options.A: the outcomes of evolution are fixed in advance by the physical shape of the environment.
options.B: the history of a lineage is of no use in understanding what that lineage became.
options.C: an end point reached by a route no one could repeat may still have been very likely to be reached.
options.D: contingency enthusiasts are wrong to claim that many forms appeared only once.

questions.correct_answer: (C) an end point reached by a route no one could repeat may still have been very likely to be reached.

option_rationales.A: The image shows only that a unique history does not prove a contingent outcome; it does not claim that all outcomes are fixed in advance.
option_rationales.B: The point is that history alone does not prove dependence, not that history is useless; the author never dismisses lineage histories.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 accepts that a 'far larger number of forms' appeared once; the image targets a different inference made by the contingency school.

questions.explanation: The image follows the charge that contingency enthusiasts treat a particular history as 'proof that its outcome depended on that history, which does not follow'. A ball's unique path can still end in 'the only hollow', so a unique route is compatible with an all but inevitable result.
questions.common_misconception: Overextending the image into a claim that outcomes are predetermined.
questions.difficulty_reason: The image must be read against the specific inference it rebuts.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the two schools is best described as

options.A: partisan, favouring the convergence school and treating the contingency school's case as anecdote.
options.B: even-handed, crediting each with a real insight while faulting how it treats evidence.
options.C: dismissive, regarding the entire debate between them as confused and not worth pursuing.
options.D: deferential, accepting the claims of each school and declining to judge between them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) even-handed, crediting each with a real insight while faulting how it treats evidence.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'each tends to treat the other's evidence as anecdote' as a fault of both, and paragraph 3 calls both views 'probably true'.
option_rationales.C: The author says only that 'much of the disagreement' dissolves, and treats the remaining question about intelligence as open and important.
option_rationales.D: The author criticises both schools' reasoning in paragraph 2 and offers a judgement of their own in paragraph 3, so the stance is not deferential.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens 'Each school has a strong case' and then criticises the convergence list as 'assembled after the fact' and the contingency inference as one that 'does not follow'. Paragraph 3 holds that both claims are compatible and 'probably true'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the reconciliation as refusal to judge, when it rests on criticism of both sides.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options capture part of the stance (no favourite; some reserve), so the correct answer must be matched to both paragraphs.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the reconciliation proposed in paragraph 3?

options.A: Intelligence that is capable of language and the making of tools has arisen in only one lineage of animals so far.
options.B: Far more forms of life have appeared once in the history of life and never recurred than have appeared repeatedly.
options.C: A replay of evolution would probably not produce birds as the main flying animals, nor backboned animals as the main swimmers.
options.D: Most supposed independent origins of eyes, wings and streamlined bodies turn out to descend from one shared ancestral form.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Most supposed independent origins of eyes, wings and streamlined bodies turn out to descend from one shared ancestral form.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 states this as a limit on what the evidence shows; it bears on the separate question of intelligence, not on the two-level reconciliation.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 already grants this, and paragraph 3 assigns such unrepeated forms to the level of particular lineages, so it is consistent with the reconciliation.
option_rationales.C: This is what paragraph 3 itself predicts at 'the level of particular lineages', so it supports rather than weakens the reconciliation.

questions.explanation: The functional-level half of the reconciliation, that a replay would 'very probably' produce seeing, swimming and flying organisms, rests on the recurrence of these designs as evidence that physical problems 'admit only a few good solutions'. If the recurrences were really inherited from a single origin, that evidence would vanish.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the unrepeated-forms option because it sounds like evidence for contingency against convergence.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options are statements the passage itself makes or accepts; the correct answer targets the evidence on which one level of the reconciliation depends.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 4 that the author regards the repeated evolution of eyes and wings as

options.A: good evidence that intelligence like ours was most probably a fluke of one lineage's history.
options.B: good evidence that intelligence like ours is a likely outcome of any rerun of evolution.
options.C: irrelevant to any question about what a replay of evolution would be likely to produce.
options.D: insufficient grounds for expecting a replay of evolution to produce a creature like us.

questions.correct_answer: (D) insufficient grounds for expecting a replay of evolution to produce a creature like us.

option_rationales.A: The author says 'a single case cannot reveal whether it was a likely destination or a fluke', so the author does not take the evidence to favour the fluke reading either.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the recurrence of eyes and wings 'does not tell us that every capacity we value is among those solutions', which denies this.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 uses that recurrence to predict that a replay would 'very probably' produce seeing and flying organisms, so it is relevant to some questions.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the recurrence shows only that 'some problems have few solutions' and that on intelligence the evidence 'does not yet discriminate between the two views'. It is relevant to broad functions but not enough to predict a creature like us.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'fluke' option, which wrongly takes the author's scepticism about convergence as support for contingency.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options sit on either side of the author's agnostic position; the third overextends the limitation.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most analogous to the reconciliation of the two schools in paragraph 3?

options.A: A town rebuilt after a flood would almost surely again have bakeries and schools, though chance would decide who ran them.
options.B: A river fed by the same snowmelt every spring rises on the same day each year and always reaches exactly the same height.
options.C: A chess game replayed from the same opening position follows a different course every time and ends in a different result.
options.D: Two engineers working apart design nearly identical bridges because both have copied the same famous earlier bridge.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A town rebuilt after a flood would almost surely again have bakeries and schools, though chance would decide who ran them.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in this case varies from year to year, so it shows only a fixed, recurring outcome; it lacks the second level at which chance decides the particular occupants of a recurring role.
option_rationales.C: This captures only contingency, with no level at which the replays reliably converge on the same broad outcome.
option_rationales.D: The similarity here comes from a shared source, which is not convergence on a solution arrived at independently.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says broad functional roles recur because problems 'admit only a few good solutions', while 'which occupants of that space history happens to supply' is contingent. Bakeries and schools are the recurring roles; who runs them is the contingent occupancy.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the river, which illustrates convergence alone, or the bridges, which mistake copying for convergence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The analogy must reproduce both levels of the reconciliation, and each wrong option reproduces at most one.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: criticise public figures who take part in planting ceremonies mainly in order to be photographed doing something popular.
options.B: argue that forest recovery should be judged by the lasting forest it produces rather than by the number of saplings that are planted.
options.C: argue that tree planting campaigns should be replaced everywhere by the protection of land, so that forests can regenerate naturally without any planting.
options.D: explain the practical techniques by which nurseries and planters can raise the survival rate of the saplings they put into the ground.

questions.correct_answer: (B) argue that forest recovery should be judged by the lasting forest it produces rather than by the number of saplings that are planted.

option_rationales.A: The minister with a spade in paragraph 1 illustrates why planting appeals to campaigns; the passage does not attack anyone's motives, and its target is the measure of success.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this means that planting is always a mistake' and names cases where planting 'may be the only way to begin', so a blanket replacement contradicts the author.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 mentions why saplings die, but only as evidence that counting plantings hides losses; the passage offers no techniques for improving survival.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the thesis: counting saplings 'has quietly confused an input with an outcome'. Paragraphs 2 and 3 show the costs of that confusion and an alternative, and paragraph 4 concludes that success should be measured by land that 'becomes, and remains, a functioning forest'.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the argument into a rejection of all planting, which the last paragraph explicitly rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated in paragraph 1 and restated in paragraph 4; wrong options are clearly too broad or too narrow.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason natural regeneration is undervalued is that

options.A: it succeeds only on grasslands, which many people wrongly assume were once covered by forest.
options.B: it usually costs more than planting because the protected land has to be guarded against grazing, fire and clearing.
options.C: for several years after protection begins, the land looks like scrub and does not resemble visible progress.
options.D: the species that arrive by themselves are often poorly suited to the soil and climate of the site where they settle.

questions.correct_answer: (C) for several years after protection begins, the land looks like scrub and does not resemble visible progress.

option_rationales.A: Grasslands appear in paragraph 2 as places where planting did harm; regeneration is said to need old roots, seed trees and living soil, not grassland.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says regeneration happens 'often more cheaply than planting', so the claim about higher cost reverses the passage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: regenerating species are 'suited to the site because they arrived there by themselves'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 ends: 'for some years the land looks like scrub, which is one reason it is undervalued: it does not look like progress.'
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the cost comparison or the point about site suitability, both stated in the same paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement 'The objection is not to the spade but to the scoreboard' means that the author

options.A: objects to competition between rival campaigns that try to outdo each other in the number of trees they plant.
options.B: objects to manual planting by volunteers and prefers that saplings be put in by trained professionals.
options.C: accepts the counting of saplings planted, provided that the trees are put in during the correct season.
options.D: objects to the way the success of forest campaigns is measured, not to the act of planting trees itself.

questions.correct_answer: (D) objects to the way the success of forest campaigns is measured, not to the act of planting trees itself.

option_rationales.A: The 'scoreboard' is the count of saplings used to report success; nothing in the passage describes campaigns competing with one another.
option_rationales.B: The spade stands for planting in general; the passage never compares volunteers with professionals.
option_rationales.C: Accepting the count is the opposite of the author's point; paragraph 4 replaces it with the area that remains forest after ten or twenty years.

questions.explanation: The sentence follows the concession that planting is sometimes necessary. The 'spade' is planting itself, which the author accepts in some cases; the 'scoreboard' is the habit of measuring success by the number planted, which the next sentence replaces with the area of land that 'becomes, and remains, a functioning forest'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'scoreboard' literally as competition rather than as the measure of success.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figure is explained by the sentences on either side of it.

questions.question: Which of the following programmes would the author of the passage most likely regard as best designed?

options.A: One that waters and tends every sapling through its first dry months, so that the number of trees reported as planted is accurate rather than inflated.
options.B: One that refuses to plant anywhere, including on badly degraded soils, and instead fences every site and waits for a forest to return on its own.
options.C: One that fences off land near surviving seed trees, plants only on degraded plots with no seed source, and reports how much forest still stands after fifteen years.
options.D: One that plants a wide mix of native species instead of a single fast-growing tree, and reports the total number of saplings put into the ground each season.

questions.correct_answer: (C) One that fences off land near surviving seed trees, plants only on degraded plots with no seed source, and reports how much forest still stands after fifteen years.

option_rationales.A: Tending saplings addresses survival, but the programme still reports trees planted and plants everywhere, ignoring both the choice of site and the long-term measure the author proposes.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says that where soils are badly degraded or no seed sources survive, 'careful planting may be the only way to begin', so refusing to plant anywhere goes against the author.
option_rationales.D: Choosing a mix of species answers the problem of 'choice', but reporting saplings planted keeps the very scoreboard that paragraph 4 rejects, so losses would still go unrecorded.

questions.explanation: The author wants campaigns judged by forest that 'becomes, and remains' after ten or twenty years, wants regeneration where seed trees and soil remain (paragraph 3), and accepts planting where no seed sources survive (paragraph 4). Only the correct answer combines all three.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the mixed-species option, which fixes one problem from paragraph 2 but keeps the count of saplings planted.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying both the measurement point and the concession; one wrong option fixes a real problem but keeps the rejected measure.

questions.question: According to the passage, protecting a large predator can benefit less appealing species because

options.A: the large area that such a predator needs, once protected, also shelters many other species living in it.
options.B: donors who first give money for the predator are later persuaded to give money for the less appealing species too.
options.C: breeding programmes and tracking collars for the predator also yield information about the other species.
options.D: the predator keeps down the animals that would otherwise eat or crowd out the less appealing species.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the large area that such a predator needs, once protected, also shelters many other species living in it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says these species are ones 'no donor would have paid to save directly'; the benefit comes through shared habitat, not through donors changing their giving.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 mentions breeding programmes and collars as spending on the animal itself, precisely the case in which 'the advertising argument does not apply'.
option_rationales.D: The passage never describes the predator's effect on other animals; its point concerns the area protected 'for its sake'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A large predator needs a large area, and the forest or grassland that is protected for its sake also shelters thousands of less appealing species'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying an ecological mechanism (predation) that the passage does not mention.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The list 'a single cave, a spring, a patch of chalk grassland, the gravel bed of one river' in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the kinds of places in which donors most often refuse to pay for conservation work of any kind.
options.B: give examples of habitats whose threatened species would gain nothing from the protection of a charismatic animal.
options.C: suggest that conservation money should be moved away from tiger reserves towards caves, springs and rivers.
options.D: show that small habitats are generally richer in species than the forests and grasslands that large predators need.

questions.correct_answer: (B) give examples of habitats whose threatened species would gain nothing from the protection of a charismatic animal.

option_rationales.A: Donors' refusals are not discussed in paragraph 3; the list describes where threatened organisms live, not where donors decline to give.
option_rationales.C: The author does not propose moving money from reserves; paragraph 4 keeps flagship species as 'a useful' tool and asks only that some effort follow need.
option_rationales.D: The passage compares no habitats for richness; the examples matter because no charismatic animal shares them, as the next sentence says.

questions.explanation: The list follows 'Some of the most threatened organisms live in habitats that no charismatic animal shares' and is followed by 'Protecting a tiger reserve will do nothing for them.' It marks the limit of the advertising defence.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the examples as a recommendation to reallocate money, which the conclusion does not make.
questions.difficulty_reason: The surrounding sentences state the function directly.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the use of flagship species in conservation is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality: the passage sets out the critics' complaint and its defence without deciding between them.
options.B: strong enthusiasm: by protecting whole landscapes they answer the critics' complaint about neglected species.
options.C: qualified approval: they are a useful means of raising attention and money but an incomplete guide to priorities.
options.D: firm disapproval: they let the tastes of donors distort priorities and should therefore be dropped from conservation appeals altogether.

questions.correct_answer: (C) qualified approval: they are a useful means of raising attention and money but an incomplete guide to priorities.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 draws an explicit conclusion of its own, 'The sensible conclusion is ...', so the author is not neutral.
option_rationales.B: The author accepts the advertising defence only 'up to a point' (paragraph 3) and lists species it leaves out, so the complaint is not answered.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the sensible course is 'neither to abandon flagship species' nor to rely on them alone, so the author does not want them dropped.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defends flagship species, paragraph 3 limits the defence, and paragraph 4 concludes they are 'a tool ... and a useful one' while insisting 'Some part of the effort has to be directed by need rather than by appeal'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing enthusiasm because of paragraph 2, without weighing the limits set out in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires weighing the defence against its stated limits; two wrong options each match one half of the argument.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a donation made in the name of a famous animal does most to answer the critics' complaint when it is

options.A: given by donors who are already aware that small and drab species are more threatened than famous ones.
options.B: spent on breeding programmes that increase the number of the famous animal itself living within its protected reserves.
options.C: raised in an appeal that features a beetle or mussel alongside the famous animal in its pictures.
options.D: spent on protecting the habitat that the animal shares with many other species, rather than on the animal alone.

questions.correct_answer: (D) spent on protecting the habitat that the animal shares with many other species, rather than on the animal alone.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not say drab species are generally more threatened, and the donor's awareness does not change what the money protects.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says that when money is spent 'on that animal directly, on breeding programmes', the advertising argument 'does not apply at all'.
option_rationales.C: Who appears in the pictures does not decide what is protected; the passage ties the benefit to how the money 'is spent'.

questions.explanation: The defence in paragraph 2 works because the money 'is spent, at least in part, on soil, water and cover that serve everything living there'. Paragraph 3 says it fails when money is spent on the animal itself. So the donation does most for neglected species when it goes to the shared habitat.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the breeding option because it helps a threatened animal, missing that paragraph 3 excludes it from the defence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the defence in paragraph 2 and its limit in paragraph 3 to be combined.

questions.question: According to the passage, compensation schemes fall short in practice partly because they

options.A: are run by conservation charities that do not understand the cost of farming close to the forest edge.
options.B: pay only for the market value of damaged crops and leave out losses such as sleep, schooling and constant fear.
options.C: pay farmers more than their crops were worth, which removes any reason for them to guard their fields at night.
options.D: reach only those farmers who have retaliated against elephants and so reward hostility rather than tolerance.

questions.correct_answer: (B) pay only for the market value of damaged crops and leave out losses such as sleep, schooling and constant fear.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not say who runs the schemes; their faults are delay, paperwork and narrow valuation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says schemes pay 'a fraction of the loss', the reverse of overpayment, and never suggests they discourage guarding.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in paragraph 3 links payment to retaliation; the obstacles named are slowness and paperwork for poor households.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: schemes 'pay for the market value of a damaged crop while ignoring the sleepless nights, the children kept from school to guard fields and the fear that hangs over every harvest'.
questions.common_misconception: Inventing a reason (who runs the schemes) that sounds plausible but is not given.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the claim that such a scheme 'does not shift the burden; it documents it' means that the scheme

options.A: records that farmers have suffered a loss while leaving most of that loss with the farmers who suffered it.
options.B: produces useful records of elephant movements that can later be used to plan deterrents for affected villages.
options.C: requires so much paperwork that farmers spend more on completing forms than they ever receive in payment.
options.D: transfers the cost of elephant damage from the farmers to the state, but only after a long and frustrating administrative delay.

questions.correct_answer: (A) records that farmers have suffered a loss while leaving most of that loss with the farmers who suffered it.

option_rationales.B: The passage never mentions records of elephant movements; what is documented is the burden itself, the farmers' loss.
option_rationales.C: Paperwork is one fault mentioned earlier, but the passage does not compare its cost with the payment; 'documents' refers to recording the loss, not to forms costing money.
option_rationales.D: To 'not shift the burden' means the cost is not transferred; a scheme that paid in full, even late, would contradict the author's point about 'a fraction of the loss'.

questions.explanation: The scheme pays 'a fraction of the loss, a year late'. The burden stays where it was (it is not shifted), and the payment serves only to acknowledge or record that the loss occurred.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'documents' literally as paperwork, a detail from the same paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option exploits the paperwork detail nearby; the correct answer needs the sense of the figure.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that hostility to elephants should not be read as ignorance?

options.A: Villages that received prompt and full compensation reported far less retaliation than villages where payments were slow and partial.
options.B: In affected villages, farmers who retaliated against elephants could describe the animals' role in spreading the seeds of forest trees as accurately as farmers who never retaliated.
options.C: Farmers who had lost nothing to elephants were as likely to retaliate as those with heavy losses, and retaliation fell sharply after lessons on the animals' role.
options.D: Tolerance of elephants differed widely between neighbouring communities that had suffered similar losses, reflecting differences in tradition.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Farmers who had lost nothing to elephants were as likely to retaliate as those with heavy losses, and retaliation fell sharply after lessons on the animals' role.

option_rationales.A: This fits the author's distributive framing in paragraphs 3 and 4, since it ties hostility to how costs are borne rather than to ignorance.
option_rationales.B: This supports the author: a farmer may 'understand their ecological importance perfectly well' and still be hostile, so knowledge and hostility coexist.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 already concedes that tolerance 'is shaped by tradition as well as by loss', so this finding is consistent with the passage and does not show hostility is ignorance.

questions.explanation: The author argues that hostility reflects inability to bear costs, not lack of understanding (paragraph 2). If hostility were unrelated to losses and disappeared once farmers were taught about elephants, ignorance would be the better explanation, which weakens the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the tradition option, which sounds like a challenge but repeats the concession the author already makes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the precise claim isolated from the concession made in the same paragraph.

questions.question: The author's remark that deterrents push 'elephants onto the next village's fields' suggests that

options.A: neighbouring villages ought to coordinate their deterrents so that elephants are steered back into the forest.
options.B: a remedy that lowers one village's losses may only pass them to neighbours, leaving the wider question of who pays unresolved.
options.C: the costs of a recovered elephant population are in fact spread evenly across the villages that border the forest.
options.D: beehive fences and chilli repellents seldom reduce losses at all, since elephants soon learn to ignore them and return to the same fields.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a remedy that lowers one village's losses may only pass them to neighbours, leaving the wider question of who pays unresolved.

option_rationales.A: The author proposes no coordination; the conclusion turns instead to whether 'the wider society' will pay those who live beside elephants.
option_rationales.C: Moving damage from one village to the next does not make costs even, and paragraph 1 says they are 'concentrated on a few villages'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says that 'where these work they reduce losses at modest cost'; the remark is about losses moving, not about deterrents failing or elephants learning.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 grants that deterrents work locally but says they 'move the problem as often as they solve it'. The next sentence states that 'The underlying question remains political', so the remark shows that technical fixes redistribute costs among those already bearing them instead of transferring them to the wider society.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the remark as saying deterrents do not work, when the passage says they do work locally.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the remark to the distributive thesis and separating 'move the problem' from 'fail'.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the frequent low-intensity fires of many dry forests

options.A: cleared away the material on the forest floor while leaving most of the older, thick-barked trees unharmed.
options.B: were started deliberately by forest agencies to reduce the fuel that had built up under years of suppression.
options.C: killed off the older trees so that young trees and undergrowth could grow in the light that was let in.
options.D: climbed into the crowns of the trees but burned out before they could spread to neighbouring stands.

questions.correct_answer: (A) cleared away the material on the forest floor while leaving most of the older, thick-barked trees unharmed.

option_rationales.B: The low-intensity fires described in paragraph 2 came before suppression; deliberate burning appears only in paragraph 4 as a modern remedy.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: these fires cleared 'young trees' and undergrowth while 'leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed'.
option_rationales.D: Climbing into the crowns is what the later, large fires did after fuel accumulated; the earlier fires stayed small and on the forest floor.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: frequent low-intensity fires 'cleared the undergrowth, fallen branches and young trees that gather on the forest floor, while leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the earlier small fires with the later crown fires described in the same paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as contributing to catastrophic fires EXCEPT

options.A: the spread of houses and settlements into land that is covered by woods and forest.
options.B: long spells of drought and heat in the seasons when the most destructive fires break out.
options.C: the build-up of undergrowth and fallen branches in dry forests after decades of fire suppression.
options.D: the planting of fast-growing, thin-barked trees in place of the older species of dry forests.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the planting of fast-growing, thin-barked trees in place of the older species of dry forests.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists 'the spread of housing into wooded land' among the causes of catastrophic fire besides suppression.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land matter as well'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 describes exactly this accumulation of fuel, which allows a fire to 'climb into the crowns of the trees'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 name accumulated fuel, drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land. No change in tree species through planting is mentioned anywhere; the thick-barked trees are said to be killed by the large fires, not replaced by planting.
questions.common_misconception: Recognising 'thick-barked' from paragraph 2 and assuming the option restates it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires checking options against two paragraphs; the correct answer borrows a passage word.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a sharp rise in burning in a wet forest where fire had historically been rare as

options.A: evidence that the rise must have been caused by housing spreading into the wooded land around it.
options.B: further proof that suppressing fires is always a mistake, since fuel must have built up there as well.
options.C: a welcome correction, because fires in every forest clear the undergrowth and protect the older trees.
options.D: a genuine danger to that forest, not a sign that fire is returning to its natural place there.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a genuine danger to that forest, not a sign that fire is returning to its natural place there.

option_rationales.A: Housing is named as one factor among several in paragraph 3; nothing allows the author to assign this single cause to an unspecified case.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the suppression lesson 'is sometimes drawn too broadly' and singles out wet forests as places where fire was rare, so the author would not extend it there.
option_rationales.C: The claim that fires do this in 'every forest' is the overbroad lesson the author rejects; paragraph 3 says the argument 'is not that fire is good'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: in 'some wet forests and many shrublands fire was historically rare, and a recent increase in burning there is a threat rather than a return to normal'. Whether a fire harms 'depends on the ecosystem in which it burns'.
questions.common_misconception: Applying the dry-forest lesson to every forest, the overgeneralisation that paragraph 3 warns against.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the qualification in paragraph 3 rather than the main narrative of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The asymmetry described in the last paragraph implies that

options.A: the public blames managers equally for escaped planned burns and for wildfires caused by accumulated fuel.
options.B: a manager may keep suppressing fires even when aware that doing so raises the risk of catastrophic fire later.
options.C: planned burns are in fact more dangerous to towns than wildfires that grow from decades of accumulated fuel.
options.D: managers continue suppressing fires mainly because they have not yet understood how fuel builds up on the floor of dry forests.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a manager may keep suppressing fires even when aware that doing so raises the risk of catastrophic fire later.

option_rationales.A: The passage says the reverse: an escaped burn 'is blamed on the people who lit it' while a fuel-driven wildfire 'is blamed on nature'.
option_rationales.C: The passage says planned burns carry visible and attributable risks, not that their total harm exceeds that of large wildfires; the asymmetry concerns blame and timing.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph opens with 'Recognising this has not made the remedy easy', so the problem is incentives, not a lack of understanding.

questions.explanation: The harm of acting (a planned burn) is 'visible and attributable', while the harm of not acting is 'deferred and diffuse', so 'the easiest course is to keep doing what made the problem worse'. This holds even for managers who recognise the problem, as the paragraph's first sentence implies.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the ignorance option, which overlooks 'Recognising this' at the start of the paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer depends on reading the asymmetry as one of incentives and blame, and wrong options distort it in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Because exclusion carries certain costs and often only assumed benefits, removing residents from protected land should be justified in each case rather than treated as the default.
options.B: Because romantic images of forest dwellers are as misleading as images of wilderness, conservation should rely on neither residents nor parks to protect species.
options.C: Because national parks were founded on a false picture of untouched nature, the model should be abandoned and replaced by community management everywhere.
options.D: Because local residents shaped many admired landscapes over centuries, they should never be removed from land that is set aside for conservation.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Because exclusion carries certain costs and often only assumed benefits, removing residents from protected land should be justified in each case rather than treated as the default.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 uses the romantic image only to qualify the critique; the passage keeps both protection and residents' share in management, rejecting neither.
option_rationales.C: The author concludes with 'not a rule but a burden of proof'; replacing parks with community management everywhere is itself a rule the passage does not propose.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 rejects the view that 'exclusion is never justified', and paragraph 4 allows exclusion where use is absent or demonstrably incompatible.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 sums up: the critique establishes 'not a rule but a burden of proof'. Exclusion has 'certain and heavy costs' while its benefits 'are often assumed rather than shown', so it 'must be defended, case by case, rather than taken as the natural form of protection'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that matches the critique in paragraph 2 and missing the qualification in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: All options borrow genuine premises from the passage; the correct answer alone keeps the balance of the conclusion.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, removing residents from landscapes that had long been shaped by them

options.A: allowed grasslands to stay open because grazing animals could now move freely without being herded.
options.B: was generally carried out with fair compensation for the homes, graves and sacred places that were lost.
options.C: started an unplanned change in which some of the qualities that made the places worth protecting declined.
options.D: returned the land to the original state that visitors had admired before the residents first arrived.

questions.correct_answer: (C) started an unplanned change in which some of the qualities that made the places worth protecting declined.

option_rationales.A: Grasslands were kept open 'by grazing and deliberate burning' under the residents; the passage says nothing of grazing animals moving freely after removal.
option_rationales.B: The passage says these losses came 'often with little or no compensation', the reverse of fair compensation.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says removal 'did not return the land to an original state'; it began 'a new and unplanned experiment'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: removal 'began a new and unplanned experiment, and in some cases the very qualities that had made the place worth protecting began to decline'.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the founding picture of the parks, which the paragraph says was 'historically false'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Directly stated in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It offers new evidence that most forest communities now hunt and clear land at rates that the land can no longer sustain.
options.B: It explains why the founders of national parks believed that nature was most fully itself where people were absent.
options.C: It abandons the critique of fortress conservation and argues that strict exclusion is usually the more effective form of protection.
options.D: It guards the critique of fortress conservation against an opposite oversimplification before the author states a conclusion.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It guards the critique of fortress conservation against an opposite oversimplification before the author states a conclusion.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says a population 'may, under new pressures' overharvest; it is a possibility, not evidence about most communities.
option_rationales.B: The founders' picture is described in paragraph 1 and refuted in paragraph 2; paragraph 3 turns to a different error, the romantic image of the forest dweller.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says it would be 'too simple' to treat residents as always the best stewards; it does not make exclusion usually better, and paragraph 4 keeps the presumption in favour of residents with a compatible record.

questions.explanation: After paragraph 2 criticises the image of untouched wilderness, paragraph 3 warns that 'The romantic image of the timeless forest dweller can be as misleading', and concedes that some exclusion may be justified. This prepares the balanced 'burden of proof' conclusion in paragraph 4.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a concession as a reversal of the author's position.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing the paragraph as a qualification rather than a change of side.

questions.question: In which of the following cases would the reasoning of the passage most clearly support excluding people from an area?

options.A: A cliff used by a seabird that deserts its nests at slight disturbance, where counts show breeding fails whenever people enter, and which no community has ever used.
options.B: A river valley whose fishing families have lived there for centuries, where a recent survey found fish numbers stable and a proposal to remove them cites the general belief that wildlife does better alone.
options.C: A grassland that herders have grazed and burned for centuries, which visitors admire as wilderness and would prefer to see without any settlements.
options.D: A forest from which a village has gathered fruit and firewood for generations, where officials hold that the rare birds living there are probably disturbed by people.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A cliff used by a seabird that deserts its nests at slight disturbance, where counts show breeding fails whenever people enter, and which no community has ever used.

option_rationales.B: The fishing record is long and compatible with stable fish numbers; relying on a general belief is exactly the assumption paragraph 4 rejects as a basis for exclusion.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 suggests such grassland may depend on the herders' grazing and burning, and visitors' preferences are not a reason the passage accepts for exclusion.
option_rationales.D: The village has a long record of use and the harm is only 'probably' so, a benefit 'assumed rather than shown'; paragraph 4 puts the presumption with the residents here.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 allows exclusion 'Where that record is absent, or where a species' needs are demonstrably incompatible with human use'. The seabird case meets both conditions: no history of use, and evidence that any presence causes breeding to fail.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the forest case because it mentions rare birds, overlooking that the harm is only assumed and that use is long established.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each case has a feature that seems to favour exclusion; only one meets the passage's conditions with evidence rather than assumption.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the description of keystone status as 'a property of a relationship in a particular setting' means that

options.A: a species keeps its keystone role wherever it lives, once that role has been demonstrated in one setting.
options.B: whether a species has outsized influence depends on the community and conditions in which it lives.
options.C: a keystone species is one that forms close partnerships with a small number of other species.
options.D: keystone species are found only in particular kinds of habitat, such as rocky shores, and not elsewhere.

questions.correct_answer: (B) whether a species has outsized influence depends on the community and conditions in which it lives.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'fixed attribute' view the sentence rejects; paragraph 2 says the same species may have 'a minor one in another' place.
option_rationales.C: 'Relationship' refers to a species' role within a given community, not to partnerships; the rocky-shore example concerns predators and prey in different places.
option_rationales.D: The rocky shore is one example of a setting; the passage does not limit keystones to any habitat type.

questions.explanation: The sentence sums up paragraph 2: the same species 'may have a dominant influence in one place and a minor one in another, depending on what else lives there, on the climate and on the history of the site'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'relationship' in its everyday sense of a partnership.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase restates the sentences just before it.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard the unqualified statement that 'a certain predator is a keystone species' as

options.A: adequate, provided that the predator's effect has been carefully measured in at least one community.
options.B: false, because the passage shows that no species really has an influence larger than its abundance suggests.
options.C: incomplete, since it leaves out the particular system in which the predator's influence was found.
options.D: harmful, because naming keystone species always draws money away from the diffuse interactions in a community.

questions.correct_answer: (C) incomplete, since it leaves out the particular system in which the predator's influence was found.

option_rationales.A: Measuring it in one community is exactly what the author warns against generalising from, since the role may be 'minor' elsewhere.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'Some species really do have outsized and well-documented effects', so the author does not deny keystone effects.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says a keystone strategy 'may' neglect diffuse interactions; 'always' overstates it, and paragraph 4 values naming species.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 warns against 'treating the label as a discovery about a species' nature rather than a finding about a particular system'. An unqualified statement does just that, so the author would see it as missing the setting.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing 'false', which overstates the critique into a denial that keystones exist.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires distinguishing the author's scope objection from a denial of the concept.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the argument of paragraph 3?

options.A: On one coast, removing a single predator led to the collapse of a mussel bed, but on another coast removing the same predator had little effect.
options.B: In a meadow, removing any single species of grazing insect changed little, but removing several of them together altered the plant community sharply.
options.C: In a lake, removing a single fish species that was rare but fed on grazing animals caused a large growth of algae within a few seasons.
options.D: Conservation funding in one region rose sharply after a campaign that described a single bird as the keystone of its forests.

questions.correct_answer: (B) In a meadow, removing any single species of grazing insect changed little, but removing several of them together altered the plant community sharply.

option_rationales.A: This supports paragraph 2's point that influence depends on the setting; it says nothing about influence being spread across several species, which is the claim of paragraph 3.
option_rationales.C: This is a classic keystone case of one species with outsized effect; it illustrates the concept the paragraph says is not the only pattern, so it does not strengthen that paragraph.
option_rationales.D: This illustrates the persuasive value of the label mentioned in paragraphs 1 and 4; it does not show that influence is diffuse or that diffuse interactions are neglected.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that in many communities 'influence is spread across several species, each of moderate importance, whose combined effects' keep the system stable. A case where no single removal matters but the joint removal does is direct evidence of such diffuse influence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the two-coasts finding, which is true to the passage but supports paragraph 2 rather than paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options support other parts of the passage, so the precise claim of paragraph 3 must be isolated.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the keystone concept is best described as

options.A: indifferent, regarding the question of whether it is accurate as less important than whether it raises funds.
options.B: dismissive, regarding it as a misleading metaphor that ecology would be better off discarding entirely.
options.C: appreciative of its value as a memorable idea but wary of its being taken as a general model of communities.
options.D: admiring, regarding it as an accurate account of how most ecological communities are actually held together.

questions.correct_answer: (C) appreciative of its value as a memorable idea but wary of its being taken as a general model of communities.

option_rationales.A: The author cares a great deal about accuracy, devoting paragraphs 2 and 3 to its misleading assumptions.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 begins 'None of this means the concept should be discarded', so the author is not dismissive.
option_rationales.D: The final sentence says it should not be used 'as a model of how communities are generally built', the opposite of this view.

questions.explanation: The author credits the concept with being 'enormously useful' (paragraph 1) and refuses to discard it (paragraph 4) while warning against treating it as a fixed property or a general model.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the strong criticism in paragraphs 2 and 3 as a rejection.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires balancing praise and criticism across the passage.

questions.question: The contrast between a plant that crosses a mountain range by itself and one that crosses in a shipment of grain (paragraph 1) serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate that species carried by people usually spread faster and farther than those moving by natural means.
options.B: suggest that plants arriving in shipments of grain should be protected in the same way as native plants are protected.
options.C: show that species which spread on their own as the climate warms are less harmful than those carried by trade.
options.D: show that the label of invader turns on how a species travelled rather than on anything about the species or what it does.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that the label of invader turns on how a species travelled rather than on anything about the species or what it does.

option_rationales.A: Speed and distance of spread are never compared; the example sets two plants making the same crossing side by side to show that only the means of travel differs.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 makes no recommendation about protection; the author's own position, given in paragraph 4, allows a presumption against newly arrived species.
option_rationales.C: The passage compares no harms in paragraph 1; the example concerns what the plant is called, and paragraph 3 later says even newcomers are not 'more likely to be harmful'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 argues that native status 'rests on a choice that is not itself ecological'. The two plants make the same crossing, and only the one carried by people is called an invader, so the label depends on the manner of arrival, not on the plant or its effects.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a claim about harm or speed of spread, which the paragraph does not discuss.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example's function follows from the preceding sentence about the convention behind native status, but wrong options attach plausible ecological claims to it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the author's main disagreement with the ecologists described in paragraph 2 concerns

options.A: whether the effects of an introduced species can be known at the time when a decision about it has to be taken.
options.B: whether the origin of a species is in itself a form of harm to the ecosystem into which it has been introduced.
options.C: whether introduced species are, as a rule, more likely than native species to damage the communities they enter.
options.D: whether many eradication campaigns have been carried out without first asking if the targeted species was causing damage.

questions.correct_answer: (A) whether the effects of an introduced species can be known at the time when a decision about it has to be taken.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 opens 'The critics are right that origin is not itself a harm', so on this point the author agrees with them.
option_rationales.C: The author denies this in paragraph 3: the lack of shared history 'does not make the newcomer more likely to be harmful', so it is not what divides the author from the critics.
option_rationales.D: The author concedes this too, saying the critics are 'right that much eradication has been undertaken without asking whether the target was doing any damage'.

questions.explanation: After two concessions, paragraph 3 states the objection: 'their alternative assumes that effects can be known at the moment a decision has to be made, and this is often false'. The rest of the passage builds on this point about timing and knowledge.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about newcomers being more harmful, which sounds like the traditional view the critics attack but which the author explicitly rejects.
