option_rationales.C: The dust reply occupies only part of paragraph 2 and is quickly rejected; the option takes one rejected response for the purpose of the whole passage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says outright that it 'would be an exaggeration to say that the darkness of the night proves that the universe had a beginning'; the option claims what the author disowns.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 sets out why an infinite, evenly stocked, unchanging universe predicts a bright sky; paragraph 2 rejects attempts to block the light; paragraph 3 gives the accepted resolution; paragraph 4 concludes that the dark sky 'rules out only one combination of assumptions' but that this 'is no small thing'. The passage is about what this everyday fact tells us.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the conclusion into a proof of a beginning, or mistaking the dust reply for the main subject.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option turns the hedged conclusion into a proof, another overgeneralises the closing lesson; both use the passage's own words.

questions.question: According to the passage, interstellar dust cannot resolve the puzzle of the dark sky because

options.A: the dust between the stars is spread far too thinly to absorb any significant share of the light of distant stars.
options.B: clouds of dust would hide nearby stars as well as distant ones, making the sky far darker than it is actually observed to be.
options.C: dust absorbs only some wavelengths of starlight, so that the remaining wavelengths still reach the earth unhindered.
options.D: over an unlimited time the dust would be heated by the light it absorbs until it shone as brightly itself.

questions.correct_answer: (D) over an unlimited time the dust would be heated by the light it absorbs until it shone as brightly itself.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says the dust is too thin; its objection in paragraph 2 is that absorbing dust is 'warmed' and 'eventually it glows'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 raises no worry about nearby stars or about the sky being too dark; the failure it describes is that absorption only 'delays the problem'.
option_rationales.C: Nothing is said about dust absorbing selected wavelengths; the only wavelength point, in paragraph 3, concerns the expansion of space.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'dust that absorbs light for long enough is warmed by it, and eventually it glows as brightly as the light it swallows. Over an unlimited span of time, absorption delays the problem; it does not remove it.'
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible physical objection from outside the passage instead of the one the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the proposal to arrange stars in 'clusters within clusters' was regarded with suspicion mainly because it

options.A: was contradicted by observations showing that stars are in fact spread evenly through space.
options.B: seemed to have been devised only to dispose of the puzzle, with no other reason to believe it.
options.C: required the universe to have a finite age, an assumption that the astronomers of the period regarded as unacceptable.
options.D: conflicted with the dust explanation, which most astronomers of the time preferred to accept.

questions.correct_answer: (B) seemed to have been devised only to dispose of the puzzle, with no other reason to believe it.

option_rationales.A: No such observations are mentioned; the passage objects to the proposal as 'contrived', not as refuted by evidence.
option_rationales.C: Finite age belongs to the accepted resolution in paragraph 3, not to the cluster proposal, which was meant to keep the infinite universe.
option_rationales.D: The passage reports no rivalry or preference between the two replies; both are presented as failed attempts to rescue the infinite universe.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the cluster proposals 'seemed contrived, a geometry invented to answer a single awkward question'. The suspicion is that the arrangement was adopted only because it solved this one problem.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the finite-age idea of paragraph 3 to the wrong proposal.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in one phrase at the end of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the reasoning set out in paragraph 1?

options.A: In a large but walled garden, a visitor can see open sky between the trees because the planting stops at the wall some distance away.
options.B: In a city at night, the lamps of distant buildings look fainter than nearby ones, so that the skyline appears brightest close at hand.
options.C: A lamp seen through thick fog grows dimmer the farther the observer walks from it, until at last it cannot be seen at all.
options.D: In a forest that extends without limit in every direction, a walker anywhere would find that every line of sight ends, sooner or later, at a tree trunk.

questions.correct_answer: (D) In a forest that extends without limit in every direction, a walker anywhere would find that every line of sight ends, sooner or later, at a tree trunk.

option_rationales.A: A limit beyond which there is nothing to see parallels the finite reach of paragraph 3, the resolution, not the reasoning of paragraph 1 that produces the puzzle.
option_rationales.B: This captures only the dimming of remote sources and ignores the compensating increase in their number, which paragraph 1 says 'grows in step with the dimming'.
option_rationales.C: Fog absorbing light parallels the dust reply of paragraph 2, a rejected attempt to block the light, not the argument of paragraph 1.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 argues that if stars fill boundless space uniformly, 'any direction in which an observer looks, pursued far enough, must sooner or later meet the bright disc of a star'. The endless forest, in which every line of sight ends at a trunk, has the same structure.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an analogy for the resolution or for the dust reply instead of for the original reasoning.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is a faithful analogy for a different paragraph, so the reader must match structure to the right part.

questions.question: According to the passage, differences in local time between towns became a problem when

options.A: the market, the place of worship and the field in a single town began to keep different times.
options.B: astronomers found that solar noon falls at different moments in different seasons of the year.
options.C: people and goods began moving between towns quickly enough for a difference of minutes to matter.
options.D: governments began to require one uniform time for keeping official records and collecting taxes.

questions.correct_answer: (C) people and goods began moving between towns quickly enough for a difference of minutes to matter.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: noon 'meant the same thing in the market, the place of worship and the field'.
option_rationales.B: Seasonal variation of noon is never mentioned; paragraph 2 ties the problem to faster movement between towns.
option_rationales.D: Records and taxes are not discussed, and paragraph 3 says governments 'followed' the railways rather than starting the change.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends: 'The differences between towns became a problem only when goods and people began to move between them quickly enough for a few minutes to matter.'
questions.common_misconception: Reaching for an outside reason, or reversing the order in which railways and governments acted.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of one sentence.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward standard time is best described as

options.A: appreciative of its benefits but critical of the claim that it corrected an earlier error.
options.B: hostile, regarding it as a needless break with the natural rhythm of daylight in each town.
options.C: indifferent, treating the choice between local and standard time as having no real practical consequence.
options.D: enthusiastic, celebrating it as the triumph of common sense over a long period of local confusion.

questions.correct_answer: (A) appreciative of its benefits but critical of the claim that it corrected an earlier error.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 begins 'Nothing here suggests that standard time was a mistake' and credits it with saving lives, so hostility is ruled out.
option_rationales.C: The author says coordinated schedules 'saved lives' and made later systems 'workable', which is far from indifference.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'usual story' of paragraph 1, which the author says 'misdescribes what was replaced'.

questions.explanation: The author grants that standard time saved lives and was needed (paragraph 4) but denies that it was 'the discovery of a correct time hidden beneath local error'. The attitude is approval of the practice combined with criticism of the usual story told about it.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the reported 'usual story' as the author's own view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession and the criticism are both stated plainly in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The mention of 'single tracks' in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that railway accidents were caused chiefly by poor engineering rather than by timekeeping.
options.B: illustrate how governments compelled reluctant railway companies to adopt a single standard time.
options.C: explain why railways in regions that kept local time were built more slowly than those elsewhere.
options.D: show that mismatched local times created a real danger on the railways, not merely an inconvenience.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that mismatched local times created a real danger on the railways, not merely an inconvenience.

option_rationales.A: The example makes timekeeping the hazard: a mismatch 'could put two trains on the same stretch of line', which is the reverse of the option.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the companies began keeping a single time themselves and governments 'eventually followed them', so there was no compulsion.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about the speed of railway construction; the point concerns trains meeting on the same line.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that on single tracks 'a mismatch of a few minutes could put two trains on the same stretch of line', which is a safety hazard; paragraph 4 later notes that coordinated schedules 'saved lives'. The example gives the railways a concrete reason for a single time.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the roles of railways and governments in the change.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is clear from the sentence in which the phrase appears.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A way of setting clocks should be judged by how well it suits the needs of those who keep it, not by its closeness to a true time.
options.B: Solar time is the true time, and standard time is merely a convenient approximation that the railways adopted for their own purposes.
options.C: Standard time corrected errors in local timekeeping that small towns had failed to notice because they traded mainly with themselves.
options.D: Once the railways had spread, the position of the sun ceased to have any importance for daily life.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A way of setting clocks should be judged by how well it suits the needs of those who keep it, not by its closeness to a true time.

option_rationales.B: The author calls neither system true; paragraph 4 rejects the idea of 'a correct time', and this applies to solar time as much as to standard time.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 denies that standardisation corrected 'local error'; local time was 'the most sensible time to keep' for such towns.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the network became 'more important to daily life than the position of the sun', a comparison, not a claim that the sun ceased to matter.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says local time was 'the most sensible time to keep' for self-contained communities, and paragraph 4 says standard time was chosen because the network had become more important. Each system suited the needs of its users; neither was correct in itself.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about correcting unnoticed errors, which restates the 'usual story' in subtler words.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining paragraphs 2 and 4 and noticing that the author rejects 'correct time' for both systems; one wrong option overstates a comparison.

questions.question: According to the passage, the value assigned to the constant in the new definition of the kilogram was chosen

options.A: by a calculation that made no reference to any earlier measurement of the mass of physical objects.
options.B: to correct for the mass that the cylinder near Paris was believed to have lost over the decades.
options.C: so that the new kilogram would agree with the old one as closely as instruments could tell.
options.D: to match the average mass of the official copies, which were thought more reliable than the cylinder.

questions.correct_answer: (C) so that the new kilogram would agree with the old one as closely as instruments could tell.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the value was fixed precisely to 'match the old one', so earlier measurements were the reference.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says there was 'no way, even in principle, to say that it had changed', so no known loss could be corrected for.
option_rationales.D: The passage never ranks the copies above the cylinder; paragraph 2 speaks of matching 'the old one', the cylinder's kilogram.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'the value assigned to the constant was chosen precisely so that the new kilogram would match the old one as closely as instruments could tell. Nobody wanted bags of flour to change weight overnight.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the redefinition was meant to fix a known drift.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'a peculiar kind of blindness' refers to

options.A: the general public's ignorance of the fact that all the world's measurements of mass led back to one cylinder.
options.B: the impossibility, in principle, of detecting any change in a standard that served as its own definition.
options.C: the failure of the officials in charge to notice that the official copies were drifting away from the cylinder.
options.D: the inability of most laboratories in the world to realise the kilogram directly from a constant of nature.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the impossibility, in principle, of detecting any change in a standard that served as its own definition.

option_rationales.A: Public awareness is never discussed; paragraph 3 explains the blindness as a feature of a self-defining standard.
option_rationales.C: The drift was noticed: paragraph 3 says the copies 'were found to have drifted apart'; what could not be seen was whether the cylinder itself had changed.
option_rationales.D: That limitation is conceded in paragraph 4 about the new system, whereas the blindness is something the redefinition 'removed'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the phrase: 'because the cylinder was the kilogram by definition, there was no way, even in principle, to say that it had changed. A standard that defines itself cannot be found wanting.'
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'blindness' as human inattention rather than a limitation built into the definition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is given in the next paragraph, and one wrong option confuses the detected drift with the undetectable change.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the drift between the cylinder and its official copies?

options.A: It proved that the copies had gained mass over the decades while the cylinder itself stayed unchanged.
options.B: It showed that something had changed, without making it possible to establish what.
options.C: It was the reason the constant was given a value slightly different from the one that matched the cylinder.
options.D: It was too slight to have any bearing on scientific measurement, which is why the redefinition changed little.

questions.correct_answer: (B) It showed that something had changed, without making it possible to establish what.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists three possibilities, 'Either the copies had gained mass, or the cylinder had lost it, or both', and says none could be settled; 'proved' overstates.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the value was chosen to 'match the old one', not to depart from it because of the drift.
option_rationales.D: The passage calls the drift 'small but measurable' and treats its significance in principle as the point; the redefinition is said to have removed a real defect.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the copies and cylinder 'were found to have drifted apart' and that either the copies gained mass, or the cylinder lost it, or both; but since the cylinder defined the unit, there was no way to say it had changed. The drift revealed change but not its location.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about the copies gaining mass because the cylinder was officially unchanging, confusing the definition with the physical object.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option confuses 'officially exactly one kilogram' with being physically unchanged.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's final claim about what the redefinition achieved?

options.A: Ordinary users of balances and scales noticed no change at all in their measurements when the new definition came into force.
options.B: Most of the world's weighing instruments are still calibrated against physical masses rather than against direct realisations of the unit.
options.C: The constant was assigned a value chosen to reproduce the old kilogram, so the new unit simply inherits the size of the cylinder.
options.D: Each of the few laboratories that can realise the kilogram uses a unique design whose results no other laboratory is able to reproduce or check.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Each of the few laboratories that can realise the kilogram uses a unique design whose results no other laboratory is able to reproduce or check.

option_rationales.A: This is what paragraph 2 says was intended ('Nobody wanted bags of flour to change weight overnight'), so it is consistent with the author's account.
option_rationales.B: The author concedes exactly this in paragraph 4 ('most of the world still calibrates against physical masses') and still maintains the claim, so it does not weaken it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 makes this point itself; the author's claim concerns dependence on an object, not the size of the unit, so the fact is already accommodated.

questions.explanation: The final claim is that dependence is now 'on a procedure that can be checked and repeated'. If no laboratory's realisation can be reproduced or checked by another, the new dependence would be no more checkable than dependence on the cylinder, which strikes at the claimed gain.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a fact the author has already conceded, mistaking a concession for an objection.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options restate points the passage itself concedes; only one attacks the specific property the author claims for the new system.

questions.question: The analysis of steam engines mentioned in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: show that a result reached within the caloric framework could outlast the framework itself.
options.B: prove that caloric gave a correct account of heat at least in so far as engines were concerned.
options.C: illustrate how close study of engines eventually exposed the caloric theory as mistaken.
options.D: explain why heat moves from hot bodies to cold ones in the way that water runs downhill.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that a result reached within the caloric framework could outlast the framework itself.

option_rationales.B: The passage says caloric was wrong about what heat is and, in paragraph 4, that it 'could make no sense of heat turning into work'; only the result survived.
option_rationales.C: That point belongs to paragraph 4; in paragraph 2 the engine analysis is an achievement of caloric, not its refutation.
option_rationales.D: The flow of heat is explained earlier in paragraph 2 by the fluid picture itself; the engine analysis concerns how much work an engine can extract.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the engine analysis 'was framed entirely in its terms' and adds: 'That result survived the theory's collapse.' Its role is to show that caloric produced lasting results.
questions.common_misconception: Merging the engine example of paragraph 2 with the engine-related failure of paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence that follows the example.

questions.question: The author's view of the defenders of caloric who answered the cannon-boring objection is that they

options.A: were right to dismiss the observations of cannon boring as the product of careless experimental work.
options.B: were being stubborn in refusing to accept evidence that plainly and decisively refuted their theory.
options.C: acted reasonably in retaining a productive theory while no rival yet explained as much.
options.D: produced replies that were uniformly ingenious and that fully disposed of the objection for decades.

questions.correct_answer: (C) acted reasonably in retaining a productive theory while no rival yet explained as much.

option_rationales.A: The passage calls the difficulties 'real' and never suggests the observations were faulty or dismissed as such.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 mentions this description only to set it aside: 'It is easy to call this stubbornness. It is more accurate to say ...'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the replies were 'some ingenious and some strained', and the objection was survived, not fully answered.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 rejects the charge of stubbornness and says a theory 'which organises a large body of successful work is not abandoned because of one anomaly, particularly when no rival yet explains everything the old theory explained'. The author regards their persistence as reasonable.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the 'stubbornness' label, which the author raises in order to reject.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option uses a word from the passage that the author explicitly sets aside; another overstates a mixed judgement.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the cannon-boring observations troubled the caloric theory chiefly because

options.A: they demonstrated that heat has a measurable weight, whereas caloric was supposed to be weightless.
options.B: a fluid that is merely conserved and released should not be available in a supply without limit.
options.C: they showed that heat could pass from colder bodies into hotter ones when metal was being bored.
options.D: they were carried out by investigators who had already rejected caloric in favour of another theory.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a fluid that is merely conserved and released should not be available in a supply without limit.

option_rationales.A: Weight is never measured in the observations described; the difficulty is that friction produced heat 'apparently without limit'.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in paragraph 3 concerns the direction of heat flow; the problem was the apparently unlimited quantity of heat.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about who made the observations or what they believed, so this cannot be inferred.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: friction produced heat 'apparently without limit', and 'If heat were a conserved fluid squeezed out of the metal, the supply should eventually have run out.' The conflict is between conservation of a finite fluid and unlimited production.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible-sounding physical objection not given in the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the conditional in paragraph 3 to be connected to the observation before it.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the author's account of the caloric theory?

options.A: An old map drawn on a mistaken belief about the shape of the land records routes between towns accurately, and later mapmakers keep the routes while redrawing the outline.
options.B: An old map is mistaken in places, but mapmakers keep using it unchanged for generations only out of loyalty to the person who drew it.
options.C: An old map records accurate routes but a mistaken outline of the land, and later mapmakers throw it away entirely because the outline is wrong.
options.D: An old map is accurate in every detail but is replaced because a newer method of printing makes it cheaper to draw a fresh one.

questions.correct_answer: (A) An old map drawn on a mistaken belief about the shape of the land records routes between towns accurately, and later mapmakers keep the routes while redrawing the outline.

option_rationales.B: This casts persistence as mere loyalty, the 'stubbornness' reading that paragraph 3 rejects, and leaves out that the theory organised much successful work.
option_rationales.C: The author says the behavioural truths 'pass, nearly intact, to its successor'; discarding the whole map, routes included, is the 'series of failures' view the author rejects.
option_rationales.D: Caloric was replaced because it was wrong about what heat is and could not handle heat turning into work, not for reasons unconnected with its accuracy.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'A theory can be wrong about what something is while being right about many of the ways it behaves, and those behavioural truths can pass, nearly intact, to its successor.' The map wrong about the outline but right about routes, whose routes are kept, matches both halves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the map with right routes and wrong outline that is thrown away, which matches the first half of the account but not the handing on.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options share the right-routes, wrong-outline structure; only one also includes the transfer to the successor, which the reader must see is essential.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pulsating stars can serve as measures of distance because

options.A: their shift against the background as the earth travels around the sun can be converted into a distance.
options.B: they shine so brilliantly when they explode that they can be seen across much of the universe.
options.C: their light, unlike that of ordinary stars, is not dimmed by the dust lying between the stars.
options.D: the timing of their cycle of brightening and fading reveals how bright they truly are.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the timing of their cycle of brightening and fading reveals how bright they truly are.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 gives that geometric method for the nearest stars, the bottom rung; the pulsating stars are useful because their rhythm 'is tied to their true brightness'.
option_rationales.B: That description belongs to the 'class of exploding stars' on the next rung, which the pulsating stars calibrate, not to the pulsating stars themselves.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 mentions dust only as an assumption once neglected; nothing says pulsating stars are exempt from its dimming.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: their 'rhythm of brightening and fading is tied to their true brightness, so that once the rhythm has been timed, a comparison of true with apparent brightness yields a distance'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching to the pulsating stars a property the passage gives to a different rung of the ladder.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 1; two wrong options borrow details from neighbouring rungs.

questions.question: By saying that the chain image is apt 'but only half of it' (paragraph 3), the author means that

options.A: the image fits the lower rungs of the ladder well but fails for the upper rungs that rely on exploding stars.
options.B: only about half of the rungs rest on the rungs beneath them, while the others are measured independently.
options.C: the rungs do depend on one another, but that dependence also lets them test one another, as links cannot.
options.D: the ladder is far stronger than its weakest rung, because errors made at the bottom are never carried upward.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the rungs do depend on one another, but that dependence also lets them test one another, as links cannot.

option_rationales.A: The passage draws no line between lower and upper rungs; its objection is that the rungs check one another, which a chain's links do not.
option_rationales.B: This reads 'half' as a count of rungs; the passage says every rung 'rests on the one beneath' and uses 'half' of the image, not of the ladder.
option_rationales.D: The author grants that interdependence is 'a route by which errors travel upward'; denying that errors are carried upward contradicts paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 accepts the part of the image about dependence and rejects the rest: a chain's links are 'tested by nothing except the load', whereas 'The rungs of the distance ladder are tested by one another'. Interdependence carries errors upward but also catches them.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'half' literally, or taking the author to deny the half of the image that is conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning has to be assembled from the contrast that follows the phrase; one wrong option overstates the author's defence.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the discovery that two kinds of pulsating star had been taken for one

options.A: showed that the ladder as a whole is too unreliable to be used in measuring how fast the universe expands.
options.B: was made by geometry alone, without any appeal to the other methods by which astronomers measure distance.
options.C: is an instance of an error common to every rung, of the kind that comparisons between methods could not catch.
options.D: came about because distances found by different rungs for the same objects failed to agree.

questions.correct_answer: (D) came about because distances found by different rungs for the same objects failed to agree.

option_rationales.A: The author cites such revisions as evidence that the ladder corrects itself, and paragraph 4 treats its expansion rate as worth taking 'so seriously'.
option_rationales.B: The passage presents it as the product of comparing methods, not of a single method working on its own.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 offers it as an error exposed by 'a comparison between overlapping rungs'; paragraph 4 says shared errors 'pass each comparison untouched', so this reverses its role.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says several large revisions came about 'when a comparison between overlapping rungs exposed a hidden assumption', naming 'the confusion of two kinds of pulsating star with one' as an example. It was caught because methods applied to the same objects disagreed.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the errors that cross-checks catch (paragraph 3) with the shared errors that escape them (paragraph 4).
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option uses the language of paragraph 4 and requires the reader to keep the two kinds of error apart.

questions.question: The claim in paragraph 3 that interdependence is 'the means by which they are caught' depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Methods that can be applied to the same objects nearly always give answers that agree within their stated uncertainties.
options.B: At least some of the errors that affect one method of finding distances do not also affect another method used on the same objects.
options.C: The geometric measurements of the nearest stars are free from any error that could be carried up the ladder.
options.D: The expansion rate inferred from the early universe is more trustworthy than the rate found with the ladder.

questions.correct_answer: (B) At least some of the errors that affect one method of finding distances do not also affect another method used on the same objects.

option_rationales.A: Catching errors requires that faulty methods sometimes disagree; if overlapping methods nearly always agreed, comparisons would rarely expose anything, so this works against the claim.
option_rationales.C: The argument does not need this: paragraph 2 contemplates 'A small mistake in the geometry of nearby stars', and paragraph 3 explains how errors anywhere can be caught.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 leaves open whether the disagreement reveals 'a flaw common to the ladder's rungs' or 'something new about the cosmos', and the claim in paragraph 3 does not concern it.

questions.explanation: A comparison can expose a fault only if the fault does not afflict both methods alike. Paragraph 4 makes the point explicit: 'Cross-checks catch only the errors that differ between methods'. If every error were shared, interdependence would catch nothing, so the claim assumes that some errors differ between methods.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that sounds like a precondition for a reliable ladder rather than one the specific claim requires.
questions.difficulty_reason: An assumption question whose answer is made explicit only in the next paragraph; wrong options are plausible conditions for reliability that the argument does not need.

questions.question: The passage is chiefly concerned with

options.A: arguing that conservation laws are better understood as consequences of symmetries, a shift that alters how they explain rather than proving them.
options.B: demonstrating that the conservation of energy is a truth of logic, which no observation of nature could ever overturn.
options.C: recounting how a mathematician's theorem persuaded physicists who had long doubted the conservation laws to accept them.
options.D: explaining how the expansion of the universe has forced physicists to give up the conservation of energy altogether.

questions.correct_answer: (A) arguing that conservation laws are better understood as consequences of symmetries, a shift that alters how they explain rather than proving them.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls this conclusion 'a mistake' and insists that only observation can tell us whether the underlying symmetry holds.
option_rationales.C: No earlier doubt about the conservation laws is reported; paragraph 1 says they were taught as 'bedrock' and the theorem relocates rather than restores them.
option_rationales.D: The expanding universe appears only in paragraph 4 as an application, and the passage says merely that a universal law is unclear 'there', not that it has been abandoned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the theorem 'puts the foundations in the wrong place'; paragraph 2 shows conservation laws following from symmetries; paragraph 3 says the change is in 'the direction of explanation', not a proof; paragraph 4 shows the payoff. The correct answer covers both the reframing and its limit.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the application in paragraph 4 for the subject, or overreading the theorem as a proof.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option states the very conclusion the author rejects, in confident terms; the correct answer must hold both halves of the argument.

questions.question: The passage pairs each of the following features of the laws of nature with the quantity it implies is conserved EXCEPT

options.A: laws that ignore which way a system is facing, with the conservation of angular momentum.
options.B: laws that are the same here as in the next room, with the conservation of momentum.
options.C: laws that stay the same however fast a system is moving, with the conservation of energy.
options.D: laws that are the same today as they were yesterday, with the conservation of energy.

questions.correct_answer: (C) laws that stay the same however fast a system is moving, with the conservation of energy.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says that if the laws 'do not depend on which way a system happens to be facing, angular momentum is conserved'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 gives this pairing in so many words: 'If they are the same here as in the next room, momentum is conserved.'
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 states this pairing directly: 'If the laws are the same today as they were yesterday, energy is conserved.'

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists three pairings: sameness in time with energy, sameness in place with momentum, and independence of orientation with angular momentum. The passage never mentions laws that are unchanged by a system's speed, so that pairing is not one it makes.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that energy, which appears twice among the options, must be correctly paired both times.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each correct pairing is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, convincing evidence that the laws of physics had changed slightly over time would

options.A: count as evidence against the strict conservation of energy, since evidence about the symmetry is in effect evidence about conservation.
options.B: leave the conservation of energy untouched, since the theorem establishes conservation as a matter of logic alone.
options.C: show that the theorem itself had been mathematically mistaken when it linked the symmetries of laws with quantities that are conserved.
options.D: cast doubt on the conservation of momentum while leaving the conservation of energy secure.

questions.correct_answer: (A) count as evidence against the strict conservation of energy, since evidence about the symmetry is in effect evidence about conservation.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls the idea that energy 'must be conserved as a matter of logic' a mistake, so the author would not hold conservation immune.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 treats a failure of symmetry as exactly what the theorem leads us to expect, a loss of footing for the conservation law, not a refutation of the theorem.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 ties momentum to sameness from place to place and energy to sameness over time, so a change over time bears on energy.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'the evidence for the symmetry and the evidence for the conservation law are, in effect, the same evidence', and paragraph 2 ties energy to laws being 'the same today as they were yesterday'. Evidence against that sameness would therefore be evidence against strict energy conservation.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the theorem as a proof of conservation, the reading paragraph 3 rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the 'same evidence' claim of paragraph 3 to the time symmetry of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The discussion of the expanding universe in paragraph 4 functions mainly to

options.A: concede that the theorem breaks down on the largest scales and therefore holds only for systems of modest size.
options.B: report evidence that the conservation of energy has been observed to fail throughout the expanding universe.
options.C: illustrate the 'scandal' that has led physicists to doubt the conservation laws they once treated as bedrock.
options.D: show that treating conservation as resting on symmetry pays off, by telling us where a conservation law should lose its hold.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that treating conservation as resting on symmetry pays off, by telling us where a conservation law should lose its hold.

option_rationales.A: It is the symmetry, not the theorem, that is said to be absent on the largest scales; the author calls the result 'just what one should expect' from the theorem.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says only that it is 'far from clear that a universal law of energy conservation can even be stated there', which is not an observed failure.
option_rationales.C: The scandal is how the case 'would look' 'On the older view'; the author rejects that framing, and no physicists are said to have lost faith in the laws.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the theorem lets us 'ask whether time is uniform'; paragraph 4 opens 'That question has teeth' and shows the answer bearing on the expanding universe. Its final sentence states the function: the principle has become 'a claim whose limits can be foreseen'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the failure of a symmetry with a failure of the theorem that links symmetry and conservation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The most tempting wrong option turns the author's illustration of the theorem's value into a concession against it; telling them apart needs paragraphs 3 and 4 together.

questions.question: The observation in paragraph 2 that the boundary 'can be drawn anywhere convenient without altering the predicted statistics' serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that measuring devices, unlike the particles they record, do not obey the smooth equation of the theory.
options.B: show that the measurement problem has in effect been solved, since the location of the boundary makes no difference.
options.C: explain why a gap in the theory's foundations makes so little difference to how the theory is used.
options.D: support the claim that rival interpretations differ in their predictions only for sufficiently large systems.

questions.correct_answer: (C) explain why a gap in the theory's foundations makes so little difference to how the theory is used.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: a device 'is made of atoms, and atoms obey the smooth equation'.
option_rationales.B: The next sentence says this is 'precisely what makes the problem so easy to ignore', and paragraph 5 calls it 'a gap in the statement of the physics itself', so the problem is not solved.
option_rationales.D: That claim, made in paragraph 4, concerns theories that modify the equation; paragraph 2 is about the textbook rule's undefined boundary.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 sets out the gap (the theory does not say where measurement happens) and then notes that 'In practice nothing hangs on the answer', because the boundary can be moved without changing predictions. The following sentence draws the consequence: that 'is precisely what makes the problem so easy to ignore'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking practical irrelevance as a solution, the confusion the author is arguing against.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by the sentence that follows, but one wrong option turns it into the dismissive view the passage rejects.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the process, described in paragraph 3, in which a system's entanglement with its surroundings suppresses the signs of superposition?

options.A: It is the means by which the theories that modify the smooth equation produce their spontaneous tendency to collapse.
options.B: It deals with one part of what the measurement problem asks but, on most accounts, leaves the occurrence of a particular outcome unexplained.
options.C: It makes the textbook rule unnecessary, because it shows why an apparatus records one result rather than a superposition.
options.D: It is dismissed by most physicists as irrelevant, since superpositions of large objects are in fact readily observed.

questions.correct_answer: (B) It deals with one part of what the measurement problem asks but, on most accounts, leaves the occurrence of a particular outcome unexplained.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 credits the modified theories with 'adding a tiny spontaneous tendency to collapse'; the entanglement process is described separately, as 'A widely discussed physical process', not as their mechanism.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says that on most accounts it 'does not explain why one outcome occurs rather than another', so it does not replace the rule's selection of a result.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the process explains 'why superpositions of large objects are never seen' and is 'widely discussed', the reverse of being dismissed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the process 'explains why superpositions of large objects are never seen, but on most accounts it does not explain why one outcome occurs rather than another'. The measurement problem includes both the absence of visible superpositions and the occurrence of 'exactly one result' (paragraph 1); the process addresses the first but not the second.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that explaining why superpositions are never seen is the same as explaining why one definite result occurs.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer states a partial success that must be distinguished from a full solution, and a wrong option plausibly links the process to the collapse theories.

questions.question: The author regards the view that the dispute over interpretations is 'metaphysics' as

options.A: correct about the theories that modify the equation but mistaken about those that leave the equation untouched.
options.B: a sound conclusion, given that the rival pictures agree with one another in every experiment ever performed.
options.C: a dishonest evasion by physicists who privately believe the theory to be false but prefer not to admit it.
options.D: a natural reaction that wrongly treats one incomplete interpretation as if it were a neutral standard.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a natural reaction that wrongly treats one incomplete interpretation as if it were a neutral standard.

option_rationales.A: The author does not divide the verdict between families of interpretation; the objection in paragraph 4 is to the treatment of the textbook rule as a baseline.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the pictures agree in 'nearly every experiment so far performed', not every one, and calls the response 'confused'.
option_rationales.C: The author calls the response 'understandable'; nothing suggests dishonesty or a private belief that the theory is false.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'The response is understandable but confused. It treats the textbook rule as a neutral baseline from which the interpretations depart, when the rule is itself an interpretation, and an incomplete one'. The attitude combines sympathy with a specific diagnosis of the error.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'sound conclusion' option by overlooking 'nearly' and the author's word 'confused'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases a two-part judgement; one wrong option depends on missing a single qualifying word.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim in paragraph 4 that the rival pictures are not 'strictly equivalent'?

options.A: Most working physicists compute reaction rates successfully without committing themselves to any interpretation.
options.B: The theories that modify the equation can always be adjusted so that their departures fall below anything experiment could detect.
options.C: The smooth equation has been confirmed to great precision in experiments on single particles and small molecules.
options.D: Experiments of increasing delicacy, carried out on ever larger systems, have so far found no departures from standard behaviour at all.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The theories that modify the equation can always be adjusted so that their departures fall below anything experiment could detect.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 concedes this; it bears on the practical irrelevance of the debate, not on whether the interpretations make different predictions.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the modified theories' tendency to collapse is 'negligible for single particles', so precise confirmation at that scale does not tell against them.
option_rationales.D: The author says such experiments 'are now searching' for departures; a null result so far is compatible with departures that are smaller or that arise in larger systems.

questions.explanation: The author's ground for non-equivalence is that modified theories 'predict small departures from standard behaviour in sufficiently large systems'. If those departures could always be tuned below any detectable level, the theories would make no difference that experiment could register, undercutting that ground.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the null experimental result, which is consistent with the author's claim that the search is still under way.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options look like evidence against the modified theories but are neutralised by details in paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Physicists ought to settle which interpretation is correct before they rely on the predictions that the theory makes.
options.B: The measurement problem would vanish if experiments confirmed that all the rival pictures make identical predictions.
options.C: The chief defect the author finds in the textbook rule would be removed if the theory stated precisely what counts as a measurement.
options.D: The interpretations that leave the equation untouched are to be preferred, because they alone avoid an undefined notion of measurement.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The chief defect the author finds in the textbook rule would be removed if the theory stated precisely what counts as a measurement.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says the debate does not oblige 'the working physicist to choose a side before computing a reaction rate'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 holds that a theory that works 'has not thereby been shown to need no description'; agreement in predictions would leave the gap in its statement.
option_rationales.D: The author compares the families of interpretation without endorsing any; the passage never says that only one family avoids the undefined term.

questions.explanation: The author's central complaint against the textbook rule is that it 'invokes a notion the theory never defines' (paragraph 2) and 'relies on a word it cannot define' (paragraph 4). A precise definition would remove that specific objection, whatever other questions remained.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about identical predictions, which repeats the dismissive view of paragraph 4 in a new form.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is a conditional inference from the author's specific objection; the strongest wrong option restates the view that paragraph 5 rejects.

questions.question: The comparison with the swimming pool in paragraph 2 is used to illustrate

options.A: how conclusions drawn from a sample selected by the conditions of observation can mislead.
options.B: the claim that the constants of nature fall within narrow ranges that permit observers to exist.
options.C: why living things are more likely to arise on some planets than on others in the same system.
options.D: how the ambitious form of anthropic reasoning accounts for the fine tuning of physical constants.

questions.correct_answer: (A) how conclusions drawn from a sample selected by the conditions of observation can mislead.

option_rationales.B: That claim belongs to paragraph 1; the pool comparison illustrates the 'warning about bias' of paragraph 2.
option_rationales.C: The comparison is about a biased sample of residents, not about where life arises; the planet remark only sets up the point about bias.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 concerns only the 'modest form'; the attempt to explain the constants begins in paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says treating our surroundings 'as a fair sample of the cosmos' would be like judging a town's fitness from people met at the pool, and concludes that the principle is 'a warning about bias'.
questions.common_misconception: Linking the comparison to the fine tuning of the constants rather than to the modest principle.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is named in the sentences around the comparison.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the lottery example that, in the author's view, the existence of observers would explain nothing about the constants if

options.A: ours were the only universe there is, with its constants fixed once and for all.
options.B: the other regions of a large ensemble turned out to be unobservable to us in principle.
options.C: a great many universes existed whose constants differed from ours, most of them hostile to life.
options.D: the constants permitted observers to exist only within some very narrow range of values.

questions.correct_answer: (A) ours were the only universe there is, with its constants fixed once and for all.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says unobservability means the evidence for the ensemble 'must come from somewhere else', not that the explanation would fail if the ensemble existed.
option_rationales.C: This is the case in which, according to paragraph 3, anthropic reasoning 'dissolves the puzzle'; it corresponds to millions of tickets sold.
option_rationales.D: That narrowness is the puzzle itself, set out in paragraph 1; it is not the condition under which the selection effect fails to explain.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: with a single ticket, the winner's existence 'explains nothing about why that ticket was drawn', and a selection effect 'does explanatory work only when there are many draws'. A single universe is the one-ticket case.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing a lack of evidence for an ensemble (paragraph 4) with the absence of an ensemble (paragraph 3).
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires mapping the analogy onto the cosmic case and keeping apart two distinct difficulties the passage raises.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: Selection effects belong to sound reasoning in the empirical sciences, and neglecting them leads to error.
options.B: Some claims that the constants of nature are set with extreme precision have not held up under examination.
options.C: Anthropic reasoning is unscientific, since the many universes it relies on can never be observed.
options.D: The modest form of anthropic reasoning is a correct and useful warning about a bias in what we observe.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Anthropic reasoning is unscientific, since the many universes it relies on can never be observed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says selection effects 'are a respectable part of reasoning in every empirical science' and that ignoring them 'produces errors'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says 'some claims of extreme precision have not survived scrutiny', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says that 'as a warning it is both correct and useful', so the author agrees.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 opens: 'None of this shows that the approach is unscientific, a charge often levelled against it with more heat than precision.' The author grants that the other regions are 'unobservable in principle' on most versions (paragraph 4) but draws only the narrower conclusion that the evidence must come from elsewhere.
questions.common_misconception: Moving from the author's point about unobservable regions to the stronger charge the author explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer echoes paragraph 4's language about unobservability, so it can look like the author's own conclusion.

questions.question: The statement at the end of paragraph 4 that 'Anthropic reasoning cannot certify its own premise' means that

options.A: the cosmological theories that imply many regions were devised only in order to rescue anthropic reasoning.
options.B: the varied ensemble on which the ambitious explanation depends needs support from evidence other than the fact that we exist.
options.C: anthropic reasoning is circular and therefore can never form any part of a good scientific explanation of the constants of nature.
options.D: the modest principle cannot be shown to be true, because its truth would depend on the existence of observers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the varied ensemble on which the ambitious explanation depends needs support from evidence other than the fact that we exist.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 reports that these theories were 'developed to address quite different problems', and the author grants that the reply 'has force'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the explanation is 'exactly as good as the theory that supplies the ensemble', so it can be good if that theory is; 'never' contradicts this.
option_rationales.D: The statement concerns the ensemble needed by the ambitious version; paragraph 5 calls the modest principle 'nearly beyond dispute'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 makes a varied ensemble the premise of the ambitious explanation; paragraph 4 says the explanation is only as good as the theory supplying that ensemble, whose evidence 'must come from somewhere else'. Our existence as observers cannot itself be the evidence that the ensemble exists.
questions.common_misconception: Inflating the limited point into a charge of circularity or attaching it to the modest principle.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the premise identified in paragraph 3 to the burden described in paragraph 4; two wrong options overextend the claim in different directions.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Anthropic reasoning explains fine tuning wherever many regions exist, and current cosmological theories have now shown that such regions exist.
options.B: The apparent fine tuning of the constants is largely an illusion, produced by selection effects that physicists have so far failed to take into account.
options.C: The modest form of anthropic reasoning is an empty truism, while the ambitious form is speculation that has no place in science.
options.D: Reasoning from our existence rightly corrects for bias, but it explains fine tuning only given a varied ensemble that it cannot itself establish.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Reasoning from our existence rightly corrects for bias, but it explains fine tuning only given a varied ensemble that it cannot itself establish.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the explanation comes free only 'if those theories are right' and that evidence for them 'must come from somewhere else'; 'have now shown' overstates.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says 'Enough of the pattern has held up' to pose a real question, and the passage never calls fine tuning an illusion.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 calls the modest form 'correct and useful', and paragraph 5 denies that the approach is unscientific.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 endorses the modest principle as 'a warning about bias'; paragraph 3 shows that explaining the constants needs many universes or regions with different values; paragraph 4 says reasoning from observers 'cannot certify its own premise'; paragraph 5 separates the two claims. The correct answer holds all three elements: the correction for bias, the need for an ensemble, and the inability to establish that ensemble.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about current cosmological theories, which keeps the author's conditional structure but quietly drops the 'if'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches part of the argument but distorts one element of it: the condition, the reality of fine tuning, or the value of the modest principle.

questions.question: The central concern of the passage is that

options.A: officials who run prevention programmes deserve far more public trust than they now receive, since their claims about averted outbreaks are accurate.
options.B: the benefits of preventive measures are hard to perceive, which erodes support for them unless their record can be checked.
options.C: governments spend too much on hospitals and should move that money to food inspection, where it would buy more health.
options.D: vaccines against rare diseases have become more dangerous than the diseases themselves, which explains why many parents now hesitate.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the benefits of preventive measures are hard to perceive, which erodes support for them unless their record can be checked.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the public should not 'simply take officials at their word' and warns that such claims 'can be inflated', so the passage asks for checkable records, not more trust.
option_rationales.C: Food inspection is one illustration in paragraph 3, and the passage makes no recommendation to transfer hospital budgets; the option is too narrow and adds a prescription.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the vaccine becomes more 'noticeable' than the disease, not more dangerous; the option turns a point about perception into a claim about actual risk.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the problem (success in prevention is 'an absence'), paragraphs 2 and 3 show how this invisibility distorts parents' judgements and budgets, and paragraph 4 proposes making the record 'legible' rather than demanding trust. The correct answer captures both the problem and the author's remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Taking one illustration (food inspection budgets) for the whole argument, or missing the author's refusal to endorse deference.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure is signposted and each wrong option conflicts with an explicit sentence.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the doubting parent's calculation is 'not foolish' because

options.A: health officials have exaggerated the dangers of diphtheria in order to protect their budgets.
options.B: the parent has personally watched a child struggle to breathe and so understands the risk at first hand.
options.C: the disease really has become uncommon in the parent's daily life, so its danger seems remote.
options.D: the side effects of the vaccine are in fact more serious than the disease would have been for the child.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the disease really has become uncommon in the parent's daily life, so its danger seems remote.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 warns in general that claims about averted disasters can be inflated, but nothing suggests that the danger of diphtheria has been exaggerated.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the passage, which describes a parent 'who has never seen a child struggle to breathe with diphtheria'.
option_rationales.D: The passage never compares the actual severity of the two; it says the parent weighs 'something vivid against something abstract', which concerns perception.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'From where that parent stands, the calculation is not foolish; the danger really has receded from ordinary experience.' The correct answer restates that reason.
questions.common_misconception: Importing paragraph 4's caution about inflated claims into paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in the same sentence as the quoted phrase.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a food inspection service is especially easy to cut because

options.A: the harm done by weakening it appears slowly and thinly and is usually blamed on something else.
options.B: it usually costs considerably more to run than treating the illnesses that contaminated food would otherwise cause.
options.C: the public has come to believe that contaminated food no longer poses any real danger in modern shops.
options.D: its officials have often been caught exaggerating the number of outbreaks it has prevented.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the harm done by weakening it appears slowly and thinly and is usually blamed on something else.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 suggests the opposite, noting that prevention is often 'the cheaper way to buy the same health'.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about public beliefs on food safety; the vulnerability it describes comes from how slowly and diffusely the costs of neglect appear.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such claims can be inflated by any agency, but it does not say that inspection officials have been caught doing so, nor that this explains the cuts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the year after a cut 'looks much like the year before it' and that the costs of neglect 'arrive slowly, are spread thinly, and are usually blamed on something else'. The correct answer combines these points.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about inflated claims because it echoes paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is assembled from two adjacent sentences.

questions.question: Which of the following actions best fits the response to invisibility that the author recommends in the final paragraph?

options.A: A health department launches a campaign in which senior doctors explain why the public should trust their expertise on vaccination.
options.B: A health department stops publishing any estimates of illnesses averted, since such estimates concern events that never happened and can be inflated.
options.C: A health department shifts much of its budget from prevention to treatment so that its spending produces results people can see.
options.D: A health department reports outbreaks averted alongside comparisons with similar districts that lacked the measure and an account of its side effects.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A health department reports outbreaks averted alongside comparisons with similar districts that lacked the measure and an account of its side effects.

option_rationales.A: The author says 'The answer to invisibility is not deference'; a campaign asking for trust is exactly the response the passage rejects.
option_rationales.B: The author wants 'better ways of making the counterfactual visible', not silence about it; dropping the estimates leaves prevention as invisible as before.
option_rationales.C: This yields to the drift towards cure that paragraph 3 criticises; the author wants prevention made legible, not abandoned for more visible spending.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists the remedy: 'comparisons with places and periods that lacked the measure, honest accounting of the measure's own costs and side effects, and records kept carefully enough that a sceptic could check them'. Only the correct answer does this.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that stops publishing estimates, because it seems to answer the worry about inflated claims.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option plausibly responds to the author's concession, so the reader must keep hold of the stated remedy.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is most striking about the historical references to waking in the night?

options.A: They attribute the waking interval to the spread of cheap artificial light in the evenings.
options.B: They treat the waking interval as a normal part of the night, not as a cause for complaint.
options.C: They come mainly from medical advice written for people who could not manage to sleep through the whole night.
options.D: They describe in close detail the prayers and conversations with which people filled the interval.

questions.correct_answer: (B) They treat the waking interval as a normal part of the night, not as a cause for complaint.

option_rationales.A: Artificial light is an explanation offered later for the interval's disappearance, not something the historical sources themselves say.
option_rationales.C: The sources listed are 'diaries, legal testimony and household advice', and the passage says the interval was mentioned 'not as a complaint'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says what is striking 'is not their content but their tone', so the activities described are explicitly not the striking feature.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'What is striking about these references is not their content but their tone: the waking interval is mentioned as an ordinary feature of the night, not as a complaint.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about activities because the passage lists them just before the sentence that answers the question.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence.

questions.question: The author mentions that people used the night-time interval 'to pray, tend the fire, talk quietly, or simply lie in the dark and think' in order to

options.A: show that the interval was filled with everyday activities, consistent with its being treated as ordinary.
options.B: prove that the waking interval was caused by household duties such as keeping the fire alight.
options.C: argue that people in pre-industrial Europe spent their nights more usefully than people do today.
options.D: suggest that waking in the night was a religious custom observed mainly by devout households.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that the interval was filled with everyday activities, consistent with its being treated as ordinary.

option_rationales.B: Tending the fire is listed as one way the interval was used, not as its cause; the passage offers no cause for the interval itself.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no comparison of how usefully nights are spent; the list illustrates how routine the interval was.
option_rationales.D: Prayer is one item in a list that also includes talking and thinking; nothing restricts the practice to devout households.

questions.explanation: The list of activities precedes the remark that the interval is mentioned 'as an ordinary feature of the night'. Its function is to show that people simply got on with things during it, which supports the point about tone.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a cause or a value judgement into a descriptive list.
questions.difficulty_reason: The role of the list is clear from the sentence that follows it.

questions.question: The reasoning in paragraph 3 implies that a person who regularly wakes for an hour in the night would probably sleep better if he or she

options.A: got up and kept busy until feeling tired again, because lying awake in the dark is what makes the waking last longer.
options.B: went to bed much earlier and avoided artificial light altogether, so as to restore the pre-industrial pattern of two sleeps.
options.C: sought medical treatment for insomnia at once, since any waking during the night is a disorder that needs correcting.
options.D: regarded the waking as an unremarkable part of the night rather than as a sign that something had gone wrong.

questions.correct_answer: (D) regarded the waking as an unremarkable part of the night rather than as a sign that something had gone wrong.

option_rationales.A: The passage blames worry, not lying in the dark; it notes that people once simply lay in the dark and thought, and treated that as ordinary.
option_rationales.B: The light explanation is called 'suggestive rather than conclusive', and paragraph 4 rejects treating segmented sleep as a true pattern to restore; paragraph 3's point concerns worry.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 suggests that labelling such waking a disorder can itself worsen sleep, so this option runs against the reasoning.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that 'worry about sleep is itself a powerful disrupter of sleep' and that a person who 'concludes that something has gone wrong' stays awake longer than 'one who regards the waking as unremarkable'. The correct answer applies this directly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about artificial light, which uses paragraph 2's material but ignores paragraph 4's warning against restoring a supposed natural pattern.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options use real passage material; the reader must identify that paragraph 3's mechanism is worry.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the idea that segmented sleep is the natural human pattern is best described as

options.A: approving, since the idea provides a welcome corrective to the modern insistence on eight unbroken hours.
options.B: indifferent, since the author regards historical evidence about sleep as having no bearing on medicine.
options.C: sceptical, since the historical evidence shows sleep taking several forms rather than one original form.
options.D: hostile, since the author believes that consolidated sleep is the biologically correct pattern for adults.

questions.correct_answer: (C) sceptical, since the historical evidence shows sleep taking several forms rather than one original form.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls this idea a second 'myth' to be avoided; the author criticises the eight-hour rule without endorsing a rival natural pattern.
option_rationales.B: The author uses historical evidence to argue that some insomnia may be 'a mismatch between a person and a norm', which is a medical point.
option_rationales.D: The author says consolidated sleep is 'partly a product of custom' and does not call either pattern correct.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'It would be a mistake, however, to replace one myth with another', and the record 'shows that sleep has taken more than one form'. This is measured scepticism grounded in the evidence.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because the author criticises the eight-hour rule, he or she must favour segmented sleep.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the author's critique of one norm from any endorsement of its rival.

questions.question: In context, the words 'It is both' at the start of paragraph 2 assert that the improvement seen in a placebo group is

options.A: genuine, and also worth investigating in its own right.
options.B: unreal, though it remains of some interest to researchers.
options.C: a measure of the drug and of the context at the same time.
options.D: produced partly by deception and partly by honest explanation.

questions.correct_answer: (A) genuine, and also worth investigating in its own right.

option_rationales.B: The sentence answers the assumption that the improvement is 'not real, or at least not interesting'; 'both' affirms that it is real and interesting, not unreal.
option_rationales.C: The placebo group receives no drug, so its improvement cannot measure the drug; paragraph 2 calls it a measure of 'the context of care'.
option_rationales.D: Deception is not discussed until paragraph 3, and 'both' refers back to the two qualities just denied, real and interesting.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 ends with the assumption that the improvement 'is not real, or at least not interesting'. 'It is both' rejects this: the improvement is real and it is interesting.
questions.common_misconception: Losing track of what 'both' refers back to.
questions.difficulty_reason: The referent is the immediately preceding clause.

questions.question: The passage implies that the open-label trials are important chiefly because they

options.A: prove that inert pills can relieve the symptoms of an infection even when patients know they are inert.
options.B: establish that the novelty of taking part in an unusual study is the real source of placebo responses.
options.C: cast doubt on the belief that using placebo effects on purpose requires misleading patients.
options.D: show that symptoms reported by patients themselves are too unreliable to be used in clinical trials.

questions.correct_answer: (C) cast doubt on the belief that using placebo effects on purpose requires misleading patients.

option_rationales.A: The findings are called 'preliminary', so 'prove' overstates them, and paragraph 4 says the meaning of a consultation is unlikely to 'clear an infection'.
option_rationales.B: Novelty is raised as an open question ('it is not clear how much of the effect survives'), not established as the source of the response.
option_rationales.D: The passage treats self-reported symptoms as the area where placebo responses are most consistent; it never calls such reports unreliable.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the standard objection rested on the assumption that a placebo 'works only if the patient is deceived', and that the open-label trials 'have unsettled this assumption'. The correct answer states that significance.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the novelty option because the passage mentions novelty as a caveat, and mistaking a caveat for a conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options overstate hedged statements; the reader must track the degree of the passage's claims.

questions.question: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: recommend that doctors use inert pills more often in order to replace the time lost from shorter consultations.
options.B: draw a practical consequence from the argument that the context of care has effects of its own.
options.C: concede that the evidence for placebo responses is too weak to have any bearing on medical practice.
options.D: show that clinical trials have systematically overstated the effects of the drugs they test.

questions.correct_answer: (B) draw a practical consequence from the argument that the context of care has effects of its own.

option_rationales.A: The sentence before it says the conclusion 'is not that doctors should prescribe sugar pills'; the final sentence makes no such recommendation.
option_rationales.C: The sentence draws a consequence for practice, warning about shorter consultations, so it does not deny that the evidence bears on practice.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 calls the subtraction of placebo improvement 'sound for its purpose'; the final sentence concerns consultations, not the accuracy of drug trials.

questions.explanation: Having argued that the placebo arm measures 'how much the context of care can do by itself', the author concludes that 'the manner of care is itself a part of treatment', and the final sentence applies this: shortening consultations may remove 'an active ingredient' unrecorded.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the final sentence as a criticism of drug trials because it echoes the 'nothing' of paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the last sentence back to the reframing in paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the suggestion in paragraph 3 that 'the ritual may matter more than the belief that the pill is active'?

options.A: Improvements among patients openly given inert pills persisted for several months, well after the novelty of the study had worn off.
options.B: Patients openly given inert pills reported less pain and nausea but showed no change in laboratory measures of their underlying disease.
