options.C: Patients given longer and more attentive consultations improved more than those given brief ones, whether or not they also received any pill at all.
options.D: Patients openly given inert pills improved no more than patients given identical consultations without pills, while patients told the pills were active improved markedly.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Patients openly given inert pills improved no more than patients given identical consultations without pills, while patients told the pills were active improved markedly.

option_rationales.A: This answers the novelty caveat in paragraph 3 and so, if anything, strengthens the open-label findings rather than weakening the claim about ritual.
option_rationales.B: This fits paragraph 4's claim that placebo responses are strongest for reported symptoms; it says nothing about whether ritual or belief drives the response.
option_rationales.C: This supports the broader claim that the context of care has effects of its own, and does not set the ritual of pill-taking against belief in an active pill.

questions.explanation: The claim contrasts two possible sources of the response: the ritual of taking a pill and the belief that it is active. The correct answer shows that the ritual of pill-taking added nothing beyond the consultation, while belief in an active pill produced a large effect, which directly reverses the suggested ranking.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the laboratory-measures option because it seems to limit placebo effects, without noticing that it does not bear on ritual versus belief.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option concerns placebo effects and two appear to limit or qualify them; only the correct answer isolates the specific comparison the claim makes.

questions.question: According to the passage, responsible use of a new antibiotic harms the finances of the company that makes it because

options.A: responsible use allows bacteria to develop resistance to the new drug more quickly than careless use would.
options.B: health systems refuse to pay more for a new antibiotic than they already pay for older and cheaper ones.
options.C: regulators prevent companies from promoting reserve antibiotics to doctors during the life of the patent.
options.D: it recovers its costs by selling in quantity while its patent lasts, and responsible use keeps sales low.

questions.correct_answer: (D) it recovers its costs by selling in quantity while its patent lasts, and responsible use keeps sales low.

option_rationales.A: This reverses the passage: holding the drug back is recommended precisely because 'every use exerts selective pressure'.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about health systems refusing higher prices; the problem it identifies is low volume, not low price.
option_rationales.C: Regulation of promotion is never mentioned; doctors are 'urged not to use' the drug for medical reasons, not because of a ban on marketing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A company recovers the cost of developing a drug by selling it in quantity during the years its patent protects it, and a drug that doctors are urged not to use cannot be sold in quantity.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the resistance option by reversing the direction of the stewardship argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The mechanism is stated in one sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements is closest in principle to the payment scheme described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A city pays a builder a single fixed price to construct a flood wall, after which the builder has no further role.
options.B: A publisher pays an author a royalty on every copy of the author's book that is sold, for as long as it stays in print.
options.C: A hospital pays a supplier a yearly fee to keep a standby generator ready for it, whether or not the power ever fails.
options.D: A pharmacy receives a fee from the health system for each prescription that it fills during the year.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A hospital pays a supplier a yearly fee to keep a standby generator ready for it, whether or not the power ever fails.

option_rationales.A: The scheme is a recurring payment 'for access' to something kept available; a one-off construction price rewards completing a job, not maintaining a reserve.
option_rationales.B: A royalty rises with each sale, which ties income to consumption; the scheme in paragraph 3 is designed to break exactly that link.
option_rationales.D: A fee per prescription is a payment by volume, the very model that paragraph 2 says makes reserve antibiotics a commercial disaster.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes 'a fixed annual sum for access' paid whether the drug is used 'on a thousand patients or on ten', which 'rewards the existence of the drug rather than its consumption'. A yearly standby fee paid whether or not the generator is used has the same structure.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the flood wall because it involves a fixed price, without noticing that the scheme pays repeatedly for continued availability.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option shares the 'fixed sum' feature, so the reader must identify the full principle.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the forms of misuse listed in paragraph 1 as

options.A: genuine causes of resistance that have nonetheless drawn attention away from a separate economic problem.
options.B: the main reason that large pharmaceutical firms have stopped developing new antibiotics.
options.C: exaggerated worries that distract attention from what is in fact the true and only cause of antibiotic resistance.
options.D: problems that the payment schemes in paragraph 3 would largely solve once they were adopted.

questions.correct_answer: (A) genuine causes of resistance that have nonetheless drawn attention away from a separate economic problem.

option_rationales.B: The author says the economic problem 'has nothing to do with carelessness' and would arise 'Even if every prescription were perfectly judged', so misuse is not the reason firms left.
option_rationales.C: The author says each practice 'deserves the attention it receives' and gives bacteria opportunities to evolve defences, so misuse is not dismissed.
option_rationales.D: The schemes address the incentive to develop drugs, not prescribing habits or animal dosing; the passage never claims they would reduce misuse.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 grants that misuse 'deserves the attention it receives' and then turns to 'a quieter problem' that is 'Less often discussed'. The author therefore sees misuse as real but as having overshadowed the economic problem.
questions.common_misconception: Overreading the turn to 'a quieter problem' as a dismissal of misuse.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the concession and the turn of paragraph 1 together.

questions.question: The argument in paragraph 2 that responsible use makes a new antibiotic 'a commercial disaster' depends most on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Older and cheaper antibiotics will soon stop working against most common infections, leaving doctors with no alternative to the new drug.
options.B: The price per course of a reserve antibiotic cannot be set high enough to recover its costs from a few patients.
options.C: Medicines for chronic conditions cost more to develop than new antibiotics do, which gives their makers stronger incentives.
options.D: A genuinely new antibiotic will usually prove less effective against common infections than the older and cheaper drugs it backs up.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The price per course of a reserve antibiotic cannot be set high enough to recover its costs from a few patients.

option_rationales.A: If older drugs failed widely, the new drug would be used far more, which would ease the commercial problem rather than underlie it; the argument assumes older drugs still work for most patients.
option_rationales.C: The contrast with chronic medicines turns on how often they are taken, not on what they cost to develop; the argument works whatever the relative costs.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 holds the new drug back because 'every use exerts selective pressure', not because it works less well; the commercial problem arises however effective the drug is.

questions.explanation: The step from 'cannot be sold in quantity' to 'commercial disaster' holds only if low volume cannot be offset by a high price per course. If a company could charge enough per course to recover its costs from a small number of patients, responsible use would not be ruinous. That unstated premise is what the correct answer states.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about older drugs failing, which sounds like a premise of any argument about resistance but would in fact ease the commercial problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: The needed premise is unstated, and two wrong options sound like natural premises of an argument about resistance and drug development.

questions.question: According to the passage, the ecological vocabulary accounts for the intestinal infection that can follow a broad course of antibiotics by pointing out that

options.A: the drug directly strengthens the harmful species that it fails to kill in the gut.
options.B: the drug clears away resident species that had been keeping a harmful one under control.
options.C: the harmful species is carried into the gut along with the antibiotic during treatment.
options.D: the immune system is weakened by the drug and can no longer repel invading microbes.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the drug clears away resident species that had been keeping a harmful one under control.

option_rationales.A: The passage says the drug removes 'the competitors' of the harmful species; it says nothing about the drug strengthening that species directly.
option_rationales.C: Nothing suggests the antibiotic introduces the harmful species; the passage says resident competitors 'had kept a harmful one in check', so it was already present.
option_rationales.D: This is an explanation in the language of war, and the passage does not give it; the mechanism described is the loss of competing resident species.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'by clearing out the resident species, the drug removes the competitors that had kept a harmful one in check.'
questions.common_misconception: Reaching for a familiar immune explanation instead of the one the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The mechanism is stated in a single sentence.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the war metaphor is best described as

options.A: nostalgic, since the author wishes that medicine would return to the clarity of its older language.
options.B: neutral, since the author declines to judge whether the war picture or the ecological picture explains more.
options.C: dismissive, since the author treats it as a piece of decoration that held back medical research for decades.
options.D: appreciative of what it achieved, while holding that it misdescribes most of the body's microbes.

questions.correct_answer: (D) appreciative of what it achieved, while holding that it misdescribes most of the body's microbes.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 opens by saying 'The lesson is not that medicine should return to the language of war'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the war metaphor now looks 'crude' and that the ecological vocabulary 'explains things the older one could not', which is a clear judgement.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says 'The metaphor was not idle decoration' and credits its programme with saving 'an enormous number of lives'.

questions.explanation: The author credits the war metaphor in paragraph 1 ('saved an enormous number of lives') but says in paragraph 2 that most resident microbes 'are not enemies' and that the metaphor now looks 'crude'. The attitude is respect for its record combined with a judgement that it is inadequate.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the author's criticism of the ecological metaphor in paragraph 3 for nostalgia about the war metaphor.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining a credit in paragraph 1 with a criticism in paragraph 2 and a disclaimer in paragraph 4.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author objects to products that promise to 'rebalance' the gut chiefly because

options.A: their promises are too vague to be tested, so no evidence could show that they fail.
options.B: ecologists have shown that no community of microbes in the gut can ever remain stable for long.
options.C: they rely on the language of war while presenting themselves as products based on ecology.
options.D: they contain species of bacteria that are known to harm the gut when taken in large amounts.

questions.correct_answer: (A) their promises are too vague to be tested, so no evidence could show that they fail.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says real ecosystems 'have many stable states', the reverse of saying none can remain stable.
option_rationales.C: The products are criticised for borrowing the popular ecological idea of balance, not for using the war metaphor.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no claim about what such products contain or whether they cause harm; its objection is to how their promise is framed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says such products specify 'nothing that could be measured' and that 'the vagueness of the promise protects it from ever being shown false'. Paragraph 4 condemns images that no experiment 'could ever contradict'. The objection is untestability.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the stability option by misreading 'many stable states' as a claim that no stable state exists.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option distorts a precise phrase; the correct answer requires linking paragraph 3 to the criterion in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following uses of the ecological picture would the author most clearly endorse?

options.A: A textbook that swaps its talk of invading germs for talk of an unbalanced gut while leaving its explanations otherwise unchanged.
options.B: A clinic that advises patients to restore their gut to its natural original community through a carefully planned diet.
options.C: A study that predicts how quickly particular gut species return after antibiotic treatment and then tests the prediction against measurements.
options.D: A public campaign that urges people to refuse antibiotics because the bacteria in their bodies are partners rather than enemies.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A study that predicts how quickly particular gut species return after antibiotic treatment and then tests the prediction against measurements.

option_rationales.A: Changing the vocabulary without importing working concepts brings only 'the mood of ecology'; nothing in the revised textbook generates a testable prediction.
option_rationales.B: This assumes that each body has 'a single proper community to which it should be restored', the popular error paragraph 3 criticises.
option_rationales.D: The author credits the antibiotic programme with saving many lives and says the lesson is not a simple reversal; the campaign uses the ecological image to blur a question, not sharpen it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the ecological picture is valuable when it brings concepts 'such as competition, succession and the effects of disturbance, which generate predictions that can be tested'. Recolonisation after antibiotic disturbance is succession after disturbance, and the study tests a prediction.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the textbook revision because it moves away from war language, which the author also wants, without noticing that it adds no testable concept.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options look ecological; separating 'working concepts' from 'mood' is the fine distinction tested.

questions.question: The example of pain felt in amputated limbs (paragraph 2) is used to

options.A: suggest that surgical amputation is a common cause of pain that lasts for many years.
options.B: show that the brain suppresses pain during moments of danger or intense concentration.
options.C: present a case in which pain occurs although no tissue remains that could be damaged.
options.D: illustrate the claim that pain normally fades once the injured tissue has healed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) present a case in which pain occurs although no tissue remains that could be damaged.

option_rationales.A: The passage does not discuss how common such pain is or blame surgery; it uses the case only to show pain where 'there is no tissue left to report anything'.
option_rationales.B: That point is made by the separate example of serious wounds felt little 'in moments of danger'; the amputation example concerns pain without tissue.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the role of the example, which is offered as a difficulty for the gauge picture, not as support for it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists cases where 'the gauge picture fails', and says of amputated limbs that 'there is no tissue left to report anything'. The example shows pain without damaged tissue.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the amputation example with the neighbouring example about moments of danger.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence that gives the example.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, calling pain a 'verdict' rather than a 'reading' suggests that pain is

options.A: a final judgement that, once reached, cannot be revised however circumstances change.
options.B: a faithful report that passes on the exact extent of the damage done to the tissues.
options.C: a penalty that the body imposes on itself whenever some part of it has been injured.
options.D: a conclusion that the brain reaches by weighing several kinds of information together.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a conclusion that the brain reaches by weighing several kinds of information together.

option_rationales.A: The passage treats the verdict as revisable: paragraph 4 suggests that treatment aimed at the protective system 'may help', so the verdict is not fixed.
option_rationales.B: This describes a 'reading', the gauge picture that the word 'verdict' is chosen to replace.
option_rationales.C: The legal sense of punishment is not intended; the passage describes the brain combining 'context, expectation and memory' to judge threat, not penalising injury.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the term: tissue signals are 'one input among several', and the brain 'combines them with context, expectation and memory' and produces pain 'when it concludes' the body is under threat. A verdict is a conclusion drawn from evidence.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'verdict' to mean something final and unchangeable, as in its courtroom sense.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option uses a familiar connotation of the word that the passage's own argument rules out.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that, for a patient whose pain has continued long after an injury has healed,

options.A: a scan that shows no damaged structure does not show that the pain is imaginary.
options.B: operating on whatever abnormality a scan reveals is the most promising route to relief.
options.C: the original injury was probably far more severe than any of the doctors had realised.
options.D: the pain is best treated by persuading the patient that it has no real basis in the body.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a scan that shows no damaged structure does not show that the pain is imaginary.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says that 'operating on whatever turns up in a scan, may do little good' when the alarm itself is oversensitive.
option_rationales.C: This reasons from the gauge picture, which the passage rejects; on the verdict account, pain can outlast damage without the damage having been underestimated.
option_rationales.D: The author denies that the account means 'the pain is imaginary' and insists that the verdict 'hurts just as much'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a verdict produced by the nervous system 'is as real as any other bodily event' and that searching harder for a damaged structure may do little good. So the absence of a visible structure does not make the pain unreal.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the persuasion option, which mirrors the misunderstanding the author explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options express views the passage reports in order to reject; the reader must hold the author's reply.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Long-lasting pain is caused by damage too small for present scans to detect, so better imaging is the most urgent need.
options.B: Pain is better seen as the brain's judgement about threat than as a measure of injury, which bears on treating pain that outlasts healing.
options.C: The gauge picture of pain is mistaken even for everyday injuries, which is why burns and scratches are so poorly understood.
options.D: Pain that continues after healing is largely imaginary, and patients should be helped to understand that it can be safely ignored.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Pain is better seen as the brain's judgement about threat than as a measure of injury, which bears on treating pain that outlasts healing.

option_rationales.A: This keeps the gauge picture; the author suggests the alarm itself 'has become oversensitive' and doubts that searching harder for damage will help.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the gauge picture is 'roughly accurate' for 'a great many everyday injuries'; the passage says it fails in particular cases.
option_rationales.D: The author says the account is not 'a polite way of saying that the pain is imaginary' and that such pain 'hurts just as much'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 sets out the gauge picture, paragraph 2 gives cases where it fails, paragraph 3 proposes the verdict account, and paragraph 4 defends it against the charge that it makes pain imaginary and draws a consequence for treatment. The correct answer covers both the thesis and its consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about imaginary pain because the passage discusses that interpretation at length.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is a misreading the passage itself anticipates, and another overstates the scope of the critique.

questions.question: In the hypothetical case of the woman described in paragraph 2, detection by scan at sixty-three

options.A: adds five years to her life by allowing treatment to begin before symptoms appear.
options.B: fails her because the tumour is found too late in its course to be treated successfully.
options.C: shows that her tumour must have belonged to the slow-growing kind that repeated tests tend to catch.
options.D: lengthens the survival recorded after her diagnosis without postponing her death.

questions.correct_answer: (D) lengthens the survival recorded after her diagnosis without postponing her death.

option_rationales.A: The case stipulates that the tumour 'will kill a woman at seventy whatever is done', so no years are added to her life; only the measured survival grows.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about the timing being too late; the point of the case is that the timing makes no difference to when she dies.
option_rationales.C: Slow tumours are the 'second distortion', introduced after the example; the woman's case illustrates the earlier starting of the clock, not tumour speed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Nothing about her death has changed, but the survival figure has more than tripled, simply because the clock was started earlier.' Her survival after diagnosis rises from two years to seven while she still dies at seventy.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the seven years of survival as five extra years of life.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must apply the stipulation 'whatever is done' to the figures.

questions.question: When the author says that the comparison in paragraph 1 is 'rigged' (paragraph 2), the point is that

options.A: comparisons of survival are worthless for judging any medical treatment, whether or not it involves screening.
options.B: the way it is made favours screening whether or not screening saves lives, though nobody intends this.
options.C: researchers have deliberately arranged survival figures so as to make screening programmes look successful.
options.D: patients whose cancers are found by screening receive better treatment than patients who come with symptoms.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the way it is made favours screening whether or not screening saves lives, though nobody intends this.

option_rationales.A: The passage criticises survival after diagnosis as a measure of screening; it makes no claim about every other use of survival comparisons.
option_rationales.C: The author says the comparison is rigged 'by the arithmetic of detection rather than by anyone's intent', which rules out deliberate manipulation.
option_rationales.D: The passage attributes the better survival to when the clock starts and to what is found, 'rather than what was done', not to differences in treatment.

questions.explanation: The author immediately qualifies 'rigged' with 'by the arithmetic of detection rather than by anyone's intent', and then shows how lead time and tumour speed improve the figures regardless of benefit.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'rigged' in its usual sense of deliberate fraud, ignoring the qualification that follows it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The ordinary sense of the word is cancelled by the clause after it.

questions.question: The observation that 'every overdiagnosed patient experiences the treatment as a rescue' (paragraph 3) contributes to the argument chiefly by

options.A: explaining why the harm of overdiagnosis tends to build support for screening rather than doubts about it.
options.B: showing that overdiagnosed patients are simply wrong to believe that they were ever found to have cancer.
options.C: suggesting that patients ought to be told at diagnosis whenever their tumour is of the harmless kind.
options.D: revealing that screening programmes recruit their former patients as advocates in order to protect their funding.

questions.correct_answer: (A) explaining why the harm of overdiagnosis tends to build support for screening rather than doubts about it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the cells 'are what the pathologist says they are'; the patients' error, if any, concerns whether they were in danger, not whether they had the abnormality.
option_rationales.C: The same sentence says 'no individual can know' that his or her tumour was harmless, so the passage cannot be recommending that patients be told.
option_rationales.D: The passage calls these advocates 'sincere' and describes an unintended effect; it attributes no strategy or motive to the programmes.

questions.explanation: The sentence leads straight into 'Screening thus produces its own most sincere advocates, and the more it overdiagnoses, the more grateful survivors it creates.' Its role is to show that overdiagnosis, a harm, is experienced as a benefit and so generates support.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about patients being wrong to believe they had cancer, which confuses being 'never in danger' with never having had the abnormality.
questions.difficulty_reason: The first wrong option turns on the passage's fine distinction between the diagnosis being accurate and the prediction being wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following findings would the author regard as the strongest evidence that a particular screening programme is beneficial?

options.A: Patients whose cancers were found by the programme survived, on average, twice as long after diagnosis as patients found through symptoms.
options.B: People who chose to attend the programme were less likely to die of the disease than people in the same area who chose not to attend.
options.C: When comparable populations were assigned at random to be screened or not, fewer people in the screened population died of the disease.
options.D: After the programme began, far more cancers were diagnosed each year than before, and a much larger share of them were at an early stage.

questions.correct_answer: (C) When comparable populations were assigned at random to be screened or not, fewer people in the screened population died of the disease.

option_rationales.A: This is the survival comparison that paragraph 4 says 'cannot answer that question', because lead time, slow tumours and overdiagnosis inflate it even when no death is prevented.
option_rationales.B: The author asks whether fewer people 'in the population it serves' die, a question answered only by 'comparisons between whole populations'; attenders and non-attenders are self-selected parts of one population, so the gap may reflect who chooses to attend rather than what screening does.
option_rationales.D: More and earlier diagnoses are exactly what overdiagnosis and the bias towards slow tumours would produce, so this finding cannot distinguish benefit from distortion.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the right question is 'whether fewer people in the population it serves die of the disease', and cites 'carefully conducted trials comparing large screened and unscreened populations' as the evidence that justifies some programmes. A randomised comparison of mortality between populations is that kind of evidence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the attenders comparison because it measures deaths, without noticing that it compares self-selected groups rather than whole populations.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options reflect the distortions the passage describes, and the third measures mortality but in the wrong comparison, so the reader must apply the full criterion.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the passage's account of overdiagnosis EXCEPT:

options.A: It can lead people to undergo surgery or radiation that they did not in fact need.
options.B: It improves a screening programme's survival figures without preventing any deaths.
options.C: It cannot be recognised in any individual patient at the time the patient is treated.
options.D: It occurs when a pathologist mistakes harmless cells for cancerous ones under the microscope.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It occurs when a pathologist mistakes harmless cells for cancerous ones under the microscope.

option_rationales.A: Consistent: paragraph 3 says such people 'are treated, sometimes with surgery or radiation', though 'they were never in danger'.
option_rationales.B: Consistent: overdiagnosed patients 'appear in the statistics as survivors', and paragraph 4 lists overdiagnosis among the influences that improve survival 'even when not a single death has been prevented'.
option_rationales.C: Consistent: paragraph 3 says 'no individual can know that his or her own tumour was of this harmless kind'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says overdiagnosis 'is not an error in the usual sense, since the cells are what the pathologist says they are', and that 'The error lies in the prediction that they would have mattered'. A misreading by the pathologist is therefore exactly what overdiagnosis is not.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that overdiagnosis must be a laboratory mistake, since the word suggests a wrong diagnosis.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer reads like a natural definition of the term, and the passage's own definition must be applied to reject it.

questions.question: According to the passage, a doctor's personal experience is a weak guide to who benefits from a treatment because it

options.A: cannot be written down or shared with colleagues and so cannot be checked by anyone.
options.B: rests on few patients, has no comparison group and is shaped by memorable cases.
options.C: is biased in particular towards remembering those patients whom the treatment harmed.
options.D: covers too few patients with any one condition for a doctor to form an impression at all.

questions.correct_answer: (B) rests on few patients, has no comparison group and is shaped by memorable cases.

option_rationales.A: Whether experience can be recorded or shared is never discussed; the weaknesses listed concern sample size, comparison and memory.
option_rationales.C: The passage says memory 'favours vivid cases', which may be successes or failures; it does not say the bias runs towards harms.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the sample is small, not that it is too small to yield any impression; doctors do form impressions, which the passage calls a 'poor instrument'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls a doctor's experience a trial 'without randomisation, with a small sample, no comparison group and a memory that favours vivid cases'.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'vivid cases' into a specific bias towards harms.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer restates one sentence.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining why analysis of subgroups is the most reliable way to identify which patients benefit from treatment.
options.B: defending the clinical judgement of experienced doctors against the growing authority of randomised trials.
options.C: showing how evidence from trials about groups should, and should not, guide decisions about individual patients.
options.D: arguing that trials within single patients should replace large randomised trials for most medical conditions.

questions.correct_answer: (C) showing how evidence from trials about groups should, and should not, guide decisions about individual patients.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says subgroup analysis is not 'as reliable as it appears' and produces 'mirages' by chance.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 presents reliance on clinical judgement as 'The second error' and calls the clinician's impression 'a poor instrument'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says such designs suit only 'some chronic conditions' and 'are not always practical'; they illustrate what individual evidence requires.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 sets up the gap between the group question and the individual question; paragraphs 2 to 4 reject two errors and a tempting remedy; paragraph 5 states the author's position on how averages should be used. The correct answer covers that whole structure.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about clinical judgement because the passage criticises over-literal use of averages in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option takes one part of the passage and reverses or inflates it.

questions.question: The discussion of the stroke drug in paragraph 2 implies that promising a patient that the drug will cut his own risk by three points is unjustified because

options.A: the trial result fits patterns of benefit under which that patient's own risk would not fall by three points.
options.B: no individual patient's risk can be changed by a drug whose effects are known only as averages.
options.C: the drug actually harms more patients than it helps, a fact that the favourable average conceals.
options.D: the true average benefit of the drug is probably smaller than the three points the trial estimated.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the trial result fits patterns of benefit under which that patient's own risk would not fall by three points.

option_rationales.B: The passage says the average may conceal a minority who 'benefited a great deal', so individual risks can change; what the trial cannot reveal is whose risk changes and by how much.
option_rationales.C: The passage says only that the same average could arise 'if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed'; it never says harms outnumber benefits.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not question the trial's estimate of the average; its objection is to applying a correct average to each patient.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the same average 'would result if a small minority benefited a great deal and everyone else not at all, or if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed'. Under these patterns a given patient might gain far more, nothing, or be harmed, so promising three points claims 'knowledge the trial does not contain'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that no individual's risk can be changed, which mistakes uncertainty about whose risk changes for a claim that no individual's risk changes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options exaggerate possibilities the passage merely mentions, and the first sounds like a deep statistical point while contradicting the passage.

questions.question: Which of the following doctors is reasoning in the way the author would most clearly endorse?

options.A: One who withholds the drug from a patient because three earlier patients of hers who took it suffered outcomes she vividly remembers.
options.B: One who departs from the trial-based default for a patient whose genetic variant is known to block the drug's mechanism, an effect confirmed in a later trial.
options.C: One who prescribes the drug to an elderly woman because, among many subgroups in the original trial, women over eighty benefited most.
options.D: One who prescribes the drug and assures the patient that his own risk of a stroke will now fall by exactly three points.

questions.correct_answer: (B) One who departs from the trial-based default for a patient whose genetic variant is known to block the drug's mechanism, an effect confirmed in a later trial.

option_rationales.A: This relies on a small, unrandomised sample and on 'a memory that favours vivid cases', which paragraph 3 calls a poor instrument.
option_rationales.C: A single striking subgroup among many divisions is the kind of finding paragraph 4 says may be a chance 'mirage' and has 'often failed to reappear when tested again'.
option_rationales.D: This is 'The first error' of paragraph 2: applying the average 'as though it were a fact about each patient'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says departures from the average need 'a plausible mechanism together with a difference that recurs in a fresh trial', and paragraph 5 says departures should be justified by reasons. A known mechanism plus a confirming later trial meets both conditions.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the subgroup option because it appears to use trial evidence rather than intuition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The subgroup wrong option looks evidence-based; rejecting it requires applying paragraph 4's warning about multiple divisions.

questions.question: The reference to trials within a single patient in the final paragraph serves mainly to

options.A: propose a design that should take the place of large trials for chronic conditions whose symptoms are stable.
options.B: show that the average from a large trial is of no value whenever a patient's symptoms come and go quickly.
options.C: indicate what a genuinely individual conclusion would demand, by contrast with a mere claim that a patient is different.
options.D: concede that, for chronic illnesses at least, a doctor's intuition about an individual patient is a reliable guide.

questions.correct_answer: (C) indicate what a genuinely individual conclusion would demand, by contrast with a mere claim that a patient is different.

option_rationales.A: The design is described for conditions whose symptoms 'come and go quickly', not stable ones, and is said to be 'not always practical'; no replacement is proposed.
option_rationales.B: The author calls the average 'the best default available when nothing more is known'; the single-patient design adds information rather than showing the average worthless.
option_rationales.D: A single-patient trial uses alternating treatment and placebo and compares results, which is the opposite of relying on intuition.

questions.explanation: The paragraph says such designs 'show what an answer to the individual question would actually require, and how little the bare assertion of individuality provides'. The reference sets a standard against which the second error of paragraph 3 falls short.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a recommendation of a new standard method rather than as an illustration of what individual evidence requires.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options each misread the example's scope or purpose, and the first copies a passage detail with one word changed.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: trace how the word 'computer' came to name a machine instead of the occupation that it originally described.
options.B: claim that electronic machines added little to calculation apart from a gain in speed over the offices they displaced.
options.C: show that human computing offices produced more reliable results than the first electronic machines that replaced them.
options.D: argue that electronic computers took over a way of organising calculation that human computing offices had already developed.

questions.correct_answer: (D) argue that electronic computers took over a way of organising calculation that human computing offices had already developed.

option_rationales.A: The change in the word's meaning is only the opening observation of paragraph 1; the passage does not trace the history of the word but uses it to introduce a claim about how calculation was organised.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 denies that 'the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly' and says their speed 'changed which problems were worth posing at all'.
option_rationales.C: The passage never compares the reliability of offices and machines; paragraph 3 says only that designers borrowed the offices' 'conception of what it meant to make a calculation reliable'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the electronic computer 'inherited an idea that human computing offices had already worked out in detail'; paragraphs 2 and 3 describe that idea (division of labour, rules, checking by redundancy) and show it anticipated programming; paragraph 4 qualifies but keeps the continuity. The purpose is to argue this continuity.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the opening remark about the word for the purpose, or reading the passage as belittling the machines.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated plainly in paragraph 1 and restated in paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, how were errors caught in the human computing offices?

options.A: The same column was worked out by two people separately, and any mismatch sent it back to be redone.
options.B: Results were compared against published tables of positions and tides that earlier offices had already computed.
options.C: The planner who designed the procedure checked every finished sheet against their own understanding of the problem.
options.D: Workers were trained to understand the purpose of each step so that they would notice when a result looked wrong.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The same column was worked out by two people separately, and any mismatch sent it back to be redone.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 mentions such tables as the products of the offices' work, not as a means of checking it; the checking method in paragraph 2 is duplicate computation.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says errors were caught 'not by insight but by procedure'; a planner reviewing sheets through understanding is the opposite of what is described.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the workers 'did not have to understand why a step was there' and that the scheme was designed so that they would not need to.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'two people would compute the same column independently, and any disagreement sent the column back.' The correct answer restates this.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that checking must involve someone who understands the problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The opening sentence of the final paragraph ('None of this is to say that the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly') serves mainly to

options.A: summarise the evidence that the designers of electronic machines borrowed techniques from the offices.
options.B: concede that the computing offices were in fact slower and less accurate than is usually assumed.
options.C: head off an overstatement that the passage's stress on continuity might otherwise invite.
options.D: introduce a new thesis that replaces the claim of continuity made in the preceding paragraphs.

questions.correct_answer: (C) head off an overstatement that the passage's stress on continuity might otherwise invite.

option_rationales.A: The borrowing is described in paragraph 3; this sentence does not summarise it but guards against reading the continuity as mere sameness.
option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about what is usually assumed about the offices' speed or accuracy; the sentence qualifies the author's own argument.
option_rationales.D: The same paragraph goes on to say 'But the continuity matters', so the earlier claim is kept, not replaced.

questions.explanation: Having argued for continuity between offices and machines, the author forestalls the inference that machines were nothing more than faster offices, and then explains that speed changed which problems were posed, before reaffirming that 'the continuity matters'. The sentence is a qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a qualifying sentence as a change of thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'None of this is to say' and the following 'But'.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that, in the computing offices, a worker's not understanding why a step was there was

options.A: an intended feature of the method, since the procedure was meant to yield correct results without that understanding.
options.B: a temporary arrangement that the offices dropped once their workers had grown familiar with the problems.
options.C: a weakness that planners put up with only because workers with mathematical training were too scarce to hire.
options.D: the main source of the errors that the practice of computing each column twice was intended to catch.

questions.correct_answer: (A) an intended feature of the method, since the procedure was meant to yield correct results without that understanding.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage suggests the arrangement was abandoned; it is presented as the defining feature of the offices, later carried over into programming.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the scheme 'was in fact designed so that they would not need to' understand; nothing is said about a shortage of trained workers or about planners merely tolerating the arrangement.
option_rationales.D: The passage never links errors to the workers' lack of understanding; duplicate computation catches disagreements whatever their cause, and the passage treats non-understanding as part of the design.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the scheme was 'designed so that they would not need to' understand, and that the result was 'a method in which correctness no longer depended on anyone grasping the whole'. Non-understanding was therefore built in, not a flaw.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that lack of understanding must be a defect, which makes the error-source option tempting.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading 'in fact designed' together with the closing sentence of paragraph 2; one wrong option plausibly links ignorance to error.

questions.question: The example of the two songs in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: illustrate the fragmentation of a shared public into sealed niches tuned to individual listeners.
options.B: suggest that the second song was neglected because early listeners judged it to be the weaker work.
options.C: prove that listeners cannot tell apart songs of equal appeal without guidance from an algorithm.
options.D: show how an accidental early advantage can grow into a large gap when ranking rewards prior engagement.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show how an accidental early advantage can grow into a large gap when ranking rewards prior engagement.

option_rationales.A: Fragmentation is the familiar view of paragraph 1 that the author revises; the example shows concentration on one song, the opposite tendency.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the second song may disappear 'not because anyone judged it worse but because no one was shown it'.
option_rationales.C: The example is hypothetical and concerns exposure, not listeners' powers of discrimination; the passage proves nothing about what listeners can tell apart.

questions.explanation: The example follows directly on the description of the feedback loop and shows 'the small, accidental difference' hardening 'into an enormous gap'. It illustrates the mechanism of concentration.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the example with the fragmentation view it is meant to correct.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence after the example states its point.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the 'early hope' mentioned in paragraph 3 has been undermined chiefly because

options.A: digital platforms have, in practice, offered far fewer obscure works than their early promoters had claimed.
options.B: making a vast catalogue available does little for obscure work if ranking keeps people from encountering it.
options.C: personalised systems confine each user to a narrow niche that obscure work is unable to reach.
options.D: users, left to themselves, prefer familiar and popular works to obscure ones that might suit them better.

questions.correct_answer: (B) making a vast catalogue available does little for obscure work if ranking keeps people from encountering it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 speaks of 'the vast catalogue that digital distribution made available'; the problem is that it 'sits largely unvisited', not that it is small.
option_rationales.C: This is the fragmentation picture of paragraph 1; the author says the characteristic risk is 'less fragmentation than concentration'.
option_rationales.D: The author locates the cause in a ranking system 'that rewards prior popularity', not in users' preferences; the two-songs example stresses that neglect need not reflect anyone's judgement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the hope 'depended on people actually encountering that work', and ranking that rewards popularity 'makes such encounters rarer than the size of the catalogue suggests'. Availability without exposure does not help obscure work.
questions.common_misconception: Blaming users' tastes, or reverting to the fragmentation account the author has set aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options offer familiar explanations; the correct answer requires the author's specific mechanism of exposure.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that an automated ranking is 'partly manufacturing' what people want?

options.A: Bestseller lists in the decades before online platforms also showed a few large successes and a great many neglected works.
options.B: When the same new songs were ranked separately for several groups of listeners, different songs became hits in each group, depending on early chance.
options.C: Most users of streaming services now listen to a narrower range of genres than they did before such services became common.
options.D: Listeners who rely on recommendation engines report that they enjoy the suggested songs more than songs that were picked for them at random.

questions.correct_answer: (B) When the same new songs were ranked separately for several groups of listeners, different songs became hits in each group, depending on early chance.

option_rationales.A: This supports the concession in paragraph 4 that concentration is not new, but it says nothing about whether automated rankings shape demand.
option_rationales.C: Narrowing of individual taste bears on the fragmentation view of paragraph 1 and does not show that rankings produce the popularity they appear to report.
option_rationales.D: Greater enjoyment of suggestions is consistent with the ranking merely reporting real preferences; it does not show that exposure created the demand.

questions.explanation: If identical songs become hits or flops depending on early chance, popularity is in part produced by the loop rather than reflecting fixed appeal. That is exactly what 'partly manufacturing it' claims.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is on topic (recommendation, concentration) but does not separate created demand from reported demand.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing what evidence would distinguish manufacture from accurate reporting.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's view of the 'remedy' mentioned in the final paragraph?

options.A: It would aim chiefly at showing users fewer of the items that match the tastes they have already displayed.
options.B: It would remove popularity from rankings entirely, since amplifying success is a harm peculiar to algorithms.
options.C: It would be achieved once automated rankings were made as slow to respond as the choices of booksellers.
options.D: It would ask whether apparent popularity shows real preference or just the prominence an item had earlier.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It would ask whether apparent popularity shows real preference or just the prominence an item had earlier.

option_rationales.A: The author says the remedy lies 'less in protecting users from their own tastes'; limiting matches to past taste is the response to fragmentation that the author downgrades.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'It would be wrong to present this as something algorithms invented'; the author also proposes no removal of popularity signals.
option_rationales.C: The author hedges ('if there is one') and identifies invisibility as well as speed as what is new; nothing suggests that slowing the loop would be enough.

questions.explanation: The final sentence locates any remedy in 'asking how much of what looks like popular demand is an echo of earlier exposure', that is, whether popularity reflects preference or prior prominence. The correct answer says this in other words; it neither promises success nor prescribes a mechanism.
questions.common_misconception: Taking one of the two new features (speed) as the whole problem, or reading the remedy as protection from one's own tastes.
questions.difficulty_reason: The hedged 'if there is one' and the 'less ... than' contrast must both be respected; two wrong options use the paragraph's own vocabulary.

questions.question: According to the passage, a person who submits a sample to a genetic testing service

options.A: gives up legal ownership of the sample and of any information that may later be drawn from it.
options.B: reveals information only about themselves, provided that they have read the privacy notice first.
options.C: may disclose facts about relatives, some of whom may not even know that the test was taken.
options.D: can protect their relatives fully by refusing permission for the results to be used in research.

questions.correct_answer: (C) may disclose facts about relatives, some of whom may not even know that the test was taken.

option_rationales.A: Legal ownership of samples is never discussed; 'ownership' in paragraph 1 is an image of privacy, not a legal claim about samples.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the person 'reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins', whatever notice they have read.
option_rationales.D: No such option is described; the passage's point is that the disclosure about relatives happens through the test itself.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: such a person 'reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins, some of whom may not know the test was taken.'
questions.common_misconception: Bringing in outside ideas about legal ownership or research consent.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement that 'consent cannot carry the load it has been given' means that

options.A: consent has been relied on to provide more protection than individual choices are able to supply.
options.B: consent has turned out to be worthless and ought to be dropped in favour of rules on inference.
options.C: consent forms have grown too long and too complicated for most people to read with any care.
options.D: people are now asked for consent so often that they agree to requests without considering them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) consent has been relied on to provide more protection than individual choices are able to supply.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens 'This does not make individual consent worthless' and says 'Being asked still matters'; rules are to be added, 'not merely' substituted.
option_rationales.C: The length or complexity of forms is never mentioned; the problem described is structural, that others' choices reveal what a refuser withholds.
option_rationales.D: Fatigue with consent requests is an outside idea; the passage's argument holds even for people who decide carefully.

questions.explanation: The 'load' is the 'whole burden of protection' that paragraph 3 says the framework places on individual decisions. Because data is collective, individual consent cannot bear that burden alone, though it still matters.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the sentence as a rejection of consent, against the opening of paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor is explained by paragraph 3's 'whole burden of protection'; one wrong option overstates it into worthlessness.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the condition the author has in mind when comparing privacy to 'clean air or quiet streets'?

options.A: A tenant who refuses to sign an unfair lease is turned away, and so ends up with no flat on that street at all.
options.B: A shopper who reads the terms carefully before signing is later charged a fee that the terms had deliberately concealed.
options.C: A gardener who fences her own plot keeps out the deer that go on damaging the unfenced plots beside it.
options.D: A household that stops burning wood in its stove still breathes smoky air, because most of the town keeps burning wood.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A household that stops burning wood in its stove still breathes smoky air, because most of the town keeps burning wood.

option_rationales.A: This concerns the cost of refusing, not the futility of refusing; the tenant's refusal does secure what it aims at, freedom from the lease.
option_rationales.B: This is deception, which paragraph 4 treats as a separate wrong that 'the collective character of data does not erase'; it is not a case of others' conduct defeating a private choice.
option_rationales.C: Here the private choice succeeds in protecting its maker, the reverse of a condition that 'no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes privacy as 'a condition that each person's conduct affects for others, and that no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone'. The household's private choice cannot secure clean air while others keep burning wood, mirroring a refuser whose traits are inferred from others' data.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the deception case because it is about consent, though the analogy concerns collective conditions.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires abstracting the structure of the comparison and testing each scenario against it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3?

options.A: Deceiving people about how their information will be used remains a serious wrong even when the data involved is collective.
options.B: Traits inferred about non-sharers from others' data prove so unreliable that they seldom reveal what a refuser meant to hide.
options.C: Many people who upload their contact lists do not realise that they are disclosing information about other people.
options.D: Systems that infer traits from shared data become steadily more accurate as more people choose to disclose those traits.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Traits inferred about non-sharers from others' data prove so unreliable that they seldom reveal what a refuser meant to hide.

option_rationales.A: This is the author's own concession in paragraph 4 and does not bear on whether refusals protect anything.
option_rationales.C: This illustrates the relational character of data described in paragraph 2 and leaves untouched the claim that a refusal secures little.
option_rationales.D: Growing accuracy makes it more likely that a refused fact 'can be known anyway', which strengthens rather than weakens the argument.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 concludes that a refusal 'has secured very little' on the condition 'If it can be known anyway, through the choices of others'. If inferences about non-sharers are unreliable, the fact cannot in practice be known anyway, and the refusal does protect it.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the true-sounding concession about deception, which is consistent with the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires locating the conditional premise on which paragraph 3 rests; one wrong option is the author's own concession and another strengthens.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that failures blamed on operators often stem from how automation shapes their role, and to suggest design responses.
options.B: show that operators of automated systems are usually careless and need stricter supervision and training.
options.C: argue that automated systems are more dangerous than manual ones and should be introduced only where unavoidable.
options.D: explain why official accident reports are required to name a single cause for every failure they describe.

questions.correct_answer: (A) argue that failures blamed on operators often stem from how automation shapes their role, and to suggest design responses.

option_rationales.B: The passage shifts blame from the individual to 'the design of the whole arrangement'; it does not call operators careless.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this is a case against automation', which has removed 'many kinds of mistake'.
option_rationales.D: The passage notes that reports end with 'human error' but says nothing about any requirement to name a single cause.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 explain how automation leaves operators the hardest situations while eroding their skill and attention, so that 'human error' misplaces the fault; paragraph 4 proposes designing systems 'around the people who must step in'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading criticism of the 'human error' label as criticism of automation itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession in paragraph 4 rules out the main tempting wrong option directly.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, why do people supervising a highly reliable machine tend to monitor it poorly?

options.A: They trust the machine so completely that they decide there is no longer any need to watch it closely.
options.B: They have been given less training than the operators who used to do the work by hand.
options.C: Attention drifts when nothing happens for long stretches, and a reliable machine makes such stretches longer.
options.D: The displays they watch are usually too complicated to be read quickly when an emergency arises.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Attention drifts when nothing happens for long stretches, and a reliable machine makes such stretches longer.

option_rationales.A: The passage describes drifting attention, not a deliberate decision to stop watching; trust is never mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says skill decays through lack of exercise, not that training was reduced; and that point concerns control, not monitoring.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 suggests better displays as a remedy, but paragraph 2 does not give complex displays as the reason monitoring is poor.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Attention drifts when nothing happens for hours, and the more reliable the machine, the longer the stretches in which nothing happens.'
questions.common_misconception: Importing the familiar idea of over-trust in machines, which the passage does not use.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in the last two sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage suggests that an improvement in how well an automated system works under ordinary conditions could

options.A: make supervisors more attentive, since a dependable machine frees them to concentrate on what remains.
options.B: remove the need for human supervisors, since rare emergencies would then be handled entirely by the machine itself.
options.C: leave its overseers worse equipped for unusual crises, so that their lapses come as more of a shock.
options.D: make emergencies so infrequent that the skill of the people supervising the system would hardly matter.

questions.correct_answer: (C) leave its overseers worse equipped for unusual crises, so that their lapses come as more of a shock.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: a more reliable machine lengthens the stretches in which 'nothing happens', during which attention drifts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says what remains for humans are the situations 'in which the machine gives up'; nothing suggests better ordinary performance removes these.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the rare moments 'are the ones in which the most is at stake', so rarity does not make skill unimportant.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'The better the automation works in ordinary conditions, the less prepared its human supervisors may be for the extraordinary ones, and the more surprising their failure will look when it comes.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that better automation must make the whole system safer in every respect.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inversion is stated in paragraph 3 but must be matched to a paraphrase; one wrong option reverses paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the label 'human error' is best described as

options.A: approving, since it correctly points to the operator as the part of the system most in need of reform.
options.B: indifferent, treating it as a harmless habit of official reports that has no real effect on what happens.
options.C: dismissive, on the ground that operators are never really responsible for what goes wrong in such systems.
options.D: sceptical of it as an explanation of failure, while granting that it is accurate in a narrow sense.

questions.correct_answer: (D) sceptical of it as an explanation of failure, while granting that it is accurate in a narrow sense.

option_rationales.A: The author says the label 'hides the way the situation was produced' and that 'the design of the whole arrangement deserves scrutiny'.
option_rationales.B: The author holds that the label misdirects scrutiny 'at the very moment' it is needed, which is not indifference.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 grants that 'a person did do the wrong thing'; the author does not deny the operator's part, only that it is the whole story.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 calls the phrase 'accurate in a narrow sense' but says it 'hides the way the situation was produced'; paragraph 3 says it 'locates the fault in the individual' when the design deserves scrutiny. This is qualified scepticism.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the author's criticism into a denial of any operator responsibility.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the concession ('accurate in a narrow sense') together with the criticism.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as part of the material reality behind the cloud EXCEPT

options.A: satellites that relay stored data between continents when undersea links fail.
options.B: water drawn from local supplies to keep buildings full of servers cool.
options.C: sites chosen because they offer cheap power or favourable taxes.
options.D: cables laid along railway lines as well as across sea floors.

questions.correct_answer: (A) satellites that relay stored data between continents when undersea links fail.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says servers 'must be kept cool, often with water drawn from local supplies'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 mentions 'particular sites chosen for cheap power, favourable taxes or stable ground'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 mentions 'cables laid across sea floors and along railway lines'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists buildings of servers, cooling water, cables across sea floors and along railway lines, and sites chosen for power, taxes or ground. Satellites are never mentioned.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting a plausible piece of real-world infrastructure that the passage does not name.
questions.difficulty_reason: A list in one paragraph; each option can be checked directly.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the final paragraph in the argument?

options.A: It brings forward fresh evidence about the environmental costs of data centres to reinforce the claims of paragraph 2.
options.B: It answers a defence of the metaphor by separating what users need from what those who govern the infrastructure need.
options.C: It concedes that hiding complexity is what good computing does and therefore withdraws the earlier criticism of the metaphor.
options.D: It argues that ordinary users ought to learn where their data is physically stored before they make use of online services.

questions.correct_answer: (B) It answers a defence of the metaphor by separating what users need from what those who govern the infrastructure need.

option_rationales.A: No new evidence about costs appears in paragraph 4; it addresses an objection about the value of abstraction.
option_rationales.C: The author grants the point ('That is true') but adds 'it confuses two audiences', so the criticism is kept and narrowed, not withdrawn.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'Nobody wants to think about the location of a server before sending a message' and calls abstraction 'a gift to the user'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with what 'Defenders of the metaphor might point out', accepts it for users, and replies that abstraction 'becomes a liability' for 'citizens, regulators and planners'. It is an objection and a reply by distinction.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the concession ('That is true') for a retreat from the thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the concession is limited by the distinction between audiences.

questions.question: The author's remark that a cloud 'is diffuse, which suggests resilience' implies that

options.A: users are unable to tell where their files travel between one of their devices and another.
options.B: storing old files indefinitely uses up so much energy that the system will eventually be unable to cope.
options.C: the image invites a belief that services are widely spread, when they may hinge on a few points of failure.
options.D: data centres are often built on unstable ground, which makes them liable to sudden and widespread failure across a region.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the image invites a belief that services are widely spread, when they may hinge on a few points of failure.

option_rationales.A: That users need not know where files go is the part of the metaphor the author accepts in paragraph 1; it does not bear on resilience.
option_rationales.B: Energy cost is a separate effect of the metaphor ('A cloud uses nothing'); it is not what makes the impression of resilience misleading.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says sites are chosen partly for 'stable ground'; the resilience point concerns concentration in few companies and sites.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 contrasts the suggestion of resilience with the fact that 'a large share of the services people rely on may depend on a small number of companies and sites, so that a single failure can ripple outward'. The image of diffusion hides concentration.
questions.common_misconception: Mixing up the three separate ways the metaphor misleads in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Paragraph 3 lists three effects; the solver must keep resilience apart from location and energy.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely parallels the author's reply to the defenders of the metaphor?

options.A: A map that leaves out minor roads misleads every traveller, since it gives a false picture of the ground to anyone who uses it.
options.B: A driver who knows nothing about engines is a worse driver than one who understands how the car works under the bonnet.
options.C: A city that buries its power lines for the sake of appearance pays more to repair them, since faults become harder to find.
options.D: Using a tap without a thought for reservoirs is a convenience, but a water board that planned as if water came from taps would plan badly.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Using a tap without a thought for reservoirs is a convenience, but a water board that planned as if water came from taps would plan badly.

option_rationales.A: The author says the cloud image 'is not simply wrong' and serves users well; an abstraction that misleads every audience is the opposite of the reply.
option_rationales.B: The author accepts that users need not know what lies behind the abstraction; the reply concerns a different audience, not users' competence.
option_rationales.C: This concerns the cost of hiding infrastructure physically; it lacks the distinction between an abstraction that helps one audience and harms another.

questions.explanation: The reply in paragraph 4 is that abstraction is 'a gift to the user at the moment of use' but 'a liability' for those who must decide about the infrastructure. The tap is convenient for the user and misleading only if carried into planning, matching that two-audience structure.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the buried power lines because it is about hidden infrastructure, though it lacks the two-audience distinction.
questions.difficulty_reason: Several options share the surface theme of hidden systems; only one preserves the structure of the argument.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that both sides in the debate wrongly treat understanding as all-or-nothing, and to propose mapping separate abilities instead.
options.B: show that fluent machines lack the grounding in perception and action without which there can be no genuine understanding.
options.C: argue that no question about machine understanding can be answered until the nature of inner experience has been settled.
options.D: defend the view that behaviour indistinguishable from that of a competent person is sufficient evidence of genuine understanding.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that both sides in the debate wrongly treat understanding as all-or-nothing, and to propose mapping separate abilities instead.

option_rationales.B: This is the second reported answer; the author says its verdict 'merely manipulates symbols' flattens the profile 'in the opposite direction'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the question of experience 'should not be allowed to stand in for' the tractable question of what a system can do.
option_rationales.D: This is the first of the 'Two answers' in paragraph 1, which the author reports; paragraph 3 says the verdict 'really understands' tells us little.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 identifies the 'shared assumption' that understanding is 'a single property'; paragraph 3 concludes that 'The useful work lies in mapping which abilities are present'. The correct answer captures both moves.
questions.common_misconception: Taking one of the reported views for the author's own.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options state the reported positions accurately; the solver must see that the author rejects both.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, saying that a system 'really understands' is said to flatten 'this profile into a verdict'. This means that the claim

options.A: exaggerates what the system can do by ignoring the failures that it shows on trivial variations.
options.B: reduces an uneven pattern of strengths and weaknesses across abilities to a single yes or no judgement.
options.C: replaces a careful technical description of the system with an emotional reaction to its fluency.
options.D: simplifies the technical vocabulary of research so that readers without special training can follow it.

questions.correct_answer: (B) reduces an uneven pattern of strengths and weaknesses across abilities to a single yes or no judgement.

option_rationales.A: The author says the opposite verdict 'does the same in the opposite direction', so the fault is not exaggeration in one direction but collapsing the profile either way.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in paragraph 3 concerns emotion; the contrast is between a detailed map of abilities and a single verdict.
option_rationales.D: The 'profile' is the system's pattern of abilities, not a body of vocabulary; the passage does not discuss popularisation.

questions.explanation: The 'profile' is the description just given: some abilities 'to a high degree and others hardly at all'. A verdict of 'really understands', like its opposite, collapses this into one answer that 'tells us little'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'flattens' as 'flatters', that is, as exaggeration, which the parallel with the opposite verdict rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is half right for one verdict; the parallel clause excludes it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument of paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: The abilities by which we judge understanding always come together, each present to exactly the degree the others are.
options.B: Some machines that converse fluently fail at trivial variations of problems that they otherwise solve quickly and with ease.
options.C: Many people who exercise a practical skill expertly are unable to explain the principles on which it rests.
options.D: Philosophers continue to disagree about whether an inner experience of meaning could ever be detected from behaviour.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The abilities by which we judge understanding always come together, each present to exactly the degree the others are.

option_rationales.B: This is exactly the uneven profile paragraph 3 describes, so it supports rather than weakens the argument.
option_rationales.C: This repeats the mechanic example of paragraph 2 and confirms that the abilities 'can come apart'.
