option_rationales.D: This concerns the objection of paragraph 4, which the author sets aside as a separate question; it leaves paragraphs 2 and 3 untouched.

questions.explanation: The argument rests on the premise that the abilities 'can come apart' (paragraph 2), which is why a single verdict is 'badly posed' (paragraph 3). If they always occurred together in matching degrees, understanding would behave like a single property and a single verdict would lose little.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about inner experience because it sounds like a challenge to the author.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying the unstated load-bearing premise; two wrong options restate supporting evidence in new words.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the question of whether understanding involves an inner experience of meaning as

options.A: decisive, so that practical decisions about such systems ought to wait until the question has been resolved.
options.B: perhaps a real question, but not one peculiar to machines or one on which most practical decisions turn.
options.C: a question that arises only for machines, because only their inner workings are closed to inspection.
options.D: meaningless, since nothing that cannot be inspected from outside could ever be the subject of a sensible question at all.

questions.correct_answer: (B) perhaps a real question, but not one peculiar to machines or one on which most practical decisions turn.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the question 'should not be allowed to stand in for' the tractable one on which 'most practical decisions' depend.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says it 'arises equally for any being whose inner life we cannot inspect', so it is not peculiar to machines.
option_rationales.D: The author answers the objection with 'Perhaps it does', allowing that the question may be real and 'whatever its answer' may matter.

questions.explanation: 'Perhaps it does' concedes the question may be untouched by mapping abilities; 'arises equally for any being' shows it is not specific to machines; and the final sentence says practical decisions depend on the other question. The correct answer combines these.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's setting aside of the question as a dismissal of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three distinct cues in paragraph 4 must be combined; each wrong option violates exactly one.

questions.question: According to the passage, the criteria of fairness described in paragraph 1 cannot all be met together when

options.A: the lender relies on more than one measure of creditworthiness when it decides whether to approve a loan.
options.B: the difference in default rates between the groups is itself the result of earlier unfair treatment.
options.C: the groups differ in how often their members actually default and the predictions are less than perfect.
options.D: the scoring system has been poorly engineered or built from too small a body of past lending records.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the groups differ in how often their members actually default and the predictions are less than perfect.

option_rationales.A: The number of measures a lender uses is never mentioned; the condition given concerns base rates and imperfect prediction.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 raises earlier unfairness as a consideration in choosing which criterion gives way, not as the condition under which the conflict arises.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the conflict 'is not a defect of any particular system that better engineering might remove'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'When the groups' underlying default rates differ and the prediction is less than perfect', the criteria conflict; it 'follows from the arithmetic of prediction under unequal base rates'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the condition for the conflict with a consideration relevant to resolving it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The reference to the conflict between honesty and kindness in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: suggest that fairness, like kindness, ought to give way whenever it comes into conflict with truthfulness.
options.B: illustrate that everyday moral notions are too vague to offer any guidance to those who design algorithms.
options.C: show that the builders of scoring systems ought to be guided by their personal virtues rather than by arithmetic.
options.D: support the claim that a conflict between two demands does not show that either demand is empty.

questions.correct_answer: (D) support the claim that a conflict between two demands does not show that either demand is empty.

option_rationales.A: The comparison concerns whether conflicting values are real, not which should prevail; the author says which criterion yields depends on harm to those affected.
option_rationales.B: The author holds that fairness 'bundles together several demands' that are each meaningful; the comparison defends, rather than dismisses, everyday notions.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 rejects leaving the choice to builders as a technical matter; it says nothing about their personal virtues.

questions.explanation: The sentence reads: 'Discovering that two values can conflict is not the same as discovering that one of them is empty, any more than the occasional conflict between honesty and kindness shows that one of these is an illusion.' The analogy rebuts the conclusion that fairness is incoherent.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the analogy as ranking the values instead of defending their reality.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is given by the sentence in which the comparison appears.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the decision about which fairness criterion should give way

options.A: cannot be made on any principled basis, because the competing criteria have been shown to be incompatible.
options.B: would rest partly on how heavily each kind of mistaken decision falls on those who must bear it.
options.C: should favour whichever criterion produces the smallest total number of errors across both groups combined.
options.D: should be left to those who build the scoring system, since they understand the arithmetic of prediction best.

questions.correct_answer: (B) would rest partly on how heavily each kind of mistaken decision falls on those who must bear it.

option_rationales.A: This is close to the 'incoherent' conclusion the author rejects; paragraph 3 names the principles, harm and responsibility, on which the choice should rest.
option_rationales.C: The author ties the choice to 'who bears the cost' and 'how severe that cost is'; a total count of errors ignores how costs are distributed and is the kind of technical rule the author resists.
option_rationales.D: This is the second of the 'two conclusions' that paragraph 3 rejects: 'Nor does the need to choose make the choice technical'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the choice 'depends on what the decision does to the people it touches: who bears the cost of being wrongly refused, how severe that cost is', and calls these 'questions about harm and responsibility, not about arithmetic'. The correct answer captures this concern with how the burden of errors falls on applicants.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the total-error rule, which sounds neutral but replaces questions about who bears harm with a single technical figure.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the author reports and rejects; the third is an outside rule that sounds principled, and the correct answer must be recognised as a paraphrase of the list in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the formal analysis of fairness criteria is best described as

options.A: appreciative of its having exposed a hidden trade-off, but wary that the clarity it brings may be wasted.
options.B: dismissive, since it only restates a dilemma that loan officers had always acknowledged openly in their decisions.
options.C: enthusiastic, regarding it as having shown how every reasonable demand of fairness can at last be met together.
options.D: suspicious, holding that its technical vocabulary was deliberately designed to hide choices that belong to discretion.

questions.correct_answer: (A) appreciative of its having exposed a hidden trade-off, but wary that the clarity it brings may be wasted.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the loan officer 'does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know', so the dilemma had not been openly acknowledged.
option_rationales.C: The analysis shows the opposite: it 'removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once'.
option_rationales.D: The author fears the choice may be 'buried again' under technical vocabulary, a danger to be avoided, not a purpose the analysis was designed to serve.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'the formal analysis has done something valuable' by making the conflict explicit, but 'The danger is that the explicitness is squandered'. The attitude is appreciation with a caution.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the author's warning about a future danger into an accusation about the analysis itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The suspicious option uses the paragraph's own words; the solver must separate a risk from an intent.

questions.question: The passage implies that a loan officer who judges applicants by experience, when the groups differ in base rates,

options.A: treats applicants more fairly than an algorithm, since personal discretion allows the special features of each case to count.
options.B: escapes the trade-off, because without an explicit score none of the criteria is ever strictly applied to the decisions.
options.C: sacrifices at least one of the criteria just as a scoring system must, though possibly without knowing which one.
options.D: can satisfy every criterion together, provided that the officer takes enough care over each individual application.

questions.correct_answer: (C) sacrifices at least one of the criteria just as a scoring system must, though possibly without knowing which one.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no comparison of fairness between officers and algorithms; its point is that both face the same dilemma.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the officer 'faces exactly the same trade-off'; not declaring the criterion does not remove the conflict.
option_rationales.D: The author says the analysis 'removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: the officer 'faces exactly the same trade-off' but 'does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know'. The correct answer combines both parts.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a choice not made explicitly is not made at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option turns the officer's silence into an escape; the passage's 'exactly the same trade-off' must be weighed against it.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, a file left on an old disk

options.A: survives neglect better than a paper letter, because a digital copy does not decay in the way that paper does.
options.B: can be read a century later by anyone who knows the language in which the file was originally written.
options.C: becomes unreadable within a few years, however carefully the disk itself is stored and looked after over time.
options.D: can be read later only if the disk, a machine able to read it and software able to interpret the file all survive.

questions.correct_answer: (D) can be read later only if the disk, a machine able to read it and software able to interpret the file all survive.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: 'A single digital copy is, if anything, more perishable than a sheet of paper. Paper survives neglect'.
option_rationales.B: This is what paragraph 2 says of 'a letter left in a drawer', not of a file on a disk.
option_rationales.C: The passage gives no time limit and says the dependencies decay 'on its own schedule'; it does not say care is useless.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: a file 'depends on the disk surviving, on a machine that can still read the disk, and on software that can still interpret the file'.
questions.common_misconception: Transferring the description of the paper letter to the digital file.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence that sits beside the contrasting paper case.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: The belief that the internet never forgets is a myth, since nearly everything posted online eventually disappears without a trace.
options.B: Whether digital material lasts turns on reasons to copy it, which explains both complaints and makes preservation an institutional task.
options.C: Digital records are far less durable than paper and should be printed out whenever they need to be kept for the long term.
options.D: Libraries and archives should copy everything that appears on the web so that no record of the present is ever lost to historians.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Whether digital material lasts turns on reasons to copy it, which explains both complaints and makes preservation an institutional task.

option_rationales.A: The author accepts that embarrassing material does persist; the argument reconciles the two complaints rather than denying one.
option_rationales.C: The passage contrasts single copies with paper but never recommends printing; it locates persistence in copying and institutions, not in a change of medium.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says archives 'must choose' because of 'the sheer volume of material'; copying everything is presented as impossible.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 locates persistence in 'whether enough people, or enough systems, have reasons to keep making copies'; paragraph 3 shows this explains both complaints; paragraph 4 concludes that preservation is 'less a technical problem than an institutional one'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that takes one half of the opening puzzle for the conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures one paragraph's material; the correct answer must span the whole argument.

questions.question: The claim that digital persistence 'tracks attention and interest rather than value' implies that

options.A: material may matter a great deal for later understanding and still be among the first things to be lost.
options.B: the value of a piece of material can be judged reliably by counting how often it has been copied.
options.C: material that attracts a lot of attention is generally of little value to anyone who studies it later.
options.D: valuable material is always lost before trivial material, whatever efforts are made to preserve it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) material may matter a great deal for later understanding and still be among the first things to be lost.

option_rationales.B: This reverses the claim: if copying tracks attention 'rather than value', the number of copies is not a reliable measure of value.
option_rationales.C: The passage says persistence follows attention 'rather than value', not that attention and value are inversely related.
option_rationales.D: 'Always' overstates the passage, which says such material is 'often' most likely to vanish, and paragraph 4 describes institutions that can preserve it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 follows the phrase with 'the material most likely to vanish is often the unglamorous record that matters most to a historian a generation later'. Value and persistence can come apart.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'rather than' into an inverse relation, or reading 'often' as 'always'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading 'rather than' precisely; two wrong options distort it in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the first paragraph?

options.A: It rejects both of the familiar complaints about digital information as exaggerations that do not survive scrutiny.
options.B: It states the author's thesis that digital information is more durable than paper and then lists evidence for it.
options.C: It sets out two complaints that seem to contradict each other, a tension that the following paragraphs then resolve.
options.D: It describes a puzzle about digital information that the author concedes in the end cannot be fully resolved.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It sets out two complaints that seem to contradict each other, a tension that the following paragraphs then resolve.

option_rationales.A: The author goes on to say that 'the two complaints describe the same mechanism working on different material', so both are kept, not rejected.
option_rationales.B: The author says in paragraph 2 that a single digital copy is 'more perishable than a sheet of paper'; paragraph 1 states no thesis of its own.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 opens 'The puzzle dissolves', so the author does resolve it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 presents the two complaints and ends 'it is puzzling to hear the same medium accused of both'; paragraph 2 begins 'The puzzle dissolves'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that an author who presents two views must reject at least one of them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The link 'The puzzle dissolves' must be connected back to paragraph 1; one wrong option is tempting because the passage does contrast media.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT

options.A: an organisation that preserves material must be willing to keep paying for it after interest in it has faded.
options.B: an archive's decision about what to copy from the web is in effect also a decision about what to let vanish.
options.C: the ease of copying is what allows some digital material to outlast the efforts made to delete it.
options.D: print archives never had to choose what to keep, since the volume of print was small enough to preserve in full.

questions.correct_answer: (D) print archives never had to choose what to keep, since the volume of print was small enough to preserve in full.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says preservation needs an organisation that 'will go on paying for that duty when the material has ceased to be interesting'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'every choice about what to copy is also, in effect, a choice about what to let disappear'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the photograph 'is duplicated faster than any single copy can be deleted', which depends on the capacity to copy described in paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says archives face 'a difficulty that print archives faced less acutely', which implies print archives faced it to some degree; 'never had to choose' is not supported.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'less acutely' as 'not at all'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported option turns on a comparative of degree; the other three paraphrase scattered statements and must each be checked.

questions.question: The central claim of the passage is that

options.A: publishing papers before they are reviewed is better than any arrangement that relies on the private judgement of specialists.
options.B: anonymous review becomes hard to defend chiefly when secret reports also decide whether a paper is published at all.
options.C: junior researchers need the protection of anonymity, since senior figures in their fields often control decisions about their promotion.
options.D: anonymous review should be abolished outright, because referees routinely use their concealment to suppress the work of their rivals.

questions.correct_answer: (B) anonymous review becomes hard to defend chiefly when secret reports also decide whether a paper is published at all.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 notes that such arrangements 'are not free of costs' and uses them only to reveal an assumption; the author never ranks them above every alternative.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'usual defence' reported in paragraph 1, which the author grants force but then qualifies; it is one step in the argument, not its central claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'Most referees, of course, do nothing of the kind', and paragraph 3 says it would be 'wrong to infer' that 'anonymity is, in itself, the problem', so both the call for abolition and the claim of routine abuse misstate the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the thesis: anonymity is not itself the problem; 'What makes it dangerous is its combination with gatekeeping power.' Paragraph 4 restates it: if review only improves papers 'a mask does little harm', but if it decides 'which papers exist' it deserves suspicion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that sounds most critical of anonymous review and missing the qualification in paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated almost verbatim in paragraph 3; the other options are clearly too strong or too narrow.

questions.question: According to the passage, the usual defence of anonymity in peer review is that it

options.A: ensures that a manuscript is judged by its arguments rather than by the reputation of whoever wrote it.
options.B: spares referees the labour of explaining their recommendations to authors and readers in public.
options.C: lets less powerful researchers criticise the work of influential authors without having to fear for their own careers.
options.D: prevents editors from choosing referees who have close personal ties to the authors of a manuscript.

questions.correct_answer: (C) lets less powerful researchers criticise the work of influential authors without having to fear for their own careers.

option_rationales.A: The passage concerns hiding the referee's name, not the author's; nothing in paragraph 1 says anonymity shields authors' reputations from view.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 mentions that a referee need not 'explain himself in public', but as a danger of anonymity, not as the defence offered for it.
option_rationales.D: The passage never discusses how editors choose referees or personal ties; paragraph 1 grounds the defence in the junior referee's fear for her promotion.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says a young researcher 'may hesitate to point out its flaws if her name is attached', since the powerful author 'may one day sit on the committee that decides her promotion'. Anonymity 'allows candour to flow upward'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option taken from paragraph 2, which describes a cost of anonymity, not its defence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The defence is stated in two consecutive sentences of paragraph 1.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, 'candour to flow upward' refers to

options.A: honest criticism travelling from junior researchers toward the people who hold power over them.
options.B: junior researchers gaining promotion more quickly once they have refereed for prominent journals.
options.C: the quality of published research rising steadily as referees become more experienced over time.
options.D: frank opinions passing from journal editors to the specialists whom they invite to assess papers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) honest criticism travelling from junior researchers toward the people who hold power over them.

option_rationales.B: Promotion is mentioned only as something the powerful figure could later affect; paragraph 1 does not say that refereeing speeds anyone's promotion.
option_rationales.C: This reads 'upward' as improvement in quality; the sentence is about who may safely criticise whom, as the preceding example of the young researcher shows.
option_rationales.D: The editor is not the subject of the defence; paragraph 1 concerns a young researcher assessing 'the most powerful figure in her field', and editors are not described as speaking upward.

questions.explanation: The phrase sums up the example just given: a young researcher can criticise 'the most powerful figure in her field' only if her name is hidden. Candour flows 'upward' from the less powerful to the more powerful.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'upward' literally as improvement or advancement instead of as direction in a hierarchy.
questions.difficulty_reason: The image is explained by the sentence immediately before it.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard the anonymity of referees as largely harmless in a system where

options.A: referees remain unnamed and their reports, seen only by the editor, settle whether a paper appears in print.
options.B: referees remain unnamed but are chosen only from researchers who are in the early years of their careers.
options.C: editors keep the names of referees secret even from one another, so that no outside pressure can be applied to them.
options.D: every paper is published, with the unsigned referee reports printed beside it and the authors free to reply.

questions.correct_answer: (D) every paper is published, with the unsigned referee reports printed beside it and the authors free to reply.

option_rationales.A: This is exactly the arrangement paragraph 3 condemns: a report that 'decides, in secret, whether anyone will read the paper', where 'the absence of a name becomes the absence of accountability'.
option_rationales.B: Choosing junior referees might answer the remark in paragraph 2 that 'the established' usually referee, but the reports would still decide in secret, which paragraph 3 identifies as the real danger.
option_rationales.C: Greater secrecy does nothing to remove the gatekeeping power that, according to paragraph 3, makes anonymity dangerous; if anything it reduces accountability further.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that when a report 'merely advises', being 'published alongside the paper as one reader's criticism that the authors can answer', the critic's identity 'matters far less'. Reports printed beside papers that are published regardless, with a right of reply, fit that description even though the reports are unsigned.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the junior-referee option because it seems to fix the problem of the established refereeing, while missing that the author locates the danger in secret gatekeeping.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the paragraph 3 distinction to new arrangements; one wrong option addresses a real point from paragraph 2.

questions.question: According to the passage, a published literature from which failed studies are missing leads its readers to

options.A: treat the positive studies they read as if those studies had been conducted with unusually large samples.
options.B: overestimate both how frequently the effect being studied occurs and how strong it tends to be when it does.
options.C: doubt the positive findings they read, because they suspect that many failed studies have been quietly hidden from them.
options.D: assume that journals reject every study that fails to find a difference between the groups it compares.

questions.correct_answer: (B) overestimate both how frequently the effect being studied occurs and how strong it tends to be when it does.

option_rationales.A: Sample size appears only in paragraphs 3 and 4 as a matter of study design; nothing in paragraph 1 links the missing failures to beliefs about sample size.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the reader 'will then overestimate' the effect, which is the opposite of doubting the positive findings.
option_rationales.D: The passage attributes no such assumption to readers; the preference of editors is part of 'the complaint' about journals, not a belief readers form.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the reader 'will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about readers' suspicion, which reverses the effect described.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a close paraphrase of the last sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a researcher who obtains a null result often leaves it unwritten mainly because

options.A: she fears that publishing it would contradict the published findings of senior colleagues in her field.
options.B: editors have made it clear in advance that they will not consider studies that find no effect.
options.C: she herself often cannot tell what the absence of the expected effect actually means.
options.D: she is too occupied with newer projects to spend time on work that has already failed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) she herself often cannot tell what the absence of the expected effect actually means.

option_rationales.A: Fear of contradicting colleagues is never mentioned; paragraph 3 explains abandonment by the ambiguity of the result and the poor return on writing it up.
option_rationales.B: This is the conventional account that paragraph 2 says 'places the drawer in the wrong office'; the study is abandoned 'before any journal had a chance to reject it'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 begins 'The reason is not laziness' and locates the reason in the result being 'mute about its own meaning'; being busy is not the explanation offered.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a null result 'is mute about its own meaning': it may reflect no effect, a small sample, contamination or a misread protocol, and the researcher 'is often the person least able to tell which'. An uninterpretable finding is not worth the weeks of writing.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the journal-rejection option because it is the familiar explanation, though the passage argues against it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting the claim in paragraph 2 to the explanation in paragraph 3 and setting aside the view the author reports in order to reject.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: In fields where sample sizes and procedures must be declared before data are collected, researchers submit a far larger share of their null results.
options.B: Researchers whose null results came from carefully designed studies report that journals still often refuse to publish such results.
options.C: Most researchers say they would write up their null results if doing so counted toward their promotion and toward their chances of winning grants.
options.D: Null results that have appeared in print are cited much less often than positive results on the same research questions.

questions.correct_answer: (A) In fields where sample sizes and procedures must be declared before data are collected, researchers submit a far larger share of their null results.

option_rationales.B: This suggests that journal rejection persists even for informative null results, which supports the conventional account and so tends to weaken the author's claim that design is what empties the drawer.
option_rationales.C: This points to career incentives, not interpretability, as the obstacle; it offers a rival explanation to the one in paragraphs 3 and 4 rather than support for it.
option_rationales.D: Citation after publication does not bear on the claim that null results are published once they become informative; it concerns how such results are received.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 claims that the drawer 'will empty only when null results become informative', which depends on decisions 'made before any data are collected', such as adequate samples and procedures 'specified in advance'. A finding that such pre-declared design is followed by many more null results being submitted directly supports this causal claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is on topic but supports a different explanation (journal bias or career incentives) from the one the author defends.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are tempting because they concern why null results go unpublished; only the correct answer supports the specific mechanism in paragraph 4, and one option actually weakens it.

questions.question: Each of the following is mentioned in the passage as something a null result might reflect EXCEPT

options.A: too few cases having been studied for a real effect to show up.
options.B: a person running the study having misunderstood its procedure.
options.C: a material used in the experiment having been impure.
options.D: a hypothesis framed too loosely for any experiment to count against it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a hypothesis framed too loosely for any experiment to count against it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 lists 'that the sample was too small to detect it', so this is mentioned.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 lists 'that a student misread the protocol', which this paraphrases, so this is mentioned.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 lists 'that a reagent was contaminated' among the possibilities, so this is mentioned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a null result 'may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol'. A loosely framed hypothesis is not among these possibilities.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking a paraphrase of one listed item and choosing it as the exception.
questions.difficulty_reason: The listed items are paraphrased in the options, so each must be matched to its phrase in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The example of the two similar warblers in paragraph 1 serves to

options.A: illustrate the kind of error that critics expected untrained volunteers to make when recording what they saw.
options.B: show that bird song is a more dependable guide to identifying species than a bird's appearance.
options.C: explain why well-run projects began asking volunteers to photograph what they had observed.
options.D: prove that volunteer records of birds have turned out to be less accurate than records of flowers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) illustrate the kind of error that critics expected untrained volunteers to make when recording what they saw.

option_rationales.B: The passage makes no comparison between song and appearance; the fragment of song only shows what the trained expert can do.
option_rationales.C: Photography is mentioned in paragraph 2 as a later response to hard identification; the warbler example belongs to the critics' objection in paragraph 1.
option_rationales.D: Accuracy is never compared across groups of organisms, and the claim of proof is far stronger than anything in paragraph 1.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 reports 'the objection most often raised' that amateurs would err; the warbler example shows the kind of misidentification feared: the expert distinguishes two species that the walker 'may not know' exist.
questions.common_misconception: Linking the example to the photographing practice of paragraph 2 rather than to the objection it sits in.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is clear from the sentences before and after the example.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a bird which 'seems to be thriving in the suburbs'

options.A: is probably being confused by volunteers with a rarer species that looks very similar to it.
options.B: may appear common there partly because the suburbs are where many observers happen to be.
options.C: is recorded accurately because suburban volunteers tend to be more skilled than rural ones.
options.D: has been driven out of farmland and into gardens by the spread of industrial estates.

questions.correct_answer: (B) may appear common there partly because the suburbs are where many observers happen to be.

option_rationales.A: This is misidentification, which paragraph 3 explicitly sets aside: the stubborn problem 'lies not in what volunteers see but in where and when they look'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says that 'no amount of skill in identification' will correct this distortion, and it compares the places observers visit, not their skill.
option_rationales.D: The passage mentions farmland and industrial estates only as places volunteers visit less; it makes no claim about birds moving between habitats.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a map of sightings is 'partly a map of the observers', and the bird 'may simply be living where the watchers live'. Its apparent abundance may reflect where people look.
questions.common_misconception: Reverting to misidentification, the problem the paragraph has just moved past.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer follows from the sentence quoted and the one before it.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the early objection that amateurs would make mistakes is best described as

options.A: fully supportive, since the author believes misidentification remains the chief threat to such projects.
options.B: dismissive, since the author holds that volunteers make no more errors than trained specialists do.
options.C: sympathetic to why it was raised, while holding that another weakness of volunteer data matters more.
options.D: puzzled, since the author cannot understand why scientists ever doubted the abilities of volunteers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) sympathetic to why it was raised, while holding that another weakness of volunteer data matters more.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 calls the sampling problem 'more stubborn' and paragraph 4 says it is 'harder to correct than misidentification', so the author does not rank misidentification first.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'Errors do not vanish' and calls the worry 'reasonable'; the author never claims volunteers are as accurate individually as specialists.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 opens 'The worry was reasonable', which shows the author understands the doubt perfectly well.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 grants that 'The worry was reasonable' but says it was 'aimed at the lesser target'; paragraphs 3 and 4 identify sampling as the 'more stubborn' problem. The attitude is respectful but corrective.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's answer to the objection in paragraph 2 as outright dismissal, or as full agreement.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires weighing 'reasonable' against 'lesser target' and the later comparison in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following projects would best address the concern raised in paragraphs 3 and 4?

options.A: A bird survey in which specialists examine each unusual record before it is added to the shared database.
options.B: A flower survey that invites as many people as possible to send in photographs from wherever they choose to walk.
options.C: A butterfly survey that trains its volunteers for several weeks so that they can identify every species they meet.
options.D: A frog survey in which each volunteer visits an allocated pond on set evenings, wherever that pond happens to lie.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A frog survey in which each volunteer visits an allocated pond on set evenings, wherever that pond happens to lie.

option_rationales.A: Checking improbable records is the paragraph 2 remedy for misidentification; it does not change where and when observations are made.
option_rationales.B: Open recording from chosen places reproduces the bias of paragraph 3, since people walk 'along popular footpaths' and near their homes.
option_rationales.C: Training improves identification, but paragraph 3 says 'no amount of skill in identification' separates the map of species from the map of observers.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says projects that take the sampling bias seriously 'ask some volunteers to survey assigned locations at fixed times', giving 'a sample whose shape is known'. Allocated ponds on set evenings do exactly this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that improves accuracy of identification, which answers the earlier concern, not the one in paragraphs 3 and 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options offer real improvements, but to the wrong problem; the solver must keep the two problems distinct.

questions.question: The description of the public as 'a vessel with a hole in it' (paragraph 1) suggests that the deficit model

options.A: regarded scientists as having failed to notice what the public already knew about many scientific matters.
options.B: regarded ordinary people as unable to retain scientific facts however often these were explained to them.
options.C: regarded the press as distorting expert opinion on its way from the laboratory to ordinary readers.
options.D: regarded ordinary people as defined only by an absence of knowledge that experts were expected to fill.

questions.correct_answer: (D) regarded ordinary people as defined only by an absence of knowledge that experts were expected to fill.

option_rationales.A: The image describes how the model saw the public, not a failing of scientists; that criticism comes later and is the author's, not the model's.
option_rationales.B: This reads the hole as a leak; the same sentence glosses the image as being 'defined entirely by what it lacked', which is about emptiness, not about failing to retain.
option_rationales.C: The press is never mentioned; the image concerns the supposed emptiness of the public mind.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the model assumed resistance came from not understanding, to be fixed by 'supplying the missing facts', and it 'treated the public as a vessel with a hole in it, defined entirely by what it lacked'. The image means the public was seen only as a lack to be filled.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'hole' to mean a leak and so choosing the option about retaining facts.
questions.difficulty_reason: The image is glossed in the same sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Engineers and public officials ought to be held legally responsible whenever the assurances they give to the communities near their projects prove wrong.
options.B: Well-informed people are generally more likely than poorly informed people to reject the considered consensus of scientific experts.
options.C: Public resistance to expert conclusions often reflects judgements about trust and risk, so supplying facts is at best a partial remedy.
options.D: Scientific explanations rarely change anyone's mind, so communicators should give up explaining and concentrate on negotiating with their audiences.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Public resistance to expert conclusions often reflects judgements about trust and risk, so supplying facts is at best a partial remedy.

option_rationales.A: The dam example in paragraph 3 illustrates why scepticism may be rational; the passage proposes no legal remedy, so this adds an outside prescription.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says only that it is 'easy to find' well-read people who reject the consensus; it makes no claim that the well informed are generally more likely to do so.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says some people need 'a good explanation' and that good communication 'will sometimes end in explanation', so giving up explaining contradicts the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows that knowledge does not guarantee acceptance, paragraph 3 that scepticism may be 'a judgement about whom to trust and who pays', and paragraph 4 concedes that explanation is sometimes what is needed but rejects making it 'the whole story'.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating the author's critique into a rejection of explanation altogether.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the critique and the concession of paragraph 4 together; one wrong option distorts a detail of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The example of the village and the dam in paragraph 3 is used to

options.A: illustrate the claim in paragraph 2 that people who read widely become more certain as they learn more.
options.B: show that scepticism can rest on considerations of trust and fairness that a technical briefing leaves out.
options.C: show that villagers often understand engineering better than the officials who are sent to reassure them.
options.D: suggest that the dam is in fact unsafe and that the assurance given by the engineers is mistaken.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that scepticism can rest on considerations of trust and fairness that a technical briefing leaves out.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 introduces 'The deeper failure', a different point from paragraph 2; the villagers' doubts rest on past assurances and the distribution of benefits and losses, not on extra reading.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says only that the villagers 'may follow the hydrology perfectly well'; it does not rank their understanding above the engineers'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the scepticism 'may be quite rational even when the hydrology is sound', so the example does not depend on the dam being unsafe.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the villagers understand the hydrology but also know that past assurances failed, that benefits go elsewhere and that they would bear the loss. Their scepticism is 'a judgement about whom to trust and who pays', which the engineers' presentation 'omits'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the example must show the dam to be dangerous, and missing 'even when the hydrology is sound'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by 'The deeper failure concerns what the model leaves out', but one wrong option misreads the claim about the villagers' understanding.

questions.question: The author's claim that communication which starts from the audience's concerns 'will at least explain the right thing' implies that

options.A: a briefing under the deficit model can be accurate and still address a question other than the one troubling its audience.
options.B: communicators should explain only those matters about which the members of an audience have asked them directly and in advance.
options.C: an audience will come to accept a scientific conclusion once its fears and its experiences have been properly listened to.
options.D: explanations given under the deficit model usually contained factual errors that, once discovered, did lasting damage to public trust.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a briefing under the deficit model can be accurate and still address a question other than the one troubling its audience.

option_rationales.B: The author says communication should begin by 'asking what an audience already knows, fears and has experienced'; restricting explanation to direct questions is an extreme rule the passage does not state.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says such communication 'will sometimes end in explanation', not that acceptance will follow; the option promises an outcome the author does not.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage says deficit-model explanations were inaccurate; in paragraph 3 the hydrology may be 'sound'. The phrase 'the right thing' concerns relevance, not accuracy.

questions.explanation: In paragraph 3 the engineers explain hydrology, which the villagers already follow, while omitting the matters of trust and loss that drive their doubt. To 'at least explain the right thing' implies that the alternative can explain something true but beside the point, as in the dam example.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'right' as 'factually correct' rather than 'relevant to the audience's actual concern'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires connecting a phrase in paragraph 4 to the example in paragraph 3 and distinguishing relevance from accuracy; the wrong options overstate the phrase in different directions.

questions.question: According to the passage, the geologist judges her work successful when

options.A: her hypothesis survives a controlled experiment that has been designed in order to refute it.
options.B: she can find natural cases that differ from one another in just the one respect she wishes to compare.
options.C: her account of past events hangs together and explains the scattered evidence she has found.
options.D: the instruments she has built for the purpose can be made to work reliably in the field and laboratory.

questions.correct_answer: (C) her account of past events hangs together and explains the scattered evidence she has found.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the geologist 'is not testing a hypothesis by experiment' at all, so this cannot be her standard.
option_rationales.B: This is the ingenuity paragraph 2 attributes to the astronomer, who 'cannot intervene' and must find suitable natural cases.
option_rationales.D: Making instruments work is what paragraph 2 says occupies the chemist; it is not given as the geologist's standard.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the geologist assembles 'a history from traces' and that 'her standard of success is the coherence of a narrative that accounts for scattered evidence'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the three scientists of paragraph 2 with one another.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option describes another scientist in the same paragraph; the correct answer is a direct paraphrase.

questions.question: The author's remark that a single recipe may become 'so general that it no longer guides anyone' suggests that

options.A: the textbook sequence has been revised so many times that it has become too complicated to be followed.
options.B: every science would be better served by a recipe written specifically for its own distinctive subject matter.
options.C: researchers in most fields disregard general instructions and rely instead on intuition and luck when they work.
options.D: a description broad enough to fit every science would be too vague to tell any researcher what to do next.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a description broad enough to fit every science would be too vague to tell any researcher what to do next.

option_rationales.A: The passage calls the sequence 'tidy' and 'easy to examine', the opposite of too complicated; the remark describes a hypothetical broader recipe.
option_rationales.B: The author does not recommend separate recipes; paragraph 4 says what the sciences share are norms that 'cannot be captured in a flowchart'.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says scientists rely on intuition or luck; the remark concerns the usefulness of a description, not how researchers actually proceed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 offers a dilemma: a single recipe 'either excludes much of their work or becomes so general that it no longer guides anyone'. The second horn means that a recipe stretched to cover astronomy, geology and chemistry alike would say too little to direct anyone's work.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about separate recipes, which turns a criticism into a prescription the author does not make.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the remark as one half of a dilemma and not as a claim about how scientists behave.

questions.question: The author objects to the textbook account of the scientific method on all of the following grounds EXCEPT that it

options.A: gives too much weight to criticism by colleagues as a way of testing scientific claims.
options.B: overlooks the considerable effort of getting instruments and procedures to function in the first place.
options.C: fails to prepare people for long periods in which results conflict and experts disagree with one another.
options.D: implies that sciences which are unable to run experiments are of lower standing than those that can.

questions.correct_answer: (A) gives too much weight to criticism by colleagues as a way of testing scientific claims.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the chemist spends much time on something 'the textbook sequence ignores entirely: making instruments and procedures work at all', so this is an objection.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the sequence 'leaves the public poorly prepared' for research in which 'experts disagree for long periods', so this is an objection the author makes.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the sequence 'encourages the view that sciences which cannot experiment are somehow lesser', so this is one of the author's objections.

questions.explanation: The textbook sequence makes no mention of criticism by colleagues; in paragraph 4 the author names exposure 'to colleagues who are expected to attack' claims as one of the norms the sciences genuinely share. The author therefore could not object that the sequence overstates it.
questions.common_misconception: Missing that the correct answer reverses the author's own positive account in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three objections are spread over two paragraphs, and the exception must be recognised as the author's own view reversed.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about what the sciences have in common?

options.A: Students who were taught the norms of criticism and revision did no better on tests of experimental procedure than students who had memorised the steps.
options.B: In one long-established and productive science, central claims are customarily shielded from colleagues' attacks and are not expected to be revised in the light of evidence.
options.C: Geologists, unlike chemists, seldom run controlled experiments in a laboratory and rely mainly on traces left by events in the distant past.
options.D: Some eminent scientists who were shown to be wrong took many years to accept the evidence against their views, and a few never accepted it.

questions.correct_answer: (B) In one long-established and productive science, central claims are customarily shielded from colleagues' attacks and are not expected to be revised in the light of evidence.

option_rationales.A: The author claims such students would 'understand science better', not that they would perform procedures better; tests of procedure do not touch the claim about shared norms.
option_rationales.C: This agrees with paragraph 2, which describes the geologist as assembling 'a history from traces'; it confirms the variety of methods rather than weakening the claim about shared norms.
option_rationales.D: The norms are things scientists are 'expected' to do; individual lapses are compatible with the norm, and paragraph 3 already allows that experts may 'disagree for long periods'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says what 'unites' the sciences is a set of communal norms: claims are exposed to attack, stated so that evidence could tell against them, and given up when it does. A productive science in which the community itself does not hold these expectations would show that the norms are not common to the sciences.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about stubborn individuals, which concerns lapses from a norm rather than the absence of the norm.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting option about stubborn scientists seems to contradict the norms but does not, because the norms concern what a community expects; this distinction between norm and behaviour must be drawn.

questions.question: The passage suggests that readers who give priority to papers by well-known authors are

options.A: responding sensibly to the impossibility of reading everything that is published in their field.
options.B: unaware that the unknown co-authors of such papers usually did most of the work that the papers report.
options.C: behaving unfairly and ought to be trained to ignore the names that are attached to the research they read.
options.D: motivated mainly by admiration for eminent figures rather than by any practical consideration of their own.

questions.correct_answer: (A) responding sensibly to the impossibility of reading everything that is published in their field.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the unknown co-author 'did much of the work' in one illustrative case; readers' awareness is never discussed, and 'usually' generalises the example.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says forbidding readers to notice names 'would be both futile and costly', so the author would not recommend training them to ignore names.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 rejects 'Condemning it as mere snobbery' and explains the habit as 'a reasonable strategy for coping with abundance', which is a practical consideration.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the literature is 'far larger than anyone could read', that a familiar name is 'a cheap signal' of worth, and that readers who rely on it 'are not being foolish'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the author condemns the readers because the effect is unfair to unknown researchers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that the Matthew effect is 'a problem of fairness' is best described as

options.A: treating it with open contempt as a complaint voiced only by those who have themselves been denied credit.
options.B: rejecting it entirely, on the ground that credit in science is in fact distributed according to merit.
options.C: accepting it as accurate as far as it goes, while holding that it misses the more serious harm.
options.D: endorsing it fully, since the author regards the effect chiefly as an injustice done to unknown researchers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) accepting it as accurate as far as it goes, while holding that it misses the more serious harm.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage scorns the fairness view or its holders; the author calls it accurate and builds on it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 calls the description 'correct within its limits', and paragraph 3 shows careers diverging for reasons 'partly accidental', so the author does not think credit tracks merit.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the effect is 'less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets', so the author does not regard it chiefly as an injustice.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the fairness description 'is correct within its limits, but it understates what is at stake'. Paragraphs 3 and 4 then identify the larger cost: a field's resources are committed for 'reasons that are partly accidental'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'endorsing it fully' option because the author agrees that the effect is unfair.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires distinguishing partial agreement from full endorsement across paragraphs 2 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following measures is most in keeping with the remedy the author proposes?

options.A: A university that awards prizes to junior co-authors whose contributions to celebrated papers went unrecognised.
options.B: A journal that prints every paper without the names of its authors, so that readers cannot be swayed by reputation.
options.C: A professional society that publishes a yearly ranking of the most frequently cited researchers in each field.
options.D: A funding agency that assesses a share of the applications it receives with the applicants' names and records removed.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A funding agency that assesses a share of the applications it receives with the applicants' names and records removed.

option_rationales.A: This addresses credit owed to individuals, which paragraph 4 calls the lesser issue; it does nothing to loosen the link between attention and money.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the remedy 'is not to forbid readers from noticing names, which would be both futile and costly'; hiding authors from readers is exactly that.
option_rationales.C: A citation ranking advertises the attention already received and would strengthen, not loosen, the conversion of attention into resources.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the remedy is 'to loosen the link between attention and money', for example 'to judge some grant proposals without knowing who wrote them'. Blind assessment of some applications does this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the anonymous journal because it also hides names, without noticing that the author rejects hiding names from readers.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options hide or correct names; the solver must see that the remedy targets funding, not reading.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, the most serious consequence of the Matthew effect is that

options.A: unknown researchers leave science altogether because they receive too little credit for the work they have done.
options.B: a field may commit its resources to some ideas and neglect others for reasons that have little to do with their merit.
options.C: well-known researchers gradually come to believe that their own ideas are better than those of their colleagues.
options.D: readers stop judging papers for themselves and simply accept whatever a famous author happens to have written.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a field may commit its resources to some ideas and neglect others for reasons that have little to do with their merit.

option_rationales.A: Departure from science is not mentioned; the passage describes ideas waiting 'years for a hearing', not people leaving the profession.
option_rationales.C: The passage never discusses what eminent researchers believe about themselves; the harm it describes lies in how resources are allocated.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 warns against treating a name as 'a reason to believe', but paragraph 2 calls attention to names reasonable, and the passage says the effect is above all 'a distortion in how a field allocates its bets'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says compounding advantage means a field 'has placed a heavy bet on one line of work for reasons that are partly accidental', while ideas from less visible researchers go untested. Paragraph 4 states that the effect is 'less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about readers' credulity, which draws on the last sentence but is not what the author ranks as the main harm.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option uses a real phrase from paragraph 4; the correct answer requires combining paragraph 3's account of compounding with paragraph 4's explicit ranking.

questions.question: According to the passage, panels judging research proposals are reasonably good at

options.A: separating proposals that are scientifically sound from those that are not, at the threshold of quality.
options.B: ranking the strongest proposals in the order of their likely scientific value to the field.
options.C: recognising when their own preferences have influenced a decision about where the funding line falls.
options.D: predicting which of the riskier projects before them will eventually produce the largest payoff.

questions.correct_answer: (A) separating proposals that are scientifically sound from those that are not, at the threshold of quality.

option_rationales.B: Paragraphs 1 and 2 say the opposite: near the top, the line 'often separates projects that no one present could distinguish with any confidence'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the biases at the margin need not be 'deliberate', which suggests panels may not notice them, not that they recognise them.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 describes panels as wary of 'projects whose payoff is uncertain'; nothing says they predict payoffs well.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says judgement 'is exercised in full at the threshold, where panels are reasonably good at separating the sound from the unsound'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that panels which judge soundness well must also rank well, which paragraphs 1 and 2 deny.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one clause of paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author mentions the efficiency argument for lotteries in paragraph 2 primarily in order to

options.A: concede that lotteries are cheaper but argue that their savings in cost outweigh the loss of careful judgement.
options.B: show that funding agencies adopted lotteries mainly in order to reduce the workload of their panels.
options.C: grant it but set it aside as a weak justification before presenting what the author considers the stronger one.
options.D: refute the common view that ranking proposals costs panels a great deal of time and careful effort.

questions.correct_answer: (C) grant it but set it aside as a weak justification before presenting what the author considers the stronger one.

option_rationales.A: The author does not argue that savings outweigh anything; the efficiency case is called 'the weakest part of the case', and paragraph 4 denies that judgement is lost.
option_rationales.B: The passage never says why agencies adopted lotteries; paragraph 1 links the experiments to the 'predicament' of indistinguishable proposals, not to workload.
option_rationales.D: The author accepts this view ('This is true'), so the purpose is not to refute it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 reports the efficiency defence, grants it ('This is true'), calls it 'the weakest part of the case', and then says 'The stronger argument is about honesty'. Its role is to be set aside in favour of the honesty argument.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'concede' option, which captures the grant but invents a weighing the author never performs.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options partly fit (the author does grant the point); the solver must see how the paragraph ranks the arguments.

questions.question: The sentence 'Hidden chance is not neutral chance' (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: panels deliberately favour applicants whom they know personally whenever the funding line is close.
options.B: lotteries are themselves biased, because the proposals entered into them are chosen by cautious panels.
options.C: chance plays a smaller part in conventional ranking than defenders of lotteries usually suppose.
options.D: when merit cannot settle a decision, the outcome is shaped by systematic leanings rather than by pure luck.

questions.correct_answer: (D) when merit cannot settle a decision, the outcome is shaped by systematic leanings rather than by pure luck.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the biases are mild and that 'none need be deliberate', so deliberate favouritism misstates it.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says a lottery 'removes this tilt at the margin'; the threshold is described in paragraph 4 as the place where panels judge well, not as a source of bias.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says ranking 'already contains a large element of chance'; the sentence adds that this chance is tilted, not that it is small.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the sentence: when merit cannot separate proposals, 'other preferences fill the gap', which together 'tilt the funding line toward the safe and the recognisable'. The 'chance' in ranking is therefore not random but leans in a consistent direction.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'not neutral' as deliberate unfairness, or as a criticism of lotteries.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence is explained by the rest of the paragraph, but each wrong option misreads it in a plausible direction.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the objection that lotteries will corrode scientists' motivation?

options.A: Some researchers say they would rather lose a draw than be told that their proposal was ranked just below the funding line.
options.B: Projects ranked just above the funding line have consistently gone on to outperform those ranked just below it.
options.C: Agencies that fund by lottery spend considerably less on assessing proposals than agencies that rank every proposal they receive.
options.D: Members of a panel sometimes disagree about whether a borderline proposal is sound enough to be entered into the draw.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Projects ranked just above the funding line have consistently gone on to outperform those ranked just below it.

option_rationales.A: This supports the reply, which holds that the loser of a draw 'has at least been told the truth'; a preference for that outcome strengthens rather than weakens it.
option_rationales.C: This concerns the efficiency argument of paragraph 2, which the author calls the weakest part of the case; it does not touch the reply about motivation.
option_rationales.D: This bears on the claim that panels judge well at the threshold, which answers a different objection in paragraph 4; occasional disagreement is also compatible with being 'reasonably good'.

questions.explanation: The reply in paragraph 4 rests on the premise that the belief that reward follows merit 'is, at the margin, already false'. If projects just above the line reliably outperform those just below, the ranking near the line does track merit, and a lottery would then replace a meaningful judgement; the premise, and with it the reply, collapses.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about disagreement at the threshold because it is about panels' judgement, without noticing that it addresses a different objection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must identify which premise the reply depends on and separate the two objections handled in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Agencies should publish how close their decisions near the funding line were instead of adopting lotteries at all.
options.B: Where panels cannot reliably separate good proposals, drawing lots is preferable to a ranking that disguises chance as judgement.
options.C: The main advantage of funding by lottery is that it saves both agencies and panels a great deal of time and money.
options.D: Funding by lottery should replace ranking by expert panels, because the judgements of such panels are shaped by bias at every stage.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Where panels cannot reliably separate good proposals, drawing lots is preferable to a ranking that disguises chance as judgement.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 offers publication as something agencies 'that decline to draw lots might still learn'; the author does not recommend it in place of lotteries, which the passage defends where 'judgement has reached its limit'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 calls efficiency 'the weakest part of the case'; the author's central argument is about honesty.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says panels judge well 'at the threshold', and paragraph 5 says lotteries are not recommended 'everywhere', so both the call for wholesale replacement and the claim of bias at every stage overstate the case.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 to 4 argue that near the funding line ranking 'already contains a large element of chance' that is hidden and tilted, so an open lottery above a threshold is more honest; paragraph 5 limits this to cases 'where judgement has reached its limit'. The correct answer keeps both the claim and its scope.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option drawn from paragraph 5 because it echoes 'the pretence of precision', without seeing that it reverses the author's support for lotteries.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option overstates the scope and another misreads the closing suggestion as the thesis; the correct answer must be chosen on scope.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'the promise' that 'is only partly kept' is the idea that

options.A: a competent reader who follows a paper's written methods will be able to obtain the findings it reports.
options.B: researchers will share their materials and equipment with any laboratory that asks to repeat their work.
options.C: scientific knowledge will in time be cleared of the errors made by the people who first produced it.
options.D: a failed replication shows that either the original claim or the replicators' own care must be at fault.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a competent reader who follows a paper's written methods will be able to obtain the findings it reports.

option_rationales.B: Sharing materials is never mentioned; the promise in paragraph 1 is that anyone 'who follows' the listed methods 'will see what the authors saw'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 describes knowledge as 'independent of the particular people who first produced it', which concerns independence from persons, not the correction of their errors.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'natural suspicion' that paragraph 1 says follows from the promise; it is a consequence of believing the promise, not the promise itself.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'the implicit promise is that anyone competent who follows them will see what the authors saw', and paragraph 2 says this promise 'is only partly kept' because tacit skills cannot be written down.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'natural suspicion', which is closely tied to the promise but is what follows from it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The referent lies in the previous paragraph, and one wrong option is the consequence stated two sentences after the promise.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the groups that succeeded after a visit

options.A: were given secret details that the original laboratory had deliberately kept out of its published papers.
options.B: had discovered errors in the published descriptions, which the original authors then went on to correct.
options.C: may have acquired the decisive skill without identifying which part of the procedure it concerned.
options.D: were more careful and more competent than the groups that had worked only from the published papers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) may have acquired the decisive skill without identifying which part of the procedure it concerned.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says such knowledge 'is not secret', and paragraph 3 says the authors themselves 'did not know' which of their actions mattered, so nothing was deliberately withheld.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'the written instructions were not wrong', only incomplete, so there were no errors to discover.
option_rationales.D: The passage attributes success to contact with the original laboratory, not to greater care; paragraph 2 says the missing knowledge is 'acquired by doing and by watching others do'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the successful groups often could not 'say afterwards what the crucial difference was', because even the original authors 'did not know which of the many things they did without thinking were the things that mattered'. The skill was transferred without being identified.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that success after a visit must mean that information was hidden or that the published account was mistaken.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining paragraph 2's claim that the knowledge is not secret with paragraph 3's account of why it could not be specified.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the account of instrument-building in paragraph 3?

options.A: A baker refuses to reveal one key ingredient, and rivals who copy her bread cannot match its flavour until a former employee discloses what it is.
options.B: Cooks who follow a recipe all succeed at the first attempt, but only those with many years of experience are able to explain why each of its steps matters.
options.C: A recipe is printed with a wrong oven temperature, and the cooks who follow it keep failing until the publisher prints a correction in the next edition.
options.D: Cooks using a baker's detailed recipe keep failing to match her bread until one spends a week in her kitchen, after which he succeeds without knowing what he changed.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Cooks using a baker's detailed recipe keep failing to match her bread until one spends a week in her kitchen, after which he succeeds without knowing what he changed.

option_rationales.A: This depends on deliberate secrecy, whereas paragraph 2 says the knowledge 'is not secret' and paragraph 3 says even the authors did not know what mattered.
option_rationales.B: In paragraph 3 the readers of the instructions fail; here they succeed, so the situation reverses the pattern the passage describes.
option_rationales.C: Here the instructions are wrong and a written correction fixes them; paragraph 3 says 'the written instructions were not wrong', and the missing element could not be written down.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes groups that fail from written descriptions alone and succeed after time in the original laboratory, 'often without being able to say afterwards what the crucial difference was', while the instructions themselves 'were not wrong'. Only the baker's kitchen case has all three features: accurate but insufficient instructions, success through presence, and an unidentified difference.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the secret-ingredient case because a visit or an insider also brings success there, overlooking that the passage rules out secrecy.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches part of the pattern; the correct answer must match failure from accurate text, success through presence, and an unarticulated difference all at once.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Failed replications should generally be blamed on the replicators' lack of skill rather than on any weakness in the original claim.
options.B: Knowledge carried in the skills of practitioners is less reliable than knowledge that has been stated explicitly in published papers.
options.C: A field could report its techniques far more fully than it now does and still find that some of its results are hard to reproduce elsewhere.
options.D: Because tacit skills cannot be written down, efforts to improve the way methods are reported in papers are largely a waste of effort.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A field could report its techniques far more fully than it now does and still find that some of its results are hard to reproduce elsewhere.

option_rationales.A: The author explains why replication can fail even for sound claims but never says failures should as a rule be blamed on replicators; the option turns a possibility into a general verdict.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says this 'is not a reason to distrust that knowledge, since skills can be tested by their results as surely as statements can'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'A great deal that is now left out of papers could be written down' and that omitting it 'deserves the criticism it receives', so reporting reform is not wasted.
