questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says longer methods sections 'will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was'. Fuller reporting is worthwhile, but tacit skill would still be missing, so some results could remain hard to reproduce.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that dismisses reporting reform, which ignores the concession at the start of paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding together the concession and the limit stated in paragraph 4; two wrong options are plausible extensions of the argument that the author explicitly rules out.

questions.question: Each of the following is proposed or endorsed by the author as a way of helping others check published results EXCEPT

options.A: paying for researchers to spend time working in one another's laboratories.
options.B: counting the training of those who attempt a replication as part of what the replication costs.
options.C: including in papers the details that are now omitted to save space or to keep an advantage.
options.D: lengthening methods sections until each of them captures the whole of the technique it describes.

questions.correct_answer: (D) lengthening methods sections until each of them captures the whole of the technique it describes.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 proposes 'funding researchers to visit one another's laboratories', so this is endorsed.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 proposes 'treating the training of a replicator as part of the cost of a replication', so this is endorsed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says much that is left out 'could be written down' and that omitting it 'whether to save space or to protect an advantage, deserves the criticism it receives', so the author endorses including it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that 'Demanding ever longer methods sections will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was'. A methods section that captures the whole of a technique, tacit portion included, is what the author argues is impossible, so this is not endorsed.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the endorsement of fuller reporting as an endorsement of complete reporting, and so picking the option about omitted details as the exception.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer and one wrong option both concern writing more down; the solver must separate the author's support for fuller reporting from the claim that reporting can be complete.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that an unreliable narrator's deepest effect is to make readers question the trust they give to all narration.
options.B: explain the techniques by which novelists plant the clues that let readers reconstruct the true events behind a distorted account.
options.C: condemn novels that hold back a revelation until their final chapters, since such books give their readers no real pleasure.
options.D: show that novels told by unreliable narrators are generally inferior to those told by calm and impersonal third-person narrators.

questions.correct_answer: (A) argue that an unreliable narrator's deepest effect is to make readers question the trust they give to all narration.

option_rationales.B: This is the 'game of detection' of paragraph 1, which paragraph 2 calls 'thin'; the passage moves beyond it rather than setting out to explain it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says such books 'can be thrilling once', so they do give pleasure; the paragraph is a concession, not the purpose of the passage.
option_rationales.D: The passage never ranks the two kinds of novel; paragraph 3 mentions the calm third-person narrator only as a voice we trust too readily, not as a superior model.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the usual view (a puzzle), paragraph 2 calls it 'thin', and paragraph 3 gives the author's position: the best uses of the device bring 'a change in how the reader regards narration as such'. Paragraph 4 is a concession that supports the same point.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the detection view the author reports, or the concession in paragraph 4, for the passage's purpose.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated plainly in paragraph 3; each wrong option is tied to a single paragraph and is easy to rule out.

questions.question: According to the passage, novels that keep a revelation for their final chapters tend to go flat on a second reading because

options.A: the clues planted in the early chapters become obvious once the reader knows where to look for them.
options.B: the one question they raised has been answered, leaving the reader nothing to wonder about.
options.C: their narrators turn out to have been lying, whereas the narrators of better novels merely select and omit.
options.D: readers resent having been misled for so long and are unwilling to trust the narrator a second time.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the one question they raised has been answered, leaving the reader nothing to wonder about.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about clues becoming obvious; it explains the flatness by the answered question alone.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 contrasts lying with selecting only when discussing ordinary narrators; that contrast is not the reason given for these novels going flat.
option_rationales.D: Resentment is never mentioned; paragraph 4 gives a different reason, that 'the only question they posed has been answered'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'On a second reading, however, they tend to go flat, because the only question they posed has been answered.' The correct answer restates this reason.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a plausible reason from general reading experience instead of the one the passage states.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in a single sentence introduced by 'because'.

questions.question: The observation that the clues to a narrator's distortions 'are supplied by the same narrator' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: unreliable narrators usually intend their distortions to be noticed by an attentive reader of the novel.
options.B: novelists who employ unreliable narrators ought to include a second, trustworthy voice to settle what happened.
options.C: the reader can confirm the true story by comparing the narrator's account with the account of another character.
options.D: the reader's version of what really happened rests on testimony that the reader has already decided to doubt.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the reader's version of what really happened rests on testimony that the reader has already decided to doubt.

option_rationales.A: The narrator's intentions are never discussed; the point concerns where the reader's evidence comes from, not what the narrator means to reveal.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no recommendation to novelists; it describes the reader's position without proposing a remedy.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: 'we have no other witness'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 goes on to say that the true story we assemble is 'built from the materials of the account we have decided to distrust'. The correct answer states this consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the remark as a claim about the narrator's intentions rather than about the reader's evidence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The implication is spelled out in the sentences that follow the quoted phrase.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the effect that the author attributes to the best uses of the unreliable narrator?

options.A: A detective who exposes a lying suspect closes the case, confident that the full sequence of events is now known.
options.B: A juror who catches one witness contradicting himself concludes that all the remaining witnesses must therefore be telling the whole truth.
options.C: A juror who catches one witness contradicting himself starts to ask what the apparently consistent witnesses may also have left out.
options.D: A reader who discovers that one memoir contains invented episodes resolves never to trust any memoir again.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A juror who catches one witness contradicting himself starts to ask what the apparently consistent witnesses may also have left out.

option_rationales.A: This matches the view in paragraph 1, where the reader who spots the discrepancy 'has finished the work'; the author rejects that as the device's best effect.
option_rationales.B: This replaces a bad witness with trusted ones, which is the 'thin' detection picture; the author's point is that distrust should extend to voices 'that give no sign of strain'.
option_rationales.D: The effect the author describes is awareness that every narrator will 'select, arrange and omit' (paragraph 3), a sharper attention to all voices, not a wholesale rejection of one genre.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that having learned to read one voice against itself, 'we begin to notice how much we ordinarily grant to voices that give no sign of strain'. The juror who turns his scrutiny to the consistent witnesses mirrors this extension of attention from one untrustworthy voice to all voices.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the detective or the first juror, who stop at catching one liar, which is the view the author calls thin.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options reproduce the view the author reports; the correct answer requires matching the extension of distrust in paragraph 3, and the third wrong option overshoots it.

questions.question: The example of the woman packing a suitcase (paragraph 2) serves primarily to

options.A: demonstrate that short stories most often take domestic life and the breakdown of marriages as their subject.
options.B: show that a story grows more moving once the backgrounds of its characters have been explained in some detail.
options.C: illustrate how a story makes an unstated history felt through what it chooses to show and leave out.
options.D: suggest that photographs and other personal objects are the most effective details a writer can place in a scene.

questions.correct_answer: (C) illustrate how a story makes an unstated history felt through what it chooses to show and leave out.

option_rationales.A: One example cannot establish what stories most often concern, and the passage makes no claim about the usual subjects of stories.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 argues the reverse: giving the woman 'a history' makes the photograph 'one detail among many'.
option_rationales.D: The photograph matters because of what it implies, not because objects of that kind are better than others; the passage ranks no types of detail.

questions.explanation: The example comes straight after the claim that 'selection pressed hard enough becomes a kind of meaning in itself', and the passage says the eleven years 'are present precisely because they are withheld'. It illustrates meaning made by omission.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example literally, as a point about subject matter or objects, rather than about method.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is announced by the sentence that introduces the example.

questions.question: According to the passage, a novel earns its effects chiefly through

options.A: the very large amount of background information it supplies about the earlier lives of its characters.
options.B: the length of time over which the reader lives alongside its characters and watches them change.
options.C: the pressure of selection, which turns a few chosen details into a kind of meaning.
options.D: the variety of minor characters and subplots that its greater length allows it to sustain.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the length of time over which the reader lives alongside its characters and watches them change.

option_rationales.A: Information is discussed only in paragraph 3, as what weakens an expanded story; it is never named as the novel's source of effect.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 assigns selection to the short story: 'What it has instead is selection'. The novel is contrasted with it.
option_rationales.D: Subplots and minor characters are not mentioned; the passage names duration, not variety, as the novel's resource.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A novel accumulates; it earns its effects through duration, letting the reader live alongside its people for enough days that change in them can be felt as change.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the novel's method with the story's, since the two are described in adjacent sentences.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of one sentence; the main lure is the story's method in the next line.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a critic's praise of a story as 'as rich as a novel' as

options.A: evidence that most critics do not read short stories with any real attention or care.
options.B: an accurate account of what the best short stories manage to achieve within their few pages.
options.C: a sign that publishers have at last begun to value collections of short stories as highly as novels.
options.D: a compliment that measures the story by a standard that belongs to a different form.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a compliment that measures the story by a standard that belongs to a different form.

option_rationales.A: The passage criticises the standard such critics apply, not their attentiveness, and a claim about most critics goes beyond anything stated.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the praise treats 'richness of that kind' as the measure of success 'as though' it were, signalling disagreement; the story's force lies elsewhere.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says publishers regard collections as 'harder to sell' and that the habit is 'reinforced' by them, so the praise belongs to the same habit, not to a change in it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 cites the phrase as an example of the habit of treating the story as a smaller novel, and paragraph 4 concludes that 'judging it by the novel's standards will reliably mistake its strengths for omissions'. The praise is such a judgement.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the praise at face value because it sounds generous to the story.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer requires linking a phrase in paragraph 1 to the conclusion in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about expanding fine stories?

options.A: Readers comparing admired stories with later full-length versions by the same writers mostly found the longer versions stronger, because of the added history.
options.B: Publishers continue to report that collections of short stories sell fewer copies than novels by the same writers.
options.C: Several admired novels are known to have grown out of rough, unfinished short pieces that their authors went on revising, sometimes for many years, before finally publishing them.
options.D: Writers who began with short stories and later turned to novels often say that the shorter form taught them economy.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Readers comparing admired stories with later full-length versions by the same writers mostly found the longer versions stronger, because of the added history.

option_rationales.B: Sales concern the trade's habit in paragraph 1, not whether expansion improves a story; the fact is irrelevant to the claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 already concedes that 'more than one long novel began as a few pages', so this is consistent with the argument and does not show that expansion improves fine stories.
option_rationales.D: This supports, if anything, the value of the story's method and says nothing about whether expanded stories are better or worse.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that 'expanding a fine story so rarely improves it' because filling the gaps with information weakens implication. Evidence that expanded versions are generally found more powerful, precisely because of the added history, strikes at both the claim and its reason.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the novels that grew from short pieces, which the author has already conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option restates a concession, which tempts readers who do not check what the author already allows.

questions.question: The heroine 'killed by a runaway carriage' (paragraph 2) is mentioned in order to

options.A: prove that tragic endings are in general less honest than the happy endings that serious readers distrust.
options.B: show that an unhappy ending forced on a story from outside is as arbitrary as a contrived happy one.
options.C: suggest that sudden accidental deaths are seldom believable in novels whose stories are set in earlier centuries.
options.D: illustrate the kind of courageous ending that serious readers are right to admire in a novel.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that an unhappy ending forced on a story from outside is as arbitrary as a contrived happy one.

option_rationales.A: The author says such a catastrophe is 'no more truthful', not less, and paragraph 4 allows that some tragic endings are honest; the option overstates and ranks.
option_rationales.C: The period setting is incidental; the point is that the death is imposed 'because the author wanted the book to feel weighty', not that accidents are unbelievable.
option_rationales.D: This is the view of paragraph 1 that the example is meant to unsettle; the carriage death is called 'arbitrary', not courageous.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the fault of contrived happy endings is that 'nothing in the preceding chapters made them necessary', and then offers the carriage death as 'A catastrophe imposed in the same way', 'no less arbitrary'. The example extends the fault to unhappy endings.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the example as a general verdict on tragic endings rather than as a parallel case.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase 'imposed in the same way' states the function directly.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, an ending is said to 'console' when it

options.A: makes up to the reader for the sadness and suffering of the earlier chapters.
options.B: rewards the characters the reader likes and punishes those the reader has come to dislike.
options.C: marks clearly the point beyond which the story will not go on being told.
options.D: leaves the reader reassured about the world that the novel has depicted.

questions.correct_answer: (D) leaves the reader reassured about the world that the novel has depicted.

option_rationales.A: This is an everyday sense of consoling, but the passage defines the word differently, as leaving the reader 'reassured about the world the book has shown'.
option_rationales.B: Rewards and punishments are not mentioned; the passage defines consolation by its effect on the reader's view of the world.
option_rationales.C: This is what the passage calls closing: 'it marks the point after which the story will not be told'. The author separates it from consoling.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 defines the term: 'Some endings also console; they leave the reader reassured about the world the book has shown.' The correct answer paraphrases this definition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the definition of closure, which sits in the preceding sentence, or the everyday sense of the word.
questions.difficulty_reason: The passage's own definition must be preferred over the ordinary sense, and closure is defined in the adjacent sentence.

questions.question: The author makes each of the following claims EXCEPT that

options.A: readers ought to prefer novels that end in marriage or reconciliation to novels that end in failure.
options.B: some endings that arrive from outside the story deserve the reader's feeling of having been cheated.
options.C: every story, whatever its tone or subject, has to stop at some point and leave the rest untold.
options.D: an unhappy ending can meet the expectations of some readers as predictably as a happy one can.

questions.correct_answer: (A) readers ought to prefer novels that end in marriage or reconciliation to novels that end in failure.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says readers 'are right to feel cheated' by endings that 'arrive from outside the story', so the author does make this claim.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 calls closure 'a formal necessity, since a story must stop somewhere', so the author makes this claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the unhappy note 'can be just as comfortably familiar to readers who have learned to expect gloom', so the author makes this claim.

questions.explanation: The author's test in paragraph 4 is indifferent to tone: an ending is honest 'whether that place is a marriage or a grave'. Nowhere does the author rank happy endings above unhappy ones; the passage defends happy endings only against blanket suspicion.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the defence of happy endings against prejudice for a preference for them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported option is a plausible overextension of the author's sympathy for happy endings.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the 'suspicious reader' described in paragraph 3?

options.A: Such a reader is right to object to consolation in fiction but mistaken in admiring unhappy endings for their courage.
options.B: Such a reader believes that every serious novel must end in death, separation or failure if it is to count as honest fiction.
options.C: Such a reader treats a dislike of reassurance as if it were an objection to bringing a story to a definite end.
options.D: Such a reader consciously prefers novels that refuse to finish at all, ranking them above both happy and tragic ones.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Such a reader treats a dislike of reassurance as if it were an objection to bringing a story to a definite end.

option_rationales.A: The author never endorses the objection to consolation, calling consolation merely 'a choice'; the option assigns the author a verdict the passage does not give.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says unhappy endings are 'credited with courage', but a requirement on every serious novel is far stronger than anything attributed to the reader.
option_rationales.D: The phrase 'as though the honest book would be the one that refused to finish' is the author's account of where the reader's confusion leads, not a preference the reader holds; paragraph 1 shows this reader admiring tragic endings.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the suspicious reader 'objects to the consolation, and then mistakes the objection for an argument against closure itself'. The correct answer restates this confusion of the two functions the author has just distinguished.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's 'as though' clause as a description of the reader's actual taste.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to the text: one turns the author's reductio into the reader's stated preference, the other grants the author a verdict on consolation that is never given.

questions.question: According to the passage, a turn in the ninth line of a sonnet registers as a turn because

options.A: the reader already knows the point in the poem at which a turn is expected.
options.B: readers of sonnets are taught to look for a contradiction of the poem's opening.
options.C: the ninth line is by tradition the longest and most emphatic line of the poem.
options.D: the poet abandons the rhyme scheme at that line so as to mark the change clearly.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the reader already knows the point in the poem at which a turn is expected.

option_rationales.B: The passage does not describe what a turn contains or how readers are taught; it says only that they know 'where turns are expected'.
option_rationales.C: Line length is never mentioned; the passage says only that the length of the whole poem is fixed.
option_rationales.D: The passage says nothing about abandoning the rhyme scheme; it attributes the effect to the reader's expectation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'a turn in the ninth line registers as a turn only because the reader knows where turns are expected'. The correct answer restates this.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying outside knowledge about sonnets instead of the reason the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in one clause beginning 'only because'.

questions.question: The author lists 'the fractured chronology' and 'the unnamed narrator' (paragraph 4) in order to

options.A: illustrate the inventions by which literary novels create their own shape instead of inheriting one.
options.B: show that literary fiction also depends on inherited conventions that can be followed mechanically.
options.C: argue that literary fiction has become more formulaic than any of the popular genres it looks down on.
options.D: identify techniques that genre writers have recently borrowed from the literary novel.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that literary fiction also depends on inherited conventions that can be followed mechanically.

option_rationales.A: This is the view of paragraph 1 that the author rejects; the devices are offered as conventions, and the author adds that some writers 'complete them dutifully', so they are not inventions.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'the same is true' of literary fiction, an equivalence, not a claim that it is more formulaic than every genre.
option_rationales.D: Borrowing between the two is never discussed; the devices are presented as literary fiction's own conventions.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the hardening of conventions into formula is 'the same' in literary fiction, 'which has its own conventions', and gives these devices as examples, adding that some writers 'complete them dutifully'. They support the conclusion that no books lack conventions.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the examples as an attack that ranks literary fiction below genre fiction.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function depends on the 'same is true' clause; one wrong option overstates it into a ranking.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the pleasure of the devoted genre reader as

options.A: confined to checking whether a writer has followed every rule of the genre correctly.
options.B: lesser than the pleasure of meeting an unconventional novel for the first time without expectations.
options.C: depending on close knowledge of the conventions against which a particular book can be measured.
options.D: arising chiefly from the comfort of meeting familiar situations and outcomes once again.

questions.correct_answer: (C) depending on close knowledge of the conventions against which a particular book can be measured.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 describes alertness to 'the smallest variation', not to compliance; checking rules is closer to the formula writer's 'checklist' in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.B: The passage never compares these pleasures; it says only that the unconventional novel cannot make departures felt so precisely.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the pleasure is 'not the passive pleasure of repetition', which this option describes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says devoted readers, having read 'a hundred novels built on the same frame', notice the smallest variation, and that their pleasure is 'the active one of comparison'. Comparison requires knowledge of the frame against which each book is measured.
questions.common_misconception: Equating familiarity with repetition, which the passage explicitly rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires inferring what 'comparison' presupposes; one wrong option is the reading the passage denies.

questions.question: The claim that a departure from convention in a detective story 'is felt with a precision no unconventional novel can command' depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Readers of unconventional novels generally read with less attention and care than the devoted readers of detective stories.
options.B: Detective stories that break their conventions are more highly valued than detective stories that keep them.
options.C: Most readers of detective stories have read more widely than most readers of literary fiction.
options.D: How sharply a departure is felt depends on how firmly the reader expected the thing departed from.

questions.correct_answer: (D) How sharply a departure is felt depends on how firmly the reader expected the thing departed from.

option_rationales.A: The author explains the difference by the absence of 'settled expectation', not by inattention; the argument would stand even if both readers were equally attentive.
option_rationales.B: The claim concerns how precisely a departure is felt, not how much the book is valued; the argument needs no ranking of books.
option_rationales.C: Breadth of reading is not needed; even a reader of a few detective stories knows that 'the culprit must be among the people introduced'.

questions.explanation: The author's reason is that 'the unconventional novel has no settled expectation to depart from'. For that to explain the difference in precision, the strength of a felt departure must depend on the strength of the prior expectation, which is what the correct answer states.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option about readers' qualities instead of the link between expectation and effect that the reason requires.
questions.difficulty_reason: The assumption must be extracted from a 'because' clause; the wrong options offer alternative explanations that the argument does not need.

questions.question: According to the passage, during the pause after the line 'she said she would not leave', the reader takes the woman to be

options.A: forbidden by someone else in the house from leaving until it is safe to go out.
options.B: agreeing to leave the house as soon as the rain outside has finally stopped falling.
options.C: refusing to leave at all, until the next line narrows her refusal to the weather.
options.D: speaking insincerely, so that the reader begins to doubt whether she means what she says.

questions.correct_answer: (C) refusing to leave at all, until the next line narrows her refusal to the weather.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the example suggests anyone else forbids her; the refusal is her own ('she said').
option_rationales.B: This is the reading the whole sentence finally gives; paragraph 2 says that during the pause 'the woman refuses to leave at all'.
option_rationales.D: Sincerity is never raised; the example concerns how the line break changes the scope of the refusal.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'For the length of the pause the woman refuses to leave at all; the next line shrinks the refusal to a matter of weather.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the meaning of the completed sentence instead of the meaning the single line has during the pause.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence; the lure is the full-sentence reading.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, line breaks that were 'decoration' are breaks that

options.A: restore some of the rhyme and regular metre that free verse otherwise abandons.
options.B: give a text the look of verse while adding nothing to its meaning or its pace.
options.C: make a poem visually attractive on the page, which the author treats as a legitimate secondary aim.
options.D: enrich a poem's language with ornamental words that make its images more vivid.

questions.correct_answer: (B) give a text the look of verse while adding nothing to its meaning or its pace.

option_rationales.A: Rhyme and metre are what free verse has given up (paragraph 1); decorative breaks are defined by doing no work, not by reintroducing them.
option_rationales.C: The author uses 'decoration' as a verdict of failure ('then the breaks were decoration') and nowhere calls appearance a legitimate aim.
option_rationales.D: The word refers to the breaks, not to the poem's vocabulary; ornamental diction is never discussed.

questions.explanation: The sentence defines the term by its condition: 'If nothing is lost, if no meaning that the breaks created has vanished and no pace has been flattened, then the breaks were decoration.' Decorative breaks are those that contribute neither meaning nor pace.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'decoration' in its neutral everyday sense rather than as the failure the test detects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the conditional sentence; one wrong option keeps the everyday sense and adds a judgement the author does not make.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author regard as the best evidence that the line breaks in a particular free verse poem are doing real work?

options.A: When the poem is printed as a continuous paragraph, a second sense that one of its lines had carried disappears.
options.B: Readers who are shown the poem set out as prose still recognise it at once and find it just as effective.
options.C: The poet explains in an interview that every break in the poem was chosen with great care over many drafts.
options.D: The lines of the poem are strikingly unequal in length, some a single word long and some running nearly to the margin.

questions.correct_answer: (A) When the poem is printed as a continuous paragraph, a second sense that one of its lines had carried disappears.

option_rationales.B: If the prose version is just as effective, nothing has been lost, which by the author's test would show the breaks were 'decoration'.
option_rationales.C: The test in paragraph 4 is applied to the text by a reader, not to the poet's account of intentions; care in choosing does not show the breaks work.
option_rationales.D: Unequal lines show only that breaks exist; the author's test asks whether anything is lost when they are removed, which this does not establish.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4's test is to 'set the poem out as prose, read it again, and ask what has gone'; the breaks were doing work if some 'meaning that the breaks created has vanished'. A lost second sense, of the kind shown in paragraph 2, is exactly such a meaning.
questions.common_misconception: Taking visible features of the lines, or the poet's testimony, as evidence instead of applying the author's own test.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the prose test to new cases; one wrong option is the test's negative result.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the objection that free verse is 'merely prose with the margins moved' is best described as

options.A: partial agreement: it succeeds against free verse in general, though a few exceptional poems happen to escape it.
options.B: reluctant sympathy: poets have generally failed to answer it, so it remains in effect unanswered by anyone.
options.C: firm rejection: it rests on a misunderstanding and in practice holds against almost none of the poems published today.
options.D: qualified acceptance: it is fair against many poems but cannot become a verdict on the form itself.

questions.correct_answer: (D) qualified acceptance: it is fair against many poems but cannot become a verdict on the form itself.

option_rationales.A: The final sentence says the test 'cannot do' this: it cannot 'condemn the form as such'. The option makes the objection a general verdict with exceptions, which reverses the author's position.
option_rationales.B: The author grants that poets give a weak answer ('deserves a better answer than poets usually give it') but then supplies one in paragraphs 2 and 3.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'A good deal of what is published as free verse' fails the test and that there 'the objection is simply correct'.

questions.explanation: The author answers the objection with the principle of the line as 'a unit of attention' (paragraph 2), yet concedes in paragraph 4 that for much published free verse 'the objection is simply correct'. The test, however, 'cannot do' the work of condemning 'the form as such'. The attitude is acceptance limited to particular poems.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the partial agreement option, which sounds balanced but makes the objection right about the form in general.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two attitude options are both mixed; separating them needs the scope distinction between particular poems and the form.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Round characters succeed only when a novel first presents them as flat and later reveals their hidden depth.
options.B: Flat characters do work of their own in fiction, so treating roundness as the only mark of achievement misreads many novels.
options.C: Flat characters are more lifelike than round ones, because people in ordinary life are known to us only by their habits.
options.D: The best novels are those that portray a whole society rather than the inner life of a single individual.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Flat characters do work of their own in fiction, so treating roundness as the only mark of achievement misreads many novels.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says that one particular effect depends on first taking a figure as simple; it does not say round characters in general succeed only this way.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 offers this only as 'a case that' flatness is closer to experience, and paragraph 4 says 'This is not to invert the hierarchy'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the inner-life tradition is 'one powerful tradition' among others; the author does not rank the two kinds of novel.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 give flat characters functions (registering a society, comedy, fidelity to how others appear), and paragraph 4 concludes that flat and round 'are not grades of achievement but different tools' and that a criticism rewarding only one 'will misread every novel in which both are at work'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that inverts the hierarchy, which the author explicitly declines to do.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option overstates one supporting point; the correct answer needs the conclusion of paragraph 4.

questions.question: The man who consults the same almanac after every misfortune (paragraph 3) is introduced in order to

options.A: suggest that superstition was a favourite target of the satirical fiction of earlier periods.
options.B: demonstrate that comic novels seldom contain any round characters at all among their casts.
options.C: show how a character's comic effect can depend on his being unable to act in any other way.
options.D: argue that a novel always gains in seriousness when its comic figures are given moments of inner doubt.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show how a character's comic effect can depend on his being unable to act in any other way.

option_rationales.A: No historical claim about satire is made; the almanac simply gives the man a fixed habit to repeat.
option_rationales.B: The passage makes no claim about the casts of comic novels; it shows how one flat figure produces comedy.
option_rationales.D: The passage says such deepening 'may be a gain, but it is a different book'; it does not claim the novel always gains.

questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that fiction's comedy 'depends on repetition', and the passage says the man is funny 'precisely because he could not have done otherwise'. It illustrates comedy arising from fixity.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the follow-up remark about deepening him as the purpose of the example.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option draws on the sentence after the example and adds 'always'.

questions.question: The passage suggests that characters such as the aunt and the official in paragraph 2 contribute to a novel chiefly by

options.A: embodying an unyielding social world against which the changing characters can be measured.
options.B: delivering the novelist's moral message more directly than the major characters ever could.
options.C: standing in for the reader, who also experiences the society of the novel from outside it.
options.D: revealing, late in the story, depths that overturn the reader's first impression of them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) embodying an unyielding social world against which the changing characters can be measured.

option_rationales.B: Delivering a message is the use the dismissive view in paragraph 1 allows flat characters; paragraph 2 gives them a different role.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in paragraph 2 links these figures to the reader's position; they represent the society, not the outsider.
option_rationales.D: That effect belongs to the figure 'we had thought simple' in paragraph 4; the aunt and the official are valued for their 'fixity'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says their fixity 'is how the novel registers the pressure of a world that does not bend, against which its few changing figures can be measured'. The correct answer restates this role.
questions.common_misconception: Assigning to these figures a function the passage reserves for other characters or for the view it rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The role is stated, but two wrong options borrow functions from paragraphs 1 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 2?

options.A: Novels centred on the inner life of one individual have been studied far more often than novels about societies.
options.B: Several critics who prefer round characters also count novels portraying an entire society among their favourite books.
options.C: In many novels about a society, the unchanging minor figures are also among the funniest characters in the book.
options.D: Readers of novels about whole societies report learning the society's pressures almost entirely through the changing main characters, and barely recall the fixed minor ones.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Readers of novels about whole societies report learning the society's pressures almost entirely through the changing main characters, and barely recall the fixed minor ones.

option_rationales.A: How often a kind of novel is studied is irrelevant to whether fixed characters convey a society's pressure.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 is about how such novels work, not about which books critics like; a critic's taste does not bear on how a society is felt in fiction.
option_rationales.C: This is consistent with paragraph 3, which links flatness to comedy, and does not challenge the claim that such figures register a society.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 claims that 'a society is felt in fiction partly through the people who never change'. If readers in fact grasp the society through the changing characters and scarcely notice the fixed ones, the proposed function of flat characters is undercut.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about critics' preferences, which touches the passage's subject but not the mechanism paragraph 2 asserts.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires isolating the causal claim of paragraph 2 from the critical preference it is used to challenge.

questions.question: According to the passage, the essay taught in schools and universities

options.A: encourages students to record the abandoned lines of thought by which they reached their conclusions.
options.B: was first designed in order to replace the treatise as the standard form of academic writing.
options.C: opens with a thesis and restates it at the close, after setting out evidence and dealing with objections.
options.D: has no real virtues that could justify the place it now holds in teaching and examination.

questions.correct_answer: (C) opens with a thesis and restates it at the close, after setting out evidence and dealing with objections.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: writers learn to treat 'any movement of thought' as a defect 'to be removed in revision'.
option_rationales.B: The passage calls it 'a miniature treatise', not a replacement for one, and says nothing about its origin.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says its virtues 'are real virtues, and there are good reasons to teach them'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: it 'opens with a thesis, marshals evidence in its favour, dispatches objections and restates the thesis at the close'.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the author's concession that the school essay has real virtues.
questions.difficulty_reason: A paraphrase of a single sentence; wrong options contradict nearby statements.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the phrase 'a standpoint from nowhere in particular' refers to

options.A: a voice that remains vague about which subject or question it is actually addressing.
options.B: a writer who conceals his own name and publishes his work anonymously or under another name.
options.C: a writer who declines to commit to any definite conclusion about the matter under discussion.
options.D: a voice that presents its claims as if they did not depend on anyone's particular position or experience.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a voice that presents its claims as if they did not depend on anyone's particular position or experience.

option_rationales.A: The phrase concerns where the claims are made from, not what they are about; the treatise is credited with 'clarity of claim' in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: This reads the phrase literally; the contrast is with the essayist's 'I', a matter of voice, not of authorship.
option_rationales.C: That describes the 'meandering essay' of paragraph 5, not the impersonal treatise, which states its conclusion plainly.

questions.explanation: The phrase is set against the essayist's 'I', which 'marks the scope of a claim: this is how the matter looks from here'. The treatise's impersonal voice instead claims no particular location, which is why its claims are 'harder to locate'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the impersonal treatise with the evasive essay of paragraph 5.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning depends on the contrast with the first person drawn in the same paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the author's view of the treatise?

options.A: Its manner of presentation can make a conclusion seem more inevitable than the evidence by itself warrants.
options.B: Its impersonal voice is always a form of self-display disguised as a neutral and objective manner.
options.C: It is an inferior kind of writing that schools ought to stop teaching in favour of the provisional essay.
options.D: Its conclusions are, as a rule, less reliable than those reached by writers of the provisional essay.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Its manner of presentation can make a conclusion seem more inevitable than the evidence by itself warrants.

option_rationales.B: Self-display is said of the essay's 'I'; paragraph 4 allows that the treatise's objectivity 'is sometimes real', so calling it a disguise in every case contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 grants that its virtues are real and that 'there are good reasons to teach them'; the author regrets what was lost, not that the treatise is taught.
option_rationales.D: The author contrasts how visible the route to a conclusion is, not how reliable conclusions are; nothing is said about which form reaches truer conclusions.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The treatise presents its conclusion as if it were the only place the evidence could lead', and paragraph 4 adds that its objectivity is 'always also a manner' that can be adopted by writers 'whose claims have not earned it'. Together these imply that the form can lend a conclusion more inevitability than it has.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the author's comparison of forms into a verdict on their reliability or their place in teaching.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer needs two paragraphs combined; the reliability wrong option is a natural but unsupported extension of the comparison.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the claim that the provisional essay leaves the reader 'better placed to disagree'?

options.A: Readers shown an argument that included the writer's abandoned paths were more likely than other readers to accept its final conclusion.
options.B: Readers shown an argument that included an alternative the writer had rejected could state reasoned objections to its conclusion more readily than readers shown the conclusion alone.
options.C: Readers generally report finding essays written in the first person more enjoyable and more personal than essays written in an impersonal voice.
options.D: Students who are trained to write thesis-first essays score higher than other students on tests of clarity and economy in writing.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Readers shown an argument that included an alternative the writer had rejected could state reasoned objections to its conclusion more readily than readers shown the conclusion alone.

option_rationales.A: Greater acceptance does not show readers were better able to disagree; if anything it points the other way.
option_rationales.C: Enjoyment is not the claim; the question is whether seeing the route to a conclusion equips readers to contest it.
option_rationales.D: This bears on the virtues of the school essay granted in paragraph 2, not on the reader's capacity to disagree with a provisional essay.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that by 'showing the alternatives it passed through' the essay equips the reader to contest its conclusion. A finding that readers who see a rejected alternative can object more readily is direct evidence for that mechanism.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the finding about abandoned paths and agreement, which shares the correct answer's setup but measures the wrong outcome.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options describe the same kind of experiment; only one measures the ability to disagree.

questions.question: The final paragraph functions chiefly to

options.A: concede that the thesis-first essay is, after all, more useful than the provisional essay the author has praised.
options.B: guard the argument against being taken as a defence of writing that never commits itself to a claim.
options.C: summarise the historical change in how essays are taught that was first described in the second paragraph.
options.D: introduce a fresh objection to the provisional essay which the author admits cannot be satisfactorily answered.

questions.correct_answer: (B) guard the argument against being taken as a defence of writing that never commits itself to a claim.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says the meandering essay is 'less useful' than the rigid one; it does not say the thesis-first essay is more useful than the provisional essay at its best.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 does not return to schooling or to history; it sets a limit on the author's own thesis.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph answers the objection itself: a thought must be 'stated with enough definiteness to fail', and the best essay is 'argument conducted in the open'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 opens 'None of this licenses formlessness' and distinguishes genuine provisionality from 'the meandering essay that circles its subject without ever risking a claim'. Its role is to block a misreading of the argument as a defence of non-commitment.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the comparison with the 'rigid' essay as a reversal of the author's preference.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option misapplies a comparison between two bad forms to the author's preferred form.

questions.question: According to the passage, recurring characters with distinctive habits of speech helped readers of serial novels by

options.A: making it easier to find their place in the story after a month away from it.
options.B: signalling which of the many characters would turn out to matter by the end of the novel.
options.C: allowing authors to fill the length they were paid for without having to invent any new plots.
options.D: giving readers figures whose opinions and manners resembled those of the readers themselves.

questions.correct_answer: (A) making it easier to find their place in the story after a month away from it.

option_rationales.B: The passage says nothing about foreshadowing; the figures help a returning reader 'find her place'.
option_rationales.C: Padding is discussed in paragraph 4 as a cost of fixed lengths, but the passage never links it to recurring characters.
option_rationales.D: Resemblance to readers is never mentioned; the habits of speech help readers recognise characters, not identify with them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'recurring figures with distinctive habits of speech helped her find her place', the reader in question being one 'returning after a month's absence'.
questions.common_misconception: Linking the recurring figures to padding because both concern serial length.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in one clause of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author suggests that the critical view described in paragraph 1 assumes that

options.A: authors who wrote in instalments were on the whole indifferent to the quality of what they produced.
options.B: a chapter that ends in suspense is always a sign of poor craftsmanship in a novel of any kind.
options.C: the serial novel that readers actually have falls short of a better book its author would otherwise have written.
options.D: serial novels were read less carefully by their first readers than they are read by modern critics.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the serial novel that readers actually have falls short of a better book its author would otherwise have written.

option_rationales.A: The view blames deadlines and payment, external pressures, not indifference; it excuses authors rather than accusing them.
option_rationales.B: The view objects to 'a contrived moment of suspense', and paragraph 4 objects only to cliffhangers 'the story did not need'; the claim that such endings are always a fault in any kind of novel goes far beyond either.
option_rationales.D: The first readers' care is never compared with critics'; paragraph 1 concerns how critics explain the novels' faults.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The implication is that the real novel, the one the author would have written in better conditions, lies somewhere beneath the one we have'. The correct answer restates this hidden assumption.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the excuse as an accusation against the authors.
questions.difficulty_reason: The assumption is spelled out as an 'implication', but the wrong options are close in subject.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that adjusting a novel in response to readers is 'a surrender of artistic control' is best described as

options.A: indifferent, since the author regards the question of control as irrelevant to a novel's merits.
options.B: contemptuous, since the author treats it as a confusion that no serious critic could still hold.
options.C: approving, since the author agrees that serial novelists gave up too much to their audiences.
options.D: even-handed, since the author grants it as one possible reading while offering an alternative that is equally reasonable.

questions.correct_answer: (D) even-handed, since the author grants it as one possible reading while offering an alternative that is equally reasonable.

option_rationales.A: The author engages the question directly and reframes it; nowhere is it called irrelevant.
option_rationales.B: The author writes 'A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control', which allows the reading; there is no contempt and no claim about what critics still hold.
option_rationales.C: The author immediately offers the alternative of 'a kind of conversation', which does not endorse the purist's verdict.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control. It can as easily be seen as a kind of conversation'. The phrase 'as easily' grants the purist's reading while presenting an equally available alternative.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the author's reframing for outright rejection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tone turns on the force of 'may' and 'as easily'.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT that

options.A: some cliffhangers in serial novels read badly once the instalments had been collected into a volume.
options.B: the ideal of the unified novel arose because serial publication had made novels too long to plan in advance.
options.C: readers' responses to early instalments could influence the later course of a serial novel.
options.D: a feature that looks like digression in a bound volume may have served a purpose for the novel's first readers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the ideal of the unified novel arose because serial publication had made novels too long to plan in advance.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says some cliffhangers 'read awkwardly once the parts were bound together', which supports this.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says authors 'sometimes did' adjust their plans 'in light of how readers responded', which supports this.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such material could, 'at the pace of first reading, serve as the texture of a world one returned to', which supports this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says only that the ideal 'has a history of its own' and 'gained much of its authority later, among writers and critics who worked for a different market and under different conditions'. The passage gives no cause for its rise, and certainly not the length of serial novels.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a causal story for the unified-design ideal because the passage places it after the serial era.
questions.difficulty_reason: The unsupported option borrows the passage's terms and adds a cause that is never given; the supported options are paraphrases across three paragraphs.

questions.question: The reference to long television dramas in the final paragraph serves mainly to

options.A: argue that television has now replaced the novel as the principal home of serial storytelling for most audiences.
options.B: suggest that modern critics have become less demanding than those who once apologised for the instalment novel.
options.C: suggest that serial forms can succeed only where audiences are able to discuss each episode before the next one appears.
options.D: point out that qualities once excused in the instalment novel are now admired when they appear in a similar form.

questions.correct_answer: (D) point out that qualities once excused in the instalment novel are now admired when they appear in a similar form.

option_rationales.A: The passage makes no claim about which medium dominates; the comparison concerns how critics judge the same qualities.
option_rationales.B: The author's point is that the old standard was misapplied, not that today's critics have lowered theirs; the irony targets the earlier embarrassment.
option_rationales.C: Discussion between episodes is mentioned as a shared feature, not as a necessary condition; 'only' is unsupported.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 calls it 'an irony in the critical embarrassment': television dramas are praised 'for the very qualities' that 'the instalment novel was once thought to need excusing for'. The comparison reinforces the claim of paragraph 4 that the unified-design standard converts differences into faults.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the irony as a complaint about falling standards rather than as support for the author's critique of the old standard.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are plausible cultural claims; the correct answer requires linking paragraph 5 to the argument of paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, lists of untranslatable words tend to undermine their own claim because they

options.A: explain each supposedly untranslatable word clearly in the very language said to have no equivalent for it.
options.B: present foreign words without examples, so that readers never learn how the words are used in daily speech.
options.C: include many words that are invented or exaggerated and that ordinary speakers of the original language never use.
options.D: show that speakers of every language share exactly the same experiences, which makes the special words unnecessary.

questions.correct_answer: (A) explain each supposedly untranslatable word clearly in the very language said to have no equivalent for it.

option_rationales.B: The passage never complains about missing usage examples; its point in paragraph 2 is that the lists succeed in explaining the words.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says 'most of the words in them are real', so the author does not fault the lists for inventing words.
option_rationales.D: The author claims neither that all experiences are identical nor that the words are unnecessary; paragraph 3 even treats a word's existence as cultural information.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 notes that each entry pairs the foreign word with an English explanation that readers grasp at once: 'The list, in other words, translates every word it calls untranslatable.' The lists thus refute the claim they are meant to illustrate.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a criticism that sounds reasonable in general but is not the one the passage makes.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, the word 'packages' refers to

options.A: the cultural information that a word conveys about the community that first found an experience worth naming.
options.B: the process by which a translator compresses a long explanation of a word into a brief footnote.
options.C: the way one language bundles into a single word a meaning that another language spreads across several words.
options.D: the attractive manner in which popular articles present foreign words so that they seem more exotic than they are.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the way one language bundles into a single word a meaning that another language spreads across several words.

option_rationales.A: That idea belongs to paragraph 3; in paragraph 2 the word contrasts a single word with a phrase expressing the same meaning.
option_rationales.B: Footnotes appear only in paragraph 3, and there they fail to restore losses; 'packages' describes how vocabularies are divided, not a translator's technique.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 does call the lists charming, but in paragraph 2 the subject of 'packages' is a language, not an article.

questions.explanation: The sentence says 'one language packages in a single word what another expresses in a phrase', and the next calls this 'a fact about how vocabularies happen to be divided up'. The word therefore means bundling a meaning into one word.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying over associations of the word (marketing, wrapping) instead of reading the sentence it sits in.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contrast with 'expresses in a phrase' in the same sentence fixes the meaning.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It argues that explanatory footnotes are the most effective means a translator has of restoring what is lost.
options.B: It abandons the argument of paragraph 2 by admitting that some experiences cannot be grasped outside their own language.
options.C: It gives the example of a particular poem whose translation failed because it contained a single untranslatable word.
options.D: It concedes that something is lost in translation, while locating that loss in qualities other than a word's basic sense.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It concedes that something is lost in translation, while locating that loss in qualities other than a word's basic sense.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says the opposite: 'no amount of explanation in a footnote restores them'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 opens 'But the losses are of degree, not of kind', so the concession limits the argument rather than abandoning it, and paragraph 3 never says experiences cannot be grasped.
option_rationales.C: No particular poem is discussed; the paragraph speaks generally of 'a translator working on a poem'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'This is not to say that nothing is lost' and lists ease of use, register, sound and associations as what a paraphrase cannot reproduce. The meaning itself was shown in paragraph 2 to cross, so the concession relocates the loss rather than reversing the thesis.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a concession as a reversal of the author's position.
questions.difficulty_reason: The opening phrase of the paragraph signals its role.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: A translation may render a word's sense accurately and yet fail to carry over much of what that word does in the original.
options.B: The real difficulties of translation are confined mostly to rare words that name experiences peculiar to one culture.
options.C: Languages with larger vocabularies allow their speakers to perceive a wider range of experiences than other languages do.
options.D: Since every language lacks words for many things, the presence or absence of a word reveals nothing about a community.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A translation may render a word's sense accurately and yet fail to carry over much of what that word does in the original.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the losses 'are not peculiar to exotic words' and occur whenever any word is rendered by another.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the way vocabularies are divided 'tells us very little about what their speakers are able to think or feel', which contradicts this.
option_rationales.D: This is too absolute: paragraph 3 says a word's existence is 'a small piece of cultural information', and paragraph 2 says vocabulary tells us 'very little', not nothing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 holds that meaning crosses between languages, and paragraph 3 that a word's register, sound, ease and associations are lost even so. Together these support the correct answer; paragraph 4 sums it up as 'always possible and never complete'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the absolute version of the author's claim over the hedged one.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs paragraphs 2 and 3 together, and one wrong option exaggerates a real point of the passage.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: defending film directors against the charge that they borrow the titles of famous books merely to attract an audience.
options.B: explaining why novels narrated by untrustworthy characters can rarely be adapted successfully for the screen.
options.C: arguing that adaptations should be judged by whether they achieve what their source achieved, not by how little they change.
options.D: showing that film is an inferior medium to the novel because it cannot represent what happens inside a character's mind.

questions.correct_answer: (C) arguing that adaptations should be judged by whether they achieve what their source achieved, not by how little they change.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says the complaint against such films 'is fair', so the author does not defend them.
option_rationales.B: The unreliable narrator is an illustration, and paragraph 3 describes how a director could adapt such a novel well.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says a film 'must find something for the camera to look at', and paragraph 3 shows it can succeed; the author never ranks the media.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 rejects the checklist standard, paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that a film must find 'its own means of doing what the book did', and paragraph 4 restates fidelity as 'a matter of purpose rather than of inventory'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the central example or the concession for the purpose of the whole passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated in paragraph 1 and restated at the end.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is a difference between novels and films?

options.A: A novel is written for a small circle of devoted readers, whereas a film is made for a large and ready-made audience.
options.B: A novel can linger over or summarise events as it likes, whereas a film moves at a pace the viewer cannot slow.
options.C: A novel must preserve every one of its incidents, whereas a film is free to drop a subplot or merge characters.
options.D: A novel depends on a narrator to tell its story, whereas a film can show events only plainly and from the outside.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A novel can linger over or summarise events as it likes, whereas a film moves at a pace the viewer cannot slow.

option_rationales.A: The 'ready-made audience' in paragraph 4 is what a famous title brings to some films; it is not offered as a general difference between the media.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says novels must preserve incidents; dropped subplots are mentioned only as items on the critics' checklist.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 describes a director framing scenes so the viewer doubts them, so the passage denies that film can show events only from the outside.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states: 'A novel handles time loosely, lingering or summarising as it likes, while a film runs at a pace the viewer cannot slow.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that reuses passage phrases in a claim the passage does not make.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following adaptations would the author most likely regard as the most faithful to its source?

options.A: A film of a comic novel that keeps every scene and nearly every line of dialogue but is acted so solemnly that the book's humour disappears.
options.B: A television series that keeps the title and the characters' names of a famous satirical novel but turns its story into a simple romance.
options.C: A film of a novel about a child's confused view of adult quarrels, shot from the adults' side, with added scenes that explain each quarrel.
options.D: A play based on a novel told in letters, which cuts several letters but has each actor speak straight to the audience, so each character's partial view is felt.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A play based on a novel told in letters, which cuts several letters but has each actor speak straight to the audience, so each character's partial view is felt.

option_rationales.A: This keeps the inventory and loses what the book does, which is exactly the failure paragraph 2 describes.
option_rationales.B: This matches paragraph 4's case of 'keeping the label and throwing away the substance', which the author calls a fair target of complaint.
option_rationales.C: The book's effect lies in the child's confusion; explaining every quarrel from outside discards it, much as the plain staging in paragraph 2 loses the unreliable narrator.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the right question is 'whether the film has found its own means of doing what the book did'. The play drops material but invents a stage device that reproduces the novel's effect of partial, first-person views, so it is the faithful adaptation in the author's sense.
questions.common_misconception: Equating faithfulness with keeping scenes, which the author rejects as a checklist.
questions.difficulty_reason: The principle must be applied to new cases; one wrong option keeps almost everything and so looks faithful.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the complaint against adaptations that merely borrow a famous title as

options.A: understandable but unfair, since such films often lead viewers to read the book they are based on.
options.B: misguided, because a film is entitled to change whatever it wishes once it has acknowledged its source.
options.C: justified, though for a reason that a checklist of departures from the book does not capture.
options.D: justified, because such adaptations usually depart from the book on more points than other adaptations do.

questions.correct_answer: (C) justified, though for a reason that a checklist of departures from the book does not capture.

option_rationales.A: The passage never discusses films sending viewers to books, and it calls the complaint fair, not unfair.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says 'the complaint against them is fair', and the opening sentence 'None of this means that every liberty is defensible' rules this out.
option_rationales.D: Counting departures is the checklist reasoning the author rejects; paragraph 4 says such films fail 'not because they changed things'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: the complaint 'is fair', 'But it is fair for a different reason than the checklist suggests': these films changed 'the wrong things', keeping the label and discarding the substance.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the right verdict with the wrong reason, the very move the author warns against.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options share the verdict 'justified'; they must be told apart by the reason.

questions.question: According to the passage, those who favour silence over negative criticism argue that

options.A: critics who write unfavourably about books are usually settling personal scores with their authors.
options.B: the space available for criticism is scarce and should go to books that deserve attention.
options.C: readers stop trusting critics who praise too many of the books that they choose to discuss.
options.D: unfavourable notices damage the sales of small publishers who take risks on unknown writers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the space available for criticism is scarce and should go to books that deserve attention.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 mentions only 'the pleasure that some critics take in wounding', not personal scores, and this is not the core of the argument.
option_rationales.C: The devaluation of praise is the author's own point against silence in paragraph 3, not part of the argument for it.
option_rationales.D: Sales and publishers' risks are never mentioned in the argument for silence in paragraph 1.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: so many books appear that 'the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious', and spending it on a bad book 'is to deny it to a book that deserves attention'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the author's counter-argument to the side the author is answering.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument is laid out in paragraph 1; one wrong option borrows a point from paragraph 3.

questions.question: The remark that such a reader 'will read the next novel more alertly' (paragraph 2) suggests that

options.A: a reasoned negative argument can be of use even to a reader whom it fails to persuade.
options.B: the chief value of criticism lies in helping readers choose more wisely which novel to read next.
options.C: readers ought to be suspicious of any novel that they find themselves admiring on a first reading.
options.D: readers who disagree with a careful critic will usually come round to that critic's view in time.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a reasoned negative argument can be of use even to a reader whom it fails to persuade.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 rejects the view that guiding choice is the only job of criticism; the alertness meant is a way of reading, not a way of choosing.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not advise distrust of one's own admiration; it says the reader gains standards to test and dispute.
option_rationales.D: The sentence allows that the reader 'may end unconvinced'; nothing says he will later be converted.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a careful negative account makes standards public for readers to 'test, dispute and apply'. The reader who 'may end unconvinced' still gains those standards, so the argument is useful even where it does not persuade.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'next novel' as a buying decision and so choosing the guide-to-choice view the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase must be read against the concessive 'may end unconvinced' and the rejection of criticism as sorting.

questions.question: According to the author, the argument for silence rests on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Criticism exists solely to help readers decide which books are worth their time.
options.B: Most of the books published each year are of poor quality and deserve no attention.
options.C: A poor book that is ignored will sell fewer copies than one that is attacked in print.
options.D: Critics take more pleasure in writing unfavourable notices than favourable ones.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Criticism exists solely to help readers decide which books are worth their time.

option_rationales.B: The argument appeals to the number of books and the scarcity of space, not to the proportion that are bad; the author never says it assumes most books are poor.
option_rationales.C: The passage never discusses sales; the argument says a neglected book 'simply sinks' but does not compare it with an attacked one.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 mentions that 'some critics' enjoy wounding as the only thing lost by silence; it is not something the argument depends on.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens: 'it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read.' The correct answer restates that assumption.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a premise that sounds congenial to the argument but that the author does not identify.
questions.difficulty_reason: The assumption is named by the author, but wrong options offer premises the argument might seem to need.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: contesting the reputation of a heavily promoted book can be one of the most useful acts of criticism.
options.B: the case for keeping silent about a weak book is strongest when few people are likely to read it.
options.C: criticism that never says no can inform readers just as well as criticism that sometimes dissents, provided its praise is carefully argued.
options.D: an account of why a book fails also indicates, at least implicitly, what success would have required.

questions.correct_answer: (C) criticism that never says no can inform readers just as well as criticism that sometimes dissents, provided its praise is carefully argued.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 calls contesting a reputation that shapes public taste 'among the most useful things criticism can do'.
