option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 grants that restraint 'does have force' for a modest first novel 'which few people will encounter anyway'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such an account 'is also an account of what success would have looked like', so the author agrees.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way.' Careful argument does not remedy this, since the problem is that the verdict could never have been negative. The author would reject this statement; the other three restate paragraphs 2 and 4.
questions.common_misconception: Taking careful argument as enough to rescue praise, and missing that paragraph 3 locates the problem in the impossibility of dispraise.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer sounds moderate and reasonable; rejecting it requires applying the reason given in paragraph 3 rather than its surface wording.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that a canonical work's status is 'less a medal than a position in a network of replies' means that the work

options.A: has been awarded prizes less often than it has been attacked by the readers who came after it.
options.B: has a reputation that rises and falls as each new generation of critics comments upon it.
options.C: is valued chiefly for its own replies to earlier books rather than for any originality of its own.
options.D: matters because so many later works respond to it, not because it has been judged to excel.

questions.correct_answer: (D) matters because so many later works respond to it, not because it has been judged to excel.

option_rationales.A: This takes 'medal' literally; the passage never mentions prizes or attacks by readers.
option_rationales.B: The replies are by 'later writers' who rewrite and parody the work, not by critics, and no rise and fall is described.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the direction: paragraph 2 describes later writers replying to the canonical work, not the work replying to its predecessors.

questions.explanation: The surrounding sentences say a work becomes canonical 'because later writers cannot leave it alone' and is 'the one you must have read in order to understand a great many others'. A medal is a verdict of excellence; a position in a network is defined by the replies the work receives.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the direction of the replies, which run from later works to the canonical one.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor is explained by the sentences on either side of it.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about a highly polished novel that later writers never took up?

options.A: It would become canonical once a syllabus committee had placed it on a sufficient number of reading lists.
options.B: On the conversational account it would probably not be canonical, however excellent it is judged to be.
options.C: Defenders of the list model would rank it above many canonical works, and they would be wrong about its quality.
options.D: It must have been neglected because its author belonged to a group that was denied access to publishers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) On the conversational account it would probably not be canonical, however excellent it is judged to be.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says a committee 'cannot make a book canonical by placing it on a reading list'.
option_rationales.C: The author does not dispute judgements of quality; the claim is only that quality does not explain canonical status.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such works 'simply provoked no answer'; paragraph 4 describes exclusion in general, and 'must' asserts a cause the passage does not.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says canons 'exclude works of great finish that simply provoked no answer', since status comes from being answered, not from being judged excellent.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a causal story from paragraph 4 and treating it as necessary.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the paragraph 2 model to a new case and resisting a cause borrowed from paragraph 4.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: reject the conversational account in favour of the view that the canon simply records the tastes of a narrow group of readers.
options.B: set out a specific programme of reforms to publishing and education that would make future canons fairer than past ones.
options.C: qualify the conversational account by showing that it inherits, in a new location, the exclusions that critics of the canon object to.
options.D: show that the critics of the canon were right all along about the biased judgements of tastemakers and teachers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) qualify the conversational account by showing that it inherits, in a new location, the exclusions that critics of the canon object to.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the account 'relocates' the complaint; it does not abandon the account or return to the list model.
option_rationales.B: No programme is proposed; the paragraph says only where 'the remedy, if there is one, must be sought'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph moves the complaint away 'from the judgements of tastemakers' to the conditions under which people could write.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens with 'Yet the conversational canon is not thereby cleared' and argues that access to education, publishing and preservation shaped who joined the conversation, so the conversational canon still reflects exclusion, now located in the conditions of writing.
questions.common_misconception: Taking a qualification for a rejection, or the hedge 'if there is one' for a proposal.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options each overstate one strand of a carefully hedged paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the account of canons defended in paragraph 2?

options.A: Reading lists drawn up by syllabus committees have changed considerably over the course of the last century.
options.B: Many works that all parties agree are canonical turn out to have been almost never quoted, imitated, parodied or answered by later writers.
options.C: Several works of great finish that provoked no answer from later writers have stayed popular with ordinary readers for centuries.
options.D: Some of the most firmly canonical works are regarded by most readers as clumsy and tedious for long stretches.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Many works that all parties agree are canonical turn out to have been almost never quoted, imitated, parodied or answered by later writers.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says committees cannot confer canonical status, so changing lists are compatible with the account and do not bear on it.
option_rationales.C: Popularity with readers is not canonical status on either model discussed; the account only predicts such works are not canonical, which this does not deny.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 cites exactly this as something the conversational account explains and the list model cannot, so it supports the account.

questions.explanation: The account claims a work is canonical because later writers 'answer it, parody it, borrow its situations'. If many undisputed canonical works received no such replies, canonical status would not track replies, which strikes at the account's central claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about polished but unanswered works because it sounds like a counter-example, without noticing that it concerns popularity rather than canonical status.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option looks like a counter-example but changes the property in question; another is evidence the passage itself uses in support.

questions.question: According to the passage, the 'usual answer' to why translations age is that

options.A: translators of earlier generations were simply less skilled, and less faithful to their originals, than the translators who are at work today.
options.B: each generation of readers demands a translation that reflects its own concerns and preoccupations.
options.C: the originals are now read mainly by scholars, who are unusually tolerant of difficult and archaic language.
options.D: a translation uses the idiom of its own time, which changes, while the original is read with allowance for its age.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a translation uses the idiom of its own time, which changes, while the original is read with allowance for its age.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says 'retranslation is not a sign that earlier translators failed', and the usual answer in paragraph 2 concerns language, not skill.
option_rationales.B: This is close to the author's own 'deeper reason' in paragraph 3, which is offered precisely because the usual answer 'cannot be the whole story'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says readers return to originals 'century after century'; nothing restricts them to scholars.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The usual answer is linguistic: a translation is written in the language of its own moment', whose idioms change, whereas the original is read 'as a historical text' whose strangeness is forgiven.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the usual answer with the author's deeper explanation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated directly in paragraph 2; one wrong option is the passage's other explanation.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Translations date because each must settle what its original leaves open, and so preserves one period's reading of it.
options.B: Translations date chiefly because the idioms of the language into which they are made keep changing over time.
options.C: The best translations are those that become works of literature in their own right and so stop ageing.
options.D: Great works can never be adequately translated, because no translator is able to preserve their openness.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Translations date because each must settle what its original leaves open, and so preserves one period's reading of it.

option_rationales.B: This is the 'usual answer', which paragraph 2 says 'cannot be the whole story'.
option_rationales.C: Too narrow, and the author does not rank translations; this reversal is called 'occasional' in paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: Too absolute: the author treats each translation as a valuable reading and retranslation as a way 'a classic stays alive'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives the 'deeper reason': translation 'forces choices', each choice 'settles a question the original left unsettled', and the result 'records one generation's reading'. Paragraph 4 draws the consequence for retranslation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the explanation the author qualifies, or overstating the author's claim into impossibility.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's view must be separated from the view the author reports and partly accepts.

questions.question: The passage suggests that an old translation which is 'perfectly intelligible' may 'still feel inadequate' because

options.A: it was made from an unreliable copy of the original that later scholarship has corrected.
options.B: its translator misread the original language at important points and introduced errors.
options.C: the decisions it made about undecided passages reflect concerns its present readers no longer share.
options.D: its language, though understandable, sounds too formal and dignified to a modern reader's ear.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the decisions it made about undecided passages reflect concerns its present readers no longer share.

option_rationales.A: The state of the original text is never discussed; this is outside the passage.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the translator's choices 'are not arbitrary'; mistranslation is never suggested.
option_rationales.D: This restates the linguistic explanation, which the author introduces this very observation to show is incomplete.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 offers the observation as evidence against the purely linguistic answer, and paragraph 3 supplies the explanation: a translation's choices are 'shaped by what the translator's own age finds plausible or important', and 'When the concerns of that generation fade' it looks like an interpretation.
questions.common_misconception: Falling back on the linguistic answer for a fact the author cites against it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The question links a detail in paragraph 2 to the explanation in paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the process described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A dictionary is revised every few decades to record the words and senses that have entered the language since its last edition.
options.B: A historian rereads old letters and finds that a phrase she took for sarcasm was, in its own period, an ordinary courtesy.
options.C: A painting darkens as its varnish yellows with age, so that restorers must clean it every so often to recover its original colours.
options.D: Actors staging an old play must decide how each ambiguous line is spoken, so every production shows its own era's reading while the script stays open.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Actors staging an old play must decide how each ambiguous line is spoken, so every production shows its own era's reading while the script stays open.

option_rationales.A: This tracks change in the language itself, which corresponds to the 'usual answer' of paragraph 2, not the deeper reason of paragraph 3.
option_rationales.B: Here the phrase had a settled meaning that she corrects; paragraph 3 concerns places 'where its sense is undecided', which a translator must settle without being wrong.
option_rationales.C: This is physical decay with a recoverable original state; the passage concerns choices forced on an interpreter where the original has no single settled sense.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the original 'can leave such places open', but writing in another medium 'forces choices at every point', shaped by the interpreter's age. A performance must likewise fix tone where the script does not, and the script remains open for the next production, as the original remains for the next translator.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the historian, who is also reading across time, without noticing that she recovers a fixed meaning rather than settling an open one.
questions.difficulty_reason: The analogy turns on the structure of forced choice in a new medium; two wrong options share the surface theme of ageing or period meaning.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the intentionalist and anti-intentionalist positions is best described as

options.A: firm support for the anti-intentionalist position, tempered by some sympathy for the intentionalist's concern with an author's purpose.
options.B: partial acceptance of each, joined to the claim that both rest on the same mistaken picture of intention.
options.C: impatience with both, on the ground that the question they dispute cannot in principle ever be answered.
options.D: neutral detachment, setting out the strongest form of each position without deciding between them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) partial acceptance of each, joined to the claim that both rest on the same mistaken picture of intention.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 rejects a premise the anti-intentionalist shares, and paragraph 4 keeps a role for the author, so the author does not side with either camp.
option_rationales.C: The author answers the question in paragraphs 3 and 4 by redefining intention; nothing says it is unanswerable.
option_rationales.D: The passage is not neutral: paragraph 3 names 'The mistake common to both' and offers the author's own account.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'each is right about what it denies', and paragraph 3 says 'The mistake common to both is to picture intention as a private event lying behind the text'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the even-handed paragraph 2 as the author's final stance.
questions.difficulty_reason: The stance is stated outright but must be distinguished from neutrality and from partisanship.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would treat a novelist's public statement about what her book means as

options.A: evidence worth weighing, which counts only insofar as it helps to reveal patterns that are present in the work.
options.B: decisive whenever it is sincere, since the intention that matters to criticism is the one the novelist actually held.
options.C: entirely irrelevant, since the meaning of a published work is fixed by the public language in which it is written.
options.D: more reliable than the novel itself, because the novelist has access to choices that the text cannot show.

questions.correct_answer: (A) evidence worth weighing, which counts only insofar as it helps to reveal patterns that are present in the work.

option_rationales.B: This is the private-event picture paragraph 3 rejects, and paragraph 2 says authors 'misremember' and 'misjudge what they have made', so sincerity does not settle meaning.
option_rationales.C: This is the anti-intentionalist view; paragraph 4 says the view 'does not make the author irrelevant' and that notebooks 'may help us see a pattern'.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the author's view that intentions 'are public because the work is' and that the work's design can be taken 'more seriously' than the author's account.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 denies such statements 'special authority over the book', yet paragraph 4 says notebooks may help 'as the testimony of a witness may help a court, but the evidence is then the pattern, not the testimony'. A public statement is thus admissible but subordinate to what the work shows.
questions.common_misconception: Collapsing the author's middle position into one of the two positions the passage reports.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer combines two hedged claims from paragraphs 2 and 4, and the two strongest wrong options are the reported views.

questions.question: The example of the novel written to celebrate a way of life (paragraph 4) serves mainly to

options.A: establish that novelists are in general unaware of the social costs of the ways of life they choose to depict.
options.B: demonstrate that a writer's private notebooks can expose patterns that the finished work keeps hidden.
options.C: illustrate the anti-intentionalist claim that an author's purpose has no bearing on what a work means.
options.D: show that a work can mean more than its author meant without that reading being a defiance of the work's design.

questions.correct_answer: (D) show that a work can mean more than its author meant without that reading being a defiance of the work's design.

option_rationales.A: The example concerns one hypothetical novel and what it can reveal; it makes no general claim about novelists' awareness.
option_rationales.B: The notebooks appear in the previous sentence as an aid to seeing patterns in the work; the novel example involves no notebooks at all.
option_rationales.C: The author says the reading takes 'the work's design more seriously', so purpose embodied in the work still matters; this is not the anti-intentionalist claim.

questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that 'a work may carry implications its author never foresaw', and the paragraph concludes that pointing these out 'is not to defy the author's intention but to take the work's design more seriously than its author's later account of it'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading an example of meaning beyond the author's foresight as support for the anti-intentionalist view.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the author's notion of embodied intention differs from both reported views.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the author's account of intention EXCEPT

options.A: a work may support a reading that its author, if asked, would have rejected outright.
options.B: recognising a repetition in a poem as deliberate already involves attributing a purpose to the text.
options.C: the intentions that matter to criticism lie hidden behind a text, which can at best report them faithfully.
options.D: an author's diary can sometimes help a critic notice a pattern in the work that had been overlooked.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the intentions that matter to criticism lie hidden behind a text, which can at best report them faithfully.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says a work may carry implications 'its author never foresaw and would perhaps have disowned'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says noticing 'that a repetition is deliberate' is 'already to treat the text as the product of choices'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 grants that 'A writer's notebooks may help us see a pattern we had missed', and a diary serves the same role.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 identifies 'The mistake common to both' as picturing intention 'as a private event lying behind the text, which the text either reports faithfully or conceals'. The correct answer states exactly that picture, so it is inconsistent with the author's account.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the diary option because paragraph 2 denies such entries 'special authority', missing that paragraph 4 still allows them an evidential role.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer restates the shared premise of two views the author partly accepts, and one wrong option seems to clash with paragraph 2.

questions.question: According to the passage, a first reading typically involves

options.A: forming judgements of characters that the book later shows to be mistaken.
options.B: recognising which of the passages one most admires are in fact the weakest.
options.C: dwelling on descriptions in order to anticipate how the story will end.
options.D: noticing images that return later in the book with an altered meaning.

questions.correct_answer: (A) forming judgements of characters that the book later shows to be mistaken.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 presents this as a discovery made on rereading, not during a first reading.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says that on a first reading 'We skim descriptions to reach events'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 lists returning images among what we can attend to 'Only when we know the ending'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: on a first reading we 'form judgements of characters that the book later overturns'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a rereading experience because it appears in the same list.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that knowing the outcome 'does not empty these details; it fills them' means that

options.A: rereaders tend to supply from their own imagination whatever an author has left unsaid in a scene.
options.B: such details gain significance once a reader can see what they were preparing for.
options.C: a reader who knows the ending will find such details tedious, though still necessary to the book.
options.D: the suspense of a first reading is replaced on rereading by a complete knowledge of the plot's events.

questions.correct_answer: (B) such details gain significance once a reader can see what they were preparing for.

option_rationales.A: Nothing in the passage concerns readers inventing material; the details meant are those already in the text.
option_rationales.C: This is close to the opposite: the sentence denies that knowledge of the outcome empties the details.
option_rationales.D: The rereader does know the events, but the sentence is about what that knowledge does to 'these details', namely make them meaningful.

questions.explanation: The 'details' meant are the preparing scene, the returning image and the idle remark that 'turns out to state the novel's theme'. Their importance 'has not yet been revealed' on a first reading; knowing the ending reveals it, so the details are filled with meaning.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that is true of rereading in general but is not what the sentence says about the details.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor must be read against the list it concludes; one wrong option states a true but different point.

questions.question: The example of the story of a marriage (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: a reader's growing experience can reveal qualities in a book that were present but unseen before.
options.B: young readers are usually right to find stories about ordinary people rather dull.
options.C: novels about marriage are best understood by readers who are themselves married.
options.D: the meaning of a book changes as the culture surrounding it changes over time.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a reader's growing experience can reveal qualities in a book that were present but unseen before.

option_rationales.B: The older reader finds the story 'almost unbearably exact', so the passage implies the young reader missed something.
option_rationales.C: The example contrasts a younger and an older reader, not married and unmarried ones; this generalises beyond the passage.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the book 'has not altered a word' and locates the change in 'the person reading it', not in the culture.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the reader 'has acquired experiences that let different passages speak', and the marriage story becomes 'almost unbearably exact'. The exactness was there; the young reader lacked the experience to see it.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the change to the book or the culture rather than to the reader.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires locating the source of change the paragraph identifies.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that rereading is 'a kind of nostalgia' is best described as

options.A: sympathetic, since the author shares the regret that a first encounter with a book cannot be repeated.
options.B: critical, though willing to grant that a first reading has a real value of its own.
options.C: neutral, since the passage lays out the arguments for both kinds of reading without favouring either.
options.D: dismissive, holding that a first reading offers nothing that a later reading cannot supply better.

questions.correct_answer: (B) critical, though willing to grant that a first reading has a real value of its own.

option_rationales.A: The author argues for 'the opposite view' in paragraph 2 and does not share the lament.
option_rationales.C: The author argues that 'in an important sense only rereading is reading' and ends by urging distrust of first-reading verdicts.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the first reading 'has a quality nothing later can supply', so the author is not dismissive of it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues against the nostalgia view, and paragraph 4 concedes that the first reading has 'an innocence about what is coming that the writer counted on'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the concession and choosing an extreme, or mistaking the concession for neutrality.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tone combines a firm position with a real concession.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as the best evidence that a novel is more than 'a mechanism for producing suspense'?

options.A: Readers who begin it find themselves unable to put it down until they have reached the last page.
options.B: Critics praised it highly on its first appearance, well before its ending had become widely known.
options.C: Readers who already know how it ends report finding more in it on a third reading than on a second.
options.D: Its final twist recasts the earlier chapters so completely that first-time readers are astonished by it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Readers who already know how it ends report finding more in it on a third reading than on a second.

option_rationales.A: Compulsive reading is what suspense produces; it is a first-reading effect and is what a mere mechanism would also achieve.
option_rationales.B: These are verdicts reached 'from inside a first reading', which the author says we should distrust.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such a twist 'can surprise only once'; it is an effect designed for the first reading and says nothing about later ones.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 makes the test whether a book 'offers nothing on a second reading' or 'gives more each time'. Only the correct answer reports what readers find after the ending is known, and it shows the book giving more each time.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the twist because recasting earlier chapters sounds like what rereading does, though it happens on the first reading.
questions.difficulty_reason: The test must be applied precisely; the twist wrong option borrows the language of rereading.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is an objection that has been made to distant reading?

options.A: The charts that such studies produce are too complex for most literary scholars to interpret.
options.B: Computers are not yet able to process anything close to the full output of a century of novels.
options.C: Distant reading has been applied mostly to canonical novels and has neglected forgotten ones.
options.D: A frequency count cannot register the irony or dramatic context on which a word's meaning depends.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A frequency count cannot register the irony or dramatic context on which a word's meaning depends.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 complains of 'a modest result dressed in charts', a point about the modesty of results, not the difficulty of charts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 presents processing a century's output as what the method makes possible; no one in the passage objects that it cannot be done.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says this; paragraph 4 credits the method with reaching 'the much larger body of books that the canon left out'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The meaning of a word depends on its context, on irony, on the dramatic situation in which it is spoken, none of which a frequency table records.'
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option that echoes the word 'charts' or 'century' from the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: The objection is stated directly in paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author values the anomalies mentioned in paragraph 3 chiefly because they

options.A: prove that the canon was assembled by readers whose tastes were narrow and unrepresentative.
options.B: point readers towards particular books that then repay being read closely.
options.C: can be interpreted with confidence without anyone reading the books in which they occur.
options.D: show that machines detect features of style that human readers are incapable of perceiving.

questions.correct_answer: (B) point readers towards particular books that then repay being read closely.

option_rationales.A: The anomalies are said to mean 'little until someone goes back and reads the books'; they prove nothing by themselves.
option_rationales.C: This contradicts paragraph 3: 'Such a finding means little until someone goes back and reads the books in question'.
option_rationales.D: The features are ones 'nobody had thought to examine', not ones humans cannot perceive; the claim is too strong.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the anomalies matter because they send someone 'back' to read, and 'it is that return which produces understanding'. 'The count poses a question; it does not answer one.'
questions.common_misconception: Overstating what the anomalies show, or confusing features nobody examined with features nobody could perceive.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the function of the anomalies from the last two sentences of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.A: The objections to computational reading are decisive, since counting words can never produce any understanding of literature.
options.B: The literary canon is an unrepresentative sample, and its study should give way to the study of forgotten novels.
options.C: Computational reading should take the place of close reading, since it can study the entire output of a period instead of a sample.
options.D: Computational reading cannot interpret texts by itself, but it can pose questions for close reading and test claims drawn from a biased sample.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Computational reading cannot interpret texts by itself, but it can pose questions for close reading and test claims drawn from a biased sample.

option_rationales.A: The author grants that some objections 'are serious' but calls the debate 'a false picture of the choice' and credits the method with real contributions.
option_rationales.B: The passage diagnoses the sampling problem but never recommends abandoning study of the canon; this adds a prescription.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says distant reading 'does not replace close reading', so this contradicts the author.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives the method the role of posing questions that close reading answers, and paragraph 4 its 'independent contribution' of testing generalisations against the books 'the canon left out'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the strong prescription built on paragraph 1, or the objections the author reports and answers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must hold together two separate claims of paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim made in paragraph 4 about the independent contribution of distant reading?

options.A: Some canonical novels turn out to cluster with obscure ones on features of style that critics had never before thought to examine.
options.B: Scholars who use computational methods also spend much of their working time reading individual novels closely.
options.C: The novels available in digital form for analysis are mostly the same books that later readers chose to keep in print.
options.D: Many of the patterns reported by computational studies merely confirm what attentive readers had already suspected.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The novels available in digital form for analysis are mostly the same books that later readers chose to keep in print.

option_rationales.A: This is the kind of anomaly paragraph 3 describes, and it presupposes access to obscure novels, so it is consistent with the claim.
option_rationales.B: This fits the author's view that the two kinds of reading work together and has no bearing on the sampling claim.
option_rationales.D: This is the objection of paragraph 2 about trivial results; it does not touch the claim about testing generalisations against a wider sample.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the method can test canonical generalisations against 'the much larger body of books that the canon left out'. If the machine-readable corpus is largely the kept-in-print canon, the machine would be testing claims against the same selection, and the independent contribution would vanish.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the objection from paragraph 2 because it is critical of distant reading, without checking whether it bears on the specific claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer weakens an unstated premise (that the larger body is available to machines); wrong options are critical or on topic but irrelevant.

questions.question: The statement that a claim about 'the novel' which describes only the surviving books 'was never a claim about the novel at all' implies that such a claim

options.A: while offered as a history of a form, in fact describes the preferences that decided which books were kept.
options.B: could be made responsibly only by a scholar who had personally read every novel of the period concerned.
options.C: is simply false, because the canonical novels are unlike the rest of the period's output in every respect.
options.D: reveals that the idea of a single literary form called the novel is an illusion produced by the syllabus.

questions.correct_answer: (A) while offered as a history of a form, in fact describes the preferences that decided which books were kept.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says no scholar can do this, and the author proposes testing by machine instead, so this is not implied.
option_rationales.C: The passage says such a claim may 'describe' the surviving books accurately; it does not say they differ in every respect.
option_rationales.D: The author questions generalisations about the form, not the existence of the form; this over-reads the sentence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 completes the sentence: the claim was 'about the tastes of the readers who did the selecting'. A generalisation from a selected sample describes the selection and hence the selectors' preferences, not the whole form.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'never a claim about the novel' as 'false', when the point concerns what the claim is about.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires distinguishing a claim's scope from its truth, a fine distinction.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that visitors who read labels before looking at a painting understand it less well than those who do not.
options.B: propose that a label should be judged by whether it sends the visitor back to the work, not by its length.
options.C: argue that museums should replace long wall labels with audio guides and screens that visitors can consult at will.
options.D: defend the purist view that a painting should be encountered without any written explanation beside it.

questions.correct_answer: (B) propose that a label should be judged by whether it sends the visitor back to the work, not by its length.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 describes the habit of reading first and glancing after, but the passage never compares the understanding of two groups of visitors; the claim invents a finding.
option_rationales.C: Audio guides and screens appear in paragraph 1 only as part of the expansionist camp's proposal, which the author goes on to criticise in paragraph 2; the author recommends nothing of the kind.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 rejects the purist assumption, saying an unexplained altarpiece makes a visitor feel 'excluded', and paragraph 4 keeps a place for historical information on the wall.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says both camps wrongly treat quantity as the label's 'only variable'; paragraph 3 replaces that with the question of 'what the label asks the visitor to do'; paragraph 4 concludes that information belongs on the wall 'when it changes what the visitor notices'. The purpose is to reframe how labels should be judged.
questions.common_misconception: Taking one camp described in paragraph 1 as the author's own position.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated outright in paragraphs 3 and 4 and the two camps are clearly marked as views the author rejects.

questions.question: The passage suggests that removing labels altogether would most likely

options.A: encourage most visitors to spend longer with each painting, since they would have nothing else to read.
options.B: make visitors rely more heavily on catalogues, which the author regards as the proper home for all information.
options.C: leave many visitors feeling shut out, so that they pass the work more quickly instead of studying it.
options.D: have little effect on visitors, who already pay more attention to paintings than to the panels beside them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) leave many visitors feeling shut out, so that they pass the work more quickly instead of studying it.

option_rationales.A: This is the purist's assumption, which paragraph 2 contradicts: an unexplained work does not make a visitor 'look harder'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 sends only facts that do not change what one notices to the catalogue, and the passage never predicts that visitors would turn to catalogues.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says the opposite: labels are read often while the paintings are 'looked at as little', with only a glance to confirm what the label said.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that a visitor faced with an unexplained altarpiece 'feels excluded and walks faster'. Removing labels would produce exactly this case.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the purist premise that less text automatically means more looking.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer restates one sentence in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The two sentences about the merchant's portrait in paragraph 3 are used to

options.A: contrast a statement that can be taken in without looking with one that sends the reader to the canvas.
options.B: suggest that labels about portraits should avoid biographical facts about the people who commissioned them.
options.C: show that the merchant's marriage is more important to the meaning of the portrait than the objects he holds.
options.D: prove that painters of merchants used lighting to signal which of the sitter's possessions mattered most.

questions.correct_answer: (A) contrast a statement that can be taken in without looking with one that sends the reader to the canvas.

option_rationales.B: The author objects to facts that merely 'sit beside the object', not to biography as such, and paragraph 4 explicitly defends information that changes what is noticed.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not rank the marriage against the ledger and glove; the example concerns what each sentence makes the reader do, not which fact matters more.
option_rationales.D: The second sentence asks the reader to decide which hand is lit more brightly; it makes no general claim about painters, and the portrait is only 'imagined'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph introduces the contrast between labels that 'close' and labels that 'open' a picture, and the closing sentence makes the point of the example: 'The first sentence can be absorbed without raising one's eyes; the second cannot be finished without looking.'
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example for its content (the merchant, his marriage) rather than for its role in the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is spelled out in the sentence that ends the paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following labels for a painting of a busy kitchen would the author most likely approve for the gallery wall?

options.A: Critics have long agreed that this is the most accomplished of the painter's works and a turning point in his career.
options.B: The crowded kitchen expresses the painter's lifelong anxiety about poverty, which haunted him after his father's business failed.
options.C: The painting passed through the hands of four private collectors in three countries before the museum acquired it in a recent sale.
options.D: Figures by the window are in quick, broken strokes, those in shadow smooth; which group does your eye reach first?

questions.correct_answer: (D) Figures by the window are in quick, broken strokes, those in shadow smooth; which group does your eye reach first?

option_rationales.A: A verdict borrowed from critics directs the eye to nothing checkable on the canvas, so it fails the test in paragraph 3 that a label should 'open' the picture.
option_rationales.B: This label would 'close' the picture by telling the viewer what it means; it can be absorbed without looking, which paragraph 3 counts against it.
option_rationales.C: A chain of owners is the kind of fact paragraph 2 says gives 'a great deal to know and very little to see'; by paragraph 4 it belongs in the catalogue.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 praises a label that directs 'attention to something that can be checked against the canvas itself' and that 'cannot be finished without looking'. The correct label points to a visible contrast in brushwork and asks the viewer to test it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the label that sounds most informative or most authoritative.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must apply the open/close test to new cases, and two wrong options contain accurate-sounding information that the author would still exclude.

questions.question: According to the author's reasoning, public disputes over removing old statues become bitter chiefly because

options.A: the statues offer no built-in occasion for reconsideration, so disagreement is held back until it bursts out all at once.
options.B: bronze and stone are expensive materials, and removing works made of them wastes the money a town once spent.
options.C: the statues are usually so unfamiliar to passers-by that few people are able to say why they were put up.
options.D: later generations change their opinions too quickly to respect the judgements of the people who raised the statues.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the statues offer no built-in occasion for reconsideration, so disagreement is held back until it bursts out all at once.

option_rationales.B: Cost is never raised; the passage treats durable materials as a statement of respect and of permanence, not as an expense to be protected.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says many such figures become unrecognised, but paragraph 2 locates the cause of the crisis in the absence of any 'procedure' for reconsideration, not in ignorance.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 opens by denying exactly this: 'The problem is not that later generations are fickle.'

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a permanent work 'asks only to be accepted' with 'no procedure built into it for being reconsidered', and so 'When disagreement finally arrives, it therefore arrives as a crisis'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the explanation the author explicitly rules out (fickleness), or taking a detail from paragraph 1 as the cause.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be reconstructed from the causal chain in paragraph 2, and one wrong option reuses a real detail from paragraph 1.

questions.question: The author accepts permanence as appropriate for which kind of public work?

options.A: A mural that residents have grown fond of during the years it has been on display.
options.B: A statue of a civic leader whose reputation has stayed secure for several generations.
options.C: A sculpture commissioned for a central square that is visited by large numbers of tourists.
options.D: A memorial to the dead of a disaster, since its purpose is to resist forgetting.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A memorial to the dead of a disaster, since its purpose is to resist forgetting.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 describes murals 'painted on the understanding that it will be painted over'; fondness is part of the conversation, not a reason to fix the work.
option_rationales.B: The passage nowhere exempts secure reputations; paragraph 1 warns that any monument may outlast the judgement it records.
option_rationales.C: Attracting visitors is mentioned in paragraph 4 only as a danger of temporary art sliding into spectacle, not as a reason for permanence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'a memorial to the dead of a war or a disaster is meant to resist the passing of time, because forgetting is precisely the danger it guards against.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the author would protect works that are popular or long-respected.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 4.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'an occasion rather than a verdict' most nearly means that temporary public art

options.A: is judged by experts once the work has been removed, rather than by the people who saw it in place.
options.B: is an event that invites the public to respond and argue, not a settled judgement handed down to be accepted.
options.C: avoids taking any position at all, rather than making a claim that some members of the public might dispute.
options.D: is held for special celebrations only, rather than being on view to the public throughout the year.

questions.correct_answer: (B) is an event that invites the public to respond and argue, not a settled judgement handed down to be accepted.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 stresses the 'collective judgement' of the public while the work is up; experts and post-removal judgement are not mentioned.
option_rationales.C: The passage does not say temporary art is neutral; its value is that people 'argue about the new piece', which implies it can provoke disagreement.
option_rationales.D: The phrase is not about festivals; paragraph 3 explains it as people arguing about, liking or being relieved to lose a work.

questions.explanation: The next sentence explains the phrase: people 'argue about the new piece, grow fond of it or feel relieved to see it go', practising the 'collective judgement' that a permanent statue, which 'asks only to be accepted', forecloses.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'occasion' as a special celebration instead of as an event that prompts response.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is given by the sentence immediately after the phrase.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that a city expecting its public art to change would face no crisis over what stands in its squares?

options.A: Several temporary sculptures have provoked angry letters to newspapers and heated public meetings while they were on display.
options.B: Visitors to war memorials often say that the permanence of the stone is what makes the place feel solemn to them.
options.C: A city with a rotating plinth for decades still endured years of bitter petitions over removing a nearby statue.
options.D: Most of the works shown on rotating plinths are forgotten by the public within a year or two of being removed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A city with a rotating plinth for decades still endured years of bitter petitions over removing a nearby statue.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 welcomes argument about the new piece; lively debate over a temporary work is the habit the author wants, not the crisis he warns against.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 already grants that memorials to the dead aim at permanence for good reason, so this agrees with the author rather than weakening him.
option_rationales.D: Forgetting a temporary work after it leaves is compatible with the author's view that such works matter as the 'conversation' they start, so it does not touch the claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 claims that a city used to change 'would already possess a habit of revisiting' and so would avoid crisis. A city with exactly that habit that still suffered a prolonged crisis is a direct counterexample.
questions.common_misconception: Treating any public argument as the 'crisis' the author predicts, when he welcomes argument about temporary works.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must separate the debate the author welcomes from the crisis he says the habit prevents.

questions.question: Which point in favour of the cleaners does the author accept?

options.A: Varnish yellows with age, so preferring the darkened colours can mean preferring an accident to the painter's choice.
options.B: Cleaned paintings are in every respect identical to the pictures as they looked when they left the studio.
options.C: Cleaners have never removed the final glazes that painters used to soften their effects.
options.D: Admirers of the darkened pictures are moved by sentiment and have no real reason for their preference.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Varnish yellows with age, so preferring the darkened colours can mean preferring an accident to the painter's choice.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 denies this directly: cleaning 'does not take it back to the day it left the studio' because pigments have also changed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 reports the mourners' suspicion that cleaners have removed final glazes, and the author never dismisses it, so the passage gives no such guarantee.
option_rationales.D: The author reports the 'truth and sentiment' framing as 'tempting' and grants only part of it; he never says the mourners have no reason, and paragraph 1 records their worry about lost glazes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'Natural resin varnishes do yellow and darken with age' and adds that 'to prefer the olive because one is used to it is to prefer an accident over a decision.'
questions.common_misconception: Stretching the author's partial concession into full agreement with the cleaners.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession is stated in one place and introduced by 'There is something to this.'

questions.question: The author implies that a freshly cleaned painting

options.A: will usually be darker and less harmonious than it was before its old varnish was removed.
options.B: is in most cases a closer approximation to the original than the same painting before cleaning.
options.C: should be covered again with a varnish so that its appearance matches what earlier viewers loved.
options.D: may present colour relationships the painter never saw, because faded and unfaded parts now appear together.

questions.correct_answer: (D) may present colour relationships the painter never saw, because faded and unfaded parts now appear together.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says cleaning reveals 'colours far brighter', and the passage makes no claim that cleaned pictures are less harmonious overall.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the bright painting 'may therefore be no closer to the original', and the author never claims which state is usually closer.
option_rationales.C: The author recommends reversibility, documentation and honest language in paragraph 4, not a return to the old appearance.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says cleaning 'produces a new object, one in which unchanged passages and altered ones sit side by side in proportions the painter never saw'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the author favours either the cleaned state or the darkened state, when he denies that either is the original.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases a dense sentence; one wrong option overstates the cleaners' case in a milder, plausible form ('closer approximation').

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the cleaners is best described as

options.A: enthusiastic agreement: he believes they have recovered what the painters intended and should say so with confidence.
options.B: outright hostility: he regards them as zealots whose work has destroyed much of what earlier painters achieved.
options.C: qualified support: he accepts their practice and results but rejects the strength of their central claim.
options.D: detached neutrality: he reports both parties' views without indicating which arguments he finds more persuasive.

questions.correct_answer: (C) qualified support: he accepts their practice and results but rejects the strength of their central claim.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 asks restorers to 'abandon the language of revelation' and calls 'this is what the painter meant' a claim beyond the evidence.
option_rationales.B: The charge of 'zeal' belongs to the mourning party in paragraph 1; the author himself says the lesson is 'not that cleaning should stop' and credits it with real discoveries.
option_rationales.D: The author takes clear positions: he endorses the point about varnish in paragraph 2 and rejects the claim of original state in paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 grants that cleaning has shown painters to be 'bold colourists'; paragraph 3 says the claim to restore the 'original state' is 'harder to sustain than it sounds'; paragraph 4 says cleaning should continue but be 'described honestly'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing to the author the hostility of the party he reports in paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the whole arc: concession, critique and recommendation together.

questions.question: The argument in paragraph 3 that cleaning cannot return a painting to its original state relies on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: The varnish on old paintings was not applied by the painters themselves as part of the finished work.
options.B: Removing varnish does not also undo the fading and browning that the pigments themselves have undergone.
options.C: Viewers who knew the painting before cleaning were mistaken about the colours the painter had chosen.
options.D: The darkened state of a painting before cleaning was closer to its original appearance than the cleaned state.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Removing varnish does not also undo the fading and browning that the pigments themselves have undergone.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 rests on changes in the pigments, so the argument would hold whoever applied the varnish; this matters to the dispute over glazes in paragraph 1, not to this claim.
option_rationales.C: Earlier viewers' beliefs play no role in paragraph 3; the argument concerns physical change in the picture, not anyone's opinion of it.
option_rationales.D: The author says the two are 'differently distant' from the original and needs no ranking between them; asserting this would actually go beyond his argument.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 moves from 'Pigments themselves change' to the conclusion that removing varnish 'produces a new object'. This step works only if cleaning leaves the altered pigments altered. If cleaning also reversed the fading, the cleaned picture could match the original and the conclusion would fail.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a claim that is related to the debate (who applied the varnish, which state is closer) but that the argument does not need.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires identifying a necessary, unstated link and rejecting two options that strengthen or extend the case without being required.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Viewers should learn to check images for doctored pixels, because unaltered photographs are always accurate about the events they record.
options.B: Concern with doctored images neglects the commoner danger of selective framing, so a photograph's worth as evidence rests on its context.
options.C: Photographers who choose where to stand and when to press the shutter are mainly responsible for the dishonest stories told with images.
options.D: Software that can alter photographs invisibly has made every image unreliable, so photographs should no longer count as evidence.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Concern with doctored images neglects the commoner danger of selective framing, so a photograph's worth as evidence rests on its context.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 warns that passing this check gives a 'false sense of security', and paragraph 2 says an unaltered image can mislead about the event.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 notes that 'the frame is chosen by someone', but the passage never blames photographers; its point is about how viewers should weigh images.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'None of this makes photographs worthless as evidence', and paragraph 1 calls manipulation 'the least interesting way' a photograph misleads.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the manipulation worry leaves 'the more ordinary and more pervasive problem almost untouched'; paragraphs 2 and 3 identify that problem as framing and selection; paragraph 4 locates evidential value 'in its surroundings'.
questions.common_misconception: Fixing on the manipulation theme of paragraph 1 or on the photographer's choice in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must combine the critique and the positive conclusion; two wrong options exaggerate claims the passage actually makes.

questions.question: The example of the photograph of a crowded square in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: show that an image with nothing added or removed can still leave the event unclear.
options.B: illustrate how software can be used to add figures to a crowd without leaving a visible trace.
options.C: argue that photographs of demonstrations are less reliable than photographs of other public events.
options.D: suggest that most demonstrations are smaller than the photographs published of them make them appear.

questions.correct_answer: (A) show that an image with nothing added or removed can still leave the event unclear.

option_rationales.B: The photograph is stipulated to be 'unaltered'; adding figures is the manipulation worry of paragraph 1, which the example is meant to move beyond.
option_rationales.C: The demonstration is just a convenient case; the passage draws a general conclusion about every photograph, not a comparison between kinds of event.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph raises the possibility that a square was not full only as one unanswerable question; it makes no claim about most demonstrations.

questions.explanation: The example begins by granting that 'Every figure in it was really there' and the image is 'entirely truthful', then lists what it cannot tell us, ending with the general claim that a photograph is 'wholly silent about what falls outside' its frame.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking an illustrative question in the example for a factual claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is set up by the contrast in paragraph 1 and stated in the last sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a viewer who has confirmed that an image has not been digitally altered

options.A: should go on to assume that the image was staged, since honest photographs are more misleading than forged ones.
options.B: has wasted effort, because doctored images are now so rare that checking them is no longer worth doing.
options.C: has done all that can reasonably be asked, since an unaltered image cannot be used to support a false account.
options.D: has settled one real question but has learnt little about whether the story built on the image is true.

questions.correct_answer: (D) has settled one real question but has learnt little about whether the story built on the image is true.

option_rationales.A: The author says honest images can mislead 'often more easily' because they survive scrutiny, not that they are more misleading in general or that one should presume staging.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 calls the worries about manipulation 'reasonable' and says the tools 'have become more powerful'; the author never says forgeries are rare.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'An honest photograph can support a dishonest story as easily as a forged one can', so the check is far from sufficient.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says such a check 'has said nothing about selection, timing or framing'; paragraph 1 still grants the manipulation worry is 'reasonable'. So the check settles something, but not what matters most.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'often more easily' into a general ranking, or turning 'least interesting' into a claim that checking is pointless.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are distortions of degree of claims the passage actually makes.

questions.question: Which of the following best exemplifies the 'false sense of security' described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A reader who learns that one picture in a newspaper was retouched decides to distrust every photograph that the paper prints afterwards.
options.B: A photographer who arrived too late restages a scene with volunteers and publishes it with a caption calling it a reconstruction.
options.C: An editor, told that a photograph of empty shelves is unaltered, runs it as proof of a citywide shortage without asking where it was taken.
options.D: A court admits a photograph after an expert confirms it is unaltered and the photographer testifies to exactly when and where she took it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) An editor, told that a photograph of empty shelves is unaltered, runs it as proof of a citywide shortage without asking where it was taken.

option_rationales.A: This is excessive suspicion after detecting manipulation, the opposite of the misplaced confidence paragraph 3 describes.
option_rationales.B: The staging is openly declared, so no viewer is lulled into trusting the image as a record; the case does not involve the pixel check at all.
option_rationales.D: Here the check is joined by the caption-like facts that paragraph 4 calls the image's 'surroundings', so confidence is grounded rather than false.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes a viewer who concludes that 'an image which passes the check is reliable, when the check has said nothing about selection, timing or framing'. The editor relies on the check while ignoring exactly those questions about the shelves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the court case because it shares the forensic check, without noticing that it also supplies the context the author requires.
questions.difficulty_reason: The nearest wrong option shares the decisive feature (a passed check) and differs only in the presence of context, so the solver must apply paragraph 4 as well as paragraph 3.

questions.question: According to the passage, a newly accepted attribution can raise a painting's price sharply because

options.A: the painting becomes scarcer once it is known to be by a celebrated artist who produced very few works.
options.B: museums begin competing to acquire the painting so that they can display it to large numbers of visitors.
options.C: buyers pay partly for the name on a work, which can change while the picture stays the same.
options.D: experts who examine the painting again find qualities in its brushwork that earlier owners had failed to notice.

questions.correct_answer: (C) buyers pay partly for the name on a work, which can change while the picture stays the same.

option_rationales.A: The passage treats scarcity and the name as separate features with separate effects; the attribution example is explained by the name alone.
option_rationales.B: Museum competition is not given as the cause; paragraph 4 mentions institutions only as hesitating over works with unmanageable insurance values.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 stresses that the price rises 'without a single brushstroke changing' and that no one's 'experience of looking at the picture altered'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the buyer acquires an object that 'carries a name capable of conferring distinction', and 'the name explains why a newly accepted attribution can multiply a canvas's price overnight'.
questions.common_misconception: Running the scarcity example and the attribution example together.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause is stated in the same sentence as the example.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that two paintings of equal artistic merit

options.A: would reach equal prices at auction, since informed buyers pool their judgements of quality.
options.B: would eventually fetch similar prices once critics had studied both of them for long enough.
options.C: could not be compared at all, because artistic merit has no connection with what buyers pay.
options.D: might fetch very different prices if one were by a far more famous artist than the other.

questions.correct_answer: (D) might fetch very different prices if one were by a far more famous artist than the other.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'verdict' view of paragraph 1, which the author says rests on 'a mistaken premise'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says prices and esteem converge 'Over long periods' for artists, through reputation; it makes no promise about equal works, and paragraph 2 shows the name can outweigh merit.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says 'This does not mean that prices float free of critical judgement'; the author rejects the view that price measures 'nothing at all'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'a minor work by a celebrated painter can outsell a masterpiece by an obscure one', because price follows ownership features such as the name. Equal merit therefore does not guarantee equal price.
questions.common_misconception: Adopting one of the two responses in paragraph 1 that the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must extend the paragraph 2 example to a new case and resist the long-run convergence in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The comparison with a credit rating in paragraph 3 is used to

options.A: illustrate how one thing can track another at second hand while remaining a different kind of thing.
options.B: warn that the art market, like the market for company debt, is liable to sudden collapses in value.
options.C: suggest that auction prices are as carefully calculated by experts as the ratings given to companies.
options.D: argue that buying paintings is a sounder investment than lending money to companies with good ratings.

questions.correct_answer: (A) illustrate how one thing can track another at second hand while remaining a different kind of thing.

option_rationales.B: No collapse is mentioned; the danger the author identifies in paragraph 4 is that prices shape judgement, not that they crash.
option_rationales.C: The comparison concerns the relation between a measure and what it tracks, not the expertise or care involved in setting either.
option_rationales.D: The passage gives no investment advice and draws no comparison of returns; the rating is an analogy for indirect measurement only.

questions.explanation: The sentence says the market 'registers critical judgement at second hand, much as a credit rating registers a company's prospects without being the same thing as its earnings'. The analogy shows a real but indirect connection.
questions.common_misconception: Reading a financial analogy as a financial claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The analogy is explained within its own sentence, but the solver must abstract its point.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as an effect of treating prices as verdicts EXCEPT:

options.A: people gathering in front of the most expensive work in a gallery while neighbouring works go unvisited.
options.B: galleries raising the asking prices of other works whose style resembles that of the record-breaking canvas.
options.C: artists early in their careers taking note of what kinds of work the market rewards.
options.D: museums becoming reluctant to put certain works on display or send them to other institutions.

questions.correct_answer: (B) galleries raising the asking prices of other works whose style resembles that of the record-breaking canvas.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4: 'Visitors crowd around the record-breaking canvas while the room beside it stands empty'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4: 'young artists learn which styles sell'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4: 'institutions hesitate to show or lend works whose insurance values have become unmanageable'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 gives three effects: visitors crowding one canvas, institutions hesitating to show or lend, and young artists learning 'which styles sell'. Nothing is said about galleries repricing similar works; the option borrows the idea of style from the third effect and the record price from the first, but describes a market reaction the passage never mentions.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting an option because it combines familiar words from paragraph 4 ('styles', 'record-breaking') and sounds like a natural consequence, without checking it against the three effects actually listed.
questions.difficulty_reason: All options are paraphrased and the correct answer is assembled from words in the same paragraph, so the solver must check each against the text rather than against plausibility.

questions.question: The remark that 'a theory that can detect a difference only once it has been told where to look is not much of a theory' serves to

options.A: cast doubt on the second explanation by pointing out that the supposed visible flaws are noticed only after exposure.
options.B: introduce the author's own account, which holds that forgeries can always be distinguished by close study.
options.C: reject the first explanation by showing that critics who praised the forgery were not motivated by snobbery.
options.D: support the second explanation by showing that trained eyes can find the deadness of a forgery once they are alerted.

questions.correct_answer: (A) cast doubt on the second explanation by pointing out that the supposed visible flaws are noticed only after exposure.

option_rationales.B: The author's account in paragraph 3 says the two canvases 'may look alike' and locates the difference in achievement, not in anything visible.
option_rationales.C: The remark concerns the claim of visible difference, the second explanation; the snobbery explanation is answered separately with the 'proves too much' objection.
option_rationales.D: The remark comes after 'yet' and undercuts the explanation; the author grants only that 'Sometimes this is so'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents the second explanation, that forgeries 'differ visibly after all', concedes 'Sometimes this is so', and then objects that the deadness 'is usually perceived only after the verdict is known'. The quoted remark completes that objection.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the 'yet' and reading the remark as support, or attaching it to the wrong explanation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The remark's target is clear once the two explanations in paragraph 2 are kept apart.

questions.question: In objecting that the snobbery explanation 'proves too much', the author implies that a satisfactory account of the reaction to forgery must

options.A: show that snobbery and the wish to resell play no part in the fall in a forgery's price.
options.B: allow that someone could mind the difference for reasons other than prestige or resale.
options.C: establish that the pleasure visitors took in the forgery was not genuine pleasure but a kind of mistake.
options.D: explain why historians are better placed than collectors to judge whether a painting is a forgery.

questions.correct_answer: (B) allow that someone could mind the difference for reasons other than prestige or resale.

option_rationales.A: The author concedes that 'much of the fall in price' reflects the lost signature, so he does not require snobbery to play no part.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 insists that 'the pleasure that thousands took in it was genuine pleasure', and nothing in the objection depends on denying this.
option_rationales.D: The historian is cited as someone who minds 'with no money at stake', not as a better judge of authenticity; detection is not at issue in this objection.

questions.explanation: An explanation 'proves too much' when it covers cases it should not. The snobbery account would make 'the scrupulous historian with no money at stake' a snob, so an adequate account must leave room for a motive that is neither status nor money; paragraph 3 then supplies one.
questions.common_misconception: Over-reading the objection as a total rejection of snobbery, when the author grants it explains much of the price fall.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires understanding the logical form of a 'proves too much' objection and keeping the concession in view.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the author's own account of why the exposure of a forgery changes our appreciation?

options.A: Students who build an exact model of a famous building as an exercise are praised by teachers for the skill of their copy.
options.B: A copy of a novel loses most of its value to collectors when it turns out to be a later printing, though its text is identical.
options.C: A chess game admired as brilliant play in an unforeseen position is found to have been copied move for move from an older game.
options.D: A wine praised in a blind tasting is revealed to be a cheap one, after which the same tasters begin to describe it as thin.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A chess game admired as brilliant play in an unforeseen position is found to have been copied move for move from an older game.

option_rationales.A: This matches the concession in paragraph 4 that imitation can be 'a considerable achievement of its own kind', not the account of why exposure changes appreciation.
option_rationales.B: This mirrors the snobbery explanation: the loss reflects the market for a desirable label, the part the author grants but calls inadequate.
option_rationales.D: This mirrors the second explanation, where a flaw is 'perceived only after the verdict is known', which the author rejects.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says we admire a work partly as 'a problem of light or space confronted at a particular moment' by someone 'who did not know how it would turn out', and that a forgery answers a different question. The copied chess game has identical moves, but the achievement admired, solving an unforeseen position, never took place.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the case that fits one of the explanations the author reports and rejects, or the concession in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every wrong option maps onto a real element of the passage, so the solver must match the specific structure of the author's own account.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that 'what matters in a painting is what can be seen in it' is best described as

options.A: endorsing it reluctantly, since the reaction to forgery cannot be explained without some appeal to visible features.
options.B: dismissing it as a form of snobbery that values the label over the evidence of the eye.
options.C: accepting it for ordinary visitors while holding that experts must also weigh facts about a painting's making.
options.D: rejecting it as a full account, while admitting his alternative makes value rest partly on unseen facts.

questions.correct_answer: (D) rejecting it as a full account, while admitting his alternative makes value rest partly on unseen facts.

option_rationales.A: The author's account explicitly makes value depend on 'facts that cannot be seen in it', which is the opposite of endorsing the view.
option_rationales.B: The view prizes the eye, not the label: paragraph 1 says that on this view the reaction to forgery looks like 'a triumph of the label over the eye'. Snobbery is the label-loving attitude, so the option inverts the view.
option_rationales.C: The author draws no line between ordinary visitors and experts; he says 'looking alone can never be the whole of appreciation' for anyone.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says that on this view the reaction 'looks irrational'; paragraph 3 replaces it with the idea of paintings as achievements; paragraph 4 admits the 'cost' that 'looking alone can never be the whole of appreciation' and judges it 'worth paying'.
