questions.common_misconception: Confusing which side of the label versus eye contrast each view occupies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The view is stated hypothetically in paragraph 1 and rejected only through the account and its admitted cost in paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: arguing that older portraits are artistically superior to modern ones because they honestly record a sitter's social position.
options.B: explaining how photography destroyed the market for painted portraits in the nineteenth century and after.
options.C: describing the symbols, such as dogs and columns, that court painters used to signal their sitters' virtues.
options.D: showing that the demand for psychological insight in portraits is a historical development, not a timeless standard for the genre.

questions.correct_answer: (D) showing that the demand for psychological insight in portraits is a historical development, not a timeless standard for the genre.

option_rationales.A: The author ranks neither period; paragraph 5 says modern portraits also display position and older ones could show character.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says photography took over 'much of the trade in cheap likenesses', one of several changes; it does not say the market for painted portraits was destroyed, and this is not the passage's focus.
option_rationales.C: The symbols in paragraph 2 support the claim that portraits established position; listing them is too narrow to be the passage's concern.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the modern standard; paragraphs 2 and 3 show older portraits served a different purpose; paragraph 4 says the psychological portrait 'is not the essence of the genre finally achieved but one of its historical forms'; paragraph 5 draws the lesson that we should judge a portrait 'by the question it was asked to answer'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a supporting detail (photography, symbols) or turning the author's relativising point into a ranking.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is explicit in paragraph 4 but the wrong options draw on real material from paragraphs 2, 4 and 5.

questions.question: According to paragraph 3, likeness mattered in older commissioned portraits chiefly because

options.A: the purpose of such portraits was to reveal the sitter's private character to later generations.
options.B: the face had to be recognisable enough for the role shown to be attached to the right person.
options.C: patrons insisted that painters should show exactly how the sitter looked, without any flattery at all.
options.D: painters were judged mainly by their skill in capturing the particular features of each sitter's face.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the face had to be recognisable enough for the role shown to be attached to the right person.

option_rationales.A: This is the modern standard the passage contrasts with older practice; paragraph 2 says the aim was 'less to record a personality than to establish a position'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says painters could be criticised for flattering 'too much or too little', which implies some flattery was expected, not none.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says likeness 'served the larger purpose rather than defining it', so painters were not judged mainly on it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'A face had to be recognisable enough to attach the role to the right person, and beyond that the painter's task was to make the person fit the role.'
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'Likeness was not irrelevant' as a claim that likeness was the main aim.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a direct paraphrase of one sentence.

questions.question: When the author says such a portrait 'was closer to a document than to a confession' (paragraph 2), the point is that it

options.A: was a truthful account of the sitter, while psychological portraits are works of imaginative fiction.
options.B: was valued mainly as a legal record that could be used to prove a family's ownership of land.
options.C: recorded the sitter's public standing in a readable form instead of disclosing his inner life.
options.D: was painted from written descriptions of the sitter rather than from the sitter in person.

questions.correct_answer: (C) recorded the sitter's public standing in a readable form instead of disclosing his inner life.

option_rationales.A: The contrast is between recording position and revealing inner life, not between truth and fiction; the author never calls modern portraits fictional.
option_rationales.B: The estate glimpsed through a window is one symbol of position; the passage never says portraits served as legal proof, so this takes 'document' too literally.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage concerns how portraits were produced; paragraph 3 even mentions families wanting to know what a bride 'looked like'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the sitter appeared 'as a holder of office, an heir, a bride' and that objects 'carried meanings that contemporaries could read'. A 'confession' would reveal the private self, which paragraph 1 associates with the modern standard.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'document' literally as a legal paper.
questions.difficulty_reason: The metaphor must be read against both the surrounding sentences and the modern standard in paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the arrival of photography affected portrait painting by

options.A: taking over the trade in cheap likenesses, so that painters turned to offering what a camera seemed unable to give.
options.B: bringing to an end the tradition of painting sitters with symbols of office, such as chains and columns.
options.C: making painted portraits more truthful, because painters could now correct their work against photographs.
options.D: introducing the belief that a person's truth lies within, which painters then tried to express in their portraits.

questions.correct_answer: (A) taking over the trade in cheap likenesses, so that painters turned to offering what a camera seemed unable to give.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says a present-day portrait of a chairman still 'documents a position', so the display of position did not end.
option_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about painters using photographs as references; it describes a change in the market for likenesses.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 lists 'New ideas about the self' as a separate change from photography; the option merges two distinct causes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: photography 'took over much of the trade in cheap likenesses, leaving painters free, or obliged, to offer something a camera seemed unable to supply'. The passage connects this to the rise of the psychological portrait.
questions.common_misconception: Running together the separate causes listed in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option fuses two causes the paragraph lists separately, which a quick reader may accept.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The similarity among many older portraits reflects an intention of the patrons rather than a lack of skill.
options.B: A painter working within the conventions of a court portrait could still let something of the sitter's character appear.
options.C: Older portrait painters were largely indifferent to whether the people they painted could be recognised.
options.D: A portrait made today for a company boardroom may serve much the same purpose as a portrait made for a royal court.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Older portrait painters were largely indifferent to whether the people they painted could be recognised.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'Its sameness was not a failure of observation but a deliberate placing of the individual within a recognisable type'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5: 'A shrewd painter could let a sitter's character show through the conventions'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says such a portrait 'documents a position as surely as any court painting did', so the author agrees.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'Likeness was not irrelevant' and says a face 'had to be recognisable enough to attach the role to the right person'. Indifference to recognisability contradicts this, so it is the one statement the author would reject.
questions.common_misconception: Overextending the thesis that portraits established position into the claim that likeness did not matter at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer sounds like a natural summary of the passage's thesis and is refuted only by the qualification in paragraph 3; the true statements are all paraphrased.

questions.question: Which of the following does the author mention as a merit of slow looking?

options.A: It gives visitors who seem to need it permission to remain with a single work.
options.B: It replaces the reading of labels, which visitors often do in place of looking.
options.C: It trains beginners to ask where the light in a painting comes from.
options.D: It guarantees that whoever stays long enough will discover something new in the picture.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It gives visitors who seem to need it permission to remain with a single work.

option_rationales.B: Labels are mentioned in paragraph 1 only to describe brief viewing; slow looking is never said to replace them.
option_rationales.C: Asking about the light is the art historian's learned question in paragraph 3, an example of expertise, not something slow looking is said to teach.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says it 'does sometimes yield discoveries' and that fifteen minutes can be spent in reverie; there is no guarantee.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists the merits, including: 'It gives permission to stay, which many visitors seem to need.'
questions.common_misconception: Upgrading 'sometimes' to a guarantee, or crediting slow looking with what paragraph 3 attributes to expertise.
questions.difficulty_reason: The merit is stated in a single sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The statement 'Time is a condition of seeing, not a cause of it' (paragraph 2) most nearly means that

options.A: seeing a painting well takes no time at all once the viewer has the right questions in mind.
options.B: seeing requires time but time does not by itself produce seeing, since something else must turn it into perception.
options.C: the conditions in a gallery, such as crowding and noise, affect seeing more than the time spent there.
options.D: people who spend more time in front of a picture always see less than those who spend less time.

questions.correct_answer: (B) seeing requires time but time does not by itself produce seeing, since something else must turn it into perception.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says 'questions without time confirm what they expected', so time remains necessary even for the expert.
option_rationales.C: The word 'condition' here means a necessary requirement, not the physical setting of the gallery; crowding is mentioned only as encouraging hurried viewing.
option_rationales.D: The author denies only that time is sufficient; he never says more time reduces seeing, and paragraph 2 grants that it 'does sometimes yield discoveries'.

questions.explanation: The sentence closes a paragraph showing that fifteen minutes can be spent in reverie. Paragraph 3 then names what does turn time into seeing: 'What turns time into seeing is a question.'
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'condition' as the surrounding circumstances, or reversing the claim into one about time harming perception.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase uses a technical sense of 'condition' that must be recovered from the argument.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a beginner who sits before a painting for an hour is likely to

options.A: look less carefully than an expert, since beginners give up their attention sooner than trained viewers.
options.B: discover the features that experts miss, since he has no expectations that tell him where not to look.
options.C: see as much as an expert does in a few seconds, provided that he keeps looking attentively.
options.D: dwell on whatever is most conspicuous or familiar, since no question is directing where he looks.

questions.correct_answer: (D) dwell on whatever is most conspicuous or familiar, since no question is directing where he looks.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says outright 'The beginner is not looking less'; the difference is the absence of a question, not effort.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says setting expertise aside can produce surprise, but paragraph 3 says an unguided gaze settles on the obvious; the beginner is not credited with seeing what experts miss.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says experts 'see in seconds what a patient beginner misses in an hour', which contradicts this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the beginner is 'looking without a question, and an unguided gaze tends to settle on whatever is largest, brightest or most familiar'.
questions.common_misconception: Importing the point of paragraph 4 about expert blindness and giving it to the beginner.
questions.difficulty_reason: The third wrong option draws on paragraph 4 and is tempting because the passage does value a lack of expectation, though not in a beginner's unguided gaze.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 4 about the risk carried by expertise?

options.A: Experts told in advance to search for an anomaly in a painting found it much faster than untrained viewers did.
options.B: Experts identified the school of an unfamiliar painting far more quickly and accurately than untrained viewers did.
options.C: Untrained viewers who looked at a painting for fifteen minutes listed more details than those who looked for two minutes.
options.D: Shown a painting with an odd detail clashing with its school, experts noticed the detail less often than untrained viewers did.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Shown a painting with an odd detail clashing with its school, experts noticed the detail less often than untrained viewers did.

option_rationales.A: This shows that a question directs the eye, the advantage in paragraph 3; it does not show expectations blinding experts to what they were not looking for.
option_rationales.B: Quick and correct classification supports paragraph 3 on the expert's advantage; it shows nothing about failing to notice what 'does not fit'.
option_rationales.C: This bears on the premise of slow looking, which paragraph 2 questions, and says nothing about experts or their expectations.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 claims an expert 'may stop looking once she has found' what she expected and fail 'to notice what does not fit'. Experts missing an anomaly that untrained viewers caught is direct evidence of that risk.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing evidence of expert skill, which belongs to paragraph 3, instead of evidence of expert blindness.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options concern experts and anomalies yet support the other half of the argument; the solver must isolate the precise claim of paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?

options.A: A defence of expertise against slow looking, concluding that guided questions should replace the habit of long and unstructured contemplation.
options.B: A criticism of museums for allowing visitors to glance at pictures briefly and spend most of their time reading the labels instead.
options.C: An assessment of a museum practice that grants its value, disputes the reasoning behind it, and recommends combining it with what expertise supplies.
options.D: An argument that slow looking matters chiefly because it lets trained viewers set aside the expectations that their knowledge creates.

questions.correct_answer: (C) An assessment of a museum practice that grants its value, disputes the reasoning behind it, and recommends combining it with what expertise supplies.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 credits slow looking with correcting the expert's blindness, and paragraph 5 rejects 'the quick classification that expertise permits' as the sole practice.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 describes brief viewing only to introduce slow looking; the passage does not blame museums and focuses on how seeing happens.
option_rationales.D: This is one point from paragraph 4; the passage also criticises the premise of slow looking and ends by recommending alternation, so the option is too narrow.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 concedes 'real merits' but calls the premise 'weaker than it looks'; paragraph 3 says questions turn time into seeing; paragraph 4 says slow looking can correct expertise; paragraph 5 recommends 'an alternation between them'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option that captures only one stage of a dialectical argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow wrong option states a true point the author makes, so the solver must weigh whole-passage scope.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: challenge a popular picture of improvisation by arguing that its freedom rests on conventions the performer has fully absorbed.
options.B: argue that improvisers are best understood as skilled recombiners of phrases that they have memorised during long training.
options.C: show that improvisation in Indian classical music is more tightly governed by rules than improvisation in jazz.
options.D: recommend that teachers of improvisation stop encouraging students to imitate and instead train them to recall the rules.

questions.correct_answer: (A) challenge a popular picture of improvisation by arguing that its freedom rests on conventions the performer has fully absorbed.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 explicitly denies this: 'None of this is to say that improvisation is merely the recombination of stored parts'.
option_rationales.C: The passage presents the raga and the jazz tune as parallel cases of the same point ('What these traditions share'); it never ranks one tradition as more rule-bound.
option_rationales.D: The passage endorses imitation as 'the means by which the constraints are absorbed' and says fluent players do not consult rules, so the recommendation reverses its view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 names the image of 'pure spontaneity' and says it 'badly misdescribes' improvisers; paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that the constraints are internalised like grammar; paragraph 4 concludes that freedom is 'a fluency so complete that form can be played with'. The purpose is to correct the popular picture.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the comparison of two traditions, or the stress on imitation, for the purpose, or overstating the thesis into the claim that improvising is only recombination.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option (recombination) uses the passage's own emphasis on absorbed vocabulary and must be rejected through the concession in paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to the passage, a student of improvisation who is told simply to be free is likely to

options.A: imitate the phrases of established players more closely than a student given strict exercises.
options.B: produce something without shape or rely on a few habits acquired by chance.
options.C: discover a personal style sooner, though at the cost of breaking with the tradition.
options.D: learn the rules of the tradition more slowly, but understand them more deeply in the end.

questions.correct_answer: (B) produce something without shape or rely on a few habits acquired by chance.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 presents imitation as what teachers prescribe instead of the instruction to be free, not as its result.
option_rationales.C: The passage says the result is usually 'something shapeless', not an early personal style; no trade-off of this kind is described.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in paragraph 3 says such a student eventually learns the rules at all, let alone more deeply; the outcome described is wholly negative.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states that such a student 'usually produces something shapeless, or falls back on a handful of habits picked up by accident'. The correct answer paraphrases this directly.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that freedom in training must have some compensating benefit.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is located in a single sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the years of imitation in an improviser's training as

options.A: an inefficient custom that persists mainly because teachers in both traditions were trained in the same way.
options.B: the main source of what listeners value most in a great improvised performance.
options.C: a stage that suppresses creativity, which the student must later unlearn in order to improvise freely.
options.D: the way the conventions of a tradition become second nature, which later makes confident variation possible.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the way the conventions of a tradition become second nature, which later makes confident variation possible.

option_rationales.A: The passage gives a reason for imitation (absorbing constraints) and never calls it inefficient or explains it by teachers' habits.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 locates what listeners value in a convention 'stretched or bent', which imitation only prepares for; the option confuses the preparation with the valued moment.
option_rationales.C: The author concedes that imitation 'can look like the opposite of creativity' to an outsider, but argues it is in fact what makes later variation possible; nothing is to be unlearned.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'imitation here is the means by which the constraints are absorbed, and only once they have been absorbed can the student vary them with confidence'. The correct answer restates this relation.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the outsider's view of imitation that the author reports and then rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The relevant sentence states the relation almost directly; one wrong option borrows the outsider's view.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the author's account of what makes a great improvised moment?

options.A: A poet who has written strict sonnets for decades breaks the expected rhyme in the final line, and readers feel the break as deliberate and apt.
options.B: A beginner who has never studied verse writes a poem with no metre or rhyme, and some readers find its roughness refreshing and honest.
options.C: A poet with an exceptional memory for other people's verse assembles a new poem entirely from lines borrowed from famous earlier poems.
options.D: A translator who looks up every word in a dictionary produces a version that is accurate in each line but stiff when read aloud as a whole.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A poet who has written strict sonnets for decades breaks the expected rhyme in the final line, and readers feel the break as deliberate and apt.

option_rationales.B: The author says a performer without absorbed constraints 'usually produces something shapeless'; this case lacks the mastery of form that the passage makes essential.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 denies that the best improvisers are 'simply those with the largest memories' or that improvising is 'the recombination of stored parts'.
option_rationales.D: This depicts rules consulted rather than internalised, which the passage contrasts with fluency; it involves no meaningful bending of a convention.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says listeners value 'a moment at which a convention is stretched or bent in a way that still makes sense within the tradition', possible 'only for someone who knows exactly where the boundaries lie'. The sonneteer has internalised the form and departs from it at one point in a way readers recognise as meaningful.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the untrained poet because the passage praises freedom, or the memorising poet because it stresses absorbed vocabulary.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches one strand of the passage (freedom, rules, memory); only the correct answer matches the full account.

questions.question: According to the passage, many companies that hold detailed records of their repertoire

options.A: use notation to correct the drift that has crept in through generations of teaching.
options.B: regard the notated record as the authoritative version of a dance when teachers disagree.
options.C: still revive works through direct teaching and use the written record to support memory.
options.D: have abandoned studio teaching now that film and video can capture complete performances.

questions.correct_answer: (C) still revive works through direct teaching and use the written record to support memory.

option_rationales.A: No such use of notation is described; paragraph 4 discusses drift without proposing documents as a corrective.
option_rationales.B: The passage says companies treat the record 'as an aid to memory rather than as the work itself', the reverse of making it authoritative.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says these tools 'have not displaced the older method of transmission'; companies 'still rely on such teaching'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: such companies 'still rely on such teaching when a work is revived, and they tend to treat the written record as an aid to memory rather than as the work itself'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that better tools must have replaced older methods.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2; wrong options contradict it plainly.

questions.question: The author would most likely expect a revival staged by dancers who learned a role only from a film of one performance to

options.A: fail chiefly because film cannot show the position of each part of the body over time.
options.B: risk copying one performer's personal habits and errors as though they were part of the choreography.
options.C: convey the weight and timing of each movement more faithfully than a revival taught in the studio, since film records every detail.
options.D: be closer to the choreographer's original intentions, since the film is free of the drift that teaching introduces.

questions.correct_answer: (B) risk copying one performer's personal habits and errors as though they were part of the choreography.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 credits film with capturing performances; the limitation the passage identifies is the weight, attention and reasons behind movements, and the inability to separate dancer from dance.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 lists 'the weight of a movement' and 'the reasons a gesture is timed as it is' among the things a recording 'captures poorly or not at all', so the author would expect the reverse.
option_rationales.D: A film preserves one dancer's version, including 'her idiosyncrasies and her mistakes', so it is not free of distortion; the passage gives no ground for thinking it closer to the maker's intention.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a film shows 'what a particular dancer did on a particular night, including her idiosyncrasies and her mistakes' and 'cannot say which of those features belong to the choreography and which belong to her'. Without a teacher to draw that line, the revival is likely to treat the dancer's habits as the dance.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a complete visual record of one performance must preserve the dance itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the paragraph 3 distinction to a new case and rejecting a plausible but differently grounded criticism.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the transmission of dance from dancer to dancer is best described as

options.A: nostalgic, regretting that newer tools such as film and notation are steadily replacing it in most companies.
options.B: ambivalent, finding its losses roughly equal to its gains and declining to prefer it to documentation.
options.C: defensive, insisting that the method causes no real change to the dances handed down by it.
options.D: appreciative, while openly admitting that the method gradually alters the works it preserves.

questions.correct_answer: (D) appreciative, while openly admitting that the method gradually alters the works it preserves.

option_rationales.A: The passage says these tools 'have not displaced the older method', so there is no replacement to regret, and the author calls the tools 'valuable'.
option_rationales.B: The author does prefer it: the archive of dance is 'not mainly a shelf of documents but a lineage of people', and the drift 'is not simply a corruption'.
option_rationales.C: The author concedes that 'a dance may drift a long way from what its maker first set', so the method is not claimed to leave dances unchanged.

questions.explanation: The author defends studio teaching ('The reason is not mere conservatism') and ends by calling the lineage of dancers the real archive, while conceding that 'This method has an obvious cost' and that drift occurs. Appreciation with an acknowledged cost fits.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the concession in paragraph 4 as evenly balanced ambivalence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The ambivalent wrong option is tempting because the author does name a cost; the final sentences settle the author's preference.

questions.question: In the first paragraph, the suggestion that the remedy for dance's fragility is 'simply better documentation' functions as

options.A: the thesis that the author defends throughout the remaining paragraphs.
options.B: a natural conclusion that the rest of the passage goes on to qualify.
options.C: a historical claim about how choreographers once preserved their work.
options.D: an objection to the view that dance has the most fragile relation to its past.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a natural conclusion that the rest of the passage goes on to qualify.

option_rationales.A: Paragraphs 2 to 4 argue that documentation has not displaced studio teaching and records much 'poorly or not at all', so the author does not defend this remedy.
option_rationales.C: The sentence is introduced as what 'It is tempting to conclude', a line of reasoning, not a report of past practice.
option_rationales.D: The suggestion accepts that fragility and proposes a cure; it does not object to the opening claim.

questions.explanation: The sentence begins 'It is tempting to conclude', marking a plausible inference; paragraph 2 grants that documentation is 'valuable' but shows it has not displaced teaching, and paragraph 3 explains why. The suggestion is set up to be qualified.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the first view mentioned as the author's thesis.
questions.difficulty_reason: The signal phrase 'It is tempting to conclude' and the turn in paragraph 2 make the function clear.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a wrong note matters more on a recording than in a concert because

options.A: on a recording it is heard every time the performance is replayed, instead of passing once and being forgotten.
options.B: listeners at home concentrate harder than audiences in a hall, who are distracted by their surroundings.
options.C: recording equipment exaggerates small errors that the acoustics of a concert hall would soften.
options.D: performers who record are expected to be more skilled than those who play only in concerts.

questions.correct_answer: (A) on a recording it is heard every time the performance is replayed, instead of passing once and being forgotten.

option_rationales.B: The passage never compares the attention of home and concert listeners; it explains the difference by repetition alone.
option_rationales.C: No claim is made about equipment distorting sound; the blemish is permanent because it is replayed, not because it is amplified.
option_rationales.D: The passage does not rank recording artists above concert performers; the same performers learned that slips acceptable in a hall became 'intolerable on disc'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A live performance is heard once; its slips pass and are forgotten', whereas on a recording 'on the tenth hearing a wrong note ... is no longer a passing accident but a permanent blemish'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying an outside explanation (attention, equipment) instead of the one the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause is stated in adjacent sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The 'curious inversion' mentioned in paragraph 3 refers to the fact that

options.A: performers who once took risks in the concert hall now take them only in the recording studio.
options.B: editing, once used to remove errors from recordings, is now used to add effects that cannot be produced live.
options.C: a recording, intended to copy a performance, now serves many listeners as the model that live performances are judged against.
options.D: listeners who once went to concerts to hear new works now go mainly to hear works they already know.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a recording, intended to copy a performance, now serves many listeners as the model that live performances are judged against.

option_rationales.A: The passage says the opposite tendency exists: some performers play 'more cautiously' live; it never says risk has moved into the studio.
option_rationales.B: Editing is described as assembling 'a single flawless performance from many takes'; adding effects is never mentioned, and this is not what 'inversion' refers to.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says many know a work first through a recording, but the inversion it names is between copy and original, not between new and familiar works.

questions.explanation: The sentences after the phrase explain it: 'The recording was meant to be a copy of the performance; it has become, for many listeners, the original, and the performance its imperfect copy.'
questions.common_misconception: Picking a change that the passage mentions nearby (familiar works, caution) instead of the one the phrase names.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the following sentence, but two wrong options use real details from the same paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that some performers have responded to recordings by playing more cautiously in concerts?

options.A: Many listeners now say that they prefer recordings to concerts because recordings are free of the slips that so often occur in live performance.
options.B: A few celebrated performers refused to make recordings at all because they disliked the conditions of the studio.
options.C: Recordings have allowed students of music to compare dozens of interpretations of the same work in a single afternoon.
options.D: Broadcasts of live concerts from before and after edited recordings became common show that the same kinds of performers took risks just as often.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Broadcasts of live concerts from before and after edited recordings became common show that the same kinds of performers took risks just as often.

option_rationales.A: This fits the passage's account of audiences learning to expect a 'clean surface', so it supports rather than weakens the pressure towards caution.
option_rationales.B: Refusals by a few performers do not touch the claim about those who did respond to recordings; the passage says only that 'some' became more cautious.
option_rationales.C: This is a benefit the passage itself grants in paragraph 4; it says nothing about how performers behave in concerts.

questions.explanation: The claim in paragraph 3 is a causal one about change in live playing after recordings became the norm. Evidence that live risk-taking did not change across that period directly undercuts it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about recordings in general that does not bear on live behaviour.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the precise claim to be isolated; two wrong options are on topic and one even supports the passage.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the effects of recording on musical life is best described as

options.A: a qualified appreciation that values what recording made possible while rejecting the view that it left performing and listening unchanged.
options.B: a guarded scepticism that doubts recording has widened access to music as much as is often claimed, though it accepts its value for comparison.
options.C: a neutral detachment that describes the effects of recording on performers and listeners without judging whether any of them is desirable.
options.D: a regretful nostalgia that concedes the conveniences of recording but holds that musical life has on balance declined since concerts lost their place.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a qualified appreciation that values what recording made possible while rejecting the view that it left performing and listening unchanged.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the claim about access 'is true as far as it goes' and the gain 'enormous', so the author does not doubt it.
option_rationales.C: The author does judge: the gain in access is 'enormous', caution comes 'at the cost of' spontaneity, and an account that ignores the change has 'mistaken a transformation for a mere extension'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says 'It would be wrong to treat this as a simple story of decline', and the author never weighs gains against losses to reach a verdict of decline.

questions.explanation: The author grants the enormous gain in access and the benefits of comparison and preservation (paragraphs 1 and 4), yet insists that 'recording is not neutral' and transformed what a performance is. That combination is qualified appreciation joined to a rejection of the 'window' view.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the account of lost spontaneity as nostalgia, or the balanced survey as neutrality.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options (nostalgia, neutrality) each capture part of the tone; separating them needs the explicit denial of decline and the evaluative language across the passage.

questions.question: The reference to a carved mask in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: support the second view that sadness is enjoyable when it arrives without a real loss behind it.
options.B: illustrate the first view's claim that listeners recognise sadness in music without themselves feeling it.
options.C: show that visual art expresses sadness less powerfully than music, which can move listeners to tears.
options.D: express the author's own position that the pleasure of sad music lies in skill rather than feeling.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate the first view's claim that listeners recognise sadness in music without themselves feeling it.

option_rationales.A: The mask appears in the account of the first view, which denies the listener feels sad; the second view accepts the feeling is real.
option_rationales.C: The mask is not compared with music for power; it is offered as a parallel case of recognising an expression without sharing it.
option_rationales.D: The author reports this view and then says it 'fits poorly' with listeners' reports; the author's own account, in paragraph 3, concerns the form given to a real feeling.

questions.explanation: The sentence presents the first response: the listener 'recognises sadness in the music, much as she might recognise a sorrowful expression on a carved mask'. The mask is an analogy for recognition without feeling.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing a reported view to the author, or attaching the example to the wrong view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example sits inside a clearly labelled account of the first view.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the pleasure a listener takes in a lament depends chiefly on

options.A: the listener's recognition of the composer's skill in depicting sorrow without being affected by it.
options.B: the listener's confidence that the sorrow has no real cause and will have no consequences afterwards.
options.C: the way the music leads a real sorrow through an ordered course from beginning to resolution.
options.D: the intensity of the sorrow the music arouses, so that the most moving laments are the most enjoyed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the way the music leads a real sorrow through an ordered course from beginning to resolution.

option_rationales.A: This is the first response, which the author says 'fits poorly' with listeners' reports of being moved.
option_rationales.B: This is the second response, which the author says captures something but misses the shaping of emotion and fails the test of grieving listeners.
option_rationales.D: The author criticises both rival views for treating emotion as a state 'mild or intense' and locates the pleasure 'less in the feeling than in the form', so intensity is not the decisive factor.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the author's account: music gives an emotion 'a shape over time', leading the listener through sorrow with 'a beginning, an end and a recognisable order', so that 'The pleasure ... lies less in the feeling than in the form the feeling is given'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the two reported views, each of which the author grants may 'capture something'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are views the author partly credits; the correct answer requires separating the author's account from them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why some grieving people cannot bear sad music?

options.A: Listeners who are not grieving often report being moved to tears by laments, and not merely noticing that the music is sad.
options.B: Some listeners enjoy sad music most when they hear it in a concert hall among strangers rather than alone at home.
options.C: Grieving listeners who avoid sad music for a time usually return to it once their own grief has become less raw.
options.D: Grieving listeners find sad music that wanders without clear form or resolution just as unbearable as laments that move to a settled close.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Grieving listeners find sad music that wanders without clear form or resolution just as unbearable as laments that move to a settled close.

option_rationales.A: This tells against the first response, which the author also rejects; it leaves the account of grieving listeners untouched.
option_rationales.B: The setting of listening is not part of the author's explanation, so this finding neither supports nor undermines it.
option_rationales.C: This is consistent with the author's account: once the listener's own sorrow takes some shape, the contrast with the music's shaped sorrow would be less sharp.

questions.explanation: The author explains the grieving listener's distress by 'the contrast' between the music's 'shaped and completed sorrow' and the listener's sorrow, which 'has no shape yet'. If formless, unresolved sad music were equally unbearable, the music's shape could not be what produces the distress, and the explanation would lose its basis.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about tears, which is a real objection in the passage but aimed at a different view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must identify which explanation is being tested, what it depends on (the contrast of shape) and which finding removes that dependence; two wrong options are on topic and one is consistent with the account.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: The frame view correctly predicts that people in grief will find sad music harder to bear than before.
options.B: On the frame view, the sadness of music can be savoured because no loss causes it and no consequences follow.
options.C: A lament may return to a phrase heard earlier in the piece before it finally comes to rest.
options.D: The view that listeners only recognise sadness can explain why sad music does not spoil a listener's day.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The frame view correctly predicts that people in grief will find sad music harder to bear than before.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 states the frame view in these terms: the sadness 'arrives without a loss to cause it and without consequences to follow'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 describes a lament that 'returns to a phrase heard earlier and comes to rest'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 grants that this view 'has the merit of explaining why sad music does not ruin anyone's day'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a frame that keeps sadness at a safe distance 'should make such music easier to bear in grief, not harder'. The frame view therefore predicts the opposite of what grieving listeners report, which is why the author treats their experience as a check on it.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the 'not harder' and assuming that every view in the passage accounts for the grieving listener.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are direct paraphrases; the correct answer reverses a prediction stated in the final paragraph.

questions.question: According to the passage, one result of performing older music on period instruments was that

options.A: audiences came to prefer small ensembles to large orchestras for music of every period.
options.B: textures that had seemed heavy under large modern orchestras came to sound transparent.
options.C: composers' written complaints about their instruments were finally resolved by better reconstructions.
options.D: dissonances that later audiences had stopped noticing began to startle listeners once again.

questions.correct_answer: (B) textures that had seemed heavy under large modern orchestras came to sound transparent.

option_rationales.A: The passage speaks only of music written before about 1800 and says nothing about a general preference for small ensembles.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 mentions composers' dissatisfaction to show that their wishes cannot be inferred from their circumstances; it says nothing about resolving it.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: a dissonance that once startled 'may now pass unnoticed', and reconstruction cannot restore the original listeners.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Textures that had sounded thick and heavy when played by large modern orchestras became transparent'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a detail about dissonance from paragraph 2 and reversing it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in a single sentence of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The argument of paragraph 2 implies that a perfect reconstruction of the instruments and tempi of an early work would still

options.A: sound less transparent to modern ears than a performance by a large modern orchestra.
options.B: be impossible to achieve, because the treatises written in the period are too vague to guide performers.
options.C: fail to reproduce the original listeners' experience, because later music has shaped how modern audiences hear it.
options.D: contradict the composer's intentions, since composers disliked the instruments of their own time.

questions.correct_answer: (C) fail to reproduce the original listeners' experience, because later music has shaped how modern audiences hear it.

option_rationales.A: The passage reports that period performance made textures 'transparent'; nothing implies a perfect reconstruction would sound heavier than a modern orchestra.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 grants the reconstruction for the sake of argument ('Even if every instrument and every tempo could be reconstructed exactly'); the vagueness of treatises is never claimed.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says only that some composers were dissatisfied, and argues that their preferences cannot be inferred; it does not claim reconstruction contradicts their intentions.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that even with exact reconstruction 'the listeners could not be' reconstructed: a modern audience hears an older piece against the music of the following two centuries, so 'The same sounds, entering differently formed ears, do not produce the same experience'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the second objection (composers' wishes) with the first, or mistaking a hypothetical concession for a claim of impossibility.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires following a conditional argument and keeping the two objections of paragraphs 2 and 3 apart.

questions.question: Which of the following arguments makes the same error that paragraph 3 identifies?

options.A: A playwright's audiences knew stories that modern audiences do not, so modern productions cannot recreate the effect the plays first had.
options.B: A playwright's early productions were praised by critics, so modern productions that copy them will be equally admired today.
options.C: A playwright whose plays were first staged in small rooms lit by candles must have wanted them staged that way, so modern productions should do the same.
options.D: A playwright left detailed notes on how certain scenes should be staged, so directors who follow those notes are closer to the writer's stated wishes.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A playwright whose plays were first staged in small rooms lit by candles must have wanted them staged that way, so modern productions should do the same.

option_rationales.A: This parallels paragraph 2's point about differently formed listeners, which the author endorses; it is not the error of inferring a preference from a circumstance.
option_rationales.B: This assumes that past success guarantees present success, a different flaw from confusing 'what a composer was given with what he would have chosen'.
option_rationales.D: Here the preference is documented, not inferred from what happened to be available, so the inference does not commit the error described.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 criticises the step from the fact that a composer wrote for the instruments available to the conclusion that he wanted exactly those instruments: 'To infer a preference from a circumstance'. The candle-lit staging argument makes the same step.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about audiences, which matches a different argument in the passage.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option mirrors the passage's other objection, so the solver must identify which reasoning paragraph 3 attacks.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Because authenticity is unreachable, performers should set historical research aside entirely and judge each interpretation solely by whether it succeeds as music.
options.B: Authentic performance of early music is possible only if modern audiences are first taught to hear it as its original listeners did.
options.C: Period-instrument performances, however vivid and revealing, are on the whole less faithful to what composers intended than careful performances on modern instruments.
options.D: Period-instrument performances are valuable for the musical possibilities their research uncovered, not for any success in reproducing how the music first sounded.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Period-instrument performances are valuable for the musical possibilities their research uncovered, not for any success in reproducing how the music first sounded.

option_rationales.A: The author values the research as 'a provocation' that 'led performers to hear possibilities'; setting it aside reverses the conclusion even though musical success is the final test.
option_rationales.B: The passage treats the original listeners as impossible to reconstruct and proposes no programme of re-education; this distorts paragraph 2 into a prescription.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 argues only that preferences cannot be inferred from circumstances; it does not claim modern instruments are more faithful, and paragraph 4 praises the performances.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 separates the performances, 'among the most vivid of the past century', from 'a particular way of justifying them', and concludes that they persuade 'not because they are correct ... but because the research behind them led performers to hear possibilities that habit had concealed'. The correct answer states this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about setting research aside, because it echoes 'succeed or fail as music'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option borrows the passage's final words but drops the value it places on research; separating them needs the whole of paragraph 4.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a singer who replaced the name of a town in a ballad with one her listeners knew was

options.A: following an ordinary practice of fitting the song to the audience in front of her.
options.B: damaging the song in the way the collectors feared, though for an understandable reason.
options.C: departing from the custom of her tradition, which required songs to be sung as they were learned.
options.D: making an error that later singers corrected when they learned the song from printed texts.

questions.correct_answer: (A) following an ordinary practice of fitting the song to the audience in front of her.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says such a singer 'was not corrupting a text'; the author rejects the collectors' view of change as damage.
option_rationales.C: The passage says she 'was doing what singers of such songs had always done', so she was following the custom, not breaking it.
option_rationales.D: The passage mentions later singers learning from print as an irony of fixing the songs, not as a correction of earlier errors.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the singer who 'changed the name of a town to one her listeners knew, was not corrupting a text. She was doing what singers of such songs had always done'.
questions.common_misconception: Adopting the collectors' view of variation, which the passage reports in order to reject.
questions.difficulty_reason: The relevant sentences state the point almost directly.

questions.question: The reference to the editing of ancient manuscripts in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: provide evidence that the collectors were trained as classical scholars before they turned to rural music.
options.B: trace the collectors' method to a field where it suited its object, and so show why it misfitted songs.
options.C: show that folk songs, like classical texts, descend from single originals that careful editing can recover.
options.D: suggest that the editing of manuscripts is as flawed a method as the collectors' reconstruction of songs.

questions.correct_answer: (B) trace the collectors' method to a field where it suited its object, and so show why it misfitted songs.

option_rationales.A: The passage says the picture 'borrowed its method' from manuscript editing, which concerns ideas, not the collectors' training; no biographical claim is made.
option_rationales.C: The passage draws the opposite conclusion: 'A folk song is a fundamentally different kind of object' and 'was never fixed in a single authoritative form'.
option_rationales.D: The author says the method 'makes good sense' for manuscripts, so the comparison does not criticise manuscript editing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the picture 'borrowed its method from the editing of ancient manuscripts, where it makes good sense', because a classical text was written once and copies are more or less faithful, and then states that 'A folk song is a fundamentally different kind of object'. The comparison explains the method's origin and why it does not transfer.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the comparison as a likeness between songs and texts, or as an attack on manuscript editing.
questions.difficulty_reason: The comparison works by contrast; one wrong option reads it as similarity and another over-extends the critique.

questions.question: In the final sentence, the word 'noise' refers to

options.A: differences between versions, which the collectors' theory treated as interference obscuring an original song.
options.B: the names of individual singers, which the collectors considered irrelevant to the songs themselves.
options.C: the sound of rural performances, which the collectors found rough compared with concert singing.
options.D: the many songs the collectors judged too corrupt to record and therefore left out of their notebooks.

questions.correct_answer: (A) differences between versions, which the collectors' theory treated as interference obscuring an original song.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says some collectors 'took care to record ... the names of the singers'; 'noise' is tied to 'variety', not to names.
option_rationales.C: The passage never comments on the quality of rural singing; 'noise' is used figuratively for what the theory dismissed, not for actual sound.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the collectors' notebooks saved 'a great many songs'; it does not say they rejected whole songs, and 'noise' refers to variety within songs.

questions.explanation: The sentence speaks of 'the variety which the collectors' theory taught them to regard as noise'. Paragraph 1 explains that theory: 'Variation between versions was evidence of decay' from 'an original'. Noise here means meaningless interference hiding the signal of the original.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'noise' literally as sound.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative sense must be traced back to the theory set out in paragraph 1.

questions.question: Which of the following records of a folk song would the author most likely judge the most valuable?

options.A: A single printed text carefully assembled from the best verses of several singers, with notes explaining each editorial choice.
options.B: The oldest written version of the song that survives, found in a manuscript that predates every known rural performance.
options.C: A sound recording, made with modern equipment, of the version that most singers in the region now agree is the standard and correct one.
options.D: Handwritten transcriptions of the song from six singers in different villages, each kept separate and noted with the singer's name and the occasion.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Handwritten transcriptions of the song from six singers in different villages, each kept separate and noted with the singer's name and the occasion.

option_rationales.A: This is the collectors' method criticised in paragraph 3: 'a single standard text, often assembled from several singers'; explaining the choices does not restore the variety.
option_rationales.B: Valuing the oldest version assumes an authoritative original, but the passage says a folk song 'was never fixed in a single authoritative form'.
option_rationales.C: However faithful as sound, it preserves a single version chosen as standard, which repeats the collectors' error of fixing one form and discards the variety the author values.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a record of oral music is valuable 'precisely to the extent that it preserves the variety', and praises collectors who recorded 'variants and the names of the singers'. Separate transcriptions with singers and occasions preserve exactly that variety and its context.
questions.common_misconception: Preferring the sound recording because it seems more accurate than writing, which ignores that it keeps only one version.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sound recording looks technically superior; the solver must apply the author's criterion (variety) rather than fidelity of medium.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following does a score specify with the greatest precision?

options.A: The exact speed at which a lively movement should be taken.
options.B: The pitches of the notes and the order in which they come.
options.C: How loud a passage should be in a given performance space.
options.D: How long a performer should linger at the high point of a phrase.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The pitches of the notes and the order in which they come.

option_rationales.A: A tempo word 'admits a range of speeds wide enough' to make performances sound urgent or relaxed, so speed is not exactly fixed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says a marking for a loud passage 'does not say how loud', and the right loudness depends on the room.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says 'Nothing in the marks tells the player exactly how long to linger at the high point of a phrase'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A score fixes pitches and their order with considerable precision, and durations rather less'. Every other feature listed is said to be left open or indicated only roughly.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a feature that a score does mark (loudness, tempo) without noticing that the passage says it is marked only roughly.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in the opening sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The example of a performer who takes a slow movement at double speed is used to

options.A: support the claim that a performer who alters the notes has made a mistake whatever the result sounds like.
options.B: illustrate how imprecise tempo markings allow performances of one piece to differ widely in character.
options.C: show that the view that the work is the performance cannot account for judgements musicians routinely make.
options.D: suggest that informed listeners disagree too often about tempo for any standard of performance to exist.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that the view that the work is the performance cannot account for judgements musicians routinely make.

option_rationales.A: That claim belongs to the first view, in paragraph 1; in the double-speed case the notes are not altered, and the example is aimed at the opposite view.
option_rationales.B: Imprecise tempo words are discussed in paragraph 2 as a problem for the first view; the double-speed case in paragraph 3 is a judgement of error that tells against the second view.
option_rationales.D: The passage stresses that musicians make such judgements 'constantly and with considerable agreement', the opposite of persistent disagreement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that if the score were 'merely a recipe to be finished at will, there would be no ground for such judgements', yet the double-speed performance is plainly 'worse than ... an unusual choice'. The example exposes a weakness of the view that the work simply is the performance.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the example to the wrong view, since tempo also figures in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Tempo appears in two paragraphs serving opposite purposes; the solver must track which view each example is aimed at.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a performer who plays every note exactly as written but ignores the conventions by which the style is ordinarily read has

options.A: been faithful to the work, since a performance is good to the degree that it delivers what the notation contains.
options.B: created a new work, because a work changes whenever the practice used to read its score changes.
options.C: been accurate to the marks on the page without being faithful to the work they belong to.
options.D: exercised a performer's right to complete the score in whatever way she judges best.

questions.correct_answer: (C) been accurate to the marks on the page without being faithful to the work they belong to.

option_rationales.A: This is the first view, set out in paragraph 1; the author argues that notation 'specifies far less than the view requires', so delivering the notation is not enough.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says works change only as shared practices change, 'slowly'; one performer's departure does not change the practice, and the author never says it creates a new work.
option_rationales.D: This is the second view, which the author rejects in paragraph 3; paragraph 5 adds that crossing a practice's lines 'knowingly' is 'not exercising a right'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the work is 'the marks as a practice reads them' and that 'Fidelity is owed to that combination'. A performer who honours the marks but ignores the practice satisfies only half of what fidelity requires, which is also why paragraph 3 says some performances seem 'wrong-headed even when every note is in place'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about a new work by over-reading the reply to the objection in paragraph 5.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the definition in paragraph 4 with paragraph 3 and the limits set in paragraph 5; each wrong option is a view or a distortion found in the passage.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument against the view that the work simply is the performance?

options.A: Performers and critics often disagree about the best tempo for particular movements, and both sides defend their choices at length in print.
options.B: When informed listeners independently judge performances of the same piece, their verdicts on which are wrong-headed agree no more than chance would predict.
options.C: Some modern scores specify loudness and tempo far more exactly than older scores, using numbers rather than words.
options.D: Some performers have deliberately ignored the conventions of a style and later persuaded many listeners that their readings were justified.

questions.correct_answer: (B) When informed listeners independently judge performances of the same piece, their verdicts on which are wrong-headed agree no more than chance would predict.

option_rationales.A: Disagreement about the best tempo is compatible with broad agreement that some choices are wrong; the author even notes that musicians 'argue' about performances.
option_rationales.C: This bears on the imprecision argued in paragraph 2 against the first view, not on the argument in paragraph 3 against the second.
option_rationales.D: The author allows for this: a performer who crosses the lines 'is making a claim that must be argued for', so successful argument fits the account.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 rejects the second view because it 'cannot explain' judgements of wrong-headedness that musicians make 'constantly and with considerable agreement'. If such judgements showed no real agreement, there would be nothing for the second view to fail to explain, and the argument would collapse.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about tempo disputes, which looks like disagreement but does not touch the agreement the argument relies on.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must locate the specific premise (agreement in judgements) and distinguish it from ordinary disputes and from the argument against the other view.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: propose that a work is its score as read within a shared practice, after showing two simpler views fail.
options.B: argue that because performing practices keep changing, musical works can have no stable identity from one generation to the next.
options.C: defend the traditional view that the score is the work against critics who would grant performers unlimited interpretive freedom.
options.D: show that musical notation is too imprecise to guide performers and should be made far more exact.

questions.correct_answer: (A) propose that a work is its score as read within a shared practice, after showing two simpler views fail.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 5 says only that a work's identity is 'less fixed than the first view supposed' and insists 'What does not follow is that anything goes'.
option_rationales.C: The author rejects the traditional view as well, since notation 'specifies far less than the view requires'; the passage is not a defence of either extreme.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 notes imprecision to criticise the first view, but the passage never recommends more exact notation; the practice, not better marks, fills the gap.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 set out and reject the view that the score is the work and the view that the work is the performance; paragraph 4 offers 'the marks as a practice reads them'; paragraph 5 answers an objection to that account. The purpose is to propose and defend the middle account.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the traditional-view option because the author's account preserves standards of fidelity.
questions.difficulty_reason: The traditional-view wrong option is tempting because the author keeps the idea of fidelity; the correct answer needs the full three-step structure.

questions.question: According to the passage, the length of the pause that comic actors leave before a line varies between performances because

options.A: directors change the timing of each scene during a run to keep the actors alert.
options.B: comedies are drilled less precisely than other plays and leave actors more freedom.
options.C: actors in large houses cannot see the audience and must guess when to continue.
options.D: the laughter at the previous line differs from one night to the next.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the laughter at the previous line differs from one night to the next.

option_rationales.A: No director is mentioned; paragraph 2 ties the pause to the audience's laughter, not to instructions.
option_rationales.B: The passage never compares how precisely comedies and other plays are rehearsed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says performers in large houses 'can barely see past the first rows', but this is not offered as the reason pauses vary.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: actors 'hold a line until the laughter at the previous one has crested and begun to fall, and the length of that pause differs from night to night because the laughter does'.
questions.common_misconception: Importing a detail from paragraph 4 as the cause.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence that states the cause with 'because'.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, a silence that tells the performers 'they have the room' indicates that

options.A: the performers have more physical space to move about than in a smaller theatre.
options.B: the audience has stopped responding and the actors may now ignore it.
options.C: the audience's attention is fully held by what is happening on stage.
options.D: the auditorium is full and the production has sold every seat in the house.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the audience's attention is fully held by what is happening on stage.

option_rationales.A: The sense is figurative; the paragraph contrasts this silence with a 'restless audience', not a large stage with a small one.
option_rationales.B: The silence is a response of 'a particular quality' that leads actors to stretch a moment, the opposite of an audience that has disengaged.
option_rationales.D: The phrase concerns the quality of a silence during a tense scene, not ticket sales; nothing in the paragraph refers to attendance.

questions.explanation: The silence is contrasted with 'a restless audience' and leads performers to 'let a moment stretch further'. To 'have the room' is to hold the audience's attention completely.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the idiom literally (space or seats).
questions.difficulty_reason: The idiom must be read from the contrast with a restless audience.

questions.question: The comparison with a lecture delivered in person (paragraph 1) is meant to show that

options.A: lectures, like plays, lose much of their value when they are recorded for a screen.
options.B: being physically present does not by itself make an event more valuable.
options.C: theatre is valuable chiefly because it teaches its audiences, as a lecture does.
options.D: audiences respond to lecturers in the same way that they respond to actors.

questions.correct_answer: (B) being physically present does not by itself make an event more valuable.

option_rationales.A: The author says an in-person lecture 'is not obviously better than the same lecture recorded', which denies this loss of value.
option_rationales.C: The passage nowhere assigns theatre a teaching role; the lecture is a test case for the claim that presence confers value.
option_rationales.D: Audience response is introduced only in paragraph 2 and is never attributed to lectures; the comparison concerns presence alone.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'A great many things are physically present to us without being valuable for that reason', and offers the lecture as such a case, concluding that presence alone would make the case for theatre 'something close to a superstition'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the comparison likens lectures to plays rather than testing the appeal to presence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point follows from the sentence that introduces the example, but a wrong option reverses its claim about recordings.

questions.question: Which of the following productions would the author regard as making the fullest use of what the stage offers and the screen does not?

options.A: A play in a mid-sized theatre whose cast is rehearsed to let the pacing of scenes follow the audience's reactions each night.
options.B: A play staged in a tiny room with spectators an arm's length from the actors, who are directed never to vary the timing of any line.
options.C: A play performed with such precision that critics who attend on different nights report seeing an identical performance.
options.D: A play that projects close-ups of the actors' faces onto large screens so that every spectator can see the smallest expression.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A play in a mid-sized theatre whose cast is rehearsed to let the pacing of scenes follow the audience's reactions each night.

option_rationales.B: This offers maximum proximity but suppresses responsiveness; the author says presence alone is 'close to a superstition' and that a production which suppresses responsiveness 'has given up the main thing that the stage offers'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 treats productions 'drilled to such precision that they vary little from night to night' as the case in which the live capacity goes unused.
option_rationales.D: The close-up is named in paragraph 4 as one of film's 'resources of its own'; borrowing it does not use what is distinctive to the stage.

questions.explanation: The author locates the distinctive value of the stage in 'the performance and its audience' remaining 'capable of affecting one another' (paragraph 5), a capacity a production 'can choose to use ... or to suppress'. A cast trained to let pacing follow the house uses it most fully.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the tiny-room production because it maximises presence, the argument the author rejects in paragraph 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tiny-room option matches the popular defence of theatre; rejecting it requires the passage's distinction between presence and responsiveness.

questions.question: The author would be LEAST likely to agree with which of the following?

options.A: The quality of an audience's silence can affect how long performers sustain a moment.
options.B: The familiar appeal to presence, though weak as usually stated, points the way towards a stronger defence of theatre.
options.C: Film possesses expressive means of its own, such as the close-up, that the stage does not share.
options.D: Every live production is responsive to its audience to some degree, even when spectators do not notice it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Every live production is responsive to its audience to some degree, even when spectators do not notice it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says such a silence tells performers 'they have the room', and 'they may let a moment stretch further'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'A more promising answer begins from what presence makes possible', so the author builds the better argument from the weak one.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'Film ... has resources of its own, the close-up and the edit among them'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 calls responsiveness 'a capacity of the live form, not a guarantee', adding that 'a production can choose to use it or to suppress it' and that one may suppress it 'entirely'. The claim that every production is responsive contradicts this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the presence option because the author criticises the appeal to presence, missing that paragraph 2 develops it into the better answer.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer sounds sympathetic to the author's account of liveness; it is refuted only by the qualification in paragraph 4, while one wrong option seems to clash with paragraph 1 but is endorsed in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that

options.A: a mistake that many people repeat with one object usually signals poor design rather than personal carelessness.
options.B: every error that people make with everyday objects is the fault of the designers who made those objects.
options.C: written signs and printed warnings are useless and should be removed from doors, appliances and public buildings.
options.D: designers ought to test every new product on hurried first-time users before it is allowed to reach the market.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a mistake that many people repeat with one object usually signals poor design rather than personal carelessness.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that 'every mistake is the designer's fault' and allows that 'some carelessness is simply carelessness'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says only that people follow the hardware when it disagrees with the sign; it does not call signs useless or propose removing them, so the option is extreme.
option_rationales.D: The passage explains why designers misjudge their objects but never proposes a testing rule; the option turns a diagnosis into a prescription the author does not make.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 questions the automatic verdict of carelessness, paragraph 2 explains why designers misjudge what their objects say, paragraph 3 shows the cost of blaming users, and paragraph 4 concludes that repeated mistakes point 'less at the people than at the thing they all share'. The correct answer states this central claim with its limit.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the absolute version of the thesis and missing the concession in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated plainly in the first and last paragraphs; one wrong option is a clear overstatement.

questions.question: According to the passage, when the hardware on a door and the sign above it give conflicting messages, people tend to

options.A: stop and read the sign with care before deciding whether they should push the door or pull it.
options.B: wait until someone else uses the door so that they can copy whatever that person does first.
