options.C: act on what the shape of the hardware suggests, since form is read faster than printed words.
options.D: push the door whatever its fittings, since pushing is the most natural movement for someone in a hurry.

questions.correct_answer: (C) act on what the shape of the hardware suggests, since form is read faster than printed words.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: 'people follow the hardware', since 'the shape of a thing is read faster than words are'.
option_rationales.B: Copying other people is never mentioned; paragraph 2 says people simply follow the hardware.
option_rationales.D: The passage says a flat plate invites pushing and a vertical bar invites pulling; it never claims that people push regardless of the fittings.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'When the hardware and the sign disagree, people follow the hardware, and they are not foolish to do so, since the shape of a thing is read faster than words are.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that careful people would obey the written sign, which is the assumption the passage rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer is located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: At a railway station, many passengers keep inserting their tickets upside down into the entry gates. Which response would the author most clearly favour?

options.A: Placing staff beside each gate to remind passengers, politely but firmly, how to hold their tickets.
options.B: Fining passengers who jam the gates, so that they learn to take more care with their tickets next time.
options.C: Printing a large red arrow on every ticket showing passengers which way up it should be inserted.
options.D: Reshaping the slot and ticket so that a ticket can enter the gate only the right way up.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Reshaping the slot and ticket so that a ticket can enter the gate only the right way up.

option_rationales.A: This asks individuals to try harder, the remedy paragraph 3 says leaves the error in place for the next person; it does not change the design.
option_rationales.B: Penalising individuals is the response of an organisation that blames users, like the hospital that disciplines the nurse in paragraph 3.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 lists 'more signs' and 'warnings printed in red' as the remedies of the blaming habit, and paragraph 2 says people follow form rather than written cues.

questions.explanation: The author argues that errors attributed to design are cured by 'changing the design, which removes the error for everyone at once' (paragraph 3), and that a repeated mistake points at the shared object (paragraph 4). Reshaping the slot so the wrong insertion is impossible is that kind of change.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the printed arrow because it seems like a design change, when the passage classes signs and warnings with the blaming response.
questions.difficulty_reason: The printed arrow is tempting; the solver must recall that paragraph 3 groups signs and warnings with asking people to try harder.

questions.question: The hospital example in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: show that hospital staff are, as a rule, more careless than the people working in most other occupations.
options.B: contrast what follows from treating a mistake as a personal failing with treating it as a design problem.
options.C: illustrate the claim that look-alike containers are the most common cause of serious errors in hospitals.
options.D: prove that disciplining an employee never does anything at all to reduce the number of mistakes made at work.

questions.correct_answer: (B) contrast what follows from treating a mistake as a personal failing with treating it as a design problem.

option_rationales.A: The example is introduced as an imagined case about bottles, and nothing in it compares the carefulness of nurses with that of other workers.
option_rationales.C: No claim about the most common cause of hospital errors is made; the bottles are one hypothetical case.
option_rationales.D: The passage says the hospital 'may' still find the confusion repeated; the option's never and prove overstate this hedged illustration.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 first states that individual blame leads to more signs and training while design blame leads to a changed design. The hospital case then shows both paths: disciplining the nurse leaves the confusion to recur, while making the bottles different 'removes the occasion for the mistake altogether'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the illustration as a factual claim about hospitals instead of as an illustration of the two remedies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by the sentences that immediately precede the example.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the admirers' account of vernacular building is best described as

options.A: dismissive, since the author regards their claims about the climatic benefits of traditional building forms as simply mistaken.
options.B: indifferent, since the author treats vernacular building as a subject of purely historical interest today.
options.C: appreciative of what it gets right, but critical of the idealised picture of the past that it presents.
options.D: wholly approving, since the author endorses their call for modern builders to copy traditional forms directly in their own work.

questions.correct_answer: (C) appreciative of what it gets right, but critical of the idealised picture of the past that it presents.

option_rationales.A: The author grants 'There is much truth in this' and does not dispute that thick walls keep rooms cool; the objection is to how kindly the story is told.
option_rationales.B: The author says vernacular building remains 'worth studying' and draws a lesson from it for modern builders, so indifference is wrong.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says a builder who copies the outward shape of a courtyard house elsewhere 'has learned nothing from it', which rejects that call.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens 'There is much truth in this, but the story is told too kindly', then explains how the record is filtered and how scarcity shaped the forms. The author keeps the account's insight while rejecting its idealisation.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the criticism in paragraph 2 as a total rejection and overlooking 'much truth'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tone is announced in a single signposted sentence at the start of paragraph 2.

questions.question: According to the passage, village builders used earth for their walls chiefly because

options.A: it was found close at hand and cost nothing to bring to the building site.
options.B: the hot climate made thick earth walls the only kind that could keep their rooms cool.
options.C: it was the walling material that took the least labour to keep in good repair from year to year.
options.D: they had compared it with the other available materials and judged it to be the best of them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) it was found close at hand and cost nothing to bring to the building site.

option_rationales.B: The passage says earth walls keep rooms cool but attributes the choice of earth to its availability and cost, not to its being the only cooling option.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says an earth wall may be 'laborious to patch every year', which is the reverse of this.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 denies this directly: 'not because they had compared it with every other material and found it best'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'People built with earth because earth lay underfoot and cost nothing to carry, not because they had compared it with every other material and found it best.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that because thick walls are cool, coolness must have been the reason for choosing earth.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is stated in one sentence, and two wrong options are explicitly contradicted.

questions.question: The remark that the failures 'left nothing for us to photograph' (paragraph 2) suggests that

options.A: most of the vernacular buildings ever put up have since collapsed or been abandoned by their communities.
options.B: a judgement of traditional building drawn only from surviving examples is likely to overstate how well it worked.
options.C: early photographers of the countryside chose to record only the most handsome and best built village houses they found.
options.D: traditional communities deliberately destroyed their failed buildings in order to hide their mistakes from later generations.

questions.correct_answer: (B) a judgement of traditional building drawn only from surviving examples is likely to overstate how well it worked.

option_rationales.A: The passage says failures existed and left no trace; it says nothing about their proportion, so the claim about most such buildings is unsupported.
option_rationales.C: The remark is about what survived to be seen, not about choices made by photographers, who are never discussed.
option_rationales.D: Nothing suggests deliberate destruction or concealment; the failures simply collapsed or were abandoned.

questions.explanation: The next sentence explains the remark: 'What we see is therefore a filtered record, and it flatters the past.' Because only successes survive, a view based on what survives will judge the tradition too favourably.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'photograph' literally and choosing the option about photographers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figurative remark must be connected to the 'filtered record' sentence; one wrong option overstates by quantity.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as having genuinely learned from vernacular building?

options.A: A builder who uses thick earth walls on every project in every region, on the ground that earth is the traditional material.
options.B: A developer who reproduces the domed earth roofs of a desert village on a housing estate in a cold and rainy northern city.
options.C: An engineer who abandons all traditional materials and relies on mechanical cooling, since village forms were shaped by poverty.
options.D: An architect in a humid coastal town who records how a trial house behaves through a monsoon and revises the next design.

questions.correct_answer: (D) An architect in a humid coastal town who records how a trial house behaves through a monsoon and revises the next design.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 praises knowledge that is 'local by necessity'; applying one traditional material everywhere ignores local conditions.
option_rationales.B: This copies 'the outward shape' into 'a different climate', which paragraph 4 says means having 'learned nothing'.
option_rationales.C: The author says vernacular building remains 'worth studying' and holds a lesson in its method; rejecting it outright learns nothing from it.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 3 and 4 locate the lesson in the method: adjusting 'slowly and continuously to the conditions in front of them', and a builder who 'builds, watches what happens and is willing to revise'. The coastal architect does exactly this, even though the building need not look like a village house.
questions.common_misconception: Equating learning from tradition with reproducing traditional forms or materials.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options honour tradition on the surface; the solver must apply the method versus form distinction.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'an undifferentiated cliff' refers to

options.A: a wall whose stone has weathered so unevenly over the years that it now resembles a natural rock face.
options.B: a facade so heavily carved and moulded that the eye can no longer pick out its individual parts.
options.C: a tall wall offering no visible divisions by which someone passing could judge how big it is.
options.D: a building constructed on the edge of a steep slope, so that it seems to rise directly from the rock.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a tall wall offering no visible divisions by which someone passing could judge how big it is.

option_rationales.A: Weathering is discussed in a separate sentence about mouldings; the cliff image is about the absence of divisions that show scale.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the image: the cliff is what a wall becomes without the band of moulding, not a wall with too much ornament.
option_rationales.D: The phrase is a metaphor for a featureless wall; nothing in paragraph 2 concerns a site on a slope.

questions.explanation: The phrase is contrasted with sensing 'the height of the building in storeys', which the band of moulding makes possible. Without such divisions, the wall reads as one featureless mass that the eye cannot measure.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the metaphor literally as a geological or site feature.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contrast that defines the phrase sits in the same sentence.

questions.question: The author implies that the progressive architects described in paragraph 1

options.A: recognised as genuine uses only those functions that would show up in a structural calculation.
options.B: produced no buildings of lasting value, since their designs ignored what people on the street needed.
options.C: eventually gave up their position once the shortcomings of plain buildings became widely known.
options.D: were motivated above all by a wish to lower building costs and only later found moral reasons for their view.

questions.correct_answer: (A) recognised as genuine uses only those functions that would show up in a structural calculation.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 grants that the argument 'produced buildings of great clarity', so the author does not deny them all value.
option_rationales.C: The passage never says the architects changed their minds; their later history is outside its scope.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 lists cost as one strand of their argument and says it 'had moral force'; nothing suggests cost was the main motive or that morality came later.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says their argument 'rested on a narrow idea of what counts as use', and paragraph 2 lists the work ornament does before concluding 'These are uses, though not of the kind that appear in a structural calculation'. The implication is that the critics counted only the calculable kind.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the cost option because cost appears in the critics' argument, without noticing that the author's objection concerns the definition of use.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer joins a phrase in paragraph 1 with the last sentence of paragraph 2; the cost option reuses a real detail.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claims about blank walls in paragraph 3?

options.A: Much of the ornament on older commercial buildings was copied from pattern books with no thought for its purpose.
options.B: Strangers asked to find the entrances of plain modern buildings do so as quickly as visitors to richly ornamented ones.
options.C: Several plain modern buildings are widely admired by the public for the clarity and simplicity of their design.
options.D: Ornamented buildings turn out to cost considerably more to build and to maintain than plain buildings of a similar size.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Strangers asked to find the entrances of plain modern buildings do so as quickly as visitors to richly ornamented ones.

option_rationales.A: The author already concedes that applied ornament of this kind is dishonest, so the finding is consistent with the passage.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 already grants that the plain approach 'produced buildings of great clarity'; admiration does not show that blank walls tell strangers where to go in.
option_rationales.D: Cost was the critics' argument, and the author never denies it; it leaves untouched the claim that blank walls fail people on the street.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims a blank wall 'tells the stranger nothing about where to go in'. If strangers find the entrances of plain buildings as easily as those of ornamented ones, a central part of that claim fails.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a fact that favours the critics in general (cost, admiration) rather than one that hits the specific claim about blank walls.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are all pro-critic facts; only one bears on the author's specific claim.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the position the passage argues for?

options.A: Ornament and structural honesty are incompatible, so every architect must decide which of the two a building will sacrifice.
options.B: Traditional ornament should now be revived everywhere, because plain modern buildings have proved to be dishonest about their structure and their purposes.
options.C: The critics of ornament were right in principle but wrong to apply their principle to the commercial building of their own day.
options.D: Ornament should be judged by what it does for people at street level, a test that some ornamented and some plain buildings fail.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Ornament should be judged by what it does for people at street level, a test that some ornamented and some plain buildings fail.

option_rationales.A: The author never says they conflict; ornament that does real work is not called dishonest, and the conclusion asks what ornament is for rather than forcing a choice.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls the plain building 'honest about its structure', and paragraph 4 rules out pastiche, so neither the charge nor the call for revival is the author's.
option_rationales.C: This reverses paragraph 3, which says the critics were right precisely about the commercial ornament of their day and wrong in the remedy they chose.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 replaces the question 'whether a building should be ornamented' with 'what its ornament is for', and says this rules out both 'pastiche' and 'austerity that passes itself off as rigour'. Paragraphs 2 and 3 supply the test: what ornament does for a stranger, for the eye at walking pace, for weathering.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the defence of ornament as a call to revive it, and missing that the test cuts against pastiche too.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option captures part of the debate; the correct answer needs the two-sided conclusion and the redefinition of use together.

questions.question: According to the passage, in earlier periods irregularity in a crafted object was generally regarded as

options.A: a decorative effect that weavers and potters added at the end to make each piece distinctive.
options.B: a welcome trace of the material's character that a master would leave deliberately in place.
options.C: a sign of inexperience or haste, which skilled makers took pride in removing from their work.
options.D: the proof that a person rather than a machine had made the object, which buyers valued most of all.

questions.correct_answer: (C) a sign of inexperience or haste, which skilled makers took pride in removing from their work.

option_rationales.A: Irregularity is never described as an added decoration in the past; regularity was the aim.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says 'the master's pride lay in eliminating it', which contradicts deliberate preservation.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says this is how irregularity is regarded 'Today, by contrast', not in earlier periods.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Irregularity was the mark of an apprentice or of a hurried job, and the master's pride lay in eliminating it.'
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the past view with the present one that the paragraph contrasts it with.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer is stated in one sentence; the most tempting wrong option is the 'today' view in the same paragraph.

questions.question: The phrase 'a premium paid for a story' (paragraph 2) implies that, if irregularity is what buyers value,

options.A: the extra price buys a belief about how an object was made, not a quality visible in it.
options.B: buyers knowingly pay more for objects whose irregularities they understand to be produced by machines.
options.C: the prices of handmade goods are set mainly by advertising rather than by the cost of the materials used.
options.D: handmade goods are usually sold together with invented accounts of the lives of the people who made them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the extra price buys a belief about how an object was made, not a quality visible in it.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says buyers 'cannot tell' simulated irregularity from the real thing, so they are not paying knowingly.
option_rationales.C: Advertising and material costs are never discussed; the point concerns what the premium is paid for, not how prices are set.
option_rationales.D: The 'story' is the buyer's belief that a person made the object, not a sales narrative; invented biographies are never mentioned.

questions.explanation: If irregularity can be forged undetectably, an irregular object looks the same whether a person or a machine made it. What the extra money secures is then only the account of its origin, not anything visible in the object.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'story' literally as marketing copy.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires linking the forgery argument to the meaning of the metaphor.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: An ordinary buyer is generally unable to distinguish simulated irregularity from that of a hand-thrown piece.
options.B: A weaver may adjust the work in progress in response to changes in the moisture of the surrounding air.
options.C: Some goods that are sold as handmade are produced without any attention to the particular piece being made.
options.D: Machines are in principle incapable of responding to the particular qualities of the material they work on.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Machines are in principle incapable of responding to the particular qualities of the material they work on.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'an ordinary buyer cannot tell it from the real thing', so this is supported.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says a weaver 'feels the tension of the warp change with the damp in the air and corrects for it', so this is supported.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'much of what is sold as handmade' would fail the test of attention to the particular, so this is supported.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states that 'Machines can be built to sense and respond to their material', which contradicts the correct answer. Paragraph 3 says only that a machine-made irregularity 'responds to nothing', which concerns simulated irregularity, not what machines can do in principle.
questions.common_misconception: Generalising the remark in paragraph 3 about machine-made irregularity into a claim about all machines.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer echoes paragraph 3 and must be checked against the concession in paragraph 4.

questions.question: By the test proposed in the final paragraph, which of the following would most clearly count as craft?

options.A: A factory press that stamps a different random dent into every metal bowl so that no two bowls are ever identical.
options.B: A bread machine that measures the moisture of each batch of flour and changes its kneading time to suit that batch.
options.C: A hand-knitted scarf made by repeating a fixed chart row after row, without any notice taken when the yarn thickens.
options.D: A workshop in which each worker performs one hand motion all day on identical parts that have been cut in advance.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A bread machine that measures the moisture of each batch of flour and changes its kneading time to suit that batch.

option_rationales.A: This is the forged irregularity of paragraph 2: a pattern 'generated in advance and imposed on material treated as uniform', responding to nothing.
option_rationales.C: The knitting is done by hand but without 'attention to the particular' material, which paragraph 4 says decides the matter, not the hand.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 names this as hand production 'as mechanical as anything in a factory', which the test excludes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the line 'is not drawn by the presence of a hand' but by 'whether the making involved attention to the particular', and that machines 'can be built to sense and respond to their material'. The bread machine responds to each batch, so by that test it counts as craft.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a handmade option because it involves a hand, which the final paragraph says is not the criterion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Counter-intuitive answer: the only machine option is right and the hand-made options are wrong, which requires applying the final test strictly.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, 'strangely inert' describes manuals that

options.A: are rarely read, because they sit unopened in libraries long after their publication.
options.B: fail to make their readers competent even though what they record is accurate.
options.C: are written in such dry and technical prose that ordinary readers lose interest in them.
options.D: contain so many errors of measurement that following them leads readers astray.

questions.correct_answer: (B) fail to make their readers competent even though what they record is accurate.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says readers do follow the manuals, step by step; the problem is the result, not neglect.
option_rationales.C: Nothing is said about the style of the prose; 'inert' refers to the manuals' failure to produce competent work.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 calls the manuals 'careful, accurate and lovingly illustrated', so errors are not the problem.

questions.explanation: The colon after 'strangely inert' explains it: 'the reader can follow every step and still produce work that a practitioner would reject at a glance', even though the manuals are 'careful, accurate'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'inert' to mean dull or unused rather than ineffective.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is glossed in the same sentence.

questions.question: The example of metal that 'turns the colour of straw' (paragraph 2) is used to show that

options.A: a spoken or written instruction can rely on the very perception that it is meant to pass on.
options.B: manuals would succeed if their authors replaced comparisons with precise measurements of temperature.
options.C: colour is a less dependable guide to the heat of iron than the sound or feel of the work.
options.D: smiths historically chose vague comparisons on purpose, so as to keep their methods secret from outsiders.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a spoken or written instruction can rely on the very perception that it is meant to pass on.

option_rationales.B: The passage proposes no such fix, and its argument implies that the difficulty lies in perception, not in imprecise wording.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 gives sight, sound and touch as parallel examples and does not rank them for reliability.
option_rationales.D: Secrecy appears only in paragraph 4, about guilds; the straw example concerns a limit of description, not a deliberate choice.

questions.explanation: The sentence before the example says 'the description presupposes the perception it describes'. The straw instruction illustrates this: it helps only someone who 'already knows which straw, in which light, and how much variation is allowed'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the example as evidence about smithing itself rather than about the limits of description.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the link between the example and the general claim that precedes it; two wrong options offer plausible practical readings.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the master's repeated 'now' and 'not yet' were valuable chiefly because they

options.A: reminded the apprentice of rules that he had already learned from older written sources on the craft.
options.B: kept the apprentice obedient and dependent on the master during the long years of his training.
options.C: joined words to what the apprentice was perceiving at that instant, gradually training where he looked.
options.D: supplied a fixed technical vocabulary that could later be collected and published in manuals.

questions.correct_answer: (C) joined words to what the apprentice was perceiving at that instant, gradually training where he looked.

option_rationales.A: The passage treats apprenticeship as an alternative to written instruction, so recalling written rules is not its role.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 calls apprenticeship 'often exploitative', but paragraph 3 explains the value of the words as guidance of perception, not control.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the words worked 'as pointers to experiences the learner was having at that very moment', not as a vocabulary for later writing.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the words mattered 'chiefly as pointers to experiences the learner was having at that very moment', and what passed on was 'a trained attention'. Their value lay in fixing the apprentice's attention on the right perception at the right moment.
questions.common_misconception: Importing the criticism in paragraph 4 into the explanation of how apprenticeship worked.
questions.difficulty_reason: The exploitation option uses a genuine claim from another paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's argument?

options.A: Some tasks, such as baking a cake from a printed recipe, can be learned almost entirely from written instructions.
options.B: Many apprentices in earlier centuries left their masters before finishing their training because they were badly treated and poorly fed.
options.C: Experienced joiners who read a good manual improved their technique noticeably over the following months of ordinary work.
options.D: Novices who studied only a detailed manual for a year matched, in masters' judgement, apprentices trained for that year.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Novices who studied only a detailed manual for a year matched, in masters' judgement, apprentices trained for that year.

option_rationales.A: The author contrasts craft with 'a recipe', implying recipes can be stored in text; the finding agrees with the passage.
option_rationales.B: This fits paragraph 4, which calls apprenticeship 'often exploitative'; it says nothing about whether texts can transmit craft perception.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 already grants that a written account helps 'a learner who has already begun to see', so this is consistent with the argument.

questions.explanation: The argument holds that craft knowledge is trained perception that texts cannot supply to a beginner. If complete novices reached apprentice standard from a manual alone, the central claim that a craft 'cannot be stored in a text' would be undermined.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a fact that is critical of apprenticeship, which the author has already conceded, instead of one that attacks the thesis about texts.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options concern the right topics and match concessions in the passage; only the correct answer strikes the core claim.

questions.question: According to the passage, those who favour conserving a building's layers want new work to be distinguishable from old work so that

options.A: visitors can see the building as it was meant to be seen by its very first builders.
options.B: the cost of each repair can be estimated separately from the value of the surviving parts.
options.C: later additions such as staircases and windows can be removed easily whenever they are no longer wanted.
options.D: nobody later takes a modern reconstruction for part of the building's original fabric.

questions.correct_answer: (D) nobody later takes a modern reconstruction for part of the building's original fabric.

option_rationales.A: This is the aim of restoration, described in paragraph 1, not of the conservers in paragraph 2.
option_rationales.B: Cost is never mentioned; paragraph 2 gives the reason as preventing anyone from mistaking 'a modern guess for an original fact'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 wants later additions kept, and the distinguishability rule concerns new work, not removal of earlier layers.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: new work should be 'distinguishable from the old, so that no one mistakes a modern guess for an original fact'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the restorers' goal from paragraph 1 to the conservers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reason is given in a single clause of paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a conservator who leaves a hurried partition in place over an important painted ceiling has

options.A: made a judgement about which part of the building's past matters, though it may look like simple restraint.
options.B: acted correctly, since a conservator's first duty is to keep every layer that happens to have survived.
options.C: behaved exactly as a restorer would, by imposing a modern idea of the past upon the building.
options.D: avoided interpreting the building at all, leaving the question of its meaning to later generations.

questions.correct_answer: (A) made a judgement about which part of the building's past matters, though it may look like simple restraint.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'Not every layer is worth keeping' and gives this very case as one where keeping is questionable.
option_rationales.C: A restorer strips later additions; leaving the partition is the opposite act, even though both involve a choice.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says 'refusing to remove it is itself a choice about which history matters', so the conservator has interpreted.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 uses this example to show that conservation 'is not as neutral as its defenders sometimes suggest': refusing to remove the partition 'is itself a choice about which history matters'.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the conservators' claim to neutrality, which the author is qualifying.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting 'acted correctly' option matches the author's general preference for conservation but not this case.

questions.question: The sentence 'Keeping everything is also an interpretation' (paragraph 3) functions to

options.A: give a practical example of a layer that ought to be removed in order to reveal something older.
options.B: extend the author's qualification by showing that even refusing to remove anything involves a judgement.
options.C: withdraw the author's earlier preference for conservation and move the argument towards restoration instead.
options.D: introduce a criticism of restoration that the defenders of conservation had not previously considered.

questions.correct_answer: (B) extend the author's qualification by showing that even refusing to remove anything involves a judgement.

option_rationales.A: The practical example is the partition in the previous sentence; this sentence generalises from it to a claim about interpretation.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph opens 'I find the second answer more persuasive', and paragraph 4 confirms the preference, so nothing is withdrawn.
option_rationales.D: The sentence criticises an assumption of conservation's defenders, namely its neutrality, not restoration.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 qualifies the author's support for conservation by denying its neutrality. After the partition example, this sentence generalises: keeping everything 'values continuity over quality' and so is itself an interpretation, leading to 'The conservator, no less than the restorer, decides what the building will say'.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a qualification of the preferred view for a change of side.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing the sentence as part of a concession that sets up the final paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Restoration is preferable whenever reliable evidence of a building's original state survives, and conservation is preferable otherwise.
options.B: Neither approach can be preferred to the other, since each of them is equally an interpretation of a building's past.
options.C: Both approaches interpret the past, but conservation is preferable because it leaves its interpretations open to later correction.
options.D: Conservation is preferable to restoration because, unlike restoration, it preserves buildings without imposing any interpretation on their history.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Both approaches interpret the past, but conservation is preferable because it leaves its interpretations open to later correction.

option_rationales.A: The passage never makes the choice depend on the evidence available; it prefers conservation on the ground of reversibility.
option_rationales.B: The author does prefer one, saying conservation 'deserves the benefit of the doubt' because its mistakes can be corrected.
option_rationales.D: Paragraphs 3 and 4 deny exactly this: 'The conservator, no less than the restorer, decides', and the difference 'is not that one interprets and the other does not'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 concedes that conservation also interprets; paragraph 4 locates the difference in visibility and reversibility and concludes that 'the approach that allows its mistakes to be corrected deserves the benefit of the doubt'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that states the author's preference with the usual justification, which the author explicitly rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The strongest wrong option gets the preference right and the reason wrong; another gets the premise right and the conclusion wrong.

questions.question: According to the passage, people who appear in the typical photographs of a new building are there mainly to

options.A: make the empty rooms look warmer and more welcoming than they would otherwise appear.
options.B: hide the defects in finishes and furnishings that had not yet been completed on the day.
options.C: indicate the size of the spaces rather than to show how the building is actually used.
options.D: show prospective occupants what it will feel like to live or work in the building.

questions.correct_answer: (C) indicate the size of the spaces rather than to show how the building is actually used.

option_rationales.A: No such purpose is mentioned; the passage states that people are included only to give scale.
option_rationales.B: The passage never says the photographs conceal unfinished work; people are small and blurred and serve to give scale.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 says people are 'present to give scale rather than to show use', which rules this out.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'people, if they appear at all, are small and blurred, present to give scale rather than to show use'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that people in a photograph must be there to show occupation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one clause of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The contrast between white render and brick at the end of paragraph 3 suggests that

options.A: photographers deliberately light brick buildings so that they look duller than they really are on opening day.
options.B: brick should be preferred to white render in all new buildings, whatever their purpose or setting.
options.C: occupants are usually happier in buildings faced with brick than in those finished with white render.
options.D: how a material looks when new can mislead about its long-term merits, which opening-day images cannot reveal.

questions.correct_answer: (D) how a material looks when new can mislead about its long-term merits, which opening-day images cannot reveal.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'There is nothing sinister' in the photographer's work; the dullness of new brick is a property of the material.
option_rationales.B: The author draws no universal prescription; the contrast illustrates a point about judging at opening, and render 'often', not always, weathers badly.
option_rationales.C: The satisfaction of occupants with materials is never discussed; the contrast concerns appearance over time.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists 'the dignity with which a material ages' among qualities a single frame cannot register. Render photographs well but 'often weathers badly', while brick 'may look better in its fiftieth year than in its first', so judging at opening favours the wrong one.
questions.common_misconception: Turning an illustration into a recommendation about materials.
questions.difficulty_reason: The illustration must be tied back to the claim about single-frame qualities; the prescription option is tempting.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It grants the factual claims of the photograph's defenders while arguing that they leave the author's real objection untouched.
options.B: It argues that critics should judge only those buildings that they have visited and experienced in person over time.
options.C: It admits that the author's criticism of photography has been overstated and partly withdraws the charge made in paragraph 3.
options.D: It shows that architectural drawings were a more honest medium than photographs for judging the merits of buildings.

questions.correct_answer: (A) It grants the factual claims of the photograph's defenders while arguing that they leave the author's real objection untouched.

option_rationales.B: This is the alternative the defenders call 'parochial', and the author does not contest it; the remedy offered is a second look, not personal visits.
option_rationales.C: The author says 'none of them reaches the central point', so nothing is withdrawn; paragraph 5 goes on to propose a remedy for the problem.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says photographs flatter just as 'drawings did too', so drawings are not presented as more honest.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 reports three points made by defenders and calls them 'fair', then adds that 'none of them reaches the central point': the complaint is about photographing becoming 'the moment of judgement', not about flattery.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'Each of these points is fair' as a retreat, or attributing the defenders' rejected alternative to the author.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph both concedes and rebuts, and the solver must separate the defenders' claims from the author's reply.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that architects have come to 'design for the photograph'?

options.A: Buildings that win major architectural awards are photographed far more often, and more widely published, than ordinary buildings.
options.B: Over several decades, award-winning designs show ever more dramatic visual features alongside steadily less attention to acoustics and weathering.
options.C: Many prominent architects say in interviews that they dislike the way photographers present their completed buildings.
options.D: Occupants of celebrated buildings report problems with heat and leaks at about the same rate as occupants of ordinary buildings.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Over several decades, award-winning designs show ever more dramatic visual features alongside steadily less attention to acoustics and weathering.

option_rationales.A: This fits the claim that rewards follow the photograph but shows no change in how architects design, which is what the claim asserts.
option_rationales.C: Architects' views of photographers do not show that their designs have shifted toward photogenic qualities; it is beside the point.
option_rationales.D: If anything this suggests celebrated buildings perform no worse in use, which cuts against rather than supports the author's concern.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that a profession 'whose rewards follow the photograph' will favour single-frame qualities over those experienced 'over time or through the other senses', naming acoustics and ageing. Evidence that rewarded designs moved toward visual drama while attention to acoustics and weathering fell supports exactly that shift.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about awards and photographs, which confirms the incentive but not the change in design that the claim is about.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option supports a premise but not the conclusion; separating the two requires precise reading of the claim.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: showing how judging buildings through opening-day images skews both criticism and design toward what one frame can show.
options.B: contrasting the honesty of architects' hand drawings with the distortions that were later introduced by the camera.
options.C: exposing the ways in which architectural photographers misrepresent buildings so that their clients' work becomes easier to sell.
options.D: arguing that critics ought to visit buildings in person instead of relying on published photographs of them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) showing how judging buildings through opening-day images skews both criticism and design toward what one frame can show.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says drawings idealised buildings too; the passage does not contrast their honesty with photography.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'There is nothing sinister in this'; the author does not accuse photographers of misrepresentation.
option_rationales.D: The author accepts that judging only what one has visited would be 'parochial' and proposes a second photographed look instead.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 describe how photographs fix reputations at opening, paragraph 3 extends the effect to design, paragraph 4 defends the point against objections, and paragraph 5 proposes a second look. The correct answer covers both criticism and design.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the personal-visits option because it sounds like a natural cure, though the author accepts the objection to it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are plausible attitudes toward photography that the passage explicitly sets aside.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'slack' most nearly means

options.A: carelessness in construction that leaves a building unfinished or poorly fitted for its purpose.
options.B: a period of low demand during which an old building stands empty before it is converted.
options.C: spare capacity in a building's dimensions and structure beyond what its first use demanded.
options.D: the freedom given to occupants to move partitions and walls to wherever they please.

questions.correct_answer: (C) spare capacity in a building's dimensions and structure beyond what its first use demanded.

option_rationales.A: The author praises slack as the source of adaptability; it is not presented as a fault of workmanship.
option_rationales.B: The passage defines slack by listing physical features: larger dimensions, simple structure, surfaces that can be cut into.
option_rationales.D: This is 'flexibility in the engineered sense', which paragraph 3 explicitly contrasts with slack.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 defines the term with a colon: 'dimensions a little larger than any one use required, a structure simple enough to be understood by ordinary builders, and surfaces that can be cut into without catastrophe'.
questions.common_misconception: Equating slack with the engineered flexibility that the passage sets it against.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option describes the very idea the term is contrasted with.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, an old mill and a flexible-plan office differ chiefly in that

options.A: the mill fitted its original use exactly, whereas the flexible-plan office failed to fit any particular use at all.
options.B: the mill is built of more durable materials, which is the main reason it has outlasted the flexible-plan office.
options.C: the mill's builders anticipated the uses it would later be put to, whereas the office's designers did not foresee change.
options.D: the mill adapts because it is generously and simply built, whereas the office relied on mechanisms its users seldom worked.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the mill adapts because it is generously and simply built, whereas the office relied on mechanisms its users seldom worked.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says such buildings 'fit their first use loosely'; an exact fit is what paragraph 4 calls brittle.
option_rationales.B: Thick walls are mentioned, but the passage attributes adaptability to slack, not durability, and never says the offices failed to last.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says the adaptable buildings 'were never designed with change in mind', while the flexible offices were designed for change; this reverses both.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the flexible plans depended on partitions that 'were seldom moved', and paragraph 3 attributes the mills' adaptability to 'slack' rather than 'flexibility in the engineered sense'. The difference lies in where adaptability comes from.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the adaptable building must have been designed for change, the opposite of the passage's paradox.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining paragraphs 2 and 3; each wrong option misplaces one element of the contrast.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to what the author calls loose fit?

options.A: A jacket with zip-off sleeves and detachable panels for every season, which most of its owners never trouble to change.
options.B: A suit cut with generous seam allowances, so that tailors in later years can let it out or take it in as its wearer changes.
options.C: A coat made in a single standard size that hangs badly on every customer and offers no margin at all for alteration.
options.D: A suit tailored precisely to its wearer's measurements for a wedding day and much admired for the perfection of its fit.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A suit cut with generous seam allowances, so that tailors in later years can let it out or take it in as its wearer changes.

option_rationales.A: This parallels the flexible plan of paragraph 2, with movable parts that are 'seldom moved', which the author contrasts with loose fit.
option_rationales.C: Loose fit suits its first use and leaves room to alter; this coat fits nobody and cannot be altered, so it shares neither feature.
option_rationales.D: This is the exact fit of paragraph 4, 'admirable on the day of opening and brittle thereafter'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes buildings that 'fit their first use loosely' and have spare dimensions and fabric 'that can be cut into without catastrophe', so ordinary builders can adapt them. A suit with generous seams fits now and can be altered later by ordinary tailoring.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the detachable jacket because it seems adaptable, when it corresponds to engineered flexibility.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option maps onto a concept in the passage, so the solver must match the precise structure of loose fit.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why old warehouses and mills proved so adaptable?

options.A: Warehouses with low ceilings and irregular columns proved as easy to convert as those with generous ceilings and regular grids.
options.B: Most warehouses and mills were built without the slightest expectation that people would one day live or work in them.
options.C: Flexible-plan offices built in recent decades have been demolished far more often than old warehouses in the same districts.
options.D: Some warehouses converted into flats were later returned to storage when the demand for housing in their district fell.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Warehouses with low ceilings and irregular columns proved as easy to convert as those with generous ceilings and regular grids.

option_rationales.B: This matches paragraph 3, which says such buildings 'were never designed with change in mind'.
option_rationales.C: This fits the author's contrast between engineered flexibility and slack, and so if anything supports the account.
option_rationales.D: Being converted again shows further adaptability, which is consistent with the author's account rather than a challenge to it.

questions.explanation: The author attributes the warehouses' adaptability to slack, including 'regular grids of columns' and 'generous ceiling heights'. If buildings lacking those features converted just as well, those features would not explain the result.
questions.common_misconception: Selecting a fact about warehouses that seems surprising but is consistent with the author's account.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options are all on topic and two of them sound like evidence; only the correct answer breaks the causal link.

questions.question: The author's attitude to precision in architectural design is best described as

options.A: enthusiastic endorsement, since precision is the profession's distinctive strength and its main source of pride.
options.B: qualified scepticism: precision suits uses that are fixed and exacting but burdens most ordinary buildings.
options.C: outright rejection, on the ground that a precise fit makes every kind of building brittle once its use changes.
options.D: indifference, since the author regards the closeness of fit as irrelevant to how well a building adapts.

questions.correct_answer: (B) qualified scepticism: precision suits uses that are fixed and exacting but burdens most ordinary buildings.

option_rationales.A: The author calls the lesson 'an uncomfortable one for a profession that prides itself on precision', which is critical, not enthusiastic.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says 'This is not an argument against all precision' and names operating theatres and laboratories as exceptions.
option_rationales.D: The whole argument links loose fit to adaptability and close fit to brittleness, so fit is central, not irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 criticises buildings 'tailored exactly' to a brief as 'brittle' but limits the point: 'an operating theatre or a laboratory must fit its use closely'. The attitude is sceptical with a stated exception.
questions.common_misconception: Ignoring the concession and choosing outright rejection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession must be weighed against the main critical thrust.

questions.question: According to the passage, a lack of craft cannot be what makes an object kitsch because

options.A: judgements of craft vary so widely between viewers that they cannot ground any definition.
options.B: clumsy work usually provokes stronger feelings in its viewers than skilful work does.
options.C: most kitsch objects are produced by trained artists rather than by amateurs or children.
options.D: skilfully made objects can be kitsch, while much clumsy work is not.

questions.correct_answer: (D) skilfully made objects can be kitsch, while much clumsy work is not.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 never says that judgements of craft are unreliable; it treats the skill of the shepherdess and the clumsiness of the watercolour as plain facts.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 makes no comparison of the feelings that clumsy and skilful work provoke; its argument rests only on which objects count as kitsch.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says many kitsch objects are made 'with considerable skill', not that most are made by trained artists; the claim about who makes them is the option's addition.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives skilful kitsch (the shepherdess, the sunset, the verse that 'scans perfectly') and clumsy work that 'is not kitsch at all', and concludes that whatever makes an object kitsch 'it is not a lack of craft'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading in a general scepticism about craft, or turning many skilful kitsch objects into a claim about who usually makes them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in paragraph 1 and the wrong options add claims absent from it.

questions.question: The reference to a serious painting that shows grief 'in a particular face' (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the technical skill that the makers of kitsch characteristically lack.
options.B: suggest that portraits are a more truthful form of art than scenes of soldiers and kittens.
options.C: show that a work can move us deeply while still demanding close attention.
options.D: demonstrate that serious art, unlike kitsch, almost never moves its viewers to tears.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that a work can move us deeply while still demanding close attention.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 has already said that kitsch is often made with considerable skill, so the example cannot be about a lack of skill.
option_rationales.B: No ranking of genres is made; the example contrasts a demanding treatment of feeling with a ready-made one, whatever the subject.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such a painting 'may also move us to tears'; the contrast is in how the tears are earned, so the option reverses the point.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says kitsch lacks 'resistance', and the painting of grief is the contrasting case: it 'may also move us to tears' but 'makes us work for them' by showing a face that does not match our expectation. It shows feeling joined to attention.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the example as a contrast of emotion versus no emotion, when the contrast is between earned and ready-made emotion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentence containing the example states its role.

questions.question: The passage suggests that kitsch 'tends to flatter' its viewers because it

options.A: is made by people who copy the tastes of wealthy buyers in order to sell their work.
options.B: deals with sentimental subjects, which are by their nature more pleasing than serious ones.
options.C: portrays its viewers as more refined and better educated than they really are.
options.D: calls up feelings viewers already hold and approve of, making their pleasure a kind of self-approval.

questions.correct_answer: (D) calls up feelings viewers already hold and approve of, making their pleasure a kind of self-approval.

option_rationales.A: The makers' motives and markets are never discussed; the explanation in paragraph 3 concerns the viewer's response.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says 'Sentiment as such is not the problem'; the flattery comes from approved feelings detached from attention, not from sentiment itself.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 locates the flattery in the emotions kitsch calls up, 'tenderness towards the innocent or pride in sacrifice', not in any picture of the viewer's refinement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'Because the emotion it calls up is one we already possess and approve of ... we come away feeling good not about the work but about ourselves.' The flattery is that the viewer enjoys his or her own approved feelings.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the sentiment option, which blames sentiment as such, the very view paragraph 3 rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer paraphrases a causal sentence; one wrong option uses the passage's own word 'sentimental' against its qualification.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an instance of the danger described in the final paragraph?

options.A: A national memorial service that leaves its audience proud and tearful but tells them nothing about the events it commemorates.
options.B: A gifted painter who sells many technically polished sunsets to tourists visiting a lakeside town.
options.C: An elderly widow who treasures a cheap mass-produced figurine on her shelf because it reminds her of her late husband.
options.D: A news report on a distant famine that sets out detailed causes and interviews several aid workers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A national memorial service that leaves its audience proud and tearful but tells them nothing about the events it commemorates.

option_rationales.B: This is kitsch on the mantelpiece, the setting the author treats as harmless; nothing in it concerns suffering, history or the replacement of finding out by feeling.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says such an object 'may carry real memories' and that comfort is 'a legitimate thing to want', so this is the harmless case the author excuses.
option_rationales.D: Such a report demands the 'harder work of finding out what actually happened', which is the opposite of the danger the author describes.

questions.explanation: The danger arises when ready-made feeling spreads to places where attention matters, such as 'the way public ceremonies ask us to feel about history', so that the feeling stands in for 'finding out what actually happened'. A ceremony that supplies emotion without information fits exactly.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the figurine or the sunsets because they are typical kitsch, though the author says kitsch at home is not the danger.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the distinction between harmless and dangerous settings to new cases.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining why children, unlike adults, enjoy hearing the same story told many times over.
options.B: questioning the belief that knowing a story's outcome destroys its value, while granting that something real is lost.
options.C: arguing that stories built around a single surprise are inferior to stories that reward rereading.
options.D: defending the etiquette against spoilers as the necessary protection of what gives every story its value for an audience.

questions.correct_answer: (B) questioning the belief that knowing a story's outcome destroys its value, while granting that something real is lost.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 gives children and adults as parallel cases of the same behaviour, and the point is only one piece of evidence, so the option is both distorted and too narrow.
option_rationales.C: The author never ranks the two kinds of story; paragraph 4 treats the shock of a reversal as 'a real pleasure', not as a mark of inferiority.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the etiquette protects only 'a narrow and unrepeatable pleasure, not the whole value of a story', so the option inflates the concession into the thesis.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the theory that a known story is 'used up', paragraphs 2 and 3 argue against it, and paragraph 4 concedes that some stories lose a genuine but narrow pleasure. The correct answer captures both the critique and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the defence of the etiquette because paragraph 4 says it 'protects something genuine'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure of the passage is simple and the concession is clearly marked as limited.

questions.question: The bedtime story and the tragedies drawn from well-known legends (paragraph 2) are offered as

options.A: illustrations of how the customs of storytelling have changed over the centuries.
options.B: examples of stories built around a single reversal that cannot be enjoyed twice.
options.C: evidence that people seek out and enjoy stories whose outcomes they already know.
options.D: support for the view that suspense depends entirely on uncertainty about the final scene.

questions.correct_answer: (C) evidence that people seek out and enjoy stories whose outcomes they already know.

option_rationales.A: The examples span children, adults and audiences 'for centuries' to show a constant behaviour, not a change in custom.
option_rationales.B: Such stories appear only in paragraph 4 as the exception; a tragedy whose end everyone knows is the reverse of a story that depends on surprise.
option_rationales.D: The examples are used against that view; paragraph 3 draws from them that 'suspense is not simply uncertainty about outcome'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens by saying the theory is 'difficult to square with how people actually behave' and closes with 'If knowing the ending destroyed the pleasure, none of this would make sense'. The examples are evidence of people enjoying known outcomes.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the examples of paragraph 2 with the exception introduced in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph's first and last sentences state the examples' role.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the comparison with 'a lottery ticket that has already been scratched' conveys the idea that

options.A: stories, like lotteries, reward only a lucky few among those who take part in them.
options.B: revealing a story's ending is a theft that ought to be punished like any other.
options.C: the author regards watching films as a form of gambling with one's time and money.
options.D: a story, on the theory described, is worthless once its outcome is known.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a story, on the theory described, is worthless once its outcome is known.

option_rationales.A: The image concerns what remains after the outcome is revealed, not how rewards are distributed among an audience.
option_rationales.B: The theft image is a separate one describing how spoiling friends are treated; the ticket image explains why, on the theory, the story is 'used up'.
option_rationales.C: The image belongs to the theory the author goes on to reject ('On this view'), and it says nothing about gambling with time or money.

questions.explanation: The sentence reads: 'once the outcome is known the thing is used up, like a lottery ticket that has already been scratched.' A scratched ticket has no further value once its result is seen, which is what the theory says about a known story.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the ticket image to the earlier theft image, or taking the reported theory as the author's own view.
questions.difficulty_reason: The meaning is fixed by the clause the image completes.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a reader rereading a mystery novel whose solution she remembers

options.A: can still take pleasure in its telling, though not in the shock of first discovering the solution.
options.B: will feel no suspense of any kind, since suspense is no more than uncertainty about outcome.
options.C: will enjoy it more than on a first reading, because the plot no longer distracts her attention.
options.D: gains nothing from the experience, since a mystery depends entirely on the reader's ignorance.

questions.correct_answer: (A) can still take pleasure in its telling, though not in the shock of first discovering the solution.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says that 'suspense is not simply uncertainty about outcome', so the option rests on the view the author rejects.
option_rationales.C: The author never claims that a second reading is better; paragraph 4 treats the first encounter as offering a pleasure that rereading 'does not restore'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says such a mystery 'loses something', not everything, and paragraph 3 says the manner of telling is untouched by knowing the plot.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a mystery whose solution is known 'loses something that rereading does not restore', namely the shock of the first encounter, while paragraph 3 says the pleasures of 'the manner of its telling' are not spoiled by knowing the plot. Both halves of the correct answer are supported.
questions.common_misconception: Over-reading the concession in paragraph 4 as total loss, or over-reading paragraph 3 as a claim that rereading is better.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the concession in paragraph 4 with the argument of paragraph 3.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, confessing to a guilty pleasure works as 'a kind of insurance' because

options.A: it guarantees that the listener will forgive the speaker for her lapse of taste.
options.B: the speaker is safe whether her listener shares the enthusiasm or scorns it.
options.C: it allows the speaker to abandon her stated opinion later without any embarrassment.
options.D: it obliges the listener to confess an embarrassing enthusiasm of his own in return.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the speaker is safe whether her listener shares the enthusiasm or scorns it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says only that the smile 'asks to be forgiven'; paragraph 2 says the speaker is safe even if the listener sneers, so no forgiveness is guaranteed or needed.
option_rationales.C: Changing one's opinion later is never mentioned; the protection described concerns the listener's immediate reaction.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 imposes no obligation on the listener; it considers only two possible reactions, sharing the enthusiasm or sneering.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'if her listener turns out to share the enthusiasm, nothing is lost; if the listener sneers, she has already sneered first.' Either way the speaker is covered, which is what insurance does.
questions.common_misconception: Borrowing 'asks to be forgiven' from paragraph 1 and treating a request as a guarantee.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is in the two sentences after the phrase.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 suggests that the author suspects the ranking which the phrase depends on

options.A: has been carefully examined by critics over many years and found to be broadly sound in most of its judgements.
options.B: places every predictable work below every unpredictable one, whatever audience it attracts.
options.C: is shaped partly by the social standing of the audiences associated with works, not only by the works themselves.
options.D: is imposed on the rest of the public by teenagers and provincial and domestic audiences.

questions.correct_answer: (C) is shaped partly by the social standing of the audiences associated with works, not only by the works themselves.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says that 'the ranking itself is rarely examined', which is the opposite of the option.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 notes that respected pleasures escape the label 'however predictable they may be', so predictability is precisely not what the ranking tracks.
option_rationales.D: Those audiences are named as the ones whose pleasures get labelled guilty, so they are on the receiving end of the ranking, not its authors.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls it 'striking' that the pleasures labelled guilty are those of audiences 'who have little cultural prestige', while respected people's predictable pleasures are not so labelled. The author's point is that prestige of audience, not only quality of work, seems to drive the ranking.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the predictability option because the passage mentions predictability, without noticing that it is cited as the feature the ranking ignores.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference requires reading the contrast in the final sentence of paragraph 3 correctly.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the phrase 'guilty pleasure' is best described as

options.A: approving, because the author sees it as a healthy awareness of the limits of one's taste.
options.B: amused and tolerant, since the author regards it as a harmless habit of polite talk.
options.C: openly contemptuous of the people who use it, whom the author treats as snobs.
options.D: sceptical of its apparent modesty, while allowing that some pleasures do deserve genuine unease.

questions.correct_answer: (D) sceptical of its apparent modesty, while allowing that some pleasures do deserve genuine unease.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 calls the confession 'very often, a display of good taste' and a kind of insurance, which is the reverse of approval of its humility.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says the phrase 'tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question', which is a substantive objection, not amused tolerance.
option_rationales.C: The author analyses what the phrase does, not the character of its users, and paragraph 4 even suggests that the singing contest may need 'no apology'.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 argue that the phrase is less modest than it looks; paragraph 4 begins 'It does not follow that no pleasure should ever make us uneasy', allowing real scrutiny of some pleasures. Scepticism with a qualification fits.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing contempt because the analysis is critical, though the criticism is aimed at the phrase rather than at people.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires weighing the critical thrust against the qualification in paragraph 4.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 that the phrase 'tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question'?

options.A: Habitually confessing a pleasure as guilty is found, over time, to make people rate that work as highly as the approved ones.
options.B: The works that are most often called guilty pleasures turn out in fact to be associated mainly with audiences of very little cultural prestige.
options.C: Many people who use the phrase do so without any conscious wish to display their own good taste to others.
options.D: Some enjoyments, such as laughing at another person's humiliation, really do deserve to make us uneasy.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Habitually confessing a pleasure as guilty is found, over time, to make people rate that work as highly as the approved ones.

option_rationales.B: This matches the observation in paragraph 3 and so supports, rather than weakens, the author's account of the ranking.
option_rationales.C: The claim in paragraph 3 concerns what the phrase does to the ranking, which 'needs the ranking in order to mean anything' whatever the speaker intends. Even the point of paragraph 2 is that the confession displays knowledge of the rankings, which it does whether or not the speaker wishes it to.
option_rationales.D: The author grants this in paragraph 4, and it concerns a different kind of unease; it leaves the claim about prestige rankings untouched.

questions.explanation: The claim is that the confession 'leaves that ranking intact'. Evidence that habitual use of the phrase leads people to raise the confessed works to the level of approved ones would show the phrase eroding the hierarchy, directly weakening the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about speakers' motives, which bears on the display argument of paragraph 2 but not on the structural claim of paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the motive-based point of paragraph 2 from the structural claim of paragraph 3; one wrong option attacks the wrong claim.

questions.question: According to the passage, an explained joke usually fails to produce a laugh because

options.A: analysis damages the fragile, almost mystical quality on which all humour depends.
options.B: the listener is denied the chance to discover the second meaning for himself.
options.C: most listeners resent being told something that they were perfectly able to work out.
options.D: the explanation offered is usually far less clever than the joke it tries to rescue.

questions.correct_answer: (B) the listener is denied the chance to discover the second meaning for himself.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 reports this as the usual inference and says it 'does not follow'; the author's own explanation is different.
option_rationales.C: Resentment is never mentioned; paragraph 2 says the pleasure is lost, not that the listener is offended.
option_rationales.D: The cleverness of explanations is never compared with that of jokes; paragraph 2 locates the failure in who does the work, not in the quality of the explanation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The pleasure lies largely in the listener's own discovery of the second meaning ... Explanation takes this work away from him.' The joke dies because the examination 'has been done for the listener'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'fragile, almost mystical' option because it is a familiar view, though the passage reports it only to reject it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in paragraph 2; one wrong option is the view the author rejects.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the argument of the passage?

options.A: It concedes that the study of comedy is self-defeating but defends that study on other grounds.
options.B: It offers a second explanation of why explained jokes fail, independent of the one in paragraph 2.
options.C: It turns the account of why explained jokes fail into grounds for thinking humour can be analysed.
options.D: It introduces circumstances in which explaining a joke at the moment of telling can be helpful.

questions.correct_answer: (C) It turns the account of why explained jokes fail into grounds for thinking humour can be analysed.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'There is nothing self-defeating in studying how jokes work', so it makes no such concession.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 begins 'Seen in this way', building on the explanation of paragraph 2 rather than offering a rival one.
option_rationales.D: That is the role of paragraph 4, which begins 'There is even a case for explanation in the moment'; paragraph 3 concerns analysis afterwards.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the failure of explained jokes 'tells us something about humour ... and this is exactly the kind of thing analysis can discover', and then answers the charge that studying comedy is 'a contradiction in terms' from paragraph 1. It converts the explanation into a defence of analysis.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing analysis afterwards (paragraph 3) with explanation in the moment (paragraph 4).
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires tracking how paragraph 3 uses paragraph 2 to answer paragraph 1.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: A listener may laugh at a joke after being told what an unfamiliar allusion in it refers to.
options.B: Being told the answer to a riddle tends to take away the satisfaction of solving it.
options.C: A joke that has once been closely examined can never again amuse anyone who has studied it.
options.D: Analysing a comic routine afterwards can deepen one's understanding of a laugh already enjoyed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A joke that has once been closely examined can never again amuse anyone who has studied it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says such a listener 'will sometimes laugh a moment later, on his own', so this is consistent.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says being told a riddle's answer 'deprives one of the satisfaction of solving it', so this is consistent.
