It does not show that the pattern 'governs how people reason when they are not speaking', so it would not show more combative arguing.
questions.common_misconception: Taking productivity, which the author does accept, as proof of the stronger claim the author withholds.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer applies the author's distinction between availability and influence to a new case; one wrong option takes the step the author refuses.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would supply the kind of evidence the author says is needed to support the mapping view's stronger claims?

options.A: Asked to invent new expressions about time, speakers produced spatial ones far more often than any other kind.
options.B: In a wordless task, people set pictures of earlier events in the direction that their language's time expressions assign to the past.
options.C: Asked about their own speech, most speakers said they did not picture space when talking about deadlines.
options.D: A large survey found that spatial expressions for time outnumber all other kinds in every language examined.

questions.correct_answer: (B) In a wordless task, people set pictures of earlier events in the direction that their language's time expressions assign to the past.

option_rationales.A: This is evidence of productivity, which paragraph 4 says shows only that a pattern is available for making expressions.
option_rationales.C: Speakers' reports of what they picture are still testimony about their use of the expressions, not observation of non-verbal reasoning, and would tell against the mapping view rather than for it.
option_rationales.D: This is frequency evidence drawn from the expressions themselves, which paragraph 3 calls circular and paragraph 4 sets aside.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the stronger claims 'can be settled only by evidence that does not itself consist of the very expressions in question', such as how people 'solve problems, judge situations or remember events'. A wordless picture-arranging task whose results track the language's spatial metaphor for time is evidence of exactly that non-linguistic kind.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the invention task, which feels experimental but still measures expressions, the very evidence the author says cannot settle the question.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three options are empirical findings; only one escapes the linguistic evidence the author rules insufficient.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the author's claim that many everyday metaphors are 'alive' means that they

options.A: occur in ordinary speech more often than the dead metaphors that speakers no longer notice.
options.B: are still felt by speakers as figurative, so that their origin is present to mind whenever used.
options.C: can serve speakers as patterns for forming and understanding new expressions, whatever their effect on reasoning.
options.D: govern how speakers reason about argument and time even when they are not speaking at all.

questions.correct_answer: (C) can serve speakers as patterns for forming and understanding new expressions, whatever their effect on reasoning.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 opens by setting frequency aside: 'Productivity, then, rather than frequency, is the better test'.
option_rationales.B: Felt origin is the sceptic's criterion in paragraph 2; the author's test is whether the pattern can be extended, not whether its origin is felt.
option_rationales.D: The author separates this from being alive: availability 'is not to show that it governs how people reason when they are not speaking'.

questions.explanation: The author qualifies the word at once: alive 'at least in the sense that speakers can use them as patterns for making and understanding new expressions', and then says this 'is also less than the mapping view claims'. The sense is restricted to productivity and leaves influence on reasoning open.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the felt-origin reading, because paragraph 2 defines dead metaphors as those whose 'figurative origin is no longer felt'; the author replaces that criterion with productivity.
questions.difficulty_reason: The strongest wrong option uses a definition the passage itself supplies, but from the sceptic rather than the author.

questions.question: The passage gives each of the following as a reason why mutual intelligibility fails as a test for separating languages from dialects EXCEPT that

options.A: speakers often pretend not to understand a variety they dislike.
options.B: neighbours along a chain may understand each other when the ends cannot.
options.C: how well people understand depends on topic and speed of speech.
options.D: one group may understand another better than it is understood.

questions.correct_answer: (A) speakers often pretend not to understand a variety they dislike.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says intelligibility 'is not transitive' and describes the chain of villages.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says intelligibility 'varies with the topic, the speed of speech and the listener's experience'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says intelligibility 'is frequently lopsided', which is exactly this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists degree, variation with topic, speed and experience, lopsidedness and non-transitivity. Nothing in the passage says speakers pretend not to understand varieties they dislike.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that attitudes towards a variety, which are plausible in the world, are among the reasons the passage gives.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reasons are listed together in paragraph 2 and paraphrased in the options.

questions.question: The example of the traveller passing from village to village in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: show that people living in villages understand neighbouring varieties better than city dwellers do.
options.B: show that intelligibility gives no principled point at which to divide a continuous chain of varieties.
options.C: suggest that the borders of states were first drawn to follow the boundaries between languages.
options.D: prove that every variety along such a chain must be treated as a separate language in its own right.

questions.correct_answer: (B) show that intelligibility gives no principled point at which to divide a continuous chain of varieties.

option_rationales.A: The passage contrasts neighbouring villages with the two ends of the chain; it says nothing about city dwellers.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says map boundaries 'tend to coincide' with state borders, but makes no claim about which came first.
option_rationales.D: The author draws no such conclusion; the example shows that intelligibility 'alone gives no answer', not that there are many languages.

questions.explanation: The example illustrates the claim that intelligibility 'is not transitive' and is followed by the question 'Where on such a chain does one language stop and the next begin?' and the answer that 'Intelligibility alone gives no answer'.
questions.common_misconception: Reversing the relation between state borders and language boundaries.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is set by the claim before the example and the question after it.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a variety now commonly called a dialect

options.A: is usually harder for outsiders to understand than a variety that is commonly called a language.
options.B: has a less fully developed grammar than the standard variety from which it is distinguished.
options.C: will in most cases die out within a few generations unless its speakers succeed in having it recognised as a separate language.
options.D: could come to be called a language by gaining a written standard and a place in schooling, its grammar unchanged.

questions.correct_answer: (D) could come to be called a language by gaining a written standard and a place in schooling, its grammar unchanged.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 notes Chinese varieties called dialects that are mutually unintelligible and Scandinavian languages that are intelligible; the label does not track difficulty.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says these are 'facts about the social life of a variety, not about its grammar', so no grammatical inferiority is implied.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says institutions affect 'whether it survives', but the passage does not predict that most dialects will die out.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a dialect is 'very often simply a variety that lacks the institutions which would have entitled it to be called a language', and paragraph 5 says recognition requires 'a change in those arrangements' rather than in 'the linguistic facts'.
questions.common_misconception: Moving from the point that institutions affect survival to a prediction that most dialects will die.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires combining the definition in paragraph 3 with the conclusion in paragraph 5; one wrong option overstates a real point in paragraph 4.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the writers who conclude that the distinction is 'empty' is best described as

options.A: uncertain, since the author thinks that the question of whether the distinction is real cannot yet be settled.
options.B: dismissive of both their starting point and their conclusion, which the author thinks rest on bad evidence.
options.C: in full agreement, since the author also regards the distinction as politics dressed up as science.
options.D: accepting the observation they start from while firmly rejecting the conclusion they draw from it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) accepting the observation they start from while firmly rejecting the conclusion they draw from it.

option_rationales.A: The author is not undecided: paragraph 4 states that institutional facts 'are facts' and paragraph 5 says what the distinction is.
option_rationales.B: The author shares their starting point: paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that the boundaries are drawn by institutions, not by sound systems.
option_rationales.C: The author answers their conclusion with 'It does not follow' and argues that institutional boundaries are real.

questions.explanation: The writers' premise, that the line is drawn by institutions, is the author's own conclusion from paragraphs 2 and 3. The author rejects only the inference to emptiness: 'It does not follow', because a boundary 'drawn by institutions rather than by sound systems' is not thereby 'unreal'.
questions.common_misconception: Missing that the author agrees with the premise, and so choosing outright dismissal.
questions.difficulty_reason: The attitude has two parts that point in opposite directions, and two wrong options each capture only one of them.

questions.question: A campaign argues that a regional variety deserves recognition as a language because linguists have measured large differences between its grammar and that of the standard. The author would most likely respond that the campaign

options.A: rests its case on the wrong ground, since recognition turns on a society's arrangements rather than on measured features of speech.
options.B: is illegitimate, since the line between a language and a dialect is in the end nothing more than politics.
options.C: should first establish whether speakers of the standard can understand the variety without any difficulty.
options.D: is well founded, since measured grammatical distance is the most objective basis there is for applying the label.

questions.correct_answer: (A) rests its case on the wrong ground, since recognition turns on a society's arrangements rather than on measured features of speech.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 rejects the view that the distinction is 'empty', and paragraph 5 says such requests 'should be judged on those terms', not dismissed.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 argues that intelligibility 'does not deliver what it promises', so the author would not propose it as the decisive test.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says the difference 'is not a property of the speech itself, waiting to be measured', which rules out this response.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says a community seeking recognition 'is asking not for a correction of the linguistic facts but for a change in those arrangements'. A campaign that argues from grammatical measurements treats the question as one of linguistic fact, which is where the author says the mistake lies.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the response that calls the campaign illegitimate, which treats the author as the sceptic of paragraph 4 whom the author answers.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option applies one of the positions the passage examines, so the solver must apply the author's final view precisely.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Typing should replace handwriting in early schooling, since writing is mainly a way of getting words from the mind onto a surface.
options.B: Joined handwriting should again be made compulsory in schools because it preserves an elegant tradition that a keyboard culture is losing.
options.C: Handwriting deserves a place in schooling because writing by hand supports learning in ways that an argument from speed and efficiency overlooks.
options.D: Students who take notes by hand always understand lectures better than students with laptops, so laptops should be kept out of classrooms.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Handwriting deserves a place in schooling because writing by hand supports learning in ways that an argument from speed and efficiency overlooks.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'narrow idea' that paragraph 2 sets out in order to reject; the author argues for keeping handwriting, while adding that 'children need both'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the insistence on 'one elegant joined style' belongs to 'the manners of an earlier age' and can go, and it denies that the case rests on beauty or tradition.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says the laptop user 'may understand far less', a hedged claim about one setting; the passage proposes no ban and makes no claim about every case.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 sets up the efficiency objection and says it rests 'on a narrow idea'; paragraphs 2 and 3 give two learning benefits (letter recognition, note-taking as compression); paragraph 4 states the 'modest' case that handwriting is useful because it is slow. The correct answer captures this whole argument.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the tradition option because the passage defends handwriting, without noticing that it explicitly drops the defence from tradition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated almost directly in the final paragraph and each wrong option is plainly contradicted or overstated.

questions.question: According to the passage, students who take notes by hand are forced to compress what they hear because

options.A: forming each letter by hand fixes its shape in memory and leaves little attention for the lecture itself.
options.B: they cannot write quickly enough to record a lecture word for word, so they must select and rephrase.
options.C: their teachers deduct marks for notes that are untidy or that do not follow a single joined style.
options.D: lectures are usually designed with summaries that students are expected to rewrite in their own words.

questions.correct_answer: (B) they cannot write quickly enough to record a lecture word for word, so they must select and rephrase.

option_rationales.A: Fixing letter shapes in memory is the benefit for young children in paragraph 2; it is not offered as the reason older students compress their notes.
option_rationales.C: Marks lost for 'an untidy loop' belong to the old handwriting curriculum in paragraph 4, not to note-taking; paragraph 3 gives slowness as the reason.
option_rationales.D: Nothing in the passage describes how lectures are designed; paragraph 3 attributes compression only to the hand being 'too slow'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: older students writing by hand 'cannot transcribe a lecture word for word, because the hand is too slow. They are forced to choose, compress and rephrase'.
questions.common_misconception: Carrying the memory point from paragraph 2 into the note-taking discussion of paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in two adjacent sentences.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'a delivery system' describes handwriting understood as

options.A: a set of rules for joined script that schools impose on their pupils.
options.B: a method of teaching young children the shapes and directions of letters.
options.C: a way of sending written messages to people who live far away from the writer.
options.D: nothing more than a means of moving words from the mind onto a page.

questions.correct_answer: (D) nothing more than a means of moving words from the mind onto a page.

option_rationales.A: The rules of joined script are discussed in paragraph 4 as an outdated feature of the curriculum, not as the meaning of 'delivery system'.
option_rationales.B: That is the broader view the author defends against the 'narrow idea'; the delivery-system view leaves out exactly this learning role.
option_rationales.C: The phrase is not about posting letters; the passage glosses it at once as 'a way of getting words from a head onto a surface'.

questions.explanation: The phrase is explained in the same sentence: 'a way of getting words from a head onto a surface'. It names the narrow, purely functional view of handwriting.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'delivery' literally as sending messages instead of using the gloss that follows it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is defined immediately in its own sentence.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: Research has firmly established that writing letters by hand is how children first learn to recognise them.
options.B: A practice can be valuable partly because of the very slowness that makes it look outdated.
options.C: Typing lessons should be postponed until children have fully mastered a neat and consistent joined hand.
options.D: The old emphasis on elegant script did real harm to children's learning and explains why many of them read poorly.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A practice can be valuable partly because of the very slowness that makes it look outdated.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 reports only that researchers 'have suggested' this and adds that the evidence 'is far from settled', so calling it firmly established overstates it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says typing should not be neglected and that 'children need both'; it never asks for typing to wait, and it drops the demand for a neat joined style.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says that emphasis had more to do with manners than learning and 'can be abandoned without much loss'; it does not say it harmed learning or caused poor reading.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'The slowness that makes handwriting look obsolete is, in this setting, precisely its use', and paragraph 4 says the hand helps 'in ways that are useful precisely because they are inefficient'. The correct answer generalises this view without adding to it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the research option because the passage does discuss research on letter recognition, missing the explicit hedge.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the author's general position rather than a single line; one wrong option upgrades a hedged claim.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that, before it became the dominant form, the codex was regarded as

options.A: a modest format suited to practical, everyday writing rather than to works of literary standing.
options.B: an expensive luxury that only wealthy communities could afford to adopt for their sacred texts.
options.C: the preferred format for prestigious literature, which was too long to fit on a single roll.
options.D: a format that every community took up at the same moment once its savings became clear.

questions.correct_answer: (A) a modest format suited to practical, everyday writing rather than to works of literary standing.

option_rationales.B: The passage calls the codex economical and 'humble'; nothing suggests it was a costly luxury, and the early Christian example is explained by 'identity and use'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the reverse: 'prestigious literature stayed on the roll' while the codex served humbler uses.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 stresses that adoption was 'uneven' and that some communities took it up 'well before their neighbours'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the codex 'lingered for generations as a humble format for notebooks, accounts and school exercises, while prestigious literature stayed on the roll'. Its standing was therefore modest and practical.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing which form held prestige at the time.
questions.difficulty_reason: One sentence settles it once read carefully.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the economic explanation of the codex's success is best described as

options.A: endorsing it as the best account of literary adoption while thinking it irrelevant to everyday documents.
options.B: treating it as the most convincing account of why early Christian communities adopted the codex first.
options.C: accepting the facts it relies on while denying that they account for the pattern and pace of the change.
options.D: rejecting it outright on the grounds that the codex did not in fact use writing material more economically.

questions.correct_answer: (C) accepting the facts it relies on while denying that they account for the pattern and pace of the change.

option_rationales.A: The passage applies no such split; it says the codex served everyday documents first and that cost fails to explain the uneven timing overall.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says those communities' reasons 'probably had as much to do with identity and use as with price', which limits rather than favours the economic account.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 lists the codex's savings and says 'All of this is true', so the author does not dispute the facts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 grants the savings ('All of this is true') but adds 'none of it is quite enough'; paragraph 2 then argues that the economic story 'struggles with timing' and with uneven adoption. The author accepts the premises and denies their sufficiency.
questions.common_misconception: Treating criticism of an explanation as a denial of its facts.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the truth of a premise from its explanatory sufficiency across two paragraphs.

questions.question: The examples of a legal compilation, a book of scripture cited in argument and a technical manual (paragraph 3) serve mainly to

options.A: show that lawyers, clergy and engineers were the first groups to adopt the codex before it spread to other readers.
options.B: identify works that readers consult at chosen points rather than read through, and which therefore suited the codex.
options.C: prove that a scroll was physically unable to hold the long texts that such specialised works usually required.
options.D: illustrate the prestigious literature that, according to the passage, remained on the roll for generations.

questions.correct_answer: (B) identify works that readers consult at chosen points rather than read through, and which therefore suited the codex.

option_rationales.A: The passage gives no order of adoption by profession; the examples illustrate a mode of use, not a history of who adopted the form first.
option_rationales.C: Length and capacity are not the point of paragraph 3; the contrast is between continuous reading and consultation, and the passage offers nothing as proof.
option_rationales.D: The prestigious literature of paragraph 2 stayed on the roll, whereas these works are said to 'suit the codex far better than the roll'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that the codex 'made the text navigable'. The three examples are introduced as 'works one enters at a point rather than travels through', showing what navigability was good for.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the examples as a history of adoption instead of as illustrations of a way of reading.
questions.difficulty_reason: Function is signalled by the sentence the examples sit in, but two wrong options invent plausible roles.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument against a purely economic explanation in paragraph 2?

options.A: The codex spread to literature fastest where papyrus was dearest, and almost as soon as its savings were understood.
options.B: Because of their wide margins, early codices saved much less writing material than historians have usually supposed.
options.C: Some early Christian communities that favoured the codex continued to keep a few of their texts on rolls.
options.D: Page numbers and indexes did not become common in codices until many centuries after the codex had become dominant.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The codex spread to literature fastest where papyrus was dearest, and almost as soon as its savings were understood.

option_rationales.B: If the savings were small, a purely economic explanation becomes weaker still, so this supports the author rather than weakening the argument.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says only that such communities took up the codex earlier; keeping some rolls is compatible with that and leaves the timing argument intact.
option_rationales.D: This concerns the 'later apparatus' of paragraph 4, which the passage already treats as later; it has no bearing on the timing argument of paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that if thrift 'alone had driven the change', the codex should have spread 'fastest where writing material was scarce' and triumphed 'as soon as its savings were obvious', and that this did not happen. Evidence that exactly this pattern occurred removes the author's ground for rejecting the economic account.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the wide-margins option because it attacks the economic explanation, without noticing that the question asks what weakens the author's attack on it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the conditional structure of the paragraph 2 argument and a careful reading of whose argument is to be weakened; the most tempting wrong option works in the opposite direction.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, in the large historical dictionaries a definition was written

options.A: before volunteer readers were sent out to find quotations that would confirm the editors' chosen meaning.
options.B: by the volunteer readers themselves, who copied out each quotation together with its source and date.
options.C: only once the quotations gathered for a word had been sorted by the senses they seemed to show.
options.D: only for those senses of a word that the editors judged to be correct and respectable usage.

questions.correct_answer: (C) only once the quotations gathered for a word had been sorted by the senses they seemed to show.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 reverses this order: the slips were gathered and sorted first, and 'A definition was written only after' that.
option_rationales.B: The volunteers supplied the slips; the passage says definitions were written after sorting and does not assign that work to the volunteers.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says editors did not define 'from their own sense of correctness' and that an unapproved sense 'went in regardless'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'A definition was written only after the slips for a word had been sorted into piles according to the senses they seemed to show.'
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the familiar order in which a meaning is decided and then illustrated.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in a single sentence.

questions.question: In saying that the printed quotations are 'not decoration but the grounds on which it rests' (paragraph 2), the author means that the quotations

options.A: matter more than the definitions themselves, which careful readers can safely ignore.
options.B: guarantee that each definition is correct and will not need to be revised in the future.
options.C: were included chiefly to display the range of the editors' literary reading to the dictionary's users.
options.D: are the evidence that a definition summarises and against which it can be tested.

questions.correct_answer: (D) are the evidence that a definition summarises and against which it can be tested.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 asks readers to 'notice the quotations as well as the definitions', not instead of them, so this overstates the point.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says a dictionary's claims 'can be revised when new evidence arrives', so evidence does not make a definition final.
option_rationales.C: That is the 'decoration' reading the author explicitly rejects; the quotations are called 'the grounds' of the definition.

questions.explanation: On the model of paragraph 2, a definition 'is a summary of a body of quotations'; the quotations are its basis. Paragraph 4 adds that the claims 'can be checked against the citations'.
questions.common_misconception: Inflating 'grounds' into a guarantee of correctness, or into a claim that the quotations replace the definition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The literal sense is easy, but two wrong options overstate it in ways the last paragraph rules out.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a dictionary's label 'nonstandard' as

options.A: a purely factual report that follows mechanically from the quotations gathered for the word.
options.B: proof that the dictionary has abandoned its evidential method and turned itself into a court.
options.C: a reliable sign that careful writers ought to avoid the word in serious work.
options.D: a judgment by the dictionary's makers, even though it is presented as a plain description of usage.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a judgment by the dictionary's makers, even though it is presented as a plain description of usage.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says such labels 'are themselves verdicts', and that sorting senses is 'a judgment the slips cannot make for themselves'.
option_rationales.B: The author treats labels as an unavoidable point of view within an evidence-based dictionary, not as an abandonment of the method; paragraph 4 still calls it 'an argument from evidence'.
option_rationales.C: The author never advises on usage; treating the label as a binding instruction is the 'court' view the passage criticises.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that the labels a dictionary attaches 'are themselves verdicts, even when they are offered as descriptions', and 'nonstandard' is one of the labels it names.
questions.common_misconception: Moving from the idea that a label is a judgment to the idea that the dictionary has stopped being evidential, which overstates the author's point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is stated, but one wrong option pushes the same idea to an extreme the author avoids.

questions.question: Which of the following has an authority most like the one the author attributes to a good dictionary in paragraph 4?

options.A: A respected elder whose rulings on proper manners are followed because of his long standing in the community.
options.B: A coastal survey trusted because its measurements are recorded, can be rechecked and are redrawn when the shoreline shifts.
options.C: A referee whose decision on a disputed goal stands as final, whatever later replays of the match may show.
options.D: A photograph that records a street scene exactly as it was, without any choice made by the photographer.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A coastal survey trusted because its measurements are recorded, can be rechecked and are redrawn when the shoreline shifts.

option_rationales.A: This authority rests on status, not on checkable evidence, and its rulings settle questions; the author's dictionary earns trust by citations that can be checked.
option_rationales.C: This is the authority of a judge or court, which paragraph 4 contrasts with that of 'a careful witness'; it also cannot be revised.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'neutral mirror' that paragraph 3 rejects, since a dictionary's collectors and editors inevitably make choices.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes a dictionary as 'an argument from evidence' whose claims 'can be checked against the citations' and 'revised when new evidence arrives', with the authority of 'a careful witness rather than a judge'. The survey shares all three features: recorded evidence, checkability and revision.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the photograph because it seems purely descriptive, missing that the author rejects the mirror view as firmly as the court view.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding both rejected models (court and mirror) and the positive model at once and mapping them onto unfamiliar cases.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that weaker reading on screens stems largely from trained habits, while granting that paper keeps some genuine advantages.
options.B: show that screens are destroying the capacity of a generation raised on phones to follow long arguments.
options.C: recommend that schools return to printed books because paper gives readers a better sense of place in a text.
options.D: demonstrate that the medium of reading makes no difference to comprehension once habits are corrected.

questions.correct_answer: (A) argue that weaker reading on screens stems largely from trained habits, while granting that paper keeps some genuine advantages.

option_rationales.B: This is the lament of paragraph 1 that the author calls 'too quick'; paragraph 4 says screens 'are not destroying our capacity to read deeply'.
option_rationales.C: Paper's sense of place is one concession in paragraph 4; the passage asks for deliberate deep reading on screens and recommends no return to print.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 opens by denying that 'the medium makes no difference at all'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 questions the view that 'the screen itself damages comprehension'; paragraph 2 offers the habit explanation; paragraph 3 draws its hopeful consequence; paragraph 4 concedes paper's real advantages and gives 'a qualified' conclusion. The correct answer covers both the thesis and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'no difference' option by ignoring the concession in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Paragraph structure is clearly signposted and the concession is explicit.

questions.question: According to paragraph 4, which advantage does paper offer that a scrolling screen supplies only weakly?

options.A: A greater willingness among readers to slow down and summarise what they have read.
options.B: Faster reading of long and demanding texts when the reader is working against the clock.
options.C: Physical cues of position and length that help some readers recall where an idea appeared.
options.D: Freedom from the headlines, messages and feeds that interrupt reading on a device.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Physical cues of position and length that help some readers recall where an idea appeared.

option_rationales.A: Slowing down and summarising appear in paragraph 3 as ways to narrow gaps on screens, not as an advantage of paper.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says comprehension on screens suffers under time pressure; it says nothing about paper making reading faster.
option_rationales.D: Headlines and feeds appear in paragraph 2 as what people usually read on screens, not as interruptions that paper removes; paragraph 4 is about a sense of place.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: paper offers 'a sense of place', 'the thickness of the pages already read, the position of a passage on the left or right page', cues that 'help some readers remember where an idea appeared', and 'a screen supplies them only weakly'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a detail from another paragraph that also contrasts screens and paper.
questions.difficulty_reason: Answer located in two sentences of one paragraph.

questions.question: A habitual phone reader is asked to read a long essay on a tablet and then write a summary of it. Based on the passage, the author would most likely expect this reader's comprehension to be

options.A: closer to what the same reader would manage on paper than if no summary had been asked for.
options.B: no better than with no summary at all, because the screen itself is what damages understanding.
options.C: markedly better than the same reader would achieve when reading the essay on paper.
options.D: unchanged, since the passage says that only extra time, not a change of task, narrows the gap.

questions.correct_answer: (A) closer to what the same reader would manage on paper than if no summary had been asked for.

option_rationales.B: This is the interpretation the author calls 'too quick'; paragraph 3 says gaps 'seem to narrow' when readers are asked to summarise.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says such a reader 'may perform nearly as well' as with the book, not better; paragraph 4 also grants paper some advantages.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 names both more time and being 'asked to slow down and summarise', so the claim misreports the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says gaps 'seem to narrow when readers are given more time, or are asked to slow down and summarise', and that a reader with the right intentions 'may perform nearly as well' as with a book. The summary task should therefore move the reader toward paper-level comprehension, without exceeding it.
questions.common_misconception: Overshooting to comprehension better than on paper, or misremembering the conditions that narrow the gap.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying a hedged finding to a new case and stopping at the right degree.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the explanation offered in paragraph 2?

options.A: Readers of printed books were better than screen readers at remembering on which page an idea had appeared.
options.B: Adults who had seldom used screens before showed the same comprehension gap on tablets as habitual screen readers did.
options.C: Readers given extra time to finish a long text on a screen understood noticeably more of it than readers who were hurried.
options.D: Most of the material that people read on their phones each day consists of short headlines, messages and search results.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Adults who had seldom used screens before showed the same comprehension gap on tablets as habitual screen readers did.

option_rationales.A: This fits the concession in paragraph 4 about paper's sense of place; it does not bear on whether skimming habits explain the gap.
option_rationales.C: This agrees with paragraph 3, which says gaps narrow 'when readers are given more time'; it is consistent with the habit explanation.
option_rationales.D: This repeats the premise of paragraph 2 ('Most of what they encounter there is brief') and so supports rather than weakens it.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains the screen gap by a skimming habit built up through years of screen use. If people without that habit show the same gap, the habit cannot be what produces it, and something about the screen itself becomes the likelier cause.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the page-memory option because it favours paper, though it targets paragraph 4 rather than the habit explanation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The explanation must be identified as habit-based and tested with a group lacking the habit.

questions.question: The comparison of a good edit to 'good stage lighting' in paragraph 2 is used to suggest that

options.A: editors make weak passages look more impressive than they really are to the reader.
options.B: editing is a theatrical skill that most authors lack and must therefore hire from others.
options.C: editors are chiefly responsible for the visual design and layout of the printed page.
options.D: editorial work is successful when readers of the finished book are not aware of it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) editorial work is successful when readers of the finished book are not aware of it.

option_rationales.A: The passage never says editing disguises weakness; the point of the image is that a good edit 'is meant to pass unnoticed'.
option_rationales.B: Nothing in the passage calls editing theatrical or says authors lack the skill; the image only explains why the work is 'deliberately invisible'.
option_rationales.C: The comparison concerns visibility, not design; paragraph 2 describes editors' work on structure, characters and sentences, not layout.

questions.explanation: The image follows the sentence 'The work is deliberately invisible' and is glossed at once: a good edit 'is meant to pass unnoticed'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the stage image literally, as a point about appearance or performance.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is spelled out in the sentence containing the image.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the exceptions mentioned in paragraph 3?

options.A: They have become more frequent as publishing has grown more commercial and more dependent on editors.
options.B: They show that the solitary author is usually a fraud whose books are largely written by others.
options.C: Their unsettling effect reveals an ordinary expectation that the author, not the editor, is a book's main maker.
options.D: They arise when editors who want their contribution celebrated insist on rewriting large parts of an author's manuscript.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Their unsettling effect reveals an ordinary expectation that the author, not the editor, is a book's main maker.

option_rationales.A: The passage says nothing about how often such cases occur over time or about commercial pressures; this is outside its scope.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 calls that conclusion an overcorrection; the exceptions are rare cases, and the author says that 'In most cases the author supplies the material'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 mentions editors who want recognition, but the passage never links them to the extensive rewriting in paragraph 3.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the exceptions are 'exceptions precisely because they unsettle us'. Being unsettled by a heavy editorial hand implies that the normal expectation, which paragraph 3 also states, is that 'the author supplies the material, the voice and the governing intention'.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the exceptions as evidence for the overcorrection the author rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires reading the force of 'precisely because they unsettle us' rather than any stated fact.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that editors are 'secret co-authors' is best described as

options.A: strict neutrality, since the author reports the view without passing any judgment on it.
options.B: understanding why it appeals but rejecting it as an overstatement of a real point.
options.C: wholehearted agreement, since the finished text is rarely the text that the author first submitted.
options.D: contemptuous dismissal, on the ground that editors' contributions to a book are in fact trivial.

questions.correct_answer: (B) understanding why it appeals but rejecting it as an overstatement of a real point.

option_rationales.A: The author does judge the view: 'This overcorrects', and paragraph 4 offers what it calls 'The real lesson' in its place.
option_rationales.C: The author grants that books change in editing but says the co-author view 'overcorrects', so agreement is not wholehearted.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 describes substantial editorial contributions, from structure to commas, so the author does not regard them as trivial.

questions.explanation: The author calls the view 'tempting', which concedes its appeal, and then says 'This overcorrects', which accepts that there is something to correct while denying the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the author's emphasis on editing for agreement with the stronger claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Tone must be read from two words ('tempting', 'overcorrects') and the paragraph around them.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Authors are best understood as directors of an editorial process rather than as the source of their books' material and voice.
options.B: Editors deserve the same credit as authors, because the finished book is seldom the manuscript that was first submitted.
options.C: Publishers should print editors' names on covers so that readers stop skipping the acknowledgements page.
options.D: Treating authorship as one person's undivided possession hides the graded collaboration through which most books are made.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Treating authorship as one person's undivided possession hides the graded collaboration through which most books are made.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says authors 'direct a process', but paragraph 3 says that in most cases 'the author supplies the material, the voice and the governing intention', so the contrast drawn here contradicts the passage.
option_rationales.B: The author denies this in paragraph 3 ('This overcorrects') and says the lesson is about how credit is assigned 'rather than who deserves the most of it'.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no recommendation about covers; the acknowledgements page is one detail illustrating how the solitary picture is reinforced.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the lesson: 'Our habits treat authorship as an all-or-nothing property, possessed entirely by one person, when the making of most books is a graded collaboration'. Paragraphs 1 to 3 lead up to this by showing the solitary picture, the editor's real role and the error of the opposite extreme.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about directing a process because it echoes paragraph 4, without noticing it denies authors the material and voice that paragraph 3 gives them.
questions.difficulty_reason: The strongest wrong option reuses the passage's final sentence but sets it against paragraph 3; separating them needs the whole argument.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that a modern scholar who wants to know exactly what a hand-press edition printed on a particular page should

options.A: consult any one surviving copy, since every copy of an edition was printed from the same type.
options.B: prefer a manuscript copy of the work, since manuscripts were more dependable than early printed books.
options.C: compare several surviving copies of that edition, since they may not agree on that page.
options.D: rely on a later reprint of the edition, since reprints corrected the errors of the original printing.

questions.correct_answer: (C) compare several surviving copies of that edition, since they may not agree on that page.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says copies of one edition 'may therefore differ on any number of pages' because of corrections made during the run, so one copy may mislead.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: a printed book was 'a more dependable object than a manuscript', though not a guaranteed replica.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says reprints 'introduced fresh errors and silent improvements of their own', so a reprint is a further source of variation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that corrected and uncorrected sheets were bound together, so 'Two copies of the same edition may therefore differ on any number of pages'. Only by comparing copies can one establish what was printed, which is also what paragraph 3 says scholarly editors learned to do by 'collating copies'.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the commonplace of identical copies that the paragraph is written to undo.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires applying the mechanism of stop-press correction to a practical question.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement that 'the same commonplace is now being run in reverse' means that

options.A: the belief that technology alone decides textual stability now yields a forecast of instability for digital texts.
options.B: digital texts are being converted back into print so that they will become stable once again.
options.C: the history of printing is now being read backwards, starting from the digital present.
options.D: historians are now arguing that the printing press made texts less stable than hand copying had ever done.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the belief that technology alone decides textual stability now yields a forecast of instability for digital texts.

option_rationales.B: Nothing in paragraph 4 describes converting digital texts to print; the remedy proposed is institutions such as archives and citation conventions.
option_rationales.C: The phrase concerns the direction of the argument (stability to instability), not the order in which history is studied.
option_rationales.D: The passage nowhere reports such a reversal among historians; paragraph 2 still holds print 'more dependable' than manuscript.

questions.explanation: The commonplace of paragraph 1 holds that a machine fixed texts. Paragraph 4 says 'Digital texts, we are told, are inherently unstable', which applies the same technology-decides reasoning with the opposite outcome. The author's reply is that institutions, not the machine alone, will 'settle the outcome'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking 'reverse' to mean a reversal of historical judgment rather than the same reasoning applied with the opposite result.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase can only be decoded by linking paragraph 4 back to the thesis of paragraph 1.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim in paragraph 3 that fixity was a social achievement the technology 'made possible but did not by itself deliver'?

options.A: Hand-press printers in fact seldom stopped the press to correct errors, so most copies of an edition were identical.
options.B: Some medieval copyists produced manuscripts so accurate that later scholars could find very few errors in them.
options.C: When powered presses replaced hand presses, variation between copies of one edition largely vanished even before any rights over copies were enforced.
options.D: Where presses were common but rights over copies and collation were absent, printed texts of one work kept varying for generations.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Where presses were common but rights over copies and collation were absent, printed texts of one work kept varying for generations.

option_rationales.A: This undermines the evidence of paragraph 2 that copies differed, and it would make the press itself look like the source of fixity.
option_rationales.B: The claim concerns what made print fixed; the accuracy of individual manuscripts is irrelevant to whether institutions or the press delivered fixity.
option_rationales.C: This credits the technology alone with producing fixity, without institutions, so it weakens the paragraph 3 claim rather than strengthening it.

questions.explanation: The claim has two parts: the press enabled fixity, but institutions were needed to deliver it. A case in which presses existed without those institutions and texts still varied shows that the technology was not sufficient, which is precisely what the claim asserts.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the powered-press option because it mentions copies becoming identical, missing that it makes the machine sufficient.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options concern fixity and one of them reverses the claim; the solver must isolate necessity versus sufficiency.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that digital texts are inherently unstable, unlike printed books, which became fixed as soon as the press was invented.
options.B: refute the thesis that printed books were more dependable than manuscripts, and argue that digital texts are equally unreliable.
options.C: qualify a common thesis about print by crediting institutions as well as the press with fixity, and extend the lesson to digital texts.
options.D: describe in detail the methods by which printers in the hand-press period corrected errors while their sheets were still being printed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) qualify a common thesis about print by crediting institutions as well as the press with fixity, and extend the lesson to digital texts.

option_rationales.A: This states the two commonplaces the author challenges; paragraph 3 says fixity took a 'slowly assembled set of expectations and institutions'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the thesis 'in its broad outline' is 'not wrong', and paragraph 2 calls print 'a more dependable object than a manuscript'; nor does the author call digital texts unreliable.
option_rationales.D: Stop-press correction is evidence used in paragraph 2; describing it is too narrow to be the purpose of a passage that moves on to institutions and digital texts.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 grants the commonplace in outline but says it credits the machine with too much; paragraphs 2 and 3 show variation in print and the institutions that produced fixity; paragraph 4 applies the lesson to digital texts. The correct answer names the qualification, its basis and the application.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the author's critique of the commonplace as an outright refutation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author's position is a qualification rather than a rejection, and the wrong options are rejection, narrow detail and the reported view.

questions.question: The author suggests that the uneven division of the religion class in the scheme described in paragraph 2 is best explained by

options.A: the collections and assumptions of the libraries that were familiar to the person who devised the scheme.
options.B: the technical limits of decimal notation, which could not divide a single class into more than a few parts.
options.C: a deliberate effort by its maker to push the world's other religious traditions to the margins of libraries.
options.D: the near absence, anywhere in the nineteenth century, of published books about religions other than Christianity.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the collections and assumptions of the libraries that were familiar to the person who devised the scheme.

option_rationales.B: Notation is never blamed; the passage treats the allocation as a judgment reflecting assumptions, not as a technical constraint.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says 'Nobody needs to suppose malice to explain this', which rules out deliberate intent as the explanation offered.
option_rationales.D: The passage makes no claim about what books existed; it attributes the imbalance to the libraries 'its maker knew', not to the world's output.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'the scheme reflected the collections and the assumptions of the libraries its maker knew'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying malice where the passage explicitly says none need be supposed.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence immediately after the example.

questions.question: The hypothetical study of household labour in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: show that schemes allot too little shelf space to subjects that their makers did not consider central.
options.B: illustrate how a scheme, by deciding a book's neighbours, frames the way browsing readers meet its argument.
options.C: suggest that authors, rather than librarians, should decide where their books are placed on the shelves.
options.D: argue that studies of household labour belong among works on economics rather than among works on the family.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate how a scheme, by deciding a book's neighbours, frames the way browsing readers meet its argument.

option_rationales.A: Space allocation is the topic of paragraph 2; paragraph 3 opens by saying the effect 'is not confined to how much space a subject receives' and turns to adjacency.
option_rationales.C: The passage notes that the scheme 'rather than the author' chooses the conversation, but it proposes no transfer of that choice to authors.
option_rationales.D: The author takes no side on where the study belongs; the point is that either placement shapes how it is read, and 'The book is the same'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 claims that 'Classification also governs adjacency, and adjacency governs discovery'. The household-labour example shows one book met 'as an argument about production and value' in one place and 'as an argument about domestic life' in another.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the adjacency point of paragraph 3 with the space point of paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option uses the neighbouring paragraph's point; another turns an observation into a proposal.

questions.question: The passage offers each of the following as a reason not to replace classification with keyword search EXCEPT that

options.A: without some order, readers could find only what they already knew to ask for.
options.B: search systems rank their results, and ranking involves choices just as shelving does.
options.C: a collection without any arrangement would be unusable rather than neutral.
options.D: keyword search cannot cope with subjects that older schemes had crammed into long, unwieldy numbers.

questions.correct_answer: (D) keyword search cannot cope with subjects that older schemes had crammed into long, unwieldy numbers.

option_rationales.A: This is stated in paragraph 4: 'a reader can then find only what she already knows to ask for'.
option_rationales.B: This is stated in paragraph 4: 'ranking embodies choices just as surely as shelving does'.
option_rationales.C: This is stated in paragraph 4: 'a collection with no arrangement is not neutral but unusable'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 gives three reasons against abandoning classification: ranking embodies hidden choices, an unarranged collection is unusable, and without order a reader finds only what she already knows to ask for. The 'long, unwieldy numbers' belong to paragraph 2's discussion of space and are never offered as a limitation of keyword search.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting an option because its wording comes from the passage, without checking whether it is used as a reason in paragraph 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer reuses passage wording from a different paragraph and context.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A classification scheme revised often enough could eventually achieve complete neutrality about knowledge.
options.B: Giving a book several subject headings partly offsets its being able to stand in only one place.
options.C: Local fixes to an inherited scheme are the best way for a library in a diverse city to correct its biases.
options.D: Keyword search, unlike shelving, allows readers to meet books without any viewpoint being imposed on them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Giving a book several subject headings partly offsets its being able to stand in only one place.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 5 says flatly that 'No scheme will ever be neutral', however often it is revised.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 presents local fixes as a cost, since they 'make its shelves harder to share with other libraries'; they are not recommended.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says search systems rank results and that ranking 'embodies choices just as surely as shelving does'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 notes, as part of making classification revisable and visible, that 'catalogues increasingly allow a book to carry several subject headings even though it can stand in only one place', which presents multiple headings as a partial remedy for the single physical location that paragraph 3 shows to be so consequential.
questions.common_misconception: Reading paragraph 5's call for revision as a promise of eventual neutrality.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be inferred from how paragraph 5 uses a detail, and each wrong option is ruled out by a different paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the point about adjacency made in paragraph 3?

options.A: A museum shows one painting among devotional works, then among portraits, and visitors see it as worship in one room and a likeness in the other.
options.B: A curator labels a painting with the wrong date, and the error is corrected decades later after visiting scholars point it out to the museum.
options.C: A museum has wall space for only a fraction of its paintings, so works from traditions its founders neglected stay in storage while others are displayed.
options.D: A visitor uses the museum's search terminal to locate a painting she already knows by name and goes straight to it without looking at anything else.

questions.correct_answer: (A) A museum shows one painting among devotional works, then among portraits, and visitors see it as worship in one room and a likeness in the other.

option_rationales.B: This resembles the revisions of paragraph 5, prompted by outsiders, but a mistaken date is a factual error, not a framing produced by placement.
option_rationales.C: This parallels the allocation of space in paragraph 2, not adjacency; paragraph 3 explicitly turns away from 'how much space a subject receives'.
option_rationales.D: This mirrors the reader who finds 'only what she already knows to ask for' in paragraph 4; it involves no effect of neighbouring works on interpretation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that the same book is understood differently depending on its neighbours: 'The book is the same, but the conversation it is placed in is not'. The painting read as devotional in one room and as a portrait in another has exactly this structure: the object is unchanged, and the placement chooses how it is met.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the storage option because it is also about bias in a collection, though it concerns space rather than neighbours.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option maps onto a different paragraph of the passage, so the solver must isolate the specific relation in paragraph 3.

questions.question: According to the passage, the characters of Chinese are

options.A: signs that stand only for syllables, which places them one rung below the alphabet.
options.B: for the most part pictures of the things they name, much as the ladder described them.
options.C: in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another loosely indicates sound.
options.D: an early and incomplete stage in a development that leads naturally toward the alphabet.

questions.correct_answer: (C) in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another loosely indicates sound.

option_rationales.A: The passage describes the characters as meaning-and-sound compounds; it never says they stand only for syllables.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the ladder presented them this way but that the scripts on its lower rungs 'were seldom what it said they were'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 denies this: such a script 'is not a halting step toward phonetic writing but a different and highly developed answer'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the characters are 'in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another indicates, however loosely, sound.'
questions.common_misconception: Taking the ladder's description, which the passage reports in order to reject, as the passage's own.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, to 'mistake a family tree for a law of nature' is to

options.A: confuse the biological ancestry of peoples with the history of the scripts that those peoples happen to use.
options.B: regard scripts that are historically related to one another as if they had developed quite independently.
options.C: assume that scripts change by a process of natural selection in which the fittest systems survive.
options.D: treat the particular line of descent of some scripts as a sequence through which every writing system must pass.

questions.correct_answer: (D) treat the particular line of descent of some scripts as a sequence through which every writing system must pass.

option_rationales.A: The 'family tree' is a lineage of scripts, 'one lineage of scripts in one region', not the ancestry of peoples.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the error: the ladder over-generalises one lineage, rather than overlooking relations between scripts.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no claim about selection; 'law of nature' refers to a universal rule that all writing 'must follow'.

questions.explanation: The sentence explains itself: the sequence is 'the history of one lineage of scripts in one region', and the error is 'to present it as the path that all writing must follow'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'family tree' and 'law of nature' as biological terms instead of as figures for local history and universal rule.
questions.difficulty_reason: The figure must be decoded from its sentence; wrong options exploit biological readings.

questions.question: The discussion of the Korean script in paragraph 4 implies that

options.A: judging one script better than another can be defensible when the judgment is tied to particular users and ends.
options.B: the ladder was right to rank phonetic scripts above others, since the Korean designers reached the same view.
options.C: scripts that were deliberately designed are in general better than scripts that developed gradually over centuries.
options.D: once the costs of learning are taken into account, every script turns out to be equally suited to every language.

questions.correct_answer: (A) judging one script better than another can be defensible when the judgment is tied to particular users and ends.

option_rationales.B: The designers' belief is called 'a ranking relative to a purpose, which is precisely what the ladder lacked', so it does not vindicate the ladder's absolute ranking.
option_rationales.C: The passage contrasts purpose-relative and absolute rankings, not designed and evolved scripts; this generalisation is outside its scope.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 begins by denying that 'scripts are equal in every respect' and says the costs of learning differ.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the designers 'believed that some ways of writing were better than others for certain ends', and that this 'is a ranking of a kind, but it is a ranking relative to a purpose'. The author therefore accepts comparisons tied to purposes and users while rejecting the ladder's purpose-free ranking.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the example as support for the ladder because it involves a phonetic script judged superior.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer turns on the difference between an absolute and a purpose-relative ranking; the strongest wrong option blurs exactly that difference.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim in paragraph 5 about what literacy rates chiefly depend on?

options.A: Several societies using alphabets but lacking widespread schooling have had low adult literacy for long periods.
options.B: With schooling, reading matter and rewards for reading held equal, societies using regularly spelled alphabets had far higher adult literacy.
options.C: Children learning an alphabet with regular spelling begin decoding unfamiliar words earlier than children learning a script that represents meaning.
options.D: Learners of English must memorise many irregularly spelled words almost as wholes before they can read fluently.

questions.correct_answer: (B) With schooling, reading matter and rewards for reading held equal, societies using regularly spelled alphabets had far higher adult literacy.

option_rationales.A: This fits the author's claim that schooling matters more than script, so it supports rather than weakens paragraph 5.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 already concedes this advantage of economy; an earlier start in decoding does not show that literacy rates depend chiefly on script.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 makes this point itself; it concerns the cost of one alphabet and does not bear on what literacy rates chiefly depend on.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 claims that literacy rates 'owe much more to schools, to the availability of reading matter and to whether reading pays' than to scripts. If, with those conditions held equal, script type still produced large differences in literacy, script would emerge as a major cause, which directly undercuts the claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the decoding option because it shows an advantage of alphabets, without noticing that the author grants it and that it concerns speed of learning, not rates of literacy.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding the claim's comparative form ('much more') and seeing that only a controlled comparison tests it; the most tempting wrong option is a conceded point.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following claims EXCEPT that

options.A: how economical an alphabet is depends partly on how closely its spelling follows pronunciation.
options.B: the ladder's ordering of scripts carried an implicit judgment about the peoples who used them.
options.C: the mixed system used for Japanese is easier for beginners to learn than an alphabet with regular spelling.
options.D: rejecting the ladder is compatible with holding that some scripts suit certain purposes better than others.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the mixed system used for Japanese is easier for beginners to learn than an alphabet with regular spelling.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says 'an alphabet is only as economical as its spelling permits', which supports this claim.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 notes that the peoples on 'the topmost rung were, in most such accounts, the authors' own', implying a self-flattering judgment.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the Korean designers' belief was 'a ranking relative to a purpose', which the author accepts while rejecting the ladder.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the mixed Japanese system aids 'rapid reading once the system is mastered'; it makes no claim that the system is easier to learn, and paragraph 3 credits ease of early decoding to a regularly spelled alphabet instead. The other three claims are each supported by the paragraph cited.
questions.common_misconception: Turning an advantage for mastered readers into an advantage for beginners.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer distorts a real advantage the passage grants, and the supported claims require inference from tone (paragraph 1) and concession (paragraph 4).

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Journalism should stop treating novelty as a test of newsworthiness and should report events in proportion to how often they occur.
options.B: Readers misjudge risks mainly because they follow too little news, and wider and more regular reading would correct their sense of how often events occur.
options.C: The news misleads chiefly because of how news is defined, and the fault is better corrected by adding context than by seeking cheerful stories.
options.D: Editors favour bad news because it attracts paying readers, and this commercial taste is the main reason that audiences overrate rare and dramatic dangers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The news misleads chiefly because of how news is defined, and the fault is better corrected by adding context than by seeking cheerful stories.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 calls novelty 'a legitimate test', and paragraph 4 says the news should not try to be 'a faithful miniature of the world'.
option_rationales.B: The passage argues that reading the news is what makes rare events 'feel common'; nothing suggests that reading more would correct the skew.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 1 grants that the accusation is 'not exactly false' but says it 'misplaces the problem'; the skew comes from the definition of news, not a taste for bad tidings.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 locates the skew in 'a definition of news itself', paragraph 2 shows its effects on perceived risk and trends, paragraph 3 rejects demanding 'more good news' and abandoning the unusual, and paragraph 4 proposes reporting 'the denominator alongside the numerator'. The correct answer holds both the diagnosis and the remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the accusation the author reports in paragraph 1 as if it were the author's own diagnosis.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option restates a view the author partly grants and then sets aside; the correct answer needs both halves of the argument.

questions.question: According to the passage, gradual improvements tend to go unreported because

options.A: editors deliberately hold them back, believing that cheerful stories sell far fewer copies than alarming stories about decline.
options.B: they are spread thinly over time, so that no single day offers an event the definition of news can register.
options.C: readers distrust any outlet that reports good news, so publications avoid such stories in order to protect their credibility.
options.D: they are usually too technical to explain clearly in the limited space that an ordinary news story can allow them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) they are spread thinly over time, so that no single day offers an event the definition of news can register.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the skew does not come mainly from 'a taste for bad tidings', and paragraph 2 says its effects are ones 'no individual editor intends'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says readers distrust outlets 'managing their mood' with stories chosen for cheerfulness, not that they distrust good news as such.
option_rationales.D: The passage never mentions technical difficulty or space; it explains the omission by the definition of news.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says news privileges what is 'attributable to a single moment', so the firms that open over a decade are not news 'because no single day contains their story'; paragraph 2 adds that improvements are 'gradual and diffuse'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the passage as a complaint about editorial motives rather than about a definition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is stated in paragraph 1 and echoed in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author's observation that improvements are 'gradual and diffuse' while deteriorations are 'often abrupt' implies that

options.A: abrupt deteriorations matter less than gradual improvements and should therefore receive less space in the news.
options.B: most news reports about social trends contain errors of fact that systematically exaggerate how far things have declined.
options.C: societies are in fact improving in most respects, whatever impression their news happens to give them.
options.D: a society's news can mislead it about the direction of change even when each individual report is accurate.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a society's news can mislead it about the direction of change even when each individual report is accurate.

option_rationales.A: The author never ranks the two; paragraph 3 defends reporting the fire that did happen, so the option invents a prescription.
option_rationales.B: The passage never says reports are inaccurate; the distortion comes from which events count as news, not from false statements.
option_rationales.C: The passage says a society 'that is slowly getting better at something' can believe it is getting worse; it makes no claim that most things are improving.

questions.explanation: Because deteriorations arrive as datable events and improvements do not, the news registers the first and misses the second, so a society 'can easily believe, from its news, that it is getting worse' without any single story being false.
questions.common_misconception: Turning a conditional point about perception into a factual claim that the world is improving.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing that the mechanism is selection, not error, and rejecting an overstatement of the conditional.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, 'report the denominator alongside the numerator' most nearly means

options.A: present an event together with the wider count of cases against which its frequency can be judged
options.B: divide the space available evenly between rare events and the common events that seldom make headlines
options.C: balance each day's alarming stories with an equal number of cheerful stories about the same subjects
options.D: publish the statistics behind a story in place of the narrative account of what actually happened on the day

questions.correct_answer: (A) present an event together with the wider count of cases against which its frequency can be judged

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the news should not try to be a 'faithful miniature', and nothing proposes an even division of space.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 rejects stories 'chosen because they are cheerful', so a quota of good news is the remedy the author dismisses.
option_rationales.D: The examples in paragraph 4 add figures to the story ('can say whether such crimes are rising'); they do not replace the story.

questions.explanation: The examples that follow explain the phrase: a crime story says 'whether such crimes are rising or falling', and a side-effect story says 'how many people take the drug without harm'. The single case is set against the larger total.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the metaphor as a call for balancing good news against bad.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is glossed by the two examples that follow it.

questions.question: According to the passage, one advantage of funding news through subscriptions is that a publication

options.A: becomes answerable to its own readers and has less reason to chase brief online clicks.
options.B: can make sure that its best reporting reaches readers who could not otherwise afford it.
options.C: can target its advertising at particular audiences far more precisely than printed newspapers could.
options.D: can lower the price that readers pay for careful reporting and so share it more widely.

questions.correct_answer: (A) becomes answerable to its own readers and has less reason to chase brief online clicks.
