option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the wall excludes readers who cannot pay; reaching them is the problem paragraph 4 tries to solve.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 credits precise targeting to the online platforms that drew advertising away, not to subscription-funded publications.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the opposite: it was advertising that 'made news cheap for the reader', while subscriptions put careful reporting behind a wall.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says a subscription-funded publication 'answers to the people who read it rather than to the firms that want to sell them things' and has 'less incentive to chase the cheap, fleeting clicks'.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing to subscriptions an effect that the passage attributes to advertising or to online platforms.
questions.difficulty_reason: Stated in two adjacent sentences of paragraph 1.

questions.question: The passage implies that readers who do not pay for subscriptions

options.A: are mostly people who prefer opinion to reporting and would not read careful journalism if it were free.
options.B: are likely to depend more on cheaply produced material such as opinion, rumour and aggregation.
options.C: are largely protected from misinformation by the better-informed subscribers who live around them.
options.D: tend to stop following public affairs altogether once careful reporting is placed behind a wall.

questions.correct_answer: (B) are likely to depend more on cheaply produced material such as opinion, rumour and aggregation.

option_rationales.A: The passage says they cannot 'or will not' pay, but it never says they prefer opinion; their reliance on it follows from what is free.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 says that even the well-informed 'are not fully protected' when those around them are misinformed; nothing suggests that subscribers shield anyone else.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says plainly that 'The second group does not stop reading'; it turns to free material instead.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says non-paying readers turn 'to whatever is free', which is 'increasingly material that is cheap to produce: opinion, aggregation, rumour and content funded by people with something to promote'.
questions.common_misconception: Inferring a preference from a pattern the passage explains by price.
questions.difficulty_reason: The inference follows directly from two sentences of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following is most similar to the author's reason, in paragraph 3, for treating news differently from most products?

options.A: A restaurant meal, which costs more at a better restaurant but satisfies the diner's hunger whichever one is chosen.
options.B: A gym membership, whose benefits go to the member alone and in proportion to how often the member actually attends.
options.C: A luxury watch, whose value to its owner is quite unaffected by whether anyone else in the town owns one or not.
options.D: Fire safety in a block of flats, where a household that takes every precaution is still endangered if its neighbours take none.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Fire safety in a block of flats, where a household that takes every precaution is still endangered if its neighbours take none.

option_rationales.A: This concerns price and quality for a single buyer, not the way one person's lack of a good harms those who have it.
option_rationales.B: The benefit here stays with the buyer, whereas paragraph 3 stresses that the value of reporting 'does not stay with the person who buys it'.
option_rationales.C: This is a purely private good, the kind of product the author contrasts news with; its value does not depend on others.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that 'the well-informed are not fully protected if those around them are not', comparing news to public health. Fire safety in shared housing has the same structure: one party's protection depends on what others do.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about price or quality, which is the theme of paragraph 2, rather than the spillover of paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Only one option has the spillover structure the paragraph describes.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the shift to subscription funding is best described as one of

options.A: enthusiastic endorsement, treating it as the solution to the problems that the advertising era left behind.
options.B: nostalgic regret, wishing that the advertising arrangement it replaced could somehow be brought back again.
options.C: qualified approval, valuing the independence it brings while insisting that the exclusion it causes be reduced.
options.D: resigned pessimism, doubting whether any measure could do much to reduce the exclusion it creates.

questions.correct_answer: (C) qualified approval, valuing the independence it brings while insisting that the exclusion it causes be reduced.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 sets out 'a cost that its admirers tend to pass over', so the author does not endorse the shift without reservation.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the conclusion is not that news 'should go back to an advertising model that has largely collapsed'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 lists several remedies; 'None is sufficient alone' calls for combining them, which is not a counsel of despair.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 grants that the change has been welcomed 'with some reason'; paragraph 2 names its cost; paragraph 4 asks 'how to keep the independence that reader revenue brings while limiting the exclusion it creates'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'None is sufficient alone' as pessimism, or the praise of advertising's reach as nostalgia.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options exploit isolated phrases; the correct answer requires the balance of paragraphs 1, 2 and 4.

questions.question: The example of the council's road proposal in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that disputes in local politics turn on questions of fact rather than of values.
options.B: illustrate a kind of dispute in which giving the competing cases equal space is appropriate.
options.C: show that local reporters tend to favour the views of residents over those of officials.
options.D: demonstrate how the habit of balance misleads readers about the true weight of opinion.

questions.correct_answer: (B) illustrate a kind of dispute in which giving the competing cases equal space is appropriate.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 offers the road as a disagreement 'about values or interests', the reverse of a question of fact.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 has the reporter call residents on both sides; no preference for residents over officials is suggested.
option_rationales.D: That is the point of paragraph 2 about lopsided scientific questions; the road example shows where balance works.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 uses the road and the minister as cases where 'the disagreement is about values or interests', concluding that there 'readers are entitled to hear the competing cases at comparable length'.
questions.common_misconception: Attaching the example to the paragraph 2 criticism instead of the paragraph 1 concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is signalled by the sentence that follows the example.

questions.question: The passage suggests that in a report giving equal time to one scientist from each camp, the misleading element lies chiefly in

options.A: the statements of the dissenting scientist, who misrepresents the evidence in order to seem credible.
options.B: the reporter's decision to quote any dissenting scientist at all on a question that is largely settled.
options.C: the reader's unreasonable belief that a newspaper would never stage a contest between unequal parties.
options.D: the arrangement of the report, which implies a parity between the two camps that does not exist.

questions.correct_answer: (D) the arrangement of the report, which implies a parity between the two camps that does not exist.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says the format 'communicated a falsehood that neither speaker uttered', so the speakers' statements are not the source.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says the critique requires 'not the exclusion of minority views but their placement', so quoting a dissenter is acceptable.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 calls the reader's assumption reasonable ('reasonably assuming'), so the fault is not placed on the reader.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the report is 'scrupulously fair to the two individuals and seriously misleading about the state of knowledge', and 'The format has communicated a falsehood that neither speaker uttered'. The equal allotment implies an even split.
questions.common_misconception: Blaming the dissenter or the reader, or treating any mention of a dissenter as the fault.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the format from the content of what is said; one wrong option reverses 'reasonably'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the first point of the objection in paragraph 3?

options.A: In many fields there is no reliable way to tell how researchers' views are distributed, since such opinion is seldom surveyed.
options.B: Several majorities in the history of science later abandoned their views after new and unexpected evidence came to light.
options.C: Many journalists who report on science have no formal training in any of the fields that they cover.
options.D: Readers say that they trust reports quoting two scientists more than reports quoting only a single scientist.

questions.correct_answer: (A) In many fields there is no reliable way to tell how researchers' views are distributed, since such opinion is seldom surveyed.

option_rationales.B: This is the second point of the objection, which the author concedes and answers separately; it does not touch the reply about distribution.
option_rationales.C: The author already grants that journalists are 'poorly placed' to judge; the reply is that they need not judge, so this leaves it intact.
option_rationales.D: Readers' trust in a format does not bear on whether a reporter can check how opinion in a field is distributed.

questions.explanation: The reply is that the reporter need only describe 'how opinion within a field is distributed, which is itself a matter of fact that can be checked'. If that distribution often cannot be reliably checked, the reply loses its footing.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a restatement of the objection itself, which the author has already conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires isolating the precise premise of the reply and separating it from the conceded points.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: If a minority scientific view later prevails, the way the question is reported ought to change.
options.B: Giving rival positions comparable space is appropriate when the dispute concerns values or interests.
options.C: Where researchers disagree, reporters should present the majority view in a field as the settled answer.
options.D: A report can be entirely fair to each person it quotes and yet leave its readers with a false picture.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Where researchers disagree, reporters should present the majority view in a field as the settled answer.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says that if a dissent prevails 'the reporting can change with it', so the author accepts this.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 calls the habit 'a good one wherever the disagreement is about values or interests', so the author agrees.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says such a report is 'scrupulously fair to the two individuals and seriously misleading', so the author agrees.

questions.explanation: The author rejects 'reflexive deference' as well as 'reflexive balance' (paragraph 4) and says that where science is 'genuinely unsettled', rival hypotheses belong side by side. Treating the majority as settled whenever researchers disagree is therefore not the author's view.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a critic of false balance must favour deference to the majority in every case.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is tempting because the passage criticises false balance; rejecting it needs the final paragraph's two-sided qualification.

questions.question: According to the passage, the click on a headline measures

options.A: how much better informed a reader has become after finishing the article that the headline introduced.
options.B: the importance that editors attach to a story compared with the other stories on the page.
options.C: how many of the readers who opened a story were disappointed by what they found in it.
options.D: how strongly a headline draws a reader at the moment of deciding which article to open.

questions.correct_answer: (D) how strongly a headline draws a reader at the moment of deciding which article to open.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says a click measures 'still less whether the reader was better informed for having read it'.
option_rationales.B: Clicks record readers' decisions, 'made by a real person'; editors' judgements of importance are not what is measured.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says a disappointing story can 'outperform' a rewarding one, so clicks do not record disappointment.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: a click 'measures the pull of a headline at the instant of choice, not the worth of what follows'.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing what a click records with what newsrooms wrongly take it to record.
questions.difficulty_reason: Located in one sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that coverage of foreign elections tends to shrink mainly because

options.A: resources follow a measure that cannot register the value such coverage has for readers.
options.B: readers have shown through their choices over many years that they no longer want to read it.
options.C: editors have concluded after deliberation that such subjects are no longer worth the effort of reporting.
options.D: such stories cost far more to produce than the lighter stories that tend to perform well on screens.

questions.correct_answer: (A) resources follow a measure that cannot register the value such coverage has for readers.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 says such coverage is vulnerable 'not because readers have rejected it', which rules this out directly.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 begins 'No editor decides to abandon difficult subjects'; the thinning happens without any such decision.
option_rationales.D: Production costs are never mentioned; the passage explains the decline by how performance figures are read.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says poorly performing stories receive 'less space, fewer reporters and less prominent positions', and that the vulnerable subjects decline 'because the measure in use was never designed to register its value'.
questions.common_misconception: Supplying a deliberate editorial decision or a reader rejection that the paragraph explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are ruled out by explicit denials; the correct answer requires linking the allocation to the measure.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Audience figures have damaged journalism, and newsrooms would serve the public better by returning to editorial instinct.
options.B: Audience figures record genuine choices but are misused when newsrooms treat them as a verdict on value.
options.C: Headline testing misleads readers by promising stories that the articles behind the headlines fail to deliver.
options.D: Refined measures such as return visits and subscriptions can at last settle what a public needs to know.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Audience figures record genuine choices but are misused when newsrooms treat them as a verdict on value.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says it 'would be naive' to switch the screens off, since the old instincts 'were not neutral'.
option_rationales.C: This enlarges one illustration in paragraph 2 into the thesis; the passage is about how newsrooms read the figures.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 calls these 'improvements' that 'can be gamed' and says 'no figure, however refined' can settle this.

questions.explanation: The passage opens by granting that 'the numbers are not lies', argues that a newsroom treating them 'as a verdict on its journalism' misreads curiosity as value, traces the gradual damage, and concludes that judgement 'cannot be handed to the instruments'.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the critics' conclusion in paragraph 1, which the author answers rather than adopts.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options take the critics' side, overstate the remedy, or narrow to one example.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation in paragraph 3 of why some subjects thin out?

options.A: Stories about committee hearings draw fewer clicks than stories about celebrities, although their readers stay with them longer.
options.B: Headline testing has raised the total number of readers that most news websites attract each month, sometimes by a wide margin.
options.C: In newsrooms that never adopted live audience figures, coverage of the same subjects declined over the same years at the same pace.
options.D: Some editors privately regret the shrinking space given to foreign elections but feel unable to do anything to reverse the trend.

questions.correct_answer: (C) In newsrooms that never adopted live audience figures, coverage of the same subjects declined over the same years at the same pace.

option_rationales.A: This fits the author's account that the click misses the value such stories have, so it supports rather than weakens it.
option_rationales.B: Total traffic says nothing about which subjects lose resources or why, so it leaves the explanation untouched.
option_rationales.D: This is consistent with 'No editor decides to abandon difficult subjects'; regret without decision is what the author describes.

questions.explanation: The author attributes the thinning to resources being allocated by a measure that cannot register value. If newsrooms without such measures show the same decline, some other cause is at work and the explanation is undermined.
questions.common_misconception: Picking an option that mentions the vulnerable subjects but is consistent with, or supports, the author's account.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer works by removing the proposed cause while the effect persists; the topical wrong options all fit the author.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, the phrase 'the story cannot be stood up' indicates that

options.A: the reporters cannot gather enough evidence to justify publishing the story they had suspected was there.
options.B: the person at the centre of the story has refused every request from the reporters to be interviewed about it.
options.C: the story has grown far too long to fit into the limited space that the publication has made available for it.
options.D: a rival publication has already reported the same story before the team could finish its own work.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the reporters cannot gather enough evidence to justify publishing the story they had suspected was there.

option_rationales.B: Reluctant sources are mentioned, but the phrase names the outcome of the checking, not a refusal by one person.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 concerns months of 'checking figures' that may come to nothing; the length of the story is never at issue.
option_rationales.D: Rivals appear only in paragraph 2, reporting a finding after it is published; they are not part of this phrase.

questions.explanation: The phrase follows months of 'requesting documents, cultivating reluctant sources and checking figures' and is paired with the story proving 'smaller and duller than it seemed'. It means the evidence does not hold up enough to publish.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the idiom literally, or attaching it to a detail from a later paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The surrounding sentence makes the sense clear.

questions.question: The author's remark that 'a quiet year may be evidence of its success' suggests that

options.A: a lack of published exposures proves that the deterrent effect of investigative reporting is working as it should.
options.B: a lack of published exposures indicates that the publication has failed to fund enough investigations to be effective.
options.C: a lack of published exposures shows that officials have learned to conceal their wrongdoing more skilfully than they once did.
options.D: a lack of published exposures need not mean the reporting was idle, since it may have prevented wrongdoing.

questions.correct_answer: (D) a lack of published exposures need not mean the reporting was idle, since it may have prevented wrongdoing.

option_rationales.A: The author says a quiet year 'may be' evidence of success; claiming proof turns that possibility into a certainty.
option_rationales.B: This is the unfair judgement by 'visible output' that the author warns against, not the author's own inference.
option_rationales.C: Concealment is never discussed; the passage's point is that wrongdoing may not have occurred at all.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says officials who expect scrutiny behave differently and that 'the corruption that never takes place leaves no story behind it'. A year without exposures is therefore compatible with the reporting doing its job.
questions.common_misconception: Hardening the author's 'may be' into 'proves'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option matches the author's direction but overstates the degree.

questions.question: Paragraph 2 contributes to the argument of the passage chiefly by

options.A: establishing that most investigations fail to produce a story that a publication is able to print.
options.B: explaining why the market tends to supply less investigative work than a society would want.
options.C: demonstrating that readers place little value on the results that investigative reporting produces for them.
options.D: showing that rival publications act unfairly when they repeat findings that another paper paid to uncover.

questions.correct_answer: (B) explaining why the market tends to supply less investigative work than a society would want.

option_rationales.A: Failure rates belong to paragraph 1; paragraph 2 is about who receives the benefits of the investigations that succeed.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the benefits reach people 'who did not pay for them', not that anyone values them little.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 describes rivals reporting a finding 'within hours' as a fact about where rewards go; it passes no moral judgement.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that the rewards of a successful investigation do not return to the publisher, because rivals copy it and the beneficiaries are not its readers; such spillover goods 'tend to be supplied in smaller quantities' than a society would choose.
questions.common_misconception: Confusing the content of paragraph 1 with that of paragraph 2, or reading a factual point as a complaint.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option belongs to the neighbouring paragraph; another misstates spillover as low valuation.

questions.question: Which of the following policies most closely reflects the reasoning of the final paragraph?

options.A: A city publishes every inspection report online so that diners can compare kitchens and choose the cleanest restaurants for themselves.
options.B: A city awards a public prize each year to the inspector whose findings led to the most dramatic and widely reported restaurant closure.
options.C: A city keeps a small team of inspectors visiting restaurants unannounced all year round, instead of a large campaign every few years.
options.D: A city trains its food inspectors so thoroughly that their findings against restaurants are almost never overturned when owners appeal against them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A city keeps a small team of inspectors visiting restaurants unannounced all year round, instead of a large campaign every few years.

option_rationales.A: This disciplines restaurants through consumer choice, a different mechanism from the continuous possibility of scrutiny the paragraph describes.
option_rationales.B: Rewarding the spectacular case is the reverse of valuing 'a steady capacity for inquiry above the occasional prize-winning scoop'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 says the case for such work 'does not depend on its infallibility'; accuracy is not the feature it rests on.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 holds that 'Deterrence works only if the possibility of scrutiny is continuous' and that a 'modest but permanent habit of looking' beats a rare brilliant exposure. Year-round unannounced visits by a small team embody that reasoning.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the infallibility option, which addresses the objection the author sets aside rather than the conclusion the author draws.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option picks up a real theme of the passage; only one matches the specific claim about continuity.

questions.question: The passage implies that a reader who, after seeing the correction, still blames the stored chemicals for the warehouse fire

options.A: probably never saw the correction at all, since notices of this kind are seldom noticed or read by anyone.
options.B: may well accept that the correction is true while having no other account to put in place of the old one.
options.C: has rejected the correction because it was printed too late and too far away from the original report it was meant to correct.
options.D: trusts the original report more than the correction simply because the original report happened to be published first.

questions.correct_answer: (B) may well accept that the correction is true while having no other account to put in place of the old one.

option_rationales.A: The scenario in paragraph 2 is about readers who were 'told to discard' the claim; the passage never says corrections go unread.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says the complaint about size and timing 'misses the more interesting difficulty', and paragraph 2 says readers do not disbelieve the correction.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says readers return to the claim 'not because they disbelieve the correction', so a judgement of greater trust is ruled out.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: readers 'reach for the explanation they were told to discard, not because they disbelieve the correction but because the correction left them with no story at all'.
questions.common_misconception: Explaining the persistence by distrust of the correction, which the passage expressly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The trust wrong option echoes the 'first explanation' advantage of paragraph 4; the correct answer needs the precise mechanism of paragraph 2.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the explanation offered in paragraph 2?

options.A: Readers who saw the correction on the same page as the original report remembered it better than readers who saw it elsewhere.
options.B: Readers recalled retracted claims more often when the original report had been repeated by several different outlets before the retraction.
options.C: Readers whose correction named another cause of the fire later cited the discarded cause far less often than readers whose correction named none.
options.D: Readers who refused to accept the correction were mostly those who already distrusted the particular newspaper that had printed it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Readers whose correction named another cause of the fire later cited the discarded cause far less often than readers whose correction named none.

option_rationales.A: This concerns prominence, which the author treats as secondary; it does not show that a gap in the account keeps the false claim alive.
option_rationales.B: This points to repetition and familiarity, a different mechanism from the missing link that paragraph 2 describes.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 explains persistence among readers who do accept the correction, so findings about those who reject it are beside the point.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the false claim survives 'because it was doing work that the retraction did not take over'. If filling the gap with another cause sharply reduces reliance on the false one, that explanation is directly supported.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing a finding about prominence, which matches the conventional complaint the author sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option names a real factor in how corrections fail; only one tests the gap mechanism.

questions.question: The author would endorse each of the following practices EXCEPT

options.A: stating in a correction what the investigators now think likely, even when the true cause is not yet certain.
options.B: holding back a causal explanation of an event until the facts on which it depends are better established.
options.C: explaining, when no alternative cause is yet known, why the original claim was made and why it seemed plausible.
options.D: wording a correction so that it avoids restating the false claim, to keep that claim from growing more familiar.

questions.correct_answer: (D) wording a correction so that it avoids restating the false claim, to keep that claim from growing more familiar.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says a retraction can state 'what did cause the fire, or at least what the investigators now think likely'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 tells reporters to 'be slower to supply a cause', so the author endorses this practice.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 recommends exactly this, so that 'the discarded belief is accounted for rather than merely forbidden'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls the worry about repetition 'reasonable' but says it 'should not lead editors to issue vague notices that never say what was wrong', because 'a denial that does not name its target cannot replace anything'.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the author's concession that the worry is 'reasonable' as an endorsement of the practice it motivates.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer rests on a view the author grants partial weight and then rejects; the wrong options are all endorsed in paraphrase.

questions.question: A paper wrongly reported that a train was delayed by a signal failure, and the real cause is still unknown. Which correction would the author regard as most likely to work?

options.A: One saying the cause is still being investigated and explaining that a signal switched off for repairs had been mistaken for a fault.
options.B: One that avoids any mention of signals and says simply that an earlier report about the delay contained an error.
options.C: One printed prominently on the front page the following morning, stating only that the earlier report of a signal failure was wrong.
options.D: One issued within the hour, saying that the signal report was wrong and apologising for the haste with which it had been published.

questions.correct_answer: (A) One saying the cause is still being investigated and explaining that a signal switched off for repairs had been mistaken for a fault.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 rejects 'vague notices that never say what was wrong', since such a denial 'cannot replace anything'.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 1 says even a 'prominent and prompt' correction may fail; a bare denial leaves the gap that paragraph 2 describes.
option_rationales.D: Speed and an apology do not supply an account; the author says the remedy 'lies less in the size of the correction than in its content'.

questions.explanation: With no alternative cause known, paragraph 3 recommends that the correction 'explain why the original claim was made and why it seemed plausible', so the discarded belief is 'accounted for'. Only one option does this.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the promptest or most prominent notice, which addresses the conventional complaint the author says misses the point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The usual remedy (supply the real cause) is unavailable, so the solver must apply the author's fallback recommendation.

questions.question: The comparison with a laboratory in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: argue that scientists, unlike reporters, are free of the personal ambitions that would otherwise distort their judgement.
options.B: illustrate how the labour of verification usually remains invisible to the people who go on to read the results.
options.C: show that trust can rest on how work is arranged rather than on the character of the people doing it.
options.D: suggest that newsrooms should adopt the full experimental methods of the natural sciences in their daily reporting work.

questions.correct_answer: (C) show that trust can rest on how work is arranged rather than on the character of the people doing it.

option_rationales.A: The passage says laboratories are trusted 'not because its scientists lack ambitions', which is the opposite of this claim.
option_rationales.B: Invisibility of verification is a point made in paragraph 3 about journalism; the laboratory comparison makes a different point.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says the method resembled empirical inquiry only 'in a modest way'; no full adoption of experimental method is proposed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'the objectivity belonged to the procedure, not to the person', and the laboratory is trusted because 'their work is arranged so that others can repeat it'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the comparison as praise of scientists' personal virtue, which the sentence denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence containing the comparison.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the author's account, a story that quotes two officials making incompatible claims and checks neither

options.A: is preferable to a story in which the reporter states, on the evidence, which of the two officials is right.
options.B: meets the standard of objectivity as its early champions understood it, though not as its critics understand it.
options.C: fails mainly because the reporter allowed strong personal opinions to shape the way the story was framed.
options.D: displays the outward signs of objectivity while lacking the practice that those signs were supposed to indicate.

questions.correct_answer: (D) displays the outward signs of objectivity while lacking the practice that those signs were supposed to indicate.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 regrets that a reporter who had established which official was wrong 'was discouraged from saying so'.
option_rationales.B: The early champions defined objectivity as checking claims against sources; a story that checks neither claim fails that standard.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the method was designed for reporters with strong opinions; the failure here is the absence of checking, not opinion.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives exactly this case as one that can 'still look objective' without 'any verification at all': 'The appearance had detached itself from the practice it was supposed to indicate'.
questions.common_misconception: Diagnosing the failure as bias, when the passage locates it in the missing verification.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option blends the historical and critical senses of the word; another imports a cause the author rejects.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Objectivity was always an impossible pose, and journalists should replace it by stating their own commitments openly to readers.
options.B: Objectivity as a checkable method rather than personal neutrality remains worth defending, though much criticism fairly targets a debased form of it.
options.C: Objectivity declined because reporters abandoned the flat tone and balanced quotation that had once made their fairness visible to readers.
options.D: Objectivity is valuable because a disciplined method of verification allows newsrooms to become impartial in choosing their stories.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Objectivity as a checkable method rather than personal neutrality remains worth defending, though much criticism fairly targets a debased form of it.

option_rationales.A: This is the critics' alternative, which paragraph 4 rejects because it leaves readers 'no common procedure by which to test' anything.
option_rationales.C: This reverses paragraph 3, where the flat tone and paired quotations are the degraded signs that displaced verification, not what was lost.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 concedes that verification 'governs how a story is reported, not which stories are chosen', so impartial selection is denied.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 separates the impossible 'pose' from objectivity as 'a remedy for the journalist's limitations'; paragraphs 2 and 3 describe the method and its decay into outward signs; paragraph 4 grants that much criticism targets 'this degraded form' but rejects its remedy; paragraph 5 restates the case as answerability.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the critics' view, which the author partly endorses, as the author's conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating three positions: the critics', the degraded practice and the author's; two wrong options are near-misses on scope.

questions.question: The statement in paragraph 5 that the concession 'limits the claim rather than defeating it' implies that

options.A: the defence of objectivity survives once it is confined to making reports answerable and no longer promises impartiality.
options.B: the critics of objectivity were right after all to say that it cannot be defended against the charge of bias.
options.C: the concession is too slight to affect the argument for objectivity in any way that a reader would need to notice.
options.D: the bias shown in choosing stories can in time be brought under the same discipline of verification as reporting.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the defence of objectivity survives once it is confined to making reports answerable and no longer promises impartiality.

option_rationales.B: The author says the concession does not defeat the claim; the case is restated, not abandoned.
option_rationales.C: The concession does change the claim: it gives up impartiality in story selection, which is why the author says it 'limits' the claim.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 5 says 'No procedure can remove that influence', so extending verification to story selection is ruled out.

questions.explanation: Having conceded that method cannot govern which stories are chosen, the author narrows the case: objectivity as method 'is not that it makes journalism impartial but that it makes journalism answerable'. The claim is reduced in scope, not refuted.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the concession as either trivial or fatal, rather than as a narrowing of scope.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer turns on the difference between limiting and defeating a claim; each wrong option errs in a different direction.

questions.question: Which of the following practices best fits objectivity as the passage says its early champions understood it?

options.A: A reporter refuses to state any conclusion and gives each side of a dispute exactly the same number of paragraphs.
options.B: A reporter declines to cover any subject on which she holds strong opinions, so as to keep her own work neutral.
options.C: A reporter known for strong views publishes an investigation listing the documents and named sources behind each of its claims.
options.D: A reporter begins every story by declaring her political commitments, so that readers can make allowance for them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A reporter known for strong views publishes an investigation listing the documents and named sources behind each of its claims.

option_rationales.A: These are the 'outward signs' of paragraph 3, which can be produced 'without any verification at all'.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says 'the method existed for such reporters'; avoiding the subjects mistakes objectivity for personal neutrality.
option_rationales.D: This is the critics' remedy in paragraph 4; candour 'is not a substitute for evidence' and is not the early method.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes the method: checking claims, preferring documents and saying 'where each piece of information came from, so that a reader or a rival could test it', and adds that a reporter with strong opinions 'could practise the method'.
questions.common_misconception: Equating objectivity with neutral tone or with the avoidance of opinion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option matches a different position in the passage; the correct answer needs the specific content of paragraph 2.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'a common silence' refers to

options.A: the shared absence from public discussion of matters that the gatekeepers chose not to raise.
options.B: the reluctance of mass audiences to criticise the broadcasters whose bulletins they listened to every evening.
options.C: the quiet that settled over public life once the coffeehouses and reading societies had finally closed.
options.D: an agreement freely reached among citizens to avoid raising the topics that most divided them from one another.

questions.correct_answer: (A) the shared absence from public discussion of matters that the gatekeepers chose not to raise.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 says the silence concerned 'matters that the gatekeepers did not think worth raising', not audiences withholding criticism.
option_rationales.C: The phrase describes the broadcast era's 'common ground', not the end of early modern gatherings.
option_rationales.D: The silence was set by 'a small number of editors and producers', so it was imposed by gatekeepers, not freely agreed.

questions.explanation: The sentence reads: 'What looks in retrospect like common ground was in part a common silence about matters that the gatekeepers did not think worth raising'. The silence is the shared omission imposed by those who controlled the forum.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the silence as chosen by citizens rather than set by gatekeepers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is defined within its own sentence.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the lament described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: wholly supportive, endorsing both its account of the shared past and its proposal to restore that past.
options.B: dismissive, treating its concern about lost common ground as a misunderstanding that has no real basis at all.
options.C: detached, describing the lament and its critics without committing to a view of its own on the question.
options.D: sympathetic to the worry it expresses but critical of the history it assumes and of the remedies it suggests.

questions.correct_answer: (D) sympathetic to the worry it expresses but critical of the history it assumes and of the remedies it suggests.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 questions its picture of the past, and paragraph 5 calls its remedy 'impossible' and risky.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says the lament 'contains a real worry', and paragraph 3 says the loss 'should not be dismissed'.
option_rationales.C: The author takes clear positions, for instance that fragmented standards matter more than fragmented audiences.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The lament contains a real worry, but it rests on a picture of the past that deserves scrutiny, and the remedies it suggests follow from the picture rather than from the worry'. Paragraphs 2, 3 and 5 develop each part of this attitude.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the critique of the lament's history as a dismissal of its concern.
questions.difficulty_reason: The balance is set out in paragraph 1 and confirmed in paragraph 3.

questions.question: The passage implies that the breadth of broadcast-era audiences

options.A: made public discussion more inclusive than the coffeehouse gatherings in every respect that mattered for democracy.
options.B: came at the cost of narrowing who could take part in public discussion as speakers rather than listeners.
options.C: resulted from the efforts of editors and producers to widen the range of views considered respectable.
options.D: was achieved by excluding from the audience those who lacked the leisure and literacy to take part.

questions.correct_answer: (B) came at the cost of narrowing who could take part in public discussion as speakers rather than listeners.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says broadcast breadth 'was purchased by a different narrowing', so it was not more inclusive in every respect.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says editors and producers set and limited that range; nothing says they tried to widen it.
option_rationales.D: That exclusion is attributed to the early modern gatherings; broadcast audiences numbered 'millions' who listened.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'their breadth was purchased by a different narrowing: millions listened, while very few were permitted to speak'.
questions.common_misconception: Transferring the exclusion described for the coffeehouses onto the broadcast audience.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option uses the right paragraph's language about the wrong period.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the author's argument EXCEPT:

options.A: Groups that read quite different publications may still resolve their factual disputes with one another if they accept the same rules of evidence.
options.B: The decline of the mass audience is to be regretted mainly because it ended the experience of a nation attending to the same events.
options.C: An attempt to restore a few dominant news outlets could also bring back the exclusions that once accompanied their authority.
options.D: A shared body of reported facts, even one assembled selectively, made it easier for political opponents to argue usefully about policy.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The decline of the mass audience is to be regretted mainly because it ended the experience of a nation attending to the same events.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 says such a society 'is plural, not broken', so this is consistent with the argument.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 5 says nostalgia 'risks restoring the exclusions along with the authority', so this matches.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 grants that a shared stock of facts 'gave opponents something definite to disagree about'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says what was lost 'was not chiefly that everyone attended to the same things', which 'was never a requirement of self-government'; the real loss was shared procedures for settling disputes of fact. Locating the main regret in common attention contradicts this.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting this statement because the author does admit a genuine loss, without noticing that the author locates that loss elsewhere.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer overlaps the author's concession; rejecting it requires the precise 'not chiefly' distinction of paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the fragmentation of audiences matters less than the fragmentation of standards?

options.A: In the broadcast era many citizens distrusted the bulletins they watched yet still accepted the facts those bulletins reported.
options.B: Several plural democracies contain many small publics that settle their disputes through courts and statistical offices trusted by all.
options.C: The coffeehouse debates of early modern Europe were in fact far less exclusive than their modern critics have usually supposed.
options.D: Groups that rarely encounter one another's news gradually stop accepting the same rules of evidence, so separate audiences breed separate standards.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Groups that rarely encounter one another's news gradually stop accepting the same rules of evidence, so separate audiences breed separate standards.

option_rationales.A: This concerns trust within a shared audience and leaves untouched the claim that separate audiences need not mean separate standards.
option_rationales.B: This illustrates the author's picture of plural publics with shared standards, so it supports rather than weakens the claim.
option_rationales.C: This bears on the history in paragraph 2, not on the comparison between audiences and standards in paragraph 4.

questions.explanation: The author treats the two kinds of fragmentation as separable: many publics are fine if standards are shared. If audience fragmentation itself causes standards to fragment, it cannot matter less, since it produces the very danger the author ranks higher.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the coffeehouse option because it attacks part of the author's argument, though not the claim in question.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer works by linking the two variables the author treats as independent; one wrong option attacks the wrong claim.

questions.question: The author's main point about the cycle of replacement terms is that it

options.A: shows that renaming alone cannot change attitudes, though each new term briefly allows more courteous speech.
options.B: reflects a dishonest habit through which speakers flatter themselves while only appearing to spare their listeners.
options.C: can be halted altogether once schools and officials agree to adopt one carefully chosen set of terms.
options.D: proves that renaming is futile and that reformers should give up trying to replace words that have become offensive.

questions.correct_answer: (A) shows that renaming alone cannot change attitudes, though each new term briefly allows more courteous speech.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 reports that 'some go further and call it dishonest'; the author rejects this as part of the hasty second half of the critics' argument.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 says the cycle slows only 'when the thing named stops being a mark of shame'; agreement on vocabulary is never offered as a cure.
option_rationales.D: This is the conclusion of the critics in paragraph 2, and paragraph 3 calls that half of their argument 'too hasty', so it is not the author's point.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 accepts that 'a new word cannot by itself change what people feel' but insists the treadmill 'is not simply a record of failure', since each term creates an interval in which conversations 'become possible'. Paragraph 4 sums up: renaming is 'a temporary courtesy' that cannot 'carry the whole burden of reform'. The correct answer holds both halves of this position.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the critics' view, reported in paragraph 2, as the author's own.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author states the position explicitly; two wrong options restate the reported critics' view, which is clearly marked as rejected.

questions.question: According to the usual explanation described in the passage, replacement terms lose their neutrality because

options.A: the reformers who choose replacement terms misjudge how ordinary speakers will actually use them.
options.B: each new term is usually borrowed from an older vocabulary that already carried traces of contempt.
options.C: attitudes towards the thing a word names pass, while they last, to any word that reliably refers to it.
options.D: speakers soon grow tired of any word that is introduced through official forms and school teaching.

questions.correct_answer: (C) attitudes towards the thing a word names pass, while they last, to any word that reliably refers to it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 locates the cause in attitudes towards the thing named, not in any misjudgement by reformers, who are never blamed for the choice of words.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 1 says each coinage arrives 'clean'; the passage never suggests that new terms are borrowed from tainted vocabularies.
option_rationales.D: Weariness with official words is not mentioned; forms and teachers appear in paragraph 3 only as places where a fresh term does some good.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Attitudes towards the thing named are what give a word its colouring, and so long as those attitudes persist, any word that reliably points at the thing will soon absorb them.' The correct answer paraphrases this sentence.
questions.common_misconception: Inventing a cause about reformers or about where words come from instead of locating the sentence that states the explanation.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer paraphrases a single sentence in paragraph 2.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'displacement activity' refers to

options.A: an action that gives a sense of having dealt with a problem while leaving its cause untouched.
options.B: a process through which the meaning of one word is gradually transferred to another.
options.C: a deliberate effort to push a disliked word out of polite speech and into the slang of everyday talk.
options.D: an activity that shifts the work of reform from public officials onto ordinary speakers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) an action that gives a sense of having dealt with a problem while leaving its cause untouched.

option_rationales.B: This describes the treadmill itself, not the phrase, which the passage applies to the act of replacing terms as a substitute for changing attitudes.
option_rationales.C: The phrase is glossed in the same sentence as 'a way of feeling that something has been done while the underlying attitude goes untouched'; it is not about moving words between registers.
option_rationales.D: No transfer of responsibility between groups is described; the phrase concerns a feeling of accomplishment that leaves attitudes unchanged.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains the phrase immediately: replacing terms is 'a way of feeling that something has been done while the underlying attitude goes untouched'. The correct answer captures that sense of apparent action without effect on the cause.
questions.common_misconception: Reading 'displacement' literally as the moving of a word, instead of using the gloss that follows it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is defined in the clause that follows it.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would expect a replacement term to keep its neutrality longest in a society where

options.A: the term has been chosen by a body of experts rather than by reformers.
options.B: what the term names has largely ceased to be treated as something shameful.
options.C: the new term is gentler and more delicate than any of the terms before it.
options.D: officials use the term consistently on forms and in their public documents.

questions.correct_answer: (B) what the term names has largely ceased to be treated as something shameful.

option_rationales.A: Who chooses the term plays no part in the passage's account; paragraph 2 says any word pointing at the thing absorbs the attitudes towards it.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 suggests the reverse: a gentle name for a harsh reality may sour 'perhaps faster', since the gap 'invites irony'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 mentions official forms as a place where a fresh term helps, not as something that preserves the term's neutrality.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says words absorb the attitudes held towards what they name, and paragraph 4 adds that the cycle slows 'when the thing named stops being a mark of shame. The word then has nothing to absorb.' A term therefore stays neutral longest where the shame has gone.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the gentler term on the assumption that a softer word lasts longer, which paragraph 4 contradicts.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires joining the mechanism in paragraph 2 to the conclusion in paragraph 4 and rejecting a tempting option about gentler words.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is one of the efforts required to follow an argument one disagrees with?

options.A: Taking written notes so that each of the speaker's points can be checked against the evidence later.
options.B: Asking the speaker to slow down so that the separate parts of the argument can be connected.
options.C: Holding back from preparing a reply while the speaker is still partway through a sentence.
options.D: Agreeing provisionally with the speaker until the whole of the argument has been stated.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Holding back from preparing a reply while the speaker is still partway through a sentence.

option_rationales.A: Note-taking and checking evidence are never mentioned; paragraph 2 lists holding parts in mind, resisting a premature reply and noticing what was actually said.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 asks the listener to hold the parts in mind to see how they connect; it says nothing about asking the speaker to change pace.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 3 says 'Listening is not the same as agreeing', so provisional agreement is not one of the efforts described.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists three efforts, one of which is to 'resist the urge to compose a reply while the speaker is still in the middle of a sentence'. The correct answer restates it.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a plausible listening habit from general experience rather than from the list in paragraph 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is a paraphrase of one item in a list in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The reference to 'a meeting in which three people answer a point that nobody made' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: support the objection that a culture of listening lets persistent speakers exhaust others.
options.B: show that meetings are an unsuitable setting for arguments between people who disagree.
options.C: suggest that public meetings should be made smaller so that every participant can be heard.
options.D: illustrate what follows when the effortful work of listening is carried out poorly.

questions.correct_answer: (D) illustrate what follows when the effortful work of listening is carried out poorly.

option_rationales.A: That objection is raised only in paragraph 3, and the example in paragraph 2 concerns misheard points, not persistent speakers.
option_rationales.B: The passage does not reject meetings as a setting; the example is offered as what happens 'when it is done badly', that is, when listening fails.
option_rationales.C: No proposal about the size of meetings is made; paragraph 3 even warns against meetings in which everyone must be 'fully heard'.

questions.explanation: The sentence ends 'has seen what happens when it is done badly', where 'it' is the effortful listening just described. The meeting is an illustration of failed listening.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the example as a claim about meetings themselves rather than about listening.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function is stated in the sentence that contains the example.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the suggestion made in paragraph 4?

options.A: Most people who had been trained in debating at school said they rarely used those skills in their later working lives.
options.B: Committees required to restate one another's points before replying reached decisions in fewer total hours than similar committees without the rule.
options.C: Committees that allowed every member unlimited time to speak took far longer to reach decisions than committees with strict time limits.
options.D: Members of committees required to restate one another's points before replying said they found the meetings more pleasant than before.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Committees required to restate one another's points before replying reached decisions in fewer total hours than similar committees without the rule.

option_rationales.A: The usefulness of debating training is irrelevant to the claim that restating before answering saves time overall.
option_rationales.C: This concerns time limits, not restating the other's point, and it echoes the paragraph 3 worry about endless meetings rather than supporting paragraph 4.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 4 is about time: restating might take 'less time overall'. Pleasantness does not bear on that claim.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 suggests that a discussion in which each participant 'first restated the other's point before answering it might take longer at each step and less time overall'. Evidence that the restating rule shortened total decision time directly supports that suggestion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option about meetings in general, or about the satisfaction of participants, instead of one that tests the specific claim about total time.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options concern meetings and listening but miss the precise claim about overall time; the reader must isolate that claim.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the objection discussed in paragraph 3 is best described as

options.A: complete dismissal of it as a misunderstanding of how deliberation in meetings actually proceeds.
options.B: reluctant agreement that it shows that teaching people to listen would do more harm to public argument than good.
options.C: partial acceptance of the concern it raises combined with rejection of its view of what listening is for.
options.D: neutral reporting of it without any indication of whether the author finds it persuasive.

questions.correct_answer: (C) partial acceptance of the concern it raises combined with rejection of its view of what listening is for.

option_rationales.A: The author says 'There is something to this' and grants that a meeting that cannot end is no model of deliberation, so the dismissal is not complete.
option_rationales.B: The author goes on to say the objection 'mistakes the purpose' and ends by urging that listening be taught, so the author does not agree with it.
option_rationales.D: The author evaluates it explicitly, first conceding a point and then saying it 'mistakes the purpose', which is not neutral.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 concedes 'There is something to this' and that listening is not agreeing, but then says 'the objection mistakes the purpose': listening matters because it is 'useful to the listener', not because it is fair to the speaker. That is partial acceptance plus a rejection of the objection's assumption about purpose.
questions.common_misconception: Missing the concession and choosing complete dismissal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires weighing a concession against a rebuttal within one paragraph.

questions.question: The contrast between the villager and the commuter in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: argue that online platforms ought to be designed to resemble small villages rather than trains.
options.B: illustrate that being anonymous has no effect at all on how people speak to strangers.
options.C: show that people who live in villages are by nature more courteous than people who live in cities.
options.D: suggest that the prospect of meeting people again restrains behaviour more than being identifiable does.

questions.correct_answer: (D) suggest that the prospect of meeting people again restrains behaviour more than being identifiable does.

option_rationales.A: The example comes before any proposal, and paragraph 4 speaks of identities that persist, not of imitating villages; the option turns an illustration into a prescription.
option_rationales.B: Paragraph 2 opens by granting that 'Anonymity does loosen some restraints', so the example cannot be meant to show anonymity has no effect.
option_rationales.C: The passage makes no claim about anyone's nature; the villager is restrained by having to 'live beside her the next day', a situation, not a character trait.

questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that the most important restraint 'is the expectation of meeting the same people again'. The villager faces her neighbour the next day; the commuter does not. The sentence that follows draws the point: what disinhibits is 'the absence of a future'.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the example as a comment on rural and urban character.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point of the contrast is stated in the sentences on either side of it.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a pseudonymous account would be most likely to be used with restraint if

options.A: it had been used in the same community long enough to carry a reputation its owner valued.
options.B: it was used mainly to post on large platforms that reach a broad and constantly changing audience.
options.C: its owner's legal name could be discovered by the platform whenever a complaint was made about it.
options.D: its owner had been required to verify an identity with the platform before choosing the pseudonym.

questions.correct_answer: (A) it had been used in the same community long enough to carry a reputation its owner valued.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 3 suggests the opposite: on vast, transient platforms 'no particular reader's opinion' seems to count, which weakens restraint.
option_rationales.C: This rests on the fear of being named, which paragraph 2 says is not the restraint that matters most; the passage ties restraint to durability, not to the threat of exposure.
option_rationales.D: Verification is the remedy the author treats as incomplete; paragraph 3 says the relevant distinction is durable versus disposable, not verified versus unverified.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a pseudonym 'used for years in a small forum accumulates a reputation as surely as a name does, and its owner has much to lose by squandering it'. Restraint follows from a durable identity with something to lose, which the correct answer describes.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing an option based on traceability, the commonplace reasoning the passage calls incomplete.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options use the identification logic of paragraph 1, which looks sensible unless the reader holds on to the author's durable/disposable distinction.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: Legal action against online abusers proved easier to bring on platforms that required every user to verify an identity.
options.B: Many employees who had reported misconduct online said they would not have done so if made to use their own names.
options.C: On one forum, users who kept the same pseudonym for years proved as abusive as users whose accounts were created and abandoned within a week.
options.D: On large platforms, users posting under their real names proved slightly less abusive than anonymous users posting on the same platforms.

questions.correct_answer: (C) On one forum, users who kept the same pseudonym for years proved as abusive as users whose accounts were created and abandoned within a week.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 concedes that identity rules 'would make legal remedies easier to pursue', so this finding agrees with the passage.
option_rationales.B: This supports the cost described in paragraph 4 and does not touch the claim about durable and disposable identities.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 already grants that anonymity 'does loosen some restraints', so a slight difference is consistent with the argument rather than damaging to it.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that durable identities restrain behaviour because their owners have a reputation to lose. If long-kept pseudonyms were as abusive as throwaway accounts, durability would make no difference, which strikes at the core of the argument.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the finding about named users being less abusive without noticing that the author has already conceded it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option bears on anonymity in general, and the reader must see that the passage has conceded that point and rests its argument on durability.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: The civility of an online space depends chiefly on whether its members could be identified by outsiders.
options.B: Real-name rules might curb some of the most severe abuse while imposing burdens on speakers who need cover.
options.C: Being unidentifiable does make some people more willing to say harsh things to others.
options.D: Courtesy between strangers who do not expect to meet again cannot be taken for granted.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The civility of an online space depends chiefly on whether its members could be identified by outsiders.

option_rationales.B: Paragraph 4 says identity requirements 'might deter some of the worst abuse' but carry costs falling on the employee, the young person and the dissenter, so the author agrees.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 grants that 'Anonymity does loosen some restraints', so the author agrees with this.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 notes that 'commuters are not famous for their courtesy', so the author agrees with this.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says many civil forums have members few of whom 'could be identified by an outsider', and that the relevant distinction 'is not between named and anonymous accounts but between identities that are durable and identities that are disposable'. The author therefore rejects this statement; the other three restate the concession in paragraph 2, the commuter example and the trade-off in paragraph 4.
questions.common_misconception: Rejecting one of the author's concessions as if it were the commonplace view, because it seems to favour anonymity's critics.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three statements the author accepts are concessions and asides scattered across three paragraphs; a reader who keeps only the thesis may wrongly think the author denies them.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'a tacit rule about what kind of thing goes in the slot' refers to

options.A: the original caption, which every later version of the meme must repeat.
options.B: a written guideline issued by the platform on which the meme first appeared.
options.C: an agreement among sharers to keep the meme's message the same in each version.
options.D: an unstated shared sense of which contents suit a particular template.

questions.correct_answer: (D) an unstated shared sense of which contents suit a particular template.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 1 says the photograph soon carries 'hundreds of other captions', so later versions do not repeat the original.
option_rationales.B: The word 'tacit' means unstated; nothing in the passage suggests that any platform issues rules about memes.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 2 says the messages 'are all different and many contradict one another', so there is no agreement to keep the message constant.

questions.explanation: The slot in the cat template takes 'any experience of disappointed expectation' (paragraph 1). The rule is 'tacit', unspoken, and it governs what fits the slot; sharers show skill by filling it 'aptly'.
questions.common_misconception: Ignoring the word 'tacit' and choosing a formal or written rule.
questions.difficulty_reason: The phrase is explained by the cat example and by the word 'aptly' in the next sentence.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, a person who shares a version of a political meme

options.A: is usually trying to ridicule the view that the original version of the meme expressed.
options.B: may be showing skill with a familiar form rather than declaring support for the view its caption expresses.
options.C: has in effect cast a small vote that analysts can reliably count as a sign of agreement with the meme's sentiment.
options.D: is generally unaware that earlier versions of the same template carried quite different messages.

questions.correct_answer: (B) may be showing skill with a familiar form rather than declaring support for the view its caption expresses.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 3 says an inverted version 'may' be passed along by the other side; the passage does not say this is the usual motive for sharing.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 3 calls this a tempting mistake: shares measure 'the vitality of the form far more reliably than the distribution of belief'.
option_rationales.D: Paragraph 2 says sharers are 'demonstrating that they know the form', which implies familiarity with its many uses, not ignorance of them.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says sharers 'are not endorsing a claim; they are demonstrating that they know the form and can fill it aptly', and paragraph 3 adds that a template 'can carry a sentiment its sharers do not hold'. The hedged 'may' in the correct answer matches the passage's 'in such cases'.
questions.common_misconception: Turning a possibility the passage mentions (inverted versions) into the usual case.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option converts a 'may' in paragraph 3 into 'usually'; the reader must notice the change of degree.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the spread of the cat photograph as the passage describes it?

options.A: A rumour changes a little with every retelling until its original source can no longer be traced at all.
options.B: A melody becomes the basis of hundreds of new songs whose lyrics are unrelated to each other and often contradictory.
options.C: A news photograph is shared widely because it records an important event that many people wish to remember.
options.D: A campaign slogan is repeated, word for word, by thousands of supporters who all agree with what it says.

questions.correct_answer: (B) A melody becomes the basis of hundreds of new songs whose lyrics are unrelated to each other and often contradictory.

option_rationales.A: A rumour remains one story that drifts by accident; the meme is a deliberate frame filled with many different messages.
option_rationales.C: This photograph spreads for what it shows, whereas paragraph 1 says the cat 'stopped meaning anything about cats'.
option_rationales.D: Here a single message spreads with endorsement, which is exactly what paragraph 2 says has not happened with the meme.

questions.explanation: The cat image becomes 'a recognisable structure with a slot in it' that carries many different, even contradictory, messages (paragraph 2). A melody reused for unrelated and contradictory lyrics is the same relation: the form spreads, the content varies.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the rumour because it involves change across versions, without seeing that the meme's variation is a deliberate refilling of a fixed frame.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires abstracting the relation between fixed form and varying content and testing each analogy against it.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how paragraph 4 relates to paragraph 3?

options.A: It reverses it by showing that the reach of a meme does after all indicate how widely its sentiment is held.
options.B: It illustrates it with a case in which a meme's sharers held the opposite view to the one the meme expressed.
options.C: It extends it by adding a second reason for thinking that memes have no effect on what people believe.
options.D: It qualifies it by granting that memes can sway opinion while placing that influence where share counts cannot capture it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) It qualifies it by granting that memes can sway opinion while placing that influence where share counts cannot capture it.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 4 never says reach indicates belief; it says influence works through familiarity and is 'so hard to measure and so easy to misread'.
option_rationales.B: The repeated use of the cat's bowl for a government's policies illustrates the influence of repetition, not sharers who disagree with the meme.
option_rationales.C: Paragraph 4 opens by rejecting that conclusion: 'It would be too quick to conclude that memes persuade nobody'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 argues that shares do not measure belief. Paragraph 4 heads off the inference that memes therefore persuade nobody: repetition can make a view 'feel natural', but this power 'lies in the frame's quiet familiarity' and is 'hard to measure'. That is a qualification which keeps paragraph 3's point about measurement intact.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the concession in paragraph 4 as a reversal of paragraph 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must see that paragraph 4 both concedes influence and reaffirms the measurement problem; the reversal and extension options each catch half of this.

questions.question: According to the passage, the logician's attitude to the speaker's character is appropriate when

options.A: the claim being made concerns a practical matter on which the listener must act.
options.B: the speaker has already built up a long record of honesty in the field concerned.
options.C: the listener is in a position to examine the whole argument for himself or herself.
options.D: the audience has been warned in advance against appeals to emotion and to character.

questions.correct_answer: (C) the listener is in a position to examine the whole argument for himself or herself.

option_rationales.A: Paragraph 2 says 'most of the claims on which people must act are not like proofs', which is where the logician's attitude fails.
option_rationales.B: A speaker's record is what paragraph 2 says listeners must rely on when the argument is out of reach, which is the opposite situation.
option_rationales.D: Warnings to the audience are never mentioned; the condition the passage gives is the listener's ability to examine the argument.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens: 'The logician's attitude is correct for a particular situation: one in which the listener can examine the argument fully.' The geometry proof illustrates it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about an honest record, which belongs to the rhetorician's side of the argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: The condition is stated in the first sentence of paragraph 2.

questions.question: A listener follows a retired judge's advice about how a legal dispute is likely to be decided, relying on the judge's long record. The author would most likely regard this listener as

options.A: reasoning soundly, since the judge's credibility was earned in the very domain the advice concerns.
options.B: relying on character improperly, since a long career shows sincerity rather than the truth of a belief.
options.C: justified only if the listener has first worked through all the legal reasoning behind the advice.
