questions.difficulty_reason: The chain is carried by 'That speed', the contrast with handwriters and 'This selection and rephrasing'.

questions.subtopic: Worked solutions help beginners but hinder those who already command the patterns, so the best method depends on the learner.

sentences.text: Learners who already command the patterns are in the opposite position, since every worked step repeats what they could have supplied themselves.

questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: 'them' and 'they' could grammatically point to either group, so the reader must use what is claimed about each group to decide.

questions.subtopic: The nocebo effect makes informing patients of side effects partly harmful, and the answer lies in framing rather than silence.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Patients warned that a drug may cause headaches or nausea report those symptoms more often than patients given no warning, even when their pills contain no active ingredient.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.difficulty_reason: A dilemma is posed, one answer rejected and a better one offered; the comparative 'more promising' fixes the last pair.

questions.subtopic: Surgical checklists protect what experts already know from ordinary lapses of attention.

sentences.text: Surgical teams are made up of highly trained people, so it can seem odd to ask them to work through a simple checklist before an operation.

questions.subtopic: Mountain passes concentrated trade, enriching the towns beside them but making their wealth insecure.

questions.subtopic: Every flat map sacrifices some property, so the sea chart's inflation of high latitudes is a trade-off, though misused as a picture of the world.

sentences.text: No flat map can show the curved surface of the earth without distortion; it can keep shapes true over small regions, or keep areas true, but never both at once.

Every projection is therefore a choice about which property to sacrifice, and the right choice depends on what the map is meant to do.
The price is that lands far from the equator are drawn much larger than they really are, an exaggeration that grows steadily towards the poles.

questions.subtopic: Moral luck sets the principle that we are judged only for what we control against our harsher verdict on unlucky wrongdoers.

questions.subtopic: Because our choices decide who will exist, duties to future generations must be owed to whoever comes to live, not to particular people.

questions.subtopic: Longitude at sea depended on knowing home-port time, which needed clocks steady enough to keep it.

questions.difficulty_reason: A problem, its explanation, a method, the obstacle to the method and the solution follow in sequence, with 'The difficulty' and 'however' as clear markers.

questions.subtopic: Habits are triggered by cues, so changing surroundings helps to break them.

questions.subtopic: The ozone layer is recovering slowly after damaging chemicals were phased out.

questions.subtopic: Hindsight bias makes past decisions look worse than they were, so fair judgement must ask what was knowable then.

questions.subtopic: Witnesses help less in crowds because responsibility is diffused and hesitation is contagious.

Sentence 2 turns with 'however': for merchants and officials 'that same variety', named in 4, caused disputes. Sentence 1 proposes 'a remedy' for those disputes, units based on nature rather than custom. Sentence 3 refers to 'that very detachment', the break from custom in 1, and explains its appeal.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 straight after sentence 5 as the obvious complaint, then sentence 4 as a concession, which leaves 'however' in sentence 2 with no defence of the units to answer and puts the defence of custom just before the remedy it is meant to motivate.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession and reply must be ordered by the logic of the argument: the defence of local custom comes first, the commercial objection answers it, and the remedy answers the objection.

questions.subtopic: Shared pastures are overgrazed because each user gains fully but bears only part of the cost.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The cost of that animal, a slight thinning of the grass, is spread across everyone who uses the pasture.
Consider a pasture open to every herder in a village, where each additional animal brings its owner the full gain from its grazing.
The result is a field grazed bare by people who each acted sensibly, which is why shared resources often need rules that limit what each user may take.
Each herder thus has reason to add animals even when the pasture as a whole is already strained, and so does every other herder.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. The cost of that animal, a slight thinning of the grass, is spread across everyone who uses the pasture.
2. Consider a pasture open to every herder in a village, where each additional animal brings its owner the full gain from its grazing.
3. The result is a field grazed bare by people who each acted sensibly, which is why shared resources often need rules that limit what each user may take.
4. Each herder thus has reason to add animals even when the pasture as a whole is already strained, and so does every other herder.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 draws its 'thus' from the contrast between full private gain and spread cost; without sentence 1 the reason to overload a strained pasture is missing, and 'that animal' in sentence 1 would then follow a sentence about many animals.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 sets up the hypothetical pasture and the private gain from each animal. Sentence 1 gives the other half of the calculation, the shared cost of 'that animal'. Sentence 4 combines the two with 'thus': gain is private and cost is shared, so each herder keeps adding animals. Sentence 3 states 'The result' and the lesson. The argument needs both the gain and the cost before the conclusion in 4.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 straight after sentence 2, although the herder's reason to add animals 'even when the pasture as a whole is already strained' depends on the cost being shared, which only sentence 1 states.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order follows the logic of the argument: private gain, shared cost, the incentive that follows from both, then the outcome.

questions.subtopic: Rent control protects sitting tenants but can disadvantage newcomers by discouraging supply.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: For those who hold a controlled lease, the policy often delivers exactly that, and they may stay put for decades at a modest rent.
The difficulty lies with the people who do not yet have such a lease, since landlords facing capped returns have less reason to build, maintain or let new flats.
Rent control appeals to a simple sense of fairness: tenants should not be priced out of homes they already occupy.
A city may thus end up protecting its current tenants at the expense of newcomers, who face fewer and costlier homes to choose from.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. For those who hold a controlled lease, the policy often delivers exactly that, and they may stay put for decades at a modest rent.
2. The difficulty lies with the people who do not yet have such a lease, since landlords facing capped returns have less reason to build, maintain or let new flats.
3. Rent control appeals to a simple sense of fairness: tenants should not be priced out of homes they already occupy.
4. A city may thus end up protecting its current tenants at the expense of newcomers, who face fewer and costlier homes to choose from.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4's 'thus' requires the reason newcomers lose, the reduced supply of flats, which only sentence 2 gives.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the fairness argument. Sentence 1 says the policy 'delivers exactly that' for current leaseholders. Sentence 2 turns to people 'who do not yet have such a lease' and the effect on supply. Sentence 4 draws the conclusion with 'thus', contrasting current tenants with newcomers, which needs both 1 and 2.
questions.common_misconception: Ending with sentence 2 after sentence 4, although the newcomers' shortage of homes in sentence 4 follows from the reduced supply described in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The last three sentences must be ordered by the logic of winners, losers and the trade-off between them.

questions.subtopic: Earthworms improve soil by burrowing, pulling down leaves and leaving rich casts.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Over many years, this ceaseless digging, feeding and excreting can turn over the whole upper layer of a field, which is why farmers have long welcomed worms.
They also drag fallen leaves down into their tunnels, carrying dead plant matter from the surface into the soil where it can decay.
The leaves they swallow, along with the soil around them, pass through their bodies and emerge as casts that are richer in nutrients than the surrounding earth.
As they burrow, they open channels through which air and rainwater can reach the roots below.
Earthworms are easily dismissed as humble creatures, yet few animals do more to shape the soil in which plants grow.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. Over many years, this ceaseless digging, feeding and excreting can turn over the whole upper layer of a field, which is why farmers have long welcomed worms.
2. They also drag fallen leaves down into their tunnels, carrying dead plant matter from the surface into the soil where it can decay.
3. The leaves they swallow, along with the soil around them, pass through their bodies and emerge as casts that are richer in nutrients than the surrounding earth.
4. As they burrow, they open channels through which air and rainwater can reach the roots below.
5. Earthworms are easily dismissed as humble creatures, yet few animals do more to shape the soil in which plants grow.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 speaks of 'The leaves they swallow' before any leaves have been mentioned; they enter the soil in sentence 2.
Sentence 2 says the worms 'also' drag leaves down, which presupposes the first activity, burrowing, in sentence 4; and 'their tunnels' needs the burrows of sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 introduces the claim that worms shape the soil. Sentence 4 gives the first effect, burrowing. Sentence 2 adds a second ('also'): pulling leaves into the tunnels. Sentence 3 follows those leaves through the worm's body ('The leaves they swallow'), so it must come after 2. Sentence 1 sums up the 'digging, feeding and excreting' of 4, 2 and 3 in that order and concludes.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 before sentence 2 because casts seem a separate effect, although 'The leaves they swallow' presupposes the leaves dragged underground in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The three effects look like a list that could be reordered; the reader must see that the leaves dragged underground are what pass through the worm to form casts, and that 'also' places leaf-dragging after burrowing.

questions.subtopic: Batteries let weather-dependent power match demand on a grid that must balance supply instantly.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Large batteries help to close this gap by storing surplus power when the sun shines or the wind blows and releasing it later.
Power stations that burn fuel can meet this requirement by raising or lowering output as demand changes through the day.
Electricity is unusual among goods in that, on a conventional grid, it must be produced at the very moment it is consumed.
Solar panels and wind turbines cannot be steered in the same way, since their output follows the weather rather than the needs of consumers.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Large batteries help to close this gap by storing surplus power when the sun shines or the wind blows and releasing it later.
2. Power stations that burn fuel can meet this requirement by raising or lowering output as demand changes through the day.
3. Electricity is unusual among goods in that, on a conventional grid, it must be produced at the very moment it is consumed.
4. Solar panels and wind turbines cannot be steered in the same way, since their output follows the weather rather than the needs of consumers.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 says solar and wind cannot be steered 'in the same way', which presupposes the adjustable stations of sentence 2; sentence 1 would also follow a sentence about fuel stations, which create no gap.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the requirement that supply match demand instantly. Sentence 2 calls it 'this requirement' and shows how fuel-burning stations meet it. Sentence 4 contrasts solar and wind, which 'cannot be steered in the same way' as the stations of 2. Sentence 1 refers to 'this gap', the mismatch between weather-driven output and demand, and gives the remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 before sentence 2 because both concern power sources, although 'in the same way' needs the adjustable stations of sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order follows the problem: the requirement, a source that meets it, a source that does not, and the remedy for the mismatch.

questions.subtopic: Standard containers cut handling, and standardisation let all transport be built around them.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Standard steel containers changed the job entirely, since a sealed box could be lifted by crane from a lorry to a ship and back without its contents being touched.
Loading a single vessel in this way could take days, and goods were often damaged or stolen while they sat on the quay.
Because the boxes were all the same size, ports, ships, trains and lorries could be built around them, and the cost of moving goods across the world fell sharply.
Until the middle of the twentieth century, cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece, with dockworkers carrying sacks, barrels and crates by hand or on slings.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Standard steel containers changed the job entirely, since a sealed box could be lifted by crane from a lorry to a ship and back without its contents being touched.
2. Loading a single vessel in this way could take days, and goods were often damaged or stolen while they sat on the quay.
3. Because the boxes were all the same size, ports, ships, trains and lorries could be built around them, and the cost of moving goods across the world fell sharply.
4. Until the middle of the twentieth century, cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece, with dockworkers carrying sacks, barrels and crates by hand or on slings.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2's 'in this way' refers to manual loading, so it must follow sentence 4; after sentence 1 it would describe container loading as slow, the opposite of the point.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 describes piece-by-piece loading. Sentence 2 says loading 'in this way' was slow and risky. Sentence 1 introduces containers, which answer both problems of 2: sealed boxes are moved by crane and untouched. Sentence 3 refers to 'the boxes' and adds the further effect of standard size.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 before sentence 1, although 'the boxes' in sentence 3 are introduced as containers only in sentence 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must see that the container sentence answers both problems of manual loading (delay and theft) and that the effect of standard size builds on the containers already introduced.

questions.subtopic: Dark patterns steer users by making the company's preferred option the easiest, which is what makes them troubling.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Designers of websites and apps have learned that small choices about layout can steer users without their noticing.

Such designs, often called dark patterns, do not forbid anything, since the subscriber can still cancel and the box can still be unticked; they simply make the option the company prefers the easiest one to take.
A subscription that takes one click to start but several screens to cancel, or a box pre-ticked to accept marketing emails, works this way.
Critics argue that this is precisely what makes them troubling, since a user who never noticed being steered has no reason to object.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Designers of websites and apps have learned that small choices about layout can steer users without their noticing.
2. Such designs, often called dark patterns, do not forbid anything, since the subscriber can still cancel and the box can still be unticked; they simply make the option the company prefers the easiest one to take.
3. A subscription that takes one click to start but several screens to cancel, or a box pre-ticked to accept marketing emails, works this way.
4. Critics argue that this is precisely what makes them troubling, since a user who never noticed being steered has no reason to object.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 cannot open: 'Such designs' needs the examples of sentence 3 before it.

Sentence 2 speaks of 'the subscriber' who can still cancel and 'the box' that can still be unticked, which are introduced only in the examples of sentence 3; and sentence 4's 'this' would then point at the examples rather than at the steering without prohibition.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states that layout can steer users unnoticed. Sentence 3 gives examples that work 'this way'. Sentence 2 names 'Such designs' as dark patterns and, referring to 'the subscriber' and 'the box' of the examples in 3, says they forbid nothing. Sentence 4 says 'this is precisely' what makes them troubling, referring to the quiet steering of 2, and links back to the unnoticed steering of 1.
questions.common_misconception: Starting with sentence 2 because it names the subject, although 'Such designs' requires the examples in sentence 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Students must see that the examples come before the naming of the category, and that the critics' point refers to the description of how dark patterns work.

questions.subtopic: Gossip enforces good conduct as an informal reputation system, at the cost of spreading falsehoods.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Since any lapse may become common knowledge in this way, most people have a strong motive to behave well even when no one is watching at the moment.
Gossip has a poor reputation, yet in small communities it has long done work that no formal institution could do as cheaply.
Talk about who failed to repay a loan or broke a promise spreads knowledge of people's conduct far beyond those who witnessed it.
Gossip thus acts as an informal system of reputation, though the same mechanism that punishes cheats can also spread falsehoods about the innocent.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Since any lapse may become common knowledge in this way, most people have a strong motive to behave well even when no one is watching at the moment.
2. Gossip has a poor reputation, yet in small communities it has long done work that no formal institution could do as cheaply.
3. Talk about who failed to repay a loan or broke a promise spreads knowledge of people's conduct far beyond those who witnessed it.
4. Gossip thus acts as an informal system of reputation, though the same mechanism that punishes cheats can also spread falsehoods about the innocent.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 says lapses become known 'in this way', but the way, talk spreading knowledge beyond witnesses, is described only in sentence 3.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 claims gossip does useful work. Sentence 3 shows what that work is: talk spreads knowledge of conduct. Sentence 1 draws the effect 'in this way': lapses become known, so people behave well. Sentence 4 concludes with 'thus' that gossip is a reputation system and adds a qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 1 before sentence 3 because the motive to behave well seems to follow from gossip in general, although 'in this way' refers to the spreading of knowledge described in sentence 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must follow the mechanism (talk spreads knowledge, so lapses are costly, so gossip works as reputation) rather than rely on topic words.

questions.subtopic: Beliefs direct the search for confirming cases, so a real test asks what would be seen if the belief were false.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: When people test a belief, they tend to look for cases that would fit it rather than cases that would refute it.
Evidence gathered in answer to that question can genuinely test a belief, because it was not selected by the belief it is meant to judge.
Each late arrival then feels like fresh proof of laziness, although it was noticed only because the belief directed where to look.
The remedy is not to have fewer beliefs but to ask, deliberately, what one would expect to see if the belief were false.
Someone convinced, say, that a colleague is lazy will notice each late arrival and pass over the many mornings when the colleague came early.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. When people test a belief, they tend to look for cases that would fit it rather than cases that would refute it.
2. Evidence gathered in answer to that question can genuinely test a belief, because it was not selected by the belief it is meant to judge.
3. Each late arrival then feels like fresh proof of laziness, although it was noticed only because the belief directed where to look.
4. The remedy is not to have fewer beliefs but to ask, deliberately, what one would expect to see if the belief were false.
5. Someone convinced, say, that a colleague is lazy will notice each late arrival and pass over the many mornings when the colleague came early.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 5 contains 'say', which marks it as an illustration of a claim already made; it cannot open before the general tendency in sentence 1.
Sentence 2 refers to 'that question', which is the question proposed in sentence 4; before it, there is no question to answer.
Offering the remedy before the example leaves the illustration marked by 'say' far from the tendency it illustrates, and the paragraph would end on the flaw after its cure had already been given.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states the tendency. Sentence 5 illustrates it ('say') with the colleague. Sentence 3 picks up 'Each late arrival' from 5 and explains why such cases feel like proof though the belief chose them. Sentence 4 offers the remedy, and sentence 2 explains why the remedy works, referring to 'that question' asked in 4. The closing reason in 2, evidence 'not selected by the belief', answers exactly the flaw identified in 3.
questions.common_misconception: Opening with the concrete case of the colleague, or treating sentence 2 as a general claim that could come before the remedy, although 'that question' needs the question posed in sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Difficult because the paragraph turns on the idea that the belief itself selects its evidence; the reader must see that the remedy and its justification answer that flaw, and resist the tempting example-first opening.

questions.subtopic: Whether a minimum wage cuts jobs depends on whether local employers can set wages.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The debate is thus less about whether the textbook logic is valid than about which kind of labour market a particular town actually resembles.
Yet that prediction assumes employers have no power to set wages, competing for workers so fiercely that each is paid exactly what the market will bear.
Where a few employers dominate a local labour market, they have exactly such power, and a modest minimum may then draw more people into work rather than fewer.
The simplest textbook model predicts that a minimum wage set above the market rate must reduce employment, since labour has become more expensive.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. The debate is thus less about whether the textbook logic is valid than about which kind of labour market a particular town actually resembles.
2. Yet that prediction assumes employers have no power to set wages, competing for workers so fiercely that each is paid exactly what the market will bear.
3. Where a few employers dominate a local labour market, they have exactly such power, and a modest minimum may then draw more people into work rather than fewer.
4. The simplest textbook model predicts that a minimum wage set above the market rate must reduce employment, since labour has become more expensive.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 says dominant employers have 'exactly such power', but no power has been mentioned until sentence 2; and sentence 2's 'Yet' would then contrast with a sentence that already makes its point.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 gives the textbook prediction. Sentence 2 identifies the assumption behind 'that prediction', that employers cannot set wages. Sentence 3 describes a market where that assumption fails: dominant employers have 'exactly such power', the power to set wages denied in 2. Sentence 1 concludes with 'thus' that the question is which kind of market a town is, a conclusion that needs both the textbook case and the exception.
questions.common_misconception: Treating sentence 3 as an immediate counterexample to sentence 4 and placing sentence 2 after it, although 'such power' in sentence 3 refers to the wage-setting power named only in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: The economic reasoning (prediction, hidden assumption, case where the assumption fails, reframed debate) is abstract, and the sentence about dominant employers looks at first like a direct reply to the textbook prediction.

questions.subtopic: Specialisation pays only where the market is large enough, so it grows with trade.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Specialisation is thus less a choice that any workshop can make than a reward that grows as trade widens the circle of buyers.
But the gain depends on the size of the market, since a specialist is worth employing only if there is enough demand to keep him busy at his one task.
A village blacksmith must therefore do every kind of metalwork himself, while a large city can support separate makers of nails, locks and hinges.
Dividing a task among specialists raises output, because each worker becomes quicker at a narrow job than anyone could be at the whole.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Specialisation is thus less a choice that any workshop can make than a reward that grows as trade widens the circle of buyers.
2. But the gain depends on the size of the market, since a specialist is worth employing only if there is enough demand to keep him busy at his one task.
3. A village blacksmith must therefore do every kind of metalwork himself, while a large city can support separate makers of nails, locks and hinges.
4. Dividing a task among specialists raises output, because each worker becomes quicker at a narrow job than anyone could be at the whole.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3's 'therefore' needs a reason why the village smith cannot specialise; sentence 4 gives only the benefits of specialisation, and it is the market-size condition in sentence 2 that explains the village case.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 states the benefit of dividing work. Sentence 2 qualifies it with 'But the gain depends on the size of the market'. Sentence 3 applies that condition ('therefore') to the village and the city: the small market cannot keep specialists busy, the large one can. Sentence 1 concludes with 'thus' that specialisation depends on the extent of trade.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the blacksmith of sentence 3 as an illustration of sentence 4, although the village smith is the opposite of a specialist and his case follows only from the market-size condition in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Difficult because the economic reasoning is abstract and the example of the village and the city can look like an illustration of specialisation in general rather than of its dependence on market size.

questions.subtopic: Network effects both enlarge and protect an early lead, so such markets settle on early winners.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: A loaf of bread is worth no more to its buyer because millions of other loaves are sold the same day.
Because such a lead both grows and protects itself, these markets tend to settle on one or two dominant providers, which need not be the best ones, only the ones that grew large first.
Where value grows with the number of users in this way, an early lead tends to feed on itself, as each new user makes the service more attractive to the next.
A telephone is another matter: owned by one person, it is useless, and it grows more useful with every new subscriber who can be called.
The same feature that rewards the leader also shields it, since a rival must persuade people to leave the network where their contacts already are.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. A loaf of bread is worth no more to its buyer because millions of other loaves are sold the same day.
2. Because such a lead both grows and protects itself, these markets tend to settle on one or two dominant providers, which need not be the best ones, only the ones that grew large first.
3. Where value grows with the number of users in this way, an early lead tends to feed on itself, as each new user makes the service more attractive to the next.
4. A telephone is another matter: owned by one person, it is useless, and it grows more useful with every new subscriber who can be called.
5. The same feature that rewards the leader also shields it, since a rival must persuade people to leave the network where their contacts already are.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 calls the telephone 'another matter', which needs the contrasting case of bread in sentence 1 before it.
Sentence 2 says the lead 'protects itself', but the protection is first explained in sentence 5; placed after the conclusion, sentence 5 would merely repeat a point already drawn.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 gives the ordinary case of bread. Sentence 4 says the telephone is 'another matter', so it must follow the case it contrasts with. Sentence 3 generalises from the telephone ('in this way') to the self-reinforcing lead. Sentence 5 adds that 'The same feature that rewards the leader' also protects it, which assumes the leader rewarded in 3. Sentence 2 concludes from a lead that 'both grows and protects itself', so it needs both the growth of 3 and the protection of 5.
questions.common_misconception: Opening with the telephone because it introduces the real subject, or placing the conclusion of sentence 2 before sentence 5, although sentence 2's claim that the winners 'grew large first' and stay dominant needs both growth and protection.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order of the last three sentences depends on the idea: growth of a lead, then its protection, then the market outcome that follows from both; the bread sentence is an unusual, low-key opener.

questions.subtopic: An iridium anomaly suggested an impact, and finding the predicted crater made it the leading explanation.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Geologists studying rock laid down at the time the dinosaurs vanished found a thin band of clay unusually rich in iridium, a metal rare in the earth's crust but common in asteroids.
If the hypothesis was right, however, so violent an impact should have left a crater of enormous size, of the right age, somewhere on the planet.
The later identification of a buried crater of the predicted size and age, beneath the Yucatan coast of Mexico, turned a bold conjecture into the leading explanation.
This suggested that a large asteroid had struck the earth, scattering its dust worldwide, and that the impact might explain the extinction.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Geologists studying rock laid down at the time the dinosaurs vanished found a thin band of clay unusually rich in iridium, a metal rare in the earth's crust but common in asteroids.
2. If the hypothesis was right, however, so violent an impact should have left a crater of enormous size, of the right age, somewhere on the planet.
3. The later identification of a buried crater of the predicted size and age, beneath the Yucatan coast of Mexico, turned a bold conjecture into the leading explanation.
4. This suggested that a large asteroid had struck the earth, scattering its dust worldwide, and that the impact might explain the extinction.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 speaks of 'the predicted size and age', but nothing has been predicted until sentence 2 says what the hypothesis requires.
Sentence 4 begins 'This suggested', which needs the iridium-rich clay of sentence 1 as its referent.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 reports the observation, the iridium-rich clay. Sentence 4 draws the hypothesis from it ('This suggested'). Sentence 2 derives a test from the hypothesis: a crater should exist. Sentence 3 reports that the predicted crater was found, which only makes sense once the prediction of 2 has been made.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 before sentence 2 because the discovery seems to follow the hypothesis directly, although 'the predicted size and age' refers to the prediction set out only in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Difficult because the order follows the logic of scientific testing (observation, hypothesis, prediction, confirmation), and the reader must see that the 'however' of the crater sentence marks a test of the hypothesis rather than an objection to it.

questions.subtopic: Spam filtering is an endless contest because each side's moves teach the other.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Early filters for junk email worked by blocking messages that contained words commonly found in advertising, such as offers of free money.
The contest has no final victory for either side, because a filter that learns and an adversary who adapts each supply the other with the lessons it needs.
Each improvement, however, taught senders what the filter was now looking for, and the advantage passed back to them until the next adjustment.
Filters then began to learn from examples, weighing hundreds of features of each message instead of a few forbidden words.
Senders quickly learned to misspell those words or hide them in images, so that their messages slipped past the lists.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. Early filters for junk email worked by blocking messages that contained words commonly found in advertising, such as offers of free money.
2. The contest has no final victory for either side, because a filter that learns and an adversary who adapts each supply the other with the lessons it needs.
3. Each improvement, however, taught senders what the filter was now looking for, and the advantage passed back to them until the next adjustment.
4. Filters then began to learn from examples, weighing hundreds of features of each message instead of a few forbidden words.
5. Senders quickly learned to misspell those words or hide them in images, so that their messages slipped past the lists.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: After sentence 5, no filter has yet been improved, so 'Each improvement' in sentence 3 has nothing to refer to; sentence 4 must supply the first improvement.
Sentence 2 would conclude that the contest never ends before sentence 3 has shown that improvements keep handing the advantage back to senders.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 describes word-list filters. Sentence 5 gives the senders' response to 'those words'. Sentence 4 gives the filters' counter-move ('then'), learning from examples. Sentence 3 says that 'Each improvement', the filters' upgrades just described, in turn taught senders, so the cycle repeats. Sentence 2 generalises the cycle into the claim that neither side can win.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 straight after sentence 5, although 'Each improvement' refers to improvements in filters, and the first improvement appears only in sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Difficult because the paragraph is a cycle of move and counter-move; the reader must see that the 'Each improvement' sentence generalises a cycle that the senders' evasion and the learning filters have begun and that the conclusion explains why it never ends.

questions.subtopic: Repairing an undersea cable is a sequence: locate the fault, hook the cable, splice and relay it.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: When an undersea communications cable breaks, the first task is to work out where along its great length the fault actually lies.
The two severed ends are then hauled aboard, joined with a new section, and lowered back to the bottom.
Once the position is known, a repair ship sails to the spot and lowers a grapnel to drag the seabed and hook the damaged cable.
Engineers do this from the shore, sending a pulse down the line and timing the reflection that comes back from the break.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

2. The two severed ends are then hauled aboard, joined with a new section, and lowered back to the bottom.
3. Once the position is known, a repair ship sails to the spot and lowers a grapnel to drag the seabed and hook the damaged cable.
4. Engineers do this from the shore, sending a pulse down the line and timing the reflection that comes back from the break.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 needs the position to be known already, which happens only through the shore measurement in sentence 4; and 'do this' in 4 would then follow the hooking of the cable in 3, though it can only mean locating the fault.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 opens by stating the first task, locating the fault. Sentence 4 says engineers 'do this', which can only refer to locating the fault. Sentence 3 begins 'Once the position is known', the result of the timing method in 4, and brings the cable up by grapnel. Sentence 2 follows with 'then', splicing the 'severed ends' that the grapnel in 3 has hooked.
questions.common_misconception: Starting with the ship sailing out, as if the repair began at sea, which leaves 'Once the position is known' with nothing before it.
questions.difficulty_reason: A plain procedure with clear sequence markers ('the first task', 'do this', 'Once', 'then').

questions.subtopic: Predictive text suits formulaic writing but pulls personal writing towards cliche.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Accept enough suggestions while writing one, and the letter drifts, word by word, towards what everyone says, which is the one thing it should not be.
For a note confirming a meeting this is exactly what is wanted, since such notes are formulaic and nobody reads them for their style.
A letter of condolence is another matter, because what makes it worth receiving is precisely the phrase that most people would not have thought to use.
Predictive text offers, at each point, the words that most often follow what a writer has already typed.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Accept enough suggestions while writing one, and the letter drifts, word by word, towards what everyone says, which is the one thing it should not be.
2. For a note confirming a meeting this is exactly what is wanted, since such notes are formulaic and nobody reads them for their style.
3. A letter of condolence is another matter, because what makes it worth receiving is precisely the phrase that most people would not have thought to use.
4. Predictive text offers, at each point, the words that most often follow what a writer has already typed.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 calls the condolence letter 'another matter', so a first case must come before it; that case is the meeting note in sentence 2, which cannot be postponed to the end.
Sentence 1 says 'while writing one', and the only thing it can mean is the letter of condolence introduced in sentence 3.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 describes the mechanism: the words that 'most often follow'. Sentence 2 judges that mechanism ('this') well suited to formulaic notes. Sentence 3 sets up the contrasting case with 'another matter', which needs the routine case of 2 before it, and explains that a condolence letter is valued for the unusual phrase. Sentence 1 applies the mechanism to that case: 'writing one' refers to the letter, and drifting 'towards what everyone says' is bad only because of the value named in 3.
questions.common_misconception: Ending with the meeting note, as a concession, which leaves 'another matter' in the condolence sentence with no prior case to contrast with.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order depends on the logic of the contrast (routine note, then personal letter, then the cost to that letter); the tempting order puts the concession about routine notes last.

questions.subtopic: Digital copying preserves bits but not readability, so archivists favour open formats.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: To guard against such losses, archivists concerned with centuries rather than years prefer plain, openly documented formats to convenient proprietary ones.
A file in a format that no surviving program can read is in practice as lost as a letter that has been burned, even though every bit is intact.
Copying, however, preserves only the sequence of bits, and a sequence of bits means nothing without a program that knows how to interpret it.
We tend to think of digital records as safer than paper, since they can be copied any number of times without the slightest loss.
Their reasoning is that a published specification allows the file to be read again by anyone willing to write a new program, even after every original program has vanished.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. To guard against such losses, archivists concerned with centuries rather than years prefer plain, openly documented formats to convenient proprietary ones.
2. A file in a format that no surviving program can read is in practice as lost as a letter that has been burned, even though every bit is intact.
3. Copying, however, preserves only the sequence of bits, and a sequence of bits means nothing without a program that knows how to interpret it.
4. We tend to think of digital records as safer than paper, since they can be copied any number of times without the slightest loss.
5. Their reasoning is that a published specification allows the file to be read again by anyone willing to write a new program, even after every original program has vanished.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 applies the principle that bits mean nothing without an interpreting program, which is stated only in sentence 3; placed straight after the opening belief, it asserts a loss the paragraph has not yet explained, and the 'however' of 3 then has nothing left to qualify.
Sentence 5 begins 'Their reasoning', and the only people whose reasoning it can be are the archivists introduced in sentence 1.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 states the common belief. Sentence 3 qualifies it with 'however': copying keeps bits but not their meaning. Sentence 2 draws the consequence of 3, a file with intact bits that is still lost. Sentence 1 gives the practical response 'To guard against such losses', which needs the lost file of 2 before it, and sentence 5 explains the archivists' reasoning, 'Their' referring to the archivists of 1.
questions.common_misconception: Putting the burned-letter sentence directly after the opening belief because both talk about loss, which makes the 'however' of the bits sentence redundant.
questions.difficulty_reason: The sentences share vocabulary (copying, bits, programs), so the reader must follow the argument from belief to qualification to consequence to remedy; the burned-letter sentence is a tempting second sentence.

questions.subtopic: Spreadsheets changed office work with figures from arithmetic to analysis rather than ending it.

Recalculating a large ledger by hand had taken days, and the new programs did it in seconds whenever a single figure was changed.
When electronic spreadsheets first appeared on personal computers, many predicted that they would make the clerks who kept ledgers redundant.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 supports the prediction of redundancy, not the outcome, so it must come before the 'Yet' of sentence 4; placed after it, it would separate 'change its shape' from 'The new shape' in sentence 1.

questions.common_misconception: Placing the 'Yet' sentence immediately after the prediction, before the reason for the prediction has been given.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order follows the logic of prediction, its ground, its failure and the explanation; the sentence giving the ground for the prediction could be misplaced as evidence for the outcome.

questions.subtopic: Pneumatic tube post was fast but fixed, and lost to the flexible telephone.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: In several large cities of the late nineteenth century, letters were sent through networks of underground tubes by compressed air, crossing town in minutes.
The weakness lay in what made the tubes fast: each was a fixed physical route that had to be dug, and reaching a new district meant digging again.
For urgent messages within a crowded centre, nothing else available at the time came close to that speed.
The tubes were therefore not beaten at their own game of speed so much as made beside the point by a medium that could reach almost everywhere.
Telephone wires, by contrast, needed no digging, since they could be strung cheaply along existing streets, and they carried not a written message but the conversation itself.

The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

4. The tubes were therefore not beaten at their own game of speed so much as made beside the point by a medium that could reach almost everywhere.
5. Telephone wires, by contrast, needed no digging, since they could be strung cheaply along existing streets, and they carried not a written message but the conversation itself.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 5 says the telephone 'needed no digging', a contrast that only makes sense after sentence 2 has explained that the tubes had to be dug.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 introduces the tube networks. Sentence 3 refers to 'that speed' and states their strength. Sentence 2 gives the weakness, the need to dig. Sentence 5 contrasts the telephone, which 'needed no digging', so it must follow 2. Sentence 4 concludes with 'therefore', combining the strength of 3 with the reach of 5.
questions.common_misconception: Setting the telephone against the tubes immediately after their speed is praised, which leaves 'needed no digging' with nothing to contrast with.
questions.difficulty_reason: Reference words help, but the reader must see that the telephone sentence contrasts with the cost of digging, not with speed.

questions.subtopic: The turn in the Italian sonnet makes the poem enact a change of mind.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: A reader who knows this learns to hold the opening lines provisionally, as positions the poem may yet abandon.
In the first group the poet usually lays out a situation, a question or a complaint.
The Italian sonnet divides its fourteen lines into a group of eight and a group of six, and the shift between them is traditionally called the turn.
The second group then answers, qualifies or overturns what has been set up, so that the poem enacts a change of mind rather than merely describing one.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. A reader who knows this learns to hold the opening lines provisionally, as positions the poem may yet abandon.

4. The second group then answers, qualifies or overturns what has been set up, so that the poem enacts a change of mind rather than merely describing one.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 treats the opening lines as positions the poem may 'abandon', which presupposes the overturning described in sentence 4; placed second, it anticipates a claim the paragraph has not made.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 introduces the two groups and the turn. Sentence 2 describes the first group and sentence 4 the second, which 'then' responds to it. Sentence 1 draws the consequence for the reader: the opening lines are 'positions the poem may yet abandon', which depends on 4 having said that the second group may overturn them.
questions.common_misconception: Moving the reader sentence up to follow the description of the structure, before the paragraph has said that the second group can overturn the first.
questions.difficulty_reason: The final sentence's place follows from the idea, not a pronoun alone: reading the opening as provisional only makes sense once overturning has been described.

questions.subtopic: An audiobook narrator interprets the text rather than delivering it neutrally.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Listening to an audiobook is often described as reading by ear, as though the narrator merely delivered the text unchanged.
These choices settle questions the printed page leaves open, so that an ironic line read sincerely can become a different line altogether.
The listener therefore receives not only the author's book but also one performer's interpretation of it.
In fact, every narrator must make decisions that a silent reader makes privately, such as where to pause, which word to stress and how each character should sound.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 begins 'In fact', which corrects a view; that view is the description in sentence 1, so 1 must open.

questions.common_misconception: Opening with the narrator's decisions, which leaves 'In fact' correcting nothing.
questions.difficulty_reason: Clear chain of common view, correction ('In fact'), reference ('These choices') and conclusion ('therefore').

questions.subtopic: Darkening the auditorium changed how audiences behaved, not only how they saw.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Gas, and later electric, lighting changed this by allowing the house to be darkened while the stage stayed bright.
In such a hall spectators could see one another as clearly as they saw the actors, and an evening at the theatre was as much about being seen as about watching.
If so, habits now regarded as simple good manners, such as silence and stillness during a scene, may owe as much to lighting as to any refinement of taste.
The change was social as well as technical, for an audience sitting in darkness cannot watch itself and is left with nothing to attend to but the play.
For most of theatrical history the auditorium stayed lit throughout a performance, since candles and oil lamps could not easily be dimmed and relit.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. Gas, and later electric, lighting changed this by allowing the house to be darkened while the stage stayed bright.
2. In such a hall spectators could see one another as clearly as they saw the actors, and an evening at the theatre was as much about being seen as about watching.

4. The change was social as well as technical, for an audience sitting in darkness cannot watch itself and is left with nothing to attend to but the play.
5. For most of theatrical history the auditorium stayed lit throughout a performance, since candles and oil lamps could not easily be dimmed and relit.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 opens 'If so', conditional on the claim that darkness leaves an audience nothing to watch but the play; that claim is made only in sentence 4.
Sentence 1 says the new lighting 'changed this', so something must precede it; and sentence 4 must follow 1 directly, because 'The change' is the darkening of the house.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 describes the lit auditorium and why it stayed lit. Sentence 2 begins 'In such a hall' and draws the social consequence. Sentence 1 says new lighting 'changed this'. Sentence 4 calls 'The change' social as well as technical, and sentence 3 draws a tentative conclusion with 'If so', which rests on the claim in 4.
questions.common_misconception: Jumping from the new lighting straight to modern manners, which leaves the 'If so' of the last sentence resting on a claim not yet made.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five sentences in historical order; the reader must see that the conclusion about manners depends on the social claim, not on the technical one.

questions.subtopic: The blank between comic panels is where readers supply the story.

sentences.text: Acts of completion as small as this one are the medium's real material, and much of a cartoonist's craft lies in judging how many of them to ask for.
Show a raised fist in one panel and a man rubbing his jaw in the next, and the reader imagines the punch without any sense of having done work.
Yet it is there that much of the story happens, since whatever occurs between one frozen moment and the next must be supplied by the reader.
Nothing is drawn in the narrow blank between two comic panels, and most readers never consciously look at it.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 speaks of 'Acts of completion as small as this one', which needs the single imagined punch of sentence 2 before it.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 introduces the blank between panels. Sentence 3 turns with 'Yet' to claim that the story happens there. Sentence 2 illustrates the claim with the imagined punch. Sentence 1 generalises from 'this one', the punch, to the cartoonist's craft.
questions.common_misconception: Placing the general point about the craft before the example, which leaves 'this one' with no single act to refer to.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example must sit between the claim it illustrates and the generalisation that refers back to it; the order follows the logic of claim, illustration, lesson.

questions.subtopic: Newspapers prepare obituaries of prominent people in advance for the sake of accuracy.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: This practice can look macabre to outsiders, as if journalists were simply waiting for people to die.
Most newspaper obituaries are written quickly, within a day or two of the death they report.
For prominent figures, many papers avoid that rush by preparing obituaries years in advance and quietly updating them as their subjects' lives go on.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 avoids 'that rush', which is the haste described in sentence 2; and 'This practice' in sentence 1 means advance preparation, so 1 must follow 3.

questions.common_misconception: Starting with advance preparation, which leaves 'that rush' without a referent.
questions.difficulty_reason: Reference words ('that rush', 'This practice', 'Its real purpose') fix the order.

questions.subtopic: The semicolon joins two independent statements and leaves their connection to the reader.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The semicolon sits between these options, telling the reader that the statements belong together without spelling out how.
The semicolon is often treated as an ornament, a mark that careful writers use to show off and everyone else can safely ignore.
That last feature is both its strength and its risk, because the reader must work out the connection that a word like 'because' or 'but' would have supplied.
Its actual job is more modest and more useful: it joins two statements that could each stand alone as sentences.
A full stop between them would present the two as separate thoughts, while a comma alone would usually be a grammatical error.

The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 places the semicolon 'between these options', the full stop and the comma, which are named only in sentence 5.

Sentence 1 places the semicolon 'between these options', the full stop and comma of 5. Sentence 3 takes up 'That last feature', not spelling out the connection, from the end of 1.
questions.common_misconception: Putting the semicolon's position between the options before the options have been named.
questions.difficulty_reason: A chain of references ('between them', 'these options', 'That last feature') across five sentences.

questions.subtopic: Cryptic clues look lawless but their two converging routes make answers certain.

sentences.text: A well-made clue in fact offers two independent routes to one word: a plain definition at one end, and wordplay that assembles the answer from its parts.
Where the two routes meet, however, there is usually just one word, and a solver who finds it can be surer of it than of any answer to an ordinary riddle.
To a newcomer, a cryptic crossword clue reads like a riddle without rules, a sentence whose answer could be almost anything.
Taken alone, either route would leave the solver guessing, since many words fit a brief definition and most wordplay can be parsed in several ways.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.subtopic: A percentage chance of rain describes frequency, not duration.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Understood this way, the number tells a reader whether to carry an umbrella, not how long the shower will last.
What the figure actually expresses is how often rain falls at a given place on days with conditions like the ones expected.
On seven such days in ten it rains at least a little there, and on the other three it stays dry.

questions.subtopic: Debasing coinage gave rulers a short-lived profit that hoarding and rising prices soon erased.

questions.subtopic: Railway timetables made local solar time unworkable, leading to standard time.

questions.subtopic: Belief in other minds is better defended as an explanatory theory than by analogy from one's own case.

sentences.text: On this view my belief rests not on my own case at all but on the same kind of reasoning that leads us to accept unseen causes elsewhere in science.

questions.subtopic: Repetition in oral epics looks like padding only by the standards of writing; it enabled composition in performance.

4. Because the substitute is a real word, it passes the quick glance that would have caught an ordinary typing error.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 says the errors are 'subtle' and 'the harder kind to notice', which is a conclusion from sentence 4; and 'the substitute' in sentence 4 needs the substitution of sentence 2 immediately before it.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the design. Sentence 2 says the weakness 'follows from the same design', so it must come after the design is described. Sentence 4 explains why 'the substitute' escapes notice. Sentence 1 sums up with 'thus': fewer but subtler errors, which rests on 4.
questions.common_misconception: Ending with sentence 4 after sentence 1, which puts the reason after the conclusion drawn from it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reasoning about why a real-word error is hard to see fixes the last two sentences.

questions.subtopic: Paywalls steady newspaper finances but divide readers by what they can trust.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The worry is that the second group, often the larger, is left with the material least worth trusting.
Advertising revenue, however, flowed increasingly to the large platforms that controlled where readers found the news.
This has steadied the finances of some titles, but it has also divided readers into those who pay for careful reporting and those who rely on whatever is free.

Many papers responded by putting their reporting behind a paywall and asking readers to subscribe.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

4. For years newspapers gave their articles away online, hoping that advertising would pay for the journalism.
5. Many papers responded by putting their reporting behind a paywall and asking readers to subscribe.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 5 says papers 'responded', and the problem they responded to, advertising moving to platforms, is stated in sentence 2.
Sentence 1 mentions 'the second group' before sentence 3 has divided readers into two groups.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 describes the free model. Sentence 2 says, with 'however', that advertising did not stay with newspapers. Sentence 5 gives the response, paywalls. Sentence 3 states the effects of 'This', including the division of readers. Sentence 1 refers to 'the second group', which exists only after sentence 3 names two groups.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 5 before sentence 2, which offers a response before the problem it responds to.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five sentences in a chain of problem, response and consequence; the middle requires seeing why papers 'responded'.

questions.subtopic: Negative marking removes the gain from blind guessing but rewards nerve as well as knowledge.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Negative marking is meant to remove this advantage by deducting marks for each wrong answer.
In a multiple-choice test, a candidate who knows nothing can still score by guessing.
That reward reaches only those willing to claim it, however: some cautious candidates leave blank even questions they could narrow down, so the scheme measures nerve as well as knowledge.
Set at the right level, the penalty makes blind guessing worthless on average, while still rewarding a candidate who can eliminate some options.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: After sentence 1, 'That reward' in sentence 3 has no referent: the reward for eliminating options is introduced only in sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the problem of guessing. Sentence 1 introduces negative marking to remove 'this advantage'. Sentence 4 explains how a well-set penalty works and notes that it still rewards partial knowledge. Sentence 3 begins 'That reward', the reward for eliminating options in 4, and qualifies it, so it must come last.
questions.common_misconception: Treating sentence 3 as a general objection that could follow sentence 1, when 'That reward' points only to the reward described in sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The closing qualification depends on seeing what 'That reward' refers to and why caution undercuts it.

questions.subtopic: Gift cards profit retailers through unspent value whose loss no one feels.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: One might expect such losses to make people wary of the cards, but the loss is spread thinly and felt by no one in particular, since the giver never sees it and the recipient rarely notices it.
For the retailer, however, its chief attraction lies less in the sale it records than in the spending it never has to honour.
A gift card looks like a sensible compromise between a present and cash: it lets the recipient choose, while still showing that the giver thought of a particular shop.
Retailers can therefore promote the cards energetically without provoking the resentment that a visible charge of the same size would arouse.
A noticeable share of cards is lost, forgotten or left with a balance too small to bother with, and the value they carry then stays with the seller.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. One might expect such losses to make people wary of the cards, but the loss is spread thinly and felt by no one in particular, since the giver never sees it and the recipient rarely notices it.
2. For the retailer, however, its chief attraction lies less in the sale it records than in the spending it never has to honour.
3. A gift card looks like a sensible compromise between a present and cash: it lets the recipient choose, while still showing that the giver thought of a particular shop.
4. Retailers can therefore promote the cards energetically without provoking the resentment that a visible charge of the same size would arouse.
5. A noticeable share of cards is lost, forgotten or left with a balance too small to bother with, and the value they carry then stays with the seller.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 5 cannot come straight after sentence 3: the value it says 'stays with the seller' is the point of sentence 2, whose 'however' marks the turn from the recipient's view to the retailer's and must come first.

Sentence 4 says retailers can 'therefore' promote the cards without resentment, but the reason, that the loss is 'felt by no one in particular', is given only in sentence 1; placed last, sentence 1 would reopen a doubt the paragraph has already settled.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 introduces the gift card from the point of view of the giver and the recipient. Sentence 2 turns, with 'For the retailer, however', to the seller's interest, stated compactly as 'the spending it never has to honour'. Sentence 5 unpacks that phrase: cards that are lost, forgotten or left with small balances leave their value 'with the seller'. Sentence 1 raises the expectation that 'such losses' would make people wary and answers it: the loss is 'felt by no one in particular'. Sentence 4 draws the consequence with 'therefore': because the loss is invisible, retailers can push the cards without provoking resentment.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 last as a closing remark on the retailer's motive, which leaves 'For the retailer, however' contrasting with a sentence that is already about retailers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The second sentence states the retailer's interest in a compact phrase that only the third unpacks, and the close runs from an objection to its answer to the consequence, so the order rests on the logic of invisible loss rather than on pronouns.

questions.subtopic: A magnetic sense in birds was doubted because no organ for it could be found.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: That migrating birds find their way across continents has never been in doubt; what has resisted explanation is the means.
The trouble was that no one could find the organ responsible, and a sense without an organ struck many biologists as no sense at all.
Experiments that altered the magnetic field around caged birds changed the direction in which they tried to fly, which pointed to a magnetic sense.
That objection assumed that a sense must be housed in some visible structure, whereas this one might operate through molecules in the eye or particles scattered in tissue.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.
