2. The trouble was that no one could find the organ responsible, and a sense without an organ struck many biologists as no sense at all.
3. Experiments that altered the magnetic field around caged birds changed the direction in which they tried to fly, which pointed to a magnetic sense.
4. That objection assumed that a sense must be housed in some visible structure, whereas this one might operate through molecules in the eye or particles scattered in tissue.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 can look like a lively opener, but sentence 1 cannot then follow it: its contrast between the undoubted fact and the unexplained 'means' frames the question that the experiments begin to answer.
Sentence 2 speaks of 'the organ responsible', which presupposes the magnetic sense proposed in sentence 3.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 separates the established fact of navigation from the open question of how. Sentence 3 gives experimental evidence for one answer, a magnetic sense. Sentence 2 raises 'The trouble': no organ could be found, so the sense was doubted. Sentence 4 identifies the assumption behind 'That objection' and answers it. Each step depends on the previous claim: evidence, then doubt about the evidence, then a reply to the doubt.
questions.common_misconception: Reading sentence 4 as background that could come before the doubt, when it rebuts the specific objection voiced in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Abstract claim, evidence, objection and reply; the reader must track which sentence answers which and resist placing the evidence first.

questions.subtopic: A strict poetic form can aid invention by forcing poets past obvious phrases.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: If that is right, free verse, which offers no such instrument, may be harder to write well than it looks.
It is tempting to think that a strict form, with its fixed count of lines and its demanding rhyme scheme, can only hamper a poet.
The form, on this view, is less a cage than an instrument of search, a way of making the mind try possibilities it would have skipped.
Yet the constraint can work the other way, since the need to find a rhyme pushes the poet past the first, obvious phrase towards one that would otherwise never have been reached.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

4. Yet the constraint can work the other way, since the need to find a rhyme pushes the poet past the first, obvious phrase towards one that would otherwise never have been reached.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 cannot open: 'on this view' points back to the argument of sentence 4 that constraint aids invention.
Sentence 1 speaks of 'no such instrument', and the form is described as an instrument only in sentence 3.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the tempting view that form only hampers. Sentence 4 counters it with 'Yet': the constraint can push the poet past the obvious. Sentence 3 generalises 'on this view' that form is an instrument of search. Sentence 1 draws an implication for free verse, 'which offers no such instrument', so it must follow the image of the instrument in 3. The order moves from a view, to its reversal, to the general principle, to its implication.
questions.common_misconception: Starting with sentence 3 because it sounds like a thesis, when 'on this view' requires the view argued in sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order rests on the movement from a rejected view to the principle and its consequence; the thesis-like sentence is a tempting wrong opener.

questions.subtopic: Popular volunteer software can collapse when the burden on its few maintainers grows.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The few volunteers end up answering complaints instead of writing code, and some of them simply walk away.
A great deal of the code that businesses rely on every day is maintained, without pay, by a handful of volunteers.
As the project grows popular, its users multiply far faster than its maintainers, and most of them contribute nothing but requests.
In the early life of a project this arrangement works well enough, since the people who write the code are also the people who use it.
When they do, companies that had treated the software as free discover that it was free only because someone else was paying with time.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

5. When they do, companies that had treated the software as free discover that it was free only because someone else was paying with time.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 says the volunteers 'end up' answering complaints; the complaints come from the flood of users described in sentence 3, so the effect cannot precede its cause.
Sentence 4 describes the 'early life' of a project, and placing it after the growth of sentence 3 reverses the chronology the paragraph depends on.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the situation of unpaid maintenance. Sentence 4 says 'this arrangement' works early on, because writers and users coincide. Sentence 3 describes growth, which breaks that coincidence. Sentence 1 gives the effect on the volunteers. Sentence 5 begins 'When they do', referring to volunteers walking away, so it must follow 1. The middle three follow the life of a project from early to popular to strained.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 1 straight after sentence 4, which makes the volunteers overworked before the paragraph has introduced the growth in users that overworks them.
questions.difficulty_reason: Few connectives: the middle of the paragraph is ordered by the logic of a project's growth, and the reader must see that the burden comes from the surge of users.

questions.subtopic: Ability grouping can become self-confirming because placement shapes what pupils learn.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: A judgement made at eleven can thus become self-confirming, as the groups grow further apart each year and seem to prove the original sorting right.
Grouping pupils by ability appears to help everyone, since teachers can pitch each lesson to the level of the class in front of them.
In practice the placement also shapes what the pupil will be able to do, because lower groups are usually taught less and expected to achieve less.
The appearance depends on treating a pupil's placement as a measurement of what that pupil can do.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 says placement 'also' shapes ability, which adds to the view of placement as a measurement stated in sentence 4; and 'The appearance' must follow 'appears' in sentence 2.
Sentence 1 concludes that the sorting is self-confirming, which follows only once sentence 3 has shown that placement shapes what pupils can do.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the apparent benefit. Sentence 4 exposes the assumption behind 'The appearance': placement is treated as a measurement. Sentence 3 challenges that assumption, since placement also shapes ability. Sentence 1 draws the conclusion, 'thus', that the sorting confirms itself, which follows only from the claim that placement shapes ability.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 before sentence 4 because it sounds like the main criticism, which separates 'The appearance' from the claim in sentence 2 and gives 'also' nothing to add to.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order turns on the distinction between measuring and shaping ability; 'also' in the third sentence only makes sense after the measuring view is stated.

questions.subtopic: A franchise trades the owner's freedom for reduced uncertainty.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The owner of a franchised cafe, for instance, may not change the menu, the decor or the opening hours, even where local customers would plainly prefer something else.
The fees, though, are not the real price; what the franchisee surrenders in exchange for less uncertainty is the freedom to decide.
A franchise lets an entrepreneur buy into a proven formula rather than invent one, paying fees in return for the brand, the methods and the suppliers.
Whether the bargain is a good one depends on which a particular entrepreneur values more: freedom to experiment or protection from the cost of experiments that fail.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

4. Whether the bargain is a good one depends on which a particular entrepreneur values more: freedom to experiment or protection from the cost of experiments that fail.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: After sentence 3, the cafe example would be an instance of buying a proven formula, but it shows a restriction, which is the loss of freedom stated in sentence 2.
Sentence 1 after sentence 4 would illustrate the general weighing of freedom against protection, and the paragraph would end on an example instead of the judgement it leads to.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 describes what a franchise offers for its fees. Sentence 2 turns, with 'though', to the real price: loss of the freedom to decide. Sentence 1 illustrates that loss with a cafe owner who cannot change the menu. Sentence 4 weighs 'the bargain', freedom against protection, so it must come after both sides are stated. The example must follow the claim about lost freedom, since it shows nothing about the fees of sentence 3.
questions.common_misconception: Putting the cafe example after sentence 3, where 'for instance' would illustrate the benefits of a proven formula, which the example does not show.
questions.difficulty_reason: The example's position depends on recognising which claim it illustrates, and the closing sentence weighs two sides that must both be in place.

questions.subtopic: Respelling dialect speech makes characters seem ignorant, so writers often keep standard spelling.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Respelling words as they are pronounced looks like the most faithful course, and many earlier novelists took it freely.
Its cost is that the reader meets the speech as a page of misspellings, and misspelling, on the page, suggests ignorance rather than an accent.
Many later writers have therefore kept conventional spelling for dialogue and conveyed the region through vocabulary, idiom and the rhythm of the sentence.
Worse, characters rendered this way can come to seem less intelligent than the narrator who describes them in standard spelling, an effect the novelist seldom intends.
A novelist who wants readers to hear the speech of a region must decide how far to let spelling follow sound.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

4. Worse, characters rendered this way can come to seem less intelligent than the narrator who describes them in standard spelling, an effect the novelist seldom intends.
5. A novelist who wants readers to hear the speech of a region must decide how far to let spelling follow sound.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 begins 'Worse', which needs a first cost before it; that cost, misspelling suggesting ignorance, is stated in sentence 2.
Sentence 3 says later writers 'therefore' kept standard spelling, which must follow the full case against respelling, including the further cost in sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 sets out the novelist's decision. Sentence 1 gives the apparently faithful option, respelling. Sentence 2 states 'Its cost': misspelling suggests ignorance. Sentence 4 escalates with 'Worse', a further cost that builds on the first, the contrast with a standard-spelling narrator. Sentence 3 draws the consequence, 'therefore', in the practice of later writers, which needs both costs before it.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 before sentence 2 because 'rendered this way' can refer to the respelling of sentence 1, which leaves 'Worse' escalating from nothing and makes 'Its cost' ambiguous.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two costs must be ordered by degree; 'rendered this way' and 'Its' could both attach to the respelling sentence, so the reader must use 'Worse' and the logic of escalation.

questions.subtopic: Teaching to a single high-stakes test is an understandable temptation whose cost falls on pupils.

sentences.text: Yet the cost of giving in to it is borne by the pupils, who learn to recognise question formats instead of understanding the subject behind them.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 needs a concession before its 'Yet', which sentence 2 supplies; placed last, sentence 2 also refers to a temptation mentioned two sentences earlier.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 introduces the situation and names 'a strong temptation'. Sentence 2 picks it up as 'This temptation' and concedes that it is understandable. Sentence 1 turns with 'Yet' from that concession to the cost of 'giving in to it'. Sentence 3 describes 'Such pupils', the pupils of sentence 1 who recognise formats without understanding.

questions.subtopic: Snow's cholera map mattered because it treated the pattern of cases as evidence.

sentences.text: When he persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle, he was acting on his rival view that the disease travelled through contaminated water.

Sentence 1 continues with 'he' and 'the pump's handle', which need sentence 2, and names his 'rival view'. questions.subtopic: Obsolete city walls were replaced by ring boulevards still visible on maps.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: For centuries, many European cities were enclosed by thick walls that protected their inhabitants but also confined their growth.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.subtopic: The spotlight effect makes us overrate how much others notice us.

sentences.text: In fact, the other guests are largely occupied with their own worries about how they themselves are coming across.

Someone who arrives at a party with a stain on a shirt, for instance, may spend the evening convinced that everyone has seen it.

questions.question:

questions.subtopic: The veil of ignorance does not settle justice by itself but exposes each side's attitude to risk.

sentences.text: Suppose you had to choose the rules of a society without knowing what place you would occupy in it: your class, talents, sex or health.
Critics reply that this conclusion owes less to the veil than to an assumed horror of risk, since a chooser willing to gamble might prefer greater rewards at the top.
Unable to favour yourself, you would have to consider how the rules looked from every position, including the worst.
The device, then, does not settle what justice requires by itself, but it does force each side to state openly the attitude to risk on which its answer depends.
Fearing that the worst position might be their own, prudent choosers behind such a veil, it has been argued, would insist that the least advantaged be made as well off as possible.

3. Unable to favour yourself, you would have to consider how the rules looked from every position, including the worst.
4. The device, then, does not settle what justice requires by itself, but it does force each side to state openly the attitude to risk on which its answer depends.
5. Fearing that the worst position might be their own, prudent choosers behind such a veil, it has been argued, would insist that the least advantaged be made as well off as possible.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 speaks of 'the attitude to risk on which its answer depends', a notion that only sentence 2 introduces.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 sets up the thought experiment. Sentence 3 draws its first implication: one must consider every position 'including the worst'. Sentence 5 picks up 'the worst position' and states the argued conclusion. Sentence 2 reports the critics' reply to 'this conclusion', introducing risk. Sentence 4 is the author's verdict: the device does not settle justice but forces each side to state its 'attitude to risk', which needs sentence 2.
questions.common_misconception: Ending with sentence 2 because a critics' reply often closes a debate, although the verdict of sentence 4 turns on the risk point that sentence 2 introduces.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends on the logic of the argument: the verdict balances the argued conclusion against the critics' point about risk, so it must follow both.

questions.subtopic: On the dirty hands view, necessary political wrongs remain wrongs and good leaders bear the guilt.

sentences.text: Some have concluded that public office simply suspends private morality, so that what would be wrong for a citizen is permitted to a minister.

A politician who refuses ever to lie, bargain with scoundrels or break a promise may keep a clean conscience while the people they serve pay for those scruples.
The more troubling view is that the act remains wrong even when it is necessary, so that a good politician must sometimes do wrong and know it.

4. The more troubling view is that the act remains wrong even when it is necessary, so that a good politician must sometimes do wrong and know it.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 reports what 'Some have concluded', but the conclusion needs a premise; sentence 3's dilemma supplies it and must come first.
'The more troubling view' needs a less troubling view before it, and sentence 2's guilt cannot belong to the view that office suspends morality.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the dilemma that gives rise to the debate. Sentence 1 reports one conclusion drawn from it ('Some have concluded'). Sentence 4 offers 'The more troubling view', which is defined against the view of sentence 1. Sentence 2 develops 'this account'; its talk of guilt fits only sentence 4, since on the view of sentence 1 there would be no wrong to feel guilty about.
questions.common_misconception: Opening with sentence 1 because it states a general position, although 'concluded' presupposes the dilemma of sentence 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends on the logic of two rival views: the student must see that the talk of guilt belongs to the view that necessary acts remain wrong, not to the view that office suspends morality.

questions.subtopic: Equivalent risk frames change choices by shifting attention, not by conveying different information.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: If arithmetic is not what fails, then what the framing alters is not the information people receive but the feature of the situation on which their attention settles.
Told that ten out of a hundred will die within five years, many of the same people hesitate, although the two statements describe exactly the same outcome.
A tempting conclusion is that people are simply careless with numbers, but the effect has been reported even among doctors who understand that the figures are equivalent.
Told that a treatment gives ninety out of a hundred patients five more years of life, most people find it attractive.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

4. Told that a treatment gives ninety out of a hundred patients five more years of life, most people find it attractive.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 refers to 'the same people' and 'the two statements', so the first frame in sentence 4 must precede it.
Sentence 1 begins from the premise that arithmetic does not fail, which only the evidence about doctors in sentence 3 establishes.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 gives the positive frame. Sentence 2 gives the negative frame, mentions 'the same people' and notes that the statements are equivalent. Sentence 3 considers and rejects the explanation that people cannot handle numbers. Sentence 1 follows from that rejection ('If arithmetic is not what fails') and offers the alternative explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Placing the explanation of sentence 1 before the objection in sentence 3, although sentence 1 presupposes that the arithmetic explanation has already been ruled out.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends on the logic of eliminating one explanation before offering another; the two frames could seem to swap until 'the same people' is noticed.

questions.subtopic: False consensus persists because believing one's views common is comforting, not only because of exposure.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: People tend to assume that their own opinions and habits are more widely shared than they actually are.
One likely addition is motive: believing that one's views are common is comforting, because it makes them seem normal and therefore reasonable.
A belief that serves such a need is not easily corrected by information, since it was never held merely on the strength of information.
But if exposure were the whole story, the bias should vanish once people learn the true figures, and it often seems not to.
Part of the explanation is simply exposure, since we spend our time among people who resemble us and so mistake our circle for the world.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

4. But if exposure were the whole story, the bias should vanish once people learn the true figures, and it often seems not to.
5. Part of the explanation is simply exposure, since we spend our time among people who resemble us and so mistake our circle for the world.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2's 'addition' answers the claim in sentence 4 that exposure is not the whole story, and sentence 3's 'such a need' must follow sentence 2 immediately.
Sentence 4 tests exposure as an explanation, which has not been proposed until sentence 5.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states the bias. Sentence 5 gives 'Part of the explanation', exposure. Sentence 4 shows that exposure cannot be 'the whole story'. Sentence 2 supplies 'One likely addition', the comfort motive. Sentence 3 uses 'such a need' to explain the observation in sentence 4 that information does not cure the bias, and so closes the argument.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 straight after sentence 5 as a second cause, although 'addition' answers the gap that sentence 4 opens.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends on the logic of a partial explanation, its failure, and a supplement; two causes look listable in either order.

questions.subtopic: Rivers make attractive borders but move, turning their visibility into a source of dispute.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Such stranded villages turn the river's chief merit as a frontier, its plain visibility, into a source of dispute, since anyone can see that the water no longer runs where the treaty says.
Yet a river is not a line but a process, forever eroding one bank, building up the other and occasionally abandoning its bed altogether.
Rivers seem ideal boundaries, visible to everyone and hard to cross, which is why so many treaties have fixed borders along them.
A border drawn along the channel as it ran on the day of signing may within a generation leave fields and villages on the wrong side of the water.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

3. Rivers seem ideal boundaries, visible to everyone and hard to cross, which is why so many treaties have fixed borders along them.
4. A border drawn along the channel as it ran on the day of signing may within a generation leave fields and villages on the wrong side of the water.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 takes for granted that the channel shifts after signing; only sentence 2 establishes that rivers move, and its 'Yet' must answer sentence 3.
Sentence 1 begins 'Such stranded villages', which needs the villages left on the wrong side of the water in sentence 4; as a closing example sentence 4 would also follow the conclusion it supports.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 gives the case for rivers as borders. Sentence 2 objects ('Yet') that a river moves. Sentence 4 draws the practical consequence of that movement for a border fixed on one day. Sentence 1 refers to 'Such stranded villages' from sentence 4 and closes by turning the original advantage of sentence 3, visibility, into the source of the problem.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 before sentence 2, as if the misplaced villages were the objection, although sentence 4 presupposes the movement of the channel that sentence 2 explains.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends on the logic of the idea: the consequence presupposes the process, and the conclusion ties back to the opening advantage.

questions.subtopic: A fixed retirement age is a recent arrangement whose original assumptions have changed.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: A fixed age at which working life ends seems to many people a natural feature of the life course, like adolescence or old age itself.
When those schemes began, the qualifying age was set high enough that relatively few workers could expect to draw a pension for many years.
Debates about raising that age are therefore not attempts to abolish a timeless right, but disputes over how to adjust an arrangement whose original assumptions no longer hold.
Life expectancy has since risen greatly, but in many countries the qualifying age has risen far less, turning retirement from a brief coda into a long stage of life.
It is in fact a fairly recent invention, which spread with state pension schemes from the late nineteenth century onwards.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

5. It is in fact a fairly recent invention, which spread with state pension schemes from the late nineteenth century onwards.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 says life expectancy has risen 'since', and that the age has risen less, which needs the original setting of the age in sentence 2.
Sentence 5 begins 'It is in fact', a correction that needs the belief stated in sentence 1.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states the common belief that retirement is natural. Sentence 5 corrects it ('in fact') and links it to pension schemes. Sentence 2 describes the conditions when 'those schemes' began. Sentence 4 describes what has changed 'since'. Sentence 3 concludes ('therefore') by rejecting the 'timeless right' framing of sentence 1 and naming the changed assumptions of sentences 2 and 4.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 before sentence 2, although 'since' and 'has risen far less' measure change from the starting point that sentence 2 fixes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five sentences; the student must see that the conclusion answers the opening belief and needs the historical comparison.

questions.subtopic: Treating money by its source looks irrational but may be a serviceable defence against temptation.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Yet people treat money differently according to where it came from, spending a windfall freely while guarding wages with care.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2's 'On reflection, though' revises a verdict; only sentence 4 gives one, and after sentence 2 the dismissal would end the paragraph on a view the author has already answered.
'such habits' in sentence 4 requires the behaviour described in sentence 1.

questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends on separating the reported judgement from the author's revision of it; the last two sentences look reversible.

questions.subtopic: Labour-saving appliances raised standards of cleanliness, so they saved less labour than promised.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The effort saved on each task was thus spent on doing more tasks more often, which is how a labour-saving device can fail to save labour at all.

4. Washing machines, vacuum cleaners and electric irons were sold to households with the promise that they would free people from the drudgery of domestic work.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 explains why hours did not fall; placed before sentence 2 it answers a question nobody has yet asked, and 'Yet' in sentence 2 then has nothing to contrast with except an explanation that already concedes the point.

Sentence 3 offers 'The explanation': the machines eased each task but raised standards. A puzzle must be stated before its solution, so sentence 3 cannot come before sentence 2.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 straight after sentence 4 because both describe the machines, which puts 'The explanation' before the puzzle it explains.
questions.difficulty_reason: The middle pair is fixed by the logic of puzzle followed by explanation rather than by a reference word.

questions.subtopic: Sports fans stay loyal through every change because the team carries a story about themselves.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Players come and go, owners sell up, and the team may even move its ground to another part of the city.
Through all these changes the fan's loyalty often survives, attaching itself to the name and colours rather than to any particular people.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 cannot open: 'the team' and 'its ground' assume a club that only sentence 3 introduces, and 'all these changes' in sentence 2 must follow the list directly.

Sentence 2 refers to 'all these changes' and says loyalty survives them. Sentence 4 begins 'In this sense' and interprets that survival as loyalty to a story about oneself.

questions.subtopic: Given names rise and fall like fads because parents of a generation independently seek the same kind of freshness.

sentences.text: A name picked for its distinctiveness thus becomes common, and in becoming common it begins to sound dated to the next cohort of parents, who avoid it for the very reason it was once chosen.

Yet the popularity of a name rises and falls on the familiar curve of a fad, climbing slowly, peaking and fading within a generation, as though someone were marketing it.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. A name picked for its distinctiveness thus becomes common, and in becoming common it begins to sound dated to the next cohort of parents, who avoid it for the very reason it was once chosen.

4. The puzzle dissolves once we notice how parents tend to choose: they look for a name that is uncommon but not strange, one that sounds fresh to their ear.
5. Yet the popularity of a name rises and falls on the familiar curve of a fad, climbing slowly, peaking and fading within a generation, as though someone were marketing it.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 repeats the rise and fall of sentence 5 but its 'thus' and 'distinctiveness' depend on the preference for freshness in sentence 4 and the convergence in sentence 2, so it cannot follow sentence 5 directly.

Sentence 2 says the parents' 'ears agree', but what their ears are listening for, a fresh but not strange name, is introduced only in sentence 4, which also names 'the puzzle' and so must come right after sentence 5.

After sentence 4 the 'thus' of sentence 1 has no ground, because a preference for fresh names does not make any one name common until sentence 2 shows that parents converge on the same choices; sentence 2 placed last would explain a result already narrated.

Sentence 4 calls this 'the puzzle' and begins the answer with the way parents choose, seeking freshness. Sentence 2 adds why many parents converge on the same names. Sentence 1 concludes with 'thus': the name chosen as distinctive becomes common and then dated, which completes the rise and the fall described in sentence 5.
questions.common_misconception: Putting sentence 1 immediately after sentence 5 because both describe a name rising and falling, which leaves 'distinctiveness' and 'thus' without the reasoning of sentences 4 and 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five abstract sentences; the closing sentence echoes the fad curve and tempts an early placement, and the two explanatory sentences must be ordered by seeing that convergence presupposes the preference for freshness.

questions.subtopic: Open-plan offices can reduce conversation because being overheard makes people guarded; privacy enables collaboration.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 says 'on this view', but at that point no view has been offered, only an observation; the explanation in sentence 4 must come first.

questions.difficulty_reason: The connectives help, but the step from the observed reversal to its explanation and then to a general view must be followed.

questions.subtopic: Natural ice was harvested, stored and shipped until mechanical ice-making ended the trade.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 assumes that insulation preserves ice, which sentence 3 establishes, and 'these blocks' in sentence 3 must follow sentence 1 directly.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 contrasts ('however') with a benefit that has not yet been stated, and 'thus' in sentence 2 must follow the accumulation in sentence 3, not the general claim in sentence 1.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states the benefit of irrigation with a warning hedge ('at least for a while'). Sentence 4 introduces the problem with 'however': the irrigation water leaves salt. Sentence 3 describes 'these deposits' accumulating. Sentence 2 concludes with 'thus' that irrigation can undo itself.
questions.common_misconception: Starting with sentence 4 because it explains the mechanism, though 'the water brought to the fields' and 'however' presuppose the irrigation introduced in sentence 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: A cause-and-effect chain; the concluding irony requires the mechanism first.

questions.subtopic: As software improves, tests meant to tell humans from machines increasingly frustrate the humans.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 presents 'the odd result', but the cause, puzzles growing harder as software improves, appears only in sentence 3; and 'such tasks' in sentence 3 needs sentence 2.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 describes the tests. Sentence 2 names the assumption behind 'These tests'. Sentence 3 says, with 'however', that improving software shrinks 'such tasks', forcing harder puzzles. Sentence 1 states 'the odd result' of that escalation.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 1 before sentence 3, although the frustration it describes is a result of puzzles growing harder, which sentence 3 explains.
questions.difficulty_reason: Back-references fix the first three sentences; the conclusion requires the escalation to precede it.

questions.subtopic: Because collisions in orbit can multiply debris past a threshold, the risk grows faster than the number of satellites.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: When two such objects collide, they do not simply vanish but shatter into thousands of fragments travelling at enormous speeds.
Every satellite launched into low orbit adds to a population of objects that will remain there, in many cases, for years or decades.
A fragment no larger than a coin can disable a satellite, and a disabled satellite struck again becomes a fresh source of fragments.
Because of this tipping point, the danger does not grow in step with the number of objects in orbit, which is why a modest rise in launches may matter far more than it seems.
Beyond a certain density, then, collisions could feed on themselves, multiplying debris faster than it falls back to Earth.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. When two such objects collide, they do not simply vanish but shatter into thousands of fragments travelling at enormous speeds.
2. Every satellite launched into low orbit adds to a population of objects that will remain there, in many cases, for years or decades.
3. A fragment no larger than a coin can disable a satellite, and a disabled satellite struck again becomes a fresh source of fragments.
4. Because of this tipping point, the danger does not grow in step with the number of objects in orbit, which is why a modest rise in launches may matter far more than it seems.
5. Beyond a certain density, then, collisions could feed on themselves, multiplying debris faster than it falls back to Earth.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 says danger does not grow in step with numbers, which follows from the existence of a runaway threshold; that threshold is introduced only in sentence 5, so sentence 4 cannot precede it.
Sentence 3 speaks of fragments before any collision has produced them; the fragments come from the collision described in sentence 1.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 establishes the growing population of orbiting objects. Sentence 1 says collisions between 'such objects' create fragments. Sentence 3 says fragments disable satellites that then produce more fragments. Sentence 5 draws the first inference ('then'): past a certain density the process becomes self-sustaining. Sentence 4 draws the second inference, 'Because of this tipping point', which refers to the density threshold of sentence 5: because there is such a threshold, danger does not rise in proportion to numbers.
questions.common_misconception: Swapping the last two sentences because both are conclusions, although the claim that danger is not proportional to numbers depends on the threshold described in sentence 5.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two successive conclusions must be ordered by which one depends on the other; both carry inference words.

questions.subtopic: Touchscreens cut costs for carmakers but distract drivers, so some physical controls are returning.

sentences.text: Manufacturers favour the change because one screen is cheaper to build than dozens of separate controls and can be updated with new features.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: 'For this reason' in sentence 4 must refer to the distraction described in sentence 3; the cost savings in sentence 1 are a reason to keep touchscreens, not to remove them.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 describes the change to touchscreens. Sentence 1 gives the manufacturers' reason for 'the change'. Sentence 3 gives the drawback for drivers with 'however'. Sentence 4 says 'For this reason', referring to that drawback, some carmakers are restoring controls.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 after sentence 1, although bringing back physical controls is a response to the drivers' problem in sentence 3, not to the manufacturers' savings.
questions.difficulty_reason: Clear connectives and a simple advantage, drawback and response structure.

questions.subtopic: Sequels must balance familiarity and surprise; the best keep the characters and change the situation.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The familiarity that guarantees this audience also sets a trap, since viewers want both to recognise what they loved and to be surprised.

Studios favour sequels because an audience that enjoyed the first film is a market that already exists.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 speaks of 'the first desire' and 'the second', which only make sense after sentence 1 has said viewers want both recognition and surprise.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 gives the commercial reason for sequels. Sentence 1 says the familiarity behind 'this audience' also sets a trap, because viewers want two things. Sentence 2 refers to 'the first desire' and 'the second', which are the two wants named in sentence 1. Sentence 4 says how the best sequels escape 'this bind'.

questions.difficulty_reason: The middle sentences are linked by the logic of the two competing desires rather than by an obvious pronoun.

questions.subtopic: Direct address to the audience is older than the realist fourth wall it is said to break.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: An actor who turns to address those people directly is therefore described as breaking the wall, and the device is usually called modern and disruptive.
What is modern, then, is not the broken wall but the wall itself, a convention that became dominant only when realism made the stage resemble a room with one side removed.
Yet direct address is far older than the convention it supposedly breaks, since actors in many earlier theatres delivered asides and soliloquies straight to the crowd.
Theatre audiences are often said to watch a play through a 'fourth wall', an imaginary barrier that keeps the characters from seeing the people who look at them.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. An actor who turns to address those people directly is therefore described as breaking the wall, and the device is usually called modern and disruptive.
2. What is modern, then, is not the broken wall but the wall itself, a convention that became dominant only when realism made the stage resemble a room with one side removed.
3. Yet direct address is far older than the convention it supposedly breaks, since actors in many earlier theatres delivered asides and soliloquies straight to the crowd.
4. Theatre audiences are often said to watch a play through a 'fourth wall', an imaginary barrier that keeps the characters from seeing the people who look at them.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 concludes 'then' that the wall is modern, but nothing before it has shown that direct address is old; and 'Yet' in sentence 3 would then oppose a conclusion it supports.
'the convention it supposedly breaks' in sentence 3 needs the claim that direct address breaks the wall, which is made in sentence 1; and 'those people' in sentence 1 must follow sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 introduces the idea of the fourth wall. Sentence 1 follows with 'therefore': addressing 'those people', the audience, counts as breaking the wall, a device called modern. Sentence 3 objects with 'Yet' that direct address is older than the wall. Sentence 2 draws the reversed conclusion with 'then': the wall, not its breaking, is the modern thing. The conclusion needs the historical evidence of sentence 3 before it.
questions.common_misconception: Treating sentence 2 as the direct reply to the claim of novelty in sentence 1 and leaving the historical evidence of sentence 3 to the end, which makes 'Yet' contradict a conclusion it actually supports.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion reverses the common view, and solvers must see that the historical evidence must precede the reversal, since both answer the claim that direct address is modern.

questions.subtopic: Sample-clearance requirements changed the sound of sample-based music, not merely its legality.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Once courts in some countries held that even short samples could infringe copyright, record labels began to insist that every fragment be cleared and paid for.
In its early years, producers often borrowed drum breaks and vocal phrases freely, treating old records as raw material.
The fees made dense collages of dozens of samples prohibitively expensive, and producers turned instead to a few licensed loops or to replaying the parts themselves.
Sampling, the practice of building a new track from fragments of existing recordings, became central to several genres of popular music.
The law, in other words, did not merely regulate a style of music; by pricing certain sounds out of reach, it changed what that style sounded like.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. Once courts in some countries held that even short samples could infringe copyright, record labels began to insist that every fragment be cleared and paid for.
2. In its early years, producers often borrowed drum breaks and vocal phrases freely, treating old records as raw material.
3. The fees made dense collages of dozens of samples prohibitively expensive, and producers turned instead to a few licensed loops or to replaying the parts themselves.
4. Sampling, the practice of building a new track from fragments of existing recordings, became central to several genres of popular music.
5. The law, in other words, did not merely regulate a style of music; by pricing certain sounds out of reach, it changed what that style sounded like.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 5 claims the law changed the sound, which restates the turn to loops and replayed parts in sentence 3; and 'The fees' in sentence 3 needs the clearance requirement in sentence 1 directly before it.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 defines sampling. Sentence 2 describes its early, free-borrowing years. Sentence 1 describes the legal change that ended free borrowing. Sentence 3 gives the effect of the clearance fees on how tracks were made. Sentence 5 restates that effect as a general point ('in other words'): the law changed the sound itself.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 5 after sentence 1 because it mentions the law, although 'changed what that style sounded like' restates the change in production described in sentence 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five sentences in chronological order; the closing restatement must follow the effect it restates.

questions.subtopic: Because authors blurb their friends, blurbs reveal connections more than quality.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The back cover of almost any new novel carries short words of praise from other writers.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.common_misconception: Putting sentence 4 before sentence 3, which leaves 'however' with nothing to contrast and 'These blurbs' far from its referent.
questions.difficulty_reason: Clear reference and contrast words.

questions.subtopic: Letters in an epistolary novel seem to offer direct access to a mind but are always shaped for a reader.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: A novel told entirely in letters seems, at first, to offer the most direct access a reader could want to a character's private thoughts.
What looks like a window into the heart is therefore always partly a performance, and the attentive reader learns to read between the lines.
Yet that very spontaneity carries a hidden constraint, because every letter is addressed to someone and is shaped for that person's eyes.
Each letter is written in the heat of the moment, before its writer knows how events will turn out.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Here sentence 4 is left stranded at the end, after the conclusion; its point about writing in the moment supports the first impression and cannot follow the verdict of sentence 2.
Sentence 3 needs a spontaneity already described, and that description is in sentence 4; placing 4 after 3 also separates the constraint from the 'therefore' of sentence 2.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 introduces the novel in letters and its apparent directness. Sentence 4 supports that impression: 'Each letter' refers back to the letters of 1, and writing 'in the heat of the moment' explains the sense of directness. Sentence 3 turns with 'Yet that very spontaneity', which needs the spontaneity of writing 'in the heat of the moment' described in 4; the 'direct access' of 1 is a reader's impression, not the writer's spontaneity. Sentence 2 draws the conclusion ('therefore') that the letter is partly a performance, which follows only from the constraint in 3.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 straight after sentence 1, so that the objection arrives before the spontaneity it turns against has been described.
questions.difficulty_reason: The supporting sentence about writing in the moment must precede 'that very spontaneity', and the conclusion needs the constraint before it; one step of inference beyond pronoun matching.

questions.subtopic: Invented ruins in eighteenth-century landscapes offered a mood of pleasurable decay rather than a lesson in history.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Painters of the eighteenth century often placed a crumbling temple or a broken arch in the corner of an otherwise ordinary pastoral scene.
A ruin that commemorates nothing in particular can hardly be a lesson in history, so its appeal must lie elsewhere.
Many of the ruins in these pictures, however, belong to no identifiable building, and some were simply invented by the painter.

The real attraction, it seems, was the chance to contemplate decay from a safe distance, as a mood to be savoured rather than a loss to be mourned.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

4. The usual explanation is that such ruins invited the viewer to reflect on the grandeur of lost civilisations.
5. The real attraction, it seems, was the chance to contemplate decay from a safe distance, as a mood to be savoured rather than a loss to be mourned.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 5 names the real attraction, so sentence 2 saying the appeal 'must lie elsewhere' would come after the question is already settled; the inference must precede the answer.
Sentence 3 objects to an explanation with 'however', but placed second it has no explanation to object to; the usual view in sentence 4 must come first.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 sets the scene with the painted ruins. Sentence 4 gives 'The usual explanation' of 'such ruins', so it needs 1. Sentence 3 objects with 'however': the ruins often depict no real building. Sentence 2 infers from that objection that a ruin commemorating nothing cannot teach history, and so its appeal 'must lie elsewhere'. Only then can sentence 5 name 'The real attraction'. Reversing the last two would have the paragraph name the attraction and then announce that it must lie somewhere not yet found.
questions.common_misconception: Putting sentence 5 before sentence 2 because both concern the true appeal, which makes 2 announce as an open question something already answered.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: the last two sentences have no pronoun lock, and the solver must see that 'must lie elsewhere' is a step that precedes naming the real attraction.

questions.subtopic: Dutch vanitas still lifes turn a display of plenty into a reminder of mortality.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 introduces the paintings and their first impression. Sentence 1 describes 'Their tables', the evidence of plenty. Sentence 4 turns with 'Look closer, however' and 'the same tables', which need the tables of 1. Sentence 2 explains what 'These objects', the skull, candle and watch of 4, do to the meaning of the picture.
questions.common_misconception: Reading sentence 4 before sentence 1, although 'the same tables' only makes sense once the tables have been described.
questions.difficulty_reason: Clear opener and reference words ('Their tables', 'the same tables', 'These objects') fix every link.

questions.subtopic: The chorus in Greek tragedy, often thought an interruption, models how citizens should respond to events.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Seen this way, the chorus is less an interruption of the tragedy than a guide to how the tragedy should be received.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 begins 'Seen this way', which needs the reinterpretation in sentence 3; it cannot open the paragraph.
Sentence 3 refers to 'That pause', and the halting of the story that creates the pause is described only in sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the modern complaint about the chorus. Sentence 4 develops it: the songs 'seem to halt the story'. Sentence 3 reinterprets 'That pause', which refers to the halting described in 4, as purposeful. Sentence 1 sums up the reinterpretation ('Seen this way'): the chorus is a guide rather than an interruption, which depends on the purpose given in 3.
questions.common_misconception: Starting with sentence 1 because it sounds like a thesis, though 'Seen this way' requires a way of seeing already offered.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: complaint, its development, reinterpretation and verdict; the verdict cannot open because it answers the complaint.

questions.subtopic: Children who grow up with a pidgin turn it into a full creole, showing that they impose structure on language.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: When people with no shared language must trade or work together, they often improvise a simplified tongue known as a pidgin.

The change suggests that children do not merely copy the language around them but actively impose structure on it.

The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

5. Something remarkable can happen, though, when children grow up hearing a pidgin as the main language of their community.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 5 contrasts with the fact that nobody grows up speaking a pidgin, so the description of the pidgin's limits in sentence 2 must come before it.

Sentence 5 contrasts ('though') with exactly that limit: children who grow up hearing it. Sentence 4 says what 'those children' do, turning the pidgin into a creole. Sentence 3 draws the general conclusion from 'The change'.
questions.common_misconception: Putting sentence 3 immediately after sentence 5, so that a conclusion about what children do is drawn before anything they do has been described.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: definition, limitation, the contrasting circumstance, the transformation and the inference drawn from it.

questions.subtopic: The footnote lets readers verify a claim rather than simply trust the author.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: With that information, a sceptical reader can go to the original source and check whether it says what the author claims.
Yet its main purpose is a simple one: to show readers exactly where a claim comes from.
In this sense, the humble footnote turns an argument from a request for trust into an invitation to verify.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: After all, no listener seriously takes such a question as an inquiry into their physical abilities.

questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: the solver must see that the 'After all' sentence supports the dismissive view, not the reply, and that 'even when it is never used' presupposes it.

questions.subtopic: The passive voice survives in lab reports because it puts the repeatable procedure ahead of the person.

sentences.text: Still, the passive survives in laboratory reports for a reason: it keeps attention on the procedure rather than on the person who carried it out.

The advice has merit, since a paper full of phrases like 'it was observed that' can be tiring to read.
Style guides have long urged scientists to abandon the passive voice in favour of livelier sentences that say who did what.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 presents the unnamed experimenter as making a point, but the link between the passive and the procedure is first made in sentence 1; and 'Still' in 1 needs the concession of sentence 3 directly before it.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 states the advice of style guides. Sentence 3 concedes that 'The advice has merit'. Sentence 1 turns with 'Still': the passive persists for a reason, keeping attention on the procedure. Sentence 2 explains why that focus matters, since a method should be repeatable by anyone, and so must follow 1.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 before sentence 1 because it states a general principle, though its 'grammar that leaves the experimenter unnamed' presupposes the reason given in 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Concession then counter-claim then justification; the final sentence elaborates the reason in the third and cannot stand before it.

questions.subtopic: Cramming feels effective but spaced review produces more lasting learning.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.difficulty_reason: Simple problem and solution sequence with a reference word ('That familiarity').

questions.subtopic: Rubrics make marking consistent but can penalise originality as students write to the list.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Students, being sensible, soon learn to write towards the rubric, ticking off each listed feature in turn.
Their essays grow more uniform, and the rare piece that succeeds by doing something unlisted risks being marked down.
Detailed marking rubrics were introduced in many schools to make the grading of essays fairer and more consistent.

By spelling out in advance what earns each mark, such rubrics reduce the weight of any single teacher's personal taste.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 says the fairness is 'thus' bought by penalising originality, but at that point no penalty has been described; the marking down appears only in sentence 2.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the purpose of rubrics. Sentence 5 explains how 'such rubrics' serve it, by limiting individual taste, so it must follow 3. Sentence 1 describes the students' response, writing towards the rubric, and sentence 2 its effect ('Their essays'): uniformity, and penalties for the unlisted. Sentence 4 concludes with 'thus' that fairness is 'purchased by penalising' originality, which depends on the marking down described in 2.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 third as a thesis, although its 'thus' and 'penalising' depend on the consequence described in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: purpose, mechanism, response, effect, verdict; few pronouns help, and the verdict is tempting as an early thesis.

questions.subtopic: Recipe-style school practicals teach pupils to reproduce known answers, the reverse of real inquiry.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Pupils who follow such a recipe learn to reproduce an answer already known, and a reading that deviates from it is treated as a mistake.
School science practicals are usually defended as a way of teaching pupils how scientists actually find things out.
In many classrooms, though, the practical arrives as a worksheet listing the apparatus, the steps and even the result that should be obtained.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: After sentence 2, sentence 4 would say real inquiry runs 'the other way' from the defence of practicals, which is the reverse of the point; it contrasts with the recipe practice described in sentence 1.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the usual defence of practicals. Sentence 3 contrasts ('though') with how they are actually run. Sentence 1 describes the effect of 'such a recipe', the worksheet of 3, including that a deviating reading counts as a mistake. Sentence 4 says real inquiry 'runs the other way', which only makes sense against the treatment of deviation in 1.
questions.common_misconception: Reading sentence 4 as a natural second sentence because it describes real science, although 'the other way' needs the contrary practice described in sentence 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: the closing contrast hinges on the treatment of an unexpected reading.

questions.subtopic: A longer pause after a teacher's question lets more pupils think and answer.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The silence that feels awkward to the teacher is, for the class, the time in which thinking actually happens.
Such a brief pause rewards the quickest pupils and gives the others little reason to think at all.
If the teacher instead waits several seconds in silence, more pupils attempt an answer, and their answers tend to be fuller.
When a teacher asks the class a question, the pause before someone is called on, or before the teacher answers, is often very short.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 second, which leaves 'Such a brief pause' in sentence 2 after the longer wait has already been described.
questions.difficulty_reason: Reference words ('Such a brief pause', 'instead', 'The silence') fix the order.

questions.subtopic: Pain scores are useful for tracking one patient over time, not for comparing patients.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The score is therefore most useful for tracking change in one patient over time, not for comparing one patient with another.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 objects to comparing patients, and that only makes sense once sentence 2 has claimed the number is easy to compare; placed after 4, sentence 2 also breaks the 'therefore' link to sentence 1.

Sentence 1 concludes ('therefore') where the score is useful, which follows from the objection in 4 and limits the claim about comparison in 2.

questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: the conclusion narrows the use of the score, which needs both the claimed comparability and the objection to it.

questions.subtopic: Bed rest after surgery was replaced by early walking once its dangers became clear.

sentences.text: Prolonged bed rest, however, turned out to carry dangers of its own, including blood clots, weakened muscles and chest infections.

questions.difficulty_reason: Chronology (last century, today) and 'however' make the order clear.

questions.subtopic: Variolation protected against smallpox at real risk and was abandoned once cowpox inoculation offered the same protection.

sentences.text: The resulting illness was usually milder than smallpox caught in the ordinary way, and those who recovered were protected against the disease.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 begins 'Yet', which needs a benefit to set against; placed before sentence 1 it follows only the procedure, and the risks appear before any reason for running them.
Ending with the risks in sentence 3 after the practice has been abandoned leaves the abandonment unexplained and makes 'Yet' contrast with the arrival of a better method.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 names variolation. Sentence 2 describes the procedure. Sentence 1 gives 'The resulting illness', which needs the procedure of 2, and its benefit. Sentence 3 sets the risks against the benefit with 'Yet'. Sentence 4 explains why the practice ended: a safer method, which the risks in 3 make decisive.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 before sentence 1, although 'Yet' must contrast with the benefit, and the illness it concerns has not yet been described.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: procedure, benefit, cost and replacement; the replacement makes sense only after the cost.

questions.subtopic: The danger of many prescriptions for an elderly patient lies in nobody overseeing the whole list.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: An elderly patient who sees several specialists often leaves each appointment with one more prescription.

Each of these prescriptions, considered by itself, may be entirely appropriate to the condition it was written for.
No single doctor need be at fault, and the danger therefore lies in the absence of anyone whose job is to look at the whole list.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

4. No single doctor need be at fault, and the danger therefore lies in the absence of anyone whose job is to look at the whole list.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 is neutral, so 'Taken together, however' in sentence 2 has nothing favourable to turn against; the contrast is with 'considered by itself' in sentence 3.
Sentence 4 locates 'the danger' before any danger has been described; the interactions of sentence 2 must come first.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 sets up the situation: several specialists, one more prescription each. Sentence 3 grants that 'Each of these prescriptions, considered by itself' may be sound, and 'these' ties it to 1. Sentence 2 turns with 'Taken together, however', a contrast that needs the 'by itself' of 3. Sentence 4 concludes that no doctor need be at fault, since each acted soundly as 3 says, and that the danger lies in the missing overview, the harm of the combination described in 2.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 directly after sentence 1 because both concern several medicines, which leaves 'however' with no favourable judgement to contrast with.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: the mandatory pair is 'considered by itself' followed by 'Taken together', and the conclusion draws on both halves of that contrast.

questions.subtopic: Colonial hill stations in India were built as imitations of home as much as refuges from heat.

sentences.text: These hill stations, as they came to be called, soon grew beyond simple retreats, and some even served as seats of government for part of the year.

Ending with sentence 1 leaves 'each hill station' and 'seasonal capital' in sentence 2 without anything to refer to, and the name the towns 'came to be called' would arrive only after they had been discussed.

Sentence 2 ('Whether summer retreat or seasonal capital, each hill station') picks up both the name and the government role introduced in 1, and describes how the towns were designed. Sentence 4 interprets 'Such deliberate imitation', which is the imitation described in 2.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 second, although 'each hill station' and 'seasonal capital' in it presuppose the name and the government role that sentence 1 introduces.
questions.difficulty_reason: The naming phrase, the echo of 'seasonal capital' and 'Such deliberate imitation' fix the order.

questions.subtopic: Planned capitals seem sterile because the neutrality for which their sites were chosen left them no local life.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Visitors often find these planned capitals sterile, with grand avenues that seem to lead nowhere and few signs of ordinary street life.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Chronology tempts students to give the motive before the result, but sentence 3 opens with 'That reason', and no reason has been mentioned until sentence 4 speaks of 'the reason the sites were chosen'.
Sentence 4 reads 'this' as a failure of design, but the sterility it refers to is described only in sentence 1.

Sentence 4 rejects the obvious reading of 'this' sterility and points to 'the reason the sites were chosen'. Sentence 3 begins 'That reason', so it must come straight after 4, and supplies the political motive that explains the emptiness.
questions.common_misconception: Following chronology and putting the political motive of sentence 3 second, although 'That reason' needs the reason first mentioned in sentence 4.

questions.subtopic: Artists revive cheap districts and are then priced out, a cycle that consumes its own makers.

questions.subtopic: Embankments that make floods rarer encourage building that makes the eventual flood more destructive.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 says the flood finds 'far more to destroy than before', which only follows once sentence 4 has described development spreading across the floodplain; and 'duly' in 4 needs the sense of safety of sentence 2 directly before it.
