Sentence 1 shows the consequence when a large flood comes: 'far more to destroy', which presupposes the development of 4. Sentence 3 states the general paradox with 'thus'.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 1 before sentence 4 because floods becoming rarer seems to follow the embankment directly, which leaves 'far more to destroy than before' unexplained.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: the greater destruction in the flood sentence depends on the development sentence, without any pronoun to signal it.

questions.subtopic: Oasis towns flourished on desert caravan trade and shrank when trade found other routes.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Across the great deserts, towns grew up wherever a reliable spring or well made a stopping place possible.
That prosperity, however, depended on the trade routes that passed through them.
When ships and later railways carried goods by other paths, many of these towns shrank to a fraction of their former size.
Caravans crossing the sand had to rest and water their animals, and these oasis towns grew rich supplying food, shelter and markets.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Across the great deserts, towns grew up wherever a reliable spring or well made a stopping place possible.
2. That prosperity, however, depended on the trade routes that passed through them.
3. When ships and later railways carried goods by other paths, many of these towns shrank to a fraction of their former size.
4. Caravans crossing the sand had to rest and water their animals, and these oasis towns grew rich supplying food, shelter and markets.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 explains why the towns were vulnerable, so it must come before the decline in sentence 3, not after it.
Sentence 2 refers to 'That prosperity', but no prosperity has been mentioned until the towns grow rich in sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 explains where the towns grew. Sentence 4 describes the caravan trade that made the towns rich. Sentence 2 qualifies 'That prosperity' with 'however': it depended on those routes. Sentence 3 shows the consequence when trade moved elsewhere.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 last, which leaves the decline in sentence 3 stated before the dependence that explains it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Clear chronology and 'however' make the order plain.

questions.subtopic: A whistleblower who reports fraud may be the most loyal employee, if loyalty is owed to an institution's purpose.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Whistleblowers are often accused of disloyalty, as though exposing wrongdoing were a betrayal of their colleagues.
But loyalty to an institution is usually loyalty to its stated purpose, whether that is healing patients or serving customers honestly.
On that view, the employee who reports fraud may be the most loyal person in the building.
The charge assumes that loyalty is owed to the people of an organisation, whatever they happen to be doing.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Whistleblowers are often accused of disloyalty, as though exposing wrongdoing were a betrayal of their colleagues.
2. But loyalty to an institution is usually loyalty to its stated purpose, whether that is healing patients or serving customers honestly.
3. On that view, the employee who reports fraud may be the most loyal person in the building.
4. The charge assumes that loyalty is owed to the people of an organisation, whatever they happen to be doing.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 answers the assumption about whom loyalty is owed to, which is stated only in sentence 4; and 'On that view' in sentence 3 must follow the view of 2, not the assumption.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states the accusation of disloyalty. Sentence 4 identifies the assumption behind 'The charge'. Sentence 2 challenges that assumption with 'But', offering a different object of loyalty. Sentence 3 draws the conclusion 'On that view', which refers to the view of 2.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 before sentence 4, so that the rival account of loyalty is offered before the assumption it challenges has been exposed.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: accusation, hidden assumption, rival account and its consequence.

questions.subtopic: The transitivity objection suggests memory is evidence of personal identity rather than what identity consists in.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Since sameness cannot behave like this, memory may be evidence of who someone is without being what personal identity consists in.
A well-known objection imagines an old general who remembers his first battle but has forgotten his boyhood, which the young officer at that battle recalled clearly.
One influential view holds that what makes you the same person as some earlier individual is your ability to remember that individual's experiences from the inside.
If remembering is what identity consists in, the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy.
The view has obvious appeal, since memory seems to be what binds the separate episodes of a life into a single story.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. Since sameness cannot behave like this, memory may be evidence of who someone is without being what personal identity consists in.
2. A well-known objection imagines an old general who remembers his first battle but has forgotten his boyhood, which the young officer at that battle recalled clearly.
3. One influential view holds that what makes you the same person as some earlier individual is your ability to remember that individual's experiences from the inside.
4. If remembering is what identity consists in, the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy.
5. The view has obvious appeal, since memory seems to be what binds the separate episodes of a life into a single story.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 speaks of 'the general', 'the officer' and 'the boy' as already known, but they are introduced only in sentence 2.

Granting the view 'obvious appeal' in sentence 5 after the objection has been raised breaks the argument; the concession belongs before the objection, and sentence 4 must follow the case in sentence 2 directly.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the memory view. Sentence 5 grants its appeal. Sentence 2 introduces the objection with the general, the officer and the boy. Sentence 4 works through the case: by the memory view the general is the officer and the officer the boy, yet the general is not the boy. Sentence 1 concludes from 'this' failure of sameness that memory is evidence of identity rather than its substance.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 4 before sentence 2 because it states the logic of the objection, though the general, the officer and the boy are introduced only in sentence 2.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: the solver must follow a transitivity argument, setting the case before its analysis and the analysis before the verdict.

questions.subtopic: Deferring to experts is rational but shifts the layperson's judgement to choosing whom to trust.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The layperson's task is thus shifted rather than abolished: from weighing the evidence to weighing the track records and incentives of those who report it.
Deference does not free us from judgement entirely, however, because experts sometimes disagree and someone must decide whom to believe.
Most of what any of us believes about medicine, climate or economics rests not on our own investigation but on the word of experts.
This is not a failing, since no one could check more than a tiny fraction of such claims for themselves.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. The layperson's task is thus shifted rather than abolished: from weighing the evidence to weighing the track records and incentives of those who report it.
2. Deference does not free us from judgement entirely, however, because experts sometimes disagree and someone must decide whom to believe.
3. Most of what any of us believes about medicine, climate or economics rests not on our own investigation but on the word of experts.
4. This is not a failing, since no one could check more than a tiny fraction of such claims for themselves.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: With sentence 2 second, 'This is not a failing' in sentence 4 would refer to the need for judgement rather than to reliance on experts, and 'however' in 2 would have no defence to qualify.
Sentence 1 says the task is 'thus shifted rather than abolished', but without sentence 2 before it nothing has shown that any task remains.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 observes that most beliefs rest on experts. Sentence 4 defends 'This' reliance. Sentence 2 qualifies the defence with 'however': deference still requires judgement when experts disagree. Sentence 1 concludes ('thus') that the task is 'shifted rather than abolished', which presupposes both that deference is reasonable (4) and that judgement remains (2).
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 second, so that the qualification arrives before the defence it qualifies, and 'This is not a failing' then seems to defend the need for judgement.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: defence must precede qualification, and the conclusion combines both; the word 'Deference' first appears in the qualifying sentence, which tempts solvers to place it early.

questions.subtopic: A duty of gratitude makes sense as a duty to acknowledge a benefit, not to feel an emotion on demand.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Yet we do blame people who accept great kindness and then behave as though nothing had been done for them.
Understood this way, a duty of gratitude no longer clashes with the spontaneity that makes thanks valuable.
Perhaps the duty is not to feel a particular emotion on cue but to acknowledge the benefit and not act against the benefactor.
It seems odd to speak of a duty of gratitude, since thanks extracted by obligation hardly feel like thanks at all.
The blame suggests that gratitude is owed after all, even if it cannot be demanded in the way a debt can.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. Yet we do blame people who accept great kindness and then behave as though nothing had been done for them.
2. Understood this way, a duty of gratitude no longer clashes with the spontaneity that makes thanks valuable.
3. Perhaps the duty is not to feel a particular emotion on cue but to acknowledge the benefit and not act against the benefactor.
4. It seems odd to speak of a duty of gratitude, since thanks extracted by obligation hardly feel like thanks at all.
5. The blame suggests that gratitude is owed after all, even if it cannot be demanded in the way a debt can.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 proposes what 'the duty' consists of, but that there is a duty at all is first inferred in sentence 5; and 'The blame' in 5 must follow the blaming described in sentence 1.
Sentence 5 refers to 'The blame', which needs the blaming of the ungrateful in sentence 1 before it.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 raises the puzzle: a duty of gratitude seems self-defeating. Sentence 1 counters with 'Yet': we blame the ungrateful. Sentence 5 interprets 'The blame' as evidence that gratitude is owed. Sentence 3 proposes what the duty might be. Sentence 2 shows that, 'Understood this way', the duty resolves the puzzle of 4.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 before sentence 5, so that the duty is redefined before the paragraph has shown that there is any duty to redefine.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: puzzle, counter-evidence, inference, proposal and resolution; the proposal must follow the inference that a duty exists.

questions.subtopic: Neither logic nor experience can justify the premise that the future will resemble the past, and philosophers respond in two ways.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Faced with this dilemma, some philosophers have concluded that inductive inference is not rationally justified at all, but merely a habit of mind.
Experience is no better placed, for to argue that the future will resemble the past because it always has done so is to assume the very premise in question.
Our confidence that bread will nourish us tomorrow, or that the sun will rise, rests on an unstated premise: that the future will resemble the past.
Logic cannot supply that premise, since there is no contradiction in supposing that nature might change its course tomorrow.
A second response holds that the demand was misplaced from the start, since induction is part of what we mean by reasoning well and needs no deeper foundation.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. Faced with this dilemma, some philosophers have concluded that inductive inference is not rationally justified at all, but merely a habit of mind.
2. Experience is no better placed, for to argue that the future will resemble the past because it always has done so is to assume the very premise in question.
3. Our confidence that bread will nourish us tomorrow, or that the sun will rise, rests on an unstated premise: that the future will resemble the past.
4. Logic cannot supply that premise, since there is no contradiction in supposing that nature might change its course tomorrow.
5. A second response holds that the demand was misplaced from the start, since induction is part of what we mean by reasoning well and needs no deeper foundation.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Experience cannot be 'no better placed' when nothing has yet been tried; the comparison needs the failure of logic in sentence 4 first.
Sentence 5 calls itself 'A second response', so it cannot precede the first response given in sentence 1.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the unstated premise behind everyday expectations. Sentence 4 tries the first possible source of justification, logic, and refers to 'that premise'. Sentence 2 says experience is 'no better placed', a comparison that only makes sense after one source has already failed, so it follows sentence 4. The two failures together form 'this dilemma' of sentence 1, which gives the first response. Sentence 5, 'A second response', must come after the first.
questions.common_misconception: Putting sentence 2 straight after sentence 3 because experience seems the obvious first place to look, missing that 'no better placed' compares experience with a source already rejected.
questions.difficulty_reason: Abstract argument with few explicit connectives; the order of the two horns depends on the comparative 'no better placed', and 'this dilemma' needs both horns before it.

questions.subtopic: Whether a slippery slope argument fails depends on what is supposed to carry us from one step to the next.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Such arguments are often dismissed as fallacies, but whether they fail depends on what is supposed to carry us down the slope, and two cases must be distinguished.
Slippery slope arguments warn that a modest step, harmless in itself, will lead by stages to an outcome that nobody wants.
If each step merely makes the next one conceivable, the warning is weak, since conceivability is cheap and most conceivable steps are never taken.
If, however, each step changes the incentives or precedents that govern the next decision, the slope may be real and the warning deserves a hearing.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Such arguments are often dismissed as fallacies, but whether they fail depends on what is supposed to carry us down the slope, and two cases must be distinguished.
2. Slippery slope arguments warn that a modest step, harmless in itself, will lead by stages to an outcome that nobody wants.
3. If each step merely makes the next one conceivable, the warning is weak, since conceivability is cheap and most conceivable steps are never taken.
4. If, however, each step changes the incentives or precedents that govern the next decision, the slope may be real and the warning deserves a hearing.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 announces that two cases 'must be distinguished'; placed last it introduces a distinction that has already been drawn.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 defines the slippery slope argument. Sentence 1 refers to 'Such arguments' and announces that 'two cases must be distinguished'. Sentences 3 and 4 are those two cases, and sentence 4 begins 'If, however', contrasting with the weak case of sentence 3, so it comes last.
questions.common_misconception: Ending with sentence 1 as a summary, which leaves its announcement of 'two cases' pointing at nothing.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order depends on the logic of setting up a distinction and then giving its two branches; the sentence that announces the distinction can look like a closing judgement.

questions.subtopic: The parable of the starving donkey shows that the ability to choose without a reason supports rationality.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The real animal's escape, an arbitrary choice, suggests that the capacity to pick without a reason is not a flaw in rationality but one of its necessary supports.
The story is absurd as zoology, since any real animal would simply start eating, but it poses a genuine puzzle for theories of rational choice.
Put abstractly, the puzzle is this: if rational agents act only on reasons, an agent facing two perfectly equal options seems to have no rational way to begin.
An old parable describes a donkey placed exactly midway between two identical bales of hay, which starves because it has no reason to prefer either.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. The real animal's escape, an arbitrary choice, suggests that the capacity to pick without a reason is not a flaw in rationality but one of its necessary supports.
2. The story is absurd as zoology, since any real animal would simply start eating, but it poses a genuine puzzle for theories of rational choice.
3. Put abstractly, the puzzle is this: if rational agents act only on reasons, an agent facing two perfectly equal options seems to have no rational way to begin.
4. An old parable describes a donkey placed exactly midway between two identical bales of hay, which starves because it has no reason to prefer either.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 answers the puzzle, so it cannot come before sentence 3, which first states what the puzzle is.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 tells the parable. Sentence 2 calls it 'The story', notes that 'any real animal would simply start eating' and says it poses 'a genuine puzzle'. Sentence 3 states 'the puzzle' abstractly. Sentence 1 resolves it by returning to 'The real animal's escape' mentioned in sentence 2; a resolution must follow the statement of the problem.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 1 right after sentence 2 because both mention the real animal, so that the resolution comes before the puzzle has been stated.
questions.difficulty_reason: The last two sentences must be ordered by the logic of problem before solution; the shared mention of the real animal tempts students to put the resolution straight after the story.

questions.subtopic: The universalisability test condemns lying promises but also harmless policies, so it needs a better way of describing actions.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: What the test needs, then, is a way of describing actions that separates the deceiver's principle from the tennis player's, and supplying it has proved harder than it first appears.
A lying promise fails the test neatly: if everyone made promises they meant to break, nobody would accept a promise, and the lie could not even be told.
One influential test in ethics asks whether the principle behind an action could be willed as a rule that everyone follows.

Critics point out that the test seems to condemn harmless policies just as readily, such as playing tennis on Sunday mornings because the courts are empty, which would defeat itself if everyone did it.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. What the test needs, then, is a way of describing actions that separates the deceiver's principle from the tennis player's, and supplying it has proved harder than it first appears.
2. A lying promise fails the test neatly: if everyone made promises they meant to break, nobody would accept a promise, and the lie could not even be told.
3. One influential test in ethics asks whether the principle behind an action could be willed as a rule that everyone follows.
4. Critics point out that the test seems to condemn harmless policies just as readily, such as playing tennis on Sunday mornings because the courts are empty, which would defeat itself if everyone did it.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: The objection says the test condemns harmless policies 'just as readily' as something else; that something is the lying promise of sentence 2, which must come first.
Sentence 1 refers to 'the deceiver', who appears only in sentence 2, so sentence 2 cannot come after it.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 introduces the test. Sentence 2 shows the test working on a lying promise, which defeats itself when universalised. Sentence 4 says the test condemns harmless policies 'just as readily', a comparison that requires the successful case of sentence 2 to come first. Sentence 1 draws the conclusion 'then' and names both 'the deceiver' and 'the tennis player', so it must come last.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the critics' objection as the natural follow-up to the definition and placing sentence 4 second, which leaves 'just as readily' without anything to compare with.
questions.difficulty_reason: Students must see that the tennis case has the same self-defeating structure as the lying promise; the order turns on the comparison 'just as readily' rather than on pronouns.

questions.subtopic: A decoy option is added not to be bought but to make a neighbouring option look better.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Having done its work without being bought, the six-month plan is what marketers call a decoy, an option whose job is to flatter a rival placed beside it.
The owner then introduces a six-month plan that costs almost as much as the annual membership.
Imagine a gym offering two memberships, a monthly plan and a much pricier annual one, and finding that most new members pick the monthly plan.
Hardly anyone signs up for the new six-month plan, but annual memberships climb, because the annual plan now looks generous beside its costly neighbour.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Having done its work without being bought, the six-month plan is what marketers call a decoy, an option whose job is to flatter a rival placed beside it.
2. The owner then introduces a six-month plan that costs almost as much as the annual membership.
3. Imagine a gym offering two memberships, a monthly plan and a much pricier annual one, and finding that most new members pick the monthly plan.
4. Hardly anyone signs up for the new six-month plan, but annual memberships climb, because the annual plan now looks generous beside its costly neighbour.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 says the six-month plan worked 'without being bought'; that cannot be said until sentence 4 reports that hardly anyone signed up for it.
Sentence 1 refers to 'the six-month plan' and its work, neither of which exists until sentences 2 and 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 sets up the hypothetical gym. Sentence 2 adds the six-month plan ('then'). Sentence 4 reports the result for 'the new six-month plan'. Sentence 1 says the plan did its work 'without being bought', which is known only once sentence 4 has reported that hardly anyone chose it, and then names the device, so it closes the paragraph.
questions.common_misconception: Placing the definition in sentence 1 straight after the new plan appears in sentence 2, although 'without being bought' needs the sales result reported in sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: A simple narrative with time order and clear back-references ('then', 'the new six-month plan', 'without being bought').

questions.subtopic: Unfinished tasks linger in the mind, which can help or burden, and planning can relieve the burden.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: It can also be a burden, as anyone who has lain awake rehearsing tomorrow's unfinished chores will know.
Psychologists have long observed that an interrupted task tends to linger in the mind longer than one brought to completion.
This persistence can be useful, since a problem left open overnight is sometimes solved in the morning without further effort.
The interrupted task, whether a half-written letter or an unsolved puzzle, keeps returning to awareness, as though the mind were reluctant to let go of an unreached goal.
The burden, interestingly, often lifts once a person writes down a concrete plan for completing the task, even before any of the work is done.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. It can also be a burden, as anyone who has lain awake rehearsing tomorrow's unfinished chores will know.
2. Psychologists have long observed that an interrupted task tends to linger in the mind longer than one brought to completion.
3. This persistence can be useful, since a problem left open overnight is sometimes solved in the morning without further effort.
4. The interrupted task, whether a half-written letter or an unsolved puzzle, keeps returning to awareness, as though the mind were reluctant to let go of an unreached goal.
5. The burden, interestingly, often lifts once a person writes down a concrete plan for completing the task, even before any of the work is done.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 says the persistence 'can also be a burden', so it must follow the first effect given in sentence 3.
Sentence 5 explains how 'The burden' lifts, but no burden has been mentioned until sentence 1.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the general observation. Sentence 4 picks up 'The interrupted task' and illustrates it. Sentence 3 calls this 'This persistence' and gives its benefit. Sentence 1 adds 'also' a cost, which needs the benefit before it. Sentence 5 says how 'The burden' of sentence 1 lifts, so it comes last.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 5 after sentence 4 because both describe how the mind holds on to a task, which leaves 'The burden' without a referent.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five sentences with a benefit and cost pair and a final remedy; students must track 'This persistence', 'also' and 'The burden' across the chain.

questions.subtopic: Crediting successes to oneself and failures to circumstance may be a protective buffer rather than vanity.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: People tend to credit their successes to their own ability and effort while blaming their failures on bad luck, unfair tests or difficult circumstances.
Yet the habit may serve a purpose, because someone who reads every failure as proof of personal inadequacy may stop trying altogether.
The bias, on this view, is less a defect of reasoning than a buffer that keeps people persisting long enough to improve.
At first sight this looks like simple vanity, a refusal to face unwelcome truths about oneself.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

3. The bias, on this view, is less a defect of reasoning than a buffer that keeps people persisting long enough to improve.
4. At first sight this looks like simple vanity, a refusal to face unwelcome truths about oneself.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Placed last, sentence 4 offers a first impression ('At first sight') after the considered view has already been reached, and the 'Yet' of sentence 2 then has no earlier judgement to push against.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 describes the tendency. Sentence 4 gives the first, unflattering reading of 'this'. Sentence 2 answers it with 'Yet', proposing a purpose. Sentence 3 states 'this view', the buffer interpretation that sentence 2 introduced, and so comes last.
questions.common_misconception: Following sentence 1 with sentence 2, since 'Yet the habit' seems to contrast with the description, and then ending with the vanity reading.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order rests on the logic of a first reading followed by a reinterpretation; 'Yet' could attach to the opening description on a quick reading.

questions.subtopic: Tip-of-the-tongue states show that word meaning and word sound are retrieved in separate stages.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Most people know the frustration of a word that seems about to surface but refuses to appear, a state psychologists call being on the tip of the tongue.
When the state occurs, then, the meaning has been found but the route to the sound has briefly failed.
Such partial knowledge suggests that retrieving a word happens in stages, with its meaning and its sound stored somewhat separately.
In this state, people can often report the first letter of the missing word, or how many syllables it has, though the word itself stays out of reach.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

2. When the state occurs, then, the meaning has been found but the route to the sound has briefly failed.

questions.subtopic: Expertise works around the limit of working memory by packing information into larger meaningful units.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: The chess master's patterns 'count as a single item' only because of the distinction drawn in sentence 1; placed earlier, the example contradicts the limit just stated.

questions.difficulty_reason: The order depends on the logic of the idea: the chess example only makes sense once the distinction between items and information has been drawn.

questions.subtopic: The local rules of street cricket record the geography and people of the lane.

questions.subtopic: Libraries should protect silence in some rooms rather than restore it everywhere.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 begins 'Their complaint', which has no referent until the users in sentence 4 complain.

questions.subtopic: The tea stall is a meeting place because using it creates no obligation of hospitality.

questions.subtopic: Athenian ostracism removed dangerously influential men without punishing them, but it could be abused by factions.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: 'The procedure was thus not a punishment' follows from the exile keeping his property and citizenship, not from the abuse described in sentence 2.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 introduces the vote to exile a prominent man. Sentence 3 explains how 'Each voter' took part and who had to leave. Sentence 1 says what 'the exile' kept. Sentence 4 draws the conclusion 'thus' from the fact that nothing was confiscated: the procedure was not a punishment. questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 before sentence 4 because both evaluate the procedure, which leaves 'thus' in sentence 4 drawing its conclusion from a weakness rather than from the kept property.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five sentences of description and evaluation; the conclusion 'not a punishment' must be drawn from the kept property before the weakness can be weighed.

questions.subtopic: Private insurance fire brigades gave way to public fire services because fire spreads beyond insured property.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 describes the earliest, improvised firefighting. Sentence 1 moves forward in time to insurers' own teams. Sentence 2 refers to 'These private brigades' and names their limitation. Sentence 4 concludes 'Over time' with the public service that answered it.

questions.subtopic: Medieval fairs secured trust among strangers through recorded reputations, which worked only because the fairs mattered.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Merchants who met at the great medieval fairs faced a problem that had little to do with goods: how to trust partners they might never see again.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

Sentence 2 gives 'The fairs' answer', which must follow the full statement of the problem. Sentence 4 states the condition under which 'Exclusion', the barring described in sentence 2, could work.

questions.difficulty_reason: Problem, failed remedy, solution and the condition of the solution; the order follows the logic of the argument, and the condition sentence can look like a free-standing opener.

questions.subtopic: Imperial examinations favoured the wealthy in practice, yet kept the ideal of merit believable, binding ambitious men to the state.

sentences.text: That belief may have been its most important product, binding ambitious men across a vast empire to the state that examined them.

questions.subtopic: For some luxury goods a high price is part of what is bought, so demand can fall when the price is cut.

questions.subtopic: Lean inventory saved money but removed the buffer that protects production when a supplier fails.

questions.subtopic: Publishing salaries narrows unjustified gaps but also discourages justified ones, making pay uniform rather than fair.

The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

questions.subtopic: Stretching a brand saves money but can empty the name of meaning and destroy the trust it rests on.

questions.subtopic: Straightening rivers sped water downstream and worsened floods there, so some regions are restoring bends and wetlands.

sentences.text: In the past, engineers straightened many winding rivers, cutting through their bends so that floodwater would be carried away faster.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. In the past, engineers straightened many winding rivers, cutting through their bends so that floodwater would be carried away faster.
2. Some regions are therefore restoring the bends and wetlands that earlier generations of engineers removed, accepting slower drainage in return for safer towns.
3. The straightened channels did move water quickly past the farms beside them, but they delivered it all the sooner to the towns downstream.
4. Floods that the old meanders and marshes had once spread out and slowed now arrived downstream higher and faster, sometimes overwhelming defences built for gentler peaks.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 says regions are 'therefore' restoring bends; the reason is the higher, faster floods of sentence 4, which must come first.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 describes the straightening. Sentence 3 refers to 'The straightened channels' and states the drawback. Sentence 4 spells out the effect on floods downstream. Sentence 2 gives the response 'therefore'.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 before sentence 4, though the restoration is a response to the worsened floods described in sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Cause, effect and response in time order with 'The straightened channels' and 'therefore' as markers.

questions.subtopic: Mixed planting trades some yield in good years for protection against a disease that could wipe out a uniform field.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: A field planted with a single high-yielding variety is easy to sow, tend and harvest, and in a good year it outproduces any mixed planting.
Its uniformity is also its weakness, because a disease that can infect one plant in such a field can infect every plant in it.
The farmer who grows a mixture thus accepts a smaller harvest in good years in exchange for protection against the bad year that could destroy everything.
In a mixed field, by contrast, susceptible plants are separated by resistant ones, which slow the spread of the disease from neighbour to neighbour.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. A field planted with a single high-yielding variety is easy to sow, tend and harvest, and in a good year it outproduces any mixed planting.
2. Its uniformity is also its weakness, because a disease that can infect one plant in such a field can infect every plant in it.
3. The farmer who grows a mixture thus accepts a smaller harvest in good years in exchange for protection against the bad year that could destroy everything.
4. In a mixed field, by contrast, susceptible plants are separated by resistant ones, which slow the spread of the disease from neighbour to neighbour.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: The farmer's trade-off in sentence 3 weighs yield against 'protection', which means nothing before the disease risk of sentence 2 and the mixed field's defence in sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 gives the advantage of a single-variety field. Sentence 2 names the weakness of 'Its uniformity'. Sentence 4 contrasts the mixed field and refers to 'the disease' of sentence 2. Sentence 3 draws the trade-off 'thus', which needs both the yield advantage and the protection already stated.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 3 after sentence 1 because both compare yields, although 'protection against the bad year' depends on the disease argument of sentences 2 and 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order follows the logic of a trade-off: advantage, weakness, the alternative's defence, then the farmer's choice.

questions.subtopic: Eruptions cool the planet through long-lived stratospheric sulphur haze rather than through short-lived ash.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: That is why an eruption in the tropics can be followed by failed harvests on the other side of the world in the following summer.
Above the weather, with no rain to wash it out, this haze can linger for a year or more and spread around the globe.
The lasting effect comes from sulphur gases carried high into the stratosphere, where they form a fine haze of droplets that reflects sunlight back into space.
Ash is heavy and falls out of the air within days or weeks, long before it could affect the climate of distant continents.
A great volcanic eruption can cool the whole planet, but not, as one might expect, because of the ash that darkens the sky around it.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. That is why an eruption in the tropics can be followed by failed harvests on the other side of the world in the following summer.
2. Above the weather, with no rain to wash it out, this haze can linger for a year or more and spread around the globe.
3. The lasting effect comes from sulphur gases carried high into the stratosphere, where they form a fine haze of droplets that reflects sunlight back into space.
4. Ash is heavy and falls out of the air within days or weeks, long before it could affect the climate of distant continents.
5. A great volcanic eruption can cool the whole planet, but not, as one might expect, because of the ash that darkens the sky around it.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: With sentence 4 after sentence 3, 'this haze' in sentence 2 is separated from its referent, and the reason for denying the role of ash comes after the real cause has already displaced it.
Sentence 1 explains effects 'on the other side of the world' a season later, which requires the haze to linger and spread as sentence 2 says.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 says eruptions cool the planet but 'not' through ash. Sentence 4 justifies that denial: ash falls out within weeks. Sentence 3 gives 'The lasting effect', contrasting with the short-lived ash. Sentence 2 explains why 'this haze' persists and spreads. Sentence 1, 'That is why', draws the distant consequence that needs both persistence and global spread.
questions.common_misconception: Following sentence 5 with the sulphur explanation of sentence 3 because it gives the real cause, which leaves the ash sentence stranded between the haze and 'this haze'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The order depends on the logic of the explanation: the denial in the opener must be justified before the real cause is given, and the consequence needs both the persistence and the spread of the haze.

questions.subtopic: Failed replications can arise from publication bias without misconduct, so the remedy lies in what journals publish.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Repairing such a field, then, requires changing what gets published, not merely policing the people who publish it.
If many teams test unlikely ideas and only the lucky successes are printed, the literature will fill with flukes even if every study was conducted honestly.
A more troubling explanation needs no wrongdoing at all, only journals that prefer striking positive results to dull null ones.
When many published findings in a field fail to reappear on repetition, the natural suspicion is that some researchers have been careless or dishonest.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Repairing such a field, then, requires changing what gets published, not merely policing the people who publish it.
2. If many teams test unlikely ideas and only the lucky successes are printed, the literature will fill with flukes even if every study was conducted honestly.
3. A more troubling explanation needs no wrongdoing at all, only journals that prefer striking positive results to dull null ones.
4. When many published findings in a field fail to reappear on repetition, the natural suspicion is that some researchers have been careless or dishonest.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 describes selective printing, the mechanism of the journal explanation, before sentence 3 has introduced that explanation; 'A more troubling explanation' would then arrive after it had already been set out.
Sentence 3 is 'more troubling' than something, so it cannot open; it is compared with the suspicion of carelessness or dishonesty in sentence 4.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 gives the 'natural suspicion' of misconduct. Sentence 3 offers 'A more troubling explanation', a comparison with the suspicion already stated. Sentence 2 works through the mechanism of that explanation, showing how flukes accumulate 'even if every study was conducted honestly'. Sentence 1 concludes 'then' that the remedy lies in publishing practice.
questions.common_misconception: Placing the mechanism of sentence 2 right after sentence 4, so that the selective printing appears before the explanation it belongs to is introduced.
questions.difficulty_reason: Abstract argument comparing two explanations; the order rests on 'more troubling' needing the first explanation and on the mechanism elaborating the second.

questions.subtopic: Seed vaults preserve old crop varieties but freeze their evolution, so they should complement farmers who keep varieties growing.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Crop seed vaults store frozen samples of thousands of plant varieties, many of which are no longer grown by any farmer.
The reasoning behind them is simple: a variety that has vanished from the fields may one day carry a trait, such as drought tolerance, that breeders urgently need.
For this reason, many agronomists argue that vaults should support, not replace, the farmers who keep old varieties alive in their fields.
Yet a seed kept in a freezer is cut off from the pests, climates and growers that shaped it, and so it stops adapting.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Crop seed vaults store frozen samples of thousands of plant varieties, many of which are no longer grown by any farmer.
2. The reasoning behind them is simple: a variety that has vanished from the fields may one day carry a trait, such as drought tolerance, that breeders urgently need.
3. For this reason, many agronomists argue that vaults should support, not replace, the farmers who keep old varieties alive in their fields.
4. Yet a seed kept in a freezer is cut off from the pests, climates and growers that shaped it, and so it stops adapting.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 says vaults should not replace living fields; that conclusion follows from the frozen seed ceasing to adapt in sentence 4, so it cannot precede it.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 introduces crop seed vaults and what they hold. Sentence 2 gives 'the reasoning behind them', where 'them' needs the vaults of sentence 1. Sentence 4 opens with 'Yet' and states the limitation: a frozen seed stops adapting. Sentence 3 begins 'For this reason' and draws the conclusion that only follows from that limitation, namely that living fields must continue alongside the vaults.
questions.common_misconception: Putting sentence 3 straight after sentence 2, although the case for keeping varieties alive in fields rests on the problem raised in sentence 4, not on the rationale for vaults.
questions.difficulty_reason: The opener is clear and 'them', 'Yet' and 'For this reason' fix every link.

questions.subtopic: Flight data recorders let investigators reconstruct crashes, and the lessons drawn feed back into safety rules.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: The lessons drawn from such reconstructions are then turned into new rules and training, which is one reason air travel has grown steadily safer.
These records allow investigators to reconstruct the final minutes in detail, even when no one on board survives to describe what happened.
Throughout every flight the device logs hundreds of measurements, from engine temperature to the position of each control surface.
After an airliner crashes, investigators search the wreckage first for its flight data recorder, a box built to survive fire, impact and deep water.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. The lessons drawn from such reconstructions are then turned into new rules and training, which is one reason air travel has grown steadily safer.
2. These records allow investigators to reconstruct the final minutes in detail, even when no one on board survives to describe what happened.
3. Throughout every flight the device logs hundreds of measurements, from engine temperature to the position of each control surface.
4. After an airliner crashes, investigators search the wreckage first for its flight data recorder, a box built to survive fire, impact and deep water.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 speaks of 'These records' before any record has been described; the measurements it refers to appear only in sentence 3.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 introduces the flight data recorder. Sentence 3 describes what 'the device' logs. Sentence 2 refers to 'These records', the logged measurements of sentence 3, and says what they make possible. Sentence 1 refers to 'such reconstructions' from sentence 2 and says how their lessons are used.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 2 before sentence 3 because both concern investigators, which leaves 'These records' with nothing to refer to.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each sentence names something introduced by the one before it ('the device', 'These records', 'such reconstructions').

questions.subtopic: A concert hall's sound depends on the timing and amount of reflected sound, which architects balance.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Sound reaches that listener twice: directly from the stage, and a fraction of a second later as reflections from the walls and ceiling.
Architects therefore shape surfaces and choose materials with great care, aiming at a balance between clarity and warmth.
A concert hall is judged not only by how it looks but, above all, by how it sounds to a listener in an ordinary seat.
If the reflections arrive too late, the music turns muddy; if there are too few of them, it sounds thin and dry.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Sound reaches that listener twice: directly from the stage, and a fraction of a second later as reflections from the walls and ceiling.
2. Architects therefore shape surfaces and choose materials with great care, aiming at a balance between clarity and warmth.
3. A concert hall is judged not only by how it looks but, above all, by how it sounds to a listener in an ordinary seat.
4. If the reflections arrive too late, the music turns muddy; if there are too few of them, it sounds thin and dry.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 cannot open because 'that listener' points back to the listener in an ordinary seat named in sentence 3.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 introduces the subject, how a hall sounds to a listener. Sentence 1 refers to 'that listener' and introduces reflections. Sentence 4 describes what goes wrong when 'the reflections' are badly timed or too few. Sentence 2 draws the practical consequence with 'therefore': architects must balance them.
questions.common_misconception: Opening with sentence 1 because it explains the physics, although 'that listener' needs the listener introduced in sentence 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: Back-references ('that listener', 'the reflections') and 'therefore' make the chain direct.

questions.subtopic: Subtitling and dubbing each trade one kind of loss for another, and habit decides which an audience accepts.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Dubbing, by contrast, frees the eye but substitutes a new voice, which may match neither the face nor the feeling of the original.
Countries differ sharply in how they present foreign films and television: some prefer subtitles, while others replace the original voices through dubbing.
Neither method is simply better, then; each trades one kind of loss for another, and habit largely decides which loss an audience will accept.
Subtitles keep the actors' own performances, but they ask viewers to read quickly, often at the cost of missing details in the picture.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Dubbing, by contrast, frees the eye but substitutes a new voice, which may match neither the face nor the feeling of the original.
2. Countries differ sharply in how they present foreign films and television: some prefer subtitles, while others replace the original voices through dubbing.
3. Neither method is simply better, then; each trades one kind of loss for another, and habit largely decides which loss an audience will accept.
4. Subtitles keep the actors' own performances, but they ask viewers to read quickly, often at the cost of missing details in the picture.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 says 'Dubbing, by contrast'; placed before sentence 4 it has nothing to contrast with, since sentence 2 only names both practices.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 introduces the two practices. Sentence 4 takes subtitles first. Sentence 1 turns to dubbing 'by contrast', which presupposes that subtitles have already been discussed. Sentence 3 concludes with 'then' that neither method is better, a verdict that needs both descriptions before it.
questions.common_misconception: Treating sentences 4 and 1 as interchangeable, although 'by contrast' ties the dubbing sentence to a preceding account of subtitles.
questions.difficulty_reason: The general opener and the contrast marker settle the order quickly.

questions.subtopic: Arguing an assigned side in school debating is better seen as training in intellectual sympathy than in insincerity.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Many schools run debating societies in which students argue for positions assigned to them, whatever they personally believe.
Supporters reply that defending an unfamiliar view forces students to understand it from the inside, which is the first step towards judging it fairly.
On this account, debating is less a training in insincerity than an exercise in intellectual sympathy.
Critics say that this practice teaches young people to value clever argument over honest conviction.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Many schools run debating societies in which students argue for positions assigned to them, whatever they personally believe.
2. Supporters reply that defending an unfamiliar view forces students to understand it from the inside, which is the first step towards judging it fairly.
3. On this account, debating is less a training in insincerity than an exercise in intellectual sympathy.
4. Critics say that this practice teaches young people to value clever argument over honest conviction.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 is a reply; before sentence 4 it answers nothing, and 'insincerity' in sentence 3 then echoes a charge made only after the defence.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 describes the practice of arguing assigned positions. Sentence 4 gives the critics' objection to 'this practice'. Sentence 2 gives the supporters' 'reply', which must follow the objection it answers. Sentence 3 begins 'On this account', the supporters' account, and restates their view as a conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Placing the supporters' reply in sentence 2 before the critics' objection in sentence 4, although one cannot reply to a charge that has not yet been made.
questions.difficulty_reason: Objection, reply and 'On this account' give a standard and well-signalled sequence.

questions.subtopic: A fixed daily step target hides the fact that the first extra steps matter most, so increases should be rewarded.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: For a sedentary person, however, that belief is badly wrong: the first few thousand extra steps are likely to matter far more than the last few hundred before the goal.
Fitness apps commonly set a single daily step target and congratulate their users only when they reach it.
Such a target is easy to remember, but it invites the belief that walking which falls short of it brings no benefit at all.
A better message, then, might reward any increase over a person's usual level rather than a fixed and arbitrary line.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. For a sedentary person, however, that belief is badly wrong: the first few thousand extra steps are likely to matter far more than the last few hundred before the goal.
2. Fitness apps commonly set a single daily step target and congratulate their users only when they reach it.
3. Such a target is easy to remember, but it invites the belief that walking which falls short of it brings no benefit at all.
4. A better message, then, might reward any increase over a person's usual level rather than a fixed and arbitrary line.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 offers a remedy with 'then', but the reason for rewarding any increase is given only in sentence 1, so the remedy cannot come first.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 introduces the single step target. Sentence 3 refers to 'Such a target' and names the false belief it invites. Sentence 1 says 'that belief', the belief named in sentence 3, is wrong. Sentence 4 proposes, with 'then', a better message that follows from the counter-argument.
questions.common_misconception: Ending with sentence 1 after sentence 4, although the proposal in sentence 4 is drawn from the point about the first extra steps and so must come after it.
questions.difficulty_reason: 'Such a target', 'however' and 'then' fix the order once the opener is identified.

questions.subtopic: Legumes enrich the soil with nitrogen captured from the air, which explains the old practice of rotating cereals with pulses.
questions.instructions: The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: A wheat or rice crop sown in the same field the following season can draw on this store, and so needs less fertiliser than it otherwise would.
When these plants die back or are ploughed in, part of that captured nitrogen is left behind in the soil.
Nitrogen makes up most of the air around every plant, yet most crops cannot use it in that form and must draw it from the soil instead.
Plants of the pea and bean family are an exception, because bacteria living in small swellings on their roots convert the nitrogen of the air into a form the plant can use.
This is why farmers in many regions have alternated cereals with pulses for centuries, long before anyone could explain what the roots were doing.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of five numbers as your answer.

1. A wheat or rice crop sown in the same field the following season can draw on this store, and so needs less fertiliser than it otherwise would.
2. When these plants die back or are ploughed in, part of that captured nitrogen is left behind in the soil.
3. Nitrogen makes up most of the air around every plant, yet most crops cannot use it in that form and must draw it from the soil instead.
4. Plants of the pea and bean family are an exception, because bacteria living in small swellings on their roots convert the nitrogen of the air into a form the plant can use.
5. This is why farmers in many regions have alternated cereals with pulses for centuries, long before anyone could explain what the roots were doing.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 draws on 'this store', which is the nitrogen left in the soil in sentence 2; placed after sentence 5, it is cut off from that referent, and 'This is why' would then come before the benefit to cereals that it explains.
Sentence 4 calls legumes 'an exception', which needs the general rule of sentence 3 that crops cannot use the nitrogen of the air.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the general problem: crops cannot use the nitrogen of the air. Sentence 4 names 'an exception', which needs the general rule of sentence 3 before it. Sentence 2 refers to 'these plants' and 'that captured nitrogen' from sentence 4. Sentence 1 says the next crop draws on 'this store', the nitrogen left in the soil in sentence 2. Sentence 5 explains the farming practice with 'This is why', which needs the benefit to the following cereal crop described in sentence 1.
questions.common_misconception: Placing sentence 5 straight after sentence 2 because both seem to sum up the value of legumes, although the practice of alternating cereals with pulses is explained only by the benefit to the next cereal crop in sentence 1.
questions.difficulty_reason: Five sentences, but each is tied to the previous one by 'an exception', 'these plants', 'this store' or 'This is why'.

questions.subtopic: A sunken whale carcass feeds a succession of deep-sea communities, from scavengers to bone bacteria.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: With the flesh gone, smaller animals move in to colonise the exposed bones and the sediment enriched by the scavengers' leftovers.
Large scavengers such as hagfish and sleeper sharks arrive first, stripping away most of the soft tissue within months.
When a whale dies in the open ocean, its body usually sinks to the deep seafloor, where food is otherwise extremely scarce.
Long after that, bacteria begin to break down the fats stored inside the bones themselves, sustaining a distinctive community for decades.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. With the flesh gone, smaller animals move in to colonise the exposed bones and the sediment enriched by the scavengers' leftovers.
2. Large scavengers such as hagfish and sleeper sharks arrive first, stripping away most of the soft tissue within months.
3. When a whale dies in the open ocean, its body usually sinks to the deep seafloor, where food is otherwise extremely scarce.
4. Long after that, bacteria begin to break down the fats stored inside the bones themselves, sustaining a distinctive community for decades.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 needs 'the flesh gone' and 'the scavengers' leftovers' to have just been described; after sentence 4 the narrative would jump back decades.
Sentence 1 says the flesh is already gone and mentions the scavengers' leftovers, so it cannot come before the scavengers of sentence 2 arrive.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 sets the scene: a carcass reaching a food-poor seafloor. The rest is a succession that follows from what each stage consumes. Sentence 2 has large scavengers arrive 'first' and remove the soft tissue. Sentence 1 can only come next, since its animals colonise bones that are exposed only once 'the flesh' is gone and feed on 'the scavengers' leftovers'. Sentence 4 describes the last stage, bacteria feeding on fats inside the bones themselves, 'Long after that'.
questions.common_misconception: Placing the bacteria of sentence 4 before the bone colonisers of sentence 1 because both concern the bones, although the fats inside the bones are the last resource to be used.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of ecological succession: soft tissue, then exposed bones and sediment, then the fats within the bones.

questions.subtopic: Frequent update prompts train users to postpone them, which attackers exploit, so updates may be best installed silently.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: Software companies release security updates frequently, and each one asks users to stop what they are doing and restart their devices.
Since delay is so costly, some designers argue that the safest update is the one the user never notices, installed quietly while the device is idle.
Faced with constant interruptions, many people learn to postpone updates by reflex, without reading what they fix.
The habit is dangerous precisely because attackers study published fixes to learn which weaknesses remain open on machines that have not been patched.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Software companies release security updates frequently, and each one asks users to stop what they are doing and restart their devices.
2. Since delay is so costly, some designers argue that the safest update is the one the user never notices, installed quietly while the device is idle.
3. Faced with constant interruptions, many people learn to postpone updates by reflex, without reading what they fix.
4. The habit is dangerous precisely because attackers study published fixes to learn which weaknesses remain open on machines that have not been patched.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 rests on 'delay is so costly', but the cost of delay is established only by sentence 4; and sentence 4's 'The habit' would then refer back past the proposal.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 introduces frequent updates that interrupt work. Sentence 3 describes the user response those 'constant interruptions' produce. Sentence 4 explains why 'The habit' of postponing is dangerous. Sentence 2 proposes silent installation 'Since delay is so costly', a premise established only by sentence 4.
questions.common_misconception: Putting sentence 2 right after sentence 3 on the thought that postponement alone motivates silent updates, although the cost of delay that sentence 2 relies on is shown only in sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: Order depends mainly on the logic of the idea: a behaviour, why it is harmful, and a design response that presupposes the harm.

questions.subtopic: Publishing a dead novelist's unfinished manuscript is best done with a frank account of its state.
questions.instructions: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.text: When a novelist dies leaving a manuscript unfinished, heirs and publishers must decide whether readers should ever see it.
Against this, the writer may have regarded the draft as a failure, and an author's silence on the matter is not the same as consent.
Publishing the fragment honours the labour that went into it and may satisfy a genuine public interest in the writer's last work.
The most defensible course may be to publish with a clear account of the manuscript's condition, so that readers judge a draft as a draft.

questions.question:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in the sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. When a novelist dies leaving a manuscript unfinished, heirs and publishers must decide whether readers should ever see it.
2. Against this, the writer may have regarded the draft as a failure, and an author's silence on the matter is not the same as consent.
3. Publishing the fragment honours the labour that went into it and may satisfy a genuine public interest in the writer's last work.
4. The most defensible course may be to publish with a clear account of the manuscript's condition, so that readers judge a draft as a draft.

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 4 already answers the worry that a draft may be mistaken for finished work; placed before sentence 2 it solves a problem not yet raised, and 'Against this' would then oppose the compromise rather than the case for publishing.
Sentence 2 begins 'Against this' but sentence 1 states only a question, not a position that can be argued against.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 poses the decision. Sentence 3 gives the case for publishing 'the fragment'. Sentence 2 opens 'Against this' and gives the case against, which must answer a case already made. questions.subtopic: Hidden photo data is a useful but fallible clue for verifiers, to be weighed with evidence in the picture itself.

questions.subtopic: Folk tale variants cannot be traced to one original because tellers combine versions; the better question is why variants took root.

Sentence 3 judges 'That explanation' incomplete and introduces the reverse mechanism, anxiety using up working memory. Sentence 2 illustrates that mechanism with a worrying student.
