options.A: Open plans often cut face-to-face talk, though not for every team, since closeness yields interaction only where work demands it and people feel unobserved.
options.B: Bringing colleagues physically closer together reliably multiplies the chance conversations from which ideas emerge, which is why open plans suit most companies better than walled offices.
options.C: Newsrooms and trading floors gain from open-plan layouts because their teams need to coordinate constantly and quickly, unlike most office workers, who would prefer walls.
options.D: Open-plan offices always reduce collaboration among colleagues, because employees who fear being overheard retreat behind headphones and communicate only through written messages.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Open plans often cut face-to-face talk, though not for every team, since closeness yields interaction only where work demands it and people feel unobserved.

option_rationales.B: This is the original promise, which the paragraph says has often turned out 'the reverse'.
option_rationales.C: This is the exception the paragraph mentions, not its point, and the claim about what most workers prefer is not in the paragraph.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'It would be wrong, however, to conclude that open plans always reduce collaboration', and it names teams that 'may genuinely benefit'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports that open plans have often reduced face-to-face talk, qualifies this (some teams 'may genuinely benefit'), and draws the lesson that closeness produces interaction only depending on the work and on whether people feel 'free to talk without being observed'. The correct answer keeps the finding, the qualification and the lesson.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'always reduce' option, which keeps the finding but drops the qualification.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph reports a finding, qualifies it and generalises; the wrong options each keep one stage.

questions.subtopic: Reputation enforces informal credit cheaply but only in dense communities, excluding newcomers.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: In many markets, small traders lend goods to one another on credit without any written contract, and the arrangement works far better than an outsider might expect. The reason is that these traders deal with each other repeatedly and talk constantly. A trader who fails to repay does not merely lose one partner; word spreads, and soon no one in the market will extend credit to them. The threat of losing that reputation enforces the debt more cheaply than a court could. The system has limits. It works only within a community dense enough for news to travel, and it tends to exclude newcomers, who have no reputation to lose and therefore little to offer as security.

options.B: A trader who fails to repay a debt in a close-knit market soon finds that no other trader there is willing to sell goods to them on credit.
options.C: Informal credit among traders works because repeated dealing and gossip make a lost reputation a strong penalty, but it holds only in close-knit groups and tends to shut out newcomers.
options.D: Informal credit based on reputation is cheaper and more reliable than legal contracts, and so it should replace the courts as the main way of enforcing debts everywhere.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Informal credit among traders works because repeated dealing and gossip make a lost reputation a strong penalty, but it holds only in close-knit groups and tends to shut out newcomers.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the system 'tends to exclude newcomers, who have no reputation to lose', which is the reverse of this option.
option_rationales.B: This is one step in the explanation; it leaves out why the system works overall and the limits the paragraph sets on it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the system 'works only within a community dense enough for news to travel', so recommending it everywhere ignores its stated limits.

questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about a defaulting trader, which is a step in the argument rather than its point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The mechanism and the limits are both stated in plain sentences.

questions.subtopic: Omitting unpaid household work from national income is a flaw, but pricing it brings its own distortion.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: National income accounts leave out the cooking, cleaning and care done unpaid within households, and the omission is often called a simple bias that a better statistic would correct. The criticism is right that something valuable goes unmeasured, and that this can distort judgements: when a family starts paying for childcare it once provided itself, measured output rises though little more care may be given. But the remedy is less simple than it sounds. To add household work to the accounts one must price it, and every method of pricing an hour of unpaid care, whether at what a hired carer would earn or at what the carer could have earned elsewhere, imposes a market valuation on activity whose meaning to those who do it is often precisely that it is not done for money. The omission is a real flaw, but the obvious fix may trade one distortion for another.

The omission is a real flaw, but the obvious fix may trade one distortion for another.

options.A: Leaving unpaid household work out of national income is a genuine and misleading flaw, yet including it would require market prices that misrepresent such work, so the fix may bring a distortion of its own.
options.B: Unpaid household work cannot be valued in money at all, so national income accounts are right to leave it out, and the critics of the omission are simply mistaken.
options.C: When families begin to pay for childcare they previously provided themselves, measured national output rises even though little additional care may actually be given to the children.
options.D: Leaving out unpaid household work is a simple bias in national income figures, which statisticians could correct by pricing each hour at what a hired carer would earn.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Leaving unpaid household work out of national income is a genuine and misleading flaw, yet including it would require market prices that misrepresent such work, so the fix may bring a distortion of its own.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says 'The criticism is right that something valuable goes unmeasured' and calls the omission 'a real flaw', so it does not defend leaving the work out.
option_rationales.C: This is the paragraph's illustration of the distortion; it omits the main point that the obvious remedy has a problem of its own.
option_rationales.D: This is the view the paragraph reports and then qualifies with 'the remedy is less simple than it sounds'; it treats the hired-carer rate as one of the methods that impose a market valuation.

questions.explanation: The paragraph agrees with critics that omitting household work is a flaw that 'can distort judgements', then argues that the remedy is not simple: any price for unpaid care 'imposes a market valuation' on work valued because 'it is not done for money'. It concludes that the fix 'may trade one distortion for another'. The correct answer states both the flaw and the problem with the fix.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that treats the omission as a simple bias with an easy fix, which is the view the paragraph qualifies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author agrees with a criticism but rejects its remedy; the wrong options take either side too far or keep only the example.

questions.subtopic: Introduced species should be judged by their effects, not their origin.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Any species that arrives in a new region with human help is now often labelled invasive and treated as a threat to be removed. Some newcomers deserve that reputation: a predator introduced to an island can wipe out birds that evolved without defences against it. But many introduced plants and animals settle in without causing measurable harm, and some come to fill roles left empty by the loss of native species, providing food for pollinators or shelter for birds. Judging a species by its origin rather than its effects can waste money on removing harmless arrivals while drawing attention from the damaging ones. The useful question is not where a species came from but what it actually does.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Any species that arrives in a new region with human help is now often labelled invasive and treated as a threat to be removed. Some newcomers deserve that reputation: a predator introduced to an island can wipe out birds that evolved without defences against it. But many introduced plants and animals settle in without causing measurable harm, and some come to fill roles left empty by the loss of native species, providing food for pollinators or shelter for birds. Judging a species by its origin rather than its effects can waste money on removing harmless arrivals while drawing attention from the damaging ones. The useful question is not where a species came from but what it actually does.

options.A: Because they arrive with human help rather than naturally, introduced species should be removed as soon as they are found in a new region.
options.B: Introduced species should be judged by their effects rather than their origin, since while some are destructive, many are harmless or even useful, and blanket removal wastes effort.
options.C: Introduced species are generally good for the regions they reach, so efforts to remove them do more harm than good and should be given up altogether.
options.D: Predators that people introduce to remote islands can wipe out native birds that evolved without any means of defending themselves against such attackers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Introduced species should be judged by their effects rather than their origin, since while some are destructive, many are harmless or even useful, and blanket removal wastes effort.

option_rationales.A: This is the attitude the paragraph criticises; it says 'The useful question is not where a species came from but what it actually does'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'Some newcomers deserve that reputation', such as island predators, so it does not oppose all removal.
option_rationales.D: This is the paragraph's example of a harmful newcomer; it leaves out the main point about judging species by their effects.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises treating every introduced species as a threat. It concedes that some are harmful, notes that many are harmless or useful, and concludes that species should be judged by 'what it actually does'. The correct answer captures the conclusion and its basis.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that all introduced species are good, which ignores the concession about harmful predators.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated in the last sentence and the wrong options fail on explicit lines.

questions.subtopic: Filtering results by excitement distorts the scientific record without any individual dishonesty.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Journals are more likely to publish studies that find an effect than studies that find none, and researchers, knowing this, are less likely to write up their null results at all. Each choice seems reasonable, since a finding that nothing happened looks less interesting than a discovery. Together, however, they distort the record. If twenty teams test a useless remedy and one obtains a positive result by chance, that one study may be the only one anyone reads, and the remedy will appear to work. The problem lies not in any single dishonest scientist but in a system that filters results by whether they are exciting rather than by whether they are sound.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Each choice seems reasonable, since a finding that nothing happened looks less interesting than a discovery. Together, however, they distort the record. If twenty teams test a useless remedy and one obtains a positive result by chance, that one study may be the only one anyone reads, and the remedy will appear to work. The problem lies not in any single dishonest scientist but in a system that filters results by whether they are exciting rather than by whether they are sound.

options.A: When many research teams test a useless remedy, one of them is likely to obtain a positive result purely by chance, and that study may be the one that is widely read.
options.B: Scientists frequently falsify their data in order to obtain positive results, since journals refuse to publish any study that fails to find an effect for its treatment.
options.C: Because journals and researchers both favour positive findings over null ones, the published record can make useless treatments look effective, a fault of the system rather than of dishonest individuals.
options.D: Journals should be required by law to publish every study submitted to them, whatever its results, so that null findings are no longer lost to other researchers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Because journals and researchers both favour positive findings over null ones, the published record can make useless treatments look effective, a fault of the system rather than of dishonest individuals.

option_rationales.A: This is the illustration; it omits the cause the paragraph identifies, the shared preference for positive findings.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the problem lies 'not in any single dishonest scientist', and it says journals are 'more likely' to publish positive results, not that they refuse all others.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph diagnoses a problem and makes no proposal, least of all a legal one, so this adds a prescription.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains how two individually reasonable choices, journals preferring positive results and researchers not writing up null ones, together 'distort the record', and it places the fault in 'a system that filters results by whether they are exciting'. The correct answer gives the cause, the effect and the point about the system.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the falsification option, which the last sentence explicitly rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated in the last sentence; wrong options are a distortion, the example and a prescription.

questions.subtopic: Seed banks should back up, not replace, conservation of wild plant populations.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Two strategies compete for the limited money available to protect plant diversity. Seed banks store frozen samples of thousands of species in secure vaults, offering insurance against extinction at modest cost. Conservation in the wild protects plants where they grow, along with the insects, fungi and soils they depend on. The seed bank's great advantage is security, but its samples are frozen in time: a population kept in a vault stops adapting to changing climate and pests, and some species have seeds that cannot survive drying and freezing at all. Wild populations go on evolving, but they are exposed to every threat the vault avoids. Neither strategy can substitute for the other. The vault is best understood as a backup for living populations, not a replacement for them.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The vault is best understood as a backup for living populations, not a replacement for them.

options.A: Because frozen seeds stop adapting and some cannot be stored at all, money spent on seed banks would be better spent entirely on protecting wild habitats instead.
options.B: Since seed banks protect their samples from every threat at modest cost, they are a more efficient way to safeguard plant diversity than conservation in the wild.
options.C: Some plant species produce seeds that cannot survive being dried and frozen, so these species cannot be kept in seed banks and must be conserved in the wild.
options.D: Seed banks are secure but halt adaptation and miss some species, while wild populations evolve but stay exposed, so vaults should back up, not replace, wild conservation.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Seed banks are secure but halt adaptation and miss some species, while wild populations evolve but stay exposed, so vaults should back up, not replace, wild conservation.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph calls the vault 'a backup for living populations' and notes that wild populations are 'exposed to every threat the vault avoids', so it does not favour dropping seed banks.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says samples in vaults stop adapting and that some seeds cannot be stored, and it concludes that 'Neither strategy can substitute for the other'.
option_rationales.C: This is one detail among the weaknesses of seed banks; it misses the comparison and the conclusion that the two strategies complement each other.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares two strategies, giving each an advantage and a weakness: vaults are secure but static and incomplete, wild populations evolve but are exposed. It concludes that the vault is 'a backup for living populations, not a replacement for them'. The correct answer holds the comparison and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the one-sided options because the paragraph's criticism of seed banks seems to favour the wild, or its praise of security seems to favour the vault.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph balances two strategies; two wrong options each take one side, and one is a detail.

questions.subtopic: Many disputes over species boundaries are about definitions, though classification is not arbitrary.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Naturalists have long divided into those who tend to lump similar organisms into one broad species and those who split them into many narrow ones. The dispute is often presented as a quarrel of temperaments, as if one side were simply careless and the other fussy. In fact it reflects something real about living things. Populations diverge gradually, and at any moment some pairs are clearly distinct, some clearly the same, and many lie in between, interbreeding a little or differing in a few traits. For these intermediate cases no fact of nature settles whether there are one species or two; the answer depends on which criterion one adopts. This does not make classification arbitrary, since the clear cases are clear. But it means that some disputes about species are disagreements about definitions rather than about the organisms.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Because populations diverge gradually, many borderline species cases depend on the criterion chosen, so some lumper and splitter disputes concern definitions, though clear cases prevent arbitrariness.
options.B: Since populations diverge gradually, the division of living things into species is entirely arbitrary and reflects only the preferences of the naturalists who classify them.
options.C: Naturalists who lump organisms into broad species tend to be careless, while those who split them into many narrow species are excessively fussy about small differences.
options.D: Disagreements between lumpers and splitters could be settled if naturalists studied the disputed organisms more closely and gathered more evidence about how often and how freely they interbreed.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Because populations diverge gradually, many borderline species cases depend on the criterion chosen, so some lumper and splitter disputes concern definitions, though clear cases prevent arbitrariness.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says 'This does not make classification arbitrary, since the clear cases are clear', which this option contradicts.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'quarrel of temperaments' picture that the paragraph reports and then corrects with 'In fact it reflects something real about living things'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says that for intermediate cases 'no fact of nature settles' the question, so more evidence about the organisms would not resolve a dispute about definitions.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the view that the lumper and splitter dispute is about temperament: gradual divergence leaves many intermediate cases where 'the answer depends on which criterion one adopts'. It limits the claim (clear cases keep classification from being arbitrary) and concludes that some disputes are 'about definitions rather than about the organisms'. The correct answer keeps the reason, the conclusion and the limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'more evidence' option, which assumes the dispute is factual when the paragraph says it is partly definitional.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option treats a definitional dispute as factual, which requires grasping the paragraph's central distinction.

questions.subtopic: Volunteer biological records are limited less by individual error than by uneven coverage.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Projects that recruit volunteers to count birds, record flowering dates or photograph insects are often dismissed by professional researchers on the grounds that amateurs make mistakes. The objection is true and largely beside the point. Individual records from volunteers are indeed less reliable than those of trained surveyors, but the errors tend to be random rather than systematic, and random errors shrink in importance as the number of observations grows. A thousand imperfect counts spread across a region can reveal a trend that a handful of expert surveys, confined to a few accessible sites, would miss altogether. The real weakness of such data lies elsewhere: volunteers go where it is pleasant to go, at weekends and in good weather, so the gaps in their coverage are anything but random. The question to ask of citizen science is therefore not how careful each participant is but where and when the participants chose to look.

A thousand imperfect counts spread across a region can reveal a trend that a handful of expert surveys, confined to a few accessible sites, would miss altogether. The real weakness of such data lies elsewhere: volunteers go where it is pleasant to go, at weekends and in good weather, so the gaps in their coverage are anything but random. The question to ask of citizen science is therefore not how careful each participant is but where and when the participants chose to look.

options.A: Because the errors volunteers make are random, large citizen science projects produce records more trustworthy than professional surveys, and they should replace such surveys.
options.B: Since volunteers survey pleasant places at convenient times, citizen science records reveal more about the leisure habits of people than about birds, plants or insects.
options.C: Volunteer records suffer less from individual error, which large numbers offset, than from uneven coverage of the places and times volunteers choose to survey.
options.D: Citizen science records are unreliable because amateurs make frequent identification mistakes, and these mistakes become more serious as the number of volunteers grows.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Volunteer records suffer less from individual error, which large numbers offset, than from uneven coverage of the places and times volunteers choose to survey.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph never ranks volunteer data above expert data overall or recommends replacing surveys; it also says the coverage of volunteer data has a serious weakness of its own.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says coverage gaps are non-random and must be examined; it does not say the records are mainly about human leisure, and it credits them with revealing real trends.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the paragraph, which says random errors 'shrink in importance as the number of observations grows' and calls the objection about mistakes 'largely beside the point'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph concedes that volunteers make more mistakes but argues that random errors average out over many records, and it locates 'the real weakness of such data' in where and when volunteers choose to look. The correct answer keeps both the dismissal of the usual objection and the relocated weakness.
questions.common_misconception: Seizing on the strength of large numbers and forgetting the weakness the paragraph identifies, or seizing on the weakness and overstating it.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option overstates the defence and another overstates the criticism; the correct answer must hold both halves.

questions.subtopic: Rewilding is better justified by the processes it allows than by a claim to restore an original state.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Advocates of rewilding sometimes speak as though removing fences and reintroducing a few large animals will return a landscape to the condition it was in before human interference. The promise is appealing but confused. There is no single earlier condition to return to: the landscapes in question have changed continuously for thousands of years, with shifts in climate, in the species present and in the ways people used them. Choosing a baseline is therefore a decision about which past to prefer, not a discovery of the true one. This does not make rewilding pointless. Letting natural processes such as flooding, grazing and decay operate with less management can produce richer and more resilient ecosystems. But the honest case for it is about the processes it allows, not about a lost original it claims to restore.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Choosing a baseline is therefore a decision about which past to prefer, not a discovery of the true one. This does not make rewilding pointless. Letting natural processes such as flooding, grazing and decay operate with less management can produce richer and more resilient ecosystems. But the honest case for it is about the processes it allows, not about a lost original it claims to restore.

options.A: Rewilding succeeds best when planners first establish the true condition of a landscape before human interference and then reintroduce the animals that lived there.
options.B: Rewilding may be worth doing for the processes it frees, but promising to restore an original landscape misleads, since any baseline is a chosen past.
options.C: Because landscapes have always been changing, rewilding has no coherent goal at all, and its supporters cannot justify it on ecological or on any other grounds.
options.D: Over thousands of years, shifts in climate, in the species present and in human uses of the land have kept altering the landscapes that rewilding now targets.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Rewilding may be worth doing for the processes it frees, but promising to restore an original landscape misleads, since any baseline is a chosen past.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph denies that there is a 'true' prior condition to discover, so this reverses its central claim.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'This does not make rewilding pointless' and gives a reason for it, so the option contradicts its concession.
option_rationales.D: This is only the supporting detail used to show there is no single earlier state; it leaves out both the critique of the restoration claim and the positive case.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the promise of return to a pre-human state ('There is no single earlier condition'), adds that a baseline is a choice, and then concedes that rewilding can still be justified by 'the processes it allows'. The correct answer captures the critique and the concession together.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the critique of the restoration claim as a rejection of rewilding itself.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession in the second half must be kept; one wrong option drops it and turns the critique into outright rejection.

questions.subtopic: A forest offset is a reversible delay, not a cancellation of a fossil emission.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: An offset that pays to plant a forest is often treated as cancelling an equivalent quantity of emissions from a flight or a factory. The equivalence is only arithmetical. Carbon released from burning fossil fuel stays in the atmosphere for centuries, while carbon stored in trees is held only as long as the trees survive fire, disease, drought and the decisions of future landowners. The two quantities are measured in the same tonnes, yet one is a near-permanent addition and the other a reversible loan. None of this means that planting forests is worthless; a stored tonne buys time, and time has value. It means that an offset should be counted as a delay whose worth depends on how securely the storage can be guaranteed, rather than as an erasure that lets the original emission be forgotten.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

An offset that pays to plant a forest is often treated as cancelling an equivalent quantity of emissions from a flight or a factory. The equivalence is only arithmetical. Carbon released from burning fossil fuel stays in the atmosphere for centuries, while carbon stored in trees is held only as long as the trees survive fire, disease, drought and the decisions of future landowners. The two quantities are measured in the same tonnes, yet one is a near-permanent addition and the other a reversible loan. None of this means that planting forests is worthless; a stored tonne buys time, and time has value. It means that an offset should be counted as a delay whose worth depends on how securely the storage can be guaranteed, rather than as an erasure that lets the original emission be forgotten.

options.A: Forest offsets are valuable chiefly because they buy time, so a tonne of carbon stored in trees should be counted as equal to a tonne released by burning fuel.
options.B: The weakness of forest offsets lies in measurement, since the carbon held in trees cannot be counted as accurately as the carbon released when fuel is burned.
options.C: Because trees can burn or be felled, forest offsets do nothing to address emissions, and they should be abandoned in favour of directly cutting the use of fossil fuel.
options.D: Because forest storage is reversible while fossil carbon persists, an offset is a delay whose value depends on secure storage, not a cancellation of the emission.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Because forest storage is reversible while fossil carbon persists, an offset is a delay whose value depends on secure storage, not a cancellation of the emission.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph calls the equivalence 'only arithmetical' and contrasts a 'near-permanent addition' with a 'reversible loan', so equal counting is exactly what it rejects.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says both are 'measured in the same tonnes'; the problem it identifies is how long the storage lasts, not the accuracy of counting.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says planting forests is not 'worthless' because 'a stored tonne buys time', and it makes no recommendation about abandoning offsets.

questions.explanation: The paragraph distinguishes the permanence of fossil carbon from the reversibility of carbon in trees, concedes that storage 'buys time', and concludes that an offset is 'a delay whose worth depends on how securely the storage can be guaranteed'. The correct answer states the contrast, the conclusion and its dependence on security of storage.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that repeats the concession ('buys time') and missing that it is attached to the very equivalence the paragraph rejects.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each take one half of the argument (worthless, or equal) and the solver must see why both halves are needed.

questions.subtopic: Biology's reliance on a few convenient species makes its knowledge deep but of assumed generality.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Much of what biologists know about how genes, cells and nervous systems work comes from a small number of species: a fruit fly, a roundworm, a small weed of the mustard family, the laboratory mouse. These organisms were not chosen because they are typical of life. They were chosen because they breed quickly, survive in captivity and can be manipulated easily, and once a community of researchers had built tools and stocks around them, each new study was cheaper to do in the same species than in a new one. The result is a body of knowledge that is deep but narrow, and whose generality is often assumed rather than tested. Findings that hold in a mouse may hold in people, and frequently do; but the reasons the mouse was studied had little to do with its resemblance to us.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

These organisms were not chosen because they are typical of life.
