Findings that hold in a mouse may hold in people, and frequently do; but the reasons the mouse was studied had little to do with its resemblance to us.

options.A: Because model organisms were selected for convenience rather than typicality, findings from them rarely apply to people, and medical research should turn to other species.
options.B: Researchers keep studying the same few species because tools and breeding stocks already exist, which makes each further study cheaper than starting with a new organism.
options.C: Biology relies on a few species chosen for convenience rather than typicality, so its knowledge is deep but its generality is often assumed, not tested.
options.D: Model organisms were selected because they represent living things in general, which is why discoveries made in them so often extend to human beings.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Biology relies on a few species chosen for convenience rather than typicality, so its knowledge is deep but its generality is often assumed, not tested.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says findings from a mouse 'frequently do' hold in people and recommends no change of species, so the option contradicts it and adds a prescription.
option_rationales.B: This gives only the mechanism by which the species stayed in use; it omits the paragraph's point about narrow knowledge whose generality is assumed.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the organisms 'were not chosen because they are typical of life', so this reverses the stated reason for their selection.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why a few species dominate (convenience, then accumulated tools) and draws the consequence: knowledge 'deep but narrow' whose 'generality is often assumed rather than tested', while conceding that findings frequently transfer. The correct answer carries cause and consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the accurate account of why the species persisted and missing that the paragraph's point is the consequence for generality.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow wrong option is accurate and tempting; the correct answer must be preferred for including the consequence.

questions.subtopic: Accurate predictive text could make prose more uniform through the cumulative pull of common phrasing.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Writing tools that suggest the next word or complete a sentence are usually judged by whether their suggestions are accurate, that is, whether they offer what the writer was about to type. By that standard they are improving quickly. But accuracy measured this way rewards the most probable continuation, and the most probable continuation is, by definition, the one that most writers have already used. A tool that is perfectly accurate in this sense would steer each writer a little towards the common phrase and away from the unusual one, and across millions of documents these small nudges could make prose more uniform without anyone deciding that it should be. The danger lies not in any single suggestion, which the writer is free to refuse, but in the cumulative pull of accepting the easy option many times a day.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Writing tools that suggest the next word or complete a sentence are usually judged by whether their suggestions are accurate, that is, whether they offer what the writer was about to type. By that standard they are improving quickly. But accuracy measured this way rewards the most probable continuation, and the most probable continuation is, by definition, the one that most writers have already used. A tool that is perfectly accurate in this sense would steer each writer a little towards the common phrase and away from the unusual one, and across millions of documents these small nudges could make prose more uniform without anyone deciding that it should be. The danger lies not in any single suggestion, which the writer is free to refuse, but in the cumulative pull of accepting the easy option many times a day.

options.A: Writers ought to switch off predictive suggestions altogether, since every suggestion forces common phrases on them and takes away their freedom to choose their own words.
options.B: Predictive writing tools are dangerous because their suggestions are often inaccurate, leading writers to type words and phrases they never intended to use at all.
options.C: Predictive writing tools have become accurate enough to anticipate what most writers were about to type, which shows how rapidly the technology is now improving.
options.D: Since predictive writing tools favour the most common continuation, their cumulative pull could make prose more uniform, even though each single suggestion is easy enough to refuse.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Since predictive writing tools favour the most common continuation, their cumulative pull could make prose more uniform, even though each single suggestion is easy enough to refuse.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says each suggestion is one 'the writer is free to refuse' and gives no advice to switch tools off, so the option is both extreme and prescriptive.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the tools are 'improving quickly' in accuracy and locates the danger in accuracy itself, so inaccuracy is not its concern.
option_rationales.C: This restates the opening concession only; it misses the argument that this kind of accuracy pulls prose towards uniformity.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that accuracy rewards 'the most probable continuation', which nudges writers towards common phrasing, and that the danger is 'the cumulative pull' rather than any 'single suggestion'. The correct answer keeps the mechanism, the effect and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the worry is about bad suggestions, when the paragraph's worry is that good suggestions homogenise.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument turns on a counter-intuitive link between accuracy and uniformity.

questions.subtopic: Repair restrictions mainly secure manufacturers' control; genuine hazards can be met by standards for repairers.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Manufacturers who make devices hard to open, refuse to sell spare parts or tie components to software locks usually justify these choices on grounds of safety and quality. Some of the concern is genuine: a badly fitted battery can catch fire. Yet the same arguments were once made about cars, and an independent repair trade grew up around them without the roads becoming notably more dangerous. What restrictions on repair reliably achieve is not safety but control over the after-sales market, together with shorter lives for the products themselves. Where real hazards exist, they can be handled by setting standards for repairers rather than by excluding everyone but the original maker.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Manufacturers who make devices hard to open, refuse to sell spare parts or tie components to software locks usually justify these choices on grounds of safety and quality. Some of the concern is genuine: a badly fitted battery can catch fire. Yet the same arguments were once made about cars, and an independent repair trade grew up around them without the roads becoming notably more dangerous. What restrictions on repair reliably achieve is not safety but control over the after-sales market, together with shorter lives for the products themselves. Where real hazards exist, they can be handled by setting standards for repairers rather than by excluding everyone but the original maker.

options.A: The history of car repair proves that independent repairers are always as safe and as skilled as manufacturers, whatever kind of product happens to be repaired.
options.B: Although defended on safety grounds, repair restrictions chiefly secure makers' control and shorten product lives; real hazards could be handled by standards for repairers instead.
options.C: Independent repair of devices is dangerous, as the risk of battery fires shows, so manufacturers are right to restrict who may obtain spare parts and open devices.
options.D: Manufacturers restrict repair mainly because they want to protect their customers from badly made spare parts that could damage expensive modern devices.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Although defended on safety grounds, repair restrictions chiefly secure makers' control and shorten product lives; real hazards could be handled by standards for repairers instead.

option_rationales.A: The car example is used as a comparison, not as proof that repairers are 'always' as safe; the paragraph also admits that some hazards are genuine.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph grants that a badly fitted battery is a real risk but argues that restriction is not the right answer, so this reverses its conclusion.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says restrictions achieve 'not safety but control over the after-sales market', so it rejects this as the main effect.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the safety justification, concedes part of it (battery fires), undercuts it with the car example, names what restrictions actually achieve, and proposes standards for repairers. The correct answer covers the claim and the alternative.
questions.common_misconception: Being swayed by the concession about batteries into taking the manufacturers' side.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument is stated directly in the fourth and fifth sentences.

questions.subtopic: Digital records survive only while the means of interpreting them is maintained.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is often assumed that digital records, because they can be copied without loss, are safer than paper ones. A manuscript can burn; a file can be duplicated a thousand times. But a copy is only useful if something can still read it. Files depend on formats, formats on software, and software on machines and operating systems that are replaced every few years, so a perfectly preserved sequence of bits can become unreadable simply because the programs that understood it have gone. Paper asks nothing of its reader except literacy and light. Digital preservation is therefore less a matter of storing data than of continually maintaining the conditions under which data can be interpreted, a task that never finishes and is easy to neglect.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is often assumed that digital records, because they can be copied without loss, are safer than paper ones. A manuscript can burn; a file can be duplicated a thousand times. But a copy is only useful if something can still read it. Files depend on formats, formats on software, and software on machines and operating systems that are replaced every few years, so a perfectly preserved sequence of bits can become unreadable simply because the programs that understood it have gone. Paper asks nothing of its reader except literacy and light. Digital preservation is therefore less a matter of storing data than of continually maintaining the conditions under which data can be interpreted, a task that never finishes and is easy to neglect.

options.A: Digital records are not safe merely because they copy without loss; they remain readable only while the software and systems that interpret them are continually maintained.
options.B: Digital files are fragile because copying them again and again introduces small errors that accumulate until the original data can no longer be recovered.
options.C: Paper is a better medium than digital storage for every kind of record, because it never depends on a machine and so can never become unreadable.
options.D: The main threat to digital archives is that storage hardware wears out quickly, so institutions have to keep buying new disks to hold their collections of files.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Digital records are not safe merely because they copy without loss; they remain readable only while the software and systems that interpret them are continually maintained.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph grants that files 'can be copied without loss'; the threat it describes is loss of the software that reads them, not copying errors.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph admits that 'A manuscript can burn' and does not rank paper above digital storage for all records; it only contrasts what each asks of the reader.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says even 'a perfectly preserved sequence of bits' can become unreadable; its point is about interpretation, not the wear of storage devices.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts that copies are lossless, then argues that a copy is useless without something to read it, and concludes that preservation means 'continually maintaining the conditions under which data can be interpreted'. The correct answer states this.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming the threat to digital records is physical decay or copying error, which the paragraph sets aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion is stated in the last sentence and the wrong options are clearly off.

questions.subtopic: Recommendation systems shape preferences as well as reflect them, so they are not neutral mirrors.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Defenders of recommendation systems argue that they merely give people more of what they already like, and that this is a service rather than a manipulation. The claim assumes that preferences exist fully formed before the recommendations arrive. Taste, however, is partly made by exposure: people come to like music, food or films they have encountered repeatedly, and they rarely develop a liking for what they never meet. A system that learns from what someone has chosen, and then shows them more of the same, is therefore not simply reflecting a preference but helping to fix it, narrowing the range of encounters from which future preferences could grow. This need not be sinister, and the user remains free to search elsewhere. But it means the defence of such systems as neutral mirrors is mistaken.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Defenders of recommendation systems argue that they merely give people more of what they already like, and that this is a service rather than a manipulation. The claim assumes that preferences exist fully formed before the recommendations arrive. Taste, however, is partly made by exposure: people come to like music, food or films they have encountered repeatedly, and they rarely develop a liking for what they never meet. A system that learns from what someone has chosen, and then shows them more of the same, is therefore not simply reflecting a preference but helping to fix it, narrowing the range of encounters from which future preferences could grow. This need not be sinister, and the user remains free to search elsewhere. But it means the defence of such systems as neutral mirrors is mistaken.

options.A: Recommendation systems deliberately manipulate users into liking content they would otherwise reject, and in doing so they deprive people of any real freedom of choice.
options.B: Because taste grows partly from exposure, systems that offer more of what people chose help fix and narrow their preferences, so they are not neutral mirrors.
options.C: Recommendation systems serve users well by supplying more of what they already like, though people should still search elsewhere if they wish to broaden their tastes.
options.D: Because people come to like what they meet repeatedly, recommendation systems are now the main force that decides which music, food and films people enjoy.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Because taste grows partly from exposure, systems that offer more of what people chose help fix and narrow their preferences, so they are not neutral mirrors.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the effect 'need not be sinister' and that 'the user remains free to search elsewhere', so deliberate manipulation and loss of all choice go beyond it.
option_rationales.C: This is the defenders' view, which the paragraph calls 'mistaken', combined with advice the paragraph does not give.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says such systems help to fix preferences; it never ranks them as 'the main force' over every other influence on taste, so the option overstates its claim.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the defence, exposes its assumption that preferences exist 'fully formed', argues that taste is 'partly made by exposure', and concludes that such systems help 'fix' preferences, so the 'neutral mirrors' defence fails, while conceding the effect need not be sinister. The correct answer keeps the reason, the conclusion and the moderate scope.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating a measured critique into a charge of manipulation, or upgrading 'helping to fix' into 'the main force'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options overstate the critique in different directions and must be separated from its exact scope.

questions.subtopic: Deciding about a dead writer's drafts involves how to present them, not only whether to publish.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a writer dies leaving a novel unfinished, or instructs that drafts be destroyed, those who hold the papers face a familiar dilemma. Publishing seems to betray the author's wishes or, at least, to present as a book what the author never judged to be one. Suppressing seems to deprive readers of work that may be among the best the writer produced. The dilemma is usually framed as loyalty against value, but this framing overlooks a third consideration: how the work is presented. An unfinished draft printed as a draft, with its gaps visible and its status made plain, misrepresents the author far less than the same text smoothed by an editor into the appearance of completion. The question is not only whether to publish but in what form.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a writer dies leaving a novel unfinished, or instructs that drafts be destroyed, those who hold the papers face a familiar dilemma. Publishing seems to betray the author's wishes or, at least, to present as a book what the author never judged to be one. Suppressing seems to deprive readers of work that may be among the best the writer produced. The dilemma is usually framed as loyalty against value, but this framing overlooks a third consideration: how the work is presented. An unfinished draft printed as a draft, with its gaps visible and its status made plain, misrepresents the author far less than the same text smoothed by an editor into the appearance of completion. The question is not only whether to publish but in what form.

options.A: The fate of a dead writer's unfinished work involves more than loyalty against value; whether it is printed openly as a draft also matters.
options.B: Editors who complete a dead author's unfinished novel betray that author, so any drafts left at death ought to be destroyed as the author wished.
options.C: Those who inherit a writer's papers must choose between honouring the author's wishes and giving readers access to work of possibly great literary value.
options.D: Unfinished manuscripts should always be published, because readers' interest in a writer's best work outweighs any instruction the author left about destroying the drafts.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The fate of a dead writer's unfinished work involves more than loyalty against value; whether it is printed openly as a draft also matters.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph criticises smoothing a draft into apparent completion but does not conclude that drafts should be destroyed; it says a draft 'printed as a draft' misrepresents the author far less.
option_rationales.C: This is the usual framing, 'loyalty against value', which the paragraph says 'overlooks a third consideration'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph does not settle the dilemma in favour of publication; it argues that the dilemma omits the question of form.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets out the familiar dilemma, then says the 'framing overlooks a third consideration: how the work is presented', and ends 'The question is not only whether to publish but in what form.' The correct answer captures this addition to the debate.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the accurate statement of the dilemma, which the paragraph presents in order to say it is incomplete.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option restates the very framing the paragraph sets out to correct.

questions.subtopic: The lost esteem of an exposed forgery is partly snobbery and partly a response to a real absence of achievement.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a painting long admired as the work of a master is shown to be a forgery, its price collapses, and many viewers report that it now looks worse to them. Sceptics take this as proof that the art world values names rather than pictures, since the canvas itself has not changed. The inference is too quick. What we admire in a work is not only the arrangement of paint before us but also an achievement: a solution to a problem, reached at a certain time by a certain person. A forger who copies a style after it has been invented has not achieved what the original painter achieved, even if the surfaces are indistinguishable. Some of the lost esteem is snobbery, no doubt; but some of it tracks a real difference that the eye alone cannot see.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a painting long admired as the work of a master is shown to be a forgery, its price collapses, and many viewers report that it now looks worse to them. Sceptics take this as proof that the art world values names rather than pictures, since the canvas itself has not changed. The inference is too quick. What we admire in a work is not only the arrangement of paint before us but also an achievement: a solution to a problem, reached at a certain time by a certain person. A forger who copies a style after it has been invented has not achieved what the original painter achieved, even if the surfaces are indistinguishable. Some of the lost esteem is snobbery, no doubt; but some of it tracks a real difference that the eye alone cannot see.

options.A: Viewers who find an exposed forgery less beautiful are responding correctly, because every forgery contains visible flaws that an attentive eye will eventually detect.
options.B: The collapse in the value of exposed forgeries shows that collectors and viewers care about famous names far more than about the paintings that hang before them.
options.C: The fall in esteem for an exposed forgery is not pure snobbery about names; it partly reflects that admiring a work includes admiring an achievement the forger never made.
options.D: A forgery that cannot be told apart from an original has exactly the same artistic worth, since the value of a painting lies wholly in what the eye can see.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The fall in esteem for an exposed forgery is not pure snobbery about names; it partly reflects that admiring a work includes admiring an achievement the forger never made.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph allows that the surfaces may be 'indistinguishable' and places the real difference beyond what the eye can see, so visible flaws are not its reason.
option_rationales.B: This is the sceptics' inference, which the paragraph calls 'too quick'; it grants only that 'some' of the lost esteem is snobbery.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph argues the opposite, that admiration includes 'an achievement' and that there is a difference 'the eye alone cannot see'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the sceptics' conclusion, rejects it as 'too quick', and argues that admiration includes 'an achievement' that a later copyist cannot share, while conceding 'Some of the lost esteem is snobbery'. The correct answer keeps both the rejection and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the sceptics' view because the paragraph grants part of it, or defending the drop in esteem for the wrong reason (visible flaws).
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph reports a view and then partly rejects it; one wrong option defends the author's conclusion with a reason the author denies.

questions.subtopic: The white-walled gallery is a setting with strong effects of its own, not a neutral one.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: The bare, white-walled gallery with even lighting and no decoration is often described as a neutral setting, one that lets the art speak for itself. It is better understood as a setting with very strong effects of its own. By removing every sign of daily life, it tells visitors that what hangs there is set apart, to be contemplated rather than used, touched or talked over. Objects that were made to be handled in a home, carried in a procession or worn on the body take on a different character when isolated on a plinth under a spotlight. The white room is not wrong for that reason, and for some works it may be ideal. But it is a choice that shapes what we see, and calling it neutral hides that choice from view.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The bare, white-walled gallery with even lighting and no decoration is often described as a neutral setting, one that lets the art speak for itself. It is better understood as a setting with very strong effects of its own. By removing every sign of daily life, it tells visitors that what hangs there is set apart, to be contemplated rather than used, touched or talked over. Objects that were made to be handled in a home, carried in a procession or worn on the body take on a different character when isolated on a plinth under a spotlight. The white room is not wrong for that reason, and for some works it may be ideal. But it is a choice that shapes what we see, and calling it neutral hides that choice from view.

options.A: Objects made for everyday use lose their meaning entirely when placed in galleries, so museums inevitably distort the cultures whose objects they claim to present.
options.B: The white gallery is ideal for displaying art because its bare walls and even lighting let every work speak for itself without the distraction of daily life.
options.C: Galleries should give up white walls and show objects in the settings for which they were made, such as homes, processions and ceremonies of every kind.
options.D: The bare white gallery is not neutral: stripping away everyday context sets objects apart, which may suit some works but changes how others are seen.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The bare white gallery is not neutral: stripping away everyday context sets objects apart, which may suit some works but changes how others are seen.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says such objects 'take on a different character', not that they lose all meaning, and it draws no conclusion about museums distorting cultures.
option_rationales.B: This is the common description the paragraph corrects; it allows that the room may be ideal only 'for some works'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'The white room is not wrong' and makes no recommendation to abandon it, so the option adds a prescription it rejects.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the description of the white room as 'a neutral setting', explains its effect (objects are 'set apart'), concedes it is 'not wrong' and may be ideal for some works, and concludes that it is 'a choice that shapes what we see'. The correct answer keeps the claim and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Turning a critique of the word 'neutral' into a rejection of white galleries altogether.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession must be kept; the prescriptive wrong option is tempting.

questions.subtopic: Prize shortlists may concentrate an existing readership more than they enlarge it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is widely observed that a novel's sales rise sharply once it is shortlisted for a major literary prize, and rise again if it wins. This is often cited as evidence that prizes help good writing find readers. That is partly true, but the effect is concentrated. Because a shortlist directs attention to a handful of books rather than spreading it across hundreds, the gain for those chosen may come partly at the expense of comparable books that narrowly missed out, whose sales are not lifted at all. Prizes, in other words, may do less to enlarge the audience for serious fiction than to redistribute an existing audience towards a few titles.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is widely observed that a novel's sales rise sharply once it is shortlisted for a major literary prize, and rise again if it wins. This is often cited as evidence that prizes help good writing find readers. That is partly true, but the effect is concentrated. Because a shortlist directs attention to a handful of books rather than spreading it across hundreds, the gain for those chosen may come partly at the expense of comparable books that narrowly missed out, whose sales are not lifted at all. Prizes, in other words, may do less to enlarge the audience for serious fiction than to redistribute an existing audience towards a few titles.

options.A: Literary prizes harm serious fiction, because the books chosen for their shortlists are usually weaker than many of the books that narrowly miss out.
options.B: Literary prizes are the most effective way of bringing good writing to readers, since shortlisted and winning novels always enjoy a sharp rise in their sales.
options.C: A novel's sales rise once it is shortlisted for a major literary prize and then rise a second time if it goes on to win that prize.
options.D: Shortlists lift the chosen books' sales by concentrating attention on them, so prizes may redistribute an existing readership more than they enlarge it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Shortlists lift the chosen books' sales by concentrating attention on them, so prizes may redistribute an existing readership more than they enlarge it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph calls the books that miss out 'comparable' and says nothing about shortlisted books being weaker, so the claim is outside its scope.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph grants that the claim about prizes is only 'partly true' and says the effect is concentrated; it never calls prizes the most effective means, and 'always' overstates it.
option_rationales.C: This repeats the opening observation only; it misses the paragraph's point that the gain is concentrated and may be redistributive.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts that shortlisting lifts sales, then qualifies the inference: attention is concentrated, so gains may come 'at the expense of comparable books', and prizes may 'redistribute an existing audience'. The correct answer states the finding and its qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the opening observation for the point, when the paragraph uses it to set up a qualification.
questions.difficulty_reason: The qualification is stated plainly in the last two sentences.

questions.subtopic: Dictionaries describe usage; advice on appropriateness is a separate job.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a dictionary adds a slang term or records a new sense for an old word, complaints follow that it has abandoned standards. The complaint misunderstands what most modern dictionaries are for. They aim to record how a language is actually used, much as a map records where roads actually run, and a map that omitted a busy road because planners disapproved of it would simply be a bad map. Recording a usage is not endorsing it. Readers who want advice on what is appropriate in formal writing are entitled to it, and usage notes and style guides exist to provide it. The mistake lies in expecting one book to do both jobs and then blaming it for doing the one it set out to do.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a dictionary adds a slang term or records a new sense for an old word, complaints follow that it has abandoned standards. The complaint misunderstands what most modern dictionaries are for. They aim to record how a language is actually used, much as a map records where roads actually run, and a map that omitted a busy road because planners disapproved of it would simply be a bad map. Recording a usage is not endorsing it. Readers who want advice on what is appropriate in formal writing are entitled to it, and usage notes and style guides exist to provide it. The mistake lies in expecting one book to do both jobs and then blaming it for doing the one it set out to do.

options.A: Because language is always changing, there is no such thing as correct usage, and style guides that offer advice on formal writing are therefore misguided.
options.B: A dictionary resembles a map, and a map that left out a busy road because its planners disliked that road would mislead everyone who relied on it.
options.C: Recording new or informal usages does not lower a dictionary's standards, since its task is to describe use; advice on appropriateness belongs to other guides.
options.D: Dictionaries ought to refuse slang entries until such words have been accepted in formal writing, so that readers are not misled about what counts as correct usage.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Recording new or informal usages does not lower a dictionary's standards, since its task is to describe use; advice on appropriateness belongs to other guides.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says readers 'are entitled to' advice on formal writing and that style guides 'exist to provide it', so it does not reject correctness or such guides.
option_rationales.B: This restates the supporting analogy only; it omits the paragraph's conclusion about separating description from advice.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph defends recording usages that are actually in use and says 'Recording a usage is not endorsing it', so this reverses its view.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the complaint that dictionaries abandon standards, argues by the map analogy that their aim is to record use, states 'Recording a usage is not endorsing it', and places advice in usage notes and style guides. The correct answer keeps the defence and the division of labour.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a defence of description as a denial that any usage is better than another.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme wrong option sounds like the paragraph's side of the debate and must be rejected on its denial of correctness.

questions.subtopic: Compressed headline style outlived its original constraint, at the cost of occasional ambiguity.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Newspaper headlines have long had a grammar of their own: articles and linking verbs drop out, short words such as 'bid', 'probe' and 'row' replace longer ones, and the present tense is used for events that are already over. These habits arose from a practical constraint, the need to fit a message into a narrow column in large type. They persist on screens, where space is less tight, partly because readers have learned to decode them and partly because brevity still helps a headline compete for attention. The cost is ambiguity: a compressed headline can sometimes be read in two ways, and the reader must open the story to find out which was meant.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Newspaper headlines have long had a grammar of their own: articles and linking verbs drop out, short words such as 'bid', 'probe' and 'row' replace longer ones, and the present tense is used for events that are already over. These habits arose from a practical constraint, the need to fit a message into a narrow column in large type. They persist on screens, where space is less tight, partly because readers have learned to decode them and partly because brevity still helps a headline compete for attention. The cost is ambiguity: a compressed headline can sometimes be read in two ways, and the reader must open the story to find out which was meant.

options.A: Headline grammar, born of narrow columns, persists on screens through readers' familiarity and the value of brevity, though compression can cause ambiguity.
options.B: Headlines put past events in the present tense because editors want every story to seem more urgent and more recent to readers than it really is.
options.C: Now that screens have removed the old shortage of space, compressed headlines no longer serve any purpose and survive purely through readers' habit.
options.D: Compressed headlines are made deliberately ambiguous, since forcing readers to open the story is the main reason editors choose to write them that way.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Headline grammar, born of narrow columns, persists on screens through readers' familiarity and the value of brevity, though compression can cause ambiguity.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph traces headline habits to the constraint of column space, not to a wish to exaggerate urgency, so the motive is outside its scope.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph gives a second reason for their survival, that 'brevity still helps a headline compete for attention', so 'no longer serve any purpose' contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph presents ambiguity as a 'cost' of compression, not as its purpose, so the option reverses the relation.

questions.explanation: The paragraph describes headline grammar, explains its origin in space constraints, gives two reasons it persists online, and names its cost, ambiguity. The correct answer covers origin, persistence and cost.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking a side effect (ambiguity) for a purpose, or ignoring the second reason for survival.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure is stated sentence by sentence; wrong options are clearly off once read.

questions.subtopic: Teaching a standard language threatens dialects only when dialects are treated as mistakes.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Schools that teach a standard form of a language are sometimes accused of destroying the regional dialects their pupils bring from home. The charge contains a truth: children who are told that their way of speaking is wrong often come to feel that it is, and may abandon it. But the fault lies in the telling, not in the teaching of the standard itself. Learning a second variety of one's language, useful in examinations, offices and correspondence with strangers, need not displace the first, any more than learning a second language erases one's mother tongue. Many speakers move between dialect and standard with ease, choosing according to company. What threatens a dialect is the attitude that treats it as a mistake, not the addition of another way of speaking.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Schools that teach a standard form of a language are sometimes accused of destroying the regional dialects their pupils bring from home. The charge contains a truth: children who are told that their way of speaking is wrong often come to feel that it is, and may abandon it. But the fault lies in the telling, not in the teaching of the standard itself. Learning a second variety of one's language, useful in examinations, offices and correspondence with strangers, need not displace the first, any more than learning a second language erases one's mother tongue. Many speakers move between dialect and standard with ease, choosing according to company. What threatens a dialect is the attitude that treats it as a mistake, not the addition of another way of speaking.

options.A: Children who are told that their way of speaking is wrong tend to believe it and may then give up the dialect they first learned at home.
options.B: Teaching a standard variety need not erase dialects, since people can use both; what endangers dialects is treating them as errors rather than as varieties.
options.C: Speakers who move easily between dialect and standard show that regional dialects face no real threat from schools or from any other source.
options.D: Schools should stop teaching the standard form of the language, because doing so inevitably destroys the regional dialects that pupils bring with them from home.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Teaching a standard variety need not erase dialects, since people can use both; what endangers dialects is treating them as errors rather than as varieties.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'truth' the paragraph concedes in its second sentence; it omits the argument that teaching the standard is not itself the cause.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph names a real threat, 'the attitude that treats it as a mistake', so 'no real threat' contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the fault 'lies in the telling, not in the teaching of the standard itself', so this contradicts its main claim.

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants part of the charge, relocates the fault from teaching the standard to telling children their speech is wrong, supports the point with the analogy of a second language, and concludes that the threat is an attitude. The correct answer keeps the distinction.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the conceded truth as if it were the conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession is accurate and tempting; the correct answer turns on the distinction between teaching and telling.

questions.subtopic: Podcasts create one-sided intimacy, mostly harmless but powerful for advertising.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Listeners often describe a favourite podcast host as a friend, and the feeling is not hard to explain. Audio reaches us at close range, frequently through earphones, while we are alone and doing something else: driving, cooking, walking. The host's voice is unpolished and conversational, with hesitations and jokes that a scripted broadcast would remove, and it returns at regular intervals for hours each week. These conditions mimic the circumstances of real friendship closely enough that the mind responds as if to one. The relationship is, of course, one-sided: the host does not know the listener exists. That asymmetry is harmless for most people, but it is also what makes the medium so effective for advertising, since a recommendation from a 'friend' carries unusual weight.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Listeners often describe a favourite podcast host as a friend, and the feeling is not hard to explain. Audio reaches us at close range, frequently through earphones, while we are alone and doing something else: driving, cooking, walking. The host's voice is unpolished and conversational, with hesitations and jokes that a scripted broadcast would remove, and it returns at regular intervals for hours each week. These conditions mimic the circumstances of real friendship closely enough that the mind responds as if to one. The relationship is, of course, one-sided: the host does not know the listener exists. That asymmetry is harmless for most people, but it is also what makes the medium so effective for advertising, since a recommendation from a 'friend' carries unusual weight.

options.A: The way podcasts are heard and voiced makes hosts feel like friends; this one-sided closeness is mostly harmless but gives their spoken advertising recommendations unusual force.
options.B: Podcasts are usually heard at close range through earphones, while listeners are alone and busy with other tasks such as driving, cooking or walking.
options.C: Podcast hosts deliberately keep hesitations and jokes in their shows in order to make their listeners trust the advertisements that they read out on air.
options.D: Podcast listeners wrongly believe that their favourite hosts know and care about them personally, and they are harmed by a relationship that can never be returned.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The way podcasts are heard and voiced makes hosts feel like friends; this one-sided closeness is mostly harmless but gives their spoken advertising recommendations unusual force.

option_rationales.B: This is one of the conditions offered to explain the feeling of friendship; it leaves out the one-sided relationship and its use for advertising.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph attributes no such motive to hosts; it explains the informal style as a contrast with scripted broadcasts.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls the asymmetry 'harmless for most people', so the claim of harm contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains the feeling of friendship by the conditions of listening and of the host's voice, then notes that the relationship is 'one-sided', 'harmless for most people', and 'effective for advertising'. The correct answer covers the explanation and both consequences.
questions.common_misconception: Picking a single explanatory detail or reading a motive into the hosts' style.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is plainly narrow, contradictory or unsupported.

questions.subtopic: The homework-achievement association partly reflects prior advantage and fades beyond a point, so it supports moderate homework.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Studies of homework have tended to find that the amount of homework older pupils do is associated with higher achievement, while for young children the link is weak or absent. It is tempting to conclude that more homework simply works for teenagers. But an association of this kind can arise in several ways: pupils who are already motivated, or whose families support study, both do more homework and do better at school, so the homework may be partly a sign of advantage rather than its cause. And beyond a certain amount, the association often fades. The evidence supports homework that is moderate, purposeful and suited to the pupil's age, not the belief that more is always better.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Studies of homework have tended to find that the amount of homework older pupils do is associated with higher achievement, while for young children the link is weak or absent. It is tempting to conclude that more homework simply works for teenagers. But an association of this kind can arise in several ways: pupils who are already motivated, or whose families support study, both do more homework and do better at school, so the homework may be partly a sign of advantage rather than its cause. And beyond a certain amount, the association often fades. The evidence supports homework that is moderate, purposeful and suited to the pupil's age, not the belief that more is always better.

options.A: Pupils from supportive families do better at school whether or not they do homework, which shows that homework has no effect on achievement.
options.B: Homework's link with older pupils' achievement may partly reflect motivation and family support and fades beyond a point, so evidence favours moderate homework.
options.C: Since homework does nothing for young children and its benefits for teenagers are an illusion, schools should abolish homework at every stage of education.
options.D: Because older pupils who do more homework achieve better results, schools ought to keep increasing the amount of homework they set for their teenage pupils.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Homework's link with older pupils' achievement may partly reflect motivation and family support and fades beyond a point, so evidence favours moderate homework.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph offers family support as one possible source of the association, not proof that homework has no effect; it still endorses moderate homework.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the homework may be 'partly' a sign of advantage, not wholly, and it ends by supporting moderate homework, so abolition contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: This is the tempting conclusion the paragraph warns against; it rejects 'the belief that more is always better'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the association, warns against reading it causally, notes that it fades beyond a certain amount, and concludes that evidence 'supports homework that is moderate, purposeful and suited to the pupil's age'. The correct answer keeps the caution and the measured conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Swinging from 'more is better' to 'homework is useless', when the paragraph takes a middle position.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options take each extreme; the correct answer depends on the word 'partly' and the final sentence.

questions.subtopic: Grade inflation's main cost is lost discrimination between candidates, which shifts advantage to the privileged.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Complaints about grade inflation usually focus on fairness to earlier generations, whose hard-won marks now look ordinary beside the higher grades awarded today. The more serious cost falls elsewhere. A grade is useful to an employer or a university chiefly as a way of telling candidates apart, and when most candidates crowd into the top band, it stops doing that job. Selectors then fall back on other evidence, such as the standing of the institution, interviews, or the polish of a personal statement, which tend to favour candidates from privileged backgrounds more than marks did. Inflation that looks generous to every student can thus end up shifting advantage towards those who needed it least.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Complaints about grade inflation usually focus on fairness to earlier generations, whose hard-won marks now look ordinary beside the higher grades awarded today. The more serious cost falls elsewhere. A grade is useful to an employer or a university chiefly as a way of telling candidates apart, and when most candidates crowd into the top band, it stops doing that job. Selectors then fall back on other evidence, such as the standing of the institution, interviews, or the polish of a personal statement, which tend to favour candidates from privileged backgrounds more than marks did. Inflation that looks generous to every student can thus end up shifting advantage towards those who needed it least.

options.A: Once grades rise, employers and universities stop using them altogether and rely solely on interviews and personal statements whenever they select among candidates.
options.B: Since higher grades are awarded to every student, grade inflation helps disadvantaged students most of all, because it narrows the gap between them and others.
options.C: Grade inflation's worse harm is not to past students: crowded top grades stop separating candidates, so selectors turn to signals that tend to favour the privileged.
options.D: Grade inflation is unfair chiefly to earlier generations, whose hard-earned marks now look ordinary when set beside the higher grades handed out to students today.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Grade inflation's worse harm is not to past students: crowded top grades stop separating candidates, so selectors turn to signals that tend to favour the privileged.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says selectors 'fall back on other evidence' when grades stop telling candidates apart; 'altogether' and 'solely' overstate this, and it lists the standing of the institution too.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph concludes that inflation shifts advantage 'towards those who needed it least', which is the reverse of this option.
option_rationales.D: This is the usual complaint, which the paragraph sets aside: 'The more serious cost falls elsewhere.'

questions.explanation: The paragraph dismisses the usual fairness complaint as the lesser cost, explains that crowded grades cannot separate candidates, and traces how the substitute signals favour the privileged. The correct answer keeps the contrast with the usual complaint and the mechanism.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the familiar complaint that the paragraph mentions only to set aside.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph opens with a view it rejects, and the reversal wrong option trades on the point that inflation 'looks generous to every student'.

questions.subtopic: Tests of matching teaching to learning styles have generally failed; material, not learner, decides presentation.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many teachers have been trained to identify each pupil's learning style, whether visual, auditory or kinaesthetic, and to match lessons to it. The idea is attractive because it seems to respect individual differences. Yet when it has been tested by teaching pupils in a style that matches their supposed preference and comparing them with pupils taught in a mismatched style, the expected advantage has generally failed to appear. People certainly have preferences about how they like to learn; what is doubtful is that those preferences determine how well they learn. More often, the best form of presentation depends on the material: maps are best shown and pronunciation is best heard, whoever the learner is.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many teachers have been trained to identify each pupil's learning style, whether visual, auditory or kinaesthetic, and to match lessons to it. The idea is attractive because it seems to respect individual differences. Yet when it has been tested by teaching pupils in a style that matches their supposed preference and comparing them with pupils taught in a mismatched style, the expected advantage has generally failed to appear. People certainly have preferences about how they like to learn; what is doubtful is that those preferences determine how well they learn. More often, the best form of presentation depends on the material: maps are best shown and pronunciation is best heard, whoever the learner is.

options.A: The learning styles approach appeals to teachers because it seems to respect individual differences, which explains why so many of them have been trained in it.
options.B: Teachers should present every lesson in visual, auditory and kinaesthetic forms at once, so that the learning style of every pupil is properly served.
options.C: Pupils have no real preferences about how they learn, so teachers who ask about learning styles are wasting their own time and the time of their pupils.
options.D: Matching lessons to supposed learning styles has generally not helped when tested; people have preferences, but the material, not the learner, usually decides the best presentation.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Matching lessons to supposed learning styles has generally not helped when tested; people have preferences, but the material, not the learner, usually decides the best presentation.

option_rationales.A: This restates the paragraph's explanation of the idea's appeal; it omits the finding that matching has not helped.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph doubts that learning styles determine learning at all, so a prescription to serve every style is not its conclusion.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'People certainly have preferences about how they like to learn', so this contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains the appeal of matching lessons to learning styles, reports that tested matching 'has generally failed', grants that preferences exist, and concludes that 'the best form of presentation depends on the material'. The correct answer states the finding and its qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Over-reading the finding into a denial that preferences exist.
questions.difficulty_reason: The finding and qualification are stated directly.

questions.subtopic: Memory serves understanding rather than opposing it, though disconnected drilling is still poor practice.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Memorisation has a poor reputation in modern education, where it is often set against understanding as the lower activity against the higher. The opposition is overdrawn. Understanding works on material held in mind: a pupil who must look up every multiplication fact or every date has little attention left for noticing patterns or weighing causes. Knowledge stored securely in memory is what frees thought to operate on something. None of this justifies drilling facts that are never connected to anything, which is as dull as its critics claim and is quickly forgotten. The case is for memory in the service of understanding, not memory in its place.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Memorisation has a poor reputation in modern education, where it is often set against understanding as the lower activity against the higher. The opposition is overdrawn. Understanding works on material held in mind: a pupil who must look up every multiplication fact or every date has little attention left for noticing patterns or weighing causes. Knowledge stored securely in memory is what frees thought to operate on something. None of this justifies drilling facts that are never connected to anything, which is as dull as its critics claim and is quickly forgotten. The case is for memory in the service of understanding, not memory in its place.

options.A: Memorising is not the opposite of understanding, since securely remembered knowledge frees attention for thought, though drilling disconnected facts remains as poor a practice as its critics say.
options.B: Facts drilled without connection to anything else are dull and quickly forgotten, which is why memorisation has acquired such a poor reputation in schools.
options.C: Understanding is a higher activity than memorisation, so pupils should be taught to look facts up when they need them rather than commit them to memory.
options.D: Schools should return to drilling facts, because pupils who memorise multiplication tables and dates always understand their subjects better than pupils who do not.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Memorising is not the opposite of understanding, since securely remembered knowledge frees attention for thought, though drilling disconnected facts remains as poor a practice as its critics say.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph grants that disconnected drilling is dull but does not say this explains memorisation's reputation, and the option omits its main claim.
option_rationales.C: This is the opposition the paragraph calls 'overdrawn'; it argues that a pupil who must look everything up has little attention left for thought.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph rejects drilling 'facts that are never connected to anything' and claims no such 'always'; it argues for memory 'in the service of understanding'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph calls the opposition between memory and understanding 'overdrawn', argues that remembered knowledge 'frees thought', and concedes that disconnected drilling is dull and forgotten. The correct answer holds the claim and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the defence of memory as a defence of drilling, or choosing the concession as the point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession wrong option borrows the paragraph's words and attaches an unsupported causal link.

questions.subtopic: The fairness and validity objections to exam coaching cannot both be pressed at full strength.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Coaching for entrance examinations is criticised on two different grounds that are often run together. One is that it is unfair: families who can pay for it buy their children an advantage that others cannot. The other is that it defeats the purpose of the test, which was meant to measure ability, by inflating scores without improving the underlying skills. The two objections pull in different directions. If coaching genuinely builds skills, the second objection fails, but the first becomes stronger, since a real advantage is being bought. If coaching merely teaches tricks, the second objection holds, but the unfairness is less troubling, because the advantage it buys is partly illusory. Critics who press both at full strength at once owe an account of how coaching can be both useless and decisive.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Coaching for entrance examinations is criticised on two different grounds that are often run together. One is that it is unfair: families who can pay for it buy their children an advantage that others cannot. The other is that it defeats the purpose of the test, which was meant to measure ability, by inflating scores without improving the underlying skills. The two objections pull in different directions. If coaching genuinely builds skills, the second objection fails, but the first becomes stronger, since a real advantage is being bought. If coaching merely teaches tricks, the second objection holds, but the unfairness is less troubling, because the advantage it buys is partly illusory. Critics who press both at full strength at once owe an account of how coaching can be both useless and decisive.

options.A: Exam coaching is unfair because only families who can afford it gain an advantage, and it should therefore be restricted or else made freely available to everyone.
options.B: The fairness and validity objections to coaching pull against each other, since what strengthens one weakens the other, so critics cannot press both fully.
options.C: Exam coaching inflates scores without improving the skills that tests are meant to measure, so it both defeats the purpose of testing and wastes families' money.
options.D: Because coaching either builds real skills or teaches mere tricks, both objections to it fail, and critics have no sound reason to oppose coaching at all.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The fairness and validity objections to coaching pull against each other, since what strengthens one weakens the other, so critics cannot press both fully.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph presents the fairness objection as one of two and analyses how it interacts with the other; it neither endorses it outright nor proposes any remedy.
option_rationales.C: This adopts the second objection as fact, whereas the paragraph treats it as holding only if coaching 'merely teaches tricks'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says that in each case one objection holds or grows stronger; it denies only that both can hold fully at once.

questions.explanation: The paragraph separates two objections and shows that they 'pull in different directions': if coaching builds skill, unfairness grows and the validity objection fails; if it teaches tricks, the reverse. It concludes that critics cannot press both 'at full strength at once'. The correct answer states this tension.
questions.common_misconception: Taking one of the reported objections as the author's view, or concluding that the tension defeats both objections.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph is a dilemma; the solver must see that it limits the critics' case without dismissing it.

questions.subtopic: Open-label placebo results show effects of care, mostly on self-reported symptoms, not of the pill.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Some small trials have reported that patients given pills they are told openly contain no active ingredient nonetheless describe their symptoms as improved. The finding seems to dissolve the ethical objection to placebos, which rested on the need to deceive. It should be read with care. The improvements reported have mainly been in symptoms that patients assess themselves, such as pain or discomfort, rather than in measures of underlying disease, and in trials where patients cannot be blinded to what they received, expectations can colour reports. The pills may also work less through the pill than through the ritual around it: a consultation, an explanation, a doctor's attention. What the trials suggest is that care itself has effects, not that sugar does.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The improvements reported have mainly been in symptoms that patients assess themselves, such as pain or discomfort, rather than in measures of underlying disease, and in trials where patients cannot be blinded to what they received, expectations can colour reports. The pills may also work less through the pill than through the ritual around it: a consultation, an explanation, a doctor's attention. What the trials suggest is that care itself has effects, not that sugar does.

options.A: Because patients knew the pills were inactive, the improvements they reported must be due only to expectation, so the trials show nothing about placebo effects at all.
options.B: Open-label placebo trials prove that placebos can treat disease without deceiving anyone, which removes every ethical objection to prescribing them in practice.
options.C: Open placebo trials seem to remove the need for deception, but their gains are mostly in self-reported symptoms and may stem from surrounding care, not pills.
options.D: The effects of placebos depend chiefly on consultation and attention, so doctors should spend more time with their patients instead of prescribing them drugs.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Open placebo trials seem to remove the need for deception, but their gains are mostly in self-reported symptoms and may stem from surrounding care, not pills.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says expectations 'can colour reports', not that they explain everything, and it draws a positive conclusion: 'care itself has effects'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the finding 'should be read with care' and notes that improvements were mainly in self-assessed symptoms 'rather than in measures of underlying disease'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph suggests the ritual of care may matter but makes no recommendation, and it says nothing about replacing active drugs.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the finding and its apparent ethical consequence, then qualifies it: gains are mainly in self-assessed symptoms, unblinded reports can be coloured by expectation, and the effect may come from 'the ritual around it'. It concludes 'care itself has effects, not that sugar does'. The correct answer holds the finding with both qualifications.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a hedged finding either as proof or as worthless.
questions.difficulty_reason: A finding and its layered qualification; the wrong options overstate in opposite directions and one adds a prescription.

questions.subtopic: Counting detections overstates screening's benefit because overdiagnosed patients look like saved ones.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Screening programmes are usually judged by how many cases of disease they find, and by that measure more sensitive tests always look better. But some conditions that screening detects would never have caused harm in a person's lifetime: small, slow-growing abnormalities that would have stayed silent until the person died of something else. Finding these is not a benefit; it converts healthy people into patients, exposing them to anxiety and to treatments with real side effects. Because no one can tell, in an individual case, whether a detected abnormality would have progressed, the overdiagnosed patient is indistinguishable from one whose life was saved, and may well believe that screening saved them. Counting detections therefore overstates what screening achieves, without implying that screening is never worthwhile.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
