Because no one can tell, in an individual case, whether a detected abnormality would have progressed, the overdiagnosed patient is indistinguishable from one whose life was saved, and may well believe that screening saved them. Counting detections therefore overstates what screening achieves, without implying that screening is never worthwhile.

options.A: More sensitive screening tests find more cases of disease, which is why they are generally judged superior by the people who design and run screening programmes.
options.B: Patients who have been overdiagnosed usually know that their treatment was unnecessary, which makes them suspicious of screening and unwilling to return for tests.
options.C: Screening programmes do more harm than good, because the abnormalities they detect are usually harmless and the treatments that follow them are dangerous.
options.D: Counting detections overstates screening's value, since some detected conditions would never have caused harm, and those treated for them look just like patients truly helped.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Counting detections overstates screening's value, since some detected conditions would never have caused harm, and those treated for them look just like patients truly helped.

option_rationales.A: This repeats the paragraph's opening description of how screening is judged; it omits the argument that this measure overstates the benefit.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the overdiagnosed patient 'may well believe that screening saved them', which is the reverse.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says only 'some' detected conditions are harmless and says its argument does not imply that screening is 'never worthwhile', so this overstates it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that detection counts include harmless conditions whose treatment harms people, that such cases cannot be told apart from lives saved, and that counting detections 'overstates what screening achieves', while not condemning screening. The correct answer captures the claim and its reasons.
questions.common_misconception: Turning the critique of a measure into a rejection of screening.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be told apart from an overstated wrong option by the paragraph's final qualification.

questions.subtopic: Because every use spreads resistance, antibiotics are a shared resource whose use carries a common cost.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Every time an antibiotic is used, bacteria that happen to resist it gain an advantage over those that do not, so resistance spreads in proportion to use, including use that does the patient no good, as when antibiotics are taken for viral infections they cannot touch. This makes antibiotics unlike most medicines. A painkiller taken unnecessarily affects only the person who takes it; an antibiotic taken unnecessarily slightly reduces the usefulness of the drug for everyone. Decisions that look private, between one doctor and one patient, therefore have a shared cost. Treating antibiotics as a common resource, to be used when needed but not casually, is not excessive caution but a recognition of how they work.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Every time an antibiotic is used, bacteria that happen to resist it gain an advantage over those that do not, so resistance spreads in proportion to use, including use that does the patient no good, as when antibiotics are taken for viral infections they cannot touch. This makes antibiotics unlike most medicines. A painkiller taken unnecessarily affects only the person who takes it; an antibiotic taken unnecessarily slightly reduces the usefulness of the drug for everyone. Decisions that look private, between one doctor and one patient, therefore have a shared cost. Treating antibiotics as a common resource, to be used when needed but not casually, is not excessive caution but a recognition of how they work.

options.A: Antibiotics should be withheld from patients except in life-threatening cases, since every single use of them helps resistant bacteria spread further through the population.
options.B: Antibiotics have no effect on viral infections, so patients with colds and similar illnesses gain nothing at all from taking a course of them.
options.C: Unnecessary painkillers are as harmful to society as unnecessary antibiotics, since both kinds of medicine lose their usefulness when they are used too freely.
options.D: Since every use of an antibiotic, even a needless one, helps resistance spread, prescribing carries a shared cost, and the drugs should be treated as a common resource.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Since every use of an antibiotic, even a needless one, helps resistance spread, prescribing carries a shared cost, and the drugs should be treated as a common resource.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says antibiotics should be 'used when needed but not casually', which is far wider than life-threatening cases only.
option_rationales.B: This is an example of needless use given in passing; it leaves out the paragraph's point about the shared cost of every use.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph contrasts the two: a needless painkiller 'affects only the person who takes it', while a needless antibiotic affects everyone.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why resistance tracks use, contrasts antibiotics with painkillers, concludes that private prescribing decisions 'have a shared cost', and recommends treating antibiotics 'as a common resource'. The correct answer states the reason and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the example of viral infections, or overstating the recommendation into near-total restriction.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated directly in the last two sentences.

questions.subtopic: Many patients stop medicines by choice, so adherence depends more on learning their reasons than on reminders.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When patients fail to take medicines as prescribed, the problem is commonly described as one of forgetfulness or carelessness, and the proposed remedies are reminders: alarms, pill boxes, text messages. These help some people. But many patients who stop taking a drug have not forgotten it; they have decided, for reasons that seem good to them, such as side effects, cost, doubts about whether it works, or a regimen that clashes with their working day. Reminders do nothing for a patient who has chosen not to take a pill and may irritate one who has. Improving adherence therefore depends less on prompting patients than on finding out why they stop, which requires asking them.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When patients fail to take medicines as prescribed, the problem is commonly described as one of forgetfulness or carelessness, and the proposed remedies are reminders: alarms, pill boxes, text messages. These help some people. But many patients who stop taking a drug have not forgotten it; they have decided, for reasons that seem good to them, such as side effects, cost, doubts about whether it works, or a regimen that clashes with their working day. Reminders do nothing for a patient who has chosen not to take a pill and may irritate one who has. Improving adherence therefore depends less on prompting patients than on finding out why they stop, which requires asking them.

options.A: Many patients stop their medicines by choice rather than forgetfulness, so reminders help only some, and adherence depends more on learning why they stop.
options.B: Patients who stop taking their medicines are acting irrationally, since side effects and costs are seldom good reasons for abandoning a course of treatment.
options.C: Most failures to take medicines as prescribed arise from forgetfulness, which is why alarms and text messages are the most effective remedy for them.
options.D: Reminders such as alarms, pill boxes and text messages are ineffective, and they should no longer be offered to patients who fail to take their medicines.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Many patients stop their medicines by choice rather than forgetfulness, so reminders help only some, and adherence depends more on learning why they stop.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph describes the patients' reasons as ones 'that seem good to them' and does not judge them irrational.
option_rationales.C: This is the common description the paragraph corrects: 'many patients who stop taking a drug have not forgotten it'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says reminders 'help some people', so calling them ineffective and withdrawing them contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the usual diagnosis (forgetfulness) and remedy (reminders), grants that reminders 'help some people', argues that many patients stop deliberately, and concludes that adherence depends on 'finding out why they stop'. The correct answer covers the correction and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the common diagnosis the paragraph sets out to correct.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion is stated in the last sentence and wrong options are clearly off.

questions.subtopic: Open visiting in intensive care has mostly helped, but only where units prepare for it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: For much of the twentieth century, intensive care units kept families at a distance. Visiting was confined to short, fixed periods, on the reasoning that relatives would spread infection, tire patients and get in the way of urgent work. As more units have experimented with open visiting, these fears have largely failed to materialise: patients with family nearby tend to be calmer, and relatives who watch the care being given often understand and trust it better. Yet the case for openness is not unconditional. Nurses in units that opened their doors overnight without adding staff or space have described exhaustion from the constant presence of anxious onlookers, and some patients want rest more than company. The lesson is not that restriction was simply wrong, but that flexible visiting works when units plan for it rather than merely permit it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

For much of the twentieth century, intensive care units kept families at a distance. Visiting was confined to short, fixed periods, on the reasoning that relatives would spread infection, tire patients and get in the way of urgent work. As more units have experimented with open visiting, these fears have largely failed to materialise: patients with family nearby tend to be calmer, and relatives who watch the care being given often understand and trust it better. Yet the case for openness is not unconditional. Nurses in units that opened their doors overnight without adding staff or space have described exhaustion from the constant presence of anxious onlookers, and some patients want rest more than company. The lesson is not that restriction was simply wrong, but that flexible visiting works when units plan for it rather than merely permit it.

options.A: Open visiting in intensive care exhausts nurses and disturbs patients, so the fears of infection and disruption behind the old restrictions have turned out to be justified.
options.B: Relaxing intensive care visiting rules has mostly brought benefits, not the feared harms, but those benefits depend on units preparing for open visiting rather than merely allowing it.
options.C: Families who stay close by in intensive care units help patients remain calm, and by watching the treatment closely they come to understand and trust the staff far better.
options.D: The old restrictions on intensive care visiting were mistaken from the start, and units should now allow families unlimited access at every hour of the day.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Relaxing intensive care visiting rules has mostly brought benefits, not the feared harms, but those benefits depend on units preparing for open visiting rather than merely allowing it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the old fears 'have largely failed to materialise'; the exhaustion it mentions arises only where units opened without adding staff or space, so this reverses its finding.
option_rationales.C: This keeps only the benefits listed in the third sentence and drops the qualification that follows 'Yet the case for openness is not unconditional', so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'The lesson is not that restriction was simply wrong' and warns that opening doors overnight without preparation exhausted nurses, so this contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (the feared harms of open visiting 'have largely failed to materialise' and patients and relatives benefit) and then qualifies it: openness is 'not unconditional', and 'flexible visiting works when units plan for it rather than merely permit it'. The correct answer keeps both the finding and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that lists the benefits and forgetting the qualification, or swinging to the claim that the old fears were right.
questions.difficulty_reason: The finding and its qualification are both stated plainly in the last two sentences; wrong options are clearly one-sided.

questions.subtopic: Defensive medicine is sustained by professional culture, not only by fear of lawsuits.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Defensive medicine is usually described as a doctor's rational response to the threat of lawsuits: order the extra scan, refer to the specialist, and no court can say you overlooked anything. The description is accurate as far as it goes, but it locates the problem too narrowly. Many doctors who practise in places where litigation is rare still order tests whose results will not change what they do. What they fear is less a judge than a colleague's raised eyebrow, a patient's disappointment, or their own memory of the one case that went wrong. Reforming malpractice law may therefore reduce unnecessary testing less than its advocates expect. The habit is sustained by a professional culture in which doing more is felt as diligence and doing less as risk, and a culture is not dismantled by a statute.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Defensive medicine is usually described as a doctor's rational response to the threat of lawsuits: order the extra scan, refer to the specialist, and no court can say you overlooked anything. The description is accurate as far as it goes, but it locates the problem too narrowly. Many doctors who practise in places where litigation is rare still order tests whose results will not change what they do. What they fear is less a judge than a colleague's raised eyebrow, a patient's disappointment, or their own memory of the one case that went wrong. Reforming malpractice law may therefore reduce unnecessary testing less than its advocates expect. The habit is sustained by a professional culture in which doing more is felt as diligence and doing less as risk, and a culture is not dismantled by a statute.

options.A: Even in places where lawsuits are rare, many doctors still order tests and referrals whose results are unlikely to change the treatment they finally choose.
options.B: Because doctors order unnecessary tests chiefly to protect themselves in court, reforming malpractice law is the most direct and effective way to reduce defensive medicine.
options.C: Excess testing owes much to a medical culture that equates doing more with diligence, not just to fear of lawsuits, so changing malpractice law alone will achieve less than hoped.
options.D: Doctors who order extra tests are acting irrationally, since such tests never alter treatment and serve only to calm their own anxiety about mistakes in past cases.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Excess testing owes much to a medical culture that equates doing more with diligence, not just to fear of lawsuits, so changing malpractice law alone will achieve less than hoped.

option_rationales.A: This is the supporting observation in the third sentence; it omits the conclusion about professional culture and the limits of legal reform, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.B: This is the usual description the paragraph says 'locates the problem too narrowly'; it also predicts that legal reform will 'reduce unnecessary testing less than its advocates expect'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'Many doctors' order some tests that will not change what they do; it does not say all extra tests are useless or call doctors irrational, so 'never' overstates it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants that the lawsuit explanation is 'accurate as far as it goes' but argues it is too narrow: doctors fear colleagues, patients and their own memories, and 'doing more is felt as diligence'. Hence legal reform will achieve less than expected, because 'a culture is not dismantled by a statute'. The correct answer keeps both the wider cause and the consequence for reform.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that repeats the familiar lawsuit explanation, which the paragraph mentions first but then qualifies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The opening states the conventional view at length; the reader must see that the paragraph widens it rather than endorses it, and one wrong option is only the evidence.

questions.subtopic: Objections to diagnosing grief overlook that a label can secure help for the minority whose mourning is stuck.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a bereaved person is still unable to work or sleep months after a death, there is a growing tendency to describe the condition as a disorder and to offer treatment. Critics object that this turns an ordinary human experience into a pathology, and that sorrow proportionate to a loss is not something to be cured. The objection has force, but it assumes that the only alternative to a diagnosis is respect. In practice the alternative is often neglect: a person whose grief has hardened into years of isolation may receive nothing, because friends have stopped asking and no institution recognises the need. A label can be misused, and grief that is merely intense should not be hurried. Yet a name can also be what makes help available to the minority for whom mourning has stopped moving.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a bereaved person is still unable to work or sleep months after a death, there is a growing tendency to describe the condition as a disorder and to offer treatment. Critics object that this turns an ordinary human experience into a pathology, and that sorrow proportionate to a loss is not something to be cured. The objection has force, but it assumes that the only alternative to a diagnosis is respect. In practice the alternative is often neglect: a person whose grief has hardened into years of isolation may receive nothing, because friends have stopped asking and no institution recognises the need. A label can be misused, and grief that is merely intense should not be hurried. Yet a name can also be what makes help available to the minority for whom mourning has stopped moving.

options.A: Though merely intense grief should not be hurried into treatment, critics of diagnosis overlook that a label may secure help for those whose mourning has become stuck.
options.B: Diagnoses of grief are usually misused, yet they still matter because the friends of the bereaved gradually stop asking after them and leave them isolated.
options.C: Calling prolonged grief a disorder wrongly turns a normal and proportionate response to loss into a pathology, and so the practice ought to be resisted by doctors.
options.D: Every bereaved person who is still struggling months after a death should be diagnosed and treated, since friends and institutions otherwise abandon the grieving.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Though merely intense grief should not be hurried into treatment, critics of diagnosis overlook that a label may secure help for those whose mourning has become stuck.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says only that a label 'can be misused', not that it usually is, and it ties the value of a diagnosis to the minority whose mourning has stopped moving, which this option drops.
option_rationales.C: This is the critics' objection, which the paragraph grants 'has force' but then rebuts by pointing out that the real alternative to a diagnosis is 'often neglect'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph insists that 'grief that is merely intense should not be hurried' and confines the benefit of a label to 'the minority', so 'every bereaved person' contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports an objection to diagnosing grief, concedes its force, and then argues that it wrongly assumes 'the only alternative to a diagnosis is respect'. Its conclusion is qualified both ways: intense grief 'should not be hurried', yet a name can make help available 'to the minority for whom mourning has stopped moving'. The correct answer keeps the concession, the counterpoint and the restricted scope.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the critics' view, stated early and sympathetically, for the author's conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: A critique of a critique: the reported objection is stated persuasively, and one wrong option gets the conclusion half right while distorting degree and scope.

questions.subtopic: Consent fails mainly through conversation: doctors forget their words are technical and patients do not ask.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Patients often sign consent forms for procedures they do not understand, and the usual explanation is that the forms are badly written. That is part of it, but the deeper difficulty lies in conversation. Doctors learn a technical vocabulary so thoroughly that words like 'benign', 'negative' or 'unremarkable' stop sounding specialised to them, even though a patient may hear a negative result as bad news. Meanwhile patients, unwilling to appear slow or to waste a busy doctor's time, nod rather than ask. Each side leaves believing that information has been exchanged. Consent obtained in this way satisfies the paperwork while missing its purpose, which is that the person agreeing should know what they are agreeing to.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Patients often sign consent forms for procedures they do not understand, and the usual explanation is that the forms are badly written. That is part of it, but the deeper difficulty lies in conversation. Doctors learn a technical vocabulary so thoroughly that words like 'benign', 'negative' or 'unremarkable' stop sounding specialised to them, even though a patient may hear a negative result as bad news. Meanwhile patients, unwilling to appear slow or to waste a busy doctor's time, nod rather than ask. Each side leaves believing that information has been exchanged. Consent obtained in this way satisfies the paperwork while missing its purpose, which is that the person agreeing should know what they are agreeing to.

options.A: Patients sign consent forms they do not understand mainly because doctors deliberately use technical language to discourage questions and to save their own time.
options.B: Consent often fails less through bad forms than because doctors forget their words are technical and patients are reluctant to ask, so the gap goes unnoticed.
options.C: Consent forms should be rewritten in plain language and patients trained to question doctors, since only then can hospitals be sure that consent is truly informed.
options.D: Medical words such as 'negative' and 'unremarkable' mean something quite different to patients than they do to the doctors who have long used them at work.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Consent often fails less through bad forms than because doctors forget their words are technical and patients are reluctant to ask, so the gap goes unnoticed.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says technical words 'stop sounding specialised' to doctors, an unnoticed habit, not a deliberate tactic; it is patients who worry about wasting the doctor's time.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph proposes no remedy and treats the forms as only 'part of it'; the prescription and the word 'only' add what the paragraph does not say.
option_rationales.D: This is one illustration from the third sentence; it leaves out the patients' silence and the conclusion that consent misses its purpose, so it is too narrow.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets aside badly written forms as only 'part of it' and locates 'the deeper difficulty' in conversation: doctors no longer hear their vocabulary as technical, and patients 'nod rather than ask', so that 'Each side leaves believing that information has been exchanged'. The correct answer states this two-sided mechanism and its result.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the vivid example of 'negative' results instead of the general mechanism it illustrates.
questions.difficulty_reason: The central contrast is announced in the second sentence; the wrong options fail on plainly stated points.

questions.subtopic: The scarcity of public toilets quietly restricts the city for many residents.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Discussions of what makes a city welcoming tend to dwell on parks, transport and housing, and rarely mention public toilets. Yet their absence quietly shapes who can use the city at all. A healthy young commuter can manage a long day out on the strength of a visit to a cafe; an elderly person, a parent with small children, someone with a medical condition or a delivery rider on a twelve-hour shift often cannot. Such people learn to plan their routes around the few places they may use, or to stay at home. Toilets are expensive to build and to keep clean, and badly managed ones become a nuisance, so their scarcity is understandable. But a city that leaves this need to the goodwill of cafes has, without ever deciding to, made its streets less open to some of its residents than to others.

options.A: Public toilets are seldom built because they are costly and soon become a nuisance, which shows that cities are right to leave this need to cafes.
options.B: Elderly people, parents with young children and delivery riders on long shifts often plan their routes around the few toilets they can use, or else stay at home.
options.C: Though costly to provide well, public toilets matter more than urban debates admit, because their scarcity quietly limits the city for many residents who cannot rely on cafes.
options.D: Every city should build free public toilets on every street, since leaving the need to cafes is a deliberate policy of excluding poorer residents from public space.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Though costly to provide well, public toilets matter more than urban debates admit, because their scarcity quietly limits the city for many residents who cannot rely on cafes.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph grants the costs only to reject the conclusion: leaving the need to cafes has made the streets less open to some residents, so this reverses its point.
option_rationales.B: This repeats the illustration in the fourth sentence but leaves out the point it supports, that scarcity makes the streets 'less open to some of its residents than to others'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the exclusion happens 'without ever deciding to' and calls the scarcity 'understandable'; a deliberate policy and a demand for toilets on every street both distort it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that a neglected amenity shapes 'who can use the city at all': people who cannot rely on cafes plan around the few toilets or stay home. It concedes that toilets are costly and that scarcity is 'understandable', but concludes that leaving the need to cafes makes the city less open to some residents. The correct answer keeps the claim, who is affected and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the list of affected people, which is accurate but is only the evidence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The claim is stated in the second sentence and restated at the end; the wrong options fail on plainly worded points.

questions.subtopic: Regulating street vendors should begin from accommodation, not removal, while protecting pedestrians.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: City authorities often treat street vendors as a nuisance to be cleared: they block pavements, avoid taxes and make a district look disorderly. Each charge contains some truth, but together they describe vendors only from the point of view of those who drive past them. For the office cleaner who needs a cheap meal at six in the morning, or the migrant who cannot yet afford a shopfront, the stall is part of how the city works. Vendors also keep streets watched and lit after shops close, a service no budget pays for. None of this means pavements should belong to whoever claims them first; pedestrians have rights too. It means that regulation which begins from the goal of removal will usually destroy more than it orders, whereas regulation that begins from accommodation can address congestion without abolishing a livelihood.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Street vendors block pavements and avoid taxes, so although they serve poorer residents, city authorities are justified in clearing them from busy districts.
options.B: Street vendors provide cheap meals for early workers, a foothold for migrants, and an informal watch over streets that stay open after the shops have closed.
options.C: Pavements should be left free for vendors to use as they wish, since the cheap food and safety they provide outweigh any inconvenience caused to pedestrians.
options.D: Since vendors serve many residents and keep streets safer, cities should regulate them with the aim of accommodating rather than removing them, while protecting pedestrians.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Since vendors serve many residents and keep streets safer, cities should regulate them with the aim of accommodating rather than removing them, while protecting pedestrians.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph grants that each charge 'contains some truth' but argues that regulation aimed at removal 'will usually destroy more than it orders', so this reverses its conclusion.
option_rationales.B: This lists the supporting points from the middle sentences but omits the argument about how regulation should begin, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph explicitly says 'None of this means pavements should belong to whoever claims them first; pedestrians have rights too', so this contradicts its qualification.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the case against vendors, concedes that it 'contains some truth', shows what it leaves out (cheap meals, livelihoods, watched streets), limits its own claim with 'pedestrians have rights too', and concludes that regulation should begin 'from accommodation' rather than 'from the goal of removal'. The correct answer keeps the reason, the conclusion and the limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the list of benefits, which is accurate but leaves out what the paragraph argues for.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each capture one side of a balanced argument; the correct answer must hold the conclusion and the concession together.

questions.subtopic: Rivers mostly joined communities historically; their role as frontiers is largely a later political choice.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Atlases encourage us to see rivers as natural boundaries: a blue line on the map separates one province or country from the next, and it is tempting to assume the line was drawn there because the water divided people. For most of history the reverse was closer to the truth. Before railways, moving goods by water was far cheaper than moving them by land, so a river bound the communities along its banks into a single zone of trade, kinship and shared speech, while the hills on either side were the real obstacles. Rivers became frontiers largely when states, wanting lines that were easy to describe in treaties and to defend, chose them for that purpose. The division we read into the landscape is therefore often an administrative choice laid over a geography that once worked the other way. This is not to deny that some rivers, wide or violent, have always separated peoples.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Atlases encourage us to see rivers as natural boundaries: a blue line on the map separates one province or country from the next, and it is tempting to assume the line was drawn there because the water divided people. For most of history the reverse was closer to the truth. Before railways, moving goods by water was far cheaper than moving them by land, so a river bound the communities along its banks into a single zone of trade, kinship and shared speech, while the hills on either side were the real obstacles. Rivers became frontiers largely when states, wanting lines that were easy to describe in treaties and to defend, chose them for that purpose. The division we read into the landscape is therefore often an administrative choice laid over a geography that once worked the other way. This is not to deny that some rivers, wide or violent, have always separated peoples.

options.A: Before railways, carrying goods by water cost much less than carrying them overland, which is why hills rather than rivers were the main barriers to trade.
options.B: Rivers have never truly divided human communities, and borders drawn along them are wholly artificial lines imposed by states that ignored how settlement actually took shape.
options.C: The habit of seeing rivers as natural dividers mostly reflects later choices by states, since rivers usually joined the communities along them, though some have genuinely kept peoples apart.
options.D: States drew borders along rivers because, long before railways, river valleys already separated distinct communities that differed in their trade, kinship and speech.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The habit of seeing rivers as natural dividers mostly reflects later choices by states, since rivers usually joined the communities along them, though some have genuinely kept peoples apart.

option_rationales.A: This is accurate but is only the supporting reason in the third sentence; it says nothing about the paragraph's main claim that river frontiers are largely political choices.
option_rationales.B: The last sentence concedes that 'some rivers, wide or violent, have always separated peoples', and the paragraph says the division is 'often', not always, an administrative choice, so 'never' and 'wholly' overstate it.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the relation: the paragraph says a river bound riverside communities 'into a single zone of trade, kinship and shared speech' and that states chose rivers for ease of description and defence.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the view that rivers are natural boundaries. Its claim is that 'the reverse was closer to the truth' because water transport joined riverside communities, that rivers 'became frontiers largely when states' chose them, and, as a qualification, that some rivers 'have always separated peoples'. The correct answer keeps the reversal, the political explanation and the concession; the closest wrong option drops the concession and turns 'largely' and 'often' into absolutes.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the absolute version, which sounds like a bold restatement of the thesis but contradicts the final sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer and the strongest wrong option differ only in degree; the reader must weigh the hedges 'largely', 'often' and the closing concession.

questions.subtopic: For many shrinking cities, planning for a smaller population is costly but more honest than chasing growth.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Cities that lose population are usually discussed as patients awaiting a cure: planners draw up schemes to attract new industry, new residents and new investment, measuring success by whether the numbers start rising again. A different approach, tried in some declining industrial towns, accepts that the population may not return and asks how a smaller city can be a good one. Vacant blocks become parks or allotments, services are concentrated in the districts that remain lived in, and the city plans for the people it has rather than those it lost. The first approach keeps hope alive but often spends heavily on growth that never arrives; the second risks being read as surrender and can abandon residents of emptying neighbourhoods. Neither is costless, but only the second is honest about the likely future of many such places.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Cities that lose population are usually discussed as patients awaiting a cure: planners draw up schemes to attract new industry, new residents and new investment, measuring success by whether the numbers start rising again. A different approach, tried in some declining industrial towns, accepts that the population may not return and asks how a smaller city can be a good one. Vacant blocks become parks or allotments, services are concentrated in the districts that remain lived in, and the city plans for the people it has rather than those it lost. The first approach keeps hope alive but often spends heavily on growth that never arrives; the second risks being read as surrender and can abandon residents of emptying neighbourhoods. Neither is costless, but only the second is honest about the likely future of many such places.

options.A: Though it has costs, planning for a smaller but liveable city is more realistic for many declining cities than spending heavily on growth that may never come.
options.B: Accepting decline is a form of surrender that abandons residents of emptying districts, so declining cities should keep investing in bringing back residents and industry.
options.C: Shrinking cities may either pursue renewed growth or adapt to a smaller population, and each of these two strategies has distinct advantages as well as distinct costs.
options.D: Declining cities should concentrate services in occupied districts and turn empty blocks into parks, since trying to attract new industry is always a waste of public money.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Though it has costs, planning for a smaller but liveable city is more realistic for many declining cities than spending heavily on growth that may never come.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph mentions that the second approach 'risks being read as surrender' as a cost, not as its conclusion, and it ends by favouring that approach, so this reverses it.
option_rationales.C: This reports the comparison but drops the verdict in the last sentence that 'only the second is honest about the likely future of many such places'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says growth schemes 'often' spend on growth that never arrives, not always, and it admits the second approach has costs; 'always a waste' overstates it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares two responses to population loss, gives each a cost ('Neither is costless'), and then judges that 'only the second is honest about the likely future of many such places'. The correct answer keeps the preference, the admitted costs and the scope ('many').
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the even-handed comparison and missing that the paragraph ends with a verdict.
questions.difficulty_reason: A neutral wrong option describes the comparison accurately; it is wrong only because the paragraph takes a side in its final clause.

questions.subtopic: Inability excuses only when a duty was never within one's power, not when one destroyed one's own ability.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A familiar principle in ethics holds that 'ought' implies 'can': it makes no sense to say that someone ought to do what they are unable to do. Nobody blames a person for failing to rescue a drowning child from a river on the other side of the world. The principle seems obvious, but it needs care. A man who could have repaid a loan but carelessly made himself unable to, by spending the money he had set aside for it, is not excused by his present inability. What the principle rules out, properly understood, is an obligation that was never within a person's power to meet, not an obligation that a person has put beyond his own reach.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A familiar principle in ethics holds that 'ought' implies 'can': it makes no sense to say that someone ought to do what they are unable to do. Nobody blames a person for failing to rescue a drowning child from a river on the other side of the world. The principle seems obvious, but it needs care. A man who could have repaid a loan but carelessly made himself unable to, by spending the money he had set aside for it, is not excused by his present inability. What the principle rules out, properly understood, is an obligation that was never within a person's power to meet, not an obligation that a person has put beyond his own reach.

options.A: The principle that duty requires ability is mistaken, since people are often rightly blamed for failing to do things that they were in fact unable to do.
options.B: Inability cancels a duty only when the person never had the power to meet it, not when the person has carelessly made the duty impossible.
options.C: Nobody can reasonably be blamed for failing to rescue a drowning child whom they could not possibly have reached in time to save from the water.
options.D: Whenever people are unable to do what is asked of them, they cannot be blamed for failing, whatever the reason they now find themselves unable to act.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Inability cancels a duty only when the person never had the power to meet it, not when the person has carelessly made the duty impossible.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph keeps the principle and says it 'needs care'; it narrows what the principle rules out rather than calling it mistaken.
option_rationales.C: This restates the opening illustration only; it misses the refinement that makes up the rest of the paragraph, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph denies that inability always excuses: the man who spent the money set aside for his loan 'is not excused by his present inability'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states the principle, grants its obvious core, and then refines it with the example of the man who spent the money for his loan: what the principle rules out is an obligation 'never within a person's power to meet, not an obligation that a person has put beyond his own reach'. The correct answer states exactly this refinement.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the unqualified version of the principle, which the paragraph sets up only to refine.
questions.difficulty_reason: The refinement is stated outright in the last sentence; wrong options are the unrefined principle, the opening example and a reversal.

questions.subtopic: Hypocrisy undermines a critic's authority, not the truth of the criticism, and admission can restore standing.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is widely held that a hypocrite has no standing to blame: the smoker who lectures his son about cigarettes, we say, should keep quiet. There is something right in this. Blame from someone who excuses the same fault in himself rings false, and it invites the reply 'Look who is talking'. But the view goes wrong if it implies that the criticism itself is mistaken. The son's smoking is no healthier because his father smokes, and a fault does not become acceptable merely because the person naming it shares it. What hypocrisy damages is the critic's authority to demand change, not the truth of what he says, and even that damage can be repaired if the critic admits his own failing. A hypocrite who says 'I do it too, and I am wrong to' has not forfeited the right to speak.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is widely held that a hypocrite has no standing to blame: the smoker who lectures his son about cigarettes, we say, should keep quiet. There is something right in this. Blame from someone who excuses the same fault in himself rings false, and it invites the reply 'Look who is talking'. But the view goes wrong if it implies that the criticism itself is mistaken. The son's smoking is no healthier because his father smokes, and a fault does not become acceptable merely because the person naming it shares it. What hypocrisy damages is the critic's authority to demand change, not the truth of what he says, and even that damage can be repaired if the critic admits his own failing. A hypocrite who says 'I do it too, and I am wrong to' has not forfeited the right to speak.

options.A: A hypocrite's criticism may be correct but carries no weight, and since nothing can restore his authority, he should leave the task of blaming to others.
options.B: People who share a fault have no right to criticise it in others, because blame from anyone guilty of the same failing always rings false to those who hear it.
options.C: Since a criticism is no less true when the critic shares the fault, hypocrisy does nothing to weaken anyone's standing to blame other people for that fault.
options.D: Hypocrisy weakens a critic's authority to demand change but not the correctness of the criticism, and a critic who admits sharing the fault can recover the standing to speak.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Hypocrisy weakens a critic's authority to demand change but not the correctness of the criticism, and a critic who admits sharing the fault can recover the standing to speak.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the damage to authority 'can be repaired if the critic admits his own failing', so the claim that nothing can restore it is false.
option_rationales.B: This is the widely held view the paragraph qualifies; it ends by saying a hypocrite who admits the fault 'has not forfeited the right to speak'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph grants 'There is something right in this' and says hypocrisy 'damages' the critic's authority to demand change, so 'does nothing to weaken' contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph separates two things the common view runs together: the truth of a criticism, which hypocrisy leaves untouched ('The son's smoking is no healthier because his father smokes'), and the critic's 'authority to demand change', which hypocrisy damages. It then adds that this damage 'can be repaired' by admitting the fault. The correct answer holds all three parts; each wrong option gets one part wrong.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that defends the criticism's truth and overlooking that the paragraph does concede a real loss of authority.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option is right about one of the paragraph's three claims and wrong about another; the reader must track the distinction between truth and authority and the closing repair.

questions.subtopic: Since many interests are not interests in experiences, death need not end them, so the dead can be harmed.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Can the dead be harmed? The sceptic replies that harm requires someone to suffer it, and the dead suffer nothing. Yet we do seem to wrong a person when, after her death, we break the promise we made to her, scatter the collection she spent her life assembling, or spread lies about her. One way to make sense of this is to notice that many of our interests are not interests in experiences. A woman who wants her life's work to survive wants something to be true of the world, not merely to feel that it is; that is why being deceived about it during her lifetime would also harm her. If interests of this kind can be set back without the person's knowledge, then death, which ends experience, need not end every interest.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Can the dead be harmed? The sceptic replies that harm requires someone to suffer it, and the dead suffer nothing. Yet we do seem to wrong a person when, after her death, we break the promise we made to her, scatter the collection she spent her life assembling, or spread lies about her. One way to make sense of this is to notice that many of our interests are not interests in experiences. A woman who wants her life's work to survive wants something to be true of the world, not merely to feel that it is; that is why being deceived about it during her lifetime would also harm her. If interests of this kind can be set back without the person's knowledge, then death, which ends experience, need not end every interest.

options.A: The dead can be harmed because some form of experience continues after death, which is why lies told about them seem to wrong them so deeply.
options.B: A person who wants her life's work to survive is harmed if she is deceived about its fate, even if she never discovers the deception during her life.
options.C: Because many interests concern how the world goes rather than what a person experiences, they can be set back after death, so the dead may genuinely be harmed.
options.D: Since harm needs someone who suffers it and the dead experience nothing, breaking promises made to them can wrong only the living people who remember them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Because many interests concern how the world goes rather than what a person experiences, they can be set back after death, so the dead may genuinely be harmed.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph describes death as that 'which ends experience' and rests its case on interests that do not depend on experience, so this contradicts its reasoning.
option_rationales.B: This is the supporting case about deception during a lifetime; it omits the conclusion about death, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.D: This is the sceptic's reply from the second sentence, extended; the paragraph argues against it by distinguishing interests from experiences.

questions.explanation: The paragraph answers the sceptic by noting that 'many of our interests are not interests in experiences'; such interests can be set back 'without the person's knowledge', as the case of deception shows, so 'death, which ends experience, need not end every interest'. The correct answer gives the premise and the conclusion together.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the deception example because it is the paragraph's most concrete step, and missing the conclusion it leads to.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument is abstract and runs through an analogy; one wrong option is the analogy without the conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Pity and compassion differ in stance, not warmth: only compassion treats the sufferer as an equal.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Pity and compassion are often treated as the same feeling, but they place the one who feels them differently. Pity looks down. It registers another's misfortune from a position of safety, and it often carries a quiet relief that the misfortune belongs to someone else; this is why people who are pitied so often resent it. Compassion stands alongside. It begins from the recognition that the other person's suffering is the kind of thing that could befall anyone, oneself included, and so it treats the sufferer as an equal rather than as an object of concern. The difference is not that one is warmer than the other, for pity can be intensely felt. It is that only compassion leaves the dignity of the sufferer intact.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Pity and compassion are often treated as the same feeling, but they place the one who feels them differently. Pity looks down. It registers another's misfortune from a position of safety, and it often carries a quiet relief that the misfortune belongs to someone else; this is why people who are pitied so often resent it. Compassion stands alongside. It begins from the recognition that the other person's suffering is the kind of thing that could befall anyone, oneself included, and so it treats the sufferer as an equal rather than as an object of concern. The difference is not that one is warmer than the other, for pity can be intensely felt. It is that only compassion leaves the dignity of the sufferer intact.

options.A: Pity is a selfish emotion that ought to be suppressed entirely, since it involves relief at another's suffering and treats the sufferer as an object of concern.
options.B: People who are pitied often resent it, because pity registers their misfortune from a position of safety and carries relief that the misfortune is not one's own.
options.C: Compassion is a deeper and warmer feeling than pity, which is why people who are pitied resent it while those who receive compassion feel respected by it.
options.D: Pity and compassion differ less in intensity than in stance: pity regards the sufferer from above, while compassion sees an equal and so preserves the sufferer's dignity.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Pity and compassion differ less in intensity than in stance: pity regards the sufferer from above, while compassion sees an equal and so preserves the sufferer's dignity.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says pity 'often' carries relief, not always, and it recommends nothing; calling it selfish and urging its suppression goes beyond the text.
option_rationales.B: This describes pity alone and leaves out compassion and the contrast that is the paragraph's point, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'The difference is not that one is warmer than the other, for pity can be intensely felt', so this misstates the basis of the contrast.

questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts the two feelings by where they place the one who feels them: pity 'looks down', compassion 'stands alongside'. It then rules out the obvious alternative ('not that one is warmer than the other') and ends with the real difference: 'only compassion leaves the dignity of the sufferer intact'. The correct answer captures the stance contrast and the denial that it is about warmth.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that ranks compassion as warmer, which the paragraph explicitly denies.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option states the contrast in terms of warmth, which the paragraph rules out in one clause near the end.

questions.subtopic: Impostor feelings are often a reasonable response to exclusionary settings, not only an individual fault.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Impostor feelings, the private conviction that one's success is undeserved and will soon be exposed, are commonly described as a disorder of self-perception to be corrected by building confidence. The description fits some cases. But it treats as a fault in the individual a response that is often a reasonable reading of the situation. A first-generation student surrounded by peers who seem to know unspoken rules, or the only woman in a department, may feel out of place because she has been placed in a setting that signals, in many small ways, that she does not belong. Confidence training alone asks her to stop noticing those signals. It would be wiser to treat persistent impostor feelings as information about environments as well as about the people in them.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Impostor feelings, the private conviction that one's success is undeserved and will soon be exposed, are commonly described as a disorder of self-perception to be corrected by building confidence. The description fits some cases. But it treats as a fault in the individual a response that is often a reasonable reading of the situation. A first-generation student surrounded by peers who seem to know unspoken rules, or the only woman in a department, may feel out of place because she has been placed in a setting that signals, in many small ways, that she does not belong. Confidence training alone asks her to stop noticing those signals. It would be wiser to treat persistent impostor feelings as information about environments as well as about the people in them.

options.A: First-generation students and women in departments dominated by men are especially likely to feel that their success is undeserved and will soon be exposed.
options.B: Impostor feelings are not only a distorted self-image but often a sensible response to settings signalling exclusion, so they also carry information about environments.
options.C: Impostor feelings are a distorted way of seeing oneself, and the best remedy is training that builds the confidence of the individuals who privately experience them.
options.D: Impostor feelings are never really about the individual but are created entirely by unwelcoming institutions, so confidence training is pointless and should be abandoned.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Impostor feelings are not only a distorted self-image but often a sensible response to settings signalling exclusion, so they also carry information about environments.

option_rationales.A: These are illustrations, and the paragraph makes no claim about which groups are most likely to have such feelings; the option misses its point about remedies.
option_rationales.C: This is the common description the paragraph says fits only 'some cases'; it argues that confidence training 'alone' misses what the feelings reveal about environments.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph concedes that the individual description 'fits some cases' and asks for attention to environments 'as well as' people, so 'never' and 'entirely' overstate it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the usual view (a disorder of self-perception, fixed by confidence), grants that it 'fits some cases', and then argues that the feelings are 'often a reasonable reading of the situation' in settings that signal non-belonging. It concludes that they should be treated as 'information about environments as well as about the people in them'. The correct answer keeps the reinterpretation, its hedges and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Swinging from the individual view to the opposite extreme and ignoring 'fits some cases' and 'as well as'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer and the extreme wrong option share the reinterpretation; they differ only in degree, which turns on two short qualifiers.

questions.subtopic: Actions are regretted more in the short run, inactions more over a lifetime.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: People asked about a recent decision usually regret what they did more than what they failed to do: the hasty purchase or the unwise remark stings more than the opportunity let pass. Asked to look back over their lives, however, many report the reverse; the courses not taken, the things left unsaid, come to dominate. One explanation is that the consequences of an action are bounded and visible, so they can be repaired, excused or absorbed into a story of learning, while the consequences of inaction remain open, an unlived alternative that imagination keeps improving. If so, the familiar finding that actions are regretted more is not false, but it describes only the short run; over time the balance appears to shift.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

People asked about a recent decision usually regret what they did more than what they failed to do: the hasty purchase or the unwise remark stings more than the opportunity let pass. Asked to look back over their lives, however, many report the reverse; the courses not taken, the things left unsaid, come to dominate. One explanation is that the consequences of an action are bounded and visible, so they can be repaired, excused or absorbed into a story of learning, while the consequences of inaction remain open, an unlived alternative that imagination keeps improving. If so, the familiar finding that actions are regretted more is not false, but it describes only the short run; over time the balance appears to shift.

options.A: Actions tend to be regretted more in the short term but inactions more over a lifetime, perhaps because unchosen paths stay open to imagination while the results of actions are settled.
options.B: Because the results of actions can be repaired or excused, people regret their actions less as time passes and, in the end, cease to regret them at all.
options.C: People regret what they fail to do more than what they actually do, so the familiar claim that actions are regretted more reflects a mistake about human memory.
options.D: Short-term regret centres on actions and long-term regret on inactions, which shows that memory distorts the past and makes early judgements of our choices unreliable.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Actions tend to be regretted more in the short term but inactions more over a lifetime, perhaps because unchosen paths stay open to imagination while the results of actions are settled.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says only that 'the balance appears to shift' towards inaction; it never says regret for actions disappears, and the option drops inaction entirely.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the familiar finding 'is not false' but 'describes only the short run', so declaring it a mistake reverses the paragraph's qualification.
option_rationales.D: The first half is right, but the paragraph explains the shift by the open-endedness of inaction, not by a failure of memory, and it says the short-run finding 'is not false', so it does not call early judgements unreliable.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (recent decisions: actions regretted more), sets beside it a reversal over a lifetime ('many report the reverse'), offers a tentative explanation ('One explanation is', 'If so'), and concludes that the familiar finding 'describes only the short run'. The correct answer keeps both time scales, the tentative cause and the hedged tone; the closest wrong option has the right pattern but attaches an explanation the paragraph does not give.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the first half of an option and not checking the explanation it adds.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options have the correct short-run and long-run pattern in part; one is separated from the correct answer only by the cause it supplies.

questions.subtopic: Satisfaction depends on whom people compare themselves with; upward comparison can motivate but often breeds discontent.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: People rarely judge their own situation in isolation; they compare it with that of others, and the others they choose are usually those slightly better off. Such upward comparison can motivate, since a colleague who is a little more skilled shows what is within reach. But when the comparison is constant and the gap seems fixed, it breeds dissatisfaction even among people who are doing well by any absolute measure. A worker whose salary rises may feel poorer if her neighbours' salaries rise faster. Contentment, on this account, depends less on what one has than on whom one measures oneself against.

options.A: A worker whose pay increases may still feel poorer than before if the neighbours living around her are receiving larger increases each year than her own.
options.B: People usually compare themselves with those who are worse off, which motivates them to work harder and keeps them content even when their own incomes fall.
options.C: Since people measure themselves against those slightly better off, contentment depends on whom they compare with; such comparison can motivate but, when constant, breeds discontent.
options.D: Comparing oneself with others is always harmful, since it makes even prosperous people dissatisfied, so people should judge their lives by absolute standards of wealth alone.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Since people measure themselves against those slightly better off, contentment depends on whom they compare with; such comparison can motivate but, when constant, breeds discontent.

option_rationales.A: This is the illustration in the fourth sentence; it omits the general claim about comparison and its two effects, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says people compare with 'those slightly better off', so this reverses the direction of comparison and its effect.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says upward comparison 'can motivate', so 'always harmful' contradicts it, and it offers no advice about absolute standards.

questions.common_misconception: Choosing the salary example, which is vivid but only illustrates the point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated in the first and last sentences; each wrong option is a detail, an absolute or a reversal.

questions.subtopic: Corrected analyses suggest a modest hot hand exists: the belief is exaggerated, not baseless.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: For decades the belief that basketball players get a 'hot hand', becoming more likely to score after a run of successes, was a textbook example of people seeing patterns in randomness. Analyses of shooting records found that hits did not cluster more than chance would predict, and the belief was filed alongside other errors of intuition. Later work identified a subtle flaw in the way those records had been analysed: the method used was biased toward finding no streakiness. Corrected analyses suggest that a modest hot hand may exist after all. This does not vindicate the fans entirely, since the effect appears far smaller than players and spectators believe. The episode shows instead that a debunking can itself rest on an error, and that a belief may be exaggerated without being baseless.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: People readily see patterns in random events, as belief in the basketball hot hand shows, since shooting records reveal no clustering of successful shots at all.
options.B: The hot hand, dismissed as an illusion, may exist in modest form once a flaw in earlier analyses is corrected, so the belief is exaggerated, not baseless.
options.C: Later research has shown that sports fans were right all along about the hot hand, and that the earlier studies dismissing it should now simply be disregarded.
options.D: Since debunkings can rest on errors, beliefs that experts dismiss as illusions usually turn out to be correct once the original evidence is analysed again.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The hot hand, dismissed as an illusion, may exist in modest form once a flaw in earlier analyses is corrected, so the belief is exaggerated, not baseless.

option_rationales.A: This is the earlier view the paragraph reports and then revises: corrected analyses 'suggest that a modest hot hand may exist after all'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the correction 'does not vindicate the fans entirely', since the effect 'appears far smaller' than they believe, so 'right all along' overstates it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph draws a lesson from one episode, that a debunking 'can' rest on an error; 'usually turn out to be correct' generalises far beyond it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph traces a finding and its revision: the hot hand was dismissed, a flaw in the method was found, and corrected analyses suggest 'a modest hot hand may exist after all'. It then qualifies the revision ('does not vindicate the fans entirely') and ends that the belief 'may be exaggerated without being baseless'. The correct answer keeps the revision and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the revision as a full vindication, or stopping at the earlier debunking reported in the first two sentences.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph moves through three positions; wrong options capture the first, an overstated second and an overgeneralised lesson.

questions.subtopic: Haggling, which looks wasteful to outsiders, discovers prices and builds customer relationships.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: To a visitor used to fixed prices, haggling in a bazaar can look like inefficiency, a waste of time over sums too small to matter. For the trader it does useful work. In a market without price tags, the opening figure lets the seller learn what a customer is willing to pay, so that the wealthy visitor and the local regular can be charged differently without either being told so. The exchange also builds a relationship: a buyer who returns and bargains well is recognised, and the next deal starts from a friendlier figure. What seems like friction is, in such markets, the means by which prices are discovered and loyalty is formed.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

To a visitor used to fixed prices, haggling in a bazaar can look like inefficiency, a waste of time over sums too small to matter. For the trader it does useful work. The exchange also builds a relationship: a buyer who returns and bargains well is recognised, and the next deal starts from a friendlier figure. What seems like friction is, in such markets, the means by which prices are discovered and loyalty is formed.

options.A: Bazaar traders use haggling mainly to cheat wealthy visitors, charging them far more than local customers while pretending that the price is the same for all.
options.B: Haggling over small sums wastes the time of buyers and sellers alike, which is why most modern markets have replaced it with fixed and clearly labelled prices.
options.C: A buyer who returns to the same trader and bargains well is recognised, so that the next deal between them begins from a friendlier opening price.
options.D: Haggling, which outsiders see as wasteful, lets traders learn what each buyer will pay and build ties with returning customers, so it serves real purposes.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Haggling, which outsiders see as wasteful, lets traders learn what each buyer will pay and build ties with returning customers, so it serves real purposes.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph notes that different buyers can be charged differently but treats this as price discovery, not cheating; the moral charge and 'mainly' are added.
option_rationales.B: This is the visitor's impression that the paragraph sets aside; the claim about modern markets replacing haggling is not made at all.
option_rationales.C: This is one of the two functions the paragraph describes; it leaves out price discovery and the general point, so it is too narrow.

questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts the visitor's view of haggling as 'inefficiency' with the work it does for the trader: it discovers what each customer will pay and builds a relationship with returning buyers. The last sentence sums up: what 'seems like friction' is how 'prices are discovered and loyalty is formed'. The correct answer states both functions against the outsider's view.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the relationship detail, which is only half of what the paragraph claims.
questions.difficulty_reason: The two functions are named in the final sentence; wrong options are the rejected view, a moral distortion and one half.

questions.subtopic: Monetising a hobby suits some, but for many it destroys the freedom from obligation that made it valuable.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It has become common advice that anyone with a hobby should turn it into a side income: sell the pottery, charge for the baking, open a channel for the guitar playing. The advice is not foolish, and for some people a pastime becomes a satisfying second livelihood. But it rests on the assumption that an activity is improved by acquiring a market price, and for many people the opposite is true. A hobby is valuable partly because nothing depends on it; one can do it badly, stop for a month, or follow a whim without disappointing anyone. Once customers, ratings and deadlines arrive, the activity begins to resemble the work it once offered relief from. Some pursuits are worth keeping precisely because they earn nothing.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
