options.A: Turning hobbies into income suits some people, but for many it destroys what made the hobby valuable, its freedom from obligation, by making it resemble ordinary work.
options.B: Hobbies are valuable mainly because people can do them badly or drop them for a month, which is why they make poor businesses that seldom earn money.
options.C: People should never sell what they make in their spare time, since earning money from any activity inevitably destroys the pleasure it once gave them.
options.D: A hobby is a valuable source of extra income, and people who develop their pastimes into small businesses often find in them a satisfying second livelihood.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Turning hobbies into income suits some people, but for many it destroys what made the hobby valuable, its freedom from obligation, by making it resemble ordinary work.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says a hobby is valuable 'partly', not mainly, because nothing depends on it, and it says nothing about hobbies making poor businesses or earning little; that conclusion is added.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph grants that 'for some people a pastime becomes a satisfying second livelihood', so 'never' and 'inevitably' contradict it.
option_rationales.D: This is the common advice and its best case, which the paragraph concedes for 'some people' before arguing that for many 'the opposite is true'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports common advice, concedes that it works for 'some people', and then challenges its assumption: a hobby is valuable 'partly because nothing depends on it', and once customers and deadlines arrive it 'begins to resemble the work it once offered relief from'. The correct answer keeps the concession, the scope 'many' and the reason.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the conceded best case, stated early, for the paragraph's view.
questions.difficulty_reason: A concession and a reported view precede the argument; one wrong option borrows the argument's premise and attaches an outside conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Casual dress codes replace learnable written rules with unwritten ones that still sort people, less visibly.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When offices relax their dress codes, the change is usually welcomed as a move towards equality: without suits and ties, the argument goes, the junior clerk and the senior partner look alike, and people are judged by their work rather than their clothes. The intention is sincere, but the result is often a code that has become harder, not easier, to read. A formal rule could be learned once and followed by anyone who could afford a suit; the new norms, which separate the right kind of casual from the wrong kind, are rarely written down and are absorbed mostly by those already at home in the social world that sets them. The newcomer who arrives in the wrong trainers has broken no stated rule and cannot easily find out which unstated one she has broken. Relaxing a code, in short, need not relax its power to sort people; it may only make that power less visible.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Abolishing suits and ties in offices removes the visible markers of rank, so that junior and senior staff look alike and are judged mainly on the quality of their work.
options.B: Relaxed dress codes, though meant to equalise, often swap learnable written rules for unwritten ones that favour insiders, so clothing may sort people as before, only less visibly.
options.C: Casual dress codes are adopted insincerely by employers who wish to keep newcomers out of senior roles while appearing to treat all their staff as equals.
options.D: Offices should return to formal dress codes, because written rules about clothing are fairer than casual norms and can be followed by anyone who wishes to.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Relaxed dress codes, though meant to equalise, often swap learnable written rules for unwritten ones that favour insiders, so clothing may sort people as before, only less visibly.

option_rationales.A: This is the hope the paragraph reports in its first sentence; it goes on to argue that the result is 'often a code that has become harder, not easier, to read'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'The intention is sincere'; the sorting it describes is an unintended effect of unwritten norms, not a hidden aim.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph prescribes nothing, and it limits the virtue of formal rules to those 'who could afford a suit', so 'anyone who wishes to' and the recommendation both go beyond it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the egalitarian case for relaxed codes, grants that 'The intention is sincere', and argues that the result is often harder to read: formal rules could be 'learned once', while casual norms are unwritten and 'absorbed mostly by those already at home' in the world that sets them. Its conclusion is hedged: relaxing a code 'need not relax its power to sort people; it may only make that power less visible'. The correct answer keeps the sincere intention, the mechanism, the hedges and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the prescription to restore formal codes, which reads the comparison as a recommendation, or the insincerity reading, which ignores an explicit concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close inferences a reader might draw (go back to formal codes; the policy is a cover) and are ruled out only by a short concession and the limited claim made for formal rules.

questions.subtopic: Urban anonymity costs loneliness but gives a freedom close-knit towns seldom allow.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Small towns are often praised for their closeness: everyone knows your name, and help is never far away. Large cities are faulted for the opposite, a crowd in which no one notices whether you thrive or fail. The contrast is fair as far as it goes, but it leaves out what anonymity gives. To be known by everyone is also to be watched by everyone, and for a young person whose ambitions, beliefs or way of life depart from the local norm, the town's closeness can feel like a cage. The indifference of the city is what allows such people to try out a new self without asking permission. Loneliness is a real cost of urban life, but it is the price of a freedom that intimate communities rarely offer.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Small towns are often praised for their closeness: everyone knows your name, and help is never far away. Large cities are faulted for the opposite, a crowd in which no one notices whether you thrive or fail. The contrast is fair as far as it goes, but it leaves out what anonymity gives. To be known by everyone is also to be watched by everyone, and for a young person whose ambitions, beliefs or way of life depart from the local norm, the town's closeness can feel like a cage. The indifference of the city is what allows such people to try out a new self without asking permission. Loneliness is a real cost of urban life, but it is the price of a freedom that intimate communities rarely offer.

options.A: Urban anonymity, usually counted only as a cause of loneliness, also gives people who depart from local norms a freedom that close-knit towns seldom allow.
options.B: Anonymity makes city life better than small town life in every respect, since the loneliness that people complain of in large cities is largely imagined.
options.C: Young people whose ambitions or beliefs differ from those of their home town often experience its closeness as a cage from which they long to escape.
options.D: Large cities are lonely places where nobody notices anyone else, whereas small towns provide the closeness and ready help that people need in order to thrive.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Urban anonymity, usually counted only as a cause of loneliness, also gives people who depart from local norms a freedom that close-knit towns seldom allow.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph calls loneliness 'a real cost of urban life', so calling it imagined, and the city better 'in every respect', contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: This is one step of the argument; it leaves out the city's side of the comparison and the weighing of loneliness against freedom, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.D: This is the familiar contrast the paragraph calls 'fair as far as it goes' before adding what it 'leaves out', the freedom anonymity gives.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts the usual contrast as 'fair as far as it goes', then adds what it omits: being known is also being watched, and the city's indifference lets nonconforming people 'try out a new self'. It ends by weighing the two: loneliness is 'a real cost' but 'the price of a freedom that intimate communities rarely offer'. The correct answer keeps the added point and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the extreme option because it favours the city, which seems to be the paragraph's side, without noticing it denies the conceded cost.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph takes a side while conceding a cost; the extreme wrong option is on the right side but drops the concession.

questions.subtopic: Period labels are indispensable but carry their coiners' judgements, which unwary historians inherit.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Historians divide the past into periods, and the names they choose do more than organise it. To call a thousand years of European history the 'Middle Ages' is to describe them as an interval between two more important times, a long pause between the classical world and its supposed rebirth. The label was coined by people who wished to see themselves as reviving antiquity, and it carried their judgement into textbooks for centuries. Periods are indispensable; without them the past would be an undifferentiated stream. But a period name is never a neutral container. It embeds a view about what mattered, and the historian who uses it without noticing this inherits a verdict rather than reaching one.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Historians should abandon period labels such as the 'Middle Ages', since dividing the past into named periods inevitably distorts how students and scholars understand it.
options.B: Because history without periods would be an undifferentiated stream, the names that historians give to periods are neutral containers that help to organise the past.
options.C: The term 'Middle Ages' was coined by people who saw themselves as reviving antiquity, and it presents a thousand years as a pause between two greater eras.
options.D: Period labels are needed to organise history, yet they carry their coiners' judgements, so historians who use them unthinkingly adopt verdicts they never examined.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Period labels are needed to organise history, yet they carry their coiners' judgements, so historians who use them unthinkingly adopt verdicts they never examined.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'Periods are indispensable'; its complaint is against using names 'without noticing' what they embed, not against periods or names as such.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the reverse: 'a period name is never a neutral container', even though periods themselves are indispensable.
option_rationales.C: This is the example the paragraph uses; it leaves out the general claim about all period names and what historians inherit, so it is too narrow.

questions.explanation: The paragraph uses the 'Middle Ages' to show that period names 'do more than organise' the past. It concedes that 'Periods are indispensable', but insists that a name 'embeds a view about what mattered', so a historian who uses it unawares 'inherits a verdict rather than reaching one'. The correct answer keeps the concession and the warning.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that rejects period labels altogether, which ignores the concession that periods are indispensable.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession and the warning sit in adjacent sentences; one wrong option keeps the warning and drops the concession, another keeps the concession and drops the warning.

questions.subtopic: Famines are often failures of access to food by particular groups rather than overall shortages.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It seems obvious that famines happen when there is not enough food. Yet several major famines have occurred in regions where the total supply of food was not much lower than in normal years, and some while food was being exported. What collapsed was not the harvest but the ability of particular groups to obtain food: labourers whose wages fell, artisans whose customers vanished, herders whose animals lost value as grain prices rose. A famine, on this view, is less a shortage of food than a failure of access to it, concentrated on those whose means of buying or growing it have broken down. This does not mean harvests are irrelevant, for a poor harvest is often what sets the collapse in motion; it means that counting the grain is not enough to predict who will starve.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

This does not mean harvests are irrelevant, for a poor harvest is often what sets the collapse in motion; it means that counting the grain is not enough to predict who will starve.

options.A: Harvest failures play no real part in causing famines, which are produced entirely by falling wages and the loss of customers among the poorest groups of people.
options.B: Famines occur when the total supply of food in a region falls below what its people need, so the size of the harvest is the best guide to who will starve.
options.C: Famines often stem less from an overall lack of food than from the collapse of particular groups' ability to obtain it, though a poor harvest may set that collapse off.
options.D: During famines, labourers, artisans and herders suffer most because their wages, customers and animals lose their value just as the price of grain is rising.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Famines often stem less from an overall lack of food than from the collapse of particular groups' ability to obtain it, though a poor harvest may set that collapse off.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'This does not mean harvests are irrelevant', since a poor harvest 'is often what sets the collapse in motion', so 'no real part' and 'entirely' contradict it.
option_rationales.B: This is the 'obvious' view the paragraph challenges; it ends by saying 'counting the grain is not enough to predict who will starve'.
option_rationales.D: These are the examples of collapsed access in the third sentence; the option omits the general reinterpretation and the place of harvests, so it is too narrow.

questions.explanation: The paragraph challenges the view that famines are simply shortages: several have occurred without a large fall in total supply, and what failed was 'the ability of particular groups to obtain food'. It then qualifies the thesis: harvests are not 'irrelevant', since a poor one 'is often what sets the collapse in motion'. The correct answer keeps the reinterpretation and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the absolute version that dismisses harvests, which overlooks the final sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is clear, but the correct answer must be told apart from an extreme version by the closing qualification.

questions.subtopic: Factories replaced task-based work with clock discipline, so punctuality began as an imposed habit.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Before factories, most work was organised by the task rather than by the hour. A farmer milked when the cows needed milking, and a weaver at home worked hard before a delivery and slackly after it. The factory changed this because its machines were expensive and had to be kept running, which required many workers to be present at the same moment. Clocks, bells and fines for lateness taught people to treat time as something owned by the employer and measured in units. The punctuality now regarded as a personal virtue was, in large part, a discipline that industrial work had to impose.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Before factories, most work was organised by the task rather than by the hour. A farmer milked when the cows needed milking, and a weaver at home worked hard before a delivery and slackly after it. The factory changed this because its machines were expensive and had to be kept running, which required many workers to be present at the same moment. Clocks, bells and fines for lateness taught people to treat time as something owned by the employer and measured in units. The punctuality now regarded as a personal virtue was, in large part, a discipline that industrial work had to impose.

options.A: Before factories, workers were idle and unreliable, and only clocks, bells and fines for lateness finally taught them the value of working hard every day.
options.B: A farmer milked his cows when they needed milking, and a weaver at home laboured hard before a delivery and slackly after it had been made.
options.C: Punctuality is a natural personal virtue, and factories prospered because they could attract and keep workers who already possessed that virtue in abundance.
options.D: Clock-measured work replaced task-based rhythms because costly factory machines needed workers present together, so punctuality began largely as imposed discipline.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Clock-measured work replaced task-based rhythms because costly factory machines needed workers present together, so punctuality began largely as imposed discipline.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph describes task-based work, in which people worked hard when the task required; it never calls earlier workers idle, and its point is about punctuality, not effort.
option_rationales.B: This restates the examples of task-based work in the second sentence and leaves out the change and its cause, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says punctuality was 'in large part, a discipline that industrial work had to impose', which is the reverse of a virtue workers already had.

questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts task-based work with factory time, gives the cause (expensive machines needing many workers 'present at the same moment'), names the means (clocks, bells, fines), and concludes that punctuality was 'in large part' imposed. The correct answer gives the change, its cause and the hedged conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the examples of pre-industrial work, which are vivid but only set up the contrast.
questions.difficulty_reason: The causal chain runs in order through short sentences; wrong options are a detail, a reversal and a moral distortion.

questions.subtopic: A tradition's recent origin corrects a belief about its history but does not make it a sham.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many customs presented as ancient turn out, on inspection, to be quite recent: a ceremony said to go back centuries may have been devised a few generations ago, often at a moment when a group felt its identity threatened. Debunkers enjoy pointing this out, as if exposing the recent origin of a tradition exposed it as a fraud. The inference is too quick. A tradition does not need to be old to do what traditions do, which is to bind people to one another and to a shared past, and a recent invention that people adopt wholeheartedly is no less real in its effects than one inherited unbroken. What the discovery should change is not our regard for the practice but our belief about its history; the claim to antiquity may be false while the attachment it supports is genuine.

options.A: Traditions are usually invented when a group's identity is threatened, which explains why such new customs are adopted more wholeheartedly by their members than inherited ones.
options.B: Traditions that claim ancient roots but were in fact devised recently are frauds, since their whole appeal depends on a false story about their origins in the distant past.
options.C: Showing that a supposedly ancient tradition is recent should correct beliefs about its history, but it does not make the tradition a sham, since the bonds it creates are real.
options.D: Because recent traditions bind people as effectively as ancient ones, the false claims of antiquity attached to them are harmless and need not be corrected.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Showing that a supposedly ancient tradition is recent should correct beliefs about its history, but it does not make the tradition a sham, since the bonds it creates are real.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says such inventions 'often' come at such moments and that adopted inventions are 'no less real', not more wholehearted; the comparison is added.
option_rationales.B: This is the debunkers' inference, which the paragraph calls 'too quick': a recent tradition can bind people just as an inherited one does.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the discovery 'should change' our 'belief about its history', so it does want the false claim corrected; only our regard for the practice should stay.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (many 'ancient' customs are recent), rejects the debunkers' inference that recency means fraud ('The inference is too quick'), and draws a two-sided conclusion: the discovery should change 'not our regard for the practice but our belief about its history'. The correct answer keeps both halves; the hardest wrong option keeps the first half and drops the second.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that defends recent traditions so fully that it excuses the false history, missing that the paragraph still wants the belief corrected.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer's two halves are each mirrored in a wrong option that keeps one and inverts the other; the reader must hold the closing distinction exactly.

questions.subtopic: The name 'Silk Road' misrepresents a shifting network of short relays as one planned route.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: The phrase 'the Silk Road' suggests a single highway along which caravans carried silk from China to Rome. The reality was a shifting web of routes, by land and sea, along which most goods travelled only short distances before changing hands. Few merchants made the whole journey; a bale might pass through a dozen markets, each trader knowing only the next stage. Silk was one commodity among many, and ideas, technologies and diseases moved along the same paths. The single name is convenient, but it can make a loose and long-lived network sound like a planned route.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Silk was one commodity among many, and ideas, technologies and diseases moved along the same paths. options.A: Few merchants ever travelled the whole distance between China and Rome, so a bale of goods might pass through a dozen markets before it reached its final buyer.
options.B: The name 'Silk Road' can suggest one planned highway, but trade actually moved in short relays along a shifting web of land and sea routes, carrying many goods.
options.C: Silk was a minor commodity on the routes between China and Rome, which carried chiefly ideas, technologies and diseases rather than goods meant for sale.
options.D: Historians should stop using the name 'Silk Road' altogether, since it is a myth with no connection to any trade that really took place along those routes.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The name 'Silk Road' can suggest one planned highway, but trade actually moved in short relays along a shifting web of land and sea routes, carrying many goods.

option_rationales.A: This is a supporting detail from the third sentence; it omits the paragraph's point about the misleading name, so it is too narrow.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says silk was 'one commodity among many' and that 'most goods travelled only short distances', so goods were central; this distorts it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls the name 'convenient' and describes real trade along the routes; it neither calls the trade a myth nor asks for the name to be dropped.

questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts what the name 'suggests' (a single highway carrying silk) with what it calls 'The reality': a shifting web of routes, short-distance relays and many kinds of cargo. It ends that the 'convenient' name can make a network 'sound like a planned route'. The correct answer states the contrast and its elements.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the detail about merchants, which supports the point but is not the point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The contrast between name and reality is announced in the first two sentences and restated at the end.

questions.subtopic: The competence objection to choosing officials by lot wrongly compares lot with ideal expertise rather than with elections as they actually filter candidates.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Critics of choosing public officials by lot usually object that it ignores competence: a random citizen, they say, is no more fit to govern than a random passenger is to fly an aircraft. The objection assumes that election reliably selects for the relevant competence, and that assumption deserves more scrutiny than it receives. Elections reward the ability to win elections, which overlaps with the ability to deliberate well on public questions but is not the same thing; they also filter heavily for wealth, connections and an appetite for publicity. Lot has its own weaknesses, and nobody sensible proposes drawing a finance minister from a hat. But for bodies whose task is to weigh evidence and represent a cross-section of opinion, such as panels reviewing a contested policy, the comparison that matters is not lot against an ideal of expertise but lot against the electoral filter as it actually operates.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Lot has its own weaknesses, and nobody sensible proposes drawing a finance minister from a hat. But for bodies whose task is to weigh evidence and represent a cross-section of opinion, such as panels reviewing a contested policy, the comparison that matters is not lot against an ideal of expertise but lot against the electoral filter as it actually operates.

options.A: The objection that lot ignores competence assumes elections select for it; for deliberative bodies, lot should be weighed against how elections really filter, not against ideal expertise.
options.B: Selection by lot is better than election for every public office, because elections favour wealth, connections and a taste for publicity over genuine ability.
options.C: Since a random citizen is as unfit to govern as a random passenger is to fly, lot should be confined to advisory panels that hold no real authority.
options.D: Elections reward the skill of winning votes instead of the skill of deliberating, which is why elected officials are usually less competent than citizens chosen at random.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The objection that lot ignores competence assumes elections select for it; for deliberative bodies, lot should be weighed against how elections really filter, not against ideal expertise.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph limits its case to deliberative bodies and says 'nobody sensible proposes drawing a finance minister from a hat', so 'every public office' contradicts its stated scope.
option_rationales.C: The passenger analogy is the critics' view, which the paragraph scrutinises rather than accepts, and it says nothing about denying such panels authority.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the two abilities overlap 'but' are 'not the same thing'; it never claims elected officials are less competent than random citizens, so this overstates the point.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the critics' objection, then attacks its hidden assumption that elections select for competence, noting that they reward 'the ability to win elections' and filter for wealth and publicity. It concedes lot's weaknesses and restricts its case to deliberative bodies, concluding that the right comparison is 'lot against the electoral filter as it actually operates'. The correct answer keeps the critique, the scope and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that turns a qualified critique of the objection into a sweeping endorsement of lot.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the author's scope limit (deliberative bodies only) to reject the sweeping option and to see that the passenger analogy belongs to the critics.

questions.subtopic: Wars are decided more by supply than by battlefield brilliance.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Popular accounts of war dwell on generals and battles, but campaigns are more often decided by supply. An army that cannot feed its soldiers, replace its ammunition or move fuel to its vehicles loses the capacity to fight long before it loses a battle. Many celebrated offensives stalled not because the enemy stopped them but because they outran the roads, railways or wagons that sustained them. Brilliant tactics can win an engagement; only a working system of supply can turn a run of engagements into a victory. This is why careful commanders tend to plan the movement of food and fuel before the movement of troops, and why the study of logistics, though unglamorous, explains more about the outcome of wars than the study of battlefield genius.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

This is why careful commanders tend to plan the movement of food and fuel before the movement of troops, and why the study of logistics, though unglamorous, explains more about the outcome of wars than the study of battlefield genius.

options.A: Careful commanders plan the movement of food and fuel before the movement of troops, and this habit makes them more successful than commanders who plan otherwise.
options.B: Popular histories of war ought to be rewritten to drop accounts of generals and battles and to concentrate instead on roads, railways and supplies.
options.C: Wars are usually decided less by tactical brilliance in battle than by keeping armies supplied, so logistics explains their outcomes better than generalship does.
options.D: Generals who win battles through clever tactics are overrated, since nearly every famous offensive failed once enemy forces managed to cut its lines of supply.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Wars are usually decided less by tactical brilliance in battle than by keeping armies supplied, so logistics explains their outcomes better than generalship does.

option_rationales.A: This takes one illustrative detail as the point and adds a comparison of commanders that the paragraph never makes.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph makes a claim about what explains outcomes; it prescribes no rewriting of popular histories, and it grants that tactics can win engagements.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says offensives stalled 'not because the enemy stopped them' but because they outran their own supply, and it speaks of 'Many celebrated offensives', not nearly every one.

questions.explanation: The opening sentence states the thesis that 'campaigns are more often decided by supply', the middle sentences support it, and the last sentence concludes that logistics 'explains more about the outcome of wars than the study of battlefield genius'. The correct answer restates exactly this comparison.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option about commanders' planning because it repeats a detail from the final sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis is stated in the first and last sentences; wrong options are a misread detail, a narrow detail and an added prescription.

questions.subtopic: Premodern empires valued courier relays because faster information let rulers oversee distant officials.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Large premodern empires often invested heavily in relay systems of couriers and stations long before they built much else in common. The reason is less obvious than it seems. A ruler far from his provinces faced a problem not of force but of information: governors might rebel, under-report taxes or simply act on stale orders, and the centre could not correct what it could not see. A fast relay shortened the delay between an event and the capital's knowledge of it, and so shrank the room in which local officials could act unobserved. The roads and horses carried letters, but what they really delivered was the credible prospect of timely oversight. That is why such systems were often reserved for official use rather than opened to merchants and private correspondents.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Large premodern empires often invested heavily in relay systems of couriers and stations long before they built much else in common. The reason is less obvious than it seems. The roads and horses carried letters, but what they really delivered was the credible prospect of timely oversight. That is why such systems were often reserved for official use rather than opened to merchants and private correspondents.

options.A: Courier relays in premodern empires were closed to merchants because private letters would have crowded the roads and delayed the government's own messages.
options.B: Premodern empires prized courier relays mainly because quicker news let distant rulers watch provincial officials, narrowing the room for disobedience or deceit to go unnoticed.
options.C: Because distant governors routinely rebelled and concealed taxes, premodern rulers came to treat fast relays as their only effective means of keeping control.
options.D: Premodern empires built courier relays chiefly to move troops and tax revenue quickly between capital and provinces, which made any rebellion much harder to sustain.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Premodern empires prized courier relays mainly because quicker news let distant rulers watch provincial officials, narrowing the room for disobedience or deceit to go unnoticed.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph explains the restriction by the relays' role in oversight; congestion of the roads is a reason it never gives.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says governors 'might' rebel or under-report, not that they routinely did, and it never calls relays the only means of control.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the ruler's problem was 'not of force but of information' and that the relays 'carried letters', so troops and revenue misstate their purpose.

questions.explanation: The paragraph poses a puzzle (why relays came early), answers it by recasting the ruler's problem as one of information, and explains that speed 'shrank the room in which local officials could act unobserved'. Its last line, 'what they really delivered was the credible prospect of timely oversight', is the point the correct answer captures.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the troops-and-revenue option because relays sound like military infrastructure.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer depends on the reframing from force to information; one wrong option uses the force reading and another inflates 'might' into 'routinely'.

questions.subtopic: The cartel and trust views of craft guilds can coexist; which function dominated likely depended on how hard quality was to observe.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Two accounts of medieval craft guilds have long competed. On one, guilds were cartels: they restricted entry, fixed prices and kept outsiders from the trade, enriching masters at the expense of customers and would-be rivals. On the other, they were institutions of trust: in markets where buyers could not easily judge the quality of cloth or metalwork, a guild's standards and inspections gave its mark a meaning that no single workshop could establish alone. The two accounts are usually presented as rivals, but they describe mechanisms that can coexist in the same institution, and the more useful question is which one predominated under which conditions. Where quality was easy to observe, the trust function had little to add and restriction was likely to dominate; where quality stayed hidden until long after purchase, the same barriers to entry may have been the price of a reputation worth having.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Two accounts of medieval craft guilds have long competed. On one, guilds were cartels: they restricted entry, fixed prices and kept outsiders from the trade, enriching masters at the expense of customers and would-be rivals. On the other, they were institutions of trust: in markets where buyers could not easily judge the quality of cloth or metalwork, a guild's standards and inspections gave its mark a meaning that no single workshop could establish alone. The two accounts are usually presented as rivals, but they describe mechanisms that can coexist in the same institution, and the more useful question is which one predominated under which conditions. Where quality was easy to observe, the trust function had little to add and restriction was likely to dominate; where quality stayed hidden until long after purchase, the same barriers to entry may have been the price of a reputation worth having.

options.A: The cartel and trust views of guilds need not be rivals; which function prevailed probably depended on how hard buyers found it to judge quality before buying.
options.B: Guilds were primarily institutions of trust rather than cartels, since their limits on entry were simply the price buyers paid for reputations that benefited every customer.
options.C: Where the quality of goods could be judged at a glance, guilds served no useful purpose at all, and towns would have done better without them.
options.D: The cartel and trust accounts of guilds are both partly right, because every guild restricted entry to some extent and every guild also inspected its members' goods.

questions.correct_answer: (A) The cartel and trust views of guilds need not be rivals; which function prevailed probably depended on how hard buyers found it to judge quality before buying.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph refuses to choose one account and says restriction 'was likely to dominate' where quality was easy to observe, so siding wholly with trust contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says only that the trust function 'had little to add' there; 'no useful purpose at all' and the verdict on towns go beyond it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph's point is conditional, that the balance depended on how observable quality was; it makes no universal claim about what every guild did.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets out the cartel view and the trust view, then argues that they 'describe mechanisms that can coexist' and that the useful question is 'which one predominated under which conditions'. Its final sentence ties the answer to whether quality was easy to observe or 'stayed hidden until long after purchase'. The correct answer captures both the reconciliation and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'both partly right' option, which sounds balanced but replaces the paragraph's conditional answer with an unsupported universal claim.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options sound like reconciliations; only one keeps the condition (observability of quality) that decides between the mechanisms.

questions.subtopic: The advantage of entering a market first is conditional, and the anecdotes offered for it suffer from survivorship bias.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Business writing often treats being first to market as a decisive advantage, and the stories it tells are memorable: the pioneer that defined a category and never let go. Yet such stories are drawn disproportionately from survivors. Pioneers that created a market and were then overtaken by better-funded or more careful followers are forgotten, or are remembered as footnotes to the followers' success, so the sample from which the lesson is drawn is tilted in its favour. Followers also enjoy real benefits: they can learn from the pioneer's mistakes, wait for customers to understand the product and adopt technology that has become cheaper. This does not mean that entering first is never valuable; where customers face high costs of switching, an early lead can harden into dominance. It means that the advantage is conditional, and that the anecdotes usually offered for it cannot establish how often it holds.

options.A: Business writers deliberately exaggerate the value of being first to market, picking pioneer stories that suit the lessons they already wish to teach.
options.B: Firms that follow a pioneer into a new market generally outperform it, because they learn from its mistakes and adopt technology after it has become cheaper.
options.C: Entering a market first pays off only when customers find switching costly, and in every other market it is a handicap that sensible firms ought to avoid.
options.D: Entering a market first helps only in some conditions, such as high switching costs; belief in its power rests on stories that forget overtaken pioneers.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Entering a market first helps only in some conditions, such as high switching costs; belief in its power rests on stories that forget overtaken pioneers.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph describes a sampling bias toward survivors, not deliberate exaggeration; it attributes no motive to business writers.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph lists followers' benefits but never says they generally outperform pioneers; it says only that the first-mover advantage is conditional.
option_rationales.C: Switching costs are offered as one example ('where customers face high costs'), not the sole condition, and the paragraph never calls early entry a handicap to avoid.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises the belief in first-mover advantage on two grounds: the stories behind it come from survivors, and followers have real benefits. It then concedes that early entry can matter 'where customers face high costs of switching' and concludes that 'the advantage is conditional'. The correct answer holds the critique and the concession together.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the follower option, which turns 'Followers also enjoy real benefits' into a general claim of superiority.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option reverses the myth instead of qualifying it; the correct answer must keep the concession.

questions.subtopic: Counterfeits hurt luxury brands less by lost sales than by eroding the status signal of the genuine article.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It might seem that counterfeits can only harm the luxury brands they copy, since each fake sold appears to be a sale lost. But most people who buy an obvious imitation for a small fraction of the price were never going to pay for the original, so the lost sale is often imaginary. The more serious threat is subtler. A luxury good is bought partly for what it signals, and the signal depends on the belief that the item is scarce and costly to obtain. When copies become common enough that observers can no longer tell who paid full price, the original loses part of what its buyers were paying for, even though none of them has been deceived. The harm, in other words, falls not on any transaction between the brand and the buyer of a fake but on the meaning of the logo for everyone else.

options.A: Counterfeits harm luxury brands less through lost sales, often illusory, than by blurring which items are genuine and so weakening the status the logo signals.
options.B: Luxury brands begin to lose sales to counterfeits once copies become common enough that observers can no longer tell genuine items from imitations.
options.C: Counterfeit luxury goods do little real harm to the brands they copy, because the people who buy fakes could never have paid for the genuine articles anyway.
options.D: The chief damage done by counterfeits falls on buyers of genuine luxury goods, who are misled into paying full price for items that are no longer scarce.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Counterfeits harm luxury brands less through lost sales, often illusory, than by blurring which items are genuine and so weakening the status the logo signals.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph locates the harm 'not on any transaction' but on the logo's meaning; recasting it as lost sales reverses the distinction it draws.
option_rationales.C: This keeps the first half of the argument and drops the 'more serious threat' to the meaning of the logo, so it contradicts the paragraph's conclusion that harm does occur.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says genuine buyers lose part of what they paid for 'even though none of them has been deceived', so 'misled' contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph first dismisses the obvious harm (lost sales are 'often imaginary'), then identifies 'The more serious threat': a luxury good's signal depends on perceived scarcity, and common copies blur who paid full price. Its last sentence locates the harm in 'the meaning of the logo for everyone else'. The correct answer states both moves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the lost-sales option because it mentions the right condition (copies becoming indistinguishable) while getting the kind of harm wrong.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every wrong option reuses the paragraph's terms; separating them needs the distinction between harm to sales, harm through deception and harm to a signal.

questions.subtopic: Resentment of surge pricing reflects fairness norms about emergencies, not economic confusion, and ignoring it costs goodwill.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Economists tend to defend surge pricing on grounds of efficiency: when demand for rides or rooms spikes, a higher price rations the scarce supply to those who value it most and draws more suppliers in. The reasoning holds within its own terms, but it explains less of the public reaction than its defenders suppose. People who resent a tripled fare during a storm are not usually confused about supply and demand; they are objecting to what the price seems to say, that a seller is profiting from their predicament. Norms of fairness in many communities treat raising prices in an emergency differently from raising them on a busy Saturday, even when the economics are identical. A pricing scheme that ignores this distinction may be efficient on paper and still erode the goodwill on which the seller depends.

Norms of fairness in many communities treat raising prices in an emergency differently from raising them on a busy Saturday, even when the economics are identical. options.A: Customers accept higher prices on busy weekends but reject them in storms because the increases charged during emergencies tend to be far larger than weekend ones.
options.B: Surge pricing may ration supply efficiently, but anger at it stems from fairness norms about profiting from emergencies, which sellers ignore at the cost of goodwill.
options.C: Surge pricing is both unfair and inefficient in emergencies, so sellers should hold prices fixed whenever customers are caught in storms or similar predicaments.
options.D: Public opposition to surge pricing arises mainly because customers misunderstand how higher prices ration scarce supply and attract extra sellers when demand spikes.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Surge pricing may ration supply efficiently, but anger at it stems from fairness norms about profiting from emergencies, which sellers ignore at the cost of goodwill.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the norms differ 'even when the economics are identical', so explaining the difference by the size of the increase contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph grants that the efficiency reasoning 'holds within its own terms' and offers no rule about fixing prices, so both halves misstate it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says resentful customers 'are not usually confused about supply and demand', so this states the opposite of its explanation.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts the efficiency case, then argues that it misses the source of public anger: people object to 'what the price seems to say', and fairness norms treat emergencies differently 'even when the economics are identical'. It ends by warning that such a scheme may 'erode the goodwill on which the seller depends'. The correct answer includes the concession, the explanation and the consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'unfair and inefficient' option by forgetting that the efficiency argument is conceded.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires separating the conceded efficiency point from the fairness explanation; one wrong option contradicts each.

questions.subtopic: Suppressing every fire in fire-adapted forests lets fuel accumulate and produces larger fires.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: In many forests that evolved with frequent low-intensity fire, decades of putting out every blaze have made fires worse rather than rarer. Small fires once cleared away dead wood, needles and young trees at regular intervals, keeping the fuel on the forest floor thin. When those fires were suppressed, the fuel kept accumulating, and dense undergrowth formed a ladder by which flames could climb into the canopy. A fire that would once have crept harmlessly along the ground now meets years of stored fuel and becomes the kind of blaze that kills mature trees and resists control. The policy succeeded at its immediate aim, stopping each fire, while creating the conditions for larger ones. The lesson applies chiefly to fire-adapted forests; in ecosystems where fire was naturally rare, suppression does not have the same effect.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

In many forests that evolved with frequent low-intensity fire, decades of putting out every blaze have made fires worse rather than rarer. Small fires once cleared away dead wood, needles and young trees at regular intervals, keeping the fuel on the forest floor thin. When those fires were suppressed, the fuel kept accumulating, and dense undergrowth formed a ladder by which flames could climb into the canopy. A fire that would once have crept harmlessly along the ground now meets years of stored fuel and becomes the kind of blaze that kills mature trees and resists control. The policy succeeded at its immediate aim, stopping each fire, while creating the conditions for larger ones. The lesson applies chiefly to fire-adapted forests; in ecosystems where fire was naturally rare, suppression does not have the same effect.

options.A: Putting out forest fires is always counterproductive, because fuel builds up in every kind of forest whenever small fires are prevented from burning.
options.B: Forest managers should stop fighting fires altogether and let every blaze burn, since small fires once kept forests thin and safe from larger ones.
options.C: In forests adapted to frequent small fires, suppressing every blaze lets fuel pile up, so later fires grow larger and more destructive.
options.D: Dense undergrowth lets flames climb from the forest floor into the canopy, where they kill mature trees and become very hard to bring under control.

questions.correct_answer: (C) In forests adapted to frequent small fires, suppressing every blaze lets fuel pile up, so later fires grow larger and more destructive.

option_rationales.A: The last sentence restricts the point to fire-adapted forests and says that where fire was rare 'suppression does not have the same effect', so 'always' and 'every kind' contradict it.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph explains a consequence of suppression but prescribes no policy, and letting every blaze burn goes well beyond anything it says.
option_rationales.D: This describes one step in the mechanism and leaves out the cause, suppression of small fires, which is the paragraph's point.

questions.explanation: The first sentence states the phenomenon, the middle sentences explain how fuel accumulates when small fires are suppressed, and the last two sentences draw the paradox and limit it to fire-adapted forests. The correct answer states the cause, the effect and the scope.
questions.common_misconception: Overlooking the final sentence's limit to fire-adapted forests.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point and its scope are stated plainly; wrong options are an overgeneralisation, a detail and a prescription.

questions.subtopic: Repetition reveals precision but not accuracy; systematic error needs an independent check.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A measurement can be precise without being accurate. If a scale consistently reads two kilograms too heavy, repeated weighings of the same object will agree closely with one another, and that agreement may inspire confidence, yet every reading is wrong by the same amount. Precision describes how tightly repeated results cluster; accuracy describes how close they lie to the true value. The distinction matters because the usual way of checking a result, repeating it, reveals only the first. A systematic error survives any number of repetitions untouched, and can be exposed only by comparing the instrument with an independent standard or a different method. Consistency is therefore reassuring about random noise but silent about bias.

options.A: A scale that reads two kilograms too heavy gives readings that agree closely with one another, which is why such scales are trusted more than they deserve.
options.B: Scientists should stop repeating measurements and rely only on comparisons with independent standards, since repetition cannot reveal any kind of error.
options.C: Precise instruments tend to be inaccurate, because the consistency of their readings conceals errors that less precise instruments would reveal through their scatter.
options.D: Repeating a measurement shows whether results agree, not whether they are correct; systematic bias can be exposed only by an independent standard or method.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Repeating a measurement shows whether results agree, not whether they are correct; systematic bias can be exposed only by an independent standard or method.

option_rationales.A: This repeats the illustration without the general point it serves, that repetition cannot reveal systematic error.
option_rationales.B: The last sentence says consistency is 'reassuring about random noise', so repetition does reveal one kind of error, and the paragraph prescribes nothing.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says precision and accuracy are independent ('can be precise without being accurate'), not that precise instruments tend to be inaccurate.

The correct answer captures this distinction and its consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that stretches the paragraph into a rejection of repetition, missing that it still detects random noise.
questions.difficulty_reason: A single clearly stated distinction; wrong options misread, narrow or overstate it.

questions.subtopic: Trees do cool streets, but only when mature and watered, so counting saplings planted overstates the relief.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Measurements in many cities have found that streets shaded by mature trees are noticeably cooler on summer afternoons than nearby streets without them, and planting trees has accordingly become a favoured response to urban heat. The finding is robust, but it is easy to draw more from it than it supports. Much of the cooling comes from shade and from water evaporating through leaves, and both depend on the tree being large, healthy and adequately watered; a newly planted sapling in a paved pit provides little of either for years, and in a drought a stressed tree may provide less still. Trees therefore help most where there is space, soil and water for them to mature, and planting programmes judged only by the number of saplings put in the ground may promise relief that arrives late or not at all.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Mature, well-watered trees do cool city streets, but young or stressed trees give little cooling, so counting saplings planted overstates the relief that planting brings.
options.B: Streets shaded by mature trees are cooler on summer afternoons mainly because their leaves release water that evaporates and draws heat from the air around them.
options.C: Planting trees is an ineffective answer to urban heat, since saplings in paved pits give almost no shade and stressed trees provide no cooling in a drought.
options.D: Cities should plant trees only where soil and water are plentiful, and should abandon programmes that put saplings into narrow pits in paved streets.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Mature, well-watered trees do cool city streets, but young or stressed trees give little cooling, so counting saplings planted overstates the relief that planting brings.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph credits both 'shade' and 'water evaporating through leaves', and in any case this mechanism is a detail, not the paragraph's point about overreading the finding.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph calls the cooling finding 'robust' and says trees 'help most' in suitable places, so calling planting ineffective contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph warns against judging programmes by sapling counts but never tells cities to abandon any programme; the rule is an added prescription.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states a finding (mature trees cool streets), affirms it, then qualifies what follows from it: cooling depends on size, health and water, so saplings give little for years. Its conclusion is that programmes 'judged only by the number of saplings' may over-promise. The correct answer keeps both the finding and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the qualification as a refutation of the finding, or picking the mechanism detail.
questions.difficulty_reason: A finding-and-qualification paragraph; the strongest wrong option overturns the finding instead of qualifying it.

questions.subtopic: Because the fossil record is a sparse and biased sample, gaps in it cannot alone decide between gradual and abrupt change.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is sometimes argued that the scarcity of transitional fossils counts against gradual evolutionary change: if lineages changed slowly, the rocks should be full of intermediate forms. The argument assumes that the fossil record is a fair sample of past life, and it is not. Fossilisation requires rapid burial, suitable sediments and the absence of scavengers, conditions met for a tiny fraction of organisms and far more often for hard-shelled marine animals than for soft-bodied or upland ones. Erosion and the movement of the earth's crust have since destroyed much of what was preserved. Given a record this patchy, gaps are what one would expect under almost any account of change, so their presence cannot by itself decide between gradual and abrupt models. The question has to be settled by those parts of the record that are dense enough to test it.

The question has to be settled by those parts of the record that are dense enough to test it.

options.A: The fossil record is too incomplete to tell us anything about how evolutionary change happened, so the dispute between gradual and abrupt models cannot be settled.
options.B: The scarcity of transitional fossils shows that evolutionary change was abrupt rather than gradual, because slow change would have left many intermediate forms behind.
options.C: Since fossils form rarely and unevenly, gaps would appear under nearly any model of change, so only densely preserved sequences can show whether change was gradual.
options.D: Gaps in the fossil record arise chiefly because erosion and movements of the crust destroyed most fossils of soft-bodied and upland organisms after they had formed.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Since fossils form rarely and unevenly, gaps would appear under nearly any model of change, so only densely preserved sequences can show whether change was gradual.

option_rationales.A: The last sentence says the question can be settled by 'those parts of the record that are dense enough to test it', so declaring it unsettleable contradicts the paragraph.
option_rationales.B: This is the argument the paragraph reports and rejects, on the ground that it wrongly assumes the record 'is a fair sample of past life'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says such organisms rarely fossilised in the first place; erosion is a further cause, and in any case the option omits the conclusion about testing models.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports an argument from missing intermediates, rejects its assumption that the record is a fair sample, explains why it is sparse and biased, and concludes that gaps 'cannot by itself decide' the question, which must be settled by dense parts of the record. The correct answer captures the reason, the limited conclusion and the way forward.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'too incomplete to tell us anything' option, which overstates the paragraph's scepticism and ignores its final sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are close to the correct answer in different directions (the rejected argument, and excessive scepticism); the final sentence decides.

questions.subtopic: Software accumulates features because benefits are concentrated and costs diffuse, while removal creates visible losers.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Software products tend to accumulate features over time, and the process is hard to reverse. Each addition is usually requested by some group of users and can be justified on its own terms, while the costs it imposes are spread thinly: a slightly more crowded menu, a little more to test, one more interaction that can fail. Because no single feature seems to be the one that made the product cluttered, there is rarely a moment at which anyone decides to stop. Removing a feature, on the other hand, produces a visible loss for identifiable users, who complain. The result is a steady drift toward complexity that no one chose, driven by an imbalance between concentrated benefits and diffuse costs.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Removing a feature, on the other hand, produces a visible loss for identifiable users, who complain. The result is a steady drift toward complexity that no one chose, driven by an imbalance between concentrated benefits and diffuse costs.

options.A: Software companies add needless features on purpose in order to justify new versions, even when most users would much prefer a simpler and more reliable product.
options.B: Every feature added to a software product makes it harder to test and more likely to fail, so developers ought to turn down most requests from users.
options.C: Users of software complain more about features being taken away than about menus becoming crowded, because people feel losses more keenly than gains.
options.D: Software grows cluttered because each feature has clear backers while its costs are small and scattered, and removal angers known users, so complexity builds unchosen.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Software grows cluttered because each feature has clear backers while its costs are small and scattered, and removal angers known users, so complexity builds unchosen.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph describes a drift 'that no one chose', not a deliberate strategy, and it never mentions users preferring simplicity.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph explains why features accumulate; it offers no advice to developers about refusing requests.
option_rationales.C: Complaints about removal are one part of the mechanism; the option drops the main point and adds a general claim about losses and gains.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a phenomenon: additions have visible justifications while their costs are 'spread thinly', no single addition is decisive, and removal creates identifiable losers. Its last sentence names the cause, 'an imbalance between concentrated benefits and diffuse costs'. The correct answer restates this explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the deliberate-strategy option and missing 'that no one chose'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The explanation is summarised in the final sentence; wrong options add a motive, a prescription or a narrow detail.

questions.subtopic: Spreadsheets that inform big decisions should be reviewed like software, since their ease of use breeds unwarranted trust.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Spreadsheets are among the most widely used analytical tools in business and government, and also among the least scrutinised. A model built in one can be shared, extended and relied upon for years by people who never inspect its formulas, and a single misplaced cell reference can spread silently through every figure that depends on it. The danger is not that spreadsheets are unusually prone to error in the hands of careful users but that their ease of use invites a level of trust that their lack of checks does not justify. Code written by programmers is usually reviewed and tested; a spreadsheet that informs a large decision often has no comparable safeguard, simply because it does not look like software. Treating important spreadsheets as programs, subject to review, would not remove error, but it would bring their scrutiny closer to their influence.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Spreadsheets are more prone to error than programs written in code, so important decisions in business and government should not be based on them at all.
options.B: Important spreadsheets deserve software-style review, since their ease of use breeds trust their lack of checks does not warrant, though review would not end error.
options.C: A single misplaced cell reference can spread silently through every dependent figure, which is why spreadsheet models are usually discarded after a few years.
options.D: Reviewing spreadsheets in the way software is reviewed would eliminate the errors that now pass unnoticed into the decisions that rely on them.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Important spreadsheets deserve software-style review, since their ease of use breeds trust their lack of checks does not warrant, though review would not end error.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the danger is 'not that spreadsheets are unusually prone to error', and it proposes reviewing them, not abandoning them.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says models are relied upon 'for years'; the claim that they are discarded is invented, and the error-propagation detail is not the main point.
option_rationales.D: The last sentence says such review 'would not remove error'; it would only bring scrutiny closer to influence, so 'eliminate' contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph identifies the gap between the influence of spreadsheets and the scrutiny they receive, locates the danger in misplaced trust rather than in unusual error rates, contrasts them with reviewed code, and recommends treating important spreadsheets as programs while conceding this 'would not remove error'. The correct answer keeps the recommendation, its reason and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'eliminate the errors' option by overlooking the concession in the final sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer and one wrong option share the recommendation; only the correct answer respects the concession, and another wrong option reverses the 'not unusually prone' qualification.

questions.subtopic: Batteries handle daily swings in wind and solar output well but not long lulls, so they are only part of the answer to intermittency.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Batteries are often presented as the answer to the intermittency of wind and solar power: store the surplus when the sun shines and release it when it does not. For smoothing variation over hours they are increasingly effective, absorbing the midday peak of solar output and covering the evening rise in demand. But the harder problem of intermittency is not the daily cycle. It is the windless, overcast week in winter, or the season in which output stays low for months, and covering gaps of that length with batteries of the kind now installed would require storage on a scale that is, at present, very costly. Batteries, then, solve one part of the problem well, and success with that part should not be mistaken for a solution to the whole, which will also need other means such as long-distance transmission, flexible demand or different forms of storage.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Batteries, then, solve one part of the problem well, and success with that part should not be mistaken for a solution to the whole, which will also need other means such as long-distance transmission, flexible demand or different forms of storage.

options.A: Long-distance transmission and flexible demand deal with every form of intermittency in renewable electricity more effectively than batteries are able to.
options.B: Batteries smooth the hourly swings of wind and solar power well, but not, at present, lulls lasting weeks or seasons, so other measures will also be needed.
options.C: Batteries already shift midday solar surplus into the evening, so continued investment in them will in time overcome the seasonal shortfalls of renewable power.
options.D: Batteries do little to solve the intermittency of wind and solar power, because the real difficulty lies in long winter lulls rather than in daily swings.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Batteries smooth the hourly swings of wind and solar power well, but not, at present, lulls lasting weeks or seasons, so other measures will also be needed.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph lists these as additional means for the long gaps; it never ranks them above batteries, and certainly not for every form of intermittency.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph warns that success with the daily cycle 'should not be mistaken for a solution to the whole', which is the mistake this option makes.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says batteries are 'increasingly effective' for hourly variation and 'solve one part of the problem well', so calling them of little help contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants that batteries smooth hourly variation, then identifies the harder problem of week-long and seasonal gaps, which current batteries could cover only at very high cost, and concludes that the daily success 'should not be mistaken for a solution to the whole'. The correct answer keeps the concession, the limit and the need for other means.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that dismisses batteries, which turns a limit on their role into a denial of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options err in opposite directions (too dismissive, too hopeful); the correct answer sits between them.

questions.subtopic: Because spammers adapt to filters, filtering success decays and must be renewed, though filtering is not futile.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Spam filtering differs from most problems of classification in one important respect: the things being classified fight back. A filter that learns to recognise the features of unwanted messages changes the environment it was trained on, because senders whose messages are blocked alter them until they pass. Each improvement therefore tends to erode its own basis, and a filter that performed superbly when it was built may decline without any change to its code. This is why accuracy measured on yesterday's messages is a weak guide to tomorrow's, and why effective filtering is better understood as a continuing contest than as a solved problem. The point is not that filtering is futile, since raising the cost of evasion still reduces what gets through, but that its success has to be renewed rather than achieved once.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
