options.A: Since senders adapt to what filters detect, filtering success decays and must be continually renewed; past accuracy predicts little, though filtering still cuts spam.
options.B: Filters should be judged on future messages rather than past ones, because a filter trained on yesterday's messages will always misclassify those of tomorrow.
options.C: Spam filters lose accuracy over time mainly because their code grows outdated as email software and the habits of ordinary users gradually change.
options.D: Spam filtering is ultimately futile, since every improvement in detection is soon cancelled out by senders who alter their messages in order to evade it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Since senders adapt to what filters detect, filtering success decays and must be continually renewed; past accuracy predicts little, though filtering still cuts spam.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph calls past accuracy 'a weak guide', not a guarantee of failure, so 'always misclassify' overstates it, and it proposes no rule for judging filters.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a filter may decline 'without any change to its code' and blames adapting senders, not outdated code or ordinary users.
option_rationales.D: The last sentence says 'The point is not that filtering is futile', because raising the cost of evasion still reduces spam, so this contradicts the paragraph.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why spam filtering is unusual: blocked senders adapt, so 'Each improvement therefore tends to erode its own basis'. It draws two consequences (past accuracy is 'a weak guide', filtering is 'a continuing contest') and adds a qualification, that filtering is not futile. The correct answer holds the mechanism, the consequence and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the futility option by missing the final qualification.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must keep a qualification that the most tempting wrong option denies; the others misplace the cause or overstate.

questions.subtopic: An unreliable narrator works only because a reliable author plants clues that let readers see past the narration.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A narrator who misleads the reader would seem to undermine the trust on which fiction depends, yet some of the most admired novels are told by narrators whose accounts cannot be taken at face value. The effect works because the author has not deceived the reader in the way the narrator has. Small inconsistencies, the reactions of other characters and gaps between what is said and what is shown allow an attentive reader to reconstruct what the narrator cannot or will not admit. The pleasure lies in that reconstruction, and in watching a mind reveal itself through the very effort of self-justification. An unreliable narrator, in other words, depends on a reliable author: if the clues were absent, the reader would simply be lied to, and the device would collapse into a trick.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A narrator who misleads the reader would seem to undermine the trust on which fiction depends, yet some of the most admired novels are told by narrators whose accounts cannot be taken at face value. The effect works because the author has not deceived the reader in the way the narrator has. The pleasure lies in that reconstruction, and in watching a mind reveal itself through the very effort of self-justification. An unreliable narrator, in other words, depends on a reliable author: if the clues were absent, the reader would simply be lied to, and the device would collapse into a trick.

options.A: An unreliable narrator weakens the trust between author and reader, which is why only a few highly skilled novelists have attempted to use the device.
options.B: Novels with unreliable narrators are admired more than other novels because readers enjoy being misled and then surprised by the truth near the end.
options.C: Unreliable narration rewards readers because the author plants clues that expose the narrator's distortions; without such clues the device would be mere deception.
options.D: Unreliable narrators reveal their characters through self-justification, which makes them more psychologically convincing than the narrators of novels who report events accurately and fully.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Unreliable narration rewards readers because the author plants clues that expose the narrator's distortions; without such clues the device would be mere deception.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph argues that the author 'has not deceived the reader', so trust between them survives; how many novelists use the device is never discussed.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph locates the pleasure in the reader's ongoing reconstruction, not in being misled and surprised, and it compares these novels with no others.
option_rationales.D: Self-justification is one source of the pleasure the paragraph mentions, but the comparison with accurate narrators is invented and the central point about clues is missing.

questions.explanation: The paragraph raises an apparent paradox (a misleading narrator in admired fiction), resolves it by distinguishing narrator from author, explains how clues let the reader reconstruct the truth, and concludes that 'An unreliable narrator ... depends on a reliable author'. The correct answer captures that resolution and its condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the trust option, which repeats the apparent paradox the paragraph goes on to dissolve.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer turns on the distinction between narrator and author; one wrong option restates the paradox as if it were the conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Item-by-item fidelity is a confused test of a film adaptation; the right test is comparable achievement in the film's own medium.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Reviews of film adaptations often turn on fidelity: whether the film kept the plot, the characters and the ending of the book. The criterion is natural but confused. A novel can spend pages inside a character's thoughts, stretch a single moment or move freely across decades; a film must render most of this through image, sound and duration, and a scene transferred unchanged may carry quite different weight on screen. Literal faithfulness can therefore betray what made the book matter, while a film that alters events may preserve it. This does not make every departure justified, and some adaptations change a story for no better reason than convenience. But the question worth asking is whether the film achieves in its own medium something comparable to what the book achieved in its, not whether the two can be matched item by item.

options.C: Film adaptations should depart freely from their source books, since altering plot and characters is the only way to keep what made the original matter.
options.D: Since novels and films work differently, point-by-point fidelity is a poor test of an adaptation; what matters is whether the film achieves something comparable in its own medium.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Since novels and films work differently, point-by-point fidelity is a poor test of an adaptation; what matters is whether the film achieves something comparable in its own medium.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph argues that 'Literal faithfulness can therefore betray what made the book matter', which is the reverse of this claim.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says a film 'must render' inner life through image and sound, not that it cannot, and it argues that a film can achieve something comparable.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says only that a film that alters events 'may' preserve the book's value, and it adds that not 'every departure' is justified, so 'only way' and 'freely' overstate it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects fidelity as 'natural but confused', explains why (the two media render thought, time and weight differently), concedes that some departures are unjustified, and proposes a better question: whether the film 'achieves in its own medium something comparable'. The correct answer states the rejection and the replacement test without overstating it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'depart freely' option, which keeps the criticism of fidelity but ignores the concession that not every change is justified.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is the correct answer's critique pushed one step too far; spotting it needs the concession in the second-last sentence.

questions.subtopic: Jazz improvisation is spontaneous recombination of a long-practised vocabulary, and that preparation makes spontaneity possible.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Improvisation in jazz is often imagined as pure spontaneity, music invented from nothing in the moment of performance. The reality is closer to the opposite. Improvisers spend years absorbing scales, harmonic patterns, phrases from recordings and the habits of other players, until a large vocabulary is available to them without conscious thought. What happens on stage is the fresh combination of this material in response to the other musicians and the shape of the tune, not creation from a blank page. Far from diminishing the achievement, this explains it: spontaneity of the kind audiences admire is possible only because so much has been prepared that the performer is free to listen and respond.

options.A: Jazz improvisation is far less spontaneous than audiences believe, which means that the achievement of improvising musicians has been greatly overestimated.
options.B: Jazz musicians learn phrases from recordings and from other players so that they can reproduce them exactly whenever they perform before an audience.
options.C: Jazz improvisation is not invention from nothing but the live recombination of a long-practised musical vocabulary, and that preparation is what frees performers to respond spontaneously.
options.D: Improvising musicians respond to one another and to the shape of the tune, which is why the same jazz piece sounds different every time it is played.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Jazz improvisation is not invention from nothing but the live recombination of a long-practised musical vocabulary, and that preparation is what frees performers to respond spontaneously.

questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'overestimated' option by reading the correction as a debunking.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated directly; the main wrong option reverses the final sentence.

questions.subtopic: Both sides of the varnish-cleaning dispute appeal to the artist's intention; they differ over trust in present reconstructions.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Few decisions in the care of old paintings provoke as much argument as the removal of discoloured varnish. Those who favour cleaning point out that yellowed varnish distorts colour and flattens depth, so that a viewer sees the grime of centuries rather than the painting. Those who resist it reply that cleaning is irreversible, that it can strip away thin final glazes the artist applied, and that our idea of what the painting originally looked like is itself a guess. Both sides appeal to the artist's intention, which is part of what makes the dispute so stubborn: the cleaner trusts present knowledge to recover it, the sceptic distrusts that knowledge enough to leave the surface alone. What separates them is less a disagreement about values than about how much confidence our reconstructions deserve.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Advocates and opponents of cleaning old paintings both aim to honour the artist's intention; they differ mainly over how far present knowledge can reconstruct the original.
options.B: The dispute over cleaning old paintings sets those who value the artist's original intention against those who value the marks that age leaves on a surface.
options.C: Because yellowed varnish distorts colour and flattens depth, cleaning lets viewers see old paintings as they first appeared rather than the grime of centuries.
options.D: Discoloured varnish should be left in place, because cleaning cannot be reversed and may strip away the thin final glazes that the artist applied.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Advocates and opponents of cleaning old paintings both aim to honour the artist's intention; they differ mainly over how far present knowledge can reconstruct the original.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says 'Both sides appeal to the artist's intention'; neither side is described as valuing the marks of age, so the opposition is invented.
option_rationales.C: This is the cleaners' argument presented as fact; the paragraph notes that our idea of the original appearance 'is itself a guess'.
option_rationales.D: This adopts the sceptics' side, while the paragraph reports both positions without endorsing either and locates the dispute in confidence, not in a verdict.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets out the case for and against cleaning, then observes that 'Both sides appeal to the artist's intention' and concludes that the disagreement is 'less ... about values than about how much confidence our reconstructions deserve'. The correct answer states this shared aim and the real point of difference.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the intention-versus-age option, which sounds like a neat summary of a dispute but contradicts 'Both sides appeal to the artist's intention'.
questions.difficulty_reason: A comparison of two views; two wrong options each state one side, and a third misdescribes what divides them.

questions.subtopic: The literary canon is shaped by institutional access and sustained by readers' continued use.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Defenders of the literary canon sometimes speak as if it were simply the record of quality, the works that survived because they were best. Critics reply that it is the record of power, the works that those with influence over schools, publishers and reviews chose to preserve. Each picture captures something and each is too simple. Survival does depend on institutions, and works by people excluded from those institutions often failed to be printed, taught or kept; to that extent the canon reflects who was in a position to choose. But institutions do not keep works alive by decree alone. A book that generations of readers find inert will drop out of the curriculum however prestigious its origins, and the works that last tend to be those that keep rewarding new readers with questions their makers never imagined. The canon is shaped by access and sustained by use.

options.A: Prestigious institutions keep the canon alive by deciding which books are taught, but readers now increasingly reject those choices in favour of newer works.
options.B: The canon reflects both institutional power, which decided whose works were preserved and taught, and readers' continuing engagement, which decides which of them stay alive.
options.C: The works that remain in the literary canon are those of the highest quality, because books that readers find inert sooner or later drop out of the curriculum.
options.D: The literary canon is above all a record of power, since works by people shut out of schools, publishers and reviews were never printed, taught or preserved.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The canon reflects both institutional power, which decided whose works were preserved and taught, and readers' continuing engagement, which decides which of them stay alive.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says institutions do not keep works alive 'by decree alone', and it reports no trend of readers rejecting canonical choices for newer works.
option_rationales.C: This is the defenders' picture, which the paragraph also calls 'too simple'; it ignores the role of access in deciding which works were ever kept and taught.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls this picture 'too simple' and says excluded works 'often' failed to survive, not that they never did; it adds that institutions cannot keep works alive 'by decree alone'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets two pictures of the canon against each other, calls each 'too simple', grants the power view its due (exclusion limited what survived) and the quality view its due (inert books drop out), and concludes that 'The canon is shaped by access and sustained by use'. The correct answer restates that synthesis.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing one of the two pictures the paragraph explicitly calls 'too simple'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each capture half the synthesis with plausible support; only the correct answer keeps both halves and their division of labour.

questions.subtopic: Borrowing words rarely threatens a language; languages die when speakers abandon them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Campaigns to protect a language from foreign words usually rest on the fear that borrowing will dilute it or eventually destroy it. The history of languages gives little support to this fear. Most major languages have absorbed large numbers of words from their neighbours, conquerors and trading partners, and they have remained recognisably themselves, because what makes a language distinct lies far more in its grammar and sound system than in the origin of its vocabulary. Borrowed words are typically reshaped to fit the borrowing language's pronunciation and grammatical endings until speakers no longer notice where they came from. Languages do die, but they die when their speakers abandon them for another language, not when they take in words from outside.

Languages do die, but they die when their speakers abandon them for another language, not when they take in words from outside.

options.A: Campaigns to keep foreign words out of a language do real harm, because a language that refuses to borrow will lose its speakers to its neighbours and die.
options.B: Most major languages consist largely of borrowed words, which shows that vocabulary has no connection at all with what makes a language distinct.
options.C: Borrowed words are usually reshaped to fit the pronunciation and grammar of the language that takes them in, until speakers forget where the words came from.
options.D: Taking in foreign words seldom endangers a language, whose identity lies mainly in grammar and sound; languages die when their speakers abandon them, not through borrowing.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Taking in foreign words seldom endangers a language, whose identity lies mainly in grammar and sound; languages die when their speakers abandon them, not through borrowing.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says languages die when speakers abandon them, but it never claims that refusing to borrow causes this; the causal link is invented.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says distinctness lies 'far more' in grammar and sound, not that vocabulary has 'no connection' to it, and it says languages absorbed many words, not that they consist largely of them.
option_rationales.C: This repeats one supporting detail and leaves out the paragraph's point, that borrowing does not threaten a language's survival.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states a fear (borrowing destroys languages), rejects it with historical evidence and an explanation (identity lies in grammar and sound; loans are adapted), and ends by naming what does kill languages. The correct answer captures the rejection, its reason and the contrast in the last sentence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reshaping option because it is a true statement from the paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is explicit in the second and last sentences; wrong options add a cause, overstate, or narrow.

questions.subtopic: Emoji supply the tone that casual writing lacks, so judging them by formal prose misunderstands them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Complaints that emoji are degrading written language tend to miss what they are for. Spoken conversation carries much of its meaning in tone of voice, facial expression and gesture, which tell a listener whether a remark is a joke, a rebuke or a kindness. Casual written messages, exchanged quickly between people who know each other, lost most of these signals, and misunderstandings followed: a brief reply could read as cold, an ironic one as sincere. Emoji and similar marks restore part of that missing layer, which is why they cluster in informal messages and are rare in contracts or reports. They are less a replacement for words than a substitute for the face, and judging them by the standards of formal prose mistakes their function.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Emoji are acceptable in informal messages between friends, but they degrade written language now that they are spreading into contracts and formal reports.
options.B: Because casual written messages are often misread, people ought to add emoji whenever a remark they write might be taken in the wrong way.
options.C: Emoji have improved written language by replacing many words with symbols that express meaning more quickly and more precisely than formal prose can.
options.D: Emoji chiefly restore the tone and expression that quick informal messages lose, so condemning them by the standards of formal prose misunderstands their purpose.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Emoji chiefly restore the tone and expression that quick informal messages lose, so condemning them by the standards of formal prose misunderstands their purpose.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says emoji 'are rare in contracts or reports' and rejects the complaint that they degrade language, so both halves contradict it.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph explains why emoji exist and where they appear; it gives no advice about when people should use them.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says emoji are 'less a replacement for words than a substitute for the face', so describing them as replacing words reverses its point.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rebuts a complaint by explaining the function of emoji: casual writing lost the cues of tone, face and gesture, and emoji 'restore part of that missing layer'. It concludes that 'judging them by the standards of formal prose mistakes their function'. The correct answer states both the function and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'improved written language' option by confusing a defence of emoji with a claim that they replace words.
questions.difficulty_reason: The function and conclusion are stated directly; each wrong option contradicts a specific sentence or adds advice.

questions.subtopic: Sign languages are full natural languages, and treating them as lesser codes has harmed deaf education.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Sign languages are often assumed to be a gestured version of the spoken language around them, or a simple system of mime that anyone could follow. Both assumptions are mistaken. Sign languages used by deaf communities have their own grammars, with rules for word order, agreement and the use of space that differ from those of the local spoken language, and they cannot be understood by untrained hearing observers any more than an unfamiliar spoken language can. They also vary from country to country and change over time, as all natural languages do. Treating them as lesser codes has had practical costs, since it has encouraged schooling that suppressed signing in favour of lip-reading and speech.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Sign languages used by deaf communities have their own grammars, with rules for word order, agreement and the use of space that differ from those of the local spoken language, and they cannot be understood by untrained hearing observers any more than an unfamiliar spoken language can. They also vary from country to country and change over time, as all natural languages do. Treating them as lesser codes has had practical costs, since it has encouraged schooling that suppressed signing in favour of lip-reading and speech.

options.A: Sign languages are complete natural languages with their own grammars, not gestured speech or mime, and regarding them as lesser has harmed the schooling of deaf people.
options.B: Deaf children learn better through sign language than through lip-reading and speech, so schools should teach them only in sign language from the start.
options.C: Sign languages follow the word order and grammar of the spoken language of their country, but they use space and movement where speech uses sound.
options.D: Sign languages form a universal system of gestures that deaf people from every country can use to communicate with one another without any training.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Sign languages are complete natural languages with their own grammars, not gestured speech or mime, and regarding them as lesser has harmed the schooling of deaf people.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph criticises schooling that suppressed signing but makes no comparison of learning outcomes and recommends no exclusive policy.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says their grammars 'differ from those of the local spoken language', which is the opposite of following its word order and grammar.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says sign languages 'vary from country to country' and cannot be followed by the untrained, so this states the assumption it rejects.

questions.explanation: The paragraph names two mistaken assumptions, refutes them (independent grammars, unintelligible without training, variation and change) and ends with a practical consequence of the error for schooling. The correct answer keeps the refutation and the consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the schooling option because it echoes the last sentence while adding a comparison and a policy.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated in the second sentence and supported plainly; wrong options restate the rejected views or add a prescription.

questions.subtopic: Radio drama's lack of images is both its strength and its limitation.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Radio drama is sometimes regarded as a poor relation of film and television, a form that lasted only until pictures could be added. Yet the absence of images is not simply a lack. Because the listener must supply faces, rooms and landscapes, each production is completed in a different imagination, and the scenes that would be most expensive or least convincing on screen, a battle at sea or a city on another planet, cost a radio producer little more than a few sounds and a sentence. What radio cannot do is control exactly what the audience sees, and so it suits stories that depend on voice, suggestion and inner life better than those that depend on precise visual spectacle. Its limitations and its strengths are, in large part, the same feature viewed from two sides.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Its limitations and its strengths are, in large part, the same feature viewed from two sides.

options.A: Radio drama lasted only until pictures could be added to broadcasts, after which film and television replaced it for most of its former audience.
options.B: Lacking pictures both frees radio drama, letting listeners imagine any setting cheaply, and limits it, suiting stories of voice and suggestion over precise spectacle.
options.C: Radio drama is superior to film and television, because listeners can picture any scene, however vast or costly, without the limits that images impose.
options.D: Radio producers favour scenes such as sea battles and alien cities because these can be created with a few sounds and at very little expense.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Lacking pictures both frees radio drama, letting listeners imagine any setting cheaply, and limits it, suiting stories of voice and suggestion over precise spectacle.

option_rationales.A: This is the dismissive view the paragraph reports and then disputes with 'Yet the absence of images is not simply a lack'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph presents the absence of images as both a strength and a limit; it never ranks radio above film and television.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says such scenes cost radio little, not that producers favour them, and the option drops the limitation entirely.

questions.explanation: The paragraph disputes the view of radio as a poor relation, shows how the absence of images is a strength (imagination, low cost of spectacle) and a limitation (no control over what is seen), and concludes that these are 'the same feature viewed from two sides'. The correct answer keeps both sides and the resulting fit with certain stories.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'superior' option, which keeps the strength and forgets the limitation.
questions.difficulty_reason: A comparison with a two-sided conclusion; the strongest wrong option keeps only one side.

questions.subtopic: The conglomerate discount alone cannot show that diversification destroys value, because selection may explain part of it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many analyses of stock markets have reported that diversified conglomerates tend to be valued below what their separate divisions would be worth as independent firms, and the finding has often been read as proof that diversification destroys value. The reading moves too quickly. Firms do not diversify at random: companies that expand into unrelated businesses may already have been struggling in their core activity, and the divisions conglomerates acquire may have been weaker than the independent firms used as benchmarks. If so, part of the discount reflects who chooses to diversify and what they buy, not damage done by diversification itself. None of this shows that conglomerates are efficient; managers of sprawling firms may well misallocate capital among divisions. It shows only that a lower valuation, on its own, cannot tell the two explanations apart.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The reading moves too quickly. Firms do not diversify at random: companies that expand into unrelated businesses may already have been struggling in their core activity, and the divisions conglomerates acquire may have been weaker than the independent firms used as benchmarks. If so, part of the discount reflects who chooses to diversify and what they buy, not damage done by diversification itself. None of this shows that conglomerates are efficient; managers of sprawling firms may well misallocate capital among divisions. It shows only that a lower valuation, on its own, cannot tell the two explanations apart.

options.A: Firms that are struggling in their core activity ought to avoid expanding into unrelated businesses, because doing so pushes their market valuation lower still.
options.B: The discount reported for conglomerates is an illusion produced by comparing weak acquired divisions with strong independent firms, so diversification does no harm.
options.C: A conglomerate's lower valuation need not mean diversifying destroyed value, since weaker firms and divisions may be the ones that diversify; the discount alone cannot separate selection from harm.
options.D: Diversified conglomerates are worth less than their separate divisions because the managers of sprawling firms misallocate capital among businesses they do not understand.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A conglomerate's lower valuation need not mean diversifying destroyed value, since weaker firms and divisions may be the ones that diversify; the discount alone cannot separate selection from harm.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph gives no advice to firms and asserts no causal effect of diversifying on valuation; that is exactly what it says the evidence cannot establish.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says 'part of the discount' may reflect selection and that 'None of this shows that conglomerates are efficient', so 'illusion' and 'no harm' overstate it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph offers misallocation only as something that 'may well' happen, and its point is that the discount 'cannot tell the two explanations apart', so asserting this cause contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (the conglomerate discount), rejects the inference that diversification destroys value, offers a selection explanation, concedes that conglomerates may still misallocate capital, and concludes that the discount alone 'cannot tell the two explanations apart'. The correct answer keeps the finding, the alternative and the limited conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'illusion' option, which turns the selection argument into a full acquittal and ignores the concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each assert one of the explanations the paragraph says cannot be separated; the correct answer must stay agnostic between them.

questions.subtopic: Polite replacement words inherit the stigma of what they replace, because words take colour from attitudes.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Each generation seems to need new polite words for things that make people uncomfortable, and each new word eventually acquires the sting of the one it replaced. A term coined to soften the description of a disability or a humble occupation begins neutral, but because it is used to refer to the same people, held in the same regard, it gradually absorbs the attitudes attached to them. Within a few decades the once-gentle term is heard as an insult, and reformers propose another. This cycle does not show that changing words is pointless; a fresh term can briefly signal respect and break a habit of mockery. It does show that vocabulary cannot carry the burden of changing attitudes on its own, since words take their colouring from the attitudes they name rather than the other way round.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

This cycle does not show that changing words is pointless; a fresh term can briefly signal respect and break a habit of mockery. It does show that vocabulary cannot carry the burden of changing attitudes on its own, since words take their colouring from the attitudes they name rather than the other way round.

options.A: Polite replacement terms tend to inherit the stigma of the words they displace, because meaning follows attitudes; renaming can help briefly but cannot by itself change how people are regarded.
options.B: Words gradually shape the attitudes people hold, so a polite term that stays in use long enough will eventually soften the regard in which the people it names are held by others.
options.C: Since every new polite term eventually becomes an insult, efforts to replace offensive vocabulary are pointless and merely give reformers an illusion of changing attitudes.
options.D: Terms for disabilities and for humble occupations are especially prone to becoming insults, so reformers working in these two areas must keep proposing fresh and gentler vocabulary.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Polite replacement terms tend to inherit the stigma of the words they displace, because meaning follows attitudes; renaming can help briefly but cannot by itself change how people are regarded.

option_rationales.B: This reverses the direction of influence: the last sentence says words take their colouring from attitudes 'rather than the other way round'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph explicitly says the cycle 'does not show that changing words is pointless', since a fresh term 'can briefly signal respect', so this option contradicts its qualification.
option_rationales.D: Disabilities and humble occupations are only the paragraph's examples, not a special class, and the paragraph does not prescribe an endless supply of new terms; it says vocabulary 'cannot carry the burden' alone.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why polite terms keep turning into insults: they refer to the same people held in the same regard, so they absorb the existing attitudes. It then qualifies the point: renaming is not pointless, since it can briefly signal respect, but vocabulary cannot change attitudes on its own because 'words take their colouring from the attitudes they name'. The correct answer keeps the mechanism, the direction of influence and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that calls renaming pointless, missing the explicit concession that a fresh term can briefly signal respect.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each catch half of the paragraph (the cycle, the direction of influence) but distort the qualification; the reader must hold both the mechanism and the concession.

questions.subtopic: A serious correction should reach roughly the audience the original error reached.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Newspapers often print an error on the front page and the correction, days later, in a small box near the back. Editors defend this as routine: corrections are numerous, and giving each one the prominence of the original story would crowd out the news. Yet the practice means that most readers who absorbed the mistake never meet the fix, so the record the paper leaves in its readers' minds stays wrong even after the paper itself has set it right. If a correction is meant to repair the harm an error caused, rather than merely to place the truth somewhere on file, it should reach roughly the audience the error reached. A serious mistake deserves a correction as visible as the story that carried it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Newspapers often print an error on the front page and the correction, days later, in a small box near the back. Editors defend this as routine: corrections are numerous, and giving each one the prominence of the original story would crowd out the news. Yet the practice means that most readers who absorbed the mistake never meet the fix, so the record the paper leaves in its readers' minds stays wrong even after the paper itself has set it right. If a correction is meant to repair the harm an error caused, rather than merely to place the truth somewhere on file, it should reach roughly the audience the error reached. options.A: Newspapers print so many corrections that giving each one prominence would crowd out the news, so placing them in a small box near the back is reasonable.
options.B: Every correction a newspaper prints, however trivial, should appear on the front page so that no reader is ever left with an inaccurate picture of events.
options.C: Editors bury corrections in small boxes at the back of the paper chiefly because they wish to hide their mistakes from readers and protect the paper's reputation.
options.D: Because a buried correction rarely reaches readers who absorbed the original error, serious corrections deserve prominence comparable to the stories they correct.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Because a buried correction rarely reaches readers who absorbed the original error, serious corrections deserve prominence comparable to the stories they correct.

option_rationales.A: This is the editors' defence, which the paragraph reports and then rejects with 'Yet the practice means that most readers who absorbed the mistake never meet the fix'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph limits its demand to 'a serious mistake' and asks only that a correction reach 'roughly' the original audience, so 'every correction, however trivial' on the front page overstates it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph reports the editors' stated reason, that prominent corrections 'would crowd out the news', and never attributes a wish to hide mistakes; the motive is outside the paragraph.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states the editors' defence of burying corrections and answers it: a buried correction leaves the error in readers' minds, so if a correction is meant to 'repair the harm', it should reach roughly the same audience. Its conclusion is limited to 'a serious mistake'. The correct answer gives the reason and the scoped conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the editors' defence because it is stated clearly in the paragraph, without noticing that the 'Yet' sentence rejects it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The central claim is stated in the last two sentences and each wrong option is clearly off once the 'Yet' turn is noticed.

questions.subtopic: Subtitling and dubbing each lose something different, so preferring one is a judgement of what matters in a film.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Audiences who grow up with subtitled foreign films often regard dubbing as a betrayal: the actor's voice, half the performance, is replaced by a stranger's. Audiences raised on dubbing reply that subtitles betray the image instead, since the viewer's eyes spend much of each scene at the bottom of the frame and miss faces, gestures and composition. Each side is right about what the other loses and quiet about what its own method loses. Subtitles preserve the sound of a performance but condense its words, often dropping a good deal of the dialogue to suit the reading speed of viewers; dubbing keeps more of the dialogue and the whole image but sacrifices the voice. Neither is a transparent window onto the original. The choice is between two different losses, and preferring one is a judgement about which part of a film matters most, not a recognition that one method is faithful and the other is not.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Audiences who grow up with subtitled foreign films often regard dubbing as a betrayal: the actor's voice, half the performance, is replaced by a stranger's.
