The irony is that the moments when automation hands control back are precisely the unusual and difficult ones, so the human is asked to perform best in the situations for which their recent experience has least prepared them. The answer is not to abandon automation, whose benefits are real, but to design training and routine work so that people keep exercising the abilities they will need when the machine gives up.

options.A: Because pilots lose their manual skills when automated systems fly the aircraft, airlines should reduce their reliance on automation and return to more flying by hand.
options.B: Automated cockpit systems often fail during routine flights, so pilots must watch them constantly and be ready to take over control at a moment's notice.
options.C: Pilots who spend most of each flight watching automated systems get little practice in flying by hand, and so their manual skills gradually fade as a result.
options.D: Cockpit automation improves safety but lets manual skill fade just when hard situations demand it, so training and work should keep those skills in regular use.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Cockpit automation improves safety but lets manual skill fade just when hard situations demand it, so training and work should keep those skills in regular use.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'The answer is not to abandon automation, whose benefits are real', so cutting back on it is the remedy it rejects.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph describes 'a system that rarely fails' and says control returns in 'unusual and difficult' moments, not routine ones.
option_rationales.C: This is one step of the argument; it omits the irony that skill is needed most in the hardest moments and the proposed remedy.

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants that automation 'has made flying far safer', explains that manual skill 'fades' with disuse, and notes the irony that control returns in 'the unusual and difficult' moments. Its remedy is not to abandon automation but to design training so people 'keep exercising the abilities they will need'. The correct answer holds the benefit, the problem and the remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the remedy the paragraph explicitly rejects because it follows naturally from the problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option draws a natural but rejected conclusion and another is an accurate partial step.

questions.subtopic: Following app directions teaches less about a route, but the effect depends on how the tool is used.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: People who follow turn-by-turn directions from a phone tend to remember less about the route afterwards than people who found their own way with a map. This is hardly surprising: following instructions requires attention to the next turn, not to the layout of the streets, and what we do not attend to we do not learn. It would be wrong, though, to conclude that navigation apps are steadily damaging our brains. The finding concerns what is learned on a given trip, and someone who uses an app to get around a new city but then explores it on foot can build a perfectly good mental map. The effect depends on how the tool is used, not merely on whether it is used.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Paper maps are a better guide than navigation apps for travellers in unfamiliar cities, because they help such travellers reach their destinations more quickly.
options.B: A traveller who uses an app to reach places in a new city and then explores the streets on foot can still build a perfectly good mental map of it.
options.C: Following app directions teaches less about a route because attention goes to the next turn, but this reflects how the tool is used, not lasting harm from using it.
options.D: Navigation apps steadily weaken the brain's ability to form mental maps, so that people who rely on them gradually lose their sense of direction altogether.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Following app directions teaches less about a route because attention goes to the next turn, but this reflects how the tool is used, not lasting harm from using it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph compares what people remember, not how quickly they arrive, and it does not rank maps above apps as guides.
option_rationales.B: This is the example used to qualify the finding; it omits the finding itself and the general point about how the tool is used.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'It would be wrong, though, to conclude that navigation apps are steadily damaging our brains', which this option asserts.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports that app users 'remember less about the route', explains this by attention, and then qualifies it: the finding 'concerns what is learned on a given trip', and 'the effect depends on how the tool is used'. The correct answer states the finding and its qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Overstating a trip-level finding into a claim of lasting brain damage.
questions.difficulty_reason: The finding and its qualification are both stated outright; the extreme wrong option is explicitly denied.

questions.subtopic: Technical debt is like a loan in buying speed now, but unlike one its cost is hidden, so teams take on too much.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Software engineers speak of technical debt: the future cost created when code is written quickly rather than well. The metaphor is apt in one respect, since like a loan a shortcut lets a team deliver something sooner in exchange for paying more later, and taking it on can be a sensible choice. But it misleads in another. A financial debt has a known balance and a schedule of payments, so a borrower can decide whether it is worth it. The cost of hasty code is rarely visible; it shows up as features that take longer than expected and failures nobody can easily trace, and it grows in ways no one has agreed to. Teams therefore tend to take on far more of it than they would if the bill arrived in writing.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The cost of hasty code is rarely visible; it shows up as features that take longer than expected and failures nobody can easily trace, and it grows in ways no one has agreed to. Teams therefore tend to take on far more of it than they would if the bill arrived in writing.

options.A: Technical debt closely resembles financial debt, since both have a known balance and a schedule of payments that let a team judge whether a particular shortcut is worthwhile.
options.B: Writing code quickly rather than well is always a mistake, because the hidden costs of shortcuts eventually exceed any benefit gained by delivering software sooner.
options.C: Hasty code reveals its cost through features that take longer than expected to build and through failures that nobody in the team is able to trace easily.
options.D: Like a loan, a coding shortcut can sensibly buy speed at a later price, but its cost is hidden and grows unchecked, so teams take on too much.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Like a loan, a coding shortcut can sensibly buy speed at a later price, but its cost is hidden and grows unchecked, so teams take on too much.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the metaphor 'misleads' precisely because the cost of hasty code, unlike a loan, has no known balance and 'is rarely visible'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says taking on technical debt 'can be a sensible choice', so 'always a mistake' contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: This describes how the cost appears; it leaves out the comparison with a loan and the conclusion that teams take on too much.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares technical debt with a loan: apt because a shortcut buys speed 'in exchange for paying more later' and 'can be a sensible choice'; misleading because a loan has 'a known balance', while the cost of hasty code 'is rarely visible' and grows 'in ways no one has agreed to'. So teams 'take on far more of it'. The correct answer holds both sides of the comparison and the consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Keeping only the apt half of the metaphor and missing where it misleads.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must hold where an analogy fits and where it fails; one wrong option keeps only the fit.

questions.subtopic: Clumsy standards survive because wide adoption gives them dependants, so their persistence records success.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Engineers often speak of legacy systems as if they were merely old, but what makes a legacy difficult is not its age but the number of things that have come to depend on it. A file format, a connector or a programming interface that was widely adopted becomes a promise to everyone who built on it, and each new version must keep that promise or break their work. This is why designs that almost everyone agrees are clumsy survive for decades: the cost of changing them would be borne not by the designer but by thousands of users who would all have to adapt at once. The awkwardness of a long-lived standard is therefore less a sign of poor judgement than a record of its success; only what was widely adopted acquires enough dependants to become impossible to fix.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The awkwardness of a long-lived standard is therefore less a sign of poor judgement than a record of its success; only what was widely adopted acquires enough dependants to become impossible to fix.

options.A: Awkward standards endure because wide adoption gives them many dependants who would bear the cost of any change, so their persistence reflects success, not poor design.
options.B: A widely adopted file format or connector becomes a promise to its users, and every later version of it has to remain compatible with their work.
options.C: Old technical systems are hard to replace mainly because of their age, since the knowledge needed to modify them is lost as their original designers retire.
options.D: Designers of widely used standards should refuse to change them at all, because every new version breaks the work of the users who built on them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Awkward standards endure because wide adoption gives them many dependants who would bear the cost of any change, so their persistence reflects success, not poor design.

option_rationales.B: This restates only the second sentence and omits the paragraph's conclusion that a standard's awkwardness is 'a record of its success'.
option_rationales.C: The first sentence says the difficulty is 'not its age but the number of things that have come to depend on it', so this option names the very cause the paragraph rejects.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph explains why clumsy standards persist; it prescribes nothing, and it says each new version 'must keep that promise', which implies versions are made, not refused.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a phenomenon: clumsy standards survive because adoption creates dependants, the cost of change falls on those many users, and so awkwardness that cannot be fixed is evidence of success. The correct answer keeps the mechanism (dependants bearing the cost) and the conclusion (success, not poor judgement).
questions.common_misconception: Picking the compatibility option because it uses the paragraph's own terms, without noticing that it drops the conclusion about success.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow wrong option is a faithful paraphrase of one sentence, so the reader must test for the paragraph's conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Tracking consent banners give only the appearance of control because their design steers the answer.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is often said that the banners asking website visitors to accept or refuse tracking have handed people control over their personal data. The claim assumes that a choice offered is a choice made. In practice, a visitor who wants to read an article is asked, at the worst possible moment, to weigh consequences that are invisible and distant against an obstacle that is immediate and irritating. Many banners make acceptance a single click while refusal requires several screens of toggles. Unsurprisingly, most people click whatever makes the banner disappear. A mechanism built in this way records the visitor's impatience rather than the visitor's preference, and it lends the appearance of consent to an outcome largely decided by the design of the box.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is often said that the banners asking website visitors to accept or refuse tracking have handed people control over their personal data. The claim assumes that a choice offered is a choice made. In practice, a visitor who wants to read an article is asked, at the worst possible moment, to weigh consequences that are invisible and distant against an obstacle that is immediate and irritating. Many banners make acceptance a single click while refusal requires several screens of toggles. Unsurprisingly, most people click whatever makes the banner disappear. A mechanism built in this way records the visitor's impatience rather than the visitor's preference, and it lends the appearance of consent to an outcome largely decided by the design of the box.

options.A: On many websites accepting tracking takes a single click, while refusing it requires the visitor to work through several screens of separate toggles.
options.B: Consent banners only appear to give control: their timing and lopsided design lead people to click whatever removes them, so answers reflect impatience, not preference.
options.C: Most internet users do not really care about their personal data, which is why they accept tracking without reading what the banners on websites ask them.
options.D: Websites should be banned from tracking visitors altogether, since no banner, however carefully it was designed, could ever obtain genuine consent from a reader.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Consent banners only appear to give control: their timing and lopsided design lead people to click whatever removes them, so answers reflect impatience, not preference.

option_rationales.A: This is one supporting detail; it leaves out the central claim that the resulting 'consent' records impatience and only appears to give control.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph attributes the clicks to timing and design ('an obstacle that is immediate and irritating'), not to indifference about data, so this supplies a cause the paragraph does not give.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph blames a mechanism 'built in this way', which implies that design matters; it neither says consent is impossible nor proposes a ban.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the view that banners give people control. Its reasons are the timing of the request and the asymmetry between accepting and refusing, and its conclusion is that the banner records impatience and lends 'the appearance of consent'. The correct answer states the critique, the reasons and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the ban because the paragraph is critical of banners, although it criticises a particular design, not consent as such.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion is stated outright in the last sentence and each wrong option is plainly narrow, extreme or off-cause.

questions.subtopic: Efficiency savings are partly eaten by extra use, but the size of the rebound varies, so estimate honestly.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Making a machine more efficient seems an obvious way to reduce the energy it consumes, but economists have long noted an awkward complication. When a service becomes cheaper to run, people tend to use more of it: a more economical car makes longer journeys affordable, and cheaper lighting invites more of it. Some of the expected saving is therefore taken back in additional use. It does not follow, as enthusiasts of the idea sometimes conclude, that efficiency is futile. Whether the rebound swallows a small or a large part of the saving depends on how much more of the service people actually want once its price falls, and for many household uses that appetite is limited; nobody keeps the fridge door open because the fridge is economical. The finding is a reason to estimate savings honestly, not a reason to abandon the pursuit of them.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Making a machine more efficient seems an obvious way to reduce the energy it consumes, but economists have long noted an awkward complication. When a service becomes cheaper to run, people tend to use more of it: a more economical car makes longer journeys affordable, and cheaper lighting invites more of it. Some of the expected saving is therefore taken back in additional use. It does not follow, as enthusiasts of the idea sometimes conclude, that efficiency is futile. Whether the rebound swallows a small or a large part of the saving depends on how much more of the service people actually want once its price falls, and for many household uses that appetite is limited; nobody keeps the fridge door open because the fridge is economical. The finding is a reason to estimate savings honestly, not a reason to abandon the pursuit of them.

options.A: The rebound in use is larger for cars and lighting than for refrigerators, so policy on efficiency should concentrate on household appliances rather than on transport.
options.B: Cheaper services get used more, so some efficiency savings are lost, but how much depends on how much extra use people want, which calls for realistic estimates rather than abandoning efficiency.
options.C: Gains in efficiency cut energy use roughly in proportion to the improvement, since for most household devices people do not use them more when running costs fall.
options.D: Because cheaper energy services are always used more, gains in efficiency end up raising total consumption, so efforts to save energy through better machines defeat themselves.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Cheaper services get used more, so some efficiency savings are lost, but how much depends on how much extra use people want, which calls for realistic estimates rather than abandoning efficiency.

option_rationales.A: Cars, lighting and fridges are illustrations, not a ranking, and the paragraph makes no recommendation about where policy should concentrate.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'Some of the expected saving is therefore taken back', so savings are not proportional; the fridge shows that the appetite for some uses is limited, not that rebound is absent.
option_rationales.D: This is the conclusion of the 'enthusiasts' whom the paragraph corrects when it says 'It does not follow' that 'efficiency is futile'. The paragraph says only 'some' of the saving is taken back.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (cheaper services are used more, so some saving is lost) and then qualifies it against two misreadings: it is not proof that efficiency is futile, and its size depends on how much extra use people want. The correct answer holds the finding, the condition and the closing moral ('estimate savings honestly').
questions.common_misconception: Taking the efficiency defeats itself option because the paragraph spends its first half on the rebound, missing the turn at 'It does not follow'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are the opposite overreadings (rebound is total; rebound is absent), and the correct answer must sit between them with the right condition.

questions.subtopic: Code maintained by a few volunteers is not a free good; popularity raises its upkeep.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Much of the software that businesses rely on is maintained by a handful of volunteers, sometimes by a single person working in spare hours. Companies that would never run a factory on an unpaid supplier routinely build products on such code and treat it as a free natural resource, like air. The comparison flatters them. Air does not need anyone to fix it; code does, and the work of fixing security flaws, answering bug reports and keeping up with changes elsewhere does not get easier as more people use a project. It gets harder. Popularity, which looks like a sign of health, can thus be precisely what exhausts the few people who keep a project alive. A firm that depends on such work and contributes nothing to it is not enjoying a free good but drawing down a stock that someone else is paying to replenish.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Much of the software that businesses rely on is maintained by a handful of volunteers, sometimes by a single person working in spare hours. Companies that would never run a factory on an unpaid supplier routinely build products on such code and treat it as a free natural resource, like air. The comparison flatters them. Air does not need anyone to fix it; code does, and the work of fixing security flaws, answering bug reports and keeping up with changes elsewhere does not get easier as more people use a project. It gets harder. Popularity, which looks like a sign of health, can thus be precisely what exhausts the few people who keep a project alive. A firm that depends on such work and contributes nothing to it is not enjoying a free good but drawing down a stock that someone else is paying to replenish.

options.A: Firms treat volunteer-maintained code as free like air, yet its upkeep rests on a few people and grows with popularity, so taking without contributing depletes their effort.
options.B: Popular open software tends to be healthier and more secure than obscure software, because its many users report bugs and help its small group of volunteers fix them.
options.C: Businesses ought to stop using software maintained by volunteers and should buy commercial products whose suppliers are contractually responsible for fixing security flaws.
options.D: Many companies build their products on code that unpaid volunteers maintain, and sometimes one person looks after an entire project in spare hours.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Firms treat volunteer-maintained code as free like air, yet its upkeep rests on a few people and grows with popularity, so taking without contributing depletes their effort.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the reverse: maintenance 'does not get easier as more people use a project. It gets harder', and popularity 'can thus be precisely what exhausts' the maintainers.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph criticises firms that contribute 'nothing'; it does not tell them to abandon volunteer code or switch to commercial suppliers, so this adds a prescription.
option_rationales.D: This restates the opening facts and omits the argument: that popularity increases the burden and that taking without contributing draws down someone else's effort.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues against the 'free natural resource' picture: unlike air, code needs upkeep, the upkeep grows with popularity, and a firm that only takes is consuming a stock others replenish. The correct answer keeps the rejected comparison, the reason and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the popular software is healthier option because popularity is usually a sign of health, which is the very assumption the paragraph overturns.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must combine the rejected analogy, the counter-intuitive role of popularity and the conclusion; the narrow option is accurate as far as it goes.

questions.subtopic: An ending should be faithful to what the novel is about; openness is not a virtue in itself.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Readers who complain that a novel simply stops often assume that an ending exists to settle what the story has raised: who is guilty, who marries whom, whether the journey succeeds. Some endings do that, and do it well. But an ending can also be judged by whether it completes the shape of the book's attention. A novel that has spent three hundred pages showing how hard it is to know another person would contradict itself if its last chapter revealed everything; the unresolved close is then not a failure of nerve but the argument carried through. Openness is not a virtue in itself, and a writer who withholds an answer merely to seem profound has evaded rather than completed the work. The question is not whether an ending is closed but whether it is faithful to what the novel has been about.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A novel that has spent three hundred pages showing how hard it is to know another person would contradict itself if its last chapter revealed everything; the unresolved close is then not a failure of nerve but the argument carried through. Openness is not a virtue in itself, and a writer who withholds an answer merely to seem profound has evaded rather than completed the work. The question is not whether an ending is closed but whether it is faithful to what the novel has been about.

options.A: Readers who complain about unresolved endings are usually right, because a novel that withholds its answers has generally failed to finish what its early chapters began.
options.B: Open endings are artistically superior to tidy ones, since resolving every question that a story raises insults the intelligence of its serious readers.
options.C: A novel about how difficult it is to know another person would contradict itself if its final chapter revealed everything about its characters' hidden inner lives and motives.
options.D: An ending should be judged by its fit with the novel's concerns; an unresolved close can complete a book's argument, but openness adopted merely for effect is evasion.

questions.correct_answer: (D) An ending should be judged by its fit with the novel's concerns; an unresolved close can complete a book's argument, but openness adopted merely for effect is evasion.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph rejects this complaint's assumption; it says an unresolved close can be 'the argument carried through' rather than a failure.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says 'Openness is not a virtue in itself' and grants that some closed endings settle questions 'and do it well', so it ranks neither kind above the other.
option_rationales.C: This is the paragraph's example only; it omits the general criterion of faithfulness and the warning about openness used merely to seem profound.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues for a criterion: an ending is good if it is 'faithful to what the novel has been about'. It illustrates with a novel whose open close completes its theme, and it qualifies the point by denying that openness is good in itself. The correct answer carries the criterion, the illustration's lesson and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the defence of one open ending as a general preference for open endings, and so picking the 'artistically superior' option.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option overgeneralises the example; only the qualification in the penultimate sentence rules it out.

questions.subtopic: Strict poetic forms can prompt invention rather than cage it, though they do not guarantee good work.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A familiar view holds that strict poetic forms, with their fixed line counts and rhyme schemes, are cages that a free imagination must escape. Poets who have worked in such forms often describe the opposite experience. The need to find a rhyme or to fit a thought into a fixed number of syllables pushes them away from the first phrase that comes to mind, which is usually the most worn, and towards words and connections they would not otherwise have found. The constraint works less as a wall than as a prompt. This does not make every sonnet good; a form can be filled mechanically. But the assumption that freedom from rules is the natural condition of creativity mistakes the absence of resistance for the presence of invention.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The need to find a rhyme or to fit a thought into a fixed number of syllables pushes them away from the first phrase that comes to mind, which is usually the most worn, and towards words and connections they would not otherwise have found. The constraint works less as a wall than as a prompt. This does not make every sonnet good; a form can be filled mechanically. But the assumption that freedom from rules is the natural condition of creativity mistakes the absence of resistance for the presence of invention.

options.A: Poets who write in fixed forms often say that hunting for a rhyme leads them away from the first words that occur to them while they compose.
options.B: Fixed forms such as the sonnet restrict what poets can say, so a truly free imagination needs to set aside rhyme schemes and fixed line counts altogether.
options.C: Strict forms are not simply cages: by blocking the first, most worn phrase they can push poets towards fresh language, though a form can still be filled mechanically.
options.D: Poets write better in strict traditional forms than in free verse, because rhyme and fixed syllable counts guarantee that their work avoids worn and predictable phrasing.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Strict forms are not simply cages: by blocking the first, most worn phrase they can push poets towards fresh language, though a form can still be filled mechanically.

option_rationales.A: This reports the poets' experience but leaves out the paragraph's point about creativity and its qualification that forms can be filled mechanically.
option_rationales.B: This is the 'familiar view' stated in the first sentence, which the rest of the paragraph argues against.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'This does not make every sonnet good; a form can be filled mechanically', so 'guarantee' overstates it, and it makes no comparison with free verse.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises the view that forms are cages. It argues that constraint works 'as a prompt' against worn phrasing, concedes that a form can be filled mechanically, and concludes that freedom from rules is not the natural condition of creativity. The correct answer keeps the reversal and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'guarantee' option because it agrees with the paragraph's direction, without noticing that the concession rules out any guarantee.
questions.difficulty_reason: The view under attack is labelled 'A familiar view', and the concession is explicit.

questions.subtopic: Intention-based and reader-based accounts of meaning each explain one feature of interpretation; a sound view needs both.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: One school of critics holds that a poem means what its author intended, and that interpretation is the patient reconstruction of that intention from the text and its circumstances. Another holds that once a work is published its meaning belongs to its readers, so that the author's own account is just one reading among many. Each position captures something the other cannot. The first explains why we can be wrong about a poem, as we are when we take an ironic line for a sincere one; the second explains why a work can say more than its author knew, as when a later age sees in an old novel a pattern its writer never noticed. What neither can do alone is account for both experiences, of being corrected by the text and of being surprised by it, and a defensible view of interpretation will have to make room for both.

options.A: The view that a poem means what its author intended is the better supported one, since only the author's intention can explain how a reader comes to misread an ironic line.
options.B: A satisfactory account of interpretation should divide the work between the two, treating intention as decisive for older works and readers' responses as decisive for recent ones.
options.C: Intention-centred and reader-centred views of meaning each explain one real feature of reading, that we can misread and that works can exceed their authors, so an adequate theory must accommodate both.
options.D: Since critics disagree so deeply about where meaning lies, no interpretation of a poem can be judged more correct than another, and every reading stands on equal terms.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Intention-centred and reader-centred views of meaning each explain one real feature of reading, that we can misread and that works can exceed their authors, so an adequate theory must accommodate both.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph credits the intention view with explaining error but says 'Each position captures something the other cannot', so it does not declare either view better supported.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph asks for a view that makes room for both experiences; it never divides authority by the age of a work, and its own example of surprise involves an 'old novel'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph treats 'being corrected by the text' as a real experience any defensible view must explain, which presupposes that some readings are wrong.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares two views and concludes that each explains something the other cannot: intention explains error, reader-centred meaning explains surplus meaning. It ends by requiring a view that makes room for both. The correct answer states this comparison and the conclusion without inventing how the combination would work.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the divide by age compromise because it sounds like making room for both, although the paragraph proposes no such rule and its own example cuts against it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The compromise wrong option mimics the conclusion's spirit, and rejecting it requires noticing that the 'old novel' example contradicts it.

questions.subtopic: Amateur choirs attract hesitant singers because choral singing asks for mutual listening and gives belonging.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Why do people who insist they cannot sing keep turning up, week after week, to rehearse with amateur choirs? Part of the answer lies in what choral singing asks of them. Unlike a solo performance, it does not demand that any one voice be remarkable; it demands that each voice listen to the others and adjust, breathing and entering together. The individual's weaknesses are absorbed into the sound of the group, while the group's sound depends on everyone's attention. Members describe the result less as a musical achievement than as a feeling of belonging that few other activities supply so directly. The music matters, but for many singers it is the occasion for the coordination, and the coordination is what they come back for.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Why do people who insist they cannot sing keep turning up, week after week, to rehearse with amateur choirs? Part of the answer lies in what choral singing asks of them. Unlike a solo performance, it does not demand that any one voice be remarkable; it demands that each voice listen to the others and adjust, breathing and entering together. The individual's weaknesses are absorbed into the sound of the group, while the group's sound depends on everyone's attention. Members describe the result less as a musical achievement than as a feeling of belonging that few other activities supply so directly. The music matters, but for many singers it is the occasion for the coordination, and the coordination is what they come back for.

options.A: Choral singing is a more valuable musical activity than solo performance, because it requires every singer to listen carefully and adjust to the voices nearby.
options.B: People join amateur choirs mainly to improve their singing voices, since regular rehearsal with others gradually turns weak singers into capable soloists.
options.C: In a choir the weaknesses of any individual singer are absorbed into the sound of the whole group, so that no single voice has to be remarkable.
options.D: People unsure of their voices keep joining choirs because group singing asks for mutual listening rather than individual brilliance, and that coordination gives them belonging.

questions.correct_answer: (D) People unsure of their voices keep joining choirs because group singing asks for mutual listening rather than individual brilliance, and that coordination gives them belonging.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph contrasts what the two demand but never ranks their musical value; this adds a judgement it does not make.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says members value 'a feeling of belonging' more than 'a musical achievement' and says nothing about becoming soloists.
option_rationales.C: This is one step in the explanation and omits the answer the paragraph gives to its question: belonging produced by coordination.

questions.explanation: The paragraph asks why hesitant singers keep coming and answers: choral singing asks for listening and adjustment rather than a remarkable voice, and the coordination yields belonging, which is what members return for. The correct answer gives the question's answer with both parts.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the 'weaknesses are absorbed' option because it is accurate, without checking whether it answers the paragraph's question.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer is spelled out in the last two sentences; wrong options are clearly narrow or out of scope.

questions.subtopic: Borrowing does not erode a language; preferring native words is a matter of taste, not defence.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Campaigns to purify a language usually begin from the fear that borrowed words are a kind of erosion, each foreign term a small loss of the native stock. The fear misdescribes how languages grow. A borrowed word rarely displaces an existing one outright; more often it settles beside it and the two divide the territory, one taking a formal shade and the other an everyday one, so that the language ends up able to say more rather than less. Borrowing is also old: most languages that purists wish to protect were themselves assembled from earlier contacts. None of this means that every borrowing is welcome or that speakers cannot reasonably prefer a native coinage. It means that the decision is one of taste, not a defence against decay.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Campaigns to purify a language usually begin from the fear that borrowed words are a kind of erosion, each foreign term a small loss of the native stock. The fear misdescribes how languages grow. A borrowed word rarely displaces an existing one outright; more often it settles beside it and the two divide the territory, one taking a formal shade and the other an everyday one, so that the language ends up able to say more rather than less. Borrowing is also old: most languages that purists wish to protect were themselves assembled from earlier contacts. None of this means that every borrowing is welcome or that speakers cannot reasonably prefer a native coinage. It means that the decision is one of taste, not a defence against decay.

options.A: The languages that purists protect were themselves formed through earlier contacts, which shows that campaigns for purity misunderstand the history of the languages they defend.
options.B: Purists wrongly treat borrowing as erosion, since loanwords usually add distinctions beside native words and languages have always borrowed; preferring native words is legitimate, but only as taste.
options.C: When a foreign word enters a language it usually replaces a native word, but the loss is made good because the newcomer tends to carry a more formal shade of meaning.
options.D: Borrowed words enrich every language they enter, so efforts by speakers to prefer native coinages over foreign terms are misguided and ought to be abandoned.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Purists wrongly treat borrowing as erosion, since loanwords usually add distinctions beside native words and languages have always borrowed; preferring native words is legitimate, but only as taste.

option_rationales.A: This is the supporting point about history only; it omits the main mechanism (loanwords add distinctions) and the concession that preference is a matter of taste.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a borrowed word 'rarely displaces an existing one outright'; it settles beside it, so 'usually replaces' reverses the claim.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph concedes that not 'every borrowing is welcome' and that it does not mean speakers cannot 'reasonably prefer a native coinage', so it does not call such preferences misguided.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the purist fear of erosion with two reasons (borrowings add distinctions; languages were always assembled by borrowing) and then limits its own claim: preferring native words is reasonable, but it is taste rather than defence. The correct answer holds the critique, both reasons and the limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'enrich every language' option and missing the concession in the last two sentences.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option follows the argument but drops the concession; another reverses a single word ('rarely' to 'usually').

questions.subtopic: Lower incivility under real names may be confounded and has hidden costs, so it does not settle anonymity.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Comparisons of online discussions are often said to show that comment threads in which participants use their real names contain fewer insults than anonymous ones, and the point is regularly offered in support of ending anonymity. The inference moves too fast. Sites that require real names tend to differ from anonymous ones in other ways as well: they are often smaller, more closely moderated and frequented by people who already know one another, any of which could explain the gentler tone. Even where the effect is genuine, it is bought at a price that the comparison does not measure, since the people most likely to fall silent when they must identify themselves include those with the most to fear from speaking, such as an employee criticising an employer. Less abuse in the threads that remain is not the same as better discussion overall.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Comparisons of online discussions are often said to show that comment threads in which participants use their real names contain fewer insults than anonymous ones, and the point is regularly offered in support of ending anonymity. The inference moves too fast. Sites that require real names tend to differ from anonymous ones in other ways as well: they are often smaller, more closely moderated and frequented by people who already know one another, any of which could explain the gentler tone. Even where the effect is genuine, it is bought at a price that the comparison does not measure, since the people most likely to fall silent when they must identify themselves include those with the most to fear from speaking, such as an employee criticising an employer. Less abuse in the threads that remain is not the same as better discussion overall.

options.A: Gentler named threads may owe their tone to other features of such sites, and even a real effect could silence vulnerable speakers, so the comparison alone does not justify ending anonymity.
options.B: Requiring real names does nothing to reduce abuse in online comment threads, since the gentler tone of named forums comes entirely from closer moderation and smaller size.
options.C: Anonymity should be kept in online discussion because it protects vulnerable people such as employees criticising employers, and this benefit plainly outweighs any increase in abuse.
options.D: Real-name rules make online discussion less abusive, but because they also deter some people from posting, sites should use them only together with strict moderation.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Gentler named threads may owe their tone to other features of such sites, and even a real effect could silence vulnerable speakers, so the comparison alone does not justify ending anonymity.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says other features 'could explain' the tone and then considers the case 'Even where the effect is genuine', so it does not assert that the effect is absent or wholly due to moderation.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the price 'the comparison does not measure', which means the balance is unknown; it argues that the case for ending anonymity is incomplete, not that the benefit plainly outweighs the abuse.
option_rationales.D: This treats the effect as established and adds a recommendation about moderation that the paragraph never makes; it uses moderation only as a possible confounder.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques an inference from a reported comparison. It gives two objections: confounding (named sites differ in size, moderation and familiarity) and an unmeasured cost (vulnerable speakers fall silent). Its conclusion is limited: less abuse is not the same as better discussion, so the comparison does not settle the matter. The correct answer states both objections and the limited conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that defends anonymity outright, because the paragraph clearly leans that way, and missing that it claims only that the cost is unmeasured.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each overstate one of the paragraph's two objections into a firm conclusion, and the correct answer must keep both hedges ('could explain', 'does not measure').

questions.subtopic: Equal airtime misleads when experts largely agree; fairness to evidence requires proportion.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Giving each side of a dispute equal time looks like the essence of fair reporting, and on questions where informed opinion is genuinely divided it is. But when nearly all of those who have studied a matter agree and a small minority dissents, presenting the two positions as evenly matched misinforms the audience about the very thing it most needs to know: where the weight of evidence lies. The audience leaves believing that experts are split when they are not. Fairness to persons, letting each view be heard, has been confused with fairness to the evidence, which requires that views be presented in proportion to their support. A report can include a dissenting voice and still be accurate, provided it does not pretend that the dissent is as strong as the consensus.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Giving each side of a dispute equal time looks like the essence of fair reporting, and on questions where informed opinion is genuinely divided it is. But when nearly all of those who have studied a matter agree and a small minority dissents, presenting the two positions as evenly matched misinforms the audience about the very thing it most needs to know: where the weight of evidence lies. The audience leaves believing that experts are split when they are not. Fairness to persons, letting each view be heard, has been confused with fairness to the evidence, which requires that views be presented in proportion to their support. A report can include a dissenting voice and still be accurate, provided it does not pretend that the dissent is as strong as the consensus.

options.A: Giving each side of a dispute equal time is the essence of fair reporting, because it lets every view be heard and leaves audiences free to weigh the evidence themselves.
options.B: Journalists should leave dissenting views out of their reports whenever most experts agree, since giving such views any airtime misleads the audience about the evidence.
options.C: Equal coverage suits disputes where informed opinion is truly divided, but under near consensus it misleads audiences about the evidence; dissent may be reported without being made to look equal.
options.D: Audiences often come away believing that experts are deeply divided on questions where nearly everyone who has studied the matter in fact agrees.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Equal coverage suits disputes where informed opinion is truly divided, but under near consensus it misleads audiences about the evidence; dissent may be reported without being made to look equal.

option_rationales.A: This is the appearance the first sentence describes and the rest of the paragraph rejects for cases of near consensus, where equal time 'misinforms the audience'.
option_rationales.B: The last sentence says 'A report can include a dissenting voice and still be accurate', which this option contradicts.
option_rationales.D: This is the consequence the paragraph describes, but it omits the cause (equal time for unequal support) and the remedy of proportion that the paragraph argues for.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that equal time is fair only when opinion is truly divided; under near consensus it misleads, because fairness to evidence requires proportion. It ends by allowing dissent to be reported if not inflated. The correct answer captures the condition, the harm and the allowance.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the leave dissent out option because it follows from the paragraph's direction, overlooking the explicit allowance in the final sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer's condition ('truly divided') and allowance (dissent reported) must both be checked against wrong options that drop one of them.

questions.subtopic: Spelling reform weighs future learners' convenience against continuity with existing writing and varied speech.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Proposals to make English spelling match pronunciation have a strong case on one side and a stubborn obstacle on the other. In favour, a regular system would spare children years of memorising exceptions and would make reading easier to learn. Against it stands not mere habit but the sheer amount already written: every reform would make the existing stock of books, signs and records look strange to the next generation, and the more successful the reform, the more foreign the past would become. There is also the awkward question of whose pronunciation should be the standard, since speakers in different regions say the same words differently. The case for reform rests on the convenience of future learners; the case against rests on continuity with what has been written and the variety of present speech.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Proposals to make English spelling match pronunciation have a strong case on one side and a stubborn obstacle on the other. In favour, a regular system would spare children years of memorising exceptions and would make reading easier to learn. Against it stands not mere habit but the sheer amount already written: every reform would make the existing stock of books, signs and records look strange to the next generation, and the more successful the reform, the more foreign the past would become. There is also the awkward question of whose pronunciation should be the standard, since speakers in different regions say the same words differently. The case for reform rests on the convenience of future learners; the case against rests on continuity with what has been written and the variety of present speech.

options.A: Spelling reform has repeatedly failed in English because speakers from different regions could never agree on one standard for how words are pronounced.
options.B: Children learning English spend years memorising irregular spellings, which a regular system matching spelling to pronunciation would allow them to avoid.
options.C: English spelling should be reformed to match pronunciation, because the only real obstacle to such a change is the habit of adult readers who dislike unfamiliar forms.
options.D: Phonetic spelling would make reading easier for future learners, but it would estrange readers from existing writing and would require choosing one region's pronunciation as the standard.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Phonetic spelling would make reading easier for future learners, but it would estrange readers from existing writing and would require choosing one region's pronunciation as the standard.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says nothing about past attempts failing; it mentions regional pronunciation as one difficulty a reform would face, not as the cause of a history of failure.
option_rationales.B: This gives only the case in favour and omits the two objections that make up most of the paragraph.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the obstacle is 'not mere habit but the sheer amount already written', and it also raises the problem of whose pronunciation to use.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares the case for reform (easier learning) with the case against (estrangement from existing writing, and no neutral pronunciation to follow), summarising them in its last sentence. The correct answer gives both sides.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the one-sided option about children because it is the first point the paragraph makes.
questions.difficulty_reason: The last sentence states both sides directly; wrong options are one-sided, contradicted, or about history not discussed.

questions.subtopic: Recall beats rereading, but it strengthens learning only after understanding and cannot replace teaching.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Memory researchers have repeatedly found that trying to recall material, for example by answering questions on it, fixes it in memory better than reading it again for the same amount of time. Students tend to resist the finding because rereading feels productive: the text grows familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. Recall, by contrast, is effortful and exposes gaps, which feels like failure. The finding has limits that its enthusiasts sometimes forget. Testing oneself helps most when the material has first been understood; quizzing a student on ideas that were never properly explained simply rehearses confusion. Recall is a way of strengthening learning, not a substitute for the teaching that makes something worth recalling.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Memory researchers have repeatedly found that trying to recall material, for example by answering questions on it, fixes it in memory better than reading it again for the same amount of time. Students tend to resist the finding because rereading feels productive: the text grows familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. Recall, by contrast, is effortful and exposes gaps, which feels like failure. The finding has limits that its enthusiasts sometimes forget. Testing oneself helps most when the material has first been understood; quizzing a student on ideas that were never properly explained simply rehearses confusion. Recall is a way of strengthening learning, not a substitute for the teaching that makes something worth recalling.

options.A: Testing oneself improves memory only for students who already understand the material very well, so it is of little use to most learners in an ordinary classroom.
options.B: Recall fixes material in memory better than rereading, though it feels less productive, but it works best after understanding and cannot replace teaching.
options.C: Students prefer rereading to testing themselves because the familiarity of a reread text feels like knowledge, while the effort of recalling it feels like failure.
options.D: Students should stop rereading their notes entirely and should quiz themselves on new topics before any explanation, since effortful recall always beats passive review.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Recall fixes material in memory better than rereading, though it feels less productive, but it works best after understanding and cannot replace teaching.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says self-testing 'helps most' after understanding, not 'only', and it says nothing about most learners lacking understanding.
option_rationales.C: This explains the students' resistance only and omits both the finding's main claim and its limits.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph warns that quizzing on ideas 'never properly explained simply rehearses confusion', so testing before explanation is exactly what it cautions against.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states a finding (recall beats rereading), explains why students resist it, and qualifies it: recall works best after understanding and is no substitute for teaching. The correct answer holds the finding, the resistance in brief and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'only for students who already understand' option, which turns 'helps most' into 'only'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Finding and limit are each stated in a single sentence; wrong options are plainly extreme or narrow.

questions.subtopic: What a school does with ability groups matters more than whether it groups.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Arguments over whether schools should group pupils by ability usually proceed as if the choice were between two outcomes: grouping helps able pupils and harms the rest, or mixing helps the rest at some cost to the able. Both sides assume that the group itself does the work. Yet much of what happens to a pupil placed in a lower group depends on what the school then does with that group: whether it is given the most experienced teachers or the least, a demanding curriculum or a diluted one, and whether pupils can move up when they improve. A lower set taught ambitiously and kept open differs more from a lower set treated as a holding pen than either does from a mixed class. Asking whether grouping works is therefore a less useful question than asking what it is used to do.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Arguments over whether schools should group pupils by ability usually proceed as if the choice were between two outcomes: grouping helps able pupils and harms the rest, or mixing helps the rest at some cost to the able. Both sides assume that the group itself does the work. Yet much of what happens to a pupil placed in a lower group depends on what the school then does with that group: whether it is given the most experienced teachers or the least, a demanding curriculum or a diluted one, and whether pupils can move up when they improve. A lower set taught ambitiously and kept open differs more from a lower set treated as a holding pen than either does from a mixed class. Asking whether grouping works is therefore a less useful question than asking what it is used to do.

options.A: Debates on ability grouping wrongly assume grouping itself decides outcomes, when the teaching, curriculum and mobility given to each group matter more, so its effects depend on its use.
options.B: Grouping by ability helps only when lower groups receive the most experienced teachers and a demanding curriculum, so schools unable to provide these should teach mixed classes.
options.C: Mixed-ability classes and ability groups yield broadly similar results for pupils, since what matters is the quality of teaching rather than the way classes are formed.
options.D: Ability grouping helps able pupils at the expense of the others, but schools can reduce the harm by letting pupils in lower groups move up as they improve.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Debates on ability grouping wrongly assume grouping itself decides outcomes, when the teaching, curriculum and mobility given to each group matter more, so its effects depend on its use.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph lists conditions that shape outcomes, but it never makes them the sole condition of benefit or tells any school to adopt mixed classes.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says outcomes within grouping vary widely, with two lower sets differing 'more' from each other than from a mixed class; that is a claim about variation, not that grouped and mixed classes produce similar results.
option_rationales.D: This adopts one side's framing, that 'the group itself does the work', which the paragraph rejects as an assumption shared by both sides.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares the two usual positions, finds a shared assumption (the group itself does the work), and replaces it: what the school does with the group matters more, as the comparison of two kinds of lower set shows. The correct answer states the rejected assumption, what matters instead and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'broadly similar results' option because the paragraph downplays the grouping decision, without seeing that it stresses wide variation rather than equal results.
questions.difficulty_reason: The 'similar results' wrong option sounds like the paragraph's deflation of the debate; separating it needs a precise reading of the lower-set comparison.

questions.subtopic: Teenagers' later body clocks make early starts harmful, but a later bell alone may not add sleep.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Sleep researchers broadly agree that during adolescence the body clock shifts later, so that teenagers who are sent to bed early often lie awake and then struggle to wake for an early start. This has led to calls for secondary schools to begin later in the morning, in the expectation that pupils will then sleep longer. The expectation is reasonable but less simple than it looks. A later start helps only if bedtimes do not drift later in step, and the gain can be eroded by evening screens or by family and transport timetables that a school cannot alter. The biological finding is sound; what it shows is that early starts work against teenagers, not that moving the bell alone will give them the sleep they lack.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Sleep researchers broadly agree that during adolescence the body clock shifts later, so that teenagers who are sent to bed early often lie awake and then struggle to wake for an early start. This has led to calls for secondary schools to begin later in the morning, in the expectation that pupils will then sleep longer. The expectation is reasonable but less simple than it looks. A later start helps only if bedtimes do not drift later in step, and the gain can be eroded by evening screens or by family and transport timetables that a school cannot alter. The biological finding is sound; what it shows is that early starts work against teenagers, not that moving the bell alone will give them the sleep they lack.

options.A: Teenagers who are sent to bed early often lie awake and then find it difficult to get up in time for lessons that begin early in the morning.
options.B: Secondary schools should start later in the morning, because the shift in teenagers' body clocks means that a later bell will by itself give them the sleep they need.
options.C: Teenagers' later body clocks make early school starts a real burden, but starting later will add sleep only if bedtimes and other evening pressures do not shift along with it.
options.D: The claim that teenagers' body clocks shift later is doubtful, because their shortage of sleep is better explained by evening screens and family timetables.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Teenagers' later body clocks make early school starts a real burden, but starting later will add sleep only if bedtimes and other evening pressures do not shift along with it.

option_rationales.A: This restates the opening observation and omits the paragraph's point, which is the limit on what a later start can achieve.
option_rationales.B: The last sentence says the finding does not show 'that moving the bell alone will give them the sleep they lack', which this option asserts.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls the biological finding 'sound'; screens and timetables are factors that can erode the benefit of a later start, not rival explanations of the finding.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts a finding about adolescent body clocks and qualifies the policy drawn from it: a later start adds sleep only if bedtimes and evening pressures do not drift later too. The correct answer keeps the accepted finding and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that doubts the finding, because the paragraph raises screens and timetables, while it explicitly calls the finding 'sound'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must separate doubt about the policy from doubt about the finding.

questions.subtopic: Rubrics give consistency, but for original work they reward template-matching, which is not fairness.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Detailed marking rubrics are usually defended as a protection for students: they make expectations explicit, reduce the influence of a marker's mood and allow two examiners to reach the same grade. These are real gains, especially for routine tasks. The trouble begins when the same apparatus is applied to work whose value lies in doing something unexpected. A rubric can list only the qualities its authors anticipated, and a student who learns to satisfy each line, an introduction here, three examples there, is rewarded for matching the template rather than for thinking. An essay that takes an original route may score worse than a dutiful one because its strengths fall between the boxes. Consistency is worth having, but a scheme that is perfectly consistent about the wrong things is not fair; it is reliably unfair.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Detailed marking rubrics are usually defended as a protection for students: they make expectations explicit, reduce the influence of a marker's mood and allow two examiners to reach the same grade. These are real gains, especially for routine tasks. The trouble begins when the same apparatus is applied to work whose value lies in doing something unexpected. A rubric can list only the qualities its authors anticipated, and a student who learns to satisfy each line, an introduction here, three examples there, is rewarded for matching the template rather than for thinking. An essay that takes an original route may score worse than a dutiful one because its strengths fall between the boxes. Consistency is worth having, but a scheme that is perfectly consistent about the wrong things is not fair; it is reliably unfair.

options.A: Rubrics protect students by making expectations explicit and by ensuring that two examiners who mark the same piece of work will arrive at the same grade.
options.B: Rubrics bring real clarity and consistency, but for original work they reward conformity to anticipated features and may penalise unexpected strengths, so consistency need not mean fairness.
options.C: Detailed rubrics should be abolished, because a marker's own judgement is always fairer than any fixed scheme that tries to list the qualities of good work in advance.
options.D: Rubrics are unreliable because markers read their criteria differently, so two examiners using the same scheme often give an original essay quite different grades.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Rubrics bring real clarity and consistency, but for original work they reward conformity to anticipated features and may penalise unexpected strengths, so consistency need not mean fairness.

option_rationales.A: This is the defence the paragraph reports and accepts only in part; it omits the central objection about original work.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph calls the rubric's benefits 'real gains, especially for routine tasks' and says 'Consistency is worth having', so it does not call for abolition or claim judgement is always fairer.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph grants that rubrics 'allow two examiners to reach the same grade'; its complaint is that they are consistent about the wrong things, not inconsistent.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the standard defence of rubrics. It accepts the gains, then argues that for original work a rubric rewards matching a template and can penalise unexpected strengths, concluding that consistency about the wrong things is 'reliably unfair'. The correct answer holds the concession, the objection and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'unreliable' option, which confuses the paragraph's charge of misdirected consistency with a charge of inconsistency.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option reverses the kind of fault (inconsistency instead of consistency about the wrong things), which needs careful reading.

questions.subtopic: Handwritten notes help memory because slowness forces selection and rephrasing, which a typist can also do.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is often observed that students who take notes by hand remember a lecture better than classmates who typed nearly every word. The explanation is not that pens are magical but that they are slow. Unable to keep up with the speaker, the student writing by hand must decide what matters, compress it and put it in their own words, and this selecting and rephrasing is itself a form of learning. The fast typist can record the lecture almost verbatim without having to think about it at all. The advantage, then, belongs to the mental work rather than to the instrument, and a typist who deliberately summarises instead of transcribing can recover much of it.

The fast typist can record the lecture almost verbatim without having to think about it at all. The advantage, then, belongs to the mental work rather than to the instrument, and a typist who deliberately summarises instead of transcribing can recover much of it.

options.A: Typing students remember lectures poorly because the screen distracts them with messages and other material that has nothing to do with the speaker.
options.B: A typist can record a lecture almost word for word, whereas a student writing by hand cannot keep up with the speaker and has to leave things out.
options.C: Students should always take lecture notes by hand, because typing on a laptop prevents them from learning anything from the lectures that they attend.
options.D: Handwritten notes aid memory because slowness forces students to select and rephrase, and typists who summarise rather than transcribe can gain much of the same benefit.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Handwritten notes aid memory because slowness forces students to select and rephrase, and typists who summarise rather than transcribe can gain much of the same benefit.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph gives a different cause, verbatim recording without thought, and never mentions distraction by other material.
option_rationales.B: This describes the difference in speed but omits why it matters (selection and rephrasing are learning) and the point that typists can recover the advantage.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a typist who summarises 'can recover much of' the advantage, so typing does not prevent learning and handwriting is not required.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why handwriting helps: its slowness forces the mental work of selection and rephrasing, and that work, not the pen, is the cause, so a summarising typist can recover much of the advantage. The correct answer gives the cause and the consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the always by hand option and overlooking the final clause about typists who summarise.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause and the qualification are stated directly in the last sentence.

questions.subtopic: Symptom checkers should be judged against realistic alternatives, not doctors.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Online symptom checkers are usually compared with doctors, and by that standard they look poor: they miss diagnoses a clinician would catch and raise alarming possibilities a clinician would dismiss. But for most people the realistic alternative to a symptom checker is not a consultation; it is a search engine, a relative's opinion or simply waiting. Against those alternatives, a tool that asks structured questions and advises when to seek care may do better, even if it diagnoses worse than a doctor. The relevant question is not whether such tools match professionals but whether they improve the decisions people would otherwise make, and in particular whether they send the right people to a clinic and reassure the right people to stay at home.

options.A: Symptom checkers should be judged against what people would realistically do without them, not against doctors, so the test is whether they improve decisions about seeking care.
options.B: People should use structured symptom checkers in place of search engines or a relative's advice, since such tools will always give them better guidance about when to seek care.
options.C: Online symptom checkers are unreliable tools, because they miss diagnoses that clinicians would catch and raise alarming possibilities that clinicians would quickly dismiss.
options.D: Symptom checkers are now accurate enough to replace a first consultation with a doctor for most people, provided that they ask structured questions.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Symptom checkers should be judged against what people would realistically do without them, not against doctors, so the test is whether they improve decisions about seeking care.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says such a tool 'may do better', which is a question to be tested, not a guarantee, and it gives no instruction to users.
option_rationales.C: This judges the tools by the comparison with doctors, which the paragraph describes in its first sentence and then sets aside as the wrong standard.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph concedes that such a tool 'diagnoses worse than a doctor'; its claim is about the realistic alternative, not replacing consultations.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares two standards for judging symptom checkers and argues for the realistic one: what people would otherwise do. Its conclusion is a test, whether the tools improve care-seeking decisions. The correct answer states the change of standard and the test.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the always better guidance option because the paragraph favours the tools over search engines, overlooking that it says only 'may'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer is a change of comparison; one wrong option overstates 'may do better' into 'always', which needs a careful eye.

questions.subtopic: A daily step target is an encouragement, not a threshold, and treating it as a pass mark discourages beginners.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A round daily target of steps has become, for many people, the definition of an active day, and falling short of it can feel like failure. The number is better treated as a convenient goal than as a threshold. Nothing happens to the body at the moment the counter reaches it; the benefits of walking appear to rise gradually with activity, and an inactive person who adds a modest amount of walking gains something real even if the target remains far off. Treating the figure as a pass mark can discourage exactly the people who stand to gain most, by making their improvement look like a shortfall. A target is useful as an encouragement and harmful only when it is mistaken for a line between health and its absence.
