options.A: The benefits of walking seem to rise gradually as activity increases, rather than appearing all at once when a step counter reaches a particular figure.
options.B: People who do not reach a daily step target gain no real health benefit from their walking, so the target marks the minimum level of useful activity.
options.C: Daily step targets are harmful and should be abandoned, because they make people who fall short of them feel that they have failed to take enough exercise.
options.D: A daily step target is a useful encouragement rather than a health threshold, since benefits rise gradually, and treating it as a pass mark can discourage those who would gain the most.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A daily step target is a useful encouragement rather than a health threshold, since benefits rise gradually, and treating it as a pass mark can discourage those who would gain the most.

option_rationales.A: This is the supporting reason only; it omits the paragraph's point about how targets should be treated and the harm of treating them as pass marks.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says an inactive person who walks a little more 'gains something real even if the target remains far off', the opposite of this option.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a target 'is useful as an encouragement and harmful only when it is mistaken for a line', so it does not call for abandoning targets.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques treating a step target as a threshold. Because benefits rise gradually, the target is best seen as encouragement, and a pass-mark reading discourages those who gain most. The correct answer keeps both the reframing and the harm.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the abandon targets option because the paragraph lists a harm, missing the word 'only' in the last sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The final sentence states the conclusion; wrong options are extreme, reversed or narrow.

questions.subtopic: Warnings lose force because overuse makes them uninformative, so the fault lies with issuers.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Why do warnings that once alarmed people come to be ignored? The usual answer is that people grow careless, but the process is more reasonable than that. A warning that appears everywhere, on products that are mostly harmless as well as on ones that are genuinely dangerous, teaches its readers that it carries little information. Each false alarm lowers the value of the next, and a sensible person learns to discount the signal. The fault then lies less with the reader than with the issuers, who, wishing to cover every conceivable risk, spend the credibility that a warning needs in order to work. A label that warned about fewer things would protect people better, because they would have reason to believe it.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The fault then lies less with the reader than with the issuers, who, wishing to cover every conceivable risk, spend the credibility that a warning needs in order to work. options.A: Warnings lose force not through carelessness but because, placed on harmless and dangerous things alike, they carry little information; issuers who overuse them squander their credibility.
options.B: Each false alarm lowers the value of the next warning, so a sensible reader slowly learns to discount the warnings that appear on many different products.
options.C: People ignore health warnings because familiarity breeds carelessness, so warnings must be redesigned regularly with fresh images and wording to keep catching attention.
options.D: Warning labels should be removed from products altogether, since readers have learned that such labels carry little information and no longer pay any attention to them.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Warnings lose force not through carelessness but because, placed on harmless and dangerous things alike, they carry little information; issuers who overuse them squander their credibility.

option_rationales.B: This describes the reader's learning but omits the paragraph's main conclusion, that the fault lies with issuers who spend the credibility of warnings.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph rejects carelessness as 'The usual answer' and says the reader's response is 'more reasonable than that'; it proposes fewer warnings, not redesigned ones.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'A label that warned about fewer things would protect people better', so it wants warnings used sparingly, not removed.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a phenomenon: warnings are ignored because overuse makes them uninformative, so discounting them is reasonable and the fault lies with issuers. It ends by suggesting fewer warnings. The correct answer carries the rejected explanation, the real mechanism and where the fault lies.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'false alarm' option because it describes the mechanism accurately, while it leaves out the shift of blame to the issuers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow wrong option is an accurate paraphrase of the mechanism; the correct answer must be chosen for including the conclusion.

questions.subtopic: The free-rider charge fits those who could be vaccinated, not those who cannot, whose need is why protection must be kept.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When most of a community is vaccinated against a contagious disease, the few who are not are protected too, because the infection struggles to find a path to them. This makes refusal look costless to the refuser, and some ethicists describe the unvaccinated as free riders on the efforts of others. The label is apt for some and unjust to others. It fits a person who could safely be vaccinated and declines because others have made the risk small, since that person's safety is borrowed from neighbours who accepted the minor burden. It does not fit an infant too young for the vaccine or a patient whose treatment rules it out; for them, the protection of the crowd is not a free ride but the only protection available, and it is precisely the reason the rest of us have to keep it intact.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When most of a community is vaccinated against a contagious disease, the few who are not are protected too, because the infection struggles to find a path to them. This makes refusal look costless to the refuser, and some ethicists describe the unvaccinated as free riders on the efforts of others. The label is apt for some and unjust to others. It fits a person who could safely be vaccinated and declines because others have made the risk small, since that person's safety is borrowed from neighbours who accepted the minor burden. It does not fit an infant too young for the vaccine or a patient whose treatment rules it out; for them, the protection of the crowd is not a free ride but the only protection available, and it is precisely the reason the rest of us have to keep it intact.

options.A: Everyone who stays unvaccinated in a well-vaccinated community is a free rider, since each of them benefits from protection created by neighbours who accepted the burden of vaccination.
options.B: The free-rider charge fits those who could safely be vaccinated but rely on others' immunity, not those medically unable to be, whose dependence on shared protection is why it must be maintained.
options.C: Vaccination should be compulsory for everyone who can safely receive it, since those who decline borrow safety from others, including infants and patients who cannot be vaccinated.
options.D: Since community immunity protects people who are not vaccinated, an individual's choice to decline a vaccine has little effect on others and remains a private matter.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The free-rider charge fits those who could safely be vaccinated but rely on others' immunity, not those medically unable to be, whose dependence on shared protection is why it must be maintained.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the label is 'apt for some and unjust to others' and excludes infants and patients who cannot be vaccinated, so 'everyone' contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph judges when the free-rider label is fair and says the protection must be kept intact, but it proposes no means of doing so; compulsion is a policy it never mentions.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says only that this 'makes refusal look costless', and it says those who decline borrow safety from neighbours; it ends by saying 'the rest of us have to keep it intact', which treats the matter as shared, not private.

questions.explanation: The paragraph takes a reported view (the unvaccinated are free riders) and draws a distinction: the label fits those who could safely be vaccinated and decline, but not those who cannot, for whom communal protection is the only protection and the reason it must be maintained. The correct answer states the distinction and the closing point; it adds no policy.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the compulsion option because its reasoning echoes the paragraph, without noticing that it adds a specific policy the paragraph does not propose.
questions.difficulty_reason: The compulsion wrong option shares the correct answer's moral reasoning and must be rejected for adding a prescription; the 'everyone' option is the reported view.

questions.subtopic: A bypass hurts trade that served passing traffic but may help trade that depends on lingering; early losses mislead.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a bypass takes through traffic away from a small town, shopkeepers on the old main road often predict ruin, and in the first months after it opens some of them do lose trade from passing motorists. Yet the longer story is frequently different. Freed from heavy lorries, the main street grows quieter and safer to walk along, and the visitors who now stop do so because they mean to, staying longer than the drivers who once paused for fuel. Businesses that served passing traffic, such as filling stations and roadside cafes, tend to suffer most, while those that depend on people lingering may gain. Whether a town is helped or harmed thus depends on which kind of trade it lived on, and the early losses are a poor guide to the eventual result.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Whether a town is helped or harmed thus depends on which kind of trade it lived on, and the early losses are a poor guide to the eventual result.

options.A: Building a bypass around a small town eventually improves trade for all the businesses on its old main road, once the early losses from passing motorists are recovered.
options.B: Planners should build bypasses only around towns whose shops depend on lingering visitors, and should keep through traffic in towns that serve passing motorists.
options.C: A bypass harms businesses that served passing motorists but may help those depending on visitors who linger in a quieter centre, so early losses poorly predict the outcome.
options.D: Shopkeepers are right to fear bypasses, since the trade lost from passing motorists in the first months after opening usually proves permanent for the town.

questions.correct_answer: (C) A bypass harms businesses that served passing motorists but may help those depending on visitors who linger in a quieter centre, so early losses poorly predict the outcome.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says businesses serving passing traffic 'tend to suffer most', so the gain is not shared by 'all' the businesses.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph explains who gains and who loses but makes no recommendation about where bypasses should be built.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'the longer story is frequently different' and that 'the early losses are a poor guide to the eventual result', which this option contradicts.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports an early finding (some shops lose trade) and qualifies it: over time the effect splits by kind of business, so the result depends on the town's trade and early losses mislead. The correct answer states the split and the warning about early losses.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the all businesses improve option because the paragraph's turn is optimistic, overlooking the businesses it says suffer most.
questions.difficulty_reason: The 'all businesses' wrong option shares the paragraph's optimism; the differentiation in the fourth sentence rules it out.

questions.subtopic: Moving behind gates is reasonable for each household but corrosive for the shared city.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Residents who move into walled housing estates with guarded gates usually describe their decision as a private one: they want safety for their families and are willing to pay for it. Taken one by one, such decisions are understandable. Their sum is something none of the residents chose. As more households withdraw behind walls, the streets outside lose the people whose presence made them feel safe, the public parks and schools lose the residents best placed to demand that they be improved, and the city comes to be organised around the boundaries between enclaves rather than the spaces they once shared. The insecurity that drove people indoors grows in the areas they left. A choice can be reasonable for each household and still be corrosive for the city they share.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Gated housing estates make cities safer overall, because the residents they protect are no longer exposed to the dangers found on public streets and in parks.
options.B: Families who move into gated estates are acting selfishly, since they choose their own safety while knowingly abandoning the parks and schools that others rely on.
options.C: Governments should ban walled housing estates, because the security they offer their residents is outweighed by the damage they do to the surrounding streets.
options.D: Each household's move behind gates is understandable, but together such moves drain public streets and services and deepen insecurity outside, harming the city they share.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Each household's move behind gates is understandable, but together such moves drain public streets and services and deepen insecurity outside, harming the city they share.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the insecurity 'grows in the areas they left', so the city as a whole is not made safer.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph calls such decisions 'understandable' and says their sum is 'something none of the residents chose', so it rejects both the charge of selfishness and 'knowingly'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph diagnoses a collective harm but proposes no ban or any other policy.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that individually reasonable choices add up to an unchosen collective harm: public streets, parks and schools decline and insecurity grows outside the walls. The correct answer keeps the individual reasonableness and the collective harm.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the 'selfish' option because the paragraph is critical of the result, missing that it explicitly calls each decision understandable.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer turns on the contrast between individual reason and collective effect; the moralising wrong option drops that contrast.

questions.subtopic: Plans that see informal settlements as disorder erase the order they contain; improvement should start by learning it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: City master plans often treat informal settlements as blank spaces awaiting proper development, marking them for clearance or for replacement by orderly blocks of housing. The view assumes that what is unplanned is unorganised. Settlements that grew without permission frequently contain dense networks of their own: workshops next to homes, credit circles, arrangements for sharing water and minding children, all of them fitted to the needs of people with little money and long working days. Clearing such a place and rehousing its residents in tidier flats on the city's edge can improve their buildings while destroying the arrangements that made their lives workable. This is not an argument for leaving dangerous housing alone. It is an argument that improvement should begin by learning what a settlement already does, since a plan that sees only the absence of order will fail to notice the order it erases.

options.A: Plans that treat informal settlements as mere disorder can destroy the arrangements they contain, so improving unsafe housing should begin by understanding how a settlement already works.
options.B: Informal settlements should be upgraded where they stand rather than cleared, since residents moved to the city's edge lose the workshops and credit circles near their homes.
options.C: Rehousing the residents of informal settlements in flats on the city's edge fails because the new buildings are usually of poorer quality than the homes they replace.
options.D: Informal settlements are better organised than planned housing, so cities should leave them as they are rather than clearing them or rehousing their residents elsewhere.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Plans that treat informal settlements as mere disorder can destroy the arrangements they contain, so improving unsafe housing should begin by understanding how a settlement already works.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph asks that improvement 'begin by learning what a settlement already does'; it does not settle in advance that upgrading in place is the answer or rule out relocation.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says rehousing 'can improve their buildings'; the loss it describes is of social and economic arrangements, not of building quality.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'This is not an argument for leaving dangerous housing alone', and it never ranks informal settlements above planned housing.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the assumption that the unplanned is unorganised, shows the networks such settlements contain, concedes that dangerous housing must not be left alone, and concludes that improvement should start by learning how the place works. The correct answer holds the critique, the harm and the method-level conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the upgrade in place option because it follows the paragraph's sympathies, though the paragraph prescribes a starting point (learning), not a specific outcome.
questions.difficulty_reason: The upgrade wrong option is a plausible policy consistent with the paragraph's tone; telling it apart requires noticing that the conclusion is about how to begin, not what to decide.

questions.subtopic: Cities treat the night as disorder or as opportunity; each sees something real and either alone backfires.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Cities tend to think about their evenings in one of two ways. Some treat the hours after dark as a problem to be contained, a time of noise, drinking and disorder to be managed with closing times and police patrols. Others treat them as an opportunity, encouraging late markets, theatres and restaurants that bring life and employment to streets otherwise deserted after the offices close. Each view sees something real; the first notices the residents kept awake, the second the workers and visitors who depend on the night. A city that adopts only one tends to get its worst version: enforcement alone empties the streets and makes them less safe, while promotion alone pushes disorder onto the people who live nearby.

options.A: Strict closing times and police patrols are the most effective way for a city to keep its streets safe and to protect residents from noise at night.
options.B: Some cities manage the hours after dark through closing times and police patrols, treating evening activity as noise, drinking and disorder to be contained.
options.C: Cities see the night as disorder to contain or opportunity to promote; each view captures something real, and relying on only one tends to backfire.
options.D: Cities should promote late markets, theatres and restaurants after dark, since bringing activity to the streets at night creates jobs and makes those streets safer.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Cities see the night as disorder to contain or opportunity to promote; each view captures something real, and relying on only one tends to backfire.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'enforcement alone empties the streets and makes them less safe', the opposite of this claim.
option_rationales.B: This describes only the first of the two approaches and leaves out the comparison and the warning against relying on either alone.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph warns that 'promotion alone pushes disorder onto the people who live nearby', so it does not endorse promotion as the answer.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares two approaches to the night, grants that each sees something real, and warns that either alone produces its worst version. The correct answer gives both views, the concession and the warning.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the promotion option because the paragraph describes it warmly, overlooking the last sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both approaches and the warning are stated plainly; wrong options are one-sided or narrow.

questions.subtopic: Closing a shopping street to cars tends to help its trade, but only where customers can already reach it without driving.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Shopkeepers often resist plans to close a street to cars, fearing that customers who cannot park outside will go elsewhere. In many towns where such schemes have gone ahead, the fear has proved exaggerated: people on foot linger, return more often and spend more over a month than drivers who stop briefly, and footfall on the closed street tends to rise. Yet the gains are not automatic. A pedestrian street works when it already sits within walking distance of homes, offices or public transport, so that people arrive on foot anyway. Where a high street serves mainly shoppers who drive in from scattered suburbs, closing it to traffic without offering another way to reach it can empty it, and the shopkeepers' fear turns out to be justified.

options.A: Closing shopping streets to cars always increases trade, because shoppers on foot linger longer and spend more than drivers, so shopkeepers' fears are unfounded.
options.B: Closing a shopping street to traffic tends to help its trade, but only where enough customers can reach it on foot or by public transport.
options.C: Towns should build large car parks beside pedestrian streets so that suburban drivers can still reach the shops after traffic is banned.
options.D: Shoppers who arrive on foot tend to return more often and spend more over a month than drivers, who usually stop at shops only briefly.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Closing a shopping street to traffic tends to help its trade, but only where enough customers can reach it on foot or by public transport.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'the gains are not automatic' and that for car-dependent high streets 'the shopkeepers' fear turns out to be justified', so 'always' and 'unfounded' contradict its qualification.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph mentions 'another way to reach it' only as a condition and never recommends car parks; the option adds a prescription the paragraph does not make.
option_rationales.D: This repeats one supporting detail from the second sentence and leaves out the central claim and its condition about how customers reach the street.

questions.explanation: The paragraph corrects the shopkeepers' fear (pedestrian streets usually gain trade) and then limits the correction: it holds only where the street is 'within walking distance of homes, offices or public transport'. The correct answer keeps both the claim and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the first half as the whole point and ignoring 'Yet the gains are not automatic'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The qualification is stated in one plain sentence beginning 'Yet', and each wrong option is clearly off once it is read.

questions.subtopic: Blaming by outcome conflicts with the control principle, but applying that principle strictly would leave little to blame.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Two drivers take the same corner too fast after the same glass of wine; one reaches home, the other strikes a cyclist who appears suddenly from a side lane. Most people blame the second driver far more, even though the two drivers made identical choices and differ only in what happened next, which neither controlled. This reaction sits uneasily with the widely held principle that people should be judged only for what is within their control. If we applied that principle strictly, we would have to say the drivers are equally culpable, and that our sharper condemnation of the second is a kind of error. The difficulty is that almost everything we do has consequences shaped by circumstance, so a strict rule of control would leave very little that anyone could be blamed or praised for at all.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Two drivers take the same corner too fast after the same glass of wine; one reaches home, the other strikes a cyclist who appears suddenly from a side lane. Most people blame the second driver far more, even though the two drivers made identical choices and differ only in what happened next, which neither controlled. This reaction sits uneasily with the widely held principle that people should be judged only for what is within their control. If we applied that principle strictly, we would have to say the drivers are equally culpable, and that our sharper condemnation of the second is a kind of error. The difficulty is that almost everything we do has consequences shaped by circumstance, so a strict rule of control would leave very little that anyone could be blamed or praised for at all.

options.A: Judging people by outcomes they did not control clashes with the principle of judging only what is controlled, yet applying that principle strictly would leave almost nothing to blame.
options.B: Since the two drivers made identical choices, our harsher condemnation of the one who struck the cyclist is simply an error that careful moral reasoning ought to correct and remove.
options.C: Because consequences are always shaped by circumstance, nobody can ever be held morally responsible for anything they do, whether it turns out well or badly.
options.D: Drinking before driving is wrong whatever happens on the road, and drivers who take corners too fast deserve blame even when nobody is hurt at all.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Judging people by outcomes they did not control clashes with the principle of judging only what is controlled, yet applying that principle strictly would leave almost nothing to blame.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says only that the strict principle 'would' force this verdict, and then raises 'The difficulty' with that principle; it does not endorse calling the reaction an error.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a strict rule of control 'would leave very little' to blame; it presents this as a problem for the rule, not as a conclusion that no one is ever responsible.
option_rationales.D: The example is used to test how we assign blame; the paragraph makes no argument about the wrongness of drink-driving, so the option is out of scope.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets an intuition (blame the driver who struck the cyclist more) against a principle (judge only what is controlled), and then shows that resolving the conflict in favour of the principle has a heavy cost. The point is the unresolved tension, which the correct answer states with both sides.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the paragraph as siding with the control principle, when its last sentence turns against applying it strictly.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option states the conditional verdict as the author's conclusion; the solver must notice the final 'difficulty' that keeps the tension open.

questions.subtopic: Knowing the outcome makes it look predictable, which leads to unfair judgements of past decisions.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: After learning the outcome of an event, people find it remarkably hard to recover how uncertain it looked beforehand. The outcome reorganises our memory of the evidence: signs that pointed towards it now seem obvious, while signs that pointed elsewhere fade or are reinterpreted as noise. As a result we tend to believe that we, and others, should have seen it coming. This matters most when we judge decisions. A doctor whose patient suffered a rare complication, or a manager whose project failed, is likely to be faulted for missing warnings that were, at the time, mixed in with many others pointing the opposite way.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

As a result we tend to believe that we, and others, should have seen it coming. This matters most when we judge decisions. A doctor whose patient suffered a rare complication, or a manager whose project failed, is likely to be faulted for missing warnings that were, at the time, mixed in with many others pointing the opposite way.

options.A: Doctors and managers are often blamed for failures that resulted from rare complications or unforeseeable events rather than from any error in their own decisions.
options.B: Since no outcome can ever be predicted in advance, decision makers should never be held responsible when the results of their choices turn out badly.
options.C: Knowing an outcome makes it seem more predictable than it was, so we judge past decisions too harshly for missing signs that were unclear at the time.
options.D: People who know how an event turned out tend to forget the outcome and remember instead the warning signs that pointed in other directions.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Knowing an outcome makes it seem more predictable than it was, so we judge past decisions too harshly for missing signs that were unclear at the time.

option_rationales.A: The doctor and the manager are examples; the paragraph's point is a general distortion of memory caused by knowing the outcome, which this option leaves out.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph claims only that outcomes look more predictable afterwards than they were; it neither says nothing is predictable nor proposes that no one be held responsible.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the paragraph, which says signs pointing towards the outcome 'now seem obvious' while those that 'pointed elsewhere fade'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a bias (the outcome 'reorganises our memory of the evidence') and its main consequence (unfair judgement of decisions). The correct answer states both.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option built from the examples instead of the general mechanism.
questions.difficulty_reason: The mechanism and its consequence are stated directly; the wrong options are a detail, a reversal and an overstatement.

questions.subtopic: Wedding spending is an investment in standing rather than mere imprudence, though competition makes it a burden on the poor.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Lavish weddings are often criticised as a simple failure of prudence: families spend their savings, or borrow, for a single day that leaves nothing behind. The criticism misreads what the money buys. In many communities a wedding is the occasion on which a family displays its standing to a wide network of relatives, neighbours and future in-laws, and that standing affects the marriages its other children can make, the help it can call on and the credit it is offered. Seen this way, the spending is less a lapse than an investment in reputation. None of this makes it harmless. When every family must match its neighbours, the display that once signalled standing becomes a cost that all must pay merely to avoid falling behind, and the people least able to afford it are pressed hardest.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Lavish weddings are often criticised as a simple failure of prudence: families spend their savings, or borrow, for a single day that leaves nothing behind. The criticism misreads what the money buys. In many communities a wedding is the occasion on which a family displays its standing to a wide network of relatives, neighbours and future in-laws, and that standing affects the marriages its other children can make, the help it can call on and the credit it is offered. Seen this way, the spending is less a lapse than an investment in reputation. None of this makes it harmless. When every family must match its neighbours, the display that once signalled standing becomes a cost that all must pay merely to avoid falling behind, and the people least able to afford it are pressed hardest.

options.A: Communities should agree to limit wedding spending so that poorer families are no longer forced to borrow simply in order to keep up with richer neighbours.
options.B: Heavy wedding spending is better seen as an investment in social standing than as mere imprudence, though competition can make it a burden falling hardest on poorer families.
options.C: Families who spend heavily on weddings are making a sensible investment, since the reputation they gain brings them better marriages, more help and easier credit.
options.D: Lavish weddings are a wasteful habit in which families recklessly give up their savings and take on heavy debt for one celebration that leaves them with nothing of lasting value.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Heavy wedding spending is better seen as an investment in social standing than as mere imprudence, though competition can make it a burden falling hardest on poorer families.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph diagnoses a competitive burden but proposes no remedy; the agreement to limit spending is a prescription it does not make.
option_rationales.C: This keeps the reinterpretation but drops the qualification 'None of this makes it harmless' and the point that competition presses the poorest hardest.
option_rationales.D: This is the criticism the paragraph says 'misreads what the money buys'; it is reported in order to be corrected, not endorsed.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the 'failure of prudence' reading, reinterprets the spending as an 'investment in reputation', and then qualifies that the competition makes it a cost 'all must pay', heaviest on the poor. The correct answer holds all three moves.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that agrees with the reinterpretation but ignores the qualification that follows it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option matches the paragraph's main turn; it is wrong only because it omits the final qualification.

questions.subtopic: Structures set the range of outcomes; how much an individual mattered depends on how wide that range was.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It has become routine to dismiss the history of great individuals as naive, on the ground that leaders merely ride forces (economic, demographic, technological) that would have produced much the same results without them. The correction was needed, but it has been pushed too far. Structural forces set the range of what is possible; they rarely settle which possibility is realised. At moments of crisis, when institutions are weak and outcomes hang on a few decisions, the character and judgement of particular people can tip events one way or another, and the effects can last for generations. The sensible position is not to return to heroic biography but to ask, case by case, how wide the range left open by circumstance actually was, since that width determines how much any individual could matter.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It has become routine to dismiss the history of great individuals as naive, on the ground that leaders merely ride forces (economic, demographic, technological) that would have produced much the same results without them. The correction was needed, but it has been pushed too far. Structural forces set the range of what is possible; they rarely settle which possibility is realised. At moments of crisis, when institutions are weak and outcomes hang on a few decisions, the character and judgement of particular people can tip events one way or another, and the effects can last for generations. The sensible position is not to return to heroic biography but to ask, case by case, how wide the range left open by circumstance actually was, since that width determines how much any individual could matter.

options.A: History is driven chiefly by the character and judgement of exceptional leaders, whose decisions at moments of crisis shape events far more than economic or technological forces do.
options.B: Individuals shape history only during crises, while in ordinary times structural forces alone decide which of the possible outcomes is actually realised in the end.
options.C: Leaders largely ride economic, demographic and technological forces, which would have produced broadly similar historical outcomes whatever particular individuals happened to be in charge.
options.D: Structural forces limit what can happen but seldom fix the outcome, so an individual's influence depends on how much room circumstances left, which tends to be widest in crises.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Structural forces limit what can happen but seldom fix the outcome, so an individual's influence depends on how much room circumstances left, which tends to be widest in crises.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph explicitly declines 'to return to heroic biography' and says structural forces 'set the range of what is possible', so it does not rank leaders above structures.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says structures 'rarely settle which possibility is realised' in general and asks 'case by case' how much room was left; 'only' and 'alone' turn its emphasis on crises into a rule it never states.
option_rationales.C: This is the dismissive view the paragraph says 'has been pushed too far'; it is reported in order to be corrected.

questions.explanation: The paragraph corrects an overcorrection: structures bound the possible but 'rarely settle' the outcome, and the room left to individuals varies, being largest in crises. The correct answer keeps the general principle, the variable room and the role of crisis without making crisis the sole condition.
questions.common_misconception: Selecting the 'only during crises' option because crises are the paragraph's illustration, missing that the paragraph treats room for individuals as a matter of degree in every case.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are the two positions the paragraph sits between, and the third hardens a matter of degree into an absolute; separating them needs the whole argument.

questions.subtopic: Evidence of small job losses from modest minimum wage rises undercuts the simple prediction but has limited scope.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A standard textbook argument holds that raising the minimum wage must reduce employment, since employers buy less of anything that becomes more expensive. Comparisons of neighbouring areas where the wage floor rose in one and not the other have often found smaller job losses than that argument predicts, and sometimes none at all. One explanation is that where few employers compete for workers, wages were held below what a competitive market would pay, so a modest floor can raise pay without cutting jobs. But this evidence concerns modest increases in places where the floor was low relative to local wages. It says little about large rises, or about poorer regions where a single national floor sits close to the typical wage, and treating it as proof that minimum wages never cost jobs stretches it beyond what it shows.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A standard textbook argument holds that raising the minimum wage must reduce employment, since employers buy less of anything that becomes more expensive. Comparisons of neighbouring areas where the wage floor rose in one and not the other have often found smaller job losses than that argument predicts, and sometimes none at all. One explanation is that where few employers compete for workers, wages were held below what a competitive market would pay, so a modest floor can raise pay without cutting jobs. But this evidence concerns modest increases in places where the floor was low relative to local wages. It says little about large rises, or about poorer regions where a single national floor sits close to the typical wage, and treating it as proof that minimum wages never cost jobs stretches it beyond what it shows.

options.A: Since employers buy less of whatever becomes more expensive, a higher minimum wage does reduce employment, although in some neighbouring areas the losses have been smaller than expected.
options.B: Evidence that modest minimum wage rises cost few jobs undercuts the simple prediction of job losses, but cannot be extended to large rises or to regions where the floor nears typical wages.
options.C: Studies of neighbouring areas have shown that raising the minimum wage does not reduce employment at all, because employers facing little competition have always paid workers less than they are worth.
options.D: Where only a few employers compete for workers, wages tend to be held below competitive levels, which allows a modest minimum wage to raise pay without cutting any jobs.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Evidence that modest minimum wage rises cost few jobs undercuts the simple prediction of job losses, but cannot be extended to large rises or to regions where the floor nears typical wages.

option_rationales.A: This affirms the textbook argument that the evidence is presented as undercutting; the paragraph says the comparisons found losses 'smaller ... than that argument predicts', not that the argument holds.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph found 'smaller job losses', 'sometimes none', and warns against 'treating it as proof that minimum wages never cost jobs'; the option turns that evidence into the very proof it rejects and adds 'always'.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'One explanation' offered for the finding; it omits the finding's challenge to the textbook view and the scope limit that is the paragraph's main qualification.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding that weakens the textbook prediction, offers a possible mechanism, and then fences the finding in: it concerns modest rises where the floor is low, and says 'little about large rises' or regions near the typical wage. The correct answer carries both the finding and its scope.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that states the mechanism, which is accurate but only one step of the paragraph, or the option that turns 'smaller job losses' into 'does not reduce employment'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option reproduces one stage of the argument (finding overstated, original theory, mechanism); only the correct answer holds the finding together with its limits.

questions.subtopic: Port-city openness comes from the practical needs of trade, which is why it can fade when trade declines.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Port cities have long been more open to strangers than inland towns of similar size, and the usual explanation credits the sea with broadening minds. The cause is more practical. A port lives by trade with people it cannot choose, and its merchants, dock workers and officials learn that a ship's crew from a distant coast must be housed, fed, paid and understood if business is to continue. Tolerance there begins as a working habit, enforced by self-interest, before it becomes a value anyone defends. This also explains why such openness can be fragile. When trade declines or shifts to other harbours, the practical reason for accommodating outsiders weakens, and port cities have sometimes turned as suspicious of strangers as any inland town.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Port cities have long been more open to strangers than inland towns of similar size, and the usual explanation credits the sea with broadening minds. The cause is more practical. A port lives by trade with people it cannot choose, and its merchants, dock workers and officials learn that a ship's crew from a distant coast must be housed, fed, paid and understood if business is to continue. Tolerance there begins as a working habit, enforced by self-interest, before it becomes a value anyone defends. This also explains why such openness can be fragile. When trade declines or shifts to other harbours, the practical reason for accommodating outsiders weakens, and port cities have sometimes turned as suspicious of strangers as any inland town.

options.A: Port cities welcome foreigners only out of self-interest and never come to regard tolerance as a value that is worth defending for its own sake.
options.B: Merchants and officials in ports must house, feed, pay and understand foreign crews, since otherwise the trade on which their city depends would stop.
options.C: Port cities are more open to strangers because trade demands it, not because the sea broadens minds, which is why that openness can fade when trade declines.
options.D: Living beside the sea broadens the outlook of a city's inhabitants, which is why port cities have long been more welcoming to strangers than inland towns are.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Port cities are more open to strangers because trade demands it, not because the sea broadens minds, which is why that openness can fade when trade declines.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says tolerance 'begins as a working habit ... before it becomes a value anyone defends', which implies it can become such a value; 'never' contradicts this.
option_rationales.B: This restates one supporting detail and omits both the contrast with the usual explanation and the point about fragility.
option_rationales.D: This is 'the usual explanation' that the paragraph sets aside with 'The cause is more practical'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph replaces the romantic explanation (the sea broadens minds) with a practical one (trade forces accommodation) and draws a consequence: openness built on trade 'can be fragile'. The correct answer states the cause and the consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'only out of self-interest' option, which sounds like the paragraph's practical explanation but overstates it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme wrong option echoes the paragraph's emphasis on self-interest; it fails on 'before it becomes a value', which takes a careful reading.

questions.subtopic: A justified political wrong still wrongs someone: justification overrides a claim without cancelling it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is sometimes said that a politician who lies to the public or bargains with a ruthless faction to prevent a greater harm has simply done the right thing, and that once the calculation favours the act, no moral residue remains. This tidy view misdescribes the situation. The act may be justified, all things considered, and still involve doing something wrong: deceiving people who were owed the truth, or lending strength to people who deserved none. A leader who felt nothing after such a choice would be more worrying than one who felt the weight of it, because that weight is how a person registers that a real claim was overridden rather than dissolved. Justification answers whether one should act; it does not erase what the act cost those it wronged.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is sometimes said that a politician who lies to the public or bargains with a ruthless faction to prevent a greater harm has simply done the right thing, and that once the calculation favours the act, no moral residue remains. This tidy view misdescribes the situation. The act may be justified, all things considered, and still involve doing something wrong: deceiving people who were owed the truth, or lending strength to people who deserved none. A leader who felt nothing after such a choice would be more worrying than one who felt the weight of it, because that weight is how a person registers that a real claim was overridden rather than dissolved. Justification answers whether one should act; it does not erase what the act cost those it wronged.

options.A: Politicians who deceive the public or bargain with ruthless factions act wrongly whatever their reasons, because no greater good can ever justify overriding the real moral claims of other people.
options.B: Leaders who feel the weight of their hard choices are more trustworthy than those who feel nothing, since remorse is a reliable sign of good political character.
options.C: Once a politician's lie or compromise is justified by preventing a greater harm, it is simply the right thing to do and leaves nothing behind to regret.
options.D: A politician may be right overall to deceive or compromise for a greater good yet still have wronged someone, since justification overrides a real claim without cancelling it.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A politician may be right overall to deceive or compromise for a greater good yet still have wronged someone, since justification overrides a real claim without cancelling it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph grants that 'The act may be justified, all things considered'; it denies only that justification erases the wrong, so this option reverses its concession.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph uses the leader's feeling as evidence that 'a real claim was overridden'; it says nothing about trustworthiness or character in general, so the option shifts the point to a side remark.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'tidy view' that the paragraph says 'misdescribes the situation', because it denies any 'moral residue'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the view that justification leaves 'no moral residue' while keeping the claim that the act 'may be justified'. Its point is the distinction in the last sentence: justification settles whether to act, not whether anyone was wronged. The correct answer states both halves.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the paragraph's rejection of the tidy view as a claim that such acts are never justified, or mistaking the remark about feeling for the main point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must be told apart from a reversal that also stresses the wrong; the solver must hold 'may be justified' and 'does not erase' together.

questions.subtopic: Later work suggests passivity under stress is the default and that what is learned is control.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Early laboratory work on helplessness suggested a simple lesson: animals exposed to shocks they could not escape learned that nothing they did mattered, and later failed to escape even when escape became easy. The idea spread quickly into accounts of human depression and of children who stop trying at school. Later research reversed the emphasis. Passivity in the face of prolonged stress, it now appears, is the default response, and what is learned is the opposite: that one's actions can make a difference. Experiences of control teach organisms to override the default. The practical implication shifts accordingly. Rather than looking only for the damage done by uncontrollable events, one should ask whether a person has had enough experiences of mastery to learn that effort pays.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Early laboratory work on helplessness suggested a simple lesson: animals exposed to shocks they could not escape learned that nothing they did mattered, and later failed to escape even when escape became easy.
