Passivity in the face of prolonged stress, it now appears, is the default response, and what is learned is the opposite: that one's actions can make a difference. Experiences of control teach organisms to override the default. The practical implication shifts accordingly. Rather than looking only for the damage done by uncontrollable events, one should ask whether a person has had enough experiences of mastery to learn that effort pays.

options.A: Later work suggests passivity is not learned from uncontrollable events but is the default response to stress, and what experiences of control teach is that action helps.
options.B: Animals and people repeatedly exposed to events that they cannot control learn that their own actions are useless, and so they stop trying even when escape becomes easy.
options.C: Prolonged stress is what teaches organisms that their efforts make a difference, which is why passivity appears only when such stressful experiences are absent.
options.D: Depression in adults and lack of effort among schoolchildren are both caused mainly by too few experiences of mastery during the early years of childhood.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Later work suggests passivity is not learned from uncontrollable events but is the default response to stress, and what experiences of control teach is that action helps.

option_rationales.B: This is the 'simple lesson' of the early work, which the paragraph says later research 'reversed'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says passivity under 'prolonged stress' is the default and that 'Experiences of control' teach efficacy; the option garbles the relation between stress and learning.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph mentions depression and schoolchildren only as places where the early idea 'spread'; it makes no causal claim about either and says nothing of early childhood.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (helplessness is learned) and then its revision: passivity is 'the default response', and what is learned is 'that one's actions can make a difference'. The correct answer states the revision, which is the paragraph's point.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the early finding because it is described in the most detail.
questions.difficulty_reason: The solver must see that the first half of the paragraph is superseded; the option repeating it is detailed and plausible.

questions.subtopic: Authentic food cannot mean one original recipe, but it can mean a cook's understanding of a tradition.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Diners often praise a restaurant for serving the authentic version of a dish, meaning the one that matches how it is made in its place of origin. The standard is harder to apply than it sounds. Most celebrated dishes have changed repeatedly, absorbing ingredients that arrived through trade or conquest, and cooks in the same region disagree about the correct recipe. What is called authentic is usually one moment in that history, often the version a visitor first encountered, fixed and treated as the original. This does not make every claim of authenticity empty. A cook who learned a tradition from the inside and respects its logic is doing something different from one who merely borrows a name; but the difference lies in that understanding, not in matching a single correct recipe.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Diners often praise a restaurant for serving the authentic version of a dish, meaning the one that matches how it is made in its place of origin. The standard is harder to apply than it sounds. Most celebrated dishes have changed repeatedly, absorbing ingredients that arrived through trade or conquest, and cooks in the same region disagree about the correct recipe. What is called authentic is usually one moment in that history, often the version a visitor first encountered, fixed and treated as the original. This does not make every claim of authenticity empty. A cook who learned a tradition from the inside and respects its logic is doing something different from one who merely borrows a name; but the difference lies in that understanding, not in matching a single correct recipe.

options.A: Food authenticity cannot mean fidelity to one original recipe, since dishes keep changing, but it can still mark a cook's real understanding of a tradition rather than mere borrowing.
options.B: A dish is authentic when it is cooked exactly as the people of its region made it at the moment a visitor first tasted it there.
options.C: Since every celebrated dish has changed over time and cooks disagree about recipes, the very idea of authentic food is meaningless and ought to be abandoned by diners altogether.
options.D: Many famous dishes have absorbed ingredients brought by trade or conquest, so the recipes now served in their places of origin are themselves fairly recent.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Food authenticity cannot mean fidelity to one original recipe, since dishes keep changing, but it can still mark a cook's real understanding of a tradition rather than mere borrowing.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph describes this as the mistake: one moment 'fixed and treated as the original'. The option presents the error as the definition.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'This does not make every claim of authenticity empty', so calling the idea meaningless contradicts its qualification.
option_rationales.D: This takes one supporting detail and adds a claim about recipes being 'fairly recent' that the paragraph does not make; it misses the point about what authenticity can mean.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises the recipe-matching notion of authenticity and then rescues a different notion: understanding a tradition 'from the inside'. The correct answer states the critique and the rescue.
questions.common_misconception: Stopping at the critique and choosing the option that throws the idea away.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme wrong option follows the paragraph's critique faithfully until the last sentence reverses it.

questions.subtopic: Overextension is applied after the fact; loyalty of elites and revenue capacity explain imperial survival better than size.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A familiar account of why great empires fall points to overextension: they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, and the cost of holding distant frontiers drains the centre. The account is attractive because it turns decline into a lesson about limits. Its weakness is that it is applied after the fact. Empires that collapsed are described as having overreached, while others that held equally vast and costly territories for centuries are not, and the difference is rarely explained by size alone. What seems to matter more is whether the centre could keep the loyalty of provincial elites and raise revenue without provoking revolt, capacities that some large empires possessed and some small ones lacked.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A familiar account of why great empires fall points to overextension: they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, and the cost of holding distant frontiers drains the centre. The account is attractive because it turns decline into a lesson about limits. Its weakness is that it is applied after the fact. Empires that collapsed are described as having overreached, while others that held equally vast and costly territories for centuries are not, and the difference is rarely explained by size alone. What seems to matter more is whether the centre could keep the loyalty of provincial elites and raise revenue without provoking revolt, capacities that some large empires possessed and some small ones lacked.

options.A: Modern states should learn from the fall of empires that expanding beyond their means invites collapse, and should keep their commitments within their capacities.
options.B: Great empires fall because they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, so that the cost of their distant frontiers gradually drains the centre.
options.C: The size of an empire has no bearing on its survival, which depends entirely on the loyalty of its provincial elites and the willingness of its subjects to pay taxes.
options.D: Overextension explains imperial collapse less well than it seems, being invoked only after the fact; keeping provincial elites loyal and raising revenue peacefully matter more than an empire's size.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Overextension explains imperial collapse less well than it seems, being invoked only after the fact; keeping provincial elites loyal and raising revenue peacefully matter more than an empire's size.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph draws no lesson for modern states, and it doubts the 'lesson about limits' that this option recommends.
option_rationales.B: This is the 'familiar account' whose weakness the paragraph exposes: it 'is applied after the fact' and does not explain why equally large empires survived.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the difference is 'rarely explained by size alone' and that loyalty and revenue 'matter more'; 'no bearing' and 'entirely' overstate a comparative claim.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques a popular explanation on two grounds (it is applied only after collapse, and size does not separate failures from survivors) and offers an alternative: elite loyalty and the capacity to raise revenue. The correct answer keeps the critique and the alternative while keeping the comparative 'matter more'.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the absolute option because it names the alternative factors, without noticing that the paragraph only ranks them above size.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme wrong option names the right factors but changes 'matter more' into 'entirely'; the solver must catch the degree.

questions.subtopic: Mission statements tell outsiders something only when they rule out choices a competitor might make.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Almost every company now publishes a mission statement, and most of them sound alike: commitments to customers, integrity, innovation and people. Because the words cost nothing and exclude nothing, they tell an outsider very little about how the firm will behave. A statement becomes informative only when it rules something out, when it commits the company to a choice that a competitor might reasonably make differently, such as refusing a profitable line of business or accepting slower growth for some stated reason. Statements of that kind are rare precisely because they constrain the people who write them, and that constraint is what gives them meaning.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Almost every company now publishes a mission statement, and most of them sound alike: commitments to customers, integrity, innovation and people. Because the words cost nothing and exclude nothing, they tell an outsider very little about how the firm will behave. A statement becomes informative only when it rules something out, when it commits the company to a choice that a competitor might reasonably make differently, such as refusing a profitable line of business or accepting slower growth for some stated reason. Statements of that kind are rare precisely because they constrain the people who write them, and that constraint is what gives them meaning.

options.A: Most corporate mission statements sound much alike, promising customer focus, integrity, innovation and care for people, because firms tend to copy their competitors' wording.
options.B: Most mission statements reveal little because they commit firms to nothing; a statement means something only when it rules out choices a reasonable competitor might make.
options.C: Firms that refuse profitable business or accept slower growth for stated reasons are more ethical than competitors whose mission statements promise nothing specific.
options.D: Mission statements are a useless corporate ritual, and companies would lose nothing by abandoning them altogether and simply describing the products and services they sell instead.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Most mission statements reveal little because they commit firms to nothing; a statement means something only when it rules out choices a reasonable competitor might make.

option_rationales.A: This repeats the opening observation and adds a cause, copying, that the paragraph never gives; it misses the point about what makes a statement informative.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph is about whether a statement carries information, not about which firms are more ethical; the comparison is outside its scope.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says a statement 'becomes informative' when it rules something out, so it does not call all mission statements useless or propose abandoning them.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that cheap, inclusive wording conveys nothing and that a statement gains meaning only by constraining the firm. The correct answer states that criterion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'useless ritual' option because the paragraph is critical of most statements.
questions.difficulty_reason: The criterion is stated in one sentence ('informative only when it rules something out'); the wrong options are clearly off once it is read.

questions.subtopic: Planned capitals are judged unfairly early, but their thin street life is partly fixed in their layout.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Capitals built from scratch, on open land chosen by the state, are usually judged against old capitals that grew over centuries, and they usually lose: their avenues are wide and empty, their ministries far apart, their street life thin. The comparison is partly unfair. An old capital is the survivor of many cities that never grew; the planned capital is judged in its first decades, before people have had time to adapt it to their purposes. Yet the unfairness cuts only so far. The features that make a planned capital feel lifeless (the separation of government from commerce, a scale designed for ceremony rather than walking) are fixed in its layout, and time can fill the spaces between buildings without changing how far apart they are.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Capitals built from scratch, on open land chosen by the state, are usually judged against old capitals that grew over centuries, and they usually lose: their avenues are wide and empty, their ministries far apart, their street life thin. The comparison is partly unfair. An old capital is the survivor of many cities that never grew; the planned capital is judged in its first decades, before people have had time to adapt it to their purposes. Yet the unfairness cuts only so far. The features that make a planned capital feel lifeless (the separation of government from commerce, a scale designed for ceremony rather than walking) are fixed in its layout, and time can fill the spaces between buildings without changing how far apart they are.

options.A: Old capitals are lively because they grew over centuries alongside commerce, while planned capitals fail because the state chose open land far from existing cities.
options.B: Since the layouts of planned capitals are fixed, comparisons with old capitals are entirely fair, and their lifelessness is permanent whatever people later do with them.
options.C: Planned capitals are judged too early and against survivors, yet their thin street life is partly built into layouts that time can fill in but cannot fundamentally change.
options.D: Planned capitals compare poorly with old capitals only because they are judged in their first decades; given enough time, they will develop an urban life every bit as rich as that of old capitals.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Planned capitals are judged too early and against survivors, yet their thin street life is partly built into layouts that time can fill in but cannot fundamentally change.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph locates the problem in layout (separation of functions and ceremonial scale), not in the choice of site, and the option drops the point that the comparison is partly unfair.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph calls the comparison 'partly unfair' and says time 'can fill the spaces between buildings', so both 'entirely fair' and 'permanent whatever people later do' contradict it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'the unfairness cuts only so far' because the lifeless features 'are fixed in its layout'; promising a life 'every bit as rich' ignores that limit.

questions.explanation: The paragraph makes a concession and then limits it. The concession: planned capitals are judged against survivors and too early. The limit: their lifeless features are 'fixed in its layout'. The correct answer keeps both, including the precise point that time can fill gaps but not move buildings.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that stops at the concession, since the paragraph spends several sentences defending planned capitals before turning.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each keep one half of a concession-and-limit structure, and the third misplaces the cause; the correct answer is fixed only by holding both halves.

questions.subtopic: Moral deference troubles us because moral belief should rest on one's own understanding, not because no experts exist.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: We defer to experts on bridges and medicines without hesitation, yet many people feel that deferring to someone else on a moral question (adopting a view on the ethics of eating meat simply because a thoughtful philosopher holds it) would be a failing. One explanation is that there are no moral experts to defer to. That seems too quick: some people have plainly thought harder and more carefully about such questions than others. A better explanation is that moral belief is meant to be connected to one's own understanding of why something is wrong; a person who refrains from cruelty only on someone's say-so seems to have the right belief in the wrong way. On this account deference may sometimes be prudent, when one must act and cannot work the question through, but it cannot be the end of the matter.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

We defer to experts on bridges and medicines without hesitation, yet many people feel that deferring to someone else on a moral question (adopting a view on the ethics of eating meat simply because a thoughtful philosopher holds it) would be a failing. One explanation is that there are no moral experts to defer to. That seems too quick: some people have plainly thought harder and more carefully about such questions than others. A better explanation is that moral belief is meant to be connected to one's own understanding of why something is wrong; a person who refrains from cruelty only on someone's say-so seems to have the right belief in the wrong way. On this account deference may sometimes be prudent, when one must act and cannot work the question through, but it cannot be the end of the matter.

options.A: Moral deference troubles us not because moral expertise is impossible but because moral belief should rest on one's own understanding, so deference can be a stopgap, never a final answer.
options.B: Since moral belief must rest on one's own understanding, it is always wrong to adopt any moral view on the authority of another person, however thoughtful or well informed that person may be.
options.C: Moral experts deserve the same deference we give engineers and doctors, since some people have thought harder about ethics than others and so are more likely to be right.
options.D: People rightly hesitate to defer to others on moral questions, because unlike engineering or medicine, ethics has no experts whose judgement is any better than anyone else's.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Moral deference troubles us not because moral expertise is impossible but because moral belief should rest on one's own understanding, so deference can be a stopgap, never a final answer.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph allows that 'deference may sometimes be prudent, when one must act'; 'always wrong' contradicts that concession.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph grants that moral expertise exists but argues that deferring to it differs from deferring on bridges, because belief should be 'connected to one's own understanding'.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'One explanation' the paragraph calls 'too quick', since 'some people have plainly thought harder and more carefully' about moral questions.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects one explanation of our unease about moral deference (no experts exist), offers another (moral belief should be grounded in one's own understanding), and limits it (deference may be prudent when one must act). The correct answer states all three.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'always wrong' option, which follows the paragraph's preferred explanation but ignores its final concession.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph weighs two explanations and then concedes a limit; each wrong option captures one of these moves in isolation and the strongest one fails only on 'always'.

questions.subtopic: Cohesion alone does not cause bad group decisions; its combination with a directive leader or isolation does.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Close-knit teams are often blamed for poor decisions, on the theory that members who like one another suppress doubts to preserve harmony. Yet many of the most effective teams are also highly cohesive, and their members argue fiercely because they trust that disagreement will not cost them their place. Cohesion, it seems, is not the culprit by itself. The trouble comes when cohesion is combined with a dominant leader who signals the preferred answer early, or with isolation from outside views, so that loyalty to the group comes to mean agreeing with it. Breaking up close teams to prevent bad decisions would therefore sacrifice the trust that makes candid disagreement possible.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Close-knit teams are often blamed for poor decisions, on the theory that members who like one another suppress doubts to preserve harmony. Yet many of the most effective teams are also highly cohesive, and their members argue fiercely because they trust that disagreement will not cost them their place. Cohesion, it seems, is not the culprit by itself. The trouble comes when cohesion is combined with a dominant leader who signals the preferred answer early, or with isolation from outside views, so that loyalty to the group comes to mean agreeing with it. Breaking up close teams to prevent bad decisions would therefore sacrifice the trust that makes candid disagreement possible.

options.A: Members of close-knit teams suppress their doubts in order to preserve harmony, which is why such teams tend to make poorer decisions than looser and less friendly groups of colleagues do.
options.B: Leaders should avoid stating their preferred answer early in a discussion, since doing so leads loyal team members to agree with them instead of openly voicing their own doubts.
options.C: Highly cohesive teams always make better decisions than loose ones, because members who trust one another feel free to argue fiercely about every question they face.
options.D: Cohesion alone does not cause poor group decisions; harm comes from combining it with a dominant leader or isolation, and breaking up close teams would destroy the trust behind candid dissent.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Cohesion alone does not cause poor group decisions; harm comes from combining it with a dominant leader or isolation, and breaking up close teams would destroy the trust behind candid dissent.

option_rationales.A: This is the theory the paragraph reports and then rejects with 'Cohesion, it seems, is not the culprit by itself'.
option_rationales.B: The dominant leader is one of two conditions the paragraph names; it gives no advice to leaders, so this option is both narrow and a prescription it does not make.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says cohesion causes trouble when 'combined with a dominant leader' or 'isolation', so 'always' better contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the view that cohesion causes groupthink, locates the harm in cohesion combined with other conditions, and concludes against breaking up close teams. The correct answer states the diagnosis and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the advice to leaders, which sounds like a sensible lesson from the paragraph but is not its point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reported view is described in detail first, and a narrow prescription is plausible; the solver must follow the paragraph's turn at 'Yet'.

questions.subtopic: Fashion changes because styles stop being distinctive once they spread, not because they stop being attractive.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Fashion moves in cycles because it serves two opposed wishes at once: to resemble the people one admires and to stand apart from the people one does not. A style adopted by a small, admired group spreads as others imitate it; but the more widely it spreads, the less it distinguishes anyone, and the group that began it abandons it for something new. The style then lingers among late adopters until it seems dated, and it becomes available for revival only once it has been forgotten long enough to look fresh. The engine of change is therefore social rather than aesthetic: styles are dropped not because they stop being attractive but because they stop being distinctive.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Fashion moves in cycles because it serves two opposed wishes at once: to resemble the people one admires and to stand apart from the people one does not. A style adopted by a small, admired group spreads as others imitate it; but the more widely it spreads, the less it distinguishes anyone, and the group that began it abandons it for something new. The style then lingers among late adopters until it seems dated, and it becomes available for revival only once it has been forgotten long enough to look fresh. The engine of change is therefore social rather than aesthetic: styles are dropped not because they stop being attractive but because they stop being distinctive.

options.A: Out-of-date styles linger among late adopters until they look dated, and they can be revived only after being forgotten long enough to seem fresh again.
options.B: Fashions change because people want both to imitate admired groups and to stand out, so a style is dropped once its spread means it sets nobody apart.
options.C: Fashion is controlled by small, admired groups who deliberately invent new styles every season in order to stay ahead of the many people who keep imitating them.
options.D: Styles go out of fashion when people stop finding them attractive, and they return only once tastes have changed enough for them to look appealing to people again.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Fashions change because people want both to imitate admired groups and to stand out, so a style is dropped once its spread means it sets nobody apart.

option_rationales.A: This restates one stage of the cycle described in the third sentence and leaves out the two opposed wishes that drive it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the admired group abandons a style once it spreads; it says nothing about control, deliberate invention or seasons, so the option adds an outside idea.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says styles are dropped 'not because they stop being attractive but because they stop being distinctive', which this option reverses.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains the fashion cycle by two opposed wishes (imitation and distinction) and concludes that change is 'social rather than aesthetic'. The correct answer states the mechanism and its consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about revival, which is accurate but describes only the tail of the cycle.
questions.difficulty_reason: The final sentence states the point outright, and the wrong options are a reversal, a detail and an addition.

questions.subtopic: Revolutions follow improvement because discontent tracks the gap between expectations and reality.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It seems natural to expect revolutions where misery is deepest, yet they have often broken out in societies that were growing richer and whose rulers had begun to reform. The puzzle dissolves once one considers what people compare their situation with. Long and settled hardship tends to produce resignation, because it is all that people expect. When conditions start to improve, expectations rise faster than conditions can, and when a reforming regime then stalls or reverses course, the gap between what people now think possible and what they actually have becomes intolerable. Discontent, on this view, tracks the distance between hopes and reality, not the absolute level of hardship.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It seems natural to expect revolutions where misery is deepest, yet they have often broken out in societies that were growing richer and whose rulers had begun to reform. The puzzle dissolves once one considers what people compare their situation with. Long and settled hardship tends to produce resignation, because it is all that people expect. When conditions start to improve, expectations rise faster than conditions can, and when a reforming regime then stalls or reverses course, the gap between what people now think possible and what they actually have becomes intolerable. Discontent, on this view, tracks the distance between hopes and reality, not the absolute level of hardship.

options.A: Revolutions break out where misery is deepest and most prolonged, since the people who have suffered longest and worst have the strongest reasons to overthrow their rulers.
options.B: Rulers who wish to avoid revolution should never begin to reform, since any improvement in their subjects' conditions will inevitably provoke a rebellion against them.
options.C: Revolutions often follow improvement rather than settled misery because rising conditions raise expectations, and unrest grows from the gap between those hopes and what people actually have.
options.D: People who have lived through long and settled hardship usually become resigned to it, because such hardship is all that they have ever learned to expect.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Revolutions often follow improvement rather than settled misery because rising conditions raise expectations, and unrest grows from the gap between those hopes and what people actually have.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'natural' expectation the paragraph corrects; it says long hardship 'tends to produce resignation'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph explains a pattern; it gives no advice to rulers, and it says unrest follows when reform 'stalls or reverses course', not that any improvement 'inevitably' provokes rebellion.
option_rationales.D: This is one step in the explanation; it leaves out the central claim that discontent tracks 'the distance between hopes and reality'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph poses a puzzle (revolutions in improving societies) and resolves it: rising conditions raise expectations, and a stalled reform opens an intolerable gap. The correct answer states the pattern and its explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the prescription for rulers, which seems to follow from the paragraph but overstates it and ignores the role of a stalled reform.
questions.difficulty_reason: The prescription wrong option is a tempting overextension of the explanation, and the detail about resignation is accurate but partial.

questions.subtopic: Remittances help households in ways aid does not, but cannot replace public investment and may weaken pressure for reform.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Money sent home by migrants now reaches many poor countries in larger sums than foreign aid, and it has advantages aid lacks: it goes directly to households, it tends to rise when the home country suffers a disaster, and it pays for food, school fees and medical care that families choose for themselves. It is tempting to conclude that remittances can do the work of development. The conclusion overreaches. Remittances smooth and raise household consumption, but they do not build roads, courts or power grids, and a country that comes to depend on exporting its workers may find that its most enterprising people, and the political pressure they might have exerted for reform, are abroad.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Money sent home by migrants now reaches many poor countries in larger sums than foreign aid, and it has advantages aid lacks: it goes directly to households, it tends to rise when the home country suffers a disaster, and it pays for food, school fees and medical care that families choose for themselves. It is tempting to conclude that remittances can do the work of development. The conclusion overreaches. Remittances smooth and raise household consumption, but they do not build roads, courts or power grids, and a country that comes to depend on exporting its workers may find that its most enterprising people, and the political pressure they might have exerted for reform, are abroad.

options.A: Remittances help poor households more directly than aid and hold up in crises, but cannot supply public infrastructure or institutions, and reliance on emigration may drain pressure for reform.
options.B: Remittances harm poor countries, since they drain away their most enterprising workers and lead families to spend on consumption instead of building the roads and power grids the country needs.
options.C: Because remittances now exceed foreign aid and reach households directly, they can replace aid as the main engine of development in many poor countries.
options.D: Migrants tend to send more money home after a disaster, which makes remittances a more dependable source of support in hard times than foreign aid is.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Remittances help poor households more directly than aid and hold up in crises, but cannot supply public infrastructure or institutions, and reliance on emigration may drain pressure for reform.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph lists real advantages of remittances and never says they harm countries or that families should build roads; it says only that remittances do not supply such public goods.
option_rationales.C: This is the conclusion the paragraph calls tempting and then says 'overreaches', since remittances 'do not build roads, courts or power grids'.
option_rationales.D: This picks out one advantage from the first sentence and omits the paragraph's main point, that remittances cannot 'do the work of development' because they do not build public goods and may export would-be reformers.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets out the advantages of remittances, rejects the inference that they can 'do the work of development', and gives two reasons: they do not fund public goods, and dependence on emigration may export reformers. The correct answer holds the advantages and both limits.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that treats the paragraph's criticism as a claim that remittances do harm, when it says they help households.
questions.difficulty_reason: The 'harm' wrong option uses the paragraph's own words about enterprising people and roads but reverses its overall assessment.

questions.subtopic: Gentrification may not push many residents out, yet it excludes poorer newcomers, transforming areas gradually.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a poor neighbourhood starts to attract wealthier residents, the common fear is that existing tenants are driven out. Some careful tracking of households has found something less dramatic: long-standing residents of gentrifying areas move away at rates not much higher than those in similar neighbourhoods that are not changing, and those who stay benefit from safer streets and better shops. This finding is real but easy to misread. It concerns whether people leave, not who arrives. As rents rise, the poorer households who would have moved in, replacing those who leave for ordinary reasons, can no longer afford to, so the neighbourhood is transformed over a decade without any dramatic eviction. Displacement, in other words, may happen less at the door than in the queue for vacant homes.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a poor neighbourhood starts to attract wealthier residents, the common fear is that existing tenants are driven out. Some careful tracking of households has found something less dramatic: long-standing residents of gentrifying areas move away at rates not much higher than those in similar neighbourhoods that are not changing, and those who stay benefit from safer streets and better shops. This finding is real but easy to misread. It concerns whether people leave, not who arrives. As rents rise, the poorer households who would have moved in, replacing those who leave for ordinary reasons, can no longer afford to, so the neighbourhood is transformed over a decade without any dramatic eviction. Displacement, in other words, may happen less at the door than in the queue for vacant homes.

options.A: Fears about gentrification are largely mistaken, since long-standing residents rarely leave changing neighbourhoods and those who stay go on to enjoy safer streets and better shops.
options.B: When wealthier people move into a poor neighbourhood, existing tenants are soon driven out by rising rents, which is why such areas change so quickly and so visibly.
options.C: Gentrification displaces poor households less through eviction than through rising rents that steadily push existing tenants out of their homes over the course of a decade.
options.D: Gentrification may not push out many existing residents, yet it can shut out poorer newcomers who can no longer afford to move in, transforming an area gradually.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Gentrification may not push out many existing residents, yet it can shut out poorer newcomers who can no longer afford to move in, transforming an area gradually.

option_rationales.A: This stops at the finding that the paragraph says is 'easy to misread'; it ignores the point that the neighbourhood is still 'transformed' as poorer households can no longer move in.
option_rationales.B: This is 'the common fear' that the tracking contradicts, and the paragraph says the change takes 'over a decade without any dramatic eviction'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says existing residents leave at rates 'not much higher' than elsewhere; the displacement it describes falls on would-be newcomers, not on existing tenants, so the option misplaces it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding that undercuts the fear of eviction, then shows its scope: it measures who leaves, not who arrives, and rising rents exclude poorer newcomers. The correct answer keeps the finding, the shift of focus to arrivals, and the gradual transformation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about rents pushing tenants out 'over a decade', which borrows the paragraph's timescale and its downplaying of eviction but applies them to the wrong group.
questions.difficulty_reason: The subtle wrong option has the right mechanism (rents, gradual change) attached to the wrong households; it is separated from the correct answer only by 'not who arrives'.

questions.subtopic: Neither our ignorance of future people's wants nor their non-existence frees us from duties to them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is sometimes argued that we owe nothing to people who do not yet exist, since they cannot make claims on us and we cannot know what they will want. The second point is weaker than it looks. We do not know the tastes of people a century from now, but we know with some confidence that they will need breathable air, fertile soil and a climate in which crops grow, just as we do. Obligations of that basic kind do not depend on knowing anyone's particular preferences. And the first point proves too much: a person who buries a hazard that will harm whoever digs there in fifty years seems clearly to wrong that future person, even though no one yet exists to complain.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is sometimes argued that we owe nothing to people who do not yet exist, since they cannot make claims on us and we cannot know what they will want. The second point is weaker than it looks. We do not know the tastes of people a century from now, but we know with some confidence that they will need breathable air, fertile soil and a climate in which crops grow, just as we do. Obligations of that basic kind do not depend on knowing anyone's particular preferences. And the first point proves too much: a person who buries a hazard that will harm whoever digs there in fifty years seems clearly to wrong that future person, even though no one yet exists to complain.

options.A: We should give the wishes of future generations the same weight as our own, since we can know with confidence what people a century from now will need and prefer.
options.B: We owe nothing to people who do not yet exist, since they cannot make any claims on us and we have no way of knowing what they will want.
options.C: Neither our ignorance of future people's wants nor their present non-existence frees us from duties to them, since their basic needs are knowable and harming them is plainly wrong.
options.D: Burying a hazard that will harm whoever digs there in fifty years wrongs a future person, even though nobody yet exists to complain about it.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Neither our ignorance of future people's wants nor their present non-existence frees us from duties to them, since their basic needs are knowable and harming them is plainly wrong.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'We do not know the tastes of people a century from now'; it claims knowledge only of basic needs, and it says nothing about equal weight.
option_rationales.B: This is the argument the paragraph reports in its first sentence and then rebuts point by point.
option_rationales.D: This is the example used against the first point; it omits the reply to the argument from ignorance of future preferences.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rebuts both premises of the argument that we owe future people nothing: ignorance of preferences does not touch basic needs, and the buried-hazard case shows non-existence does not cancel wrongs. The correct answer keeps both replies.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that overstates our knowledge of future people, treating knowledge of basic needs as if it covered preferences.
questions.difficulty_reason: The overreaching wrong option sounds like a strong version of the author's view; it fails on the distinction between needs and tastes.

questions.subtopic: Habits form through repetition in a stable setting, so a change of circumstances is a chance to change them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: People trying to build a habit usually rely on willpower and reminders, but habits form most reliably when a behaviour is repeated in the same setting, at the same time or after the same prompt, until the setting itself begins to trigger it. Once that link is established, the behaviour needs little deliberate effort; the cue does the work. This is why habits are often easiest to change when circumstances change anyway. Someone who moves house or starts a new job has lost many of the old cues at once, and for a while their routines are open to revision in a way they rarely are otherwise.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

People trying to build a habit usually rely on willpower and reminders, but habits form most reliably when a behaviour is repeated in the same setting, at the same time or after the same prompt, until the setting itself begins to trigger it. Once that link is established, the behaviour needs little deliberate effort; the cue does the work. This is why habits are often easiest to change when circumstances change anyway. Someone who moves house or starts a new job has lost many of the old cues at once, and for a while their routines are open to revision in a way they rarely are otherwise.

options.A: Habits form most reliably when people rely on strong willpower and regular reminders to repeat a behaviour over and over until it no longer requires any deliberate effort.
options.B: Habits form when a behaviour is repeated in a stable setting until the setting triggers it, which is why a change of circumstances offers a rare chance to change routines.
options.C: Anyone who wants to change a bad habit should move house or change jobs, since such routines can never be broken while the old surroundings remain.
options.D: People who move house or start a new job lose many of their old cues all at once, so their daily routines become open to revision for a while.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Habits form when a behaviour is repeated in a stable setting until the setting triggers it, which is why a change of circumstances offers a rare chance to change routines.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph contrasts what people 'usually rely on', willpower and reminders, with what actually works, repetition in 'the same setting'; the option reverses this.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says habits are 'often easiest to change' after a move, not that they 'can never be broken' otherwise, and it recommends no such step.
option_rationales.D: This is the illustration in the last sentence; it omits the explanation of how habits form, which is what makes the illustration matter.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains habit formation (repetition in a stable setting until 'the cue does the work') and draws a consequence: lost cues make routines easier to revise. The correct answer states both.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the illustration about moving house because it is the most concrete sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The mechanism is stated in the first sentence and the consequence is flagged by 'This is why'; wrong options are a reversal, a detail and an extreme prescription.

questions.subtopic: Retirement is hardest for those who relied on work for structure, company and identity, whatever their savings.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Retirement is usually planned as a financial problem: whether savings will last. For many people the harder adjustment turns out to be of another kind. Work supplies more than income; it gives the week a shape, provides daily contact with people one did not choose but comes to rely on, and answers the question of what one does. Those who retire from jobs that supplied these things, and who have not built other sources of them, can find that a secure income leaves them oddly adrift. People whose sense of themselves was already rooted in family, hobbies or community tend to make the transition more easily, whatever their savings.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Work gives the week its shape, provides daily contact with colleagues and answers the question of what one does, as well as supplying the income people live on.
options.B: Financial planning for retirement is pointless, because people with ample savings are just as likely as anyone else to feel adrift once they stop working.
options.C: People with large savings adjust to retirement more easily than others, because a secure income lets them develop new hobbies and ties in their community.
options.D: Beyond money, retirement removes the structure, company and identity work provided, so it is hardest for those without other sources of these, whatever their savings.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Beyond money, retirement removes the structure, company and identity work provided, so it is hardest for those without other sources of these, whatever their savings.

option_rationales.A: This restates the list in the third sentence and leaves out the point about who struggles in retirement and why.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the non-financial adjustment is often 'the harder' one; it never calls financial planning pointless, and it says those with other sources of identity adjust 'more easily'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'a secure income leaves them oddly adrift' and that ease of transition holds 'whatever their savings', which contradicts this option.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares the financial and the non-financial sides of retirement and argues that the second is often harder, especially for people whose identity rested on work. The correct answer states the comparison and who is most affected.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'pointless' option because the paragraph downplays money, when it only says money is not the whole problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is plain once the phrase 'whatever their savings' is read; the wrong options are an overstatement, a list and a contradiction.

questions.subtopic: Dissenters show that a past age's views could be seen past, so the standards of the time lessen blame without removing it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Two responses are common when a celebrated figure from the past is found to have held views now regarded as abhorrent. One insists that such people be judged by the standards of their own time, since no one can be expected to see beyond the moral horizon of their age. The other holds that wrong is wrong, and that admiration should be withdrawn. Both overlook something. Any age contains dissenters, people who did see past the prevailing view, often at some cost, and their existence shows that the horizon was not closed. It does not follow that every figure who failed to join them was a villain; it does follow that 'they were of their time' is a partial excuse, which lessens blame without removing it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Two responses are common when a celebrated figure from the past is found to have held views now regarded as abhorrent. One insists that such people be judged by the standards of their own time, since no one can be expected to see beyond the moral horizon of their age.
