Any age contains dissenters, people who did see past the prevailing view, often at some cost, and their existence shows that the horizon was not closed. It does not follow that every figure who failed to join them was a villain; it does follow that 'they were of their time' is a partial excuse, which lessens blame without removing it.

options.A: A figure who held views now seen as abhorrent deserves no admiration, since wrong is wrong whatever the standards of the age in which that person lived.
options.B: Past figures should be judged only by the moral standards of their own age, since nobody can reasonably be expected to see beyond the outlook of their time.
options.C: Because dissenters in every age saw past its accepted wrongs, the standards of a figure's own time can lessen blame for abhorrent views but cannot remove it.
options.D: Since some people in every age saw past its prevailing views, those who failed to join these dissenters deserve the same blame as anyone holding such views today.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Because dissenters in every age saw past its accepted wrongs, the standards of a figure's own time can lessen blame for abhorrent views but cannot remove it.

option_rationales.A: This is the second common response; the paragraph rejects it too, saying it 'does not follow that every figure who failed to join them was a villain'.
option_rationales.B: This is the first common response, which the paragraph says overlooks the dissenters whose existence 'shows that the horizon was not closed'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls the appeal to the time 'a partial excuse, which lessens blame'; 'the same blame' as today denies that it lessens anything.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets out two opposed responses and rejects both. The existence of dissenters shows the moral horizon was open, so the standards of the time are 'a partial excuse, which lessens blame without removing it'. The correct answer states this middle position and its ground.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that uses the paragraph's own argument about dissenters but draws the stronger conclusion that the excuse counts for nothing.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are the two views the paragraph rejects, and the third uses its own premise to reach a conclusion it denies; separating them needs the exact force of 'partial excuse'.

questions.subtopic: The high cost of artillery-proof fortresses shifted power from local lords to tax-raising rulers, without any plan to centralise.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When cannon became powerful enough to batter down tall stone walls, the castle of a local lord lost much of its value as a refuge. The answer was a new kind of fortification: low, thick ramparts with angled bastions that deflected shot and allowed defenders to cover every approach. Such works were enormously expensive to build and to garrison, far beyond the means of most nobles, and so the ability to hold territory passed increasingly to rulers who could raise taxes across a whole realm. A change in military technology thus did political work, strengthening central authority at the expense of local power, not by any decision to centralise but through the rising cost of defence.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When cannon became powerful enough to batter down tall stone walls, the castle of a local lord lost much of its value as a refuge. The answer was a new kind of fortification: low, thick ramparts with angled bastions that deflected shot and allowed defenders to cover every approach. Such works were enormously expensive to build and to garrison, far beyond the means of most nobles, and so the ability to hold territory passed increasingly to rulers who could raise taxes across a whole realm. A change in military technology thus did political work, strengthening central authority at the expense of local power, not by any decision to centralise but through the rising cost of defence.

options.A: The new fortifications had low, thick ramparts and angled bastions, which deflected cannon shot and allowed the defenders to cover every approach to the walls.
options.B: Cannon made castles obsolete, and the costly fortresses replacing them were affordable only to rulers taxing whole realms, so defence costs moved power from lords to the centre.
options.C: Rulers deliberately adopted artillery and expensive new fortresses as part of a long-term plan to centralise their realms and break the power of local nobles.
options.D: Gunpowder weapons ended warfare between local lords altogether, since no noble could any longer build walls that were able to withstand a sustained bombardment.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Cannon made castles obsolete, and the costly fortresses replacing them were affordable only to rulers taxing whole realms, so defence costs moved power from lords to the centre.

option_rationales.A: This describes the design of the new fortresses from the second sentence and omits the political consequence that the paragraph builds towards.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says central authority grew 'not by any decision to centralise but through the rising cost of defence', so a deliberate plan contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says castles 'lost much of' their value and that power passed 'increasingly' to rulers; it says nothing about warfare between lords ending, so the option overstates and adds.

questions.explanation: The paragraph traces a chain: cannon made tall walls vulnerable, the replacement fortifications were too costly for most nobles, and so holding territory passed to rulers with realm-wide taxes. Its last sentence names the point: technology 'did political work' through cost, not design. The correct answer states the chain and its result.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming that a political outcome must have been intended, and so choosing the option about a deliberate plan.
questions.difficulty_reason: The last sentence states the point and rules out the 'deliberate plan' reading; the other wrong options are a detail and an overstatement.

questions.subtopic: Network effects make platform leadership durable but not permanent, depending on the cost of using several platforms.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Platforms that grow more valuable as more people use them, such as messaging services or marketplaces, are often said to be unassailable once they lead: every new user makes the leader more attractive, so challengers cannot catch up. The record is less kind to that claim. Leading platforms have lost their position when a rival offered something the leader could not easily match, or when users could belong to several platforms at once at little cost, so that joining a newcomer did not mean abandoning the old network. Network effects make leadership durable, not permanent; how durable depends largely on how costly it is for users to use more than one platform.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Platforms that grow more valuable as more people use them, such as messaging services or marketplaces, are often said to be unassailable once they lead: every new user makes the leader more attractive, so challengers cannot catch up. The record is less kind to that claim. Leading platforms have lost their position when a rival offered something the leader could not easily match, or when users could belong to several platforms at once at little cost, so that joining a newcomer did not mean abandoning the old network. Network effects make leadership durable, not permanent; how durable depends largely on how costly it is for users to use more than one platform.

options.A: Network effects make a leading platform hard but not impossible to displace, its security depending largely on how costly users find it to join more than one platform.
options.B: Once a platform leads its market, every new user makes it more attractive, so rivals can never catch up with it and its dominance soon becomes effectively permanent.
options.C: Regulators should require platforms to let users belong to several networks at once, since this is the only way to keep markets for messaging services competitive.
options.D: Network effects give leading platforms no real protection, since users will always move to whichever new rival offers something the leader cannot easily match.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Network effects make a leading platform hard but not impossible to displace, its security depending largely on how costly users find it to join more than one platform.

option_rationales.B: This is the claim the paragraph says 'The record is less kind to'; its conclusion is that network effects make leadership 'durable, not permanent'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph mentions low-cost multiple membership as a condition under which leaders have lost ground; it makes no recommendation to regulators and no 'only way' claim.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says network effects make leadership 'durable'; 'no real protection' and 'always move' reverse that.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the view that leading platforms are unassailable, citing cases where leaders lost ground, and concludes that leadership is 'durable, not permanent', with durability depending on the cost of using several platforms. The correct answer states both parts.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the regulatory option, which draws a policy from the paragraph's condition rather than stating its point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reported view and its reversal flank the correct answer, and a plausible policy wrong option tempts readers who infer a remedy; the paragraph's final sentence settles it.

questions.subtopic: The winner of an auction for an item of uncertain value has probably guessed too high, so offers should be shaded more as bidders increase.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Imagine a sealed jar of coins auctioned to a room of thirty people, each of whom guesses its contents by eye. Their guesses will fall on both sides of the real sum, and taken together they may average out remarkably well. Yet the person who takes the jar home is the one who guessed highest, and so, even if every guesser is sensible and the crowd as a whole is accurate, the buyer has very probably paid more than the jar holds. Victory in such a contest is itself evidence of having guessed too high. Better guessing cannot cure this, since no guess is free of error; what helps is to offer less than one's own guess, and to hold back further when the room is larger, because a bigger crowd throws up a more extreme top guess.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Imagine a sealed jar of coins auctioned to a room of thirty people, each of whom guesses its contents by eye. Their guesses will fall on both sides of the real sum, and taken together they may average out remarkably well. Yet the person who takes the jar home is the one who guessed highest, and so, even if every guesser is sensible and the crowd as a whole is accurate, the buyer has very probably paid more than the jar holds. Victory in such a contest is itself evidence of having guessed too high. Better guessing cannot cure this, since no guess is free of error; what helps is to offer less than one's own guess, and to hold back further when the room is larger, because a bigger crowd throws up a more extreme top guess.

options.A: When many bid on something of uncertain value, the winner has probably guessed too high, so bidders should offer below their guesses, more so in larger crowds.
options.B: The person who wins the jar of coins usually does so because he or she is a worse judge of quantities than the others in the room.
options.C: Guesses about the contents of the jar fall on both sides of the real sum, and when they are taken together they tend to average out quite accurately.
options.D: Since every guess contains some error, bidders should study the jar more carefully until their estimates of its contents become reliable enough to bid on.

questions.correct_answer: (A) When many bid on something of uncertain value, the winner has probably guessed too high, so bidders should offer below their guesses, more so in larger crowds.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the buyer has probably overpaid 'even if every guesser is sensible', so the problem is selecting the highest of honest errors, not poor judgement.
option_rationales.C: This restates only the second sentence; it omits the central point that the winner is the highest guesser and the remedy that follows.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph rejects this remedy outright: 'Better guessing cannot cure this, since no guess is free of error'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a selection effect: guesses scatter around the truth, but the highest one wins, so the winner has probably paid too much; 'Victory in such a contest is itself evidence of having guessed too high.' It then gives the remedy, offering less than one's guess and holding back further in a larger room. The correct summary keeps both the mechanism and the scaled remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the outcome as a sign of poor judgement, or picking the option that restates the scatter of guesses without the selection effect.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires seeing the selection logic and the scaled remedy; the narrow option restates accurate details.

questions.subtopic: Extended warranties are overpriced for most buyers but may suit those who cannot absorb a large repair bill.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Shops selling televisions and washing machines press customers hard to buy an extended warranty at the till, and the reason is simple: these contracts are among the most profitable things the shop sells. The price is set well above the expected cost of repairs, because most appliances that survive their first months go on working for years, and those that fail early are already covered by the maker's own guarantee. A buyer who can afford an occasional repair bill is therefore better off keeping the money and paying for repairs if they come. The case changes only for someone who could not absorb a sudden large expense; for that buyer, paying a premium to avoid the risk may be sensible.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Shops selling televisions and washing machines press customers hard to buy an extended warranty at the till, and the reason is simple: these contracts are among the most profitable things the shop sells. The price is set well above the expected cost of repairs, because most appliances that survive their first months go on working for years, and those that fail early are already covered by the maker's own guarantee. A buyer who can afford an occasional repair bill is therefore better off keeping the money and paying for repairs if they come. The case changes only for someone who could not absorb a sudden large expense; for that buyer, paying a premium to avoid the risk may be sensible.

options.A: Appliances rarely fail after their first few months, which is why their makers are willing to offer a guarantee covering only the early period of use.
options.B: Extended warranties are a dishonest sales trick, and no buyer of a household appliance, whatever their circumstances, should ever agree to buy one.
options.C: Extended warranties cost more than expected repairs, so buyers able to pay for repairs should decline them, though they may suit someone who cannot bear a large expense.
options.D: Shops push extended warranties chiefly because customers who buy them are more likely to return to the same shop when they come back to buy their next household appliances.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Extended warranties cost more than expected repairs, so buyers able to pay for repairs should decline them, though they may suit someone who cannot bear a large expense.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph mentions early failures and the maker's guarantee only as a reason the warranty is overpriced; it does not explain why makers offer guarantees, and the option misses the main point.
option_rationales.B: The last sentence makes an exception for 'someone who could not absorb a sudden large expense', so 'whatever their circumstances' contradicts the paragraph.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph gives a different reason: the contracts are 'among the most profitable things the shop sells'. Repeat custom is never mentioned.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that extended warranties are priced 'well above the expected cost of repairs', so a buyer who can afford occasional repairs should keep the money; it then qualifies this for buyers who cannot absorb a large expense. The correct summary states the claim and the exception.
questions.common_misconception: Ignoring the final qualification and choosing the absolute rejection of all warranties.
questions.difficulty_reason: The claim and its single exception are stated directly in the last two sentences.

questions.subtopic: Supply shocks discredit a cost-cutting imitation of lean production, not the method that relied on supplier knowledge.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It became common, after a run of supply disruptions, to say that lean manufacturing had been exposed as a mistake: firms that held almost no inventory had saved money in calm years and paid for it many times over when deliveries stopped. The charge contains a truth but misplaces it. Holding little stock was never the whole of the method; its purpose was to make problems visible quickly so that they could be fixed, and the firms that practised it most seriously also cultivated close, long relationships with a few suppliers and knew in detail where their parts came from. What failed in many cases was a cheaper imitation: low inventory adopted as a cost target, combined with suppliers chosen solely on price and scattered across distant regions that nobody had mapped. The lesson, then, is less that buffers are always wise than that thin buffers are safe only where the knowledge and relationships the method assumed are actually present.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It became common, after a run of supply disruptions, to say that lean manufacturing had been exposed as a mistake: firms that held almost no inventory had saved money in calm years and paid for it many times over when deliveries stopped. The charge contains a truth but misplaces it. Holding little stock was never the whole of the method; its purpose was to make problems visible quickly so that they could be fixed, and the firms that practised it most seriously also cultivated close, long relationships with a few suppliers and knew in detail where their parts came from. What failed in many cases was a cheaper imitation: low inventory adopted as a cost target, combined with suppliers chosen solely on price and scattered across distant regions that nobody had mapped. The lesson, then, is less that buffers are always wise than that thin buffers are safe only where the knowledge and relationships the method assumed are actually present.

options.A: Lean manufacturing remains sound in every setting, since its critics have simply confused the genuine method with the cost-cutting targets that careless imitators pursued.
options.B: Lean manufacturing failed during the recent disruptions because the firms practising it most seriously relied on a handful of suppliers they knew too closely.
options.C: Recent supply disruptions have shown that holding minimal inventory was a costly error, and that manufacturers ought to return to keeping large buffers of stock.
options.D: The disruptions discredit less lean production itself than a version that cut stock while neglecting the supplier knowledge and ties on which thin inventories safely depend.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The disruptions discredit less lean production itself than a version that cut stock while neglecting the supplier knowledge and ties on which thin inventories safely depend.

option_rationales.A: The last sentence makes the safety of thin buffers conditional: they are safe 'only where' the assumed knowledge and relationships exist, so 'sound in every setting' overstates the defence.
option_rationales.B: This reverses the paragraph, which presents close, long supplier relationships and detailed knowledge as what made thin stocks safe; the failures came from imitators with unmapped, price-chosen suppliers.
option_rationales.C: This is the common charge the paragraph reports and then says 'misplaces' the truth; the conclusion explicitly denies that 'buffers are always wise'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the charge that lean manufacturing was a mistake, concedes it 'contains a truth', and relocates the failure to an imitation that cut inventory without the supplier relationships and knowledge the real method relied on. Its conclusion is conditional: thin buffers are safe only where those conditions hold. The correct summary keeps the relocation of blame and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the unconditional defence of lean manufacturing, which sounds like the author's side but drops the 'only where' condition.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two options side against the critics; only one keeps the conditional conclusion, so scope must be read precisely.

questions.subtopic: Franchise uniformity solves the problem of buying from strangers, which is why chains and independents locate differently.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A traveller who eats at a franchised restaurant in an unfamiliar town is buying something an independent cafe cannot easily offer: the assurance that the meal will be much like the one eaten at the same chain elsewhere. The independent may cook far better, but the stranger has no way of knowing that in advance, whereas the franchise's sameness is precisely what makes its quality knowable. This is why chains cluster along highways and near stations, where most customers are passing through, while independent places flourish more often in neighbourhoods whose residents return often enough to learn which kitchens are good. Uniformity, so often mocked, is less a failure of taste than an answer to the problem of buying from strangers.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A traveller who eats at a franchised restaurant in an unfamiliar town is buying something an independent cafe cannot easily offer: the assurance that the meal will be much like the one eaten at the same chain elsewhere. The independent may cook far better, but the stranger has no way of knowing that in advance, whereas the franchise's sameness is precisely what makes its quality knowable. This is why chains cluster along highways and near stations, where most customers are passing through, while independent places flourish more often in neighbourhoods whose residents return often enough to learn which kitchens are good. Uniformity, so often mocked, is less a failure of taste than an answer to the problem of buying from strangers.

options.A: Franchised restaurants generally serve better food than independent cafes do, which explains why travellers so often choose them along highways and near stations.
options.B: Franchises thrive among passing strangers because uniformity makes their quality predictable, while independents do better with returning locals who can learn which kitchens are good.
options.C: Chain restaurants tend to cluster along highways and near railway stations, while independent cafes are found more commonly in the quieter residential neighbourhoods of most towns and cities.
options.D: Towns should protect independent cafes from franchised competitors, since the uniformity of chains steadily erodes local taste and the variety of neighbourhood kitchens.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Franchises thrive among passing strangers because uniformity makes their quality predictable, while independents do better with returning locals who can learn which kitchens are good.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph concedes that 'The independent may cook far better'; travellers choose chains for predictability, not superior food.
option_rationales.C: This reports the pattern but drops the explanation, that uniformity makes quality knowable to strangers, which is the paragraph's point.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph makes no policy proposal and explicitly says uniformity is 'less a failure of taste than an answer' to a problem, so this contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains franchise success by the problem of buying from strangers: sameness makes quality knowable. It uses this to explain why chains cluster where customers pass through and independents thrive where residents return. The correct summary links the mechanism to the location pattern.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that states the location pattern accurately but leaves out why it arises.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow option is factually accurate to the paragraph; the correct answer must be preferred for including the explanation.

questions.subtopic: Coral gardening is a useful holding action but cannot match the scale of reef loss; only curbing warming addresses the cause.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Coral gardening, in which fragments are grown in underwater nurseries and then fixed onto damaged reefs, has become the most visible form of reef restoration, and its photographs of divers planting coral are genuinely encouraging. Yet its scale should be kept in view. A well-run project may replant a few hectares, while the reefs being lost to warming seas are measured in thousands of square kilometres, and transplanted corals die in the next marine heatwave as readily as wild ones. None of this makes the work pointless: nurseries can preserve heat-tolerant strains and keep particular reefs alive for tourism or fisheries. But treating gardening as a solution to reef decline mistakes a holding action for a cure, since only reducing the warming itself addresses the cause.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Coral gardening has real but local value, such as preserving tolerant strains, yet it cannot match the scale of reef loss, and only curbing warming tackles the cause.
options.B: Coral gardening is a wasteful distraction from the real problem, and conservation groups should abandon it entirely in favour of campaigning for lower emissions.
options.C: Because transplanted corals are more vulnerable to heatwaves than wild ones, coral gardening tends to speed up rather than slow down the decline of reefs.
options.D: With enough funding and divers, coral nurseries could be expanded to replant reefs as quickly as warming seas are destroying them across the world.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Coral gardening has real but local value, such as preserving tolerant strains, yet it cannot match the scale of reef loss, and only curbing warming tackles the cause.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says 'None of this makes the work pointless' and lists its uses, so calling it wasteful and urging its abandonment contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says transplanted corals die 'as readily as wild ones', not more readily, and never claims gardening accelerates decline.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph's contrast of 'a few hectares' with 'thousands of square kilometres', and its description of gardening as 'a holding action', run against this optimistic claim.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises the view that coral gardening solves reef decline: its scale is tiny compared with losses and transplants die in heatwaves. It concedes local value (tolerant strains, particular reefs) and concludes that only reducing warming addresses the cause. The correct summary keeps the concession and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Overreading the criticism into a call to abandon gardening, ignoring the concession 'None of this makes the work pointless'.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option captures the critical tone but drops the concession; the reader must hold both.

questions.subtopic: Pollinator concern wrongly centres on honeybees; wild pollinators are the ones declining and are helped by planting, not hives.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Public concern about the decline of pollinators has fastened almost entirely on the honeybee, and campaigns urge people to keep hives in gardens and on city rooftops. The honeybee, however, is a managed farm animal, kept in large numbers by beekeepers and in little danger of disappearing. The pollinators that are genuinely declining are mostly wild: solitary bees, bumblebees, hoverflies and moths, many of which need particular flowers and undisturbed nesting ground. Adding hives can even make matters worse for these species, because dense colonies of honeybees compete with them for the same nectar and pollen. Those who wish to help pollinators would do better to plant varied native flowers and leave patches of ground untidy.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Public concern about the decline of pollinators has fastened almost entirely on the honeybee, and campaigns urge people to keep hives in gardens and on city rooftops. The honeybee, however, is a managed farm animal, kept in large numbers by beekeepers and in little danger of disappearing. The pollinators that are genuinely declining are mostly wild: solitary bees, bumblebees, hoverflies and moths, many of which need particular flowers and undisturbed nesting ground. Adding hives can even make matters worse for these species, because dense colonies of honeybees compete with them for the same nectar and pollen. Those who wish to help pollinators would do better to plant varied native flowers and leave patches of ground untidy.

options.A: Many wild pollinators, including solitary bees, bumblebees and hoverflies, depend on particular flowers and on undisturbed patches of nesting ground in order to survive.
options.B: Concern for pollinators wrongly centres on the managed honeybee, when the declining species are wild ones that extra hives may harm and varied planting would help.
options.C: Honeybee colonies are the main cause of the decline of wild pollinators, so beekeeping both in towns and in the countryside ought to be banned.
options.D: The honeybee is the pollinator most at risk of disappearing, so keeping more hives on rooftops and in gardens is the best way to help pollinators.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Concern for pollinators wrongly centres on the managed honeybee, when the declining species are wild ones that extra hives may harm and varied planting would help.

option_rationales.A: This is one supporting detail from the third sentence; it omits the paragraph's point that concern is misdirected at honeybees.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says hives 'can' make matters worse through competition, not that they are the main cause, and it proposes planting flowers, not a ban.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the honeybee is 'in little danger of disappearing' and that adding hives 'can even make matters worse', so this reverses it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises the popular focus on honeybees: they are managed and not endangered, the declining pollinators are wild, extra hives can harm those, and native planting would help. The correct summary contains the critique, the reason and the better course.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the accurate but narrow detail about wild pollinators' needs.
questions.difficulty_reason: The stance is explicit from the second sentence and the wrong options are clearly narrow, reversed or extreme.

questions.subtopic: New instruments often set the agenda of science, though theory is still needed to interpret what they show.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is tempting to describe the history of science as a sequence of ideas, each tested by instruments built to check it. Often the order runs the other way. A new instrument, made for some modest practical purpose, reveals phenomena that no existing theory anticipated, and theory then scrambles to absorb them; the instrument, in effect, sets the agenda. This does not make theories mere reflections of the tools available, for a device shows nothing until someone has ideas about what its readings mean, and the same image has been read differently by observers holding different views. But it does suggest that the questions a science finds pressing at any moment depend heavily on what it has lately become able to see, and that some questions remain unasked not because they are unimportant but because nothing yet exists to make them answerable.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is tempting to describe the history of science as a sequence of ideas, each tested by instruments built to check it. Often the order runs the other way. A new instrument, made for some modest practical purpose, reveals phenomena that no existing theory anticipated, and theory then scrambles to absorb them; the instrument, in effect, sets the agenda. This does not make theories mere reflections of the tools available, for a device shows nothing until someone has ideas about what its readings mean, and the same image has been read differently by observers holding different views. But it does suggest that the questions a science finds pressing at any moment depend heavily on what it has lately become able to see, and that some questions remain unasked not because they are unimportant but because nothing yet exists to make them answerable.

options.A: Scientific theories are largely reflections of the instruments available at the time, since what scientists come to believe is fixed by what their devices display.
options.B: The most important scientific questions have often gone unasked because scientists preferred building practical instruments to speculating about what they could not see.
options.C: Science advances as theories are proposed first and instruments are then built to test them, which is why its history is best told as a history of ideas.
options.D: Instruments often shape which questions science pursues by revealing what theory had not foreseen, though theory is still needed to interpret what instruments show.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Instruments often shape which questions science pursues by revealing what theory had not foreseen, though theory is still needed to interpret what instruments show.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph explicitly denies this: 'This does not make theories mere reflections of the tools available', because readings need interpretation and the same image is read differently.
option_rationales.B: The last sentence says such questions go unasked 'because nothing yet exists to make them answerable', not because of a preference, and it does not call them the most important.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'tempting' description in the first sentence, which the author immediately qualifies with 'Often the order runs the other way'.

questions.explanation: The author qualifies the idea-first picture of science: instruments often reveal unanticipated phenomena and so set the agenda of questions. A concession follows, that theories are not mere reflections of tools since readings need interpretation. The correct summary holds both the claim and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the claim about instruments to its extreme and ignoring the concession about interpretation, or mistaking the opening description for the author's view.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options take one half of the argument each (reported view, overstated claim); the third distorts the final clause.

questions.subtopic: Urban animals' boldness has several possible causes that only careful study can separate.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Animals living in cities often seem bolder than their rural relatives: urban birds let people approach more closely before flying off, and town foxes raid bins in daylight. It is natural to conclude that city life has bred a new temperament, and in some populations there may be genuine inherited change. But at least two other explanations fit the same observation. Individual animals may simply learn, over a lifetime of harmless encounters, that people pose little threat; or the city may attract the bolder individuals from the surrounding countryside while the timid ones stay away. Each would produce bold urban animals, and only careful study, such as raising young from both settings under identical conditions, can tell them apart.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Animals living in cities often seem bolder than their rural relatives: urban birds let people approach more closely before flying off, and town foxes raid bins in daylight. It is natural to conclude that city life has bred a new temperament, and in some populations there may be genuine inherited change. But at least two other explanations fit the same observation. Individual animals may simply learn, over a lifetime of harmless encounters, that people pose little threat; or the city may attract the bolder individuals from the surrounding countryside while the timid ones stay away. Each would produce bold urban animals, and only careful study, such as raising young from both settings under identical conditions, can tell them apart.

options.A: Urban animals merely appear bolder than rural ones because observers in cities are more likely to notice and record their encounters with wildlife.
options.B: Raising young animals from the city and the countryside under identical conditions is the most reliable method of studying the temperament of wildlife in general.
options.C: Urban animals' boldness may reflect inherited change, but learning or the arrival of bolder individuals could equally explain it, and only careful study can separate these causes.
options.D: City life has bred a genuinely new and inherited temperament in urban birds and foxes, and this explains why they tolerate people far more readily than their relatives in the countryside do.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Urban animals' boldness may reflect inherited change, but learning or the arrival of bolder individuals could equally explain it, and only careful study can separate these causes.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph accepts the observation of boldness and debates its cause; observer bias is never raised, so this is out of scope.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph offers this only as an example of the careful study needed for this question; it makes no general claim about studying wildlife temperament.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'natural' conclusion the paragraph reports and then challenges with two alternative explanations; it allows inherited change only 'in some populations'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph presents a finding (urban animals seem bolder), the natural inference (an inherited temperament), and then two rival explanations, learning and selective settlement, that fit equally. It concludes that careful study is needed to tell them apart. The correct summary keeps the finding, the rivals and the methodological conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reported 'natural' conclusion as if it were the author's.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph reports a conclusion before qualifying it; the reader must separate report from stance.

questions.subtopic: Subscription sites deliberately make cancelling hard, keeping customers through their impatience rather than their choice.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many websites make it easy to sign up for a subscription and remarkably hard to leave it. Joining takes a single click; cancelling requires finding a link buried in account settings, passing through several screens that ask whether the user is sure, and sometimes telephoning a support line during office hours. None of this is accidental. Designers know that each additional step causes some users to give up, and a user who gives up remains a paying customer. Such designs work not by persuading people that they want to stay but by exploiting the effort and impatience that make people abandon a task half done.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many websites make it easy to sign up for a subscription and remarkably hard to leave it. Joining takes a single click; cancelling requires finding a link buried in account settings, passing through several screens that ask whether the user is sure, and sometimes telephoning a support line during office hours. None of this is accidental. Designers know that each additional step causes some users to give up, and a user who gives up remains a paying customer. Such designs work not by persuading people that they want to stay but by exploiting the effort and impatience that make people abandon a task half done.

options.A: Websites make cancellation difficult mainly because their designers pay far less attention to the exit process than to the work of attracting new subscribers.
options.B: Websites deliberately make cancelling far harder than joining, keeping subscribers not by persuading them to stay but by counting on them to give up.
options.C: Governments should require every website to let subscribers cancel with a single click, since making cancellation difficult is a form of fraud.
options.D: Cancelling some online subscriptions requires users to telephone a support line, which is often open only during ordinary office hours on weekdays.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Websites deliberately make cancelling far harder than joining, keeping subscribers not by persuading them to stay but by counting on them to give up.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'None of this is accidental': designers add steps knowingly, so neglect is the wrong explanation.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph describes and explains the design; it proposes no law and does not call it fraud, so this adds an outside prescription.
option_rationales.D: This is one detail from the second sentence; it leaves out that the obstacles are deliberate and how they retain customers.

questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts easy joining with hard cancelling, states that this is deliberate, and explains the mechanism: each extra step makes some users give up, and they keep paying. The correct summary contains the asymmetry, the intent and the mechanism.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the neglect explanation, which overlooks 'None of this is accidental'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Key points are stated in consecutive sentences; wrong options are clearly narrow, contradicted or out of scope.

questions.subtopic: If defaults are read as advice, designers who set self-serving defaults are giving misleading advice.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When software ships with a setting already chosen, most users never change it, and this is often described as laziness. A more charitable reading is available. A default carries an implicit message that this is what the makers, who presumably understand the product, consider suitable, and many users reasonably treat it as advice. That reading, however, cuts both ways. If defaults function as recommendations, then the people who set them bear something like the responsibility of an adviser, and a default chosen because it serves the maker's interest in data or revenue, rather than the user's, is not a neutral starting point but a misleading recommendation. The defence of inert users thus becomes a charge against designers.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When software ships with a setting already chosen, most users never change it, and this is often described as laziness. A more charitable reading is available. A default carries an implicit message that this is what the makers, who presumably understand the product, consider suitable, and many users reasonably treat it as advice. That reading, however, cuts both ways. If defaults function as recommendations, then the people who set them bear something like the responsibility of an adviser, and a default chosen because it serves the maker's interest in data or revenue, rather than the user's, is not a neutral starting point but a misleading recommendation. The defence of inert users thus becomes a charge against designers.

options.A: Users who leave software settings unchanged are behaving reasonably, because a default implicitly signals what the makers of a product consider suitable for them.
options.B: Defaults are neutral starting points that users would be wise to treat as advice, since software makers understand their products better than the people using them.
options.C: If users keep defaults because they reasonably take them as the makers' advice, then designers who choose defaults to serve themselves are giving misleading advice.
options.D: Most users never change software defaults because they are too lazy to explore the settings, which leaves designers free to choose whatever settings suit them.

questions.correct_answer: (C) If users keep defaults because they reasonably take them as the makers' advice, then designers who choose defaults to serve themselves are giving misleading advice.

option_rationales.A: This captures only the first move, the charitable reading of users; it misses the turn 'That reading, however, cuts both ways' and the conclusion about designers' responsibility.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph denies that a self-serving default is 'a neutral starting point' and never advises users to trust defaults; it turns the point into a charge against designers.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph mentions laziness only as the common description that the next sentence replaces with a more charitable reading, and it argues designers are not free of responsibility.

questions.explanation: The paragraph replaces the laziness explanation with a charitable one, that users treat defaults as advice, and then turns it: if defaults are advice, those who set them carry an adviser's responsibility, so self-serving defaults are misleading. The final sentence states the point: 'The defence of inert users thus becomes a charge against designers.' The correct summary includes the turn.
questions.common_misconception: Stopping at the charitable reading of users and missing that the paragraph's conclusion concerns designers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The too-narrow option states a true premise accurately; the correct answer requires following the argument's turn to its conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Hiring software applies past biases consistently, and its apparent impartiality hides them from correction.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Firms that screen job applications with software trained on the records of past hires often defend the practice as more objective than human judgement, since the program applies the same rule to every applicant and cannot be swayed by a candidate's charm. Consistency, however, is not the same as fairness. A program that learns which applicants were hired in the past learns whatever preferences shaped those decisions, including any unjustified ones, and then applies them with perfect regularity. Human recruiters are inconsistent, but their inconsistency at least leaves room for a manager to notice and correct a pattern; a rule embedded in software may go unexamined precisely because it looks impartial.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Firms that screen job applications with software trained on the records of past hires often defend the practice as more objective than human judgement, since the program applies the same rule to every applicant and cannot be swayed by a candidate's charm. Consistency, however, is not the same as fairness. A program that learns which applicants were hired in the past learns whatever preferences shaped those decisions, including any unjustified ones, and then applies them with perfect regularity. Human recruiters are inconsistent, but their inconsistency at least leaves room for a manager to notice and correct a pattern; a rule embedded in software may go unexamined precisely because it looks impartial.

options.A: Hiring software trained on past decisions applies their biases consistently, and its look of impartiality may shield those biases from scrutiny that human judgement still allows.
options.B: Firms should stop using software to screen job applications altogether and return to human recruiters, whose judgement is both more reliable and more fair.
options.C: Screening software is fairer than human recruiters because it applies one identical rule to every single applicant and can never be swayed by a candidate's personal charm, however persuasive it is.
options.D: Human recruiters are inconsistent in their decisions, and this inconsistency is the main source of the unfairness that appears in the hiring records of firms.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Hiring software trained on past decisions applies their biases consistently, and its look of impartiality may shield those biases from scrutiny that human judgement still allows.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph calls human recruiters 'inconsistent' and claims only that their errors are easier to notice; it neither calls them fairer nor proposes abandoning software.
option_rationales.C: This is the defence the paragraph reports in its first sentence and rejects with 'Consistency, however, is not the same as fairness'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph treats human inconsistency as leaving 'room for a manager to notice and correct a pattern', not as the main source of unfairness.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the claim that screening software is more objective: consistency differs from fairness, the software learns and applies past preferences including unjustified ones, and its impartial appearance can keep the rule from being examined. The correct summary keeps both the inheritance of bias and the concealment.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the 'more objective' defence, or turning the critique into a blanket preference for human recruiters.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is the reported view and another overextends the critique; both are tempting.

questions.subtopic: Version control keeps every change with its reasons, which encourages experiment and explains code to newcomers.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A writer revising a manuscript on paper keeps, if anything, a few dated drafts, and the reasons behind each change are lost unless recorded separately. Software teams that use version control keep something quite different: every change, however small, is stored with its author, its time and a short note explaining it, so that any earlier state of the work can be recovered and the history of a single line traced. The difference is not merely one of convenience. Because nothing is irretrievably lost, programmers can experiment boldly, abandoning a failed approach without fear; and because each change is explained, a newcomer can learn why the code is as it is rather than only what it does.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The difference is not merely one of convenience. Because nothing is irretrievably lost, programmers can experiment boldly, abandoning a failed approach without fear; and because each change is explained, a newcomer can learn why the code is as it is rather than only what it does.

options.A: Version control stores each change made to a piece of software together with the name of its author, the time it was made and a short explanatory note.
options.B: Writers revising manuscripts ought to adopt the version control tools used by software teams, since dated paper drafts lose the reasons behind every change.
options.C: The chief advantage of version control over paper drafts is convenience, since earlier versions of the work can be recovered quickly whenever they are needed.
options.D: Unlike a few paper drafts, version control keeps every change with its reasons, which both frees programmers to experiment and shows newcomers why code is as it is.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Unlike a few paper drafts, version control keeps every change with its reasons, which both frees programmers to experiment and shows newcomers why code is as it is.

option_rationales.A: This describes only the mechanism in the second sentence; it omits the paragraph's point that the difference is 'not merely one of convenience' and its two consequences.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph compares the two practices but recommends nothing to writers; this adds a prescription it does not make.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says explicitly 'The difference is not merely one of convenience' and stresses bold experiment and understanding instead.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares paper drafts with version control, describes what version control records, and argues that the difference matters beyond convenience: it permits bold experiment and lets newcomers learn why the code is as it is. The correct summary keeps the comparison and both consequences.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the accurate description of the mechanism, which leaves out what the paragraph says follows from it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow option is an accurate paraphrase of one sentence; the correct answer is preferred for including the consequences.

questions.subtopic: A cover version is an interpretation and should be judged by what it reveals in the song.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A cover version of a song is often treated as a lesser thing than the original, a copy made by musicians who could not write their own material. Yet many of the most admired recordings in popular music are covers, and what makes them admired is precisely what they change: a different tempo, an unexpected arrangement, a singer who finds sorrow in a lyric that was first sung cheerfully. A good cover is an interpretation, in the way that a pianist's performance of a sonata is an interpretation, and it should be judged by what it reveals in the song rather than by whether its performers also wrote it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A cover version of a song is often treated as a lesser thing than the original, a copy made by musicians who could not write their own material. Yet many of the most admired recordings in popular music are covers, and what makes them admired is precisely what they change: a different tempo, an unexpected arrangement, a singer who finds sorrow in a lyric that was first sung cheerfully. A good cover is an interpretation, in the way that a pianist's performance of a sonata is an interpretation, and it should be judged by what it reveals in the song rather than by whether its performers also wrote it.

options.A: Cover versions are usually better than the original recordings, because later musicians are able to correct the mistakes of the songwriters who came before them.
options.B: Pianists who perform sonatas and singers who record cover songs are alike in being performers who have failed to compose any original music of their own.
options.C: Cover versions deserve to be judged as interpretations, by what they reveal in a song, not dismissed as copies by musicians lacking material of their own.
options.D: Many admired cover versions change the tempo or the arrangement of a song, or find sorrow in a lyric that was first sung in a cheerful manner.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Cover versions deserve to be judged as interpretations, by what they reveal in a song, not dismissed as copies by musicians lacking material of their own.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph defends covers as interpretations; it never ranks them above originals or speaks of correcting songwriters' mistakes.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph uses the pianist to show that a cover is a legitimate interpretation; this turns the comparison into the dismissive view it rejects.
option_rationales.D: These are the examples in the second sentence; the option leaves out the paragraph's conclusion about how covers should be judged.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a dismissive view of covers, counters it with the observation that admired covers are admired for what they change, and concludes that a cover is an interpretation to be judged 'by what it reveals in the song'. The correct summary gives the rejected view and the alternative standard.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the list of changes, which supports the point but does not state it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion is stated plainly in the final sentence.

questions.subtopic: Whether ghostwriting deceives depends on what readers of a given kind of book actually expect.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Critics of ghostwriting say that a memoir written by someone other than its named author deceives readers, who believe they are reading the subject's own words. The charge assumes a convention that many readers do not share. Few people who buy the autobiography of a famous athlete suppose that the athlete sat alone composing sentences; what they expect is that the story, the opinions and the memories are genuinely the athlete's, and that he or she has approved the result. Measured against that expectation, a ghostwritten memoir deceives only when the content is invented or the subject has not endorsed it. Where readers do expect sole authorship, as with a novel or a scholarly article, concealed ghostwriting remains a real deception.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Critics of ghostwriting say that a memoir written by someone other than its named author deceives readers, who believe they are reading the subject's own words. The charge assumes a convention that many readers do not share. Few people who buy the autobiography of a famous athlete suppose that the athlete sat alone composing sentences; what they expect is that the story, the opinions and the memories are genuinely the athlete's, and that he or she has approved the result. Measured against that expectation, a ghostwritten memoir deceives only when the content is invented or the subject has not endorsed it. Where readers do expect sole authorship, as with a novel or a scholarly article, concealed ghostwriting remains a real deception.

options.A: Ghostwriting is never truly deceptive, since readers of every kind of book understand that named authors routinely depend on hidden professional writers for help.
options.B: Ghostwriting deceives only when it breaks what readers expect: memoir readers expect the subject's story and approval, not the subject's own prose, while novels still imply sole authorship.
options.C: Readers of celebrity memoirs care only that the memories are broadly genuine, so a ghostwriter may freely invent minor details and whole scenes provided the subject approves the finished book.
options.D: A memoir written by someone other than its named author deceives its readers, who believe that they are reading the subject's own words throughout the book.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Ghostwriting deceives only when it breaks what readers expect: memoir readers expect the subject's story and approval, not the subject's own prose, while novels still imply sole authorship.

option_rationales.A: The last sentence says that where readers expect sole authorship, 'as with a novel or a scholarly article', concealed ghostwriting 'remains a real deception'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a memoir deceives 'when the content is invented', so invented details remain deceptive even with approval.
option_rationales.D: This is the critics' charge from the first sentence, which the paragraph says 'assumes a convention that many readers do not share'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the blanket charge against ghostwriting by tying deception to readers' actual expectations. For memoirs readers expect genuine content and the subject's approval, so ghostwriting deceives only when those fail; for novels and scholarly articles sole authorship is expected, so concealed ghostwriting does deceive. The correct summary keeps the principle and both sides of its application.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the blanket defence of ghostwriting and missing the final sentence's limit, or the approval option and missing that invented content still deceives.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options take the author's side but each breaks one stated limit; separating them needs close reading of the last two sentences.

questions.subtopic: A conductor's beat solves a timing problem in large orchestras, but the main work is done in rehearsal.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Audiences sometimes wonder what a conductor does, since the players have the notes in front of them and could, it seems, keep together by listening to one another. In a small ensemble they often do. But in an orchestra of eighty or more, spread across a wide stage, sound takes a noticeable time to travel, and players at the back may hear their colleagues at the front slightly late; following the ear alone would make the orchestra drag. The conductor's beat gives everyone a visual signal that arrives at once. Most of the conductor's work, however, happens earlier, in rehearsal, where decisions about balance, tempo and phrasing are made and agreed, so that the gestures in performance mainly remind players of what has already been settled.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
