Most of the conductor's work, however, happens earlier, in rehearsal, where decisions about balance, tempo and phrasing are made and agreed, so that the gestures in performance mainly remind players of what has already been settled.

options.A: Every musical ensemble, however small, needs a conductor to lead it, because players cannot keep together simply by listening to one another while performing.
options.B: The conductor's most important contribution is made during the performance itself, when gestures decide the balance, tempo and phrasing that the audience hears.
options.C: In a large orchestra, players at the back of a wide stage hear their colleagues at the front slightly late, because sound takes a noticeable time to travel.
options.D: A large orchestra needs a visible beat since sound reaches distant players late, but a conductor's main work is settling interpretation in rehearsal.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A large orchestra needs a visible beat since sound reaches distant players late, but a conductor's main work is settling interpretation in rehearsal.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says that in a small ensemble players 'often do' keep together by listening, so this contradicts it.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says these decisions are 'made and agreed' in rehearsal and that gestures in performance 'mainly remind players' of them, so this reverses it.
option_rationales.C: This is the mechanism in the third sentence only; it leaves out the role of the beat and the paragraph's point that most of the work happens in rehearsal.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why large orchestras need a conductor's beat (sound reaches distant players late, so following the ear makes the orchestra drag) and then adds, with 'however', that most of the conductor's work happens in rehearsal. The correct summary keeps both parts.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the acoustic detail and missing the 'however' sentence that shifts the emphasis to rehearsal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two-part explanation with a turn; the narrow option is an accurate detail.

questions.subtopic: Untitled and evocative titles for abstract works each have a benefit and a cost; neither is simply correct.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Two habits divide painters of abstract pictures. Some call their works 'Untitled' or give them only numbers, on the ground that a title would tell viewers what to see and so narrow a picture meant to be met on its own terms. Others give evocative titles, a word or phrase that suggests a mood or a landscape. The first habit protects the viewer's freedom but can leave the uncertain viewer with nothing to hold on to; the second offers a way in but risks fixing one reading so firmly that others become hard to notice. Neither is simply correct, and the choice reveals less about the picture than about how much guidance the painter believes a viewer wants.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Two habits divide painters of abstract pictures. Some call their works 'Untitled' or give them only numbers, on the ground that a title would tell viewers what to see and so narrow a picture meant to be met on its own terms. Others give evocative titles, a word or phrase that suggests a mood or a landscape. The first habit protects the viewer's freedom but can leave the uncertain viewer with nothing to hold on to; the second offers a way in but risks fixing one reading so firmly that others become hard to notice. Neither is simply correct, and the choice reveals less about the picture than about how much guidance the painter believes a viewer wants.

options.A: Leaving abstract works untitled preserves viewers' freedom but may leave them lost, while evocative titles give entry but may fix a reading; neither choice is simply right.
options.B: Some painters of abstract pictures give their works only numbers, believing that any title would narrow what viewers are able to see in the work.
options.C: The title that an abstract painter chooses reveals more about the meaning of the picture itself than any careful study of its colours and forms could do.
options.D: Painters who give abstract works evocative titles help their viewers, whereas painters who leave works untitled leave their audience without any guidance at all.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Leaving abstract works untitled preserves viewers' freedom but may leave them lost, while evocative titles give entry but may fix a reading; neither choice is simply right.

option_rationales.B: This describes only the first habit and its rationale; it omits the comparison and the conclusion that neither habit is simply correct.
option_rationales.C: The last sentence says the choice 'reveals less about the picture' than about the painter's view of viewers, so this reverses it.
option_rationales.D: This takes one side, while the paragraph gives each habit a cost: evocative titles risk 'fixing one reading', and it says 'Neither is simply correct'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares two titling habits, gives each a benefit and a cost, and concludes that neither is simply correct. The correct summary keeps the balanced comparison.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the one-sided option, which sounds sensible but ignores the cost the paragraph assigns to evocative titles.
questions.difficulty_reason: Balanced comparison; wrong options are one-sided, reversed or narrow, with the one-sided option tempting.

questions.subtopic: Longer visits by audio guide users support only a weak claim, because of self-selection and the gap between time and attention.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Museums that track visitors often find that those using audio guides spend longer in the galleries than those without, and this is readily taken as proof that the guides deepen engagement. The figure deserves a second look. Visitors who choose to rent a guide may already be the more interested ones, so the longer visits might have occurred anyway. And time is an uncertain measure of attention: a visitor can stand before a painting for the full length of a recorded commentary while looking at the floor, listening rather than seeing. The finding is not worthless, since it shows at least that guided visitors are not hurrying through, but it supports a weaker claim than the one usually drawn from it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Museums that track visitors often find that those using audio guides spend longer in the galleries than those without, and this is readily taken as proof that the guides deepen engagement. The figure deserves a second look. Visitors who choose to rent a guide may already be the more interested ones, so the longer visits might have occurred anyway. And time is an uncertain measure of attention: a visitor can stand before a painting for the full length of a recorded commentary while looking at the floor, listening rather than seeing. The finding is not worthless, since it shows at least that guided visitors are not hurrying through, but it supports a weaker claim than the one usually drawn from it.

options.A: Because visitors with audio guides spend longer in the galleries, museums can be confident that the guides deepen their engagement with the works on display.
options.B: Audio guides reduce visitors' engagement with art, because those who listen attend to recorded commentary rather than looking at the paintings in front of them.
options.C: The longer visits of audio guide users reveal nothing at all about their experience, since the visitors who rent guides were already far more interested in art before they arrived.
options.D: Guide users' longer visits show they are not hurrying but support less than deeper engagement, since self-selection and the gap between time and attention weaken that inference.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Guide users' longer visits show they are not hurrying but support less than deeper engagement, since self-selection and the gap between time and attention weaken that inference.

option_rationales.A: This is the inference the paragraph says 'deserves a second look' and finally calls stronger than the finding supports.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says only that a visitor 'can' listen rather than look, as a reason time is an uncertain measure; it does not conclude that guides reduce engagement.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'The finding is not worthless' and that guide users 'may' already be more interested; this denies all value and turns a possibility into a fact.

questions.explanation: The paragraph presents a finding, notes the inference usually drawn, and gives two reasons to doubt it: self-selection of interested visitors and time being an uncertain measure of attention. It then qualifies its own doubt: the finding shows guided visitors are not hurrying, but supports only a weaker claim. The correct summary keeps the finding, both doubts and the limited conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Swinging from the overclaim to the opposite extreme, calling the finding worthless or the guides harmful.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three wrong options are near positions (overclaim, worthless, harmful); only the correct answer keeps 'not worthless' with 'weaker claim'.

questions.subtopic: Probability forecasts confuse listeners who are not told what the percentage is out of.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a forecast announces a seventy per cent chance of rain, many listeners are unsure what has been promised. Some suppose it will rain over seventy per cent of the area, others that it will rain for seventy per cent of the day. The intended meaning is different: on days when conditions resemble today's, rain falls at the given place on about seven days in ten. The confusion arises because the number answers a question listeners did not know had been asked, namely 'out of what?', and forecasters seldom say. A forecast can be perfectly accurate in its own terms and still mislead an audience that supplies the wrong reference class.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a forecast announces a seventy per cent chance of rain, many listeners are unsure what has been promised. Some suppose it will rain over seventy per cent of the area, others that it will rain for seventy per cent of the day. The intended meaning is different: on days when conditions resemble today's, rain falls at the given place on about seven days in ten. The confusion arises because the number answers a question listeners did not know had been asked, namely 'out of what?', and forecasters seldom say. A forecast can be perfectly accurate in its own terms and still mislead an audience that supplies the wrong reference class.

options.A: Forecasters should abandon numerical probabilities altogether and return to plain verbal descriptions of the weather, which all listeners can understand without any confusion.
options.B: A seventy per cent chance of rain means that, on days resembling today, rain falls at the given place on about seven days out of every ten.
options.C: Rain probabilities mislead because listeners, never told what the figure is out of, supply their own basis such as area or duration, even when forecasts are accurate.
options.D: Forecasts that announce a percentage chance of rain are frequently inaccurate, which is why so many listeners have learned not to trust what they are promised.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Rain probabilities mislead because listeners, never told what the figure is out of, supply their own basis such as area or duration, even when forecasts are accurate.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph notes that forecasters 'seldom say' what the number refers to but recommends nothing, least of all giving up numbers.
option_rationales.B: This gives only the correct meaning from the third sentence and omits the paragraph's point about why listeners misread it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says a forecast 'can be perfectly accurate in its own terms and still mislead'; the problem is interpretation, not inaccuracy.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a confusion: listeners read a rain probability as a share of area or time, while it means a frequency over similar days, and they err because they are not told what the number is 'out of'. Its last sentence stresses that accuracy and clarity differ. The correct summary keeps the cause of the confusion and the point about accuracy.
questions.common_misconception: Selecting the correct definition of the forecast, which is true but is not the paragraph's point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow option is an exact and correct detail; the correct answer must be preferred for the explanation of the confusion.

questions.subtopic: Radio and television commentary differ because each responds to what its audience can already see.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Radio and television commentary on the same match sound strikingly different. The radio commentator must describe almost everything: where the ball is, who has it, which way the play is moving, because the listener has no other way of knowing. The television commentator, whose audience can see all this, would be tiresome doing the same, and so speaks less, leaving silences and using words to add what the picture cannot show, such as a player's record, a tactical change or the significance of the moment. Each style is a response to what its audience already possesses.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Radio and television commentary on the same match sound strikingly different. The radio commentator must describe almost everything: where the ball is, who has it, which way the play is moving, because the listener has no other way of knowing. The television commentator, whose audience can see all this, would be tiresome doing the same, and so speaks less, leaving silences and using words to add what the picture cannot show, such as a player's record, a tactical change or the significance of the moment. Each style is a response to what its audience already possesses.

options.A: Radio commentators describe play constantly since listeners cannot see it, while television commentators say less and add what the picture lacks; each suits its audience.
options.B: Television commentators often use their words to add information such as a player's record, a tactical change or the significance of the moment.
options.C: Radio commentary is more skilful than television commentary, since describing every movement of play demands far greater talent than adding a few occasional remarks.
options.D: Television commentators speak less than radio commentators mainly because broadcasters wish to reduce their costs by shortening the spoken commentary on all televised matches.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Radio commentators describe play constantly since listeners cannot see it, while television commentators say less and add what the picture lacks; each suits its audience.

option_rationales.B: This covers only the television half; it leaves out the contrast with radio and the explanation that each style responds to its audience.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph explains the difference by the audience and makes no judgement about which style needs more skill.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph gives a different reason: the audience 'can see all this', so describing it would be 'tiresome'. Cost is never mentioned.

questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts the two styles and explains both by the same principle: 'Each style is a response to what its audience already possesses.' The correct summary keeps the contrast and the principle.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the television detail, which is accurate but covers only half the comparison.
questions.difficulty_reason: The principle is stated in the last sentence and the wrong options are clearly narrow or out of scope.

questions.subtopic: Corporate jargon is evasive rather than empty, which makes it worse than critics allow.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Corporate jargon is usually mocked as empty: phrases about 'leveraging synergies' and 'circling back' are taken to show that those who use them have nothing to say. The mockery misses what the vocabulary does. Much of it serves to soften or blur, so that a decision to close a department can be announced as a 'realignment' without anyone having to state plainly that people will lose their jobs. Such language is not empty but evasive, and evasion has uses for the speaker. This makes it more troubling than the critics allow, not less: an empty phrase merely wastes time, whereas an evasive one shifts the burden of understanding onto listeners, who must work out for themselves what is being done to them.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Corporate jargon is usually mocked as empty: phrases about 'leveraging synergies' and 'circling back' are taken to show that those who use them have nothing to say. The mockery misses what the vocabulary does. Much of it serves to soften or blur, so that a decision to close a department can be announced as a 'realignment' without anyone having to state plainly that people will lose their jobs. Such language is not empty but evasive, and evasion has uses for the speaker. This makes it more troubling than the critics allow, not less: an empty phrase merely wastes time, whereas an evasive one shifts the burden of understanding onto listeners, who must work out for themselves what is being done to them.

options.A: Firms often announce the closure of a department as a 'realignment', so that nobody has to state plainly that people will lose their jobs.
options.B: Corporate jargon is less empty than evasive, sparing speakers from stating unwelcome facts, which makes it worse than its mockers think, since listeners must decode it.
options.C: Critics who mock corporate jargon overstate its harm, since phrases that merely blur unwelcome news serve useful purposes and waste very little of anyone's working time.
options.D: Corporate jargon shows that the managers who rely on phrases such as 'circling back' usually have nothing of real substance to say to their staff.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Corporate jargon is less empty than evasive, sparing speakers from stating unwelcome facts, which makes it worse than its mockers think, since listeners must decode it.

option_rationales.A: This is the illustrating example only; it leaves out the general claim that jargon is evasive and the conclusion about why that is worse than emptiness.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says evasive jargon is 'more troubling than the critics allow, not less'; the uses it mentions are uses 'for the speaker', not a defence.
option_rationales.D: This is the mockery the paragraph reports and says 'misses what the vocabulary does'; the author holds the language does a great deal.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the view that jargon is empty, argues it is evasive and useful to the speaker, and concludes this makes it 'more troubling than the critics allow, not less', because it shifts the burden of understanding to listeners. The correct summary keeps the reclassification and the conclusion about degree.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the rejection of the critics as a defence of jargon, when the author thinks the critics understate the problem.
questions.difficulty_reason: The author disagrees with the critics but in the direction of greater, not lesser, concern; one wrong option exploits that.

questions.subtopic: Obituary discretion is defensible for private failings but not for the public harms of the powerful.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Newspaper obituaries have long followed a convention of discretion: the dead are praised for their achievements, while their failings are passed over or hinted at in phrases that knowing readers decode. The convention is defended as kindness to grieving families, and kindness is a real consideration. But an obituary is also the first draft of a public record, often consulted later by people who never knew the subject. When it omits the serious harm a powerful person did, it does not merely spare feelings; it misinforms everyone who relies on it afterwards. Discretion is defensible for private failings that harmed no one beyond the household, far less so for public conduct that harmed many.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Newspaper obituaries have long followed a convention of discretion: the dead are praised for their achievements, while their failings are passed over or hinted at in phrases that knowing readers decode. The convention is defended as kindness to grieving families, and kindness is a real consideration. But an obituary is also the first draft of a public record, often consulted later by people who never knew the subject. When it omits the serious harm a powerful person did, it does not merely spare feelings; it misinforms everyone who relies on it afterwards. Discretion is defensible for private failings that harmed no one beyond the household, far less so for public conduct that harmed many.

options.A: Obituaries should record every failing of the person who has died, since any omission at all betrays the readers who rely on the newspaper for accurate information.
options.B: Obituaries rightly pass over the failings of the dead in silence, because kindness to grieving families matters more than the completeness of any public record.
options.C: Obituaries often hint at the failings of the dead in coded phrases that knowing readers can decode, while openly praising their achievements and careers.
options.D: Since obituaries become a public record, discretion that hides the serious public harms of the powerful misinforms later readers, though private failings may be spared.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Since obituaries become a public record, discretion that hides the serious public harms of the powerful misinforms later readers, though private failings may be spared.

option_rationales.A: The last sentence says discretion 'is defensible for private failings that harmed no one beyond the household', so 'every failing' contradicts it.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph grants that kindness is 'a real consideration' but argues that for public harms omission 'misinforms everyone', so this reverses its conclusion.
option_rationales.C: This describes the convention in the first sentence only; it omits the argument about the public record and where discretion stops being defensible.

questions.explanation: The paragraph describes the convention of discretion, concedes its justification in kindness, and argues that because obituaries form a public record, omitting serious public harms by powerful people misinforms later readers. It ends by drawing the line between private failings and public conduct. The correct summary keeps the reason and the line.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the extreme option that every failing must be reported, which ignores the private failings exception.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options take each extreme of a position that draws a line, plus a narrow description.

questions.subtopic: Effort praise helps only when it links what a child did to the result, not when used as a formula.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Teachers are now widely advised to praise children for effort rather than for cleverness, on the reasoning that a child told she is clever may avoid hard tasks for fear of disproving it, while one praised for trying learns that ability grows with work. The advice has something in it, but it is easily turned into a formula. Praise for effort that is given regardless of outcome can teach a child that trying is what counts even when the method is hopeless, and children are quick to notice when 'good effort' is offered as consolation for failure. What seems to matter is less the word used than whether praise connects what the child did to what resulted, so that the child learns which kinds of effort work.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Teachers are now widely advised to praise children for effort rather than for cleverness, on the reasoning that a child told she is clever may avoid hard tasks for fear of disproving it, while one praised for trying learns that ability grows with work. The advice has something in it, but it is easily turned into a formula. Praise for effort that is given regardless of outcome can teach a child that trying is what counts even when the method is hopeless, and children are quick to notice when 'good effort' is offered as consolation for failure. What seems to matter is less the word used than whether praise connects what the child did to what resulted, so that the child learns which kinds of effort work.

options.A: Praising effort has merit, but as a formula it can reward hopeless methods or sound like consolation; praise works best when it ties children's actions to results.
options.B: The precise words that teachers choose when praising children matter more than anything else, so 'good effort' should be replaced by more specific phrases.
options.C: Children praised for cleverness avoid hard tasks, so teachers should always praise effort rather than intelligence, whatever the result of the child's work.
options.D: Praising children for effort is generally harmful, because they soon recognise it as consolation for failure and then stop trying hard at difficult tasks.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Praising effort has merit, but as a formula it can reward hopeless methods or sound like consolation; praise works best when it ties children's actions to results.

option_rationales.B: The last sentence says what matters is 'less the word used than whether praise connects what the child did to what resulted', so this inverts the priority.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph reports this reasoning and grants it 'something', but warns precisely against effort praise 'given regardless of outcome'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the advice 'has something in it' and that formulaic praise 'can' mislead; it neither calls effort praise harmful in general nor says children stop trying.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the advice to praise effort and its rationale, grants it merit, then warns that as a formula it can mislead children and be read as consolation. It concludes that what matters is whether praise connects action to result. The correct summary keeps the concession, the warning and the alternative principle.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about precise wording, which sounds like a refinement but reverses the final sentence's 'less the word used'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every wrong option uses the paragraph's terms; separating them needs the concession and the exact contrast in the last sentence.

questions.subtopic: Peer tutoring benefits tutors when, and only when, it requires them to explain.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Schools that pair older pupils with younger ones for tutoring usually set out to help the younger children, and they often do. A recurring observation, however, is that the tutors gain as much or more: having to explain an idea to someone who does not yet grasp it forces the tutor to organise what he or she half knows, to notice gaps and to find examples. This benefit is not automatic. A tutor who merely supplies answers, or who is given material far below his or her own level with no need to explain it, gains little. The gain comes from the effort of explanation, and schools that want it must design tutoring so that explanation is actually required.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Schools that pair older pupils with younger ones for tutoring usually set out to help the younger children, and they often do. A recurring observation, however, is that the tutors gain as much or more: having to explain an idea to someone who does not yet grasp it forces the tutor to organise what he or she half knows, to notice gaps and to find examples. This benefit is not automatic. A tutor who merely supplies answers, or who is given material far below his or her own level with no need to explain it, gains little. The gain comes from the effort of explanation, and schools that want it must design tutoring so that explanation is actually required.

options.A: Peer tutoring helps younger children only when their older tutors are given material well above their own level, which forces the tutors to work harder.
options.B: Peer tutoring always benefits the older tutors more than the younger pupils, whatever material they are given or whatever method they follow in the sessions.
options.C: Peer tutoring can help tutors as much as tutees, but only when tutors must truly explain, so schools should design it to require explanation.
options.D: Older pupils who tutor younger children are made to organise what they half know, to notice gaps in their understanding and to search for suitable examples.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Peer tutoring can help tutors as much as tutees, but only when tutors must truly explain, so schools should design it to require explanation.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph speaks of material 'far below' the tutor's level as a problem when no explanation is needed; it never requires material above their level or ties the tutees' gain to it.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says tutors gain 'as much or more' and that a tutor who merely supplies answers 'gains little', so 'always' and 'whatever' contradict it.
option_rationales.D: This lists the benefits in the second sentence but drops the paragraph's qualification, 'This benefit is not automatic', and its conclusion about design.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (tutors gain at least as much as tutees), explains it by the work of explanation, and qualifies it: the benefit is not automatic and disappears when no explanation is required. It concludes that tutoring must be designed to require explanation. The correct summary keeps the finding, its condition and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the list of benefits, which is accurate but omits the condition on which they depend.
questions.difficulty_reason: A finding with a qualification; the narrow option reads as a fair summary until the qualification is noticed.

questions.subtopic: Multiple-choice tests can test demanding reasoning; their weakness lies in poor writing, not the format.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Multiple-choice tests are commonly dismissed as measuring only recognition: the answer is on the page, the critics say, so the student need only spot it. This is true of badly written questions, whose wrong options are obviously absurd. A well-made question is different. If its wrong options reflect the mistakes that students actually make, choosing correctly requires the student to tell a sound piece of reasoning from several plausible but flawed ones, which is itself a demanding skill. The weakness of many such tests lies in the craft of writing them, not in the format.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Multiple-choice tests are commonly dismissed as measuring only recognition: the answer is on the page, the critics say, so the student need only spot it. This is true of badly written questions, whose wrong options are obviously absurd. A well-made question is different. If its wrong options reflect the mistakes that students actually make, choosing correctly requires the student to tell a sound piece of reasoning from several plausible but flawed ones, which is itself a demanding skill. The weakness of many such tests lies in the craft of writing them, not in the format.

options.A: Multiple-choice tests can measure only the recognition of answers, because the correct answer is always printed somewhere on the page right in front of the student taking the test.
options.B: Multiple-choice tests need not measure mere recognition; with options built on real mistakes they test demanding judgement, so weak tests reflect poor writing, not the format.
options.C: Badly written multiple-choice questions often contain wrong options so obviously absurd that students can reject them without giving the matter much thought.
options.D: Multiple-choice tests are the most demanding form of assessment available, since every question requires students to weigh several flawed lines of reasoning.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Multiple-choice tests need not measure mere recognition; with options built on real mistakes they test demanding judgement, so weak tests reflect poor writing, not the format.

option_rationales.A: This is the critics' view in the first sentence, which the paragraph accepts only for 'badly written questions' and rejects for well-made ones.
option_rationales.C: This restates the concession in the second sentence; it omits the paragraph's main claim about well-made questions and where the weakness lies.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph grants that badly written questions are easy and never ranks the format above others, so 'most demanding' and 'every question' overstate it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph critiques the view that multiple-choice tests measure only recognition, concedes it for badly written questions, and argues that well-made questions test the demanding skill of telling sound reasoning from plausible errors. It concludes that the weakness lies in the writing, not the format. The correct summary keeps the rejection, the concession and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that restates the concession about badly written questions.
questions.difficulty_reason: The critique and conclusion are explicit in the first and last sentences.

questions.subtopic: School trips are real learning, anchoring later lessons and reaching pupils who would otherwise miss such experiences.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: School trips to museums, factories and nature reserves are often the first thing cut when budgets tighten, on the ground that they are enjoyable outings rather than real learning. That judgement undervalues what a visit can do. A child who has stood in a working mill or watched a river carry silt remembers it vividly, and the memory gives later lessons something concrete to attach to; an abstract idea in a textbook becomes an explanation of something the child has seen. For pupils whose families cannot afford such visits themselves, the school trip may be the only chance of these experiences.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

School trips to museums, factories and nature reserves are often the first thing cut when budgets tighten, on the ground that they are enjoyable outings rather than real learning. That judgement undervalues what a visit can do. A child who has stood in a working mill or watched a river carry silt remembers it vividly, and the memory gives later lessons something concrete to attach to; an abstract idea in a textbook becomes an explanation of something the child has seen. For pupils whose families cannot afford such visits themselves, the school trip may be the only chance of these experiences.

options.A: Field trips teach children far more than classroom lessons do, so schools should spend a larger share of their budgets on visits than on textbooks.
options.B: Children who visit a working mill or watch a river carrying silt are likely to remember the experience vividly for a long time after the visit.
options.C: School trips are wrongly cut as mere outings, since vivid visits anchor later lessons and may be poorer pupils' only chance of such experiences.
options.D: School trips are enjoyable outings rather than real learning, so they are sensibly the first expense to be cut when a school's budget becomes tight.

questions.correct_answer: (C) School trips are wrongly cut as mere outings, since vivid visits anchor later lessons and may be poorer pupils' only chance of such experiences.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says trips give lessons 'something concrete to attach to'; it does not rank trips above lessons or propose shifting budgets from textbooks.
option_rationales.B: This is the example in the third sentence; it omits the argument against cutting trips and the point about pupils who cannot otherwise go.
option_rationales.D: This is the judgement the paragraph says 'undervalues what a visit can do', so it reverses the author's view.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the view that school trips are mere outings to be cut first. It gives two reasons: vivid memories anchor later lessons, and for some pupils the trip may be the only such chance. The correct summary keeps the rejection and both reasons.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the prescription about budgets, which goes further than the paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The stance and both reasons are explicit; wrong options are clearly reversed, narrow or extreme.

questions.subtopic: Age-graded classes rest on a false premise, and mixed-age classes justify training teachers for them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Schools sort children by year of birth so routinely that the practice seems like a law of nature rather than an administrative convenience. Yet grouping by age assumes that children born within the same twelve months are ready for the same material at the same moment, an assumption that every experienced teacher knows to be false. In classrooms that deliberately mix ages, the older children consolidate what they know by explaining it, and the younger ones see, in the work of those just ahead of them, what the next step looks like. None of this makes mixed-age teaching easy: it demands careful planning and a teacher able to manage several levels at once, and without these it can fail badly. But that difficulty is a reason to prepare teachers for the task, not a reason to treat the age-graded class as the only sensible arrangement.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Yet grouping by age assumes that children born within the same twelve months are ready for the same material at the same moment, an assumption that every experienced teacher knows to be false. But that difficulty is a reason to prepare teachers for the task, not a reason to treat the age-graded class as the only sensible arrangement.

options.A: Sorting pupils by age rests on a convenient but false premise; mixed-age classes bring real benefits, and their demands call for trained teachers rather than rejection.
options.B: Mixed-age teaching usually fails because teachers cannot manage several levels at once, which is why schools still sort their pupils by year of birth.
options.C: Schools should abolish grouping by birth year and adopt mixed-age classes everywhere, since every teacher knows that children of one age differ in readiness.
options.D: Older pupils in a mixed-age class gain more than younger ones, since explaining material to others is the surest way of consolidating one's own understanding of it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Sorting pupils by age rests on a convenient but false premise; mixed-age classes bring real benefits, and their demands call for trained teachers rather than rejection.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says such teaching fails only without planning and skilled teachers, and it attributes age sorting to 'administrative convenience', not to the failure of mixed-age classes.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph concedes that mixed-age teaching 'can fail badly' and argues only against treating the age-graded class as 'the only sensible arrangement'; it never calls for abolition everywhere.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph names benefits for the younger children as well ('see ... what the next step looks like') and never ranks the two groups; it also leaves out the central claim about age grading.

questions.explanation: The paragraph attacks the assumption behind age grading, gives the benefits of mixing ages, concedes the difficulty, and concludes that the difficulty calls for preparing teachers rather than abandoning the idea. The correct summary keeps the critique, the benefit, the concession and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that turns the argument into a call for abolition, missing the concession that mixed-age teaching can fail.
questions.difficulty_reason: The prescriptive wrong option overstates a moderate conclusion and must be rejected on degree.

questions.subtopic: Evidence of holiday learning loss has been tempered by measurement concerns.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Comparisons of test scores taken at the end of one school year and the start of the next have often suggested that children lose ground over the long holiday, and that children from poorer homes lose more. The finding has been used to argue that much of the gap between richer and poorer pupils opens not in school but outside it. Later work has complicated the picture. Some of the apparent loss depends on which tests are used and how their scores are scaled, and some estimates shrink considerably when the same children are measured in a different way. What survives scrutiny is more modest: holiday loss is real for some children, but it is smaller and less consistent than first reported, so it cannot by itself account for the gap, even if the long break remains a time when unequal home resources count for more than usual.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Comparisons of test scores taken at the end of one school year and the start of the next have often suggested that children lose ground over the long holiday, and that children from poorer homes lose more. Some of the apparent loss depends on which tests are used and how their scores are scaled, and some estimates shrink considerably when the same children are measured in a different way. What survives scrutiny is more modest: holiday loss is real for some children, but it is smaller and less consistent than first reported, so it cannot by itself account for the gap, even if the long break remains a time when unequal home resources count for more than usual.

options.A: Because most of the gap between richer and poorer pupils opens outside school, schools ought to shorten the long holiday to protect children from poorer homes.
options.B: Early evidence that long holidays widen the gap between richer and poorer pupils has been tempered by measurement concerns, leaving a smaller, less uniform effect that cannot alone explain it.
options.C: Test scores taken at the start and end of school years are unreliable, and research on education should stop using them to compare different groups of pupils.
options.D: The idea that children lose learning over the long holidays has been shown to be an artefact of test scaling, so the long break has no effect whatever on the gap between richer and poorer pupils.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Early evidence that long holidays widen the gap between richer and poorer pupils has been tempered by measurement concerns, leaving a smaller, less uniform effect that cannot alone explain it.

option_rationales.A: This repeats the earlier argument that later work 'complicated', and it adds a prescription about shortening holidays that the paragraph never makes.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says only that some estimates depend on test choice and scaling; it neither condemns such scores in general nor recommends abandoning them.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says holiday loss 'is real for some children' and that the break is a time when home resources 'count for more'; it denies only that the loss explains the gap by itself.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding, notes the use made of it, then qualifies it: the loss is real for some but smaller and less consistent, so it cannot alone explain the gap. The correct summary states the finding and the qualification with its scope.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that turns 'smaller and less consistent' into no effect at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme wrong option reuses the measurement point; the reader must notice that the loss is qualified, not denied.

questions.subtopic: Rewriting textbooks to improve readability scores can remove the links that comprehension needs.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A familiar remedy for textbooks that students find hard is to rewrite them in shorter sentences with commoner words, guided by formulas that score a text by the length of its words and sentences. The formulas do measure something, but what makes a passage hard to understand is often not its vocabulary so much as the gaps it leaves for the reader to fill. Cutting one long sentence into three short ones frequently removes the very words, such as because, although and therefore, that told the reader how the ideas were related; the result scores as easier and is harder to follow. None of this means that dense prose is a virtue or that difficult words never obstruct learning. It means that a readability score measures surface features, and a text revised to improve its score can lose the connective tissue on which comprehension depends.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A familiar remedy for textbooks that students find hard is to rewrite them in shorter sentences with commoner words, guided by formulas that score a text by the length of its words and sentences. The formulas do measure something, but what makes a passage hard to understand is often not its vocabulary so much as the gaps it leaves for the reader to fill. Cutting one long sentence into three short ones frequently removes the very words, such as because, although and therefore, that told the reader how the ideas were related; the result scores as easier and is harder to follow. None of this means that dense prose is a virtue or that difficult words never obstruct learning. It means that a readability score measures surface features, and a text revised to improve its score can lose the connective tissue on which comprehension depends.

options.A: Short sentences make textbooks harder to follow than long ones, so formulas that reward brevity measure the opposite of what makes a text truly difficult.
options.B: Readability formulas are worthless guides for textbook writers, since the length of the words and sentences in a passage has no bearing at all on how easily students can understand what it says.
options.C: Textbooks should be written in long and complex sentences, since students learn more from dense prose that forces them to work out the meaning for themselves.
options.D: Revising textbooks to raise readability scores can backfire, because the scores track surface features, and shortening sentences may strip out the links between ideas that understanding needs.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Revising textbooks to raise readability scores can backfire, because the scores track surface features, and shortening sentences may strip out the links between ideas that understanding needs.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says splitting sentences 'frequently' removes connectives, not that short sentences are always harder, and it grants that the formulas 'do measure something', not the opposite of difficulty.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the formulas 'do measure something' and concedes that 'difficult words' can 'obstruct learning', so calling them worthless contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph explicitly denies that 'dense prose is a virtue'; its point concerns lost connectives, not the value of difficulty.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises the readability-formula remedy: the formulas capture surface features, and splitting sentences can delete the connectives that show how ideas relate, so a text can score as easier yet be harder to follow. The concession keeps the claim from becoming a defence of dense prose. The correct summary keeps the mechanism and the hedge 'can'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that inverts the formulas wholesale, missing that the paragraph says they 'do measure something' and that the harm is frequent, not universal.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options sit close to the author's critique and fail only on degree ('opposite', 'worthless') against the paragraph's concessions.

questions.subtopic: Teacher expectations affect pupils, but modestly and unevenly.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is widely believed that a teacher's expectations can shape how well pupils perform: tell a teacher that certain children are about to blossom, and they will. There is evidence that expectations matter, since teachers who expect more of a pupil may give that pupil more attention, more time to answer questions and more demanding work. But the effects found in careful studies are usually modest, and they tend to be larger for younger children and for pupils whom the teacher does not yet know well. Expectations, in other words, are one influence among many, not a force that can by itself transform a child's results.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is widely believed that a teacher's expectations can shape how well pupils perform: tell a teacher that certain children are about to blossom, and they will. There is evidence that expectations matter, since teachers who expect more of a pupil may give that pupil more attention, more time to answer questions and more demanding work. But the effects found in careful studies are usually modest, and they tend to be larger for younger children and for pupils whom the teacher does not yet know well. Expectations, in other words, are one influence among many, not a force that can by itself transform a child's results.

options.A: Teachers' expectations have no real effect on how pupils perform, since careful studies have failed to find any difference in their results.
options.B: Telling teachers that certain children are about to blossom reliably causes those children to perform far better than the rest of their classmates.
options.C: Teachers' expectations do affect pupils' performance, through how teachers treat them, but the effect is usually modest and uneven rather than transformative.
options.D: Younger children need more attention and more demanding work than older pupils, because they are more easily influenced by what their teachers expect.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Teachers' expectations do affect pupils' performance, through how teachers treat them, but the effect is usually modest and uneven rather than transformative.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says there 'is evidence that expectations matter' and that the effects are modest, not absent.
option_rationales.B: This is the popular belief the paragraph opens with and then qualifies; careful studies find effects that are 'usually modest', not reliable large gains.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says only that expectation effects are larger for younger children; it says nothing about what younger children need, so this distorts a detail.

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants that expectations matter through how teachers treat pupils, then limits the claim: effects are modest, larger in some groups, and one influence among many. The correct summary gives the effect and its limits.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting the popular opening claim as the paragraph's own conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The qualification is stated directly in the last two sentences.

questions.subtopic: Improvement after surgery needs sham-controlled trials to show the procedure itself works.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It seems obvious that an operation cannot work by suggestion: the knife either repairs the tissue or it does not. For this reason, many surgical procedures entered routine use on the strength of surgeons' observations that their patients felt better afterwards. But patients who undergo surgery also receive attention, hope and a period of rest, and their symptoms often fluctuate and improve on their own. When some procedures have been tested against sham operations, in which patients are anaesthetised and given an incision but the key step is omitted, the improvement in the two groups has turned out to be similar. Such trials raise real ethical questions, since the sham group bears risk without the prospect of direct benefit. Yet without them, it is hard to know whether an operation helps because of what the surgeon does or because of everything that surrounds it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It seems obvious that an operation cannot work by suggestion: the knife either repairs the tissue or it does not. For this reason, many surgical procedures entered routine use on the strength of surgeons' observations that their patients felt better afterwards. But patients who undergo surgery also receive attention, hope and a period of rest, and their symptoms often fluctuate and improve on their own. When some procedures have been tested against sham operations, in which patients are anaesthetised and given an incision but the key step is omitted, the improvement in the two groups has turned out to be similar. Such trials raise real ethical questions, since the sham group bears risk without the prospect of direct benefit. Yet without them, it is hard to know whether an operation helps because of what the surgeon does or because of everything that surrounds it.

options.A: Improvement after surgery does not prove an operation works, since hope and natural recovery also play a part; sham-controlled trials, though ethically fraught, are needed to separate them.
options.B: Most surgical procedures now in routine use are no better than sham operations, and each of them should be withdrawn from practice until it has been properly tested against a placebo operation.
options.C: Surgery works mainly through suggestion, since the attention and hope that patients receive matter more than the repair the surgeon actually performs.
options.D: Sham surgery is unethical because patients in the control group bear the risks of an operation without any prospect of benefiting from it directly.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Improvement after surgery does not prove an operation works, since hope and natural recovery also play a part; sham-controlled trials, though ethically fraught, are needed to separate them.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph reports similar results only for 'some procedures' and makes no call for withdrawal; 'most' and the prescription go beyond it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says it is 'hard to know' which factor helps; it does not claim that suggestion is the main mechanism.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph raises this as a concession ('real ethical questions') and then answers it with 'Yet without them'; making it the conclusion reverses the argument.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that post-operative improvement is not proof of effect because attention, hope and natural recovery also contribute, and that sham-controlled trials, despite their ethical cost, are needed to tell these apart. The correct summary states this with the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the ethical concession as the paragraph's conclusion, overlooking the 'Yet' that answers it.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option is a concession the paragraph raises and answers; the reader must follow the turn at 'Yet'.

questions.subtopic: Systematic misreporting in diet surveys can create or hide associations, and big samples do not cure it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Much of what is believed about diet and health rests on asking people what they eat. The objection usually raised against such surveys is that people forget, and forgetting, being random, merely adds noise. The deeper difficulty is that the errors are not random. People tend to under-report foods they regard as unhealthy and over-report those they think virtuous, and the size of the distortion varies with body weight, with education and with how much a person cares about appearing healthy. Since those same characteristics are themselves linked to health, the error can manufacture associations or hide real ones, rather than simply blurring them. This does not make dietary surveys useless; for some questions they are the only practical source. But it means that a large sample, which cures random error, offers no protection against this kind.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Much of what is believed about diet and health rests on asking people what they eat. The objection usually raised against such surveys is that people forget, and forgetting, being random, merely adds noise. The deeper difficulty is that the errors are not random. People tend to under-report foods they regard as unhealthy and over-report those they think virtuous, and the size of the distortion varies with body weight, with education and with how much a person cares about appearing healthy. Since those same characteristics are themselves linked to health, the error can manufacture associations or hide real ones, rather than simply blurring them. This does not make dietary surveys useless; for some questions they are the only practical source. But it means that a large sample, which cures random error, offers no protection against this kind.

options.A: People who care about appearing healthy are healthier than others, which is why diet surveys consistently overstate the benefits of foods regarded as virtuous.
options.B: Diet surveys are unreliable mainly because people forget what they have eaten, which is an error that larger samples can correct but that researchers seldom trouble to address properly.
options.C: Because people misreport their diets, dietary surveys are useless for health research and ought to be replaced by direct measurement of what people actually eat.
options.D: Diet surveys suffer from systematic, not random, misreporting tied to traits that also affect health, so the errors can create or hide associations that large samples cannot remove.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Diet surveys suffer from systematic, not random, misreporting tied to traits that also affect health, so the errors can create or hide associations that large samples cannot remove.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the error 'can manufacture associations or hide real ones', not that it consistently inflates benefits, and it never says image-conscious people are healthier.
option_rationales.B: Forgetting is the 'usual' objection that the paragraph sets aside for 'The deeper difficulty' of non-random error; the claim about researchers is also unsupported.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph states that this 'does not make dietary surveys useless' and that for some questions they are 'the only practical source'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets aside the familiar objection (random forgetting) for a deeper one: misreporting is systematic and tied to traits that also bear on health, so it can create or mask associations, and large samples do not help. The concession limits the claim. The correct summary captures the contrast, the mechanism and the point about samples.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option built on forgetting, which is the objection the paragraph calls less important.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option states the familiar objection the author demotes; separating random from systematic error needs the whole argument.

questions.subtopic: Loneliness is linked with early death, but the link is not proven to be causal.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Studies that follow people over many years have found that those who report feeling lonely or socially isolated tend to die earlier than those who do not, and the association has led some to describe loneliness as a threat to public health. The finding is consistent and worth taking seriously. It is not, however, a simple demonstration that loneliness causes illness. People who are already unwell may withdraw from others, and poverty or disability can produce both isolation and poor health. Researchers try to adjust for such factors, but the most that can be said with confidence is that loneliness and early death travel together, and that loneliness may contribute to it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Studies that follow people over many years have found that those who report feeling lonely or socially isolated tend to die earlier than those who do not, and the association has led some to describe loneliness as a threat to public health. The finding is consistent and worth taking seriously. It is not, however, a simple demonstration that loneliness causes illness. People who are already unwell may withdraw from others, and poverty or disability can produce both isolation and poor health. Researchers try to adjust for such factors, but the most that can be said with confidence is that loneliness and early death travel together, and that loneliness may contribute to it.

options.A: Loneliness directly causes illness and early death, and it should therefore be treated by governments as a threat to public health quite as serious as smoking.
options.B: Loneliness is consistently linked with earlier death, but since illness or poverty may produce both, the link does not show that loneliness itself causes ill health.
options.C: People who are already unwell tend to withdraw from friends and family, which explains why the sick are more often lonely than the healthy.
options.D: The link between loneliness and early death is unreliable, since studies that follow people over many years cannot take account of poverty or disability.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Loneliness is consistently linked with earlier death, but since illness or poverty may produce both, the link does not show that loneliness itself causes ill health.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph denies that the finding is 'a simple demonstration that loneliness causes illness', and the comparison with smoking comes from outside it.
option_rationales.C: This takes one of the alternative explanations as the whole point and omits the main finding and its qualification.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls the finding 'consistent' and says researchers 'try to adjust for such factors'; it questions the causal reading, not the link.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts a consistent association between loneliness and early death but warns that illness, poverty or disability could produce both, so causation is not established. The correct summary keeps both halves.
questions.common_misconception: Treating a qualified association as proof of cause.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph states its qualification plainly with 'It is not, however'.

questions.subtopic: Observed hand-hygiene audits measure behaviour under observation, not ordinary behaviour.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Hospitals that check whether staff clean their hands by sending observers onto the wards routinely record high rates of compliance. The rates are less impressive than they look. Staff who notice an observer wash more often while the observer is present, so the audit measures behaviour under observation, which is precisely the condition that does not hold for most of a working day. Where observed rates have been compared with counts from electronic dispensers or with unannounced checks, the observed rates have often turned out considerably higher. The point is not that staff are dishonest, nor that audits are pointless, since being watched does improve hand hygiene for a time. It is that a measure which changes the behaviour it measures cannot tell us how people behave when no one is looking.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Hospitals that check whether staff clean their hands by sending observers onto the wards routinely record high rates of compliance. The rates are less impressive than they look. Staff who notice an observer wash more often while the observer is present, so the audit measures behaviour under observation, which is precisely the condition that does not hold for most of a working day. Where observed rates have been compared with counts from electronic dispensers or with unannounced checks, the observed rates have often turned out considerably higher. The point is not that staff are dishonest, nor that audits are pointless, since being watched does improve hand hygiene for a time. It is that a measure which changes the behaviour it measures cannot tell us how people behave when no one is looking.

options.A: Hospital staff deliberately exaggerate their hand-washing during audits, so observed audits should be replaced entirely by electronic counts from dispensers.
options.B: Electronic dispensers and unannounced checks give hospitals a fully accurate picture of how often staff really clean their hands during a working day.
options.C: Sending observers onto hospital wards is the most effective way to improve hand hygiene, because staff wash their hands far more often whenever they know that they are being watched.
options.D: Observed audits overstate routine hand-washing because staff act differently when watched, so although observation briefly improves hygiene, it cannot reveal ordinary behaviour.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Observed audits overstate routine hand-washing because staff act differently when watched, so although observation briefly improves hygiene, it cannot reveal ordinary behaviour.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the point is 'not that staff are dishonest' and that audits are not 'pointless'; it recommends no replacement.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph uses these only as comparisons that showed the observed rates to be higher; it makes no claim that they are fully accurate.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says observation improves hygiene only 'for a time' and never compares methods; its point is about what the audit can measure.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why observed compliance figures are inflated: observation itself changes behaviour, so the audit samples an unusual condition. It concedes that watching helps for a while. The correct summary gives the mechanism, the concession and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the inflated figures as evidence of dishonesty, which the paragraph explicitly rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options each misread one concession; the correct answer must keep both the effect and its limit.

questions.subtopic: Cul-de-sacs give residents quiet but push the costs of distance and traffic elsewhere.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Two ideas of the residential street compete in suburban planning. The grid connects every street to several others, so drivers and walkers can take many routes and no single road carries the whole load. The cul-de-sac layout, with its looping roads and dead ends, keeps through traffic out, and residents of the closed streets often value the quiet and the safety of children playing outside. The difficulty is that the quiet is bought with distance: a shop a few hundred metres away as the crow flies may be more than a kilometre away by road, so residents drive for trips they might have walked, and the few roads that connect the loops carry heavy traffic. Each layout serves something real; the cul-de-sac simply moves its costs out of sight of those who enjoy its benefits.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Two ideas of the residential street compete in suburban planning. The grid connects every street to several others, so drivers and walkers can take many routes and no single road carries the whole load. The cul-de-sac layout, with its looping roads and dead ends, keeps through traffic out, and residents of the closed streets often value the quiet and the safety of children playing outside. The difficulty is that the quiet is bought with distance: a shop a few hundred metres away as the crow flies may be more than a kilometre away by road, so residents drive for trips they might have walked, and the few roads that connect the loops carry heavy traffic. Each layout serves something real; the cul-de-sac simply moves its costs out of sight of those who enjoy its benefits.

options.A: Grid layouts are superior to cul-de-sacs in every respect, since they let walkers and drivers take many different routes and spread the load of traffic across all the streets.
options.B: Residents prefer cul-de-sacs because children can play safely in quiet streets, which explains why the layout has spread so widely in suburban planning.
options.C: Cul-de-sacs give residents real quiet and safety, but unlike grids they lengthen trips and concentrate traffic on connecting roads, costs its beneficiaries tend not to see.
options.D: Residents of cul-de-sacs walk to nearby shops more often than residents of grids, because the absence of through traffic makes walking safer and pleasanter.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Cul-de-sacs give residents real quiet and safety, but unlike grids they lengthen trips and concentrate traffic on connecting roads, costs its beneficiaries tend not to see.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says each layout 'serves something real' and grants the cul-de-sac's quiet and safety, so 'in every respect' contradicts it.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph mentions what residents value but says nothing about why the layout spread, and it omits the central point about displaced costs.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the opposite: longer road distances mean residents 'drive for trips they might have walked'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares the two layouts, grants the cul-de-sac its benefits, and argues that those benefits are paid for in longer trips and heavy traffic on connecting roads, costs borne out of residents' sight. The correct summary keeps the comparison and the shifted costs.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that declares the grid better in every way, ignoring that each layout 'serves something real'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme wrong option matches the author's leaning, so it must be rejected on degree.

questions.subtopic: Paved surfaces cause floods by sending rain to rivers quickly.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When rain falls on a field or a forest, much of the water soaks into the soil, and what runs off reaches the streams slowly. When the same rain falls on roofs, roads and car parks, almost none of it soaks in; it is gathered by gutters and drains and delivered to the river within minutes. A city can therefore flood after a storm that would have caused no trouble before the land was built on, not because more rain falls but because the rain reaches the river all at once. Wider drains can carry more water away, but they also speed its journey, which is why some cities now try to slow runoff with green roofs, permeable paving and ponds.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When rain falls on a field or a forest, much of the water soaks into the soil, and what runs off reaches the streams slowly. When the same rain falls on roofs, roads and car parks, almost none of it soaks in; it is gathered by gutters and drains and delivered to the river within minutes. A city can therefore flood after a storm that would have caused no trouble before the land was built on, not because more rain falls but because the rain reaches the river all at once. Wider drains can carry more water away, but they also speed its journey, which is why some cities now try to slow runoff with green roofs, permeable paving and ponds.

options.A: Paved surfaces can cause urban floods by sending rain to rivers within minutes instead of letting it soak in, so some cities now try to slow runoff.
options.B: Wider drains are the most reliable way to protect a city from flooding, since they carry larger volumes of water away from its streets and car parks.
options.C: Green roofs, permeable paving and ponds have now replaced conventional drains in most cities that suffer from repeated flooding after heavy storms.
options.D: Cities flood more often than the countryside because building on land changes the local weather and causes heavier storms to fall over urban areas.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Paved surfaces can cause urban floods by sending rain to rivers within minutes instead of letting it soak in, so some cities now try to slow runoff.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph notes that wider drains 'also speed its journey', which is the problem; that is why some cities try to slow runoff instead.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says only that 'some cities now try' these methods; 'replaced' and 'most cities' overstate it, and the option omits the cause of flooding.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says floods happen 'not because more rain falls' but because water reaches the river all at once.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains that hard surfaces deliver rain to rivers in minutes rather than letting it soak in, so cities can flood without more rain; faster drains worsen the speed problem, hence efforts to slow runoff. The correct summary gives the cause and the response.
questions.common_misconception: Assuming urban floods mean more rain, which the paragraph rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause is stated directly and each wrong option contradicts or overstates a plain sentence.

questions.subtopic: Lower cycling risk where cycling is common may reflect safety attracting cyclists, not numbers alone.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: In places where many people cycle, the risk of injury for each cyclist tends to be lower than in places where few do. This pattern is often read as proof that drivers become more careful when cyclists are common, so that simply encouraging more cycling will make it safer. The pattern is real, but the causal story may run partly the other way. Cities that have built protected lanes and calmed their traffic attract more cyclists precisely because cycling there is already safer, and more cautious people take up cycling only when it feels safe. Driver adaptation may contribute as well; nobody needs to deny it. What the pattern does not support is the hope that numbers alone, without the infrastructure that draws them, will deliver safety.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
