Driver adaptation may contribute as well; nobody needs to deny it. What the pattern does not support is the hope that numbers alone, without the infrastructure that draws them, will deliver safety.

options.A: The lower injury risk in cities with many cyclists is an illusion, produced by the fact that only cautious people choose to cycle in such places.
options.B: Lower injury risk where cycling is common may partly reflect safer streets attracting cyclists, not only numbers creating safety, so numbers alone cannot be relied on to cut risk.
options.C: Protected lanes and calmer traffic, rather than any change in driver behaviour, fully explain why cycling is safer in cities where many people cycle.
options.D: Drivers become more careful when cyclists are common, so cities can make cycling safer simply by persuading many more people to take it up, whatever their streets happen to be like.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Lower injury risk where cycling is common may partly reflect safer streets attracting cyclists, not only numbers creating safety, so numbers alone cannot be relied on to cut risk.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the 'pattern is real'; it questions the direction of cause, and cautious riders are only one part of its account.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph grants that driver adaptation 'may contribute as well', so claiming infrastructure 'fully' explains the pattern contradicts its concession.
option_rationales.D: This is the reading the paragraph reports and then disputes; it ends by rejecting 'the hope that numbers alone ... will deliver safety'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts the pattern but argues that causation may run partly from safety to numbers, through infrastructure and self-selection, while allowing that drivers may adapt. Its conclusion is narrow: numbers alone cannot be relied on. The correct summary keeps 'partly' and the narrow conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that makes infrastructure the full explanation, missing the concession about drivers, or the one that calls the pattern an illusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each overcorrect the reported view in a different direction; only the correct answer preserves both the concession and the limited conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Faster transport yields bigger cities rather than shorter commutes, because people budget travel time.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Faster roads and railways are usually justified by the time they will save commuters. Yet in many cities and over long periods, the average time people spend travelling to work each day has stayed surprisingly stable. The explanation is that people treat travel time, not distance, as the quantity to be budgeted. When a new motorway cuts the journey, many households eventually move further out, to larger and cheaper homes, until the commute is roughly as long as it was before. The investment is not wasted: people gain space and a wider choice of jobs and housing. But its benefit arrives as a larger city rather than as the shorter commute that was promised.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Faster roads and railways are usually justified by the time they will save commuters. Yet in many cities and over long periods, the average time people spend travelling to work each day has stayed surprisingly stable. The explanation is that people treat travel time, not distance, as the quantity to be budgeted. When a new motorway cuts the journey, many households eventually move further out, to larger and cheaper homes, until the commute is roughly as long as it was before. The investment is not wasted: people gain space and a wider choice of jobs and housing. But its benefit arrives as a larger city rather than as the shorter commute that was promised.

options.A: Because people budget travel time, not distance, faster transport tends to yield longer distances and larger cities rather than shorter commutes, though it still brings benefits.
options.B: Public investment in faster roads and railways is largely wasted, since commuters end up spending just as much time travelling to work each day as they did before the money was spent.
options.C: People move further from city centres mainly because homes there are larger and cheaper, regardless of how long their journey to work becomes as a result.
options.D: New motorways shorten commutes permanently, giving households more free time each day and letting them choose jobs that lie closer to their homes.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Because people budget travel time, not distance, faster transport tends to yield longer distances and larger cities rather than shorter commutes, though it still brings benefits.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says plainly that the investment 'is not wasted', because people gain space and choice.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says households move out only 'until the commute is roughly as long as it was before', so travel time limits the move rather than being ignored.
option_rationales.D: This is the promise the paragraph says is not kept: commuting time returns to roughly its old level.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why commuting time stays stable: people budget time, so faster links lead them to live further away. It concedes that the investment brings benefits, but in the form of a larger city. The correct summary gives the mechanism, the result and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Concluding that the investment is wasted, overlooking the concession about space and choice.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option misreads the concession and another misreads the mechanism; both need the paragraph as a whole.

questions.subtopic: The argument that distance is morally irrelevant moves too quickly.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Most people feel that they would be obliged to help a stranger in danger in front of them, yet feel no comparable obligation to help a stranger in equal danger on another continent. Some philosophers conclude that this feeling is simply a bias: distance, they argue, cannot by itself make a moral difference, so our duties to the distant are as strong as our duties to the near. The argument is powerful, but it moves too quickly. Distance usually travels with other features that may matter, such as whether one is uniquely placed to help, whether one's help will actually arrive, and whether many others could help equally well. To show that the feeling is mere bias, one must show that it survives when these features are held constant, and that is harder than the argument assumes.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Most people feel that they would be obliged to help a stranger in danger in front of them, yet feel no comparable obligation to help a stranger in equal danger on another continent. Some philosophers conclude that this feeling is simply a bias: distance, they argue, cannot by itself make a moral difference, so our duties to the distant are as strong as our duties to the near. The argument is powerful, but it moves too quickly. Distance usually travels with other features that may matter, such as whether one is uniquely placed to help, whether one's help will actually arrive, and whether many others could help equally well. To show that the feeling is mere bias, one must show that it survives when these features are held constant, and that is harder than the argument assumes.

options.A: Our moral duties to strangers in danger on other continents are just as strong as our duties to strangers in danger in front of us, since distance by itself cannot make any moral difference.
options.B: We are more strongly obliged to help those near us than those far away, because physical distance is itself a morally relevant feature of any situation.
options.C: The feeling that we must help strangers nearby is a bias, but a useful one, since we are usually uniquely placed to help those who are in front of us.
options.D: The claim that distance makes no moral difference is too hasty: distance accompanies features that may matter, and the intuition is mere bias only if it survives once they are controlled.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The claim that distance makes no moral difference is too hasty: distance accompanies features that may matter, and the intuition is mere bias only if it survives once they are controlled.

option_rationales.A: This is the conclusion of the philosophers whose argument the paragraph says 'moves too quickly'; the author neither endorses nor fully rejects it.
option_rationales.B: The author never claims distance itself matters; the point is that distance 'travels with other features that may matter', which is a different claim.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph does not concede that the feeling is a bias; it says showing it to be one is 'harder than the argument assumes'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports an argument that the near-far intuition is mere bias, then objects that distance correlates with other possibly relevant features, so the intuition can be dismissed only if it survives when those are held fixed. The correct summary captures the critique without overstating it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that says distance itself matters, mistaking the author's methodological objection for a substantive defence of the intuition.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option reverses the reported view; the reader must see that the author only questions the argument's speed.

questions.subtopic: Delay weakens the reforming reason for punishment but not the reason of answering the wrong.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a crime is discovered decades after it was committed, it is sometimes said that punishing the offender now punishes a different person: the frail old man in the dock shares a name with the young man who did the deed, but little else. The objection has force where punishment is meant to reform, for a person who has long since changed has nothing left to reform. It has less force where punishment is meant to answer the wrong itself, to affirm that the victim mattered and that the act was not acceptable. For that purpose what matters is not whether the offender has changed but whether he is the one responsible, and a change of character, however real, does not transfer responsibility to someone else. Time may therefore weaken some reasons for punishment while leaving others intact.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It has less force where punishment is meant to answer the wrong itself, to affirm that the victim mattered and that the act was not acceptable. For that purpose what matters is not whether the offender has changed but whether he is the one responsible, and a change of character, however real, does not transfer responsibility to someone else. Time may therefore weaken some reasons for punishment while leaving others intact.

options.A: Offenders who have truly changed over the decades should not be punished for crimes they committed long ago, because punishing them now would mean punishing a different person.
options.B: Since old offenders cannot be reformed, punishment for crimes discovered decades later should aim instead at deterring others from committing similar acts.
options.C: Long delay undermines punishment's reforming purpose, since the offender may have changed, but not its purpose of answering the wrong, which rests on responsibility, not present character.
options.D: Punishment is justified only as a way of affirming that victims mattered, so whether an offender has changed is irrelevant to every reason for punishing.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Long delay undermines punishment's reforming purpose, since the offender may have changed, but not its purpose of answering the wrong, which rests on responsibility, not present character.

option_rationales.A: This is the objection the paragraph reports and then limits; it says the objection 'has less force' where punishment answers the wrong.
option_rationales.B: Deterrence is never mentioned; the paragraph contrasts reform with answering the wrong, so this adds an outside purpose.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph grants that the objection 'has force where punishment is meant to reform'; it recognises more than one purpose, so 'only' and 'every' contradict it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph distinguishes two purposes of punishment: reform, which a long delay may undercut, and answering the wrong, which depends on responsibility and so survives a change of character. Its conclusion is that time weakens some reasons but not others. The correct summary states that distinction.
questions.common_misconception: Treating the reported 'different person' objection as the author's verdict, or swinging to the claim that only retribution counts.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires holding two purposes apart; one wrong option states the reported objection and another overcorrects to a single purpose.

questions.subtopic: Misleading wrongs the listener as lying does; any difference lies in the speaker's self-imposed rule.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many people believe there is a moral difference between telling a lie and saying something true that is designed to mislead. Asked whether he has been drinking, the driver who answers 'I had a glass of water an hour ago' has not lied, though he hopes the listener will draw a false conclusion. One defence of the distinction is that the misleader leaves the listener a share of the responsibility, since the false belief comes from the listener's own inference. But the listener drew that inference precisely because the speaker counted on it. Whatever difference remains seems to lie less in the harm done to the listener than in what the speaker permits himself: a rule against outright falsehood that he keeps even while evading its purpose.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many people believe there is a moral difference between telling a lie and saying something true that is designed to mislead. Asked whether he has been drinking, the driver who answers 'I had a glass of water an hour ago' has not lied, though he hopes the listener will draw a false conclusion. One defence of the distinction is that the misleader leaves the listener a share of the responsibility, since the false belief comes from the listener's own inference. But the listener drew that inference precisely because the speaker counted on it. Whatever difference remains seems to lie less in the harm done to the listener than in what the speaker permits himself: a rule against outright falsehood that he keeps even while evading its purpose.

options.A: Misleading is morally worse than lying, because a speaker who deceives with true words adds hypocrisy to deception by pretending to honour a rule whose purpose he is evading.
options.B: Misleading with true words wrongs the listener scarcely less than lying, since it exploits the listener's inference; whatever difference remains lies mainly in the speaker's self-imposed rule.
options.C: Drivers questioned about drinking often reply with literally true statements, which shows that people prefer misleading to lying when they fear being caught.
options.D: Misleading with true statements is morally better than lying, because a listener who draws a false inference must share the responsibility for the resulting belief.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Misleading with true words wrongs the listener scarcely less than lying, since it exploits the listener's inference; whatever difference remains lies mainly in the speaker's self-imposed rule.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph locates the remaining difference in the speaker's rule but never ranks misleading as worse; the claim of added hypocrisy goes beyond it.
option_rationales.C: The driver is a single illustration; the paragraph makes no claim about how drivers usually answer or about general preferences.
option_rationales.D: This is the defence the paragraph reports and then rebuts: the listener drew the inference 'precisely because the speaker counted on it'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares lying and misleading, rejects the defence that the listener shares responsibility, and suggests that what difference remains lies in the speaker's own rule rather than in harm to the listener. The correct summary keeps both the rejection and the residual difference.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that ranks misleading as worse, reading a description of the speaker's rule as a verdict.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option builds on the author's last sentence but adds a ranking the paragraph does not make.

questions.subtopic: Since choices must be arranged somehow, the real question about nudges is who arranges them and how openly.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Arranging choices so that people are steered towards better outcomes, by setting a sensible default for pension saving or putting fruit at eye level in a canteen, is often defended on the ground that no option is forbidden and anyone can choose otherwise. Critics reply that such arrangements are manipulative, working on inertia and habit rather than on reason. The reply is weaker than it sounds, because some arrangement is unavoidable: a canteen must put something at eye level, and a pension scheme must have some default. The real question is therefore not whether choices will be shaped but by whom and for whose benefit, and whether the shaping is open enough that people could object to it if they knew of it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Arranging choices so that people are steered towards better outcomes, by setting a sensible default for pension saving or putting fruit at eye level in a canteen, is often defended on the ground that no option is forbidden and anyone can choose otherwise. Critics reply that such arrangements are manipulative, working on inertia and habit rather than on reason. The reply is weaker than it sounds, because some arrangement is unavoidable: a canteen must put something at eye level, and a pension scheme must have some default. The real question is therefore not whether choices will be shaped but by whom and for whose benefit, and whether the shaping is open enough that people could object to it if they knew of it.

options.A: Steering choices is acceptable because no option is forbidden, so people who end up with poor outcomes have only themselves to blame for not choosing otherwise.
options.B: Since choices must be arranged somehow, the charge that steering them is manipulative is weak; what matters is who shapes them, for whose benefit, and how openly.
options.C: Setting defaults and arranging goods is manipulative, since it works on inertia and habit rather than appealing to people's capacity to reason for themselves.
options.D: Governments and employers should set defaults for every important decision, because people left to choose for themselves will usually choose badly.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Since choices must be arranged somehow, the charge that steering them is manipulative is weak; what matters is who shapes them, for whose benefit, and how openly.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph reports the 'no option is forbidden' defence without adopting it, and the claim about blame is not in the paragraph at all.
option_rationales.C: This is the critics' reply, which the paragraph says 'is weaker than it sounds' because some arrangement is unavoidable.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph makes no such prescription and says nothing about people choosing badly; it asks only who shapes choices and how openly.

questions.explanation: The paragraph presents a defence and a criticism of steering choices, rejects the criticism on the ground that some arrangement is inevitable, and reframes the issue as one of who shapes choices, for whom, and how openly. The correct summary gives the reason and the reframing.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the critics' view because the paragraph discusses it at length.
questions.difficulty_reason: The critics' view is stated in the paragraph's own terms and must be recognised as the view rejected.

questions.subtopic: Experts explain badly because knowledge hides the beginner's view; checking understanding is the remedy.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A specialist asked to introduce a field to newcomers frequently leaves them more confused than before, and ill will rarely has anything to do with it. Understanding, once gained, erases the memory of what it was like to lack it. So the specialist jumps over steps that now feel self-evident, reaches for terms that have become automatic and misjudges how much time a novice needs to keep up. The mastery that earns someone the right to teach thus hides from that person the view of the subject a newcomer has. The best teachers get round this not by knowing less but by repeatedly testing what their audience has in fact understood.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A specialist asked to introduce a field to newcomers frequently leaves them more confused than before, and ill will rarely has anything to do with it. Understanding, once gained, erases the memory of what it was like to lack it. So the specialist jumps over steps that now feel self-evident, reaches for terms that have become automatic and misjudges how much time a novice needs to keep up. The mastery that earns someone the right to teach thus hides from that person the view of the subject a newcomer has. The best teachers get round this not by knowing less but by repeatedly testing what their audience has in fact understood.

options.A: The more a person knows about a subject, the worse a teacher of that subject the person is bound to be, whatever effort is made to explain it.
options.B: Beginners learn best from teachers who know only a little more than they do themselves, since such teachers can still remember clearly what it was like not to understand the subject.
options.C: Experts explain their subjects badly because they care little about beginners and are unwilling to spend the time needed to teach them properly.
options.D: Experts often explain badly because their own understanding makes a beginner's position hard to imagine, a problem overcome by checking what learners grasp, not by knowing less.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Experts often explain badly because their own understanding makes a beginner's position hard to imagine, a problem overcome by checking what learners grasp, not by knowing less.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the best teachers 'get round this', so the difficulty is not inevitable whatever the effort.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph never compares teachers by level of knowledge; its remedy is testing what the audience understands, not choosing less expert teachers.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says at the outset that 'ill will rarely has anything to do with it'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why experts explain poorly: understanding makes it hard to imagine not understanding, so they skip steps and use jargon. It names the remedy. The correct summary gives the cause and the remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Attributing the problem to indifference, which the first sentence rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: Cause and remedy are both stated in single sentences.

questions.subtopic: Ownership raises the value people place on things, but the effect depends on how the thing is regarded.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: In a familiar kind of experiment, people given a simple object such as a mug ask for considerably more to part with it than others, not given one, will pay to acquire it. The gap has been taken as evidence that owning a thing makes us value it more, simply because it is ours. The finding has proved robust in many settings, but its size depends on circumstances. It tends to shrink among experienced traders, who regard goods as stock to be sold, and it is larger for items people expect to keep and use than for those they hold only for exchange. Ownership, it seems, raises value most when a thing is seen as part of one's possessions rather than as a token in a market.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

In a familiar kind of experiment, people given a simple object such as a mug ask for considerably more to part with it than others, not given one, will pay to acquire it. The gap has been taken as evidence that owning a thing makes us value it more, simply because it is ours. The finding has proved robust in many settings, but its size depends on circumstances. It tends to shrink among experienced traders, who regard goods as stock to be sold, and it is larger for items people expect to keep and use than for those they hold only for exchange. Ownership, it seems, raises value most when a thing is seen as part of one's possessions rather than as a token in a market.

options.A: The effect of ownership disappears entirely among experienced traders, which shows that it was never more than an artefact of laboratory experiments.
options.B: Experiments with mugs show that sellers are greedier than buyers, which is why people who own goods ask higher prices than others are willing to pay.
options.C: People tend to value things more once they own them, but the effect varies, being weaker among traders and for goods held for exchange than for things owners mean to keep.
options.D: Ownership makes everyone value an object above its market price, a bias that persists unchanged among experienced traders as much as among ordinary buyers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) People tend to value things more once they own them, but the effect varies, being weaker among traders and for goods held for exchange than for things owners mean to keep.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the effect tends to 'shrink', not that it disappears, and it calls the finding 'robust in many settings'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph explains the gap by ownership raising value, not by greed; this replaces its explanation with an outside one.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the effect 'tends to shrink among experienced traders', so 'unchanged' contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a robust finding that ownership raises valuation and then qualifies its size: smaller for traders and for goods held for exchange, larger for things owners mean to keep. The correct summary states the finding and both qualifications.
questions.common_misconception: Turning 'tends to shrink' into 'disappears', and so dismissing a finding the paragraph calls robust.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options misstate the qualification in opposite directions.

questions.subtopic: People overestimate agreement with their views because of skewed company and a sense of what is natural.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: People tend to overestimate how many others share their opinions, habits and preferences. Part of the reason is that we spend most of our time with people like ourselves, so the sample of views we meet is not representative of the wider population. Part is that our own choices seem to us the natural response to a situation, so we assume that others facing it would choose the same. The tendency is not simply vanity; it arises from the limited and familiar evidence that each of us has about what other people think. It also helps explain why people are often surprised when an election or a survey reveals how divided opinion really is.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

People tend to overestimate how many others share their opinions, habits and preferences. Part of the reason is that we spend most of our time with people like ourselves, so the sample of views we meet is not representative of the wider population. Part is that our own choices seem to us the natural response to a situation, so we assume that others facing it would choose the same. The tendency is not simply vanity; it arises from the limited and familiar evidence that each of us has about what other people think. It also helps explain why people are often surprised when an election or a survey reveals how divided opinion really is.

options.A: People overestimate how widely others share their views, chiefly because the company they keep and their sense of what is natural skew their evidence.
options.B: People overestimate agreement with their views mainly out of vanity, since they like to believe that sensible people must think exactly as they do.
options.C: Elections and surveys usually surprise people, because opinion in most societies is far more divided than ordinary experience would lead them to expect.
options.D: Spending time with people unlike ourselves is the only reliable way to escape the habit of overestimating how many others agree with us.

questions.correct_answer: (A) People overestimate how widely others share their views, chiefly because the company they keep and their sense of what is natural skew their evidence.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the tendency 'is not simply vanity' and traces it to limited and familiar evidence.
option_rationales.C: This takes the final illustration as the main point and adds a claim about 'most societies'; the paragraph's subject is why people overestimate agreement.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph offers no remedy at all, and 'the only reliable way' is an outside prescription.

questions.explanation: The paragraph describes the tendency to overestimate agreement and gives two causes, an unrepresentative social sample and the sense that one's choices are natural, while denying that vanity is the explanation. The correct summary gives the tendency and its causes.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the closing example about elections as the paragraph's main point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The causes are listed plainly; wrong options contradict, narrow or add a remedy.

questions.subtopic: Familiarity is mistaken for understanding of how things work, less so where knowledge is easily self-tested.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Ask people how well they understand how a zip, a flush toilet or a bicycle works, and most will rate their understanding highly. Ask them then to explain, step by step, how the device actually works, and many find they cannot; when asked to rate their understanding again, they mark it down. The confidence was not a lie but a confusion: familiarity with using something, and knowing that an explanation exists somewhere, feels from the inside like possessing the explanation. Notably, the gap is narrower for facts and procedures, such as the names of capital cities or how to tie a knot, where people can check their knowledge by trying to recall or perform it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Ask people how well they understand how a zip, a flush toilet or a bicycle works, and most will rate their understanding highly. Ask them then to explain, step by step, how the device actually works, and many find they cannot; when asked to rate their understanding again, they mark it down. The confidence was not a lie but a confusion: familiarity with using something, and knowing that an explanation exists somewhere, feels from the inside like possessing the explanation. Notably, the gap is narrower for facts and procedures, such as the names of capital cities or how to tie a knot, where people can check their knowledge by trying to recall or perform it.

options.A: Most people understand facts such as capital cities better than they understand machines, because facts are simpler to learn than the workings of devices.
options.B: Asking people to explain step by step how something works is the best way to teach them how everyday devices such as zips and toilets function.
options.C: People overrate their grasp of how things work because familiarity feels like understanding; trying to explain exposes the illusion, which is weaker where knowledge is self-tested.
options.D: People pretend to understand everyday devices in order to avoid appearing ignorant, and they admit the truth only when they are forced to explain in detail how the devices actually work.

questions.correct_answer: (C) People overrate their grasp of how things work because familiarity feels like understanding; trying to explain exposes the illusion, which is weaker where knowledge is self-tested.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the gap between confidence and knowledge is narrower for facts because they can be self-checked, not that facts are better understood or simpler.
option_rationales.B: Explaining exposes the gap in the paragraph; it is not presented as a teaching method, and 'the best way' is outside the paragraph.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the confidence 'was not a lie but a confusion', so the claim of pretence contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports that people overrate their understanding of mechanisms until asked to explain them, attributes this to familiarity being mistaken for knowledge, and qualifies it: the gap is narrower where knowledge can be self-tested. The correct summary captures the finding, the cause and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Reading the contrast with facts as a claim that facts are better understood, rather than that confidence about them is better calibrated.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option distorts the qualification subtly from calibration to understanding.

questions.subtopic: The fate of the limited-resource account of self-control shows how small published studies can inflate an effect.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: For years it was widely accepted that self-control draws on a limited resource, so that resisting one temptation leaves a person less able to resist the next. The idea was supported by many small experiments and fitted the everyday experience of feeling worn out after a demanding day. When the effect was retested in large studies run to a common plan across many laboratories, it proved much smaller than the earlier work had suggested, and in some cases indistinguishable from zero. It would be too quick to conclude that people never tire of exercising self-control. What the episode shows is that a stack of small studies, each published because it found an effect, can make a weak or absent phenomenon look established, and that agreement with everyday experience is no substitute for a test designed in advance.

options.A: Everyday experience of tiring after effort still confirms the limited-resource view of self-control, even though large studies across many different laboratories later found only small effects.
options.B: Large replications have shown that self-control draws on no limited resource at all and that feeling worn out after a demanding day is merely an illusion.
options.C: The early experiments on self-control were biased by researchers who wanted to confirm a theory that matched their own experience of tiring after effort.
options.D: Large planned tests that failed to confirm the limited-resource view of self-control show how selectively published small studies can inflate an effect, though such fatigue may still exist.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Large planned tests that failed to confirm the limited-resource view of self-control show how selectively published small studies can inflate an effect, though such fatigue may still exist.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says agreement with everyday experience 'is no substitute for a test designed in advance', so it does not treat that experience as confirmation.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph warns that it 'would be too quick to conclude that people never tire of exercising self-control', so this overstates the result.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph blames the selective publication of small studies, 'each published because it found an effect', not the motives of individual researchers.

questions.explanation: The paragraph recounts how an accepted effect shrank under large pre-planned tests, cautions against concluding that self-control never tires, and draws a lesson about selective publication and the limits of intuition. The correct summary keeps the lesson and the caution.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that blames researchers' motives, confusing a problem of selective publication with deliberate bias.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options fail on the caution, on the role of intuition and on the mechanism of inflation; telling them apart needs the whole paragraph.

questions.subtopic: A single form of 'you' moves the marking of rank elsewhere rather than abolishing it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Languages that oblige speakers to choose between a familiar and a respectful form of 'you' are sometimes thought more hierarchical than those, like modern English, that use a single form for everyone. The comparison is misleading. Speakers of English mark distance and rank in other ways: through first names or titles, through how directly they make requests, through who may start a conversation and who may end it. A language without the grammatical choice has not abolished the social one; it has moved it elsewhere, often to places where it is harder for a newcomer to notice. If anything, the explicit pronoun makes the rules of respect easier to see and therefore easier to learn.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Having a single form of 'you' does not make a language less hierarchical, since speakers mark rank and distance by other, often less visible means that may be harder to learn.
options.B: Languages with separate familiar and respectful forms of 'you' are more hierarchical than English, because their grammar forces speakers to mark rank in every conversation.
options.C: Modern English is more hierarchical than languages with two forms of 'you', since its rules of respect are hidden and therefore harder for newcomers to learn.
options.D: Newcomers to English find titles and first names the hardest part of the language to master, harder than either its grammar or its pronunciation.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Having a single form of 'you' does not make a language less hierarchical, since speakers mark rank and distance by other, often less visible means that may be harder to learn.

option_rationales.B: This is the view the paragraph calls 'misleading'; it argues that English marks rank too, only by other means.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph's 'If anything' concerns only how easily the rules can be seen and learnt; it never claims English is more hierarchical.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph makes no comparison with grammar or pronunciation; this adds an outside claim and misses the main point.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the inference from a single pronoun to less hierarchy: English marks rank through names, directness and conversational rules, so the social distinction has moved, not vanished, and may even be harder to learn. The correct summary gives this point with its hedge.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reversal that makes English more hierarchical, mistaking a point about visibility for a point about degree of hierarchy.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reversal wrong option builds on the paragraph's final hedge and must be separated by scope.

questions.subtopic: That gossip enforces norms corrects its bad name but does not justify it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Gossip has a poor reputation: it is condemned as idle, malicious and a waste of time. A more sympathetic view, now common among those who study small communities, holds that gossip performs a social function, spreading knowledge of who can be trusted and deterring cheats who fear for their reputations. This view is a useful corrective, but it can slide into a defence of gossip as such. The same mechanism that deters the cheat also punishes the nonconformist, the newcomer and anyone whose private life departs from local expectation, and it does so without a hearing. To say that gossip enforces norms is to say nothing yet about whether the norms deserve enforcing, or whether those it targets had any chance to answer.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Gossip benefits small communities by spreading knowledge of who can be trusted, so its usefulness outweighs the harm it does to newcomers and nonconformists.
options.B: Seeing gossip as norm enforcement rightly corrects its idle image but does not justify it, since the norms may be unworthy and its targets get no hearing.
options.C: Gossip in small communities targets newcomers and nonconformists more often than cheats, and so on balance it does more harm than good to such communities.
options.D: Gossip deserves its poor reputation, because whatever it may do to deter cheats, it remains chiefly a malicious and idle waste of everyone's time.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Seeing gossip as norm enforcement rightly corrects its idle image but does not justify it, since the norms may be unworthy and its targets get no hearing.

option_rationales.A: This is the slide 'into a defence of gossip as such' that the paragraph warns against; it never weighs benefit against harm in gossip's favour.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the same mechanism reaches both groups; it makes no claim about frequency and reaches no verdict on the overall balance.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls the sympathetic view 'a useful corrective' to that reputation, so it does not endorse the old condemnation.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts the functional view as a corrective, warns that it does not amount to a defence, and gives two reasons: the mechanism also punishes harmless difference without a hearing, and enforcing norms says nothing about their merit. The correct summary keeps the corrective and the limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the net-harm verdict, which sounds like the author's critical tone but adds a balance the paragraph never strikes.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three wrong options each take a definite side on gossip, while the author's position is a carefully limited one.

questions.subtopic: Shared family meals are linked with children's wellbeing, but the meal's own effect is uncertain.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Children in families that eat together regularly tend, on average, to do better at school and to report fewer emotional difficulties. This has led to the advice that parents should make shared meals a priority. Yet families that manage regular meals together often differ in other ways too: they may have more predictable working hours, more money and less conflict at home. Some of what looks like the effect of the meal may be the effect of the kind of household that can arrange one. The meal may still help, but the evidence for it is weaker than the advice suggests.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Children in families that eat together regularly tend, on average, to do better at school and to report fewer emotional difficulties. This has led to the advice that parents should make shared meals a priority. Yet families that manage regular meals together often differ in other ways too: they may have more predictable working hours, more money and less conflict at home. Some of what looks like the effect of the meal may be the effect of the kind of household that can arrange one. The meal may still help, but the evidence for it is weaker than the advice suggests.

options.A: Families with predictable working hours and more money eat together more often than other families, because they have more time to cook.
options.B: Eating together every day is the most important thing parents can do to help their children succeed at school and stay emotionally healthy.
options.C: Shared meals are linked with children's wellbeing, but since such families differ in other ways too, the meal's own benefit is less certain than advice implies.
options.D: Shared family meals have no real effect on children, since any benefit linked to them can be fully explained by money, working hours and the level of conflict at home.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Shared meals are linked with children's wellbeing, but since such families differ in other ways too, the meal's own benefit is less certain than advice implies.

option_rationales.A: This picks out a detail and adds a cause, time to cook, that the paragraph never gives; it misses the point about weak evidence.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the evidence is 'weaker than the advice suggests'; 'the most important thing' goes far beyond it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the meal 'may still help' and that only part ('Some of what looks like the effect') may come from the household.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports an association, notes the advice drawn from it, and qualifies it: families who eat together differ in other ways, so the meal's own effect is uncertain though possible. The correct summary gives the association and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Swinging from the advice to the opposite extreme that meals have no effect.
questions.difficulty_reason: The qualification is explicit and the wrong options are clearly extreme or narrow.

questions.subtopic: Fixed mourning customs, though rigid, gave grief a shared structure that has been lost.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many traditional societies set out how long the bereaved should mourn, what they should wear and when they might return to ordinary life. Such rules are easily dismissed today as rigid impositions on private feeling. But they also did something for the grieving. They told others how to behave towards the bereaved, gave the mourner permission to withdraw for a time, and marked a point at which life could resume without guilt. Where the rules have faded, people are often left unsure how long grief is allowed to last and what their friends expect of them. The old customs had their costs, but they offered a shared structure that private feeling alone does not supply.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many traditional societies set out how long the bereaved should mourn, what they should wear and when they might return to ordinary life. Such rules are easily dismissed today as rigid impositions on private feeling. But they also did something for the grieving. They told others how to behave towards the bereaved, gave the mourner permission to withdraw for a time, and marked a point at which life could resume without guilt. Where the rules have faded, people are often left unsure how long grief is allowed to last and what their friends expect of them. The old customs had their costs, but they offered a shared structure that private feeling alone does not supply.

options.A: In traditional societies the bereaved were expected to withdraw from ordinary life for a fixed period and to wear particular clothing while mourning.
options.B: Rules about mourning dress and duration were rigid impositions that forced the bereaved to display feelings they may not actually have had.
options.C: Traditional mourning rules should be brought back, since people today have no idea how to grieve properly and their friends do not know how to help them through it.
options.D: Though fixed mourning customs can seem rigid, they gave the bereaved and those around them a shared structure for grief, which their decline has left many people without.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Though fixed mourning customs can seem rigid, they gave the bereaved and those around them a shared structure for grief, which their decline has left many people without.

option_rationales.A: This restates a descriptive detail from the first sentence and omits the paragraph's argument about what the customs did for people.
option_rationales.B: This is the dismissive view the paragraph mentions and then answers with 'But they also did something for the grieving'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph prescribes nothing, grants that the customs 'had their costs', and says people are 'often' unsure, not that they have 'no idea'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph concedes that mourning rules look rigid, then argues that they guided others, licensed withdrawal and marked an end to mourning, a structure whose loss leaves people unsure. The correct summary keeps the concession and the main point.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the dismissive view the paragraph reports in its second sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The turn at 'But' signals the point clearly.

questions.subtopic: Polite formulas are social gestures, not reports of feeling, so calling them insincere misjudges them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Critics of everyday courtesy often complain that phrases such as 'how are you' or 'thank you so much' are empty, since the speaker rarely wants a medical report and is seldom overwhelmed with gratitude. The complaint assumes that words are sincere only when they report an inner state. But many polite formulas are not reports at all; they are moves in a shared routine, closer to a handshake than to a confession. Their meaning lies in being offered and returned, and their omission is noticed precisely because nobody expects them to carry personal feeling. To call them insincere is therefore to judge them by a standard they never claimed to meet. This does not mean that every courteous word is innocent: a formula can be used to hold someone at a distance or to cover contempt. Yet that misuse is possible only because the routine itself has a recognised social meaning.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

To call them insincere is therefore to judge them by a standard they never claimed to meet. This does not mean that every courteous word is innocent: a formula can be used to hold someone at a distance or to cover contempt. Yet that misuse is possible only because the routine itself has a recognised social meaning.

options.A: Polite formulas are social gestures rather than reports of feeling, so calling them insincere misjudges them, although they can be misused to keep distance or hide contempt.
options.B: Polite formulas are valuable chiefly because they let people conceal contempt and keep strangers at a distance, which allows social life to continue without open conflict.
options.C: Because routine courtesies seldom express what speakers really feel, people ought to keep such phrases for occasions on which their words match their inner states.
options.D: No courteous expression can ever be insincere, since the meaning of every polite phrase lies wholly in social routine and never in the feelings of the speaker.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Polite formulas are social gestures rather than reports of feeling, so calling them insincere misjudges them, although they can be misused to keep distance or hide contempt.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph mentions concealing contempt only as a 'misuse' of the routine, not as the source of its value, so this reverses the relation.
option_rationales.C: This adopts the critics' assumption that the paragraph rejects as judging formulas 'by a standard they never claimed to meet', and adds a prescription the paragraph never makes.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph concedes that 'a formula can be used to hold someone at a distance or to cover contempt'; this absolute claim contradicts that qualification.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the critics' premise that sincerity means reporting an inner state, recasts polite formulas as moves in a shared routine whose meaning lies in 'being offered and returned', and then qualifies the point: formulas can be misused to keep distance or cover contempt. The correct answer keeps the central claim and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the absolute option that drops the concession about misuse, or mistaking the mentioned misuse for the point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The extreme option uses the paragraph's own idea of routine, so it must be rejected on the concession in the last two sentences.

questions.subtopic: Rules constitute a game, yet keeping their letter does not settle fairness; the spirit is read from the rules.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is tempting to think of the rules of a game as fences around an activity that exists without them, but moving a bishop diagonally is not a restriction on some freer way of moving a carved piece; outside the rules there is no bishop to move. Rules in this sense constitute a game rather than regulate it. From this some infer that whatever the rules permit is fair, and that a player who finds a loophole has simply played well. The inference is too quick. Rules are written to make a particular contest possible, and a move that satisfies their letter while dissolving that contest, such as a team deliberately losing to secure an easier opponent later, keeps the form of the game while emptying it. Still, the spirit of a game is no free-floating ideal that referees may invoke at will; it can only be read from the contest the rules were built to create, which is why the usual remedy for such an exploit is a better-drafted rule rather than an appeal to conscience.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is tempting to think of the rules of a game as fences around an activity that exists without them, but moving a bishop diagonally is not a restriction on some freer way of moving a carved piece; outside the rules there is no bishop to move. Rules in this sense constitute a game rather than regulate it. From this some infer that whatever the rules permit is fair, and that a player who finds a loophole has simply played well. The inference is too quick. Rules are written to make a particular contest possible, and a move that satisfies their letter while dissolving that contest, such as a team deliberately losing to secure an easier opponent later, keeps the form of the game while emptying it. Still, the spirit of a game is no free-floating ideal that referees may invoke at will; it can only be read from the contest the rules were built to create, which is why the usual remedy for such an exploit is a better-drafted rule rather than an appeal to conscience.

options.A: Teams that lose on purpose to obtain an easier opponent later break no rule, but their conduct shows a lack of respect for the opponents they face in that match.
options.B: Rules constitute a game, yet obeying their letter does not settle fairness, since a legal move can empty the contest, though the game's spirit is itself read from the rules.
options.C: Because written rules can always be exploited, referees should judge each contest by the spirit of the game and set aside the letter of the rules when the two conflict.
options.D: Since rules constitute a game instead of restricting it, any move the written rules permit counts as fair play, and exploiting a loophole is simply a sign of skill.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Rules constitute a game, yet obeying their letter does not settle fairness, since a legal move can empty the contest, though the game's spirit is itself read from the rules.

option_rationales.A: Deliberate losing is only an example, and the paragraph faults it for 'emptying' the contest, not for disrespecting opponents; the option is narrow and shifts the reason.
option_rationales.C: The last sentence denies that the spirit is an ideal 'referees may invoke at will' and says the remedy is 'a better-drafted rule', so this contradicts the paragraph.
option_rationales.D: This is the inference the paragraph reports and then rejects as 'too quick'; it is not the author's conclusion.

questions.explanation: The paragraph moves in three steps: rules constitute a game; it does not follow that whatever they permit is fair, because a legal move can empty the contest; and the spirit of the game is itself read from the rules, so remedies come through redrafting. The correct answer carries all three steps: the constitutive point, the objection with its reason, and the final limit on appeals to the spirit.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that rejects legalism outright and appeals to the spirit of the game, which overshoots the final qualification.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each capture one half of a balanced argument (letter only, spirit only); the reader must hold both the objection and the final qualification.

questions.subtopic: Humblebrags backfire because they add concealment to self-promotion.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A humblebrag, a boast dressed as a complaint or a confession of modesty, seems a clever way to have it both ways: the speaker gets to mention the award or the promotion while appearing not to care about it. Yet people often respond to it worse than to an honest boast. The reason is that the disguise adds a second fault to the first. An open boaster is at least straightforward about wanting admiration; the humblebragger wants admiration and also wants credit for not wanting it, and listeners who see through the manoeuvre resent being treated as too dull to notice. The attempt to escape the cost of self-promotion thus doubles it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A humblebrag, a boast dressed as a complaint or a confession of modesty, seems a clever way to have it both ways: the speaker gets to mention the award or the promotion while appearing not to care about it. Yet people often respond to it worse than to an honest boast. The reason is that the disguise adds a second fault to the first. An open boaster is at least straightforward about wanting admiration; the humblebragger wants admiration and also wants credit for not wanting it, and listeners who see through the manoeuvre resent being treated as too dull to notice. The attempt to escape the cost of self-promotion thus doubles it.

options.A: Humblebrags backfire because they seek praise while hiding that aim, so listeners who notice judge them more harshly than an open boast.
options.B: Humblebrags are an effective way to mention achievements, since they let a speaker draw attention to success while seeming indifferent to it.
options.C: Boasting openly about achievements is admirable, because honesty about wanting praise is a virtue that listeners can be relied upon to reward.
options.D: Listeners dislike complaints about success because they find it hard to feel sympathy for people who already enjoy awards and promotions.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Humblebrags backfire because they seek praise while hiding that aim, so listeners who notice judge them more harshly than an open boast.

option_rationales.B: This is how the humblebrag 'seems' at first; the paragraph goes on to argue that people often respond to it worse than to an honest boast.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says only that an open boaster is 'at least straightforward'; it never calls boasting admirable or says listeners reward it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph locates the resentment in the disguise and in being treated 'as too dull to notice', not in a lack of sympathy for the successful.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a reaction: humblebrags are judged more harshly than open boasts because 'the disguise adds a second fault to the first', so the attempt to avoid the cost of self-promotion 'doubles it'. The correct answer states the effect and its cause.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the opening description of how humblebrags seem as the paragraph's conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause is stated plainly in one sentence and each wrong option fails on a single reading.

questions.subtopic: Punctuality norms differ in what discipline serves, not in how much discipline there is.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Travellers who move between cultures with different attitudes to time often conclude that one kind of society is disciplined and the other careless. The comparison misleads. Where meetings start exactly on the hour, time is treated as a resource divided among commitments, and lateness signals that one has taken someone else's share. Where arrival times are loose, the priority is usually the relationship in hand: leaving a conversation abruptly to keep the next appointment would be the real discourtesy. Each system is strict, but about different things. Neither is without costs, since clock-bound societies can turn every encounter into a transaction while relationship-bound ones can leave outsiders and the less well connected waiting indefinitely. What looks like the presence or absence of discipline is a difference in what discipline is for.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Travellers who move between cultures with different attitudes to time often conclude that one kind of society is disciplined and the other careless. The comparison misleads. Where meetings start exactly on the hour, time is treated as a resource divided among commitments, and lateness signals that one has taken someone else's share. Neither is without costs, since clock-bound societies can turn every encounter into a transaction while relationship-bound ones can leave outsiders and the less well connected waiting indefinitely. What looks like the presence or absence of discipline is a difference in what discipline is for.

options.A: In clock-bound societies time is treated as a scarce resource, so lateness there is a serious offence against those whose share of time has been taken.
options.B: Travellers misjudge attitudes to time abroad because they lack the patience to learn the local customs that govern meetings, social visits and business appointments.
options.C: Cultures that differ over punctuality are not more or less disciplined; each is strict about a different priority, the schedule or the relationship, and each has costs.
options.D: Loose attitudes to time reflect a deeper respect for people, which makes relationship-bound societies kinder and more humane than those organised strictly by the clock.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Cultures that differ over punctuality are not more or less disciplined; each is strict about a different priority, the schedule or the relationship, and each has costs.

option_rationales.A: This restates one side of the comparison only and leaves out both the other system and the central claim that the two differ in what discipline is for.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph does not blame impatience; it says the comparison misleads because each system is strict 'about different things'. The cause offered is outside the paragraph.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'Neither is without costs' and that loose systems can leave outsiders 'waiting indefinitely', so ranking one system above the other contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph compares two attitudes to time and rejects the disciplined-versus-careless reading: each system is strict about a different priority, and each has costs. The correct answer keeps the comparison, the central claim and the balance of costs.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that praises the relationship-bound system, which ignores the stated costs on both sides.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow wrong option is accurate about one half of the comparison, and the evaluative one sounds like the paragraph's sympathy.

questions.subtopic: Decimal measures prevailed through state backing more than through their rationality.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Decimal systems of measurement are often presented as a triumph of reason over custom: once a simple, coherent set of units was available, the argument runs, the tangle of local measures was bound to give way. The history is less tidy. Traditional units were not merely clumsy; many were tied to things people actually did, a day's ploughing or a load a person could carry, and they let communities check trade by familiar standards. Where the new units spread, they often succeeded less through their logic than through the backing of states that needed uniform measures for taxation, armies and national markets, and they met long resistance where that backing was weak. None of this makes the decimal system less convenient; it suggests that its convenience was not, by itself, what made it prevail.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The history is less tidy. Traditional units were not merely clumsy; many were tied to things people actually did, a day's ploughing or a load a person could carry, and they let communities check trade by familiar standards. Where the new units spread, they often succeeded less through their logic than through the backing of states that needed uniform measures for taxation, armies and national markets, and they met long resistance where that backing was weak. None of this makes the decimal system less convenient; it suggests that its convenience was not, by itself, what made it prevail.

options.A: Once a coherent system of units became available, local measures were bound to disappear, because people readily adopt whatever system is simplest to learn and use.
options.B: Traditional measures survived for so long because they were more logical than decimal units, being based on everyday tasks such as ploughing a field and carrying loads.
options.C: Decimal measurement was forced on unwilling populations by states and offered ordinary people no practical advantage at all over the local units that it replaced.
options.D: Decimal measures prevailed less through their logic than through state enforcement, as older units had real local uses, though the new system's convenience is not denied.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Decimal measures prevailed less through their logic than through state enforcement, as older units had real local uses, though the new system's convenience is not denied.

option_rationales.A: This is the 'triumph of reason' view that the paragraph reports and then calls 'less tidy' than the history; it is not the author's position.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says traditional units were 'not merely clumsy' and had practical uses, not that they were more logical than decimal units; it explicitly grants the decimal system its convenience.
option_rationales.C: The last sentence says 'None of this makes the decimal system less convenient', so the claim of no practical advantage contradicts the paragraph.

questions.explanation: The paragraph questions the story that decimal units won by their logic: older units had real uses, and the new ones advanced mainly where states backed them. It ends by granting their convenience while denying that convenience alone explains their success. The correct answer keeps the cause, the reason and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Overreading the critique as a claim that the decimal system had no advantages at all.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader must keep the final concession, which rules out the tempting 'no advantage' option.

questions.subtopic: Classical examinations for officials served state purposes, but that does not make them open meritocracies.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Examination systems that recruited officials through tests on classical texts, as imperial China did for centuries, are sometimes dismissed as an odd way to choose administrators: what could mastery of ancient literature have to do with collecting taxes or managing floods? The objection misreads what such examinations were for. They were less a test of administrative skill, which could be learned in office, than a means of producing officials who shared a common learning and owed their position to the state rather than to birth, a valuable asset for rulers wary of entrenched aristocracies. To recognise this function, however, is not to accept the systems as meritocracies in a modern sense. Years of unpaid preparation lay beyond most families, so the examinations widened access to office without opening it to all, and the 'merit' they measured was the merit they themselves defined.
