options.A: Omitting the translator from the cover conceals, rather than removes, the person who chose every sentence, which hampers readers' judgement and translators' careers; naming them makes trust informed.
options.B: A translated novel is really the translator's book rather than the author's, so the translator's name ought to replace, or at least precede, the author's name on the cover.
options.C: Publishers hide translators' names because readers dislike translated books, and this preference, though understandable, steadily lowers the quality of the translations that publishers commission.
options.D: Because their names are hidden on covers, translators struggle to build reputations and so cannot command the fees and the projects that their considerable work on each novel deserves.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Omitting the translator from the cover conceals, rather than removes, the person who chose every sentence, which hampers readers' judgement and translators' careers; naming them makes trust informed.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the translator does 'a great deal of the work', not that the book belongs to the translator; it asks only that the translator be named, not ranked above the author.
option_rationales.C: The publishers' theory is that readers want to feel they meet the author directly, not that they dislike translations, and nothing is said about falling translation quality.
option_rationales.D: This is one of the two costs listed near the end; it leaves out the central claim that hiding the translator conceals rather than removes an intermediary, and the cost to readers.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the publishers' reasoning as resting 'on a fiction': the translator chose every sentence, so hiding the name 'is not to remove the intermediary but to conceal one'. It names two costs (readers cannot tell author from rendering; translators cannot build reputations) and ends by saying naming makes trust 'an informed one'. The correct answer holds the central claim, both costs and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about translators' careers because it is concrete and true to the paragraph, without noticing that it is only one of two supporting costs.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow wrong option is accurate and specific, so the correct answer must be preferred on scope rather than truth.

questions.subtopic: Abridged classics remove what makes a book distinctive and may deter young readers from the original.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Abridged editions of classic novels are often defended as a gentle doorway: a twelve-year-old who would abandon an eight-hundred-page original might finish a hundred-page version and come back for the real thing later. The trouble is that what abridgement removes is rarely random. Editors cut digressions, descriptions and the slow passages in which characters think, because these are what make a book long, but they are also what make it the particular book it is. What survives is the plot, and plot is the part of a classic that a film or a summary could deliver just as well. A young reader who finishes such a version may therefore conclude that they have read the book, and that it was merely a story, and see no reason to return. The doorway can easily become a wall.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Abridged editions of classic novels are often defended as a gentle doorway: a twelve-year-old who would abandon an eight-hundred-page original might finish a hundred-page version and come back for the real thing later. The trouble is that what abridgement removes is rarely random. Editors cut digressions, descriptions and the slow passages in which characters think, because these are what make a book long, but they are also what make it the particular book it is. What survives is the plot, and plot is the part of a classic that a film or a summary could deliver just as well. A young reader who finishes such a version may therefore conclude that they have read the book, and that it was merely a story, and see no reason to return. The doorway can easily become a wall.

options.A: Defended as a route to the originals, abridged classics tend to keep only plot and cut what makes each book distinctive, so young readers may see no reason to return.
options.B: Editors of abridged classics choose their cuts carelessly and at random, which is why the shortened versions of great novels so often fail to hold the interest of young readers.
options.C: Children should not be given classic novels until they are old enough to read the complete originals, since the shortened editions are written by editors rather than by the authors themselves.
options.D: Abridged editions are valuable because they let young readers finish classic stories they would otherwise abandon, and many of these readers later go on to read the full versions.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Defended as a route to the originals, abridged classics tend to keep only plot and cut what makes each book distinctive, so young readers may see no reason to return.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says what abridgement removes 'is rarely random': editors systematically cut digressions and description. It does not claim the versions fail to hold interest.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph makes no recommendation about when children should read classics, and its objection is to what abridgement removes, not to who wrote the shortened text.
option_rationales.D: This is the defence the paragraph reports in its first sentence and then rejects; the author argues that the doorway 'can easily become a wall'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states the defence (abridgements as a 'doorway'), then argues that the cuts remove exactly what makes a book 'the particular book it is', leaving plot, so a reader may think they have read the book and 'see no reason to return'. The correct answer keeps the defence, the mechanism and the consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that restates the opening defence, which the paragraph sets up only to answer.
questions.difficulty_reason: The turn ('The trouble is') is explicit and each wrong option is clearly off once it is read.

questions.subtopic: Laugh tracks persist because laughter is social and they supply company to a viewer watching alone.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Recorded laughter on television comedies is often mocked as a crude instruction to the audience, a machine telling viewers when something is funny. Yet its persistence for decades suggests it answers a real need. Laughter is overwhelmingly a social behaviour: people laugh far more readily in company than alone, and they often laugh less at a joke than at the shared recognition that a joke has been made. A viewer watching a comedy alone at home is deprived of that company, and the track supplies a substitute, a sense of sitting among others who are enjoying the same thing. This explains why the track feels most intrusive to viewers who are themselves watching in a group, since they already have the company it imitates.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Recorded laughter on television comedies is often mocked as a crude instruction to the audience, a machine telling viewers when something is funny. Yet its persistence for decades suggests it answers a real need. Laughter is overwhelmingly a social behaviour: people laugh far more readily in company than alone, and they often laugh less at a joke than at the shared recognition that a joke has been made. A viewer watching a comedy alone at home is deprived of that company, and the track supplies a substitute, a sense of sitting among others who are enjoying the same thing. This explains why the track feels most intrusive to viewers who are themselves watching in a group, since they already have the company it imitates.

options.A: Recorded laughter is a crude device that tells audiences when to laugh, and viewers have come to resent being instructed in this way by the people who make television comedies.
options.B: People laugh far more readily in company than when alone, and they often laugh more at the shared recognition that a joke has been made than at the joke itself.
options.C: Recorded laughter lasts because laughing is largely social: it gives a solitary viewer a stand-in for an audience, which is also why it irritates people already watching together.
options.D: Recorded laughter suits viewers who watch comedies in groups, since it adds to the shared enjoyment they already feel, while solitary viewers find the device intrusive and false.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Recorded laughter lasts because laughing is largely social: it gives a solitary viewer a stand-in for an audience, which is also why it irritates people already watching together.

option_rationales.A: This is the mockery the paragraph reports and then answers with 'Yet'; the author explains the device as meeting a real need, not as an instruction viewers resent.
option_rationales.B: This is the premise about laughter, not the point; it says nothing about laugh tracks, the solitary viewer or the group viewer.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the paragraph, which says the track supplies company to the viewer alone and feels 'most intrusive' to those watching in a group.

questions.explanation: After reporting the common mockery, the paragraph argues that laugh tracks persist because laughter is social; the track gives a viewer alone 'a sense of sitting among others', and this also explains why groups find it intrusive. The correct answer states the explanation and its corollary.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reversal because both groups are mentioned, without tracking which group the track is said to help.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option reverses the two groups and another states only the premise, so the reader must track the direction of the explanation.

questions.subtopic: Sampling cannot be called uncreative merely because its materials pre-exist, though quality and payment remain open.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Critics of sampling in popular music often argue that a producer who builds a track from fragments of other people's recordings is not composing at all but merely assembling, and that the result borrows its value from the originals. The argument assumes that originality lies in producing sounds no one has produced before. On that test, however, very little music of any period would pass: composers have always worked with inherited scales, forms, rhythms and even melodies, and much admired music is openly built on borrowed tunes. What distinguishes a composer is not the novelty of the materials but what is done with them, the choices of selection, placement and transformation that make a familiar element mean something new. This does not settle whether any particular sampled track is good, or whether the original performers deserve payment; those are separate questions. It shows only that sampling cannot be dismissed as uncreative merely because its raw materials already exist.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The argument assumes that originality lies in producing sounds no one has produced before. On that test, however, very little music of any period would pass: composers have always worked with inherited scales, forms, rhythms and even melodies, and much admired music is openly built on borrowed tunes. What distinguishes a composer is not the novelty of the materials but what is done with them, the choices of selection, placement and transformation that make a familiar element mean something new. This does not settle whether any particular sampled track is good, or whether the original performers deserve payment; those are separate questions. It shows only that sampling cannot be dismissed as uncreative merely because its raw materials already exist.

options.A: Whether a sampled track is creative depends on how good it is and whether the original performers were paid for their work, not on how new its raw materials happen to be.
options.B: Sampling is as creative as any other way of composing, so sampled tracks deserve the same respect as wholly original works and their producers owe nothing to the performers they borrow from.
options.C: Because composers in every period have borrowed scales, forms and melodies, no music has ever been truly original, and critics should abandon the idea of originality altogether.
options.D: The charge that sampling is uncreative locates originality in new materials, a test most music would fail; creativity lies in transforming materials, though this leaves a track's quality and payment unsettled.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The charge that sampling is uncreative locates originality in new materials, a test most music would fail; creativity lies in transforming materials, though this leaves a track's quality and payment unsettled.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph calls quality and payment 'separate questions' from creativity; this option turns them into the test of creativity, which distorts the argument.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says explicitly that whether performers 'deserve payment' is a separate question it does not settle, and it does not claim every sampled track deserves respect.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph relocates originality in 'what is done with' materials rather than discarding it; it never says no music is original.

questions.explanation: The paragraph identifies the critics' assumption (originality means new sounds), shows that almost no music meets it, relocates originality in 'selection, placement and transformation', and then limits its own conclusion: quality and payment are 'separate questions'. The correct answer keeps the refutation, the positive account and the limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that mentions quality and payment, because those words appear in the paragraph, without noticing that it makes them criteria of creativity rather than separate questions.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options reuse the paragraph's qualification and its examples while distorting their role; the correct answer depends on reading the final two sentences as a limit on the claim.

questions.subtopic: The blanket rule against the passive overstates a narrow objection; the passive has real uses.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Style manuals routinely tell writers to avoid the passive voice, and the advice has hardened into a rule that many writers apply without thinking. The case against the passive is real but narrow. A passive sentence can hide the agent ('mistakes were made'), and a long run of passives can make prose feel inert. But the passive also does work that nothing else does as neatly. It lets a writer keep the topic of a paragraph in the subject position, so that a passage about a disease can go on talking about the disease ('it is spread by mosquitoes') rather than lurching to whatever happens to cause it. It lets scientists foreground a procedure rather than the person who carried it out, when the person is irrelevant. The useful question is never whether a sentence is passive but whether the reader needs to know who acted, and what the sentence should be about.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It lets a writer keep the topic of a paragraph in the subject position, so that a passage about a disease can go on talking about the disease ('it is spread by mosquitoes') rather than lurching to whatever happens to cause it. It lets scientists foreground a procedure rather than the person who carried it out, when the person is irrelevant. The useful question is never whether a sentence is passive but whether the reader needs to know who acted, and what the sentence should be about.

options.A: Scientific writing differs from other prose because it describes procedures, so the passive voice, though unsuitable in most writing, is perfectly acceptable in laboratory reports.
options.B: The rule against the passive inflates a narrow objection: passives can hide agents or deaden prose but also keep topics in focus, so the reader's needs should decide.
options.C: Writers should generally prefer the passive voice to the active, because it keeps the topic of a passage in subject position and directs attention to procedures rather than people.
options.D: The passive voice serves mainly to conceal responsibility, as in 'mistakes were made', and style manuals are right to warn writers against using it in serious prose.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The rule against the passive inflates a narrow objection: passives can hide agents or deaden prose but also keep topics in focus, so the reader's needs should decide.

option_rationales.A: Science is one example of the passive's uses; the paragraph also gives the topic-keeping use for any passage and does not call the passive unsuitable elsewhere.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph defends the passive for particular purposes and accepts the case against it as 'real'; it never says the passive should generally be preferred.
option_rationales.D: Concealing the agent is the 'real but narrow' case against the passive; the paragraph goes on to describe work the passive does well, so endorsing the rule reverses it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants the objection ('real but narrow'), lists the passive's uses (keeping the topic in subject position, foregrounding procedure) and ends by replacing the rule with a question about what the reader needs. The correct answer captures concession, counter-case and the replacement test.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about science, which is a vivid example, and missing that it narrows a general point.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must balance the concession against the defence; two wrong options each keep only one side.

questions.subtopic: An unaltered news photograph is still shaped by its cropping, so readers should ask what the frame excludes.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A news photograph is often treated as the most neutral element of a report: the words may spin, but the camera simply records. Yet every published photograph has been cropped, and cropping is a choice about what the event was. A picture of a single protester shouting at a line of police tells one story; the same frame widened to show a quiet crowd of hundreds behind him tells another, and the wider frame may show that the shouting man was alone. Nothing in either version is false, and no pixel has been altered. The distortion, if there is one, lies entirely in the boundary. That is why a reader who wants to judge a photograph should ask not only what it shows but what its edges leave out.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A news photograph is often treated as the most neutral element of a report: the words may spin, but the camera simply records. Yet every published photograph has been cropped, and cropping is a choice about what the event was. A picture of a single protester shouting at a line of police tells one story; the same frame widened to show a quiet crowd of hundreds behind him tells another, and the wider frame may show that the shouting man was alone. Nothing in either version is false, and no pixel has been altered. The distortion, if there is one, lies entirely in the boundary. That is why a reader who wants to judge a photograph should ask not only what it shows but what its edges leave out.

options.A: A photograph of one protester shouting at police can make a peaceful demonstration of hundreds of people look violent and disorderly to those who see it in a newspaper.
options.B: News photographs are less trustworthy than written reports, because photographers routinely alter their images to make protests look more dramatic and violent than the events really were.
options.C: An unaltered news photograph is still shaped by cropping, since the frame's edges decide what the event seems to be, so readers should ask what lies beyond them.
options.D: Newspapers ought to publish every photograph uncropped, so that readers can see the whole scene for themselves and decide on their own what really happened at the event.

questions.correct_answer: (C) An unaltered news photograph is still shaped by cropping, since the frame's edges decide what the event seems to be, so readers should ask what lies beyond them.

option_rationales.A: This is the illustration only; it omits the general point that cropping, not falsification, shapes what any news photograph seems to show.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph stresses that 'no pixel has been altered' and does not rank photographs below written reports; the issue is the frame, not manipulation.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph prescribes nothing for newspapers; its advice is to readers, to ask what the edges leave out.

questions.explanation: The paragraph challenges the view that photographs are neutral: cropping 'is a choice about what the event was', the distortion 'lies entirely in the boundary', and readers should ask what the edges leave out. The correct answer states the point, the reason and the advice.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the protester example because it is the most memorable sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The thesis and the advice are stated outright; wrong options are an example, an extreme claim and an invented prescription.

questions.subtopic: The audiobook debate should turn on control of pace and rereading, which matters by kind of text.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Whether listening to an audiobook counts as reading is usually argued as a question of status, with defenders insisting that the story reaches the mind either way and sceptics treating listening as a lesser substitute. Both sides tend to miss what actually differs. For narrative of moderate difficulty, a competent listener appears to follow and remember the story about as well as a reader does, so the sceptic's claim that listening is shallower is hard to sustain as a general rule. The difference lies in control. A reader sets the pace, slows down at a difficult sentence, glances back to check who said what, and lets the eye run ahead; a listener receives the text at the narrator's speed and must make an effort to go back. For a thriller this hardly matters. For a dense argument, where comprehension depends on rereading, it may matter a great deal. The useful question is therefore not whether listening is reading, but what kind of text is being taken in.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Both sides tend to miss what actually differs. For narrative of moderate difficulty, a competent listener appears to follow and remember the story about as well as a reader does, so the sceptic's claim that listening is shallower is hard to sustain as a general rule. The difference lies in control. A reader sets the pace, slows down at a difficult sentence, glances back to check who said what, and lets the eye run ahead; a listener receives the text at the narrator's speed and must make an effort to go back. For a thriller this hardly matters. For a dense argument, where comprehension depends on rereading, it may matter a great deal. The useful question is therefore not whether listening is reading, but what kind of text is being taken in.

options.A: Listening is not generally shallower than reading, but it gives less control over pace and going back, a difference that matters little for stories and possibly much for dense argument.
options.B: Audiobooks are an inferior substitute for printed books, since listeners cannot slow down or glance back, and so they understand and remember less of whatever they hear.
options.C: Readers and listeners differ mainly in speed, since narrators read faster than most people, so audiobooks suit thrillers better than slow and descriptive literary fiction.
options.D: Listening to an audiobook is a form of reading, since the story reaches a listener's mind just as it reaches a reader's, so the debate about its status is pointless.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Listening is not generally shallower than reading, but it gives less control over pace and going back, a difference that matters little for stories and possibly much for dense argument.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the claim that listening is shallower 'is hard to sustain as a general rule'; loss of control matters mainly for dense argument, not for whatever is heard.
option_rationales.C: The difference named is control over pace and rereading, not that narrators are faster, and the contrast drawn is between stories and dense argument, not between kinds of fiction.
option_rationales.D: This is the defenders' position, which the paragraph says misses 'what actually differs'; the author insists on a real difference in control.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects both sides of the status debate: listening is not generally shallower (against the sceptics), but there is a real difference, 'control' (against the defenders), which 'hardly matters' for a thriller and 'may matter a great deal' for dense argument. The correct answer keeps both corrections and the dependence on the kind of text.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the defenders' option because the paragraph agrees that listeners follow stories well, and missing that it also insists on a real difference.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph corrects both camps; each of two wrong options is one camp's view and partly matches the text.

questions.subtopic: A correlation between texting and good spelling cannot show benefit but does count against the feared harm.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Teachers and parents have long worried that the abbreviations of text messaging, the dropped vowels and phonetic shortcuts, would corrode children's spelling. Suppose a school compares its pupils and finds that the heaviest users of such abbreviations are, if anything, slightly better spellers than the rest. It would be tempting to conclude that texting improves spelling, but the finding cannot carry that weight. To abbreviate a word playfully a child must usually know how it is spelled in full, so skill with abbreviations may simply be a sign of a comfort with language that the better spellers already had. What the finding does undermine is the fear itself: if abbreviating were steadily eroding spelling, the heaviest abbreviators should be doing worse, not better. A correlation that cannot prove benefit can still be evidence against harm.

options.A: The worry about texting and spelling has now been disproved, so schools ought to stop discouraging pupils from using abbreviations in their messages and other informal writing.
options.B: That heavy abbreviators spell slightly better cannot show texting helps spelling, since good spellers may simply abbreviate more, but it does tell against the fear that texting harms it.
options.C: Correlations between children's habits and their abilities can never tell us anything at all about causes, so a school's comparison of its own pupils is of no value in this debate.
options.D: Text messaging improves children's spelling, because abbreviating words playfully requires them to know the full spellings, and the habit keeps reinforcing that knowledge every day.

questions.correct_answer: (B) That heavy abbreviators spell slightly better cannot show texting helps spelling, since good spellers may simply abbreviate more, but it does tell against the fear that texting harms it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the finding does 'undermine' the fear and counts as 'evidence against harm', which is weaker than disproof, and it recommends nothing to schools.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph's last sentence says such a correlation 'can still be evidence against harm', which contradicts the claim that it is of no value.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls this conclusion 'tempting' and says the finding 'cannot carry that weight'; knowing full spellings is offered as a reason good spellers abbreviate, not as a benefit of texting.

questions.explanation: The paragraph uses a hypothetical finding to make a point about evidence: it cannot show texting helps (better spellers may abbreviate more), but it counts against the feared harm, since harm would predict the opposite pattern. The correct answer keeps both halves of this asymmetry.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'disproved' option because the paragraph does undermine the fear, and missing the gap between evidence against a claim and disproof of it.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is an asymmetry about evidence; wrong options take one half too far.

questions.subtopic: Interesting but irrelevant textbook asides can impair learning, unlike vivid material that carries the idea.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Textbook writers often add vivid asides to dry material: an anecdote about a scientist's eccentricities in a chapter on electricity, a dramatic photograph of lightning beside a diagram of charge. The intention is to hold interest, and readers do report finding such pages more enjoyable. Yet experiments on learning from text have repeatedly suggested that interesting but irrelevant details can reduce how much of the central explanation students remember and can apply, apparently by drawing attention and memory towards themselves. This does not mean that interest is the enemy of learning. Details that are vivid and also carry the core idea, such as an example that shows the principle at work, do not seem to carry the same cost. The lesson is that engagement should be built from the material that is to be learned, not borrowed from material beside it.

options.A: Irrelevant details in textbooks harm learning chiefly because they make pages longer, so that students spend less of their limited reading time on the central explanation.
options.B: Students enjoy textbook pages with vivid anecdotes and dramatic photographs more than plain pages, and this enjoyment makes them more willing to study the central explanation.
options.C: Textbooks should be written in plain language without anecdotes, photographs or examples, since anything that makes a page more enjoyable will distract students from what they are meant to learn.
options.D: Engaging but irrelevant textbook asides can divert attention from the explanation and weaken learning, though vivid material embodying the idea seems not to; interest should come from content.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Engaging but irrelevant textbook asides can divert attention from the explanation and weaken learning, though vivid material embodying the idea seems not to; interest should come from content.

option_rationales.A: The mechanism suggested is that such details draw 'attention and memory towards themselves', not that they lengthen the page or use up reading time.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph grants the enjoyment but says irrelevant details can reduce what students remember of the explanation; the claim of greater willingness to study is not in it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says interest is not 'the enemy of learning' and approves vivid examples that show the principle at work, so banning them contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (irrelevant but interesting details can reduce learning of the main explanation), qualifies it (relevant vivid details do not carry the same cost), and draws the lesson that engagement should come from the material itself. The correct answer holds finding, qualification and lesson.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the extreme option because the finding is against decorative detail, and ignoring the qualification about vivid examples.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer depends on keeping the qualification; one wrong option is an overstated version of the finding.

questions.subtopic: Open-book examinations shift the demand from recall to the use of understanding rather than lowering it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Open-book examinations are sometimes dismissed as easy, on the assumption that a student who may consult notes need not have learned anything. Anyone who has sat one knows otherwise. Because the facts are available, the examiner cannot reward their mere recall and must instead ask questions that require using them: applying a principle to an unfamiliar case, weighing two sources, building an argument under time pressure. A student who has not understood the material gains little from the book on the desk, since there is no time to learn a subject in the middle of the paper; such students tend to spend the hour leafing anxiously through pages. Open-book examinations do not lower the bar; they move it from remembering to thinking.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Open-book examinations are not easier but differently demanding: since facts can be looked up, they test the application of understanding, which notes cannot supply in the time available.
options.B: Students who have not understood a subject spend open-book examinations leafing anxiously through their notes, and so they often fail to finish the paper.
options.C: Open-book examinations are easy because students may consult their notes, so they reward the students who take careful notes rather than those who truly understand the subject.
options.D: Closed-book examinations ought to be abolished, since testing the recall of facts that anyone can look up wastes students' time and teaches them nothing useful.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Open-book examinations are not easier but differently demanding: since facts can be looked up, they test the application of understanding, which notes cannot supply in the time available.

option_rationales.B: This is one supporting detail, and the claim that such students fail to finish is added; the option misses the main point that the bar moves from remembering to thinking.
option_rationales.C: This is the dismissal the paragraph rejects in its second sentence; the author argues that notes help little without understanding.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph defends open-book examinations but says nothing against closed-book ones and recommends no abolition.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rebuts the view that open-book examinations are easy: available facts force questions that require using them, and notes cannot substitute for understanding under time pressure. Its last sentence states the point: the bar moves 'from remembering to thinking'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the detail about students leafing through pages because it is concrete.
questions.difficulty_reason: The conclusion is stated in the last sentence and each wrong option is plainly off.

questions.subtopic: The cursive debate confuses the case for handwriting with the weaker case for the joined style.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Debates over whether schools should still teach joined-up handwriting are usually framed as a contest between tradition and efficiency: cursive is a heritage skill, keyboards are what adults actually use. The framing obscures the fact that the two sides are often talking about different things. The case for teaching some handwriting is fairly strong, since forming letters by hand appears to help young children learn to recognise them, and much early schoolwork is still done with a pencil. But that case is about handwriting in general, not about the particular joined style, and an argument for one is easily mistaken for an argument for the other. The case for cursive specifically rests on weaker grounds: claims that it is faster, or that it builds discipline, are rarely as well supported as their advocates assume. A school could therefore drop cursive and keep handwriting without any inconsistency.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The case for cursive specifically rests on weaker grounds: claims that it is faster, or that it builds discipline, are rarely as well supported as their advocates assume. A school could therefore drop cursive and keep handwriting without any inconsistency.

options.A: Cursive should continue to be taught because forming letters by hand helps young children learn to recognise them, which is a benefit that typing on a keyboard cannot provide.
options.B: Schools should stop teaching handwriting altogether, because keyboards are what adults actually use and the supposed benefits of cursive are rarely supported by evidence.
options.C: The cursive debate merges two questions: the fairly strong case for teaching handwriting does not carry over to the joined style, whose particular benefits are less well supported.
options.D: The debate over cursive is at bottom a contest between tradition and efficiency, and efficiency should prevail because most adult writing is now done on keyboards.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The cursive debate merges two questions: the fairly strong case for teaching handwriting does not carry over to the joined style, whose particular benefits are less well supported.

option_rationales.A: This makes exactly the error the paragraph identifies: it uses the case for handwriting in general as an argument for the particular joined style.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph calls the case for handwriting 'fairly strong' and says a school could keep handwriting while dropping cursive; abandoning handwriting contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says this framing 'obscures' what is at issue, so presenting the debate in these terms and picking a side misses its point.

questions.explanation: The paragraph's central move is a distinction: the case for handwriting in general is 'fairly strong', but 'an argument for one is easily mistaken for an argument for the other', and the case for cursive specifically 'rests on weaker grounds'. The conclusion follows that a school can drop cursive and keep handwriting. The correct answer states the distinction and the asymmetry of support.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the pro-cursive option because the letter-recognition point is presented as well supported, and missing that it supports handwriting, not cursive.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option uses the paragraph's strongest evidence in exactly the way the paragraph warns against; separating them needs the general versus specific distinction.

questions.subtopic: University league tables imply a single best order by fixing weights that are the compiler's choice.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: University league tables are defended as a service to applicants, who would otherwise have to choose among institutions they know little about. The defence has some force, but it overlooks what a single ranked list does. Each table combines many measures, such as research output, staff numbers per student and graduate salaries, into one score, and the weights given to each are a choice made by the compiler, not a fact about universities. Different weights would produce a different order. An applicant who wants small classes and an applicant who wants a strong research culture are served by different universities, yet both are handed the same list as if it settled which is best. A table that published its components and let readers set the weights would serve applicants better than one that pretends a single verdict exists.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A table that published its components and let readers set the weights would serve applicants better than one that pretends a single verdict exists.

options.A: Applicants who want small classes should ignore league tables, since the tables systematically favour universities with strong research over those that give students personal attention.
options.B: League tables are worthless to applicants, because the measures they combine, such as research output and graduate salaries, have nothing to do with the quality of a university's teaching.
options.C: Compilers of league tables deliberately choose their weights so that famous universities stay at the top, which misleads applicants about where they ought to apply.
options.D: League tables inform applicants, but by merging many measures into one score with weights the compiler chose, they imply one best order where other priorities would rank differently.

questions.correct_answer: (D) League tables inform applicants, but by merging many measures into one score with weights the compiler chose, they imply one best order where other priorities would rank differently.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph claims no bias toward research; its point is that any fixed weighting serves some applicants' priorities and not others'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph grants the defence 'some force' and objects to the single weighted score, not to the measures; it never says they are unrelated to teaching.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the weights are 'a choice made by the compiler', not that they are chosen dishonestly; motives are never discussed.

questions.explanation: The paragraph concedes the tables help applicants, then argues that combining measures with chosen weights produces an order that is not 'a fact about universities', so different applicants are wrongly given one verdict. It proposes publishing components so readers can set weights. The correct answer keeps the concession and the central objection.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about deliberate manipulation, reading 'a choice made by the compiler' as an accusation.
questions.difficulty_reason: Wrong options add motives or biases that the paragraph does not assert, and each looks like a natural extension of it.

questions.subtopic: For ordinary short-term back pain, staying active beats prolonged bed rest, within stated limits.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: For a long time, people who hurt their backs were told to lie down and stay down until the pain passed. Current guidance for ordinary, short-lived low back pain has largely reversed this advice: staying as active as the pain allows tends to bring a quicker recovery than prolonged rest, which can stiffen muscles and make a return to normal life harder. This does not mean that a patient should ignore pain or push through heavy work, and a day or two of reduced activity in the worst phase may be sensible. Nor does the advice apply to back pain caused by serious injury or disease, which needs proper assessment. The change is narrower than a slogan like 'keep moving' suggests, but within its range it is clear.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

For a long time, people who hurt their backs were told to lie down and stay down until the pain passed. This does not mean that a patient should ignore pain or push through heavy work, and a day or two of reduced activity in the worst phase may be sensible. Nor does the advice apply to back pain caused by serious injury or disease, which needs proper assessment. The change is narrower than a slogan like 'keep moving' suggests, but within its range it is clear.

options.A: People with back pain should keep moving and work through the pain, since rest of any kind stiffens the muscles and delays the patient's return to normal daily activity.
options.B: For ordinary short-term back pain, staying reasonably active usually aids recovery better than long bed rest, though brief rest may help and serious causes need separate assessment.
options.C: Back pain that is caused by serious injury or disease needs careful assessment by a doctor before a patient decides whether to rest or to stay active.
options.D: Doctors were wrong for many years to recommend bed rest for back pain, which shows that medical advice about common complaints should not be trusted by patients.

questions.correct_answer: (B) For ordinary short-term back pain, staying reasonably active usually aids recovery better than long bed rest, though brief rest may help and serious causes need separate assessment.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says a patient should not 'ignore pain or push through heavy work' and that a day or two of reduced activity may be sensible, so ruling out rest of any kind contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: This is one of the qualifications only; it omits the main point that for ordinary back pain activity helps recovery more than prolonged rest.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph reports a change in guidance but draws no conclusion about trusting medical advice; this lesson is outside its scope.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (activity aids recovery from ordinary back pain better than prolonged rest) and then limits it twice: brief rest may be sensible, and serious causes are excluded. It closes by saying the change is 'narrower than a slogan' but clear within its range. The correct answer keeps the finding and both limits.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'keep moving' option, which is the slogan the paragraph says overstates the change.
questions.difficulty_reason: Finding and qualifications are stated plainly; the slogan wrong option is explicitly flagged as too broad.

questions.subtopic: Instant online test results honour patients' claims but can mislead; the issue is whether interpretation comes with them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many health systems now let patients see their test results online as soon as they are ready, often before a doctor has looked at them. Supporters see this as an overdue recognition that the information belongs to the patient; critics point out that a patient may meet an alarming number, or a technical phrase like 'cannot exclude malignancy', alone at midnight with no one to explain it. Both are right about something. Early access removes delays and the paternalism of having a doctor decide what a patient may know, and many patients prefer it even when the news is bad. But a result is not the same as its meaning, and a raw value read without context can frighten patients needlessly or reassure them falsely. The choice is less between access and protection than about whether interpretation arrives with the data or only later.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

But a result is not the same as its meaning, and a raw value read without context can frighten patients needlessly or reassure them falsely. The choice is less between access and protection than about whether interpretation arrives with the data or only later.

options.A: Patients should not see their test results until a doctor has reviewed them, since alarming numbers and technical phrases read alone at night cause needless fear and confusion.
options.B: Doctors have been paternalistic about test results because they want to control what patients know, and online access has at last brought this unjustified control to an end.
options.C: Immediate online access to test results honours patients' claim to their information, yet unexplained results can mislead or alarm, so the real issue is whether interpretation comes with the data.
options.D: Most patients prefer to see test results at once, even when the news is bad, so health systems are right to release every result online immediately.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Immediate online access to test results honours patients' claim to their information, yet unexplained results can mislead or alarm, so the real issue is whether interpretation comes with the data.

option_rationales.A: This is the critics' position, which the paragraph says is right only 'about something'; it also credits early access with removing delays and paternalism.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph mentions paternalism but attributes no motive to doctors, and it does not treat online access as simply settling the matter.
option_rationales.D: This takes the supporters' side and ignores the paragraph's point that a raw result read without context can frighten or falsely reassure.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets out supporters and critics, says 'Both are right about something', grants the benefits of early access and the risk that 'a result is not the same as its meaning', and reframes the choice: whether interpretation arrives with the data. The correct answer keeps both sides and the reframing.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the supporters' option because the paragraph lists the benefits of early access first and at length.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options each give one side of a balanced comparison; the correct answer requires the reframing in the last sentence.

questions.subtopic: Individually cautious monitor alarms can together make wards less safe by teaching staff to discount them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Hospital wards are full of monitors that sound an alarm whenever a patient's heart rate, oxygen level or blood pressure crosses a threshold. Each alarm is set cautiously, on the reasonable principle that a missed emergency is worse than a false alert. Yet the sum of these cautious settings can make patients less safe. When most alarms turn out to be harmless, triggered by a patient shifting in bed or a sensor slipping, staff learn, quite rationally, to treat them as background noise, to respond slowly or to silence them. The rare alarm that signals a real crisis then arrives in an environment trained to ignore it. The problem is not careless staff but a system in which each device is designed in isolation, as though it were the only voice in the room.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Each alarm is set cautiously, on the reasonable principle that a missed emergency is worse than a false alert. Yet the sum of these cautious settings can make patients less safe. When most alarms turn out to be harmless, triggered by a patient shifting in bed or a sensor slipping, staff learn, quite rationally, to treat them as background noise, to respond slowly or to silence them. The rare alarm that signals a real crisis then arrives in an environment trained to ignore it. The problem is not careless staff but a system in which each device is designed in isolation, as though it were the only voice in the room.

options.A: Nurses and doctors on busy wards too often ignore or silence monitor alarms, and they need stricter training so that they respond promptly to every alert they hear.
options.B: Most monitor alarms on hospital wards are false, being set off when patients shift in bed or when the sensors attached to their bodies slip out of place.
options.C: Monitor alarms should be set to sound far less often, since in practice a missed emergency does less harm to patients than a steady stream of false alerts.
options.D: Cautiously set monitor alarms can together make wards less safe: frequent false alerts teach staff to discount them, a fault of system design, not of careless staff.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Cautiously set monitor alarms can together make wards less safe: frequent false alerts teach staff to discount them, a fault of system design, not of careless staff.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the problem 'is not careless staff' and calls the staff response rational; it proposes no training.
option_rationales.B: This is a supporting detail; it leaves out the central point that false alerts train staff to ignore the alarms that matter.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph calls it 'reasonable' that a missed emergency is worse than a false alert; it faults the combined effect of the settings, not this principle.

questions.explanation: Each cautious setting is reasonable, but 'the sum' can make patients less safe: harmless alarms teach staff 'quite rationally' to discount them, so real crises are missed. The last sentence places the fault in isolated device design, not staff. The correct answer gives the paradox, the mechanism and where the fault lies.
questions.common_misconception: Blaming the staff, which the paragraph explicitly rules out.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must capture an aggregate effect of individually sensible choices; one wrong option overturns the sensible principle itself.

questions.subtopic: Rare-disease drug incentives work but, keyed to patient numbers, can be gamed; they need better targeting.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Because a rare disease affects few people, a drug that treats it promises a small market, and companies left to market incentives alone have little reason to develop one. Governments in many countries have therefore offered inducements, such as extended periods of exclusive sale, to make such drugs worth developing. The policy has produced treatments for conditions that once had none, and that achievement is real. But an incentive defined by the number of patients can be met in ways its designers did not intend. A common disease can sometimes be divided into narrowly defined subtypes, each rare enough to qualify, and a drug that later proves useful for many conditions may keep the protections it earned for one. The result can be high prices on drugs whose markets are not small at all. The remedy is not to abandon the incentives but to tie them more closely to the problem they were meant to solve.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Rare-disease drug incentives have yielded real treatments, but since they turn on patient numbers they can shield high prices in large markets, so they need closer targeting.
options.B: Incentives for rare-disease drugs mainly let companies charge high prices for medicines with large markets, so they have done more harm than good and ought to be withdrawn.
options.C: Drug companies divide common diseases into rare subtypes to qualify for incentives, which shows that the industry cannot be trusted to develop any medicines responsibly.
options.D: Without government incentives no company would ever develop a drug for a rare disease, since the small number of patients makes such drugs unprofitable to produce and sell.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Rare-disease drug incentives have yielded real treatments, but since they turn on patient numbers they can shield high prices in large markets, so they need closer targeting.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph calls the policy's achievement 'real' and says 'The remedy is not to abandon the incentives', which this option directly contradicts.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a disease 'can sometimes' be divided this way and draws no conclusion about the trustworthiness of the whole industry.
option_rationales.D: This overstates the premise, since the paragraph says only 'little reason', and leaves out the paragraph's main point about how the incentives can be exploited.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why incentives exist, grants their achievement, shows how a patient-number test can be met unintentionally (subdivided diseases, drugs later used widely) and concludes that the incentives should be tied more closely to their purpose, not abandoned. The correct answer keeps achievement, flaw and remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'withdraw' option because the paragraph's longest stretch describes abuse, and overlooking the explicit rejection of abandonment.
questions.difficulty_reason: The criticism dominates the paragraph, so the tempting wrong option follows its weight; only the concession and the final sentence rule it out.

questions.subtopic: Parking minimums have hidden costs and induce driving, so parking supply should not be fixed by rule.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many cities require every new building to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, a rule meant to stop drivers from overwhelming the surrounding streets. The intention is sensible, but the rule carries costs that are easy to overlook because they are hidden in other prices. Parking takes land and money, so the requirement raises the cost of every flat and shop that is built, whether or not its occupants own a car; residents who do not drive in effect subsidise those who do. And by guaranteeing that driving will always be convenient, the rule encourages more of it, partly creating the demand it was meant to accommodate. None of this means a city should have no parking. It means that the amount should be decided by those who build and use it, rather than fixed by a rule that assumes everyone will drive.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many cities require every new building to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, a rule meant to stop drivers from overwhelming the surrounding streets. The intention is sensible, but the rule carries costs that are easy to overlook because they are hidden in other prices. Parking takes land and money, so the requirement raises the cost of every flat and shop that is built, whether or not its occupants own a car; residents who do not drive in effect subsidise those who do. And by guaranteeing that driving will always be convenient, the rule encourages more of it, partly creating the demand it was meant to accommodate. None of this means a city should have no parking. It means that the amount should be decided by those who build and use it, rather than fixed by a rule that assumes everyone will drive.

options.A: Residents who do not own cars pay more for their flats, because developers are forced to build parking spaces that only car-owning residents will ever actually use.
options.B: Required parking raises building costs for drivers and non-drivers alike and encourages driving, so though some parking is needed, its amount should not be set by rule.
options.C: Cities should ban new parking spaces altogether, because parking uses up land and money and tempts people to drive when they could walk or take public transport instead.
options.D: Rules requiring parking in new buildings have failed, because drivers still overwhelm the surrounding streets, which shows that such rules can never achieve their purpose.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Required parking raises building costs for drivers and non-drivers alike and encourages driving, so though some parking is needed, its amount should not be set by rule.

option_rationales.A: This is one of the costs described; it omits the induced driving and the conclusion about who should decide the amount of parking.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'None of this means a city should have no parking'; a ban contradicts it, and walking and public transport are never mentioned.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph does not say streets are still overwhelmed; its objection is to hidden costs and induced demand, not to failure at the stated aim.

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants the rule a sensible intention, then names two overlooked effects (higher building costs borne by non-drivers too, and induced driving) and concludes, with a qualification, that parking should be decided by builders and users rather than by a rule. The correct answer holds the two effects, the concession and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the subsidy option because it is the most striking claim in the paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must include the concession that some parking is needed; the extreme wrong option is close in spirit to the critique.

questions.subtopic: Flagship museums regenerate cities only as part of wider investment; their reputation rests on exceptions.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When a declining industrial city commissions a spectacular museum from a famous architect, the hope is that the building will draw visitors, investment and a new image, as a few celebrated examples seem to show. The trouble is that the examples are remembered precisely because they are exceptional. For every city whose flagship became a destination, others built expensive buildings that drew crowds for a season and then struggled to fill their galleries or pay their running costs. The successes, moreover, rarely depended on the building alone: they tended to come where the city was already investing in transport, housing and its existing cultural life, so that the museum crowned a wider change rather than causing it. A spectacular building is not useless. But treated as a shortcut to regeneration rather than as one part of it, it is more likely to become a monument to the hope than an instrument of its fulfilment.

options.A: Spectacular museums rarely revive declining cities, since most visitors come only once, so cities should spend on transport and housing instead of on new cultural buildings.
options.B: Famous architects design museums that cost too much to run, so many cities are left struggling to fill the galleries and to pay for the buildings they commissioned.
options.C: Cities whose flagship museums succeeded were already investing in transport, housing and culture, which proves that the museums themselves contributed nothing to their revival.
options.D: Faith that a showpiece museum will revive a declining city rests on memorable exceptions; successes usually crowned wider investment, so such buildings help as one part of regeneration, not as a shortcut.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Faith that a showpiece museum will revive a declining city rests on memorable exceptions; successes usually crowned wider investment, so such buildings help as one part of regeneration, not as a shortcut.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says such a building 'is not useless' and objects only to treating it as a shortcut; it does not set museums against such spending, and visitors coming only once is never claimed.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph does not blame architects; the struggling museums are evidence that remembered successes are exceptional, not the main point.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the museum 'crowned a wider change' and 'is not useless'; claiming proof that museums contributed nothing overstates the point about dependence on wider investment.

questions.explanation: The paragraph attacks the regeneration hope on two grounds: the famous successes are exceptions (selection), and even they depended on wider investment, the museum crowning rather than causing change. questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'proves nothing' option because the paragraph says the museum did not cause the change, and missing the gap between 'crowned' and 'contributed nothing'.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are overstatements of claims the paragraph does make; the correct answer turns on its concession and on the difference between crowning and causing.

questions.subtopic: Freezing an old quarter's buildings can drive out the mixed life that gave it character.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Protecting an old quarter of a city by freezing its buildings in their present form seems the obvious way to preserve its character. But much of what people value in such places was never a matter of facades alone. It came from the mix of uses, the workshops below flats, the small shops and cheap rooms that let all kinds of people live and work there. Strict rules that forbid any alteration can make buildings expensive to adapt and maintain, so that the craftsmen and small traders move out and the quarter fills with boutique hotels and souvenir shops behind perfectly preserved fronts. Conservation that protects the shell while losing the life it once housed has preserved less than it appears.

options.A: The character of an old quarter lies in its workshops, small shops and cheap rooms rather than in the appearance of its buildings and streets.
options.B: Old city quarters should be allowed to change freely and without restriction, since rules against alteration only raise costs and end up serving the owners of boutique hotels and souvenir shops.
options.C: Freezing an old quarter's buildings can drive out the mix of people and trades that gave it character, so preserving facades alone may lose what made it valuable.
options.D: Boutique hotels and souvenir shops are spoiling the old quarters of many cities, and strict conservation rules are needed to stop such businesses from moving in.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Freezing an old quarter's buildings can drive out the mix of people and trades that gave it character, so preserving facades alone may lose what made it valuable.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says character was 'never a matter of facades alone', not that appearance does not matter; and the option omits the argument about strict rules.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph criticises strict freezing, not all conservation, and it does not recommend letting quarters change freely.
option_rationales.D: This reverses the paragraph, which says strict rules help bring such businesses in by driving out craftsmen and small traders.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that character came from 'the mix of uses', that strict no-alteration rules push out craftsmen and traders, and that conservation which keeps 'the shell' while losing 'the life' preserves less than it seems. The correct answer states this mechanism and conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'rather than' option, which turns 'not facades alone' into 'not facades at all'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument is short and direct, and the reversal and the prescription are clearly off.

questions.subtopic: Footbridges go unused because they cost walkers far more effort than crossing at street level.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Pedestrian footbridges over busy roads are built to keep walkers safe, yet many stand almost unused while people dodge traffic at street level beneath them. This is less a sign of recklessness than of a design that ignores how walking works. A footbridge typically asks a pedestrian to climb a long flight of stairs or a ramp, cross, and descend again, adding minutes and considerable effort to a crossing that would take seconds at street level. For the elderly, people with heavy bags and parents with prams, the climb can be a real obstacle. Pedestrians weigh effort against risk, as drivers do, and when the safe route is much harder than the dangerous one, many will take the risk.

options.A: Many footbridges go unused not through recklessness but because they cost far more effort than crossing at street level, and pedestrians weigh effort against risk.
options.B: Footbridges are particularly hard for elderly people, people carrying heavy bags and parents pushing prams, who find the long stairs and ramps a real obstacle.
options.C: Drivers and pedestrians both weigh effort against risk, which is why accidents are most frequent on the busy roads that footbridges are built to cross.
options.D: Pedestrians who cross busy roads beneath footbridges are behaving recklessly and should be fined, since a safe crossing has been built for them at public expense.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Many footbridges go unused not through recklessness but because they cost far more effort than crossing at street level, and pedestrians weigh effort against risk.

option_rationales.B: This is a supporting detail about some users; it misses the general point about effort against risk for all pedestrians.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph makes no claim about where accidents are most frequent; the comparison with drivers only supports the point about pedestrians.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the behaviour is 'less a sign of recklessness than of a design that ignores how walking works'; fines are not mentioned.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a puzzle (unused footbridges): the cause is design, not recklessness, since the bridge adds much effort to a crossing, and pedestrians weigh effort against risk. The correct answer states the puzzle's explanation.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the detail about the elderly and parents because it is vivid.
questions.difficulty_reason: The explanation is signposted in the second sentence; wrong options are a reversal, a detail and an unsupported causal claim.

questions.subtopic: Impartialists can justify partiality at the level of practice, at the cost of grounding friendship in the general good.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Impartial moral theories hold that everyone's interests count equally, and they seem to imply that I should be no more concerned with my friend's welfare than with a stranger's. Critics reply that a person who really thought this way would be incapable of friendship, since to be someone's friend just is to give their good special weight. The critics are right that friendship involves partiality, but the impartialist need not concede that partiality is therefore unjustified. One can argue impartially that a world in which people form close attachments and favour those they love is better for everyone than a world of detached benefactors, and so endorse partiality at the level of the practice while denying that each act of favouritism must be weighed against strangers' claims. The cost of this reply is that the friend's special claim is defended, in the end, by appeal to the general good, which some will feel misdescribes why we help our friends.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

options.A: Impartial theories require people to weigh every act of favouritism toward a friend against the claims of strangers, which makes genuine friendship impossible to sustain.
options.B: Impartialists can grant that friendship is partial by justifying, on impartial grounds, the practice of favouring loved ones, though grounding a friend's claim in the general good may misdescribe it.
options.C: Because friendship requires giving a friend's good special weight, impartial moral theories cannot be correct, and morality must permit each person to favour those they love.
options.D: A world of close attachments is better for everyone than a world of detached benefactors, so people have no reason at all to be concerned with the welfare of strangers.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Impartialists can grant that friendship is partial by justifying, on impartial grounds, the practice of favouring loved ones, though grounding a friend's claim in the general good may misdescribe it.

option_rationales.A: The impartialist reply described explicitly denies 'that each act of favouritism must be weighed against strangers' claims'.
option_rationales.C: This is the critics' inference, which the paragraph blocks: it grants that friendship is partial but denies that partiality is 'therefore unjustified' on impartial grounds.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph uses this comparison to justify partiality within an impartial framework, where strangers' interests still count equally; denying any reason to care about strangers reverses that.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the impartial view, the critics' objection, and an impartialist reply: justify partiality 'at the level of the practice' by appeal to the general good, without weighing each act. It then names the reply's cost. The correct answer states the reply and its cost.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the critics' option because the paragraph says 'The critics are right that friendship involves partiality', and missing that it rejects their conclusion.
questions.difficulty_reason: Three positions are in play (theory, critics, reply) and the reply's cost must be kept; wrong options each present one stage as the conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Preferring anonymous gifts confuses evidence of motive with the value of a gift.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is often said that a gift made anonymously is morally superior to one made publicly, since the anonymous donor cannot be seeking praise and so must be acting from pure generosity. The reasoning confuses evidence with value. Anonymity can be good evidence that a donor is not after recognition, but a public donor is not thereby shown to be after it, and even a donor who enjoys the praise may give for reasons that are mostly good. More importantly, the recipients are fed and housed just the same either way, and a well-publicised gift may persuade others to give, multiplying its effect. There may be cases where anonymity matters, as when publicity would humiliate the person helped. But as a general ranking, the preference for anonymous giving judges a gift by what it reveals about the giver rather than by what it does.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
