There may be cases where anonymity matters, as when publicity would humiliate the person helped. But as a general ranking, the preference for anonymous giving judges a gift by what it reveals about the giver rather than by what it does.

options.A: Anonymous giving is preferable only when publicity would humiliate the people being helped, which is the one case where the donor's motive really matters morally.
options.B: Donors who give anonymously are no more generous than those who give publicly, since everyone who gives to charity enjoys receiving at least some praise for doing so.
options.C: Ranking anonymous gifts higher confuses evidence of motive with a gift's worth; public gifts help recipients equally and may inspire others, though anonymity sometimes protects recipients.
options.D: Public gifts are morally better than anonymous ones, because they encourage other people to give and so multiply the good that each donation does for those in need.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Ranking anonymous gifts higher confuses evidence of motive with a gift's worth; public gifts help recipients equally and may inspire others, though anonymity sometimes protects recipients.

option_rationales.A: The humiliation case concerns harm to the recipient, not the donor's motive, and the paragraph says 'There may be cases', not that this is the only one.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says anonymity 'can be good evidence' of not seeking recognition, and it never claims every donor enjoys praise.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph rejects the general ranking of anonymous over public giving; it does not set up the reverse ranking, and it allows that anonymity sometimes matters.

questions.explanation: The paragraph diagnoses the reasoning ('confuses evidence with value'), argues that recipients benefit equally and publicity may multiply giving, allows exceptions such as humiliation, and concludes that the ranking judges a gift by what it reveals rather than what it does. The correct answer carries the diagnosis, the reasons and the exception.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reverse ranking because the paragraph mentions that publicity can multiply giving.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph rejects a ranking without inverting it; the tempting wrong option inverts it.

questions.subtopic: Exceptions show moral rules are not absolute, not that they are dispensable, since presumptions have value.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Moral rules such as 'do not lie' or 'keep your promises' are often attacked by pointing to exceptions: surely one may lie to save a life, or break a trivial promise to help someone in danger. If a rule has exceptions, the argument runs, it was never really a rule, and we should simply weigh consequences case by case. But the existence of exceptions shows less than this suggests. A rule can be a strong presumption, one that sets the burden of argument and holds unless something weighty overrides it, and such presumptions are valuable precisely because case-by-case weighing is slow, prone to self-serving bias and impossible for others to rely on. Someone who keeps promises only when calculation favours it is not a person others can plan around. The exceptions show that rules are not absolute; they do not show that rules are dispensable.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Moral rules such as 'do not lie' or 'keep your promises' are often attacked by pointing to exceptions: surely one may lie to save a life, or break a trivial promise to help someone in danger. If a rule has exceptions, the argument runs, it was never really a rule, and we should simply weigh consequences case by case. But the existence of exceptions shows less than this suggests. Someone who keeps promises only when calculation favours it is not a person others can plan around. The exceptions show that rules are not absolute; they do not show that rules are dispensable.

options.A: Exceptions show only that moral rules are not absolute, not that they are dispensable, since as strong presumptions they guard against slow, self-serving case-by-case judgement and make people reliable.
options.B: Case-by-case moral judgement is always self-serving, so people should keep to moral rules even in emergencies where breaking a rule would save a life.
options.C: Moral rules such as keeping promises must be followed without exception, because a person who breaks one even once to help someone can never again be relied on by others.
options.D: Since one may lie to save a life, moral rules are really summaries of past calculations, and in each new case we should weigh the consequences afresh.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Exceptions show only that moral rules are not absolute, not that they are dispensable, since as strong presumptions they guard against slow, self-serving case-by-case judgement and make people reliable.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says such judgement is 'prone to' bias, not always biased, and it accepts lying to save a life as a legitimate exception.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph grants that rules 'are not absolute' and accepts the exceptions; it says only that someone who keeps promises only when calculation favours it is unreliable.
option_rationales.D: This is the attack the paragraph reports and rejects; it argues that case-by-case weighing is slow, biased and impossible to rely on.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports an argument from exceptions to case-by-case weighing, then replies that rules can be strong presumptions whose value lies in avoiding slow, biased and unpredictable judgement. Its last sentence distinguishes 'not absolute' from 'dispensable'. The correct answer keeps the distinction and the reason.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the absolutist option because the paragraph defends rules, and missing that it concedes they have exceptions.
questions.difficulty_reason: The answer turns on the distinction between 'not absolute' and 'dispensable'; one wrong option collapses it in each direction.

questions.subtopic: Consent given under desperate conditions counts, but cannot by itself justify the terms.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Consent is usually treated as transforming what would otherwise be wrong into something permissible: the surgeon's knife, the borrowed car, the signed contract. But the transforming power of consent depends on the conditions under which it is given. A worker who accepts dangerous conditions because the alternative is destitution has agreed, in a sense, and it would be odd to say his signature means nothing. Yet when one party can set the terms and the other can only take them or starve, the agreement shows mainly that the worker preferred this bargain to disaster, not that the terms were fair. To treat such consent as settling the matter is to let the stronger party borrow the moral authority of a free choice that was barely available. Consent remains important; it simply cannot do all the justifying work on its own.

To treat such consent as settling the matter is to let the stronger party borrow the moral authority of a free choice that was barely available. Consent remains important; it simply cannot do all the justifying work on its own.

options.A: Agreements made by workers facing destitution are not real consent at all, and contracts signed under such pressure ought to be treated by the courts as void and unenforceable.
options.B: Consent's power to permit depends on its conditions: agreement forced by desperation shows a preference over disaster, not fairness, so it counts but cannot justify the terms alone.
options.C: Consent always turns what would otherwise be wrong into something permissible, provided the person agreeing understands the terms and signs them of their own accord.
options.D: Employers who offer dangerous work to desperate people act wrongly, and the state should set minimum safety standards that no contract between them may lower.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Consent's power to permit depends on its conditions: agreement forced by desperation shows a preference over disaster, not fairness, so it counts but cannot justify the terms alone.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says it 'would be odd to say his signature means nothing' and that consent 'remains important'; courts and voiding contracts are not discussed.
option_rationales.C: This restates the usual view that the paragraph qualifies; it argues that consent's power 'depends on the conditions', including the alternatives available.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph makes no prescription about safety standards and does not condemn such employers outright; it argues about what consent can justify.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states the common view of consent, qualifies it (power depends on conditions), grants the worker's consent some weight, and concludes that consent extracted under desperation shows preference over disaster rather than fairness, so it cannot justify on its own. The correct answer keeps the qualification and both halves of the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'not real consent' option, which overstates the critique and ignores the concession about the signature.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer must hold a concession and a limit together; the tempting wrong option drops the concession.

questions.subtopic: Confidentiality serves the public by making disclosure possible, which is also why it yields to serious harm.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Professionals such as doctors and counsellors are bound to keep what their clients tell them confidential, and the duty is sometimes criticised as protecting secrets at others' expense. The criticism misunderstands its purpose. People disclose embarrassing symptoms, private fears and past mistakes only when they trust that the information will go no further, and without such disclosure the professional cannot help them, or help protect others from them. Confidentiality therefore serves the public as well as the client. This is also why the duty is not absolute: where keeping a secret would expose someone to serious and imminent harm, the reason for the duty, which was to make help possible, no longer supports silence.

This is also why the duty is not absolute: where keeping a secret would expose someone to serious and imminent harm, the reason for the duty, which was to make help possible, no longer supports silence.

options.A: Doctors and counsellors keep their clients' secrets mainly to protect their own reputations, which is why the duty of confidentiality is criticised as working against the public.
options.B: Clients tell doctors and counsellors about embarrassing symptoms and private fears only when they trust that the information will be kept from everyone else.
options.C: The duty of confidentiality must never be broken, since clients will stop telling professionals the truth as soon as they fear that their secrets may be revealed.
options.D: Confidentiality serves the public as well as clients by enabling disclosures that make help possible, which is why it yields when silence would permit serious, imminent harm.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Confidentiality serves the public as well as clients by enabling disclosures that make help possible, which is why it yields when silence would permit serious, imminent harm.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph never mentions professionals' reputations; it says the duty exists to make help possible.
option_rationales.B: This is a premise of the argument; it leaves out the conclusions that the duty serves the public and that it has limits.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the duty 'is not absolute' and gives way to serious and imminent harm, so an exceptionless duty contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph answers a criticism: confidentiality enables disclosure, disclosure enables help, so the duty serves the public too; and because its purpose is to make help possible, it yields when silence would cause serious harm. The correct answer gives both the purpose and the limit that follows from it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'never broken' option because the paragraph defends confidentiality, missing its final limit.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument and its limit are each signalled ('therefore', 'This is also why').

questions.subtopic: Forgetting forces the memory theory of identity into a repair that concedes identity rests on wider continuity.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A popular answer to the question of what makes someone the same person over time is memory: I am the person who did the things I can remember doing. The view has real appeal, since it explains why amnesia seems to threaten the self in a way that losing a limb does not. But it struggles with ordinary forgetting. I remember nothing of being two years old, yet I do not think the toddler in the old photographs was someone else. Defenders reply that a chain of overlapping memories, each linking to the one before, is enough. That repair helps, but it quietly concedes the original point: it is not remembering that makes me the same person, but something continuous of which remembering is only one part.

options.A: Because adults cannot remember their earliest years, the memory account wrongly implies that each of us was once a quite different person from the one we are now.
options.B: Memory plays no real part in what makes a person the same over time, as the cases of amnesia and of childhood forgetting both clearly demonstrate to us.
options.C: A chain of overlapping memories, each linked to the one before it, fully rescues the memory account from the objection that people forget their early childhood.
options.D: The memory account of identity appeals, but ordinary forgetting forces a repair conceding that identity rests on a wider continuity, of which memory is only one strand.

questions.correct_answer: (D) The memory account of identity appeals, but ordinary forgetting forces a repair conceding that identity rests on a wider continuity, of which memory is only one strand.

option_rationales.A: This states only the objection from forgetting; it leaves out the reply about overlapping memories and the conclusion that identity rests on 'something continuous of which remembering is only one part'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says memory is 'only one part' of what makes me the same person, not no part, and it uses amnesia to show the view's appeal, not to refute it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the repair 'helps' but 'quietly concedes the original point'; saying it fully rescues the account reverses the author's verdict.

questions.explanation: The paragraph states the memory view, grants its appeal, raises the problem of forgetting, considers the overlapping-chain reply and concludes that the reply gives the game away: identity depends on a broader continuity, with memory 'only one part'. The correct answer keeps all three steps and the final qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the option that restates the forgetting objection and missing the final turn, or treating the repair as a success.
questions.difficulty_reason: The argument turns once, in the last sentence, and each wrong option misstates a single clearly signposted step.

questions.subtopic: Arguments about taste cannot compel enjoyment but are worthwhile because they redirect attention.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is often said that there is no disputing about taste, and in one sense this is right: no argument will make someone enjoy a dish they find bitter. Yet people argue about taste constantly, and not pointlessly. When a friend explains what to listen for in a piece of music, or why a film's slow opening earns its later payoff, she is not trying to overrule my pleasure by decree. She is directing my attention to features I may have missed, so that my next response is better informed. Such arguments cannot compel agreement, but they can change what there is to respond to. Taste is not beyond reason; it is simply reached by reasons of a different kind, ones that work by showing rather than by proving.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is often said that there is no disputing about taste, and in one sense this is right: no argument will make someone enjoy a dish they find bitter. Yet people argue about taste constantly, and not pointlessly. When a friend explains what to listen for in a piece of music, or why a film's slow opening earns its later payoff, she is not trying to overrule my pleasure by decree. She is directing my attention to features I may have missed, so that my next response is better informed. Such arguments cannot compel agreement, but they can change what there is to respond to. Taste is not beyond reason; it is simply reached by reasons of a different kind, ones that work by showing rather than by proving.

options.A: Well-informed critics can, with enough patient explanation, eventually bring other people round to agreeing with their judgements about which films and music are good.
options.B: Argument cannot force anyone to enjoy something, yet disputes about taste remain worthwhile, because they draw attention to overlooked features and persuade by showing rather than by proof.
options.C: Since no argument can make anyone enjoy what they dislike, discussions about music or film are pointless exchanges of preference that reason is unable to touch.
options.D: A slow opening in a film can be justified by the payoff it earns later, which an attentive viewer gradually learns to notice and to appreciate.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Argument cannot force anyone to enjoy something, yet disputes about taste remain worthwhile, because they draw attention to overlooked features and persuade by showing rather than by proof.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says such arguments 'cannot compel agreement'; their value lies in informing a response, not in producing eventual agreement with the critic.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says people argue about taste 'not pointlessly' and that taste 'is not beyond reason', so this reverses its conclusion.
option_rationales.D: This is one of the paragraph's examples; it leaves out the general claim about arguing over taste and the distinction between showing and proving.

questions.explanation: The paragraph concedes that argument cannot compel enjoyment, then argues that aesthetic disputes still have a point: they direct attention to features one missed, working 'by showing rather than by proving'. The correct answer keeps the concession and the main claim.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about critics winning agreement, which sounds like a defence of aesthetic argument but contradicts 'cannot compel agreement'.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option defends argument about taste in the wrong way (as producing agreement), so the reader must notice how the paragraph limits what such argument achieves.

questions.subtopic: Respecting choices is often evidence of a person's welfare, not merely a price paid for liberty.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Critics of paternalism usually frame the issue as a contest between welfare and freedom: the state may make you better off, but only by overriding your choices. This framing concedes too much to the paternalist and too little to the person. It assumes that we already know what is good for someone independently of what they would choose, so that the only question is whether to impose it. In many cases we do not. Whether a risky career, a strict diet or a dangerous hobby serves a person's welfare depends partly on the plans and commitments that give their life its shape, and these are often visible only in their choices. Respecting someone's decisions is therefore not merely a price paid for liberty; it is frequently our best evidence of what their welfare actually is.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

This framing concedes too much to the paternalist and too little to the person. It assumes that we already know what is good for someone independently of what they would choose, so that the only question is whether to impose it. In many cases we do not. Whether a risky career, a strict diet or a dangerous hobby serves a person's welfare depends partly on the plans and commitments that give their life its shape, and these are often visible only in their choices. Respecting someone's decisions is therefore not merely a price paid for liberty; it is frequently our best evidence of what their welfare actually is.

options.A: Since only individuals can know what is good for them, any attempt by the state to protect people from their own choices is bound to leave them worse off.
options.B: Respecting people's decisions matters chiefly because liberty is a value weighty enough to justify the losses in welfare that free choices sometimes bring about.
options.C: The welfare-versus-freedom contest misleads: what benefits people often depends on their own commitments, so their choices frequently reveal their welfare rather than compete with it.
options.D: Paternalism forces a hard choice between making people better off and leaving them free, and its critics rightly hold that freedom should usually win that contest.

questions.correct_answer: (C) The welfare-versus-freedom contest misleads: what benefits people often depends on their own commitments, so their choices frequently reveal their welfare rather than compete with it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph hedges throughout ('In many cases', 'often', 'frequently'); it does not claim that only the individual can know their good or that every protective measure fails.
option_rationales.B: The last sentence says respecting decisions is 'not merely a price paid for liberty'; treating it as a price paid in welfare is exactly what the author denies.
option_rationales.D: This is the framing the author rejects in the second sentence as conceding 'too much to the paternalist', so it presents the criticised view as the author's own.

questions.explanation: The author rejects the welfare-versus-freedom framing because it assumes welfare can be known apart from choice. Since a person's good often depends on their own plans, which show up in their choices, respecting those choices is often evidence about welfare. The correct answer keeps the rejection, the reason and the hedge ('frequently').
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the liberty-as-a-price option, which defends autonomy in the conventional way the paragraph sets out to replace.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options state familiar anti-paternalist positions; only a reader who sees that the author rejects the trade-off framing itself can separate them from the correct answer.

questions.subtopic: Relativism cannot ground tolerance because urging tolerance everywhere assumes a universal standard.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Moral relativism is often defended as the natural ally of tolerance: if no culture's values are truer than another's, no one has grounds to impose their own. The alliance is less secure than it looks. If all values are merely local, then tolerance itself is just one local value among others, with no more claim on a culture that rejects it than the custom of eating with chopsticks has on a culture that uses forks. The relativist who tells an intolerant society that it ought to be tolerant is appealing to exactly the kind of cross-cultural standard that relativism denies. Tolerance, it seems, needs at least one value that holds everywhere; it cannot rest on the claim that none does.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

If all values are merely local, then tolerance itself is just one local value among others, with no more claim on a culture that rejects it than the custom of eating with chopsticks has on a culture that uses forks. The relativist who tells an intolerant society that it ought to be tolerant is appealing to exactly the kind of cross-cultural standard that relativism denies. Tolerance, it seems, needs at least one value that holds everywhere; it cannot rest on the claim that none does.

options.A: Relativism cannot support tolerance as its defenders hope, because urging tolerance on every society presupposes the very universal standard that relativism says does not exist.
options.B: Because no culture's values are truer than another's, every society has good reason to tolerate practices that differ from its own customs and beliefs.
options.C: Since relativism undermines tolerance, every society should adopt a single universal moral code and require all cultures to live by its rules and values.
options.D: Tolerance is a merely local value, comparable to a custom such as eating with chopsticks, and so it carries no special weight for societies that reject it.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Relativism cannot support tolerance as its defenders hope, because urging tolerance on every society presupposes the very universal standard that relativism says does not exist.

option_rationales.B: This is the relativist defence of tolerance that the author says is 'less secure than it looks', so it reverses the author's position.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph claims only that tolerance needs 'at least one value that holds everywhere'; it proposes no single code and no enforcement on all cultures.
option_rationales.D: This describes what tolerance would be if relativism were true, a consequence the author uses to attack relativism, not a view the author holds.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that relativism undercuts the tolerance it is meant to support: if all values are local, so is tolerance, and urging it on others appeals to a 'cross-cultural standard'. The correct answer states this self-defeat and keeps the scope (it is about grounding tolerance).
questions.common_misconception: Taking the chopsticks comparison, which describes the relativist's predicament, as the author's own claim about tolerance.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option repeats the paragraph's own words about tolerance being local, and the reader must see that it is a reductio, not a conclusion.

questions.subtopic: Expert intuition is reliable only where environments are regular and feedback is quick.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Experienced firefighters, chess players and nurses often make good decisions in seconds without being able to say why. It is tempting to conclude that intuition is a general gift that grows with years in any job. But intuition is learned pattern recognition, and it can only be learned where there are patterns to recognise and where mistakes are quickly revealed. A chess position either loses or it does not, and the player soon finds out. A long-range political forecaster or a stock picker works in a world that is noisy and slow to give feedback, and years of experience there can produce confidence without producing skill.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
