It is tempting to conclude that intuition is a general gift that grows with years in any job. But intuition is learned pattern recognition, and it can only be learned where there are patterns to recognise and where mistakes are quickly revealed. A chess position either loses or it does not, and the player soon finds out. A long-range political forecaster or a stock picker works in a world that is noisy and slow to give feedback, and years of experience there can produce confidence without producing skill.

options.A: Intuition is learned pattern recognition, so it becomes reliable only where situations are regular and mistakes show up quickly; elsewhere long experience may breed confidence without skill.
options.B: Intuition cannot be trusted in any profession, because even highly experienced experts who decide quickly are seldom able to explain the reasons behind their judgements.
options.C: Chess players develop dependable intuitions because every position either loses or does not, so players quickly discover which of their moves were mistakes.
options.D: Intuition is a general gift that steadily improves with years of experience, which explains why seasoned professionals in every field, from nursing to finance, decide well.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Intuition is learned pattern recognition, so it becomes reliable only where situations are regular and mistakes show up quickly; elsewhere long experience may breed confidence without skill.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph opens by saying firefighters, chess players and nurses 'often make good decisions' by intuition, so it does not distrust intuition everywhere.
option_rationales.C: This is only the supporting example; it omits the general condition and the contrast with forecasters and stock pickers.
option_rationales.D: This is the conclusion the paragraph calls 'tempting' and then rejects with 'But'; the stock picker example shows experience need not bring skill.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the idea that intuition grows with experience in any job and states the condition for it: patterns to learn and quick feedback on mistakes. Chess meets the condition; forecasting does not. The correct answer gives the condition and the consequence where it fails.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'general gift' option because the paragraph begins by praising intuitive experts.
questions.difficulty_reason: The turn is marked by 'But' and the wrong options are an overstatement, the rejected view and a single example.

questions.subtopic: Bystanders in crowds help less because of misread cues and diffused responsibility, not callousness.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When someone collapses on a crowded street, each passer-by is less likely to help than a person who comes upon the same victim alone. This is often read as evidence that crowds make people callous, but the mechanism looks less like indifference than like confusion. In a crowd, everyone checks everyone else's face for cues, and since each person is trying to look calm, the crowd as a whole seems to signal that nothing is wrong. Responsibility is also spread thinly: if many people could act, no one feels that the duty is specifically theirs. Where a single onlooker is singled out, say by being pointed at and asked to call for help, the effect largely disappears.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When someone collapses on a crowded street, each passer-by is less likely to help than a person who comes upon the same victim alone. This is often read as evidence that crowds make people callous, but the mechanism looks less like indifference than like confusion. In a crowd, everyone checks everyone else's face for cues, and since each person is trying to look calm, the crowd as a whole seems to signal that nothing is wrong. Responsibility is also spread thinly: if many people could act, no one feels that the duty is specifically theirs. Where a single onlooker is singled out, say by being pointed at and asked to call for help, the effect largely disappears.

options.A: Crowds tend to make individuals callous towards strangers, so a victim who collapses in a busy street is less likely to get help than one who is found alone.
options.B: Passers-by in a crowd deliberately pretend to stay calm so that they can avoid the trouble of helping, leaving each victim to be rescued by somebody else.
options.C: People in crowds help less not chiefly from indifference but because they misread one another's calm and feel responsibility spread thin; singling one out largely restores help.
options.D: Anyone who collapses in a public place ought to point at one particular onlooker and ask that person for help, rather than appealing to the crowd in general.

questions.correct_answer: (C) People in crowds help less not chiefly from indifference but because they misread one another's calm and feel responsibility spread thin; singling one out largely restores help.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph mentions this reading only to reject it: the mechanism 'looks less like indifference than like confusion'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says people try to look calm and so mislead each other; it does not say they feign calm in order to avoid helping, which would bring back the callousness it rejects.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph explains why help fails and notes what removes the effect; it gives no advice to victims, and this option drops the explanation, which is its main point.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the callousness explanation and gives two mechanisms, misread cues and diffused responsibility, then supports them with the observation that singling someone out largely removes the effect. The correct answer carries the rejection, both mechanisms and the evidence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'deliberately pretend' option, which uses the paragraph's point about calm faces but turns confusion into evasion.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option reuses the calm-face detail but changes its motive, and another turns the closing observation into a prescription.

questions.subtopic: Waiting for a bigger reward may also reflect learned trust in promises, not only self-control.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Children who can wait for a larger treat rather than take a smaller one at once have long been held up as models of self-control, and their patience has been linked to later success. Yet waiting is rational only if the promised reward is likely to arrive. A child whose adults have reliably kept their word has good reason to wait; a child whose promises have often been broken has equally good reason to take what is on the table. In versions of the test where an adult first breaks a small promise to the child, waiting times tend to fall. None of this shows that self-control is unimportant. It does suggest that a measure taken to reveal a trait of character may also be recording what the child has learned about the world.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Children who can wait for a larger treat rather than take a smaller one at once have long been held up as models of self-control, and their patience has been linked to later success. Yet waiting is rational only if the promised reward is likely to arrive. A child whose adults have reliably kept their word has good reason to wait; a child whose promises have often been broken has equally good reason to take what is on the table. In versions of the test where an adult first breaks a small promise to the child, waiting times tend to fall. None of this shows that self-control is unimportant. It does suggest that a measure taken to reveal a trait of character may also be recording what the child has learned about the world.

options.A: Patience in the waiting test is better explained by a child's rational trust than by self-control, so the test's links with later success are probably illusory.
options.B: Children who can wait for a larger treat rather than accept a smaller one at once tend to be more successful in later life than those who cannot.
options.C: Children who learn to trust adults become more patient, so parents who reliably keep their promises will raise children who go on to succeed in later life.
options.D: A child's readiness to wait for a larger reward may partly reflect a sensible judgement about whether promises are kept, not only self-control, which still matters.

questions.correct_answer: (D) A child's readiness to wait for a larger reward may partly reflect a sensible judgement about whether promises are kept, not only self-control, which still matters.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the test 'may also be recording' learned trust and that self-control is not 'unimportant'; ranking trust above self-control and dismissing the links goes beyond it.
option_rationales.B: This restates the finding in the first sentence and leaves out the paragraph's qualification, which is its point.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph links trust to waiting in the test, but it never claims that trust produces later success; the chain to adult achievement is added.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (waiting is linked to later success), then qualifies how it is read: waiting is rational only if rewards arrive, and broken promises reduce waiting. It explicitly keeps self-control in the picture. The correct answer gives the qualification at the right strength (partly, not only).
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'better explained by a child's rational trust' option, which captures the direction of the argument but overstates its strength.
questions.difficulty_reason: The correct answer and the strongest wrong option differ only in degree ('may partly reflect' versus 'better explained'), so the reader must track the paragraph's hedges.

questions.subtopic: The fuel-tank model of willpower is weaker than its fame; beliefs about effort may matter.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A popular idea holds that willpower is like a fuel tank: every decision drains it, so that by evening we are too depleted to resist temptation. The image is vivid, but the evidence for a simple reservoir has proved weaker than its fame suggests, and attempts to repeat some of the best-known experiments have produced smaller effects or none. Some studies suggest instead that expectations matter. People who believe that effort exhausts them tend to flag after demanding tasks, while those who see effort as energising flag less. Tiredness after a long day is real, but how much it governs our choices may depend partly on the story we tell ourselves about it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A popular idea holds that willpower is like a fuel tank: every decision drains it, so that by evening we are too depleted to resist temptation. The image is vivid, but the evidence for a simple reservoir has proved weaker than its fame suggests, and attempts to repeat some of the best-known experiments have produced smaller effects or none. Some studies suggest instead that expectations matter. People who believe that effort exhausts them tend to flag after demanding tasks, while those who see effort as energising flag less. Tiredness after a long day is real, but how much it governs our choices may depend partly on the story we tell ourselves about it.

options.A: Because each decision drains a limited store of willpower, people should make their most important choices early in the day, before that reserve runs low.
options.B: The notion that each decision drains a fixed store of willpower is weaker than its fame suggests; our depletion may depend partly on beliefs about effort.
options.C: Tiredness after a long working day is largely imaginary, and people who simply stop believing in it will find that effort no longer affects their self-control.
options.D: Several of the best-known experiments on willpower have since been repeated by other researchers, and the repetitions have generally found smaller effects or none.

questions.correct_answer: (B) The notion that each decision drains a fixed store of willpower is weaker than its fame suggests; our depletion may depend partly on beliefs about effort.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph casts doubt on the fuel-tank model, so advice built on it reverses the paragraph's point.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'Tiredness after a long day is real' and that beliefs matter only 'partly', so this overstates and contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: This is one piece of evidence; it leaves out the alternative account based on expectations and the closing qualification.

questions.explanation: The paragraph doubts the fuel-tank model, offers expectations as a partial alternative and keeps a qualification: tiredness is real. The correct answer captures the doubt and the hedged alternative.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'largely imaginary' option, which takes the role of belief too far.
questions.difficulty_reason: The wrong options are a reversal, an exaggeration contradicted by one sentence, and a single detail.

questions.subtopic: Small talk lets strangers safely test each other's goodwill; judging it by information misses its purpose.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Small talk is usually dismissed as the emptiest form of conversation: remarks about the weather or the traffic that convey nothing anyone did not already know. But to judge it by its information content is to mistake its purpose. When strangers exchange a few safe sentences, they are testing whether the other is friendly, cooperative and willing to follow shared rules, at almost no risk to either. The very predictability of the topics is what makes this possible, since a remark nobody could disagree with leaves room only for tone. Small talk is not a failed attempt at real conversation; it is often the means by which strangers decide whether to attempt one.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Small talk is usually dismissed as the emptiest form of conversation: remarks about the weather or the traffic that convey nothing anyone did not already know. But to judge it by its information content is to mistake its purpose. When strangers exchange a few safe sentences, they are testing whether the other is friendly, cooperative and willing to follow shared rules, at almost no risk to either. The very predictability of the topics is what makes this possible, since a remark nobody could disagree with leaves room only for tone. Small talk is not a failed attempt at real conversation; it is often the means by which strangers decide whether to attempt one.

options.A: Small talk is more informative than it seems, because remarks about the weather and traffic often tell strangers useful facts that they did not already know.
options.B: Small talk seems empty only when judged by the information it carries; its predictable topics let strangers safely gauge each other's goodwill before they risk a deeper conversation.
options.C: Remarks about the weather and the traffic are popular among strangers because nobody could reasonably disagree with them or take offence at what they say.
options.D: People ought to value small talk above serious conversation, since predictable remarks on safe subjects reveal far more about character than any discussion of ideas.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Small talk seems empty only when judged by the information it carries; its predictable topics let strangers safely gauge each other's goodwill before they risk a deeper conversation.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph accepts that such remarks convey 'nothing anyone did not already know'; its point is that information is the wrong measure.
option_rationales.C: This keeps the detail about safe topics but drops the paragraph's claim about what small talk is for, testing goodwill before real conversation.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph ranks nothing above serious conversation and gives no advice; it presents small talk as a step towards 'real conversation', not a superior substitute.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects judging small talk by its information and gives its real function: a low-risk test of the other person's goodwill, made possible by predictable topics, that often precedes real conversation. The correct answer states the rejection and the function.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'more informative' option, which defends small talk but on the very measure the paragraph says is mistaken.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options defend small talk, one by distorting its value and one by overstating it, so the reader must hold onto the exact function claimed.

questions.subtopic: One-sided bonds with media figures are usually harmless, becoming a problem when reciprocity is expected.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many people feel they know a television presenter or a radio host whom they have never met. Psychologists call these one-sided bonds parasocial relationships, and they were once treated as a sign of loneliness or confusion. Later research has painted a less alarming picture. For most people such attachments sit alongside ordinary friendships rather than replacing them, and they can offer comfort, a sense of routine and models of how to behave. The bond becomes a problem mainly when the listener or viewer begins to expect something in return, as if the familiarity ran in both directions.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many people feel they know a television presenter or a radio host whom they have never met. Psychologists call these one-sided bonds parasocial relationships, and they were once treated as a sign of loneliness or confusion. Later research has painted a less alarming picture. For most people such attachments sit alongside ordinary friendships rather than replacing them, and they can offer comfort, a sense of routine and models of how to behave. The bond becomes a problem mainly when the listener or viewer begins to expect something in return, as if the familiarity ran in both directions.

options.A: Attachments to media figures are healthier than ordinary friendships, because they supply comfort and routine without ever making demands on the people who form them.
options.B: Feeling close to a presenter one has never met is generally a sign of loneliness, since such attachments tend to replace real friendships with imagined ones.
options.C: Many viewers and listeners come to feel that they personally know the presenters of their favourite programmes, even though they have never actually met them.
options.D: One-sided attachments to media figures usually sit harmlessly beside real friendships and offer comfort and routine, becoming troublesome mainly when people expect the bond to be returned.

questions.correct_answer: (D) One-sided attachments to media figures usually sit harmlessly beside real friendships and offer comfort and routine, becoming troublesome mainly when people expect the bond to be returned.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph never compares such bonds favourably with friendships; it says they sit 'alongside' them, and it notes a way they can go wrong.
option_rationales.B: This is the older view the paragraph reports; it says later research found such bonds 'sit alongside ordinary friendships rather than replacing them'.
option_rationales.C: This restates the opening observation and omits what the paragraph says about whether such bonds are harmful.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports an older, alarmed view, replaces it with a milder one (such bonds coexist with friendships and have benefits) and adds a limit (trouble arises when reciprocity is expected). The correct answer has the milder view and the limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the loneliness option because it is mentioned with the technical term.
questions.difficulty_reason: The structure is old view, new view, limit, and each wrong option fails at one clearly stated point.

questions.subtopic: Fixed holidays coordinate shared leisure, a value to be weighed against the gains of flexibility.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Proposals to let workers choose their own days off, instead of observing fixed public holidays, sound like pure gains in freedom: each person rests when it suits them, and shops and offices need never close. What the proposal overlooks is that the value of a day off depends partly on who else has it. A free Tuesday spent alone while friends and family are at work is a different good from a holiday on which everyone is free together. Fixed holidays solve a coordination problem that individual choice cannot, by guaranteeing that leisure overlaps. Flexibility has real merits for people whose lives do not fit the common calendar, but it should be weighed against what is lost when shared time disappears.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Proposals to let workers choose their own days off, instead of observing fixed public holidays, sound like pure gains in freedom: each person rests when it suits them, and shops and offices need never close. What the proposal overlooks is that the value of a day off depends partly on who else has it. A free Tuesday spent alone while friends and family are at work is a different good from a holiday on which everyone is free together. Fixed holidays solve a coordination problem that individual choice cannot, by guaranteeing that leisure overlaps. Flexibility has real merits for people whose lives do not fit the common calendar, but it should be weighed against what is lost when shared time disappears.

options.A: Letting people choose their own days off is no simple gain in freedom, since common holidays make leisure shared, a value to weigh against flexibility.
options.B: Allowing each worker to choose when to rest would increase freedom for everyone, since shops and offices could stay open and nobody would be forced to stop.
options.C: Fixed holidays are preferable to flexible ones, because people value their rest more when it falls on the same days as the rest of their community.
options.D: Workers should never be allowed to choose their own days off, because rest has value only when it is taken at the same time as everybody else's.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Letting people choose their own days off is no simple gain in freedom, since common holidays make leisure shared, a value to weigh against flexibility.

option_rationales.B: This is the proposal as it first seems, when such plans 'sound like pure gains in freedom'; the paragraph's point is what this view overlooks.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph ends by saying flexibility 'should be weighed against' shared time; it does not declare fixed holidays the winner, so this drops the qualification.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says a day's value depends 'partly' on who else has it and grants that flexibility 'has real merits', so the words never and only go far beyond it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph corrects the view that flexible days off are a pure gain: shared leisure is a distinct good that only fixed holidays secure. It then concedes that flexibility has merits and asks for weighing. The correct answer keeps both the correction and the call to weigh.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'preferable' option, which agrees with the author's direction but turns a call to weigh costs into a verdict.
questions.difficulty_reason: The strongest wrong option is right about the value of shared time and wrong only in dropping the closing concession, a fine distinction of degree.

questions.subtopic: Heirlooms are valued for their history, which also makes them a burden when that history is unwelcome.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: An old wristwatch that no longer keeps time can be worth almost nothing on the market and still be the last thing a family would sell. Its value lies not in the object's properties, which a replica could match exactly, but in its history: it was on a grandfather's wrist, it was handed over at a particular moment. This is why a perfect copy feels like no substitute. Heirlooms work as anchors for memories that would otherwise have nothing to attach to, and they make the past something one can hold. The same feature, however, makes them a burden when the history they carry is one the inheritors would rather forget.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

An old wristwatch that no longer keeps time can be worth almost nothing on the market and still be the last thing a family would sell. Its value lies not in the object's properties, which a replica could match exactly, but in its history: it was on a grandfather's wrist, it was handed over at a particular moment. This is why a perfect copy feels like no substitute. Heirlooms work as anchors for memories that would otherwise have nothing to attach to, and they make the past something one can hold. The same feature, however, makes them a burden when the history they carry is one the inheritors would rather forget.

options.A: An old wristwatch that no longer keeps time may fetch very little if sold, yet families often refuse to part with such objects at almost any price.
options.B: Heirlooms are valued because they are rare and well made, qualities that a replica, however careful, can never fully reproduce for the family that owns them.
options.C: Heirlooms are prized for their history, not their physical qualities, so copies cannot replace them; that tie can also make them a burden when the past is unwelcome.
options.D: Families ought to keep every object handed down to them by earlier generations, since heirlooms are the only reliable way of preserving the memory of the dead.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Heirlooms are prized for their history, not their physical qualities, so copies cannot replace them; that tie can also make them a burden when the past is unwelcome.

option_rationales.A: This restates the opening example and leaves out the explanation (history, not properties) and the closing qualification.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the object's properties are ones 'a replica could match exactly'; it locates the value in history, so this contradicts it.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph gives no such advice and calls heirlooms one way of anchoring memory, not the only one; it even notes they can be a burden.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains an heirloom's value by its history rather than its properties, which is why copies fail, and then qualifies: the same link to the past can make it a burden. The correct answer keeps the explanation and the qualification.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'rare and well made' option because it also explains why copies fail, though for the wrong reason.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option offers a rival explanation of the same fact (copies do not satisfy), so the reader must identify which reason the paragraph gives.

questions.subtopic: Standard time arose from railway timetabling needs rather than a wish for uniformity.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Before the railways, most towns kept their own time, setting their clocks by the sun as it passed overhead, so that noon in one town fell some minutes after noon in a town to its east. For travellers on horseback this hardly mattered. Trains changed that. A timetable that had to coordinate departures across many towns could not work with dozens of local noons, and railway companies began to run on a single standard time. Towns gradually followed, at first for convenience and later by law. A change that now seems natural was driven less by any wish for uniformity than by the practical demands of a new technology.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Before the railways, most towns kept their own time, setting their clocks by the sun as it passed overhead, so that noon in one town fell some minutes after noon in a town to its east. For travellers on horseback this hardly mattered. Trains changed that. A timetable that had to coordinate departures across many towns could not work with dozens of local noons, and railway companies began to run on a single standard time. Towns gradually followed, at first for convenience and later by law. A change that now seems natural was driven less by any wish for uniformity than by the practical demands of a new technology.

options.A: Before the railways, each town set its clocks by the passing sun, so that noon arrived slightly later in towns lying to the west of their neighbours.
options.B: Local solar time served until railways needed timetables coordinated across many towns; standard time grew more from that practical need than from any desire for uniformity.
options.C: Railway companies were the most powerful institutions of their age, able to force towns and governments to accept any rules that they found convenient.
options.D: Governments imposed a single standard time on towns because they wanted the whole country to keep uniform hours, and the railway companies reluctantly followed.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Local solar time served until railways needed timetables coordinated across many towns; standard time grew more from that practical need than from any desire for uniformity.

option_rationales.A: This repeats the opening background and leaves out the change and its cause, which is the paragraph's point.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says towns followed 'at first for convenience', not under compulsion, and says nothing about the general power of railway companies.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph reverses this order: railway companies adopted standard time first, towns followed, and law came later; it denies that uniformity was the motive.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why standard time replaced local solar time: railway timetables could not work with many local noons, so railways adopted one time and towns followed. The last sentence names the cause as practical demand, not a wish for uniformity. The correct answer states both.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the government option, which reflects a common assumption that standard time was imposed from above.
questions.difficulty_reason: The cause is stated outright in the last sentence, and the wrong options are a reversal, background and an exaggeration.

questions.subtopic: Federalism allows instructive variety, but its lessons are harder to read and less heeded than the laboratory image implies.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Federal systems are often praised as laboratories: because each state or province can try its own policy, the country can watch what works and copy it. The metaphor flatters the arrangement. A laboratory controls its conditions, but states differ in wealth, population and history, so a policy that succeeds in one may fail elsewhere for reasons that have nothing to do with its design. Nor do governments behave like disinterested scientists; a successful reform is as likely to be ignored for partisan reasons as copied for its results. Decentralisation does allow variety, and variety can teach. But the lessons are harder to read, and less often heeded, than the laboratory image implies.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Federal systems are often praised as laboratories: because each state or province can try its own policy, the country can watch what works and copy it. The metaphor flatters the arrangement. A laboratory controls its conditions, but states differ in wealth, population and history, so a policy that succeeds in one may fail elsewhere for reasons that have nothing to do with its design. Nor do governments behave like disinterested scientists; a successful reform is as likely to be ignored for partisan reasons as copied for its results. Decentralisation does allow variety, and variety can teach. But the lessons are harder to read, and less often heeded, than the laboratory image implies.

options.A: Policies tried in one state rarely work in another, so reforms are better designed at the national level than tested locally and copied elsewhere.
options.B: Since states differ in wealth and history and governments act from partisan motives, nothing of value can be learned by comparing policies across a federal system.
options.C: Federalism permits policy variety that can be instructive, but differing local conditions and partisan motives make its lessons harder to read and less often acted on than the laboratory image suggests.
options.D: Federal systems let each state test its own policies, so that the country as a whole can observe which reforms succeed and then adopt them more widely.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Federalism permits policy variety that can be instructive, but differing local conditions and partisan motives make its lessons harder to read and less often acted on than the laboratory image suggests.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says a policy 'may fail elsewhere', not that it rarely works, and it recommends no national alternative; both the degree and the prescription are added.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph concedes that 'variety can teach'; its claim is that the lessons are harder to read, not that there are none.
option_rationales.D: This is the 'laboratory' praise the paragraph says 'flatters the arrangement', so it presents the criticised view as the conclusion.

questions.explanation: The paragraph criticises the laboratory metaphor on two grounds, uncontrolled differences between states and partisan politics, then concedes that variety can teach before concluding that its lessons are harder to read and less heeded. The correct answer keeps the concession, both grounds and the comparative conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'nothing of value can be learned' option, which follows the criticism but ignores the concession in the penultimate sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph's conclusion is comparative and hedged; the wrong options fail by deleting the concession, restating the rejected metaphor, or inflating 'may' into 'rarely' with an added remedy.

questions.subtopic: Early coins announced a ruler's authority as well as serving as money.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Coins are usually studied as tools of exchange, but for many early states they were just as much instruments of announcement. A ruler's face on a coin travelled to markets the ruler would never visit, carried by people who might never see a proclamation or a soldier. Every transaction quietly repeated the claim that this authority stood behind the value in one's hand. That is one reason why new regimes so often hurried to strike their own coins, even when the old ones worked perfectly well as money. To read coins only for their weight and purity is to miss half of what they were for.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Coins are usually studied as tools of exchange, but for many early states they were just as much instruments of announcement. A ruler's face on a coin travelled to markets the ruler would never visit, carried by people who might never see a proclamation or a soldier. Every transaction quietly repeated the claim that this authority stood behind the value in one's hand. That is one reason why new regimes so often hurried to strike their own coins, even when the old ones worked perfectly well as money. To read coins only for their weight and purity is to miss half of what they were for.

options.A: Early coins mattered far more as political symbols than as money, and their weight and purity were of little real concern to the ordinary people who used them every day.
options.B: New regimes often struck fresh coins of their own even though the coins already in circulation still worked perfectly well as a means of exchange.
options.C: Early rulers relied on coins rather than soldiers or proclamations to govern distant markets, since money alone could enforce their authority there.
options.D: Besides serving as money, coins in early states carried a ruler's claim to authority into everyday transactions, which helps explain why new regimes hurried to mint their own.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Besides serving as money, coins in early states carried a ruler's claim to authority into everyday transactions, which helps explain why new regimes hurried to mint their own.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says coins were 'just as much' instruments of announcement and that reading only weight and purity misses 'half'; it does not rank symbolism above money.
option_rationales.B: This restates the supporting observation without the explanation that coins announced authority, which is the paragraph's main claim.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says coins announced or repeated a claim of authority; it does not say they replaced soldiers or enforced rule.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that early coins had a second function besides exchange: they announced a ruler's authority wherever they circulated, which explains why new regimes struck their own. The correct answer keeps both functions and the explanatory link.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'far more as political symbols' option, which overstates the paragraph's 'just as much' and 'half'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option differs from the correct answer in degree, and another turns announcing into enforcing.

questions.subtopic: Colonial tax surveys simplified layered land rights and, by becoming law, reshaped them.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Surveys of land are often presented as neutral exercises in measurement, but when colonial administrations mapped farmland, they were rarely just recording what was there. To tax land, a state needs to know who is responsible for each plot, and so surveyors assigned single owners to fields that had been held under layered arrangements: a cultivator, a family with rights to part of the harvest, a village with rights to graze after the crop was taken in. Once written down, the simplified version became the legal one, and the rights left off the record weakened over time. The map did not merely describe the land; it helped remake the claims to it.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Surveys of land are often presented as neutral exercises in measurement, but when colonial administrations mapped farmland, they were rarely just recording what was there. To tax land, a state needs to know who is responsible for each plot, and so surveyors assigned single owners to fields that had been held under layered arrangements: a cultivator, a family with rights to part of the harvest, a village with rights to graze after the crop was taken in. Once written down, the simplified version became the legal one, and the rights left off the record weakened over time. The map did not merely describe the land; it helped remake the claims to it.

options.A: Colonial land surveys, made for taxation, recorded single owners where rights had been layered, and by becoming the legal record they reshaped the very claims they appeared to describe.
options.B: Colonial administrations deliberately designed their land surveys to strip villagers of grazing rights and to hand farmland over to a few favoured owners.
options.C: Before colonial surveys, a single field might be subject to several rights at once, held by a cultivator, a family and the surrounding village.
options.D: Because surveyors measured each field precisely, colonial land records gave an accurate and complete picture of who held rights to each plot at the time the records were made.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Colonial land surveys, made for taxation, recorded single owners where rights had been layered, and by becoming the legal record they reshaped the very claims they appeared to describe.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph traces the simplification to the needs of taxation, not to a design to dispossess; deliberate intent is added.
option_rationales.C: This gives the background example but leaves out what the surveys did to those rights, which is the paragraph's point.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says surveys were 'rarely just recording what was there' and replaced layered rights with single owners, so the records were not accurate pictures of rights.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that tax-driven surveys did more than measure: they simplified layered rights into single ownership, and once that version became law the omitted rights weakened. The correct answer keeps the cause (taxation), the simplification and the effect.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'deliberately designed' option, which reads a critical paragraph as an accusation of intent it does not make.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option matches the paragraph's critical tone but changes a structural cause into a motive.

questions.subtopic: Insurance can reduce care, so insurers leave some of the loss with policyholders.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Insurance protects people from losses they cannot control, but it can also change how carefully they behave. Someone whose bicycle is fully insured may leave it unlocked for a few minutes longer than they otherwise would, not out of dishonesty but because the cost of a theft has shifted to someone else. Insurers know this, and they rarely offer complete cover. Deductibles, which require the policyholder to bear the first part of any loss, and discounts for fitting locks or alarms keep some of the cost with the insured person, so that they keep an interest in avoiding the loss.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Insurance protects people from losses they cannot control, but it can also change how carefully they behave. Someone whose bicycle is fully insured may leave it unlocked for a few minutes longer than they otherwise would, not out of dishonesty but because the cost of a theft has shifted to someone else. Insurers know this, and they rarely offer complete cover. Deductibles, which require the policyholder to bear the first part of any loss, and discounts for fitting locks or alarms keep some of the cost with the insured person, so that they keep an interest in avoiding the loss.

options.A: Many people who buy insurance deliberately neglect their property in the hope of claiming compensation, which is why insurers insist on deductibles from all their customers.
options.B: Complete insurance cover is harmful to society and should be prohibited, since people who are fully protected against loss will take no care at all.
options.C: Bicycle owners who have fully insured their bicycles may leave them unlocked a little longer than owners who would have to bear the cost of a theft.
options.D: Insurance shifts the cost of a loss away from the insured and can make them less careful, so insurers leave part of that cost with policyholders.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Insurance shifts the cost of a loss away from the insured and can make them less careful, so insurers leave part of that cost with policyholders.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the change in behaviour is 'not out of dishonesty'; it is a response to a shifted cost, not a scheme to claim.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says insurance 'can' change behaviour slightly ('a few minutes longer'); it proposes no prohibition and does not say people take no care.
option_rationales.C: This is the illustration only; it leaves out the general mechanism and how insurers respond to it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains that insurance shifts costs and so can reduce care, and that insurers respond with deductibles and discounts that keep some cost with the insured. The correct answer states the effect and the response.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the dishonesty option, which mistakes a change in incentives for fraud.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph states its mechanism and the insurers' response plainly; the wrong options are a distortion, an example and an extreme prescription.

questions.subtopic: Unequal information can unravel a market without dishonesty; warranties and reputations repair it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: In a market for used cars, sellers know far more about their vehicles than buyers do. A buyer who cannot tell a sound car from a faulty one will offer only an average price, and that price is too low for owners of good cars, who are therefore more likely to keep them. As they withdraw, the average quality of the cars on offer falls, and buyers who sense this lower their offers further. The market does not need dishonest sellers to unravel in this way; it needs only an imbalance in what each side knows. Warranties, inspection reports and dealers with reputations to protect matter less as courtesies than as ways of restoring trade that would otherwise shrink.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

In a market for used cars, sellers know far more about their vehicles than buyers do. A buyer who cannot tell a sound car from a faulty one will offer only an average price, and that price is too low for owners of good cars, who are therefore more likely to keep them. As they withdraw, the average quality of the cars on offer falls, and buyers who sense this lower their offers further. The market does not need dishonest sellers to unravel in this way; it needs only an imbalance in what each side knows. Warranties, inspection reports and dealers with reputations to protect matter less as courtesies than as ways of restoring trade that would otherwise shrink.

options.A: Used-car markets shrink chiefly because sellers conceal faults from buyers, so laws that punish dishonest dealers are the most effective way of restoring trade.
options.B: When buyers cannot judge quality, average offers drive out sellers of good cars and trade can shrink even without dishonesty; warranties and reputations matter because they correct this imbalance.
options.C: Warranties and inspection reports are offered by sellers mainly as courtesies to reassure nervous buyers, though they do little to change the prices that cars fetch.
options.D: Owners of good used cars tend to keep them, because buyers who cannot tell good cars from bad will pay only an average price for any car offered.

questions.correct_answer: (B) When buyers cannot judge quality, average offers drive out sellers of good cars and trade can shrink even without dishonesty; warranties and reputations matter because they correct this imbalance.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the market 'does not need dishonest sellers to unravel'; the cause is unequal knowledge, and it proposes no laws.
option_rationales.C: The last sentence says these matter 'less as courtesies than as ways of restoring trade', so this reverses it.
option_rationales.D: This gives the first step of the mechanism but omits the spiral, the point that no dishonesty is needed, and the role of warranties and reputations.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a spiral: unable to judge quality, buyers offer average prices, good cars are withdrawn, quality and offers fall further. It stresses that unequal information alone is enough and that warranties and reputations restore trade. The correct answer has the mechanism, the point that dishonesty is not needed and the remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'owners of good used cars tend to keep them' option, which is true to the paragraph but only its first step.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option is accurate but partial, and the reader must see that the paragraph's point is the whole unravelling and its remedy.

questions.subtopic: Trade benefits even an all-round efficient country through relative cost, though not every group gains.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is sometimes argued that a country which can produce everything more efficiently than its neighbours has nothing to gain from trading with them. The intuition is natural and wrong. What matters for trade is not absolute efficiency but relative cost: what a country gives up to make one good instead of another. Even a country that is better at everything will be much better at some things than at others, and it gains by concentrating on those and buying the rest. The argument does not, however, promise that everyone within each country gains; workers in the industries that shrink may lose, and whether they are compensated is a political question that the logic of trade does not settle.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is sometimes argued that a country which can produce everything more efficiently than its neighbours has nothing to gain from trading with them. The intuition is natural and wrong. What matters for trade is not absolute efficiency but relative cost: what a country gives up to make one good instead of another. Even a country that is better at everything will be much better at some things than at others, and it gains by concentrating on those and buying the rest. The argument does not, however, promise that everyone within each country gains; workers in the industries that shrink may lose, and whether they are compensated is a political question that the logic of trade does not settle.

options.A: Trade benefits even a country that is better at everything, because gains depend on relative rather than absolute cost, though this does not ensure that every group inside it benefits.
options.B: A country able to make every good more efficiently than its neighbours has little reason to trade with them, since it can meet all of its own needs more cheaply.
options.C: Even a country that is better at everything gains from trade, so opening its markets benefits its citizens as long as they concentrate on what they do best.
options.D: Because workers in shrinking industries lose from trade, governments are obliged to compensate them fully before opening their home markets to more efficient foreign producers.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Trade benefits even a country that is better at everything, because gains depend on relative rather than absolute cost, though this does not ensure that every group inside it benefits.

option_rationales.B: This is the intuition the paragraph calls 'natural and wrong', so it presents the rejected view as the conclusion.
option_rationales.C: This keeps the main claim but drops the qualification that workers in shrinking industries 'may lose'; it implies that citizens generally benefit, which the paragraph refuses to promise.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph calls compensation 'a political question that the logic of trade does not settle'; it imposes no obligation, so this adds a prescription.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the idea that an all-round efficient country gains nothing from trade, explains why (relative cost), and then limits the claim: gains for the country do not mean gains for every group, and compensation is left open. The correct answer keeps the main claim, its reason and the limit.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that states the main claim correctly but quietly extends it to all citizens, missing the closing qualification.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options are each half right: one keeps the main claim but loses the limit, the other keeps the limit but adds a duty the paragraph explicitly leaves open.

questions.subtopic: Unexpected inflation shifts wealth from lenders and savers to borrowers; foreseen inflation is priced in.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Inflation is usually described as a tax on everyone, eating away at the value of money, but its effects are far from even. A household that borrowed a fixed sum to buy a house repays the loan in money that is worth less each year, so unexpected inflation quietly transfers wealth from the lender to the borrower. Savers holding cash or fixed-interest bonds lose in the same way that borrowers gain. What matters is not just how fast prices rise but whether the rise was foreseen; lenders who expect inflation can demand higher interest in advance, and the transfer then largely disappears.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Inflation is usually described as a tax on everyone, eating away at the value of money, but its effects are far from even. A household that borrowed a fixed sum to buy a house repays the loan in money that is worth less each year, so unexpected inflation quietly transfers wealth from the lender to the borrower. Savers holding cash or fixed-interest bonds lose in the same way that borrowers gain. What matters is not just how fast prices rise but whether the rise was foreseen; lenders who expect inflation can demand higher interest in advance, and the transfer then largely disappears.

options.A: A household that took out a fixed loan to buy a house repays it in money that loses some of its value with each year that passes.
options.B: Borrowers always gain from rising prices at the expense of lenders, which is why households carrying large mortgages generally welcome any increase in inflation.
options.C: Inflation does not burden everyone equally: unexpected rises move wealth from lenders and savers to borrowers, whereas inflation that was foreseen can be built into interest rates.
options.D: Inflation works as a tax that falls on everyone alike, because it steadily reduces the value of the money held by households, by lenders and by borrowers.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Inflation does not burden everyone equally: unexpected rises move wealth from lenders and savers to borrowers, whereas inflation that was foreseen can be built into interest rates.

option_rationales.A: This is the illustration only; it omits the general point about uneven effects and the role of whether inflation was foreseen.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says the transfer 'largely disappears' when inflation is foreseen, so borrowers do not always gain; the claim about what households welcome is added.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph mentions this common description only to say that inflation's effects are 'far from even'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph corrects the 'tax on everyone' view: unexpected inflation transfers wealth from lenders and savers to borrowers, and the transfer largely vanishes when inflation is expected and priced into interest. The correct answer keeps the correction and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'borrowers always gain' option, which captures the transfer but ignores the condition that it be unexpected.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option states the paragraph's mechanism but drops the condition in the final sentence.

questions.subtopic: Skilled emigration has offsetting gains and real losses; which prevails depends on place and profession.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: The departure of doctors and engineers from poorer countries is commonly called a brain drain, as if skill were simply poured out of one economy into another. The picture is incomplete. Emigrants often send money home, and the prospect of working abroad can persuade more young people to train in the first place, some of whom never leave. Those who return may bring capital, contacts and experience. None of this means the loss is imaginary: a rural district that loses its only surgeon is worse off however much is sent home. The question is not whether emigration drains or enriches a country, but which effect prevails in a given place and profession.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The departure of doctors and engineers from poorer countries is commonly called a brain drain, as if skill were simply poured out of one economy into another. The picture is incomplete. Emigrants often send money home, and the prospect of working abroad can persuade more young people to train in the first place, some of whom never leave. Those who return may bring capital, contacts and experience. None of this means the loss is imaginary: a rural district that loses its only surgeon is worse off however much is sent home. The question is not whether emigration drains or enriches a country, but which effect prevails in a given place and profession.

options.A: Fears of a brain drain are mistaken, since the money and experience that emigrants send or bring home more than make up for the skills that leave the country.
options.B: A rural district that loses its only surgeon to emigration is left worse off, regardless of how much money the departed surgeon later sends home.
options.C: When doctors and engineers emigrate from poorer countries, the skill they embody is simply lost to their home economies and gained by richer ones.
options.D: Skilled emigration brings gains such as remittances, extra training and returning talent alongside real losses, so whether it harms a country depends on the particular place and profession.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Skilled emigration brings gains such as remittances, extra training and returning talent alongside real losses, so whether it harms a country depends on the particular place and profession.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'None of this means the loss is imaginary' and gives the example of the lost surgeon; it does not say the gains always outweigh the losses.
option_rationales.B: This is the paragraph's illustration of a real loss; it omits the gains and the conclusion that the balance varies.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'brain drain' picture the paragraph calls 'incomplete', since it ignores remittances, extra training and returns.

questions.explanation: The paragraph complicates the brain-drain picture with gains (remittances, extra training, returns), then insists the losses are real, and concludes that the balance depends on the place and profession. The correct answer holds both sides and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'fears of a brain drain are mistaken' option after reading the list of gains and missing the 'None of this means' turn.
questions.difficulty_reason: The paragraph turns twice, and each wrong option stops at one side of the balance.

questions.subtopic: A failed prediction indicts a bundle of assumptions; blaming an auxiliary is legitimate if it is independently testable.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A common picture of science holds that a single failed prediction refutes a theory. In practice, no theory yields a prediction by itself; every test also relies on assumptions about the instruments, the experimental conditions and other theories taken for granted. When the prediction fails, logic tells us only that something in this bundle is wrong, not which part. Scientists who keep a theory after a failed test and blame an auxiliary assumption are therefore not necessarily being dogmatic; sometimes the faulty instrument really is the culprit. What separates a reasonable rescue from an evasive one is whether the blamed assumption can be checked independently, rather than being invoked only to save the theory.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When the prediction fails, logic tells us only that something in this bundle is wrong, not which part. What separates a reasonable rescue from an evasive one is whether the blamed assumption can be checked independently, rather than being invoked only to save the theory.

options.A: Since a failed prediction indicts a bundle of assumptions, saving a theory by blaming another of them can be legitimate, if that assumption is independently checkable.
options.B: Since logic cannot say which assumption a failed prediction refutes, no experiment can ever count against a theory, and every rescue of a theory is equally reasonable.
options.C: A theory is refuted as soon as one of its predictions fails, so scientists who keep it after a failed test are refusing to accept the evidence before them.
options.D: When a prediction fails, scientists should suspect their instruments first, since faulty equipment rather than the theory itself is usually to blame for the failure.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Since a failed prediction indicts a bundle of assumptions, saving a theory by blaming another of them can be legitimate, if that assumption is independently checkable.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph distinguishes 'a reasonable rescue from an evasive one', so it denies that every rescue is equally reasonable.
option_rationales.C: This is the 'common picture' the paragraph corrects; it says such scientists are 'not necessarily being dogmatic'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'sometimes' the instrument is the culprit; it does not say it usually is or rank what to suspect first.

questions.explanation: The paragraph replaces the simple refutation picture with the point that a failed prediction shows only that something in a bundle of assumptions is wrong. Blaming an auxiliary can therefore be reasonable, and the test of reasonableness is independent checkability. The correct answer keeps the premise, the permission and the condition.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'suspect their instruments first' option, which sounds like the paragraph's point but inflates 'sometimes' into 'usually'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The topic is abstract, and the correct answer differs from two wrong options by a condition ('if that assumption is independently checkable') and a quantifier ('sometimes' versus 'usually').

questions.subtopic: Groundwater is overused because its decline is hidden and saved water may be pumped by others.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Groundwater is easy to overuse partly because its decline is invisible. A shrinking lake or a dry riverbed is a public sight, but a falling water table shows itself only as wells that must be dug deeper and pumps that must work harder, costs that each farmer meets privately. Each user also knows that the water they leave in the ground may simply be pumped by a neighbour. Under these conditions restraint looks like a sacrifice with no reward, and depletion can continue for years before anyone acknowledges that there is a common problem at all.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Groundwater is easy to overuse partly because its decline is invisible. A shrinking lake or a dry riverbed is a public sight, but a falling water table shows itself only as wells that must be dug deeper and pumps that must work harder, costs that each farmer meets privately. Each user also knows that the water they leave in the ground may simply be pumped by a neighbour. Under these conditions restraint looks like a sacrifice with no reward, and depletion can continue for years before anyone acknowledges that there is a common problem at all.

options.A: Farmers overuse groundwater mainly because the pumps they rely on are inefficient, and replacing them with better machines would stop water tables from falling any further.
options.B: Lakes and rivers are more easily overused than groundwater, because the water in them is visible to everyone and therefore seems to be freely available.
options.C: Groundwater is overused because its decline hides in private costs and because water one user saves may be pumped by others, which makes restraint seem pointless.
options.D: As a water table falls, farmers find that their wells must be dug ever deeper and their pumps must work harder to bring the water to the surface.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Groundwater is overused because its decline hides in private costs and because water one user saves may be pumped by others, which makes restraint seem pointless.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph mentions pumps working harder as a symptom of decline, not as its cause, and it proposes no technical fix.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says visible decline in lakes and rivers is 'a public sight', which is the contrast that makes groundwater easier, not harder, to overuse.
option_rationales.D: This repeats one detail, how decline shows itself, and omits why it leads to overuse.

questions.explanation: The paragraph gives two reasons for groundwater overuse: decline is hidden in private costs, and saved water can be pumped by neighbours, so restraint seems unrewarded. The correct answer states both reasons and their effect.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the detail about deeper wells, which is vivid but only part of the first reason.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both reasons are stated in consecutive sentences, and the wrong options are a misread symptom, a detail and a reversal.

questions.subtopic: Both over- and under-attributing human-like minds to animals are errors; evidence should decide case by case.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Students of animal behaviour have long been warned against anthropomorphism, the error of reading human thoughts and feelings into animals. The warning is sound, but it has a mirror image that receives less attention. A researcher who refuses to credit an animal with any mental state resembling ours, even when the evidence points that way, also makes an error, and it is not obviously the safer one. Species that share much of our evolutionary history are likely to share some of our mental equipment too. The proper aim is not to minimise every resemblance to humans but to let the evidence decide, case by case, which resemblances are real.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Students of animal behaviour have long been warned against anthropomorphism, the error of reading human thoughts and feelings into animals. The warning is sound, but it has a mirror image that receives less attention. A researcher who refuses to credit an animal with any mental state resembling ours, even when the evidence points that way, also makes an error, and it is not obviously the safer one. Species that share much of our evolutionary history are likely to share some of our mental equipment too. The proper aim is not to minimise every resemblance to humans but to let the evidence decide, case by case, which resemblances are real.

options.A: Researchers who study animal behaviour must guard against anthropomorphism, the tempting error of reading human thoughts and feelings into the creatures they observe.
options.B: Wrongly crediting animals with human-like minds is an error, but so is withholding such credit when evidence supports it; each resemblance must be judged on its evidence.
options.C: Because many species share much of our evolutionary history, researchers should assume that animals think and feel much as humans do unless it is shown otherwise.
options.D: Denying animals any human-like mental states is a more serious error than anthropomorphism, and it ought to be the main concern of researchers today.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Wrongly crediting animals with human-like minds is an error, but so is withholding such credit when evidence supports it; each resemblance must be judged on its evidence.

option_rationales.A: This states only the familiar warning and leaves out the paragraph's main point, its 'mirror image'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says the warning against anthropomorphism 'is sound' and asks for evidence 'case by case'; it does not make human-like minds the default.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the opposite error is 'not obviously the safer one', which denies that it is safer without claiming it is worse.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts the warning against anthropomorphism, points out its neglected mirror image (refusing resemblances the evidence supports), and concludes that the evidence should decide case by case. The correct answer keeps both errors and the method.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'more serious error' option by reading 'not obviously the safer one' as 'the worse one'.
questions.difficulty_reason: The tempting wrong option turns a carefully hedged comparison into a ranking, so the reader must attend to 'not obviously'.

questions.subtopic: Soil carbon gains are real but smaller, slower and less secure than simple accounts suggest.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Farm soils can store carbon, and practices such as planting cover crops or ploughing less have been shown in many trials to raise the carbon content of the topsoil. This has made soil an attractive climate solution, since farmers can be paid for carbon they lock away. The finding needs careful handling. Gains are often measured only in the upper layers, and some of the apparent increase may be carbon moved from deeper soil rather than newly captured. Soils also reach a new balance after some years and stop accumulating, and the stored carbon can return to the air if the practices are abandoned. Soil carbon is real, but slower, smaller and less secure than a simple accounting suggests.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Farm soils can store carbon, and practices such as planting cover crops or ploughing less have been shown in many trials to raise the carbon content of the topsoil. This has made soil an attractive climate solution, since farmers can be paid for carbon they lock away. The finding needs careful handling. Gains are often measured only in the upper layers, and some of the apparent increase may be carbon moved from deeper soil rather than newly captured. Soils also reach a new balance after some years and stop accumulating, and the stored carbon can return to the air if the practices are abandoned. Soil carbon is real, but slower, smaller and less secure than a simple accounting suggests.

options.A: Claims that farm soils store carbon have turned out to be mistaken, since the gains that trials measure merely reflect carbon moved upward from deeper layers of the soil.
options.B: Practices such as cover cropping and reduced ploughing raise the carbon in topsoil, which makes paying farmers to adopt them an effective and dependable climate policy.
options.C: Carbon stored in farm soils is insecure, because it returns to the air whenever farmers abandon the practices that first allowed it to accumulate there.
options.D: Some farming practices do raise soil carbon, but shallow measurement, eventual saturation and possible reversal make the climate benefit smaller and less certain than simple accounts claim.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Some farming practices do raise soil carbon, but shallow measurement, eventual saturation and possible reversal make the climate benefit smaller and less certain than simple accounts claim.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'Soil carbon is real' and that only 'some' of the apparent increase may be carbon moved from below, so this overstates one caveat into a refutation.
option_rationales.B: This states the finding and the policy appeal but ignores the qualifications that follow 'The finding needs careful handling'; calling it dependable contradicts 'less secure'.
option_rationales.C: This captures one caveat only and leaves out the measurement and saturation problems and the affirmation that the gains are real.

questions.explanation: The paragraph reports a finding (some practices raise topsoil carbon) and its appeal, then qualifies it three ways: shallow measurement, saturation and reversibility. It ends by affirming the gain while limiting it. The correct answer keeps the finding and all three qualifications at the right strength.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that calls the claims mistaken, which seizes on the measurement caveat and loses the affirmation 'Soil carbon is real'.
questions.difficulty_reason: All three wrong options draw on true sentences of the paragraph; the correct answer alone holds the finding and the qualifications in balance, which requires reading the whole paragraph.

questions.subtopic: Removing a dam starts a slow, initially disruptive recovery rather than restoring the river at once.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: When an old dam is taken down, people often expect the river to return at once to the condition it was in before the dam was built. What usually happens is messier. Sediment that piled up behind the wall for decades is released and travels downstream, burying gravel beds and clouding the water for a season or more. Fish that had been blocked may take years to recolonise the upstream reaches, and the plants that first cover the drained reservoir bed are often weeds rather than the species that grew there before. None of this means that removal fails; on many rivers the long-term gains in fish passage and natural flow are substantial. It means that removal starts a process of recovery rather than restoring a finished state, and that the early years can look worse than what came before.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When an old dam is taken down, people often expect the river to return at once to the condition it was in before the dam was built. What usually happens is messier.
