Fish that had been blocked may take years to recolonise the upstream reaches, and the plants that first cover the drained reservoir bed are often weeds rather than the species that grew there before. None of this means that removal fails; on many rivers the long-term gains in fish passage and natural flow are substantial. It means that removal starts a process of recovery rather than restoring a finished state, and that the early years can look worse than what came before.

options.A: Taking down a dam begins a gradual, at first disruptive recovery rather than an instant return to the river's earlier state, though the long-term gains can be considerable.
options.B: Sediment released when a dam is removed travels downstream and buries gravel beds, which clouds the water and harms the river for at least a season afterwards.
options.C: Old dams ought to be removed slowly and in stages, so that sediment and weeds do not overwhelm the river and fish can return upstream more quickly.
options.D: Because the first years after removal often look worse than before, taking down old dams usually does more harm to a river and its fish than simply leaving the old walls standing.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Taking down a dam begins a gradual, at first disruptive recovery rather than an instant return to the river's earlier state, though the long-term gains can be considerable.

option_rationales.B: This is one detail from the third sentence; it leaves out the paragraph's point that removal begins a recovery whose long-term gains can be 'substantial'.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph recommends no method of removal; staged removal is an outside prescription that the text never makes.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'None of this means that removal fails' and stresses long-term gains, so this option reverses its conclusion.

questions.explanation: The paragraph corrects the expectation of an instant return: sediment, slow recolonisation and weeds make the early years 'messier', but 'None of this means that removal fails'. The correct answer keeps both halves: removal 'starts a process of recovery rather than restoring a finished state', and the long-term gains can be 'substantial'.
questions.common_misconception: Picking the vivid sediment detail, or reading the description of early damage as a verdict against removal.
questions.difficulty_reason: The point is stated in the last two sentences and each wrong option is clearly narrow, reversed or prescriptive.

questions.subtopic: Earthquake forecasts are valuable when judged as probabilities, not as failed predictions.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Seismologists distinguish between predicting an earthquake and forecasting one, and public discussion often blurs the two. A prediction would name a place, a window of days or weeks and a magnitude, precisely enough to justify evacuating a city. No method has reliably done this, and claims to the contrary have tended to collapse under scrutiny. A forecast is more modest: it estimates the probability of a strong quake in a region over years or decades, using the record of past ruptures and the strain measured on faults. A forecast cannot tell anyone to leave on Tuesday, but it can tell a city how strict its building codes should be and where a hospital ought not to be built. Judged as failed predictions, forecasts look useless; judged as what they are, they are among the most practically valuable things the science produces.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Seismologists distinguish between predicting an earthquake and forecasting one, and public discussion often blurs the two. A prediction would name a place, a window of days or weeks and a magnitude, precisely enough to justify evacuating a city. No method has reliably done this, and claims to the contrary have tended to collapse under scrutiny. A forecast is more modest: it estimates the probability of a strong quake in a region over years or decades, using the record of past ruptures and the strain measured on faults. A forecast cannot tell anyone to leave on Tuesday, but it can tell a city how strict its building codes should be and where a hospital ought not to be built. Judged as failed predictions, forecasts look useless; judged as what they are, they are among the most practically valuable things the science produces.

options.A: Claims to have predicted earthquakes have usually collapsed under scrutiny, so the public should distrust anyone who announces the date and place of a coming quake.
options.B: Although no method has reliably said when and where a quake will strike, long-range probability forecasts are very useful for decisions such as building codes, if judged on their own terms.
options.C: Better measurement of the strain on faults will soon let seismologists turn their long-range forecasts into precise predictions that justify evacuating whole cities.
options.D: Since seismologists cannot say when an earthquake will strike, their probability estimates are of little practical use and should not be allowed to guide how cities are planned or where they build.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Although no method has reliably said when and where a quake will strike, long-range probability forecasts are very useful for decisions such as building codes, if judged on their own terms.

option_rationales.A: This takes one sentence about failed predictions and adds advice; it omits the central contrast with forecasts and their practical value.
option_rationales.C: Nothing in the paragraph anticipates such progress; it says no method has reliably predicted quakes, so this is an outside speculation.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says forecasts 'look useless' only when wrongly 'Judged as failed predictions', and calls them highly valuable; this option adopts the mistaken judgement.

questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts prediction, which 'No method has reliably done', with forecasting, which estimates probabilities over 'years or decades' and guides 'building codes' and the siting of hospitals. Its conclusion is that forecasts are valuable 'judged as what they are'. The correct answer captures the contrast and that conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Equating the failure of prediction with the failure of seismology, or picking the option that dwells on discredited predictions.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow wrong option about failed predictions is partly right, so the reader must keep hold of the two-part contrast.

questions.subtopic: Captive breeding justifies zoos only under stated conditions, chiefly a wild habitat for release.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Zoos often justify themselves by pointing to captive breeding: species that have vanished from the wild survive in enclosures and may one day be returned. The argument is not empty; a handful of animals have been reintroduced after being bred in captivity. But the justification works only under conditions that are seldom stated. A captive population must be large and genetically varied enough to avoid inbreeding, the animals must keep the behaviours they need to survive outside, and, most easily forgotten, there must be a wild habitat to return them to. Where the forest has been cleared, or the threat that emptied it persists, breeding preserves a species in something like suspended animation, alive but with nowhere to go. Captive breeding, in other words, is a bridge, and a bridge is valuable only if something is being built on the far side.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Zoos often justify themselves by pointing to captive breeding: species that have vanished from the wild survive in enclosures and may one day be returned. The argument is not empty; a handful of animals have been reintroduced after being bred in captivity. But the justification works only under conditions that are seldom stated. A captive population must be large and genetically varied enough to avoid inbreeding, the animals must keep the behaviours they need to survive outside, and, most easily forgotten, there must be a wild habitat to return them to. Where the forest has been cleared, or the threat that emptied it persists, breeding preserves a species in something like suspended animation, alive but with nowhere to go. Captive breeding, in other words, is a bridge, and a bridge is valuable only if something is being built on the far side.

options.A: Money spent on breeding endangered animals in zoos would do more for conservation if it were spent instead on protecting forests and removing threats in the wild.
options.B: Captive breeding is an empty excuse for keeping zoos, because animals raised in enclosures lose the behaviours they need and can almost never be returned to the wild.
options.C: Captive breeding can really help to conserve species, but only if demanding conditions are met, above all a wild habitat fit for release; without one, it keeps a species alive but cannot restore it.
options.D: Zoos are justified chiefly by their breeding programmes, which have kept alive species that vanished in the wild and have allowed several of them to be returned to their habitats.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Captive breeding can really help to conserve species, but only if demanding conditions are met, above all a wild habitat fit for release; without one, it keeps a species alive but cannot restore it.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph never compares the value of the two kinds of spending; it says breeding needs habitat, not that habitat protection should replace breeding.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph states 'The argument is not empty' and treats lost behaviours as one condition to be met, not as a fact that defeats breeding.
option_rationales.D: This is the zoos' own justification as the first two sentences report it; it drops the paragraph's main claim that the argument 'works only under conditions that are seldom stated'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph concedes that captive breeding is 'not empty' but argues that it 'works only under conditions', the most neglected being a habitat 'to return them to'. Without it a species is 'alive but with nowhere to go'; breeding is 'a bridge' that is valuable only if the far side is built. The correct answer states the concession, the conditions and what happens when habitat is missing.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the funding comparison because it sounds like the bridge metaphor, when the paragraph sets a condition rather than ranking two policies.
questions.difficulty_reason: Two wrong options sit close to the author's stance: one repeats the reported justification, one turns the habitat condition into a spending recommendation.

questions.subtopic: Renaming eponymous species has a real record-keeping cost, so reform should look forward.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Naming a newly described species after a person is an old habit, and some critics now ask whether names honouring patrons, colonial officials or celebrities should be changed. The case for renaming is easy to feel when the honoured figure was cruel. Yet the strongest reason for caution has little to do with the reputations involved. A scientific name is a retrieval key: it links the specimen in a museum drawer to every paper ever written about it. Change the name and that chain is not cut, since the rules keep track of older names, but it is lengthened and made fragile, especially for the many species known only from a single description in an obscure journal. The more promising reform looks forward: choosing descriptive names for new species costs nothing, while renaming old ones carries a real price in scientific record-keeping.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Naming a newly described species after a person is an old habit, and some critics now ask whether names honouring patrons, colonial officials or celebrities should be changed. The case for renaming is easy to feel when the honoured figure was cruel. Yet the strongest reason for caution has little to do with the reputations involved. A scientific name is a retrieval key: it links the specimen in a museum drawer to every paper ever written about it. Change the name and that chain is not cut, since the rules keep track of older names, but it is lengthened and made fragile, especially for the many species known only from a single description in an obscure journal. The more promising reform looks forward: choosing descriptive names for new species costs nothing, while renaming old ones carries a real price in scientific record-keeping.

options.A: Changing a species' name permanently severs the link between museum specimens and the literature, making many obscure species impossible for researchers to trace.
options.B: Whatever the honoured person's record, renaming species is costly because names are stable links to the literature, so reform should target how new species are named.
options.C: Species should be given names that describe their features rather than honour people, since honouring individuals has always led to disputes over reputations.
options.D: Species named after cruel colonial officials ought to be renamed at once, since the moral offence of such names plainly outweighs the trouble of updating the scientific records.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Whatever the honoured person's record, renaming species is costly because names are stable links to the literature, so reform should target how new species are named.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says 'that chain is not cut' but 'lengthened and made fragile', so this option overstates the cost into a severed link.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph favours descriptive names because renaming is costly, not because honouring people 'always' causes disputes; it says caution 'has little to do with the reputations involved'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph grants that the case for renaming is 'easy to feel' but argues for caution; this option takes the side the author resists.

questions.explanation: The paragraph sets aside the reputation question and argues that a name's value is as a 'retrieval key'. Renaming does not cut the chain but makes it 'fragile', so the better reform 'looks forward' to new names. The correct answer gives the cost, its reason, and the forward-looking remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the 'severs the link' option because it sounds like the paragraph's concern, without noticing that the text explicitly says the chain is not cut.
questions.difficulty_reason: One wrong option differs from the text only in degree (cut versus made fragile) and another gives the right remedy for the wrong reason.

questions.subtopic: Undo makes mistakes cheap, which encourages experiment and so helps users learn software.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: The undo command looks like a minor convenience, but it changes how people use software. When every action can be reversed, users explore: they try an unfamiliar menu, apply a filter just to see what it does, delete a paragraph to judge whether the essay reads better without it. Where actions are permanent, the same users grow cautious, read instructions first and stick to the few operations they already trust. Undo, in other words, lowers the cost of a mistake, and when mistakes are cheap, experimenting becomes rational. Much of what people learn about a program they learn by just such trial and error, so a design that forgives errors also turns out to be one that teaches.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The undo command looks like a minor convenience, but it changes how people use software. When every action can be reversed, users explore: they try an unfamiliar menu, apply a filter just to see what it does, delete a paragraph to judge whether the essay reads better without it. Where actions are permanent, the same users grow cautious, read instructions first and stick to the few operations they already trust. Undo, in other words, lowers the cost of a mistake, and when mistakes are cheap, experimenting becomes rational. Much of what people learn about a program they learn by just such trial and error, so a design that forgives errors also turns out to be one that teaches.

options.A: People using software with an undo command make far more mistakes than other users do, because they know that any error they commit can be reversed at no cost at all.
options.B: Software without an undo command makes users read instructions carefully, which leaves them more skilled and confident than users who simply reverse their errors.
options.C: When the actions in a program cannot be reversed, people become cautious, read the instructions first and use only the operations they already trust.
options.D: By making mistakes cheap to reverse, the undo command encourages users to experiment, and since people learn programs largely by trial and error, this tolerance of errors also helps them learn.

questions.correct_answer: (D) By making mistakes cheap to reverse, the undo command encourages users to experiment, and since people learn programs largely by trial and error, this tolerance of errors also helps them learn.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says undo makes mistakes cheap and exploration rational; it makes no claim that users commit more errors.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph treats caution without undo as limiting, since users 'stick to the few operations they already trust'; it never says they become more skilled.
option_rationales.C: This restates one sentence about permanent actions and misses the main point that undo encourages exploration and therefore learning.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains a chain: undo 'lowers the cost of a mistake', cheap mistakes make 'experimenting' rational, and people learn programs by 'trial and error', so 'a design that forgives errors' also 'teaches'. The correct answer states the whole chain.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the narrow option about permanent actions because it is closely worded from the paragraph.
questions.difficulty_reason: The causal chain is explicit and the wrong options are plainly narrow or unsupported.

questions.subtopic: Endless scrolling reflects the removal of stopping points more than weak willpower.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: It is common to blame endless feeds on a lack of willpower, as if people who scroll for an hour simply could not stop. This misplaces the problem. Much everyday self-control depends less on resisting temptation moment by moment than on natural stopping points: the end of a chapter, the last page of a newspaper, the credits of an episode. Such boundaries invite a small decision about whether to go on, and many people, offered that decision, stop. A feed that loads new items before the old ones run out removes the boundary and with it the decision. The user never declines to stop; the moment to stop simply never arrives. Designers who wished to respect their users' time would therefore do more by restoring edges than by lecturing anyone about discipline.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is common to blame endless feeds on a lack of willpower, as if people who scroll for an hour simply could not stop. This misplaces the problem. Much everyday self-control depends less on resisting temptation moment by moment than on natural stopping points: the end of a chapter, the last page of a newspaper, the credits of an episode. Such boundaries invite a small decision about whether to go on, and many people, offered that decision, stop. A feed that loads new items before the old ones run out removes the boundary and with it the decision. The user never declines to stop; the moment to stop simply never arrives. Designers who wished to respect their users' time would therefore do more by restoring edges than by lecturing anyone about discipline.

options.A: Long spells of scrolling owe less to weak willpower than to feeds that remove the natural stopping points where people would otherwise choose to quit, so restoring them would help.
options.B: Endless feeds are built to exploit their users, and designers should be held legally responsible for the hours that people lose to scrolling every day.
options.C: People who scroll through endless feeds for hours lack the self-discipline of earlier generations of readers, who stopped at the end of a chapter or on the last page of a newspaper.
options.D: Self-control depends mainly on natural boundaries such as the ends of chapters, which is why people reading printed books rarely lose track of the time.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Long spells of scrolling owe less to weak willpower than to feeds that remove the natural stopping points where people would otherwise choose to quit, so restoring them would help.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph says nothing of exploitation or legal responsibility; it suggests designers restore 'edges', which is a design change, not liability.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph rejects the willpower explanation ('This misplaces the problem'); earlier readers stopped because boundaries offered a decision, not because they were more disciplined.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says 'Much everyday self-control' depends on stopping points and makes no claim about book readers losing track of time; this generalises one premise into an unsupported conclusion.

questions.explanation: The paragraph rejects the willpower account: stopping points 'invite a small decision', and a feed that keeps loading 'removes the boundary and with it the decision'. Hence designers should restore 'edges' rather than lecture about 'discipline'. The correct answer gives the diagnosis and the remedy.
questions.common_misconception: Taking the reported willpower view at face value, or choosing the option that stretches the premise about chapter endings into a claim about readers.
questions.difficulty_reason: The third wrong option reuses the paragraph's premise but extends it beyond what is said, which takes a careful reading to reject.

questions.subtopic: Steady satisfaction scores after chatbots may hide abandoned hard cases.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Firms that replace telephone agents with chatbots often report that customer satisfaction scores barely move, and conclude that customers do not mind. The figure is real, but what it measures deserves a closer look. Satisfaction surveys are usually sent to customers whose conversations ended, and a conversation with a bot ends in two very different ways: the problem is solved, or the customer gives up. Those who give up rarely answer a survey about an exchange they abandoned, and some of them quietly take their business elsewhere. Meanwhile the simple queries that bots handle well, such as tracking a parcel, were never the ones that tested anyone's patience. Steady scores may therefore show only that bots cope with easy cases, while the frustrations of hard cases fall outside what is being counted.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Firms that replace telephone agents with chatbots often report that customer satisfaction scores barely move, and conclude that customers do not mind. The figure is real, but what it measures deserves a closer look. Satisfaction surveys are usually sent to customers whose conversations ended, and a conversation with a bot ends in two very different ways: the problem is solved, or the customer gives up. Those who give up rarely answer a survey about an exchange they abandoned, and some of them quietly take their business elsewhere. Meanwhile the simple queries that bots handle well, such as tracking a parcel, were never the ones that tested anyone's patience. Steady scores may therefore show only that bots cope with easy cases, while the frustrations of hard cases fall outside what is being counted.

options.A: Firms deliberately send satisfaction surveys only to customers whose problems were solved, so the scores they publish for chatbots are knowingly misleading.
options.B: Satisfaction scores show that customers do not mind chatbots, because bots resolve simple queries such as tracking a parcel as well as human agents ever did.
options.C: Unchanged satisfaction scores after chatbots arrive may reflect only the easy queries that bots resolve, since customers who abandon frustrating conversations tend to go unrecorded in the surveys.
options.D: Chatbots deal badly with difficult problems, so firms that replace their telephone agents lose many customers and watch their satisfaction scores steadily fall.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Unchanged satisfaction scores after chatbots arrive may reflect only the easy queries that bots resolve, since customers who abandon frustrating conversations tend to go unrecorded in the surveys.

option_rationales.A: Surveys go to customers 'whose conversations ended', including those who gave up; the bias comes from who answers, and the paragraph alleges no deliberate deception.
option_rationales.B: This is the firms' conclusion that the paragraph questions; the author says the figure is real but that what it measures 'deserves a closer look'.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says scores 'barely move', and it claims only that 'some' customers leave; falling scores and heavy losses contradict and overstate it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph accepts the figure but questions its meaning: surveys reach conversations that ended, the customers who 'give up' rarely respond, and the easy queries bots handle were never the test. So steady scores 'may therefore show only that bots cope with easy cases'. The correct answer states this hedged reinterpretation and its mechanism.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the deliberate-deception option, which mirrors the idea of a biased sample but misplaces where the bias arises.
questions.difficulty_reason: The deception option is close to the correct answer's mechanism and must be rejected on a precise reading of who receives and who answers surveys.

questions.subtopic: Range anxiety about electric cars comes from rare trips and old habits, and fades with use.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Buyers considering an electric car often worry about range, picturing themselves stranded with a flat battery far from any charger. Yet the typical car spends most days on short trips that use a small fraction of even a modest battery, and owners who charge at home begin each morning with a full one. The worry is shaped by the rare long journey rather than the ordinary day, and by habits formed with petrol cars, for which refuelling means a special trip to a station. For many owners the anxiety fades within months, not because the battery has grown but because they have learned how their own driving actually uses it. Range does matter, but less often than the fear of it suggests.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Buyers considering an electric car often worry about range, picturing themselves stranded with a flat battery far from any charger. Yet the typical car spends most days on short trips that use a small fraction of even a modest battery, and owners who charge at home begin each morning with a full one. The worry is shaped by the rare long journey rather than the ordinary day, and by habits formed with petrol cars, for which refuelling means a special trip to a station. For many owners the anxiety fades within months, not because the battery has grown but because they have learned how their own driving actually uses it. Range does matter, but less often than the fear of it suggests.

options.A: Owners who charge their electric cars at home begin every morning with a full battery and therefore never need to visit a public charging station.
options.B: Worry about electric car range stems more from rare long trips and petrol-car habits than from daily driving, and it tends to fade as owners learn their real needs.
options.C: Electric cars now carry batteries large enough for any journey at all that a driver might plan, so every worry about being stranded far from a charger is simply mistaken.
options.D: People who mostly drive on long journeys should keep buying petrol cars for now, since they alone face a genuine risk of running out of charge far from home.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Worry about electric car range stems more from rare long trips and petrol-car habits than from daily driving, and it tends to fade as owners learn their real needs.

option_rationales.A: This expands one detail into 'never', which the paragraph does not say; it also misses the explanation of where the worry comes from.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says 'Range does matter', only 'less often than the fear of it suggests'; it never claims batteries suffice for any journey.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph gives no buying advice and does not say that only long-distance drivers face any risk.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains range worry as shaped by 'the rare long journey rather than the ordinary day' and by petrol-car 'habits', and says it 'fades within months' as owners learn their driving. The correct answer covers the cause and the fading, and by saying the worry stems more from these than from daily driving it keeps the concession that 'Range does matter'.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option that turns the reassurance into a claim that range never matters.
questions.difficulty_reason: Cause and conclusion are stated directly; wrong options are clearly extreme, narrow or prescriptive.

questions.subtopic: Apparent flaws of serial novels were sensible responses to instalment publication.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Many nineteenth-century novels first reached readers in instalments, a part at a time over many months, and the form left marks on the books that later readers of the bound volume can miss. Each part needed its own small climax to bring buyers back, so chapters often close on suspense or revelation. Because readers might forget a minor character between instalments, writers gave such figures memorable tags, a phrase or a habit repeated at each appearance. The long gaps also let an author learn how the story was being received, and plots were sometimes adjusted in response. Features that a modern critic might fault as contrived or repetitive were, in their first setting, sensible answers to the conditions of publication.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many nineteenth-century novels first reached readers in instalments, a part at a time over many months, and the form left marks on the books that later readers of the bound volume can miss. Each part needed its own small climax to bring buyers back, so chapters often close on suspense or revelation. Because readers might forget a minor character between instalments, writers gave such figures memorable tags, a phrase or a habit repeated at each appearance. The long gaps also let an author learn how the story was being received, and plots were sometimes adjusted in response. Features that a modern critic might fault as contrived or repetitive were, in their first setting, sensible answers to the conditions of publication.

options.A: Nineteenth-century novelists often wrote carelessly because they were paid by the instalment, which accounts for the contrived plots and repetitive minor characters found in their books.
options.B: Modern readers ought to read nineteenth-century novels in monthly parts, as their first readers did, in order to appreciate their suspense and their characters.
options.C: Serial publication let readers shape the plots of nineteenth-century novels, which authors rewrote every month according to what their audience demanded.
options.D: Some features of serialised nineteenth-century novels that now look like flaws, such as cliffhanger endings and repeated character tags, were sensible responses to publication in instalments.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Some features of serialised nineteenth-century novels that now look like flaws, such as cliffhanger endings and repeated character tags, were sensible responses to publication in instalments.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph never mentions payment or carelessness; it argues that such features were 'sensible answers', the opposite of careless writing.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph explains features of the books but recommends no way of reading them; this is an added prescription.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says plots were 'sometimes adjusted' in response; 'rewrote every month' and audience demands overstate one detail into the main point.

questions.explanation: The paragraph lists effects of serial publication: chapter-end suspense, 'memorable tags' for minor characters, plots adjusted to reception. It concludes that features a critic 'might fault as contrived or repetitive' were 'sensible answers to the conditions of publication'. The correct answer states that reinterpretation with its examples.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the reader-influence option, which inflates the 'sometimes adjusted' detail.
questions.difficulty_reason: The reader-influence option rests on a real detail and must be rejected for degree and narrowness.

questions.subtopic: Sympathetic villains are not a fault; the fault is letting backstory cancel judgement.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: A familiar complaint about recent fiction is that its villains have become too sympathetic: give every tyrant a sad childhood, the critics say, and evil dissolves into misfortune. The complaint mistakes explanation for excuse. To show how a person came to do terrible things is not to claim that the things were less terrible; it may make them more disturbing, since it removes the comfort of thinking that such acts belong to monsters unlike ourselves. Where the criticism does land is on stories that use the backstory to settle the moral question, inviting the reader to feel that a painful past cancels the harm done. The fault there is not sympathy but a failure of nerve: the writer has explained the villain and then flinched from judging him.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A familiar complaint about recent fiction is that its villains have become too sympathetic: give every tyrant a sad childhood, the critics say, and evil dissolves into misfortune. The complaint mistakes explanation for excuse. To show how a person came to do terrible things is not to claim that the things were less terrible; it may make them more disturbing, since it removes the comfort of thinking that such acts belong to monsters unlike ourselves. Where the criticism does land is on stories that use the backstory to settle the moral question, inviting the reader to feel that a painful past cancels the harm done. The fault there is not sympathy but a failure of nerve: the writer has explained the villain and then flinched from judging him.

options.A: Giving a villain an understandable past does not in itself excuse his deeds and may make them more unsettling; the real fault lies in stories that let such a past cancel moral judgement.
options.B: Readers find sympathetic villains more disturbing than monstrous ones, because such characters remind them that ordinary people like themselves, and not only monsters, are capable of terrible acts.
options.C: Explaining how a villain came to commit terrible acts always makes those acts more disturbing, so writers should give every villain a detailed and painful past.
options.D: Recent fiction has weakened moral judgement by giving its tyrants sad childhoods, so that readers come to regard evil as mere misfortune rather than wrongdoing.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Giving a villain an understandable past does not in itself excuse his deeds and may make them more unsettling; the real fault lies in stories that let such a past cancel moral judgement.

option_rationales.B: This reworks one supporting idea into a claim about readers' reactions and drops the central distinction between explaining and excusing, and the stated fault of flinching from judgement.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says explanation 'may' make acts more disturbing, and it recommends no backstory for every villain; 'always' and the prescription both overstate it.
option_rationales.D: This is the critics' complaint, which the author says 'mistakes explanation for excuse'; the author accepts it only for stories that let backstory settle the moral question.

questions.explanation: The paragraph separates 'explanation' from 'excuse': explaining a villain 'may make' his acts 'more disturbing'. It then concedes where the criticism lands, on stories in which 'a painful past cancels the harm done', and names that fault as flinching 'from judging him'. The correct answer keeps the distinction, the hedge and the concession.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the option about readers being disturbed, which echoes the paragraph's middle but loses its argument.
questions.difficulty_reason: Every wrong option uses the paragraph's material; the correct answer is found only by tracking the explanation-versus-excuse distinction and the concession.

questions.subtopic: Silence between movements is a recent convention, not tradition, so clappers should not be scorned.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: At a symphony concert, a burst of clapping after the opening movement is often answered by hissing from seasoned listeners, who regard unbroken quiet until the final chord as a sacred inheritance. The custom is younger than they suppose. Listeners in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries commonly clapped when a movement ended, and on occasion broke in while the orchestra was still playing. The demand for total quiet hardened only later, once the concert hall began to be approached in a mood of reverence. A case for the pause can still be made: a soft close needs a moment to fade into the room. Yet that case has to stand on its own feet rather than on a claim of antiquity, and it gives no licence for treating first-time listeners with contempt.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

At a symphony concert, a burst of clapping after the opening movement is often answered by hissing from seasoned listeners, who regard unbroken quiet until the final chord as a sacred inheritance. The custom is younger than they suppose. Listeners in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries commonly clapped when a movement ended, and on occasion broke in while the orchestra was still playing. The demand for total quiet hardened only later, once the concert hall began to be approached in a mood of reverence. A case for the pause can still be made: a soft close needs a moment to fade into the room. Yet that case has to stand on its own feet rather than on a claim of antiquity, and it gives no licence for treating first-time listeners with contempt.

options.A: Concert audiences ought to return to the older habit of clapping between and even during movements, since that is how such music was first received by the listeners who heard it when it was new.
options.B: Listeners in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries often clapped at the end of a movement and sometimes even interrupted the orchestra while it was playing.
options.C: Quiet between movements is a later custom, not an ancient one, so while the pause may be worth keeping, it must be defended on its merits and gives no excuse for scorning newcomers.
options.D: Silence between the movements of a symphony has no real justification and survives only because modern listeners approach the concert hall with a kind of reverence.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Quiet between movements is a later custom, not an ancient one, so while the pause may be worth keeping, it must be defended on its merits and gives no excuse for scorning newcomers.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph grants that 'A case for the pause can still be made' and asks only that it be argued properly; it does not urge a return to the old habit.
option_rationales.B: This repeats the historical evidence but omits the paragraph's conclusions about how the pause should be defended and how newcomers should be treated.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph concedes that a soft close 'needs a moment to fade into the room', so the claim that silence has no justification contradicts it.

questions.explanation: The paragraph shows that 'The custom is younger than they suppose', concedes that 'A case for the pause can still be made', and concludes that the case must 'stand on its own feet rather than on a claim of antiquity' and gives 'no licence' for contempt towards first-time listeners. The correct answer keeps all three parts.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the historical detail, or reading the critique of the custom as a rejection of silence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The concession and conclusion are explicit, and the wrong options fail on obvious grounds.

questions.subtopic: Ruins appeal through imaginative completion and visible time, which is why restorations can disappoint.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Why do ruins draw visitors who would walk past the same building, intact, without a glance? Part of the answer is that a ruin asks the viewer to do some work. The missing roof and broken arches invite the mind to complete them, and an image a person has helped to build feels more vivid than one simply handed over. A ruin also makes time visible: weathered stone and the roots pushing through it show at a glance the centuries that a whole building conceals. This suggests why restorations sometimes disappoint. A restored castle may be more accurate than its broken neighbour, yet it leaves nothing to imagine and hides the very history it was meant to display.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Why do ruins draw visitors who would walk past the same building, intact, without a glance? Part of the answer is that a ruin asks the viewer to do some work. The missing roof and broken arches invite the mind to complete them, and an image a person has helped to build feels more vivid than one simply handed over. A ruin also makes time visible: weathered stone and the roots pushing through it show at a glance the centuries that a whole building conceals. This suggests why restorations sometimes disappoint. A restored castle may be more accurate than its broken neighbour, yet it leaves nothing to imagine and hides the very history it was meant to display.

options.A: A building that a viewer must complete in the imagination feels more vivid than one presented whole, because people value images they have helped to create.
options.B: Visitors prefer ruins to intact buildings mainly because ruins are older, and age has always been the chief source of a building's appeal to those who travel to see it.
options.C: Ruined buildings should be left as they stand rather than restored, since restoration falsifies history and makes old castles less accurate than their broken neighbours.
options.D: Ruins appeal because viewers must imagine what is missing and because decay displays the passing of time, which also explains why faithful restorations can disappoint those who visit them.

questions.correct_answer: (D) Ruins appeal because viewers must imagine what is missing and because decay displays the passing of time, which also explains why faithful restorations can disappoint those who visit them.

option_rationales.A: This gives only the first of the two reasons and leaves out visible time and the consequence for restorations.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph gives two reasons, imaginative work and visible time; it never says ruins are older or that age 'always' governs appeal.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph says a restored castle 'may be more accurate', and it recommends no policy; this reverses one claim and adds a prescription.

questions.explanation: The paragraph gives two reasons for the pull of ruins: they ask the viewer 'to do some work' of completion, and they make 'time visible'. It then draws a consequence: a restoration 'leaves nothing to imagine and hides the very history' it was meant to show. The correct answer holds both reasons and the consequence.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the single-reason option because it paraphrases the most quotable sentence.
questions.difficulty_reason: The narrow option is accurate as far as it goes; the reader must notice the second reason and the restoration point.

questions.subtopic: Slang ages fast because its insider function ends once outsiders adopt it.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Slang tends to age quickly, and the reason lies in what it is for. A slang word marks its users as insiders: to say it is to show that one belongs to a particular group, often a young one, and knows its current code. That function depends on outsiders not using the word. Once parents, advertisers and newsreaders adopt it, the word stops marking anyone as an insider, and the group that coined it drops it for something fresh. A few slang terms survive this process by losing their flavour entirely and becoming ordinary vocabulary, but most simply fade. The speed of slang's decline is, in this sense, a sign that it worked.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Slang tends to age quickly, and the reason lies in what it is for. A slang word marks its users as insiders: to say it is to show that one belongs to a particular group, often a young one, and knows its current code. That function depends on outsiders not using the word. Once parents, advertisers and newsreaders adopt it, the word stops marking anyone as an insider, and the group that coined it drops it for something fresh. A few slang terms survive this process by losing their flavour entirely and becoming ordinary vocabulary, but most simply fade. The speed of slang's decline is, in this sense, a sign that it worked.

options.A: Slang ages fast because it marks membership of a group, a role it loses once outsiders take it up; most terms then fade, though a few become ordinary words.
options.B: Slang words fade because advertisers and newsreaders deliberately adopt them in order to make young people abandon the private vocabulary of their group.
options.C: Slang is a poor and short-lived form of speech, and its rapid decline shows that it fails to communicate as clearly as the ordinary vocabulary of a language does.
options.D: Most of the ordinary words in a language began life as slang terms that young people once coined in order to mark themselves out as members of a particular group.

questions.correct_answer: (A) Slang ages fast because it marks membership of a group, a role it loses once outsiders take it up; most terms then fade, though a few become ordinary words.

option_rationales.B: The paragraph describes outsiders adopting slang, not doing so on purpose to drive young people away; the motive is invented.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph calls the speed of decline 'a sign that it worked', the opposite of treating it as a failure to communicate.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says only 'A few slang terms' become ordinary vocabulary while 'most simply fade', so this reverses the proportion.

questions.explanation: The paragraph explains slang's short life by its function: it 'marks its users as insiders', which 'depends on outsiders not using the word'. When outsiders adopt it, the group drops it; 'A few' terms become ordinary words but 'most simply fade'. The correct answer gives the function, the mechanism and the outcome with its exception.
questions.common_misconception: Reading quick decline as a sign of failure, missing the paragraph's closing reversal.
questions.difficulty_reason: The mechanism is stated plainly, and each wrong option contradicts a specific sentence.

questions.subtopic: Accent penalties mix prejudice with processing effort, and only the latter fades with exposure.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Listeners asked to rate recorded speakers often judge those with certain accents as less competent, even when the words spoken are identical. It is tempting to read this as simple prejudice against particular regions or classes, and partly it is. But some of the effect has a duller source: listeners find an unfamiliar accent harder to process, and the extra effort of understanding is easily misattributed to the speaker, as if a message that was hard to follow had been less clearly thought. This matters because the two explanations call for different remedies. Prejudice must be confronted; mere unfamiliarity tends to shrink with exposure, so that a listener who hears an accent regularly may stop penalising it without ever having examined an attitude.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Listeners asked to rate recorded speakers often judge those with certain accents as less competent, even when the words spoken are identical. It is tempting to read this as simple prejudice against particular regions or classes, and partly it is. But some of the effect has a duller source: listeners find an unfamiliar accent harder to process, and the extra effort of understanding is easily misattributed to the speaker, as if a message that was hard to follow had been less clearly thought. This matters because the two explanations call for different remedies. Prejudice must be confronted; mere unfamiliarity tends to shrink with exposure, so that a listener who hears an accent regularly may stop penalising it without ever having examined an attitude.

options.A: Listeners rate speakers with unfamiliar accents as less competent not out of prejudice but simply because such accents take more effort to understand and process.
options.B: Lower competence ratings for some accents come partly from prejudice and partly from the effort of processing unfamiliar speech, and the difference matters because only the latter may fade through exposure.
options.C: Prejudice against regional and class accents can be overcome simply by hearing those accents regularly, without any need for listeners to examine their own attitudes.
options.D: Because speakers with unfamiliar accents are harder to follow, listeners are justified in judging the messages of such speakers as less clearly thought out.

questions.correct_answer: (B) Lower competence ratings for some accents come partly from prejudice and partly from the effort of processing unfamiliar speech, and the difference matters because only the latter may fade through exposure.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph says the effect is prejudice 'partly', and adds processing effort as a second source; denying prejudice altogether contradicts it.
option_rationales.C: The paragraph assigns exposure to unfamiliarity and says 'Prejudice must be confronted'; this option merges the two causes it is careful to separate.
option_rationales.D: The paragraph says the effort is 'misattributed to the speaker', which means the judgement is a mistake, not a justified inference.

questions.explanation: The paragraph identifies two sources of the accent penalty, prejudice ('partly it is') and processing effort that is 'misattributed to the speaker', and stresses that they 'call for different remedies': prejudice 'must be confronted', while unfamiliarity 'tends to shrink with exposure'. The correct answer states both sources and why the distinction matters.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the exposure option because exposure is the paragraph's remedy, without noticing that it is the remedy for only one cause.
questions.difficulty_reason: Each wrong option collapses or misreads the two-cause distinction in a different way, and two of them are close to the paragraph's wording.

questions.subtopic: Reality television can construct characters in the edit, so the question is assembly, not scripting.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Defenders of reality television often say that nothing in it is scripted, and in a narrow sense they may be right: the participants choose their own words. But a programme is made in the edit as much as on location. Hundreds of hours of footage are cut to a few, and the choice of which glance to keep, which remark to place after which, and what music to lay underneath can turn an ordinary disagreement into a feud or a tired participant into a villain. No line need be invented for a character to be. The question to ask of such shows is therefore not whether they are scripted but how they are assembled, and that is a question their defenders rarely answer.
questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Defenders of reality television often say that nothing in it is scripted, and in a narrow sense they may be right: the participants choose their own words. But a programme is made in the edit as much as on location. Hundreds of hours of footage are cut to a few, and the choice of which glance to keep, which remark to place after which, and what music to lay underneath can turn an ordinary disagreement into a feud or a tired participant into a villain. No line need be invented for a character to be. The question to ask of such shows is therefore not whether they are scripted but how they are assembled, and that is a question their defenders rarely answer.

options.A: Reality television is in fact secretly scripted, with participants handed lines to deliver so that their ordinary disagreements look like bitter and lasting feuds.
options.B: Editors of reality television deliberately turn innocent participants into villains to win viewers, and such programmes should be required by law to disclose how all their footage was cut.
options.C: Even if participants' words are unscripted, editing can manufacture characters and conflicts, so the real question about reality television is how it is assembled, not whether it is scripted.
options.D: Because reality television uses only the words its participants actually spoke, its portrayal of them is broadly accurate, whatever music or editing is added.

questions.correct_answer: (C) Even if participants' words are unscripted, editing can manufacture characters and conflicts, so the real question about reality television is how it is assembled, not whether it is scripted.

option_rationales.A: The paragraph grants that 'the participants choose their own words'; its point is that no scripting is needed, since 'No line need be invented'.
option_rationales.B: The paragraph says editing 'can' create villains and asks a question of the shows; legal disclosure is an outside prescription and 'deliberately' is not claimed.
option_rationales.D: This adopts the defenders' reasoning that the paragraph rejects: selection, order and music can turn 'a tired participant into a villain'.

questions.explanation: The paragraph concedes that participants 'choose their own words' but argues that 'a programme is made in the edit', where selection, order and music can create a feud or a villain. Hence the question is 'not whether they are scripted but how they are assembled'. The correct answer keeps the concession and the conclusion.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the disclosure option because it sounds like a natural next step, though the paragraph proposes no rule.
questions.difficulty_reason: The prescriptive option shares the author's suspicion and must be rejected for adding a remedy and an intention.

questions.subtopic: Voice notes shift effort from the sender to the listener.
questions.instructions: The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
questions.passage_text: Voice notes sit awkwardly between a phone call and a text, and both their appeal and their irritation come from that position. For the sender, a voice note combines the ease of talking with the freedom of a text: there is no need to type, and no need to catch the other person at a convenient moment. For the receiver, the balance often tips the other way. A text can be skimmed in seconds, read during a meeting and searched later for an address; a voice note must be played through at the speaker's pace, in a place where one can listen, and cannot easily be scanned for the one detail that matters. The format, in short, moves effort from the person speaking to the person listening, which explains how the same person can enjoy sending voice notes and dread receiving them.
