Noon in one town might therefore fall several minutes earlier or later than noon in a town a short distance to the east or west.
Such differences hardly mattered while travel was slow, but they caused real confusion once trains began to run to published timetables over long distances.
Before the railways, most towns kept their own local time, setting their clocks by the position of the sun overhead.

questions.subtopic: Archives record what institutions chose to keep, so historians read them against their purpose, within limits.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: An archive is not a neutral sample of the past but a deposit of what particular institutions thought worth writing down and keeping.
Many archives have also suffered losses through fire, flood and neglect, so that some records once carefully kept now survive only in fragments.
Historians have learned to read such records against their purpose, finding in a list of debts or a trial transcript glimpses of lives the clerks never meant to describe.
Even so, there are limits to what this method can recover, and where the documents fall silent the honest course is to mark the gap rather than fill it with conjecture.
The resulting silences are not random: a tax office records who owed what, a court records who was accused of what, and people who neither paid much nor offended anyone may leave hardly a trace.

questions.subtopic: Every causal claim in history contains a counterfactual, so the choice is to state such claims openly or leave them hidden.

sentences.text: Historians are often warned against asking what would have happened if events had gone differently, on the ground that such questions cannot be answered.
Stated openly, they can at least be tested against what is known of the period, and the most fanciful among them can be set aside.
The real choice, then, is not between using counterfactuals and avoiding them, but between stating them openly and leaving them unexamined.

Yet every claim that one thing caused another quietly contains a counterfactual, since to say a drought caused a revolt is to imply that without the drought the revolt would not have occurred, or not then.
Novelists have long been drawn to imagined histories in which a famous battle was lost or a great invention was never made.

questions.subtopic: Wartime rationing was a political instrument as well as an economic one, because visibly equal sacrifice sustained consent.

sentences.text: This sense of fairness mattered for morale, because people tend to tolerate hardship far better when they believe it is being shared.

questions.subtopic: A census does not merely record a population; the categories it counts can help to create the divisions it reports.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: A census is usually imagined as a mirror, recording a population that exists independently of the act of counting it.
Because a census depends on the willingness of households to answer truthfully, a population that distrusts officials may be badly undercounted.
Once a category appears on the form, it begins to matter: resources are allocated by it, political claims are framed in its terms, and people learn to describe themselves through it.
Over time, then, the census can help to produce the very divisions it claims merely to report, so that the mirror ends up shaping the face it reflects.
But every census must decide in advance which categories it will count, and those decisions are made by officials with administrative purposes of their own.

questions.subtopic: Cheap, uniform, prepaid postage turned the letter from a commercial luxury into a part of ordinary private life.

sentences.text: Before postal reform, sending a letter was often expensive, and the charge, which rose with distance, was commonly paid by the person who received it.

The adhesive stamp, introduced to show that the fee had been paid, soon attracted collectors, who came to prize misprinted issues above all others.

questions.subtopic: In common-value auctions, winning signals over-optimism, so a sensible bidder bids below its own estimate.

questions.subtopic: Old software often holds an organisation's only complete record of its rules, so it should be read like an archive before it is replaced.

questions.subtopic: Spam filtering is an adversarial contest, so past accuracy overstates future performance and no victory is final.

questions.subtopic: Embankments invite development onto floodplains and so raise the losses from rare floods; keeping floodplains open can be cheaper protection.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

1. When a town builds an embankment along its river, the land behind it suddenly looks safe enough for houses, shops and schools.
2. The embankment works as designed, holding back the ordinary floods of most years, but when a rare flood overtops it the damage exceeds anything the unprotected town could have suffered.
3. Development follows, and within a generation far more property stands on the floodplain than stood there before the defence was raised.
4. This is why some planners argue that keeping floodplains as parks or farmland, though it looks like a waste of valuable land, is the cheaper form of protection.
5. Earth embankments also fail far more often than their designers expect, because seepage weakens them long before the river reaches its peak.
questions.correct_answer: 5 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 concedes that embankments work, which can look out of place in a critical paragraph, but it is the hinge of the argument: the losses grow even when the defence performs, and 'This is why' in sentence 4 refers to it.
Sentence 4 introduces planners, but it is the conclusion the whole chain leads to, and without it the paragraph has no point.

questions.explanation: The paragraph's argument is behavioural: the embankment makes land look safe (sentence 1), development follows (sentence 3), and so a defence that 'works as designed' still raises losses when a rare flood overtops it (sentence 2); 'This is why' in sentence 4 draws the planning conclusion. Sentence 5 attacks embankments on engineering grounds, claiming they often fail, which contradicts the concession in sentence 2 that the embankment works as designed and replaces the paragraph's mechanism (more property exposed) with a different one (structural failure).
questions.common_misconception: Choosing the concession in sentence 2 because it seems to defend embankments, or keeping sentence 5 because it also sounds critical of embankments.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence shares the paragraph's scepticism about embankments, so it must be rejected because it changes the mechanism and clashes with the concession.

questions.subtopic: Toleration may exclude those who would destroy it, but only if the exception is drawn narrowly at organised action.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Drawn more widely, at mere disagreement with liberal values, it would license precisely the suppression that toleration was meant to prevent.
The usual answer is that toleration may refuse protection to those who would destroy it, much as a club may expel members who set out to wreck the club.
But this answer is safe only if the exception is drawn narrowly, at the point where intolerant speech becomes organised action against the freedom of others.
Historically, toleration first emerged as a truce between rival communities exhausted by war, rather than as an ideal valued for its own sake.
A society that tolerates every view, including views that seek to abolish toleration, seems to risk being undone by its own generosity.

2. The usual answer is that toleration may refuse protection to those who would destroy it, much as a club may expel members who set out to wreck the club.
3. But this answer is safe only if the exception is drawn narrowly, at the point where intolerant speech becomes organised action against the freedom of others.
4. Historically, toleration first emerged as a truce between rival communities exhausted by war, rather than as an ideal valued for its own sake.
5. A society that tolerates every view, including views that seek to abolish toleration, seems to risk being undone by its own generosity.
questions.correct_answer: 4 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 has no subject of its own until one sees that 'it' is the exception from sentence 3; it supplies the reason the exception must be narrow.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 poses the puzzle, sentence 2 gives 'the usual answer', sentence 3 ('But this answer') qualifies it, and sentence 1 ('Drawn more widely') shows the danger of an exception drawn too broadly. Sentence 4 is about toleration but gives a historical account of its origin, which does nothing to resolve or qualify the logical puzzle the paragraph works through.
questions.common_misconception: Picking sentence 1 because it seems to oppose the answer in sentence 2, when it actually completes the qualification begun in sentence 3.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence shares the key term and must be rejected because history of origins is a different question from the limits of toleration.

questions.subtopic: Choosing rules without knowing one's own position makes self-interest yield impartiality, though critics question the assumed caution.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Unable to tell whether you will be rich or poor, healthy or ill, you cannot tilt the rule toward your own advantage.
Critics reply that the device yields cautious, protective rules only if we assume that the chooser is unwilling to gamble on landing near the top.
Judges in many legal systems are expected to step aside from cases in which they have a personal stake in the outcome.
Self-interest, which normally corrupts judgements about justice, is thereby made to do the work of impartiality.
One way to test whether a rule is fair is to imagine choosing it without knowing what place you will occupy in the society it governs.

5. One way to test whether a rule is fair is to imagine choosing it without knowing what place you will occupy in the society it governs.
questions.correct_answer: 3 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 disagrees with the device, but 'the device' refers back to the thought experiment, and a reported objection is a normal part of such a paragraph.

questions.explanation: Sentence 5 sets out the thought experiment, sentence 1 explains its effect, sentence 4 ('thereby') states what it achieves, and sentence 2 reports the critics' reply to 'the device'. Sentence 3 shares the theme of impartiality, but it describes an institutional rule for judges, not the imagined choice the paragraph analyses, and nothing in the paragraph refers to it.
questions.common_misconception: Being drawn to sentence 3 by the shared idea of impartiality, or dropping the critics' sentence 2 because it disagrees with the rest.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence shares the theme of impartiality; it must be rejected because it concerns a real-world rule rather than the thought experiment.

questions.subtopic: Whistleblowing can be loyalty to an institution's purpose, though loyalty still asks for internal channels first where they work.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Yet a hospital exists to heal, and staff who hide dangers to patients betray that purpose far more deeply than anyone who brings the dangers to light.
Behind that reproach lies the idea that fidelity is owed to colleagues and superiors, regardless of their conduct.
This does not make every disclosure an act of fidelity, for the institution may still ask that warnings be raised internally first, wherever internal channels genuinely work.
A nurse who reports unsafe practices to an outside regulator will often hear that she has let down her own hospital.
In several countries the law now shields employees who report fraud from dismissal, though such protection is often hard to enforce.

questions.correct_answer: 5 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 limits the argument, but it is still about what fidelity to the institution requires, so it belongs.

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 states the accusation against the nurse, sentence 2 ('that reproach') exposes the view of loyalty behind it, sentence 1 ('Yet') reverses it by appeal to the hospital's purpose, and sentence 3 ('This does not make every disclosure') adds a qualification about internal channels. Sentence 5 is about legal protection, a practical matter, while the paragraph is a moral argument about what loyalty means.
questions.common_misconception: Mistaking the qualification in sentence 3 for a change of subject.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence moves from the ethics of loyalty to law, a clear change of focus.

questions.subtopic: Relativism adopted out of modesty undermines itself, because its ban on imposition is a universal rule relativism rejects.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: If each society's morality is valid only for itself, a society whose morality approves of conquest is, by the relativist's own standard, beyond criticism.
Yet the conclusion, that no society may force its code on others, is itself offered as binding on every society, which is the very sort of universal rule relativism rejects.
Anthropologists have recorded wide variation in moral codes, though a few values, such as care for one's own children, appear almost everywhere.
Many people adopt moral relativism out of modesty: since no society can show its own code to be superior, none is entitled to force that code on others.
The humility that drew people to relativism therefore needs a firmer footing than relativism can offer it.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

2. Yet the conclusion, that no society may force its code on others, is itself offered as binding on every society, which is the very sort of universal rule relativism rejects.
3. Anthropologists have recorded wide variation in moral codes, though a few values, such as care for one's own children, appear almost everywhere.
4. Many people adopt moral relativism out of modesty: since no society can show its own code to be superior, none is entitled to force that code on others.
5. The humility that drew people to relativism therefore needs a firmer footing than relativism can offer it.
questions.correct_answer: 3 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 1 can look like a fresh objection, but conquest is the imposition that sentence 4 said relativism forbids, so it shows relativism failing its own motive and sets up 'therefore' in sentence 5.

questions.explanation: The paragraph is a logical critique: sentence 4 gives the motive for relativism, sentence 2 ('Yet the conclusion') shows that the motive relies on a universal rule, sentence 1 shows that relativism cannot condemn conquest, the very imposition the motive objected to, and sentence 5 ('therefore') concludes. Sentence 3 reports what moral codes are actually like, a descriptive question, and its remark about near-universal values pulls in a different direction; no other sentence uses it, and it neither supports nor is answered by the critique.
questions.common_misconception: Keeping sentence 3 because it seems to give the empirical background to relativism, without noticing that the paragraph argues only about whether relativism is coherent.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence shares the subject and could pass as background; rejecting it needs the distinction between describing moral variety and the normative claim under attack.

questions.subtopic: An arbitrary number seen beforehand pulls estimates towards it, a tendency used in negotiation and hard to resist.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: When people estimate an unknown quantity, an arbitrary number they have just seen tends to pull their estimate towards it.
Negotiators exploit the same tendency when they open with an extreme offer, knowing that the counter-offer will be framed in relation to it.
Suppose a class first writes down the last two digits of their phone numbers and then guesses the price of an unfamiliar object; the guesses would be expected to drift towards those digits.
The pull is hard to resist even for people who know about it, which suggests that it works below the level of deliberate reasoning.
Many shoppers respond to prices ending in nine, which seem noticeably lower than the round number just above them.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

3. Suppose a class first writes down the last two digits of their phone numbers and then guesses the price of an unfamiliar object; the guesses would be expected to drift towards those digits.
4. The pull is hard to resist even for people who know about it, which suggests that it works below the level of deliberate reasoning.
5. Many shoppers respond to prices ending in nine, which seem noticeably lower than the round number just above them.
questions.correct_answer: 5 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 3 is hypothetical and might look like an aside, but it is the illustration of the effect that sentence 2 then calls 'the same tendency'.

questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states the anchoring tendency, sentence 3 illustrates it with a hypothetical classroom case, sentence 2 ('the same tendency') applies it to negotiation, and sentence 4 ('The pull') comments on how hard it is to resist. Sentence 5 is about prices and numbers but describes a different effect, the appeal of prices ending in nine, which involves no prior arbitrary number pulling an estimate.
questions.common_misconception: Accepting sentence 5 because it, too, is about numbers and prices.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence describes a different pricing effect; the difference is easy to see once the definition in the first sentence is read.

questions.subtopic: Repeated uncontrollable failure teaches a lesson about the self, which is why passivity persists and spreads to new settings.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: What is striking is that the passivity outlasts the circumstances that produced it, so that an escape which has become easy goes unattempted.
Because that lesson travels from one setting to another, a student who has failed again and again in mathematics may give up quickly on a history essay as well.
When effort repeatedly makes no difference to outcomes, people and animals alike may stop trying.
The lesson absorbed is not about one situation but about oneself: that one's actions do not matter.
Some failure is useful, since a task at which one never fails is probably too easy to teach one anything.

questions.correct_answer: 5 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 moves to a classroom, but 'that lesson' refers to sentence 4 and the example shows exactly the transfer the paragraph explains.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the phenomenon, sentence 1 adds its striking persistence, sentence 4 explains it as a lesson about oneself, and sentence 2 ('that lesson') shows the lesson spreading to new settings. Sentence 5 also concerns failure, but it argues that failure can be beneficial, a different point from the paragraph's account of how uncontrollable failure produces lasting passivity, and nothing before or after it connects to it.
questions.common_misconception: Choosing sentence 2 because the student example seems to shift to schooling, when it actually illustrates the generalising lesson of sentence 4.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence shares the theme of failure and is rejected on function, since it praises failure rather than explaining passivity.

questions.subtopic: Readers scrutinise unwelcome news more closely than welcome news, so more information does not correct their bias.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: A story that fits their beliefs is accepted after a quick glance, while one that challenges them is read closely for errors.
Since almost any report contains some flaw when inspected closely, this unequal scrutiny lets the reader reject unwelcome news while feeling entirely rational.
Newspapers have long competed for buyers by placing their most sensational stories on the front page.
The bias is therefore hard to correct by supplying more information, because the extra information passes through the same uneven attention.
Readers rarely meet the news as neutral judges; they arrive with views and look, often without noticing, for reports that confirm them.

questions.correct_answer: 3 (the odd sentence)

tita_common_wrong_entries.reason: Sentence 2 can look like a general claim about reports, but its phrase 'this unequal scrutiny' ties it to sentence 1 and it supplies the step that sentence 4 concludes from.

Sentence 3 is about newspapers' selling tactics, not about how readers weigh what they read.
questions.common_misconception: Being drawn to sentence 3 because it mentions the news.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence moves from readers' minds to publishers' tactics, an easy shift to spot.

questions.subtopic: Equivalent descriptions change choices, but this may reflect reasonable inference of advice from the speaker's frame rather than confusion.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: A more charitable reading notes that speakers do not choose frames at random: a doctor who mentions survival is usually signalling that she recommends the treatment.
Since the two descriptions are logically equivalent, the difference seems to show that preferences attach to words rather than to outcomes.
On this view the listener is not fooled by the wording but is reasonably inferring advice from it, even when no advice was intended.
People told that a treatment has a ninety per cent survival rate tend to accept it more readily than people told that one patient in ten dies.
Choices also shift when one option is set as the default, since many people simply accept whatever has already been selected for them.

questions.common_misconception: Treating sentence 1 as the odd one because it disagrees with sentence 2, or keeping sentence 5 because it is also about how choices are swayed.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence comes from the same field and even says 'also', so it must be rejected because the paragraph is an argument about interpreting one result.

questions.subtopic: Queues are kept orderly by the people waiting in them, showing that everyday fairness rests on shared expectations.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: That ordinary strangers police the line themselves shows how much of everyday fairness rests on shared expectations rather than rules.
A queue is a small social order maintained almost entirely without enforcement.
When someone pushes in, the response usually comes not from staff but from the other people waiting, through glances, remarks or a pointed cough.
No official assigns places; each person simply notes who was there first and takes the position behind them.
Some banks and post offices now hand out numbered tokens, which let customers sit down while they wait to be called.

questions.common_misconception: Choosing sentence 3 because it describes conflict in what is said to be an orderly system.
questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence concerns a managed system rather than the informal norm under discussion.

questions.subtopic: The claim that universal museums serve humanity fails where those closest to the objects cannot reach them, though return need not improve access.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: The claim has force only if humanity can actually reach the collection, and for many people in an object's country of origin, the cost of travel and the difficulty of obtaining a visa put it out of reach.
Some objects were bought or exchanged on terms thought legitimate at the time, which complicates any single verdict on how such collections were formed.
None of this shows that every return will improve access, since an object sent home may end up in a storeroom; it shows only that the universal argument cannot settle the question by itself.
The universal museum is thus most accessible to the people who have the least connection with many of the things it displays.
Museums that hold objects taken from other countries often defend themselves by claiming to serve all of humanity rather than any one nation.

Sentence 2 raises a different issue, the legitimacy of how objects were acquired, which the access argument never relies on; although it sounds like a balancing qualification, it qualifies nothing the paragraph has said.
questions.common_misconception: Taking sentence 2 for a qualification like sentence 3, or treating sentence 3 as odd because it seems to argue against returns.
questions.difficulty_reason: Both the odd sentence and the last coherent sentence are hedging qualifications; separating them needs a clear view of which argument is being qualified.

questions.subtopic: Adults play board games despite screens because the inconvenient gathering they require is what they actually seek.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Designers of modern board games have moved steadily away from luck towards strategy, so that the more skilful players win more consistently.
The recent popularity of board games among adults is puzzling at first, since almost any of them could be played more conveniently on a screen.
The game supplies a structure for spending an evening together, with rules that tell everyone when to speak, when to wait and when to laugh at a rival's bad luck.
The puzzle dissolves once we notice that the inconvenience is part of the appeal: players must gather in one room, around one table, at one time.
What is being bought, in other words, is less a game than a reason to be in company without the strain of keeping a conversation going unaided.

questions.question:

questions.subtopic: Tax farming gave pre-modern rulers revenue without a bureaucracy but gave collectors reason to squeeze taxpayers.

sentences.text: The arrangement gave rulers predictable revenue without the expense of maintaining a bureaucracy.
Many pre-modern states lacked the officials needed to assess and collect taxes across their territories.
Taxes on land were generally easier to assess than taxes on trade, because fields could be measured while goods kept moving.
Their solution was to auction the right to collect: a private contractor paid the treasury a fixed sum in advance and kept whatever more he could extract.
But it also gave the collector every reason to squeeze taxpayers hard during his term, since any goodwill he preserved would benefit only his successor.

questions.subtopic: Coalitions are less stable but their bargaining yields broader, more durable policy, at the cost of blurred accountability.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Less often noticed is that the need to keep partners on board forces a coalition to bargain, and bargaining tends to strip proposals of their most extreme features.
Smaller parties often agree to join a coalition in the hope of securing a ministry that matters to their own core supporters.
Policies that survive this process usually command broader support than those a single party could impose, and are therefore less likely to be reversed by the next government.
The price is that voters find it harder to tell which party is responsible for any given decision, and so harder to reward or punish it at the next election.
Coalition governments are commonly blamed for instability, since the withdrawal of a single partner can bring them down.

questions.subtopic: Imperial maps helped create the territory they seemed to describe, though published lines could also bind the states that drew them.

sentences.text: Maps are usually thought of as describing territory, but in the age of empires they often helped to create it.
Yet the power of maps cut both ways, for a line once published could be cited against the very state that drew it when that state later wished to move it.
Areas left blank were read not as places unknown to the mapmaker but as places awaiting an owner, which made them seem open to claim.
Improvements in surveying instruments made maps steadily more accurate, so that later maps of a region often corrected the outlines of earlier ones.
A boundary drawn across land that its surveyors had barely seen became, once printed, the line along which taxes were collected and soldiers posted.

questions.subtopic: Referendums force complex trade-offs into a yes or no and hide the drafter's power, so they suit ratifying detailed proposals.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Turnout in referendums varies widely, and a decision taken on a low turnout may be resented by the many who did not vote.
But a single vote can only answer yes or no, while most important questions involve trade-offs that a binary choice cannot express.
Referendums therefore work best when they ratify a detailed proposal already negotiated, rather than when they are asked to settle a vague principle.
A referendum appears to be democracy in its purest form, with citizens deciding a question directly instead of through representatives.
Whoever drafts the question, moreover, decides which options appear on the ballot and in what words, and so exercises a power that the vote itself conceals.

questions.subtopic: Whether a minimum wage costs jobs depends on its level and on employers' power over wages, not on the principle itself.

sentences.text: That prediction assumes that employers must pay whatever wage the market sets, but in a small town with one large employer, that employer can hold wages below what workers' labour is worth.
The effect of a minimum wage therefore depends less on the principle than on how high it is set and on how much power employers hold where it applies.
In such a market, a moderate minimum can raise pay without reducing employment, and may even draw in workers who were unwilling to work at the old wage.
A minimum wage also differs from a cash transfer to low earners in that its cost falls on employers and customers rather than on taxpayers.
The simplest model of the labour market predicts that a minimum wage set above the going rate will price some workers out of jobs.

questions.subtopic: Joint liability lets lenders reach borrowers without collateral, because members screen and monitor one another.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Since the members choose one another, they bring to that choice a knowledge of each other's habits and reliability that no loan officer could gather cheaply.
Banks have long refused small loans to the very poor, because such borrowers have no collateral and are costly to assess one by one.
Microfinance lenders usually charge interest well above ordinary bank rates, and critics ask whether such loans relieve poverty or merely deepen debt.
Group lending answers both difficulties by making a handful of borrowers jointly responsible, so that if one member defaults the others must repay or lose access to future credit.
The same arrangement turns neighbours into watchful monitors, which is why repayment can stay high even though no borrower has pledged anything the lender could seize.

questions.subtopic: Costly price revisions make firms change prices late and in jumps, so the main cost of inflation here is distorted relative prices.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Firms with well-known brands can raise their prices during inflation with little loss of customers, while firms selling interchangeable goods must hold back.
Labels must be changed, catalogues reprinted and customers persuaded that the new price is fair, so firms tend to put off revisions and then make them in large steps.
When prices are rising steadily, every firm must from time to time revise what it charges, and each revision has a cost of its own.
Because different firms revise at different moments, the prices of goods drift out of line with one another, and buyers react to gaps that reflect nothing but the timing of revisions.
The cost of such revisions, then, lies less in the reprinting itself than in the misleading signals that staggered price changes send to buyers.

5. The cost of such revisions, then, lies less in the reprinting itself than in the misleading signals that staggered price changes send to buyers.

questions.difficulty_reason: The odd sentence uses the paragraph's words (firms, prices, raise, inflation) and offers a rival reason for holding back prices, so it must be rejected on function.

questions.subtopic: Short product life is often a trade-off buyers choose; the charge of planned obsolescence holds only where firms block repair.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: The charge regains its force only where a firm prevents repair, by sealing in batteries or withholding spare parts, for then a short life is imposed on buyers rather than chosen by them.
Short-lived goods also impose a cost on people who never bought them, since the discarded products must be buried, burned or shipped elsewhere.
Durability, on this view, is one quality among others, and a market that supplies short-lived goods may simply be supplying what people prefer to pay for.

Much of what looks like deliberate frailty, however, reflects choices buyers make themselves, since a lighter, cheaper or more up-to-date product usually lasts less long than a heavy one built for decades.
The charge of planned obsolescence holds that manufacturers deliberately build goods to fail so that customers must buy again.

questions.subtopic: A potluck turns a dinner from one household's gift into a joint production with no debts.
questions.instructions: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.text: Its deeper effect is on the relation between host and guest: since everyone has contributed, no one leaves owing a return invitation.

This is also why a potluck tolerates wildly uneven contributions, a lavish curry beside a packet of crisps, without embarrassment: what is being shared is participation, not an exact division of costs.
The meal becomes a joint production rather than a gift from one household to the others.
Because guests cook without consulting one another, a potluck can easily end up with three rice dishes and no dessert.
A potluck, in which each guest brings a dish to share, looks at first like a simple way of spreading the cost of a dinner.

questions.subtopic: Forgiving is nearly the opposite of excusing, so excusing everything leaves nothing to forgive.

questions.passage_text: Forgiveness is often confused with excusing, but the two are closer to opposites than to near relations. (1) To excuse someone is to decide that what they did was not really their fault: they were tired, misled or under pressure, and so there is nothing to hold against them. questions.subtopic: Plans run late because the inside view leaves out the interruptions that befall nearly every project.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Real projects, by contrast, are seldom spared them: an illness, a late delivery or a resignation befalls almost every one, though no single one could have been foreseen.
questions.passage_text: People who plan a project routinely underestimate how long it will take, even when they have finished similar projects late many times before. (1) What makes the error puzzling is not its existence but its persistence, since experience ought to correct it. (2) The usual explanation is that planners take an inside view: they picture the particular steps of the task in front of them and add up the time each step seems to need. (3) The proposed remedy is to take an outside view, setting aside the details of the project and asking how long projects of the same general kind have actually taken. (4) This feels like throwing information away, because it ignores everything the planner knows about her own case. In fact it restores the information that matters most, the record of how such projects usually go wrong, which the inside view had quietly left out.

questions.subtopic: Renamed streets keep their old names in speech because a name is shared local knowledge that an order cannot erase.

questions.passage_text: When a city renames a street, the new name appears overnight on signs and maps, but it often takes a generation to appear in everyday speech. (1) That knowledge is spread across thousands of small habits: residents give directions by the old name, shopkeepers print it on their cards, and older people use it to locate their memories. questions.subtopic: The openness that lets lichens live anywhere makes them sensitive recorders of air quality.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.

questions.passage_text: A lichen looks like a single plant, a crust or a leafy fringe on a rock or a branch, but it is in fact a partnership. A fungus provides the structure and holds water, while an alga or a bacterium living inside it makes food from sunlight. (1) Together they can live where neither could survive alone: on bare stone, on desert soil, on the bark of trees in the coldest forests. (2) Because a lichen has no roots and no protective outer skin, it takes in water and nutrients directly from rain and from the air around it. (3) Many species disappear from city centres where sulphur dioxide is common, and some return when the air is cleaned. For this reason, surveys of lichens have long been used as a cheap way of reading the quality of the air in a district. A lichen does not so much measure pollution as record its history, since it grows slowly and responds to years of exposure rather than to a single bad day. (4)

questions.subtopic: Moral luck exposes a conflict between the principle of control and our actual practice of blame.

questions.passage_text: Two drivers take the same corner too fast on the same wet evening, and both are equally careless. questions.passage_text: Why is the sky dark at night? The question sounds childish, but it troubled astronomers for centuries, because a simple argument seemed to show that the night sky should blaze. If the universe were infinite, unchanging and evenly filled with stars, then every line of sight, extended far enough, would end on the surface of some star. (1) Distant stars appear fainter, but there would be more of them in proportion, and the two effects would cancel exactly. (2) The whole sky would then shine about as brightly as the surface of a typical star. The darkness we see therefore tells us that at least one of the assumptions is false. (3) The modern answer rejects the assumption that the universe is unchanging: it has a finite age, so light from stars beyond a certain distance has not yet had time to reach us. (4)

questions.subtopic: Rewilding with large herbivores aims to restore ecological processes, so unpredictable outcomes are its goal rather than its weakness.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.

questions.passage_text: Conservation has traditionally worked from a picture: a meadow, a heath or a wetland as it looked at some chosen date, to be kept that way by mowing, burning and weeding. Rewilding with large herbivores starts from a different premise. Instead of fixing a picture, it reintroduces grazing animals such as cattle, horses or bison, or their nearest modern stand-ins, and lets their feeding, trampling and wallowing decide what the land becomes. Critics point out that the results cannot be specified in advance, and that a project unable to say what it is aiming at is hard to fund, monitor or defend. (1) The objection is real, but it partly misdescribes the aim. (2) Where a traditional reserve succeeds by holding change at bay, a rewilded one succeeds if change keeps happening: patches opened by grazing, scrub returning where the animals stay away, a mosaic that never quite settles. (3) Monitoring such a site means asking whether those processes are running, not whether a list of target species has been reached. (4) None of this makes rewilding suitable everywhere; a small reserve protecting one rare orchid may need exactly the kind of fixed management that rewilding rejects.

questions.passage_text: When a mountain glacier begins to shrink, the rivers it feeds do not immediately run low. For years, sometimes decades, they may actually carry more water than before, because the ice is melting faster than snowfall replaces it. Towns and farms downstream can easily read this abundance as a sign that all is well. (1) When the ice has retreated beyond some threshold, less of it remains to melt each summer, and the flows begin to fall year after year. questions.passage_text: Predictive text is usually discussed as a convenience, a way of saving a few keystrokes on a small screen. Its subtler effect is on what gets written at all. A suggestion appears, it is roughly what the writer meant, and accepting it costs less effort than typing the word that was actually in mind. Since the system proposes whatever is most common in the text it learned from, each accepted suggestion pulls the sentence slightly towards the average. questions.subtopic: Mature software must preserve accidental behaviour users depend on, a burden worsened because maintainers cannot know which accidents matter.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Worse than either of these costs, maintainers usually cannot tell which accidents anyone relies on until they remove one and the complaints arrive.
questions.passage_text: Every widely used piece of software eventually discovers that its users depend not only on what it was designed to do but on what it happens to do. A function that returns results in a particular order, though the documentation never promised any order, will sooner or later be relied upon by someone's program. Fixing such behaviour, or merely changing it for good reasons, then breaks that program, and from the user's side a fix that breaks things is indistinguishable from a bug. (1) Maintainers of mature systems therefore end up preserving accidents alongside intentions, and the line between the two blurs with each release. (2) The cost is not only the effort of carrying old behaviour forward. Each preserved quirk constrains the design of everything built later, so that a system's newest parts are shaped by decisions nobody remembers making. (3) Some projects try to escape this guesswork by announcing in advance which behaviours are guaranteed and declaring the rest open to change, a policy that is honest but only partly effective. Users rarely read such declarations, and a change that breaks enough of them tends to be reversed, whatever the policy said. (4)

questions.subtopic: In rhymed verse the rhyme times the meaning, so a translator chooses between two kinds of meaning, not between meaning and ornament.

questions.passage_text: Translators of rhymed poetry are usually said to face a simple choice between sound and sense. Keep the rhymes, and the translator must bend the meaning to find English words that chime; keep the meaning, and the poem arrives in prose broken into lines. The framing is convenient, but it assumes that rhyme is ornament laid over a meaning that exists independently of it. (1) In much rhymed verse that assumption fails. A rhyme sets up an expectation at the end of one line and settles it at the end of another, and poets use that rhythm of suspense and resolution to time a joke, sharpen a reversal or make a conclusion feel inevitable. (2) Strip it away, and the words may survive while the timing that gave them their force does not. (3) None of this tells a translator what to do in a particular case; it only means that the choice is between two kinds of meaning, not between meaning and decoration. (4)

questions.subtopic: An unreliable narrator enriches a story because the reader reconstructs what the narrator reports but fails to understand.

questions.passage_text: A narrator who cannot be trusted would seem to be a liability for a story, since the reader depends on the narrator for nearly everything the story contains. (1) Yet a good many celebrated works of fiction are narrated by people who misunderstand themselves, conceal what they have done or simply fail to notice what is happening around them. (2) The device works because a narrator reports more than he or she understands. (3) The reader assembles a picture from these details that the narrator never draws, and the distance between the two pictures becomes the real subject of the book. (4) It also depends on trust of a different kind: the reader must believe that the author has planted the evidence deliberately, or the gaps would look like carelessness rather than design.

Sentence: A servant who insists that his employer was a man of honour may describe, in passing and without comment, the guests who were turned away and the letters that went unanswered.

Paragraph: A narrator who cannot be trusted would seem to be a liability for a story, since the reader depends on the narrator for nearly everything the story contains. (1) Yet a good many celebrated works of fiction are narrated by people who misunderstand themselves, conceal what they have done or simply fail to notice what is happening around them. (2) The device works because a narrator reports more than he or she understands. (3) The reader assembles a picture from these details that the narrator never draws, and the distance between the two pictures becomes the real subject of the book. Such reading demands a kind of double attention, following the voice while quietly checking it against the evidence it supplies. (4) It also depends on trust of a different kind: the reader must believe that the author has planted the evidence deliberately, or the gaps would look like carelessness rather than design.

options.A: Blank (1)
options.B: Blank (2)
options.C: Blank (3)
options.D: Blank (4)

questions.correct_answer: (C) Blank (3)

option_rationales.A: At gap (1) the opening claim that an untrustworthy narrator is a liability must be answered directly by 'Yet a good many celebrated works of fiction'; an example placed before that answer would illustrate a principle not yet stated.
option_rationales.B: Gap (2) is tempting because the preceding sentence mentions narrators who 'fail to notice', but the principle the servant illustrates is stated only in the next sentence, and 'these details' would then be separated from the details it refers to.
option_rationales.D: At gap (4) the sentence would come between 'Such reading demands a kind of double attention' and 'It also depends', where 'It' must refer to that reading; the example would also arrive after the details have already been used.

questions.explanation: The servant is an example of a narrator who 'reports more than he or she understands': he records the turned-away guests without seeing what they mean. The next sentence needs exactly such an example, since 'these details' has no antecedent without it. So the sentence belongs at gap (3).
questions.common_misconception: Placing the example right after the list of narrators who fail to notice things, before the principle it illustrates.
questions.difficulty_reason: Needs the reader to match the example to the principle and to see that 'these details' requires it immediately before.

questions.subtopic: Stage magic pleases by letting an audience that knows it is deceived experience being outwitted, which is why explanation spoils it.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Explaining a trick spoils it, then, not because the secret was precious but because, once the limit is removed, the mind has nothing left to confront.
questions.passage_text: Stage magic is an odd art, because its audience knows from the start that it is being deceived. No one in the theatre believes that the performer has really sawn a person in half or plucked a thought from a stranger's mind. The pleasure lies elsewhere, in the collision between that certainty and the inability to see how the effect was achieved. (1) This is why magicians guard their methods so jealously, and why exposing a trick is treated within the profession as a kind of theft. Yet the methods, when revealed, are often disappointing in a telling way: a hidden assistant, a duplicate card, a moment of misdirection lasting less than a second. (2) The disappointment shows that the audience was never really interested in the method for its own sake. (3) What it valued was the experience of a mind confronting a limit, of watching closely and still being outwitted. (4)

questions.subtopic: Arguments over cleaning old paintings go beyond taste to the question of what the painter intended.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Both reactions are matters of taste, and taste alone cannot settle whether a cleaning was right.
questions.passage_text: Few decisions in a museum provoke as much argument as the decision to clean an old painting. Over centuries, the varnish that protects a picture yellows and darkens, and grime settles into the surface, until colours that were once bright look brown and muted. Removing these layers can reveal blues and reds that no living viewer has seen. To some visitors the result is a revelation; to others it looks harsh, even garish, beside the mellow image they had grown to love. (1) The deeper dispute is about what the painter intended, since some artists may have added thin tinted layers of their own that a careless cleaning would strip away. (2) Because cleaning cannot be undone, careful restorers proceed slowly, testing small areas first. (3) They stop wherever original paint and later grime become hard to tell apart, preferring to leave a picture slightly dull rather than risk removing the painter's own work. (4)

questions.subtopic: Borrowing is a normal way languages grow, though the direction of borrowing can reflect imbalances of power that speakers may resent.

questions.missing_sentence: When words flow overwhelmingly in one direction, from the language of a powerful economy or a former ruler into everyone else's, the pattern says something about who holds prestige, and speakers may reasonably resent that.
questions.passage_text: Campaigns to keep a language free of foreign words usually present borrowing as a kind of contamination. The image suggests a pure original that was whole before outsiders arrived, but few languages have any such original to return to. (1) Most of the vocabulary that purists defend was itself borrowed at some earlier date, and has simply been around long enough to feel native. (2) Borrowed words are also rarely kept intact: they are fitted to the sounds of the language, given its endings and plurals, and often shifted in meaning until their origins are invisible to ordinary speakers. Borrowing on this view is less an invasion than a form of digestion. (3) There is, however, something in the purist's worry that this argument does not dispose of. (4)

questions.subtopic: Because many readers see only the headline, its tendency to overstate matters more than the qualifications inside the article.

questions.passage_text: A headline has a job that the article beneath it does not: it must persuade someone to read on, in a handful of words, while competing with every other headline on the page or screen. (1) That pressure pushes headlines towards the vivid and the certain. A study that found a modest link becomes a headline announcing a cause; a proposal still under discussion becomes a decision. (2) A rare side effect becomes a danger, and a single surprising case becomes a trend. The article itself may contain every necessary qualification, carefully placed in the fourth or fifth paragraph. (3) Many readers, however, never reach that paragraph, because they scroll past after the headline or share the link without opening it. (4)

questions.passage_text: A common assumption about sign languages is that they are either elaborate systems of gesture or a way of spelling out the spoken language of the surrounding community with the hands. (1) Sign languages have grammars of their own, with rules that are not borrowed from speech and that children acquire in the same stages, and at roughly the same ages, as children learning to speak. (2) Many of these rules exploit the possibilities of space. (3) A signer may place a person or object at a point in the space in front of the body and then refer back to it simply by pointing there, much as a speaker uses a pronoun. (4) Such features have no direct equivalent in the spoken language of the same region, which is one reason a sign language cannot be understood simply by knowing that spoken language.

questions.subtopic: Dictionary usage notes report attitudes as facts, yet in practice they steer usage and keep disapproval alive.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Editors who kept such a sense out would simply be left behind, defending meanings that fewer and fewer people recognise.
questions.passage_text: Modern dictionaries describe themselves as records of how a language is used rather than rulebooks for how it ought to be used. (1) If enough speakers use a word in a new sense, the new sense goes in, whatever earlier editors or schoolteachers might have thought of it. (2) Many readers, however, open a dictionary precisely to be told what is correct, and a record that merely reports usage can seem to have abandoned them. (3) The usage note is the dictionary's answer to this tension. Rather than ruling on a disputed word, it reports that some careful writers avoid it, or that it may strike certain readers as informal, and leaves the decision with the user. (4) Such notes are descriptive in form, since attitudes towards a word are themselves a fact about the language, but in practice they steer readers as firmly as any rule. A writer warned that a usage annoys some readers will usually avoid it, and the warning, repeated across editions, can help keep the disapproval alive.

questions.subtopic: Spaced study works better than cramming because of the forgetting that makes it feel less effective.

questions.passage_text: Students preparing for an examination tend to study each topic in a single long session, going over the material until it feels secure. (1) Spreading the same hours across several shorter sessions, separated by days, usually produces better recall weeks later. (2) The gaps allow some forgetting, and the effort of retrieving half-forgotten material seems to strengthen the memory more than rereading material that is already fresh. Learners themselves, however, often judge the long session to be more effective. (3) At its end the material feels familiar and easy, and that ease is mistaken for lasting knowledge. (4) Spaced sessions, by contrast, begin each time with the uncomfortable discovery of how much has slipped away. Teachers who want students to space their work therefore have to persuade them to trust a method that feels worse while it is working better.

questions.passage_text: Teachers often say that they never really understood a subject until they had to teach it. (1) Gaps that could be ignored while reading become impossible to ignore when a student asks a simple question and no answer comes. (3) The benefit seems to go mostly to the pupil doing the explaining, and only when the explaining is genuine rather than a recitation of notes. A pupil who reads out a summary to a partner has rehearsed the material without ever being forced to organise it. (4)

Sentence: Each of these demands is a test that silent study rarely sets.

Paragraph: Teachers often say that they never really understood a subject until they had to teach it. The remark sounds like modesty, but it describes something real about how understanding is built. To explain an idea to someone else, a person must put its parts in order, decide what depends on what and anticipate where a listener might go wrong. (1) Gaps that could be ignored while reading become impossible to ignore when a student asks a simple question and no answer comes. (2) Schools have tried to harness this by asking pupils to teach one another, with mixed results. (3) The benefit seems to go mostly to the pupil doing the explaining, and only when the explaining is genuine rather than a recitation of notes. A pupil who reads out a summary to a partner has rehearsed the material without ever being forced to organise it. (4)

options.A: Blank (1)
options.B: Blank (2)
options.C: Blank (3)
options.D: Blank (4)

questions.correct_answer: (A) Blank (1)

option_rationales.B: Gap (2) is tempting because the preceding sentence also contrasts reading with explaining, but it describes a moment of failure rather than demands, so 'these demands' would reach back past it, and 'Schools have tried to harness this' needs that moment immediately before it.
option_rationales.C: At gap (3) the paragraph has turned to classroom practice and its 'mixed results', so a remark about the demands of explanation would interrupt the move to who benefits.
option_rationales.D: At gap (4) the last sentence describes a pupil who was never forced to organise anything, so 'these demands' would have no list to refer to.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'these demands' points to the three demands listed in the sentence before: putting the parts in order, deciding what depends on what and anticipating where a listener might go wrong. The contrast with 'silent study' then leads into 'Gaps that could be ignored while reading'. The sentence belongs at gap (1).
questions.common_misconception: Placing the sentence after the sentence about unanswered questions, because both contrast explaining with reading.
questions.difficulty_reason: Backward reference to a list; the next gap shares the reading-versus-explaining contrast.

questions.subtopic: Homework for young children depends on unequal home support, so it can widen the gaps schooling should narrow.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: In one household those resources are plentiful and a parent explains each step; in the next, the sheet is attempted alone after a long day, or not at all.
questions.passage_text: Homework for young children is often defended as a way of extending learning beyond the school day. The case is stronger for older pupils, who can work independently and whose assignments can build directly on lessons. (1) For children in the first years of school, the benefits are much harder to find, and the costs are easy to overlook. A worksheet sent home to a seven-year-old is rarely completed by the child alone. (2) Its success depends on whether an adult has the time, the patience and the knowledge to help, and those resources are spread very unequally across households. (3) Homework at this age can therefore end up measuring the home rather than the child, and widening the very gaps that schooling is meant to narrow. Reading aloud with a parent is a partial exception, since it asks for time and warmth rather than expertise, and most families can offer some of both. (4)

questions.subtopic: Antibiotic restraint protects future strangers at a cost to the present patient, so it is best supported by systems that make restraint safe.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Persuading doctors to accept that risk depends less on warnings about resistance than on arrangements, such as quick tests and clear guidelines, that make restraint safer.
questions.passage_text: From the point of view of a single doctor facing a single patient, prescribing an antibiotic when in doubt can seem the responsible choice. If the infection turns out to be bacterial, the patient is spared days of illness; if it was viral, the drug does little harm to that patient. (1) The difficulty is that each prescription also gives resistant bacteria an advantage, and the resistance that results does not stay with the patient who received the drug. (2) It spreads through households, hospitals and communities, and eventually reaches people who never took the antibiotic at all. (3) Stewardship programmes ask prescribers to keep these absent people in mind, by testing before treating where possible, choosing narrower drugs and stopping courses when they are no longer needed. This is a hard request, because the benefit of restraint is spread thinly across strangers in the future while its risk falls on the patient in the room. (4)

questions.subtopic: Screening can look more successful than it is through overdiagnosis and earlier diagnosis, so it should be judged by deaths prevented.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: That shift in the starting point would inflate survival figures even if every tumour screening found were a dangerous one, so it is a second distortion, independent of the first.
questions.passage_text: It seems obvious that finding a cancer early is better than finding it late, and for many cancers it is. Screening programmes, however, find not only the dangerous tumours they are looking for but also small, slow-growing ones that would never have caused symptoms in the person's lifetime. Such tumours cannot usually be told apart from dangerous ones at the moment of diagnosis, so they are treated in the same way, with the same surgery, radiation and anxiety. The patients concerned are counted as cancer survivors, and their good outcomes make the programme look more successful than it is. (1) Even a measure as natural as the share of patients still alive five years after diagnosis can mislead here. (2) Diagnosing a cancer earlier starts the clock earlier, so survival from diagnosis lengthens even if the date of death has not moved at all. (3) The figure that tells us whether a screening programme helps is not how many cancers it finds or how long people live after diagnosis, but whether deaths from the disease fall among those who were screened. (4) By that standard some programmes do well and others less so, which is a reason to evaluate each one rather than to reject screening as such.

questions.subtopic: Poor hand hygiene in hospitals is a problem of ward design rather than knowledge, so changing the setting works better than reminders.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Far more often, it is the ward itself that works against the habit.
questions.passage_text: Almost every doctor and nurse knows that cleaning the hands before touching the next patient does more to stop hospital infections than almost any other single habit. Yet observations on busy wards repeatedly find that the step is skipped far more often than staff themselves believe. The gap is rarely a matter of ignorance or indifference. (1) On a crowded shift, a nurse may need to clean her hands dozens of times an hour, and each time the sink or dispenser is a few steps out of the way, the step competes with an alarm, a call or a patient in distress. (2) Campaigns that simply remind staff of the importance of hygiene therefore tend to produce short-lived improvements. (3) More lasting gains have come from changing the setting: placing alcohol rub at every bed and on every trolley, so that the right action is also the easiest one. (4)

questions.subtopic: Night workers sleep poorly because the body clock resists daytime sleep and is repeatedly pulled back towards a daytime pattern.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Two features of a night worker's life keep pulling it the other way.
questions.passage_text: Working at night would be a simple matter if sleep could be moved as easily as a work schedule. The body, however, keeps its own timetable, governed by an internal clock that is set largely by daylight. (1) A night worker who goes to bed at nine in the morning is trying to sleep at the hour when that clock is pushing hardest towards wakefulness. The sleep that results is usually shorter and lighter than night-time sleep, however dark and quiet the bedroom. One might expect the clock to adjust after a few weeks of steady night work, but it seldom does so fully. (2) Each morning's journey home in bright light nudges it back towards a daytime pattern, and on days off most workers return to sleeping at night to be with family and friends. (3) People do differ in how well they tolerate the arrangement, and some find it far easier than others, but few escape its costs altogether. (4)

questions.subtopic: Incentives for rare-disease drugs work but produce high prices whose combined cost grows, so health systems must decide how much progress to pay for.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: The question a health system must eventually face is therefore not whether any single drug is affordable, but how much it is willing to pay, in total, for the progress it asked companies to make.
questions.passage_text: A medicine for a condition found in only a few thousand patients worldwide faces an awkward arithmetic. Developing and testing it may cost nearly as much as developing a drug for a common condition, but the cost must be recovered from a tiny number of patients. Many countries have therefore offered special incentives for such drugs, including longer periods of market exclusivity and help with the expense of clinical trials. (1) The incentives have worked in the sense that they were intended to: treatments now exist for conditions that companies once had no reason to study. They have also produced prices per patient that can exceed what most families earn in a lifetime, paid in practice by insurers and health systems. (2) Defenders of these prices point out that the total spent on any one rare disease is small, precisely because the patients are few. (3) The answer is accurate but incomplete, since rare diseases are numerous, and their combined cost grows as the incentives succeed in producing more treatments. (4)

questions.subtopic: Herd immunity invites free riding, which is why vaccination cannot be treated as a purely private choice.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: This indirect shield creates a temptation that any economist would recognise at once: the chance to enjoy a benefit without paying its cost.
questions.passage_text: Vaccination is unusual among medical choices because its benefits do not stop at the person who actually receives the injection. When enough people in a community are immune, a pathogen struggles to find new hosts, and even those who were never vaccinated are shielded indirectly. (1) A parent who declines a vaccine for a child may reason that, with nearly everyone else immunised, the risk of infection is already tiny. The reasoning is not foolish for any single family, which is precisely what makes it dangerous. (2) If many families reason in the same way, the level of immunity falls below the point at which the shield holds, and outbreaks return. (3) The protection that each free rider counted on then disappears for everyone, including the infants and the sick who could never have been vaccinated in the first place. Public health policy therefore cannot treat vaccination as a wholly private decision, even when it respects the right of individuals to make it. (4)

questions.subtopic: Letting patients finish their opening account is part of diagnosis, not a courtesy that competes with it.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: A woman who begins by asking about a persistent cough, for instance, may reach her real worry, a lump she has been afraid to name, only if she is allowed to keep talking.
questions.passage_text: Medical training has long prized the ability to reach a diagnosis efficiently, and the classic consultation is built around the doctor's questions rather than the patient's story. Efficiency of this kind has obvious virtues in a crowded clinic, where every minute spent with one patient is a minute taken from the next. (1) Yet the habit of steering the conversation early can cost more time than it saves, because the complaint a patient mentions first is not always the one that matters most. (2) Cut off early, such patients leave with a remedy for whatever they happened to mention first, and the problem that really brought them in waits for another visit, or for an emergency. Allowing people to finish their opening account need not take long, and the fear that it will swallow the whole appointment is usually exaggerated. (3) The deeper lesson is that listening is not a courtesy added to diagnosis but one of its instruments, as much a part of the examination as the stethoscope. (4)

But the attitudes that gave the old word its sting have not gone anywhere, and they soon attach themselves to the replacement. (2) Within a generation the polite term is being used as a taunt in school playgrounds, and reformers begin searching for another. The cycle can be traced through the vocabulary of illness, disability and poverty, and even through the names for the lavatory, which have turned over again and again. (3) Some observers conclude from this that the effort to find kinder words is pointless, but that does not quite follow, since a new word can at least signal that the speaker means no harm, even if the signal fades. (4)

questions.passage_text: Across much of the multilingual world, pupils start their schooling in a language seldom spoken in their homes, typically because it is the language of the state, the universities and the better-paid professions. (1) The intention is to give them an early start in the language that will matter most for their futures. (2) In practice, a child who must learn to read in an unfamiliar tongue faces two tasks at once: decoding print and making sense of words she does not yet know. Children who first learn to read in their home language face only the first task, and once they can read, the skill carries over to a second language with surprising ease. (4) Parents who want their children taught in the language of opportunity from the first day are not wrong about where opportunity lies; they are mistaken only about the quickest way to reach it.

questions.passage_text: Moral philosophers are fond of strange stories: a runaway tram that can be diverted onto a side track, killing one person instead of five, or a surgeon who could save five patients by sacrificing one healthy visitor. (1) By holding fixed the number of lives at stake and varying only the manner in which they are lost, the cases let us see whether that manner matters to us morally. questions.subtopic: Deep absorption arises when challenge matches skill, which makes it designable but also open to misuse.

questions.passage_text: There is a state of mind familiar to musicians, climbers, programmers and anyone who has lost track of time while absorbed in a demanding task. (1) Attention narrows to the task at hand, the sense of self as an anxious observer fades, and effort, though real, no longer feels like a burden. (2) Such absorption seems to arise most readily when the challenge of the task roughly matches the skill of the person performing it. (4) It also carries a caution: a state that feels so rewarding can be sought in activities, from gambling to endless games, that absorb us without leaving anything of value behind.

questions.subtopic: Habits draw much of their strength from the cues in their settings, so changes of setting are chances to break or rebuild them.

questions.passage_text: (1) Habits are often described as private achievements of willpower, but much of their strength is borrowed from the settings in which they form. A behaviour repeated in the same place, at the same hour and after the same preceding action gradually comes to be triggered by those cues rather than by a decision. (2) The same dependence on context explains why habits often loosen when people move house, change jobs or go away on a long journey. With the old cues gone, behaviour that once ran automatically has to be chosen again, and for a short period it becomes open to revision. (3) Those who want to drop a habit can therefore treat such transitions as opportunities, while those who want to keep one should expect to rebuild it deliberately. (4)

questions.subtopic: Deliberate delay can protect a person's self-image by supplying an excuse for failure, but at the cost of making success meaningless.

That explanation fits some cases, but it struggles with the person who knows exactly how long the work will take and still postpones it until the last night.
