questions.missing_sentence: Why would an ambitious owner accept such tight constraints on a business that is legally theirs?
questions.passage_text: A franchise is an unusual bargain between independence and control. The franchisee owns the shop, hires the staff and bears the risk of failure, yet must follow a manual that dictates everything from the recipe to the colour of the walls. (1) The answer is that the constraints are precisely what is being bought. (2) A traveller in an unfamiliar town trusts a familiar sign because every outlet behind it behaves in the same way, and that trust is worth more than any single owner could build alone. (3) The same uniformity, however, limits what a franchisee can do when local tastes differ from the assumptions written into the manual. An owner who knows that the neighbourhood wants a different menu may be forbidden to offer it, and the independence promised at the outset turns out to be largely financial. (4)

questions.subtopic: Village irrigation systems survive through farmer-made rules, which shows the conditions under which shared resources are overused.

questions.missing_sentence: What sustains them is neither altruism nor luck but a body of rules that the farmers themselves devised and continue to adjust and enforce.
questions.passage_text: A common view holds that any resource shared by many users will be overused, because whoever draws a little extra keeps all of the gain while the harm is spread thinly across everyone else. (1) On this reasoning, a canal that waters the fields of an entire village should run dry long before the farmer at the tail end receives a share. Yet many village irrigation systems have run for generations without either private ownership or control by a distant state. (2) The rules are usually precise: turns at the sluice gate are fixed in advance, every household sends labour to clear the channels, and because the fields lie side by side, a farmer who takes water out of turn is likely to be seen by a neighbour. (3) Such systems do not refute the original argument so much as specify when it applies. Overuse becomes likely when users cannot watch one another, cannot keep outsiders away or have no voice in the rules, conditions that are sometimes created, ironically, when a well-meaning authority replaces local arrangements with a uniform code. (4)

questions.subtopic: A long warranty signals quality because it is cheap for good producers and costly for bad ones, though the signal can mislead.

questions.passage_text: A long warranty is usually advertised as a promise to the buyer, but it is also a message about the seller. (1) Repairing or replacing faulty goods costs money, and a firm that offers five years of cover is betting that few of its products will fail within that time. (2) A maker of shoddy goods could print the same promise, but honouring it would soon become ruinous. (3) Buyers who cannot inspect the inner workings of a washing machine can therefore read something about its quality from the length of its guarantee. The signal is not infallible, however. (4) A firm in difficulty may offer generous terms it never expects to honour, and a buyer who relies on the warranty alone may find that the promise was only as solid as the company behind it.

questions.subtopic: Irrigation deposits salt that only drainage removes, and because drains are costly and slow to pay off, they are often skipped, ruining land.
questions.instructions: There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence can best fit.
questions.missing_sentence: Such drains are expensive, however, and because their benefits appear only slowly, they are often the first item cut from a tight budget.
questions.passage_text: Irrigation is usually counted among agriculture's great successes, and rightly so: it has turned dry plains into some of the most productive farmland on earth. Yet all irrigation water, however fresh it looks, carries a small load of dissolved salts. When the water evaporates from the fields or is drawn up by plants, the salts stay behind, accumulating year after year in the upper layers of the soil. (1) Generous watering might seem the obvious remedy, since extra water can wash the salts downwards, beyond the reach of the roots. (2) But where the land drains poorly, the extra water raises the water table instead, and the rising groundwater carries yet more salt towards the surface. (3) Engineers therefore insist that irrigation be paired with drainage, with channels or buried pipes that carry the salty water away from the fields. (4) The result, in more than one region, has been fields once famous for their harvests turning white with salt and being abandoned.

questions.passage_text: Migratory birds cross thousands of kilometres and often return to the same nesting site year after year, a feat that long puzzled naturalists. (1) Research over the past century has shown that they rely not on one sense but on several. (2) Many species take bearings from the sun by day and from the patterns of the stars at night. Others appear to sense the earth's magnetic field, and some may use smells or the low sound of distant surf to recognise familiar regions. (3) Clouds, for example, hide the stars, magnetic storms can disturb the field, and a change of wind carries scents away from their source. A bird that can switch from one cue to another is far less likely to go astray than one that trusts a single guide. (4)
